title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Jal Jeevan Mission in Madhya Pradesh
overview:
Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) was launched on 15 August 2019 with the goal of providing a Functional Household Tap Connection (FHTC) delivering 55 litres per capita per day of safe drinking water to every rural household in India by March 2024. In Madhya Pradesh, the mission was to cover 98.28 lakh households — all but the 13.53 lakh that already had connections at launch. The audit, conducted by the Principal Accountant General (Audit II), Madhya Pradesh and countersigned by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (K. Sanjay Murthy) on 30 April 2026, examined implementation from 2019–20 to 2023–24 across eight sampled districts (Chhatarpur, Dindori, Gwalior, Jhabua, Narmadapuram, Narsinghpur, Tikamgarh, and Vidisha) through scrutiny of 28 SVS agreements (144 villages), four MVS agreements (1,009 villages), and a beneficiary survey of 629 households across 32 villages.

Against the March 2024 target, Madhya Pradesh had provided FHTCs to only 60.90 lakh households as of December 2024 — a 62 per cent completion rate — while the national average stood at approximately 80 per cent. As of September 2024, only 27 per cent of Multi-Village Schemes (MVSs) and 58 per cent of Single-Village Schemes (SVSs) were completed. Northeastern districts were particularly behind: Singrauli (38%), Chhatarpur (40%), Satna (41%), Panna (44%), Rewa (48%), and Sidhi (47%). The mission's original deadline has since been extended to March 2028, but CAG found the average MVS completion time in MP to be 80 months — well beyond even the revised target.

CAG identified systemic failures across all four mission pillars: planning, implementation, monitoring, and sustainability. Planning was top-down rather than the mandated bottom-up approach — Village Action Plans (VAPs) were absent or prepared retroactively in large numbers of villages, District and State Action Plans did not flow from VAPs, and Annual Action Plans were consistently over-optimistic relative to ground capacity. Implementation was marked by cost escalations, fund mismanagement, non-recovery of contractor penalties, and diversion of JJM funds to inadmissible activities. Water quality monitoring — the core public health safeguard of the mission — was severely underfunded and technically deficient, with laboratories lacking NABL accreditation and failing to test for critical parameters including E. coli, heavy metals, and uranium. Sustainability was compromised by over-allocation of water from dam dead storage, absent groundwater recharge structures, failure to collect O&M charges, and no water metering — with 7 of 32 surveyed schemes found entirely non-functional despite being shown as completed on government dashboards.

keyFindings.text: MP achieved only 62% FHTC coverage (60.90 lakh of 98.28 lakh target households) by December 2024, against the March 2024 deadline — lagging the national average of ~80%. Only 27% of MVSs and 58% of SVSs were completed as of September 2024.

source.quote: 98.28 lakh households were to be covered by the target date... PHED was able to provide FHTCs to 60.90 lakh rural households as of 9 December 2024

keyFindings.text: Baseline surveys were not conducted for 666 villages (14% of 4,576 SVSs in eight districts) due to incomplete or delayed ISA appointments. This caused inaccurate assessments and contributed to cost escalations of ₹328.33 crore across 853 SVSs (from ₹668.67 crore to ₹997.12 crore).

source.quote: baseline surveys for 666 villages (14 per cent of total villages)

keyFindings.text: Village Action Plans (VAPs) were not prepared for 28.95% of PHED villages and 42.14% of Jal Nigam MVS villages in sampled districts. In 47 of 144 SVS villages, VAPs were prepared retroactively after DPRs were made and tenders floated — reducing them to a paperwork formality.

source.quote: failure to prepare VAPs for 28.95 per cent of villages under PHED and for 42.14 per cent in Jal Nigam indicates significant gaps in planning

keyFindings.text: Village Water and Sanitation Committees (VWSCs) were formed in only 76.14% of villages (5,517 of 7,245) in sampled districts. In 20 of 32 surveyed villages, mandatory quarterly VWSC meetings were not held. GPs/VWSCs did not obtain 80% community consent in any of the 32 test-checked villages.

source.quote: VWSCs were formed in 5517 villages (76.14 per cent) against 7,245 villages

keyFindings.text: 520 SC/ST-majority villages with a population of 3,72,745 were not prioritised in three districts (Chhatarpur, Gwalior, Vidisha). In Dindori District, 15 of 33 fluoride-affected villages continued to receive piped water without defluoridation despite a National Green Tribunal order (2020) mandating treatment by December 2020.

source.quote: 520 SC/ST villages, with a total of 3,72,745 population were not prioritized for piped water supply

keyFindings.text: 1,907 SVSs (groundwater-based schemes) across the state were shifted to MVSs due to groundwater source failure — indicating schemes were sanctioned without hydrogeological assessments. In Vidisha, all 522 SVSs were shifted; in Jhabua, 664 of 716 (93%) were shifted. This caused wasteful expenditure of ₹19.23 crore on borewells that dried up.

source.quote: 1,907 SVSs are now being shifted to MVSs due to inadequate groundwater

keyFindings.text: Due to poor fund utilisation (the state failed to utilise 80% of available funds in any year during 2019–24), the scheme was deprived of ₹9,297.11 crore in central grants that GoI did not release. The state also released its own share with a 41% shortfall against GoI releases during 2019–23.

source.quote: This deprived the GoMP of ₹ 9,297.11 crore, being the allocated share not released

keyFindings.text: Jal Nigam withdrew ₹2,410.37 crore from the Single Nodal Account in lump sum, parked it in a separate savings account, and made contractor payments of ₹2,394.72 crore outside the PFMS framework (up to June 2022) — directly contravening JJM guidelines and obscuring financial oversight.

source.quote: Jal Nigam in violation of E-in-C's instructions, withdrew the entire allocated amount (₹ 2,410.37 crore) from the SNA in lumpsum, parked the money in a separate savings account

keyFindings.text: Liquidated damages of ₹87.46 crore were not recovered from MVS contractors despite delays of 1,155 days (Payli MVS), 1,971 days (Sagad Hinotiya MVS), and 1,901 days (Bansujara Badamalhera MVS). For SVS contracts, non/short imposition of LD amounted to ₹5.09 crore.

source.quote: This resulted in non/short imposition of LD of ₹ 87.46 crore (Appendix 8)

keyFindings.text: Community contributions — mandatory under JJM guidelines at 5–10% of capital cost — amounted to only ₹27 lakh collected against a recoverable ₹241.74 crore in 4,570 villages of the eight sampled districts. The entire infrastructure cost was effectively borne by Centre and State.

source.quote: GPs/VWSCs/PHED had collected only ₹ 27 lakh against the recoverable amount of ₹ 241.74 crore towards community contribution (CC) in 4,570 villages

keyFindings.text: JJM funds were diverted to inadmissible activities totalling ₹12.11 crore: ₹3.50 crore transferred to district administration for "Vikas Yatra", ₹1.07 crore on salaries of pre-existing staff, ₹0.48 crore on tent/religious activities (Bhoomi Pujan), ₹2.53 crore on schemes without SWSM approval, and ₹4.53 crore by Jal Nigam on staff quarters construction.

source.quote: Audit observed deviation from JJM guidelines resulting in several instances of inadmissible expenditure

keyFindings.text: The E-Jal Shakti portal misreported FHTC coverage: 11,94,063 private/own-source tap connections not benefiting from JJM were counted as JJM FHTCs. Schemes in villages where water supply had not commenced were shown as FHTC-provided on the dashboard.

source.quote: 11,94,063 private/own source tap connections were not... E-Jal shakti portal displayed FHTCs provided to the households of the concerned villages

keyFindings.text: Water quality testing fell far short of prescribed frequencies: district labs conducted only 58–99% of mandated tests, the State Lab conducted only 22–48%, and Jal Nigam WTP labs tested a mere 11–19% of required samples. NABL accreditation for E. coli and total coliform was absent in district and sub-divisional laboratories. Uranium and virological parameters were never tested.

source.quote: The GoMP spent only 0.38 per cent on DWQM&S, diverting the rest 1.62 per cent for construction activities under JJM. This led to the evaluation of an insufficient number of parameters

keyFindings.text: O&M costs were not collected or collected only partially in 24 of 32 surveyed villages. Water connections were not metered in any of the sampled villages, despite the 14th Finance Commission recommendation for 100% metering by March 2017. No O&M policy was in place at the time of the audit.

source.quote: 24 villages out of 32 surveyed villages, Audit noticed that O&M costs were either not collected

keyFindings.text: Water for five MVSs (Gandhi Sagar-1, Gandhi Sagar-2, Rajghat, Agar Malwa, Kundaliya) was allocated from the dead storage of dams — violating IS:5477 specifications. At Rajghat dam, total demand of 2,217.74 MCM exceeds the 2018 reservoir capacity of 1,945 MCM by 272.74 MCM.

source.quote: Using dead storage water not only violates IS... allocation of water for the MVSs from the dead storage

keyFindings.text: Under Kaushal Vikas Prashikshan Yojana, only 11,271 persons (22% of the 50,000 target) were trained in plumbing, masonry, electrical, and fitting skills at an expenditure of ₹402.10 lakh (23% of the approved ₹1,712.62 lakh) — hobbling the long-term O&M of completed schemes.

source.quote: The Department could, however, train 11,271 people as Electrician, Mason, Fitter, etc., at the expenditure of

keyFindings.text: Availability of groundwater was not ensured in 7 of 32 surveyed villages, resulting in wasteful expenditure. During JPI, 7 schemes out of 32 surveyed schemes were found entirely non-functional due to non-maintenance of motor pumps, pipes, overhead tanks, and other components.

source.quote: seven schemes out of 32 schemes were entirely non-functional due to non-maintenance of scheme components viz., motor pumps

keyFindings.text: Beneficiary survey of 629 households across 32 villages: 141 households (22%) were not receiving water supply; 183 stated water was not potable; 252 were unaware of the community contribution requirement; and 7 of 32 surveyed schemes were entirely non-functional at the time of Joint Physical Inspection.

source.quote: seven schemes out of 32 schemes were entirely non-functional due to non-maintenance of scheme components

recommendations: Achieve 100% VAP coverage using ISAs immediately; form/activate VWSCs in all villages and mandate 5–10% community contributions via IEC campaigns. Baseline surveys completed post-award are not acceptable as they defeat the mission's bottom-up planning mandate.

Conduct mandatory hydrogeological assessments for all new and ongoing schemes; revive traditional water bodies and implement groundwater recharge measures (rainwater harvesting, check dams) before sanctioning new SVSs in water-scarce zones.

Enforce PFMS compliance for all fund releases; impose and recover liquidated damages from delayed contractors; investigate and recover inadmissible expenditure; fix accountability for idle fund balances.
Develop and implement strict data validation protocols for the E-Jal Shakti portal; conduct regular ground-level verification audits of reported FHTCs; fix accountability for misreporting.

Equip state, district, and sub-divisional water quality laboratories with NABL accreditation for all parameters stipulated under DWQM&S; hire adequate lab personnel; mandate de-fluoridation, de-arsenification, and other remedial treatment for all quality-affected villages.

Mandatorily include provisions for recharge structures in all ongoing and operational schemes; converge with 15th Finance Commission grants and MGNREGS for greywater management and source augmentation.

Implement IoT-based flow and quality monitoring systems (SCADA) across all completed schemes to detect non-functional FHTCs in real time; upload functional and non-functional status to the JJM portal.
Provide tap connections at the prescribed location inside the house; complete coverage of all public institutions (schools, Anganwadis, health centres) as a priority.
ministry: Public Health Engineering Department (PHED), Government of Madhya Pradesh

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act in Madhya Pradesh
overview:
The CAG audited implementation of MGNREGA in Madhya Pradesh across 8 districts, 16 Janpad Panchayats and 64 Gram Panchayats for 2019-24. The scheme guarantees 100 days of wage employment per rural household, but CAG found systemic failure at every level of the delivery chain — planning, finance, employment generation and oversight — resulting in only ~2% of households receiving the guaranteed entitlement.

Financially, the state accumulated a liability of ₹1,217 crore in unpaid wages and material costs by March 2024, and made ₹12.21 crore in expenditure on Cluster Facilitation Teams that the Government of India had explicitly rejected. Penal interest of ₹10.36 crore owed by the state for delayed fund transfers was never claimed, and ₹9.07 lakh in compensation for delayed wage payments to workers remained unpaid despite ₹4.42 crore sitting idle in a dedicated bank account.

On the ground, Joint Physical Verification of 384 works found 12 completed assets non-functional or not serving their intended purpose. Works completion rates ranged from only 25% to 46% across categories. Agriculture-linked works — which must constitute 60% of expenditure — received only 31.75% of spending in sampled districts. The monitoring architecture was hollowed out: the State Employment Guarantee Council held just 1 of the 10 required General Body meetings over five years, Vigilance Committees were never constituted, and social audit coverage remained below mandated levels.

stats.note: Only 1.95% (2023-24) to 5.83% (2020-21) of households received the legally guaranteed 100 days; in Raisen district the figure was just 0.75%

stats.label: Districts failing mandatory 33% women participation
stats.note: Raisen, Sagar and Vidisha districts fell below 33%; shortfall also observed in 7 of 16 Janpad Panchayats and 16 of 64 Gram Panchayats; no worksite crèches were provided

source.quote: women's participation is below 33 per cent

stats.label: Unauthorised expenditure on Cluster Facilitation Teams (post-GoI rejection)
stats.note: GoI rejected the CFT proposal in 2017; GoMP continued to operate and fund CFTs from administrative expenditure despite the rejection; expenditure deemed inadmissible

source.quote: unauthorized expenditure of ₹12.21 crore from Administrative expenditure component

keyFindings.text: The entire planning framework mandated by MGNREGA was absent across all levels. Gram Panchayats conducted no baseline surveys or door-to-door surveys to assess actual employment demand. The state-level Information, Education and Communication (IEC) Plan was never prepared. Block Resource Centres — required as knowledge hubs for capacity building — were not set up in any of the 16 selected Janpad Panchayats. Multi-year District Perspective Plans were not prepared in any of the 8 test-checked districts.

source.quote: baseline surveys and Door-to-Door surveys were not conducted by Gram Panchayats

keyFindings.text: Labour Budgets were prepared top-down at Zila Panchayat level without any input from Gram Panchayats — the opposite of what the guidelines require. This resulted in no alignment between projected and actual person-days generated. Rozgar Diwas (mandatory monthly employment fairs to register demand) were not conducted by selected GPs, cutting off the main channel through which workers signal demand. Development Plans and Shelf of Projects were also not prepared at GP level.

source.quote: Zila Panchayats formulated the Person-Days projections and Labour Budget without incorporating inputs from the Janpad Panchayats

keyFindings.text: Staff shortages crippled implementation at every tier: 64% vacancy at MPSEGC state headquarters, 57% at Division level, 63% at District level, 44% at Janpad Panchayat level, and 11% at Gram Panchayat level. No dedicated Programme Officers were appointed exclusively for MGNREGS in any district. The manpower shortfall grew from 15.25% in 2019-20 to a peak of 21.36% in 2022-23. Departmental training programmes did not cover courses defined in the guidelines, and Human Resource Development divisions at District level were never set up.

source.quote: Shortage of 64 per cent in MPSEGC, Bhopal. Shortage of 57 per cent at Division level. Shortage of 63 per cent at District level. Shortage of 44 per cent at Janpad Panchayat level

keyFindings.text: Fund utilisation peaked at underutilisation of ₹1,703.80 crore in 2021-22. Persistent discrepancies existed between fund availability and expenditure data reported by MPSEGC and what was visible on the NREGASoft public portal — undermining the transparency mandate of the scheme. The Council used over 95% of available funds in most years, but the 2021-22 shortfall was caused by late Central releases that arrived near year-end.

source.quote: amounts unutilized during 2019-2024, with a peak of ₹1703.80 crore in 2021-22

keyFindings.text: ₹2,061.49 crore of ₹13,615.31 crore in total releases by GoMP was deposited in the State Employment Guarantee Fund with delays ranging from 3 to 76 days, creating a penal interest liability of ₹10.36 crore at 12% per annum. MPSEGC never sought this amount from GoMP despite clear instructions in GoI sanction orders. The state replied no instructions were received — the CAG rejected this, noting the obligation was explicit in every sanction order.

source.quote: MPSEGC did not seek ₹10.36 crore of interest from GoMP for delayed release of funds

keyFindings.text: ₹12.21 crore was spent on Cluster Facilitation Teams (CFTs) — a field coordination structure — after the Government of India explicitly rejected the state's proposal to continue funding CFTs in 2017. GoMP continued to deploy and pay CFTs for years post-rejection by drawing from the administrative expenditure component. The CAG deemed this expenditure inadmissible and unauthorised.

source.quote: unauthorized expenditure of ₹12.21 crore from Administrative expenditure component

keyFindings.text: As of 31 March 2024, the state carried a liability of ₹1,217.05 crore in unpaid wages and material costs — money owed to workers and vendors for work already executed. ₹54.79 crore (4.7 lakh transactions) of this was stuck due to beneficiary bank accounts not being mapped to Aadhaar. Separately, ₹9.07 lakh in legally mandated compensation for delayed wage payments to workers remained unpaid, even though ₹4.42 crore sat idle in the dedicated compensation bank account.

source.quote: liabilities of wages and material of ₹1217.058 crore as on 31 March 2024

keyFindings.text: 8,575 job card applications were left unprocessed without any documented reasons, denying those households access to the scheme. ₹1.46 crore in wages were paid on 2,426 duplicate, fake, or incorrect job cards during 2019-24. Mandatory registers required at GP level — capturing demand, attendance and payments from start to end — were not maintained or updated, preventing any audit trail of whether employment was actually provided to those who demanded it.

source.quote: Irregular wage payments of ₹1.46 crore was paid on 2,426 duplicate, fake, or incorrect job cards during 2019-24

keyFindings.text: Only ~2% of households received the legally guaranteed 100 days of employment in any year (range: 1.95% in 2023-24 to 5.83% during COVID-19 year 2020-21). In Raisen district, only 0.75% of households got 100 days. At the other end, 31.21% to 46.60% of households received less than 40 days. The primary cause identified: MGNREGS wage rates were ₹32–40 lower than prevailing agricultural market wages, making the scheme unattractive relative to private employment.

source.quote: only around two per cent of the audit period, indicating limited access or implementation of the scheme

keyFindings.text: The mandatory 33% participation of women workers was not achieved in 3 of 8 test-checked districts (Raisen, Sagar, Vidisha), 7 of 16 Janpad Panchayats, and 16 of 64 Gram Panchayats. No selected JP incurred any expenditure on worksite facilities (drinking water, shade, medical aid, crèches for children of working women) during 2019-24 — directly reducing women's participation. Registration of differently-abled persons dropped sharply in 2022-23 and 2023-24, with no inclusive work types identified for them.

source.quote: women's participation is below 33 per cent

keyFindings.text: Agriculture-linked works — legally required to constitute at least 60% of district expenditure — received only 31.75% of spending (₹350.73 crore of ₹1,104.66 crore) in Vidisha district. Category B works (individual household assets, dominated by PMAY housing) were given highest priority at 62.51% of all approved works. Category C (common infrastructure) works were almost entirely neglected at 0.10% of approved works.

source.quote: 31.75 per cent (₹350.73 crore out of ₹1104.66 crore) of expenditure was incurred on works related to agriculture and allied activities

keyFindings.text: Across all categories, only 25.02% (Category C) to 46.14% (Category B) of initiated works were completed in five years. During Joint Physical Verification of 384 works, multiple items mandated under approved Technical Sanctions were absent at the site. 12 assets that had been marked completed were either non-functional or not serving their intended purpose (including farm ponds that held no water even after the rainy season). Individual private wells were dug in areas classified as critical or over-exploited for groundwater — directly violating MGNREGA guidelines.

source.quote: only 25.02 per cent (Category C works) to 46.14 per cent (Category B works) initiated works were completed in five years

keyFindings.text: New community works were approved in Gram Panchayats even when older works remained incomplete beyond one fiscal year — violating guidelines and leading to resource fragmentation. 206 community works remained incomplete as of 31 March 2024, including 189 started before the audit period and 17 started during 2019-22. A case study in Vidisha showed nursery gardens sanctioned in 2020 and 2022 remained unfinished despite spending ₹3.76 lakh and ₹4.44 lakh, while the same GPs had 85+ new works approved in subsequent years.

source.quote: new community works were approved despite works remaining incomplete beyond one fiscal year

keyFindings.text: The Madhya Pradesh State Employment Guarantee Council (MPSEGC) — the apex oversight body — held only 1 General Body meeting against the 10 required over 2019-24, and even that single meeting (February 2022) was held without nominating non-government members from civil society. Vigilance and Monitoring Committees were not constituted at state, district, or local levels. State Quality Monitoring Cell and District Quality Monitoring Cells were not set up. Nine audit observations from previous CAG reports remained unimproved.

source.quote: against the required 10 General Body meetings during 2019-20 to 2023-24, only one meeting was held

keyFindings.text: Social audit — the scheme's key accountability mechanism — was conducted in more than 50% of Gram Panchayats in most years but with major gaps: concurrent social audits (which verify ongoing works in real time) were never done; the Social Audit Unit had large vacancies with only 35 of 37 sanctioned posts filled at state level and significant district-level gaps; social audit funds were parked in Fixed Deposits outside designated bank accounts against rules; interest earned on FDRs was not remitted to the Consolidated Fund; and ₹0.33 crore in financial misappropriation identified through audits remained unrecovered.

source.quote: social audits in more than 50 per cent of Gram Panchayats each year

recommendations: Conduct baseline and door-to-door surveys in all GPs to identify genuine employment demand, differently-abled persons, and women in vulnerable categories (widowed, deserted, destitute) before preparing Labour Budgets.

Adopt a strict bottom-up approach: GPs prepare Shelf of Projects and Development Plans with Gram Sabha approval; Janpad Panchayats consolidate; Zila Panchayats finalise Labour Budget based on GP-level demand projections.
Fill all vacant posts at state, division, district, block, and GP levels on priority; appoint dedicated full-time Programme Officers exclusively for MGNREGS in each district as mandated.
Recover penal interest of ₹10.36 crore from GoMP for delayed fund transfers; clear the ₹1,217 crore unpaid wages liability and the ₹9.07 lakh pending worker compensation immediately.
Regularise or discontinue Cluster Facilitation Teams and account for ₹12.21 crore spent post-GoI rejection; eliminate discrepancies between departmental financial data and NREGASoft records.

Sanitise the Aadhaar-payment mapping database to unblock ₹54.79 crore stuck in 4.7 lakh transactions; review and revise MGNREGS wage rates in consultation with GoI to close the gap with prevailing market wages.
Ensure agriculture-linked works constitute at least 60% of district expenditure as legally mandated; rebalance work selection away from housing (PMAY) towards water, land and plantation works.
Prohibit approval of new works in GPs with incomplete projects pending beyond one financial year; stop sanctioning individual private wells in critical or over-exploited groundwater regions.
Conduct General Body meetings of MPSEGC at least twice a year with nominated non-government members; constitute Vigilance and Monitoring Committees at state, district and local levels without delay.

Strengthen social audit by filling SAU vacancies, conducting mandated concurrent social audits, recovering all pending financial misappropriation amounts, and publishing Citizens Charter at GP offices and worksites.
ministry: Panchayat and Rural Development Department (PRDD), Government of Madhya Pradesh

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana – Gramin in Uttar Pradesh
overview:
PMAY-G replaced the Indira Awaas Yojana in November 2016, promising a pucca house with basic amenities to every houseless rural family by 2022 (extended to March 2024). In Uttar Pradesh — the scheme's largest state by target — 36.15 lakh houses were planned. The CAG audited 19 of 75 districts, 57 Blocks and 1,520 Gram Panchayats covering April 2017 to March 2023.

The state reported 98% completion — 34.18 lakh of 34.71 lakh sanctioned houses built — but the audit found significant gaps beneath that headline. 11.35 lakh households who were eligible for housing assistance were identified in the AwaasPlus survey but excluded from the beneficiary list; the Rural Development Department itself accepted that many eligible beneficiaries were erroneously deleted. Only 1,248 houses (0.04% of those sanctioned) went to persons with disabilities despite a 3–5% reservation.

Financially, administrative funds were so poorly used that the Central Government withheld ₹357.29 crore in Central share. The release of the first instalment was delayed in 79% of cases, ₹20.18 crore remained unpaid to 11,031 beneficiaries with completed houses, and ₹28.70 crore in wage compensation for mason trainees was pending as of October 2024. Joint Physical Verification of 2,079 houses found 82% without the PMAY-G logo, 74% without plastered walls, 54% without a dedicated cooking space, 58% without a bathing area, and — critically — 89% without piped drinking water.

title: Performance Audit on Ayushman Bharat-PMJAY and Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana-Gramin in Bihar
overview:
This CAG report covers two flagship national schemes in Bihar — Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY, the ₹5 lakh health insurance scheme) and PMAY-G (rural housing). The audit examined 10 districts and 63 hospitals for AB-PMJAY, and covered PMAY-G implementation across the state's 30.67 lakh sanctioned houses.

On AB-PMJAY, only 2.56 crore of the 6.18 crore targeted beneficiaries were verified by March 2024 (41%). Of those verified, only 4.89 lakh (1.91%) actually availed the scheme's health benefits. The State Health Agency admitted 19,917 time-barred claims and paid ₹33.44 crore in inadmissible payments to empanelled hospitals. 218.28 lakh beneficiaries were verified with zero or one biometric match score — meaning they were enrolled without adequate identity confirmation.

On PMAY-G, Bihar reported 94% completion (28.94 lakh houses) but Joint Physical Verification found 306 of 1,324 "completed" houses had no roof casting, and 390 beneficiaries had not started construction 34-93 months after receiving the first instalment. In 541 of 961 verified completed houses (56%), no toilet had been constructed despite Swachh Bharat Mission convergence being mandatory. Only 3,648 of 13,328 required social audits (27%) were conducted across the audit period.

title: Performance Audit on AYUSH (National AYUSH Mission) in Uttar Pradesh
overview:
National AYUSH Mission (NAM) was launched in September 2014 to promote universal access to Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy (AYUSH) services. In Uttar Pradesh, the AYUSH Department was established in April 2017, with 8 Ayurvedic, 9 Homeopathic and 2 Unani Medical Colleges & Hospitals, 324 Ayurvedic Dispensaries, 1,786 Ayurvedic Hospitals, 1,585 Homeopathic Dispensaries, 72 Unani Dispensaries, 182 Unani Hospitals, 871 Health & Wellness Centres (HWCs) and 224 Yoga Wellness Centres. The CAG audit covered the period April 2018 to March 2023.

The headline finding is a systemic failure to utilise funds allocated under NAM. Against budgetary provisions of ₹5,630 crore for Ayurveda, ₹2,598 crore for Homeopathy and ₹684 crore for Unani services over five years, the Directorates incurred savings of 30.69%, 23.68% and 33.60% respectively — and surrendered 100% of those savings on the last day of each financial year, indicating deliberate non-planning rather than genuine unavailability of work. The Executing Agency (EA) for construction activities parked released funds in a savings bank account rather than deploying them on works.

The consequences of this underutilisation were concrete and measurable. Out of 1,034 HWCs sanctioned under NAM, 219 (21%) lacked electricity and 528 (51%) lacked internet connectivity as of January 2025. The State Pharmacy produced only 59.94% of the number of approved medicine types in its target — and only 51.35% of the quantity. Against a target of 25 Fifty-Bedded Integrated AYUSH Hospitals (FIAHs), only 18 were completed by 2022-23. Across the 11 functional FIAHs, 538 of the required posts (71%) were vacant.

There was no planning in the department for creating HWCs in a phased manner: 28 of 42 HWCs proposed in 2019-21 were found not feasible for upgradation; 9 were already upgraded; 74 HWCs proposed by UPSCIDCO were not required because the work was already done or buildings were dilapidated.

keyFindings.text: There were severe staff shortages across all three AYUSH systems. Medical Officers: Ayurveda 33% vacant, Unani 12% vacant, Homeopathy 4% vacant. Chief Pharmacists: Ayurveda 88% vacant, Unani 80% vacant. Pharmacists: Ayurveda 47%, Homeopathy 45%, Unani 57% vacant. Staff Nurses: Homeopathy 100% vacant, Unani 81% vacant, Ayurveda 40% vacant. In 11 functional FIAHs, 538 of the required posts (71%) were vacant; test-check of 3 FIAHs showed average 53% manpower shortage, including no Senior MOs in several facilities.

source.quote: (Ayurveda: 88 per cent, Unani: 80 per cent), Pharmacists (Ayurveda:

keyFindings.text: Teaching faculty shortages in AYUSH Medical Colleges: Ayurvedic GMCH Banda had 53% faculty vacancy, Pilibhit 27%, Homeopathic GMCH Moradabad 48%, Prayagraj 17%. Due to non-compliance with NCISM (National Commission for Indian System of Medicine) norms, the intake capacity of Ayurvedic GMCHs at Banda and Pilibhit was reduced. Delays in construction of college buildings, hostels and residential quarters compounded these deficiencies. Funds given for research were not utilised.

source.quote: 33 per cent, Homeopathy: 4 per cent, Unani: 12 per cent), Chief Pharmacists

keyFindings.text: No Radiologist or Pathologist was available in any of the five test-checked AYUSH GMCHs except one Pathologist at Lucknow. Laboratory Technicians were absent in Moradabad; X-ray Technicians were absent in Banda, Pilibhit and Moradabad. AERB licensing for X-ray machines had not been obtained. Basic fire safety requirements were not met at test-checked hospitals — fire extinguishers were not installed as required under UP Fire Norms 2005 and National Building Code 2016, and evacuation plans were absent.

source.quote: Safety from fire

recommendations: Rationalise budget demands and deploy funds throughout the year rather than surrendering savings on the last day; take action against EAs that park released funds in bank accounts instead of deploying them on works.

Develop a phased, need-based roadmap for HWC creation in joint exercise with the Health Department; ensure electricity, internet connectivity and IT equipment in all sanctioned HWCs before they are marked functional.
Provide dedicated budget to the State Pharmacy for raw material procurement and infrastructure; stop purchasing medicines exclusively from IMPCL when the State Pharmacy is capable of producing them.
Enforce procurement discipline: blacklist firms that persistently delay supplies; forfeit performance guarantees on default; do not permit offline supply orders beyond the scope of GeM tender values.
Fill critical vacancies — particularly Pharmacists, Staff Nurses, Chief Pharmacists and Medical Officers — on urgent basis through UPPSC and direct recruitment drives.
Ensure NCISM compliance at all AYUSH Medical Colleges; complete pending construction of hostels, residential quarters and college buildings within time-bound milestones with penalty provisions.
ministry: AYUSH Department, Government of Uttar Pradesh

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Jal Jeevan Mission in Karnataka
overview:
Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) was launched by the Government of India in August 2019 with the aim of providing Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTCs) to every rural household by 2024, at a prescribed service level of 55 litres per capita per day (LPCD). Karnataka targeted FHTCs for 72.14 lakh rural households. The CAG conducted a Performance Audit covering seven districts to assess planning, financial management, water quality and sustainability.

The headline finding is a severe shortfall in physical delivery: only 47.62 lakh (66 per cent) FHTCs were provided against the target of 72.14 lakh households as of November 2024. The State received only ₹11,189 crore against the total allocation of ₹24,819.48 crore (45 per cent) from the Centre, primarily due to its inability to utilise already-released funds. Community contributions — a key funding pillar — were virtually absent: only ₹22.57 crore was collected against the expected ₹1,594.90 crore.

Quality monitoring infrastructure was completely non-functional: none of the 31 district-level and 48 taluk-level laboratories in the State were equipped to test all 13 prescribed parameters for water quality. Mandatory institutional meetings were not held in 13 of 30 districts in 2023-24. Five villages were prematurely declared 100 per cent FHTC-covered though works were not completed.

stats.label: FHTCs provided vs target of 72.14 lakh households
stats.note: 47.62 lakh FHTCs provided as of November 2024 out of 72.14 lakh targeted — a shortfall of 24.52 lakh households (34 per cent). FHTC coverage in multiple districts was below 60 per cent.

source.quote: FHTCs were provided to 47.62 lakh (66 per cent) HHs as of November 2024.

stats.label: Central allocation actually received by the State
stats.note: Karnataka received only ₹11,189 crore against an allocation of ₹24,819.48 crore — the Centre withheld funds due to the State's inability to utilise already-released amounts. State's own share contribution of ₹1,594.90 crore saw only ₹22.57 crore actually collected.

stats.label: Community contribution collected vs expected ₹1,594.90 crore
stats.note: ₹22.57 crore collected out of ₹1,594.90 crore expected as community contribution for in-village infrastructure — a near-complete failure of the participatory funding model. This also compromised the sustainability of installed schemes.

source.quote: community contribution collected was ₹22.57 crore against the estimated ₹1,594.90 crore

stats.label: District-level labs equipped for all 13 water quality parameters
stats.note: None of the 31 district-level and 48 taluk-level laboratories in Karnataka were equipped to test all 13 prescribed parameters under BIS IS:10500. 37 per cent of existing labs lacked NABL accreditation. Water testing in schools and Anganwadi centres was not done at prescribed frequency.

source.quote: none of the 31 district level and 48 taluk level laboratories in the State

stats.label: FHTC target achievement (ISRA) in selected districts by 2023-24
stats.note: The overall target achievement by the Implementation Support and Review Agency (ISRA) during 2023-24 in the selected districts was only 22 per cent. Performance fell from 103 per cent in 2021-22 to 59 per cent in 2022-23, and further to 22 per cent in 2023-24.

source.quote: performance in the test-checked districts declined from 103 per cent in 2021-22 to 59 per cent in 2022-23

stats.label: Districts that held mandated 12 District Water Sanitation Mission meetings in 2023-24
stats.note: None of the 30 districts conducted the mandated 12 DWSM meetings during 2023-24. 13 districts including 4 sampled districts held zero meetings that year. The Apex Committee lacked representation from heads of Health, Finance and Planning departments.

source.quote: none of the districts had conducted the mandated 12 meetings during the years 2019-20 and 2023-24

stats.label: Villages prematurely declared 100% FHTC complete (but works not finished)
stats.note: Audit joint physical verification found that in 5 villages declared as 100 per cent FHTC-covered, household tap connection works were in fact still incomplete. Premature certification inflated progress data on the JJM dashboard.

source.quote: in four1 of these villages, the declared 100 per cent completion

stats.label: Work contract (₹146.64 lakh) abandoned after spending ₹60.41 lakh
stats.note: One water supply scheme contract of ₹146.64 lakh was abandoned after incurring an expenditure of ₹60.41 lakh; a different contractor had to be engaged from scratch. Similar instances of abandoned and idle works were found across sampled districts.

source.quote: incurring an expenditure of ₹60.41 lakh (May 2024), towards construction

stats.label: Beneficiaries unaware of JJM planning in surveyed villages
stats.note: 27 per cent of Focus Group Discussion respondents reported non-involvement in JJM planning; 32 per cent were unaware of user charges to be collected for scheme sustainability. Only 5 per cent of surveyed beneficiaries were aware of scheme details.

source.quote: Out of the FGD respondents 27 per cent reported non-involvement

stats.label: Water schemes: GP approval of scheme contract issued to contractor
stats.note: One Gram Panchayat entrusted (October 2023) a water supply scheme worth ₹51.86 lakh to a contractor with a completion period of four months, without ensuring land availability — leading to delayed execution and non-completion.

source.quote: Gram Panchayat was entrusted (October 2023) to a contractor for ₹146.64 lakh

keyFindings.text: Only 47.62 lakh (66 per cent) FHTCs were provided against the target of 72.14 lakh households as of November 2024. The State received only ₹11,189 crore out of ₹24,819.48 crore allocated by the Centre — the Centre withheld funds specifically because Karnataka could not utilise what had already been released. Community contributions, which were to fund 15 per cent of scheme costs under in-village infrastructure, stood at ₹22.57 crore against the expected ₹1,594.90 crore (1.4 per cent), effectively nullifying a core pillar of the mission design.

source.quote: FHTCs were provided to 47.62 lakh (66 per cent) HHs as of November 2024.

keyFindings.text: Not a single one of the 31 district-level and 48 taluk-level water quality testing laboratories in Karnataka was equipped to test all 13 prescribed parameters under BIS IS:10500. 37 per cent of existing labs lacked NABL accreditation. Water quality testing was not conducted in schools and Anganwadi centres as per the prescribed frequency. Without functional quality testing, the JJM guarantee of "safe" piped water is unverifiable across the entire State.

source.quote: none of the 31 district level and 48 taluk level laboratories in the State

keyFindings.text: The Village Water and Sanitation Committees (VWSCs) and District Water Sanitation Missions (DWSMs) that are the institutional backbone of JJM were largely non-functional. None of the 30 districts held the mandated 12 DWSM meetings in 2023-24; 13 districts held zero meetings. Village Action Plans (VAPs) omitted crucial elements such as source sustainability, financial sustainability provisions and groundwater data. The Apex Committee was not represented by heads of Health, Finance and Planning departments.

source.quote: none of the districts had conducted the mandated 12 meetings during the years 2019-20 and 2023-24

keyFindings.text: Five villages were prematurely declared as 100 per cent FHTC-covered in official dashboards while tap connection works were still incomplete. Third-party evaluation reports lacked depth and independent performance assessments were delayed. 27 per cent of surveyed beneficiaries reported no involvement in JJM planning; 80 per cent community approval for scheme finalisation as required by guidelines was not obtained in many surveyed villages.

source.quote: in four1 of these villages, the declared 100 per cent completion

keyFindings.text: Implementation Support Agencies (ISRA) were severely underperforming: from 103 per cent achievement in 2021-22, their performance fell to 59 per cent in 2022-23 and further to 22 per cent in 2023-24 in the test-checked districts. Gaps in deployment of trained and skilled manpower were observed. Works were awarded to contractors without ensuring availability of land, leading to multiple instances of abandoned or partially-executed schemes.

source.quote: performance in the test-checked districts declined from 103 per cent in 2021-22 to 59 per cent in 2022-23

keyFindings.text: The State failed to leverage convergence with other schemes (MGNREGS, SBM-G, MPLADS, 15th Finance Commission tied grants) to augment financial resources. No financial plan pooling available resources was prepared in test-checked districts. The 15th Finance Commission tied grants of ₹1,358 crore and ₹2,220.18 crore in community contributions remained un-mobilised. Expenditure on water quality monitoring and surveillance was only ₹22.57 crore against a provisioned ₹1,594.90 crore.

source.quote: community contribution collected was ₹22.57 crore against the estimated ₹1,594.90 crore

recommendations: Direct DWSM committees to hold all mandated meetings; link District Action Plan approval to evidence of meetings held with minutes.
Prioritise NABL accreditation for all district and taluk labs; ensure all 13 prescribed parameters are testable before any village is certified as Har Ghar Jal.
Stop prematurely certifying villages as 100 per cent FHTC-covered; link dashboard reporting to joint physical verification by Gram Panchayats and third-party agencies.
Mobilise community contributions through Gram Sabhas and ensure user charge collection frameworks are in place before scheme hand-over.
Leverage 15th Finance Commission tied grants and MGNREGS convergence to complete incomplete water supply schemes in priority areas.
ministry: Department of Rural Development and Panchayat Raj (RDPR), Government of Karnataka

title: Performance Audit on MGNREGS in Karnataka
overview:
The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS) guarantees at least 100 days of wage employment per year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer to do unskilled manual work. The CAG conducted a Performance Audit in Karnataka covering the period 2019-20 to 2023-24, examining planning, financial management, employment generation, asset creation and social audit across six test-checked districts.

The headline finding is a near-complete failure to deliver the scheme's core entitlement: only 2 to 4 per cent of households that demanded employment were actually provided 100 days of work during the audit period. The majority of demanding households received only 1 to 30 days of employment. The State delayed releases to the State Employment Guarantee Fund, incurring ₹36.26 crore in penal interest while simultaneously recording ₹32.78 crore in inadmissible expenditure under the administrative head.

Aadhaar mapping — essential for wage payment verification — was pending for 3.11 lakh out of 84.98 lakh active workers (3.7 per cent) as of March 2024. Unemployment allowances of ₹1.28 crore, legally payable when employment is not provided within 15 days of demand, were pending disbursement. Fraudulent transactions — payment for houses already completed, payments without construction, payments in excess of prescribed limits — were observed across test-checked works.

stats.label: Households provided 100 days of employment (of total demanding households)
stats.note: Only 2 to 4 per cent of households that demanded employment under MGNREGS received the full entitlement of 100 days. The majority of households received only 1 to 30 days, defeating the livelihood security objective of the scheme.

source.quote: 2 per cent to 4 per cent households were provided employment for 100 days and

stats.label: Penal interest incurred on delayed State releases
stats.note: The State Government's delay in releasing central and state share to the State Employment Guarantee Fund entailed penal interest of ₹36.26 crore — public money wasted because of administrative delays in fund transfer.

source.quote: State Employment Guarantee Fund entailed a penal interest of ₹36.26 crore.

stats.label: Inadmissible expenditure under administrative head of scheme
stats.note: Audit observed inadmissible expenditure of ₹32.78 crore under the administrative head of the Scheme — expenditure that should not have been incurred but was, reducing funds available for actual employment and asset creation.

source.quote: Audit also observed inadmissible expenditure of ₹32.78 crore under the administrative head of the Scheme.

stats.label: Active workers with pending Aadhaar account mapping (as of March 2024)
stats.note: Out of 84.98 lakh active workers, Aadhaar mapping of 3.11 lakh workers was pending at the State level as of March 2024. Without Aadhaar mapping, no assurance can be drawn about the preparation of wage lists and payments made to these workers — creating leakage risk.

source.quote: Aadhaar mapping with the accounts of 3.11 lakh out of 84.98 lakh active workers was pending (March 2024)

stats.label: Unemployment allowances due but unpaid
stats.note: Under MGNREGA, if employment is not provided within 15 days of demand, the household is entitled to unemployment allowance. Unemployment allowances assessed as payable for 2019-20 to 2023-24 amounting to ₹1.28 crore were pending payment. Demand registers were not properly maintained, meaning actual liability is likely higher.

source.quote: unemployment allowance assessed payable for the period 2019-20 to 2023-24, amounting to ₹1.28 crore, was also pending

stats.label: Job card applications pending (as of March 2024)
stats.note: Issue of job cards was pending for 34,499 beneficiaries who had applied, as of March 2024. Special job cards were not issued to differently-abled persons. The NREGASoft system had no provision to record data of vulnerable groups (nomadic tribals, HIV-positive persons etc.) for targeted support.

source.quote: Issue of job cards was pending for 34,499 beneficiaries who had applied for jobs, as of March 2024.

stats.label: Demand for employment as fraction of issued job cards
stats.note: The demand for employment from registered households did not exceed 48 per cent of issued job cards during the audit period — indicating that either awareness of entitlements was lacking, or workers were not being encouraged to formally demand employment (which triggers the 15-day clock).

source.quote: demand for employment from the registered households did not exceed 48 per cent of the issued job cards during the audit period

stats.label: Rejection of legally due delayed-wage compensation
stats.note: When wages are paid late, MGNREGA entitles workers to compensation. Programme Officers rejected delayed compensation amounting to ₹3.29 crore on incorrect grounds. NREGASoft calculated delays partially — capturing only part of the delay period to the disadvantage of beneficiaries.

source.quote: rejection of delayed compensation amounting to ₹3.29 crore by Programme Officers on incorrect grounds

stats.label: Material component funds not utilised (released at year-end)
stats.note: The Department failed to utilise the entire amount released under the material component of MGNREGS because funds were released at the fag end of the financial year. This pattern of year-end dumps made effective planning of works impossible.

source.quote: failed to utilise the entire amount released under material component as the fund were released at the fag end of the year

stats.label: Fraudulent transactions in housing and Solid Waste Management works
stats.note: Audit noticed fraudulent transactions including: payment for houses already completed, payment to ineligible beneficiaries, payments without undertaking construction, and payments in excess of prescribed limits. Fabrication of records and fraudulent payments were also found in Solid Waste Management works.

source.quote: Fraudulent transactions under housing works such as payment for houses already completed, payment to ineligible beneficiaries

keyFindings.text: Only 2 to 4 per cent of MGNREGS-demanding households in Karnataka received the full statutory entitlement of 100 days of employment during 2019-20 to 2023-24. The majority received 1 to 30 days. The unemployment allowance that the law requires to be paid when employment is not provided within 15 days was assessed at ₹1.28 crore in payable arrears but remained unpaid. Demand registers at test-checked Gram Panchayats were not maintained, meaning the actual quantum of unfulfilled employment demand — and consequent liability — is substantially understated.

source.quote: 2 per cent to 4 per cent households were provided employment for 100 days and

keyFindings.text: The State's delay in releasing funds to the State Employment Guarantee Fund incurred ₹36.26 crore in penal interest — and simultaneously ₹32.78 crore was recorded as inadmissible expenditure under the administrative head. Contractors were found hired for manual (labour-oriented) components of works, depriving registered workers of their employment entitlement. Pending Aadhaar mapping of 3.11 lakh workers out of 84.98 lakh active workers meant no assurance could be drawn on wage payment integrity for these accounts.

source.quote: State Employment Guarantee Fund entailed a penal interest of ₹36.26 crore.

keyFindings.text: Recruitment of contractual staff under the Scheme was carried out without following the State's reservation policy, resulting in inadequate representation of women, SCs, STs and differently-abled persons. 34,499 job card applications were pending as of March 2024. Special job cards for differently-abled persons were not issued. NREGASoft had no provision to record vulnerable group data. The assessment of demand was not based on a baseline survey, meaning Labour Budgets were prepared without knowing actual employment needs at the Gram Panchayat level.

source.quote: Issue of job cards was pending for 34,499 beneficiaries who had applied for jobs, as of March 2024.

keyFindings.text: Programme Officers rejected ₹3.29 crore of legally-due delayed-wage compensation on incorrect grounds. NREGASoft calculated compensation for delayed wages capturing only partial delays, systematically underpaying workers. Pending wage payments of ₹35.10 crore in Aadhaar-based transactions (rejected and regenerated) remained unresolved. A pendency of ₹30.52 crore was observed in respect of outstanding unskilled wages in test-checked districts.

source.quote: rejection of delayed compensation amounting to ₹3.29 crore by Programme Officers on incorrect grounds

keyFindings.text: Fraudulent transactions were found in housing works (payment for already-completed houses, payment to ineligible beneficiaries, payments without construction, payments in excess of limits) and in Solid Waste Management works (fabricated records). Works contracts were extended unauthorisedly without fresh tenders. Capacity building training programmes showed significant shortfall in conduct. Convergence of MGNREGS works with other departments was ineffective due to absence of prescribed institutional support.

source.quote: Fraudulent transactions under housing works such as payment for houses already completed, payment to ineligible beneficiaries

recommendations: Conduct baseline survey of job card holders to assess actual employment demand before preparing Labour Budgets; stop using previous-year consumption as a proxy for demand.
Ensure timely release of funds throughout the year to avoid year-end dumps; stop incurring penal interest on delayed releases to the State Employment Guarantee Fund.
Pay all pending unemployment allowances immediately; maintain demand registers at every Gram Panchayat and integrate demand verification into NREGASoft.
Complete Aadhaar mapping for all 3.11 lakh pending active workers; adopt Aadhaar-based payment for all wage transactions without exception.
Investigate and recover fraudulent payments in housing and Solid Waste Management works; blacklist contractors found to have submitted fabricated records.
ministry: Rural Development and Panchayati Raj Department, Government of Karnataka

title: Performance Audit of Implementation of MGNREGS in Chhattisgarh
overview:
MGNREGS guarantees at least 100 days of wage employment per year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer to do unskilled manual work. The CAG Performance Audit covered the period 2019-20 to 2023-24 in Chhattisgarh, test-checking six districts including Raigarh and Surguja. Chhattisgarh annually spends around ₹3,400 crore on MGNREGS.

The defining failure is the complete bypass of democratic accountability: 86 per cent of all MGNREGS works in the 48 test-checked Gram Panchayats were undertaken without Gram Sabha approval — the basic democratic sanction that the MGNREGA requires before any work can begin. During 2019-24, 152.36 lakh households demanded employment; employment was not provided to 18.26 lakh (12 per cent) of them. No unemployment allowances were paid to any of these households despite a legal obligation.

Employer Provident Fund contributions of ₹29.62 crore owed to MGNREGS workers for April 2015 to March 2023 remained unpaid, accumulating into a total liability of ₹84.59 crore including penalty and interest. Capacity building training — the scheme's backbone — showed a 97 per cent shortfall: against a target of 2,93,388 trainees, only 9,331 were trained.

stats.label: Works undertaken without Gram Sabha approval (test-checked GPs)
stats.note: Out of 12,714 works sanctioned in the Annual Work Plans in 48 test-checked Gram Panchayats during 2019-24, only 1,717 (14 per cent) had Gram Sabha approval; 10,997 (86 per cent) were undertaken without the approval of the respective Gram Sabha.

source.quote: 10,997 (86 per cent) works were undertaken without approval from respective

stats.label: Employment demand unmet (2019-24)
stats.note: During 2019-24, 152.36 lakh households demanded employment under MGNREGS; 134.10 lakh were provided employment. Employment was not provided to 18.26 lakh households (12 per cent). No unemployment allowances were paid to any of these households; State budget provisions of ₹2.22 crore for unemployment allowances were fully surrendered without any expenditure.

source.quote: was not provided to 18.26 lakh HHs, indicating a significant shortfall in providing the employment to the HHs.

stats.label: EPF contributions unpaid to workers (April 2015 – March 2023)
stats.note: EPF contributions of ₹29.62 crore for the period April 2015 to March 2023 remained unpaid, accumulating to a total liability of ₹84.59 crore including ₹54.96 crore in penalty and interest. Workers earning below ₹15,000 per month are entitled to EPF at 12 per cent of wages.

source.quote: ₹ 29.62 crore for the period April 2015 to March 2023 remained unpaid.

stats.label: Capacity building training shortfall (2021-22 to 2023-24)
stats.note: Against a target of 2,93,388 trainees during 2021-22 to 2023-24, training was imparted to only 9,331 trainees — a shortfall of 97 per cent. District Quality Monitoring Cells were not constituted in any district.

source.quote: 9,331 trainees with a shortfall of 97 per cent.

stats.label: Works sanctioned in 2019-24 completed by October 2024
stats.note: Out of 20.83 lakh approved works during 2019-24, only 12.64 lakh (61 per cent) were completed as of October 2024. Joint Physical Verification of selected works showed instances of idle, non-functional and unutilised assets.

source.quote: only 12.64 lakh works (61 per cent) were completed

stats.label: Households provided employment for less than 100 days (of those employed)
stats.note: Of 134.10 lakh households that were provided some employment, 111.31 lakh (83 per cent) received less than 100 days; only 1.23 lakh (0.92 per cent) received the full 100 days; 21.56 lakh (16 per cent) received more than 100 days — showing extreme disparity in implementation.

source.quote: 111.31 lakh HHs (83 per cent) were provided employment for less than 100 days

stats.label: Social Audit coverage: GPs left unaudited in some years
stats.note: Social Audit — the grassroots accountability mechanism — was not implemented as per norms. Up to 99.97 per cent of Gram Panchayats were left unaudited in some years. Out of ₹58.68 crore earmarked for Social Audit, only ₹42.55 crore was utilised. 45 per cent of sanctioned posts in the Social Audit Unit were vacant.

source.quote: with up to 99.97 per cent of Gram Panchayats left unaudited in some years.

stats.label: Statutory oversight bodies: mandated meetings held
stats.note: The Chhattisgarh Rural Employment Guarantee Council (state-level statutory oversight body) and the State Level Empowered Committee did not hold any of their mandated meetings. Human resource shortfall at State, district, block and GP levels was 35, 37, 33 and 16 per cent respectively.

source.quote: Chhattisgarh Rural Employment Guarantee Council and the State Level Empowered Committee did not hold the mandated meetings.

stats.label: Staff vacancies (Gram Rozgar Sahayaks) against sanctioned posts
stats.note: Only 9,159 Gram Rozgar Sahayaks (GRS) were deployed as of March 2024, a shortfall of 1,703 (16 per cent) against sanctioned posts. In test-checked districts, 221 of 872 GRS posts (26 per cent) were vacant — critical frontline staff who facilitate employment demand registration and work supervision.

source.quote: 9,159 GRS were deployed as of March 2024, resulting in a shortfall of 1,703 against sanctioned posts (16 per cent).

stats.label: Declined person-day generation shortfall in 2023-24
stats.note: In 2023-24, only 700 lakh person-days (PDs) were initially approved against 1,700 lakh PDs projected. After revision to 1,250 lakh PDs, the actual generation still fell short by 423.36 lakh PDs (25 per cent). Person-day generation showed a declining trend from the pandemic peak in subsequent years.

source.quote: highest shortfall recorded in 2023-24 (423.36 lakh PDs or 25 per cent)

keyFindings.text: 86 per cent of all MGNREGS works in the 48 test-checked Gram Panchayats during 2019-24 were executed without mandatory Gram Sabha approval. Of 12,714 sanctioned works, only 1,717 had the required democratic sanction. In one GP (Pusalda, Raigarh), 23 per cent of works were carried out with some approval but 75 per cent of the works proceeded entirely without Gram Sabha sanction. This systemic bypass renders MGNREGS's bottom-up, demand-driven design meaningless.

source.quote: 10,997 (86 per cent) works were undertaken without approval from respective

keyFindings.text: EPF contributions of ₹29.62 crore for MGNREGS workers for April 2015 to March 2023 remained unpaid, accumulating to a total liability of ₹84.59 crore including ₹54.96 crore in penalty and interest. Despite State budgetary provisions of ₹2.22 crore for unemployment allowances during 2019-24, not a single rupee was actually disbursed — the entire provision was surrendered, violating the legal entitlement of the 18.26 lakh households that demanded but did not receive employment.

source.quote: ₹ 29.62 crore for the period April 2015 to March 2023 remained unpaid.

keyFindings.text: Of the 134.10 lakh households that received any employment, 83 per cent (111.31 lakh) were provided less than 100 days — the minimum statutory guarantee. Only 0.92 per cent (1.23 lakh households) received the full 100 days. Person-day generation showed a declining trend after the pandemic peak, with a shortfall of 423.36 lakh PDs (25 per cent) in 2023-24 even against a revised target. No unemployment allowances were paid despite this shortfall.

source.quote: 111.31 lakh HHs (83 per cent) were provided employment for less than 100 days

keyFindings.text: Capacity building training — essential for works quality and rights awareness — showed a 97 per cent shortfall: only 9,331 of 2,93,388 targeted trainees were trained during 2021-22 to 2023-24. Social Audit was near-absent: up to 99.97 per cent of GPs were left unaudited in some years; 53 per cent of Social Audit observations that were raised remained unaddressed. The statutory oversight bodies (Rural Employment Guarantee Council, State Level Empowered Committee) held no meetings.

source.quote: 9,331 trainees with a shortfall of 97 per cent.

keyFindings.text: Of 20.83 lakh approved works during 2019-24, only 61 per cent were completed by October 2024. Joint Physical Verification found idle, non-functional and unutilised assets — meaning even the works that were "completed" did not always deliver durable public goods. District Quality Monitoring Cells were not constituted in any of the test-checked districts. 45 per cent of sanctioned Social Audit Unit posts were vacant, and GRS shortfall was 16 per cent overall and 26 per cent in test-checked districts.

source.quote: only 12.64 lakh works (61 per cent) were completed

recommendations: Notify baseline data of households with a cut-off date; strengthen Gram Sabha involvement in Labour Budget preparation and ensure no work begins without Gram Sabha approval.
Immediately clear all pending EPF contributions and penalties; integrate EPF payment with wage disbursement so contributions cannot be deferred.
Pay all pending unemployment allowances from existing surplus; document every employment demand and ensure NREGASoft records all demand-to-fulfilment timelines.
Provide adequate manpower for biannual Social Audits of all Gram Panchayats; monitor follow-up action on observations; constitute District Quality Monitoring Cells without delay.
Convene all mandated meetings of the Chhattisgarh Rural Employment Guarantee Council; fill 37 per cent vacancy in district-level posts on priority.
ministry: Panchayat and Rural Development Department, Government of Chhattisgarh

title: Performance Audit of Jal Jeevan Mission in Chhattisgarh
overview:
Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) aimed to provide Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTCs) to all 50 lakh rural households in Chhattisgarh by March 2024, at a service level of 55 LPCD. The State relied 90 per cent on groundwater sources for its Single Village Schemes (SVS). The CAG conducted a Performance Audit covering the period 2019-20 to 2023-24 across all 33 districts of the State, test-checking 7 districts in detail.

The headline failure is the near-total absence of "Har Ghar Jal" (safe drinking water at every home) certification: against the target of certifying all 19,656 villages in Chhattisgarh as Har Ghar Jal (HGJ) by March 2024, only 716 villages (3.64 per cent) were actually certified. Of the 40.10 lakh FHTCs installed, 13.31 lakh (33 per cent) were non-functional as of January 2025, due to dry sources, incomplete overhead tanks, lack of electric connection and non-installation of solar pumps.

The State could not mobilise ₹6,480.04 crore of JJM funds (Centre: ₹3,285.38 crore, State: ₹3,194.66 crore) due to slow initialisation in the first two years. title: Performance Audit on School Education in Odisha
overview:
Article 21-A of the Constitution guarantees the Right to Education as a fundamental right for all children aged 6-14 years. The CAG conducted a Performance Audit of School Education in Odisha covering the period 2018-19 to 2022-23, examining universal access, quality of education, infrastructure, teacher deployment and monitoring under the Samagra Shiksha Scheme (which subsumed SSA, RMSA and CSSTE in April 2018).

The headline finding is persistent under-utilisation of school education funds alongside systemic infrastructure failure: fund utilisation under Samagra Shiksha ranged from only 44 to 50 per cent, with overall savings and surrender of 12 per cent during 2018-23. In 2022-23, adverse Pupil-Teacher Ratio (PTR) was found in 21,958 (48 per cent) of Primary schools and 10,022 (43 per cent) of Upper Primary schools across the State. Large numbers of students were deprived of statutory entitlements.

The Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) at Secondary and Higher Secondary levels declined in Odisha compared to an increase at the national level. 3.51 lakh eligible students were deprived of free uniforms; 1.73 lakh students were deprived of bicycle incentives. In 380 cases, transport and escort allowances for Children with Special Needs (CwSNs) were transferred to dormant or wrong bank accounts.

stats.note: Fund utilisation under Samagra Shiksha Scheme ranged between only 44 and 50 per cent during 2018-23. Overall savings and surrender of 12 per cent were recorded across the five-year period — indicating persistent planning failures, not isolated shortfalls.

stats.note: 21,958 of 45,744 Primary schools (48 per cent) had adverse PTR in the State during 2022-23. Adverse SCR (Student-Classroom Ratio) was found in 5,443 (12 per cent) Primary and 5,603 (24 per cent) Upper Primary schools. 41 of 43 per cent of test-checked schools had students sitting on the floor due to absence of furniture.

In 41 of 43 per cent of test-checked schools, students sat on the floor due to absence of furniture. Higher Secondary schools showed 89 per cent adverse PTR — meaning almost 9 in 10 higher secondary schools were understaffed.

3.51 lakh eligible students were deprived of free uniforms and 1.73 lakh students were deprived of bicycle incentives across Odisha during 2018-23. These omissions directly violate the constitutional guarantee of equal access to education for persons with disabilities.

recommendations: Immediately constitute district-level and block-level planning teams as required under Samagra Shiksha; shift to participatory, bottom-up budgeting to address actual school needs.
Deploy additional teachers in schools with adverse PTR; rationalise teacher deployment by withdrawing teachers from schools with excess staff and posting them where shortages exist.
Reconcile all CwSN bank accounts; identify and re-transfer allowances to correct accounts; provide all pending assistive aids and appliances to identified CwSNs without delay.
Implement construction norms for ramps and CwSN-friendly toilets in all schools; link infrastructure grant release to compliance with accessibility norms.
Investigate delays in uniform and bicycle distribution; establish a tracking system linked to school enrolment data for timely entitlement delivery.

title: Performance Audit on Management and Distribution of Fertilizer in Madhya Pradesh
overview:
Fertilizer is the most critical and costly input for agricultural production. The Fertilizer (Inorganic, Organic or Mixed) (Control) Order (FCO), 1985, regulates trade, price, quality and distribution. In Madhya Pradesh (MP), the MP State Co-operative Marketing Federation (Markfed) under the Co-operation Department is the nodal agency for storage and distribution in the co-operative sector. The CAG conducted a Performance Audit covering 10 districts for the period 2017-18 to 2021-22.

The headline finding is systematic governance failure in fertilizer management: requirement assessment was done without consulting soil health data, districts, farmers or Panchayats; procurement targets were massively missed; and Markfed drew ₹3,372.79 crore in loans from the Apex Bank without obtaining the required Government guarantee from the Finance Department — violating the MP State Government Guarantee Rules, 2009.

Farmers were subjected to an extra burden of ₹10.50 crore when Markfed did not pass on a supplier rebate on DAP and MOP fertilizers. 40 to 76 per cent of sanctioned posts of enforcement authorities (Fertilizer Inspectors, Lab Analysts) were vacant across different cadres — making quality enforcement impossible. 48 per cent of surveyed farmers who had soil health cards did not know how to use the information on them.

stats.label: Extra financial burden imposed on farmers (DAP and MOP rebate not passed on)
stats.note: Markfed did not pass on a rebate provided by suppliers on DAP and MOP fertilizers to farmers, leading to an extra burden of ₹10.50 crore on farmers during March to July 2019. Fertilizers were sold at higher rates than the Fertilizer Control Committee (FCC) order price.

source.quote: benefit of the rebate and paid additional amount of ₹10.50 crore.

stats.label: Loss to Markfed from selling fertilizers at below-purchase rates
stats.note: Markfed lost ₹4.38 crore for selling DAP and NPK 12:32:16 fertilizers to farmers at a lower rate than what they were purchased at during Rabi 2020-21. This loss was not recovered from suppliers. On one hand farmers were overcharged; on the other, the agency sold below cost — showing pervasive pricing mismanagement.

keyFindings.text: Fertilizer requirement assessment in MP was done entirely at State level using previous years' consumption, without consulting block-wise soil deficiency data, districts, Panchayats or farmers — violating GoI directives. Assessment also excluded the fertilizer requirement for horticulture and vegetables entirely despite this being significant acreage. 65 per cent of surveyed farmers who had soil health cards did not know how to use the recommendations on them.

keyFindings.text: Quality testing was compromised on multiple fronts: the sampling mechanism prescribed in FCO was not followed; Quality testing labs were inadequate relative to fertilizer consumption; enforcement authorities were severely understaffed with vacancies of 40-76 per cent across cadres. 48 per cent of surveyed farmers with soil health cards did not know how to use the recommendations on them — indicating that the soil health card programme had no on-ground impact on fertilizer use patterns. The NPK ratio in the State showed no significant improvement over the five-year audit period.

recommendations: Mandate block-wise fertilizer requirement assessment based on soil deficiency data; involve farmers, Panchayats and agricultural co-operatives in annual demand estimation.
Recover all pending loans drawn without Government guarantee; enforce procurement discipline so Markfed does not avail loans beyond Government-guaranteed limits.
Fill all vacant posts of Fertilizer Inspectors and Lab Analysts on priority; strengthen the FCO sampling mechanism so quality testing covers a statistically significant sample.
Redirect 100 per cent of the Fertilizer Development Fund to farmer welfare — rebates, training, agricultural implements — as mandated; stop using it for administrative vehicles.

Establish a supplier performance tracking system; blacklist suppliers that consistently fail to meet monthly allocations; escalate to GoI when national allocation decisions cause peak-season shortfalls.

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Har Ghar Nal Ka Jal Yojana in Bihar
overview:
Bihar launched Har Ghar Nal Ka Jal (HGNJ) Yojana in December 2015 with the objective of providing safe piped water to every household and ending dependency on hand pumps by 2020. As per the 2011 census, only 2.60 per cent of rural and 20 per cent of urban households in Bihar had tap water. 28 of 38 districts had poor water quality due to arsenic, fluoride and iron contamination. The CAG conducted a Performance Audit covering 12 sampled districts from June to November 2023 for the period 2017-18 to 2022-23.

The headline finding is systemic data falsification: the State reported 98.70 per cent coverage of targeted rural households as of March 2023, whereas the actual coverage as per the JJM-Har Ghar Jal dashboard as of November 2025 was only 95.71 per cent. More critically, 11.22 lakh households under 46,633 rural wards — including 8.07 lakh households in quality-affected areas — were left out of the scheme entirely due to inadequate baseline surveys.

Despite allocating ₹30,500.92 crore to implementing units, Bihar's HGNJ execution was marked by non-functional water treatment plants, absent chlorinators, incomplete schemes, and contractors being paid ₹2.31 crore for works that were never executed. The IoT-based real-time monitoring system, procured at public cost, failed due to non-standardised procurement and poor post-installation follow-up.

The State's own reporting was inflated by approximately 3 percentage points.
