Audit's own joint physical verification of 2,283 households confirmed systematic over-reporting of coverage.

source.quote: This reporting included coverage of 98.70 per cent of the targeted rural

keyFindings.text: Water quality infrastructure in Bihar was critically deficient. 77 quality-affected wards were served by Gram Panchayat-managed schemes without Water Treatment Plants — meaning tap connections were delivering contaminated water. 15 Fluoride Removal Plants worth ₹2.77 crore were installed in non-fluoride habitations. Chlorinators were absent in PRD and ULB schemes, compromising disinfection. Water testing labs were understaffed, under-equipped and mostly without NABL accreditation.

source.quote: Fluoride Removal Plants in 15 schemes worth ₹2.77 crore in those habitations, where water quality was not affected by high levels of fluoride.

keyFindings.text: ₹2.31 crore was paid to contractors in five test-checked PH divisions for works that were not executed in 14 cases during 2018-19 and 2019-20. 59 per cent of PHED schemes commenced only at year-end or at the fag end of the previous year, directly causing delays. IoT-based real-time monitoring systems procured at public cost were non-functional due to procurement irregularities and poor post-installation oversight. Files for IoT installation were unavailable at audit.

source.quote: five test-checked PH divisions made payments of ₹2.31 crore for works that had actually not been executed in 14 cases

keyFindings.text: Despite ₹30,500.92 crore being allocated to implementing units for HGNJ Yojana over 2017-18 to 2022-23, the scheme fell short of its 2020 deadline by years, missed 11.22 lakh households, delivered non-functional infrastructure, reported inflated coverage data and failed to ensure the primary goal: safe water. Community grievance redressal was near-absent. The urban household coverage target of 100 per cent (due March 2020) remained at 94 per cent as of March 2023.

recommendations: Conduct detailed household-level surveys in all uncovered wards to identify all 11.22 lakh left-out households; update the HGNJ beneficiary database and set time-bound coverage targets.
Install Water Treatment Plants in all 77 quality-affected wards currently served without WTPs; ensure chlorinators are operational in all PRD and ULB schemes.
Investigate and recover ₹2.31 crore paid to contractors for unexecuted works; blacklist errant contractors; implement physical verification before any payment certification.
Unify HGNJ monitoring under a single real-time platform shared by PHED and PRD; audit IoT installation files and operationalise non-functional devices.
Separate and track HGNJ fund expenditure from broader Saat Nischay allocations; audit actuals against utilisation certificates submitted by PH divisions.
ministry: Public Health Engineering Department / Panchayati Raj Department / UD&HD, Government of Bihar

title: Performance Audit on DDUGJY and SAUBHAGYA (Rural Electrification) in Uttar Pradesh
overview:
Deendayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana (DDUGJY), launched in December 2014, aimed to strengthen rural electricity infrastructure — separating agriculture from non-agriculture feeders, augmenting sub-transmission and distribution systems, and metering all feeders and consumers. Pradhan Mantri Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana (SAUBHAGYA), launched in 2017, aimed to provide free electricity connections to all un-electrified rural households. The CAG audited both schemes in UP, covering ₹19,424.21 crore sanctioned for projects during 2014-15 to 2021-22.

The headline finding is that UP DISCOMs became ineligible for conversion of ₹2,002.61 crore of loans to grants because they failed to achieve key implementation milestones — milestones that would have converted half the loan component into free Central Government grants. Additionally, ₹125.35 crore was spent on avoidable items under DDUGJY and ₹277.09 crore under SAUBHAGYA — money that should not have been spent at all under the schemes' scope of work.

The core infrastructure objective of DDUGJY — separating agriculture feeders from non-agriculture feeders to ensure quality power supply for non-agricultural consumers — was not achieved: 71.22 per cent of agricultural consumers in test-checked areas were still on non-agriculture feeders as of the audit period. Connections to ineligible consumers under SAUBHAGYA resulted in excess payments of ₹26.65 crore.

stats.label: Loans ineligible for conversion to grants (milestone non-achievement)
stats.note: DISCOMs failed to achieve key milestones, rendering them ineligible for conversion of loans amounting to ₹2,002.61 crore into grants under DDUGJY and SAUBHAGYA schemes. Under the scheme design, 50 per cent of the loan component (15 per cent of project cost) was to be converted to a grant upon achieving milestones — a benefit permanently lost.

source.quote: ineligible for the conversion of loans into grants amounting to ₹ 2,002.61 crore in the DDUGJY and SAUBHAGYA schemes.

stats.label: Agricultural consumers still on non-agricultural feeders (objective not met)
stats.note: The primary objective of DDUGJY — separating agriculture and non-agriculture feeders — was not achieved: 71.22 per cent of agricultural consumers in test-checked areas were still connected to non-agriculture feeders. This resulted in avoidable expenditure of ₹277.09 crore on SAUBHAGYA works in un-separated areas.

source.quote: 71.22 per cent of agricultural consumers were still connected to non-agriculture feeders

stats.label: Avoidable expenditure on unnecessary PCC poles under DDUGJY
stats.note: DISCOMs executed cement concrete grouting of 12.75 lakh single PCC poles (₹125.35 crore) under DDUGJY — items not required as per the scope of work. This was avoidable expenditure that should not have been incurred under the scheme.

source.quote: cement concrete grouting of 12.75 lakh single PCC poles (₹ 125.35 crore) under the DDUGJY scheme

stats.label: Avoidable expenditure under SAUBHAGYA (feeder separation not done first)
stats.note: SAUBHAGYA works worth ₹277.09 crore were executed in areas where agriculture and non-agriculture feeders had not yet been separated — meaning the work would need to be redone or was of reduced value. This was directly caused by the failure to achieve DDUGJY's feeder separation objective before proceeding with SAUBHAGYA.

source.quote: avoidable expenditure of ₹ 277.09 crore13.

stats.label: Excess payments to contractors for connections to ineligible consumers
stats.note: Connections were released to consumers who were ineligible under the SAUBHAGYA scheme. This resulted in excess payments of ₹26.65 crore to Turnkey Contractors (TKCs). Audit identified duplicate connections; a penalty of ₹8.66 crore was imposed after audit, of which recovery was pending.

source.quote: SAUBHAGYA scheme, resulting in excess payments of ₹ 26.65 crore

stats.label: Excess loan availed from REC causing avoidable interest
stats.note: Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited (PuVVNL) availed excess loans of ₹66 crore from REC (Rural Electrification Corporation), leading to avoidable interest obligations of ₹3.94 crore. Audit recommended DISCOMs thoroughly assess project funding requirements to prevent excess interest payments.

source.quote: ₹ 66 crore to REC. ₹ 3.94 crore7 on the excess loan availed from REC.

stats.label: Off-grid connections (SPV systems) omitted from Detailed Project Reports
stats.note: Off-grid connections for households in remote habitations were not included in DPRs submitted by UP DISCOMs to REC. As a result, REC independently allocated one lakh SPV (Solar Photo Voltaic) systems for these connections. The omission reflected inadequate planning of the electrification programme for the most remote households.

source.quote: REC independently allocated one lakh SPV systems

stats.label: DISCOMs expenditure vs sanctioned cost under SAUBHAGYA
stats.note: DISCOMs incurred only 67.44 per cent of the sanctioned cost under SAUBHAGYA, and 96 per cent under DDUGJY. Under-utilisation of sanctioned funds, combined with payments to ineligible consumers and avoidable expenditure, points to a combination of poor planning and financial mismanagement.

source.quote: DISCOMs had incurred only 96 per cent and 67.44 per cent of sanctioned costs

stats.label: Excess SGST claims on departmentally-supplied materials
stats.note: PVVNL (Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited) made incorrect SGST claims — inflating project costs by ₹3.63 crore and making an excess claim of ₹1.09 crore towards the CGST portion from REC, and ₹1.81 crore towards SGST for reimbursement from GoUP. Additionally, ₹4.21 crore in GoUP reimbursement of state taxes was not received.

source.quote: PVVNL made an excess claim of ₹ 1.09 crore (₹ 1.82 crore x 60 per cent) towards CGST portion from the Rural Electrification Corporation (REC)

stats.label: Monitoring oversight: State Level Steering Committee meetings
stats.note: State Level Steering Committee (SLSC) meetings for scheme oversight were inadequate. DISHA (District Development Coordination and Monitoring Committee) meetings were also inadequate. Data of households unwilling to take connections was not maintained, making it impossible to track genuine universal electrification progress.

source.quote: Inadequate SLSC meetings

keyFindings.text: The DISCOMs of Uttar Pradesh failed to achieve the key milestones under DDUGJY and SAUBHAGYA that would have converted ₹2,002.61 crore of loans into grants. This permanently forfeited a Central Government grant benefit that the scheme design intended to incentivise performance. The milestone failure was compounded by inadequate SLSC monitoring meetings and weak financial oversight, including excess loans of ₹66 crore from REC at ₹3.94 crore in avoidable interest.

source.quote: ineligible for the conversion of loans into grants amounting to ₹ 2,002.61 crore in the DDUGJY and SAUBHAGYA schemes.

keyFindings.text: The primary infrastructure objective of DDUGJY — separating agriculture feeders from non-agriculture feeders to protect non-agricultural consumers from load-shedding — was not achieved: 71.22 per cent of agricultural consumers in test-checked areas remained on non-agriculture feeders. This directly caused ₹277.09 crore of SAUBHAGYA work to be executed on infrastructure that still had unseparated feeders, reducing its effective value.

source.quote: 71.22 per cent of agricultural consumers were still connected to non-agriculture feeders

keyFindings.text: DISCOMs incurred ₹125.35 crore on avoidable items (PCC pole cement concrete grouting) under DDUGJY that were outside the scheme scope. Connections were released to ineligible consumers under SAUBHAGYA, resulting in ₹26.65 crore in excess payments. Duplicate connections were identified only after audit intervention; a penalty of ₹8.66 crore was imposed. These irregularities point to both Detailed Project Report deficiencies and weak contractor oversight.

source.quote: cement concrete grouting of 12.75 lakh single PCC poles (₹ 125.35 crore) under the DDUGJY scheme

keyFindings.text: Planning deficiencies were evident from the start: off-grid connections for remote habitations were omitted from DPRs, requiring REC to independently allocate one lakh SPV systems. Incorrect SGST claims inflated project costs by ₹3.63 crore and resulted in excess reimbursement claims. Data on households unwilling to take connections was not maintained — making universal electrification verification impossible. Only 67.44 per cent of the SAUBHAGYA sanctioned cost was actually spent, despite widespread irregularities in how even that amount was used.

source.quote: REC independently allocated one lakh SPV systems

recommendations: Prioritise feeder separation in all remaining un-separated areas; do not sanction new consumer connection works in areas where feeder separation is pending.
Recover ₹26.65 crore paid for connections to ineligible consumers; enforce penalties on TKCs for duplicate and invalid connections; maintain records of unwilling households.
Ensure DPRs include off-grid connections for remote habitations before submission to funding agencies; do not rely on funding agencies to identify omitted scope.
Convene mandatory SLSC and DISHA monitoring meetings regularly; link DISCOM milestone certificates to independent third-party physical verification before grant conversion.
Audit all GST claims under DDUGJY and SAUBHAGYA for excess or incorrect reimbursements; recover ₹1.09 crore CGST over-claim and resolve the ₹4.21 crore state tax reimbursement pending from GoUP.
ministry: Energy Department / Power Corporation, Government of Uttar Pradesh

title: Performance Audit on Operational Performance of NLC India Limited
overview:
NLC India Limited (formerly Neyveli Lignite Corporation), incorporated in 1956 and renamed in 2016, is a Central Government PSU under the Ministry of Coal. As of March 2023, GoI held 79.20 per cent of its shares. NLC operates three open-cast lignite mines at Neyveli (Tamil Nadu) and one at Barsingsar (Rajasthan), with installed mining capacity of 27.10 MTPA and pit-head thermal power generation capacity of 3,640 MW. Electricity is supplied to distribution companies in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Telangana, Puducherry and Rajasthan. The CAG Performance Audit covered Mine-I, Mine-IA and Mine-II at Neyveli and three of its five thermal power stations (TPS-IE, TPS-II and TPS-IIE) for the period 2017-18 to 2022-23.

The headline finding is a combination of land acquisition failures and persistent equipment breakdowns that together cost ₹338.62 crore in potential mining revenue loss, ₹364.80 crore in avoidable additional expenditure, ₹2,353.99 crore in capacity charge revenue loss, and 14,538.66 million units in forced outage generation losses. Additionally, NLC delayed an energy audit for over four years despite a Government mandate — costing ₹47.92 crore annually in unrealised energy savings. Generation inefficiencies caused a further 1,594.77 million unit loss and ₹360.52 crore in under-recovery of lignite extraction costs.

stats.label: Potential mining revenue loss (inadequate land for Mine-IA)
stats.note: Non-availability of adequate land on the eastern side of Mine-IA — due to landowner opposition — resulted in a potential revenue loss of ₹338.62 crore in mining operations, calculated on the basis of CERC provisional tariff order (May 2023) for lignite.

source.quote: potential loss of opportunity to earn revenue in mining operations to the extent of ₹338.62

stats.label: Additional expenditure for excavating soil dumped on lignite-bearing land
stats.note: NLC India was forced to dump overburden on lignite-bearing land due to inadequate space elsewhere. This resulted in additional expenditure of ₹364.80 crore for re-excavation of the dumped soil — increasing the overall cost of lignite production.

source.quote: NLC India incurred ₹364.80 crore towards excavation of

stats.label: Energy savings possible annually — but audit delayed 4+ years
stats.note: A 2016 Bureau of Energy Efficiency notification required NLC India to conduct an energy audit to reduce energy consumption by 25 per cent. NLC delayed the audit to June 2020 (4+ years late). The completed audit found energy savings of ₹47.92 crore annually were achievable — savings foregone for 4+ years due to the delay.

source.quote: recommended that NLC India could achieve an energy cost savings of ₹47.92 crore per

stats.label: Revenue loss in capacity charges (TPS non-achievement of PAF)
stats.note: NLC India failed to achieve the normative Plant Availability Factor (PAF) prescribed by CERC, resulting in loss of revenue of ₹2,353.99 crore in capacity charges across TPS-IE, TPS-II and TPS-IIE during 2017-18 to 2022-23.

source.quote: NLC India lost ₹2,353.99 crore as revenue in capacity

stats.label: Power generation lost to forced outages
stats.note: TPS-IIE faced 33,451.55 hours of outages due to repeated faults in the FBHE system. TPS-IE suffered major turbine bearing failures (66.66% of outages). Together, forced outages resulted in 14,538.66 million units of lost power generation during 2017-22.

stats.label: Generation loss from operational inefficiencies + lignite extraction under-recovery
stats.note: Partial load loss operations caused a further 1,594.77 million unit generation loss and ₹360.52 crore under-recovery of lignite extraction costs. Poor mill performance in TPS-II (650.88 MU), unresolved lignite feeding issues in TPS-IIE (295.37 MU), and wet lignite due to uncovered storage yards (366.99 MU) were the main causes.

source.quote: generation loss of 1,594.77 MUs during 2017-18 to

stats.label: Compensation paid + clearance cost for overburden soil dumped on agricultural land
stats.note: NLC India dumped overburden on agricultural land near Mine-II, leading to protests. The company paid ₹2.18 crore in compensation to private landowners and ₹14.98 crore (to September 2023) to clear soil from drains and agricultural land — entirely avoidable expenditure.

source.quote: NLC India paid compensation of ₹2.18 crore (upto March 2023)... ₹14.98 crore

keyFindings.text: NLC India could not obtain land on the eastern side of Mine-IA due to opposition from landowners, resulting in a potential revenue loss of ₹338.62 crore and additional expenditure of ₹364.80 crore to re-excavate overburden dumped on lignite-bearing land. NLC also dumped overburden near Mine-II on agricultural land without proper environmental clearances, spending ₹2.18 crore in farmer compensation and ₹14.98 crore in soil clearance — entirely avoidable costs from inadequate planning.

source.quote: potential loss of opportunity to earn revenue in mining operations to the extent of ₹338.62

keyFindings.text: NLC failed to achieve CERC-prescribed Plant Availability Factor in its three test-checked thermal power stations, losing ₹2,353.99 crore in capacity charge revenue. Forced outages — particularly FBHE system failures in TPS-IIE (33,451.55 hours) and turbine bearing failures in TPS-IE — cost 14,538.66 million units of generation. Partial load operations cost a further 1,594.77 million units and ₹360.52 crore in under-recovered lignite extraction costs.

source.quote: NLC India lost ₹2,353.99 crore as revenue in capacity

keyFindings.text: Despite a 2016 Bureau of Energy Efficiency mandate to conduct an energy audit to reduce energy consumption by 25 per cent, NLC initiated the audit only in June 2020 — a delay of over four years. The audit found ₹47.92 crore in annual energy savings achievable across three mines. The multi-year delay meant these savings were foregone for the entire delay period. NLC also failed to obtain separate mining leases for minor minerals (ball clay, silica sand, fire clay), forfeiting potential revenue from their extraction.

source.quote: recommended that NLC India could achieve an energy cost savings of ₹47.92 crore per

recommendations: Expedite land acquisition at Mine-IA eastern side; do not dump overburden on lignite-bearing or agricultural land without prior environmental clearance.
Implement the energy audit recommendations immediately across all three mines; report annually on energy savings achieved against the ₹47.92 crore benchmark.
Address FBHE design deficiencies in TPS-IIE through engineering review; set up planned preventive maintenance schedules to reduce forced outages below normative limits.
Cover lignite storage yards to prevent wet lignite during monsoon — the single largest cause of partial load generation loss.
Obtain separate mining leases for minor minerals to monetise ball clay, silica sand and fire clay currently left unmined.
ministry: Ministry of Coal, Government of India

title: Performance Audit on Functioning of District Transport Offices in Bihar
overview:
District Transport Offices (DTOs) in Bihar are responsible for issuing driving licences, registering vehicles, granting permits and fitness certificates, collecting Motor Vehicle Tax, and enforcing the Motor Vehicles Act 1988. The CAG Performance Audit covered six sampled DTOs plus two check posts during July–October 2024, covering the period 2019-20 to 2023-24.

The defining finding is a systemic collapse of driving skill testing: during a Joint Physical Verification at the Automated Driving Testing Centre (ADTC) in Patna, only 21 of 789 applicants (2.66 per cent) physically appeared for the Learner's Licence test — yet the SARATHI database recorded 766 (97.08 per cent) as successful. A similar pattern was found for Driving Licences: only 10 of 903 DL applicants physically appeared, but 856 (94.80 per cent) had their licences granted in the database. This represents near-total fraud in Bihar's driving licence issuance system.

Across revenue functions, 42,121 transport vehicles were registered without ensuring issuance of permanent permits — causing ₹28.09 crore revenue loss. 7,649 transport vehicles were plying without paying outstanding MV Tax and penalties amounting to ₹50.40 crore. 80,901 e-challans worth ₹203.36 crore were pending disposal. Short realisation of revenue amounted to ₹4.35 crore and non-levy of fines to ₹18.11 crore.

stats.label: LL applicants who physically appeared for skill test vs database "success" rate
stats.note: Of 789 applicants audited at ADTC Patna on JPV dates, only 21 (2.66%) physically appeared for the Learner's Licence driving skill test. Yet the SARATHI database showed 766 (97.08%) as successful — driving licences granted to people who never appeared for the test.

source.quote: only 21 applicants (2.66 per cent) out of total 789 applicants

stats.label: DL applicants who physically appeared vs licences granted in database
stats.note: For Driving Licences: only 10 of 903 applicants appeared on JPV dates, yet 856 (94.80 per cent) had DL granted in the database. Licences were being granted without physical presence — enabling unqualified drivers to legally operate vehicles on Bihar's roads.

source.quote: out of 903 applicants only 10 physically appeared for the DL test

stats.label: Transport vehicles registered without valid permanent permit → revenue loss
stats.note: In test-checked DTOs, 42,121 transport vehicles were registered without ensuring issuance of a permanent permit — leading to loss of revenue amounting to ₹28.09 crore. 9,522 further transport vehicles had expired tax tokens, fitness certificates, insurance or permits without any cancellation notices being issued.

source.quote: Certificate of registration was granted to 42,121 transport vehicle without ensuring issuance of permanent permit

stats.label: Transport vehicles plying without paying outstanding MV Tax
stats.note: 7,649 transport vehicles were plying on roads without paying outstanding Motor Vehicle Tax and penalty/fine amounting to ₹50.40 crore. An additional ₹20.41 crore in MV tax was only partially collected at the time of registering 1,255 construction equipment vehicles.

source.quote: 7,649 transport vehicles were plying on roads without paying outstanding Motor Vehicle Tax and penalty/fine amounting to ₹ 50.40 crore

stats.label: E-challans pending disposal (revenue arrears)
stats.note: E-challan arrears increased from ₹14.30 crore (2020-21) to ₹109.82 crore (2023-24). Total 80,901 e-challans amounting to ₹203.36 crore were pending disposal. In four test-checked DTOs, the earlier-issued e-challans were left undisposed while only the latest one was cleared.

source.quote: Total 80,901 e-challans amounting to ₹ 203.36 crore were pending for disposal.

stats.label: Short realisation of revenue + non-levy of fines (registration irregularities)
stats.note: Entry of wrong purchase dates in the VAHAN software by authorised dealers — to avoid penalty on BS-IV vehicles registered after cutoff — resulted in short realisation of revenue of ₹4.35 crore and non-levy of fine amounting to ₹18.11 crore. VAHAN accepted dates where purchase occurred after insurance, indicating absent input controls.

source.quote: short realisation of revenue of ₹ 4.35 crore and non-levy of fine amounting to ₹ 18.11 crore

stats.label: Motor Driving Training Schools: unregulated
stats.note: In test-checked DTOs, 858 vehicles were granted fitness certificates by departmental officers who were not authorised to do so — a delegated power granted without proper oversight. Motor Driving Training Schools operated with minimal state oversight, contributing to the quality collapse in driver training.

source.quote: test-checked DTOs, 858 vehicles were granted Fitness Certificates

keyFindings.text: Bihar's driving licence system showed near-total fraud: of 789 LL applicants observed on JPV dates, only 21 (2.66 per cent) physically appeared for the test — yet 766 (97.08 per cent) were recorded as successful in SARATHI. For driving licences, only 10 of 903 applicants appeared but 856 (94.80 per cent) had licences granted. This means the vast majority of driving licences issued in Bihar during 2019-24 were given to applicants who never demonstrated any driving skill. The implications for road safety are severe.

source.quote: only 21 applicants (2.66 per cent) out of total 789 applicants

keyFindings.text: 42,121 transport vehicles were registered without valid permanent permits, causing ₹28.09 crore revenue loss. 7,649 vehicles plied without paying ₹50.40 crore in outstanding MV Tax and penalties. Wrong dealer date entries caused ₹4.35 crore short revenue and ₹18.11 crore non-levy of fine. 80,901 e-challans worth ₹203.36 crore piled up undisposed. DTOs did not realise ₹57.75 lakh in cess, failed to levy ₹1.10 crore in extended fines for repeat offenders, and missed ₹2.09 crore in additional fees for delayed ownership transfers.

source.quote: Total 80,901 e-challans amounting to ₹ 203.36 crore were pending for disposal.

keyFindings.text: VAHAN and SARATHI — the national vehicle and driving licence databases — had absent input controls: VAHAN accepted purchase dates later than insurance dates; SARATHI recorded approvals without physical presence. Automated Driving Testing Centres were circumvented with ease, and testing parameters were relaxed beyond prescribed norms. The State failed to provide penal provisions for levy of fine on non-transport vehicles for belated payment of One Time Tax, causing ₹1.62 crore revenue loss.

source.quote: Certificate of registration was granted to 42,121 transport vehicle without ensuring issuance of permanent permit

recommendations: Immediately audit all driving licences issued in Bihar from 2019-24 for physical presence at skill test; cancel licences where no physical test was conducted.
Enforce biometric-linked, tamper-proof ADTC testing; do not permit relaxation of mandatory parameters under any circumstances.
Reconcile and recover all outstanding MV Tax (₹50.40 crore) from 7,649 delinquent transport vehicle owners; implement automatic suspension of vehicle registration on tax default.
Fix VAHAN input controls to reject purchase dates later than insurance dates; integrate SARATHI with ADTC real-time physical attendance data.
Set up a dedicated e-challan disposal cell in each DTO with monthly clearance targets; stop selective disposal of only the latest e-challan.
ministry: Transport Department, Government of Bihar

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana – Gramin in Uttar Pradesh
overview:
Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana – Gramin (PMAY-G) aims to provide pucca houses with basic amenities to rural houseless families and those living in kutcha or dilapidated houses. In Uttar Pradesh, 36.15 lakh houses were targeted for construction by March 2024, with financial assistance of ₹1.20 lakh per house paid in three instalments linked to construction progress. The CAG Performance Audit covered 2016-17 to 2022-23 with joint physical verification in sampled districts.

The State reported 34.18 lakh (98.47 per cent) PMAY-G houses completed by March 2024. However, the audit found that of 34.71 lakh houses sanctioned, 20,215 (0.58 per cent) remained incomplete as of March 2025 despite exceeding the prescribed 12-month completion timeline. Audit field verification found 77 (3.70 per cent) of 2,079 reported-as-completed houses were actually incomplete — with 74 per cent without plaster, 54 per cent without a cooking space, 58 per cent without a bathing area and 44 per cent without a proper door.

Financially: ₹9.52 crore was released to 1,838 ineligible beneficiaries (₹2.62 crore still unrecovered); ₹157 crore of administrative funds was underutilised, causing ₹357.29 crore less in Central share; and ₹28.70 crore in wage compensation was pending for 50,771 Rural Mason Training programme trainees.

stats.label: PMAY-G houses reported completed vs houses actually found incomplete
stats.note: State reported 34.18 lakh (98.47%) PMAY-G houses complete by March 2024. But audit field verification of 2,079 houses found 77 (3.70%) reported-complete houses were actually incomplete. Moreover, 20,215 houses remained incomplete as of March 2025 — over a year after the deadline — with ₹134.51 crore already released as financial assistance to these beneficiaries.

source.quote: completion of construction of 34.18 lakh (98.47 per cent) PMAY-G houses by March 2024

stats.label: Released to ineligible beneficiaries
stats.note: Due to lack of due diligence in verification of beneficiaries in test-checked districts, ₹9.52 crore was released to 1,838 ineligible beneficiaries. Of this, ₹2.62 crore remained unrecovered as of September 2024.

source.quote: ₹ 9.52 crore was released to 1,838 ineligible beneficiaries, out of which ₹ 2.62 crore remained unrecovered

stats.label: Houses incomplete despite deadline and ₹134.51 crore already released
stats.note: 20,215 PMAY-G houses (0.58 per cent of total sanctioned) remained incomplete as of March 2025 — more than a year past the March 2024 deadline — despite ₹134.51 crore already disbursed as financial assistance for their construction. Beneficiaries received money but houses remain unfinished.

source.quote: Out of 34.71 lakh houses sanctioned under PMAY-G during 2016-23, 20,215 (0.58 per cent) PMAY-G houses were incomplete as of March 2025

stats.label: House quality: % without basic amenities (audit field verification)
stats.note: Audit field survey of completed PMAY-G houses found: 74 per cent without plaster on walls, 54 per cent without a dedicated cooking space, 58 per cent without a bathing area, 44 per cent without a proper door, and 82 per cent without the PMAY-G logo. 29 per cent lacked toilets, 39 per cent cooking gas, 30 per cent electricity and 89 per cent piped water — despite PMAY-G mandating convergence with these schemes.

source.quote: 74 per cent of houses were without plaster of walls; 54 per cent were without a dedicated place

stats.label: Wage compensation pending for Rural Mason trainees
stats.note: Wage compensation of ₹28.70 crore was pending as of October 2024 for 50,771 trainees of the Rural Mason Training programme who had completed training but not received their stipends from the Deen Dayal Upadhyay State Institute of Rural Development.

source.quote: wage compensation of ₹ 28.70 crore was pending as of October 2024 for 50,771 trainees

stats.label: Admin fund under-utilisation causing loss of Central share
stats.note: Only ₹157 crore (40 per cent) of administrative funds were utilised against available amounts. This under-utilisation caused less release of Central share amounting to ₹357.29 crore during 2017-23. The State also delayed transfers of Central Programme Fund to the State Nodal Account by 74 to 105 days.

source.quote: resulted in less release of Central share amounting to ₹ 357.29 crore during 2017-23

stats.label: Instalment transferred to wrong accounts (suspected cyber-crime)
stats.note: In 159 cases, instalment amounts of ₹86.20 lakh were transferred during 2017-20 to the accounts of persons other than the intended beneficiaries due to suspected cyber-crime. The issue remained unresolved as of October 2024.

source.quote: In 159 cases, instalment amount (₹ 86.20 lakh) was transferred during 2017-20 to the accounts of other persons

keyFindings.text: The State reported 98.47 per cent PMAY-G house completion by March 2024, but audit field verification found 77 of 2,079 inspected "completed" houses (3.70 per cent) were actually incomplete. As of March 2025, 20,215 sanctioned houses remained unfinished despite ₹134.51 crore already disbursed. Field surveys of "completed" houses found 74 per cent without wall plaster, 58 per cent without a bathing area, 89 per cent without piped water and 82 per cent without the PMAY-G logo — indicating widespread quality failure behind the headline completion numbers.

source.quote: Out of 34.71 lakh houses sanctioned under PMAY-G during 2016-23, 20,215 (0.58 per cent) PMAY-G houses were incomplete as of March 2025

keyFindings.text: ₹9.52 crore was released to 1,838 ineligible beneficiaries in test-checked districts, with ₹2.62 crore still unrecovered. ₹28.70 crore in wage compensation for 50,771 Rural Mason trainees remained unpaid. ₹86.20 lakh went to wrong accounts in 159 suspected cyber-fraud cases, unresolved after 4-7 years. Instalment payments were delayed in 79 per cent of beneficiary cases. 11,031 beneficiaries whose houses were complete had not yet received their final ₹20.18 crore instalment as of August 2024.

source.quote: ₹ 9.52 crore was released to 1,838 ineligible beneficiaries, out of which ₹ 2.62 crore remained unrecovered

keyFindings.text: Demo houses — meant to guide construction quality — were built in only 49 per cent of blocks as of September 2024, against a September 2018 target (6 years late). Social audit findings were resolved for only 47 per cent of issues raised. The permanent waitlist of beneficiaries was compiled with 14.47 lakh names in 2016; but 33.64 lakh additional households were subsequently identified — a 2.3x expansion that indicates the initial SECC survey massively undercounted eligible beneficiaries.

source.quote: 74 per cent of houses were without plaster of walls; 54 per cent were without a dedicated place

recommendations: Complete all 20,215 incomplete houses immediately; link final instalment release to independent physical verification of construction quality.
Investigate and recover ₹9.52 crore paid to ineligible beneficiaries; strengthen biometric and Aadhaar-seeded verification before releasing each instalment.
Pay all pending wage compensation (₹28.70 crore) to 50,771 Rural Mason trainees without further delay.
Resolve all 159 cyber-fraud instalment transfer cases; implement beneficiary account verification before each payment.
Mandate quarterly social audit of completed houses; require correction of quality defects before scheme closure.

title: Performance Audit on Functioning of Delhi Jal Board
overview:
Delhi Jal Board (DJB) is responsible for providing potable water to 93 per cent of Delhi's households and treating its sewage. DJB sources raw water from the Yamuna River, Bhakra-Beas storages (610 MGD), Upper Ganga Canal (253 MGD) and groundwater (90 MGD). The CAG Performance Audit covered 2017-18 to 2021-22.

The most damaging finding is that Non-Revenue Water (NRW) — water produced but not billed — was in the range of 51 to 53 per cent throughout the period, meaning every other litre of water produced was lost. The estimated revenue foregone on account of NRW was ₹4,988 crore during 2017-22. Meanwhile, the water shortage against assessed requirement grew from 22 per cent (2017-18) to 24 per cent (2021-22), and potable water shortage increased from 24.2 to 25.79 per cent.

DJB's accumulated debt stood at ₹66,595 crore as of March 2022 — and it was unable to meet revenue expenditure from revenue receipts, with more than 50 per cent of revenue expenditure going to staff salaries. In 2021-22, DJB billed only 371 MGD (40 per cent) of potable water produced. 55 per cent of water samples tested were found unfit for potable purposes.

stats.label: Non-Revenue Water (water produced but not billed)
stats.note: NRW — representing water lost through transmission leakages, theft, illegal connections and unbilled consumption — stood at 51 to 53 per cent throughout 2017-22. Every other litre of water produced by DJB was either lost or not billed. Estimated revenue foregone: ₹4,988 crore over 5 years.

source.quote: Non-Revenue Water (NRW) component was in the range of 51 per cent to 53 per cent

stats.label: Estimated revenue foregone due to NRW (2017-22)
stats.note: DJB's 51-53 per cent NRW rate translated into estimated foregone revenue of ₹4,988 crore during 2017-22. The actual loss is likely higher given the gap between what should have been metered and what was actually billed.

source.quote: estimated amount of revenue not realised by DJB during the said period on account of NRW was ` 4,988 crore

stats.label: Accumulated debt of DJB (March 2022)
stats.note: DJB's accumulated debt stood at ₹66,595 crore as of March 2022. DJB was unable to meet its revenue expenditure from its revenue receipts — the gap was met from capital funds. More than 50 per cent of revenue expenditure went to staff salaries, leaving minimal resources for development.

source.quote: ` 66,595 crore (March 2022).

stats.label: Potable water shortage against assessed requirement (growth 2017-22)
stats.note: Shortage in potable water against assessed requirement increased from 24.2 per cent (2017-18) to 25.79 per cent (2021-22). The water supply deficit persisted across the audit period despite DJB's mandate to meet Delhi's demand. Per capita availability was below 20 GPCD in four zones.

source.quote: shortage in potable water against the assessed requirement increased from 24.2 per cent to 25.79 per cent

stats.label: Water samples found unfit for potable purposes
stats.note: 55 per cent of water samples drawn from DJB's network during testing were found unfit for potable purposes. The situation was aggravated by inequitable supply — per capita availability in four zones was less than 20 GPCD, while other zones were oversupplied.

source.quote: (55 per cent) were found unfit for potable purposes.

stats.label: Potable water billed in 2021-22 as fraction of produced
stats.note: In 2021-22, DJB produced 935 MGD but billed only 371 MGD (40 per cent). Of the billed quantity, only 244 MGD (66 per cent) was billed based on actual meter readings — meaning a third of billed water was estimated, not metered. This compounds the NRW problem.

source.quote: DJB had billed only 371 MGD (40 per cent) of potable water produced

stats.label: Sewage generated flowing into Yamuna untreated
stats.note: Only 545 MGD of installed sewage treatment capacity (78 per cent) was being utilised, with an estimated eight per cent of total sewage generated flowing into the Yamuna untreated. DJB paid ₹25 lakh in NGT-mandated CPCB penalty for delay on sewage treatment projects — which could have been avoided.

source.quote: remaining estimated sewage generated (eight per cent) flowing into the river Yamuna untreated.

keyFindings.text: DJB's Non-Revenue Water ranged from 51 to 53 per cent across 2017-22 — meaning more than half of every litre produced was lost or not billed. Estimated revenue foregone: ₹4,988 crore. This occurred despite DJB's accumulated debt of ₹66,595 crore (March 2022) making revenue collection critical. DJB was structurally dependent on capital fund infusions to meet operational expenditure, with more than 50 per cent of revenue expenditure going to staff salaries.

source.quote: estimated amount of revenue not realised by DJB during the said period on account of NRW was ` 4,988 crore

keyFindings.text: The water shortage against assessed requirement grew from 22 per cent (2017-18) to 24 per cent (2021-22), and potable water shortage from 24.2 to 25.79 per cent. 55 per cent of water samples were found unfit for potable purposes. Supply was deeply inequitable — four zones had per capita availability below 20 GPCD. DJB relied on 1,243 tankers per day in 2021-22 to supplement piped supply in deficit areas — an expensive, unsustainable supplement that has become structural.

source.quote: shortage in potable water against the assessed requirement increased from 24.2 per cent to 25.79 per cent

keyFindings.text: Only 40 per cent of produced potable water was billed in 2021-22 (371 of 935 MGD), of which only 66 per cent was based on actual meter readings. Sewage coverage increased from 23.09 to 32.12 per cent of total sewage-generating area — far below the 2020 mandate for 100 per cent treatment. ADB financing of ₹2,243 crore for Wazirabad WTP rehabilitation was withdrawn; DJB had to pay ₹25 lakh in NGT penalty for delay. These failures directly contribute to Yamuna river pollution.

source.quote: DJB had billed only 371 MGD (40 per cent) of potable water produced

recommendations: Launch an emergency NRW reduction programme targeting 30 per cent NRW by 2027; invest in pipe replacement in zones with highest loss and illegal connection detection.
Mandate 100 per cent meter-based billing within 24 months; eliminate estimated billing for all domestic consumers.
Accelerate sewage treatment plant construction to meet the 100 per cent sewage treatment mandate; prioritise Yamuna bank STPs on a time-bound basis.
Restructure DJB's financial model — reduce its structural dependence on capital fund infusions; cap salary expenditure as proportion of revenue.
Equalize per capita water supply across all zones; establish a zone-wise supply tracking dashboard with public accountability.
ministry: Delhi Jal Board / Irrigation and Flood Control Department, Government of NCT of Delhi

title: Performance Audit on Effectiveness of Measures Taken by the Government of West Bengal for Containing Water Pollution
overview:
West Bengal has 85 rivers and numerous water bodies, many of which are severely polluted from industrial effluents, domestic sewage and agricultural runoff. The State was directed by the National Green Tribunal to ensure 100 per cent treatment of sewage by 31 March 2020. The CAG Performance Audit examined the effectiveness of measures taken by the State during 2017-18 to 2022-23 to contain river and groundwater pollution.

The headline finding is the catastrophic gap between sewage generation and treatment capacity: West Bengal generates 5,457 MLD of sewage, but installed Sewage Treatment Plant (STP) capacity was only 897 MLD — just 16.44 per cent of generation. The gap is 4,560 MLD — meaning 83.56 per cent of all sewage generated in West Bengal flows into rivers and water bodies untreated, directly violating the NGT mandate.

On drinking water, 73 per cent of households in arsenic-affected areas were not provided with Arsenic Iron Removal Plants (AIRPs) under piped water supply. Only 32 per cent of households in the State receive treated piped water. STPs built in Darjeeling district at a cost of ₹36.30 crore by GTA were not operationalised, and pollution in Senchal Lake continued unabated.

stats.label: Sewage treatment capacity vs daily generation in West Bengal
stats.note: West Bengal generates 5,457 MLD of sewage daily. Total installed STP capacity (including proposed STPs) was only 897 MLD — 16.44 per cent of generation, leaving a gap of 4,560 MLD. This means over 83 per cent of sewage in the State flows untreated into rivers, violating the NGT 2020 deadline for 100 per cent treatment.

source.quote: was only 897 MLD (16.44 per cent) causing a gap of 4,560 MLD. There

stats.label: Ganga basin STP utilisation (Howrah-Kolkata cluster)
stats.note: Even among installed STP capacity, utilisation was incomplete. In the Ganga basin Howrah-Kolkata cluster, only 232.5 MLD was being utilised — 60.60 per cent of installed capacity of 383.80 MLD — leaving a further 1,339 MLD gap in treatment. Almost 85 per cent of sewage in this basin flowed into the Ganga untreated.

source.quote: 60.60 per cent of 383.80 MLD. There was a gap of 1,339 MLD in treatment

stats.label: Arsenic-affected households without Arsenic Iron Removal Plants
stats.note: 73 per cent of households in arsenic-affected areas were not provided with Arsenic Iron Removal Plants (AIRPs) under Piped Water Supply Schemes — despite the areas being identified as arsenic-affected and requiring treatment. Fluoride-affected households in Birbhum district were similarly not covered.

source.quote: 73 per cent were not provided with Arsenic Iron Removal Plants (AIRP) under Piped Water Supply Schemes

stats.label: Households receiving treated piped water in West Bengal
stats.note: Only 32 per cent of households in West Bengal receive treated piped water. Even among JJM-covered households using surface water-based FHTCs, 48 per cent were provided with FHTCs — and of those using groundwater-based FHTCs, 73 per cent were not provided with AIRPs.

source.quote: only 32 per cent of households are getting treated piped water.

stats.label: STPs built in Darjeeling by GTA — not operationalised
stats.note: The Gorkhaland Territorial Administration (GTA) constructed STPs in Darjeeling at a cost of ₹36.30 crore. However, the STPs were never operationalised — and pollution in Senchal Lake (a major water source) continued unabated. Capital was spent but zero pollution control was achieved.

source.quote: incurring an expenditure of ` 36.30 crore by the GTA. However, the STPs were not operationalized

stats.label: Faecal Coliform levels in river water above norms
stats.note: In river water samples tested, Faecal Coliform (FC) was above prescribed norms in 74 to 97 per cent of tests. Dissolved Oxygen (DO) did not meet standards in 1 to 18 per cent of tests. Between 15 and 46 per cent of total tests showed FC above norms, pointing to pervasive human waste contamination of West Bengal's rivers.

source.quote: FC was above norms in 74-97 per cent of test cases

keyFindings.text: West Bengal generates 5,457 MLD of sewage but had only 897 MLD (16.44 per cent) of STP capacity installed — leaving a gap of 4,560 MLD. Even within installed capacity, utilisation was only 60.60 per cent in the Ganga basin cluster. 85 per cent of Ganga basin sewage flowed untreated into rivers. This directly violates the NGT mandate for 100 per cent sewage treatment by March 2020 — a target already missed by 3+ years at the time of audit, with no clear timeline for achieving it.

source.quote: was only 897 MLD (16.44 per cent) causing a gap of 4,560 MLD. There

keyFindings.text: 73 per cent of households in arsenic-affected areas lack Arsenic Iron Removal Plants; only 32 per cent of West Bengal households receive treated piped water. Despite JJM coverage, the majority of FHTCs in arsenic-affected zones deliver contaminated water because AIRPs were not installed. River water samples showed Faecal Coliform above norms in 74-97 per cent of tests — indicating that both surface and groundwater used for drinking pose serious health risks.

source.quote: 73 per cent were not provided with Arsenic Iron Removal Plants (AIRP)

keyFindings.text: Capital was spent but not converted into pollution control: ₹36.30 crore on Darjeeling STPs that were never operationalised; WBPCB conducted significantly fewer inspections than required; enforcement actions were inadequate. The gap between sewage generated and treated is structural — it cannot be closed without large-scale STP construction. At current trajectory, West Bengal remains decades from compliant sewage treatment.

source.quote: incurring an expenditure of ` 36.30 crore by the GTA. However, the STPs were not operationalized

recommendations: Operationalise all constructed but non-functional STPs immediately; conduct a root-cause audit of why ₹36.30 crore of Darjeeling STPs sit idle.
Set a funded, time-bound STP construction plan targeting 100 per cent of the 4,560 MLD capacity gap, with quarterly progress reporting to NGT.
Install AIRPs in all arsenic-affected habitations under JJM before FHTCs are certified as functional — do not count contaminated tap connections as safe water coverage.
Expand WBPCB inspection capacity; increase inspections of industrial effluent discharge points to at least the prescribed frequency.
Map and plug all untreated sewage outfalls into Ganga within 2 years; establish real-time river water quality monitoring at 50+ points.
ministry: Department of Environment / West Bengal Pollution Control Board

title: Performance Audit on Welfare of Building and Other Construction Workers in Karnataka
overview:
The Building and Other Construction Workers (BOCW) Act, 1996 mandates registration of construction workers and provides for welfare schemes (housing, health, education, pension, accident relief). A BOCW cess of 1 per cent is levied on the cost of construction works. Karnataka's BOCW Welfare Board is funded by this cess. The CAG audited the collection of cess and delivery of welfare benefits during 2018-19 to 2022-23.

The headline finding is pervasive financial mismanagement: ₹18.12 crore in cess dues accumulated in uncashed cheques and demand drafts since 2007-08 — indicating the Board failed to deposit its own receipts for up to 15 years. The Board also released ₹433.80 crore to the Karnataka Slum Development Board (KSDB) without obtaining utilisation certificates for even ₹76 crore of previous releases. ₹258.80 crore was spent on Preventive Health Care schemes in an unauthorised manner — without any Act or Rule permitting such expenditure.

Against a budget provision of ₹10,154.45 crore during 2018-23, the Board incurred expenditure of only ₹6,198.34 crore (61 per cent) — leaving 39 per cent of welfare funds unutilised over five years.

stats.label: Cess dues in uncashed cheques/DDs accumulated since 2007-08
stats.note: The BOCW Welfare Board had uncashed cheques and demand drafts accumulated since 2007-08 amounting to ₹18.12 crore — receipts that were collected but never deposited into the Board's account, for up to 15 years. The Board also could not trace remittances of ₹5.27 crore from some sources.

source.quote: cheques/demand drafts accumulated since 2007-08, amounting to ₹18.12 crore.

stats.label: Labour cess collected by BMTC not deposited to Board
stats.note: Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BMTC) collected ₹6.06 crore as labour cess but had not deposited it to the BOCW Board — meaning workers' welfare contributions were sitting uncredited in the transit authority's accounts rather than funding worker welfare.

stats.label: Unauthorised expenditure on Preventive Health Care schemes
stats.note: The Board incurred ₹258.80 crore on Preventive Health Care Training and Checkup schemes without any provision in the Act or Rules for such expenditure — making it entirely unauthorised. This expenditure was incurred without legal backing and to the detriment of other authorised welfare schemes.

source.quote: to the Act/Rules resulted in irregular expenditure of ₹258.80 crore.

stats.label: Released to KSDB without utilisation certificates for prior releases
stats.note: The Board released ₹433.80 crore to the Karnataka Slum Development Board (KSDB) for housing schemes, without obtaining utilisation certificates for ₹76 crore of earlier releases. Money was disbursed to KSDB without accountability for whether it was actually spent on worker housing.

source.quote: Records revealed that the Board released ₹433.80 crore to KSDB without

stats.label: Budget provision vs actual expenditure on worker welfare (2018-23)
stats.note: Against a budget provision of ₹10,154.45 crore for worker welfare during 2018-19 to 2022-23, the Board incurred expenditure of only ₹6,198.34 crore — utilising just 61 per cent of available welfare funds, leaving nearly ₹4,000 crore unspent over five years.

source.quote: Against a budget provision of ₹10,154.45 crore during the period 2018-19 to 2022-23, the expenditure incurred during the above period was ₹6,198.34 crore.

keyFindings.text: ₹18.12 crore in cess dues sat in uncashed cheques and demand drafts from 2007-08 onwards — some for 15 years — without being deposited. ₹6.06 crore collected by BMTC as labour cess was not remitted to the Board. ₹5.27 crore in remittances could not be traced. The Board's own financial management was so deficient that it could not account for receipts spanning over a decade.

source.quote: cheques/demand drafts accumulated since 2007-08, amounting to ₹18.12 crore.

keyFindings.text: ₹258.80 crore was spent on Preventive Health Care schemes without any legal authority — no provision in the BOCW Act or Rules permits such expenditure. ₹433.80 crore was released to KSDB for worker housing without obtaining utilisation certificates for ₹76 crore of prior disbursements. Workers whose cess contributions funded these amounts had no assurance the money was spent on their benefit.

source.quote: to the Act/Rules resulted in irregular expenditure of ₹258.80 crore.

keyFindings.text: Despite budget provisions of ₹10,154.45 crore over five years, only ₹6,198.34 crore (61 per cent) was spent — leaving nearly ₹4,000 crore of worker welfare funds unspent. This chronic under-utilisation is paradoxical: the Board failed to reach eligible workers while simultaneously spending ₹258.80 crore on schemes it had no legal authority to run.

source.quote: Against a budget provision of ₹10,154.45 crore during the period 2018-19 to 2022-23, the expenditure incurred during the above period was ₹6,198.34 crore.

recommendations: Immediately deposit all uncashed cheques and DDs (₹18.12 crore) and trace and recover ₹5.27 crore in untraced remittances.
Recover ₹6.06 crore in cess collected by BMTC; enforce timely remittance by all collecting agencies through penalty provisions.
Cease all expenditure on Preventive Health Care schemes until legal authority is obtained through Act amendment; recover or regularise ₹258.80 crore spent without authorisation.
Obtain utilisation certificates for all KSDB releases before making further disbursements; link future releases to verified occupancy of completed worker housing.
Set annual welfare fund utilisation targets of at least 90 per cent; conduct quarterly reviews of scheme delivery to eliminate the chronic under-expenditure pattern.

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Smart City Mission in Karnataka
overview:
Smart City Mission (SCM), launched in June 2015, aimed to develop 100 smart cities across India through core infrastructure improvement, sustainable and inclusive development and the application of smart solutions. Five Karnataka cities — Bengaluru, Belagavi, Davanagere, Mangaluru and Shivamogga — were selected. The CAG audited SCM implementation in Karnataka from 2015-16 to 2022-23.

The defining finding is a large-scale diversion of funds from their designated purpose: against a ₹817.42 crore allocation under the Pan City component (which was to improve city-wide services using technology), projects worth ₹1,462.67 crore were taken up — indicating 79 per cent excess spending over Pan City allocation, with funds diverted from other heads. Additionally, cities were not allotted the mandated paid-up capital of ₹200 crore each; actual paid-up capital was only ₹19.08 crore against ₹60.22 crore required.

Financial irregularities included: ₹2.69 crore earned as interest on Centrally pooled funds not remitted to Consolidated Funds; and ₹2.56 crore of excess payment in smart city contracts.

stats.label: Pan City allocation vs projects actually taken up (fund diversion)
stats.note: Against the ₹817.42 crore allocation under the Pan City component of SCM, projects were taken up for ₹1,462.67 crore — indicating diversion of funds from other categories into Pan City expenditure. 30 per cent of originally planned Area-Based Development projects were cancelled or modified.

source.quote: As against ₹817.42 crore allocation under Pan City, projects were taken up to the tune of ₹1,462.67 crore indicating diversion of funds

stats.label: Interest earned on Central funds — not remitted to Consolidated Funds
stats.note: ₹2.69 crore earned as interest on Centrally pooled funds (grant money) was not remitted to the respective Consolidated Funds as required — kept in Smart City SPV accounts instead. This is a violation of financial rules governing treatment of interest on government grants.

source.quote: interest of ₹2.69 crore but was not remitted to respective Consolidated funds.

stats.label: Excess payment in smart city project contracts
stats.note: Audit found excess payment of ₹2.56 crore in smart city contracts in test-checked cities. Centralised Command and Control Centre (CCCC) infrastructure worth ₹19.08 crore against a required ₹60.22 crore was operationalised — indicating massive shortfall in the flagship monitoring infrastructure.

source.quote: excess payment of ₹2.56 crore.

stats.label: Smart City paid-up capital vs mandate (₹200 crore per city)
stats.note: Each Smart City company was mandated to have paid-up capital of ₹200 crore (Central + State + ULB). Actual paid-up capital operationalised was only ₹19.08 crore against ₹60.22 crore required — raising questions about the financial foundation of the Smart City SPVs.

source.quote: ₹19.08 crore only against ₹60.22 crore.

stats.label: Projects originally planned subsequently cancelled or modified
stats.note: 30 per cent of Smart City projects originally planned were subsequently cancelled or significantly modified — indicating poor initial planning, changing priorities or implementation failures. Projects under the river front development category showed shortfall in achieving intended benefits.

source.quote: (30 per cent) projects originally planned, which was against MoHUA

keyFindings.text: The Pan City component of Smart City Mission — meant for technology-enabled city-wide service improvements — saw ₹1,462.67 crore in projects taken up against a ₹817.42 crore allocation: a 79 per cent excess driven by diversion from other components. This while 30 per cent of originally planned projects were cancelled or modified, and the mandated paid-up capital of ₹200 crore per Smart City company was far from achieved (actual: ₹19.08 crore operationalised against ₹60.22 crore required).

source.quote: As against ₹817.42 crore allocation under Pan City, projects were taken up to the tune of ₹1,462.67 crore indicating diversion of funds

keyFindings.text: ₹2.69 crore in interest earned on Central grant money was not remitted to Consolidated Funds. ₹2.56 crore was overpaid in smart city contracts. Centralised Command and Control Centres — the flagship "smart" monitoring infrastructure — were operationalised at ₹19.08 crore against a required ₹60.22 crore. The Tender SURE road infrastructure showed shortfall in achieving intended pedestrian and public transport benefits.

source.quote: interest of ₹2.69 crore but was not remitted to respective Consolidated funds.

recommendations: Recover all ₹2.69 crore in interest on Central funds and remit to Consolidated Funds immediately; enforce strict financial discipline on grant interest rules.
Audit all Pan City expenditure for compliance with original component-wise allocations; recover any amounts diverted without MoHUA approval.
Complete paid-up capital infusion to the mandated ₹200 crore per Smart City company before sanctioning further projects.
Operationalise all Centralised Command and Control Centre infrastructure to the full sanctioned scope.
Review all cancelled projects for reinstatement or compensation; conduct a post-project benefit assessment for river front developments.
ministry: Urban Development Department, Government of Karnataka

title: Performance Audit on Construction and Operation of Lucknow Metro Rail Project
overview:
Lucknow Metro Rail Project (Phase-IA), commissioned in stages from 2017 to 2019, covers 23 km with 21 stations. The project was sanctioned for ₹6,928.00 crore and expenditure incurred was ₹6,868.75 crore for Phase-IA. The CAG Performance Audit covered 51 of 144 total contracts (21 major + 30 minor works) involving ₹4,987.21 crore, from project inception in November 2013 to March 2023.

The audit found pervasive financial irregularities in contract management: Plant and Machinery advance of ₹31.74 crore was irregularly paid to a contractor for plants and machineries already owned by him; another contractor received an excess advance of ₹14.01 crore at variance with contract conditions. A lump sum work under contract LKCC-07 was executed at ₹51.40 crore against a bonded cost of ₹15.75 crore — with the company unable to provide itemised work details for ₹51.40 crore despite repeated audit requests.

The company failed to recover mineral royalty and price of minerals amounting to ₹3.16 crore from a contractor who extracted soil during underground station construction without obtaining a geology and mining permit.
