Obtain itemised works breakdowns for all lump-sum contracts before authorising final payments; report LKCC-07 findings to the State Government for action.
Recover ₹3.16 crore in mineral royalty from the contractor who extracted ordinary soil without permit; obtain retroactive clearance from Geology and Mining Department.
Ensure adequate Advance Payment Guarantees (APGs) cover all future advance payments; implement a contract audit committee to prevent recurrence.
ministry: Lucknow Metro Rail Corporation / Infrastructure and Industrial Development Department, Government of Uttar Pradesh

title: Performance Audit on Working of Uttar Pradesh State Industrial Development Authority (UPSIDA)
overview:
UPSIDA (Uttar Pradesh State Industrial Development Authority) is responsible for developing industrial infrastructure — acquiring land, developing industrial estates and allotting plots to industries — in UP. The CAG Performance Audit covered UPSIDA's operations from 2017-18 to 2022-23, covering land acquisition, industrial area development, plot allotment, and financial management.

UPSIDA consistently missed land acquisition targets: in six years, the target was achieved only in 2020-21, with shortfall ranging from 27.60 to 100 per cent (no land acquired at all in two years). Industrial area development targets were similarly missed in all six years (shortfall: 24.67 to 92.70 per cent). 15 contracts worth ₹255.75 crore were awarded without verifying bidder documents — which were later found to be suspected fakes, requiring contract cancellation.

Short recovery of Liquidated Damages of ₹13.71 crore was observed in 16 cases. UPSIDA incurred avoidable expenditure of ₹7.67 crore from its own funds on maintenance of Industrial Areas falling under municipal bodies' jurisdiction.

stats.label: Land acquisition target achievement shortfall (6 years)
stats.note: In six years from 2017-18 to 2022-23, land acquisition targets were achieved only once (2020-21). Shortfall ranged from 27.60 to 100 per cent — with zero land acquired in 2019-20 and 2022-23. COVID-19 and ambitious target-setting were cited but do not explain the 2022-23 failure.

source.quote: achievement of targets ranged between 27.60 per cent to 100 per cent with no land being acquired in two years

stats.label: Industrial area development target shortfall (6 years)
stats.note: UPSIDA did not achieve its industrial area development targets in any of the six years from 2017-18 to 2022-23. Shortfall in achievement ranged from 24.67 per cent (best year) to 92.70 per cent. Even in the best year (2020-21), UPSIDA only achieved 75.33 per cent of target.

source.quote: shortfall in achievement of targets ranged between 24.67 per cent to 92.70 per cent

stats.label: 15 contracts awarded without verifying bidder documents (suspected fake)
stats.note: 15 contracts valuing ₹255.75 crore were awarded without verifying the documents submitted by bidders. Subsequently, these documents were found to be suspected fakes, requiring cancellation of all 15 contracts — causing project delays and financial disruption.

source.quote: Instances of award of 15 contracts valuing ` 255.75 crore without verifying the documents of the bidders were noticed

stats.label: Short recovery of Liquidated Damages (contractor performance penalties)
stats.note: Short recovery of Liquidated Damages (LD) of ₹13.71 crore was observed in 16 cases — meaning contractors who missed their completion deadlines were not charged the full prescribed penalties for delay, subsidising their non-performance at public expense.

source.quote: short recovery of Liquidated Damages (LD) of ` 13.71 crore in 16 cases

stats.label: Avoidable expenditure on Industrial Areas under municipal jurisdiction
stats.note: UPSIDA incurred avoidable expenditure of ₹7.67 crore from its own funds on maintenance of Industrial Areas that fall under the jurisdiction of municipal bodies — expenditure that should have been borne by the municipalities, not UPSIDA.

source.quote: UPSIDA incurred avoidable expenditure of ` 7.67 crore from its own funds

stats.label: GoUP loan on which interest burden increased (no repayment)
stats.note: UPSIDA carried an outstanding GoUP (Government of Uttar Pradesh) loan of ₹41 crore on which interest burden was increasing. Repayment conditions of a NOIDA loan were also not complied with. These growing interest liabilities reduce UPSIDA's capacity for development expenditure.

source.quote: Increasing burden of interest on outstanding GoUP loan of ` 41 crore

keyFindings.text: UPSIDA failed to acquire land in any meaningful way: targets missed in 5 of 6 years, with shortfalls of 27.60 to 100 per cent. Industrial area development targets were missed in all 6 years (shortfall 24.67-92.70%). 15 contracts worth ₹255.75 crore were awarded to bidders whose documents turned out to be suspected forgeries — a fundamental procurement due diligence failure causing contract cancellations and project delays. Contractors who did deliver late were also not fully penalised: ₹13.71 crore in LD was short-recovered in 16 cases.

source.quote: achievement of targets ranged between 27.60 per cent to 100 per cent with no land being acquired in two years

keyFindings.text: Plot allotment achievement ranged from only 27 to 58 per cent of target during 2017-23. An industrial plot of 3,929 sq m was allotted without obtaining complete financial details of the applicant; a plot of 5,018.65 sq m worth ₹1.10 crore was allotted to an ineligible applicant due to incorrect evaluation. 37 start-of-production permissions were granted before completion or occupancy certificates were issued. ₹7.67 crore was spent maintaining Industrial Areas that municipalities should be maintaining.

source.quote: Instances of award of 15 contracts valuing ` 255.75 crore without verifying the documents of the bidders were noticed

recommendations: Mandate mandatory document verification (physical inspection, government database cross-check) for all contracts above ₹10 crore before award.
Recover full LD (₹13.71 crore) from defaulting contractors in 16 cases; do not accept reduced LD without prior authority approval.
Charge municipal bodies for UPSIDA's ₹7.67 crore expenditure on IAs under their jurisdiction; stop bearing maintenance costs for non-UPSIDA jurisdictions.
Establish binding annual land acquisition targets with a quarterly accountability review; fix legal team capacity to handle land acquisition disputes that cause zero-acquisition years.
Repay GoUP loan of ₹41 crore on priority to stop mounting interest; honour NOIDA loan repayment schedule unconditionally.
ministry: Uttar Pradesh State Industrial Development Authority (UPSIDA) / IID Department, GoUP

title: Performance Audit on Integrated Financial Management System in Kerala
overview:
Kerala's Integrated Financial Management System (IFMS-K) is a comprehensive digital platform for managing government revenue (stamp duty, motor vehicle tax, land revenue, commercial taxes, treasury operations) and expenditure. It was intended to bring all financial transactions under a single digital platform, eliminating manual processes and improving accountability. Total project cost was ₹34.30 crore (March 2023), of which software constituted ₹14.98 crore (43.67 per cent). The CAG Performance Audit covered 2014-15 to 2022-23.

The audit found significant implementation gaps: only 44 per cent of challans (revenue collection instruments) had been defaced (post-use cancellation to prevent reuse) as required — meaning 56 per cent of challans could potentially be reused for fraudulent collection. Automatic calculation of penal interest for delayed credit of money to government accounts by agency banks had not been developed. No time limits exist for processing refund applications, and 31 per cent of refund applications were pending disposal.

Monitoring was weak: IFMS review meetings showed only 19.23 per cent of scheduled meetings held, and audit identified gaps of up to 10 months between consecutive meetings. Key functionalities relating to refund of E-challans and M-challans (Manual challans) showed systematic deficiencies.

stats.label: Challans defaced (post-use cancellation to prevent reuse)
stats.note: Timely defacement of challans (cancellation after use to prevent reuse) was not being done. Only 44 per cent of challans had been defaced. 56 per cent of challans remained undefaced — creating potential for reuse in fraudulent revenue collection.

source.quote: defacement of challans is not done and only 44 per cent of challans have been defaced

stats.label: Refund applications pending disposal
stats.note: No time limits were set for processing refund applications in IFMS-K. As a result, 31 per cent of refund applications were pending disposal. Citizens who had overpaid government dues were waiting indefinitely for refunds — a denial of legal entitlements.

source.quote: No time limits are set for processing refund applications and 31 per cent of applications are pending disposal.

stats.label: IFMS review meetings held vs scheduled
stats.note: IFMS review meetings — the primary governance mechanism for tracking implementation gaps and resolving issues — were held only 19.23 per cent of the time as scheduled. Audit identified gaps of up to 10 months between consecutive meetings, indicating systemic neglect of IFMS monitoring.

source.quote: meetings (19.23 per cent). Audit identified gaps of up to 10 months between

stats.label: IFMS-K total project cost (March 2023)
stats.note: Total project cost of IFMS-K was ₹34.30 crore as of March 2023. Software purchase constituted ₹14.98 crore (43.67 per cent) — the major share. The auto-calculation feature for penal interest on agency bank delays was not developed, despite being essential for enforcing timely government credit.

source.quote: Total cost of the Project amounted to ₹34.30 crore (March 2023). Purchase of software for ₹14.98 crore (43.67 per cent)

stats.label: Automatic penal interest on delayed bank credits — not implemented
stats.note: The functionality for automatic calculation of penal interest on delayed credit of money to government accounts by agency banks had not been developed in IFMS-K. This means agency banks that delayed crediting government revenues faced no automated penalty — creating a financial loss that is impossible to quantify without manual tracking.

source.quote: The functionality of auto calculation of penal interest for delayed credit of money to government account by agency banks has not been developed.

keyFindings.text: IFMS-K's core revenue collection safeguards have not been implemented: only 44 per cent of challans were defaced (leaving 56 per cent potentially reusable for fraud); automatic penal interest for delayed bank credits was never developed; and no time limits exist for refund processing — leaving 31 per cent of applications in permanent limbo. These are fundamental design gaps in a ₹34.30 crore government financial system covering all of Kerala's revenue streams.

source.quote: defacement of challans is not done and only 44 per cent of challans have been defaced

keyFindings.text: Governance of IFMS-K was near-absent: review meetings were held only 19.23 per cent of the time scheduled, with gaps of up to 10 months between consecutive meetings. The shortfalls identified in IFMS-K — challan defacement, refund delays, absent penal interest — were known issues that appeared in meeting agendas but were not resolved due to the infrequency of governance oversight. A ₹34.30 crore investment had not been leveraged to achieve its intended financial accountability goals.

source.quote: meetings (19.23 per cent). Audit identified gaps of up to 10 months between

recommendations: Mandate 100 per cent challan defacement within 24 hours of use; implement automatic system-level defacement on confirmation of payment receipt.
Set statutory time limits for refund processing (maximum 30 days); track and publicly report refund pendency; compensate citizens for delays beyond the prescribed period.
Develop and deploy automatic penal interest calculation for agency bank delayed credits immediately; backdate and recover all pending penal interest from audit period.
Hold IFMS review meetings monthly without exception; constitute a State-level IFMS steering committee with monthly accountability to the Finance Secretary.
Commission a third-party audit of IFMS-K implementation gaps against the original scope; publish a time-bound closure report on each identified gap.
ministry: Finance Department / Information Technology Department, Government of Kerala

title: Performance Audit of Implementation of POSHAN including Integrated Child Development Services and Mid-Day Meal
overview:
Odisha's implementation of three flagship child nutrition schemes — POSHAN (PM's Overarching Scheme for Holistic Nutrition), the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS), and the Mid-Day Meal (MDM) scheme — was audited by the CAG for the period 2018-23. The schemes collectively target pregnant and lactating mothers, children under six, adolescent girls (under SAG), and school-going children. Audit covered 30 ICDS projects across six districts and test-checked stock registers, laboratory samples, and payment records.

Audit found systematic failures across nutrition supply chains: 62,686.12 quintals of rice worth ₹20.85 crore was likely short-delivered to Anganwadi Centres (AWCs) in sampled districts based on the average shortage found in physical weighment. Rice samples collected from AWCs in Sambalpur and Mayurbhanj were found "unfit for human consumption" — one sample had moisture content of 14.9% and 24.8% damaged grains against prescribed maximums of 14% and 4% respectively.

Financial management was equally poor: Self-Help Groups (SHGs) distributing Take Home Rations (THR) were overpaid ₹5.73 crore in supervision and processing costs. The Scheme for Adolescent Girls (SAG) spent only ₹10.74 crore (54.77%) of ₹19.62 crore available funds during 2018-23. In Balangir and Rayagada districts, a mere ₹2.38 crore (1.54 per cent) of the ₹154.12 crore required for SAG beneficiaries was allotted.

stats.label: Short delivery of rice to Anganwadi Centres (AWCs)
stats.note: Physical weighment of rice bags at AWCs in sampled districts revealed actual weight was short. Based on the average shortage found in 115 rice bags test-checked at AWCs, CAG estimated a likely short delivery of 62,686.12 quintals of rice worth ₹20.85 crore to AWCs — depriving children and mothers of their entitled nutrition rations.

source.quote: 62,686.12 quintals of rice to AWCs in these districts, valued at approximately ₹20.85 crore.

stats.label: SAG scheme fund utilisation (Balangir & Rayagada)
stats.note: In test-checked districts of Balangir and Rayagada, only ₹2.38 crore was allotted against the ₹154.12 crore required to provide Supplementary Nutrition Programme (SNP) to all SAG-enrolled adolescent girls. Of this, only ₹1.99 crore was actually spent — just 1.54 per cent of the requirement. Adolescent girls in these districts were effectively denied their entitled nutritional support for the entire 2018-23 period.

source.quote: (54.77 per cent) only was incurred during 2018-23 against availability of fund

stats.label: Excess payment to SHGs for THR supervision
stats.note: Supervision and processing cost for nine SHGs distributing Take Home Rations (THR) was to be paid at ₹0.31 per beneficiary per day for 25 days/month across 36,03,184 beneficiaries during 2018-23 — entailing ₹2.79 crore. However, the SHGs were paid ₹8.52 crore, resulting in an excess payment of ₹5.73 crore. The excess inflated SHG payments came at the cost of reducing ingredient quality.

source.quote: excess payment of ₹5.73 crore to the Self-Help Groups towards supervision and processing cost

keyFindings.text: The rice supply chain for Anganwadi Centres was compromised at multiple points: physical weighment at AWCs found systematic under-delivery (estimated ₹20.85 crore shortfall); laboratory tests found rice samples "unfit for human consumption" with live infestation, 14.9% moisture and 24.8% damaged grain; and wheat stocks worth ₹41 lakh were damaged in cyclone Fani due to excess accumulation with SHGs. The nutrition programmes were failing the most vulnerable beneficiaries — under-six children and pregnant mothers — at the last mile.

source.quote: 62,686.12 quintals of rice to AWCs in these districts, valued at approximately ₹20.85 crore.

keyFindings.text: The Scheme for Adolescent Girls (SAG) was near-inoperative in sampled districts: only 1.54 per cent of the required ₹154.12 crore was spent in Balangir and Rayagada; the state-wide SAG utilisation was 54.77 per cent. The Department simultaneously overpaid SHGs ₹5.73 crore in processing costs. A ₹41 lakh wheat loss occurred during cyclone Fani from excess stock accumulation. These findings point to a system that failed both in resource mobilisation and resource utilisation for child and adolescent nutrition.

source.quote: (54.77 per cent) only was incurred during 2018-23 against availability of fund

recommendations: Establish mandatory electronic weighment at AWC level with tamper-proof records; require Transport Agents to submit GPS-tracked delivery proof and weight certificates verified by a third party.
Mandate periodic laboratory testing of all nutrition commodities (rice, wheat, edible oil) at the district level every quarter; disqualify suppliers whose samples fail quality norms.
Fix SHG processing cost payments to actual beneficiary counts, auto-calculated from the nutrition management MIS; recover the ₹5.73 crore excess from SHGs and trace diversion.
Ensure 100 per cent SAG fund utilisation; the current pattern of allotting 1.54 per cent of required funds in tribal districts must be investigated and corrected at the state budget allocation stage.
ministry: Women and Child Development Department, Government of Odisha

title: Performance Audit on Working of University of Jammu
overview:
The CAG conducted a Performance Audit of the University of Jammu (J&K UT) covering academic and research activities, human resource management, infrastructure, and financial management. The University is the affiliating body for colleges in Jammu and is governed by the J&K University of Jammu Act. The audit test-checked 33 per cent of infrastructure projects/works in the University Works Department, equipment purchased by 38 departments, and service records of employees.

Academic performance was weak: the University failed to establish industry-academia linkages to make students job-ready; its Business Incubation and Innovation Centre (UBIIC) and Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) set up for startup incubation remained non-functional despite ₹1.29 crore expenditure. In 51 physically verified colleges (17 Government, 34 Non-Government), 113 out of 331 teachers appointed in 24 Non-Government colleges did not possess prescribed qualifications.

Human Resource Management was dysfunctional: Recruitment Rules had not been framed for 77 out of 142 categories of non-teaching posts. Regularisation of adhoc/contractual staff was adopted as a mode of appointment, bypassing proper recruitment. Premature and irregular promotions were also found. The UBIIC and SPV — set up to support startups — had identified no potential startups and had incurred ₹1.05 crore on furniture, desktops, and professional services/international travel without any functional output.

stats.label: Teachers without prescribed qualifications in audit-sampled colleges
stats.note: Of 331 teachers appointed in 24 Non-Government affiliated colleges physically verified by CAG, 113 (34.1%) did not possess the UGC/AICTE-prescribed qualifications. These teachers were serving students without meeting the minimum standards required for university-level teaching. The figure represents only the audited sample — the actual extent may be higher across all 51 verified colleges.

source.quote: 113 teachers did not possess the prescribed qualifications.

stats.label: Non-teaching post categories without Recruitment Rules
stats.note: Recruitment Rules had not been framed for 77 out of 142 categories of non-teaching posts (54.2%) in the University. This absence of rules allowed arbitrary appointments, regularisations of ad hoc staff, and lateral entry to direct-entry level posts — creating systemic HR mismanagement and legal vulnerability for the University.

source.quote: Recruitment Rules had not been framed for 77 out of 142 categories of non-teaching posts.

stats.label: UBIIC/SPV startup incubator: expenditure without any functional startup
stats.note: The University Business Incubation and Innovation Centre (UBIIC) and its Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) — set up to support startups — identified no potential startups and incurred ₹1.05 crore on furniture (₹30.93 lakh), desktops (₹39.62 lakh), professional services (₹27.69 lakh), and international travel (₹7.49 lakh) with zero entrepreneurial output. In addition, ₹27.68 lakh spent on professional fee to two consultancy firms was rendered infructuous as no innovators had been enrolled.

source.quote: rendering expenditure of ` 1.05 crore11 incurred on furniture/ desktops/ professional services/ international travel unfruitful.

keyFindings.text: 34.1 per cent of teachers sampled in Non-Government affiliated colleges lacked prescribed qualifications, while Recruitment Rules had not been framed for 54.2 per cent of non-teaching post categories. Regularisation of adhoc/contractual staff was used as a mode of appointment — a practice that bypasses merit-based recruitment, creates financial liabilities, and undermines academic quality. The University's governance framework for HR was fundamentally dysfunctional.

source.quote: 113 teachers did not possess the prescribed qualifications.

keyFindings.text: The UBIIC/SPV startup incubation initiative — funded to create an entrepreneurship ecosystem — was completely non-functional. ₹1.05 crore was spent on physical infrastructure and professional services, but zero startups were incubated and zero innovators were enrolled. The University also lost a ₹2.50 crore NITI Aayog grant for an Atal Community Innovation Centre (ACIC) due to non-availability of the required 4,000 sq ft space. Public funds for innovation support were entirely wasted.

source.quote: rendering expenditure of ` 1.05 crore11 incurred on furniture/ desktops/ professional services/ international travel unfruitful.

recommendations: Immediately frame Recruitment Rules for all 142 categories of non-teaching posts; invalidate appointments made in absence of Recruitment Rules and regularise only those meeting prescribed criteria.
Mandate NAAC accreditation for all affiliated colleges; debar colleges with unqualified teachers from affiliation until deficiencies are rectified.
Operationalise UBIIC with a measurable startup enrolment target and a time-bound plan; failing which, recover public funds spent and close the SPV.
Constitute an independent academic audit committee that annually verifies teacher qualification compliance in all affiliated colleges; publish results publicly.
ministry: Higher Education Department, Government of Jammu & Kashmir

title: Performance Audit on Functioning of Universities of GNCTD
overview:
The CAG audited three Delhi government universities — Guru Gobind Singh Indraprastha University (GGSIPU), Delhi Technological University (DTU), and Delhi Pharmaceutical Sciences & Research University (DPSRU) — for the period April 2018 to March 2023. These three universities, administered by the Directorate of Higher Education (DHE) and Directorate of Training and Technical Education (DTTE) under GNCTD, receive grants-in-aid from the state government.

The audit found structural failures across all three dimensions: accreditation, human resources, and finance. None of the three universities maintained required NAAC/NBA accreditation continuously. GGSIPU lacked both NAAC and NBA accreditation from 2018 to 2023. DTU operated without NAAC accreditation 2015–2019 and without NBA accreditation 2018–2023. DPSRU had no NAAC or NBA accreditation from 2020 to 2023.

Teaching staff shortages were acute and persistent: GGSIPU saw shortages of 38.77–44.84 per cent; DTU 55–60 per cent (three-fourths of Professor and Associate Professor posts vacant); DPSRU 21.77–54.43 per cent. Despite the shortfall, GGSIPU approved 144 teaching posts in 2021 but recruited to only 32 in the next two years. Seating capacity deficits ranged from 26 per cent (GGSIPU Dwarka) to 59 per cent (DPSRU) against enrolled students.

stats.label: Teaching staff shortage — DTU (2018–23)
stats.note: DTU had teaching staff shortages ranging from 55 to 60 per cent during the audit period 2018-23. Three-fourths of Professor and Associate Professor posts at DTU remained vacant. This is a premier engineering university producing thousands of engineers annually — operating effectively at half-staff for five consecutive years.

source.quote: 38.77 per cent to 44.84 per cent in GGSIPU, 21.77 per cent to 54.43 per cent in DPSRU and 55 per cent to 60 per cent in DTU.

stats.label: Avoidable tax liability — DHESF and DKDF funds
stats.note: The Delhi Higher Education Scholarship Fund (DHESF) and Delhi Knowledge Development Foundation (DKDF) — designed to provide financial assistance to meritorious students and fund knowledge initiatives — generated an avoidable tax liability of ₹25.59 crore due to sub-optimal utilisation of receipts. These funds were also misused: ₹2.44 crore meant for student financial assistance was diverted to a certificate course at GGSIPU, with ₹2.56 crore lying unspent.

source.quote: avoidable tax liability of ₹ 25.59 crore due to sub-optimal utilisation of receipts into these Funds.

stats.label: Centre of Excellence grants — utilisation outcomes
stats.note: DKDF released ₹43.76 crore to six universities during 2020-22 for eight Centre of Excellence projects. Despite this expenditure, the projects faced implementation issues — the funds were disbursed without adequate oversight of actual establishment of Centres of Excellence, and no substantive knowledge output was confirmed.

source.quote: ₹ 43.76 crore to six Universities during 2020-22 for the execution of eight projects relating to the creation of a Centre of Excellence.

keyFindings.text: All three audited Delhi universities operated without mandatory NAAC/NBA accreditation for extended periods: GGSIPU for the entire 2018-2023 audit period (both NAAC and NBA); DTU without NAAC for 4 years and without NBA for 5 years; DPSRU without both from 2020-2023. Teaching staff shortages were persistently high (38.77%–60%) and seating capacity deficits ranged from 26% to 59% against enrolled students. DHE and DTTE failed to formulate comprehensive policies to fulfil their own vision/mission statements. These universities have been chronically under-resourced and under-regulated for five or more years.

source.quote: avoidable tax liability of ₹ 25.59 crore due to sub-optimal utilisation of receipts into these Funds.

keyFindings.text: Financial management was marked by misuse and delays: ₹25.59 crore avoidable tax liability arose from sub-optimal use of student scholarship and knowledge development funds; ₹2.44 crore meant for student financial assistance was diverted to a certificate course; ₹3.04 crore lying with DHE since 2015-16 was unused (MoU with GoI never signed); and ₹43.76 crore released for eight Centre of Excellence projects showed no confirmed output. GGSIPU made recruitment to only 32 of the 144 teaching posts it approved in 2021 — despite documented shortage. Multiple curricula had not been revised in 5–11 years.

source.quote: ₹ 43.76 crore to six Universities during 2020-22 for the execution of eight projects relating to the creation of a Centre of Excellence.

recommendations: Mandate NAAC and NBA accreditation for all three universities on a rolling basis; make accreditation a precondition for grant-in-aid disbursement and linkage to performance targets.
Fill all sanctioned teaching posts within 12 months at DTU, GGSIPU, and DPSRU; publish vacancy position and recruitment progress quarterly on DHE/DTTE websites.
Immediately sign the pending GoI-GNCTD MoU for educational initiatives to release the ₹3.04 crore already allocated; set a 6-month deadline for use of all idle scholarship funds.
Conduct third-party evaluation of all eight Centre of Excellence projects funded under DKDF; recover unspent grants where outputs have not been demonstrated.
Revise all curricula that have not been updated in 5+ years; establish a 3-year mandatory curriculum review cycle across all affiliated colleges.
ministry: Directorate of Higher Education / Directorate of Training and Technical Education, GNCTD

title: Performance Audit on Development of Roads in Madhya Pradesh by MP Public Works Department
overview:
The CAG audited road infrastructure development by Madhya Pradesh Public Works Department (MPPWD) Buildings & Roads wing — responsible for Major District Roads (MDRs), Other District Roads (ODRs), Village Roads (VRs), and minor structures. Audit scrutinised 25 of 56 PWD (B&R) divisions, examined 276 road works, and 10 New Development Bank (NDB)-funded projects, including Joint Physical Inspections (JPIs) of 51 roads.

The systemic picture is alarming: there was no long-term Master Plan or Road Asset Management System (RASM) — projects were selected without Benefit-Cost Ratio assessments, strategic frameworks, or proper land acquisition. Of 286 audited works, 240 were completed with delays ranging from 18 to 2,155 days, with an average shortfall of 424 days. Only 1 of the 10 NDB-funded projects met its deadline; others fell short of targeted road lengths, leading to unutilised loan portions and avoidable financial penalties.

Capacity building under the ₹26 crore NDB-funded component was entirely wasted: only ₹13.79 crore was spent — entirely on KPMG Advisory consultancy — but KPMG's recommendations for Road Asset Management System, Work & Accounts Management System, and Integrated Project Management System were never implemented. The balance ₹12.21 crore was surrendered after loan expiry. In Shivpuri, ₹15.02 crore was spent on a forest stretch irregularly included in a project, leaving the road incomplete and abandoned.

stats.label: Average delay in road completion (240 of 286 works delayed)
stats.note: 240 out of 286 audited road works under MPPWD were completed with delays ranging between 18 and 2,155 days during 2017-2023. The average shortfall in completion was 424 days — over a year beyond schedule. Only EPC (Engineering, Procurement and Construction) contracts consistently beat the deadline, but even these were given excess time and early-completion bonuses, conferring undue benefit to contractors.

source.quote: average shortfall of 424 days. Thus, there was a shortfall in achievement in completion of road

stats.label: Capacity building expenditure under NDB project — rendered infructuous
stats.note: MPPWD hired KPMG Advisory at a cost of ₹13.79 crore for capacity building under the NDB project. KPMG submitted detailed recommendations for a Road Asset Management System, Integrated Project Management System, and Work & Accounts Management System. None of these recommendations were operationalised. The remaining ₹12.21 crore of the ₹26 crore capacity building allocation was surrendered after loan expiry — making the entire ₹13.79 crore expenditure infructuous.

source.quote: expenditure incurred on hiring external consultants at a cost of ₹ 13.79 crore was infructuous.

stats.label: Wasteful expenditure — Jhinna–Charki Ghati Road foreclosed
stats.note: Work on the Jhinna–Charki Ghati Road was taken up in April 2017 at a cost of ₹5.72 crore. It was foreclosed in June 2022 after incurring ₹5.12 crore — with the road in a motorable state and surface wearing course completed (design life remaining: 10 years). Without assigning reasons, PWD transferred the road to MPRDC for two-lane upgradation, rendering the entire ₹5.12 crore wasteful.

source.quote: of ₹ 5.12 crore as wasteful.

keyFindings.text: MPPWD had no long-term Master Plan, no Road Asset Management System, and no strategic framework for road development. The absence of RASM — identified by KPMG consultants paid ₹13.79 crore — meant that projects were selected haphazardly, land was not secured before commencement, and completion monitoring was absent. 240 of 286 works were delayed (average 424 days); only 1 of 10 NDB-funded projects met its deadline. The state spent heavily on consultancy but ignored every recommendation.

source.quote: expenditure incurred on hiring external consultants at a cost of ₹ 13.79 crore was infructuous.

keyFindings.text: Tender processes consistently violated norms: in 59 of 61 tenders above ₹5 crore, NITs were published in only a single newspaper — violating GoMP transparency guidelines. Incorrect bid evaluation in NDB projects resulted in excess liability of ₹7.39 crore in Ratlam Division alone. Quality control was compromised by delayed laboratory setups, untested materials, and premature issuance of completion certificates. In Shivpuri, 7.40 km of forest stretch was irregularly included in a project, leaving ₹15.02 crore spent on an abandoned road.

source.quote: average shortfall of 424 days. Thus, there was a shortfall in achievement in completion of road

recommendations: Establish a Road Asset Management System (RASM) immediately — implement the KPMG recommendations already paid for; make RASM a precondition for all new road project approvals.
Mandate Benefit-Cost Ratio assessment and land clearance before any road project is sanctioned; do not commence construction without secured right-of-way.
Publish NITs in at least three newspapers and online as per GoMP guidelines; constitute tender evaluation committees with mandatory independent representation.
Introduce real-time digital monitoring of road project milestones; link contractor payments to verified physical progress; impose liquidated damages automatically on delayed contracts.
Investigate and recover ₹13.79 crore infructuous KPMG expenditure; hold accountable the officials who failed to implement RASM and surrendered ₹12.21 crore unspent.
ministry: Public Works Department (Buildings & Roads), Government of Madhya Pradesh

title: Performance Audit of Development and Allotment of Properties by Ghaziabad Development Authority
overview:
The Ghaziabad Development Authority (GDA), constituted under the Uttar Pradesh Urban Planning and Development Act 1973, is responsible for planned urban development of Ghaziabad district — preparing master plans, developing residential/commercial/industrial land, allotting properties, and recovering development levies. The CAG audited GDA's development and allotment activities for 2017-22.

Audit found chronic shortfalls against Master Plan-2021 targets: residential development at 21 per cent of target, commercial at 66 per cent, public/semi-public facilities at 39 per cent, open area/parks at 79 per cent. EWS housing was the worst performer: against a target of 25,000 EWS dwelling units during 2017-22, only 9,960 were constructed/under construction (40 per cent). Developers constructing Integrated/Hi-tech Township schemes built only 2,133 EWS/LIG units (33 per cent of their 6,382 obligation).

GDA's finances were severely stressed: receipt targets were missed by 40–58 per cent in all years except 2018-19. A ₹1,089.45 crore Hindon Elevated Road project was executed — but the project was not part of MP-2021 and had been approved contrary to NCRPB directions, meaning ₹1,089 crore was spent outside the sanctioned framework. Additionally, the State Government had not disbursed ₹347.43 crore due to GDA as 2 per cent additional stamp duty for 2017-22.

stats.note: Against the Master Plan-2021 target of constructing 25,000 Economically Weaker Section (EWS) dwelling units during 2017-22, only 9,960 were constructed or under construction (40 per cent achievement). Developers of Integrated/Hi-tech Township schemes fared worse — building only 2,133 EWS/LIG units (33 per cent) against their contractual obligation of 6,382 units. GDA took no action against defaulting developers.

stats.note: GDA prepared a proposal for a six-lane Hindon Elevated Road at an estimated cost of ₹1,200 crore, starting from NH 24. The project was approved and executed — with ₹1,089.45 crore spent as of utilisation certificate date (September 2020). However, the project was developed in a direction contrary to NCRPB guidance and was not part of the approved MP-2021 framework. Over ₹1,000 crore was committed to a project that had no place in GDA's own master plan.

For the period 2017-22, GDA had demanded ₹347.43 crore from the State Government as these dues. The State Government had not disbursed this amount, resulting in GDA being deprived of its legally mandated revenue — contributing directly to the 40–58 per cent receipt shortfalls.

keyFindings.text: GDA's Master Plan 2021 targets were comprehensively missed: residential development was at 21 per cent, public/semi-public at 39 per cent, commercial at 66 per cent, and EWS housing at just 40 per cent of targets. Developers in Integrated/Hi-tech Township schemes constructed only 33 per cent of their contractual EWS/LIG obligation, yet GDA took no action against them. The State Government simultaneously withheld ₹347.43 crore in stamp duty dues owed to GDA — compounding the authority's financial stress.

This single off-plan expenditure consumed more funds than all EWS housing targets combined, yet produced no infrastructure sanctioned under the planning framework. Financial management showed persistent shortfalls of 40–58 per cent against budgeted receipts, and 40–63 per cent shortfalls in targeted expenditure. Contract management showed instances of excess payment, faulty measurements, and irregular short-term tenders.

recommendations: Enforce compliance with EWS/LIG developer obligations in all Integrated Township schemes; levy penalties on defaulting developers and publish a compliance register publicly.
Immediately bring all GDA projects within the approved MP-2021 framework; obtain NCRPB concurrence before undertaking any infrastructure above ₹50 crore.
State Government must urgently disburse ₹347.43 crore in stamp duty arrears to GDA; institute a monthly reconciliation mechanism to prevent future arrears.
Implement digital contract management with GPS-based site inspection and independent measurement; mandate Benefit-Cost Ratio for all works above ₹10 crore.
Revise Master Plan 2041 to set binding, enforceable EWS housing obligations with developer escrow deposits linked to construction milestones.

title: Performance Audit on Performance of Blast Furnaces in Steel Authority of India Limited
overview:
Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL), a Maharatna Central PSU under the Ministry of Steel, operates blast furnaces at five integrated steel plants — Bhilai, Bokaro, Rourkela, Durgapur, and Burnpur. The blast furnace is the heart of a steel plant: it converts iron ore, sinter, coke, and other inputs into hot metal (pig iron), the primary raw material for steel. The CAG audited blast furnace operations for 2017-24 across all five plants.

Raw material management was the central failure. CDI coal (Coal Dust Injection) — a cheaper substitute for coke — was consistently under-utilised: SAIL plants consumed 2.945 million tonnes more coke than norms and 2.235 million tonnes less CDI coal than targeted over 2017-24. This imbalance resulted in a potential extra expenditure of ₹6,259.25 crore (₹8,858.45 crore excess coke cost minus ₹2,599.20 crore CDI savings foregone). Power consumption also exceeded norms at most plants, contributing ₹310.48 crore in additional avoidable expenditure.

Production shortfalls were significant: against the Ministry of Steel MoU target of 130.96 million tonne of hot metal for 2017-24, SAIL achieved only 126.15 million tonne — a shortfall of 4.81 million tonne (3.7%). SAIL had set itself an even more ambitious Annual Business Perspective target of 140.88 million tonne, against which the shortfall was 14.73 MT (10.5%). Bhilai Steel Plant — SAIL's largest — achieved only 81 per cent of its Annual Business Perspective productivity target.

stats.label: Potential extra expenditure from coke overuse vs CDI underuse
stats.note: SAIL plants consumed 2.945 million tonnes more coke and 2.235 million tonnes less CDI coal than the norms fixed by plants during 2017-24. Using coke beyond norm cost ₹8,858.45 crore; the foregone CDI saving was ₹2,599.20 crore. The net potential extra expenditure was ₹6,259.25 crore. Using 10% pellets in blast furnace input charge — as recommended by National Steel Policy 2017 — could have saved ₹268 crore annually and reduced coke rate by 1.5–2%.

source.quote: There was potential extra expenditure of ₹6,259.25 crore during 2017-24

stats.label: Avoidable power expenditure (above-norm consumption)
stats.note: Power is a major cost element in steelmaking. Specific power consumption exceeded norms at most SAIL plants in most years during 2017-24. The excess power consumption led to a potential avoidable expenditure of ₹310.48 crore over the seven-year period. Only Bhilai Steel Plant (2022-23) and Durgapur Steel Plant (2023-24) achieved the coke/CDI norm.

source.quote: Excess consumption of power than the norm in the steel plants led to potential avoidable expenditure of ₹310.48 crore during 2017-24.

stats.label: Hot metal production vs MoU target (2017-24)
stats.note: During 2017-2024, SAIL's planned production as per Annual Business Perspective was 140.88 million tonne, against which actual production was 126.15 million tonne (89.5% achievement). Against the more modest Ministry of Steel MoU target of 130.96 million tonne, actual production was 126.15 million tonne (96.3%). Blast furnace productivity at Bhilai Steel Plant ranged from only 81% of Annual Business Perspective targets — the weakest performer across SAIL's five integrated plants.

keyFindings.text: SAIL's blast furnaces wasted ₹6,259.25 crore over seven years due to systematic over-reliance on coke (2.945 MT excess) and under-utilisation of CDI coal (2.235 MT shortfall) — a result of inconsistent pellet usage and declining iron ore quality that was predictable and manageable. The National Steel Policy 2017 explicitly directed SAIL to increase pellet usage, yet pellet utilisation remained sub-optimal throughout the audit period. SAIL had the technology and the policy directive to avoid this cost; it chose not to implement them.

source.quote: There was potential extra expenditure of ₹6,259.25 crore during 2017-24

keyFindings.text: Production targets were consistently missed: SAIL achieved only 126.15 million tonne against the 130.96 MT MoU target — a shortfall of 4.81 MT (3.7%) — at a time when the National Steel Policy 2017 envisaged India's crude steel capacity reaching 300 MT by 2030-31 and SAIL was expected to secure 20 per cent of domestic demand. Bhilai, the largest plant, operated at just 81% of Annual Business Perspective targets. Power consumption exceeded norms at most plants, adding ₹310.48 crore in preventable costs. Capital repair, maintenance, and blast furnace reline scheduling were not consistently adhered to.

source.quote: was 126.15 million tonne. Budgeted and actual production of hot metal in SAIL during 2017-2024 is given in the chart 3.

recommendations: Mandate a minimum 10% pellet ratio in all blast furnace charge mixes immediately; set up pellet plants or long-term pellet procurement agreements to ensure consistent availability.
Set plant-level CDI coal utilisation targets linked to blast furnace manager performance appraisals; penalise plants that consistently miss CDI targets.
Benchmark each SAIL blast furnace against top global steel plants on coke rate, CDI rate, and specific power consumption; publish plant-wise performance scorecards annually.
Implement predictive maintenance for blast furnace lining; conduct scheduled relines at prescribed intervals to avoid forced shutdowns that worsen productivity and coke rates.
Link SAIL Chairperson MoU targets to blast furnace-level operational KPIs (not just production volumes) to hold plant-level management accountable for coke/CDI optimisation.
ministry: Ministry of Steel, Union Government

title: Performance Audit on Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana and Pradhan Mantri Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana (SAUBHAGYA)
overview:
DDUGJY (launched December 2014) and SAUBHAGYA (launched October 2017) were the two flagship schemes for rural electrification in India. DDUGJY focused on feeder separation, system strengthening, and completing rural electrification, while SAUBHAGYA targeted last-mile household electricity connections. Combined, they represented the Government of India's promise to light every village and household.

DDUGJY was approved with a total outlay of ₹75,893 crore including ₹63,027 crore in budgetary support and closed with a cost of ₹64,495 crore. SAUBHAGYA had a total outlay of ₹16,320 crore including ₹12,320 crore budgetary support and closed at ₹9,246 crore. The Government announced 100 per cent village electrification in 987 days (by April 2018), an achievement acknowledged globally by the International Energy Agency.

However, audit found significant gaps beneath the headline achievement: the household electrification target was quietly reduced from 300 lakh to 248.48 lakh households (a reduction of 51.52 lakh), and 100 per cent achievement was then declared against this lower baseline. System strengthening funds — critical for reliable power, not just connection — were severely underfunded: against ₹44,821.22 crore demanded by 19 States and 2 UTs, only ₹12,412.55 crore was sanctioned. AT&C loss reduction targets were missed in 12 of 24 States, resulting in ₹3,631.62 crore less grant being released to DISCOMs.

stats.label: Household electrification target — quietly reduced to show 100% achievement
stats.value: 248.48 lakh vs 300 lakh original (51.52 lakh removed)
stats.note: The SAUBHAGYA dashboard showed 100 per cent achievement of the electrification target. Audit found that the estimated households for electrification on the dashboard was reduced to 248.48 lakh from the 300 lakh households in the Scheme guidelines — effectively redefining 100% achievement by removing 51.52 lakh unelectrified households from the denominator. "Achievement of 100 per cent against the target was declared by March 2019 accordingly."

source.quote: reduced to 248.48 lakh from 300 lakh households contained in the Scheme guidelines.

stats.label: System strengthening costs — States' demands slashed by 72%
stats.note: REC (Rural Electrification Corporation) sanctioned only ₹12,412.55 crore of the ₹44,821.22 crore demanded by 19 States and 2 UTs for system strengthening under DDUGJY — a 72 per cent cut. The cost of feeder separation demanded at ₹11,285.78 crore by seven States was cut to ₹3,967.20 crore (65%). This underfunding meant rural areas received connections but without the distribution infrastructure for reliable, adequate power — creating "electrification on paper" in many areas.

source.quote: Against cost of ₹44,821.22 crore demanded by 19 States43 and two UTs44, a sanction of ₹12,412.55 crore was accorded.

stats.label: AT&C loss target missed — reduced grant to DISCOMs
stats.value: ₹3,631.62 Cr less grant released; 12 states failed target
stats.note: One of the performance milestones under DDUGJY was reduction of Aggregate Technical and Commercial (AT&C) losses. Audit found that target of AT&C losses in 12 States and one UT out of 24 States and two UTs was not achieved, with AT&C losses ranging between 11.08 and 59.28 per cent against the norms of 10–26 per cent as on March 31, 2022. As a consequence, ₹3,631.62 crore less grant was released to DISCOMs by Ministry of Power.

source.quote: target of AT&C losses45 in 12 States and one UT out of 24 States and two UTs was not achieved and ranged between 11.08 and 59.28 per cent against the norms

keyFindings.text: The headline "100% electrification" figure was misleading: the target was silently reduced from 300 lakh households to 248.48 lakh — removing 51.52 lakh households from the counting — and 100% was declared against this reduced baseline. System strengthening funds were cut by 72%, meaning households received connections but not reliable power. Feeder separation — critical for agricultural-power separation and 24×7 supply — achieved only 86.85% of sanctioned quantities. The rural electrification achievement was structural and real, but the headline statistics obscured major quality gaps.

source.quote: reduced to 248.48 lakh from 300 lakh households contained in the Scheme guidelines.

keyFindings.text: DDUGJY and SAUBHAGYA together represented ₹75,893 crore + ₹16,320 crore in public investment. Yet AT&C losses — a fundamental measure of power system efficiency — were not achieved in 12 States, with worst performers at 59.28% loss rate (against a norm of 10–26%). DISCOMs in these states received ₹3,631.62 crore less grant, constraining their ability to invest in infrastructure improvements. 15.33 per cent of villages surveyed in field audit lacked adequate sub-transmission and distribution infrastructure despite scheme completion.

source.quote: target of AT&C losses45 in 12 States and one UT out of 24 States and two UTs was not achieved and ranged between 11.08 and 59.28 per cent against the norms

recommendations: Restore the original SAUBHAGYA target of 300 lakh households; conduct a census to identify the 51.52 lakh households dropped from the target and electrify them on a priority basis.

Release additional system strengthening funds to close the gap between what States demanded (₹44,821.22 crore) and what was sanctioned (₹12,412.55 crore) — prioritising feeder separation in States with AT&C losses above 30%.
Set State-level AT&C loss reduction as a mandatory pre-condition for the next tranche of power sector grants; publish monthly DISCOM AT&C performance dashboards publicly.
Commission an independent household survey to verify whether connections made under SAUBHAGYA are receiving power of 8+ hours daily, and publish results at district level.
ministry: Ministry of Power, Union Government

title: Performance Audit on Skill Development under Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana
overview:
Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY) is the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship's flagship scheme, launched in July 2015. Three phases (PMKVY 1.0, 2.0, 3.0) were audited — a combined outlay of ~₹14,449 crore targeting skill training and certification for 1.32 crore candidates. Against this, ₹10,194 crore was released and 1.10 crore candidates certified. CAG tabled the report in Parliament in December 2025.

The audit's most alarming finding concerns data integrity. On the Skill India Portal (SIP), bank account details were missing, blank, null, or filled with invalid entries — such as "11111111111", "123456", single-digit numbers, names, or symbols — for 90.66 lakh out of 95.90 lakh PMKVY 2.0/3.0 certified beneficiaries. That is 94.53 per cent of all records. Among the remaining entries, 12,122 bank account numbers were reused across 52,381 different candidates; one account number was shared by 2,106 individuals. The Ministry stated in May 2023 that it had made bank details non-mandatory due to "implementation challenges" — a decision that made it impossible to verify whether ₹500 DBT incentives reached genuine trainees. As of October 2024, 34 lakh certified candidates had still not received their incentive payout.

Field inspections and beneficiary surveys uncovered systematic fraud by training partners. Training centres were found closed on dates when government records showed training in progress. The same photograph was submitted as attendance evidence in multiple states simultaneously (Bihar, UP, Maharashtra, Rajasthan). Defunct companies continued to certify candidates on the portal: Radiate Designs (struck off by Registrar of Companies in 2015) certified 15,218 people; Neelima Moving Pictures (shut for 5–6 years) claimed 33,000 trainees; Jaipur Cultural Society claimed training on 31st February — a date that does not exist. An online beneficiary survey found that responses to 36.51 per cent of emails failed to deliver, and a significant fraction of received responses originated from training centre staff email IDs rather than actual candidates.

On employment outcomes — the scheme's core purpose — CAG found that of 56 lakh candidates certified under Short-Term Training (STT) and Special Projects, only 23 lakh (41 per cent) were placed. The Ministry had publicly claimed 68 per cent placement, based entirely on unverified self-reporting by training partners who had a financial incentive to inflate figures. In a special MoU for defence personnel (PMKVY 2.0), only 7.27 per cent of 9,987 freshly trained candidates received placement. Thousands of underage candidates were enrolled and certified in violation of scheme rules: over 52,000 as Group Farming Practitioners and over 40,000 as Self-Employed Tailors, without meeting minimum age requirements.

stats.note: 90.66 lakh of 95.90 lakh PMKVY 2.0/3.0 certified beneficiaries had no valid bank account on file. Entries included "11111111111", "123456", single-digit numbers, text, names, and symbols. 12,122 account numbers reused across 52,381 candidates; one number shared by 2,106 people. Ministry made bank details non-mandatory in May 2023.

source.quote: bank account details field was either blank, marked 'Null'/ 'N/A', or filled with zeros in 94.53 per cent of 95.90 lakh beneficiary records under PMKVY 2.0 and 3.0

stats.note: Of 56 lakh candidates certified under Short-Term Training and Special Projects, only 23 lakh were placed (CAG-verified). Ministry claimed 68% in PIB press releases — based on training-partner self-reporting. In UP, state agencies had no records to support claimed placements; in Kerala, partners submitted forged placement documents.

source.quote: only 23 lakh candidates were placed, representing 41 per cent placement

stats.label: DBT incentive paid to certified candidates (as of Oct 2024)
stats.note: As of October 2024, 63.75% of 95.91 lakh certified candidates had received the ₹500 DBT incentive — leaving 34 lakh (3.4 million) still unpaid despite the relevant phases having formally concluded. In 2023, only 18.44% of certified candidates had received successful payouts.

source.quote: DBT payments were processed for only 25.58 per cent of certified candidates, with successful payouts in just 18.44 per cent of cases

stats.label: Defence MoU: placement of freshly trained candidates
stats.note: Under a special MoU for skill training and placement of defence personnel (PMKVY 2.0 Special Project), 9,987 candidates completed fresh skill training. Only 726 (7.27%) received employment placement — rendering the MoU's core objective of transitioning defence veterans into civilian employment almost entirely unachieved.

source.quote: 7.27 per cent) got placement. As such, the MoU was not able to achieve the desired goal of acquiring additional skill for defence personnel or facilitating their employment.

stats.label: Total expenditure released — 3 phases (2015–22)
stats.note: ₹10,194 crore released against ₹14,448.90 crore outlay; ₹9,261 crore actually utilised. ₹933 crore unspent despite unmet certification targets. CAG found financial controls weak — funds released in violation of receipt and payment rules, delays in state component transfers, and inconsistencies in utilisation reporting.

source.quote: the Government of India allocated ₹ 13,288 crore (BE) for the scheme, of which ₹ 10,194 crore was released, and 1.10 crore candidates were certified.

keyFindings.text: Bank account data fraud: 94.53% of 95.90 lakh PMKVY 2.0/3.0 beneficiary records had missing, blank, null or invalid bank details on the Skill India Portal — including entries like "11111111111", "123456", and single-digit numbers. 12,122 account numbers were reused across 52,381 candidates. One account number was shared by 2,106 different people. This made it impossible to verify whether public funds reached genuine trainees or were siphoned through ghost accounts.

source.quote: bank account details field was either blank, marked 'Null'/ 'N/A', or filled with zeros in 94.53 per cent of 95.90 lakh beneficiary records under PMKVY 2.0 and 3.0

keyFindings.text: Ghost training centres and defunct companies: Field inspections found training centres closed on dates SIP showed training in progress. The same photograph was used as training evidence in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Rajasthan simultaneously. Radiate Designs (struck off by Registrar of Companies in 2015) certified 15,218 people; Neelima Moving Pictures (shut for 5–6 years) claimed 33,000 trainees. Jaipur Cultural Society claimed training on 31st February — a non-existent date.

source.quote: identical photographs were submitted as evidence for multiple beneficiaries across different states

keyFindings.text: Placement failure and fabricated outcomes: Only 41% of STT-certified candidates were placed (CAG-verified), against the Ministry's claimed 68% — a figure based entirely on training-partner self-reporting. In Uttar Pradesh, state agencies had no records to support placements claimed on the SIP. In Kerala, incorrect placement documents were submitted by partners to claim disbursements. Of 56 lakh certified candidates, 33 lakh had no independently verifiable employment record.

source.quote: only 23 lakh candidates were placed, representing 41 per cent placement

keyFindings.text: Underage certifications and eligibility fraud: Over 52,000 candidates were certified as Group Farming Practitioners without meeting minimum age requirements. Over 40,000 underage candidates were certified as Self-Employed Tailors. Similar violations were found across multiple job roles and states, indicating systematic non-enforcement of eligibility criteria by Training Partners and Assessment Agencies.

source.quote: thousands of underage candidates were enrolled and certified. More than 52,000 candidates were certified as Group Farming Practitioners

keyFindings.text: DBT payment failure: As of October 2024, 34 lakh certified candidates had not received the ₹500 incentive payout despite the relevant PMKVY phases having formally concluded. In 2023, DBT was successful for only 18.44% of certified candidates. The Ministry had made bank account details non-mandatory in May 2023, citing "implementation challenges" — a decision that severed the primary mechanism for verifying beneficiary identity and tracking fund disbursal.

source.quote: DBT payments were processed for only 25.58 per cent of certified candidates, with successful payouts in just 18.44 per cent of cases

keyFindings.text: No alignment with labour market demand: Sectoral and state-wise training targets under all three PMKVY phases were not based on skill-gap studies. No long-term national skill development plan was in place. Despite ₹10,194 crore spent across three phases and a decade of operation, only 4.4% of Indians aged 15–29 had received formal vocational or technical training (Economic Survey 2023-24) — statistically unchanged from pre-PMKVY baselines.

source.quote: the Government of India allocated ₹ 13,288 crore (BE) for the scheme, of which ₹ 10,194 crore was released, and 1.10 crore candidates were certified.

recommendations: Reinstate mandatory bank account validation on the Skill India Portal with real-time NPCI/bank API verification; reject any beneficiary record with a placeholder or reused account number before certification is issued.

Conduct an independent forensic audit of all Training Partners that submitted duplicate photographs, claimed training on impossible dates, or are struck-off entities — with full recovery of disbursements from fraudulent partners.
Make CAG-verified placement at 6 months post-training the primary PMKVY disbursement trigger; eliminate upfront payments to Training Partners based on self-reported enrollment and assessment figures.
Align PMKVY sectoral quotas annually with district-level skill-gap studies; no training batch should be sanctioned in any sector or state without documented employer demand.

Publish state-wise, sector-wise, and Training-Partner-wise placement rates quarterly as open data; make the Skill India Portal's beneficiary database auditable by CAG and civil society on a continuous basis.
Debar all companies that are struck off by the Registrar of Companies from the NSDC Training Partner registry; introduce automated RoC-status checks before partner accreditation renewal.
ministry: Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, Union Government

title: Performance Audit on Solar Parks and Ultra Mega Solar Power Projects
overview:
The Solar Parks and Ultra Mega Solar Power Projects scheme was launched by MNRE in two phases: Phase I (2014, target: 20,000 MW by 2018-19) and Phase II (2017, additional 20,000 MW by 2019-20 — later extended to March 2026). The scheme was central to India's National Solar Mission and Paris Agreement commitments (40% clean energy by 2030, now 50%). By centralising land, infrastructure and approvals, it aimed to reduce per-MW costs and delays that plagued individual solar projects.

As of March 2024, 58 Solar Parks across 13 States had been allocated with a combined capacity of 40,000 MW, but only 11,491 MW (28.60%) had been installed — a shortfall of 71.4 per cent against the target. The scheme fell behind in both phases due to the same recurring failures: in-principle approvals without feasibility studies, DPRs revised multiple times without addressing underlying issues, land acquisition delays that were not proactively resolved, and financial closures tied to internal resource generation.

Case studies surfaced by audit included a 1,000 MW Solar Park in Himachal Pradesh that was cancelled in 2019 after ₹0 had been built — MNRE re-sanctioned the same park in 2020 despite HIMURJA (the State Nodal Agency) having flagged its techno-economic non-viability in its own feasibility assessment. State Level Committees (SLCs) — the primary monitoring mechanism — were not formed in time across states, creating governance vacuums. The Solar Potential Map guiding site selection was last updated in 2014, while SPV module efficiency had since improved from 15% to 19–22%.

stats.label: Solar Parks installed capacity vs 40,000 MW target (March 2024)
stats.note: As of March 2024, of the targeted 40,000 MW across 58 Solar Parks allocated in 13 States, only 11,491 MW (28.60 per cent) had been installed. The Scheme extended Phase I's 2018-19 deadline and Phase II's 2019-20 deadline multiple times, with Phase II now extended to March 2026. The objectives of the scheme could not be achieved, with underutilisation of budget reflecting the slow pace of implementation.

source.quote: only 28.60 per cent (11,491 MW) of the targeted

stats.label: Feasibility studies conducted before in-principle approval
stats.value: Not conducted — approvals given without assessment
stats.note: MNRE provided in-principle approvals for Solar Parks without conducting feasibility studies or techno-economic viability assessments. In the audited HP case, HIMURJA's own assessment noted techno-economic non-viability in 2015 — yet MNRE cancelled and then re-sanctioned the same park in 2020 without addressing the documented concerns. DPRs were revised repeatedly without resolving the underlying issues of land availability, layout and technology.

source.quote: no pre-feasibility study or techno-economic viability assessment of the 400 MW

stats.label: Solar Potential Map used for site selection — last updated
stats.note: The Solar Potential Map of India — the primary tool for identifying suitable sites for Solar Parks — was last prepared in 2014 and was not updated even as the Wasteland Atlas was updated in 2019. During this period, average efficiency of SPV modules improved from 15% to 19–22%, making many previously marginal sites viable and some previously assumed viable sites potentially sub-optimal. Site selection decisions affecting tens of thousands of MW were being made using decade-old potential maps.

source.quote: updated Wasteland Atlas of India in 2019. Further, the average efficiency of SPV modules had

keyFindings.text: The Solar Parks scheme achieved only 28.60% of its 40,000 MW target as of March 2024 — representing a failure to install 28,509 MW of renewable capacity that India needed for its Paris Agreement commitments. MNRE issued in-principle approvals without feasibility studies, then sanctioned projects that had already been cancelled for non-viability. DPRs were revised multiple times while fundamental issues (land, layout, financing) remained unresolved. MNRE, despite having overall responsibility, did not proactively resolve the impediments in either Phase I or Phase II.

source.quote: only 28.60 per cent (11,491 MW) of the targeted

keyFindings.text: Land acquisition was consistently underestimated and under-managed: in Himachal Pradesh, the Ministry was unaware that a proposed Solar Park site fell within a wildlife sanctuary boundary. State Level Committees were not formed in time across states, eliminating the monitoring layer between MNRE and State Nodal Agencies. The Solar Potential Map was not updated despite the Wasteland Atlas 2019 update — meaning site-selection for tens of thousands of MW was based on decade-old data. The only Solar Park that achieved full capacity (700 MW, Gujarat) did so through a model that required centralised state ownership and coordination.

source.quote: no pre-feasibility study or techno-economic viability assessment of the 400 MW

recommendations: Mandate feasibility studies and techno-economic viability assessment before any in-principle approval; cancel or redesign parks where the original feasibility study flagged non-viability and concerns remain unresolved.

Immediately update the Solar Potential Map using the 2019 Wasteland Atlas, current SPV efficiency norms, and updated land availability data; use this map as the mandatory basis for all new park approvals.
Constitute State Level Committees for all Solar Parks immediately; require SLC to meet monthly and report milestones directly to MNRE Secretary.
Delink financial closure from internal resource generation — enable external financing through green bonds, project finance, and InvIT structures to remove the #1 delay factor.

Adopt the Gujarat model of state-owned park developer (GPCL) in all states experiencing persistent land and coordination delays; SECI to play the role of park developer of last resort in States unable to establish SPVs.
ministry: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Union Government

title: Performance Audit on E-way Bill System under GST
ministry: Commercial Taxes Department, Government of Kerala
overview: CAG found that the E-Way Bill system in Kerala had critical design deficiencies enabling tax evasion at scale. Non-filers and cancelled taxpayers could freely generate EWBs — the primary anti-evasion control of GST. NIC Analytical Reports were never used by departmental officers. Inspection reports were not recorded online, blocking senior monitoring. The audit covered 3.29 crore outward supply EWBs across 94 Taxpayer Services Circles for 2018-19 to 2021-22.

keyFindings.text: EWB portal allowed non-filers and cancelled taxpayers to generate E-Way Bills without any system block — directly enabling GST revenue leakage.

source.quote: system allowed generation of EWBs by non-filers of returns and by taxpayers whose registrations were cancelled which resulted in leakage of revenue due to shortcomings in system design.

keyFindings.text: Taxpayers issued EWBs to inactive (cancelled) consignees — enabling tax evasion as recipients could not legitimately claim input tax credit.

source.quote: taxpayers who issued EWBs to inactive consignee taxpayers were identified as evading tax payments.

recommendations: Correct system deficiencies to prevent EWB generation by non-filers, nil-filers, and cancelled taxpayers.
Introduce robust EWB data analytics to identify and red-flag high-risk transactions and taxpayers.
Mandate online recording of all goods-in-transit inspection reports for senior-level monitoring.

stats.label: EWB system design flaw — non-filers allowed to generate bills
stats.note: The EWB portal allowed non-filers of GST returns and taxpayers with cancelled registrations to freely generate E-Way Bills — the electronic document that must accompany all goods worth ₹50,000+. This is the primary anti-evasion control of GST, and it was bypassed at the system design level. The system also permitted single EWBs clubbing multiple invoices and multiple EWBs for the same invoice — both evasion techniques.

source.quote: system allowed generation of EWBs by non-filers of returns and by taxpayers whose registrations were cancelled which resulted in leakage of revenue due to shortcomings in system design.

stats.label: EWBs issued to inactive consignees — tax evaded
stats.value: Taxpayers routed supply to cancelled GSTIN recipients
stats.note: Taxpayers issued EWBs to consignees whose GST registrations had been cancelled — meaning the recipient could not legitimately account for the input tax credit. This was a deliberate evasion technique. Audit also found ITC mismatches where taxpayers who generated EWBs utilized excess credit to offset their tax liabilities without genuine supply backing.

source.quote: taxpayers who issued EWBs to inactive consignee taxpayers were identified as evading tax payments.

stats.label: Scale of EWB transactions audited — 2018-22
stats.value: 3.29 crore EWBs across 94 Taxpayer Services Circles
stats.note: The audit covered 3.29 crore outward supply EWBs across Kerala's 94 Taxpayer Services Circles for the period 2018-19 to 2021-22. Audit selected 56 taxpayers for substantive audit — and the deviations found in this sample, if extrapolated across the full population, would represent significant revenue at risk. NIC's Analytical Reports (which track high-risk patterns) were not used by any departmental officer to identify evasion cases during this period.

source.quote: Out of 94 Taxpayer Services Circles and 3.29 crore EWBs for outward supply for 2018-2022.

title: Performance Audit on Duty Drawback Scheme
ministry: Department of Revenue (Indirect Taxes – Customs), Union Government
overview: Duty Drawback refunds customs/excise duties on imported inputs used in exports — a key incentive. CAG found the scheme riddled with delays and weak controls: ₹701.69 crore in total revenue implications, 70–78% of claims delayed beyond 6 months, irregular Brand Rate sanctions of ₹410.77 crore duty effect, and ICES system failures preventing accurate tracking of export proceeds. The report covers All Industry Rates, Brand/Special Brand Rates, Re-exports, and Deemed Exports across 22–23 Commissionerates.

keyFindings.text: Total revenue implication of the audit was ₹701.69 crore across all drawback categories — AIR (₹229.41 Cr), Brand Rate (₹410.77 Cr), and others.

source.quote: performance audit has revenue implication of ₹701.69 crore. Responses received from CBIC and DGFT have been considered and appropriately included in this report.

keyFindings.text: 70.69% of AIR claims in 23 Commissionerates and 78.70% pan-India were delayed beyond 6 months — defeating the trade facilitation objective of the scheme.

source.quote: The significant delays in processing claims (70.69 per cent in the selected 23 Commissionerates and 78.70 per cent for pan-India cases) with 543 cases and 51,252 cases respectively delayed for more than six months indicates lack of supervision and internal control.

recommendations: CBIC should establish a Standard Operating Procedure for timely processing of drawback claims within stipulated timeframes.
ICES should be upgraded to eliminate technical glitches causing incorrect classification of drawback payments.
A robust monitoring mechanism should be established to verify export proceeds realization before drawback disbursement.

stats.label: Total revenue implication of audit — Duty Drawback 2025
stats.value: ₹701.69 Cr in duty effects across all chapters
stats.note: The CAG Performance Audit of the Duty Drawback Scheme identified a total revenue implication of ₹701.69 crore across all seven chapters of the report, covering All Industry Rates (₹229.41 crore), Brand/Special Brand Rates (₹410.77 crore), Re-export (₹12.42 crore), Deemed Exports (₹49.09 crore), and monitoring failures. This is money either irregularly paid, not recovered, or at risk of never being recovered — representing direct loss to the exchequer from a scheme designed to incentivize exports.

source.quote: performance audit has revenue implication of ₹701.69 crore. Responses received from CBIC and DGFT have been considered and appropriately included in this report.

stats.label: Claims processing delays — over 6 months
stats.note: Duty Drawback claims are supposed to be processed in time to provide liquidity to exporters. CAG found 70.69% of claims in the 23 selected Commissionerates were delayed beyond 6 months; for all of India the figure was 78.70%. This covers 543 cases and 51,252 pan-India cases respectively still pending beyond 6 months. These delays defeat the purpose of the scheme — exporters who cannot recover their duty paid in a reasonable time face cash-flow problems that undermine India's export competitiveness.

source.quote: The significant delays in processing claims (70.69 per cent in the selected 23 Commissionerates and 78.70 per cent for pan-India cases) with 543 cases and 51,252 cases respectively delayed for more than six months indicates lack of supervision and internal control.

stats.label: Brand Rate & Special Brand Rate — irregular sanctions
stats.value: ₹410.77 Cr duty effect; 16 observations in 22 Commissionerates
stats.note: Brand/Special Brand Rates are customized duty drawback rates granted to exporters whose product-specific duty burden differs from the All Industry Rate. CAG examined 1,167 Brand Rate/Special Brand Rate cases and found 16 audit observations with ₹410.77 crore in duty effect — the largest single category of findings. Issues included incorrect attribution of drawback identifiers distorting data, manual processing errors persisting in ICES, and sanctioning of drawback without adequate verification of shipping bill details.

source.quote: duty effect of ₹410.77 crore and five recommendations are included in this chapter.

title: Performance Audit on Inventory Management in Steel Authority of India Limited
ministry: Ministry of Steel, Union Government
overview: SAIL maintained an average inventory of ₹21,698 crore (67% of current assets) across five integrated steel plants with no benchmark for carrying costs. CAG found: Bokaro's buffer stock failures caused blast furnace shutdowns losing ₹477.26 crore in potential revenue; excess imported coal consumption added ₹2,539.68 crore in avoidable expenditure; Rourkela Steel Plant lost ₹542.91 crore potential revenue; non-moving inventory of ₹1,022 crore sat in Central Marketing Organisation. Against a production target of 119.66 MT saleable steel, SAIL achieved only 106.15 MT (89%).

keyFindings.text: SAIL had average inventory of ₹21,698 crore (67% of current assets) with no carrying-cost benchmarks — while Bokaro blast furnace shutdowns cost ₹477.26 crore in potential revenue.

source.quote: SAIL, on an average, had an inventory of ₹ 21,698 crore during 2016-17 to 2022-23 which constitutes about 67 per cent of its current assets.

keyFindings.text: Excess consumption of imported coal beyond prescribed norms during 2016-2023 resulted in potential additional expenditure of ₹2,539.68 crore.

source.quote: Higher consumption of imported coal in the Steel Plants during 2016-2023 resulted in potential additional expenditure to the extent of ₹ 2,539.68 crore.

recommendations: SAIL should fix norms for holding stock and devise a benchmark for inventory carrying cost per tonne for better cost control.
Steel Plants should adhere to Corporate Material Management Group Guidelines to reduce non-moving/surplus inventory.
Company should monitor Fuel Supply Agreement quantities to prevent excess procurement from higher-cost suppliers.

stats.label: SAIL average inventory — 67% of current assets blocked
stats.note: SAIL maintained an average inventory of ₹21,698 crore over 2016-17 to 2022-23, constituting about 67% of its current assets — an extraordinarily high proportion for a steel company. Despite this massive inventory base, SAIL had no company-wide benchmark for inventory carrying cost per tonne. Individual plants failed to maintain even minimum buffer stocks (like 80,000 tonnes/day at Bokaro) while simultaneously accumulating excess non-moving materials worth ₹1,022 crore at its Central Marketing Organisation.

source.quote: SAIL, on an average, had an inventory of ₹ 21,698 crore during 2016-17 to 2022-23 which constitutes about 67 per cent of its current assets.

stats.label: Iron ore buffer failure — Bokaro blast furnace off-blast
stats.value: ₹477.26 Cr potential revenue lost from production inability
stats.note: Bokaro Steel Plant was required to maintain a buffer of 80,000 tonnes/day of iron ore for continuous blast furnace operation. It achieved this in only 22 of the audit months. CAG analysed delay hours of the blast furnace and found 39% of delays were due to iron ore shortages. The blast furnace was kept "off-blast" (shutdown) during this period, resulting in inability to produce 2.98 lakh tonnes of Hot Metal and consequent inability to earn potential revenue of ₹477.26 crore.

source.quote: inability to produce 2.98 lakh tonnes of Hot Metal and subsequent inability to earn potential revenue of ₹477.26 crore.

stats.label: Excess imported coal consumption — avoidable cost
stats.note: Steel production requires blending indigenous and imported coal. SAIL norms, fixed annually by management, set the proportion. CAG found that all five steel plants consumed imported coal in excess of their respective norms during 2016-17 to 2022-23. Imported coal is significantly more expensive than indigenous coal. The excess consumption resulted in potential additional expenditure of ₹2,539.68 crore over the audit period — avoidable cost that directly impacted SAIL's already declining profitability.

source.quote: Higher consumption of imported coal in the Steel Plants during 2016-2023 resulted in potential additional expenditure to the extent of ₹ 2,539.68 crore.

title: Performance Audit of Saryu Nahar Pariyojana
ministry: Irrigation and Water Resources Department, Government of Uttar Pradesh
overview: Saryu Nahar Pariyojana (SNP) was conceived in 1978 to irrigate 14.04 lakh hectares across nine eastern UP districts. It was commissioned in December 2021 — after 43 years — at ₹10,003.11 crore vs the 1982 estimate of ₹299.20 crore (33× overrun). CAG found command area development complete in only 20% of CCA, meaning most farmers still cannot receive water. Weak contract management, tenders invited without technical sanctions, overestimation in work estimates, and prolonged land acquisition drove both cost and time overruns.

keyFindings.text: SNP cost escalated from ₹299.20 crore (1982) to ₹10,003.11 crore (March 2022) — a 33× overrun — due to 43 years of delays and compounding land/contract cost escalations.
