source.quote: SNP was commissioned in December 2021 at an expenditure of ₹ 10,003.11 crore (March 2022).

keyFindings.text: Despite spending ₹10,003 crore, command area works were complete in only 20% of the CCA — most farmers still cannot receive canal water.

source.quote: Command area development works were completed only in 20 per cent CCA hindering the flow of water from canals to field.

recommendations: State Government should investigate reasons for incorrect assessment of project requirements causing significant scope variations and consequential delays.
Comprehensive field surveys should determine actual area covered under SNP for correct assessment of required development work.
Responsibility must be fixed for lapses in project execution, particularly the 43-year time overrun and contract irregularities.

stats.label: Cost overrun — 33× original estimate over 43 years
stats.value: ₹10,003.11 Cr actual vs ₹299.20 Cr estimated in 1982
stats.note: SNP was formulated in 1982 at an estimated cost of ₹299.20 crore, having started in 1978 as the Left Bank Ghaghara canal project. By March 2022, the expenditure had reached ₹10,003.11 crore — a 33-fold increase over 40+ years. Cost escalations were driven by time delays (compounding price inflation), incorrect rate analysis in estimates, overestimation in work estimates, hike in land compensation amounts, and changes in project scope due to plans finalized without proper surveys.

source.quote: SNP was commissioned in December 2021 at an expenditure of ₹ 10,003.11 crore (March 2022).

stats.label: Command area development — only 20% of CCA completed
stats.value: 80% of 11.29 lakh hectares still without functioning canals
stats.note: Even after spending ₹10,003 crore and commissioning the project in December 2021, command area development works — the local canal networks and outlets that actually carry water from main canals to farmers' fields — were completed in only 20% of the Culturable Command Area (CCA). Rapti Main Canal and its distribution system was not utilized due to want of outlets and sumps. This means the vast majority of the 11.29 lakh hectares and nine eastern districts that SNP was built to irrigate still cannot receive water, despite the project being declared "commissioned".

source.quote: Command area development works were completed only in 20 per cent CCA hindering the flow of water from canals to field.

stats.label: Time overrun — 40+ years from start to commissioning
stats.note: The project was commissioned in December 2021 after almost 40 years from the date of start of works (original project: 1978, formal SNP formulation: 1982). During this period, land acquisition dragged for decades — with the Department taking exceptionally long to purchase land from farmers, causing cost escalations and delays across all contracts. Contract management was weak: tenders were invited without technical sanctions, insufficient time was given to bidders, and quality assurance tests for earthworks and masonry were not carried out per norms.

source.quote: The project was commissioned in December 2021 after almost 40 years from the date of start of works.

title: Performance Audit on Cleanliness and Sanitation in Long Distance Trains in Indian Railways
ministry: Ministry of Railways, Union Government
overview: Indian Railways runs 12,541 passenger trains carrying 17.52 million passengers daily across 7,364+ stations. CAG found systemic cleanliness failures: 33% of inspected ACWPs non-operational; Rail Madad complaints surged 229% between 2019-20 and 2022-23; quick watering facilities absent at 26% of designated stations; budget over-runs of 100–141% in some zones; online inspection recording absent; and shortfalls in on-board housekeeping, bio-toilet maintenance and linen management. Penalties of ₹9.62 crore were recovered from contractors for deficiencies — acknowledging widespread failure.

keyFindings.text: 8 of 24 ACWPs inspected (33%) were non-operational due to breakdown or repairs, undermining the mechanised cleaning regime.

source.quote: eight (33 per cent) ACWPs were not in operation due to breakdown or repair works.

keyFindings.text: Rail Madad complaints on coach cleanliness rose 229% from 69,950 in 2019-20 to 2,42,431 in 2022-23 — evidence of worsening passenger experience despite cleaning expenditure.

source.quote: related to coach cleanliness increased by 229 per cent during 2022-23 (2,42,431) as compared to the year 2019-20 (69,950).

recommendations: Railways should ensure proper maintenance of ACWPs to prevent breakdown-related shutdowns and coach cleaning failures.
Online recording of inspection reports for goods-in-transit and cleaning activities should be mandated for senior monitoring.
Quick Watering Arrangements should be expedited at all 110 designated stations to improve onboard water availability.

stats.label: Scale: 12,541 trains, 17.52 million passengers daily
stats.note: The audit covers the entire long-distance train cleanliness regime of Indian Railways — 12,541 passenger trains passing through 7,364+ stations carrying over 17.52 million passengers per day. Despite heavy public investment in mechanized cleaning contracts, on-board housekeeping services (OBHS), and bio-toilet programs, the lived experience of passengers deteriorated sharply: Rail Madad complaints related to coach cleanliness increased 229% from 69,950 in 2019-20 to 2,42,431 in 2022-23.

source.quote: Indian Railways (IR) runs 12,541 passenger trains carrying more than 17.52 million passengers per day and passing through more than 7,364 Railway Stations over the network.

stats.label: Automatic Coach Washing Plants — 33% non-operational
stats.note: During 2018-2023, Railways commissioned 56 Automatic Coach Washing Plants (ACWPs) across zones. Each ACWP saves 7,160 litres of water per wash vs manual cleaning of a 24-coach train. CAG conducted joint inspections of 24 ACWPs with Railway Officials and found 8 (33%) were not operational due to breakdown or repair works. Railways also incurred ₹2.58 crore in Mechanised Coach Cleaning Contracts for coaches that ACWPs could not process — paying twice for a problem created by poor maintenance.

source.quote: eight (33 per cent) ACWPs were not in operation due to breakdown or repair works.

stats.label: Rail Madad complaints — cleanliness up 229%
stats.note: Rail Madad passenger complaints related to coach cleanliness increased by 229 per cent during 2022-23 (2,42,431) as compared to 2019-20 (69,950). Quick Watering Arrangement (QWA) facilities — for rapid water replenishment at stations — were in operation at only 81 of 110 designated stations (74%) as of March 2023, with 28 stations experiencing 2-4 year delays in QWA setup. Online recording of cleaning inspection reports was absent, preventing monitoring by senior officials.

source.quote: related to coach cleanliness increased by 229 per cent during 2022-23 (2,42,431) as compared to the year 2019-20 (69,950).

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Samagra Shiksha in West Bengal
ministry: School Education Department, Government of West Bengal
overview: Samagra Shiksha is India's unified school education scheme (pre-primary to senior secondary). West Bengal utilized only 46–65% of funds each year during 2019-24, surrendering ₹395 crore in civil works and failing to receive ₹2,428 crore due to execution gaps. Critically, 33,835 special educator posts (95%) remained vacant, denying education to children with special needs. Board exam failure rates of 10–17% (Class X) and 12–17% (Class XII), vocational education in only 7.92% of schools, and no perspective planning reflect systemic educational underperformance.

keyFindings.text: ₹395 crore surrendered for unexecuted civil works; ₹2,428 crore in scheme funds not received due to execution inefficiencies — restricting the scheme's entire scope.

source.quote: Non-execution of sanctioned civil works resulted in surrender of ₹395 crore for unexecuted works. Inefficiencies in execution resulted in short receipt of scheme funds of ₹ 2,428 crore which restricted the Scheme's scope and hindered achieving its objectives.

keyFindings.text: Shortage of 33,835 special educators (95% of required strength) denied quality education to children with special needs across West Bengal.

source.quote: A shortage of 33,835 special educators (95 per cent) in the State had denied quality education for CwSN in schools.

recommendations: Paschim Banga Samagra Shiksha Mission should prepare long-term perspective plans with bottom-up approach as mandated in guidelines.
Department must ensure utilisation of allocated funds within stipulated timeframes to avoid curtailment of future Central releases.
Recruitment of special educators should be prioritised urgently to restore educational access for children with special needs.

stats.label: Fund utilization — 35-54% left unspent every year
stats.value: 46–65% utilized; ₹395 Cr surrendered, ₹2,428 Cr not received
stats.note: West Bengal's Samagra Shiksha Mission (PBSSM) utilized only 46 to 65 per cent of funds during 2019-24, meaning 35-54% of school education money went unspent each year. Non-execution of sanctioned civil works (school buildings, infrastructure) resulted in ₹395 crore being surrendered back. Beyond what was allocated, execution inefficiencies meant the state received ₹2,428 crore less than entitled — restricting the scheme's scope and ability to meet targets for students across West Bengal.

source.quote: Non-execution of sanctioned civil works resulted in surrender of ₹395 crore for unexecuted works. Inefficiencies in execution resulted in short receipt of scheme funds of ₹ 2,428 crore which restricted the Scheme's scope and hindered achieving its objectives.

stats.label: Samagra Shiksha fund utilization rate (2019-24)
stats.note: Every single year from 2019-20 to 2023-24, West Bengal failed to utilize more than 65% of Samagra Shiksha funds. Delays in fund release by both Central and State Governments compounded the problem, creating fiscal indiscipline that weakened scheme outcomes. The state has no perspective plan for Samagra Shiksha (despite this being mandated), meaning the under-spending is not a temporary glitch but a structural failure of planning.

source.quote: Utilisation of funds under the Samagra Shiksha Scheme ranged between 46 and 65 per cent during 2019-24, leading to unspent balances.

stats.label: Special educators shortage — 95% posts vacant
stats.note: West Bengal had a shortage of 33,835 special educators — 95 per cent of the required strength — denying quality education to children with special needs (CwSN) in schools across the state. Physical infrastructure for CwSN was also absent: 15% of schools lacked ramps and 72% lacked CwSN-friendly toilets. Transport allowances for CwSN (which enable them to reach school) were disbursed to only 30-56% of eligible students, and escort allowances to only 35-49%. The combined effect: disabled children, already the most marginalised, were systematically excluded from even the basic entitlements of the scheme.

source.quote: A shortage of 33,835 special educators (95 per cent) in the State had denied quality education for CwSN in schools.

title: Performance Audit on Exemptions and Deductions to Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
ministry: Ministry of Finance / Income Tax Department
overview: India's banks and NBFCs — financial institutions handling crores of depositors' money — receive statutory tax exemptions and deductions under the Income Tax Act 1961. CAG conducted a Performance Audit of tax assessments of Scheduled Commercial Banks and NBFCs for 2017-18 to 2020-21. The audit found 533 compliance issues with a probable tax effect of ₹74,766.39 crore. At the Ministry level, only 25 of 533 observations were replied to. At the Income Tax Department field level, 212 observations were replied to, with ITD accepting 88 observations worth ₹28,639.13 crore — but remedial action on even the accepted observations was incomplete.

stats.label: 533 audit observations on Banks/NBFCs — ₹74,766 Cr probable tax effect
stats.value: Compliance issues across assessments of FY 2017-18 to 2020-21
stats.note: CAG's Performance Audit identified 533 compliance issues in the assessments of Banks and NBFCs by the Income Tax Department, covering financial years 2017-18 to 2020-21. The probable tax implication of these 533 issues is ₹74,766.39 crore — the amount of tax revenue potentially foregone, undercollected, or erroneously exempted. This is not a theoretical estimate — each observation represents a specific assessment where CAG found that the bank or NBFC had claimed an exemption, deduction, or relief that the audit team believed was incorrect, excessive, or improperly supported. The scale — over ₹74,000 crore — reflects the systemic nature of tax assessment weaknesses across the financial sector.

source.quote: 533 compliance issues, with a probable tax implication of ₹ 74,766.39 crore.

stats.label: Ministry replied to only 25 of 533 observations (₹1,061.58 Cr)
stats.value: Ministry accepted 21 observations (₹799.38 Cr) — 532 await action
stats.note: Of the 533 audit observations raised, the Ministry of Finance furnished replies to only 25 observations involving tax effect of ₹1,061.58 crore — leaving 508 observations (₹73,704 crore) without any Ministry response. Of the 25 observations the Ministry did engage with, it accepted 21 (involving ₹799.38 crore) and partly accepted 2 (₹24.50 crore). The remaining 2 observations (₹237.70 crore) were not accepted. This response rate — 25 of 533 at the Ministry level — indicates that the Ministry of Finance did not engage seriously with the vast majority of audit findings despite the enormous tax revenue implications.

source.quote: Ministry has furnished replies in 25 audit observations involving tax effect of ₹ 1,061.58 crore. Of these 25 audit observations, the Ministry has accepted 21 audit observations involving a tax effect of ₹ 799.38 crore.

stats.label: ITD accepted 88 observations (₹28,639 Cr) — but action still incomplete
stats.value: 212 replied to of 533; 79 remedial actions completed, 64 initiated
stats.note: At the field formations level, Income Tax Department officers furnished replies in 212 audit observations (involving ₹47,557.33 crore). Of these, ITD accepted 88 observations worth ₹28,639.13 crore, completed remedial action in 79 observations (₹5,056.59 crore), and initiated action in 64 observations (₹15,324.15 crore). But ITD did not accept 41 audit observations involving ₹13,536.92 crore. The acceptance of an observation and actual recovery of the tax revenue are two different steps — CAG found that even for accepted observations, remedial action was often incomplete. For the 321 field-level observations that received no reply at all, no action was possible.

source.quote: furnished replies in 212 audit observations involving tax effect of ₹ 47,557.33 crore. Of these 212 audit observations, ITD has accepted 88 audit observations involving tax effect of ₹ 28,639.13 crore.

keyFindings.text: 533 audit observations on Bank/NBFC tax assessments with ₹74,766.39 crore probable tax effect — Ministry replied to only 25 of them, accepting 21 worth ₹799.38 crore.

source.quote: 533 compliance issues, with a probable tax implication of ₹ 74,766.39 crore. Ministry has furnished replies in 25 audit observations involving tax effect of ₹ 1,061.58 crore.

keyFindings.text: ITD accepted 88 observations (₹28,639.13 crore) at field level but remedial action remains incomplete; 321 field-level observations received no reply at all.

source.quote: ITD has accepted 88 audit observations involving tax effect of ₹ 28,639.13 crore, completed remedial action in 79 audit observations involving tax effect of ₹ 5,056.59 crore.

recommendations: Ministry of Finance must furnish replies to all 533 CAG audit observations within a prescribed time limit; non-response cannot be the default for the vast majority of findings.
ITD must complete remedial action on all accepted observations — acceptance without recovery means the revenue effect is never realised.
Assessment quality checks for Banks and NBFCs must be strengthened to prevent systematic exemption/deduction errors of this scale.

title: Performance Audit on Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana / Pradhan Mantri Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana (SAUBHAGYA)
ministry: Ministry of Power / Rural Electrification Corporation
overview: DDUGJY (launched 2015) aimed to electrify all unelectrified villages and provide distribution infrastructure. CCEA approved ₹75,893 crore outlay including ₹63,027 crore budgetary support; it closed at ₹64,495 crore. SAUBHAGYA (launched October 2017) aimed to electrify all un-electrified households, with a sanctioned cost of ₹14,082 crore, closing at ₹9,246 crore. CAG found: 81.65% of projects faced award delays; 91.74% had completion delays; SAUBHAGYA dashboard claimed 100% achievement across 25 states but only 151.60 lakh of 262.84 lakh households were actually electrified under the scheme; grant of ₹541.56 crore was released to 6 states before execution of tripartite agreement.

stats.label: SAUBHAGYA claimed 100% in 25 states — only 151.60 lakh of 262.84 lakh HHs actually done
stats.value: 262.84 lakh claimed; 111.24 lakh households not electrified under scheme
stats.note: SAUBHAGYA was implemented with a sanctioned cost of ₹14,082 crore. Its own dashboard declared 100 per cent household electrification achieved across all 25 implementing states by March 2019 — a claim the Ministry of Power announced publicly. CAG's audit found this was false: out of 262.84 lakh households shown as electrified on the dashboard, only 151.60 lakh were actually electrified under SAUBHAGYA. The remaining 111.24 lakh households counted on the dashboard were either electrified under earlier schemes, already electrified, or not genuinely covered. All 25 states declared 100% between November 2018 and March 2019 — a politically driven closure that masked actual coverage gaps.

source.quote: out of these 262.84 lakh households, only 151.60 lakh households were electrified under SAUBHAGYA.

stats.label: 81.65% of DDUGJY projects had award delays; 91.74% had completion delays
stats.value: 494 of 605 projects delayed at award; 555 of 605 delayed at completion
stats.note: DDUGJY guidelines required work completion within 24 months (or 30 months for partial turnkey/departmental execution) from date of award. Audit found delay in award of work in 494 out of 605 projects (81.65%) across 24 states and two UTs — meaning work had not even been awarded on schedule, let alone completed. There was further delay of more than 12 months in 184 projects (30%) in 14 states. At completion stage: 555 out of 605 completed projects (91.74%) experienced delays across 27 states and three UTs. A major delay of more than 24 months occurred in 263 projects (47%) in 19 states. These systemic delays meant that the rural electrification infrastructure — though eventually built — came years after planned, deferring electricity access.

source.quote: There was delay in award of work in 494 projects (81.65 per cent) out of 605 projects in 24 States and two UTs. Further, there was also delay in completion of 555 (91.74 per cent) out of 605 completed projects in 27 States and three UTs.

stats.label: DDUGJY total outlay ₹75,893 Cr; scheme closed at ₹64,495 Cr with delayed objectives
stats.value: ₹63,027 Cr budgetary support; strengthening component demand cut from ₹44,821 Cr to ₹12,413 Cr
stats.note: CCEA approved a total outlay of ₹75,893 crore including budgetary support of ₹63,027 crore for DDUGJY/RGGVY. The scheme closed with a cost of ₹64,495 crore including budgetary support of ₹45,025 crore. States demanded ₹44,821.22 crore for strengthening of sub-transmission and distribution infrastructure — a core objective of rural electrification — but the allocated budget restricted this to ₹12,412.55 crore (cuts ranging from 14.13% to 99.05%). The feeder separation component of ₹11,285.78 crore demanded by seven states was restricted to ₹3,967.20 crore (46.27%-100% cut). The objective of strengthening and augmentation of sub-transmission infrastructure was therefore only partially achieved due to insufficient budget allocation.

source.quote: Cabinet Committee of Economic Affairs (CCEA) approved a total outlay of ₹75,893 crore including budgetary support of ₹63,027 crore for DDUGJY/ RGGVY and closed with a cost of ₹64,495 crore including budgetary support of ₹45,025 crore.

keyFindings.text: SAUBHAGYA dashboard claimed 100% electrification across 25 states — only 151.60 of 262.84 lakh households were actually electrified under the scheme, a 42% gap in real achievement vs claimed.

source.quote: out of these 262.84 lakh households, only 151.60 lakh households were electrified under SAUBHAGYA.

keyFindings.text: 91.74% of DDUGJY projects had completion delays; 47% had delays exceeding 24 months. Strengthening component demand was cut from ₹44,821 crore to ₹12,413 crore, leaving rural infrastructure underbuilt.

source.quote: there was also delay in completion of 555 (91.74 per cent) out of 605 completed projects in 27 States and three UTs.

recommendations: SAUBHAGYA dashboard data must be independently verified — states self-reporting 100% completion without third-party audit created false national claims.
Ministry of Power must commission a ground-level household survey to determine actual electrification status as of 2025 given the 111.24 lakh discrepancy.
DDUGJY strengthening and feeder separation components must be adequately budgeted in successor schemes — cutting 85% of demanded infrastructure funding defeats the electrification objective.

title: Performance Audit on Pradhan Mantri Khanij Kshetra Kalyan Yojana (PMKKKY) including District Mineral Foundation Trust (DMFT)
ministry: Department of Mines and Geology, Government of Karnataka
overview: PMKKKY (launched September 2015) requires District Mineral Foundation Trusts (DMFTs) to collect a portion of mining royalties and use them for welfare of mining-affected communities. As of March 2023, Karnataka's DMFTs collected ₹4,003.51 crore and spent ₹1,826.46 crore — only 46% utilisation. CAG found: 671 works cancelled out of 4,191 taken up in sampled districts; no baseline surveys conducted; no Master Plan or Vision Documents prepared; no nomination of stakeholder representatives in most districts; GoK never amended DMFT Rules despite central directive to do so.

stats.label: DMFTs collected ₹4,003 Cr; spent only ₹1,826 Cr (46%) — ₹2,177 Cr sitting idle
stats.value: 10,865 projects sanctioned; ₹3,902 Cr allocated as of March 2023
stats.note: Karnataka's District Mineral Foundation Trusts were created to ensure that mining royalty money is channelled into welfare of mining-affected communities — clean water, health, education, and livelihood restoration for communities that bear the costs of extraction. As of end-March 2023, DMFTs collected ₹4,003.51 crore in cumulative contributions. Of this, only ₹1,826.46 crore — 46% — had been spent. The remaining ₹2,177 crore in unspent funds represents mining communities waiting years for the roads, hospitals, and infrastructure that the legal framework promised them. 10,865 projects were sanctioned with ₹3,902 crore allocated — yet completion remained far below target in sampled districts.

source.quote: The District Mineral Foundation Trusts (DMFTs) have collected an amount of ₹ 4,003.51 crore and incurred expenditure to the tune of ₹ 1,826.46 crore since the scheme initiation till the end of March 2023.

stats.label: 671 of 4,191 works cancelled in sampled districts; 575 works yet to even commence
stats.value: Ballari alone: 421 cancellations (₹62.36 Cr approved action plan)
stats.note: In the five sampled districts (Ballari, Chitradurga, Gadag, Bengaluru Urban, Vijayanagara), 4,191 works were taken up for execution. Of these: 2,215 completed, 730 ongoing, 575 yet to commence, and 671 cancelled. Ballari — Karnataka's largest mining district — had 421 cancellations alone with an approved action plan amount of ₹62.36 crore. These cancelled projects represent both unspent fund allocation and communities who were promised welfare projects that never materialised. The ₹72.74 crore in cancelled works across all five districts cannot simply be reallocated without accountability for why the original projects failed.

source.quote: Works cancelled: 421 [Ballari], 9 [Chitradurga], 0 [Gadag], 22 [Bengaluru Urban], 219 [Vijayanagara], 671 [Total]

stats.label: No baseline survey, no Master Plan, no Vision Document — DMFT governance absent
stats.value: Stakeholder nominations only in 5 of 31 districts; GoK never amended DMFT Rules
stats.note: PMKKKY requires DMFTs to conduct baseline surveys to identify affected communities before spending — without this, projects cannot target the most vulnerable. Audit found that no baseline survey was conducted to prepare a perspective plan in any sampled district. Test-checked DMFTs prepared neither a Master Plan nor a Vision Document for planned activities, and did not prepare a list of affected persons. DMFT Rules require nomination of stakeholder representatives from affected communities, industries, lease-holders, and environmental organisations. But nominations were made in only 5 of 31 Karnataka districts. The Ministry of Mines directed state governments to amend DMFT Rules to change the governing council composition — GoK never did.

source.quote: the nominations were made only in five districts. No amendment to the DMFT Rules, 2016 was issued by the GoK even though Ministry of Mines, GoI directed the State Governments to incorporate certain changes in the rules. There was no base line survey conducted to prepare perspective plan.

keyFindings.text: Karnataka DMFTs collected ₹4,003.51 crore but spent only 46% — ₹2,177 crore unspent; 671 works cancelled in 5 sampled districts out of 4,191 taken up.

source.quote: The District Mineral Foundation Trusts (DMFTs) have collected an amount of ₹ 4,003.51 crore and incurred expenditure to the tune of ₹ 1,826.46 crore since the scheme initiation till the end of March 2023.

keyFindings.text: No baseline survey, Master Plan, or Vision Document in any DMFT; stakeholder nominations in only 5 of 31 districts; GoK never amended DMFT Rules despite central directive.

source.quote: No amendment to the DMFT Rules, 2016 was issued by the GoK even though Ministry of Mines, GoI directed the State Governments to incorporate certain changes in the rules.

recommendations: Mandatory baseline surveys must be completed in all mining districts within 6 months — without this, DMFT spending cannot be targeted at genuinely affected communities.
GoK must amend DMFT Rules as directed by the Ministry of Mines without further delay — the governance framework is non-compliant.
DMFT utilisation must be tracked monthly with public dashboards; ₹2,177 crore sitting idle for years is an inexcusable failure given mining communities' legitimate claims.

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Pradhan Mantri Khanij Kshetra Kalyan Yojana including District Mineral Foundation Trusts in Gujarat
ministry: Department of Mines and Geology, Government of Gujarat
overview: PMKKKY mandates that District Mineral Foundation Trusts (DMFTs) collect a share of mining royalties for welfare of mining-affected communities. As on March 2024, Gujarat's 32 DMFs received ₹1,608.08 crore in DMF contributions but spent only ₹756.62 crore (47.05%) — leaving ₹851.46 crore (52.95%) unutilized. The Environmental Compensation Fund accumulated ₹84.46 crore but ₹83.61 crore remained unutilized. Annual Plans were not prepared on time in 5 DMFs; ₹22.74 crore outstanding from major mineral leaseholders; ₹9.04 crore of work awarded on nomination basis without tenders.

stats.label: Gujarat DMFs collected ₹1,608 Cr — spent only 47%; ₹851 Cr unutilized
stats.value: 32 DMFs; ₹756.62 Cr spent (47.05%); ₹851.46 Cr idle (52.95%) as of March 2024
stats.note: As on March 2024, the 32 District Mineral Foundation Trusts of Gujarat collectively received DMF contributions of ₹1,608.08 crore — royalty money owed to mining-affected communities. The expenditure incurred for projects under PMKKKY was ₹756.62 crore, representing 47.05 per cent of total receipts. The unutilized DMF contribution stood at ₹851.46 crore — 52.95 per cent. With over half the corpus sitting idle, mining-affected communities in Gujarat's 32 mineral districts are not receiving the infrastructure, health services, and welfare benefits the scheme legally mandates. The highest single-category spend was Education (43% of High Priority Area expenditure), while Welfare of aged and disabled, Environment Preservation, and Sanitation together received only 7%.

source.quote: As on March 2024, the 32 DMFs of Gujarat received DMF contribution of ₹1,608.08 crore, the expenditure incurred for projects under PMKKKY was ₹756.62 crore (47.05 per cent) and unutilized DMF contribution was ₹851.46 crore (52.95 per cent).

stats.label: ₹83.61 Cr of Environmental Compensation Fund unutilized — 99% of total collected
stats.value: ₹84.46 Cr collected for environment; only ₹0.85 Cr spent
stats.note: The PMKKKY framework requires DMFs to set aside an Environmental Compensation Fund specifically for projects that mitigate environmental damage caused by mining. Gujarat's DMFs collected ₹84.46 crore in this fund — yet ₹83.61 crore of this amount remained completely unutilized. This means 99% of the money designated for environmental protection near mines sat unspent while mining operations continued. The communities bearing the direct health and ecological costs of extraction — dust, water contamination, land degradation — received virtually none of the environmental restoration funding that the scheme mandated.

source.quote: the Environmental Compensation Fund of ₹ 83.61 crore out of total collection of ₹ 84.46 crore by the DMFs in Gujarat which were to be utilized for PMKKKY projects remained unutilized.

stats.label: ₹34.19 Cr outstanding DMF contributions; ₹9.04 Cr contracts awarded without tenders
stats.value: ₹22.74 Cr from major mineral leaseholders; ₹11.45 Cr from minor mineral leaseholders
stats.note: CAG found cases of non/short payment of DMF contributions in five DMFs, resulting in ₹22.74 crore outstanding from major mineral leaseholders and ₹11.45 crore from minor mineral leaseholders — a total of ₹34.19 crore in unpaid contributions. Additionally, four DMFs did not calculate interest for delayed payment as required by rules. On procurement integrity: audit found instances of award of work worth ₹9.04 crore to agencies on nomination basis without inviting tenders — constituting undue benefit to specific contractors. A Blood Bank project at Chhotaudepur remained incomplete after more than 4 years of delay, with ₹39.53 lakh paid for it remaining unfruitful.

source.quote: There were cases of non/short payment of DMF contribution in five DMFs, resulting in outstanding DMF contribution of ₹22.74 crore from major mineral leaseholders and ₹11.45 crore from minor mineral leaseholders.

keyFindings.text: Gujarat DMFs received ₹1,608.08 crore but spent only 47.05% — ₹851.46 crore unutilized; Environmental Compensation Fund 99% unspent (₹83.61 Cr of ₹84.46 Cr collected).

source.quote: As on March 2024, the 32 DMFs of Gujarat received DMF contribution of ₹1,608.08 crore, the expenditure incurred for projects under PMKKKY was ₹756.62 crore (47.05 per cent) and unutilized DMF contribution was ₹851.46 crore (52.95 per cent).

keyFindings.text: ₹34.19 crore in outstanding DMF contributions from leaseholders; ₹9.04 crore contracts awarded on nomination without tender; Blood Bank project unfinished after 4+ years.

source.quote: outstanding DMF contribution of ₹22.74 crore from major mineral leaseholders and ₹11.45 crore from minor mineral leaseholders. Audit noticed instances of award of work worth ₹9.04 crore to agency on nomination basis without inviting tender.

recommendations: Gujarat must set mandatory annual expenditure targets for each DMF — 52.95% unspent funds represent a governance failure, not a capacity constraint.
Environmental Compensation Fund deployment must be treated as an emergency — 99% unspent over 8+ years while mining damage continues is unconscionable.
All DMF contributions outstanding from leaseholders must be recovered with penal interest; automated deduction from mining permits is the only enforceable mechanism.

title: Performance Audit on Utilisation of Central Road Fund
ministry: Public Works Department, Government of Uttar Pradesh
overview: The Central Road Fund (CRF) channels cess revenue from fuel into road upgradation. UP incurred ₹7,257.86 crore under CRF on road upgradation during 2016-17 to 2022-23 across a network of 4,42,907 km. CAG's PA (April 2016 – March 2022) found: 78% of test-checked works completed with delays of 59 to 1474 days; ₹45.68 crore paid to contractors before work was even measured; 15 of 111 tenders had Bill of Quantities revised by more than 50% after bid opening (depriving other bidders); and budget was over-provisioned at ₹20,730 crore against actual requirements of ₹6,492.09 crore (319%).

stats.label: 78% of CRF works completed late — delays of 59 to 1,474 days
stats.value: All test-checked road upgradation works reviewed for timely completion
stats.note: Seventy-eight per cent of the test-checked CRF works in UP were completed with delays ranging between 59 to 1,474 days from their scheduled date of completion. A delay of 1,474 days means a road that should have been ready in one year was completed four years and one month later. These are not small deviations — the upper range (nearly 4 years) means entire communities waited years for road connectivity they were already promised. During this delay period, existing road conditions remained substandard, logistics costs remained high, and local economic activity was suppressed. CRF's entire purpose — improving connectivity through dedicated fuel cess — is defeated when the roads are built years after schedule.

source.quote: Seventy eight per cent of the test checked works were completed with delays ranging between 59 to 1474 days from their scheduled date of completion.

stats.label: ₹45.68 Cr paid before work measurement in 8 contracts — payment without verification
stats.value: Divisional officers violated contract conditions to release payments
stats.note: CAG found that Divisional officers had paid ₹45.68 crore to contractors before the measurement of eight executed works — in direct contravention of the contract conditions that require measurement before payment. Payment before measurement is one of the most fundamental financial control violations in public works — it removes all leverage over the contractor to ensure quality and eliminates the government's ability to dispute quantities. Once a contractor has been paid for work that has not been measured, there is no basis to recover money if the work is later found to be deficient in quantity or quality. CAG also found significant differences between amounts paid to contractors and expenditure recorded in the books of accounts.

source.quote: Divisional officers had paid ` 45.68 crore to contractors before measurement of eight executed works in contravention of condition of contracts.

stats.label: Budget ₹20,730 Cr provisioned for work costing ₹6,492 Cr — 319% over-provision
stats.value: UP spent ₹7,257.86 Cr under CRF in 2016-23 on road upgradation
stats.note: For CRF works costing ₹6,492.09 crore, the Government of UP provisioned ₹20,730 crore in the budget — 319 per cent of the actual requirement — representing significant differences between budget provision and actual need during 2016-17 to 2022-23. Over-provisioning at this scale is a well-known mechanism used to inflate available budget figures and enable discretionary spending. Separately, 15 of 111 tenders had their Bill of Quantities revised by more than 50 per cent by deleting basic and essential items after bids were already opened — then executing the deleted items as high-cost "extra items" later, effectively circumventing competitive procurement for a significant portion of the work.

source.quote: to execute CRF works costing ` 6,492.09 crore, GoUP provisioned ` 20,730 crore (319 per cent) during 2016-17 to 2022-23.

keyFindings.text: 78% of test-checked CRF road works delayed 59–1474 days; ₹45.68 crore paid to contractors before measurement of 8 works — contract conditions violated.

source.quote: Seventy eight per cent of the test checked works were completed with delays ranging between 59 to 1474 days from their scheduled date of completion. Divisional officers had paid ` 45.68 crore to contractors before measurement of eight executed works.

keyFindings.text: Budget 319% over-provisioned (₹20,730 Cr vs ₹6,492 Cr actual cost); 15 of 111 tenders had BoQ revised 50%+ after bid opening — depriving other bidders of fair competition.

source.quote: to execute CRF works costing ` 6,492.09 crore, GoUP provisioned ` 20,730 crore (319 per cent) during 2016-17 to 2022-23.

recommendations: PWD must implement measurement-before-payment as a hard system control — no payment order should be processable without a verified measurement book entry signed by the divisional officer.
BoQ revision after bid opening must require re-tendering; the current practice of executing deleted items as "extras" effectively bypasses competitive procurement for the costliest items.
Budget provisioning for CRF must be evidence-based — 319% over-provision enables discretionary reallocation and undermines fiscal discipline.

title: Performance Audit on Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services
ministry: Health and Family Welfare Department, Government of Kerala
overview: Kerala's health sector spent ₹48,735.92 crore during 2016-22, yet capital expenditure was only 4.24% — meaning nearly all spending went to salaries and consumables, not infrastructure. CAG found: Public Health Centre (PHC) infrastructure availability was only 14% of IPHS norms; Community Health Centre (CHC) was 35%; 82% of drug suppliers delayed consignments without penalty; ASHA workers short by 3-33% in 13 of 14 districts; per capita out-of-pocket health expenditure was second highest in India; suicide rate per lakh population exceeded national average.

stats.label: ₹48,735 Cr spent on health in 6 years — only 4.24% was capital investment
stats.value: Health budget utilisation declined from 97.64% to 93.28%; capital share 4.24%
stats.note: Against the expenditure of ₹48,735.92 crore on health during the audit period (2016-22), capital expenditure was only 4.24 per cent. With 95.76% of all health spending going to recurring costs (salaries, drugs, consumables), the physical infrastructure — hospital buildings, equipment, beds — was chronically underfunded. The State sector health spending did not meet the National Health Policy 2017 target of more than 8 per cent of the total budget. Health expenditure as a share of allocated funds declined from 97.64 per cent in 2016-17 to 93.28 per cent in 2020-21 (recovering to 98.92% in 2021-22). The allotment of funds to Kerala Medical Services Corporation Limited (KMSCL) for drug purchase was not based on actual requirement.

source.quote: Against the expenditure of ₹48,735.92 crore on health during the Audit period, the capital expenditure was only 4.24 per cent.

stats.label: 82% of drug suppliers delayed consignments — KMSCL did not penalise them
stats.value: 46 drugs & 14 suppliers escaped quality check entirely; only 10% subjected to QC
stats.note: Suppliers of around 82 per cent of the drugs delayed their consignments to KMSCL, Kerala's medical supply agency — yet in many instances they were not penalised for the delay. The absence of penalty for delayed drug supply means contractors face no financial consequence for jeopardising patient access to medicines. The quality control policy compounded this: KMSCL subjected only 10 per cent of drugs to quality check, which CAG found did not yield desired results. All the batches of 46 drugs and all supplies from 14 suppliers escaped quality check entirely during the audit period. This means those 46 drugs and 14 suppliers' entire product lines reached patients without any laboratory verification of safety or efficacy.

source.quote: Suppliers of around 82 per cent of the drugs delayed their consignment and in many instances, they were not penalised by KMSCL for the delay. The policy of subjecting only 10 per cent of drugs to quality check (QC) did not yield desired results as all the batches of 46 drugs and all supplies from 14 suppliers escaped QC during the audit period.

stats.label: PHC infrastructure only 14% of IPHS norm; CHC only 35% — health infrastructure starved
stats.value: ASHA shortage of 3-33% in 13 of 14 districts; OPD doctor shortages at hospitals
stats.note: The Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) define the minimum infrastructure — rooms, beds, labs, operating theatres — that each level of health facility must have. CAG found that the availability of infrastructure in Primary Health Centres (PHCs) was only 14 per cent of IPHS norms, and in Community Health Centres (CHCs) was only 35 per cent. Shortages in PHCs and CHCs are particularly damaging to rural and semi-urban populations, for whom these are the primary point of care. Family Health Centres were not providing services as intended under Aardram Mission due to lack of infrastructure and manpower. ASHA worker shortages ranged from 3 to 33 per cent in 13 of 14 districts — weakening the community health link that makes primary care functional.

source.quote: The percentage of health expenditure with reference to allocated funds declined from 97.64 per cent in 2016-17 to 93.28 per cent in 2020-21... The percentage of availability of infrastructure of Primary Health Centres and Community Health Centres in the State when compared with IPHS was 14 and 35 per cent respectively.

keyFindings.text: ₹48,735.92 crore spent on health (2016-22) but only 4.24% was capital — chronic underinvestment in infrastructure; health budget share below NHP 2017's 8% target throughout.

source.quote: Against the expenditure of ₹48,735.92 crore on health during the Audit period, the capital expenditure was only 4.24 per cent.

keyFindings.text: 82% of drug suppliers delayed — not penalised; 46 drugs and 14 suppliers' entire output escaped quality check; PHC infrastructure 14% of IPHS norm; CHC 35%.

source.quote: Suppliers of around 82 per cent of the drugs delayed their consignment and in many instances, they were not penalised by KMSCL for the delay.

recommendations: Capital health expenditure must be ring-fenced at minimum 8% of health budget — infrastructure backlog at 14% of IPHS norm in PHCs cannot be remedied through salaries-only spending.
KMSCL must enforce penalty clauses for all delayed drug suppliers; quality check rate must increase to at minimum 30% with mandatory sampling from every supplier every quarter.
ASHA shortages must be treated as a recruitment emergency — the community health link in 13 of 14 districts is broken.

title: Performance Audit on Goods and Services Tax (Indirect Taxes)
ministry: Ministry of Finance / Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs
overview: GST — India's unified indirect tax system — came into force in July 2017 across 14 parameters audited by CAG. CAG's PA covered FY 2017-18 to 2021-22. Key findings: in 1,268 cases (15% of audit sample) CAG found short levy of tax of ₹2,203.57 crore; 1,368 data entry errors (17%); Central GST revenue grew 27.30% (₹1,50,558 crore) in FY22 over FY21; Indirect taxes to GDP ratio declined from 5.80% in FY18 to 1.76% in FY20 before recovering; records for 954 claims (11% of sample of 8,514) were not produced, and 2,209 claims (26%) were partially produced.

stats.label: 1,268 cases (15%) found with short levy of ₹2,203.57 Cr — systematic GST under-collection
stats.value: Top deviations across 14 GST audit parameters for FY 2017-18
stats.note: CAG's audit across 14 GST risk parameters identified 1,268 cases (constituting 15 per cent) involving a short levy of tax of ₹2,203.57 crore. A short levy means tax was either not collected, under-collected, or improperly exempted on transactions that were legally taxable. Audit queries on these cases were issued to the respective tax Ranges between January 2022 and May 2022. These 1,268 cases represent systemic patterns — the audit was not a random sample but a targeted examination of the highest-risk deviation categories across India's GST network. The figure of ₹2,203.57 crore is only for FY 2017-18 under the parameters CAG examined — the full revenue impact across all years covered would be significantly higher.

source.quote: in 1,268 cases (constituting 15 per cent) involving a short levy of tax of ₹ 2,203.57 crore.

stats.label: Central GST revenue jumped 27.30% (₹1,50,558 Cr) in FY22 — yet GDP ratio still recovering
stats.note: Central GST revenue increased by 27.30 per cent (₹1,50,558 crore) during FY22 over FY21 — a recovery after GST revenue underperformed targets for several years. During FY22, Central GST revenue as a percentage of GDP increased to 2.97 per cent from 2.79 per cent in FY21. But the broader picture of Indirect taxes to GDP ratio shows a structural decline: from 5.80 per cent in FY18 to 1.76 per cent in FY20, recovering gradually. The increase in FY22 was driven significantly by post-pandemic demand, not by improved compliance — meaning the short levies and data entry errors CAG found are ongoing drags on what GST could collect.

source.quote: Central GST revenue increased by 27.30 per cent (` 1,50,558 crore) during FY 22 over FY21. During FY22, Central GST revenue as a percentage of GDP increased to 2.97 per cent from 2.79 per cent in FY21.

stats.label: Records not produced for 954 claims (11% of 8,514 sample); 2,209 claims (26%) partially produced
stats.value: 37% of audit sample had record production failures — audit scope severely limited
stats.note: CAG faced significant record production failures that limited the scope of the GST audit. Records relating to 954 claims, constituting 11 per cent of the sample size of 8,514 claims, were not produced at all for audit. Records relating to 2,209 claims, constituting 26 per cent of the sample size, were partially produced. Together, 37% of the audit sample had either no or incomplete records available to auditors. This means for over a third of the claims audited, CAG could not conduct full verification. The scale of non-production suggests that either record-keeping systems are severely deficient, or that departments were selectively withholding records from scrutiny — both of which undermine the integrity of the GST audit process.

source.quote: records relating to 954 claims, constituting 11 per cent of the sample size of 8,514 claims, were not produced and records relating to 2,209 claims, constituting 26 per cent of the sample size were partially produced.

keyFindings.text: 1,268 cases (15% of audit sample) with short levy of ₹2,203.57 crore in GST; 1,368 data entry errors (17%) across FY 2017-18 assessment period.

source.quote: in 1,268 cases (constituting 15 per cent) involving a short levy of tax of ₹ 2,203.57 crore.

keyFindings.text: 37% of 8,514 audit sample claims had record production failures — 954 not produced at all, 2,209 partially produced — limiting CAG's ability to quantify full revenue leakage.

source.quote: records relating to 954 claims, constituting 11 per cent of the sample size of 8,514 claims, were not produced and records relating to 2,209 claims, constituting 26 per cent of the sample size were partially produced.

recommendations: CBIC must mandate digitised record-keeping for all GST claims so audit queries can be answered in real-time — non-production of 37% of records is incompatible with a modern tax system.
Short levy cases (₹2,203.57 crore identified in audit) must be recovered with interest and penalty; repeat offender taxpayer patterns must be flagged for priority enforcement.
The 1,368 data entry errors must trigger an automated validation layer in the GSTN portal — basic arithmetic and range checks would prevent systematic error categories.

title: Performance Audit on Upgradation of Rural Roads under PMGSY and Take Home Ration (ICDS)
ministry: MP Rural Road Development Authority / Women and Child Development, Government of MP
overview: CAG's PA covered two major MP schemes: PMGSY rural road upgradation (₹7,879.15 crore approved for 1,190 roads, 11,936 km) and Take Home Ration (THR) under ICDS. For PMGSY: suspected fraudulent bitumen procurement worth ₹414.94 crore was found across 71 of 75 PIUs — contractors submitted fake refinery invoices, same invoices twice/thrice, and procured from private refineries. For THR: the WCD department accepted 5.51 lakh fictitious Out-of-School/At-risk Girls (OOSAGs) (actual estimate: 0.43 lakh), causing excess expenditure of ₹110.78 crore. 10,144.35 MT of THR (₹62.53 crore) could not be found transported to anganwadi centres. All THR samples (₹237 crore worth) failed nutritional quality standards.

stats.label: ₹414.94 Cr suspected bitumen fraud in PMGSY roads — 71 of 75 PIUs affected
stats.value: Contractors submitted fake refinery invoices, double/triple invoices, private refinery substitutions
stats.note: CAG unearthed suspected fraudulent practices worth ₹414.94 crore in the procurement of bitumen for PMGSY road construction across 71 out of 75 Project Implementation Units (PIUs) in 49 of 51 districts of Madhya Pradesh. The modus operandi was multi-layered: contractors submitted fake invoices of government refineries, submitted the same invoices twice or thrice for payment, and actually procured bitumen from private refineries (which is prohibited under PMGSY norms that require use of government-refinery bitumen for quality assurance). The department had no mechanism to verify invoice authenticity — fake invoices from government refineries could be generated and submitted without detection. This affects the structural integrity of ₹22,574.21 crore worth of PMGSY roads in MP.

source.quote: Suspected fraudulent practices worth ₹414.94 crores in the procurement of bitumen for the construction of PMGSY roads in 71 out of 75 PIUs and 49 out of 51 districts.

stats.label: 5.51 lakh fictitious children accepted for THR — actual estimate was 0.43 lakh (₹110.78 Cr excess)
stats.value: WCD knew the figure was inflated 12x but accepted it anyway; OOSAG data fabricated
stats.note: For the Take Home Ration scheme, a baseline survey was required to determine the number of Out-of-School/At-risk Girls (OOSAGs) to be covered. The School Education Department estimated OOSAGs at 0.43 lakh for 2018-19 to 2020-21. However, WCD officials estimated 5.51 lakh — more than 12 times higher. The Directorate, though fully aware that the number was inflated, accepted 5.51 lakh as the official figure. This fictitious beneficiary count resulted in likely excess expenditure of ₹110.78 crore. Accepting a known-fictitious baseline inflated the entire procurement chain — more THR manufactured, more distributed, more expenditure claimed — all on a base number the department knew was wrong.

source.quote: The Directorate though aware of the inflated numbers, yet accepted a fictitious number of 5.51 lakh OOSAGs instead of 0.43 lakh OOSAGs as per data of Rajya Shiksha Kendra which resulted in likely excess expenditure of ₹110.78 crore.

stats.label: ₹62.53 Cr of THR never reached anganwadis; trucks were motorcycles and autos
stats.value: 10,144 MT THR untracked; vehicles in Vahan database were cars, bikes, tankers — not trucks
stats.note: In 8 districts, 10,144.35 MT of THR (Take Home Ration) worth ₹62.53 crore was recorded as stock taken into the system but could not be verified as transported to Anganwadi centres. Separately, 6 THR manufacturing plants claimed to have transported 883.55 MT of THR worth ₹5.46 crore — but verification of the Vahan vehicle database of respective states revealed that the trucks shown as used for transport were actually registered as motorcycles, cars, autos, and tankers. Some "trucks" did not exist at all in the Vahan database. This means THR ration packets intended for malnourished children and pregnant women were either never manufactured, never transported, or diverted — while payments were made for their transport.

source.quote: Six THR manufacturing plants/firms claimed to have transported 883.55 MTs of THR costing ₹5.46 crores. Verification of the Vahan database of respective states revealed that trucks used were actually registered as motorcycles, cars, autos, and tankers or the trucks do not exist at all in the databases.

keyFindings.text: ₹414.94 crore suspected bitumen fraud in PMGSY roads across 71 of 75 PIUs — contractors submitted fake government refinery invoices, same invoices multiple times, and used private refineries.

source.quote: Suspected fraudulent practices worth ₹414.94 crores in the procurement of bitumen for the construction of PMGSY roads in 71 out of 75 PIUs.

keyFindings.text: 5.51 lakh fictitious OOSAGs accepted for THR (actual 0.43 lakh) → ₹110.78 Cr excess; 10,144 MT THR (₹62.53 Cr) untransported; transport trucks were actually registered as motorcycles and autos.

source.quote: accepted a fictitious number of 5.51 lakh OOSAGs instead of 0.43 lakh OOSAGs...resulted in likely excess expenditure of ₹110.78 crore.

recommendations: MPRRDA must implement real-time invoice verification with IOCL/HPCL/BPCL APIs — bitumen invoice fraud at ₹414.94 crore scale is only possible without such verification.
THR beneficiary numbers must be independently verified annually by a third party — not self-reported by the same WCD officials responsible for procurement.
All THR transport must use GPS-enabled vehicles with Vahan-verified registration numbers linked to shipment receipts — motorcycles cannot carry sacks of ration food.

title: Performance Audit of Systems and Controls in Assessment and Collection of Revenue from Minor Minerals
ministry: Revenue and Disaster Management Department, Government of Odisha
overview: Minor minerals (sand, stone, clay) generate significant state revenue — Odisha collected ₹2,968.75 crore during 2015-22. CAG's PA found systemic failures: 71.73% of 520 minor mineral sources in test-checked tahasils were non-operational; ₹864.45 crore leaked due to a rules provision that allowed royalty deduction without other charges; ₹98.30 crore lost to mineral theft (8.50 lakh cubic metres of black stone); ₹58.63 crore in differential dues unrealized; ₹51.69 crore from quarrying without lawful authority; and satellite-based monitoring of mines was not adopted despite its availability.

stats.label: ₹864.45 Cr revenue leaked — OMMC Rules provision allowed royalty without other charges
stats.value: Odisha Minor Mineral Concession Rules 2016 provision exploited; now ₹864.45 Cr unrecovered
stats.note: The single largest finding is a systemic revenue leakage of ₹864.45 crore caused by a provision in the Odisha Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 2016 that allowed deduction of only royalty (not other charges) from contractors' bills when transit passes for mineral procurement were not produced. This created a perverse incentive: contractors could avoid paying cess, permit fee, and other levies by simply not producing transit passes — knowing only the royalty would be deducted. The provision, likely inserted with good intentions, was exploited at massive scale across 2015-22. The ₹864.45 crore in foregone revenue represents legitimate dues that should have been collected but were legally evaded through this loophole.

source.quote: Incorporation of provisions in the Odisha Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 2016 for deduction of royalty without other charges, from the bills of contractors, in the event of non-production of transit pass in support of procurement of minor minerals from authorised sources/ agencies, resulted in leakage of mineral revenue of ₹864.45 crore.

stats.label: 8.50 lakh cubic metres of black stone stolen — ₹98.30 Cr mineral revenue lost
stats.value: No measurement taken before/after quarrying; theft undetected across audit period
stats.note: CAG found that non-adoption of a system of taking measurements of mineral sources before commencement of quarrying and after closure of lease periods resulted in theft of 8.50 lakh cubic metres of black stone — with a resultant loss of mineral revenue of ₹98.30 crore. Without baseline and closure measurements, there is no way to verify how much mineral was actually extracted. Lessees could quarry far beyond their approved limits without accountability. Compounding this: quarrying operations in District Level Committee Forest land were allowed without prior approval of the Central Government, resulting in non-realisation of ₹51.69 crore for 4.77 lakh cubic metres quarried without lawful authority.

source.quote: Non-adoption of a system of taking measurements of the sources before commencement of quarrying and after closure of the lease periods resulted in theft of 8.50 lakh cum of black stone and loss of mineral revenue of ₹98.30 crore.

stats.label: 71.73% of minor mineral sources non-operational; ₹20.10 Cr revenue non-accrual
stats.value: 373 of 520 sources non-operational; 147 operational in 22 test-checked tahasils
stats.note: In the 22 test-checked Tahasils, out of the 520 existing minor mineral sources, only 147 (28.27 per cent) were operational, while 373 (71.73 per cent) remained non-operational as of 31 March 2022. Non-operational sources cannot generate revenue — the state is sitting on mineral wealth that is untapped. The audit found that minor mineral sources could not be made operational due to non-completion of pre-requisite formalities before invitation of bids, resulting in non-accrual of mineral revenue of ₹20.10 crore. Application of pre-revised (outdated) rates of rents and royalty after revision by GoO resulted in a further revenue loss of ₹8.40 crore.

source.quote: In the test-checked 22 Tahasils, out of the existing 520 minor mineral sources, 147 sources (28.27 per cent) had been operational, while 373 sources (71.73 per cent) had remained non-operational, as on 31 March 2022.

keyFindings.text: ₹864.45 crore revenue leaked via OMMC Rules 2016 provision (royalty-only deduction loophole); 71.73% of minor mineral sources non-operational in test-checked tahasils.

source.quote: resulted in leakage of mineral revenue of ₹864.45 crore.

keyFindings.text: 8.50 lakh cu.m. of black stone stolen (₹98.30 Cr loss) due to no pre/post-quarrying measurement; ₹51.69 Cr from forest land quarrying without Central Government approval.

source.quote: theft of 8.50 lakh cum of black stone and loss of mineral revenue of ₹98.30 crore.

recommendations: The OMMC Rules 2016 provision enabling royalty-only deduction must be amended immediately — ₹864.45 crore in leakage proves the loophole is being systematically exploited.
Mandatory pre-commencement and post-closure volumetric measurement of all mineral sources must be implemented — satellite imagery can automate this at minimal cost.

All 373 non-operational mineral sources must be audited for blocking reasons; non-completion of bid formalities is an administrative failure, not a legitimate reason to leave revenue-generating assets idle.

title: Performance Audit on Regulation and Supply of Liquor in Delhi
ministry: Excise Department, Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi
overview: Delhi's Excise Supply Chain Information Management System (ESCIMS) was implemented to enable end-to-end barcode-based tracking of every liquor bottle — from manufacturer to point of sale. CAG found the objective was systematically defeated: between April 2017 and November 2021, 14.48% to 48.41% of bottles were sold without scanning barcodes, using a loophole called "stock-take-sold" (MSR Gap). As of March 2021, 136.53 crore barcodes (28.29% of 482.62 crore sold) were sold without scanning. The New Excise Policy 2021-22 introduced additional governance failures — decisions taken without competent authority approval, excise duty delinked from actual sales volume, and wholesale licenses issued exclusively to private players.

stats.label: 28.29% of Delhi liquor sold without scanning — 136.53 crore bottles untracked
stats.value: As of March 2021: 346.09 Cr barcodes scanned; 136.53 Cr sold through "stock-take-sold" workaround
stats.note: ESCIMS was designed for end-to-end barcode scanning of every liquor bottle from warehouse to retail point-of-sale. By March 2021, 482.62 crore barcodes were shown as sold. Of these, only 346.09 crore (71.71 per cent) were actually scanned at point-of-sale or categorized after scanning. The remaining 136.53 crore (28.29 per cent) were shown as "sold" through a process called "stock-take-sold" or "MSR Gap" — a monthly reconciliation where unscanned bottles at a retail vend were simply marked as sold without scanning. This monthly reconciliation exercise was used throughout the entire implementation period, defeating the fundamental purpose of barcode tracking. A bottle marked "sold" via stock-take-sold has no audit trail of where, when, or to whom it was sold.

source.quote: Out of this, only 346.09 crore (71.71 per cent) were either scanned at POS or categorized (as damaged, expired etc.) after scanning the barcodes, while the remaining 136.53 crore (28.29 per cent) were shown as sold through 'stock-take-sold'/MSR Gap exercise.

stats.label: Bottles sold without scanning: 48.41% high (2017-21) — barcode tracking near-useless at peak
stats.value: Percentage without scanning ranged from 14.48% to 48.41% across months 2017-21
stats.note: The percentage of bottles sold without scanning through ESCIMS fluctuated between 14.48 per cent and 48.41 per cent during the period from 1 April 2017 to 15 November 2021. At the upper end — 48.41% — nearly half of all liquor sold in Delhi had no verified point-of-sale record. The department continued to use the "stock-take-sold" exercise for over seven years after ESCIMS implementation despite being aware that scanning percentages were low. The stated reason for introducing stock-take-sold in the first place was low scanning compliance during the 2014 pilot phase — yet the same workaround was never eliminated, normalising the bypass. From April 2021 to November 2022, under the new excise policy, 21.18% of 118.14 crore barcodes were still recorded as sold without scanning.

source.quote: The percentage of bottles sold without scanning remained between 14.48 per cent and 48.41 per cent during the period from 1 April 2017 to 15 November 2021.

stats.label: New Excise Policy 2021-22: decisions without competent authority; excise duty delinked from sales
stats.value: Wholesale L1 licenses only to private players; GoM recommendations varied without approval
stats.note: For the New Excise Policy 2021-22 (later scrapped and subject to CBI investigation), CAG found multiple governance failures. Decisions were taken without the approval of the competent authority. The report of the Expert Committee and the recommendations of the Group of Ministers (GoM) showed variations that were not properly authorized. Wholesale (L1) licenses were issued exclusively to private players — a departure from the earlier policy that had public-sector participation. Excise duty was delinked from actual sale of liquor — meaning the duty liability was not linked to how much was actually sold, removing a basic fiscal control. Retail licenses were issued to limited entities, reducing competition and enabling monopoly conditions.

source.quote: Decisions taken without the approval of competent authority. Issue of Wholesale (L1) licenses to private players only. Excise Duty delinked to the actual sale of liquor.

keyFindings.text: 136.53 crore Delhi liquor barcodes (28.29%) sold without scanning through ESCIMS; percentage ranged 14.48%-48.41% during 2017-21 — barcode tracking system systematically bypassed for 7+ years.

source.quote: the remaining 136.53 crore (28.29 per cent) were shown as sold through 'stock-take-sold'/MSR Gap exercise.

keyFindings.text: New Excise Policy 2021-22: decisions taken without competent authority approval; excise duty delinked from actual sales; L1 wholesale licenses exclusively to private players.

source.quote: Decisions taken without the approval of competent authority. Issue of Wholesale (L1) licenses to private players only. Excise Duty delinked to the actual sale of liquor.

recommendations: Stock-take-sold/MSR Gap mechanism must be permanently eliminated from ESCIMS — there is no legitimate reason why bottles cannot be individually scanned at retail POS.
Excise duty must be re-linked to actual verified sales volume — duty on an unknown quantity creates systematic under-realisation of revenue.
Any future excise policy must be approved by the full competent authority with Expert Committee and GoM recommendations documented and reconciled before implementation.

title: Performance Audit on Welfare of Building and Other Construction Workers
ministry: Labour, Employment, Training and Skill Development Department, Government of Jharkhand
overview: The Jharkhand Building and Other Construction Workers (BOCW) Welfare Board was constituted to protect construction workers — one of India's most vulnerable labour categories. CAG found systemic failure: the Board did not prepare annual budgets for 5 years (2017-22); average expenditure was only 50% of allocated funds; 42% of actual spending went to "additional benefits" (bicycles, sewing machines, sarees, cloth) instead of priority welfare like housing, pensions, and skills; none of 1,869 construction works in test-checked districts were registered under the BOCW Act; only 26% of workers had Aadhaar/bank account details updated for direct benefit transfer; and the Board did not obtain income-tax exemption for 12 years, losing ₹91.15 lakh in TDS from its own Welfare Fund.

stats.label: 42% of BOCW spending went to bicycles, sarees and sewing machines — not housing or pensions
stats.value: Supreme Court mandated priority welfare (housing, skills, pension) was deprioritised
stats.note: The Supreme Court of India directed (2018) a Model Welfare Scheme & Action Plan (MWS&AP) that prioritises housing, awareness, skill development and pension for construction workers. Despite this, Jharkhand's BOCW Board incurred 42 per cent of its expenditure on "additional benefits" — bicycle assistance, tool-kits assistance, marriage assistance, sewing machine assistance and distribution of sarees and cloth for shirt and pants. These are not prohibited — but they were prioritised over the Supreme Court-mandated functions. A worker who received a bicycle but was not covered by a pension plan or had no housing support after injury was not protected by the spirit of the BOCW Act. The Board also did not prepare annual budgets for any of the five financial years 2017-18 to 2021-22, and average expenditure was only 50 per cent of allocated funds.

source.quote: instead of prioritising the stated functions, like housing, awareness, skill development and pension, the Board had incurred 42 per cent of expenditure on additional benefits, viz. bicycle assistance, tool-kits assistance, marriage assistance, sewing machine assistance and distribution of sarees and cloth for shirt and pants.

stats.label: None of 1,869 construction works registered under BOCW Act — cess not assessed or collected
stats.value: Board failed to coordinate with departments; Parliamentary Committee estimate: 16.99 lakh workers in JHR
stats.note: The BOCW Act requires all construction establishments to register within 60 days of commencement. In the four test-checked districts, none of the 1,869 construction works undertaken by Building and Road Construction Divisions were found registered under the BOCW Act. Without registration, the Board could not assess or collect the mandatory construction cess — the primary source of funding for worker welfare. The Parliamentary Standing Committee (44th Report, 2014) estimated 16.99 lakh construction workers in Jharkhand. Against this, only 5.96 lakh were registered by March 2017 — and 12.57 lakh by March 2022. Hundreds of thousands of workers remained outside the system. The Board failed to conduct awareness campaigns, set up facilitation centres, or assign unique identification numbers (UINs) — leading to instances of the same beneficiaries receiving benefits multiple times.

source.quote: None of the 1,869 construction works, undertaken by the Building and Road Construction Divisions, in the four test-checked districts, were found to have been registered under the BOCW Act.

stats.label: Only 26% of workers had Aadhaar/bank details for DBT; Welfare Fund lost ₹91.15 lakh to TDS
stats.value: Board not tax-exempt after 12 years; death assistance ₹1 lakh vs recommended ₹2-4 lakh
stats.note: For Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) to work, every registered worker must have their Aadhaar number and bank account linked. Only 26 per cent of registered workers in Jharkhand had these details updated in the BOCW Board's portal. Without DBT integration, welfare payments must go through intermediaries — creating opportunities for leakage. Additionally, the Board did not complete the formalities required for income-tax exemption, despite being in operation for 12 years. As a result, the Bank deducted ₹91.15 lakh as TDS from the Board's own Welfare Fund — money that was supposed to go to construction worker welfare. The Board also paid death assistance of only ₹1 lakh to dependents of deceased workers, against the recommended ₹2 lakh or ₹4 lakh under the MWS&AP.

source.quote: For roll out of Direct Benefit Transfer, the required details (Aadhaar Number and bank account details) of only 26 per cent of workers had been updated.

keyFindings.text: None of 1,869 construction works registered under BOCW Act; 42% of Board spending went to bicycles/sarees instead of mandated priority welfare (housing, pensions, skills); average expenditure 50% of allocated funds over 5 years.

source.quote: None of the 1,869 construction works, undertaken by the Building and Road Construction Divisions, in the four test-checked districts, were found to have been registered under the BOCW Act.

keyFindings.text: Only 26% of workers had Aadhaar/bank details for DBT; Welfare Fund lost ₹91.15 lakh to TDS (no tax exemption in 12 years); death assistance ₹1 lakh vs recommended ₹2-4 lakh.

source.quote: For roll out of Direct Benefit Transfer, the required details (Aadhaar Number and bank account details) of only 26 per cent of workers had been updated.

recommendations: All construction works above ₹10 lakh in Jharkhand must have mandatory BOCW registration as a tender pre-condition — the 0/1,869 registration rate proves voluntary compliance is non-functional.
BOCW spending mix must shift: at minimum 70% must go to priority welfare (housing, pensions, skills) — bicycle and saree distribution cannot dominate where workers lack pension coverage.
The Board must complete income-tax exemption formalities immediately — keeping ₹91 lakh locked in TDS from a worker welfare fund is an administrative failure with no justification.

title: Performance Audit of Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services in Jharkhand
ministry: Health, Medical Education and Family Welfare Department, Government of Jharkhand
overview: CAG's PA on Jharkhand's health system found severe shortages across every level of care. Medical Officers/Specialists were short by 21-80% statewide; lab technicians in PHCs short by 92%; Mobile Medical Units (MMUs) — the primary rural health delivery mechanism — were 50% non-functional with 33-52% of equipment broken. For COVID-19, JRHMS spent only ₹137.65 crore (32%) of ₹436.97 crore released — while Jharkhand left ₹191.67 crore of central funds unreleased. AYUSH teachers were short by 60-66%; Medical College vacancies stood at 48% for teaching staff.

stats.label: MO/Specialist shortage 21-80%; paramedics 50-100%; PHC lab technicians 92% short
stats.value: DHs: MOs 47-66% short; CHCs: doctors 18-82% short; Medical College vacancies 48%
stats.note: Jharkhand's health system has a pervasive human resource crisis across every level of care. Statewide shortages of Medical Officers (MOs)/Specialists ranged between 21 and 80 per cent; staff nurses 14 to 76 per cent; paramedical staff 50 to 100 per cent. In test-checked District Hospitals (DHs): MOs/Specialists shortage 47 to 66 per cent, paramedics and nurses 39 to 74 per cent. In 14 test-checked Community Health Centres (CHCs): doctors and paramedics shortage 18 to 82 per cent. Shortage of lab technicians in Primary Health Centres (PHCs) was 92 per cent. Radiologists, lab technicians, x-ray technicians, and pathologists were also in shortage at DHs. In six Medical Colleges: vacancies in teaching staff 48 per cent and non-teaching staff 45 per cent. AYUSH Colleges faced teacher shortages of 60-66%; AYUSH dispensaries had MO/compounder shortages of 71-98%.

source.quote: Shortages of MOs/ Specialists, Staff nurses and paramedics, in the State, ranged between 21 to 80 per cent, 14 to 76 per cent and 50 to 100 per cent, respectively. Shortage of lab technicians in PHCs was 92 per cent.

stats.label: JRHMS spent only 32% (₹137.65 Cr) of COVID-19 funds; Jharkhand left ₹191.67 Cr central share unreleased
stats.value: GoI released ₹483.54 Cr; GoJ released ₹436.97 Cr to JRHMS; JRHMS utilised only ₹137.65 Cr
stats.note: GoI released ₹483.54 crore for COVID-19 management in Jharkhand between March 2020 and March 2022 — against which Jharkhand was required to contribute ₹272.88 crore as its state share. Against the total provision of ₹756.42 crore (GoI + state share), Jharkhand released only ₹436.97 crore to JRHMS (Jharkhand Rural Health Mission Society) — leaving the central government's share of ₹191.67 crore unreleased as of August 2022. Of the ₹436.97 crore that was released to JRHMS, the agency could utilise only ₹137.65 crore — a 32 per cent utilisation rate during FYs 2019-20 to 2021-22. During a pandemic that was stressing Jharkhand's already under-resourced health system, nearly ₹300 crore in available funds went unspent.

source.quote: GoI had released (March 2020 to March 2022) ₹ 483.54 crore for COVID-19 management, against which, GoJ had to release an amount of ₹ 272.88 crore as its share. Against the total provision of ₹ 756.42 crore, GoJ released only ₹ 436.97 crore... JRHMS utilised only ₹ 137.65 crore (32 per cent) during FYs 2019-20 to 2021-22.

stats.label: 50% of Mobile Medical Units non-functional; 33-52% of MMU equipment broken
stats.value: 22 MMUs available; only 11 operational (March 2022); no lady doctors or radiographers in MMUs
stats.note: Mobile Medical Units (MMUs) are the primary mechanism for reaching rural populations in Jharkhand — they carry doctors, equipment, and medicines to villages without health facilities. Of 22 MMUs available in Jharkhand, only 11 (50 per cent) were functional as of March 2022. Lady doctors and radiographers were not available in any MMU, meaning Antenatal Care (ANC) services and child immunisation — which require female medical staff in many rural contexts — could not be properly delivered. Among the 11 functional MMUs, 33 to 52 per cent of the equipment available was non-functional. Shortages of required equipment were 19 to 23 per cent. A non-functional MMU in rural Jharkhand often means the nearest alternative health facility is 50+ kilometres away.

source.quote: Out of 22 Mobile Medical Units (MMUs) available, only 11 MMUs (50 per cent) were functional as of March 2022. Lady doctors and radiographers were not available in MMUs to provide ANC and child immunization. Further, 33 to 52 per cent of the equipment available, was non-functional.

keyFindings.text: MO/Specialist shortages 21-80% statewide; lab technicians 92% short in PHCs; Medical College teaching vacancies 48%; 50% of MMUs non-functional with 33-52% equipment broken.

source.quote: Shortages of MOs/ Specialists, Staff nurses and paramedics, in the State, ranged between 21 to 80 per cent, 14 to 76 per cent and 50 to 100 per cent, respectively.

keyFindings.text: JRHMS spent only 32% (₹137.65 Cr) of COVID-19 funds released; GoJ left ₹191.67 Cr of central allocation unreleased as of August 2022.

source.quote: JRHMS utilised only ₹ 137.65 crore (32 per cent) during FYs 2019-20 to 2021-22.

recommendations: PHC lab technician vacancy rate of 92% must be treated as a public health emergency — sample testing and diagnostic services are foundational to disease surveillance and treatment.
MMU programme must be completely overhauled: non-functional units repaired, equipment restocked, lady doctors and radiographers mandatorily posted to each unit.
COVID-19 fund utilisation at 32% indicates a systemic weakness in planning and absorption — all emergency health fund releases must have a mandatory 90-day utilisation plan filed before disbursement.

title: Annual Audit Report on General, Social, Economic and Revenue Sectors — Manipur
ministry: Multiple Departments, Government of Manipur
overview: CAG's annual audit of Manipur's government spending uncovered failures across Tourism, Construction Worker welfare, and GST. For Tourism: against ₹1,124.59 crore budget for 2017-23, only ₹350.09 crore (31%) was spent; 13 infrastructure projects were abandoned after spending ₹50.85 crore, forfeiting ₹92.45 crore in GoI grants; a ₹6.35 crore sound-and-light show built at Kangla was never made functional. For the BOCW Board: 73 cheques (₹16.08 crore) were dishonoured; ₹37.54 crore of cess collected by the state was never released to the Board; ₹5.31 crore invested in a non-nationalised bank in violation of the Supreme Court's directive. For GST: 104 of 151 audit observations had ITC/tax mismatches of ₹34.04 crore; only ₹1.08 crore recovered.

stats.label: Tourism: ₹1,124.59 Cr allocated, only ₹350.09 Cr (31%) spent; 13 projects forfeited ₹92.45 Cr GoI grants
stats.value: Projects abandoned after spending ₹50.85 Cr; delays of 7-13 years; ₹6.35 Cr sound show never functional
stats.note: Against a total budget provision of ₹1,124.59 crore for tourism development in Manipur during 2017-18 to 2022-23, total expenditure was only ₹350.09 crore — indicating overall savings (ie. underspending) of ₹774.50 crore and sub-optimal utilisation of the budgetary allocation. The state could not avail GoI grant of ₹92.45 crore for 13 Product Infrastructure Development for Destinations and Circuits (PIDDC) projects because those projects were not completed — they were lying incomplete/abandoned after incurring ₹50.85 crore, with delays ranging from seven to 13 years from the stipulated date of completion. The light and sound show at Kangla, inaugurated on 14 August 2018, was never made operational — rendering the ₹6.35 crore expenditure wasteful. Assets worth ₹16.83 crore created under the Spiritual Circuits project were idle or not used for intended purposes.

source.quote: Against total budget provision of ₹ 1,124.59 crore during 2017-18 to 2022-23, the total expenditure was ₹ 350.09 crore, indicating overall savings of ₹ 774.50 crore and sub-optimal utilisation of the budgetary allocation.

stats.label: ₹37.54 Cr BOCW cess withheld by state; ₹16.08 Cr in dishonoured cheques; ₹5.31 Cr in non-nationalised bank (SC violation)
stats.value: Cess of ₹101.15 Cr collected; only ₹63.61 Cr released to Board; SC directed nationalised bank only
