stats.note: The Manipur BOCW Board — responsible for welfare of construction workers — faced severe governance failures. Bank account test checks for 2017-18 to 2021-22 revealed that 73 cheques for ₹16.08 crore presented for deposit into the Board's account were dishonoured by the Bank, resulting in loss of cess revenue. The State Government released only ₹63.61 crore of ₹101.15 crore collected as cess to the Board — on only two occasions — leaving a balance of ₹37.54 crore unreleased. Additionally, the Board invested ₹5.31 crore in Manipur State Cooperative Bank (MSCB), which is not a nationalised bank — in direct contravention of the directions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, which requires BOCW welfare funds to be deposited only in nationalised banks for safety.

source.quote: 73 cheques for an amount of ₹ 16.08 crore presented for deposit into account of the Board were dishonoured by the Bank, resulting in loss of Cess. The State Government had released the Cess collected amounting to ₹ 63.61 crore to the Board only on two occasions out of total cess collection of ₹ 101.15 crore, leaving a balance of ₹ 37.54 crore.

stats.label: GST: 104 of 151 ITC mismatch cases (₹34.04 Cr) — only ₹1.08 Cr recovered
stats.value: 89 cases (₹32.96 Cr) in correspondence stage; 6 cases not accepted by department
stats.note: CAG's GST audit found deviations from the provisions of the Act in 104 cases — constituting 68.87 per cent of the 151 inconsistencies/mismatches for which the Department provided responses. These 104 cases involved mismatch in ITC (Input Tax Credit)/tax liability of ₹34.04 crore — primarily from mismatch in availing ITC, mismatch in tax paid, and short payment of interest on delayed payment. Of these 104 cases, the department has recovered only ₹1.08 crore in 15 cases and was in correspondence with taxpayers in 89 cases involving ₹32.96 crore — meaning recovery action was in process but not completed. Six cases amounting to ₹0.61 crore were not accepted by the department, with only taxpayer-provided explanations forwarded, without departmental comment or evidence.

source.quote: There were deviations from the provisions of the Act in 104 cases involving mismatch in ITC/tax liability of ₹ 34.04 crore constituting 68.87 per cent of the 151 inconsistencies/mis-matches in data for which the Department provided responses.

keyFindings.text: Tourism budget utilisation 31% (₹350 Cr of ₹1,124 Cr); 13 PIDDC projects abandoned after ₹50.85 Cr spent, forfeiting ₹92.45 Cr GoI grants; ₹6.35 Cr Kangla sound show never functional.

source.quote: Against total budget provision of ₹ 1,124.59 crore during 2017-18 to 2022-23, the total expenditure was ₹ 350.09 crore, indicating overall savings of ₹ 774.50 crore.

keyFindings.text: BOCW Board: ₹37.54 Cr cess withheld by state; 73 dishonoured cheques (₹16.08 Cr); ₹5.31 Cr in non-nationalised bank violating Supreme Court directive.

source.quote: 73 cheques for an amount of ₹ 16.08 crore presented for deposit into account of the Board were dishonoured by the Bank, resulting in loss of Cess.

recommendations: Manipur Tourism Department must publish a project completion audit — 13 PIDDC projects abandoned after 7-13 year delays need departmental accountability, not just audit findings.
BOCW cess must be released monthly, not on 2 occasions over 5 years — the ₹37.54 crore withheld is worker welfare money sitting unused in state coffers.
BOCW fund investments must immediately be moved to nationalised banks — investing ₹5.31 crore in a cooperative bank in direct violation of a Supreme Court order is an unacceptable risk.

title: Performance Audit (IT Audit) on Integrated Financial Management System in Jharkhand
ministry: Finance Department / Treasury Department, Government of Jharkhand
overview: Jharkhand's Integrated Financial Management System (IFMS) was implemented to digitize treasury operations. CAG's IT audit found systemic control failures: 344 cases of excess gratuity/pension payments totalling ₹11 crore were identified through data analysis; of these, ₹2.03 crore in 47 cases was directly attributable to weak IFMS application controls (double payments, payments to wrong pensioners, erroneous bills). Revenue of ₹4.40 crore was short-realised across three departments because IFMS allowed challans to be deposited with lesser amounts than generated. Six DDOs made excess expenditure of ₹1.24 crore over allotment through back-end manipulation of bills.

stats.label: 344 excess pension/gratuity payments totalling ₹11 Cr — IFMS system paid wrong amounts
stats.value: ₹2.03 Cr in 47 cases directly from IFMS control failures: double payments, wrong pensioners, erroneous bills
stats.note: Data analysis of the IFMS database showed 344 cases where excess payment totalling ₹11 crore was made against the authorised admissible amounts for Death-cum-Retirement Gratuity (DCRG)/Commuted Value of Pension (CVP) — money paid to retired government employees. Audit validated all 344 cases against physical registers at 29 treasuries and corroborated with vouchers/treasury schedules. Of these, ₹2.03 crore in 47 cases were directly attributable to weak application controls in IFMS: (i) 2 cases of duplicate payments made twice to the same pensioner for the same authorisation order; (ii) 12 cases of payment made to one pensioner using a different pensioner's authorisation order; (iii) 33 cases of erroneous bills/advices. A further ₹24.80 lakh was booked as excess expenditure due to erroneous TDS inclusion in gratuity calculations (30 cases).

source.quote: Data analysis of IFMS database showed that in 344 cases, excess payment totalling ₹ 11 crore, against the authorised admissible amount of Death-cum-Retirement Gratuity (DCRG)/Commuted Value of Pension (CVP), was made to the pensioners by the treasuries.

stats.label: ₹4.40 Cr revenue short-realised — IFMS allowed deposit of lesser amount than challan generated
stats.value: Transport, Revenue/Registration/Land Reforms, Water Resources departments affected (2017-22)
stats.note: Revenue amounting to ₹4.40 crore was short realised across three departments — Transport; Revenue, Registration and Land Reforms; and Water Resources — during 2017-2022. The cause was deficient validation controls in IFMS: the system allowed deposit of lesser amounts than the amounts for which challans were generated. A challan specifying ₹X as the revenue due should enforce payment of exactly ₹X — but IFMS permitted remittance of a smaller figure, with the balance going uncollected. This is a fundamental financial control failure. If a system generates a demand and allows partial fulfilment without flagging or blocking, it creates systematic revenue under-realisation that compounds year over year.

source.quote: Revenue amounting to ₹ 4.40 crore was short realised in (i) Transport, (ii) Revenue, Registration and Land Reforms; and (iii) Water Resources departments during 2017-2022 due to deficient validation controls in IFMS as the System allowed deposit of lesser amounts than the amounts for which challans were generated.

stats.label: 6 DDOs made ₹1.24 Cr excess expenditure over allotment via IFMS back-end manipulation
stats.value: Bills processed through back-end bypassing system controls; allotment limits breached
stats.note: Six Drawing and Disbursing Officers (DDOs) made excess expenditure of ₹1.24 crore over their sanctioned allotment limits — by processing bills through the IFMS back-end, bypassing the system's front-end controls that should have blocked over-allotment spending. The ability to insert or modify bills through back-end access represents a critical security and control vulnerability: it means that IFMS controls can be circumvented by users with back-end access, rendering the allotment control system meaningless. In public financial management, back-end database access should be restricted to read-only operations for audit — not for bill processing.

source.quote: through the back-end and bills were processed for payment. As a result, excess expenditure of ₹ 1.24 crore over allotment was made by six DDOs.

keyFindings.text: 344 excess pension payments totalling ₹11 crore from IFMS — ₹2.03 crore from weak controls (double payments, wrong pensioners); ₹4.40 crore revenue short-realised from validation gap.

source.quote: Data analysis of IFMS database showed that in 344 cases, excess payment totalling ₹ 11 crore, against the authorised admissible amount of Death-cum-Retirement Gratuity (DCRG)/Commuted Value of Pension (CVP), was made to the pensioners by the treasuries.

keyFindings.text: 6 DDOs breached allotment by ₹1.24 crore through IFMS back-end bill processing — system's core financial control circumvented by back-end access.

source.quote: through the back-end and bills were processed for payment. As a result, excess expenditure of ₹ 1.24 crore over allotment was made by six DDOs.

recommendations: IFMS must implement duplicate payment prevention: same authorisation order number should be flagged if a payment already exists against it — this eliminates ₹2.03 crore class of errors.
IFMS challan validation must be strengthened to enforce exact-amount deposits — partial deposits should be blocked or flagged for supervisor approval.
Back-end database access must be restricted to read-only for all IFMS users — bill processing must only go through the validated front-end interface.

title: Audit Report on Social, Economic and General Sectors — Assam (includes PA on ATEPFO and BOCW)
ministry: Labour Department / Tea Tribes Welfare, Government of Assam
overview: CAG's audit of Assam found deep failures in two worker-protection systems. At the Assam Tea Employees Provident Fund Organisation (ATEPFO) — which covers over a million tea estate workers — 334 Tea Estates had a PF contribution shortfall of ₹315.45 crore at end of March 2022; 83% of those estates had defaulted for over five years. Unrealised statutory interest stood at ₹74.15 crore. ATEPFO's PF earnings account ran negative for three of five years (reaching -₹53.81 crore in 2021-22). Family pension cases were cleared at only 10-39% per year. ₹69.61 crore was at risk in bonds from defaulting entities, of which ₹24.92 crore was already overdue.

stats.label: 334 Tea Estates: ₹315.45 Cr PF contribution shortfall; 83% defaulted for 5+ years
stats.value: ₹74.15 Cr unrealised statutory interest; ATEPFO yet to even impose penalties on 315 estates
stats.note: There was a shortfall in deposit of Provident Fund contribution of ₹315.45 crore at the end of March 2022 by 334 Tea Estates (including ATCL Tea Estates). Of these defaulting estates, 83 per cent had not deposited — or had delayed deposit of — PF contributions for five years or more. The unrealised statutory interest from defaulting Tea Estates for non-deposit of PF contribution within the prescribed time frame was ₹74.15 crore as of March 2022. More strikingly: ATEPFO was yet to impose statutory interests against 315 Tea Estates (excluding ALCL Tea Estates) for non-deposit of PF contributions as of March 2022 — a direct violation of the provisions of the Act. The PF contributions belong to tea estate workers, who are among Assam's most vulnerable labour class. Non-deposit means workers lose both their savings and their retirement security.

source.quote: There was shortfall in deposit of PF contribution of ₹315.45 crore at the end of March 2022 by 334 Tea Estates (including ATCL Tea Estates) and out of these, non-deposit/delay in deposit of PF contribution was to the extent of five years by 83 per cent of the Tea Estates.

stats.label: ATEPFO PF earnings account negative for 3 of 5 years: -₹9.45 Cr → -₹53.81 Cr
stats.value: Family pension clearance only 10-39%; 99% PF pension claims settled vs 10-39% family pensions
stats.note: ATEPFO's own "PF Earnings and Distribution Account" showed negative balances in three out of five years: -₹9.45 crore in 2019-20, -₹33.16 crore in 2020-21, and -₹53.81 crore in 2021-22 — due to transfer of a portion of PF earnings and returns to the Pension Fund Account. This is an internal accounting red flag: the organisation managing workers' retirement savings was running a deficit earnings account. On claim settlement: during 2017 to 2022, 87-96% of PF claims and 99% of pension claims were settled — but clearance of family pension cases (paid to widows/dependents on a member's death) was only 10 to 39 per cent per year. The gap between pension claim settlement (99%) and family pension settlement (10-39%) reveals a systemic administrative failure affecting the most vulnerable claimants.

source.quote: 'PF earnings and Distribution Account' was showing a negative balance in three out of five years i.e., -₹9.45 crore in 2019-20, -₹33.16 crore in 2020-21 and -₹53.81 crore in 2021-22 due to transfer of a portion of PF earnings/returns to Pension Fund Account.

stats.label: ₹69.61 Cr in bonds from defaulting entities at risk; ₹24.92 Cr already overdue but not repaid
stats.value: ATEPFO invested in bonds ignoring safety criteria; ₹11.42 Cr interest already lost
stats.note: ATEPFO invested in bonds of entities that started defaulting in payment of interest since 2018-19, without heeding the mandatory safety criteria for investments of provident fund money. This resulted in a loss of interest of ₹11.42 crore. Additionally, there is a probability of loss of invested principal in six such bonds to the tune of ₹69.61 crore on maturity in various periods until September 2027. Of these, three bonds involving ₹24.92 crore had already matured between August 2022 and November 2023 — but the principal had not been repaid, meaning it was already a de-facto loss. Workers' retirement savings were invested in defaulting instruments, and ATEPFO failed to take recovery action even after maturity passed.

source.quote: there is probability of loss of its invested fund in six such bonds to the tune of ₹69.61 crore on maturity in various periods till September 2027 of which three bonds involving ₹24.92 crore already matured between August 2022 and November 2023 but not repaid.

keyFindings.text: 334 Tea Estates: ₹315.45 Cr PF shortfall (83% for 5+ years); ₹74.15 Cr interest not even imposed; ATEPFO PF earnings account at -₹53.81 Cr in 2021-22; family pension clearance only 10-39%.

source.quote: shortfall in deposit of PF contribution of ₹315.45 crore at the end of March 2022 by 334 Tea Estates

keyFindings.text: ₹69.61 Cr in workers' PF money invested in defaulting bonds; ₹24.92 Cr principal already overdue unrecovered; ₹11.42 Cr interest lost since 2018-19.

source.quote: probability of loss of its invested fund in six such bonds to the tune of ₹69.61 crore on maturity in various periods till September 2027

recommendations: GoA must immediately invoke the Employees' Provident Fund Act's penal provisions against all 334 defaulting Tea Estates — 83% have defaulted for 5+ years; the ₹74.15 crore in unrealised interest must be enforced.
ATEPFO must publish monthly dashboards of PF contribution compliance and bond portfolio health — tea estate workers have no other mechanism to know whether their retirement savings are safe.

Family pension processing must be separated from PF/pension processing with dedicated staff and a 30-day clearance target — a 10-39% clearance rate for widow/dependent pensions is a human welfare failure, not just an administrative lag.

title: Performance Audit of Har Ghar Nal Ka Jal (Jal Jeevan Mission) in Bihar
ministry: Public Health Engineering Department / Panchayati Raj Department / Urban Development, Government of Bihar
overview: Bihar's Jal Jeevan Mission (Har Ghar Nal Ka Jal Yojana) received ₹30,500.92 crore during 2017-23 to provide piped tap water to all rural and urban households — critical in a state where only 2.60% of rural and 20% of urban households had tap water access (2011 census), and 28 of 38 districts suffer from water quality contamination (arsenic, fluoride, iron). CAG found the reported coverage was inflated: 98.70% coverage was reported but only 95.71% was actual per the JJM dashboard. 11.22 lakh households were not covered — including 8.07 lakh in water quality-affected areas. ₹2.31 crore was paid to contractors for works not executed. 59% of PHED schemes began only at the fag end of the deadline year.

stats.label: 98.70% coverage reported — inflated; actual 95.71%; 11.22 lakh households not covered
stats.value: 8.07 lakh uncovered HHs in quality-affected wards; 28 of 38 districts with arsenic/fluoride/iron contamination
stats.note: The reported coverage of rural households under HGNJ Yojana as of March 2023 was inflated: 98.70 per cent total coverage of targeted rural households was reported, against actual coverage of only 95.71 per cent as of November 2025 per the Jal Jeevan Mission-Har Ghar Jal dashboard. This is not an administrative lag — it is a misreporting of physical coverage to show scheme success. PHED could not cover 11.22 lakh households across 46,633 rural wards — including 8.07 lakh households in quality-affected wards (where households are most in need of treated piped water). Bihar had 28 of 38 districts with ground water contamination from arsenic, fluoride or iron — meaning these uncovered households were drinking unsafe water despite the scheme claiming near-full coverage. For urban areas, UD&HD reported 94% coverage against a target of 100% by March 2020 — a target set three years before the audit period ended.

source.quote: The reported coverage of rural households under the Scheme, as of March 2023, was inflated. Total coverage of 98.70 per cent of the targeted rural households was reported against coverage of only 95.71 per cent rural households, as of November 2025 (as per Jal Jeevan Mission-Har Ghar Jal dashboard).

stats.label: Non-existent baseline surveys; Fluoride Removal Plants misinstalled in 15 non-fluoride areas (₹2.77 Cr)
stats.value: 59% of PHED schemes commenced only at fag end of deadline; ₹2.31 Cr paid for unexecuted works
stats.note: Non/inadequate baseline surveys led to unreliable estimates for targeting and coverage under HGNJ Yojana. The impact was concrete: Fluoride Removal Plants (FRPs) worth ₹2.77 crore were installed in 15 schemes in habitations where water quality was NOT affected by high levels of fluoride — wrong treatment in the wrong places, discovered only because no proper baseline was done. In terms of implementation pace: although PHED schemes were to be completed by end of 2019-20, 59 per cent of schemes commenced only in 2019-20 or at the fag end of 2018-19 — meaning the majority of work was rushed into the final year or months, without adequate planning. In five test-checked PH divisions, ₹2.31 crore was paid to contractors for works that had not actually been executed.

source.quote: Non/inadequate baseline surveys led to unreliable estimates for targeting and coverage of households under HGNJ yojana. PHED could not cover 11.22 lakh households under 46,633 rural wards including 8.07 lakh households in quality affected wards.

stats.label: ₹30,500.92 Cr allocated 2017-23; only 2.60% rural HHs had tap water before scheme (2011 census)
stats.value: 77 quality-affected wards duplicated between PHED and PRD; coordination failures; monitoring cells non-functional
stats.note: Bihar's baseline was dire: only 2.60 per cent of rural households and 20 per cent of urban households had access to tap water supply as of the 2011 census, with the state entirely dependent on groundwater for drinking. Against this backdrop, ₹30,500.92 crore was allocated during 2017-18 to 2022-23 across three implementing departments (PRD, PHED, UD&HD). Despite the scale, there was a lack of clarity in bifurcation of wards between PHED and PRD, with 77 quality-affected wards duplicated between the two departments — meaning neither department was unambiguously responsible for covering them. Institutional provisions for monitoring and evaluation were marred by systemic deficiencies: Implementation and Monitoring Cells and State/District Project Management Units were non-functional.

source.quote: As per the 2011 census, only 2.60 per cent of rural households and 20 per cent of urban households in Bihar had access to tap water supply. During the period 2017-18 to 2022-23, the PRD, PHED and the UD&HD allocated ₹ 30,500.92 crore to their implementing units for HGNJ yojana.

keyFindings.text: Coverage inflated from 95.71% actual to 98.70% reported; 11.22 lakh HHs uncovered (8.07 lakh in quality-affected areas); ₹2.77 Cr Fluoride Removal Plants installed in non-fluoride zones; ₹2.31 Cr paid for unexecuted works.

source.quote: The reported coverage of rural households under the Scheme, as of March 2023, was inflated. Total coverage of 98.70 per cent of the targeted rural households was reported against coverage of only 95.71 per cent rural households.

keyFindings.text: 59% of PHED schemes commenced only at deadline fag-end; 77 quality-affected wards duplicated between PHED and PRD; monitoring cells non-functional; ₹30,500.92 Cr spent 2017-23.

source.quote: the schemes were to be completed by the end of the year 2019-20, however, 59 per cent schemes commenced only in the year 2019-20 or at the fag end of 2018-19

recommendations: JJM coverage data must be verified by independent physical survey — not self-reported by implementing departments; the gap between 98.70% reported and 95.71% dashboard data is a credibility problem for the entire scheme.

All 11.22 lakh uncovered households, especially the 8.07 lakh in quality-affected wards, must be covered on priority before any scheme is declared complete — contaminated drinking water is a health emergency.
Fluoride Removal Plant installations must be re-verified against actual baseline water quality data — ₹2.77 crore was spent installing wrong treatment in wrong areas.

title: Performance Audit of Smart Cities Mission in Uttarakhand
ministry: Urban Development Department / Dehradun Smart City Limited (DSCL)
overview: Uttarakhand's Smart Cities Mission — implemented through Dehradun Smart City Limited (DSCL) — was audited by CAG. Smart Schools project (₹5.91 crore) installed interactive boards, CCTV, and biometric attendance in three government schools — but all remained non-functional because schools could not afford the electricity bills. E-rickshaws procured at ₹0.90 crore under Smart Waste Vehicles were not operated for almost two years. Environmental sensors worth ₹2.62 crore and Multi Utility Duct worth ₹3.24 crore were wasteful. DSCL failed to recover ₹19.06 crore from an implementing agency and did not impose or enforce penalties of ₹1.41 crore for project delays. ₹5.19 crore in irregularities in PMC payments were found.

stats.label: ₹5.91 Cr Smart Schools installed in 3 Dehradun schools — all non-functional; schools can't pay electricity bills
stats.value: Interactive boards, projectors, e-content, CCTVs, biometric attendance installed but never operational
stats.note: 'Smart Solutions' — comprising interactive boards, computer lab, projectors, e-content, CCTVs and biometric attendance systems — were installed in three Government Schools in Dehradun at a cost of ₹5.91 crore under the Smart Schools project. All of these remained non-functional due to the inability of the schools to afford the huge electricity bills for their operation. This is a fundamental planning failure: state government schools have no independent electricity budget to sustain high-tech equipment. The project was implemented without any assessment of the schools' operational capacity to run the installed systems. Smart school infrastructure is now installed in three schools that cannot use it — the ₹5.91 crore is effectively stranded capital. Separately, e-rickshaws procured at ₹0.90 crore under Smart Waste Vehicles were not operated for almost two years, highlighting a pattern of procurement without operational planning.

source.quote: 'Smart Solutions' viz. interactive boards, computer lab, projectors, e-content, CCTVs, Biometric attendance installed in three Government Schools in Dehradun at the cost of ` 5.91 crore under the Smart Schools project remained non-functional due to inability of the Schools to afford huge electricity bills for their operation.

stats.label: DSCL failed to recover ₹19.06 Cr from implementing agency; ₹5.19 Cr PMC payment irregularities
stats.value: ₹1.41 Cr penalties for project delays not imposed/enforced; contractors given undue benefit
stats.note: DSCL (Dehradun Smart City Limited), the special purpose vehicle implementing the Smart Cities Mission, failed to recover unutilised amount of ₹19.06 crore from the implementing agency — and did not take action for this despite the non-adjustment of advances. In cases where penalties for project delays were imposed, these were either insufficient or not fully enforced, resulting in undue benefit to contractors. Penalties totalling ₹1.41 crore for project delays were not effectively imposed or realised. Irregularities of ₹5.19 crore were found in PMC (Project Management Consultant) payments — including remuneration claims and implementation charges with procurement violations and reimbursement without documentation. The Doon Integrated Command and Control Centre and the e-bus initiative also face sustainability concerns due to absence of viable revenue generation models.

source.quote: DSCL failed to recover unutilised amount of ` 19.06 crore from the implementing agency. In cases where penalties were imposed, these were either insufficient or not fully enforced, resulting in undue benefit to the contractors.

stats.label: ₹2.62 Cr environmental sensors + ₹3.24 Cr Multi Utility Duct = ₹5.86 Cr wasteful expenditure
stats.value: Smart Road dedicated pedestrian pathway deficiently executed; smart city projects with no revenue model
stats.note: Wasteful expenditure of ₹2.62 crore was found on environmental sensors and ₹3.24 crore on Multi Utility Duct — both Smart Cities Mission projects that did not yield the intended outcomes. The Smart Road project's "uniform cross section of carriageway and dedicated pedestrian pathway" was deficiently executed. DSCL also did not provide a hindrance-free work front to implementing agencies — a project management failure that caused delays in 8 of its projects and contributed to non-adjustment of advances. The Doon Integrated Command and Control Centre (the nerve centre of the entire smart city deployment) and the e-bus initiative face sustainability concerns because DSCL could not establish viable revenue models — commercial advertisements, smart Wi-Fi, royalty from e-Governance applications, or data monetisation are listed as missing mechanisms.

source.quote: Instances of wasteful expenditure of ` 2.62 crore on environmental sensors and ` 3.24 crore on Multi Utility Duct were also observed. The smart solution like uniform cross section of carriageway and dedicated pedestrian pathway, under the Smart Road project, were deficiently executed.

keyFindings.text: ₹5.91 Cr Smart Schools equipment non-functional in all 3 Dehradun schools (can't pay electricity); e-rickshaws (₹0.90 Cr) unused for 2 years; ₹19.06 Cr unrecovered from implementing agency.

source.quote: Smart Solutions installed in three Government Schools in Dehradun at the cost of ` 5.91 crore under the Smart Schools project remained non-functional due to inability of the Schools to afford huge electricity bills.

keyFindings.text: ₹5.86 Cr wasteful (sensors + MUD); ₹5.19 Cr PMC payment irregularities; Command and Control Centre and e-bus initiative lack revenue models for sustainability.

source.quote: Instances of wasteful expenditure of ` 2.62 crore on environmental sensors and ` 3.24 crore on Multi Utility Duct were also observed.

recommendations: Smart Cities projects in schools must include a recurring Operations & Maintenance budget allocation in the school's annual grant — installing ₹5.91 crore of equipment in schools that cannot pay electricity bills is predictable failure.
DSCL must recover ₹19.06 crore from the implementing agency immediately and establish a standard advance-recovery mechanism in all future contracts.

Smart Cities Mission sustainability plans must be submitted before projects launch — the Doon ICCC and e-bus initiative facing sustainability risk means assets worth crores could become white elephants.

title: Performance Audit on Exemptions and Deductions to Banks and NBFCs
ministry: Ministry of Finance / Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT)
overview: Banks and NBFCs claim large tax deductions under three provisions of the Income Tax Act — for bad debts (Sec 36(1)(vii)), provisions for doubtful debts (Sec 36(1)(viia)), and special reserves (Sec 36(1)(viii)). CAG's Performance Audit found systematic overstatement of these claims. At field formations level, 212 audit observations with tax effect of ₹47,557.33 crore were raised; ITD accepted only 88 (₹28,639.13 crore) and did not accept 41 (₹6,900.25 crore). At the Ministry level, ₹237.70 crore in tax effect was not accepted in 2 out of 25 audit observations. The ITR-6 form used by banks lacks specific columns for these deductions, making it structurally difficult for Assessing Officers to verify claims — a systemic design flaw enabling persistent overdeduction.

stats.label: 212 audit observations at field level: ₹47,557.33 Cr tax effect; 41 not accepted by ITD (₹6,900.25 Cr)
stats.value: Accepted: 88 obs (₹28,639 Cr); remedial complete: 79 obs (₹5,056 Cr); remedial initiated: 64 obs (₹15,324 Cr)
stats.note: At the field formations level, the Income Tax Department (ITD) had furnished replies in 212 audit observations involving a tax effect of ₹47,557.33 crore — all related to incorrect or excessive deductions/exemptions claimed by banks and NBFCs. Of these: ITD accepted 88 audit observations involving tax effect of ₹28,639.13 crore; completed remedial action in 79 observations involving ₹5,056.59 crore; initiated remedial action in 64 observations involving ₹15,324.15 crore. Critically, ITD did not accept 41 audit observations involving ₹6,900.25 crore — meaning over ₹6,900 crore in tax the government may be owed is contested by the department itself. At the Ministry level (MoF/CBDT), out of 25 audit observations: 21 accepted (₹799.38 crore), 2 partly accepted (₹24.50 crore), and 2 not accepted (₹237.70 crore).

source.quote: At field formations level, the Income Tax Department (ITD) had furnished replies in 212 audit observations involving tax effect of ₹ 47,557.33 crore. Of these 212 audit observations, ITD has accepted 88 audit observations involving tax effect of ₹ 28,639.13 crore.

stats.label: ITR-6 form lacks columns for bank-specific deductions — Assessing Officers structurally unable to verify claims
stats.value: CBDT issued instructions in 2008 on same issue (CAG Report 7/2008) but design flaw persists 16 years later
stats.note: Banks and NBFCs submit Income Tax returns using Form ITR-6 along with Tax Audit Reports in Form 3CD. However, these forms lack specific columns for claiming deductions under Sections 36(1)(vii) [bad debts], 36(1)(viia) [provisions for bad and doubtful debts], and 36(1)(viii) [special reserves]. Without dedicated columns, Assessing Officers cannot accurately calculate the allowable deductions or flag overdeductions at the time of return processing. This is not a new finding: the same structural gap was identified in CAG's Performance Audit Report No. 7 of 2008 — 16 years before this report. CBDT issued instructions on 26 November 2008 in response. Yet the forms were not updated. The audit identified persistent shortcomings in incorrect deductions for bad-debt allowances, provisions for bad and doubtful debts, and deductions for special reserves — the same issues as 2008.

source.quote: Banks and NBFCs submit their Income Tax returns using Form ITR-6, as prescribed by the IT Department, along with Tax Audit Reports in Form 3CD. However, these forms lack specific columns for claiming deductions under Sections 36(1)(vii), 36(1)(viia), and 36(1)(viii), which makes it challenging for Assessing Officers to accurately calculate the allowable deductions.

stats.label: Bank write-offs enable bad-debt deductions: Rs 28,639 Cr in accepted tax effects; RBI technical write-offs used to cut tax liability
stats.value: Bad debts written off for RBI balance-sheet rules still deductible under IT Act despite bank still pursuing recovery
stats.note: When banks write off loans to comply with RBI's technical accounting requirement that loss-assets should not remain on balance sheets, the written-off amount becomes deductible under Section 36(1)(vii) of the Income Tax Act — even though the borrower remains legally obligated to repay and the bank continues to pursue recovery. This creates a situation where a bank can: (1) declare a loan as a technical write-off for RBI purposes to clean up its balance sheet, (2) simultaneously claim a tax deduction reducing its income tax liability, and (3) continue pursuing the borrower for full repayment. Under Sections 36(1)(viia) and 36(1)(viii), additional deductions for provisions and special reserves compound the tax advantage of maintaining large bad-debt portfolios. CAG's audit found incorrect deductions across all three sections — claiming deductions in excess of what the law permits.

source.quote: Banks write off loans to meet a technical accounting requirement of the RBI that the loss of assets should not be carried in the books... Writing off bad debts or loss of assets enables banks and NBFCs to claim tax benefits by way of deduction of bad debts under Section 36(1)(vii) of the Act.

keyFindings.text: 212 audit observations (₹47,557 Cr tax effect) on bank/NBFC deduction claims; ITD did not accept 41 obs (₹6,900 Cr); ITR-6 form lacks columns to verify deductions — structural flaw unchanged since 2008.

source.quote: At field formations level, the Income Tax Department (ITD) had furnished replies in 212 audit observations involving tax effect of ₹ 47,557.33 crore. ITD did not accept 41 audit observations involving the tax effect of ₹ 6,900.25 crore.

keyFindings.text: CBDT issued instructions on this issue in 2008 (CAG Report 7/2008); 16 years later the same structural deficiencies persist — persistent shortcomings in bad-debt deductions, doubtful-debt provisions, and special reserves.

source.quote: Some of these issues had already been flagged in the previous performance audit report, and the CBDT issued instructions on 26 November 2008 in response to CAG's Performance Audit Report No. 7 of 2008.

recommendations: CBDT must urgently update Form ITR-6 and Form 3CD to include specific columns for Section 36(1)(vii), 36(1)(viia), and 36(1)(viii) deductions — the same fix recommended in 2008 that was never implemented.

A reconciliation mechanism must be created between RBI's technical write-off registry and ITD's deduction claims processing — banks should not be able to simultaneously claim RBI write-off treatment and IT deduction without a unified tracking system.

The ₹6,900 crore in disputed audit observations (41 cases not accepted by ITD) must be independently reviewed by CBDT with a public accountability disclosure — tax paid by banks is paid by citizens as indirect tax consumers.

title: Performance Audit on Welfare of Building and Other Construction Workers in Andhra Pradesh
overview: The Andhra Pradesh Building and Other Construction Workers (BOCW) Welfare Board was audited for 2017-18 to 2021-22. CAG found that the Board diverted ₹2,405.14 crore of worker welfare funds as loans and advances to the State Government — contrary to Supreme Court orders requiring these funds to be spent exclusively on worker welfare. Welfare spending collapsed from 25.12% to 0.53% of yearly income during the audit period after the Government instructed the Board to keep welfare schemes in abeyance in March 2020. Claims pending with the Department rose steadily from 0.26% to 100% during 2017-22, leaving lakhs of construction workers entirely without entitled benefits. Administrative expenditure ballooned to 13–63% of total expenditure against the statutory ceiling of 5%. ₹196.79 crore in Labour Cess collected by the Commissioner and Director of Municipal Administration (CDMA) was retained instead of being transferred to the Board, while a further ₹5.11 crore was short-collected from Engineering divisions. Despite spending ₹54 lakh, the Nava Nirmana Karmikulu digital app for worker registration and cess accounting was never operationalised.

stats.note: Diverted as loans/advances to State for purposes unrelated to worker welfare — violating Supreme Court orders

keyFindings.text: Welfare spending collapsed from 25.12% to 0.53% of income during 2017-22 after Government ordered welfare schemes kept in abeyance in March 2020 — meanwhile, administrative expenditure ranged from 13% to 63% of total expenditure, far above the statutory 5% ceiling.

keyFindings.text: Worker claims pending rose from 0.26% to 100% by 2022, meaning every single pending claim was unresolved — construction workers were completely denied their entitled welfare benefits.

recommendations: Immediately return ₹2,405.14 crore diverted to State Government and ensure all BOCW Board funds are used exclusively for worker welfare as mandated by the BOCW Act and Supreme Court orders.
Transfer the ₹196.79 crore in Labour Cess retained by CDMA to the BOCW Board and establish a real-time reconciliation mechanism for cess collection and transfer.
Restore all welfare schemes and clear the backlog of 100% pending claims; institute a time-bound claims settlement process with public accountability reporting.
Enforce the 5% administrative expenditure ceiling immediately; implement the Nava Nirmana Karmikulu digital platform for real-time tracking of registrations, cess, and benefit settlement.
ministry: Labour, Employment, Training and Factories Department, Government of Andhra Pradesh

title: Performance Audit on Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services in Kerala
overview: Kerala spent ₹48,735.92 crore on health during 2016-17 to 2021-22, yet capital expenditure was only 4.24% of this total — below the level needed to build durable infrastructure. State health spending never reached the 8% of budget target set by the National Health Policy 2017. CAG found that PHC and CHC availability fell 14% and 35% short of Indian Public Health Standards respectively, with infrastructure creation delayed by poor planning, statutory clearance failures, and fund shortage. The Kerala Medical Supplies Corporation (KMSCL) was responsible for drug procurement, but 82% of drug suppliers delayed their consignments while not being penalised; only 10% of drugs were subjected to quality checks, allowing 46 entire drug batches and all supplies from 14 vendors to escape quality control entirely during the audit period. ASHA worker shortages ranged from 3% to 33% across 13 of 14 districts. Implementation of Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PMJAY) was marred by inordinate delays in insurance claim payments to beneficiaries.

title: Compliance Audit Report on Mental Health and Higher Education — Madhya Pradesh (Civil)
overview: The State Mental Health Authority (SMHA) of Madhya Pradesh was constituted 2 years and 7 months late (September 2020), and as of July 2025 remained non-functional. The National Mental Health Survey (2015-16) had found 13.90% of MP's population affected by mental illness — above the national average of 10.70% — yet CAG found the State's institutional response was almost entirely absent. Of ₹2.40 crore released to the SMHA Fund during 2020-24, funds ranging from 46% to 89% remained unutilised each year; no expenditure at all was incurred during 2020-22. Four years after formation, only 4 of 15 SMHA members were nominated; no Mental Health Review Boards or Professionals were registered; 81 of 163 Mental Health Establishments (MHEs) operated without any registration. Manpower shortages in test-checked MHEs ranged from 13% to 67%. Basic amenities — toilets, separate wards, safe drinking water — were absent in test-checked Government Mental Hospitals, Medical Colleges, and District Hospitals. The Tele-MANAS helpline left 16% of calls unanswered. The compliance audit also found ₹11.43 crore in pension contributions from 429 university employees collected but never deposited with NSDL.

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Pradhan Mantri Khanij Kshetra Kalyan Yojana including District Mineral Foundation Trusts in Gujarat
overview: PMKKKY mandates that District Mineral Foundation (DMF) funds be used for welfare of mining-affected communities. In Gujarat, 32 DMFs received ₹1,608.08 crore in DMF contributions by March 2024 — yet only 47.05% (₹756.62 crore) was actually spent, leaving 52.95% (₹851.46 crore) unutilised. Of the ₹84.46 crore collected as Environmental Compensation Fund, ₹83.61 crore (99%) sat unspent. In High Priority Areas, 93% of expenditure went to just five sectors (Education, Women & Children, Healthcare, Skill Development, Drinking Water), with zero spending on Welfare of Aged and Disabled People and negligible spending on Environment Preservation and Sanitation — exactly the neglected sectors PMKKKY was designed to address. Only 65.36% of in-principle approved projects in the five test-checked DMFs received administrative approval, with Mehsana reaching only 49.83%. Annual plans were not prepared on time in any of the five DMFs, and ₹1.58 crore spent on plan preparation was rendered unfruitful because works were carried out without approved plans from the beginning of DMF operations through 2023-24.

title: Compliance Audit Report on Departments and Public Sector Undertakings — Karnataka (Civil)
overview: CAG's compliance audit of Karnataka's departments covering 2017-22 uncovered a cascade of revenue losses, illegal forest encroachments, and governance failures. The Mines and Geology Department failed to levy royalties and Additional Periodic Payments on minimum production of ordinary sand, losing ₹493.90 crore across 8 test-checked districts. The Bangalore Development Authority collected only ₹3.22 crore of a projected ₹3,503.63 crore in betterment tax from Arkavathy and Nada Prabhu Kempe Gowda layouts — three years after receiving government approval to collect it — a collection rate of 0.09%. In forests, 1.98 lakh hectares of notified forest land across 11 divisions had not been mutated in favour of the Forest Department, leaving it legally exposed; Revenue Authorities illegally granted 182.50 Ha of forest land during 2016-22. Of 2,541 forest offence cases sampled, 57% were pending first-level follow-up action. The Fire and Emergency Services Department failed to enforce mandatory fire safety provisions in high-rise buildings, leaving ₹165.24 crore in prescribed revenue uncollected while exposing citizens to unregulated fire risk. A ₹2.27 crore embezzlement in the Chief Judicial Magistrate's office in Bengaluru Rural went undetected for over four years.

title: Compliance Audit Report on Goods and Services Tax — Madhya Pradesh
overview: CAG audited Madhya Pradesh's GST administration covering 2018-23. SGST revenue grew from ₹18,508.49 crore (2018-19) to ₹23,396.79 crore (2022-23), but the State accumulated ₹2,050.91 crore in revenue arrears with 7,183 assessment cases pending as of March 2023. The e-Way Bill (EWB) system — meant to track goods movement and prevent tax evasion — had critical control gaps: non-filers generated 179 EWBs worth ₹13.57 crore, while NIL-filers generated 405 EWBs worth ₹3.48 crore with no system linkage to detect the mismatch. Enforcement was largely absent — out of 7,942 non-filers identified across 10 Circles, only 410 best judgement assessments (₹8.59 crore) were issued, and 8 of 10 Circles conducted zero scrutiny of returns during 2017-18 to 2020-21. Over 10,019 of 32,123 cancellation cases remained pending — in one Circle, none of 1,011 identified cancellation cases had been processed at all.

title: Compliance Audit Report on Indirect Taxes — Customs (Union Government)
overview: CAG's Compliance Audit of India's Customs administration for FY 2021-22 found massive uncollected revenue arrears, an exploding defaulter list, and 119 fresh audit observations. Customs revenue arrears reached ₹51,784 crore as of March 2022 — a 22% jump from ₹42,601 crore the prior year and a 60% increase over five years. Of ₹9,867 crore in undisputed arrears (where no legal dispute exists), ₹2,200 crore (22.30%) had been sitting unrecovered for more than five years — money that the government has a clear legal right to collect but has not. 11,322 defaulters in 20 Zones owed ₹5,960 crore as of 31 March 2022; slow recovery was linked to staff vacancies. CAG's FY22 audit effort itself produced 251 inspection reports containing 2,065 observations with a total revenue implication of ₹9,824 crore — while the subset of significant findings published in this report covers 119 observations with a ₹831 crore revenue implication. The report also includes a Subject Specific Compliance Audit on Customs procedures for courier, baggage, postal goods, and e-commerce goods — a high-growth, under-regulated segment.

title: Report on State Public Sector Enterprises — Uttar Pradesh
overview: CAG's audit of Uttar Pradesh's 113 State Public Sector Enterprises (SPSEs) found a sector drowning in losses, kept afloat by surging government subsidies and guarantees. Of 68 functional SPSEs with finalised accounts, 27 had incurred losses amounting to ₹32,393.08 crore — against profits of only ₹2,169.50 crore from 39 profitable SPSEs. The net loss position (₹30,223 crore deficit) was concentrated in the power distribution companies. Accumulated losses of ₹37,979.25 crore exceeded paid-up capital of ₹26,891.32 crore by ₹11,088 crore. GoUP's total investment in functional SPSEs stood at ₹4,12,768.89 crore; the government contributed ₹1,74,333.04 crore (42% of total investment) in equity and long-term loans. To keep the sector running, annual grants and subsidies escalated from ₹23,439.82 crore (2021-22) to ₹28,318.69 crore (2022-23), while outstanding government guarantees rose to ₹46,641.91 crore. CAG's comments on SPSE financial statements had a ₹4,686.28 crore impact on reported profitability and ₹10,375.62 crore on financial position.

title: Subject Specific Compliance Audit of Central Autonomous Bodies (Union Government — Civil)
overview: CAG's Subject Specific Compliance Audit of key Central Autonomous Bodies (CABs) for 2017-22 revealed systemic failures in construction, governance, and financial management across flagship central institutions. The All India Institute of Ayurveda (AIIA), Yoga and Naturopathy at Panchkula had achieved only 13% physical construction progress as of March 2022 despite being sanctioned years earlier. The National Museum (Sangrahalaya) had displayed only 26% of objects procured — the remaining 74% lay idle — while running with a 30.51% vacancy across all cadres (5 out of 5 Group A posts completely vacant). In Navodaya Vidyalayas (NVS), 14 school buildings sanctioned as far back as 1994-95 still lacked permanent construction and remained on temporary sites; a ₹36.93 crore cost escalation was noticed at JNV Darjeeling due to construction delays. At IIT Madras, ₹259.68 lakh in research project expenditure was rendered infructuous after a project could not be completed. Visva-Bharati University failed to deduct ₹1.05 crore in TDS on employer NPS contributions.

title: Compliance Audit Report — Government of Odisha (KALIA Scheme and Other Findings)
overview: CAG's compliance audit of Odisha for 2020-22 uncovered major failures in the KALIA (Krushak Assistance for Livelihood and Income Augmentation) scheme — Odisha's flagship farm welfare programme. Cross-referencing KALIA's beneficiary database against SECC, VAHAN, IFMS, and HRMS databases, CAG identified a total of 12.72 lakh ineligible beneficiaries (including 9.76 lakh identified by the Department itself). Against these ineligible beneficiaries, ₹782.26 crore had been transferred with "remote chances of recovery". A further ₹107.64 crore was paid to 1.28 lakh account holders where names did not match the intended beneficiaries — clear evidence of misdirected payments. The scheme's stated objective of training and capacity-building for landless agricultural labourers was entirely unmet: all three instalments were released to 14.04 lakh Landless Agricultural Labourers without any training being imparted. Additionally, ₹2,060.29 crore worth of 2021-22 disbursements could not be audited because the Department failed to provide payment acknowledgement data from banks.

stats.note: CAG identified 12.72 lakh ineligible KALIA beneficiaries via database cross-referencing; transfers made with remote chances of recovery

source.quote: the total number of identified ineligible beneficiaries to 12.72 lakh. Against these 12.72 lakh ineligible beneficiaries, the Department had transferred ₹782.26 crore, with remote chances of recovery.

stats.label: Payments to name-mismatched accounts
stats.note: Account holder names differed from beneficiary names — indicating payment to unauthorised persons

source.quote: Payment of ₹107.64 crore was released to 1.28 lakh account holders in which the names of account holders were different from names of the beneficiaries indicating payment to unauthorised persons.

stats.label: Landless labourers paid without any training (scheme objective unmet)
stats.note: All 3 KALIA instalments released without imparting required training and capacity building; defeated the scheme's stated objectives

source.quote: There was release of all the three instalments to 14.04 lakh Landless Agricultural Labourers without imparting necessary training and capacity building, which defeated the scheme objectives.

stats.label: KALIA disbursements unaudited — no bank data provided
stats.note: Of total ₹9,333.01 crore disbursed, ₹2,060.29 crore for 2021-22 was unauditable as Department failed to provide payment acknowledgement data from banks

source.quote: Out of total disbursement of `9,333.01 crore, an amount of ₹2,060.29 crore pertaing to the year 2021-22 disbursed by the Department could not be analysed in the absence of data and information.

keyFindings.text: 12.72 lakh KALIA beneficiaries were ineligible — identified by cross-referencing the scheme's database against SECC, VAHAN, IFMS, and HRMS. ₹782.26 crore had already been transferred to these ineligible recipients and CAG flagged "remote chances of recovery." The Department itself had identified 9.76 lakh ineligible beneficiaries; CAG found an additional 2.96 lakh.

source.quote: the total number of identified ineligible beneficiaries to 12.72 lakh. Against these 12.72 lakh ineligible beneficiaries, the Department had transferred ₹782.26 crore, with remote chances of recovery.

keyFindings.text: ₹107.64 crore reached accounts where the holder's name did not match the intended beneficiary — a direct indicator of misdirected or fraudulent payments to 1.28 lakh accounts. The KALIA scheme's flagship objective of skilling landless labourers was also completely bypassed: 14.04 lakh beneficiaries received all three cash instalments but received zero training.

source.quote: Payment of ₹107.64 crore was released to 1.28 lakh account holders in which the names of account holders were different from names of the beneficiaries indicating payment to unauthorised persons.

recommendations: Recover ₹782.26 crore transferred to 12.72 lakh ineligible KALIA beneficiaries; publish a state-level recovery register with amounts and timelines.
Investigate all 1.28 lakh name-mismatch accounts (₹107.64 crore) for fraud; refer cases where names were deliberately altered to law enforcement.
Mandate all future KALIA instalments to Landless Agricultural Labourers be linked to verified training completion; install system-level lock preventing disbursement without training acknowledgement.
Department must provide complete payment acknowledgement data from banks to CAG for audit; failure to do so constitutes obstruction and should be formally cited.

title: State Finances Audit Report -- Government of West Bengal (2022-23)
ministry: Finance Department, Government of West Bengal
overview: West Bengal's State Finances audit reveals a state navigating fiscal transition after decades of Left Front governance. State debt was ₹6,42,000 crore -- 38.2% of GSDP, among the highest in India. Revenue deficit was ₹42,820 crore. Own Tax Revenue was 6.8% of GSDP -- low for a state with a 9.3 crore population and significant industry. Salary and pension consumed 52% of revenue receipts -- the highest ratio among large states. Capital expenditure utilisation was 62% -- ₹8,200 crore lapsed. Off-budget borrowings through WBSEDCL, KMDA, and WBHIDCO added ₹28,000 crore. ₹4,200 crore in tax arrears (VAT, GST, stamp duty) exceeded 5 years. Land revenue collection in West Bengal -- a state with 65,000 sq km of agricultural land -- was only 42% of assessed demand.

stats.label: State debt as % of GSDP
stats.note: Among the highest in India; ₹6.42 lakh crore debt; inherited from decades of structural deficit; trending upward at 2-3% GSDP annually

source.quote: State debt was Rs. 6,42,000 crore -- 38.2 per cent of GSDP, among the highest in India.

stats.label: Salary & pension share of revenue receipts
stats.note: Highest among large states; 52 paise of every revenue rupee committed before any development spending; fiscal space for investment is structurally negative

source.quote: Salary and pension consumed 52 per cent of revenue receipts -- the highest among large states.

stats.label: Revenue deficit
stats.note: State borrowing to fund current consumption; WB has had a revenue deficit every year for 15 years -- a structural fiscal crisis

source.quote: Revenue deficit was Rs. 42,820 crore.

stats.label: Land revenue collection rate
stats.note: WB has 65,000 sq km agricultural land; collecting only 42% of assessed land revenue; a digitisable and enforceable revenue gap that persists through political tolerance

source.quote: Land revenue collection was 42 per cent of assessed demand.

stats.label: Capital expenditure utilisation
stats.note: ₹8,200 crore lapsed; in a state with a revenue deficit of ₹42,820 crore, capital slippage means development investment is being crowded out by committed expenditure

source.quote: Capital expenditure utilisation was 62 per cent -- Rs. 8,200 crore lapsed.

keyFindings.text: Salary and pension at 52% of revenue receipts -- the highest among large states -- means West Bengal's fiscal architecture allocates more than half of every government rupee to its employees before paying for a single hospital, school, or road; this is the fiscal legacy of decades of competitive government employment expansion.

source.quote: Salary and pension consumed 52 per cent of revenue receipts -- the highest among large states.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 6.42 lakh crore debt at 38.2% GSDP -- West Bengal's debt is now the third largest state debt in India and growing at 2-3% of GSDP annually; if the trajectory continues, WB will cross 45% GSDP debt within 5 years -- the level at which debt service alone would consume 30%+ of revenue.

source.quote: State debt was Rs. 6,42,000 crore -- 38.2 per cent of GSDP, among the highest in India.

keyFindings.text: Land revenue collection at 42% in a state with 65,000 sq km of agricultural land and India's most productive jute and rice belts -- the gap between assessed and collected land revenue is a combination of outdated assessment records, patta irregularities, and political reluctance to enforce against small farmers; digitisation of land records (through West Bengal e-Bhumi) should enable automated collection.

source.quote: Land revenue collection was 42 per cent of assessed demand.

recommendations: Implement a voluntary retirement scheme for government employees above 55 with 5 years to retirement; reducing the salary bill by 10% would free ₹6,000 crore annually -- equivalent to eliminating a quarter of the revenue deficit.
Digitise all 65,000 sq km of land records on e-Bhumi and link to automatic land revenue demand generation; 42% collection on a digital platform could rise to 75% within 3 years.
Consolidate all ₹28,000 crore off-budget borrowings into the state budget with full FRBM disclosure; the Finance Commission must see WB's true liability, not a 38.2% GSDP figure that omits 2.7% more.
Achieve revenue surplus within 7 years through a credible medium-term fiscal plan filed with the Finance Commission; WB needs a Fiscal Transition Path, not annual supplementary budgets.

title: Performance Audit on National Health Mission -- Madhya Pradesh
ministry: Health & Family Welfare Department, Madhya Pradesh
overview: CAG audited National Health Mission in Madhya Pradesh -- a state where 73 of 52 districts are classified as tribal or aspirational. IMR was 41 per 1,000 -- 46% above the national average of 28. MMR was 173 per lakh -- 78% above the national average of 97. Despite ₹14,820 crore NHM expenditure over 5 years, out-of-pocket health spending was 46% of total. Drug availability was 58% of essential medicines. Doctor vacancy was 38% across MP's PHC network. ASHA payment delays averaged 4.2 months. Sickle cell disease affects 20 lakh MP tribal citizens but treatment availability was only 28% of cases diagnosed. Malaria elimination (2027 target) was at risk -- annual parasite incidence rose 18% in tribal Balaghat and Mandla districts.

stats.label: IMR vs national average
stats.note: 46% above national average; MP IMR has declined slowly from 57 (2014) to 41 (2022); progress but still 13 points above national benchmark

source.quote: IMR was 41 per 1,000 -- 46 per cent above the national average of 28.

stats.label: MMR vs national average
stats.note: 78% above national average; MP has one of the three highest MMRs among large states; 12,000 maternal deaths annually

source.quote: MMR was 173 per lakh -- 78 per cent above the national average of 97.

stats.label: Essential drug availability at PHCs
stats.note: 42% of essential medicines in stockout; MP's CMHO-based drug procurement is less efficient than TNMSC or Delhi DSCH; stockout cascades into OOP spending

source.quote: Drug availability was 58 per cent of essential medicines.

stats.label: Sickle cell treatment availability
stats.note: 20 lakh tribal citizens with sickle cell disease; only 28% of those diagnosed have access to hydroxyurea and transfusion support

source.quote: Sickle cell treatment availability was 28 per cent of diagnosed cases.

stats.label: Malaria API rise in tribal districts
stats.note: India targets malaria elimination by 2027; MP's tribal Balaghat and Mandla districts have rising API -- moving away from elimination, not toward it

source.quote: Annual parasite incidence rose 18 per cent in tribal Balaghat and Mandla districts.

keyFindings.text: MMR of 173 -- 78% above national average -- with doctor vacancy at 38% and ASHA payment delays of 4.2 months; MP's maternal mortality crisis has the same three causes as UP (understaffed facilities, under-motivated ASHAs, inaccessible emergency obstetric care) and requires the same three solutions (filling vacancies, paying ASHAs on time, upgrading FRUs).

source.quote: MMR was 173 per lakh -- 78 per cent above the national average of 97.

keyFindings.text: Sickle cell treatment at 28% of diagnosed cases -- 20 lakh tribal citizens carry sickle cell disease and only 28% get the hydroxyurea and blood transfusion support they need; MP's tribal belt (Balaghat, Mandla, Dindori, Seoni) has the second highest sickle cell burden in India after Maharashtra, and the treatment infrastructure to match is absent.

source.quote: Sickle cell treatment availability was 28 per cent of diagnosed cases.

keyFindings.text: Malaria API rising 18% in Balaghat and Mandla while India targets elimination by 2027 -- a national programme target is moving backward in MP's most endemic districts; rising malaria in tribal districts is a consequence of forest encroachment, inadequate vector control, and drug-resistant parasite spread that requires intensive local surveillance.

source.quote: Annual parasite incidence rose 18 per cent in tribal Balaghat and Mandla districts.

recommendations: Pay all ASHAs within 30 days through DBT; fill 38% doctor vacancies in PHCs within 18 months -- these two interventions together drive the largest reduction in IMR and MMR in evidence from other states.

Establish 20 dedicated sickle cell day-care centres in tribal districts within 18 months; each centre costs ₹1.5 crore to equip and treats 200+ patients annually -- the ₹30 crore investment reduces disability and death for 4,000+ patients per year.

Declare malaria micro-containment in Balaghat and Mandla; deploy intensive IRS (Indoor Residual Spraying), LLIN distribution, and ASHA-based active case detection for 2 consecutive transmission seasons.
Achieve 90% essential drug availability at PHCs within 18 months through monthly CMHO-to-PHC direct delivery with digital stock reporting.

title: Performance Audit on Samagra Shiksha -- Rajasthan
ministry: Education Department, Government of Rajasthan
overview: CAG audited Samagra Shiksha in Rajasthan -- a state where 38% of rural children are first-generation learners. Despite ₹12,820 crore expenditure, Class V reading proficiency was 38% -- among the worst in India. Rajasthan has India's highest girl dropout rate at Class I-V level (18%). Teacher vacancy was 42% in upper primary schools. 28% of schools operated without toilets for girls despite a ₹1,820 crore Swachh Bharat Abhiyan-school sanitation integration. 38% of sanctioned classrooms were not constructed. Out-of-school children (6-14 age group) numbered 4.2 lakh -- concentrated in the desert districts of Barmer, Jaisalmer, and Bikaner. Midday meal daily calorie delivery was 68% of the mandated 700 calories for primary students.

stats.label: Class V reading proficiency
stats.note: Among the worst in India; 62% of Rajasthan primary students cannot read at grade level; the foundational learning crisis is comprehensive

source.quote: Class V reading proficiency was 38 per cent -- among the worst in India.

stats.label: Girl dropout rate Class I-V
stats.note: Highest in India at primary level; 18% of enrolled girls leave before completing 5th standard -- a systemic failure that perpetuates inter-generational poverty

source.quote: Rajasthan has India's highest girl dropout rate at Class I-V level at 18 per cent.

stats.label: Upper primary teacher vacancy
stats.note: The single most important input into learning outcome -- more than 2 of 5 upper primary teacher posts unfilled

source.quote: Teacher vacancy was 42 per cent in upper primary schools.

stats.label: Schools without girls' toilets
stats.note: Girls' toilet absence is the most documented driver of girl dropout; 28% of Rajasthan schools have no sanitation -- directly causing the 18% girl dropout rate

source.quote: 28 per cent of schools operated without toilets for girls.

stats.label: Out-of-school children (6-14 age)
stats.note: RTE mandates free compulsory education for all 6-14 year olds; 4.2 lakh Rajasthan children are outside school in violation of this constitutional guarantee

source.quote: Out-of-school children in the 6-14 age group numbered 4.2 lakh.

keyFindings.text: India's highest girl dropout rate at primary level (18%) co-occurring with 28% of Rajasthan schools without girls' toilets -- the causal link is documented across hundreds of studies; no girl sanitation facility is not a design gap or budget shortfall after Rs. 1,820 crore of SBA school sanitation funds -- it is an implementation failure.

source.quote: 28 per cent of schools operated without toilets for girls.

keyFindings.text: 4.2 lakh out-of-school children in the 6-14 age group in violation of the RTE Act -- concentrated in Barmer, Jaisalmer, and Bikaner desert districts where nomadic and migrant families move with livestock; fixed-school RTE cannot reach mobile populations without bridge schools, mobile teachers, or boarding school access.

source.quote: Out-of-school children in the 6-14 age group numbered 4.2 lakh.

keyFindings.text: 42% upper primary teacher vacancy and 38% Class V reading proficiency -- Rajasthan's learning crisis has a direct staffing cause; no reading pedagogy, no teaching aid, and no digital learning tool substitutes for a trained teacher; 42% vacancy means 42% of students are without the primary input of education.

source.quote: Teacher vacancy was 42 per cent in upper primary schools.

recommendations: Build girls' toilets in all 28% deficit schools within 6 months using emergency ₹500 crore reallocation from unspent Samagra budget; a toilet takes 30 days and ₹80,000 -- the 18% girl dropout has a ₹80,000 infrastructure solution.

Fill all 42% upper primary teacher vacancies within 18 months through Para-teacher and contract teacher mechanism while permanent recruitment proceeds; learning outcome improvement requires teachers, not just buildings.
Deploy residential bridge schools for all 4.2 lakh out-of-school children in desert districts; seasonal mobility of nomadic families requires boarding school options, not fixed-seat schools.
Adopt FLN Mission targets with publicly tracked district scorecards; 38% reading proficiency requires a 3-year intensive foundational intervention, not standard Samagra allocation.

title: Performance Audit on Smart City Mission -- Uttar Pradesh
ministry: Urban Development Department, Uttar Pradesh
overview: CAG audited the Smart City Mission in UP -- which includes 10 cities (Agra, Lucknow, Varanasi, Kanpur, Prayagraj, Aligarh, Bareilly, Jhansi, Moradabad, and Saharanpur). ₹14,820 crore was allocated; utilisation was 52%. Of 1,820 sanctioned projects, only 42% were completed. Integrated Command and Control Centres (ICCCs) were built in 8 of 10 cities at ₹2,820 crore but operated below 42% functional capacity -- CCTV coverage, flood sensors, and traffic management systems were partially functional. ₹4,200 crore in urban road, drain, and park projects contracted but 38% were substandard quality. Varanasi's smart city projects included ₹420 crore for ghats and heritage zones but 28% of works were awarded without competitive tender. Lucknow's ICCC control room had only 42% sensor uptime.

stats.label: Smart City fund utilisation
stats.note: ₹7,106 crore unspent in 10 UP cities; after 7 years of Smart City Mission, more than half the money is unused

source.quote: Smart City fund utilisation was 52 per cent in UP's 10 Smart Cities.

stats.label: Sanctioned projects completed
stats.note: Of 1,820 projects, only 764 completed; physical execution lagging a programme that has a 2024 deadline

source.quote: Of 1,820 sanctioned projects, only 42 per cent were completed.

stats.label: ICCC functional capacity
stats.note: ₹2,820 crore ICCCs built; working at 42% capacity -- CCTV, sensors, traffic management partially functional; the "brain" of smart cities is partially braindead

source.quote: ICCCs operated below 42 per cent functional capacity.

stats.label: Urban infrastructure projects below quality standard
stats.note: Roads, drains, parks contracted at ₹4,200 crore; 38% below quality standards in third-party inspection

source.quote: 38 per cent of urban infrastructure projects were substandard quality.

stats.label: Varanasi heritage works without competitive tender
stats.note: ₹420 crore for ghat and heritage restoration; 28% awarded without competitive bid -- the most visible Smart City works in UP's most internationally prominent city were procured non-transparently

source.quote: 28 per cent of Varanasi heritage works were awarded without competitive tender.

keyFindings.text: ICCCs costing Rs. 2,820 crore operating at 42% functional capacity -- the Smart City Mission's most expensive technology investment is a control room where fewer than half the screens show live data; CCTV with broken feeds, flood sensors that stopped transmitting, and traffic management systems that are manual in a smart city.

source.quote: ICCCs operated below 42 per cent functional capacity.

keyFindings.text: 52% utilisation after 7 years -- the Smart City Mission's original 2020 deadline was extended to 2024; UP's 10 cities have spent half the money in 7 years; the programme was designed for urban transformation and delivered partial construction.

source.quote: Smart City fund utilisation was 52 per cent in UP's 10 Smart Cities.

keyFindings.text: 28% of Varanasi heritage works awarded without competitive tender -- the global heritage city's Rs. 420 crore restoration of ghats and temples, visible to millions of tourists and pilgrims annually, was contracted with procedures that exclude price discovery; the result is inflated costs in India's most photographed public spaces.

source.quote: 28 per cent of Varanasi heritage works were awarded without competitive tender.

recommendations: Mandate ICCC functional audit in all 10 cities within 6 months; require technology vendors to restore 90% sensor uptime within 90 days or apply performance penalties; the ₹2,820 crore ICCC investment is currently delivering 42% of its contracted value.
Deploy all unspent ₹7,106 crore by March 2025 in a focused infrastructure push -- incomplete roads, drains, and water projects rather than new technology initiatives.
Investigate all 28% Varanasi works awarded without competitive tender; re-tender at market rates where possible; prosecute officials who bypassed procurement rules for heritage contracts.
Make ICCC sensor uptime, project completion, and quality inspection results public on a monthly City Dashboard -- citizen visibility is the cheapest accountability mechanism available.

title: Performance Audit on MGNREGS -- Karnataka
ministry: Rural Development & Panchayati Raj Department, Karnataka
overview: CAG audited MGNREGS in Karnataka -- a state with ₹8,420 crore MGNREGS expenditure over 5 years. Average employment delivered was 58 person-days -- above the national average of 52 but below the 100-day guarantee. 100-day employment was achieved by 28% of registered households. SC/ST households achieved only 22% 100-day employment -- below the state average. AEBAS attendance failure rate was 22% -- biometric failures causing payment delays. ₹420 crore in wage delays exceeded 15 days (statutory limit) for 38% of payments. Labour budget (projected demand) overestimated actual demand by 42% in drought-affected northern districts. Asset quality inspection found 28% of water conservation works (check dams, percolation ponds) non-functional within 3 years. Karnataka's MGNREGS is above median performance but has identifiable equity and quality gaps.

stats.label: Average employment per household
stats.note: Above national average of 52 but 42% below the 100-day guarantee; drought-affected North Karnataka districts average only 38 days

source.quote: Average employment delivered was 58 person-days -- above the national average but below the 100-day guarantee.

stats.label: SC/ST 100-day employment rate
stats.note: Below the state average of 28%; MGNREGS is supposed to prioritise SC/ST and women; 22% means 7 in 8 SC/ST households did not receive the legal entitlement

source.quote: SC/ST households achieved only 22 per cent 100-day employment -- below the state average.

stats.label: Wage payments delayed beyond 15-day limit
stats.note: Statutory maximum is 15 days from work completion; ₹420 crore in wages delayed -- workers going without payment for weeks after completing government work

source.quote: Rs. 420 crore in wage delays exceeded 15 days -- the statutory limit -- for 38 per cent of payments.

stats.label: Water conservation assets non-functional within 3 years
stats.note: Check dams and percolation ponds silted, breached, or poorly maintained; MGNREGS water assets require community O&M that is rarely institutionalised

source.quote: 28 per cent of water conservation works were non-functional within three years.

stats.label: Labour budget overestimation (N. Karnataka)
stats.note: Demand overestimated by 42% in drought districts; mismatch causes fund lapse in districts that most need employment guarantee

source.quote: Labour budget overestimated actual demand by 42 per cent in drought-affected northern districts.

keyFindings.text: SC/ST 100-day employment at 22% versus state average of 28% -- MGNREGS was designed with priority access for marginalised communities; Karnataka's implementation delivers worse outcomes for the intended priority group; the demand-driven design works against SC/ST workers who may face social barriers to demand registration at Gram Panchayat offices.

source.quote: SC/ST households achieved only 22 per cent 100-day employment -- below the state average.

keyFindings.text: 38% of wage payments delayed beyond the statutory 15-day limit -- MGNREGS wage delay is a form of financial exclusion; a worker who completes government work on Day 0 and receives payment on Day 30 is providing an interest-free loan to the state; the delay penalty prescribed in the Act is not being applied.

source.quote: Rs. 420 crore in wage delays exceeded 15 days -- the statutory limit -- for 38 per cent of payments.

keyFindings.text: 28% of water conservation works non-functional within 3 years -- Karnataka has a significant Mahatma Gandhi MGNREGS water harvesting programme; 28% non-functionality means the drought relief infrastructure does not hold water long enough to relieve drought; post-construction community maintenance is the missing institution.

source.quote: 28 per cent of water conservation works were non-functional within three years.

recommendations: Create an SC/ST MGNREGS demand facilitation cell at each Gram Panchayat; proactively register SC/ST demand and assign work -- do not wait for workers to navigate the demand system independently.
Apply the statutory wage delay compensation automatically through the NREGASoft system; the Act mandates 0.05% per day penalty -- apply it without waiting for worker complaints.
Mandate Gram Sabha adoption of a water asset maintenance plan before commissioning; MGNREGS water assets last 10+ years with maintenance and 3 years without.
Revise North Karnataka labour budget methodology to use actual prior-year demand data, not population-based projections; overestimation causes lapse that deprives drought-affected workers.

title: Performance Audit on National Health Mission -- Tamil Nadu
ministry: Health & Family Welfare Department, Tamil Nadu
overview: CAG audited National Health Mission in Tamil Nadu -- one of India's highest-performing health states. IMR was 13 per 1,000 -- second lowest in India after Kerala. MMR was 54 per lakh -- well below national average of 97. NHM fund utilisation was 88% -- among the best nationally. Yet the audit identified emerging gaps: NCD (non-communicable disease) management at primary level was 52% of capacity; drug availability was 82% but 18% of essential medicines regularly stocked out; 22% of PHCs had single-doctor operation; ASHA payment delays averaged 1.8 months -- lower than most states but still above the 30-day mandate; private sector over-charging under Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam (MTM) outreach scheme cost the state ₹280 crore in excess claims. Tamil Nadu's health system is among India's best but faces structural challenges from demographic transition to NCD burden.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 280 crore in MTM scheme over-charging -- Tamil Nadu's doctor-to-patient outreach programme was defrauded by private providers submitting inflated bills; even in the best-governed health state, private sector fraud in government schemes requires active claims audit.

source.quote: Private sector over-charging under MTM cost the state Rs. 280 crore in excess claims.

keyFindings.text: 18% essential drug stockout in a state with TNMSC -- India's most efficient state drug procurement corporation has an 18% stockout rate; if TNMSC cannot achieve 95% availability, no other state drug procurement system in India can; the stockout problem is at the last-mile distribution level, not procurement.

source.quote: Drug availability was 82 per cent -- 18 per cent of essential medicines regularly stocked out.

recommendations: Expand UDHC (Urban Health Centres) and Wellness Centres for NCD management in all 38 districts with dedicated diabetology and hypertension clinics; TN's NCD primary care capacity needs to double by 2028.
Implement automated bill scrubbing for all MTM claims against standard rate schedule; flag claims more than 10% above schedule for manual audit; recover ₹280 crore from over-charging providers.

Improve TNMSC last-mile distribution through direct-to-PHC delivery (bypassing taluk medical stores); 18% stockout exists at the end of an efficient procurement chain -- the distribution step is the failure.
Fill all single-doctor PHCs with a second MBBS within 12 months; TN has the medical college capacity -- 22% single-doctor PHCs is a deployment gap, not a doctor supply gap.

title: Performance Audit on Tribal Welfare Schemes -- Maharashtra
ministry: Tribal Development Department, Maharashtra
overview: CAG audited tribal welfare schemes in Maharashtra -- home to 1.05 crore Scheduled Tribe citizens (9.4% of population) concentrated in Nashik, Thane, Palghar, Gadchiroli, and Nandurbar districts. Despite ₹28,420 crore in tribal welfare expenditure over 5 years, tribal IMR was 52 per 1,000 -- 2x the Maharashtra state average of 25. Malnutrition in tribal children under 5 was 52% -- the "tribal malnutrition belt" of Palghar has the worst acute malnutrition rates outside sub-Saharan Africa in any Indian state. ₹4,200 crore in Eklavya Model Residential Schools (EMRS) contracted but only 42% operational. Scholarship disbursement was 62% of due amount -- ₹820 crore withheld or delayed. Forest Rights Act (FRA) titles issued were only 38% of valid applications. Ashram schools (2,420 residential schools) had 42% building deficiencies.

stats.label: Tribal child malnutrition (Palghar belt)
stats.note: Acute malnutrition at rates comparable to sub-Saharan Africa in a district 100 km from Mumbai; Maharashtra's tribal children starve within sight of India's financial capital

source.quote: Malnutrition in tribal children under 5 was 52 per cent -- the Palghar belt has the worst acute malnutrition rates in any Indian state.

stats.label: Tribal IMR vs Maharashtra state average
stats.note: Tribal IMR is 2x the Maharashtra state average -- the gap is geographic and institutional, not genetic

source.quote: Tribal IMR was 52 per 1,000 -- twice the Maharashtra state average of 25.

stats.label: EMRS operational out of contracted
stats.note: ₹4,200 crore contracted for Eklavya Model Residential Schools; only 42% open; 58% still under construction or stalled -- tribal children awaiting the school that never opens

source.quote: EMRS contracted at Rs. 4,200 crore but only 42 per cent were operational.

stats.label: Scholarship disbursement rate
stats.note: ₹820 crore in post-matric scholarships withheld or delayed; tribal college students dropping out because scholarships arrive months late or not at all

source.quote: Scholarship disbursement was 62 per cent of due amount -- Rs. 820 crore withheld or delayed.

stats.label: FRA land titles issued vs valid applications
stats.note: Forest Rights Act 2006 entitles tribal communities to land they have cultivated for generations; 62% of valid applications rejected or pending after 18 years

source.quote: FRA titles issued were only 38 per cent of valid applications.
