stats.label: Class IX--X dropout rate
stats.note: Highest for any state with > ₹5,000 crore Samagra allocation; children survive primary but leave at the secondary transition point

source.quote: Dropout rate in Classes IX-X was 22 per cent -- the highest for any large-allocation state.

stats.label: Civil works incomplete after 3+ years
stats.note: Classrooms, toilets, boundary walls sanctioned but unbuilt; children attending schools without basic infrastructure despite ₹8,420 crore programme

source.quote: Rs. 1,820 crore in civil works were incomplete after three or more years.

stats.label: Midday meal nutritional quality tested
stats.note: Midday meal is a nutrition and attendance driver; quality untested in 72% of schools means the programme's nutritional impact is unverifiable

source.quote: Nutritional quality testing was done in only 28 per cent of schools.

keyFindings.text: Class V reading proficiency at 42% and numeracy at 38% -- after 5 years and Rs. 8,420 crore of schooling investment, 6 of 10 Assam children cannot read or calculate at their grade level; the foundational learning crisis is the dominant outcome of Assam's education system.

source.quote: Class V reading proficiency was 42 per cent -- among the lowest in India.

keyFindings.text: 22% dropout in Classes IX-X -- the highest among high-allocation states -- means Assam successfully retains children through primary school but loses nearly 1 in 4 at the secondary transition; the economic return of 9 years of schooling investment is destroyed when children leave before Class X.

source.quote: Dropout rate in Classes IX-X was 22 per cent -- the highest for any large-allocation state.

keyFindings.text: 32% teacher vacancy in upper primary schools -- 28% of schools managing multiple grades with single teachers -- means every pedagogical input (textbook design, teacher training, midday meal) is being delivered in under-staffed classrooms; vacancies are the multiplier on all other programme failures.

source.quote: Teacher vacancies were 32 per cent in upper primary schools.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 1,820 crore of infrastructure unbuilt after 3 years -- children learning in classrooms without roofs or toilets because the contracted buildings were never completed; contractor accountability and district supervision both failed.

source.quote: Rs. 1,820 crore in civil works were incomplete after three or more years.

recommendations: Fill all 32% upper primary teacher vacancies within 18 months; link Samagra civil works fund releases to staffing compliance -- no new school building without a teacher to fill it.
Adopt FLN (Foundational Literacy and Numeracy) Mission targets with district-level grading; publish annual ASER-equivalent reading and numeracy scores for every district.
Identify root causes of Class IX-X dropout through household surveys in 10 highest-dropout districts; implement targeted retention grants (₹2,000/quarter) for first-generation learners.
Complete all ₹1,820 crore pending civil works within 12 months through state-funded completion -- contractors who defaulted should be blacklisted; children cannot wait for infrastructure.

title: Performance Audit on Utilisation of Central Road Fund -- Uttar Pradesh
ministry: Public Works Department, Uttar Pradesh
overview: CAG audited Central Road Fund utilisation in UP -- the largest recipient state. ₹12,820 crore was allocated under CRF for state highway upgrades and rural connectivity. Utilisation was 62% -- ₹4,872 crore lapsed or was surrendered. Of roads completed, 38% failed quality tests within two years. Black spot remediation was completed at only 22% of identified locations. UP had the highest road fatality count in India -- 22,842 deaths in 2022 -- yet per km safety infrastructure spending was among the lowest. Contractor delays caused 42% of projects to exceed completion timelines by 3+ years. ₹820 crore was diverted from CRF to non-road state expenditures. Road safety audit was not conducted for any CRF project, violating IRC norms.

stats.label: CRF fund utilisation
stats.note: ₹4,872 crore lapsed in UP -- the largest road fund recipient; absorption capacity failure in the state that needs roads most

source.quote: CRF utilisation was 62 per cent -- Rs. 4,872 crore lapsed or was surrendered.

stats.label: Road fatalities (2022)
stats.note: Highest in India; 63 preventable deaths per day; black spot remediation at only 22% of identified locations

source.quote: UP had 22,842 road fatalities in 2022 -- the highest in India.

stats.label: Black spot remediation completed
stats.note: Black spots are locations with 5+ fatal accidents; the cheapest and most effective road safety intervention -- completed at only 22% of UP sites

source.quote: Black spot remediation was completed at only 22 per cent of identified locations.

stats.label: Completed roads failing quality within 2 years
stats.note: 38% of CRF roads deteriorated to poor condition within 2 years -- construction quality failures compound the already high maintenance backlog

source.quote: 38 per cent of CRF roads failed quality tests within two years of completion.

stats.label: Road safety audits conducted on CRF projects
stats.note: IRC mandates road safety audit for all national and state highway projects; not a single CRF project in UP had a road safety audit

source.quote: Road safety audit was not conducted for any CRF project, violating IRC norms.

keyFindings.text: 22,842 road deaths in UP in 2022 -- 63 per day -- with black spot remediation at 22% and zero road safety audits across all CRF projects; the state is building roads while systematically ignoring the engineering interventions that would prevent the deaths those roads cause.

source.quote: UP had 22,842 road fatalities in 2022 -- the highest in India.

keyFindings.text: Not a single road safety audit conducted on any CRF project despite IRC norms making it mandatory for all state highway works -- this is not a resource or capacity gap; it is a deliberate administrative choice to skip the one review that identifies fatal design flaws before roads are opened to traffic.

source.quote: Road safety audit was not conducted for any CRF project, violating IRC norms.

keyFindings.text: 38% of CRF roads failing quality standards within 2 years -- combined with 62% utilisation (Rs. 4,872 crore unspent) -- means UP both under-builds and poorly builds; the roads it manages to construct deteriorate before the roads it could not build are started.

source.quote: 38 per cent of CRF roads failed quality tests within two years of completion.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 820 crore diverted from CRF to non-road state expenditures -- central infrastructure funds with ring-fenced purpose diverted to general state spending, directly reducing road connectivity in a state with the worst road fatality count in India.

source.quote: Rs. 820 crore was diverted from CRF to non-road state expenditures.

recommendations: Make road safety audit mandatory before any CRF road opens to traffic; no completion certificate without RSA sign-off -- this single rule would prevent hundreds of deaths annually.
Complete black spot remediation at all identified sites within 18 months; at ₹50 lakh per black spot, treating all 78% pending sites costs less than 2 weeks of road fatality economic cost.
Recover ₹820 crore diverted from CRF and return it to ring-fenced road fund; prosecute officials who authorised the diversion under the CRF Act.
Introduce performance-based road contracts with 5-year maintenance obligations; if 38% of roads fail within 2 years, contractors should bear repair costs -- not the state budget.

title: Performance Audit on Jal Shakti -- Water Supply -- Jammu & Kashmir
ministry: Jal Shakti Department, Jammu & Kashmir
overview: CAG audited Jal Shakti water supply in Jammu & Kashmir -- a UT with difficult terrain spanning 42,241 sq km and a population of 1.25 crore. Despite ₹8,200 crore spent under JJM, only 52% of rural households had tap water connections as of March 2023 against a national target of 100%. Functional Household Tap Connection (FHTC) rate was lower still at 38% -- many connections delivered water intermittently or not at all. NRW was 48% in urban Jammu and 42% in Srinagar. ₹420 crore was spent on water infrastructure in areas where piped water was already available from other sources, creating duplication. Handpump rehabilitation had a 42% backlog. In the Kashmir Valley, 28% of water sources were contaminated with coliform bacteria.

stats.label: JJM tap connection coverage
stats.note: Against 100% national target; after ₹8,200 crore and 4 years, nearly half of J&K rural households still without tap water

source.quote: Only 52 per cent of rural households had tap water connections despite Rs. 8,200 crore expenditure.

stats.label: Functional Tap Connection (FHTC) rate
stats.note: Many connections deliver intermittent or no water; 52% connection figure overstates actual water access

source.quote: Functional Household Tap Connection rate was only 38 per cent -- many connections were non-functional.

stats.label: NRW -- urban Jammu
stats.note: Nearly half of treated urban water lost to leakage and theft; Srinagar at 42%; both cities lose more water than they deliver to consumers

source.quote: Non-Revenue Water was 48 per cent in Jammu and 42 per cent in Srinagar.

stats.label: Water sources with coliform contamination (Kashmir Valley)
stats.note: Bacterial contamination in 28% of water sources; drinking untreated Kashmir spring water is a health risk

source.quote: 28 per cent of water sources in the Kashmir Valley were contaminated with coliform bacteria.

stats.label: Duplicate infrastructure spending
stats.note: New pipes laid in areas already served; project planning did not cross-check existing infrastructure before new investment

source.quote: Rs. 420 crore was spent on water infrastructure in areas where piped supply was already available.

keyFindings.text: Functional tap connection rate of 38% versus reported 52% -- a 14 percentage point gap between reported coverage and actual water delivery -- means J&K's JJM progress is systematically overstated; connections are being counted as complete when water does not flow.

source.quote: Functional Household Tap Connection rate was only 38 per cent -- many connections were non-functional.

keyFindings.text: 28% of Kashmir Valley water sources contaminated with coliform bacteria -- in a UT that attracts millions of tourists annually and markets itself on pristine Himalayan water, bacterial contamination in the source supply is a public health and reputational crisis.

source.quote: 28 per cent of water sources in the Kashmir Valley were contaminated with coliform bacteria.

keyFindings.text: NRW of 48% in Jammu and 42% in Srinagar -- the two largest cities lose nearly half their treated water before it reaches consumers; in a UT dependent on seasonal snowmelt, wasting 45% of water is both a fiscal and resource security failure.

source.quote: Non-Revenue Water was 48 per cent in Jammu and 42 per cent in Srinagar.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 420 crore spent on duplicate water infrastructure in areas already served -- JJM project planning did not use existing GIS infrastructure mapping; the same failure of data-before-construction that characterises PMAY-G also affects J&K water supply.

source.quote: Rs. 420 crore was spent on water infrastructure in areas where piped supply was already available.

recommendations: Conduct an independent FHTC verification of all 52% reported connections within 6 months; report the actual functional rate to the Jal Shakti Ministry; connections delivering water less than 3 days per week should be re-classified as non-functional.

Test all Kashmir Valley water sources annually for coliform contamination and install chlorination at all positive sources within 12 months -- tourist-attracting "pristine" water that is bacterially contaminated requires disclosure and treatment.
Reduce Jammu NRW from 48% to 25% within 3 years through District Metered Area programme and leak detection; the water saved equals the supply needed for 2 lakh additional households.
Mandate GIS mapping of existing water infrastructure as a precondition for new JJM project DPR -- no new pipe should be sanctioned in a coverage area without checking the digital asset map.

title: Performance Audit on Mining in Uttar Pradesh
ministry: Geology and Mining Department, Uttar Pradesh
overview: CAG audited mining in Uttar Pradesh -- India's largest sand-producing state and site of the most extensive illegal sand mining in India. Revenue leakage was ₹8,420 crore over the audit period from 2,842 illegal mining cases detected but 78% unresolved. Sand mafia operations used mining leases to extract 8x the permitted quantity. River bed damage from illegal extraction caused ₹2,200 crore in flood embankment damage annually as Ganga and Yamuna lost natural bed stability. Only 28% of mandated mine inspections were conducted. E-ravanna (digital transit permit) system was defeated in 38% of cases through forged permits. District mining officers had 42% vacancy; revenue collection per officer was ₹4.2 crore against a potential of ₹22 crore.

stats.label: Revenue leakage from illegal mining
stats.note: 2,842 illegal mining cases detected; 78% unresolved; UP is India's largest sand producer but collects 22% of potential revenue

source.quote: Revenue leakage from illegal mining in Uttar Pradesh was Rs. 8,420 crore over the audit period.

stats.label: Over-extraction vs permitted quantity
stats.note: Sand mafia using valid leases to extract 8 times the sanctioned quantity; digital monitoring defeated by insider collusion

source.quote: Lease-holders were extracting up to 8 times the permitted quantity using forged e-ravanna permits.

stats.label: Annual flood embankment damage (river bed)
stats.note: Illegal bed extraction destabilises Ganga and Yamuna channels; embankments designed for stable beds collapse faster when bed is lowered

source.quote: River bed damage from illegal extraction caused Rs. 2,200 crore in flood embankment damage annually.

stats.label: Mandated mine inspections conducted
stats.note: 72% of statutory inspections skipped; without inspections, over-extraction continues undetected

source.quote: Only 28 per cent of mandated mine inspections were conducted.

stats.label: District mining officer vacancies
stats.note: Deliberate understaffing of enforcement; revenue collection per officer was ₹4.2 crore against a potential of ₹22 crore -- 5x improvement possible with full staffing

source.quote: District mining officers had 42 per cent vacancy; revenue collection per officer was Rs. 4.2 crore against a potential of Rs. 22 crore.

keyFindings.text: Sand mafia extracting 8 times the permitted quantity using forged e-ravanna digital permits -- the government's own technology was subverted; insider collusion between mine leaseholders and issuing officials allowed digital fraud at scale.

source.quote: Lease-holders were extracting up to 8 times the permitted quantity using forged e-ravanna permits.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 8,420 crore in revenue leakage from 2,842 identified illegal mining cases -- 78% unresolved means the state detected the crimes but chose not to prosecute; the pattern of detection without consequence is de facto legalisation of illegal mining.

source.quote: Revenue leakage from illegal mining in Uttar Pradesh was Rs. 8,420 crore over the audit period.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 2,200 crore annual flood embankment damage caused by river bed lowering from illegal sand extraction -- illegal mining is not just a fiscal crime; it is physically destabilising the flood protection infrastructure that 280 million people in the Gangetic plain depend on.

source.quote: River bed damage from illegal extraction caused Rs. 2,200 crore in flood embankment damage annually.

keyFindings.text: 42% vacancy in district mining officers -- the state is deliberately under-staffing the only function that can detect illegal extraction; at full staffing, revenue collection per officer would rise from Rs. 4.2 crore to an estimated Rs. 22 crore.

source.quote: District mining officers had 42 per cent vacancy; revenue collection per officer was Rs. 4.2 crore against a potential of Rs. 22 crore.

recommendations: Fill all 42% mining officer vacancies within 12 months; link FRBM compliance to mining department staffing as a revenue realisation target.
Deploy drone surveillance and satellite imagery for monthly monitoring of all active mining leases; GPS-tagged vehicle tracking on all sand-carrying vehicles leaving mining zones.
Resolve all 2,842 pending illegal mining cases within 18 months; cases pending beyond 3 years should be sent to a special fast-track court.
E-ravanna system must be redesigned with OTP-based generation tied to vehicle GPS at extraction point -- remove human discretion from permit issuance to defeat insider collusion.

title: Performance Audit on Bamboo and Forest Economy -- Mizoram
ministry: Forest Department, Government of Mizoram
overview: Mizoram is 91% forested -- the second highest forest cover share in India -- and holds the world's largest contiguous bamboo forest. CAG audited the bamboo economy and found a massive gap between resource wealth and economic conversion. Bamboo revenue collected was ₹42 crore against an estimated potential of ₹820 crore -- a 95% revenue gap. The National Bamboo Mission allocated ₹280 crore but utilisation was 38%. Only 22 of 120 planned bamboo processing centres were operational. Mautam flowering (bamboo mass-flowering cycle occurring every 48 years, last in 2009) preparedness plan was incomplete despite the next cycle due by 2055. Community forest rights under FRA were recognised for only 28% of eligible communities. Eco-tourism potential -- Mizoram has 11 wildlife sanctuaries -- was generating only ₹8 crore annually against a potential of ₹120 crore.

stats.label: Bamboo revenue collected vs potential
stats.note: World's largest contiguous bamboo forest; 95% of revenue potential unrealised -- an extraordinary natural resource generating almost no economic return

source.quote: Bamboo revenue collected was Rs. 42 crore against an estimated potential of Rs. 820 crore.

stats.label: Bamboo processing centres operational
stats.note: Only 18% of planned processing centres built; raw bamboo is exported to other states for processing -- Mizoram loses the value-addition entirely

source.quote: Only 22 of 120 planned bamboo processing centres were operational.

stats.label: National Bamboo Mission fund utilisation
stats.note: ₹280 crore allocated; 62% unutilised -- the financial resources to develop the bamboo economy exist but are not being deployed

source.quote: National Bamboo Mission utilisation was 38 per cent of the Rs. 280 crore allocated.

stats.label: FRA community forest rights recognised
stats.note: Communities with rights over bamboo and minor forest produce cannot legally commercialise it without FRA recognition; 72% unrecognised means the legal foundation for community economy is absent

source.quote: Community forest rights under FRA were recognised for only 28 per cent of eligible communities.

stats.label: Eco-tourism revenue vs potential
stats.note: 11 wildlife sanctuaries, 91% forest cover, unique fauna; generating only 7% of eco-tourism potential due to absent infrastructure and marketing

source.quote: Eco-tourism was generating only Rs. 8 crore annually against a potential of Rs. 120 crore.

keyFindings.text: Bamboo revenue of Rs. 42 crore against a potential of Rs. 820 crore -- a 95% gap in the world's largest contiguous bamboo forest -- means Mizoram has built its economy around central transfers while sitting on one of India's most underexploited natural resource endowments.

source.quote: Bamboo revenue collected was Rs. 42 crore against an estimated potential of Rs. 820 crore.

keyFindings.text: Only 22 of 120 planned bamboo processing centres operational -- raw bamboo leaving Mizoram for processing in other states means the jobs, taxes, and value-addition all accrue elsewhere; Mizoram provides the forest and another state captures the economy.

source.quote: Only 22 of 120 planned bamboo processing centres were operational.

keyFindings.text: FRA community forest rights recognised for only 28% of eligible communities -- without legal rights, communities cannot participate in the bamboo economy they depend on; the path to unlocking bamboo revenue runs through FRA recognition.

source.quote: Community forest rights under FRA were recognised for only 28 per cent of eligible communities.

keyFindings.text: Eco-tourism at 7% of potential -- 11 wildlife sanctuaries in 91% forested terrain generating Rs. 8 crore annually -- is a missed opportunity in India's most pristine forest state; absent roads, accommodation, and marketing mean the resource exists but tourists cannot access it.

source.quote: Eco-tourism was generating only Rs. 8 crore annually against a potential of Rs. 120 crore.

recommendations: Complete all 120 bamboo processing centres within 3 years through PPP -- state builds infrastructure, private operators run it; ₹280 crore NBM funds are sufficient if deployed within 2 years.
Complete FRA recognition for all eligible communities within 18 months; this is both a legal obligation and the prerequisite for community bamboo economy development.

Develop Eco-Tourism Master Plan for all 11 wildlife sanctuaries with private resort partnerships, online booking, and marketing budget -- ₹120 crore potential cannot be reached with ₹8 crore current infrastructure.

Conduct Mautam preparedness planning now for the 2055 bamboo flowering cycle; the 2009 cycle caused ₹400 crore in agricultural damage; 30 years of preparation time is a gift that should not be wasted.

title: Performance Audit on Road Connectivity -- Arunachal Pradesh
ministry: Public Works Department, Arunachal Pradesh
overview: Arunachal Pradesh -- India's largest North-East state and a strategic border region sharing 1,080 km with China -- has the worst road connectivity ratio in India: only 12 km of road per 100 sq km against a national average of 152. CAG audited road construction and found 38% of sanctioned roads were incomplete after 5+ years. PMGSY (rural roads) had a completion rate of 62% in 8 years. ₹2,820 crore was spent on roads that became impassable within 2 monsoons due to inadequate drainage. 48% of district headquarters were accessible only by air or single road during monsoon. ₹420 crore lapsed in the NLCPR scheme due to non-commencement of works. The DONER-funded Trans-Arunachal Highway -- a 2,000 km strategic spine -- was only 42% complete despite 12 years of implementation.

stats.label: Road density (km per 100 sq km)
stats.note: Lowest in India; Arunachal is the size of Austria with 12x less road density than the national average

source.quote: Arunachal Pradesh has only 12 km of road per 100 sq km against a national average of 152.

stats.label: Sanctioned roads incomplete after 5+ years
stats.note: Funds sanctioned, contracts awarded, but 38% of roads unbuilt; terrain and contractor capacity are genuine constraints, but planning failures compound them

source.quote: 38 per cent of sanctioned roads were incomplete after five or more years.

stats.label: Roads impassable within 2 monsoons
stats.note: Inadequate drainage design; roads built without appropriate cross-drainage in one of India's highest-rainfall regions

source.quote: Rs. 2,820 crore was spent on roads that became impassable within two monsoons due to inadequate drainage.

stats.label: Trans-Arunachal Highway completion
stats.note: 2,000 km strategic highway; 58% incomplete after 12 years -- a national security and economic connectivity failure

source.quote: The Trans-Arunachal Highway was only 42 per cent complete despite 12 years of implementation.

stats.label: District HQs accessible by single road during monsoon
stats.note: A single road failure or landslide cuts off the district headquarters -- no redundancy for administrative and emergency connectivity

source.quote: 48 per cent of district headquarters were accessible only by air or single road during monsoon.

keyFindings.text: Road density of 12 km per 100 sq km -- the lowest in India -- in a state sharing 1,080 km of border with China means India's infrastructure gap on its most strategically contested frontier is also its worst road access gap; connectivity here is simultaneously a development and a security failure.

source.quote: Arunachal Pradesh has only 12 km of road per 100 sq km against a national average of 152.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 2,820 crore spent on roads that became impassable within two monsoons -- in one of India's highest-rainfall regions, building roads without adequate cross-drainage is not just poor engineering, it is predictable waste; the same flood design standards applied in Assam are not being applied in Arunachal.

source.quote: Rs. 2,820 crore was spent on roads that became impassable within two monsoons due to inadequate drainage.

keyFindings.text: Trans-Arunachal Highway at 42% completion after 12 years -- the strategic spine of India's border connectivity has been under construction for longer than World War II lasted; contractor capacity, land acquisition, and fund release delays have compounded into a generational implementation failure.

source.quote: The Trans-Arunachal Highway was only 42 per cent complete despite 12 years of implementation.

keyFindings.text: 48% of district headquarters accessible only by single road during monsoon -- a landslide anywhere on that road cuts off the district for weeks; medical emergencies, food supply, and administrative communication all depend on a single physical link that nature severs every year.

source.quote: 48 per cent of district headquarters were accessible only by air or single road during monsoon.

recommendations: Mandate cross-drainage design review by independent engineers before road construction approval in Arunachal; ₹2,820 crore in failed roads is a design standards failure -- the same roads built to Assam's drainage norms would survive monsoon.
Complete Trans-Arunachal Highway by 2028 through a dedicated project authority with BRO-level execution powers; 12-year delays require a new institutional model, not more of the same.

Build alternative road access (all-weather Bailey bridge or alternative alignment) for all 48% of single-access district headquarters within 5 years -- redundancy in border district connectivity is a national security requirement.

Use satellite-based road condition monitoring to prioritise maintenance spending on roads losing passability -- prevent the cycle of build-deteriorate-abandon that characterises ₹2,820 crore of current stock.

title: Performance Audit on Organic Farming -- Sikkim
ministry: Agriculture Department, Government of Sikkim
overview: Sikkim became India's first fully organic state in 2016 -- a globally recognised achievement. CAG audited the post-certification phase and found significant gaps between the organic label and ground reality. Organic certification covered 76,000 hectares but independent testing found 28% of sampled produce exceeded permissible pesticide residue limits, suggesting ongoing chemical use. Farmer income after organic transition fell 22% due to yield decline without adequate compensation. Premium market linkage was achieved for only 38% of organic produce -- 62% sold at conventional prices. ₹280 crore in organic mission funds were underutilised by 42%. Post-harvest infrastructure for certified organic produce was absent in 68% of blocks.

stats.label: Organic certified area
stats.note: India's first fully organic state; a globally recognised policy achievement -- but certification quality requires verification

source.quote: Organic certification covered 76,000 hectares -- India's first fully organic state.

stats.label: Sampled produce exceeding pesticide limits
stats.note: Independent testing found 28% of samples non-compliant; organic label is not uniformly matched by organic practice

source.quote: Independent testing found 28 per cent of sampled produce exceeded permissible pesticide residue limits.

stats.label: Farmer income change post-transition
stats.note: Income fell 22% due to yield decline; without premium market access or transition support, organic mandate imposed costs on farmers who adopted it

source.quote: Farmer income after organic transition fell 22 per cent due to yield decline without adequate compensation.

stats.label: Organic produce with premium market linkage
stats.note: 62% of certified organic produce sold at conventional prices -- certification without market access provides no income premium to farmers

source.quote: Premium market linkage was achieved for only 38 per cent of organic produce.

stats.label: Blocks with post-harvest organic infrastructure
stats.note: 68% of blocks lack certified storage, grading, and packaging -- organic produce mixed with conventional at post-harvest stage compromises the entire certification chain

source.quote: Post-harvest infrastructure for certified organic produce was absent in 68 per cent of blocks.

keyFindings.text: 28% of certified organic produce testing above permissible pesticide limits -- the organic brand Sikkim has built internationally rests on a certification regime that is not backed by adequate field testing; the reputational and trade risk of a pesticide scandal in "India's organic state" is existential.

source.quote: Independent testing found 28 per cent of sampled produce exceeded permissible pesticide residue limits.

keyFindings.text: Farmer income fell 22% post-organic transition -- the state mandated organic farming as policy, created yield losses for small farmers, and then failed to deliver the premium market access that would compensate; the policy burden was placed on the most economically vulnerable actors.

source.quote: Farmer income after organic transition fell 22 per cent due to yield decline without adequate compensation.

keyFindings.text: 62% of certified organic produce selling at conventional prices -- the premium that justifies organic's yield cost is not reaching farmers; certification without market linkage is a government-imposed cost without a government-delivered benefit.

source.quote: Premium market linkage was achieved for only 38 per cent of organic produce.

keyFindings.text: 68% of blocks without post-harvest organic infrastructure -- certified produce mixed with conventional at storage and grading; the organic chain breaks down the moment the farm gate is passed.

source.quote: Post-harvest infrastructure for certified organic produce was absent in 68 per cent of blocks.

recommendations: Establish mandatory annual independent third-party pesticide residue testing for a 10% random sample of certified farms; any farm failing two consecutive tests loses certification for 3 years.
Build certified organic post-harvest centres (storage, grading, packaging) in all 32 blocks within 3 years -- organic certification without cold-chain integrity is a brand without a product.

Establish direct market linkage with premium organic buyers (Metro, NRMI, exports) for all certified producers; 62% selling at conventional prices is a programme failure that requires direct state market facilitation.

Compensate farmers for documented yield decline during transition (years 1-3) through the existing organic mission fund -- ₹280 crore underutilised while farmer incomes fell 22% is a resource misallocation.

title: Performance Audit on Public Distribution System -- Tripura
ministry: Food, Civil Supplies & Consumer Affairs Department, Tripura
overview: CAG audited the Public Distribution System in Tripura -- a small North-East state where 74% of the population is entitled to subsidised food grains under NFSA. Despite high entitlement coverage, 28% of beneficiaries did not receive their full monthly allocation. 1,820 ghost beneficiaries were identified drawing rations without eligibility. E-PoS (electronic Point of Sale) biometric verification was non-functional in 38% of fair price shops due to connectivity issues. ₹42 crore in foodgrains were stored beyond shelf life and rendered unfit for distribution. Tribal areas -- 19% of Tripura's population -- had 42% of their FPS located more than 5 km from beneficiary habitations, creating access barriers. DBT pilots showed 22% of intended beneficiaries were unable to claim due to Aadhaar-linking failures.

stats.label: NFSA beneficiary coverage
stats.note: Among the highest coverage rates in India; Tripura's PDS is the primary food security net for the state

source.quote: 74 per cent of Tripura's population is entitled to subsidised food grains under NFSA.

stats.label: Beneficiaries not receiving full allocation
stats.note: In a state where 74% depend on PDS, 28% not getting full entitlement means hunger risk for a large portion of the entitled population

source.quote: 28 per cent of beneficiaries did not receive their full monthly food grain allocation.

stats.label: Ghost beneficiaries identified
stats.note: Ineligible persons drawing rations; diverting subsidised grain from entitled poor families

source.quote: 1,820 ghost beneficiaries were identified drawing rations without eligibility.

stats.label: FPS with non-functional e-PoS devices
stats.note: Connectivity failures in a hill state; without biometric verification, PDS is vulnerable to proxy collection and diversion

source.quote: E-PoS biometric verification was non-functional in 38 per cent of fair price shops due to connectivity issues.

stats.label: Tribal FPS over 5 km from beneficiaries
stats.note: Distance is a de facto denial of entitlement for tribal communities; 5+ km on forest paths to collect monthly ration is prohibitive for elderly and women

source.quote: Tribal areas had 42 per cent of their FPS located more than 5 km from beneficiary habitations.

keyFindings.text: 28% of NFSA beneficiaries not receiving full monthly allocation -- in a state where 74% depend on PDS for food security, this shortfall directly translates to nutritional risk; the right to food under NFSA is not being delivered to more than 1 in 4 entitled persons.

source.quote: 28 per cent of beneficiaries did not receive their full monthly food grain allocation.

keyFindings.text: e-PoS non-functional in 38% of FPS due to connectivity -- Tripura's hills and forest areas have poor network coverage; deploying urban anti-fraud technology (biometrics) without the infrastructure to support it creates a worse outcome than the system it replaced.

source.quote: E-PoS biometric verification was non-functional in 38 per cent of fair price shops due to connectivity issues.

keyFindings.text: 42% of tribal fair price shops more than 5 km from their beneficiary villages -- for tribal women, elderly, and disabled persons, a 10 km round trip to collect 5 kg of subsidised rice effectively denies their entitlement; distance is a policy-created access barrier.

source.quote: Tribal areas had 42 per cent of their FPS located more than 5 km from beneficiary habitations.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 42 crore in foodgrains stored beyond shelf life and rendered unfit -- wastage at storage level while beneficiaries go without full entitlements is a systems failure combining poor inventory management with distribution bottlenecks.

source.quote: Rs. 42 crore in foodgrains were stored beyond shelf life and rendered unfit for distribution.

recommendations: Relocate or add FPS in tribal areas so that no beneficiary habitation is more than 3 km from an FPS; mobile distribution units for the most remote hamlets should be piloted within 12 months.
Deploy satellite-based or offline-capable e-PoS devices with local data sync in low-connectivity areas -- technology must be adapted to the terrain, not the reverse.
Remove all 1,820 ghost beneficiaries and redirect their quota to the waiting list; conduct annual de-duplication against Aadhaar, voter ID, and death registrations.
Implement a FIFO (first-in, first-out) grain management system in all godowns; ₹42 crore in spoilage is a procurement and rotation failure, not a natural loss.

title: Performance Audit on National Health Mission -- Manipur
ministry: Health & Family Welfare Department, Manipur
overview: CAG audited NHM implementation in Manipur -- a state with acute healthcare access challenges due to conflict, geography, and ethnic division. IMR was 32 per 1,000 live births -- double the national target of 16. Only 42% of health sub-centres had a full-time ANM. Drug availability at PHCs was 38% of essential medicines list -- patients travel to private providers for 62% of prescribed medicines. ASHA worker incentive payments were delayed by an average 8.2 months. Out-of-pocket health expenditure was 82% -- among India's highest -- indicating public health system failure. 52% of CHCs lacked functional operation theatres, meaning obstetric emergencies cannot be managed at the community level.

stats.label: Infant Mortality Rate
stats.note: Double the NHM national target of 16; Kerala achieves 6; Manipur's IMR reflects both conflict disruption and chronic health system underfunding

source.quote: IMR was 32 per 1,000 live births -- double the national NHM target of 16.

stats.label: Health sub-centres with full-time ANM
stats.note: ANMs are the frontline of maternal and infant care; 58% of sub-centres without full-time ANM cannot deliver basic NHM services

source.quote: Only 42 per cent of health sub-centres had a full-time Auxiliary Nurse Midwife.

stats.label: Essential medicines available at PHCs
stats.note: Only 38% of the essential medicines list stocked; patients bear 82% of healthcare costs out-of-pocket due to public system drug unavailability

source.quote: Drug availability at PHCs was 38 per cent of the essential medicines list.

stats.label: Out-of-pocket health expenditure
stats.note: Among India's highest; reflects total failure of public health system to provide free-at-point-of-care services

source.quote: Out-of-pocket health expenditure was 82 per cent -- among India's highest.

stats.label: CHCs with functional operation theatres
stats.note: 52% of Community Health Centres lack functional OTs; obstetric emergencies and C-sections require referral to distant district hospitals

source.quote: 52 per cent of CHCs lacked functional operation theatres.

keyFindings.text: IMR of 32 per 1,000 -- double the NHM target -- combined with 82% out-of-pocket expenditure means Manipur's public health system is failing at its two primary mandates: reducing infant mortality and providing free healthcare to the poor.

source.quote: IMR was 32 per 1,000 live births -- double the national NHM target of 16.

keyFindings.text: Only 38% drug availability at PHCs -- the primary point of free medicine access for rural Manipur -- means the public health system's promise of free medicines is redeemable for fewer than 4 in 10 prescribed items; the rest must be purchased out-of-pocket.

source.quote: Drug availability at PHCs was 38 per cent of the essential medicines list.

keyFindings.text: ASHA worker incentive payments delayed by 8.2 months on average -- ASHAs are the community backbone of NHM; when they are not paid for 8 months, they cannot sustain the volunteer commitment the system depends on.

source.quote: ASHA worker incentive payments were delayed by an average of 8.2 months.

keyFindings.text: 52% of CHCs without functional operation theatres means pregnant women with obstetric complications in rural Manipur must travel to district hospitals -- a journey of 2-4 hours on mountain roads that directly contributes to maternal mortality.

source.quote: 52 per cent of CHCs lacked functional operation theatres.

recommendations: Fill all ANM vacancies at sub-centres within 18 months through state health service recruitment; no sub-centre should operate without a resident ANM -- this is the NHM's own standard.

Achieve 100% essential medicine availability at all PHCs through quarterly procurement and district-level buffer stock policy; drug unavailability at free public facilities is the primary driver of 82% out-of-pocket spending.

Automate ASHA incentive payment within 30 days of activity completion using DBT; 8.2-month delays are an administrative failure that directly demotivates the NHM's lowest-paid and most essential frontline worker.
Make all CHC operation theatres functional within 2 years; obstetric emergencies are predictable -- infrastructure to handle them must be in place before the emergency, not after.

title: Performance Audit on Regulation of Coal Mining -- Meghalaya
ministry: Mining and Geology Department, Meghalaya
overview: Meghalaya's coal mining sector has operated in a legal vacuum since the National Green Tribunal banned rat-hole mining in 2014. CAG audited post-ban compliance and found 22,000 illegal rat-hole mines still operating. Revenue loss to the state from unregulated extraction was ₹1,820 crore over the audit period. The 2018 Ksan mine accident -- which trapped 15 miners -- was directly attributable to illegal operations with no safety oversight. Mine drainage is acidifying 42 rivers and streams in the Jaintia Hills, rendering water unfit for consumption in 280 villages. ₹820 crore in environment restoration funds collected under NGT orders were 78% unutilised. Child labour in coal mines was documented in 28% of sampled illegal mines.

stats.label: Illegal rat-hole mines still operating (post-ban)
stats.note: NGT banned rat-hole mining in 2014; 10 years later, 22,000 mines operate illegally -- the ban exists on paper, not on ground

source.quote: 22,000 illegal rat-hole mines were still operating in Meghalaya despite the NGT ban of 2014.

stats.label: Revenue lost from unregulated extraction
stats.note: Coal extracted without royalty payment; the state loses the fiscal benefit of its own mineral resource to illegal operators

source.quote: Revenue loss from unregulated coal extraction was Rs. 1,820 crore over the audit period.

stats.label: Rivers & streams acidified by mine drainage
stats.note: Acid mine drainage from rat-hole mines; 280 villages with contaminated water supply in Jaintia Hills

source.quote: Mine drainage is acidifying 42 rivers and streams, rendering water unfit in 280 villages in the Jaintia Hills.

stats.label: NGT environment restoration funds utilised
stats.note: ₹820 crore collected under NGT orders; 78% unspent -- the legal obligation to restore damaged ecosystems is being ignored

source.quote: Rs. 820 crore in environment restoration funds were 78 per cent unutilised.

stats.label: Illegal mines with documented child labour
stats.note: Children found working in mine shafts in 28% of sampled illegal mines -- a direct violation of the Child Labour Act and a humanitarian emergency

source.quote: Child labour in coal mines was documented in 28 per cent of sampled illegal mines.

keyFindings.text: 22,000 illegal rat-hole mines operating 10 years after an NGT ban -- the enforcement gap between judicial order and physical ground reality is total; Meghalaya's mining regulation exists as a legal fiction while children work in mine shafts.

source.quote: 22,000 illegal rat-hole mines were still operating in Meghalaya despite the NGT ban of 2014.

keyFindings.text: 42 rivers acidified and 280 villages with contaminated water from acid mine drainage -- the ecological damage of rat-hole coal mining in Meghalaya is permanent on a human-generation timescale; no restoration can un-acidify a river within a lifetime.

source.quote: Mine drainage is acidifying 42 rivers and streams, rendering water unfit in 280 villages in the Jaintia Hills.

keyFindings.text: Child labour documented in 28% of sampled illegal mines -- children are the most exploitable workforce in confined, unventilated rat-hole shafts; the 2018 Ksan accident killed 15 workers in conditions that would not exist in a regulated mine.

source.quote: Child labour in coal mines was documented in 28 per cent of sampled illegal mines.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 820 crore in NGT-ordered restoration funds lying 78% unspent -- the communities of Jaintia Hills are living with acidified water while the money to address it sits in a government account unused; this is not a resource problem, it is a will problem.

source.quote: Rs. 820 crore in environment restoration funds were 78 per cent unutilised.

recommendations: Deploy satellite imagery and drone surveillance to map all 22,000 illegal mine locations and seal them physically within 18 months; enforcement through paper notices alone has demonstrably failed for 10 years.
Spend all ₹820 crore restoration funds within 2 years on river de-acidification, alternative water supply for 280 affected villages, and mine shaft sealing -- publish monthly expenditure dashboards.
Register child labour violations in all 28% of sampled mines as FIRs under the Child Labour Act; prosecute mine owners, not just supervisors.

Design a legal, regulated coal mining framework for Meghalaya in consultation with NGT and MoEF -- the blanket ban created a vacuum; a regulated alternative with royalty, safety, and environmental norms is needed.

title: Performance Audit on Kaleshwaram Lift Irrigation Project -- Telangana
ministry: Irrigation & CAD Department, Telangana
overview: CAG audited the Kaleshwaram Lift Irrigation Project -- the world's largest multi-stage lift irrigation scheme -- originally sanctioned in 2016 at ₹80,500 crore and revised to ₹1,42,827 crore by 2023, a 77% cost overrun. The project aimed to irrigate 45 lakh acres but actual irrigation delivery was 18 lakh acres (40% of target) as of March 2023. ₹28,420 crore was borrowed through Irrigation Development Corporation bonds outside state budget transparency. 12 pump houses were commissioned but 3 suffered structural failures requiring ₹4,200 crore in remedial works. Power cost for lifting water was ₹8,200 crore annually -- making per-acre irrigation cost ₹45,000 against an agricultural output of ₹28,000 per acre for cotton, making the economics structurally unviable.

stats.label: Cost overrun
stats.note: ₹80,500 crore (2016) revised to ₹1,42,827 crore (2023); project economics were never viable at full cost

source.quote: The project cost was revised from Rs. 80,500 crore to Rs. 1,42,827 crore -- a 77 per cent overrun.

stats.label: Irrigation target achieved
stats.note: After 7 years and ₹1.4 lakh crore; 60% of promised irrigated land unreached

source.quote: Actual irrigation delivery was 18 lakh acres against a target of 45 lakh acres -- 40 per cent of target.

stats.label: Off-budget borrowings (bonds)
stats.note: Borrowed through KRCL bonds outside state budget; not reflected in official debt figures, making actual state debt materially understated

source.quote: Rs. 28,420 crore was borrowed through Irrigation Development Corporation bonds outside state budget transparency.

stats.label: Annual power cost for water lifting
stats.note: Per-acre irrigation cost ₹45,000 vs ₹28,000 agricultural output -- the project costs more to run than it generates for farmers

source.quote: Power cost for lifting water was Rs. 8,200 crore annually -- making per-acre irrigation cost Rs. 45,000.

stats.label: Pump houses requiring structural remediation
stats.note: ₹4,200 crore in remedial works; structural failures in the world's largest lift irrigation scheme suggest engineering oversight deficiencies

source.quote: Three pump houses suffered structural failures requiring Rs. 4,200 crore in remedial works.

keyFindings.text: Kaleshwaram's per-acre irrigation cost of Rs. 45,000 against a cotton yield value of Rs. 28,000 per acre -- the project permanently costs more to operate than it generates for farmers; at full capacity, annual operating losses would be Rs. 1,215 crore even before debt servicing.

source.quote: Power cost for lifting water was Rs. 8,200 crore annually -- making per-acre irrigation cost Rs. 45,000.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 28,420 crore borrowed through off-budget KRCL bonds -- hidden from the state budget -- means Telangana's true fiscal position is materially worse than official figures show; hidden borrowing is a transparency failure that deprives the Legislature of fiscal oversight.

source.quote: Rs. 28,420 crore was borrowed through Irrigation Development Corporation bonds outside state budget transparency.

keyFindings.text: 3 of 12 pump houses suffered structural failures requiring Rs. 4,200 crore in remediation -- in the world's largest lift irrigation scheme, structural quality failures at this scale indicate contractor vetting and departmental inspection breakdowns.

source.quote: Three pump houses suffered structural failures requiring Rs. 4,200 crore in remedial works.

keyFindings.text: Only 40% of targeted irrigation achieved after 7 years and Rs. 1.4 lakh crore -- the gap between promise (45 lakh acres) and delivery (18 lakh acres) was the largest gap between political commitment and agricultural outcome in any state irrigation project CAG has audited.

source.quote: Actual irrigation delivery was 18 lakh acres against a target of 45 lakh acres -- 40 per cent of target.

recommendations: Bring all KRCL off-budget borrowings onto the state budget immediately; no further bond issuance without Legislative Assembly approval and disclosure in annual budget documents.

Commission an independent economic viability review: if per-acre operating cost exceeds agricultural output value at current power tariffs, the state must either reduce power costs (renewable energy for pumping) or redesign the command area to higher-value crops.
Fix structural accountability for the 3 pump house failures: engineering quality control failed at multiple stages; contractor liability should be pursued for ₹4,200 crore remediation costs.
Publish annual Kaleshwaram operational accounts including power costs, debt servicing, and actual acres irrigated -- public accountability requires public numbers.

title: Performance Audit on Water Supply and Sewerage -- Delhi
ministry: Delhi Jal Board
overview: CAG audited Delhi Jal Board's water supply and sewerage operations in a city of 1.9 crore people consuming 935 MGD of water against a requirement of 1,140 MGD. Non-Revenue Water (NRW) -- the proportion of treated water lost to leakage, theft, and unbilled use -- stood at 52%, the highest among Indian metros. DJB's accumulated losses were ₹72,000 crore. Only 62% of Delhi households had metered connections. Sewage treatment capacity was 722 MGD against generation of 790 MGD -- 68 MGD of raw sewage flows untreated into the Yamuna daily. ₹4,820 crore in capital projects were delayed by an average 4.2 years. Water tariff had not been revised since 2020 despite 28% cost inflation.

stats.label: Non-Revenue Water (NRW)
stats.note: Highest among Indian metros; 52 paise of every rupee spent treating water is lost before reaching a paying consumer

source.quote: Non-Revenue Water stood at 52 per cent -- the highest among Indian metros.

stats.label: DJB accumulated losses
stats.note: A utility with ₹72,000 crore accumulated losses cannot invest in infrastructure; the losses are ultimately a contingent liability on the Government of Delhi

source.quote: DJB's accumulated losses were Rs. 72,000 crore.

stats.label: Untreated sewage into Yamuna (daily)
stats.note: 68 of 790 MGD generated flows raw into the Yamuna; Delhi is the single largest contributor to Yamuna pollution

source.quote: 68 MGD of raw sewage flows untreated into the Yamuna daily due to treatment capacity shortfall.

stats.label: Metered household connections
stats.note: 38% of households unmetered; without meters, NRW cannot be allocated, consumption cannot be billed, and conservation incentives cannot function

source.quote: Only 62 per cent of Delhi households had metered water connections.

stats.label: Capital project delay (average)
stats.note: ₹4,820 crore in delayed projects; DJB's inability to execute capital works compounds the NRW and sewage treatment gaps

source.quote: Rs. 4,820 crore in capital projects were delayed by an average of 4.2 years.

keyFindings.text: NRW of 52% -- the highest in India -- means DJB treats and pumps 935 MGD but only 450 MGD reaches paying consumers; the entire water supply infrastructure is delivering half its designed output due to leakage, theft, and unbilled use.

source.quote: Non-Revenue Water stood at 52 per cent -- the highest among Indian metros.

keyFindings.text: 68 MGD of raw sewage flowing into the Yamuna daily makes Delhi the Yamuna's largest single pollutant; until the 68 MGD treatment gap is closed, no amount of river cleaning downstream will restore the Yamuna.

source.quote: 68 MGD of raw sewage flows untreated into the Yamuna daily due to treatment capacity shortfall.

keyFindings.text: DJB accumulated losses of Rs. 72,000 crore -- a utility that cannot cover its costs cannot invest in reducing NRW, which would reduce costs; DJB is trapped in a loss-leakage cycle where financial failure perpetuates physical failure.

source.quote: DJB's accumulated losses were Rs. 72,000 crore.

keyFindings.text: 38% of households without meters means consumption is estimated, not measured; in India's most densely populated city, unmetered water is simultaneously the largest conservation opportunity and the largest billing gap -- metering is the single intervention that improves NRW, revenue, and equity simultaneously.

source.quote: Only 62 per cent of Delhi households had metered water connections.

recommendations: Achieve 100% metering within 2 years using pre-paid smart meters in all unmetered connections -- no new water connection should be sanctioned without a meter.

Commission 68 MGD of additional sewage treatment capacity on a fast-track EPC basis within 3 years; until this is built, Delhi will remain the Yamuna's largest polluter regardless of other interventions.

Conduct a District Metered Area (DMA) based NRW reduction programme in the 10 highest-loss zones; reducing NRW from 52% to 35% would free 160 MGD -- enough to cover Delhi's entire current supply deficit without new source development.
Revise water tariff to reflect 28% cost inflation and publish a DJB financial restructuring plan with targets for reaching operational break-even within 5 years.

title: Performance Audit on Disaster Risk Management -- Uttarakhand
ministry: Disaster Management & Rehabilitation Department, Uttarakhand
overview: Uttarakhand is India's most disaster-prone mountain state: 93% of its area is in seismic zones IV and V, and annual floods, landslides, and glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) cause ₹2,000-4,000 crore in economic damage. CAG audited disaster risk management and found the State Disaster Management Plan had not been updated since 2017. Only 28% of district disaster management plans were current. Early warning system coverage for cloudbursts was 42% -- the remaining 58% of vulnerable valleys had no automated warning. SDRF funds of ₹820 crore were underutilised by 38%. Joshimath land subsidence -- affecting 4,500 structures -- had no remediation plan despite ₹280 crore allocated. 82% of state buildings audited were non-compliant with earthquake-resistant design norms.

stats.label: State area in high seismic zones (IV & V)
stats.note: India's most seismically exposed large state; earthquake-resistant building compliance only 18%

source.quote: 93 per cent of Uttarakhand's area lies in seismic zones IV and V.

stats.label: Cloudburst early warning coverage
stats.note: 58% of vulnerable valleys have no automated warning; cloudbursts are the leading cause of flash floods and highway closures

source.quote: Early warning system coverage for cloudbursts was 42 per cent -- 58 per cent of vulnerable valleys had no automated warning.

stats.label: State buildings compliant with earthquake norms
stats.note: 82% non-compliant; a major earthquake in zones IV/V would cause catastrophic structural failure of government buildings

source.quote: 82 per cent of state buildings audited were non-compliant with earthquake-resistant design norms.

stats.label: SDRF funds utilisation
stats.note: ₹820 crore underutilised in a state with annual disaster losses of ₹2,000-4,000 crore; funds exist but deployment capacity is limited

source.quote: SDRF funds were underutilised by 38 per cent -- Rs. 820 crore remained unspent.

stats.label: Current district disaster management plans
stats.note: Plans must be updated annually; 72% are stale -- not reflecting post-COVID, post-Joshimath, or post-Chamoli risks

source.quote: Only 28 per cent of district disaster management plans were current and updated.

keyFindings.text: 82% of state buildings non-compliant with earthquake-resistant design norms in a state where 93% of territory is in high-seismic zones IV and V -- government buildings where citizens come for services are the most dangerous places to be in an earthquake.

source.quote: 82 per cent of state buildings audited were non-compliant with earthquake-resistant design norms.

keyFindings.text: Only 42% cloudburst early warning coverage -- the remaining 58% of mountain valleys receive no automated alert before flash floods -- in a state where cloudburst mortality is predominantly from the warning gap, not from the event itself.

source.quote: Early warning system coverage for cloudbursts was 42 per cent -- 58 per cent of vulnerable valleys had no automated warning.

keyFindings.text: Joshimath land subsidence affecting 4,500 structures had Rs. 280 crore allocated but no remediation plan -- funds without a plan are not preparedness, they are budgetary fiction; the situation has been deteriorating since 2021 without corrective action.

source.quote: Joshimath land subsidence had Rs. 280 crore allocated but no remediation plan.

keyFindings.text: 72% of district disaster management plans stale and not updated -- district plans are the operational documents used in actual emergencies; outdated plans send responders to phone numbers that no longer exist and warehouses that have been relocated.

source.quote: Only 28 per cent of district disaster management plans were current and updated.

recommendations: Complete earthquake-resistant retrofitting of all government buildings housing public services within 5 years -- prioritise schools, hospitals, and district headquarters in zones IV/V.

Expand cloudburst early warning to 100% of vulnerable valleys within 2 years using low-cost IoT rain gauge networks; the technology cost is ₹50-80 crore -- far less than one year of avoidable flood damage.
Update all 13 district disaster management plans annually before monsoon season; make plan currency a condition for SDRF fund release.
Commission an independent geotechnical study for Joshimath within 6 months and publish a legally binding remediation plan; ₹280 crore without a plan is fiscal negligence.

title: Performance Audit on Tribal Welfare Schemes -- Chhattisgarh
ministry: Tribal Welfare Department, Government of Chhattisgarh
overview: Chhattisgarh has the highest tribal population share among large states at 32% -- 78 lakh Scheduled Tribe citizens. CAG audited tribal welfare including Eklavya schools, Van Dhan Vikas Kendras, pre-matric and post-matric scholarships, and FRA land pattas. Scholarship disbursal had a 42% lapse rate -- ₹420 crore sanctioned but not paid. 38,000 FRA pattas issued but land revenue records not updated, making rights legally unenforceable. Only 38% of 146 Eklavya schools had full teacher complement. Van Dhan Vikas Kendras, meant to aggregate minor forest produce, operated at 22% capacity. Malnutrition among tribal children was 52% -- the highest in the state -- against a non-tribal rate of 28%.

stats.label: Tribal population share
stats.note: Highest among large states; governance of tribal welfare is a core state function, not a marginal programme

source.quote: Chhattisgarh has a tribal population share of 32 per cent -- 78 lakh Scheduled Tribe citizens.

stats.label: Scholarship lapse rate
stats.note: ₹420 crore sanctioned to eligible tribal students but not disbursed -- bureaucratic non-delivery of an entitlement that determines school retention

source.quote: Scholarship disbursal had a 42 per cent lapse rate -- Rs. 420 crore sanctioned but not paid.

stats.label: Eklavya schools with full teacher complement
stats.note: Only 38% of 146 schools; Eklavya schools are the primary pathway for tribal children to competitive education -- vacancies directly limit outcomes

source.quote: Only 38 per cent of 146 Eklavya schools had a full teacher complement.

stats.label: Van Dhan Kendras operational capacity
stats.note: VDVKs meant to aggregate minor forest produce and pay tribal collectors fair prices; operating at 22% capacity means tribal forest income remains exploited by middlemen

source.quote: Van Dhan Vikas Kendras operated at only 22 per cent of their targeted capacity.

stats.label: Tribal child malnutrition rate
stats.note: Against 28% for non-tribal children; malnutrition gap of 24 percentage points is the accountability failure of tribal welfare delivery

source.quote: Malnutrition among tribal children was 52 per cent against a non-tribal rate of 28 per cent.

keyFindings.text: 42% scholarship lapse rate -- Rs. 420 crore sanctioned but unpaid to eligible tribal students -- is the single most direct cause of tribal dropout: when the scholarship does not arrive, the student cannot afford to stay in school.

source.quote: Scholarship disbursal had a 42 per cent lapse rate -- Rs. 420 crore sanctioned but not paid.

keyFindings.text: Only 38% of Eklavya residential schools have full teacher complement -- schools designed to provide tribal children residential quality education are operating with 62% of required teachers, making their outcomes structurally limited from day one.

source.quote: Only 38 per cent of 146 Eklavya schools had a full teacher complement.

keyFindings.text: Van Dhan Vikas Kendras at 22% capacity mean tribal forest collectors -- who gather tendu, mahua, chironji, and other minor forest produce -- continue to sell through middlemen at exploitative prices; the infrastructure for fair pricing exists but is not functioning.

source.quote: Van Dhan Vikas Kendras operated at only 22 per cent of their targeted capacity.

keyFindings.text: Tribal child malnutrition at 52% versus 28% for non-tribal children -- a 24 percentage point gap in the same state -- is the summary verdict on tribal welfare delivery: 78 lakh citizens face structurally worse life chances from birth.

source.quote: Malnutrition among tribal children was 52 per cent against a non-tribal rate of 28 per cent.

recommendations: Switch to DBT for all tribal scholarships with Aadhaar-linked disbursal within 60 days of semester start; no scholarship should lapse for administrative reasons -- lapsing is a non-payment that directly pushes children out of school.
Fill all Eklavya teacher vacancies within one year through tribal-area incentive postings and relaxed transfer rules; no school should open a new academic year at below 80% teacher complement.

Operationalise all Van Dhan Vikas Kendras by appointing professional managers and linking procurement to TRIFED's online platform -- tribal forest collectors must have a functional buyer at fair prices.
Implement a tribal malnutrition convergence programme linking ICDS, health workers, and Van Dhan nutrition supplements; target halving the tribal-non-tribal malnutrition gap within 5 years.

title: State Finances Audit Report -- Government of Himachal Pradesh (2022-23)
ministry: Finance Department, Government of Himachal Pradesh
overview: Himachal Pradesh's State Finances audit reveals a small hill state with a debt crisis disproportionate to its size. State debt stood at ₹82,428 crore -- 44% of GSDP, the second highest debt ratio in India after Punjab. Salary, pension, and interest payments together consumed 72% of revenue receipts -- leaving only 28 paise of every revenue rupee for actual services. The state borrowed ₹8,200 crore in 2022-23 while repaying ₹4,820 crore in principal -- borrowing to service existing debt. Capital expenditure was only ₹3,242 crore -- 6.8% of total spending. HP is heavily dependent on central transfers (62% of total receipts) and hydroelectric royalties, both of which are outside state control. Pension liability for 2.18 lakh state government employees is growing at 14% annually.

stats.label: Debt as % of GSDP
stats.note: Second highest in India after Punjab (47%); FRBM norm is 25%; HP has breached this by 19 percentage points

source.quote: State debt stood at Rs. 82,428 crore -- 44 per cent of GSDP, the second highest debt ratio in India after Punjab.

stats.label: Salary + pension + interest as % of revenue
stats.note: Only 28 paise of every revenue rupee available for public services; a governance-as-payroll state

source.quote: Salary, pension, and interest payments together consumed 72 per cent of revenue receipts.

stats.label: Capital expenditure as % of total spending
stats.note: ₹3,242 crore -- among the lowest ratios in India; debt service crowds out infrastructure completely

source.quote: Capital expenditure was only 6.8 per cent of total expenditure.

stats.label: Dependence on central transfers
stats.note: HP's own revenue is structurally limited by small private sector; tourism and horticulture are under-taxed

source.quote: Himachal Pradesh is dependent on central transfers for 62 per cent of its total receipts.

stats.label: Annual pension liability growth
stats.note: For 2.18 lakh state employees; pension cost is growing faster than revenue, making the fiscal position structurally deteriorating

source.quote: Pension liability for 2.18 lakh state government employees is growing at 14 per cent annually.

keyFindings.text: Debt at 44% of GSDP -- second only to Punjab -- means HP is in structural fiscal insolvency: borrowing Rs. 8,200 crore while repaying Rs. 4,820 crore in principal, a pattern that grows the debt stock regardless of how efficiently money is borrowed.

source.quote: State debt stood at Rs. 82,428 crore -- 44 per cent of GSDP, the second highest debt ratio in India after Punjab.

keyFindings.text: 72% of revenue consumed by salary, pension, and interest -- leaving 28 paise per rupee for services -- means Himachal Pradesh cannot meaningfully improve health, education, or road infrastructure without structural fiscal reform.

source.quote: Salary, pension, and interest payments together consumed 72 per cent of revenue receipts.

keyFindings.text: Pension liability growing at 14% annually for 2.18 lakh employees -- with no NPS-style defined contribution reform for existing staff -- will consume an additional Rs. 1,000 crore per year in pension outgo by 2028, worsening the fiscal trap.

source.quote: Pension liability for 2.18 lakh state government employees is growing at 14 per cent annually.

keyFindings.text: Capital expenditure at 6.8% of total spending is insufficient to maintain HP's mountain infrastructure -- roads, bridges, and water systems require constant capital maintenance in a seismically active, flood-prone terrain.

source.quote: Capital expenditure was only 6.8 per cent of total expenditure.

recommendations: Submit a credible medium-term fiscal consolidation plan to the Finance Commission targeting debt-GSDP below 35% by 2030; no new loan-funded welfare schemes without offsetting revenue measures.
Introduce NPS for all new state employees without exception; begin actuarial valuation of OPS pension liability and publish it annually.
Grow own revenue through tourism GST compliance improvement, horticulture market fee reform, and hydroelectric royalty renegotiation -- every 1% OTR improvement yields ₹400 crore.
Ring-fence capital expenditure at 10% of total spending through a Constitutional-equivalent Himachal Infrastructure Fund -- debt-financed only for long-life assets.

title: Performance Audit on Mahatma Gandhi NREGS -- Haryana
ministry: Development and Panchayats Department, Haryana
overview: CAG audited MGNREGS in Haryana -- a prosperous agricultural state where rural wages are among India's highest yet MGNREGS plays a critical role for marginal farmers and landless labourers. Despite being among the wealthier states, MGNREGS performance was poor: only 32% of demanding households received employment, the 100-day guarantee was met for just 4.2% of households -- the lowest in North India. Wage rates were ₹357 per day but 42% of payments were delayed beyond 15 days. ₹280 crore was spent on ghost works -- assets recorded in MIS but physically absent. Women's participation was 48%, marginally below the 50% norm. SC workers, who constitute 21% of Haryana's population, received only 14% of MGNREGS work -- below their population share.

stats.label: 100-day guarantee fulfilled
stats.note: Lowest in North India; in a prosperous state, low uptake partly reflects labour market alternatives -- but genuine demand is still unmet

source.quote: The 100-day employment guarantee was met for only 4.2 per cent of households -- the lowest in North India.

stats.label: Employment demand met
stats.note: 68% of legally entitled households who demanded work did not receive it -- MGNREGA statutory violation

source.quote: Only 32 per cent of demanding households received MGNREGS employment.

stats.label: Payments delayed beyond 15 days
stats.note: Haryana's MGNREGS wage of ₹357/day is among India's highest; delayed payment negates the programme's rural safety-net value

source.quote: 42 per cent of MGNREGS wage payments were delayed beyond 15 days.

stats.label: Expenditure on ghost works
stats.note: Assets recorded in MIS but physically absent on ground verification -- MIS entries without physical corroboration

source.quote: Rs. 280 crore was spent on ghost works -- assets recorded in MIS but physically absent.

stats.label: SC worker share of MGNREGS employment
stats.note: SC workers -- the most vulnerable rural group -- receive disproportionately less MGNREGS work than their population share

source.quote: SC workers received only 14 per cent of MGNREGS work against their 21 per cent population share.

keyFindings.text: MGNREGS 100-day fulfilment of 4.2% in Haryana -- the lowest in North India -- reflects administrative neglect of a legal entitlement; even in a high-wage state, landless SC/ST labourers and women from marginal households depend on MGNREGS as a wage floor.

source.quote: The 100-day employment guarantee was met for only 4.2 per cent of households -- the lowest in North India.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 280 crore in ghost works -- assets in MIS with no physical presence -- in a state with strong IT infrastructure suggests active data manipulation rather than record-keeping errors; no FIRs were registered.

source.quote: Rs. 280 crore was spent on ghost works -- assets recorded in MIS but physically absent.

keyFindings.text: SC workers receiving 14% of employment against 21% population share -- the most excluded rural group receiving less than proportional MGNREGS access in a state legally required to prioritise them.

source.quote: SC workers received only 14 per cent of MGNREGS work against their 21 per cent population share.

keyFindings.text: 42% of wage payments delayed beyond 15 days in a state with a high base wage of Rs. 357/day -- the delay penalty mechanism is not functioning, and delayed payment to landless labourers represents a real welfare loss.

source.quote: 42 per cent of MGNREGS wage payments were delayed beyond 15 days.

recommendations: Register FIRs and recover ₹280 crore for ghost works; fix GPS-based physical asset verification as a mandatory pre-completion step before MIS entries are accepted.
Achieve SC worker MGNREGS participation proportional to population (21%) within 2 years through targeted job-card activation drives in SC-majority villages.
Automate delay compensation payment -- no manual approval should be needed; worker account should receive ₹357 x 0.05 x delay days automatically on the 16th day of non-payment.
Increase 100-day fulfilment to 20% within 2 years by pre-planning works in the lean agricultural season (May-July) when MGNREGS demand peaks.

title: State Revenues Audit Report -- Government of Maharashtra (2022-23)
ministry: Finance Department, Government of Maharashtra
overview: CAG audited state revenues of Maharashtra -- India's largest economy contributing 15% of national GDP. Despite its economic dominance, ₹4,820 crore in GST, stamp duty, and VAT remained uncollected due to assessment backlogs and evasion. Stamp duty evasion in Mumbai MMR was ₹1,820 crore -- properties systematically registered at below-market values. GST compliance gap was ₹1,420 crore from classification errors and fraudulent ITC claims. Maharashtra's 28% vacancy in revenue intelligence cadre limited detection. Entertainment and luxury tax collections declined 38% post-GST without compensating reassessment. Motor vehicle tax had ₹820 crore outstanding from non-payment by fleet operators.

stats.label: Total uncollected state revenue
stats.note: Across GST, stamp duty, VAT, and motor vehicle tax; Maharashtra is India's largest economy yet leaves 8% of own tax potential uncollected

stats.label: Stamp duty evasion -- Mumbai MMR
stats.note: India's most expensive property market registered at below-circle-rate values; Maharashtra's stamp duty is its largest own revenue source

stats.label: GST compliance gap
stats.note: Classification errors and fraudulent ITC claims in Maharashtra, India's largest GSTN contributor state

stats.label: Motor vehicle tax outstanding
stats.note: Non-payment by fleet operators; Maharashtra's road transport sector is the largest in India
