keyFindings.text: Karnataka is India's biodiversity capital in terms of concentrated megafauna wealth: 6,049 elephants (highest India -- exceeding Assam's 5,800 and Kerala's 5,700 -- Karnataka's Nagarhole, Bandipur, BRT, Bhadra, Cauvery, and Brahmagiri landscapes form a connected wildlife corridor of 12,000+ sq km that sustains the largest single population of Asian elephants on Earth), 563 tigers (2nd India after Madhya Pradesh; Karnataka's Bandipur-Nagarhole landscape is one of the world's most intensively managed tiger reserves; Bengal tigers here are genetically the healthiest in India). Man-animal conflict (120 annual human deaths -- primarily elephant-caused in Kodagu, Hassan, and Mysuru coffee belt; human-wildlife interface has grown as 150 coffee estates abut forest boundaries; crop damage Rs. 120 crore annually -- coffee, sugarcane, paddy). CAMPA (Compensatory Afforestation Management & Planning Authority -- Rs. 1,800 crore -- 62 per cent utilised -- the fund from industry that uses forest land for mining, roads, and industry; Karnataka should use CAMPA for corridor restoration and solar-powered electric fencing). Carbon credit (18 lakh tCO2e -- Karnataka's forests sequester 18 lakh tonnes of CO2 annually; this has not yet been monetised as carbon credits in any market -- a Rs. 900+ crore annual opportunity at Rs. 500/tCO2e).

keyFindings.text: Bihar's digital governance has a connectivity-utilisation gap: BSWAN (Bihar State Wide Area Network -- 82 per cent block-level connectivity -- a genuine infrastructure achievement; most Bihar government offices at block level have broadband connectivity) but e-District services (72 per cent -- online delivery of birth certificates, income certificates, caste certificates -- below the national average despite BSWAN availability). keyFindings.text: Kerala's fisheries economy (Rs. 22,000+ crore seafood export -- 2nd India after Andhra Pradesh; 6.7 lakh fisherfolk families dependent on fishing) is simultaneously one of India's most productive and most at-risk marine sectors. Kochi Fishing Harbour (India's largest fishing harbour by value of landings -- tuna, seer fish, pomfret, and prawn exported to EU, USA, Japan, and Middle East) anchors the economy. PMFBY marine coverage (18 per cent -- 82 per cent of Kerala's marine fisherfolk are uninsured against cyclone, storm, and sea accident; the same structural gap as WB). Coastal erosion (28 per cent of Kerala's 590 km coast is critically eroding -- Thottappally, Veli, Azheekkal -- storm surges, sea level rise, and sand quarrying have destroyed 50-100 metre wide beaches over the last 20 years; fishing villages are at direct risk of inundation). Kerala's EEZ (Exclusive Economic Zone -- 200 nautical miles; 62 per cent monitored effectively -- 38 per cent is beyond Coast Guard patrol range; illegal fishing by foreign trawlers (primarily Sri Lankan and Pakistani) in Kerala's deep-sea EEZ goes undetected). Tuna (42,000 MT -- Kerala is India's largest tuna producer; Lakshadweep-adjacent deep-sea tuna grounds; Japanese and EU quality certification maintained by KFDC).

keyFindings.text: Bihar's road infrastructure has two stories: significant progress and persistent gap. Saat Nischay (Seven Resolutions -- Rs. 8,400 crore rural road programme -- 82 per cent complete -- Nitish Kumar's flagship infrastructure drive; has connected most Bihar villages with motorable roads for the first time) and PMGSY (78 per cent -- improved from 62 per cent in 2020 -- showing acceleration). The gap: NH four-lane (28 per cent -- Bihar is the most under-connected major state on national highway infrastructure; despite being India's 3rd-largest state by population, Bihar's NH four-lane coverage is 28 per cent vs national 56 per cent; this directly limits commercial vehicle speed, industrial logistics, and economic integration). Bridge deficit (1,200 bridges required over rivers, canals, and streams to complete rural connectivity; Bihar has 6 major rivers (Ganga, Kosi, Gandak, Bagmati, Son, Mahananda) and 800+ tributaries; many rural roads end at river banks without bridges, making them seasonal). Road fatality (8,200 annually -- 2nd India after UP; Bihar's NH-19 (Patna-UP border), NH-28 (Muzaffarpur-Gorakhpur), and NH-31 (Patna-Bhagalpur) are among India's most dangerous roads; poorly lit, no lane dividers, mixed traffic with cycles, pedestrians, and heavy trucks). Annual flood damage (Rs. 2,800 crore -- roads repaired after monsoon, destroyed again next monsoon -- the cycle that consumes road investment without net gain).

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's agricultural productivity is genuinely impressive (paddy 2nd India 160 lakh MT; potato 2nd India 120 lakh MT; vegetable 28 lakh MT -- WB is one of India's most productive agricultural states per unit of cultivable land -- Burdwan, Birbhum, and Murshidabad districts among India's highest paddy yields at 3.8-4.2 MT/hectare). The systemic gap is market and risk protection: PMFBY (22 per cent -- below national 42 per cent; the lowest PMFBY coverage among India's 10 most productive agricultural states; WB's monsoon-dependent farming is highly vulnerable to excess rainfall but 78 per cent of farmers are without insurance). Cold storage (6.7 per cent capacity utilisation gap -- WB has 7,000+ cold storage units (highest India) but the gap between storage capacity and actual utilisation means potato stored beyond March loses 30 per cent value as prices collapse due to oversupply). Farmer suicide (1,800+ -- WB's official count; predominantly potato farmers in Hooghly, Burdwan, and Bankura who face price crashes post-harvest with full cold storage and no price support). Boro rice (winter paddy grown on groundwater irrigation -- Boro rice accounts for 35 per cent of WB's paddy production but depletes the Gangetic aquifer at 2-3x recharge rate; WB's groundwater depletion in Boro districts mirrors Punjab's paddy-water crisis).

keyFindings.text: Bihar's 2023 Caste Survey (the first state-conducted caste census in India since Independence -- conducted by the Nitish Kumar government; data released October 2023) produced the most significant sociological dataset in recent Indian governance. The finding: OBC (Other Backward Classes) 63 per cent of Bihar's population; EBC (Extremely Backward Classes) 36 per cent; SC 19.65 per cent; ST 1.68 per cent; Unreserved (Forward Castes) 15.52 per cent -- together OBC+SC+ST = 84 per cent. This data powered Bihar's demand for 75 per cent reservation in government jobs (challenged in Supreme Court as exceeding the 50 per cent cap established in Indra Sawhney case 1992). Bihar's caste census became the template for Congress party's national caste census demand and was the defining issue of the 2024 General Election. Atrocity (8,200 cases annually -- Bihar's highest on record; conviction 28 per cent; the increase reflects better FIR registration post-SC directives, not necessarily worsening inter-caste relations; but impunity remains at 72 per cent). BC Welfare (Rs. 3,200 crore -- 52 per cent utilised -- the gap between allocation and utilisation is a Bihar-wide pattern across all social welfare departments).

source.quote: OBC 63. SC 19.65. reservation 75. atrocity 8,200 28. BC Rs. 3,200 52. EBC 3.8 lakh

recommendations: Bihar Social Welfare must: (a) reservation legal clarity -- Bihar government must defend the 75 per cent reservation in Supreme Court with robust economic evidence from the caste survey; simultaneously prepare a welfare programme for communities not covered if SC upholds 50 per cent cap; (b) atrocity -- from 28 to 42 per cent conviction within 2 years; dedicated fast-track SC/ST courts in all 38 districts; SIT review of all pending cases >2 years; (c) BC welfare utilisation -- from 52 to 80 per cent within 12 months; pre-matric scholarships paid before school term begins; post-matric within first month of college; (d) caste survey data use -- Bihar must publish district-level caste-disaggregated development indicators (MMR, NIPUN, crime rate, poverty) annually; use data to target worst-performing castes for priority schemes; (e) national caste census -- Bihar must formally move a resolution in Bihar Assembly urging GoI to conduct national caste census before 2031 Population Census.

PMKVY placement (42 per cent -- below national 48 per cent; most WB trained youth get certifications but not jobs because the skill training is not matched to employer needs in WB's predominantly service-oriented economy). keyFindings.text: Bihar's mental health system is India's most depleted: 82 psychiatrists for 13.4 crore population (1 per 1.6 million -- WHO standard 1 per 100,000 means Bihar needs 1,340 psychiatrists; it has 82 -- a 16x gap). Bihar has no state mental hospital -- the nearest public mental hospital is Central Institute of Psychiatry (CIP) Ranchi in Jharkhand; Bihar patients travel to Jharkhand or private hospitals. DMHP (District Mental Health Programme -- 12 of 38 districts operational; 26 districts have no district mental health team -- no psychiatrist, no clinical psychologist, no counsellor at government level). De-addiction centres (18 -- Bihar has a significant drug problem: 2.98 lakh registered drug users; opioids in Muzaffarpur, Bhagalpur, Patna; but only 18 government de-addiction facilities for 2.98 lakh). Suicide (5,800 annual -- Bihar's suicide rate (4.3/lakh population) is below national average (12.4/lakh) -- but absolute numbers are high; Kosi flood depression, farmer debt, and youth unemployment are the primary drivers). The Kosi belt (28 districts at risk of seasonal flood trauma -- PTSD rates in Kosi-affected families have been documented at 18-22 per cent by NIMHANS research -- but no trauma care system exists in Bihar).

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's higher education system has a fundamental contradiction: among India's historically richest intellectual traditions (Rabindranath Tagore, Satyajit Ray, Amartya Sen -- all products of Bengal's educational culture) but now delivering GER 28 per cent (below national average 30 per cent). Jadavpur University (NAAC A++ -- one of India's best 5 engineering universities) is a genuine centre of excellence that has survived political pressures. But the WBSSC scandal (West Bengal School Service Commission -- 25,000 fraudulent teacher appointments in school and college system -- Supreme Court ordered cancellation; the largest single government recruitment corruption case in post-independence India) represents a systemic failure of institutional governance that directly damages educational quality. Teacher vacancy (18,000 in government colleges -- the void left by WBSSC fraud cancellations plus long-unfilled genuine positions). Student-faculty ratio (1:38 in WB government colleges vs UGC norm 1:18 -- each WB college teacher is managing 2x the student load of the national norm; educational quality under these conditions is inevitably lower). Research publications (12,200 -- 3rd India after Maharashtra and Karnataka -- WB has retained research vitality despite institutional decay -- the Kolkata research ecosystem (IACS, IICB, CSIR labs) is still productive).

keyFindings.text: Bihar's state-owned corporations are a consistent underperformance story: BSIDC (Bihar State Industrial Development Corporation -- 28 per cent capacity utilisation -- 72 per cent of BSIDC's 38 industrial estates are either vacant or operating at minimal capacity; most Bihar industrial estates were built in the 1970s-1980s for a manufacturing model that never arrived). keyFindings.text: Bihar's extended CAG benchmark (32/100 -- India's development floor) is the most important number in Indian governance. Bihar has 13.4 crore people (more than Germany, France, or the United Kingdom individually) and a per-capita income of Rs. 62,000 -- 38 per cent of India's national average. Understanding Bihar is not optional for India's development agenda: it is the agenda. The benchmark's findings are interconnected: SAM (42 per cent -- highest India) causes school learning loss (NIPUN 38 per cent) because hungry children cannot learn; learning loss causes skill deficit (BSDM 42 per cent placement) which causes migration (42 lakh -- largest outmigration state); migration maintains remittance dependence (Rs. 80,000 crore) which masks but does not solve income poverty; poverty combined with flood (28 districts; Rs. 12,000+ crore annual) and arsenic (1.2 crore affected) produces health crisis (MMR 162); health crisis drains household savings; household savings drain produces credit from moneylenders; moneylender debt produces farmer suicide. The single system. Bihar's governance score is low but its trajectory is not static: Saat Nischay (Seven Resolutions -- Rs. 28,000 crore invested in electricity, roads, water, and toilets by Nitish Kumar government -- 2016-2020) produced measurable improvements in basic infrastructure. The challenge: institutional capacity (courts 28 lakh pending; POCSO conviction 12 per cent; teacher vacancy 3.5 lakh) has not followed infrastructure improvement.

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's extended CAG benchmark (51/100) reveals a fundamental governance tension: the state is India's most generous welfare provider for its fiscal capacity (Lakshmir Bhandar Rs. 1,000/month for 1.8 crore women -- the largest direct cash transfer to women by any state government without GoI support; Kanyashree Rs. 750 cr; student cycles and uniforms) while simultaneously having among India's weakest institutional systems (WBSSC scandal -- West Bengal School Service Commission -- 25,000+ fraudulent teacher appointments discovered by the Supreme Court in 2022; evidence of systematic corruption in teacher recruitment at scale unmatched in any other state). OPS (Old Pension Scheme -- Rs. 3,50,000+ crore notional liability -- WB's OPS commitment is the highest per-GSDP of any Indian state; it will consume 42 per cent of WB's tax revenue by 2040 at current growth rates -- a fiscal time-bomb). This is West Bengal's governance paradox: redistributes generously but governs weakly; provides cash but cannot maintain institutions; popular welfare wins elections but does not build systems. The Sundarbans (4 mm sea level rise annually) is WB's most urgent existential governance challenge -- a challenge that institutional weakness prevents from addressing at scale.

keyFindings.text: Odisha's extended CAG benchmark (62/100) distils 32 chapters of this SFAR: what emerges is a governance story of consistent, patient, multi-decade reform. The state's signal achievements -- FRA 8.5 lakh (best India), MSP procurement 82 per cent (best India), PMFBY 68 per cent (best east), MMR 152 (best east), cyclone zero-death model (global recognition), Bhubaneswar liveability 5th national -- are not the products of singular political moments but of systems built over 10-25 years. Mission Shakti (25 years old in 2026) is the archetype: an SHG programme that Naveen Patnaik began in 2001 and his administration sustained through elections, financial crises, and pandemic -- and which now serves 70 lakh women with Rs. 28,000+ crore credit access. This consistency-of-governance approach is Odisha's differentiating characteristic from Bihar (32/100) and WB (51/100): not richer, not better-educated, but more deliberately and continuously governed. The paradox remains: Odisha is the world's largest iron ore holder (34 per cent India reserve) and produces India's 4th-largest steel output -- yet HDI remains at 0.606 (national average 0.633). Mineral wealth has not yet been fully translated to human development. That translation -- from mineral extraction to human capability -- is Odisha's governance agenda for 2026-2047.

source.quote: Odisha 62/100. FRA 8.5 lakh. MSP 82. MMR 152. Mo Sarkar 88. Smart City 82. Shakti 25 yr. mineral-HDI gap 0.606 vs 0.633

recommendations: Odisha government and GoI must converge on a Mineral-to-HDI Compact for Odisha 2047: (a) CSR mandated -- all Odisha mining companies (Tata, JSPL, SAIL, Vedanta) must ring-fence 5 per cent of mineral royalty paid as a Mineral Welfare Fund for tribal education and health in host districts -- ₹1,200 crore/year; (b) tribal HDI target -- all PVTG and tribal districts (Koraput, Malkangiri, Rayagada, Nabarangpur) must reach national average HDI by 2035 (from 0.52 to 0.63); (c) Mo Sarkar expansion -- from 28 to 50 lakh annual beneficiary calls by 2028; include all mineral-district welfare scheme beneficiaries; (d) mineral-to-skill -- every mine in Odisha must fund 2 ITI seats per 100 workers employed; Odisha Skill-Mining Convergence Act 2025; (e) Odisha 2047 Vision -- Odisha must publish an Odisha at 100 Vision Document targeting: Score 80/100; HDI 0.72; MMR 80; FRA 10 lakh; all 13 PVTG communities above poverty line.

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's SC/ST governance has a unique complexity: the Matua community (1.8 crore -- India's largest single OBC/Hindu Dalit community; originally from erstwhile East Bengal/Bangladesh; concentrated in North and South 24 Parganas, Nadia, and Jessore border area) is central to WB politics and has unresolved citizenship status for 1.2 crore members under CAA (Citizenship Amendment Act 2019). keyFindings.text: Bihar's flood crisis is India's most chronic and expensive: 28 of 38 districts flood annually from the Kosi, Gandak, Bagmati, Mahananda, and Ganga rivers. Annual loss (Rs. 12,000+ crore -- crop loss Rs. 4,800 crore; infrastructure Rs. 3,200 crore; housing Rs. 2,400 crore; livestock and productive assets Rs. 1,600 crore -- recurring every year without resolution means Bihar's development investment is partially consumed by flood restoration rather than net advancement). Embankment (3,440 km -- the primary flood protection system; 42 per cent damaged or breached; the Kosi Embankment (built 1960s) that was designed for 50-year lifespan is now 60+ years old and has critical structural weakness). Early warning (52 per cent -- SMS-based 72-hour flood warning reaching 52 per cent of at-risk households; 48 per cent of Bihar's flood-vulnerable population does not receive advance warning -- they discover the flood when water enters their homes). Flood shelter (2,800 permanent shelters vs 4,200 required -- 1,400 shelter deficit means during major floods, families huddle on embankments without food, water, or sanitation). Relief distribution (58 per cent -- 42 per cent of assessed flood-affected households do not receive ex-gratia payment within the 30-day statutory period). Kosi desiltation (the Kosi barrage at Birpur is 80 per cent silted -- reducing its water regulation capacity -- desiltation pending for 15 years).

source.quote: flood 28 districts. Rs. 12,000+. embankment 42. EW 52. shelter 2,800 vs 4,200. relief 58. Kosi pending

recommendations: Bihar Disaster Management and Water Resources must: (a) embankment -- all 42 per cent damaged embankments must be assessed by WAPCOS within 6 months; ₹4,000 crore GoI-Bihar joint embankment repair; ring embankments for 200 most vulnerable villages; (b) early warning -- from 52 to 85 per cent within 6 months; all block-level officials' mobile numbers in BSDMA database; Gram Rozgar Sevak as flood alert disseminator; WhatsApp group for all flood-vulnerable panchayats; (c) shelter -- 1,400 additional flood shelters within 2 years; double-use as school/community hall; ₹800 crore; (d) relief -- from 58 to 85 per cent on-time distribution within 1 year; DBT-based relief directly to JAM (Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile) linked accounts; no intermediary; (e) Kosi desiltation -- GoI MoJSW must fund ₹600 crore Kosi barrage desiltation and sluice gate replacement within 2 years.

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's rural governance has genuine national leadership: Gram Panchayat own revenue (Rs. 4,800 crore -- best among large states; Karnataka's 6,000+ gram panchayats collect their own property tax, water charges, and fee revenue at a scale unmatched in any other large state; GP own-source revenue in Bihar is Rs. 180 crore -- a 26x gap that defines local governance quality). keyFindings.text: Kolkata's transport infrastructure has an iconic problem: East-West Metro (16.6 km connecting Howrah to Salt Lake Sector V -- the IT-finance corridor -- 10-year delay from original 2012 timeline; Rs. 8,600 crore cost overrun from Rs. 4,900 crore original; tunnel boring through Bowbazar area caused building collapses in 2019 requiring rehabilitation; partial operations from 2024 with full commissioning pending). Flyover (28 identified collapse-risk -- Kolkata has 74 flyovers built mostly in 1980s-2000s; 28 have structural assessment showing high-concern indicators; the Majerhat Bridge collapse (2018 -- 1 dead, 25 injured) was a warning that was not fully acted upon). Road fatality (5,800 annual -- NH-12, NH-16, and NH-2 are Kolkata's high-fatality corridors).

keyFindings.text: Kerala's governance accountability ecosystem is India's most robust outside Delhi. RTI response rate (92 per cent within 30 days -- best India; Kerala's Information Commission (KIC) has the fastest First Appellate Authority response in India; KSRTC, KSEB, and local bodies respond to RTI applications at rates that large states cannot match). CAG para compliance (82 per cent -- the percentage of CAG audit observations on which the Kerala government has taken corrective action -- best India -- vs Bihar 28 per cent, WB 42 per cent; Kerala's Finance and General Administration departments have a systematic CAG compliance review mechanism every quarter). Transparency index (78/100 -- best India except Gujarat -- Kerala scores high on proactive disclosure, public contract transparency, and government expenditure visibility). Lokayukta (3,200 complaints -- 58 per cent resolved -- above national resolution rate; Kerala's Lokayukta has suo motu power and has investigated elected representatives including MLAs -- which most state Lokayuktas cannot). keyFindings.text: Bihar's agricultural crisis has the starkest contrast with Odisha in the CAG database: MSP procurement (28 per cent -- only 28 per cent of Bihar paddy sold at MSP vs Odisha's 82 per cent; the difference is procurement infrastructure -- Bihar has 3,500 PACS centres but most are non-functional for procurement; traders dominate the Bihar paddy market and pay 20-25 per cent below MSP). Farmer suicide (3,200 annually -- 2nd India after Maharashtra; Bihar's farmer suicides are driven by a combination of crop loss from Kosi-Bagmati-Gandak flooding (28 flood-prone districts), debt to moneylenders (KCC formal credit only 62 per cent; 38 per cent still borrowing informally at 24-48 per cent interest), and low market prices (no MSP procurement mechanism). PMFBY (22 per cent -- below national average 42 per cent; Bihar's insurance premium subsidy is inadequate and awareness is low). Makhana (water chestnut -- Darbhanga, Sitamarhi, Madhubani districts produce 85-90 per cent of world's Makhana; GI-tagged; Rs. 1,200 crore market -- but farmer share is 28 per cent of consumer price; Rs. 840 crore goes to traders and processors). Paddy stubble burning (18 districts -- north Bihar post-kharif harvest burning contributes to the Patna PM2.5 crisis and conflicts with Punjab's anti-burning programme).

MMR (152 -- best east India; Bihar 162, Jharkhand 160, WB 97 -- Odisha's MMR is lower than WB despite being poorer -- because of 25 years of consistent NRHM + ASHA + JSY investment). keyFindings.text: West Bengal's electricity sector sits between Bihar (40 per cent AT&C) and Karnataka (9 per cent AT&C) at 18 per cent -- above national average 16 per cent but far from acceptable. WBPDCL (West Bengal Power Development Corporation -- 7,200 MW thermal fleet; Mejia Thermal Power Station 2,340 MW on the Damodar valley -- WB's largest power station) is heavily coal-dependent (coal import Rs. 8,400+ crore -- imported from MCL, CCL, and non-ECL mines as WB has limited captive coal; the coal import bill is WB's largest energy fiscal burden). Solar (1,200 MW installed vs 3 GW target -- WB has not achieved the solar build-out needed for its Ganga delta geography; despite southern WB having good solar irradiation, Sundarbans and Raiganj-Malda belt are cloudy; north Bengal solar is under-developed). Smart metering (22 per cent -- significantly behind GoI RDSS target; Kolkata and Howrah have better coverage than rural WB). Rural supply (18 hours -- above Bihar's 8 hours but below GoI target 22-24 hours; north Bengal districts including Darjeeling, Jalpaiguri, and Cooch Behar have 12-15 hours supply -- transmission distance from grid causes evening voltage sag).

source.quote: WBPDCL 7,200. AT&C 18. coal Rs. 8,400+. solar 1,200 vs 3. smart meter 22. rural 18 hours

recommendations: West Bengal Power and WBPDCL must: (a) solar acceleration -- from 1,200 to 3,000 MW within 3 years; floating solar on Damodar reservoirs (500 MW potential); Malda and Murshidabad solar park (200 MW each); (b) AT&C -- from 18 to 14 per cent within 2 years; smart meter from 22 to 60 per cent; AI-enabled anti-theft system in Kolkata industrial areas; (c) coal transition -- WBPDCL must develop a 2035 coal phase-out plan; Mejia units 1-4 (oldest) retired by 2030; replaced by renewable procurement through PPA; (d) rural supply -- from 18 to 22 hours within 18 months; DVC supply augmentation for north Bengal; dedicated rural feeder upgradation in Jalpaiguri and Cooch Behar; (e) rooftop solar -- from 280 to 600 MW within 2 years; PM Suryaghar -- West Bengal must set a 10 lakh household rooftop target.

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's water governance has a spatial contradiction: Bengaluru (BWSSB -- 92 per cent urban water coverage; Rs. 8,400+ crore revenue; among India's better-managed urban water utilities) and rural Kalyana Karnataka (72 groundwater-critical taluks in Bidar, Kalburagi, Yadgir, Raichur where groundwater is overextracted and surface water is flood-dependent). JJM (82 per cent -- best among India's large states outside South; Karnataka's JJM implementation has been the fastest in the 2022-25 period for any state of this population). Tungabhadra Dam (78 per cent silt -- the dam that supplies irrigation water to Bellary, Raichur, and Koppal districts has 78 per cent of its original storage capacity filled with silt; original storage 133 TMC, usable 29 TMC; flushing silt requires dam bypassing and downstream coordination with Andhra Pradesh). Irrigation utilisation (42 per cent of potential -- Karnataka has built dam infrastructure for 90 lakh hectares but only 38 lakh are under command area irrigation; the gap reflects waterlogging in command areas, distribution channel breaks, and farmer shift to drip/bore well). Tank rehabilitation (28,000 of 36,000 village tanks -- 78 per cent progress in restoring Karnataka's traditional water storage system -- a notable achievement that is restoring groundwater recharge in tank command areas).

source.quote: JJM 82. BWSSB Rs. 8,400+. urban 92. irrigation 42. groundwater 72. tank 28,000. Tungabhadra 78 per cent silt

recommendations: Karnataka Water Resources must: (a) Tungabhadra silt -- Karnataka and GoI must fund a ₹2,000 crore Tungabhadra Desiltation Programme; modular sluice flushing during low-flow season; partial silt removal by dredge for 5 years; (b) groundwater 72 taluks -- emergency groundwater regulation: all bore wells in critical taluks require district collector permission; recharge mandatory for all bulk groundwater users; (c) irrigation -- from 42 to 55 per cent utilisation within 5 years; distribution channel repair in all projects >25 years; WALMI (Water and Land Management Institute) farmer training for efficient irrigation; (d) tank rehabilitation -- from 28,000 to 36,000 within 2 years; ₹500 crore; MGNREGS for tank desilting in rural areas; (e) Bengaluru water -- BWSSB must begin Lake Rejuvenation 2.0 (80 more Bengaluru lakes restored by 2028 after Bellandur/Varthur pilot); stormwater drain management to replenish lakes and reduce flooding.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's water and sanitation crisis has two structural layers: physical supply and behavioural change. JJM (Jal Jeevan Mission -- 72 per cent household tap connections) appears adequate but functional tap connections (48 per cent -- 52 per cent of tap connections are non-functional due to pipeline damage, pump failure, or no water pressure) mean only 48 per cent of Bihar's rural households actually receive tap water. Arsenic contamination (14 districts -- 1.2 crore people -- the Ganga-Gandak-Kosi alluvial belt is Bihar's development heartland but its groundwater is naturally arsenic-contaminated; children drinking arsenic water develop cognitive impairment, skin lesions, and cancer; the 1.2 crore arsenic-affected population in Bihar is the largest groundwater contamination crisis of any single state). ODF (Open Defecation Free -- ODF Plus verification 38 per cent; Bihar declared ODF in 2019 under Swachh Bharat Mission but OD return (28 per cent of households that built toilets have reverted to open defecation) shows the toilet construction was not matched by behaviour change and maintenance support). Water quality testing (18 per cent -- only 18 per cent of Bihar's JJM piped water sources are regularly tested for potability; 82 per cent untested).

source.quote: JJM 72. functional 48. arsenic 1.2 crore. ODF 38. OD return 28. quality 18

recommendations: Bihar PHED must implement a Bihar Water Emergency Programme: (a) functional taps -- from 48 to 75 per cent within 18 months; district-level PHED maintenance teams with 72-hour repair SLA; Jal Mitra (village-level water plumber) scheme for all 38 districts; (b) arsenic -- emergency surface water supply in all 14 arsenic districts; iron removal plants + reverse osmosis for 1,200 affected habitations; community water ATMs in all arsenic panchayats within 12 months; (c) ODF return -- from 28 to 10 per cent within 2 years; ASHA worker daily household sanitation monitoring; gram panchayat ODF-maintenance fund ₹50,000/year; (d) water quality -- from 18 to 60 per cent testing within 12 months; district water quality labs; portable testing kits for all Jal Mitra workers; (e) PHED UC -- from 62 to 80 per cent utilisation within 6 months; ₹3,000 crore additional JJM spending acceleration.

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's real estate market (Rs. 1.8 lakh crore annual -- India's 2nd largest after Maharashtra) has a structural affordability crisis overlaying strong market health. K-RERA (Karnataka Real Estate Regulatory Authority -- 28,000 registered projects -- India's 3rd largest RERA register after MH and UP) has a complaint backlog (8,200 -- 42 per cent) where homebuyers wait 18+ months for resolution orders. Affordable housing (28 per cent of new Bengaluru supply under Rs. 45 lakh vs 58 per cent demand from the middle-class segment -- IT employees earning Rs. 8-15 lakh/year, nurses, teachers, and government employees who cannot afford premium real estate). Whitefield premium (Rs. 15,000-28,000/sq ft -- driven by proximity to Amazon, Microsoft, and Wipro campuses; a 2 BHK in Whitefield is Rs. 1.5-2.5 crore -- beyond the reach of 80 per cent of Bengaluru's working population). BBMP OC (Occupancy Certificate -- 18,000 projects pending OC from BBMP; many Bengaluru residents have been living in completed buildings for years without OC -- because the building was completed with deviations or without BBMP completing its inspection). Homebuyer stuck (Rs. 8,400+ crore -- money paid into stalled projects; Bengaluru's scale means stuck money is higher than WB in absolute terms).

source.quote: K-RERA 28,000. complaint 42. affordable 28 vs 58. Whitefield Rs. 15,000-28,000. stuck Rs. 8,400+. BBMP 18,000

recommendations: Karnataka Housing and K-RERA must: (a) complaint -- from 42 to 20 per cent backlog within 12 months; 5 additional K-RERA adjudicating officers; online hearing system to reduce physical hearing delays; (b) affordable housing -- Karnataka Affordable Housing Policy 2025: 25 per cent floor space index (FSI) bonus for projects where 30 per cent units priced <₹40 lakh; Peripheral Ring Road zone designated affordable housing belt; (c) BBMP OC -- mass OC clearance camp; 500 projects per quarter; OC inspection team doubled; (d) stuck money -- Karnataka Homebuyer Protection Fund ₹500 crore; priority for projects >5 year delay; (e) Bengaluru affordability -- satellite town development (Tumakuru, Hoskote, Ramanagara) with metro connectivity as alternative to Bengaluru premium; IT companies incentivised to establish campuses in satellite towns.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's sports governance paradox: the state with one of the highest youth populations (18-35 age group: 4.2 crore -- national leader in youth absolute numbers) has the thinnest sports infrastructure of any major state. Patna Sports Complex (Rs. 480 crore -- announced 2019; 58 per cent complete in 2026 -- 7 years; the project delay is emblematic of Bihar's infrastructure execution capacity gap). District stadiums (38 -- one per district, which Bihar has achieved -- but most are single-sport cricket grounds without running track, swimming pool, or multi-purpose court). Khelo India centres (28 -- 42 per cent functional means 16 of 28 are either incomplete, under-staffed, or without equipment; the programme to identify Olympic-calibre talent from grassroots Bihar is non-functional in 58 per cent of its centres). Boxing (8 international medalists from Bihar -- the state's boxing tradition is genuine; Srikant Tiwari, Amit Bhardwaj and other Bihar boxers have brought medals; but without infrastructure, talent exits to Delhi, Haryana, and Punjab training centres). Youth unemployment (22 per cent -- Bihar's young people are India's most underemployed relative to population, which converts directly to outmigration, social stress, and political instability).

keyFindings.text: Kolkata's urban health system combines achievement and crisis. Kolkata's MMR (82 per lakh live births -- better than the WB state average of 97 -- showing the city's hospital infrastructure does provide better obstetric care than rural WB, but still far behind Bengaluru MMR 48 and Pune MMR 38). NUHM (National Urban Health Mission -- Rs. 1,200 crore budget for WB urban health -- 58 per cent utilisation; the programme targeting slum populations has been chronically underfunded relative to rural health). Dengue (28,000 annual cases -- 2nd India after Tamil Nadu -- Kolkata's waterlogging, abandoned construction sites, and dense housing create ideal Aedes aegypti breeding conditions; 28,000 is the official count; actual burden may be 3-4x due to underreporting and home treatment). Urban ASHA vacancy (42 per cent -- ASHAs are the community health workers who form the link between households and the health system; 42 per cent urban ASHA vacancy means Kolkata's slum areas have minimal community health outreach). Air quality (PM2.5 68 -- 70 per cent above standard 40; Kolkata's air pollution from vehicular emissions, brick kilns, and garbage burning is the highest chronic disease risk for its 15+ million metropolitan population).

keyFindings.text: Kerala's higher education system has India's best metrics on research depth (8,200 annual research publications -- best per capita of any Indian state; Kerala's 3.5 crore population produces more per-capita research output than Maharashtra's 12.5 crore) and access (GER 42 per cent -- the highest in India alongside Tamil Nadu; meaning 42 per cent of 18-23 year old Keralites are enrolled in higher education vs national average 28 per cent). Yet the system faces a structural crisis: engineering college seat fill (48 per cent -- 170+ engineering colleges with 48 per cent average seat fill; Kerala produces too many engineering graduates for its domestic economy; private engineering colleges charge Rs. 1,80,000+ per year -- many engineering graduates leave to Gulf or abroad simply to service the education loan). Brain drain (38 per cent of Kerala graduates are abroad -- the highest proportion of any Indian state; Kerala's skilled human capital powers the Gulf's construction, healthcare, and hospitality sectors while Kerala's own economy needs skilled workers; remittances fund Kerala's welfare model but the developmental brain drain is a long-term risk). PhD (3,800 annually -- best India per lakh population -- Kerala produces researchers but 60 per cent do postdoctoral work abroad and do not return; the university system cannot retain talent).

source.quote: GER 42 best. publications 8,200 best per capita. PhD 3,800. brain drain 38. engineering 48. NIRF 4 top-100

recommendations: Kerala Higher Education Council must: (a) engineering rationalisation -- from 170+ to 120 colleges within 3 years (voluntary exit with compensation for non-viable colleges); redirect surplus engineering seats to allied health, data science, and EV technology courses; (b) brain drain retention -- Kerala Knowledge Economy Programme: ₹500 crore/year for returnee fellowship (Kerala researchers abroad get 5-year fellowship to return and set up lab); (c) research excellence -- Kerala must target 2 institutions in NIRF Top-50 by 2030; KIIFB ₹500 crore for research infrastructure at University of Kerala and Calicut University; (d) PhD to industry -- all PhD students must have 1-year industry placement at Kerala IT/BT companies as part of degree; KSUM (Kerala Startup Mission) to absorb 500 PhD graduates annually; (e) NIRF 4 to 8 -- systematic NIRF improvement plan for 4 next-tier institutions with dedicated management coaching.

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's housing regulatory crisis centres on HIRA (Housing Industry Regulatory Authority -- WB's version of RERA; WB had initially passed its own HIRA 2017 instead of RERA 2016 which was ultimately struck down by the Supreme Court in 2021 as unconstitutional; WB had to reconstitute HIRA under RERA -- this 4-year regulatory gap during which homebuyers had no recourse is itself a governance failure). HIRA complaint backlog (12,000 cases -- homebuyers who paid for flats that were delayed, abandoned, or delivered defectively; each backlog case represents a family that has paid EMIs for years while living in rented accommodation waiting for a flat they already bought). Stuck homebuyer money (Rs. 4,800+ crore -- money paid by homebuyers to builders for projects that are stalled or abandoned; 18 projects in NCLT insolvency means these homebuyers are unsecured creditors in insolvency proceedings with low recovery probability). Kolkata New Town (42 per cent vacant -- Rajarhat-New Town, the planned satellite city built over the last 20 years at Rs. 15,000+ crore public investment, has 42 per cent vacancy in residential towers -- speculative investment in empty flats while Kolkata's slum population has no affordable housing).

source.quote: HIRA 3,800. backlog 12,000. PMAY-U 68. delay 3.2 yr. stuck Rs. 4,800+. NCLT 18. New Town 42

recommendations: West Bengal Housing and HIRA must: (a) backlog clearance -- from 12,000 to 5,000 pending within 12 months; 3 additional HIRA adjudicating officers; fast-track resolution for stuck cases >3 years; (b) stuck money -- GoWB must create a ₹2,000 crore Homebuyer Protection Fund (partial compensation for NCLT-insolvent projects); co-funded by real estate developer industry body CREDAI-WB; (c) NCLT 18 -- WB must appoint a special government mediator for each of the 18 NCLT projects to negotiate settlement between IRP and homebuyers before full liquidation; (d) New Town vacancy -- WB Housing Board must study why 42 per cent vacancy persists; if speculative, introduce a 2 per cent Vacant Property Tax on New Town residential properties vacant >24 months; (e) PMAY-U -- from 68 to 90 per cent within 18 months; city-wise dashboard with weekly builder accountability.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's justice system is India's most congested: 28 lakh pending cases (2nd India after UP -- Bihar has approximately 1 judge per 150,000 people vs the Law Commission's recommended 1 per 50,000). Prison occupancy (180 per cent -- 72,000 inmates in 40,000-capacity prisons; Bhagalpur Central Jail 300 per cent; Muzaffarpur at 280 per cent -- conditions that courts have termed "sub-human"). Undertrial percentage (78 per cent -- 78 per cent of Bihar's 72,000 prisoners are undertrials awaiting trial; they have not been convicted but are in prison because they cannot pay bail; many undertrial prisoners in Bihar have been in jail longer than the maximum sentence for the crime charged). Judge vacancy (38 per cent -- 300+ judicial vacancies in Bihar courts; unfilled positions cause individual judges to carry 1,500+ case dockets vs the Supreme Court's recommended 500). Bihar Police vacancy (42 per cent -- in a high-crime state, police vacancy directly reduces investigation quality, bail supervision, and deterrence). Legal aid (28 per cent -- only 28 per cent of Bihar's poor accused have access to a Legal Services Authority lawyer; 72 per cent navigate courts alone or with informal paid help who may not be lawyers).

keyFindings.text: Odisha's agricultural governance has three national benchmarks: PMFBY coverage (68 per cent -- best east India; national average 42 per cent -- Odisha has achieved near-universal crop insurance by making PMFBY opt-out rather than opt-in for KCC holders and by subsidising premium above GoI's 50 per cent), MSP procurement (82 per cent of paddy sold at MSP -- best India; Odisha's PACS and government procurement network ensures farmers receive MSP rather than distress-selling to traders), and KALIA (Krushak Assistance for Livelihood and Income Augmentation -- Rs. 5,500 crore reaching 51 lakh farmer households with Rs. 10,000/year direct income support). These three programmes together mean Odisha farmers have: income support (KALIA), crop insurance (PMFBY), and price guarantee (MSP procurement). keyFindings.text: West Bengal's revenue performance (Tax-GSDP ratio 8.8 per cent -- below national average 10.2 per cent -- means WB is collecting less tax per unit of economic output than the average Indian state) has multiple dimensions. GST compliance (68 per cent -- 32 per cent of WB GST liability goes uncollected; below MH 70 per cent, far below Karnataka 78 per cent) is the primary revenue gap. Professional tax (Rs. 1,200 crore -- WB has a professional tax on salaried employees in the private sector; 18 per cent compliance gap vs assessed liability) is a small-revenue but high-compliance-signal indicator. Land revenue (Rs. 2,800 crore -- 42 per cent of potential from WB's rural land holdings; land records digitisation Banglarbhumi 82 per cent but revenue collection is separately managed and poorly monitored). Stamp duty (Rs. 8,400+ crore -- strong collection from Kolkata real estate boom; this is WB's most buoyant own tax revenue). The combined revenue gap (if WB achieved national average tax-GSDP ratio) is Rs. 12,000+ crore/year additional revenue -- money that could fund either KIIFB debt service or welfare programme expansion.

keyFindings.text: Odisha's governance quality indicators are eastern India's benchmark. Mo Sarkar (My Government -- Odisha's unique governance accountability programme where senior government officials call beneficiaries of government schemes to verify service delivery -- 88 per cent satisfaction rate from 28 lakh calls made to JJM, PMAY-G, KALIA, and Mission Shakti beneficiaries) is India's most innovative government accountability mechanism. RTI (Right to Information -- 92 per cent response rate within 30 days -- best east India; national average 72 per cent) reflects a functional information governance culture. CM Grievance (8.2 lakh applications -- direct to CM's office; 82 per cent resolved within 60 days through SUGAM portal) is a citizen-accessible accountability system. BSKY (Biju Swasthya Kalyan Yojana -- health insurance 96 lakh households; Rs. 5 lakh/family/year government-funded insurance; covering 4.2 crore people -- 90 per cent of Odisha population -- the most universal health coverage of any Indian state outside Tamil Nadu's Chief Minister's Comprehensive Health Insurance). keyFindings.text: Bihar's 42 lakh migrant workers are India's most important labour export -- and its most unprotected workforce. Remittances (Rs. 80,000+ crore -- roughly equal to Bihar's entire state budget; remittances fund rural consumption, housing construction, education, and healthcare in Bihar's villages) show the economic significance of outmigration. Yet these workers have essentially no social protection: ESIC coverage 2.8 lakh in Bihar (workers employed and insured within Bihar) vs 42 lakh Bihari workers employed outside Bihar without any Bihar-government social protection; outside Bihar they should be covered by destination state ESIC, but registration gaps and contractor avoidance mean many are unprotected. COVID reverse migration (32 lakh returned in 2020 -- India's largest single reverse migration event; Bihar's rural economy had to absorb 32 lakh suddenly unemployed workers; MGNREGS work demand tripled; remittances dropped 40 per cent; rural poverty reversed years of gain) was a preview of the fragility of Bihar's economy due to its dependence on external employment. eMigrant Portal (18 per cent -- only 18 per cent of Bihar migrant workers registered on GoI eMigrant system despite MWPF -- Migrant Workers Welfare Fund -- benefits contingent on registration).

keyFindings.text: Kerala's tourism economy (Rs. 48,000+ crore -- 12 per cent of Kerala GSDP; 2 crore tourists including 1.2 crore domestic and 8 lakh international) has a Wayanad disaster as its defining governance failure for this period. Wayanad landslide (July 2024 -- 400+ deaths in Mundakkai and Chooralmala villages; India's worst landslide in decades; triggered by extreme rainfall on saturated slopes in already ESZ-encroached Western Ghats territory). The landslide was not unprecedented -- Wayanad has 38 of Kerala's 280+ identified landslide-prone villages; the Gadgil Committee (2011) and Kasturirangan Committee (2013) both recommended strict ESZ enforcement in Western Ghats that was not implemented. ESZ encroachment (3,800 acres -- encroachment inside Eco-Sensitive Zones adjacent to Western Ghats: plantation expansion, resort development, and unauthorized quarrying in Wayanad, Idukki, and Palakkad). Houseboat nil STP (1,400 houseboats without sewage treatment -- Vembanad and backwater ecosystem receiving untreated houseboat waste -- a tourism sector contributing to the environmental degradation of its own resource base).

source.quote: Wayanad 400+. ESZ 3,800. Western Ghats 39. houseboats nil STP. coastal 28. responsible 220

keyFindings.text: The Sundarbans (54 inhabited islands in WB's portion of the world's largest mangrove forest -- shared with Bangladesh; UNESCO World Heritage; home to Royal Bengal Tiger, Irrawaddy dolphin, and 350 bird species; 45 lakh human population entirely below 5-metre elevation) is India's most acute climate crisis geography. Sea level rise (4 mm/year at Sagar Island -- the highest coastal rise rate in India; by 2050, models predict 15-20 cm additional rise, inundating 40 per cent of current Sundarban habitation permanently). Cyclone cumulative damage (Amphan 2020 Rs. 80,000 crore; Yaas 2021 Rs. 28,000 crore; Sitrang 2022 Rs. 12,000 crore) -- every 12-18 months a major cyclone hits the Sundarbans and requires the same reconstruction. Embankment (3,500 km of earthen embankments -- the primary protection against tidal flooding; 42 per cent damaged or inadequate -- meaning 42 per cent of Sundarban islands have breached or weak embankments; every high tide at new moon threatens submergence). Freshwater dependence (38 per cent of Sundarban population depends on fresh surface water from seasonal ponds -- increasingly saline with each cyclone storm surge). Arsenic in groundwater (8 Sundarban islands) is an additional drinking water crisis.

source.quote: sea level 4 mm/yr. mangrove 4,264. cyclone Rs. 1,20,000+. embankment 42 per cent. freshwater 38 per cent. arsenic 8 districts

recommendations: Government of WB and GoI must implement an emergency Sundarban Climate Resilience Programme: (a) Embankment -- all 42 per cent damaged embankments must be repaired with concrete/stone lining (not earthen) within 18 months; ₹8,000 crore GoI-WB joint investment under Jal Jeevan Mission expansion; (b) Managed retreat -- GoI must formally develop a Sundarban Managed Retreat Policy for the 8-10 islands projected to be uninhabitable by 2040; relocation with full livelihood compensation; (c) Freshwater -- desalination units on 12 most salt-stressed islands within 24 months; rainwater harvesting cisterns for every household; (d) Mangrove restoration -- net mangrove cover from 4,264 to 4,800 sq km within 5 years (mangrove buffers storm surge by 30 per cent); MGNREGS for mangrove planting; (e) Solar Sagar -- from 28 MW to 100 MW within 3 years; make Sagar Island a model 100 per cent renewable energy island; (f) GoI Climate Finance -- WB must claim ₹20,000 crore from NCEF (National Clean Energy Fund) and Green Climate Fund for Sundarban adaptation.

keyFindings.text: Odisha's road connectivity has multiple layers. PMGSY (Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana -- rural road programme) at 82 per cent (best east India; national average 72 per cent) reflects Odisha's rural connectivity priority. keyFindings.text: Bihar's school infrastructure crisis combines physical and human capital deficits. Physical: 72,000+ government schools of which 58 per cent are single-teacher or single-room (no multi-room building -- when it rains, all children in one room; when the teacher is absent, school effectively closes), toilet functional (62 per cent -- 38 per cent toilets non-functional due to no water supply, maintenance gap, or broken infrastructure; girl dropout in Bihar is directly correlated with non-functional toilet in schools), electricity (48 per cent -- half of Bihar schools have no electricity; no fan in 45 degree May summer; no lighting for afternoon study; no digital learning device charging). Human: teacher vacancy 3.5 lakh (3 lakh primary and 50,000 secondary -- the largest unfilled teacher gap in any Indian state; some Bihar government schools have 200 students per teacher). NIPUN at 38 per cent (vs Karnataka 78 per cent -- a 40-point gap that directly reflects teacher vacancy, infrastructure, and classroom quality). MDM (Mid-Day Meal 88 per cent -- above national average -- is Bihar's single most consistent school programme; it keeps children in school even when learning quality is poor). Board exam (82 lakh appeared -- Bihar's massive education scale; Bihar has more students in Class 10 exam than all of Germany has in school).

keyFindings.text: Kerala's environmental crisis has a geographic icon: Vembanad Lake (2,100 sq km -- India's largest Ramsar-listed wetland; stretching from Kottayam to Kochi) is ecologically dead in its central sections. Dissolved oxygen <2 mg/L (WHO ecological minimum 4 mg/L -- below 2 is "dead zone" where fish cannot survive); BOD 18 mg/L (6x norm) driven by untreated sewage from 1,400 houseboats (each houseboat holding 10-40 tourists discharging directly into the lake -- zero treatment), municipal drains from Alappuzha, Kottayam, and Ernakulam, and agricultural runoff (paddy fertiliser from Kuttanad -- India's only sub-sea-level paddy field, called "the rice bowl of Kerala"). Vembanad encroachment (3,200 acres of lake bed encroached -- converted to prawn farms, paddy fields, and construction) despite Ramsar designation and Kerala High Court protection orders. Plastic waste (1,200 MT/day -- 58 per cent processed; 42 per cent going to open dumps or water bodies -- Kerala's tourism economy generates disproportionate single-use plastic). KSPCB inspection backlog (3 years -- industries, hospitality, and municipalities not inspected for compliance -- the same failure as Bihar but in India's governance-leading state).

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's fisheries economy (18 lakh MT -- 2nd India after Andhra Pradesh; inland fishery from 2.8 lakh ponds and bheries; marine from Bay of Bengal/Sundarbans) is anchored by Hilsa (Ilish in Bengali -- 72,000 MT, India's largest single-species catch; also a GI-tagged product and a cultural identity symbol). Hilsa is to Bengal what salmon is to Norway: a culinary, cultural, and economic icon. The hilsa catch is declining (from 1.2 lakh MT in 2000 to 72,000 MT in 2025 -- a 40 per cent decline in 25 years driven by over-fishing, habitat loss in spawning rivers, and climate change in the Bay of Bengal). Trawl ban compliance (38 per cent -- the monsoon trawl ban allows hilsa to spawn; 62 per cent non-compliance by mechanised boats means the ban that is supposed to protect hilsa actually fails to do so). PMFBY marine coverage (8 per cent -- 92 per cent of Sundarbans fisherfolk have no crop insurance against cyclone, storm surge, or boat loss) combined with cyclone fund disbursement (52 per cent) leaves Sundarbans fishermen perpetually vulnerable after each Amphan/Yaas/Sitrang-class cyclone.

source.quote: hilsa 72,000 MT largest. trawl ban 38 per cent. cold storage 42 per cent. PMFBY 8 per cent. cyclone 52 per cent. export Rs. 1,200

recommendations: West Bengal Fisheries must: (a) Hilsa conservation -- from 38 to 85 per cent trawl ban compliance within 2 years; marine police patrol deployment; automatic satellite tracking for all mechanised trawlers >15m; (b) Hilsa GI premium -- WB must develop a Hilsa premium export channel (live Hilsa to Bangladeshi market; processed Hilsa to UAE, USA, UK diaspora); target export from ₹1,200 to ₹3,500 crore by 2030; (c) PMFBY marine -- from 8 to 40 per cent within 2 years; ₹200 crore state subsidy to bring premium below ₹1,500/year for all Sundarbans fisherfolk; (d) cold storage -- from 42 to 70 per cent gap closure within 3 years; NABARD cold chain credit to fisher cooperatives; (e) Sundarbans resilience -- all 4.8 lakh Matua and Sundarbans fisherfolk enrolled in NDRF pre-cyclone database; evacuation simulation twice yearly.

keyFindings.text: Odisha's SC/ST welfare framework has an unambiguous achievement at its centre: FRA (Forest Rights Act) title at 8.5 lakh (best India -- vs Gujarat 3.2 lakh, Jharkhand 3.8 lakh) means Odisha has recognised tribal forest rights at the highest scale of any state. keyFindings.text: Bihar's land acquisition crisis for public infrastructure is a compound failure: NH-28 (Muzaffarpur to Barauni -- a 4-lane project critical for connecting Muzaffarpur (Bihar's 2nd city) with Begusarai and Bhagalpur) has been delayed 8 years from its original 2016 completion date; NH-31 (Patna-Bakhtiyarpur-Mokameh -- the Patna to Bhagalpur corridor) delayed 12 years. keyFindings.text: Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC -- India's oldest municipal corporation, established 1876) manages one of Asia's most complex cities: 14.8 million metropolitan area; Hooghly riverfront; colonial heritage; dense informal settlements. KMC's property tax crisis (Rs. 1,800 crore collected vs Rs. 4,200 crore assessed -- 43 per cent -- a persistent structural failure; Kolkata's property valuation system is based on Annual Rental Value from 1950s surveys for many properties; owners pay nominal tax on gross undervalued assessments) is the primary fiscal constraint. Waterlogging (280 annual incidents -- Kolkata's drainage infrastructure designed for British-era population and rainfall; climate change intensifying monsoon; Mahananda pumping station consistently overwhelmed; North Kolkata and Topsia-Tiljala are chronic flood zones). East Kolkata Wetlands (12,500 acres -- a UNESCO-recognised wetland system serving as Kolkata's natural sewage treatment; the world's largest organic sewage utilisation farm; 28 per cent under encroachment despite HC protection orders) is both an ecological and a livelihood asset (8,000+ bheri fish farmers and 300+ vegetable farmers depend on EKW). Durga Puja (KMC grants Rs. 480 crore to 3,000+ puja committees -- a cultural governance decision; Durga Puja UNESCO Intangible Heritage).

keyFindings.text: Bihar's child protection system is India's most overloaded and under-resourced. POCSO cases (3,800 annually -- 2nd India after UP; Bihar's 3,800 cases for 13 crore population is actually lower than India's worst states but the conviction rate of 12 per cent -- vs national 32 per cent -- means 88 per cent of perpetrators go unpunished). Special POCSO courts (18 vs 38 required -- the POCSO Act mandates one special court per district for Bihar's 38 districts; 20 districts have no dedicated POCSO court; their cases are handled by sessions courts with 3-5 year backlogs). JJB (Juvenile Justice Board -- handles all cases involving juvenile offenders) 8,000 case backlog means Bihar's juvenile justice system is 3 years behind. Child marriage (40 per cent) and child labour (4.8 lakh) are the root conditions that create vulnerability to exploitation.

keyFindings.text: The 10-state CAG governance scorecard reveals India's development geography with stark clarity. The spread (28 to 82 -- a 54-point range within the same federal system) is the central datum of Indian governance: a child born in Bihar (score 32) faces a 6.6x higher chance of maternal death than one born in Kerala (score 82); a child in MP rural (score 28 on water delivery) is 2.5x more likely to drink unsafe water than one in Karnataka; a construction worker in Goa earns 4x more than one in Bihar doing equivalent work. The scorecard also shows paths: Odisha (62) demonstrates that an eastern tribal state can outperform the national average through 25 years of consistent governance focus. Punjab (44) shows that per-capita prosperity does not guarantee governance quality; fiscal structure can undermine even wealthy states. Kerala (82) and Karnataka (79) show that a state can simultaneously maintain fiscal discipline (Revenue Surplus), lead on health (MMR 30), and invest in technology (IT/BT USD 90 bn) -- these are not trade-offs but a governance mode. India's development agenda for 2030 must start with this geography: get Bihar from 32 to 50; get MP JJM from 28 to 60; get Punjab from 44 to 58; sustain Karnataka/Kerala above 75. The resources exist; the governance transformation is the work.

source.quote: Kerala 82. Karnataka 79. Gujarat 67. Odisha 62. WB 51. Jharkhand 48. Nagaland 46. Punjab 44. UP 38. Bihar 32. MP 28. MMR 30-210. SAM 4-42. NIPUN 38-78

recommendations: GoI Planning Commission (NITI Aayog) must adopt the CAG cross-state governance scorecard as an official national accountability tool: (a) Annual State Governance Report -- tabled in Parliament alongside Union Budget; each state scored on 12 indicators (fiscal, health, education, water, energy, environment, labour, gender, tribal, urban, digital, and equity); (b) Convergence Fund -- ₹50,000 crore/year GoI "Governance Improvement Fund" to states below score 50 (Bihar, MP, UP) on demonstrated improvement metrics -- not just input spending; (c) Best Practice Exchange -- formal Kerala-Bihar health cooperation (Bihar sends 500 health administrators to Kerala for 6-month immersion); Karnataka-MP JJM water cooperation; (d) Viksit Bharat 2047 target -- all 10 states above score 65 by 2040; (e) Media accountability -- CAG annual state governance scores must be published as press conference data; citizen awareness of comparative governance is itself a governance improvement mechanism.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's urban local body finance crisis mirrors its state finance crisis at a smaller scale. Patna Municipal Corporation (PMC) property tax collection (Rs. 280 crore vs Rs. 840 crore assessed potential -- 33 per cent collection efficiency -- among India's worst for a state capital of 3 million people) leaves the corporation dependent on state grants for basic services. Patna's untreated sewage crisis (STP capacity 60 MLD vs 180 MLD generated -- 67 per cent untreated; directly discharging into the Ganga; NAMAMI GANGE funds Rs. 1,200 crore -- 52 per cent utilised) is both a public health emergency and a governance failure. AMRUT 2.0 (Rs. 1,800 crore for Bihar urban infrastructure) at 38 per cent utilisation reflects implementation capacity deficit: engineers, procurement, and project management are all inadequate. Patna's 8 lakh slum residents (concentrated in low-lying areas near the Ganga banks -- flood-prone, without tenure, without services) are the most vulnerable urban population in India's largest river-plain city. keyFindings.text: Karnataka's 17-point Kalyana Karnataka gap (58 vs state 75 composite score) has district-level dimensions that are as stark as the national Bihar-Karnataka comparison. keyFindings.text: Goa's BOCW audit concludes at 61/100 -- a small state with India's highest per capita income (GSDP Rs. 88,000 crore; 15 lakh population; per capita Rs. 5.87 lakh/year -- 4x national average) that has not translated prosperity into labour rights. Goa's 1.2 lakh unregistered construction workers and Rs. 107 crore idle BOCW fund stand in stark contrast to its Rs. 6,800 crore tourism economy (beach resorts, casino boats, luxury hotels consuming migrant construction labour at the highest rate). Tourism prosperity is being built on the labour of unprotected migrant workers from UP, Bihar, Odisha, Jharkhand -- workers who receive compensation below legal standard when injured or killed. Child labour (1,800 -- concentrated in tourism-adjacent domestic service, hospitality, and fishing) is illegal and invisible. Goa's 61/100 reflects its macro-governance (fiscal balance, healthcare, education) alongside specific labour rights deficit. As India's smallest and richest mainland state, Goa has the resources to achieve best-in-class labour governance; the gap is will, not capacity.

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's 9-chapter audit concludes at 46/100 -- the most contextually nuanced score in the dataset. No Indian state's governance can be understood without its history; Nagaland's history is a 70-year independence movement that has kept the state in conflict, made development implementation politically complex, and concentrated fiscal authority in GoI (91 per cent of revenue) because Nagaland's own tax base is minimal. The NSCN (National Socialist Council of Nagaland) ceasefire (27 years -- 1997 to 2025) has brought relative peace, but the peace dividend (the economic development that peace makes possible) has been partly captured by conflict-era governance structures. The paradox: Nagaland has India's best English literacy (a colonial and missionary legacy), ASER reading scores 72 per cent (best northeast), and a globally networked diaspora (Naga professionals in the US, UK, Southeast Asia). Yet Hepatitis B (18 per cent -- highest India; linked to the heroin trade route) and MMR 210 (terrain-driven) show that development quality is limited by geography and governance capacity simultaneously. Biodiversity (Nagaland -- "Land of Festivals" -- is a global biodiversity hotspot; Dzukou Valley, Japfu Peak, Shilloi Lake; 60+ bird species endemic) is an untapped green economy asset. Score 46/100 reflects the best possible governance in the most constrained context.

keyFindings.text: MP's JJM audit concludes at 28/100 -- India's worst JJM implementation score. The definitive finding: Rs. 38,000 crore spent, 78 per cent of households declared as "connections provided" in the national IMIS dashboard, yet field verification shows only 34 per cent receive functional water supply (defined as 55 litres per capita per day for minimum 5 days/week). The gap between paper achievement (78 per cent) and physical reality (34 per cent) is not rounding error -- it is a governance failure of 44 percentage points affecting 2.8 crore rural MP households. This gap was produced by: contractors declaring completion before works were actually functional (incentivised by payment-on-connection-count); IMIS data not cross-verified with actual flow measurement; VWC (38 per cent active) not present to authenticate completion; MIS reporting inaccuracy (62 per cent data quality). Phase 2 (Rs. 18,000 crore -- JJM Phase 2 without fixing Phase 1 governance would repeat the same failure at double the cost). MP's water crisis is immediate: fluoride-affected 18 districts, arsenic-affected 3 districts, and 66 per cent of rural households still without reliable water despite the expenditure.

source.quote: Rs. 38,000 crore. 78 per cent vs 34 per cent functional. 3,800 abandoned. IMIS 62 per cent. VWC 38 per cent. score 28/100

recommendations: Government of MP and GoI Jal Shakti Ministry must take extraordinary measures: (a) FREEZE Phase 2 -- no new JJM Phase 2 contracts in MP until 100 per cent of Phase 1 abandoned schemes (3,800) are completed and verified; (b) AUDIT-RESET -- GoI CAG and MP must conduct a joint physical verification of all 78 per cent "connected" households within 6 months; corrected data replaces IMIS entries; (c) CONTRACTOR ACTION -- all contractors with <60 per cent functional delivery rate must be blacklisted; performance bonds (20 per cent) must be encashed; (d) VWC REVIVAL -- all 62 per cent inactive VWCs re-constituted within 3 months with elected members; VWC empowered to certify completion before payment; (e) IMIS REFORM -- GoI must make IMIS tamper-evident; flow-sensor data from IoT meters must auto-populate IMIS rather than relying on contractor self-reporting; (f) MP JJM must recover from 34 to 60 per cent functional before any Phase 2 investment. 28/100 is not a score -- it is a call for emergency governance intervention.

keyFindings.text: Kerala's 8-chapter audit concludes at 82/100 -- India's highest governance benchmark, edging above Karnataka (79/100) on health and education metrics. Kerala is the proof of concept for India's development ambition: MMR 30 (on par with Sweden; 5x better than Bihar); longevity 77 years (Europe-equivalent); NIPUN 78 per cent (best south India); GP self-financing 42 per cent (5x national average); Kudumbashree 50 lakh women in cooperative enterprises; MILMA dairy Rs. 12,000+ crore; NHM 88 per cent utilisation. What Kerala has built over 50 years: a health system that is genuinely equitable (tribal districts have MMR <50 vs national 180+ for tribal); a local governance system where GPs make real decisions with real money; a cooperative movement that reaches 50 lakh women into economic agency; and an education system where even poor rural children read at grade level. Kerala's governance challenge: fiscal sustainability (KIIFB Rs. 40,000 crore off-budget; OPS actuarial; pension as per cent of expenditure); demographic ageing (16 per cent elderly -- the governance burden the longevity success has created); and suicide (18/lakh -- the mental health cost of a high-pressure achievement culture and elderly isolation). Score 82/100 is Kerala's achievement. The remaining 18 points require solving fiscal sustainability without destroying the welfare state that produced the 82.

recommendations: Government of Kerala must protect its 82/100 leadership while addressing the three fiscal-demographic threats: (1) KIIFB transparency -- KIIFB debt fully disclosed in FRBM budget; asset yields (toll, user charges) to cover 40 per cent of debt service by 2027; GoI-Kerala debt restructuring for existing KIIFB bonds; (2) Elderly care -- Kerala Dementia Mission (8 lakh dementia sufferers); Vayomithram to 10 lakh; Gulf diaspora elderly monitoring; mental health from 18 to 12/lakh suicide rate within 5 years; (3) Cooperative evolution -- Kudumbashree from savings-credit to enterprise (all 50 lakh women in at least one ONDC-linked enterprise by 2027); MILMA to ₹16,000 crore by 2030; (4) Fiscal own-revenue -- Kerala GST compliance, property tax, and professional tax must add ₹8,000 crore own revenue within 3 years; reduce GoI dependence from 60 to 50 per cent; (5) Kerala model export -- GoI must formally study the Kerala MMR, cooperative, and LSG models for national replication; Kerala to host an annual National Development Governance Summit. keyFindings.text: Jharkhand's audit concludes at 48/100 -- India's most vivid natural resource paradox. Jharkhand has: 40 per cent of India's coal reserves; 25 per cent of iron ore; 42 per cent of lac; uranium, copper, bauxite, limestone. Mining revenue Rs. 45,000+ crore. Yet: NIPUN 48 per cent (below Bihar 38 per cent -- wait, actually among the lowest); tribal 28 per cent unelectrified; PMAY-G 58 per cent; FRA 3.8 lakh vs 8 lakh target; JSLPS enterprise profitability 8 per cent. The mineral wealth and the human development exist in two different economies in the same geography. DMFT (District Mineral Foundation Trust) has received Rs. 12,000+ crore specifically to convert mineral royalty into local community development -- but utilisation gaps and governance failures mean the community adjacent to the mine is often the last to benefit. Jharkhand's 48/100 is better than Bihar (32/100) and below Odisha (62/100) -- both eastern neighbours with whom it shares tribal demography. Odisha's better score demonstrates that tribal geography is not destiny; it is governance that makes the difference.

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's road connectivity is India's most challenging geography: 60+ tribal districts across Naga hills (1,000-2,800 m elevation), dense forest, steep slopes, seismically active zone, and 2,500 mm annual rainfall that destroys asphalt roads. National Highway connectivity (40 per cent paved in good condition vs 85 per cent national average) and village road connectivity (28 per cent motorable -- 72 per cent of Nagaland's 1,200+ villages are accessible only by foot in monsoon) reflect terrain constraints compounded by maintenance funding gap (Rs. 380 crore/year maintenance shortfall -- roads are built but not maintained). Landslides (280 annual -- highest northeast India; closing major routes for weeks) are the primary connectivity disruptor. Kohima-Dimapur 4-lane highway (Nagaland's economic lifeline -- connecting the capital to the rail head and Assam plains) has been under construction 8 years with 6 contractor changes. Trans-Nagaland Project (Rs. 2,800 crore -- east-west connectivity across Nagaland linking Myanmar border at Moreh and Champhai) is Nagaland's most transformative infrastructure project. Myanmar border trade (Rs. 420 crore -- bamboo, cane, teak, agri produce; informal trade estimated 3x) depends entirely on road quality.

keyFindings.text: Gujarat's PMKKKY audit concludes at 67/100 -- the quintessential macro-success/micro-equity paradox. Gujarat has: GSDP Rs. 24.6 lakh crore (3rd India after Maharashtra and UP); Revenue Surplus Rs. 4,200 crore (rare -- only 3 states); solar energy 8 GW (front runner); ports 43 per cent India cargo handling (Mundra, Kandla, Pipavav); 100 per cent industrial electrification; Ease of Doing Business rank 2 (national). Yet within Gujarat, 1.5 crore tribal people (concentrated in Dahod, Narmada, Tapi, Valsad, Dang -- 5 tribal districts) remain structurally excluded from this prosperity: PMKKKY Rs. 851 crore idle (tribal welfare fund sitting unused while tribal SAM is 8.2 per cent and FRA is 41 per cent); fluoride 12 lakh tribal water-contaminated; JJM tribal 20 points below state average. Gujarat's governance score of 67/100 reflects this duality: strong fiscal, energy, and business governance; weak tribal equity delivery. The 8-point gap to Karnataka (79/100) is the tribal equity gap. If Gujarat's tribal district indicators matched its state average, the score would be 73/100.

Gujarat's 67/100 to 73/100 journey is entirely within the tribal equity dimension -- and the fiscal resources (Revenue Surplus ₹4,200 crore) are available.

keyFindings.text: Punjab's 12-chapter audit concludes at 44/100 -- the most paradoxical score in the dataset. Punjab has India's highest per-capita income (Rs. 2.3 lakh/year -- 1.8x national average), Green Revolution legacy infrastructure (canal irrigation, rural roads, mandi network), the most mechanised agriculture, and a globally networked diaspora (Punjab diaspora in Canada, UK, USA, Australia exceeds 15 lakh). Yet it scores 44/100 because its fiscal structure (debt 46 per cent GSDP; STP 114 per cent revenue; OPS Rs. 2,80,000+ crore liability) means it cannot invest in its own future. Punjab's prosperity is real but its governance is borrowing from tomorrow to fund today. The drug epidemic (2.98 lakh estimated opiate users -- 7 per cent of Punjab's adult male population; 6,000+ overdose deaths annually; linked to cross-border Pakistan heroin trade and farmers's economic distress) is the social consequence of stagnation beneath prosperity. Groundwater (80 per cent of blocks overexploited -- water table falling 0.9 m/year in Ludhiana, Jalandhar, Amritsar -- driven by free power and paddy monoculture) is Punjab's environmental bankruptcy. Score 44/100 captures Punjab as a state whose governance is spending its inheritance.

recommendations: Government of Punjab must act on all three existential crises simultaneously: (1) FISCAL -- Punjab Debt Restructuring Compact with GoI: 5-year primary surplus path; no new populist subsidies without identified revenue offset; PSPCL metering and subsidy rationalisation; (2) WATER -- paddy crop diversification (Punjab Paani Bachao campaign: ₹3,000 crore incentive for farmers switching from paddy to maize, cotton, pulse); direct seeding of rice (DSR) technology to cut water use 30 per cent; (3) DRUG -- Punjab Opioid Treatment Programme expansion to all 23 districts; 1,000 OAT (Opioid Agonist Therapy) centres; Punjab Police-NGO-health convergence; (4) Agriculture -- KCC to every farmer; crop insurance; 3-year crop diversification plan replaces Kisan Andolan grievance with economic alternative; (5) OPS -- stop OPS extension immediately; begin transition roadmap. keyFindings.text: UP's electricity governance audit concludes at 38/100 -- India's worst electricity governance score for any state with declared 100 per cent electrification. The fundamental contradiction: a state that claims 100 per cent electrification but delivers 12-hour quality supply to only 44 per cent of consumers has completed the infrastructure without the governance. AT&C loss (35 per cent -- meaning 35 paisa of every rupee of electricity generated is lost to theft, metering gaps, and transmission inefficiency) is India's worst. Agricultural subsidy (Rs. 18,000+ crore/year -- 55 per cent of UP's own tax revenue -- on unmetered flat-rate power) creates a fiscal-physical doom loop: DISCOMs cannot invest in infrastructure because subsidies consume capital; poor infrastructure increases AT&C; AT&C losses further deplete DISCOM revenue. MSME outage cost (Rs. 12,000+ crore/year -- the economic damage to UP's manufacturing sector from unreliable power; small manufacturers run diesel generators at Rs. 20/unit vs grid power at Rs. 6/unit) means UP's electricity failure directly makes its manufacturing uncompetitive. UP Reform 2030 (GoI RDSS Rs. 22,000 crore + state matching) is the investment; the governance reform (metering, AT&C, subsidy rationalisation) is the hard part.

source.quote: AT&C 35 per cent. supply 44 per cent. subsidy Rs. 18,000+. MSME Rs. 12,000+. smart meter 28 per cent. RDSS Rs. 22,000. score 38/100

recommendations: Government of UP and UPPCL must implement UP Power Reform 2030 with 5 measurable commitments: (1) Smart metering -- from 28 to 80 per cent within 3 years; GoI RDSS funding must be fully deployed; every meter is a revenue certainty; (2) AT&C from 35 to 20 per cent within 5 years through smart metering, feeder separation, and enforcement against industrial theft; ₹15,000 crore additional DISCOM revenue at current rates; (3) Supply hours -- from 44 to 70 per cent of consumers receiving 12+ hours within 3 years; feeder-level performance monitoring; (4) Agricultural subsidy metering pilot -- 5 districts (Agra, Mathura, Etawah, Bareilly, Meerut) prepaid meter pilot; direct subsidy transfer to farmer account; (5) MSME power guarantee -- industrial feeders in MSME clusters must achieve 95 per cent uptime with penalty clause on DISCOM. UP's electricity score of 38/100 is the difference between a ₹24 lakh crore GSDP state that punches at its weight and one that loses ₹30,000+ crore annually to energy inefficiency.

keyFindings.text: Punjab's fiscal position is India's most acute state finance crisis. The core problem: committed expenditure (salary + pension + interest on debt) equals 114 per cent of own revenue -- meaning even before spending a single rupee on development (roads, schools, hospitals, JJM), Punjab must borrow to pay its existing staff and debt service. This is the definition of a debt trap. Debt at Rs. 3.26 lakh crore (46 per cent of GSDP -- the highest among major non-NE states; national standard is 25 per cent) means Punjab's borrowing has been structurally funding consumption (salaries, subsidies) rather than investment. PSPCL (Punjab State Power Corporation) subsidy (Rs. 18,500 crore/year -- primarily for free power to agriculture and AAP free 300 units) is 57 per cent of Punjab's total own tax revenue of Rs. 32,500 crore. OPS actuarial liability (Rs. 2,80,000+ crore) is Punjab's invisible debt -- not on the FRBM balance sheet but representing certain future payments. RBI's annual State Finance Report has placed Punjab on fiscal stress watch consecutively for 5 years.

keyFindings.text: Gujarat's FRA implementation (41 per cent title grant rate -- 3.2 lakh of 7.8 lakh claims) has a rejection rate (59 per cent) higher than the national average (52 per cent). The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act 2006 was enacted to recognise historical forest rights of tribal communities living in forests for generations; Gujarat's high rejection rate suggests administrative bottlenecks, improper application of evidence standards, or insufficient Gram Sabha support for claims. Dang (India's only all-tribal district with 95 per cent tribal population -- primarily Bhil, Bhilala, and Kukna communities; exclusively forest-dependent; biodiversity hotspot of Western Ghats) has the most critical FRA backlog. NTFP (Non-Timber Forest Produce -- bamboo, mahua flower and seed, tendu leaf, gum, resin, honey) revenue at Rs. 280 crore (28 per cent reaching tribal collectors -- 72 per cent captured by intermediaries/contractors) is a market failure for Gujarat's forest-dependent tribals. Sickle cell (22 per cent -- Gujarat highest -- concentrated in Dahod, Narmada, Dang) is a co-inheritance of forest ancestry and malaria co-evolution.

source.quote: claims 7.8 lakh. titles 41 per cent. rejection 59 per cent. NTFP 28 per cent. sickle cell 22 per cent

recommendations: Gujarat Tribal Development and Forest must: (a) FRA rejection review -- all 4.6 lakh rejected claims must be reviewed by a State-level FRA Review Committee within 12 months; Gram Sabha decisions must be respected; rejection only if fundamental eligibility gap; (b) Dang FRA -- all Dang claims must be resolved within 6 months; District Collector personally chairs monthly FRA camp; (c) NTFP -- Gujarat NTFP Fair Price Shops (on PACS model) in all 5 tribal districts; bamboo, mahua, tendu at MSP; eliminate contractor middlemen; target NTFP tribal share from 28 to 60 per cent within 3 years; (d) Vanbandhu Kalyan -- ₹1,800 crore must show tribe-level outcome data (income, asset, education); no output-based release without outcome tracking; (e) sickle cell -- Gujarat must implement GoI Sickle Cell Mission fully; universal newborn screening in all 5 tribal districts within 12 months.
