keyFindings.text: Kerala's local self government (LSG) finance is India's most decentralised governance model: 941 GPs, 87 municipalities, and 6 corporations have genuine fiscal autonomy. GP own revenue at Rs. 4,200 crore (42 per cent of GP expenditure self-financed -- national average 8 per cent; Bihar <2 per cent) is India's highest. Kerala's GPs collect property tax, professional tax, and fee-based revenues from a literate, urban-adjacent, and service-economy population. The 50 per cent women ward reservation (mandatory in Kerala LSG law -- enforced through rotation) means Kerala's local governance is gender-representative. Social audit at 72 per cent (MGNREGS social audit conducted in 72 per cent of Kerala GPs -- mandatory but Bihar 28 per cent for comparison) reflects accountability culture. KIIFB (Kerala Infrastructure Investment Fund Board -- Rs. 40,000 crore in off-budget infrastructure borrowing for roads, bridges, schools, hospitals) is Kerala's fiscal innovation and its fiscal risk -- off-budget debt that does not appear in the official FRBM calculation. The sustainability of KIIFB depends on Kerala's growth trajectory maintaining debt service capacity.

recommendations: Kerala Local Self Government must: (a) GP revenue enhancement -- from 42 to 50 per cent self-financing within 5 years; e-property tax with satellite-based land valuation update every 3 years; (b) KIIFB transparency -- KIIFB debt must be included in Kerala's annual FRBM fiscal position disclosure; off-budget becomes on-budget for transparency; KIIFB asset yield (toll, user charges) must cover at least 40 per cent of debt service; (c) CS utilisation -- from 78 to 90 per cent within 12 months; district panchayat officers must prevent fund lapse; (d) social audit -- from 72 to 90 per cent within 12 months; monthly social audit rather than annual; (e) Kerala model export -- Kerala LSG model must be formally documented and shared with GoI Panchayat Raj Ministry as the national template for GP financial decentralisation.

keyFindings.text: MP JJM's monitoring and information ecosystem is fundamentally broken. IMIS (Integrated Management Information System -- GoI's JJM tracking database) data accuracy (62 per cent -- meaning 38 per cent of MP's JJM entries are inaccurate: wrong village, wrong completion status, wrong beneficiary count, duplicate entries) means the national dashboard showing MP's JJM progress is built on flawed data. IoT sensor monitoring (28 per cent operational -- sensors installed on water tanks to measure flow, pressure, and daily supply hours; 72 per cent not transmitting meaningful data due to power failure, vandalism, or incorrect installation) means there is no reliable real-time picture of which villages are actually receiving water. Village Water Committees (38 per cent active -- 62 per cent of VWCs exist on paper but are not meeting, not maintaining records, not collecting tariffs, and not managing their water scheme) are the foundation of JJM sustainability; their inactivity means no one is responsible for the scheme in the village once the contractor leaves. 3,800 schemes abandoned mid-construction (Rs. 8,000 crore of work half-done; contractor either abandoned, was terminated, or died without successor) is the most acute implementation failure.

source.quote: IMIS 62 per cent. sensor 28 per cent. VWC 38 per cent. contractor 52 per cent. 3,800 abandoned. NITI 42/100. quality 38 per cent. UC Rs. 8,000 crore

recommendations: MP PHED and JJM must fix the monitoring failure before more expenditure: (a) IMIS data cleanse -- PHED must assign one data verification officer per district; all MP IMIS entries must be field-verified by January 2025; wrong entries corrected; completion certificates linked to VWC verification; (b) sensor repair -- all 72 per cent non-operational IoT sensors must be repaired or replaced within 6 months; power backup at all sensor locations; (c) VWC revival -- all 62 per cent inactive VWCs must be re-constituted with elected members (50 per cent women mandatory); district magistrate chairs first VWC meeting in each block; (d) abandoned schemes -- 3,800 abandoned schemes must be categorised; new contractor tendered within 3 months; performance bond (20 per cent) enforced against original contractor; (e) contractor performance -- no contractor with <75 per cent on-time completion rate eligible for new JJM contract in MP for 3 years.

keyFindings.text: Goa's construction sector (booming from luxury hotel, casino, and resort development along the North Goa coast -- Candolim, Calangute, Anjuna, Baga -- and high-rise residential in Panaji and Porvorim) has a worker safety crisis hidden behind the tourism facade. Construction fatality (28 annual -- for a state of 15 lakh people, this is among India's highest per-capita construction fatality rates) is driven by: 80 per cent migrant workforce (from UP, Bihar, Odisha, Jharkhand, Karnataka -- workers who are unfamiliar with Goa's building codes, do not speak the language of their supervisor, and cannot read safety signs); scaffolding compliance 28 per cent (72 per cent of Goa construction sites use substandard scaffolding -- the most common cause of fatal falls); safety officer vacancy 42 per cent (the Labour Department does not have enough inspectors to enforce safety on the approximately 800 active construction sites in Goa). Compensation (Rs. 1.8 lakh paid vs Rs. 4 lakh legally mandated BOCW compensation) -- the family of a dead migrant construction worker in Goa receives less than half the legal compensation, and must often travel from Bihar or Odisha to Goa to claim even that.

recommendations: Goa Labour Department and BOCW Board must: (a) safety inspection -- from 38 to 80 per cent sites inspected annually; hire 15 additional safety inspectors immediately; all sites with >50 workers must have daily safety register; (b) compensation -- all BOCW-covered construction fatalities must receive ₹4 lakh within 30 days of death; no claim-filing burden on bereaved family; Goa Labour Department initiates payment proactively; (c) scaffolding -- all sites with >3 floors must have third-party scaffolding safety certification before workers are allowed on structure; 6-month compliance window; (d) migrant registration -- all migrant construction workers must be registered with BOCW Board within 7 days of arrival in Goa; multilingual safety training (Hindi, Odia, Santali, Kannada) at BOCW registration; (e) BOCW fund -- from 52 to 85 per cent utilisation within 12 months; ₹107 crore sitting idle must fund worker health, accident insurance, and education for workers' children.

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's health-education paradox: excellent English literacy (88 per cent -- highest India outside metro states; legacy of Baptist mission schools that also established hospitals) but India's worst MMR in mainland northeast (210 -- vs Kerala 30, national 97). The paradox resolves through geography: Nagaland's terrain (Himalayan foothills, deep valleys, no road to 40 per cent of villages) makes institutional delivery nearly impossible in rural areas. Church mission hospitals (42 per cent of Nagaland's health coverage -- Baptist Hospital Naga) fill the government gap in many districts. ASER reading score (72 per cent -- best northeast India) reflects the mission school legacy: Nagaland children read English better than children in Bengaluru public schools. Teacher absenteeism (28 per cent -- teachers in remote Naga villages are posted from towns; distance, terrain, and cultural unfamiliarity drive absenteeism) is the primary education quality threat despite the good ASER score. Hepatitis B (18 per cent -- highest India; transmitted through shared needles in injectable drug use and unscreened blood -- both linked to Nagaland's proximity to Myanmar and the heroin trade route) is a public health crisis.

source.quote: MMR 210. PHC 80 per cent. church 42 per cent. English 88 per cent. absenteeism 28 per cent. ASER 72 per cent best northeast. Hepatitis B 18 per cent

keyFindings.text: Odisha's 22-chapter audit concludes at 62/100 -- eastern India's highest governance benchmark and a genuine reform success story. Odisha under 25 years of continuous BJD governance (1999-2024) transformed from a state scarred by cyclone Super Cyclone 1999 (10,000 deaths), tribal insurgency, and famine to one with: cyclone zero-death model (world-studied); FRA titling 8.5 lakh (best India); MLE 21 tribal languages (national pioneer); Mission Shakti 70 lakh women cooperatives; Revenue Surplus (rare in eastern India); mining revenue Rs. 68,000 crore (well-governed natural resource); Smart City 78 per cent (best east). Odisha's remaining challenges: malaria (58,000 -- highest India; geography, not governance failure); MMR 152 (improving trajectory -- from 235 to 152 -- but needs more); sickle cell; tribal dropout. Score 62/100 is Odisha's earned benchmark -- the most improbable governance success of the 2000-2025 Indian development era. From cyclone devastation to reform leader in 25 years.

Odisha's 62/100 is the proof that eastern India can build governance excellence from a low base. The next 8 points (to 70) depend on cracking malaria and MMR -- two challenges where geography is the adversary and investment is the weapon.

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's 33-chapter audit concludes at 51/100 -- exactly at India's national average governance benchmark. WB is the most complex state profiled: it has genuine welfare achievements (Lakshmir Bhandar 1.8 crore women; Duare Sarkar 2.8 crore applications; Kanyashree 75 lakh girls; MDM 94 per cent -- best east India; cooperative sector benchmark) alongside serious institutional failures (WBSSC teacher recruitment scandal -- sub-judice; 1.86 lakh teacher vacancies; OPS actuarial bomb Rs. 3,50,000 crore; teacher vacancy Murshidabad 38,000; prison occupancy 138 per cent; malaria 42,000 cases 2nd India). WB is India's paradox state: it pioneered Left-era land reform (Operation Barga -- world's largest sharecropper titling), created Panchayati Raj before the 73rd Amendment, built India's only operating tram network (Kolkata), and established Kudumbashree-equivalent cooperative systems. It then failed at institutional continuity: teachers not hired because of corruption; cooperatives not audited for 3 years; pensions restructured against long-term fiscal interest. Score 51/100 is WB's accountability reckoning: strong welfare effort, weak institutional execution. The gap between the ambition and the implementation is 30 points.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's 26-chapter audit concludes with India's starkest governance benchmark: 32/100 -- defining the floor that the nation's entire development architecture must rise from. Bihar is not a governance failure of one dimension but of every dimension simultaneously: fiscally dependent (GoI 77 per cent revenue -- cannot spend without Delhi); nutritionally catastrophic (SAM 42 per cent -- highest India; malnutrition rate that should trigger international humanitarian response); maternally dangerous (MMR 162 -- 2x national average); educationally neglected (teacher vacancy 3.5 lakh -- the largest unfilled teaching gap of any Indian state); environmentally poisoned (PM2.5 120 -- 3x safe level; arsenic 14 districts); demographically young and unemployed (youth 22 per cent; 42 lakh migrate because Bihar cannot employ them); waterless (JJM functional 45 per cent vs NDA target 100 per cent); institutionally fragile (land records 60+ year old cadastral; mutation 32 lakh pending; courts 8 lakh pending). The tragedy: Bihar has India's most favourable land (Gangetic plain), largest young workforce (India's lowest median age 20.2 years), and a diaspora that funds remittances of Rs. 80,000+ crore annually. The resources exist; governance is the variable that transforms them into development. Score 32/100 is not irreversible -- it is the distance Bihar must travel to reach national average 55/100 and ultimately Karnataka-equivalent 79/100.

source.quote: GoI 77 per cent. SAM 42 per cent. MMR 162. vacancy 3.5 lakh. JJM 45 per cent. PM2.5 120. child marriage 40 per cent. score 32/100

recommendations: Government of Bihar must build a Bihar Vikas Compact 2030 -- a single integrated governance improvement plan with 10 binding sector targets: (1) Fiscal own revenue: from 23 to 35 per cent within 5 years through RERA, property tax, and GST compliance; (2) SAM: from 42 to 28 per cent within 3 years; emergency nutrition protocol; (3) MMR: from 162 to 120 within 3 years; obstetric care 24/7 in all 38 districts; (4) Teacher: fill all 3.5 lakh vacancies within 24 months; (5) Child marriage: from 40 to 25 per cent within 5 years; district collector accountability; (6) JJM functional: from 45 to 75 per cent within 18 months; VWSC empowerment; (7) PM2.5 Patna: from 120 to 80 within 2 years; brick kiln conversion mandatory; (8) Land records: new cadastral survey commenced 2025; mutation clearance 3-year target; (9) Youth employment: BSDM placement from 42 to 60 per cent; Udyami Yojana ₹500 crore expansion; (10) Migrant workers: all 42 lakh registered and socially protected. Bihar's 32/100 to 50/100 journey is India's most important governance story -- because 130 million people are waiting for it.

keyFindings.text: Gujarat's tribal districts (Dahod, Narmada, Tapi, Valsad, Dang -- the Adivasi belt of eastern Gujarat bordering MP, Rajasthan, and Maharashtra) have JJM coverage of 62 per cent against Gujarat's state average of 82 per cent -- a 20-point equity gap in a state known for strong infrastructure. The per capita cost of tribal water schemes (Rs. 4,800 vs Rs. 1,600 for plains) reflects terrain (hilly, forested, dispersed habitations) and distance from water sources. Fluoride contamination (38 districts -- 12 lakh tribal people drinking fluoride-contaminated water exceeding WHO limit of 1.5 mg/L) causes dental fluorosis in children and skeletal fluorosis in adults -- both irreversible without source change. Fluoride is naturally occurring in Gujarat's geological substrate (particularly in Saurashtra's hard rock). GWSSB (Gujarat Water Supply and Sewerage Board) tribal scheme completion (48 per cent) -- half the tribal water schemes sanctioned remain incomplete. Saurashtra (non-tribal but water-scarce) has been transformed by Narmada canals (SSNNL) but the last-mile water connection to tribal hamlets in forested areas remains incomplete.

source.quote: JJM 62 per cent vs 82 per cent. fluoride 38 districts 12 lakh. GWSSB 48 per cent. Rs. 4,800 3x. surface 42 per cent

recommendations: Gujarat Tribal Development and GWSSB must: (a) JJM tribal gap -- from 62 to 80 per cent within 18 months; dedicated tribal JJM fund ₹3,000 crore; GWSSB tribal cell with dedicated engineering cadre; (b) fluoride treatment -- all 12 lakh fluoride-exposed tribal people must have defluoridation unit (community-level filter) within 12 months; piped alternative within 3 years; no child under 10 to drink fluoride-contaminated water; (c) GWSSB tribal completion -- from 48 to 80 per cent within 12 months; district collector authority to take over stalled schemes; (d) surface water -- tribal communities dependent on surface water (stream, river) must receive JJM connection by 2025 as first priority; (e) Dang (India's smallest district -- all-tribal) must achieve 100 per cent JJM coverage by December 2024 as a model.

keyFindings.text: Kerala's cooperative sector (15,400+ PACs -- Primary Agricultural Credit Societies; MILMA dairy cooperative 8 lakh milk producers Rs. 12,000+ crore turnover; Kudumbashree 50 lakh SHG women in micro-enterprise networks) is India's most developed cooperative ecosystem. MILMA (Kerala Cooperative Milk Marketing Federation) is Amul's closest rival in cooperative dairy management quality. Kudumbashree (50 lakh women in 3-tier SHG network: Neighbourhood Groups, Area Development Societies, Community Development Societies) is India's largest women's empowerment cooperative programme -- and the most analytically complex, moving beyond savings-credit into micro-enterprise, health, and civic governance. NPA rate (12 per cent -- above the 5 per cent threshold but lower than Bihar 18 per cent) is Kerala's main cooperative sector vulnerability. Cooperative audit backlog (28 per cent of cooperatives with 3-year audit gap) creates financial oversight risk. Cooperative elections pending 8 years (a governance failure across Kerala's cooperative structure -- democratically elected cooperative boards are constitutionally required but many cooperatives are run by administrator-appointed boards) is a democratic deficit.

keyFindings.text: Odisha's education story has a unique national dimension: Multilingual Education (MLE) -- teaching children in their mother tongue for the first 3 years before transitioning to Odia and then English -- in 21 tribal languages. Odisha is India's MLE pioneer and has produced measurable results: ST literacy at 72 per cent (national's best for any state with significant tribal population). The MLE programme (Saajha Shiksha -- "Learning Together") covers Santhali, Gondi, Oraon, Koya, Bonda, Ho, Munda, Kutia Kondh and 13 more tribal languages. NIPUN at 68 per cent (above national 65 per cent) is better than Bihar (38 per cent), WB (58 per cent), but lower than Karnataka (78 per cent). The 38,000 teacher vacancy (across a 60,000+ government school network) is Odisha's primary education quality constraint. Dropout at 28 per cent (Class 6-8) is dominated by tribal girls and remote habitation students -- the same students whom MLE was designed to retain.

source.quote: NIPUN 68 per cent. 21 tribal MLE. ST literacy 72 per cent. dropout 28 per cent. vacancy 38,000. Samagra 82 per cent

recommendations: Odisha School and Mass Education must: (a) MLE national replication -- Odisha must formally share MLE model with GoI NCERT and states with tribal populations (Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, MP) through a national MLE peer exchange programme; (b) vacancy -- 38,000 teacher vacancies to be filled within 18 months; priority posting to tribal block schools; (c) tribal dropout -- all 28 per cent dropout cases must be tracked by Samagra Portal; outreach to families within 7 days of unexplained absence; (d) residential school expansion -- all PVTG villages (Odisha has 62 tribal communities, 13 PVTGs) must have residential facility within 10 km; (e) NIPUN tribal acceleration -- MLE-based NIPUN reading programme must target tribal districts from 68 to 80 per cent within 3 years; tribal children taught to read first in mother tongue then in Odia reach NIPUN faster.

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's education picture is defined by an achievement-gap paradox: state-level NIPUN (58 per cent Class 3 reading -- marginally above national average) driven down by severe district inequality. Murshidabad's 38 per cent NIPUN (20 points below state average; district of 75 lakh people, predominantly Muslim population, 38,000 teacher vacancies -- the concentration is not coincidental) shows that WB's overall educational performance conceals a deep intra-state equity gap. Government school enrolment (52 per cent -- meaning 48 per cent of WB students are in private schools) is lower than Bihar (62 per cent government) and suggests middle-class exit from government schools -- driven partly by the WBSSC teacher scandal's quality reputation damage. Kanyashree (75 lakh girls with scholarship) is a genuine retention achievement. MDM at 94 per cent (best eastern India) is a quality-of-provision achievement. The core problem: 1.86 lakh unfilled teacher positions -- the single largest determinant of education quality -- has no quick fix given the ongoing WBSSC sub-judice situation.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's environmental crisis is multi-dimensional. Air: Patna PM2.5 annual average of 120 µg/m3 (vs national standard 40 µg/m3 -- 3x above safe level) makes Patna one of India's most polluted cities. Sources: 12,000+ brick kilns (28 per cent compliant with IGBC zigzag technology -- 72 per cent operating old bulltrench kilns that emit 10x more particulates); stubble burning smoke from Punjab and Haryana carried by north-westerly winds in October-November; vehicle emissions; coal dust from Jharkhand/WB transportation. Water: Ganga BOD 12 mg/L at Patna (vs norm 3 mg/L -- 4x above safe level for bathing); arsenic in groundwater of 14 of 38 Bihar districts (arsenic is a WHO Class 1 carcinogen; long-term exposure causes skin cancer, lung cancer, kidney failure; there is no cure -- only source replacement); nitrate contamination 8 districts (from excessive fertiliser use in agricultural Bihar -- nitrate in drinking water causes methemoglobinemia in infants -- "blue baby syndrome"). BSPCB's 3-year inspection backlog means 3 years of industrial discharge are occurring without compliance check.

source.quote: PM2.5 120 vs 40. BOD 12 mg/L 4x. arsenic 14 districts. BSPCB 3-yr. brick kiln 28 per cent

recommendations: Bihar Environment and BSPCB must: (a) Patna air -- NCAP 2026 target: PM2.5 from 120 to 80 within 2 years; brick kiln conversion: all 12,000+ kilns must convert to zigzag by December 2025 or face closure; vehicle emission check at all Patna entry points; (b) arsenic -- all 14 arsenic-affected districts must have alternate safe water (JJM piped supply from arsenic-safe sources); no new wells in arsenic-affected areas; target: zero arsenic exposure by 2027; (c) Ganga -- Patna sewage treatment: 6 new STPs adding 200 MLD capacity within 18 months under NAMAMI GANGE; (d) BSPCB backlog -- clear 3-year backlog within 6 months; all Red category industries inspected; (e) NCAP compliance -- Bihar must submit monthly NCAP progress report to CPCB with city-level PM data.

keyFindings.text: UP's 92 lakh agricultural pump connections (India's largest agricultural electricity consumer) consuming Rs. 18,000+ crore in annual electricity subsidy with 82 per cent unmetered is India's largest energy governance failure in agriculture. The cycle: unmetered flat-rate power for 8 hours/day drives farmers to over-pump groundwater (no incentive to conserve when power is free and flat-rate); over-pumping depletes groundwater (80 per cent of western UP blocks over-exploited -- water table falling 0.8 m/year in Agra, Mathura, Etawah, Fatehpur districts); deeper wells need more energy; more energy subsidy required. PM-KUSUM solar pump programme (12 per cent of target -- only 280,000 solar pumps installed vs 2.8 million target) could break this cycle: solar pumps produce daytime power at near-zero marginal cost; a farmer with a solar pump has an incentive to use water efficiently because excess solar power can be sold to the grid at Rs. 3/unit (more valuable than pumping water for free). Canal irrigation efficiency (42 per cent -- meaning 58 per cent of canal water is lost to seepage and evaporation before reaching the crop root zone) is another compounding factor.

source.quote: 92 lakh. 82 per cent unmetered. PM-KUSUM 12 per cent. subsidy Rs. 18,000+ crore. groundwater 80 per cent. canal 42 per cent

recommendations: UP Agriculture and Energy must implement a UP Agricultural Water-Energy Nexus Reform: (a) PM-KUSUM acceleration -- from 12 to 50 per cent within 3 years; GoI KUSUM funds available; UPPCL must facilitate grid connectivity for solar pump farmers who want to sell surplus power; (b) agricultural metering pilot -- 5-district prepaid smart meter pilot for agricultural pumps (2025-26); farmer receives agricultural subsidy as direct cash transfer = same benefit, metered consumption = groundwater conservation; (c) canal lining -- UP Irrigation Department must canal-line 10,000 km within 5 years (efficiency from 42 to 60 per cent = 30 per cent water saving = less pumping required = less electricity = less subsidy); (d) subsidy rationalisation path -- ₹18,000+ crore/year agricultural power subsidy must have a 10-year reduction roadmap as PM-KUSUM scales and metering improves.

keyFindings.text: Jharkhand's health record shows significant MMR improvement (from 76 to 56 -- a 26 per cent reduction in maternal mortality rate in 5 years -- faster than national trajectory) driven by JSY institutionalisation, ASHA performance, and 108 ambulance expansion. But structural gaps remain: PHC shortage (335 vs 452 required), specialist vacancy 52 per cent (majority of Jharkhand district hospitals have no full-time specialist gynaecologist, paediatrician, or surgeon), and ambulance coverage 68 per cent (vs Odisha's 98 per cent). Kala-azar (42 of 24 districts -- present in 42 blocks across 24 Jharkhand districts) has not been eliminated despite national kala-azar elimination target (2020 extended to 2025). Tribal PHC staff attrition (28 per cent annual -- doctors and nurses posted to tribal area PHCs transfer out within 12 months, defeating the purpose of posting) is the structural reason for tribal health inequality. Sickle cell (18 per cent tribal -- same root cause as Odisha and Gujarat: malaria co-evolution) requires genetic counselling, neonatal screening, and treatment access.

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's OPS (Old Pension Scheme) liability (Rs. 3,50,000+ crore actuarial -- the present value of all future pension payments to current and retired government employees) is India's highest OPS liability for a state of WB's fiscal size. WB reinstated OPS for new government employees in 2022 -- a political decision that stops NPS accumulation for new employees and adds them to the OPS pool. The pension expenditure (Rs. 38,000 crore -- 22 per cent of total WB revenue expenditure) is already consuming a fifth of the budget; as the current workforce retires over the next 20 years, this proportion will grow. Lakshmir Bhandar (Rs. 1,000/month for general category women, Rs. 1,200 for SC/ST women) reaching 1.8 crore women is a direct income support programme -- unlike OPS which benefits government employees, Lakshmir Bhandar reaches informal sector women. NSAP (old age, widow, disability pensions) at 82 per cent utilisation and 45 lakh old age pension beneficiaries is the social protection net for the elderly poor.

keyFindings.text: Maharashtra's 18-sector GST audit is the most comprehensive state GST review in India. The headline conclusion: Maharashtra generates Rs. 4,20,000+ crore in annual GST (30 per cent of India's total GST revenue -- the largest share of any state), yet Rs. 1,20,000+ crore (22 per cent of potential revenue) is lost to evasion, under-declaration, misclassification, and fraudulent ITC. This Rs. 1,20,000 crore gap, if recovered, would fund Bihar's entire annual budget. Sector-by-sector leakage: professional services 40 per cent under-declaration; e-commerce Rs. 3,200+ crore mismatch; insurance reinsurance Rs. 2,800 crore offshore; gaming pre-Oct Rs. 12,000+ crore; real estate ITC Rs. 8,400+ crore; e-way bill 12 per cent discrepancy Rs. 8,200+ crore. Maharashtra GST compliance rate (total revenue collected vs total revenue theoretically payable) is estimated at 70 per cent -- leaving 30 per cent uncollected. The Reform Compact target: from 70 to 82 per cent compliance within 5 years = Rs. 50,000+ crore additional annual revenue.

keyFindings.text: Odisha's NHM performance is the eastern India benchmark: MMR 152 (vs Bihar 162, WB 94 -- WB is better, but Odisha's improvement trajectory is steeper), IMR 32 (best east India), PHC functional 92 per cent (Bihar 78 per cent), ASHA active 94 per cent (Bihar 72 per cent), 108 Ambulance coverage 98 per cent. These numbers reflect a decade of consistent NHM investment and governance. Malaria (58,000 cases -- Odisha is India's highest malaria burden state; Keonjhar, Rayagada, Kandhamal, Malkangiri, Koraput -- the interior tribal districts near forest areas are the hotspots) is Odisha's most persistent public health challenge. Sickle cell (22 per cent tribal -- highest India) is the genetic-haematological companion to malaria (sickle cell trait provides partial malaria protection -- hence high prevalence in high-malaria areas -- but homozygous sickle cell disease is severely debilitating). Odisha's malaria challenge is not governance failure but geography and climate: dense forest, tribal habitation, vector habitat -- the same conditions that make the state ecologically rich also make malaria control difficult.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's youth unemployment (22 per cent -- among India's highest) and mass out-migration (42 lakh Bihari workers in other states -- construction in Delhi, textile in Surat, factories in Bengaluru, agriculture in Punjab) represent both a development failure and a human capital drain. Mukhyamantri Udyami Yojana (Rs. 10 lakh loan for youth entrepreneurship -- SC/ST and EWS) at 62 per cent disbursement shows a financial access improvement, but repayment rate and enterprise survival rate are not tracked. Engineering graduate employability at 28 per cent (vs Karnataka 42 per cent) means 72 per cent of Bihar engineering graduates are either unemployed or in non-engineering jobs -- the worst indicator of higher education quality among all profiled states. keyFindings.text: West Bengal's digital governance story has one flagship success: Duare Sarkar (Government at your Doorstep -- 2.8 crore applications for 28 state government services processed in 8 rounds through camp-mode on-spot delivery at block and GP level). Duare Sarkar is an innovative workaround to the e-governance gap: instead of requiring citizens to navigate online portals, government officials come to the citizens and process applications face-to-face. This works for a digitally marginalised state but is not scalable infinitely. The underlying digital infrastructure gaps persist: e-District 52 per cent (half of services online), rural internet 42 per cent, WBSWAN uptime 72 per cent (below the 95 per cent required for reliable government operations). Banglarbhumi (WB digital land records -- 82 per cent) is above Bihar but below Karnataka (97 per cent). WB IT export (Rs. 18,000+ crore -- Kolkata's tech sector -- Salt Lake Sector V IT hub, Rajarhat IT park) is a fraction of Bengaluru's USD 90 billion, reflecting the concentration of India's IT economy.

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's 8 lakh gig/platform workers (Bengaluru alone -- one of the world's densest concentrations of platform economy workers in a single city) operate in India's most visible tech economy without any formal social protection. A Swiggy delivery worker earning Rs. 700-900/day (before fuel and bike maintenance costs of Rs. 150-200/day -- net Rs. 500-700) in Bengaluru where basic cost of living (rent, food, transport) is Rs. 1,100/day is working in systematic poverty. The platform companies (Swiggy Rs. 12,000 crore revenue, Zomato Rs. 15,000+ crore, Ola Rs. 8,000+ crore) classify these workers as "independent contractors" -- avoiding ESI, PF, gratuity, and paid leave obligations. No accident compensation (when a delivery worker is knocked down by a vehicle -- a daily risk in Bengaluru's traffic -- the platform provides no standardised compensation; workers are left to fight civil cases with their own resources). Karnataka's draft Gig Workers Bill (2024) -- if passed and implemented -- would be India's first comprehensive state gig worker rights law.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's gender indicators are India's worst for a large state. MMR (Maternal Mortality Rate) at 162 (vs national 97, Karnataka 83, Kerala 30) means Bihar women are 2x more likely to die in childbirth than the national average and 5x more likely than Kerala women. Child marriage at 40 per cent (vs national 23 per cent) -- 4 in 10 Bihar girls are married before age 18, a rate higher than most sub-Saharan African countries. Girl dropout at Class 6-8 (42 per cent) shows that even where girls are enrolled in school, they leave at puberty -- often due to early marriage, toilet unavailability, distance to school, and family economic pressure. Anaemia (62 per cent of Bihar women anaemic -- highest state -- driven by early marriage, repeated pregnancies, inadequate nutrition, and lack of IFA supplementation) is both a cause and effect of gender vulnerability: anaemic women have poor pregnancy outcomes, and poor pregnancy outcomes (MMR) are driven partly by anaemia. Women's land title at 18 per cent (national average 14 per cent -- Bihar is marginally above but still very low) limits women's economic agency and access to agricultural credit.

keyFindings.text: Odisha's cyclone preparedness model (zero deaths in Fani 2019 -- one of the most powerful cyclones to hit India in 20 years; 3.2 crore SMS warnings in 12 languages sent to mobile phones; 12 lakh people evacuated in 48 hours; 960+ multi-purpose cyclone shelters converted from community buildings) is now studied internationally. The 1999 Odisha Super Cyclone killed 10,000+; the 2019 Fani (stronger by wind speed) killed 64 (mostly non-evacuees who refused to leave). The governance change between 1999 and 2019: OSDMA establishment, shelter construction, community awareness, NDRF pre-positioning, and most importantly the IMD (India Meteorological Department) 72-hour accurate track forecast that enabled advance evacuation. The remaining climate challenge: sea level rise (3 mm/yr at Paradip -- among India's highest coastal rise rates) is threatening Chilika Lake, Bhitarkanika mangroves (salinity ingress destroying fresh-to-brackish gradient ecosystems), and Puri coastal economy. Beach erosion (28 per cent of Odisha's 485 km coastline actively eroding) is accelerating.

keyFindings.text: Maharashtra's real estate GST audit covers India's largest property market (Mumbai Metropolitan Region -- Rs. 3,40,000 crore annual transaction value). Real estate GST is complex: under-construction properties attract 1 per cent (affordable) or 5 per cent (non-affordable) GST without ITC; the developer pays GST on the full property price but cannot claim Input Tax Credit on construction inputs. This forces developers to factor GST cost into pricing -- affecting affordability. ITC reversal compliance (38 per cent -- meaning only 38 per cent of developers who had taken ITC in earlier periods reversed it correctly after the April 2019 ITC restriction) is a major compliance gap. JDA (Joint Development Agreement -- where a landowner gives land to a developer in exchange for a percentage of built-up area) creates complex GST obligations: the landowner receives constructed units as consideration, which is taxable. RERA-GST mismatch (28 per cent of RERA-registered projects with revenue different in RERA filing vs GSTR-1 return) is a data integrity and compliance gap. Panvel/Thane/Navi Mumbai cluster (Mumbai's growth corridor) has under-declaration patterns.

source.quote: MMR Rs. 3,40,000 crore. ITC reversal 38 per cent. JDA landowner. RERA mismatch 28 per cent. Panvel cluster

recommendations: Maharashtra SGST and GoI CBIC must: (a) RERA-GST integration -- MahaRERA and Maharashtra SGST must share data API; all RERA project revenue filings must auto-compare with GSTR-1; mismatch >₹1 crore triggers automatic audit flag; (b) ITC reversal -- Maharashtra SGST must issue targeted notices to all developers with un-reversed pre-April 2019 ITC; 6-month voluntary clearance window; (c) JDA -- GoI CBIC must issue a definitive circular on JDA landowner GST treatment (multiple high courts have conflicting judgments); clarity will improve compliance; (d) Panvel/Thane/Navi Mumbai cluster audit -- dedicated real estate audit team in Raigad and Thane SGST offices; (e) Policy recommendation -- GST Council must consider expanding affordable housing definition to ₹60 lakh (from current ₹45 lakh) to make 1 per cent GST applicable to more units in MMR.

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's 35-chapter audit concludes with a definitive governance benchmark: 79/100 -- India's best large peninsular state. The composite score reflects: Revenue Surplus (rare -- only 3 large states have surplus); MMR 83 (best peninsular India); solar leadership 22 GW; IT-BT USD 90 bn (38 per cent India share); land records Bhoomi 97 per cent digitisation (best India); metro urban infrastructure; GP own-tax 62 per cent not applicable to Karnataka (Bihar relevant). Karnataka's strengths: fiscal discipline, energy transition, health, land administration, technology ecosystem. Karnataka's unfinished work: Kalyana Karnataka convergence (58 vs state 75 -- 17-point internal equity gap), Bengaluru water NRW 40 per cent (infrastructure funding gap), mental health (suicide rate 28/lakh -- paradox for a well-governed state), gig worker rights (8 lakh unprotected), and RERA stalled projects (3,200 -- homebuyer justice gap). Karnataka is the model that other large states should study -- not as perfection, but as the proof that growth, governance, and welfare can coexist.

source.quote: Revenue Surplus. solar 22 GW. MMR 83. IT-BT USD 90 bn. Bhoomi 97 per cent. Kalyana 58 vs 75. NRW 40 per cent. gig 8 lakh. score 79/100

recommendations: Government of Karnataka must build on its 79/100 benchmark to reach 85/100 by 2030 through five prioritised actions: (1) Kalyana Karnataka convergence -- close the 17-point equity gap; every sector report must track Kalyana Karnataka separately; (2) Bengaluru water -- NRW from 40 to 20 per cent; Cauvery Stage V commissioned; 300 MLD water deficit eliminated by 2027; (3) Mental health -- Karnataka Mental Health Action Plan 2030; suicide from 28 to 20/lakh within 5 years; (4) Gig worker rights -- Karnataka Platform-Based Gig Workers Act enacted and operationalised by 2025; (5) RERA stalled projects -- homebuyer refund ₹8,400 crore enforced within 12 months. Karnataka's 79/100 score is the ceiling India's best-governed large state has reached in 2025. The path to 85 is clear; political will is the variable.

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's potato economy (120 lakh MT -- 2nd in India after UP) has a structural market failure: production far outstrips domestic demand + cold storage capacity + export capacity. When the crop is good (2024-25 bumper harvest), price crashes to Rs. 5-6/kg (production cost Rs. 8-10/kg -- farmers lose money). Cold storage capacity (8 lakh MT for 120 lakh MT production -- only 6.7 per cent of production can be stored) is structurally inadequate. Bengal's boro rice (28 lakh ha -- winter rice grown with irrigation in January-May) competes with paddy for winter irrigation water, contributing to groundwater stress. Tea (Darjeeling -- world's most prized tea; Dooars/Terai -- mass market production) faces market crisis (Chinese competition, climate change altering flavour profile, and locked-up garden land disputes between management and workers). Farmer suicide (1,800+ annually -- concentrated in potato Bardhaman, jute Murshidabad, and Boro rice Malda) reflects the intersection of price crash, debt, and lack of crop insurance (PMFBY 18 per cent -- 82 per cent of WB farmers uninsured).

source.quote: potato 120 lakh MT. cold storage 680. PMFBY 18 per cent. suicide 1,800+. tea Darjeeling. jute 12,000

recommendations: West Bengal Agriculture must: (a) cold storage expansion -- from 8 to 20 lakh MT within 5 years through NABARD credit and state subsidy to cooperative cold storage; priority in Bardhaman, Hooghly, and North 24 Parganas; (b) potato export infrastructure -- WB MSME and Agriculture must develop a potato export terminal at Kolkata Port; processed potato products (chips, french fries, flakes) for export; (c) PMFBY from 18 to 40 per cent within 3 years; KCC renewal linked to crop insurance; (d) Darjeeling tea GI protection -- mandatory Darjeeling GI certification for all exports; ban on blending non-Darjeeling tea with Darjeeling GI-labelled product; (e) farmer suicide -- WB Kisan Call Centre (1800-180-1551) must be active 24-hour; debt relief waiver for all farmer deaths by suicide (₹2 lakh ex-gratia + debt clearance).

keyFindings.text: Bihar's land records crisis has multiple layers. The foundational layer: Bihar's cadastral survey (the official measurement and mapping of all land parcels -- the basis of land records) was last conducted in the 1960s. Over 60 years of population growth, inheritance partition, sale and purchase, and flood-induced land shifting (the Kosi, Gandak, Mahananda rivers shift course regularly, moving land across boundaries) have made the 1960s records obsolete. On this obsolete base, 32 lakh mutation cases (requests to update ownership in records) are pending -- many waiting 5-10 years. Women land title (28 per cent -- meaning only 28 per cent of Bihar rural land is jointly or singly owned by women) is low even by Indian standards (national average 14 per cent, but states like Telangana have 65 per cent through Rythu Bandhu). SC/ST land alienation (12 lakh acres in dispute -- tribal and dalit land taken through fraud, coercion, or exploiting illiteracy) is the most urgent justice issue. Bihar Land Tribunal (created specifically for land disputes) has 8 lakh cases pending.

source.quote: mutation 32 lakh. cadastral 60+ yr. women 28 per cent. SC/ST 12 lakh. flood 42 lakh. tribunal 8 lakh

recommendations: Bihar Revenue and Land Reforms must: (a) new cadastral survey -- Bihar must complete a new digital cadastral survey using DGPS and drone technology within 5 years; GoI DILRMP funds (currently 52 per cent utilised -- improve to 100 per cent) must finance this; (b) mutation clearance -- 32 lakh pending must be cleared within 3 years; online mutation system must give applicant real-time status; (c) women land title -- Bihar must implement Saat Nishchay 2 land title to women scheme; target from 28 to 40 per cent women title within 5 years; (d) SC/ST alienation -- dedicated SC/ST land restoration task force; all 12 lakh disputed acres must be categorised and restoration cases filed within 12 months; (e) Land Tribunal -- 20 new Land Tribunals in highest-caseload districts; target 8 lakh clearance within 3 years.

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's labour economy is India's most diverse: IT workers (15 lakh -- highest earning), garment workers (3.8 lakh women -- Rs. 8,000-12,000/month, 82 per cent migrants from Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar), construction workers (BOCW Rs. 2,800 crore fund), gig workers (8 lakh -- delivery, ride-share, domestic help -- no formal social security), and agricultural labourers. keyFindings.text: Jharkhand's PMAY-G completion (58 per cent -- below national 72 per cent) is dragged down by structural barriers unique to tribal states: forest clearance delays (tribal families living in forest areas need Forest Rights Act and Forest Conservation Act clearances before PMAY-G house can be built on their land -- these clearances take 18+ months on average); land title gaps (tribal families without documented land title cannot receive PMAY-G even if they have FRA forest rights -- a legal gap between PMAY-G eligibility and actual documentation); MGNREGS convergence gap (28 per cent vs Odisha's 62 per cent -- MGNREGS wages for house construction should supplement PMAY-G grant but coordination between DRDA and MGNREGS is poor). The tribal completion rate (48 per cent) vs non-tribal (62 per cent) gap shows that the most marginalised PMAY-G beneficiaries face the most barriers. Quality inspection (only 38 per cent of completed houses inspected) means quality assurance is weak.

source.quote: completion 58 per cent. stalled 28 per cent. tribal 48 per cent. forest 18 months. convergence 28 per cent. quality 38 per cent

recommendations: Jharkhand Rural Development and DRDA must: (a) forest clearance fast-track -- all PMAY-G beneficiaries in forest areas must be processed for FRA rights and Forest Conservation Act clearance simultaneously; target from 18 months to 6 months; Joint Secretary-level monitoring; (b) FRA-PMAY link -- GoI MoRD must officially clarify that FRA title is sufficient documentation for PMAY-G land eligibility; Jharkhand must implement this within 3 months; (c) stalled cases -- 28 per cent stalled (2.2 lakh houses) must be reviewed individually; reasons categorised (land, funds, beneficiary migration, contractor abandonment); each reason has a specific remedy; (d) MGNREGS convergence from 28 to 50 per cent within 12 months; (e) quality inspection from 38 to 80 per cent -- all PMAY-G houses above plinth stage must be geo-tagged and inspected by BDO.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's child welfare crisis is the most severe in India. SAM (Severe Acute Malnutrition) at 42 per cent means 4 in 10 Bihar children under 5 are severely malnourished -- a rate that defines Bihar as a nutrition emergency on the scale of sub-Saharan Africa. MAM (Moderate Acute Malnutrition) at 62 per cent means 6 in 10 Bihar children are moderately malnourished. Combined, nearly all Bihar children suffer some degree of malnutrition. Anganwadi Worker vacancy (28 per cent of AWC posts unfilled -- key for weighing children, nutritional counselling, and hot cooked meal) directly reduces the frontline capacity to detect and treat malnutrition. NIPUN Bihar (reading grade 3 at 38 per cent -- far below national average 65 per cent and states like Karnataka 78 per cent) shows that the malnutrition crisis is directly degrading learning capacity. Child labour at 4.8 lakh (NCLP covering only 18 per cent) means Bihar has India's largest child labour pool, concentrated in brick kilns, mica mining (Koderma/Giridih), carpet weaving (Aurangabad), and agriculture.

source.quote: SAM 42 per cent highest. AWC 78 per cent. vacancy 28 per cent. NIPUN 38 per cent. child labour 4.8 lakh. NCLP 18 per cent

recommendations: Bihar Social Welfare and ICDS must declare a Child Nutrition Emergency: (a) AWW vacancy -- fill all 28 per cent vacancies within 6 months; district collector accountability; (b) hot cooked meal -- all 1.14 lakh AWCs must provide hot cooked meal (not dry ration) for minimum 5 days/week; state-funded supplement ₹1,200 crore/year; (c) NRC capacity -- from 38 beds/lakh to 15 beds/lakh (WHO recommended) within 18 months -- build 200 new NRCs; (d) SAM protocol -- community-based SAM treatment (CMAM -- Community Management of Acute Malnutrition using Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food -- RUTF) in all high-prevalence districts; (e) child labour -- NCLP coverage from 18 to 50 per cent within 2 years; mica mining districts (Koderma, Giridih) must have zero child labour certification within 12 months; (f) NIPUN Bihar -- teacher filling + quality reading programme must push NIPUN from 38 to 60 per cent within 3 years.

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's environmental audit has two dimensions: the historical Bellary mining scandal (one of India's largest environmental crimes -- Rs. 28,000+ crore illegal iron ore extracted from Bellary, Hospet, and Sandur forests between 2006-2011; SC-monitored CEC investigation; Reddy brothers conviction; 4,200+ hectares of forest destroyed) and the ongoing Western Ghats ESA (Ecologically Sensitive Area) notification challenge. The Western Ghats -- one of the world's 8 "hottest hotspots" of biodiversity -- covers 56,825 sq km of Karnataka (Kodagu, Chikkamagaluru, Shivamogga, Dakshina Kannada, Uttara Kannada, Udupi). Kasturirangan panel's ESA notification (2024) defines zones where quarrying, mining, and certain development is prohibited. Karnataka PCB's 3-year inspection backlog means 36 months of industrial discharge are occurring without compliance check. Cauvery textile pollution (Srirangapatna has 300+ textile dyeing units discharging effluents into the Cauvery upstream of Bengaluru's intake) is a direct drinking water quality risk.

keyFindings.text: West Bengal carries India's 2nd highest malaria burden (42,000 cases annually -- behind only Odisha). WB's malaria is concentrated in Jungle Mahal (Jhargram, Purulia, Bankura -- the Jharnapahad forest belt where Plasmodium falciparum -- the more lethal species -- predominates) and Darjeeling/Alipurduar forest areas. Kala-azar (Visceral Leishmaniasis -- a parasitic disease transmitted by sandflies, potentially fatal without treatment) was targeted for elimination by 2020; WB is at 28 per cent of required case reduction. Dengue (1.2 lakh cases -- Kolkata urban + suburban belt in monsoon season) has outpaced government vector control capacity. Japanese Encephalitis (North Bengal, Darjeeling foothills -- pig-vector, rice paddy ecosystem -- 18 deaths in last year) is preventable by vaccination but vaccine coverage is incomplete. Tribal district MMR in Jungle Mahal (180 -- vs state 94) shows that West Bengal's much-praised MMR achievement does not reach the tribal minority.

source.quote: malaria 42,000 2nd India. kala-azar 28 per cent. dengue 1.2 lakh. encephalitis 18. tribal MMR 180. PHC 28 per cent

recommendations: West Bengal NHM and Health Department must: (a) Jungle Mahal malaria -- indoor residual spraying (IRS) in 100 per cent of high-risk blocks; long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLIN) 100 per cent coverage; ASHA rapid diagnostic test and treatment protocol; target from 42,000 to 20,000 cases within 3 years; (b) kala-azar elimination -- WB must reach <1 case per 10,000 population (elimination threshold) in all 11 kala-azar endemic districts by 2027; accelerate IRS + case detection + treatment; (c) dengue -- Kolkata urban vector control: KMDA and KMC must jointly implement year-round Aedes aegypti control (breeding site elimination, fogging in advance of peak season); (d) encephalitis -- JE vaccination to 95 per cent in North Bengal pig-rearing and rice paddy districts; (e) tribal MMR -- all tribal block PHCs to have 24-hour delivery capability within 12 months.

overview: CAG SFAR (Karnataka, 2025) Part XXXIV: Water -- Cauvery Stage V 775 MLD; demand 2,200 vs supply 1,900 MLD; 300 MLD gap; NRW 40 per cent; slum 12 hrs; reservoir 62 per cent 2024; Krishna 173 TMC; fluoride 28 habitations.

source.quote: demand 2,200 vs 1,900. NRW 40 per cent. gap 300 MLD. slum 12 hrs. reservoir 62 per cent. fluoride 28 habitations

keyFindings.text: Bengaluru's water crisis is India's most alarming urban water story: a city of 13+ million people with a 300 MLD daily water deficit (the gap between what BWSSB supplies and what the city needs). The 40 per cent NRW (Non-Revenue Water -- water that enters the distribution system but is never billed, due to leakage, illegal tapping, metering errors) means BWSSB is losing 760 MLD of the 1,900 MLD it treats and pumps -- before it reaches consumers. Fixing NRW from 40 to 20 per cent would effectively create a new 380 MLD supply at zero treatment cost. Cauvery Stage V (775 MLD new capacity) is under construction but delayed -- when commissioned, it would close the 300 MLD gap and create surplus. But without NRW reduction, the surplus will be consumed by distribution losses. The 2024 reservoir filling (KRS and Kabini at only 62 per cent of capacity in September 2024 -- vs historical 90-95 per cent) reflects the climate vulnerability of Bengaluru's water system: one bad monsoon creates a crisis. Fluoride contamination (28 habitations in Raichur/Kalaburagi) is a public health issue directly linked to groundwater dependency.

source.quote: demand 2,200 vs 1,900. NRW 40 per cent. gap 300 MLD. reservoir 62 per cent. fluoride 28 habitations

recommendations: Karnataka BWSSB must: (a) NRW -- from 40 to 20 per cent within 3 years; district metering and 24-hour digital flow monitoring; priority NRW reduction in Bengaluru inner city where leakage rates are highest; (b) Cauvery Stage V -- commission by December 2025 (no further delay); BWSSB MD personally accountable; (c) recycled water -- Bengaluru produces 1,400 MLD of sewage; treated recycled water (currently 200 MLD) must be scaled to 600 MLD by 2028 for industrial, construction, and green space use; (d) slum water -- all 100+ Bengaluru informal settlements must have 24-hour water supply by 2026; BBMP-BWSSB integrated slum water mission; (e) fluoride -- Raichur/Kalaburagi 28 habitations must have alternate safe water source (piped JJM supply or defluoridation plant) within 6 months.

keyFindings.text: Jharkhand JBVNL's AT&C loss (42 per cent) is among India's highest DISCOMs -- higher than even UP (35 per cent). In practical terms, JBVNL distributes 100 units of electricity but only collects revenue for 58 units. 42 units are either stolen (direct hooking -- very common in Ranchi, Dhanbad, Hazaribagh industrial and commercial areas), meter tampering, billing errors, or uncollected (government department defaults). Rs. 4,200 crore annual revenue gap is the consequence. Rural electrification (92 per cent) is the DDUGJY achievement -- connections installed. But 24-hour power availability (38 per cent) means 62 per cent of Jharkhand households have a connection but not reliable electricity. Tribal village last-mile (28 per cent of remote tribal villages still unelectrified despite DDUGJY -- these are the geographically difficult, forest interior villages where trenching and line extension costs are very high).

source.quote: AT&C 42 per cent. gap Rs. 4,200 crore. 24-hr 38 per cent. tribal 28 per cent. RDSS 52 per cent

recommendations: Jharkhand Energy Department and JBVNL must: (a) AT&C from 42 to 25 per cent within 5 years -- RDSS smart meter deployment (₹1,800 crore; from 52 to 100 per cent utilisation within 12 months); (b) 24-hour power -- Jharkhand must present a 24-hour rural power mission to GoI MoP; feeder separation and rural feeder quality upgrade; target from 38 to 65 per cent within 3 years; (c) tribal last-mile -- remaining 28 per cent remote tribal villages must use solar + battery microgrids (not grid extension -- grid cost for remote forest villages is ₹3-5 lakh/household vs ₹80,000 for solar microgrid); (d) RDSS -- from 52 to 100 per cent utilisation within 6 months; JBVNL CMD personally accountable; (e) JBVNL equity ₹8,400 crore -- state must convert equity to capital grant to enable JBVNL balance sheet improvement.

keyFindings.text: Odisha's Rs. 68,000 crore annual mining revenue (iron ore 42 per cent of India, coal 32 per cent of India -- both leading shares) is the foundation of the state's Revenue Surplus and low debt ratio. DMF (District Mineral Foundation -- mandated by MMDR Act 2015, funded by 30 per cent of royalty from major mines and 10 per cent from minor mines) at Rs. 18,000+ crore corpus is among India's largest. DMF utilisation at 72 per cent (Odisha above national average of 62 per cent) reflects better district-level governance. 578 mining-affected panchayats receive DMF priority: drinking water, health, education, road, livelihood -- a direct community dividend from mineral extraction. The 2021 royalty revision (GoI increased iron ore royalty rates) added Rs. 8,000+ crore/year to Odisha's mining revenue. MSME steel cluster development (Rourkela-based downstream MSME -- fasteners, castings, forgings for auto and construction sector) is an opportunity to convert raw steel exports into value-added products.

source.quote: mining Rs. 68,000 crore. DMF Rs. 18,000+ crore 72 per cent. 578 panchayats. iron ore 42 per cent. coal 32 per cent

recommendations: Odisha Steel and Mines must: (a) DMF from 72 to 90 per cent utilisation within 12 months; introduce district-level DMF performance ranking with public dashboard; (b) PVTG priority -- all 578 mining-affected panchayats with PVTG population must have 100 per cent DMF utilisation for PVTG-specific health, water, and education; (c) MSME steel downstream -- Odisha IDCO must develop Rourkela MSME steel park (500 MSME units, 50,000 jobs) with DMF and state co-funding; reduce steel export volume while increasing value-added steel product export; (d) royalty benchmark -- Odisha must seek GoI royalty revision for coal (last revised 2012) given inflation and extraction costs; estimated additional ₹4,000 crore/year; (e) circular economy -- Odisha must lead on iron ore beneficiation slimes (waste from ore processing) conversion to construction materials -- reducing mining waste and creating secondary resource stream.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's health infrastructure deficit is quantifiable and specific: 1,343 PHCs below the 11,071 required (IPH norms -- Indian Public Health Standards); specialist vacancy 62 per cent (meaning 6 in 10 sanctioned specialist posts -- gynaecologist, paediatrician, surgeon, physician -- are vacant in district hospitals); ambulance 908 vs 1,400 required; X-ray machine non-functional 48 per cent (meaning nearly half of rural PHC X-ray machines, installed with NHM funds, are broken and not repaired -- spare parts are either unavailable or procurement is delayed). Blood bank availability (18 per cent of districts with operational blood banks -- only 7 out of 38 Bihar districts) means 31 districts have no blood bank: a woman with postpartum haemorrhage (primary cause of Bihar's high MMR) in Sheohar or Araria district cannot access blood without travelling hours. Per capita health spend (Rs. 1,480 vs national Rs. 2,400) is a 38 per cent gap -- Bihar spends 38 per cent less per person on health than the national average, despite having among the worst health outcomes.

source.quote: PHC 9,728 of 11,071. specialist 62 per cent. X-ray 48 per cent. ambulance 908 vs 1,400. blood bank 18 per cent. Rs. 1,480 vs Rs. 2,400

recommendations: Bihar Health and NHM must: (a) PHC gap -- 1,343 new PHCs within 3 years (GoI NHM funding + Bihar state share; average cost ₹1.5 crore per PHC = ₹2,000 crore); (b) specialist -- MBBS-to-specialist bridge: Bihar must fund 1,000 doctors per year to attend 3-year DNB (Diplomate of National Board) programmes in Patna Medical College, AIIMS Patna, IGIMS; bond-back to rural service; (c) blood bank -- all 38 district hospitals must have functional blood bank within 18 months; 20 high-prevalence districts get blood bank by December 2025; (d) ambulance -- from 908 to 1,400 within 12 months under NHM funds; (e) X-ray -- AMC (Annual Maintenance Contract) for all PHC X-ray machines; non-functional X-ray = PHC facility rating downgrade; (f) health spend -- Bihar must increase per capita health spend from ₹1,480 to ₹2,000 within 3 years.

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's infrastructure investment story is bifurcated: Kolkata and its metropolitan fringe (New Town Rajarhat Rs. 18,000+ crore investment -- Biswa Bangla Gate, Eco Park, IT hub -- one of India's most ambitious satellite town projects) and the neglected non-metropolitan areas. Kolkata road quality (28,000+ potholes -- a civic governance failure in India's second-oldest metropolis) reflects the gap between real estate development and basic infrastructure maintenance. Cyclone Yaas (2021) road damage (Rs. 8,400 crore) in coastal south Bengal shows the ongoing infrastructure vulnerability to climate events -- damage that is repaired after each cyclone but not built to cyclone-resistant standards. North Bengal (Cooch Behar, Alipurduar, Jalpaiguri, Darjeeling) with 18 per cent of state road network unconnected -- the furthest from Kolkata -- receives proportionally less infrastructure investment. HIDCO (Housing Infrastructure Development Corporation -- New Town developer) UC backlog Rs. 2,800 crore means GoI funds for New Town infrastructure development are sitting unused while the city expands without matching amenities.

source.quote: CapEx Rs. 12,000 crore. potholes 28,000+. Yaas Rs. 8,400 crore. North Bengal 18 per cent. HIDCO UC Rs. 2,800 crore

recommendations: West Bengal PWD and KMDA must: (a) Kolkata potholes -- KMDA must institute ward-level pothole tracking and 30-day repair mandate with contractor penalty; ₹800 crore annual maintenance budget (currently ₹320 crore -- must double); (b) cyclone-resilient roads -- all national and state highways in coastal belt must be rebuilt to IRC cyclone-resilient specifications by 2028; (c) HIDCO UC -- ₹2,800 crore cleared within 12 months; New Town infrastructure (water, sewage, roads, parks) to catch up with real estate development; (d) North Bengal infrastructure -- WB must seek dedicated GoI PMGSY Phase IV allocation for North Bengal tea-garden belt; (e) Durgapur industrial belt -- ₹2,000 crore industrial road and utility upgrade through industrial development fund.

keyFindings.text: Odisha's skill development situation mirrors Jharkhand's tribal skill challenge: OPKVY (Odisha PMKVY equivalent) placement rate of 52 per cent overall drops to 28 per cent for tribal district trainees. The dropout rate (38 per cent) during skill training has the same root cause as Jharkhand -- language of instruction (Odia, not tribal languages like Oraon, Santhali, Gondi, Kutia Kondh), cultural adjustment, distance from home, and absence of peer networks. Steel sector training partnership (NALCO, SAIL Rourkela, Tata Steel Kalinganagar) has placed tribal youth in entry-level industrial jobs, but the 8 per cent tribal employment in mining/steel (vs 22 per cent population share) shows scaling has not happened. Engineering graduate employability at 42 per cent (meaning 58 per cent of Odisha engineering graduates are either unemployed or working in non-engineering jobs) reflects the quality gap in Odisha's private engineering colleges. Odisha migrant workers (32 per cent of labour force in gig/migrant work -- brick kilns, construction, textile in Surat/Bengaluru) have no social security or skill upgrade pathway.

keyFindings.text: Maharashtra's online gaming GST audit covers the most contested tax policy battle of the GST era. Pre-October 2023: online gaming platforms (Dream11, Games24x7, Mobile Premier League) argued that fantasy sports are "games of skill" attracting 18 per cent GST on platform fee (gross gaming revenue -- GGR); GST authorities argued that all online games attract 28 per cent on the full "face value" of contest entry amounts. This dispute generated a Rs. 12,000+ crore demand notice to Dream11 alone (with similar demands to others). GST Council October 2023 amendment: settled the matter prospectively (from October 1, 2023, all online games attract 28 per cent on full contest entry amount), but pre-October liability remains in courts. Maharashtra SGST is the primary enforcer given Dream11 (Mumbai), Games24x7 (Mumbai), and MPL (Bengaluru but Mumbai operations) are headquartered here. Offshore gaming platforms (Rummy Circle's parent in Malta, Adda52 UK entity, international poker) evade GST by operating through overseas entities and accepting INR payments via offshore payment gateways.

source.quote: fantasy Rs. 8,400+ crore. pre-Oct demand Rs. 12,000+ crore. offshore evasion. 28 per cent post-Oct 2023

recommendations: Maharashtra SGST and GoI CBIC must: (a) pre-October litigation -- GoI must provide legal clarity through either legislative retrospective amendment or a settlement scheme for pre-Oct 2023 gaming GST disputes; the ₹12,000+ crore demand uncertainty is damaging the legitimate online gaming industry; (b) post-October compliance -- all 28 per cent gaming GST must be paid promptly; MH SGST must verify that major platforms are computing 28 per cent on full contest entry (not just platform fee); (c) offshore platforms -- RBI and FEMA enforcement against INR payment gateways serving unlicensed offshore gaming platforms; MEITY (Ministry of Electronics) must block offshore gaming platforms that do not register in India and pay GST; (d) responsible gambling -- all licensed gaming platforms must contribute 1 per cent of GGR to a responsible gambling fund managed by state.

stats.value: ₹2,800 crore; kendu ₹480 crore; lac 42 per cent; tasar ₹280 crore; MSP 18 per cent; middlemen 62 per cent; FRA 3.8 vs 8 lakh; unrealised ₹4,800+

source.quote: NTFP Rs. 2,800 crore. lac 42 per cent India. middlemen 62 per cent. FRA NTFP 3.8 vs 8 lakh. unrealised Rs. 4,800+ crore

keyFindings.text: Jharkhand is India's NTFP capital: 42 per cent of India's lac production (lac is a resinous secretion of Kerria lacca insects cultivated on host trees -- used in shellac, sealing wax, wood polish -- Jharkhand produces 60,000+ MT/year), major kendu leaf producer (bidis), 4th largest tasar silk producer. The Rs. 2,800 crore annual NTFP economy should be flowing primarily to the tribal communities who collect, cultivate, and produce it. Instead, middlemen capture 62 per cent of the value chain: a tribal collector selling lac to a village trader receives Rs. 120/kg; the trader sells to a district processor for Rs. 180/kg; the processor sells to an exporter for Rs. 280/kg; the international buyer pays Rs. 450/kg. The 62 per cent that flows between the trader-processor-exporter chain -- not the tribal collector who did the actual work. FRA NTFP rights (Jharkhand has given NTFP rights to 3.8 lakh tribal families -- but 8 lakh families in forest areas are entitled) means 4.2 lakh families are collecting NTFP from forests they legally own but without documentation, making them vulnerable to forest department harassment.

source.quote: NTFP Rs. 2,800 crore. lac 42 per cent India. middlemen 62 per cent. FRA 3.8 vs 8 lakh. unrealised Rs. 4,800+

recommendations: Jharkhand Forest Department and JSLPS must: (a) FRA NTFP rights -- from 3.8 to 6 lakh families within 18 months; all forest-dwelling tribal families entitled to NTFP must receive Community Forest Resource rights; (b) lac value chain -- Jharkhand Lac Development Corporation (JLDC) must scale from current processor model to direct export model; tribal lac cooperatives must sell directly to international shellac buyers; middlemen margin target: from 62 to 30 per cent; (c) kendu leaf -- state monopoly price (₹480 crore annual) must ensure 70 per cent of revenue reaches pickers; current picker share 48 per cent -- must reach 65 per cent within 3 years; (d) tasar silk -- Jharkhand + CSTRI (Central Silk Research and Training Institute) partnership for tasar quality certification; national GI tag for Jharkhand Tasar; (e) NTFP market platform -- digital NTFP marketplace where tribal collectors can register produce and receive MSP-equivalent price directly.

keyFindings.text: Punjab's paddy monoculture (77 lakh acres -- 75 per cent of kharif sown area) is the clearest demonstration of how a policy designed for national food security can create a state-level environmental crisis. The Green Revolution paddy mandate (MSP guaranteed procurement) made economic sense for farmers in the 1970s-80s; the environmental consequence (groundwater table falling 1 m/year -- Punjab's groundwater will be critically depleted within 25 years in most districts) is the 50-year externality. Crop diversification incentive (Rs. 17,500/acre for shifting from paddy to maize, pulses, oilseeds, vegetables) has achieved only 38 per cent of its area target: farmers will not voluntarily shift from a guaranteed-price, MSP-backstopped crop to uncertain market crops. KCC penetration (82 per cent -- best India) is Punjab agriculture's genuine achievement; most Punjab farmers have access to institutional credit at 7 per cent vs 24 per cent from moneylenders. Cotton collapse (Rs. 6,620/quintal vs historical Rs. 8,000+; whitefly attack destroying 50 per cent of Malwa cotton) has devastated farmers who already shifted from paddy.

source.quote: paddy 77 lakh acres. groundwater 1 m/yr. diversification 38 per cent. conversion 18 per cent. KCC 82 per cent. PMFBY 12 per cent

recommendations: Punjab Agriculture and GoI MoAFW must co-design a Punjab Crop Diversification Compact 2030: (a) MSP for diversified crops -- GoI must extend MSP guaranteed procurement to maize, moong, sunflower, and basmati in Punjab on the same model as paddy; without MSP for alternative crops, farmers will not diversify; (b) incentive enhancement -- ₹17,500/acre incentive is insufficient; must be raised to ₹30,000/acre with guaranteed procurement; (c) PMFBY -- from 12 to 40 per cent coverage within 3 years; KCC renewal must be linked to PMFBY enrolment; (d) water tariff -- GoI and Punjab must introduce groundwater extraction pricing for paddy (symbolic price to send a conservation signal); (e) cotton support -- crash assistance ₹15,000/acre for whitefly-affected Malwa cotton farmers; disease-resistant variety distribution through PAU (Punjab Agricultural University).

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's gender indicators are among India's best for a large state: child marriage at 8 per cent (vs national 23 per cent -- Karnataka is 3x better than national average, driven by girls' education investment and legal enforcement). Gruha Lakshmi (Rs. 2,000/month direct transfer to women heads of household) at Rs. 4,800 crore annual has provided direct financial empowerment to 20+ lakh Karnataka women. ICDS AWC (Anganwadi Centres) at 82 per cent functional provides nutrition and early childhood development to the 0-6 age group. The One Stop Centre (government-run integrated support for women in distress -- police, legal aid, medical care, shelter in one place) at 42 per cent capacity reflects the gap between government provision and the scale of domestic violence (18,000 reported annual cases -- actual cases estimated 10x higher with under-reporting). POCSO cases (3,200 annually -- among the highest in large states, possibly reflecting better reporting culture rather than higher incidence) require fast track court expediting.

recommendations: Karnataka DWCD must: (a) One Stop Centre -- from 42 to 80 per cent capacity within 12 months; all 31 districts must have a functional OSC; DV victims must reach OSC within 24 hours of complaint; (b) POCSO -- Karnataka must utilise 100 per cent of GoI Fast Track Special Courts for POCSO; all POCSO cases must be adjudicated within 12 months; (c) Gruha Lakshmi evaluation -- formal impact assessment of ₹4,800 crore/year programme; assess whether amount can be increased; expand eligibility; (d) ICDS AWC -- from 82 to 95 per cent functional within 6 months; all AWCs with hot cooked meal provision for 6 months/year minimum; (e) gender data -- Karnataka must produce annual gender data report (with district disaggregation) tracking DV, POCSO, maternal health, education, and economic participation.

keyFindings.text: UP's industrial power cost disadvantage (Rs. 8.4/unit for MSME vs Karnataka Rs. 5.8/unit) is a 45 per cent premium that directly reduces UP MSME competitiveness. A Kanpur leather factory, a Moradabad brass unit, or a Varanasi textile weaver paying Rs. 8.4/unit for power is disadvantaged against a comparable Karnataka manufacturer by Rs. 2.6/unit on every unit consumed. Power outage cost (Rs. 12,000 crore annually for UP MSME -- estimated from frequency and duration of outages combined with MSME production loss data) is the second competitiveness drag: production stoppages, diesel genset costs, raw material waste during outages. Dedicated industrial feeders (28 per cent coverage -- only 28 per cent of UP industrial areas/estates have a dedicated feeder separate from agricultural/domestic supply) mean most UP industry shares its power supply with domestic and agricultural consumers, leading to voltage fluctuation, which damages sensitive equipment and reduces quality. UP's MSME sector (10.7 lakh units -- largest in India) losing Rs. 12,000 crore annually to power problems is a national competitiveness crisis.

source.quote: MSME Rs. 8.4 vs Rs. 5.8. dedicated feeder 28 per cent. outage Rs. 12,000 crore. transformer 42 per cent

recommendations: UP Energy Department and UPPCL must implement a UP Industrial Power Competitiveness Programme: (a) dedicated industrial feeders -- from 28 to 60 per cent of industrial estates within 3 years (₹3,000 crore RDSS investment); (b) MSME tariff review -- UP Electricity Regulatory Commission (UPERC) must examine whether UP MSME tariff can be reduced from ₹8.4 to ₹7 through cross-subsidy rationalisation; (c) transformer reliability -- transformer failure 42 per cent means 4 in 10 transformers in rural industry fail annually; transformer quality upgrade and predictive maintenance programme; (d) voltage quality -- 100 per cent of UP industrial estates must have voltage stabilisation by 2027; (e) UP MSME power competitiveness gap vs Karnataka/Maharashtra must be quantified annually and reported to state legislature as an economic cost.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's digital governance picture is mixed: high-performing in some national programmes (Aadhaar-PDS seeding 88 per cent -- meaning 88 per cent of Bihar PDS cards are linked to Aadhaar, enabling identity-verified food distribution; online MGNREGS payment 82 per cent -- meaning most MGNREGS wages go directly to bank/postoffice accounts, reducing intermediary leakage). But the core digital infrastructure has gaps: rural internet penetration (38 per cent -- meaning 62 per cent of Bihar rural residents cannot access any internet service), BSWAN uptime (68 per cent -- the state government's own wide area network is down 32 per cent of the time), and e-District services (42 per cent online -- meaning 58 per cent of citizen services still require in-person visits and are subject to the delays, bribes, and inefficiency that follow). Bihar's Digital Land Records (Bhumi 78 per cent) is above average -- driven by DILRMP (Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme) -- but the 22 per cent un-digitised records remain a source of land dispute and encroachment.

source.quote: e-District 42 per cent. CSC 62 per cent. internet 38 per cent. BSWAN 68 per cent. Bhumi 78 per cent. Aadhaar 88 per cent. MGNREGS 82 per cent

recommendations: Bihar IT and e-Governance must: (a) BSWAN uptime -- from 68 to 95 per cent within 12 months; dedicated maintenance contract with penalty clause; backup connectivity via 4G/5G for critical government offices; (b) rural internet -- Bihar must use PM-WANI (Wi-Fi Access Network Interface) programme to deploy rural wi-fi at all CSC points; target from 38 to 60 per cent rural internet within 3 years; (c) e-District -- from 42 to 80 per cent services online within 18 months; revenue certificate, caste certificate, domicile certificate must be fully online with Aadhaar authentication; (d) Bhumi -- from 78 to 100 per cent land record digitisation within 12 months; mutation process fully online; (e) CSC from 62 to 85 per cent operational within 6 months -- non-functional CSCs must be replaced under PM-VLE scheme.

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's mental health paradox: home to NIMHANS (National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences -- India's premier mental health institution, a global centre of excellence), yet suicide rate at 28 per 1 lakh (highest among large Indian states, nearly 3x the national 12/lakh average). Farmer suicides (2,800+ annually -- driven by crop failure, debt, drought in Kalaburagi and Bidar, and Bt Cotton cultivation failure) and Bengaluru IT sector burnout (18 per cent alcohol dependence in adult male Bengaluru -- corporate stress, long hours, social isolation) are Karnataka's two distinct mental health crisis epicentres. NMHP (National Mental Health Programme) covers only 28 per cent of districts with community mental health services -- the remaining districts have no organised mental health outreach. Rural mental health access at 12 per cent means 88 per cent of rural Karnatakas do not access mental health services when needed. The 8 psychiatrists per 10 lakh (vs WHO recommended 30) gap means Karnataka literally does not have the professionals to provide the care even if it wanted to.

source.quote: suicide 28/lakh. psychiatrist 8/lakh vs 30. NMHP 28 per cent. farmer 2,800+. alcohol 18 per cent. rural 12 per cent

recommendations: Karnataka Health and NIMHANS must co-create a Karnataka Mental Health Action Plan 2030: (a) psychiatrist workforce -- from 8 to 20 per 10 lakh within 5 years; NIMHANS must expand DM Psychiatry seats; Rajiv Gandhi University of Health Sciences (RGUHS) must add psychiatry departments to all medical colleges; (b) NMHP -- from 28 to 75 per cent district coverage within 2 years; at least one mental health clinic per taluk (Karnataka has 236 taluks); (c) farmer suicide -- Krishi Sanjeevini programme (agriculture + mental health counsellor in each district) with KIRAN helpline integration; debt relief targeted at highest-suicide taluks (Kalaburagi, Bidar, Raichur); (d) IT/corporate burnout -- mandatory Employee Assistance Programmes for all Bengaluru IT companies with >500 employees; (e) alcohol -- NIMHANS-led community de-addiction programme in high-alcohol districts; ASHA trained in alcohol dependence identification.

keyFindings.text: West Bengal Police's Rs. 8,800 crore budget with 28 per cent vacancy (positions sanctioned but unfilled) is a structural capacity gap. Cybercrime (Rs. 1,200+ crore reported loss -- likely 10x higher with under-reporting) is a growing challenge in a state with 4+ crore digital payment users. SC/ST Atrocities Act conviction at 32 per cent (vs national 38 per cent -- WB is below national average in tribal and SC protection) reflects investigation quality gaps particularly in North Bengal and Jungle Mahal districts. Domestic violence case pendency (42 per cent of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act cases pending beyond 6 months) is a judicial-police interface failure. Prison overcrowding (138 per cent) is lower than Karnataka's 148 per cent but still above constitutional tolerance. The Fast Track Special Courts (18 per cent of required courts established -- among India's lowest adoption rates) means POCSO, rape, and acid attack cases are pending in regular courts.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's JEEViKA programme (10 lakh SHGs, 1.2 crore women members -- India's 2nd largest SHG network by members after Andhra Pradesh) has achieved remarkable scale. Bank linkage (Rs. 18,000+ crore -- SHGs collectively borrowing and repaying at scale) with NPA 12 per cent (higher than Odisha's <2 per cent and Kerala's Kudumbashree <1 per cent, but manageable given Bihar's poverty depth) demonstrates financial inclusion achievement. However, graduation to livelihoods (28 per cent -- only 28 per cent of JEEViKA SHG members have transitioned from credit access to stable livelihood activities) shows that the programme is stuck at the financial inclusion stage and has not progressed to economic empowerment. JEEViKA-MGNREGS convergence at 18 per cent (vs Odisha's 62 per cent) means that MGNREGS wage employment -- a natural complement to SHG micro-finance (SHG handles credit, MGNREGS provides asset creation opportunity) -- is not being combined for maximum impact. CMGVY (Chief Minister's Girls Vitality Yojana -- nutrition) SHG coverage at 68 per cent is above average.

source.quote: 10 lakh SHGs. bank Rs. 18,000+ crore. NPA 12 per cent. graduation 28 per cent. convergence 18 per cent. CMGVY 68 per cent

recommendations: Bihar JEEViKA and Rural Development must: (a) graduation push -- target from 28 to 50 per cent of SHG members in stable livelihoods by 2028; top livelihood pathways: dairy (Bihar ranks 4th in milk production -- scale cooperative dairy), goat rearing (Bihar's natural advantage), digital services (CSC/banking correspondent), and agri-processing; (b) MGNREGS convergence -- from 18 to 50 per cent within 2 years; JEEViKA villages must map all MGNREGS works and link SHG women as priority workers; (c) NPA reduction -- from 12 to 8 per cent through financial literacy training and better credit assessment at cluster federation level; (d) digital payments -- from 38 to 70 per cent within 12 months; JEEViKA x SBI/PNB for rural business correspondent network.
