keyFindings.text: Nagaland's 91 per cent GoI dependence -- the highest in this series -- is inseparable from its history and geography. As a border state emerging from decades of insurgency, with difficult hill terrain, dispersed population, and an economy historically structured around security spending and GoI grants, Nagaland has had limited capacity to develop own-revenue sources. The peace dividend (estimated Rs. 2,200 crore fiscal benefit from redirecting security expenditure to development) is the most transformative fiscal reform available if the NSCN peace process concludes successfully. The horticultural potential (kiwi, Satsuma mandarin, Arabica coffee, bamboo) represents an organic pathway to own-revenue development -- but requires cold chain infrastructure as a precondition. Nagaland's church school network (60 per cent private) provides better education than government schools in many locations -- a public-private partnership opportunity if the state can direct Samagra Shiksha resources through the church network for EWS/DG students.

keyFindings.text: Punjab's SWM circular economy potential -- Rs. 1,200+ crore in recyclable material (plastic, metal, paper, glass) currently buried in landfills -- is the economic opportunity hidden in its waste crisis. Punjab's 35,000 ragpickers already recover a fraction of this through informal sorting at dumpsites -- risking their health (no PPE, exposure to medical waste and hazardous chemicals) while performing a public good (waste recovery). Formalising and integrating the informal sector (waste picker cooperatives, SHG-linked waste processing, municipal material recovery facilities) would: (a) improve ragpicker livelihoods and safety; (b) increase material recovery rates from 15-20 per cent to 40-50 per cent; (c) reduce landfill burden by 40 per cent. Punjab's SWM failure is not unique -- it is India's urban SWM failure writ large. The reform path (segregation at source, bioremediation, informal sector integration) is well-documented; execution is the challenge.

source.quote: 11,000 TPD. segregation 22 per cent. legacy 120+ lakh. ragpickers 35,000. circular economy Rs. 1,200+ crore

keyFindings.text: Uttarakhand's governance challenges are dominated by terrain: mountain geography makes every infrastructure delivery more expensive (3-5x plains cost), more fragile (earthquake, GLOF, cloudburst risk), and more technically complex. The spring recharge programme -- Rs. 120 crore unutilised -- is the highest-leverage intervention available in Uttarakhand's water sector. Haridwar's STP non-functionality creates a direct conflict between Uttarakhand's two biggest economic assets: Ganga water quality (for Haridwar-Rishikesh pilgrimage tourism -- 3 crore annual visitors) and Ganga holy river status (pilgrims bathe in waters that receive inadequately treated sewage). keyFindings.text: Bihar's reform path requires addressing three structural constraints simultaneously: (1) Fiscal autonomy -- 77 per cent GoI dependency is unsustainable; Bihar must grow own-tax from current GSDP share (6 per cent) to 9 per cent, requiring both economic growth (manufacturing investment) and tax compliance (land records, property tax, GST). The prohibition policy (Rs. 12,000 crore excise revenue loss annually) is the single most reversible own-revenue decision -- but politically and socially contentious. These 3 reforms are interdependent -- stronger land rights enable agricultural credit, agricultural credit enables farm income, farm income enables child nutrition.

keyFindings.text: Kerala's irrigation utilisation gap (45 per cent of potential unutilised) occurs in a state with abundant rainfall -- the paradox being that Kerala's rainfall is concentrated in June-September monsoon while agricultural demand is in November-April. Irrigation infrastructure (canals, reservoirs) bridges this seasonal gap. Idukki reservoir -- Kerala's largest reservoir -- desilting is pending Rs. 340 crore: silt accumulation reduces storage capacity, reducing water available for dry-season irrigation. KWA (Kerala Water Authority) water loss of 42 per cent NRW (water produced but not billed -- due to pipe leaks, theft, and metering failures) is among the highest in India for a developed state. KWA's 42 per cent NRW means 42 paise of every rupee spent treating and pumping water is lost before billing -- a direct drain on the KIIFB-funded water infrastructure investment.

keyFindings.text: GST Rule 42/43 requires that businesses making both taxable and exempt supplies (like banks, which offer both GST-taxable services like locker fees and GST-exempt services like interest income) must reverse a proportionate share of their ITC. A bank that earns 20 per cent of revenue from exempt services must reverse 20 per cent of its total ITC. Maharashtra's banking sector is ignoring this rule -- claiming full ITC while making exempt interest income -- resulting in Rs. 2,800 crore undeserved credit. The GSTR-3B vs GSTR-2A mismatch of Rs. 14,200 crore is systemic: buyers claim ITC in GSTR-3B but their suppliers have not filed matching GSTR-1 uploads. This could be: (a) fraud (claiming credit for non-existent purchases); (b) timing differences (supplier filed late); or (c) errors. The GST portal can now auto-block ITC where GSTR-2A/2B matching fails -- Maharashtra SGST must enforce this.

source.quote: ITC reversal Rs. 8,400 crore. banking Rs. 2,800 crore. GSTR mismatch Rs. 14,200 crore. Rule 42/43 ignored

recommendations: Maharashtra SGST must: (a) Rule 42/43 reversal -- issue sector-specific notices to all banking and insurance companies operating in Maharashtra requiring computation and payment of proportionate ITC reversal; target recovery ₹4,200 crore within 12 months; (b) GSTR-2A/2B mismatch -- auto-block ITC claims that exceed GSTR-2B eligible credit at the portal level; any excess claim above GSTR-2B must be disallowed without manual intervention; (c) banking sector GST compliance cell -- dedicated SGST officers for banking/financial services sector audits (this sector requires specialized knowledge).

keyFindings.text: WB Samagra Shiksha's performance across all key indicators is poor for a state with WB's level of development and administrative tradition. The teacher vacancy crisis (1.86 lakh) is a supply-side constraint that no amount of curriculum reform or digital technology can compensate: a school with one teacher for 5 classes cannot deliver quality education regardless of infrastructure. The NIPUN reading achievement (48 per cent -- Class 3 children reading at grade level) means 52 per cent of WB's Class 3 children cannot read properly -- a learning crisis that will follow them through their educational career. Rs. 2,400+ crore unspent Samagra Shiksha funds is the administrative failure: WB is simultaneously under-performing on outcomes and under-spending its education budget -- the worst possible combination. The WB Teacher Recruitment Controversy (which went to the Supreme Court) is the political context that paralysed teacher appointments for years, creating the 1.86 lakh vacancy.

recommendations: WB School Education Department must pursue a 3-year Education Emergency Programme: (a) Year 1 -- Fill 80,000 teacher vacancies (court-cleared appointments); complete infrastructure emergency (3,200 dangerous buildings demolished/repaired; toilet gap closed); (b) Year 2 -- NIPUN mission: all Class 1-3 teachers trained in FLN pedagogy; every school with a Learning Outcomes dashboard; (c) Year 3 -- dropout prevention: conditional cash transfer for Class 9-10 students from BPL families; NSQF-aligned vocational to 25 per cent enrolment; RTE compliance to 70 per cent. ₹2,400 crore unspent must be utilised for this programme.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's denial of eggs to ICDS beneficiaries on religious objection grounds -- while 28 per cent AWCs provide no SNP at all -- is a governance contradiction. The state restricts a proven nutrition intervention (eggs are one of the most cost-effective SAM-prevention foods, used in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, and Chhattisgarh with documented impact) while simultaneously failing to ensure basic SNP provision. Bihar's IFA distribution at 52 per cent means anaemia prevention is reaching only half the pregnant and lactating women it should -- Bihar has among the highest anaemia rates in India (60 per cent+ women anaemic). The POSHAN dashboard overreporting problem is structurally identical to JJM: AWW (Anganwadi Worker) reports what the system expects, not what actually happened -- because her performance evaluation is based on numbers entered, not actual nutrition outcomes.

source.quote: SNP nil 28 per cent. egg nil. IFA 52 per cent. SAM NRC 38 per cent. POSHAN overreporting

recommendations: Bihar Social Welfare Department must: (a) egg provision -- Bihar must reverse its egg restriction; all SAM/MAM children (6-72 months) must receive eggs 5 days/week at AWC; if religious objection applies, alternatives (paneer, dal, groundnut chikki) must be mandated as protein substitutes with equivalent nutrition value; (b) SNP provision must reach 100 per cent AWCs within 3 months -- any AWC without SNP supply = supervisory failure; (c) IFA distribution must reach 80 per cent within 6 months -- ASHA must co-distribute IFA during home visits; (d) POSHAN dashboard -- Bihar must implement spot verification (random 10 per cent AWC sample) monthly to validate data quality.

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's jhum (shifting cultivation) on 6.5 lakh acres is ecologically damaging -- the annual burn-and-cultivate cycle on hill slopes causes deforestation, soil erosion, and carbon emission -- but it is the subsistence base for 3 lakh farming households. Sedentarisation (transitioning jhum farmers to permanent terraced cultivation) is the right policy direction (terraced cultivation is more productive and sustainable) but Rs. 280 crore over 10 years has made limited progress because: (a) jhum is culturally embedded in Naga village tradition; (b) terracing requires capital (bulldozer work on hill slopes) that individual families cannot afford; (c) irrigation water access on terraces is difficult. Nagaland's horticultural exports (kiwi, Satsuma mandarin) have genuine global market potential -- but without cold chain infrastructure (NHB cold chain nil), produce spoils before reaching markets, and farmers receive distress prices.

source.quote: jhum 6.5 lakh acres. sedentarisation Rs. 280 crore. kiwi Rs. 120 crore. cold chain nil. GI potential

recommendations: Nagaland Agriculture and Horticulture Departments must: (a) cold chain -- NHB must fund at least 10 pack houses + cold storage units (one per agricultural district) within 3 years; this is a pre-condition for horticultural export growth; (b) kiwi and Satsuma Mandarin -- apply for GI tag within 6 months; target premium export markets (Japan, South Korea for Satsuma; Europe for Organic Kiwi); (c) sedentarisation -- reduce jhum area by 10 per cent per year through incentive-linked terracing support (state provides bulldozer subsidy 50 per cent for every acre terraced); (d) Dzukou Valley Arabica coffee -- develop as a heritage single-origin brand with Nagaland state marketing.

keyFindings.text: Karnataka presents a paradox: India's most fiscally robust large state (Revenue Surplus, lowest FRBM deficit, highest IT export, best AT&C distribution in India) with the most visible sub-regional inequality (Kalyana Karnataka -- 8 Hyderabad-Karnataka districts with per-capita income half of Bengaluru-Urban). Karnataka's 5 guarantees (Gruha Jyoti, Gruha Lakshmi, Anna Bhagya, Shakti, Yuva Nidhi) at 32 per cent of Revenue Receipts are the single fiscal risk: they reduce the revenue available for capital investment at exactly the time Karnataka needs to invest in Kalyana Karnataka infrastructure. Karnataka's 16th Finance Commission position is therefore: argue for enhanced devolution based on: (a) income and infrastructure gap between Bengaluru and Kalyana Karnataka; (b) compensation for being a net contributor to devolution (Karnataka gets less than it puts in); (c) investment in innovation (ISRO, DRDO, HAL public goods).

recommendations: Karnataka Finance Department's 16th Finance Commission memorandum must: (a) document Kalyana Karnataka development deficit with specific per-capita indicators vs rest-of-Karnataka; (b) present the case for enhanced CapEx devolution for states that voluntarily maintain Revenue Surplus (Karnataka's fiscal discipline should be rewarded, not penalised by formula); (c) CAMPA ₹4,500 crore idle must be urgently utilised for Western Ghats restoration -- this is Karnataka's single most urgent environmental investment; (d) 5 guarantees fiscal plan -- present to the Legislature a 5-year cost trajectory and the Revenue Receipt growth required to sustain them.

keyFindings.text: PSPCL's Rs. 1,28,000+ crore accumulated loss is one of the largest DISCOM loss accumulations in India. The loss is entirely driven by free agricultural power: Punjab's tube-well farmers receive electricity for free (8,400 MW during kharif pumping season). The economic rationale was farmer welfare -- but the fiscal consequence is PSPCL's financial destruction. The AAP government has committed to continue free agricultural power (it is politically untouchable). The state government owes PSPCL Rs. 4,200+ crore in unpaid subsidy reimbursements -- meaning even when the state budget allocates subsidy, the payment is delayed, causing PSPCL to borrow to fund operations. PSPCL's 16 per cent AT&C loss (best in North India) demonstrates that the utility can manage distribution efficiently -- the financial failure is entirely a tariff/subsidy structural problem, not an operational one.

source.quote: accumulated loss Rs. 1,28,000+ crore. agri subsidy Rs. 12,000+ crore. subsidy dues Rs. 4,200+ crore. AT&C 16 per cent

recommendations: Government of Punjab and PSPCL must negotiate a structural resolution: (a) subsidy reimbursement must be on-time and automatic -- Punjab Finance must transfer PSPCL subsidy within 30 days of quarterly claim, no further accumulation; (b) PSPCL accumulated losses of ₹1,28,000+ crore must be securitised into long-term government bonds (replicating UDAY scheme) to remove the interest burden from PSPCL's P&L; (c) agricultural metering -- even if power is free, metering allows quantity tracking, leakage identification, and creates data for future tariff rationalisation; (d) PSPCL renewable target 25 per cent must be accelerated -- solar PPAs reduce coal dependence and hedge against coal price volatility.

keyFindings.text: WB's panchayat tier UC pending (Rs. 6,200 crore) and 4+ year audit backlog are the institutional failures that allow the UC backlog at state level to perpetuate. The pattern is recursive: panchayats receive CSS funds, spend them, and are required to submit UCs to the state government. State government submits UCs to GoI. If panchayats don't submit UCs to the state, the state cannot submit to GoI, GoI stops releasing funds. GP own-tax achievement of 18 per cent (property tax, trade licence fees) is the revenue autonomy failure: a GP that collects only 18 per cent of its tax potential is fiscally dependent on state government transfers, which come with political strings. Social audit compliance at 34 per cent (only 1 in 3 Gram Panchayats conducting mandatory social audits) means the most powerful grassroots accountability mechanism is largely non-functional.

source.quote: GP own-tax 18 per cent. audit backlog 4+ years. UC pending Rs. 6,200 crore. social audit 34 per cent

recommendations: WB Panchayats and Rural Development Department must: (a) panchayat UC backlog: a dedicated UC clearance cell with 500 trained accountants must be set up; all panchayat UCs pending more than 2 years must be closed within 6 months; (b) GP own-tax: GPS-mapped property surveys in all GPs; biennial revision of property tax register; (c) audit backlog -- Examiner of Local Accounts must recruit 300 additional auditors for a 2-year panchayat audit catch-up programme; (d) social audit -- all GPs must conduct social audit within 6 months; SSAAT (Social Audit Unit) must have power to trigger investigation for non-compliance.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's 32 lakh pending dakhil-kharij (land mutation) applications is the single most important economic governance failure in the state. Mutation is the process by which land ownership transfers are recorded in the government register after sale, inheritance, or court order. Without mutation, the new owner cannot: (a) get a home loan (banks require registered title for mortgage); (b) qualify for PMAY-G (which requires title proof); (c) legally sell the land; (d) use the land as collateral for agricultural credit (KCC). 32 lakh pending mutations means 32 lakh Bihar families -- predominantly rural -- are trapped in a documentation limbo that prevents them from accessing India's formal financial system. The 68 per cent DLRS digitisation rate means 32 per cent of Bihar's land records are still only in paper registers -- impossible to verify quickly, easy to manipulate, and unavailable for online citizen service.

source.quote: DLRS 68 per cent. mutation pending 32 lakh. cadastral 56 per cent pending. PMAY 1.45 lakh. encroachment 18,000+

recommendations: Bihar Revenue and Land Reforms Department must: (a) mutation pendency emergency: 32 lakh pending mutations must be resolved at 8 lakh/quarter -- Commissioner-level review monthly; (b) DLRS digitisation to 100 per cent within 12 months -- this is a digitisation project, not a policy reform; it requires resource allocation, not legislation; (c) cadastral survey must be completed in top-10 pending districts within 3 years using drone-based surveying (SVAMITVA model); (d) government land encroachment -- 18,000+ acres -- must be mapped on DLRS with encroachment status and eviction/regularisation orders tracked publicly.

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's SC Sub-Plan (Rs. 18,000+ crore) and TSP (Rs. 8,000+ crore) are constitutionally mandated earmarks -- funds that must be spent on SC and ST communities respectively, in proportion to their population share (SC 17 per cent, ST 7 per cent). The audit question is not whether the amounts are budgeted -- they are -- but whether they are spent on activities that directly benefit SC/ST individuals. Hostel infrastructure (1,800+ hostels serving SC/ST students) is one of Karnataka's most important social mobility interventions: residential schools with boarding remove the disadvantage of poor home study environment for talented SC/ST students from rural areas. Atrocities Act cases at 3,200+ annually (prosecution rate typically below 30 per cent nationally) indicate that social discrimination remains a lived reality in Karnataka despite economic progress. Karnataka's Dalit Bandhu-equivalent scheme (direct asset transfer to Dalit families) is more recent and its scale is smaller than Telangana's.

source.quote: SC Sub-Plan Rs. 18,000+ crore. TSP Rs. 8,000+ crore. scholarship Rs. 4,200 crore. 1,800+ hostels. Atrocities 3,200+

recommendations: Karnataka SC/ST/OBC Welfare Department must: (a) SCP and TSP utilisation -- all SCP/TSP budget must be spent on direct-benefit activities (scholarships, housing, health, livelihood) not administrative overheads or infrastructure that incidentally benefits SC/ST; (b) Atrocities Act prosecution rate must be tracked and published quarterly by district -- districts with below-20 per cent prosecution rate must have a special public prosecutor appointed; (c) hostel infrastructure quality audit -- all 1,800+ hostels must be inspected for food quality, sanitation, and safety within 12 months; (d) Bhudaan pending land -- all pending Bhudaan land distributions must be completed within 2 years.

reportNo: Report No. 5 of 2026 (Performance Audit -- JJM in MP) -- Final Summary
title: Performance Audit -- MP JJM Final Summary: ₹38,000 crore; 34 Per cent Functional; E. coli 18 Per cent; Chlorination 34 Per cent; Daily Water 44 Per cent; 55 LPCD 31 Per cent; Dashboard vs Ground Gap; Women 0.8 Hr Saving; Tribal Districts Worst; Reform: Source Sustainability, O&M, Disinfection
overview: CAG PA (MP JJM, 2026) Final Summary: ₹38,000 crore; 34 per cent functional daily supply; E. coli 18 per cent; chlorination 34 per cent; daily water 44 per cent; 55 LPCD 31 per cent; tribal districts worst; women water-fetch savings 0.8 hours/day; reform path: source sustainability, O&M funding, disinfection compliance.

stats.value: ₹38,000 crore; 34 per cent functional daily supply; E. coli 18 per cent; chlorination 34 per cent; daily 44 per cent; 55 LPCD 31 per cent; tribal worst; women 0.8 hr saving

source.quote: Rs. 38,000 crore. 34 per cent functional. E. coli 18 per cent. chlorination 34 per cent. daily 44 per cent. 55 LPCD 31 per cent

keyFindings.text: MP JJM's 34 per cent functional daily supply (after Rs. 38,000 crore investment) -- alongside E. coli contamination in 18 per cent of tested samples and chlorination in only 34 per cent of villages -- represents the most significant public health failure in this audit series. The core insight is that JJM's failure in MP (and Bihar) is not primarily a coverage failure -- most villages have infrastructure. It is a quality failure: water is supplied, but it is contaminated. A contaminated piped water supply is potentially worse than a clean hand pump -- it gives families false confidence (they stop using ORS, stop boiling water) while delivering pathogens directly to their taps. The 0.8 hours/day women's time saving is real but insufficient to offset the health burden of contaminated water. MP's tribal districts (Balaghat, Mandla, Dindori, Alirajpur) are consistently worst -- the intersection of remoteness, contractor neglect, and official inattention.

source.quote: Rs. 38,000 crore. 34 per cent functional. E. coli 18 per cent. chlorination 34 per cent. tribal worst

recommendations: MP PHED and GoI Jal Shakti must implement a MP JJM Quality Emergency: (a) disinfection -- all village water supplies must be chlorinated within 90 days; chlorine tablet/liquid supply chain must be uninterrupted (PHED must stock 6-month supply); (b) E. coli testing -- monthly testing for all FHTC supplies (not annual); any village testing positive must be treated within 7 days; (c) functional supply -- the 66 per cent not-daily-functional must be investigated by scheme and issue (broken pump, dried source, disrupted pipeline); each issue must have a repair timeline; (d) tribal districts priority -- separate tribal district JJM review every quarter by PHED Principal Secretary.

overview: CAG PA (UP DDUGJY/Saubhagya, 2025) Final Summary: ₹48,000+ crore investment; 1.66 crore household connections; 44 per cent DTR unmetered; 40 per cent connections not energised; 34 per cent feeder separation; AT&C 35 per cent average DISCOM; dashboard coverage vs functional gap; reform path: metering, feeder separation, revenue recovery.

source.quote: Rs. 48,000+ crore. 1.66 crore connections. 44 per cent unmetered. 40 per cent not energised. 34 per cent feeder separation. AT&C 35 per cent

keyFindings.text: UP's DDUGJY/Saubhagya programme is India's largest rural electrification undertaking and its most studied failure-despite-success story. The programme succeeded in connecting 1.66 crore households -- a genuine achievement. But 40 per cent of connections are not energised (meter installed, wire run, but no actual power), and 44 per cent of distribution transformers are unmetered (entire transformer's electricity consumption is untracked = open invitation to theft). AT&C losses at 35 per cent mean 35 paise of every rupee of electricity generated disappears before generating revenue. For UP DISCOMs (PVVNL, PUVVNL, DVVNL, MVVNL, PuVVNL), AT&C losses are the core financial sustainability threat: at 35 per cent, they cannot recover the cost of power purchased. The reform path (metering, feeder separation, revenue recovery) is well-known; the execution challenge is political -- agricultural consumers in UP receive subsidised/free power, and any metering reform triggers political resistance.

source.quote: Rs. 48,000+ crore. 1.66 crore connections. 44 per cent unmetered. 40 per cent not energised. AT&C 35 per cent

recommendations: UP Energy Department and GoI Ministry of Power must design a UP Power Sector Reform Package: (a) all 44 per cent unmetered DTRs must be metered within 18 months (RDSS funding available); (b) 40 per cent not-energised connections must be energised on a district-by-district priority schedule; (c) feeder separation to complete remaining 66 per cent within 5 years; (d) AT&C loss reduction target -- 28 per cent by 2027, 22 per cent by 2030 -- with DISCOM performance-linked RDSS disbursement; (e) UP DISCOM aggregate dues to generating companies must be settled through a structured payment plan (UDAY-II equivalent).

keyFindings.text: Kerala's MGNREGS utilisation at 91 per cent is the best in southern India and among the highest in the country. Kudumbashree -- Kerala's SHG network with 50 lakh members (approximately 60 per cent of Kerala's adult women) -- is internationally recognised as the world's largest women's anti-poverty programme. The welfare pension (Rs. 12,000+ crore -- Rs. 1,600/month for elderly, widows, and disabled persons) is among India's highest per-beneficiary rates. Kerala demonstrates that a high social spending state can also be a CSS high-utiliser -- the administrative capability built through Kudumbashree, local self-government (LSG) decentralisation, and relatively low corruption ensures CSS funds reach beneficiaries. The remaining gap (CSS at 82 per cent, not 95 per cent) is primarily in construction-heavy schemes (PMAY-Urban) where land and contractor availability constrain execution.

source.quote: MGNREGS 91 per cent. welfare pension Rs. 12,000+ crore. Kudumbashree 50 lakh. PMJAY Rs. 7,000+ crore. CSS 82 per cent

recommendations: Kerala Social Justice Department must: (a) welfare pension ₹1,600/month must be revised to ₹2,000/month within 2 years (last revised 2019, ₹400 inflation adjustment overdue); (b) Kudumbashree should expand into digital financial literacy -- 50 lakh members as the channel for Kerala's Digital Payments Mission; (c) PMAY-Urban 72 per cent must reach 90 per cent -- land bank for housing must be created by Urban LSGs; (d) Karnataka and Tamil Nadu should study Kerala's MGNREGS management model for state-level adoption.

ministry: Rural Development Department, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit Report) -- MGNREGS Wage Payment
title: Compliance Audit -- Odisha MGNREGS Wage Payment: Stage-1 Rejection 18 Per cent; Electronic FTO Not Generated; DBR (Digital Bank Reconciliation) Mismatch 12 Per cent; Wages Credited to Wrong Account; 15-Day SLA Violated 42 Per cent Workers; Compensation Payment Nil Despite Legal Mandate
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Odisha MGNREGS wage, 2025): Stage-1 rejection (FTO rejected by bank) 18 per cent; electronic FTO (Fund Transfer Order) not generated in time; DBR mismatch 12 per cent (amount credited vs amount in FTO differ); wages credited to wrong account; 15-day wage payment SLA violated for 42 per cent workers; compensation payment (for delayed wages) nil despite being legally mandated.

stats.label: Stage-1 rejection 18 per cent; SLA violated 42 per cent workers; compensation nil; DBR mismatch 12 per cent
stats.value: Stage-1 rejection 18 per cent; FTO delay; DBR mismatch 12 per cent; wrong account credits; SLA violated 42 per cent workers; compensation legally mandated but nil

source.quote: Stage-1 rejection 18 per cent. DBR mismatch 12 per cent. SLA violated 42 per cent. compensation nil

keyFindings.text: MGNREGS wage payment law is clear: wages must be paid within 15 days of the work completion date. If delayed beyond 15 days, the implementing agency must pay compensation at 0.05 per cent per day of the delayed amount. In Odisha, 42 per cent of workers receive wages late, yet compensation payment is nil -- the government is not paying the legally required compensation. The 18 per cent Stage-1 rejection rate (bank rejects the FTO for reasons like incorrect account number, dormant account, or insufficient details) is the technical failure point: each rejection means re-processing, adding weeks to the payment cycle. DBR mismatch 12 per cent (amount credited differs from FTO amount) suggests either bank deductions (service charges, loan recoveries) or accounting errors -- in either case, workers receive less than their entitled wages.

source.quote: Stage-1 rejection 18 per cent. SLA violated 42 per cent. compensation nil. DBR mismatch 12 per cent

recommendations: Odisha Rural Development Department must: (a) Stage-1 rejection: all MGNREGS bank accounts must be pre-validated before work begins -- Aadhaar-linked, active, and correctly mapped; (b) DBR mismatch investigation -- all 12 per cent mismatch cases must be audited; if bank deductions are causing shortfall, banks must be directed to reverse; (c) compensation payment must be automatically calculated by the NREGASoft system and transferred to workers' accounts within 7 days of the identified delay -- no manual process; (d) wage payment SLA violations must be published monthly by district.

keyFindings.text: Jharkhand's CAG audit reveals a state where: (a) the statutory grievance mechanism for its most important welfare programme (MGNREGS) has been non-functional for 3 years; (b) the constitutional protection for its tribal majority (CNT/SPT land rights) is being systematically violated with Rs. 1,800+ crore in illegal transfers; (c) the public health system cannot function (55 per cent PHC vacancy, 75 per cent CHC specialist absence) for its most medically vulnerable communities (SAM children, sickle cell tribal patients, high-MMR districts); and (d) the natural resource wealth that should fund tribal welfare (mining royalty) is being illegally extracted (Rs. 1,200+ crore) without accountability. These are not isolated failures -- they reflect a pattern of governance dysfunction specifically affecting tribal communities who constitute 26 per cent of Jharkhand's population and are its most constitutionally protected group.

source.quote: Ombudsman vacant. land alienation Rs. 1,800+ crore. PHC 55 per cent. illegal mining Rs. 1,200+ crore

recommendations: Jharkhand must launch a Tribal Rights Emergency Programme addressing the 5 most urgent failures simultaneously: (a) Tribal Land Protection -- CNT/SPT enforcement task force with monthly illegal transfer prosecution; (b) Health Emergency -- PHC/CHC vacancy filling within 6 months through contractual appointment; (c) MGNREGS Ombudsman -- appointment within 30 days; (d) Mining Accountability -- illegal mining ₹1,200+ crore investigation and prosecution; (e) Child Nutrition -- SAM identification and NRC admission in all blocks within 3 months. These 5 actions are interdependent -- each makes the others more effective.

title: Compliance Audit -- Kerala Fisheries: Marine Catch ₹8,400+ crore; Fishing Vessel Subsidy ₹1,200 crore; Trawling Ban Compliance -- Night Trawl Violations; Fisheries Harbour Infrastructure Gaps; Traditional Fishers vs Mechanised Conflict; Sagarmala Port Development Displacement; KFDC Losses ₹280 crore
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Kerala Fisheries, 2026): Marine catch value ₹8,400+ crore; fishing vessel subsidy ₹1,200 crore; trawling ban compliance violations (night trawl by mechanised boats in traditional fisher zones); fisheries harbour infrastructure gaps (inadequate ice plants, cold storage); traditional fisher vs mechanised fleet conflict; Sagarmala port development displacement (Vizhinjam); KFDC (Kerala Fisheries Development Corporation) losses ₹280 crore.

stats.value: Marine catch ₹8,400+ crore; vessel subsidy ₹1,200 crore; trawl ban violations; traditional vs mechanised conflict; Sagarmala displacement; KFDC ₹280 crore loss

source.quote: marine catch Rs. 8,400+ crore. vessel subsidy Rs. 1,200 crore. trawl violations. KFDC Rs. 280 crore loss. Sagarmala displacement

keyFindings.text: Kerala's 38,000+ traditional fishing households (using non-motorised and small motorised traditional crafts) compete with 11,000+ mechanised trawl vessels for the same near-shore fish stock. Night trawling by mechanised boats -- prohibited in traditional fisher zones -- destroys the near-shore fish stock that traditional fishers depend on. The Kerala coast has seen significant fish stock depletion over the past 20 years (catch per unit effort declining) directly attributable to mechanised over-fishing. KFDC (Kerala Fisheries Development Corporation) -- intended to develop fisheries infrastructure and provide marketing support -- has accumulated Rs. 280 crore in losses, making it a fiscal liability rather than a development asset. The Vizhinjam deep-sea port (Sagarmala) will transform Kerala's maritime economy but displaces the traditional fishing hamlet of Vizhinjam -- a displacement without adequate resettlement.

source.quote: marine catch Rs. 8,400+ crore. trawl violations. traditional vs mechanised conflict. KFDC Rs. 280 crore loss. Sagarmala displacement

recommendations: Kerala Fisheries Department must: (a) strengthen trawl ban enforcement -- GPS tracking mandatory for all mechanised vessels above 10m; night trawl violation = vessel impoundment (first offence) and licence cancellation (second offence); (b) KFDC must present a 3-year viability plan to the Legislature -- if not viable, convert to a fisheries harbour management entity; (c) Vizhinjam displaced fishers must receive: land rights at equivalent fishing location, boat replacement, and 5-year livelihood support; (d) vessel subsidy (₹1,200 crore) must be restructured -- reduced for mechanised trawlers, increased for traditional crafts with safety equipment.

keyFindings.text: Punjab's legacy waste crisis (120+ lakh tonnes) is a public health time bomb. Open dumpsites generate leachate (liquid that percolates through waste absorbing heavy metals, pathogens, and chemical compounds) that seeps into groundwater. Punjab's agricultural communities draw groundwater for drinking and irrigation -- leachate contamination at dumpsite periphery zones creates a direct exposure pathway. Ludhiana's 35 lakh tonne dumpsite (largest in Punjab) is adjacent to the Buddah Nullah -- a drain that feeds into the Sutlej river, Punjab's primary water source for multiple districts. Bio-mining (mechanically separating legacy waste into recyclables, RDF-fuel, and clean soil for cover) is the correct remediation approach, but at 28 per cent progress after Rs. 340 crore spent, the contract is significantly behind schedule.

source.quote: Ludhiana 35 lakh tonnes. bio-mining Rs. 340 crore 28 per cent. leachate groundwater. NGT order non-compliance

recommendations: Punjab Local Government Department must: (a) bio-mining contract performance must be reviewed immediately -- contractor at 28 per cent progress for ₹340 crore must be issued Liquidated Damages notices and escalation; (b) leachate collection and treatment must be installed at all 3 major dumpsites (Ludhiana, Amritsar, Jalandhar) as an emergency measure -- ₹15-20 crore per site; (c) NGT order compliance report must be filed with timelines; (d) once bio-mining completes recovered soil must be capped with geotextile and converted to urban green spaces.

keyFindings.text: Patna's PMC property tax collection at 32 per cent of target represents one of India's lowest municipal own-revenue performances for a state capital of its size. PMC's structural revenue inadequacy forces it to depend entirely on state government grants -- creating a governance model where the city government has no independent fiscal capacity for day-to-day services. Patna flood protection is a life-safety issue: Patna is built on the Ganga flood plain, and annual Ganga flooding (particularly from the Sone and Ghaghara tributaries) inundates low-lying areas where Bihar's poorest urban households live. The Smart City programme (Rs. 1,200 crore) is primarily aesthetic (River Front development, LED street lighting) rather than addressing fundamental infrastructure gaps (water supply, drainage, sewage treatment) that would improve Patna's liveability for its poorer residents.

source.quote: Smart City Rs. 1,200 crore. PMC property tax 32 per cent. flood protection critical. BSUP incomplete

recommendations: Bihar Urban Development Department must: (a) PMC property tax reform -- GIS mapping of all Patna properties (estimated 8 lakh properties) within 18 months with Annual Rental Value at current market rent; target 60 per cent collection within 3 years; (b) Smart City programme must pivot from aesthetics to infrastructure -- remaining Smart City funds must be redirected to drainage and sewage treatment; (c) Patna flood protection master plan must be prepared and funded -- embankment maintenance, pumping station upgrades, and low-lying area resilient housing; (d) AMRUT 2.0 water and sewage projects must be prioritised for Bihar's 7 AMRUT cities.

source.quote: Rs. 4,218 crore. Rs. 851.46 crore idle. High-Priority 42 per cent. malnutrition 45 per cent vs 34 per cent. silicosis 2,000+. 8 years welfare paradox

keyFindings.text: Gujarat PMKKKY's 8-year record is a policy failure deserving national attention because Gujarat is one of India's better-governed states -- if PMKKKY fails in Gujarat, it likely fails everywhere. The failure has three root causes: (1) governance deficit -- DMF is governed by district committees that include the district collector and miners, but not mining-community representatives; without community voice, spending reflects bureaucratic preferences; (2) outcome blindness -- projects are tracked by expenditure, not outcomes; a defluoridation plant built but not operational counts as utilised DMF; (3) accountability gap -- mine companies pay cess and move on; there is no mechanism for them to be held accountable for the welfare outcomes in the communities they affect. The reform path requires all three: community governance (DMF committees must have 50 per cent mining community representation), outcome monitoring (welfare surveys), and transparency (public DMF expenditure dashboard by project, not just aggregate).

source.quote: Rs. 4,218 crore. Rs. 851.46 crore idle. malnutrition 45 vs 34 per cent. silicosis 2,000+. 8 years. reform: community governance, outcome monitoring, transparency

recommendations: GoI Ministry of Mines must amend the PMKKKY Rules to: (a) mandate that DMF committees have 50 per cent mining-affected community representation (currently nil); (b) require annual welfare outcome reporting (specific indicators: malnutrition, school enrolment, water quality, health facility availability) as a condition of mine lease renewal; (c) require DMF expenditure to be published project-by-project on a public web portal (not just aggregate spending); Gujarat Mines must implement all three in 6 months as a pilot -- GoI can then mandate nationally.

keyFindings.text: WB's 12 per cent vocational enrolment (vs 30 per cent target) and 38 per cent ITI placement rate represent a significant skills development failure. The ITI network (Industrial Training Institutes) was designed to provide job-ready skills -- welding, electrical, plumbing, computer operations, garment making -- to Class 8/10 school leavers. A 38 per cent placement rate means 62 per cent of ITI graduates are not employed in their trained trade. The NSQF alignment gap (59 per cent of vocational courses not aligned to National Skills Qualifications Framework) means that many WB vocational certificates are not recognised by employers who hire by NSQF level. NEP 2020 vocational integration (from Class 6 -- pottery, agriculture, carpentry, digital skills as part of regular curriculum) not having started represents a policy implementation lag.

source.quote: vocational 12 per cent vs 30 per cent. ITI placement 38 per cent. NSQF 41 per cent. industry linkage nil 75 per cent

recommendations: West Bengal School Education and Technical Education Departments must: (a) increase vocational enrolment to 25 per cent by 2027 through mandatory vocational elective in Class 9-10 (students choose from 5 NSQF-aligned trades); (b) ITI placement must reach 60 per cent within 3 years -- all ITIs must sign Industry Partnership Agreements with at least 3 local employers within 6 months; (c) NSQF alignment for all WB vocational courses must be completed within 12 months; (d) NEP 2020 vocational integration must begin in 100 pilot schools in 5 districts within 6 months.

keyFindings.text: Odisha's Millet Mission is potentially its most impactful policy innovation: millets (ragi, bajra, jowar, kodra, sawan) are drought-resistant, nutritionally superior to paddy rice (higher protein, iron, calcium), and traditionally grown by tribal communities on dryland farms. By procuring millets at MSP and distributing them through PDS and school mid-day meals, Odisha is simultaneously supporting tribal farmer income, reviving traditional crops at risk of extinction, and addressing the PVTG malnutrition crisis (where millet-based diets have historically provided nutrition in tribal communities). The KALIA scheme (Krushak Assistance for Livelihood and Income Augmentation) is more comprehensive than PM-KISAN -- providing Rs. 25,000 per year to small/marginal farmers vs Rs. 6,000 nationally, with additional Rs. 12,500 per landless agricultural household.

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's 40 per cent Class 6-8 dropout rate is the most important signal in its education system. This is the adolescent transition -- children who complete primary school (Class 5) but leave before completing middle school (Class 8). In Nagaland, contributing factors include: (a) agricultural household labour demand (children needed for jhum cultivation); (b) conflict-area school disruptions in previous decades; (c) church school fees creating an affordability barrier for low-income households; (d) teacher vacancy (28 per cent) reducing school quality and parental confidence. The church school dominance (60 per cent private enrolment under church management) is unique in India -- the Baptist/Catholic church network in Nagaland provides better-quality education than government schools in many cases, but at a cost that excludes the poorest families.

source.quote: dropout 40 per cent. teacher vacancy 28 per cent. Samagra 68 per cent. church 60 per cent

recommendations: Nagaland School Education Department must: (a) conduct a dropout causation survey in the 5 highest-dropout districts to identify specific barriers; (b) conditional cash transfer -- ₹500/month per Class 6-8 student enrolled (payable to family) -- to offset opportunity cost of keeping children in school; (c) teacher vacancy 28 per cent must be filled within 12 months through prioritised recruitment; (d) church school partnership -- negotiate with Baptist and Catholic school networks to accept Samagra Shiksha RTE reimbursement for EWS/DG students, reducing the private school affordability barrier.

stats.value: DDUGJY feeder separation: 34 per cent rural feeders separated; separated feeders 23-hr domestic supply vs 8-hr non-separated; separation cost ₹12-18 lakh per feeder; AT&C in agricultural sector; non-separation blocking DDUGJY objective

source.quote: only 34 per cent feeders separated. separated feeders 23-hr domestic vs 8-hr non-separated. separation cost Rs. 12-18 lakh per feeder

keyFindings.text: Feeder separation is the most impactful single intervention in rural electrification quality: once agricultural and domestic feeders are separated, the DISCOM can schedule agricultural supply (6-8 hours, typically night) independently from domestic supply (24 hours). UP's 34 per cent feeder separation rate -- despite Rs. 12,000+ crore DDUGJY investment -- means that 66 per cent of rural UP households are on mixed-load feeders where their electricity supply is interrupted whenever the farmer's pump motor trips or overloads the transformer. The outcome data proves the case: separated feeders achieve 23-hour domestic supply; non-separated feeders achieve only 8 hours. Every additional percent of feeder separation directly converts 8-hour supply villages to 23-hour supply villages. Completing the remaining 66 per cent at Rs. 12-18 lakh per feeder requires Rs. 10,000-15,000 crore -- significant but worth the outcome improvement.

source.quote: 34 per cent separated. separated 23-hr vs non-separated 8-hr. separation cost Rs. 12-18 lakh

recommendations: UP UPPCL must: (a) designate feeder separation as the state's single highest rural electrification priority; (b) complete the remaining 66 per cent feeder separation within 5 years (approximately 13 per cent per year); (c) secure RDSS (Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme) funding specifically for feeder separation -- RDSS is designed for exactly this type of distribution infrastructure improvement; (d) feeder separation progress must be published monthly by district with supply hours before and after; (e) the 23-hour vs 8-hour outcome data must be presented to the Legislature as evidence of the return on feeder separation investment.

source.quote: Rs. 38,000+ crore. dashboard 98.28 per cent vs functional 45-55 per cent. arsenic/fluoride uncovered. O&M nil. VWSC non-functional. Rs. 1,800 crore idle

keyFindings.text: Bihar's JJM programme has the widest reported coverage (98.28 per cent dashboard) and among the worst functional delivery gaps in India. The combination of: (a) private existing connections counted as FHTC; (b) arsenic/fluoride areas with non-functional treatment plants; (c) 90 per cent GP tariff collection nil; (d) VWSC non-functional in majority of villages; and (e) Rs. 1,800 crore idle in PHED -- paints a picture of a programme that succeeded on data entry while failing on ground reality. Bihar's JJM is a cautionary tale for India's infrastructure programmes: when incentive structures reward reported numbers rather than verified outcomes, the gap between dashboard and ground widens. The scheme collapse risk (within 3-5 years) is not hypothetical -- piped water schemes without O&M funding deteriorate, and once they stop working, communities revert to alternative sources (hand pumps, ponds) that the scheme was supposed to replace.

source.quote: Rs. 38,000+ crore. dashboard 98.28 per cent vs functional 45-55 per cent. O&M nil. collapse risk 3-5 years

recommendations: Bihar PHED and GoI Jal Shakti Ministry must jointly address: (a) dashboard correction -- Bihar must submit revised FHTC data removing private connections; (b) O&M emergency fund -- ₹1,000 crore from the ₹1,800 crore idle PHED balance must be constituted as a 3-year Bihar Water O&M Bridge Fund until GP tariff collections are established; (c) arsenic/fluoride treatment plant operation must be centralised under PHED (not handed to VWSC) in the short term; (d) VWSC activation is a 3-year programme -- PHED must provide monthly technical support visits to all GPs in Year 1.

keyFindings.text: Maharashtra's Rs. 1,20,000+ crore GST compliance gap -- identified across phantom billing, sector under-reporting, ITC fraud, and non-filing -- represents the most significant state revenue opportunity in India. Maharashtra contributes approximately 15 per cent of national GST; improving Maharashtra's compliance would add directly to national fiscal resources and provide a template for the GST Council to implement nationally. The demand recovery rate of 18 per cent (only Rs. 18 of every Rs. 100 in demand notices actually paid) is the systemic failure that enables ongoing non-compliance: businesses learn that a GST demand notice is a negotiating opening, not a legal obligation to pay. Improving demand recovery from 18 per cent to 60 per cent alone would recover Rs. 57,600 crore annually from existing stock of demands.

recommendations: Maharashtra SGST must present this audit as a reform mandate to the GST Council: (a) national EWB-to-GSTR-1 reconciliation must be automated (currently manual in most states); (b) demand recovery must be strengthened through bank attachment as the default enforcement tool (replacing the current notice-appeal-stay-notice cycle); (c) a National Anti-Phantom Billing Task Force (Maharashtra + Karnataka + Gujarat + Delhi -- top 4 GST states) should be established; (d) ITC on exempt supplies (healthcare, education) must be blocked at the GST portal itself -- not left to audit discovery; Maharashtra targets SGST ₹2,00,000 crore by 2027 with these reforms.

keyFindings.text: Uttarakhand's two distinctive revenue sources -- tourism (Rs. 3,200+ crore from Char Dham pilgrimage, adventure tourism, and nature-based tourism) and hydropower royalty (Rs. 1,800+ crore from NHPC, SJVNL, and UPCL generation) -- are both environmentally fragile. Extreme weather events (cloudburst, glacial lake outburst flood -- GLOF) periodically destroy tourism infrastructure and disrupt hydropower generation. The 2013 Kedarnath disaster (GLOF) destroyed Rs. 4,000+ crore in tourism and public infrastructure. Uttarakhand's infrastructure construction cost premium (3-5x plains cost for equivalent roads, buildings, and bridges in mountain terrain) means that the state needs significantly higher per-capita infrastructure spending to achieve connectivity equivalent to plain states. The 16th Finance Commission must weight Uttarakhand's terrain-cost premium in its horizontal devolution formula.

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's 3 CAG reports (SFAR R2/2026, Samagra R3/2026) paint a consistent picture: a large, complex, politically important state with genuinely good administrative institutions (the IAS cadre, the WBCS) and genuine fiscal and institutional failures (OPS reversion, UC backlog, SNA idle funds). The 16th Finance Commission faces a choice: if it rewards WB's fiscal position (high deficit, OPS reversion, UC non-compliance) with standard devolution, it signals that fiscal indiscipline is manageable. If it reduces devolution, it risks triggering a social welfare collapse in a state with 100 million people. The structural answer is a multi-year fiscal consolidation agreement between WB and GoI -- similar to the Debt Consolidation and Relief Facility used after the 12th Finance Commission -- where WB commits to specific milestones (UC clearance, FRBM path, OPS actuarial disclosure) in exchange for enhanced GoI fiscal support.

source.quote: Fiscal Deficit 4.92 per cent. OPS Rs. 3,50,000+ crore. Revenue Deficit Rs. 35,962 crore. UC backlog. SNA idle

recommendations: Government of West Bengal and Government of India must jointly negotiate a West Bengal Fiscal Consolidation Agreement -- binding WB to: (a) clear all UC backlogs within 2 years; (b) submit MTFP with Primary Surplus target by Year 3; (c) disclose OPS actuarial liability annually; (d) reduce SNA idle balances below ₹2,000 crore within 1 year; (e) KMC water tariff revision within 6 months; in exchange for: GoI enhanced Revenue Deficit Grants (transition period), debt restructuring on high-cost state development loans, and ring-fenced GoI support for WB's social welfare programme.

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 117.2 crore gap between PVTG SHG production value (Rs. 160 crore) and actual sales realisation (Rs. 42.8 crore) represents both the scale of middlemen extraction and the failure of OPELIP's market linkage objective. PVTG women produce honey, tamarind, bamboo crafts, palm products, and woven textiles -- products with genuine market value and, in some cases, unique GI-protectable quality characteristics (specific Kondh or Saura weaving patterns). But without: (a) aggregation (enough volume to interest larger buyers), (b) quality grading and certification, (c) packaging and branding, and (d) digital marketplace access, tribal women sell to whoever arrives in the village -- usually a middleman who pays 30 per cent below the urban market price. The 22 per cent SHG dissolution rate suggests that OPELIP-formed groups lack the institutional resilience to survive without intensive support.

keyFindings.text: Jharkhand's constitutional protections for tribal land -- the CNT (Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act) and SPT (Santhal Parganas Tenancy Act) -- are among the strongest tribal land rights protections in India. They prohibit the transfer of tribal land to non-tribals without government approval. Yet Rs. 1,800+ crore in tribal land has been transferred in violation of these protections -- through fraudulent sale deeds, benami arrangements, and collusion with revenue officials. PESA (Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas) requires that Gram Sabhas in Fifth Schedule areas must consent to any mineral extraction, displacement, or land acquisition in their territory. This has been systematically ignored for mining projects across Jharkhand's tribal belt. The Tribal Sub-Plan diversion (Rs. 2,200 crore spent on non-tribal beneficiaries or activities) means the constitutional earmark for tribal welfare is not reaching its intended recipients.

source.quote: land alienation Rs. 1,800+ crore. CNT/SPT violated. FRA 38 per cent. TSP Rs. 2,200 crore diverted

recommendations: Jharkhand Tribal Welfare Department must: (a) all identified CNT/SPT violations must be referred to the Jharkhand Revenue Tribunal for land restoration -- tribal land restored to tribal ownership, not just fine-imposed; (b) PESA compliance must be verified for all active mining leases -- any lease granted without valid Gram Sabha consent must be reviewed by the Tribal Advisory Council; (c) FRA pending claims must be resolved within 12 months through a dedicated FRA Sub-Division level court; (d) Tribal Sub-Plan must be audited annually -- all non-tribal diversions must be reversed and reported to the Legislature.

ministry: Labour Department, Government of Goa
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (Compliance-PA on BOCW in Goa) -- Part VI
title: Compliance-PA -- Goa BOCW Part VI: Migrant Worker Housing -- Labour Camps Without Drinking Water 72 Per cent; No Sanitation; BOCW Rules Labour Camp Standards Violated; Child Labour in Construction Sites; Women Worker Safety -- No Creche Facility; No State Migrant Worker Portal Registration; Inter-State Migrant Workers Act Unenforced
overview: CAG Compliance-PA (Goa BOCW, 2025) Part VI: Migrant worker housing -- labour camps without drinking water 72 per cent; no sanitation; BOCW Rules Labour Camp Standards violated; child labour observed in construction sites; women worker safety -- no creche facility (BOCW Rules mandate creche if 5+ children under 6 at site); no State Migrant Worker Portal; Interstate Migrant Workers Act unenforced.

keyFindings.text: Goa's construction sector labour force -- 65,000+ workers, predominantly migrants from UP, Bihar, Odisha, Chhattisgarh -- lives in temporary labour camps on or near construction sites that lack basic amenities. 72 per cent of camps have no drinking water supply (workers drink from construction site water, rivers, or pay water tanker prices). No sanitation means open defecation near living areas, with direct health consequences (diarrhoea, cholera risk). Child labour in construction -- children from worker families, brought to Goa because parents cannot afford childcare at home -- is both illegal and dangerous. The creche facility mandate (BOCW Rules require a creche when 5+ children under 6 are at a site) has a zero compliance rate in Goa. These workers have no voice, no registration, and no legal representation in the state where they work.

source.quote: camps 72 per cent no water. no sanitation. child labour. creche nil. ISMW unenforced

recommendations: Goa Labour Department must: (a) conduct a 30-day all-site inspection of all active construction projects -- any camp without drinking water and sanitation must receive a stop-work order until basic amenities are provided; (b) BOCW Rules Labour Camp Standards (Schedule II) must be printed in Hindi, Odia, and Bengali and distributed to all contractors; (c) child labour on construction sites must trigger FIR under Child Labour Prohibition Act -- contractor responsible; (d) register all Goa-bound migrant workers from source states in eShram portal before departure; (e) Goa State Migrant Workers Helpline must be established (Konkani + Hindi).

title: Compliance Audit -- Kerala NHM: Palliative Care ₹320 crore -- Best in India; Non-Communicable Disease Burden (Diabetes 28 Per cent, Hypertension 35 Per cent Adults); Elderly Population 16 Per cent; PHC Doctor Attendance 82 Per cent; Private Hospital Dominance 80 Per cent IP Care; Health Expenditure 5.6 Per cent GSDP (Above National)
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Kerala NHM, 2026): Palliative care ₹320 crore (best palliative care programme in India -- community-based); NCD burden (diabetes 28 per cent adults, hypertension 35 per cent); elderly 16 per cent population (highest in India); PHC doctor attendance 82 per cent (above national average); private hospital dominance 80 per cent inpatient care; health expenditure 5.6 per cent GSDP (above national norm of 2.5 per cent government health).

keyFindings.text: Kerala's health picture is unique in India: the state has achieved near-universal literacy, low infant mortality, and high life expectancy (comparable to middle-income countries) -- but now faces the health consequences of its own success. With 16 per cent of the population above 60 years (national average 9 per cent) and among India's highest rates of diabetes and hypertension, Kerala has an epidemiological transition problem: it has eliminated most infectious disease mortality but now faces a surge in chronic disease burden (heart disease, cancer, kidney failure, stroke). Kerala's palliative care programme -- community volunteers providing home-based pain relief and end-of-life care -- is the best in India and one of the best in the world, addressing the end-stage NCD burden. The 80 per cent private hospital dominance for inpatient care means public hospitals are underutilised relative to their infrastructure, while private hospitals charge above-average prices -- creating an affordability crisis for the non-NRI population.

source.quote: health 5.6 per cent GSDP. palliative Rs. 320 crore best India. diabetes 28 per cent. elderly 16 per cent

recommendations: Kerala Health Department must: (a) strengthen NCD prevention in the PHC system -- every PHC must have a dedicated NCD clinic (diabetes + hypertension management) with a nurse-led protocol; (b) expand palliative care programme with increased funding (₹500 crore) and integration with ASHA/Kudumbashree network; (c) elderly care must be formalised -- Kerala needs a State Elderly Care Policy addressing homecare, rehabilitation, dementia management, and long-term care institutions; (d) private hospital regulation -- CGHS rates must be periodically revised and enforced as the ceiling for Ayushman+Karunya Kerala scheme reimbursement.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's annual flood damage of Rs. 6,000+ crore to agriculture -- caused by Kosi, Gandak, and Bagmati rivers flooding the North Bihar plains -- represents a recurring development setback that no amount of PM-KISAN or Fasal Bima can fully offset. Fasal Bima's 18-month claim settlement delay is particularly damaging for flood-affected farmers: a farmer whose crop was destroyed in October 2023 flood receives insurance payment in April 2025 -- by which time they have already taken emergency loans at 24-36 per cent informal interest rates to survive the winter. The insurance payment arrives too late to prevent the debt trap. Bihar's agriculture GSDP share declining from 28 to 22 per cent reflects both farm-to-non-farm transition (positive) and agricultural stagnation (concerning for the 80 per cent of Bihar's workforce dependent on agriculture).

source.quote: PM-KISAN Rs. 2,400+ crore. Fasal Bima 38 per cent. claim 18 months. flood Rs. 6,000+ crore annual

recommendations: Bihar Agriculture Department must: (a) Fasal Bima claim settlement must be reduced to 30 days for flood damage (satellite-verified yield loss -- technology already available through ISRO NADAMS); (b) Fasal Bima enrolment must be linked to KCC renewal -- all KCC holders automatically enrolled in Fasal Bima; (c) PM-KISAN beneficiary data must be Aadhaar-validated -- ghost beneficiaries must be identified and removed; (d) paddy procurement: Bihar must establish state government procurement centres in all panchayats to ensure farmers receive MSP -- current procurement through FPS dealers allows middlemen to appropriate the MSP benefit.

keyFindings.text: Maharashtra's 28 per cent non-compliance rate in GSTR-3B filing (1.8 lakh non-filers + some nil-filers who are actually transacting) is the enforcement gap that enables the phantom billing and sector under-reporting found elsewhere in this audit. The demand notice recovery rate of 18 per cent is particularly revealing: SGST officers can issue 1.2 lakh demand notices, but only 18 per cent result in actual payment. This happens because: (a) notice recipients contest demands, (b) firms close before payment, (c) enforcement action (attachment of bank accounts, property) is rarely used, (d) appeal process is slow. The Mumbai-Thane compliance gap reflects urbanisation -- Mumbai businesses are more formalized, more likely to have accountants, and more easily traceable by revenue authorities than Thane semi-urban or Pune rural businesses.

source.quote: GSTR-3B 72 per cent. 1.8 lakh non-filers. demands 18 per cent recovery. Mumbai best. Thane Pune Rural worst

recommendations: Maharashtra SGST must: (a) implement a Non-Filer Amnesty Programme -- non-filers who voluntarily file all pending returns within 60 days with 50 per cent late fee waiver; after 60 days, bank account attachment for all non-filers with EWB/GSTR-1 data suggesting transactions; (b) demand notice recovery must be improved to 50 per cent through systematic enforcement (bank attachment after 30-day demand notice without payment); (c) Thane and Pune Rural compliance must receive targeted outreach -- GST Mela (awareness camps) with assisted filing by tax practitioners.

keyFindings.text: Punjab's 82 per cent committed expenditure ratio (salary+pension+interest as percentage of Revenue Receipts) is the worst among non-special-category states covered in this series. With 82 per cent of revenue committed before any development spending begins, Punjab has effectively zero fiscal discretion -- it cannot reduce committed spending (service existing debt, pay pensions, pay current salaries) without defaulting on legal obligations. The AAP guarantee (300 units free power = approximately Rs. 7,000 crore, Rs. 1,000 women's cash transfer = approximately Rs. 5,000 crore) adds Rs. 12,000 crore annually to what was already an unsustainable fiscal trajectory. For the 16th Finance Commission, Punjab presents the most difficult case: fiscal distress that is partly structural (agriculture, industry decline), partly historical (debt accumulation), and partly political (new welfare commitments on an already-stressed base).

source.quote: Debt Rs. 3,26,000+ crore. committed 82 per cent. guarantees Rs. 12,000+ crore. Revenue Deficit Rs. 8,400 crore

recommendations: Punjab Finance Department must present a Fiscal Sustainability Plan to the Legislature within 3 months: (a) committed expenditure reduction path (pension reform -- NPS adoption for new employees; interest reduction through swap of high-cost for low-cost GoI debt; salary rationalisation); (b) guarantee financing -- ₹12,000 crore guarantees must be transparently funded from identified Revenue Receipts, not borrowings; (c) 16th Finance Commission memorandum must disclose full fiscal position including PIDB off-budget borrowings; Punjab must request a debt restructuring/moratorium mechanism under the FC award.

ministry: Jal Sansthan / PHED, Government of Uttarakhand
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit) -- JJM Himalayan Water
title: Compliance Audit -- Uttarakhand JJM: Gravity-Fed Spring Sources Declining -- 50 Per cent Springs Seasonal; Lift Irrigation High Energy Cost in Himalayan Terrain; FHTC Coverage 78 Per cent Dashboard vs 48 Per cent Functional; Spring Recharge Programme Budget ₹120 crore Unutilised; Glacial Melt Long-Run Water Security Risk
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (UK JJM, 2025) found: (1) gravity-fed spring sources declining -- 50 per cent springs seasonal (dry in summer); (2) lift irrigation high energy cost in Himalayan terrain (pumping water uphill to villages); (3) FHTC coverage 78 per cent dashboard vs estimated 48 per cent functional supply; (4) spring recharge programme (catchment treatment, bunding) budget ₹120 crore unutilised; (5) glacial melt long-run water security risk for springs fed by glacial recharge.

stats.label: 50 per cent springs seasonal; dashboard 78 per cent vs 48 per cent functional; spring recharge ₹120 crore unused
stats.value: springs: 50 per cent seasonal (dry summer); FHTC dashboard 78 per cent vs functional 48 per cent; spring recharge ₹120 crore unutilised; lift cost high Himalayan; glacial melt long-run risk

source.quote: 50 per cent springs seasonal. FHTC 78 per cent vs 48 per cent functional. spring recharge Rs. 120 crore unutilised. glacial melt risk

keyFindings.text: Uttarakhand's JJM faces a fundamental geographic challenge that other states do not: mountain springs -- the most natural and cost-effective water source for hill villages -- are themselves declining. Himalayan springs are recharged by monsoon water percolating through the watershed above the spring. Deforestation, road construction, and land use change in the catchment reduces percolation, causing springs to dry up in summer (when demand is highest). The spring recharge programme (watershed treatment, plantation, bunding) is the correct intervention -- but Rs. 120 crore is unutilised. Climate change adds a longer-term risk: springs fed by glacial melt (which supplements percolation recharge) will see reduced flow as Himalayan glaciers retreat. Uttarakhand is building a water system whose source-side reliability is declining.

source.quote: 50 per cent springs seasonal. FHTC 78 vs 48 per cent. spring recharge Rs. 120 crore unutilised. glacial melt risk

recommendations: Uttarakhand Jal Sansthan must: (a) urgently utilise spring recharge programme ₹120 crore -- all seasonal springs must have catchment treatment works (plantation, bunding, percolation ponds) within 2 years; (b) every JJM scheme dependent on a seasonal spring must have an alternative or backup source designed in; (c) FHTC dashboard accuracy must be corrected -- 78 per cent reported vs 48 per cent functional is the same data integrity failure as MP; (d) a Spring Atlas for Uttarakhand must be created -- mapping all springs, their recharge catchments, current yield, seasonal variation, and climate vulnerability.

keyFindings.text: Fluoride above 1.5 mg/L in drinking water causes dental fluorosis (mottled, brown teeth -- cosmetically disfiguring) in children and skeletal fluorosis (spinal and joint deformity -- disabling) in adults after chronic exposure. In 68 per cent of test villages in Gujarat's Panna Mehsana mining belt, the fluoride concentration exceeds the safe limit. Defluoridation plants (Nalgonda technique, bone char filters, or reverse osmosis) are technically simple and relatively affordable -- Rs. 5-15 lakh per village depending on population. With DMF water funds of Rs. 320 crore (48 per cent unutilised = Rs. 166 crore available), there is sufficient money to install defluoridation in every affected village in Gujarat. The silicosis cases among stone quarry workers represent an occupational health emergency -- silicosis (irreversible progressive lung fibrosis from silica dust inhalation) is fatal and should have been prevented with dust suppression and respirator equipment.

source.quote: fluoride 68 per cent. silicosis 2,000+ cases. DMF water Rs. 320 crore 48 per cent. no defluoridation plant

recommendations: Gujarat Mines and Geology Department must: (a) utilise the ₹166 crore unused DMF water fund to install defluoridation plants in all 68 per cent fluoride-positive villages within 18 months -- this is both the highest-priority use and the most technically straightforward; (b) silicosis survey must be completed in all Gujarat stone quarry districts within 6 months -- all confirmed cases must receive ₹3 lakh compensation and lifetime pension under Silicosis Rehabilitation Policy 2015; (c) dust suppression and PPE (P3 respirators) must be mandatory in all stone quarries -- BOCW inspection must verify compliance; (d) groundwater level monitoring in all mining districts.

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's IT sector generates Rs. 5.8 lakh crore in revenue -- making Bengaluru one of the 5 most economically productive urban centres in the world by software output. Yet the state government's revenue from this sector -- despite Professional Tax, GST on domestic IT services, and stamp duty from IT park construction -- is disproportionately low relative to the sector's economic scale. Gig workers (Swiggy, Zomato, Uber, Rapido -- all with significant Bengaluru operations) represent a large and growing workforce with no ESIC coverage because they are classified as independent contractors. A gig worker injured on delivery in Bengaluru has no health insurance, no accident compensation, and no retirement savings -- a structural welfare gap that Karnataka is uniquely positioned to address as the gig economy's national capital.

keyFindings.text: A Class 5 student who can only read a Class 2 text is 3 grade levels behind. In WB, this describes 44 per cent of Class 5 students (ASER 2023). These children have spent 5 years in school but have not acquired foundational literacy -- the ability to read and comprehend age-appropriate text that is the prerequisite for all subsequent learning. Without foundational literacy, a child cannot independently learn from a textbook, cannot complete homework, and falls progressively further behind each year. By Class 8, these students are likely to be 5+ grade levels behind and at high dropout risk. The NIPUN target (basic literacy by Class 3) is achievable -- states like Himachal Pradesh have reached 80+ per cent NIPUN levels -- but requires structured pedagogy, daily reading practice, and teacher training that WB's Samagra Shiksha programme has not systematically implemented.

source.quote: NIPUN reading 48 per cent. arithmetic 44 per cent. ASER Class 5 56 per cent. mother tongue not implemented

recommendations: West Bengal School Education Department must: (a) make FLN the state's single highest education priority -- Chief Minister's Education Mission modelled on the NIPUN framework; (b) implement structured literacy programme (SLP) in all Class 1-3 classrooms -- 45 minutes daily phonics/reading instruction, 30 minutes arithmetic; (c) all Class 1-3 teachers must receive 5-day FLN residential training within 6 months; (d) quarterly NIPUN assessments must be conducted in all schools -- district-wise results published; (e) mother tongue instruction for tribal language speakers (Santali, Kurmali, Ho) must be piloted in 3 districts within 12 months.

keyFindings.text: Odisha's fiscal summary across 3 CAG reports (SFAR R3/2026, CA R3/2025, PVTG R2/2025) presents a complex picture of a state that has achieved genuine fiscal discipline (lowest Debt-GSDP among large states, Revenue Surplus) while hosting some of India's most severe human development deficits (PVTG welfare, MGNREGS social audit gaps, OPELIP livelihood outcomes).
