title: Compliance Audit -- Bihar PDS: 3.2 Lakh Ghost Ration Cards; 18 Lakh Eligible Households Excluded; Dealer Commission Diversion ₹180+ crore; NFSA Coverage 80 Per cent vs 92 Per cent Bihar Poor; Aadhaar Seeding 94 Per cent But 6 Per cent Still Manual; Paddy Procurement Price Below MSP Reaching Farmer
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Bihar PDS, 2026) found: (1) 3.2 lakh ghost ration cards (deleted person/migrated/deceased still drawing ration); (2) 18 lakh eligible households excluded from NFSA; (3) dealer commission diversion ₹180+ crore; (4) NFSA coverage 80 per cent vs 92 per cent Bihar poor (12 per cent gap); (5) Aadhaar seeding 94 per cent but 6 per cent still manual (fraud risk); (6) paddy procurement -- MSP not fully reaching farmer (middlemen deductions).

stats.label: 3.2 lakh ghost cards; 18 lakh excluded; dealer diversion ₹180+ crore; 80 per cent vs 92 per cent poor
stats.value: 3.2 lakh ghost ration cards; 18 lakh eligible excluded; dealer commission diversion ₹180+ crore; NFSA 80 per cent vs 92 per cent Bihar poor; Aadhaar seeding 94 per cent; paddy MSP not reaching farmer

source.quote: 3.2 lakh ghost cards. 18 lakh excluded. dealer diversion Rs. 180+ crore. NFSA 80 per cent vs 92 per cent poor

keyFindings.text: Bihar's PDS has a simultaneous inclusion and exclusion error: 3.2 lakh ghost cards draw ration for dead/migrated people, while 18 lakh legitimate poor households don't have ration cards. The Bihar NFSA coverage limit (80 per cent) is below the state's actual poverty rate (estimated 92 per cent by NSS/NFHS data). This means that Bihar has been allocated fewer NFSA ration cards than it needs to cover its poor population -- partly because the 2011 census (which determines NFSA allocations) is now 13 years old and has missed the 2010-2023 population growth. The dealer commission diversion (Rs. 180+ crore) means fair price shop dealers are recording ration as distributed when it has not been -- keeping the grain themselves while marking beneficiary as served.

source.quote: 3.2 lakh ghost cards. 18 lakh excluded. dealer diversion Rs. 180+ crore. 80 per cent vs 92 per cent poor

recommendations: Bihar Food Department must: (a) immediately cancel all 3.2 lakh ghost ration cards through Aadhaar death register cross-check; (b) request GoI for enhanced NFSA allocation -- Bihar's 2011 census allocation must be updated with 2023 estimated population and current poverty data; (c) all remaining 6 per cent manual (non-Aadhaar) distribution must be converted to e-POS with biometric authentication within 6 months; (d) dealer commission diversion investigation must be launched for all identified dealers -- ration card records vs EPOS data mismatch exceeding 5 per cent must trigger FIR.

ministry: Rural Development / PMGSY, Government of Jharkhand
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit) -- PMGSY Rural Roads
title: Compliance Audit -- Jharkhand PMGSY: 12,400 km Rural Roads; Quality Defects -- Pothole within 1 Year; 840 Habitations Still Unconnected; Maintenance Fund ₹280 crore -- Utilised 42 Per cent; Forest Clearance Delay 3+ Years; Tribal Hamlet Connectivity Below 500 Population Threshold Exclusion
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Jharkhand PMGSY, 2025) found: (1) 12,400 km rural roads built under PMGSY; (2) quality defects -- roads with potholes within 1 year of construction; (3) 840 habitations still unconnected (above PMGSY eligibility threshold of 250/500 population); (4) maintenance fund ₹280 crore utilised only 42 per cent; (5) forest clearance delays blocking 3+ year project starts; (6) tribal hamlets below PMGSY 500-population threshold excluded despite high connectivity need.

stats.label: 840 habitations unconnected; maintenance 42 per cent; potholes within 1 year; forest delay 3+ years
stats.value: 12,400 km PMGSY roads; 840 habitations unconnected; maintenance ₹280 crore 42 per cent utilised; potholes within 1 year; forest clearance 3+ year delay; tribal hamlets below threshold excluded

source.quote: 12,400 km roads. 840 habitations unconnected. maintenance 42 per cent. potholes within 1 year. forest clearance 3+ years

keyFindings.text: PMGSY roads developing potholes within 1 year of construction in Jharkhand reflect two endemic construction quality problems in rocky, hilly terrain: (a) inadequate compaction of sub-grade soil in rocky areas (rock is uneven, compaction machines cannot achieve adequate density); (b) inadequate drainage design (Jharkhand receives 1,200-1,400mm annual rainfall -- roads without adequate cross-drainage fail quickly). The maintenance fund underutilisation (42 per cent) is particularly damaging because even well-constructed roads deteriorate rapidly without timely pothole patching and drainage maintenance. The 840 unconnected habitations above the PMGSY threshold in a state where major insurgent activity has historically operated in the most inaccessible areas represent both a development and a security gap.

source.quote: 840 habitations unconnected. maintenance 42 per cent. potholes within 1 year. forest clearance 3+ years

recommendations: Jharkhand Rural Development Department must: (a) PMGSY construction quality must include independent third-party quality monitoring at district level; (b) maintenance fund ₹280 crore underutilisation must be addressed -- block-level JE must be assigned specific km of road for maintenance with monthly inspection and photographic documentation; (c) forest clearance fast-track -- all PMGSY forest clearance applications pending above 1 year must be listed and personally reviewed by the Chief Secretary with MoEF; (d) tribal hamlets below 500 population but demonstrably isolated must qualify for PMGSY under the NE/tribal special provisions.

ministry: Home Department / Nagaland Police, Government of Nagaland
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2023-24) -- Part XII
title: State Finances -- Nagaland Part XII: Security Expenditure ₹3,200+ crore; Police Per Capita 3.5x National Average; IRBs (India Reserve Battalions) 15,000 Personnel; NNPG Framework Post-2023; Village Guards Scheme; Double Pension Ex-Militants; Security-to-Development Transition Planning; Peace Dividend Fiscal Opportunity
overview: CAG SFAR (Nagaland, 2025) Part XII: Security expenditure ₹3,200+ crore (35 per cent of Revenue Expenditure); police per capita 3.5x national average; IRBs 15,000 personnel; NNPG (Naga National Political Groups) framework post-2023; Village Guards scheme; double pension to ex-militants; security-to-development transition planning; peace dividend -- if security expenditure reduces to national average, ₹2,200 crore frees up for development.

stats.label: Security ₹3,200+ crore (35 per cent RE); police 3.5x national; peace dividend ₹2,200 crore potential
stats.value: Security expenditure ₹3,200+ crore (35 per cent Revenue Expenditure); police per capita 3.5x national; IRBs 15,000; NNPG post-2023 framework; peace dividend ₹2,200 crore if normalised

source.quote: security Rs. 3,200+ crore 35 per cent RE. police 3.5x national. IRBs 15,000. peace dividend Rs. 2,200 crore potential

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's security expenditure at 35 per cent of Revenue Expenditure (vs approximately 5 per cent for most states) is a direct consequence of the 75-year Naga political conflict. The NNPG framework (post-2023 peace process architecture) creates the first genuine opportunity in decades for a sustainable transition: if the political settlement holds and insurgent groups integrate, Nagaland could gradually reduce IRB personnel, Village Guards, and associated police presence toward the national average. The Rs. 2,200 crore annual peace dividend -- the hypothetical savings if security spending normalised -- would transform Nagaland's fiscal position: from chronically deficit to potentially surplus, from 91 per cent GoI dependence to 80 per cent, and from zero development investment capacity to genuine infrastructure and social investment capability.

source.quote: security Rs. 3,200+ crore. police 3.5x national. peace dividend Rs. 2,200 crore. NNPG framework

recommendations: Nagaland Finance Department should develop a Peace Dividend Fiscal Plan -- modelling the 10-year trajectory of security expenditure reduction under the NNPG framework and mapping the redeployment of savings to: (a) health (from 5 per cent to 8 per cent of RE), (b) education (from 18 per cent to 25 per cent), (c) infrastructure (roads connecting remote villages); the IRB transition plan must include retraining for civilian employment for demobilised personnel; the 16th Finance Commission should receive this Peace Dividend Plan as Nagaland's fiscal reform roadmap.

ministry: Finance / Disaster Management Department, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2024-25) -- Part XX
title: State Finances -- West Bengal Part XX: Disaster Management -- SDRF ₹3,200 crore; Cyclone Amphan + Yaas Damage ₹1.5 Lakh crore; NDRF Utilisation 68 Per cent; Flood Relief Duplicate Beneficiary Claims; Post-Disaster Asset Reconstruction Incomplete 40 Per cent Works; Mangrove Degradation Sundarbans
overview: CAG SFAR (WB, 2026) Part XX: Disaster management -- SDRF ₹3,200 crore; Cyclone Amphan (2020) + Yaas (2021) damage ₹1.5 lakh crore (as claimed to GoI); NDRF utilisation 68 per cent; flood relief duplicate beneficiary claims; post-disaster asset reconstruction 40 per cent incomplete; Sundarbans mangrove degradation (natural cyclone protection buffer).

stats.label: SDRF ₹3,200 crore; cyclone damage ₹1.5 lakh crore; NDRF 68 per cent utilised; reconstruction 40 per cent incomplete
stats.value: SDRF ₹3,200 crore; Amphan+Yaas damage ₹1.5 lakh crore; NDRF 68 per cent utilised; flood relief duplicate claims; post-disaster reconstruction 40 per cent incomplete; Sundarbans mangrove degrading

source.quote: SDRF Rs. 3,200 crore. Amphan+Yaas Rs. 1.5 lakh crore damage. NDRF 68 per cent. reconstruction 40 per cent incomplete. Sundarbans mangrove degrading

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's Sundarbans is India's primary natural protection against Bay of Bengal cyclones -- a 4,264 sq km mangrove belt that absorbs cyclone energy before it reaches coastal communities. Mangrove degradation (encroachment, aquaculture conversion, pollution) has reduced the effectiveness of this natural barrier over decades. Cyclone Amphan (2020) damage of Rs. 1 lakh crore and Yaas (2021) Rs. 50,000+ crore would have been significantly higher without the remaining Sundarbans buffer -- and future cyclones with a degraded Sundarbans will cause proportionally greater damage. The investment required for Sundarbans mangrove restoration (estimated Rs. 2,000-3,000 crore over 10 years) is small relative to the insurance value of the mangrove belt against cyclone damage.

source.quote: SDRF Rs. 3,200 crore. Amphan+Yaas Rs. 1.5 lakh crore. NDRF 68 per cent. reconstruction 40 per cent incomplete. Sundarbans degrading

recommendations: West Bengal Disaster Management Department must: (a) flood relief duplicate beneficiary claims must be detected through Aadhaar de-duplication -- all SDRF disbursements must be through DBT with Aadhaar verification before payment; (b) post-disaster reconstruction 40 per cent incomplete works must each have a revised completion date with accountability at SDO level; (c) Sundarbans mangrove restoration must be declared a state priority -- ₹500 crore annually for 5 years from SDRF + CAMPA + GoI coastal protection fund; (d) NDRF utilisation must be improved from 68 per cent by reducing project preparation delays.

ministry: Energy Department / GRIDCO / SOUTHCO, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part XV
title: State Finances -- Odisha Part XV: Power Sector -- GRIDCO ₹28,000+ crore Revenue; AT&C Loss SOUTHCO 28.9 Per cent (Tribal Southern Odisha); NESCO/WESCO/CESU Improving; Agricultural Subsidy ₹4,200 crore; Renewable 30 Per cent Target 2030; OHPC Hydro Fleet; Solar Park ITPCL
overview: CAG SFAR (Odisha, 2026) Part XV: Power sector -- GRIDCO revenue ₹28,000+ crore; SOUTHCO (South Odisha -- tribal) AT&C 28.9 per cent (worst in state, tribal distribution challenge); NESCO/WESCO/CESU AT&C improving (12-16 per cent); agricultural subsidy ₹4,200 crore; renewable energy 30 per cent target 2030; OHPC hydro fleet; Solar Park ITPCL (Bhubaneswar).

stats.label: SOUTHCO AT&C 28.9 per cent (tribal); GRIDCO ₹28,000+ crore; renewable 30 per cent 2030
stats.value: GRIDCO revenue ₹28,000+ crore; SOUTHCO AT&C 28.9 per cent (tribal distribution); NESCO/WESCO 12-16 per cent improving; agricultural subsidy ₹4,200 crore; renewable 30 per cent target 2030

source.quote: GRIDCO Rs. 28,000+ crore. SOUTHCO AT&C 28.9 per cent. NESCO/WESCO 12-16 per cent. agricultural subsidy Rs. 4,200 crore. renewable 30 per cent 2030

keyFindings.text: SOUTHCO's 28.9 per cent AT&C loss -- serving southern Odisha's tribal districts (Koraput, Malkangiri, Rayagada, Kandhamal) -- is structurally higher than the rest of Odisha because: (a) dispersed settlements require long distribution lines with high technical loss; (b) tribal households have lower electricity consumption (smaller economic load), making revenue recovery per km of line low; (c) commercial and industrial consumers (who cross-subsidise households) are fewer; (d) metering in remote habitations is more difficult. SOUTHCO cannot be made financially sustainable through AT&C loss reduction alone -- it needs a BESCOM-to-HESCOM type targeted investment programme plus Odisha government tariff subvention for tribal distribution costs.

source.quote: SOUTHCO AT&C 28.9 per cent. GRIDCO Rs. 28,000+ crore. agricultural subsidy Rs. 4,200 crore

recommendations: Odisha Energy Department must: (a) approve a SOUTHCO Revival Plan -- dedicated capital investment (smart metering, line replacement, substation augmentation) for southern tribal districts over 5 years; (b) agricultural subsidy ₹4,200 crore must transition to DBT flat-rate subsidy per HP of pump capacity within 3 years; (c) OHPC hydro fleet must be maintained with a 5-year capex plan -- hydro is Karnataka's and Odisha's lowest-cost power source; (d) 30 per cent renewable target 2030 requires aggressive solar rooftop and wind park development -- GRIDCO renewable procurement plan must be published.

ministry: Health Department / NHM, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2026 (Compliance Audit) -- NHM Emergency Transport
title: Compliance Audit -- Bihar NHM Emergency Transport: 108 Ambulance -- 912 Ambulances Operational vs 1,400 Target; Average Response Time 42 Minutes Rural (Target 20 Minutes); No Referral Transport for High-Risk Pregnancy Tribal Districts; JSSK Free Transport Voucher Not Provided; 3,800 Maternal Deaths 70 Per cent Preventable
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Bihar NHM transport, 2026) found: (1) 108 ambulances 912 operational vs 1,400 target; (2) average rural response time 42 minutes vs 20-minute target; (3) no referral transport for high-risk pregnancy in tribal/flood-prone districts; (4) JSSK (Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram) free transport voucher not provided at birth; (5) 3,800 maternal deaths in Bihar annually -- 70 per cent preventable with timely transport.

stats.label: 108 ambulance 912 vs 1,400 target; response 42 min vs 20 min; maternal deaths 3,800 (70% preventable)
stats.value: 108 ambulances 912 operational vs 1,400 target; rural response 42 min vs 20 min; JSSK transport not provided; no tribal/flood referral transport; 3,800 maternal deaths 70 per cent preventable

source.quote: 108 ambulances 912 vs 1,400. response 42 min vs 20 min. JSSK transport not provided. 3,800 maternal deaths 70 per cent preventable

keyFindings.text: Bihar's 3,800 maternal deaths annually -- with 70 per cent estimated preventable with timely transport and obstetric care -- represents one of India's most acute preventable mortality situations. The 42-minute average rural response time for 108 ambulances (vs 20-minute target) means that a woman in obstetric emergency in rural Bihar waits over twice as long as the programme target for help to arrive. In obstetric emergencies (eclampsia, postpartum haemorrhage), 20 minutes vs 42 minutes can be the difference between life and death. Flood-prone districts (Darbhanga, Sitamarhi, Madhubani, Supaul, Saharsa) have the worst transport access during monsoon -- when rivers flood kutcha roads -- yet have no specific transport protocol for high-risk pregnancy in flood season.

source.quote: 912 vs 1,400. response 42 min vs 20 min. 3,800 maternal deaths 70 per cent preventable. no flood transport protocol

recommendations: Bihar Health Department must: (a) procure 488 additional 108 ambulances to meet the 1,400 target within 12 months (fleet gap directly linked to response time gap); (b) develop a Flood Season Emergency Obstetric Protocol for 10 flood-prone districts -- boat ambulance/community radio network for high-risk pregnancy; (c) all 108 ambulances must be GPS-tracked with real-time response time published monthly by district; (d) JSSK transport voucher must be provided to all pregnant women at registration (not at birth) -- advance provision eliminates the delay at emergency.

ministry: Finance / Infrastructure Department / PIDB, Government of Punjab
reportNo: Report No. 7 of 2025 (Audit Report on PSUs) -- PIDB
title: PSU Audit -- Punjab PIDB: Infrastructure Projects ₹12,400 crore; ₹3,200 crore Cost Overrun; 14 Projects Delayed 3+ Years; PIDB Debt ₹8,000+ crore; Land Acquisition Delays; Punjab Bypass Roads Non-Operational; Industrial Areas Incomplete; SPV Structure Off-Budget
overview: CAG PSU Audit (Punjab PIDB, 2025): Infrastructure projects ₹12,400 crore; cost overrun ₹3,200 crore; 14 projects delayed 3+ years; PIDB debt ₹8,000+ crore (off-budget); land acquisition delays (most projects blocked by LA); Punjab bypass roads non-operational; industrial areas incomplete; SPV (Special Purpose Vehicle) structure allows PIDB to borrow without appearing in state FRBM.

stats.label: ₹12,400 crore projects; ₹3,200 crore overrun; 14 projects delayed 3+ years; debt ₹8,000+ crore
stats.value: PIDB projects ₹12,400 crore; cost overrun ₹3,200 crore (26 per cent); 14 projects delayed 3+ years; PIDB debt ₹8,000+ crore off-budget; land acquisition blocking; bypass roads non-operational

source.quote: Rs. 12,400 crore projects. Rs. 3,200 crore overrun. 14 projects 3+ year delays. PIDB debt Rs. 8,000+ crore. land acquisition blocking

keyFindings.text: PIDB (Punjab Infrastructure Development Board) is Punjab's infrastructure financing arm -- similar to Karnataka's KIIFB and Kerala's KIIFB in structure. By routing infrastructure investment through PIDB (an SPV), Punjab can borrow beyond FRBM limits without the borrowing appearing in state accounts. The Rs. 8,000+ crore PIDB debt is therefore the Punjab government's liability -- it will ultimately require state budget repayment -- but it is invisible in the FRBM statement. The Rs. 3,200 crore cost overrun (26 per cent) and 14 projects with 3+ year delays indicate that land acquisition is the primary bottleneck: without upfront land acquisition completion before project award, construction contracts begin with the expectation of eventual land access, and delays are baked in from Day 1.

source.quote: Rs. 12,400 crore projects. Rs. 3,200 crore overrun. 14 projects delayed. PIDB debt Rs. 8,000+ crore

recommendations: Punjab Finance Department must: (a) disclose PIDB debt in the state's Annual Fiscal Document alongside the FRBM statement as a contingent liability; (b) PIDB must publish quarterly project status reports with delay attribution (land acquisition, contractor, design change, utility shifting); (c) land acquisition must be completed before contract award -- no infrastructure contract should be awarded for a project where more than 10 per cent land acquisition is pending; (d) 14 delayed projects must each have a Chief Secretary-level review with a revised completion date.

ministry: Public Health Engineering Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh
reportNo: Report No. 5 of 2026 (Performance Audit -- Jal Jeevan Mission, MP) -- Part XIII
title: Performance Audit -- MP JJM Part XIII: Beneficiary Survey -- Only 44 Per cent Households Receiving Water Daily; 31 Per cent Receiving Minimum 55 LPCD; Women Time Savings 0.8 Hours (vs 2.5 Hours Projected); Willingness to Pay ₹55/Month; Adivasi Household Satisfaction 38 Per cent; Gram Sabha Awareness of JJM Nil in 68 Per cent Villages
overview: CAG PA (MP JJM, 2026) Part XIII: Beneficiary survey results -- only 44 per cent households receive water daily (vs 100 per cent target); 31 per cent receive minimum 55 LPCD (litre per capita per day); women time savings 0.8 hours/day (vs 2.5 hours projected); willingness to pay ₹55/month for water; Adivasi household satisfaction 38 per cent; Gram Sabha awareness of JJM (who runs it, VWSC, tariff) nil in 68 per cent villages.

stats.label: Daily water 44 per cent households; 55 LPCD only 31 per cent; satisfaction 38 per cent adivasi
stats.value: Daily water 44 per cent households; 55 LPCD minimum 31 per cent; women time savings 0.8 hrs (vs 2.5 projected); adivasi satisfaction 38 per cent; Gram Sabha JJM awareness nil 68 per cent villages

source.quote: daily water 44 per cent. 55 LPCD 31 per cent. women time savings 0.8 hrs vs 2.5 projected. adivasi satisfaction 38 per cent. Gram Sabha awareness nil 68 per cent

keyFindings.text: The beneficiary survey data from MP JJM is the most damning evidence in the audit: the programme's own intended beneficiaries report that the promised outcomes -- daily water, adequate quantity, time savings for women -- have not materialised. The 2.5-hour women's time saving was JJM's flagship welfare promise: women in rural India spend 1-3 hours daily collecting water from distant sources. JJM piped water was supposed to eliminate this burden. With actual time savings of only 0.8 hours (31 per cent of the promised benefit), millions of rural women in MP are still spending significant time and energy on water collection despite the programme being 68 per cent complete on the dashboard. Adivasi satisfaction at 38 per cent -- below even the 44 per cent daily water figure -- reflects the combined impact of lower coverage (Alirajpur 7.69 per cent), contaminated water (E. coli), and VWSC absence in tribal areas.

source.quote: daily water 44 per cent. 55 LPCD 31 per cent. women time savings 0.8 hrs vs 2.5. adivasi satisfaction 38 per cent

recommendations: MP PHED and Jal Shakti Ministry must use the beneficiary survey findings to reset programme targets from input metrics (FHTC installed) to outcome metrics: (a) daily water coverage must be tracked by district and published monthly; (b) 55 LPCD achievement must be verified by independent third-party measurement -- not self-reported; (c) women's time savings must be resurveyed annually with GPS tracking of water collection trips; (d) adivasi satisfaction must be a specific reported metric with district breakdown and corrective action plan for all adivasi blocks below 60 per cent satisfaction.

ministry: Department of School Education, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (Performance Audit -- Samagra Shiksha in WB) -- Part XIII
title: Performance Audit -- WB Samagra Shiksha Part XIII: School Infrastructure -- Girls Toilet Functional 68 Per cent; Drinking Water Functional 72 Per cent; Electricity 81 Per cent; School Building Dangerous Condition 3,200 Schools; Computer Lab No Internet 45 Per cent; Samagra Shiksha Grant Utilisation 74 Per cent
overview: CAG PA (WB Samagra Shiksha, 2026) Part XIII: School infrastructure -- girls toilet functional only 68 per cent; drinking water functional 72 per cent; electricity 81 per cent; 3,200 schools in dangerous building condition; computer labs with no internet 45 per cent; Samagra Shiksha grant utilisation 74 per cent.

stats.label: Girls toilet functional 68 per cent; drinking water 72 per cent; 3,200 dangerous schools
stats.value: Girls toilet functional 68 per cent; drinking water 72 per cent; electricity 81 per cent; 3,200 dangerous buildings; computer lab no internet 45 per cent; Samagra grant utilisation 74 per cent

source.quote: girls toilet 68 per cent. drinking water 72 per cent. electricity 81 per cent. 3,200 dangerous buildings. computer lab no internet 45 per cent

keyFindings.text: WB's 68 per cent functional girls toilet rate is directly linked to female enrolment. Research consistently shows that functional, private girls toilets are among the most important factors in retaining adolescent girls in school. Without a functional girls toilet, many girls leave school at menarche (Class 6-8) when managing menstruation in school becomes difficult or impossible. Computer labs with no internet (45 per cent) represent infrastructure investment that cannot deliver its intended outcome -- computers without internet access can be used for typing and basic computer literacy but cannot access digital educational resources, AI tools, or online assessments that the NEP envisions. The 3,200 dangerous building schools represent an immediate safety risk -- any structural failure could cause casualties.

source.quote: girls toilet 68 per cent. drinking water 72 per cent. 3,200 dangerous. computer no internet 45 per cent

recommendations: West Bengal School Education Department must: (a) prioritise girls toilet repair in all schools with non-functional toilets within 6 months -- this is the highest-impact single action for female enrollment retention; (b) all 3,200 dangerous building schools must be assessed by a structural engineer within 3 months and condemned buildings must be vacated immediately; (c) internet connectivity for computer labs must be provided through state government broadband scheme (BSNL BharatNet or WBSETCL fibre); (d) Samagra grant utilisation from 74 per cent to 90 per cent within 12 months through PMU support to districts.

ministry: Energy Department / KPTCL / BESCOM, Government of Karnataka
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part XVII
title: State Finances -- Karnataka Part XVII: Power Sector -- KPTCL/BESCOM/HESCOM AT&C Losses; BESCOM AT&C 13.1 Per cent (Best Distribution Company India); Agricultural Subsidy ₹13,000+ crore; KPTCL Transmission ₹42,000+ crore Revenue; RE Renewable Targets; Power Purchase Agreement Costs Escalating
overview: CAG SFAR (Karnataka, 2025) Part XVII: Power sector -- BESCOM (Bengaluru Electricity Supply Company) AT&C losses 13.1 per cent (best of any large distribution company in India); KPTCL transmission revenue ₹42,000+ crore; agricultural electricity subsidy ₹13,000+ crore (pump-set subsidy -- Karnataka has significant irrigated agriculture); HESCOM (Hubli-Dharwad-Belgaum) AT&C 24 per cent -- significantly worse than BESCOM; renewable energy integration; PPA cost escalation.

stats.label: BESCOM AT&C 13.1 per cent (best large DISCOM India); agricultural subsidy ₹13,000+ crore; HESCOM 24 per cent
stats.value: BESCOM AT&C 13.1 per cent (best in India); HESCOM AT&C 24 per cent; agricultural subsidy ₹13,000+ crore; KPTCL revenue ₹42,000+ crore; PPA cost escalating

source.quote: BESCOM AT&C 13.1 per cent best India. HESCOM 24 per cent. agricultural subsidy Rs. 13,000+ crore. KPTCL Rs. 42,000+ crore

keyFindings.text: BESCOM's 13.1 per cent AT&C loss rate is a genuine achievement -- among the lowest of any large distribution company in India. The contrast with HESCOM (24 per cent AT&C losses in the northern Karnataka-Hyderabad-Karnataka region) reflects the urban-rural, Bengaluru-Kalyana Karnataka divide: BESCOM serves a densely populated, industrialised, high-consumption area where metering is complete and theft is harder; HESCOM serves dispersed agricultural communities where agricultural pump sets are the primary load and AT&C loss tracking is difficult. The Rs. 13,000+ crore agricultural subsidy -- paying for unmetered or subsidised agricultural power -- is Karnataka's largest invisible PSU liability, growing with KPTCL revenue growth.

source.quote: BESCOM 13.1 per cent. HESCOM 24 per cent. agricultural subsidy Rs. 13,000+ crore. KPTCL Rs. 42,000+ crore

recommendations: Karnataka Energy Department must: (a) spread BESCOM's management practices (metering, billing efficiency, enforcement) to HESCOM and other DISCOMs through knowledge transfer and leadership rotation; (b) agricultural subsidy ₹13,000+ crore must be DBT-linked -- transition to flat-rate power subsidy per HP of pump capacity (replacing unmetered consumption tracking) within 3 years; (c) PPA costs must be reviewed -- Karnataka's renewable PPA portfolio must be renegotiated for tariff efficiency where contracts allow; (d) HESCOM AT&C loss must reach BESCOM levels (13 per cent) within 5 years.

ministry: ST and SC Development Department, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit Report) -- PVTG Livelihood
title: Compliance Audit -- Odisha PVTG Vanbandhu: Minor Forest Produce -- Tendu Leaf ₹180 crore; Bamboo ₹42 crore; Mahua ₹28 crore; TRIFED Linkage Incomplete; MFP MSP Not Reaching Collectors; Van Dhan Vikas Kendras -- 40 Per cent Non-Operational; Adivasi Marketing Infrastructure Absent
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Odisha PVTG livelihood, 2025) found: (1) Minor Forest Produce (MFP) -- Tendu leaf ₹180 crore, bamboo ₹42 crore, mahua ₹28 crore; (2) TRIFED linkage incomplete (GoI Van Dhan programme for tribal MFP marketing); (3) MFP MSP (Minimum Support Price) not reaching collectors (middlemen capture); (4) Van Dhan Vikas Kendras -- 40 per cent non-operational; (5) Adivasi marketing infrastructure (processing, storage, cold chain) absent.

stats.label: Van Dhan 40 per cent non-operational; MSP not reaching collectors; TRIFED linkage incomplete
stats.value: MFP: Tendu ₹180 crore, bamboo ₹42 crore, mahua ₹28 crore; Van Dhan Kendras 40 per cent non-operational; MSP not reaching collectors (middlemen capture); TRIFED linkage incomplete; processing absent

source.quote: Tendu Rs. 180 crore. bamboo Rs. 42 crore. mahua Rs. 28 crore. Van Dhan 40 per cent non-operational. MSP not reaching collectors. TRIFED incomplete

keyFindings.text: Odisha's tribal communities collect Minor Forest Produce -- tendu leaves (bidi wrapper), bamboo, mahua flowers (fermentable, edible), honey, sal seeds, and tamarind -- from the forests they have lived in for centuries. This is their traditional livelihood, and these are resources they have rights to under the Forest Rights Act. The MSP for MFP was designed to ensure that tribal collectors receive a fair price instead of selling at whatever the arriving trader offers (typically 20-30 per cent of market value). But the Rs. 180 crore tendu leaf, Rs. 42 crore bamboo, and Rs. 28 crore mahua are transacted at market prices -- the tribal collectors receive only a fraction because: (a) Van Dhan Kendras (government procurement centres) are 40 per cent non-operational, leaving only private traders; (b) TRIFED linkage (connecting tribal co-operatives to national markets) is incomplete.

source.quote: Tendu Rs. 180 crore. bamboo Rs. 42 crore. mahua Rs. 28 crore. Van Dhan 40 per cent non-operational. MSP not reaching collectors

recommendations: Odisha ST&SC Development Department must: (a) reactivate all 40 per cent non-operational Van Dhan Vikas Kendras within 3 months -- staffing, procurement funds, and storage must be addressed; (b) TRIFED linkage must be completed for all 10 key MFPs within 6 months -- allowing tribal co-operatives to sell directly to TRIFED at MSP; (c) primary value addition (bamboo craft, mahua liquor distillation by tribal SHGs, sal leaf plate making) must be supported with equipment grants and market linkage; (d) MFP MSP compliance must be monitored through monthly price surveys published district-wise.

ministry: Finance / Social Welfare Department, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 6 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part X
title: State Finances -- Bihar Part X: Social Welfare Spending -- SC/ST/OBC/EWS ₹28,000+ crore; Pre-Matric Scholarship Beneficiary Fraud; Post-Matric Scholarship Delay 18 Months; Mahadalit Mission ₹4,200 crore; Hostel Construction Incomplete; Social Sector 18.2 Per cent Revenue Expenditure
overview: CAG SFAR (Bihar, 2026) Part X: Social welfare spending SC/ST/OBC/EWS ₹28,000+ crore; pre-matric scholarship beneficiary fraud (ghost students); post-matric scholarship delay 18 months (students wait over a year for scholarship); Mahadalit Mission ₹4,200 crore; hostel construction incomplete (SC/ST student hostels under construction for 5+ years); social sector 18.2 per cent of Revenue Expenditure.

stats.label: Social welfare ₹28,000+ crore; scholarship delay 18 months; hostel incomplete 5+ years
stats.value: SC/ST/OBC/EWS social welfare ₹28,000+ crore; post-matric scholarship delay 18 months; Mahadalit Mission ₹4,200 crore; hostel incomplete 5+ years; pre-matric ghost students; 18.2 per cent Revenue Expenditure

source.quote: social welfare Rs. 28,000+ crore. scholarship delay 18 months. Mahadalit Rs. 4,200 crore. hostel incomplete 5+ years. 18.2 per cent Revenue Expenditure

keyFindings.text: Bihar's 18-month post-matric scholarship delay has a devastating effect on SC/ST/OBC students in higher education. A first-year engineering or medical student whose scholarship has not arrived cannot pay hostel fees, examination fees, or buy textbooks. The 18-month delay means a student who enrolled in July has not received their scholarship by the following January -- 6 months of the academic year have passed with no financial support. Bihar colleges often refuse to issue semester completion certificates to scholarship students whose fees remain unpaid -- trapping students in a cycle where the delayed scholarship prevents college cooperation, which delays the scholarship further. The 18.2 per cent social sector spending (while large in absolute terms) is not adequately reaching its intended beneficiaries due to programme execution failures.

source.quote: scholarship delay 18 months. Mahadalit Rs. 4,200 crore. hostel incomplete 5+ years. 18.2 per cent Revenue Expenditure

recommendations: Bihar Social Welfare Department must: (a) implement Direct Benefit Transfer for all scholarship schemes -- scholarship amount transferred directly to student's Aadhaar-linked bank account within 60 days of college enrollment verification; (b) all SC/ST hostels under construction for 3+ years must be reviewed -- completion in 6 months or contract terminated and re-awarded; (c) pre-matric ghost student fraud must be addressed through Aadhaar-linked school attendance verification before scholarship disbursement; (d) Mahadalit Mission must present annual welfare outcome reports (literacy, employment, health) to the Legislature.

ministry: Urban Development / Kolkata Municipal Corporation, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2024-25) -- Part XIX
title: State Finances -- West Bengal Part XIX: KMC Revenue -- Property Tax ₹2,380 crore (30-40 Per cent Undervalued); Trade Licence Revenue Below Potential; KMC Debt ₹4,200+ crore; Water Tariff Not Revised Since 2006; KMDA Borrowings Off-Book; Kolkata Infrastructure Backlog ₹18,000+ crore
overview: CAG SFAR (WB, 2026) Part XIX: KMC (Kolkata Municipal Corporation) revenue -- property tax ₹2,380 crore (30-40 per cent below market value); trade licence revenue below potential; KMC debt ₹4,200+ crore; water tariff not revised since 2006 (18 years); KMDA (Kolkata Metropolitan Development Authority) borrowings off-book; Kolkata infrastructure backlog ₹18,000+ crore (drainage, roads, sewage, parks).

stats.label: Property tax 30-40 per cent undervalued; water tariff unrevised 18 years; debt ₹4,200+ crore
stats.value: KMC property tax ₹2,380 crore (30-40 per cent undervalued); water tariff unrevised since 2006; KMC debt ₹4,200+ crore; infrastructure backlog ₹18,000+ crore; KMDA borrowings off-book

source.quote: property tax Rs. 2,380 crore 30-40 per cent undervalued. water tariff unrevised 2006. KMC debt Rs. 4,200+ crore. infrastructure backlog Rs. 18,000+ crore

keyFindings.text: Kolkata's water tariff not revised since 2006 is among India's longest gaps in urban utility pricing. In 18 years, inflation has eroded the real value of the tariff by approximately 60 per cent -- meaning that KMC is providing water at 40 per cent of its 2006 real cost today. This is financially unsustainable: KMC's water supply costs (energy for pumping, chemical treatment, pipe maintenance) have risen with inflation while revenue has been frozen. The result is chronic underinvestment in water infrastructure and a Rs. 18,000+ crore infrastructure backlog that includes critical drainage networks (Kolkata floods annually partly due to inadequate drainage). Property tax undervaluation (30-40 per cent) has the same root: annual rental value assessments not updated with market rents.

source.quote: property tax 30-40 per cent undervalued. water tariff 2006. KMC debt Rs. 4,200+ crore. infrastructure backlog Rs. 18,000+ crore

recommendations: West Bengal Urban Development Department must: (a) KMC water tariff revision is overdue -- a phased revision (20 per cent now, 15 per cent in Year 2, 10 per cent in Year 3) should be initiated with a pro-poor slab structure (lifeline 5 KL/month free, regular market rate above 5 KL); (b) property tax annual rental value must be linked to the state government's ready reckoner (circle rate) and revised annually; (c) infrastructure backlog ₹18,000+ crore requires AMRUT + state budget + KMDA borrowing -- but KMDA borrowings must be disclosed on-balance-sheet.

ministry: State Goods and Services Tax (SGST) Department, Government of Maharashtra
reportNo: Report No. 6 of 2025 (Compliance Audit -- SGST) -- Part VIII: Sector Audits
title: Compliance Audit -- Maharashtra GST Part VIII: Sector Audits -- Textile ₹22,400 crore Turnover Under-Reported; Construction ₹18,800 crore Under-Reported; Healthcare ₹6,200 crore ITC Excess Claimed; Hospitality GST Input Mismatch ₹4,100 crore; Transport Sector Fake EWB ₹9,800 crore
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (MH SGST, 2025) Part VIII: Sector-specific audits -- Textile: ₹22,400 crore turnover under-reported (yarn/fabric transactions not in GST returns vs EWB data); Construction: ₹18,800 crore under-reported (work contracts, sub-contractors); Healthcare: ₹6,200 crore ITC excess claimed (exempt supplies -- medical services -- ITC ineligible but claimed); Hospitality: ₹4,100 crore GST input mismatch; Transport: ₹9,800 crore fake EWBs.

stats.label: Textile ₹22,400 crore under-reported; Construction ₹18,800 crore; Healthcare ITC ₹6,200 crore
stats.value: Textile ₹22,400 crore under-reported; Construction ₹18,800 crore; Healthcare ITC ₹6,200 crore excess; Hospitality ₹4,100 crore mismatch; Transport fake EWB ₹9,800 crore

source.quote: Textile Rs. 22,400 crore. Construction Rs. 18,800 crore. Healthcare ITC Rs. 6,200 crore. Hospitality Rs. 4,100 crore. Transport Rs. 9,800 crore

keyFindings.text: The healthcare sector's Rs. 6,200 crore excess ITC claim is based on a simple GST provision that many healthcare businesses ignore: medical services (patient treatment, surgery, hospitalisation) are exempt from GST -- hospitals do not charge GST on their bills. But the Input Tax Credit restriction says: if your output is exempt, you cannot claim ITC on your inputs. A hospital that claims ITC on medical equipment, medicines, and construction of the hospital building is illegally claiming credit for a tax never collected from patients. Maharashtra's hospitals -- including corporate hospital chains -- have been systematically claiming ITC they are not entitled to. This is not a grey area: the GST law is unambiguous that exempt supply providers cannot claim ITC.

source.quote: Textile Rs. 22,400 crore. Construction Rs. 18,800 crore. Healthcare ITC Rs. 6,200 crore excess. Transport Rs. 9,800 crore fake EWB

recommendations: Maharashtra SGST must: (a) immediately issue demand notices to all healthcare businesses that claimed ITC on exempt medical services -- recovery of ₹6,200 crore plus interest; (b) textile sector audit must use EWB data vs GSTR-1 mismatch to identify all under-reporters; (c) construction sub-contractor chain must be audited -- every main contractor's GSTR-1 must match sub-contractors' GSTR-1 for each project; (d) a dedicated Sector Intelligence Unit must be established within the SGST Commissionerate for each of the 5 identified sectors.

ministry: Rural Development Department, Government of Jharkhand
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit) -- MGNREGS Grievance Redressal
title: Compliance Audit -- Jharkhand MGNREGS Grievance: Ombudsman Post Vacant 3 Years; 2.14 Lakh Complaints Unresolved; Job Card Deletion Without Consent; Muster Roll Fraud Undetected; 60-Day MGNREGS Wage Payment SLA Violated; Unemployment Allowance Not Paid; Worker Helpline Non-Functional
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Jharkhand MGNREGS grievance, 2025) found: (1) MGNREGS Ombudsman post vacant for 3 years; (2) 2.14 lakh complaints unresolved; (3) job card deletion without worker consent or notice; (4) muster roll fraud undetected -- names of workers not present on rolls; (5) 60-day wage payment SLA violated (MGNREGS wages must be paid within 15 days of work -- courts have extended this); (6) unemployment allowance (when work not provided within 15 days of application) not paid; (7) worker helpline non-functional.

stats.label: Ombudsman vacant 3 years; 2.14 lakh complaints unresolved; job card deleted without consent
stats.value: MGNREGS Ombudsman vacant 3 years; 2.14 lakh complaints unresolved; job card deletion without consent; muster roll fraud undetected; wage payment SLA violated; unemployment allowance unpaid; helpline non-functional

source.quote: Ombudsman vacant 3 years. 2.14 lakh complaints unresolved. job card deleted without consent. muster roll fraud. unemployment allowance unpaid

keyFindings.text: The MGNREGS Ombudsman is the statutory complaint resolution mechanism for MGNREGS workers -- a dedicated quasi-judicial authority who can investigate complaints of wage non-payment, job card deletion, muster roll fraud, and work allocation denial. With the Ombudsman post vacant for 3 years, Jharkhand's 2.14 lakh unresolved complaints have nowhere to go. Workers who have been cheated -- whose wages were diverted, whose names were entered on muster rolls without their knowledge (phantom workers), or whose job cards were deleted to reduce the government's liability -- have no effective remedy. Unemployment allowance non-payment is particularly important: when MGNREGS doesn't provide work within 15 days of a job demand, the worker is entitled to unemployment allowance at 25 per cent of wage rate. Not paying it violates the law and removes the financial incentive for the government to provide work.

source.quote: Ombudsman vacant 3 years. 2.14 lakh complaints unresolved. job card deleted. muster roll fraud. unemployment allowance unpaid

recommendations: Jharkhand Rural Development Department must: (a) appoint MGNREGS Ombudsman within 30 days (a retired district judge or senior IAS officer with MGNREGS exposure); (b) all 2.14 lakh complaints must be triaged and resolved within 90 days; (c) job card deletions without consent must be reversed -- State must send SMS/letter to all job card holders before any deletion; (d) unemployment allowance must be calculated and paid for all verified demand-work mismatch cases in the past 3 years; (e) worker helpline must be reactivated with a 24-hour response SLA.

ministry: Rural Development Department, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit Report) -- MGNREGS NRM Works
title: Compliance Audit -- Odisha MGNREGS NRM Works: Pond Desilting Without Depth Measurement; Farm Bunds Without Slope Protection; Water Harvesting Structures Non-Functional After 1 Season; 3.14 Lakh NRM Works -- 58 Per cent Without Engineering Measurement; Material Quality Unverified; Asset Register Not Maintained
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Odisha MGNREGS NRM, 2025) found: (1) Pond desilting without baseline depth measurement (no way to verify desiltation actually happened); (2) farm bunds without slope protection (erode in first rain); (3) water harvesting structures non-functional after 1 season; (4) 3.14 lakh NRM works -- 58 per cent without engineering measurement books; (5) material quality unverified; (6) asset register not maintained.

stats.label: 3.14 lakh NRM works; 58 per cent without measurement; pond desilt unverifiable; structures non-functional after 1 season
stats.value: 3.14 lakh MGNREGS NRM works; 58 per cent without engineering measurement; pond desilting without depth baseline; farm bunds without slope protection; water structures non-functional after 1 season; asset register nil

source.quote: 3.14 lakh NRM works. 58 per cent without measurement. pond desilting without depth. farm bunds without slope. non-functional after 1 season

keyFindings.text: Pond desilting without a before-and-after depth measurement is a systemic fraud enabler. The procedure requires: (a) pre-work survey measuring current pond depth at multiple points, (b) work execution (manual desilting by MGNREGS workers), (c) post-work measurement confirming depth improvement. Without the pre-work baseline, there is no way to verify whether any desiltation actually occurred -- wages can be paid for work that was not done, and the payment cannot be challenged. In 58 per cent of Odisha's 3.14 lakh NRM works without measurement books, this verification is impossible. Farm bunds without slope protection (compaction, grass lining) erode in the first monsoon -- the work undoes itself within one season, requiring repeat MGNREGS expenditure in the same location the following year. Repeat expenditure on the same non-durable works is one of MGNREGS' most persistent audit findings nationally.

source.quote: 3.14 lakh NRM works. 58 per cent without measurement. pond desilting without depth baseline. non-functional after 1 season

recommendations: Odisha Rural Development Department must mandate geotagged photographic documentation for all MGNREGS NRM works -- before, during, and after; pond desilting must include GPS-logged depth measurements at defined grid points before and after (simple GPS depth rod -- ₹500 per GP -- is adequate); farm bunds must include slope compaction and grass sowing as a mandatory component with survival verification at 3 months; NRM Asset Register must be maintained at GP level with annual condition assessment; works found non-functional within 2 years must trigger contractor/JE accountability.

ministry: Labour Department / EPFO / ESIC, Government of Goa
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (Compliance-PA on BOCW in Goa) -- Part V
title: Compliance-PA -- Goa BOCW Part V: ESI and PF Non-Registration -- 65,000+ Construction Workers Without Social Security; Principal Employer Liability Unenforcced; ₹42 crore PF Arrears Uncollected; 90 Per cent Construction Projects Without Sub-Contractor PF Compliance; ESIC Dispensary Nil Near Construction Sites
overview: CAG Compliance-PA (Goa BOCW, 2025) Part V: ESI (Employees State Insurance) and PF (Provident Fund) non-registration -- 65,000+ construction workers in Goa without social security; principal employer (project owner) liability for sub-contractor ESI/PF not enforced; ₹42 crore PF arrears uncollected; 90 per cent construction projects without sub-contractor PF compliance; no ESIC dispensary within reasonable distance of major construction sites.

stats.label: 65,000+ workers without ESI/PF; ₹42 crore PF arrears; 90 per cent projects non-compliant
stats.value: 65,000+ construction workers without ESI/PF; principal employer liability unenforced; ₹42 crore PF arrears; 90 per cent projects without sub-contractor PF compliance; no ESIC dispensary near sites

source.quote: 65,000+ workers without ESI/PF. Rs. 42 crore PF arrears. 90 per cent projects non-compliant. ESIC nil near sites

keyFindings.text: Goa's construction sector -- driven by real estate (Goa's booming coastal property market), infrastructure (national highways, Mopa airport, bridges), and tourism (hotels and resorts) -- employs 65,000+ workers, most of them migrant labourers from UP, Bihar, Odisha, Jharkhand, and Chhattisgarh. These workers travel to Goa, live in temporary labour colonies on construction sites, and work without health insurance (ESI) or retirement savings (PF). When injured on site, they have no ESI cover for hospitalisation. When they return home after the project, they have no PF savings. The principal employer (the project owner -- a developer, hotel chain, or government) is legally liable for ESI/PF compliance even of sub-contractors' workers, but this liability is systematically unenforced in Goa.

source.quote: 65,000+ workers without ESI/PF. Rs. 42 crore PF arrears. 90 per cent non-compliant. ESIC nil near sites

recommendations: Goa Labour Department must: (a) mandate ESI/PF compliance for all construction projects above ₹1 crore as a condition of building permit -- no occupation certificate without EPFO and ESIC compliance certificate; (b) ₹42 crore PF arrears must be collected within 6 months through EPFO enforcement proceedings; (c) ESIC must establish a mobile dispensary for major construction sites in Goa (Mopa, NH 66, coastal hotel projects); (d) all migrant workers must be registered under the Interstate Migrant Workers Act and given BOCW registration on arrival in Goa.

ministry: Department of School Education, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (Performance Audit -- Samagra Shiksha in WB) -- Part XII
title: Performance Audit -- WB Samagra Shiksha Part XII: Teacher Vacancy 1.86 Lakh; D.El.Ed/B.Ed Untrained Teachers 22 Per cent; DIKSHA Platform Training Completion 41 Per cent; Contractual Para-Teacher Regularisation Pending; Inservice Training Only 3 Days/Year; Teacher Absenteeism Rate 14 Per cent; Primary Schools Single-Teacher 18 Per cent
overview: CAG PA (WB Samagra Shiksha, 2026) Part XII: Teacher vacancy 1.86 lakh; untrained teachers (without D.El.Ed/B.Ed) 22 per cent; DIKSHA platform training completion 41 per cent; contractual para-teacher regularisation pending for 1.2 lakh para-teachers; in-service training only 3 days/year (RTE requires 10 days); teacher absenteeism 14 per cent; primary schools with only 1 teacher (single-teacher schools) 18 per cent.

stats.label: Teacher vacancy 1.86 lakh; untrained 22 per cent; absenteeism 14 per cent; single-teacher 18 per cent
stats.value: Teacher vacancy 1.86 lakh; untrained teachers 22 per cent; DIKSHA completion 41 per cent; in-service 3 days (vs 10 mandated); absenteeism 14 per cent; single-teacher primary schools 18 per cent

source.quote: vacancy 1.86 lakh. untrained 22 per cent. DIKSHA 41 per cent. in-service 3 days. absenteeism 14 per cent. single-teacher 18 per cent

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's 1.86 lakh teacher vacancy is one of the largest absolute shortfalls in any state -- comparable only to UP and Bihar in raw numbers, but more significant given WB's smaller school-age population. The 18 per cent single-teacher primary schools -- schools with only one teacher for all classes (Class I to V) -- represent the worst-case scenario for learning outcomes: one teacher cannot simultaneously teach five grade levels. In single-teacher schools, multi-grade teaching (all students in one room, teacher moving between groups) is the norm, and learning outcomes in these schools are typically 30-40 per cent below multi-teacher schools. The 22 per cent untrained teachers -- working in classrooms without any formal pedagogical training -- compounds the vacancy problem with a quality problem.

source.quote: vacancy 1.86 lakh. untrained 22 per cent. single-teacher 18 per cent. absenteeism 14 per cent

recommendations: West Bengal School Education Department must: (a) fill 1.86 lakh teacher vacancies over 5 years (approximately 37,000 per year) through annual SLST teacher recruitment -- no gap year; (b) all untrained teachers must complete D.El.Ed within 2 years (NIOS distance programme already available) or lose employment; (c) single-teacher schools must be merged with nearby schools (with transport arrangement) or given an additional teacher within 2 years; (d) in-service training must be increased to 10 days/year as RTE mandates -- DIKSHA completion must be tracked and published district-wise.

ministry: Revenue / Agriculture Department, Government of Kerala
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 (Compliance Audit Report) -- Plantation Lease
title: Compliance Audit -- Kerala Plantation Lease: Rubber/Tea/Coffee Lease ₹2,800 crore Market Value -- ₹12 crore Lease Rent (0.4 Per cent); 50-Year Leases Expired Without Renewal; Wayanad Plantation Arrears; Deforestation Within Lease; Social Forestry Mandate Violated; Land Back-Valuation Not Done Since 1960s
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Kerala plantation lease, 2026) found: (1) Rubber/tea/coffee plantation leases -- market value ₹2,800 crore, lease rent collected only ₹12 crore = 0.4 per cent; (2) 50-year leases expired without renewal -- continued occupation without fresh lease; (3) Wayanad plantation arrears uncollected; (4) Deforestation within leased area (private plantation on government forest land exceeding lease boundary); (5) social forestry mandate violated; (6) land lease rent not revised since 1960s.

stats.label: Lease ₹12 crore vs ₹2,800 crore market value (0.4 per cent); expired leases; arrears uncollected
stats.value: Plantation lease market value ₹2,800 crore; rent ₹12 crore (0.4 per cent); 50-year leases expired without renewal; Wayanad arrears uncollected; deforestation within lease; land value not revised since 1960s

source.quote: lease market Rs. 2,800 crore. rent Rs. 12 crore (0.4 per cent). leases expired. arrears uncollected. deforestation within lease. rent not revised 1960s

keyFindings.text: Kerala's plantation lease revenue is one of India's most egregious cases of state resource under-valuation. Government forest land leased to private rubber, tea, and coffee plantation companies at rents set in the 1960s -- and never revised -- creates a permanent subsidy to plantation owners at the cost of the Kerala public. The Rs. 12 crore annual rent on Rs. 2,800 crore market value land is a 0.4 per cent yield -- a rate lower than any bank savings account. If the land were leased at a fair market rate (even 2 per cent of market value), Kerala would collect Rs. 56 crore annually -- a 4.7x revenue increase. Deforestation within leased area (plantation companies clearing government forest land beyond the lease boundary) compounded by social forestry mandate violations (mandatory planting of native species within plantation) further reduces the ecological value of the arrangement.

source.quote: lease Rs. 12 crore vs Rs. 2,800 crore market. 0.4 per cent. leases expired. deforestation within lease. rent not revised 1960s

recommendations: Kerala Revenue Department must: (a) complete land valuation of all plantation leases within 12 months -- engage a certified valuer for each district; (b) revise lease rent to minimum 1.5 per cent of current market value (from 0.4 per cent) for all leases; (c) all expired leases must be formally renewed with revised rent before continuation is allowed -- continued occupation without valid lease is illegal possession of government land; (d) deforestation within lease areas must be prosecuted under Kerala Forest Act; social forestry mandate compliance must be verified annually by Forest Range Officer.

ministry: Urban Development Department, Government of Nagaland
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2023-24) -- Part XI
title: State Finances -- Nagaland Part XI: Urban Infrastructure -- Kohima Municipal Council Budget ₹80 crore; Dimapur Urban; Solid Waste ₹120 Tonnes/Day Unmanaged; Water Supply 4-6 Hours/Day; No Sewage Treatment; Property Tax Collection 35 Per cent Target; AMRUT Funds Underutilised
overview: CAG SFAR (Nagaland, 2025) Part XI: Urban infrastructure -- Kohima Municipal Council budget ₹80 crore; 120 tonnes/day solid waste in Kohima + Dimapur largely unmanaged; water supply only 4-6 hours/day (demand far above capacity); no sewage treatment plant in either city; property tax collection 35 per cent of target; AMRUT (Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation) funds underutilised; urban growth without urban services.

stats.label: SWM 120 tonnes/day unmanaged; water 4-6 hrs; no STP; property tax 35 per cent; AMRUT underutilised
stats.value: Kohima+Dimapur SWM 120 tonnes/day unmanaged; water supply 4-6 hrs/day; no STP; property tax 35 per cent collection; AMRUT underutilised; KMC budget ₹80 crore

source.quote: 120 tonnes/day solid waste unmanaged. water 4-6 hrs/day. no STP. property tax 35 per cent. AMRUT underutilised

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's urban infrastructure deficit reflects a common pattern in small NE state capitals: rapid in-migration from rural areas (war-affected, agricultural decline) has outpaced urban services capacity. Kohima's population growth over the past 20 years has not been accompanied by proportionate water supply augmentation (4-6 hours/day is inadequate for any modern urban household), waste management expansion (120 tonnes/day unmanaged means most waste is dumped in valleys and streams), or sanitation (no STP means all sewage enters the Dzukou and other rivers raw). AMRUT -- designed precisely to address this urban infrastructure deficit -- is underutilised because of limited institutional capacity in ULBs to prepare projects, tender, and execute within AMRUT's timelines.

source.quote: SWM 120 tonnes/day unmanaged. water 4-6 hrs. no STP. property tax 35 per cent. AMRUT underutilised

recommendations: Nagaland Urban Development Department must: (a) prioritise AMRUT utilisation -- engage a Project Management Unit (PMU) to assist KMC and Dimapur Municipal Council with DPR preparation, tendering, and execution; (b) water supply augmentation must be fast-tracked -- springs and small dams in the Kohima-Mao ridge area must be assessed for additional capacity; (c) SWM: a sanitary landfill at Kohima is the minimum requirement within 3 years; (d) property tax: all properties must be GIS-mapped and assessed by the municipal council -- targeted enforcement for large commercial properties first.

ministry: Rural Development Department, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2026 (Compliance Audit) -- MGNREGS-PMAY Convergence
title: Compliance Audit -- Bihar MGNREGS-PMAY Convergence: 1.89 Lakh Houses Incomplete; MGNREGS Labour Not Used in PMAY Construction; Convergence Norms Violated; MGNREGS 90 Days Not Provided to PMAY Beneficiaries; Multiple Scheme Duplication -- Same Household MGNREGS + PMAY + PMJAY Without Coordination
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Bihar MGNREGS-PMAY convergence, 2026) found: (1) 1.89 lakh PMAY-G houses incomplete; (2) MGNREGS labour not used in PMAY house construction (convergence norm requires PMAY beneficiary to receive 90 MGNREGS days for construction labour); (3) convergence norms violated; (4) MGNREGS 90 days not provided to PMAY beneficiaries; (5) same household receiving MGNREGS + PMAY + PMJAY benefits without inter-scheme coordination -- potential duplication.

stats.label: 1.89 lakh PMAY incomplete; MGNREGS 90 days not provided; convergence violated
stats.value: 1.89 lakh PMAY-G houses incomplete; MGNREGS labour not used in PMAY construction; 90-day convergence norm violated; same household multiple scheme coordination absent

source.quote: 1.89 lakh PMAY incomplete. MGNREGS 90 days not provided. convergence violated. same household multiple schemes without coordination

keyFindings.text: The MGNREGS-PMAY convergence design is elegant: PMAY provides Rs. 1.20-1.30 lakh for materials, and MGNREGS provides 90 days of wages (approximately Rs. 18,000 at Bihar minimum wage) for the beneficiary household's own construction labour -- so the household builds its own house using both material grant and wage payment. When convergence fails (MGNREGS 90 days not provided), the household either: (a) builds the house using private hired labour (reducing the effective housing subsidy by Rs. 18,000 -- a significant sum for a BPL household), or (b) doesn't build because they can't afford to hire labour. Bihar's 1.89 lakh incomplete PMAY houses are partly explained by this convergence failure -- households expected MGNREGS wages during construction but didn't receive them.

source.quote: 1.89 lakh PMAY incomplete. MGNREGS 90 days not provided. convergence violated

recommendations: Bihar Rural Development Department must: (a) link PMAY-G beneficiary list with MGNREGS MIS -- every PMAY beneficiary must automatically receive 90 MGNREGS days during construction; (b) BDO must verify convergence for each PMAY house -- PMAY second instalment release should require confirmation that MGNREGS 90 days have been provided; (c) 1.89 lakh incomplete houses must be reviewed -- for each, identify whether convergence failure contributed to incompletion and provide missed MGNREGS wages with enhanced work allocation.

ministry: Forest / Tourism Department, Government of Uttarakhand
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit) -- Ecotourism/Forest Revenue
title: Compliance Audit -- Uttarakhand Ecotourism: Forest Entry Fee ₹73+ crore; Permit Quota Violated -- Bedni-Roopkund 150 Per Cent Over Limit; Van Gujjar Displacement Without Resettlement; CAMPA ₹1,200+ crore Idle; Forest Fire Loss 1.28 Lakh Hectares; Tourism Revenue Not Shared With Local Communities
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Uttarakhand ecotourism, 2025) found: (1) Forest entry fees ₹73+ crore; (2) Bedni-Roopkund trek permit quota violated -- 150 per cent above permitted carrying capacity; (3) Van Gujjar (nomadic forest community) displacement from Reserved Forests without resettlement; (4) CAMPA ₹1,200+ crore idle; (5) Forest fire loss 1.28 lakh hectares in test period; (6) Tourism revenue not shared with local Van Gujjar/gram sabha communities.

stats.label: Bedni-Roopkund 150 per cent over-capacity; CAMPA ₹1,200+ crore idle; forest fire 1.28 lakh ha
stats.value: Forest entry fee ₹73+ crore; Bedni-Roopkund 150 per cent over carrying capacity; Van Gujjar displaced without resettlement; CAMPA ₹1,200+ crore idle; forest fire 1.28 lakh hectares; revenue unshared

source.quote: entry fee Rs. 73+ crore. Bedni-Roopkund 150 per cent over capacity. CAMPA Rs. 1,200+ crore idle. forest fire 1.28 lakh hectares

keyFindings.text: The Bedni-Roopkund carrying capacity violation is both an ecological and safety issue. Carrying capacity limits for Himalayan treks are calculated based on: trail width, water source capacity, waste disposal infrastructure, and ecological fragility of alpine meadows (bugyals). At 150 per cent above permitted carrying capacity, the trail infrastructure is overwhelmed -- solid waste accumulates, water sources are contaminated, and trampling damage to fragile bugyal ecosystems accelerates. The Roopkund glacier area (the famous skeleton lake) contains irreplaceable archaeological material that is being permanently damaged by uncontrolled tourist traffic. Van Gujjar displacement without resettlement -- a tribal community whose seasonal migration routes pass through Reserved Forests -- is both a human rights and ecological issue (Van Gujjars have historically maintained forest ecosystems through controlled grazing).

source.quote: Bedni-Roopkund 150 per cent over capacity. CAMPA Rs. 1,200+ crore idle. forest fire 1.28 lakh hectares. Van Gujjar displaced

recommendations: Uttarakhand Forest Department must: (a) immediately enforce Bedni-Roopkund carrying capacity limits -- implement mandatory digital permit booking with daily cap; (b) Van Gujjar resettlement and Forest Rights Act pattas must be issued within 6 months for displaced families; (c) CAMPA ₹1,200+ crore must be utilised for forest fire prevention (fire lines, watch towers, trained fire watchers) -- 1.28 lakh hectare fire loss is preventable; (d) 30 per cent of forest entry fees must be shared with gram sabhas of villages adjacent to protected areas.

ministry: Local Government / Punjab Municipal Infrastructure Development Company, Government of Punjab
reportNo: Report No. 5 of 2025 (Performance Audit -- SWM in Punjab) -- Part V
title: Performance Audit -- Punjab SWM Part V: GIS Waste Mapping Not Done; Door-to-Door Collection 68 Per cent ULBs; Wet-Dry Segregation at Source -- Only 22 Per cent Households; SWM Bylaws Not Enforced; House Tax-SWM Charge Linkage Missing; Private Concession Revenue Unshared; Swachh Survekshan Ranking Manipulation Alleged
overview: CAG PA (Punjab SWM, 2025) Part V: GIS waste mapping (identifying all waste generation points) not done in any Punjab ULB; door-to-door collection 68 per cent ULBs (32 per cent have no D2D); wet-dry segregation at source only 22 per cent households; SWM bylaws (mandating source segregation) not enforced; house tax-SWM charge linkage missing (SWM charge not recovered separately); private concession revenue not shared with ULBs as required; Swachh Survekshan ranking process concerns.

stats.label: GIS mapping nil; D2D collection 68 per cent ULBs; source segregation 22 per cent; bylaws unenforced
stats.value: GIS mapping nil; D2D collection 68 per cent ULBs; wet-dry segregation 22 per cent households; SWM bylaws unenforced; SWM charge not recovered; concession revenue unshared

source.quote: GIS mapping nil. D2D 68 per cent ULBs. segregation 22 per cent. bylaws unenforced. SWM charge not recovered

keyFindings.text: Punjab's 22 per cent household segregation rate is the fundamental obstacle to its SWM programme. Without source segregation (wet waste = kitchen scraps to composting, dry waste = recyclables to MRF/recyclers), all waste arrives at the Waste Processing Facility or landfill as mixed waste -- making composting impossible (compost from mixed waste is contaminated with metals and plastic), recycling uneconomical (recyclables contaminated), and landfill the only option (which both MRFs and landfills are designed to avoid). The entire downstream SWM infrastructure (MRFs, composting plants, bio-gas plants) depends on upstream segregation. Punjab's MRF non-operational finding (previous entry) is a direct consequence of 22 per cent segregation -- without clean dry waste, MRFs have nothing to process.

source.quote: GIS nil. D2D 68 per cent. segregation 22 per cent. bylaws unenforced. SWM charge not recovered

recommendations: Punjab Local Government Department must launch a Source Segregation Mission -- targeting 60 per cent household segregation within 2 years; enforcement: SWM bylaws must be activated -- ULBs must issue notice-and-penalty for non-segregating households (₹50 first offence, ₹200 repeat); all D2D collection vehicles must have 2 compartments (wet + dry) -- single-compartment vehicles defeat the purpose of segregation; GIS waste mapping must be done in all 167 ULBs within 12 months; SWM charge must be added to house tax bills as a separate line item.

stats.value: Tariff collection nil 90 per cent panchayats; VWSC non-functional; O&M ₹2,400+ crore annual need vs ₹0 collected; pump operators unpaid; JJM scheme collapse 2-3 years without funding

keyFindings.text: Bihar's JJM scheme faces a post-construction sustainability collapse: the infrastructure has been built (at enormous cost), connections have been made, but there is no revenue to pay for the electricity (pumping), chemicals (chlorination), and labour (operations and maintenance) that keep the water flowing. A piped water scheme is not like a hand pump -- it requires ongoing energy input (electric pump), chemical input (disinfection), and skilled maintenance (pipe repairs, pump servicing). Without tariff collection, none of these can be sustained. The 90 per cent nil tariff collection rate means that within 2-3 years of GoI's JJM operational support ending, the majority of Bihar's Rs. 38,000+ crore JJM infrastructure will be non-functional -- reverting communities to the same situation they were in before JJM.

source.quote: Tariff nil 90 per cent panchayats. O&M Rs. 2,400+ crore. Rs. 0 collected. scheme collapse 2-3 years

recommendations: Bihar PHED must immediately implement a Gram Panchayat Water Tariff Programme: every GP must adopt a minimum tariff resolution (recommended ₹50/month per FHTC) within 3 months; VWSC must be constituted in every village with JJM infrastructure within 60 days; O&M funding shortfall (₹2,400+ crore minus tariff collection) must be covered by a Bihar Water Supply Maintenance Fund -- funded 50:50 by state budget and GP tariff collections; pump operators must be formally employed under state PHED with monthly salary from the maintenance fund.

keyFindings.text: Odisha's DMF at 74 per cent High-Priority spending is the strongest performance among states covered in this series -- significantly above Gujarat (42 per cent) and the 60 per cent national mandate. This relative success is partly explained by OMBADC: Odisha established OMBADC to coordinate mineral revenue-funded development in mining-affected districts, creating an institutional layer between DMF receipts and project implementation. The DMF governance in Odisha also benefits from a more specific project-level tracking system. However, even at 74 per cent High-Priority, 26 per cent of DMF spending goes to non-priority activities (administrative costs, infrastructure not directly benefiting mining communities). The welfare paradox -- mining communities remaining poorer than non-mining communities -- persists even in the better-performing states.

reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2024-25) -- Part XVIII
title: State Finances -- West Bengal Part XVIII: Pension Liability ₹28,000+ crore Annual OPS; Pension-GDP Trajectory; WB Reverts to OPS 2022 -- Long-Run Actuarial Liability ₹3,50,000+ crore; NPS Transition Employees ₹4,200 crore Corpus Not Transferred; Pension Time Bomb 2035-2050
overview: CAG SFAR (WB, 2026) Part XVIII: WB reverted to OPS (Old Pension Scheme) in 2022 from NPS (National Pension System) for state employees; annual OPS pension outgo ₹28,000+ crore; long-run actuarial unfunded liability ₹3,50,000+ crore (pension promises to current employees not backed by any fund); NPS employees' corpus ₹4,200 crore not transferred to PFRDA (employees who enrolled NPS but state reverted them to OPS); pension trajectory to become 40 per cent of Revenue Receipts by 2040.

stats.label: Annual OPS pension ₹28,000+ crore; actuarial unfunded ₹3,50,000+ crore; NPS ₹4,200 crore unresolved
stats.value: OPS pension ₹28,000+ crore annual; actuarial unfunded liability ₹3,50,000+ crore; NPS corpus ₹4,200 crore not transferred; pension-RR trajectory 40 per cent by 2040; OPS reversion 2022

source.quote: OPS pension Rs. 28,000+ crore. actuarial unfunded Rs. 3,50,000+ crore. NPS Rs. 4,200 crore unresolved. pension trajectory 40 per cent by 2040

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's reversion to OPS in 2022 -- a politically popular decision that reversed NPS adoption -- creates a Rs. 3,50,000+ crore unfunded actuarial liability. Under OPS, every employee hired today generates a pension commitment (50 per cent of last salary, dearness relief adjusted, for life plus family pension) that is entirely unfunded -- no corpus, no investment, just future budget appropriation. Under NPS, the employee and government contribute monthly to a corpus that grows and is available at retirement. By reverting to OPS, WB eliminated the annual NPS contribution saving (approximately Rs. 3,000-4,000 crore) but created an exponentially larger future liability. The 16th Finance Commission cannot ignore this: WB's pension explosion (pension already 18 per cent of Revenue Receipts, headed to 40 per cent by 2040) will crowd out every other state expenditure priority.

source.quote: OPS Rs. 28,000+ crore. actuarial unfunded Rs. 3,50,000+ crore. NPS Rs. 4,200 crore unresolved. trajectory 40 per cent by 2040

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must commission an independent actuarial valuation of the OPS reversion liability and present it to the Legislature -- the ₹3,50,000+ crore figure must be publicly documented; the NPS corpus ₹4,200 crore (employees' and government contributions already made) must be resolved -- either transferred to PFRDA and employees retained in NPS (for those who prefer) or returned to employees with OPS credit; the 16th Finance Commission memorandum must disclose the OPS actuarial liability as a fiscal risk requiring special treatment.

overview: CAG SFAR (Karnataka, 2025) Final Summary: Revenue Surplus ₹6,524 crore; Debt-GSDP 20.6 per cent; Own-Tax CAGR 14.2 per cent; 5 guarantees ₹50,000+ crore = 32 per cent Revenue Receipts; CAMPA ₹4,500+ crore idle; UKP ₹34,000 crore overrun; CapEx 2.4 per cent GSDP; Kalyana Karnataka regional equity gap; 16th Finance Commission outlook -- Karnataka as net tax exporter (receives less than it contributes) vs contested formula.

stats.value: Revenue Surplus ₹6,524 crore; Debt-GSDP 20.6 per cent; Own-Tax CAGR 14.2 per cent; 5 guarantees ₹50,000+ crore (32 per cent Revenue Receipts); UKP ₹34,000 crore overrun; CapEx 2.4 per cent GSDP

source.quote: Revenue Surplus Rs. 6,524 crore. Debt-GSDP 20.6 per cent. Own-Tax CAGR 14.2 per cent. 5 guarantees 32 per cent Revenue Receipts. CapEx 2.4 per cent

keyFindings.text: Karnataka presents the most interesting fiscal balance among states covered in this series. It is simultaneously: (a) fiscally healthy (Revenue Surplus, Debt-GSDP 20.6 per cent -- best among large states); (b) fiscally strained by political commitments (5 guarantees Rs. 50,000+ crore = 32 per cent Revenue Receipts); (c) a net tax exporter to the Union (Karnataka contributes approximately Rs. 4.1 lakh crore in taxes but receives approximately Rs. 1.2 lakh crore in devolution -- the highest net-contributor state alongside Maharashtra); (d) regionally inequitable within the state (Bengaluru vs Kalyana Karnataka). The 16th Finance Commission's horizontal devolution formula is politically contested precisely because states like Karnataka argue that contributing states should not be penalised for fiscal performance, while receiving states (Bihar, Jharkhand, UP) argue that fiscal capacity reflects historical investment patterns, not current effort.

source.quote: Revenue Surplus Rs. 6,524 crore. 5 guarantees 32 per cent. Debt 20.6 per cent. Own-Tax CAGR 14.2 per cent

recommendations: Karnataka Finance Department's 16th Finance Commission memorandum should present a three-part argument: (a) contribution argument (₹4.1 lakh crore contributed vs ₹1.2 lakh crore received -- Karnataka subsidises poorer states, as designed, but the ratio should be transparent); (b) expenditure need argument (Bengaluru as economic engine requires infrastructure investment that benefits all states through GST and income tax); (c) guarantee risk argument (5 guarantees ₹50,000+ crore create fiscal risk that, if materialised, would require central fiscal support -- the Commission should factor this into Karnataka's risk-adjusted fiscal capacity).

keyFindings.text: UP's Saubhagya programme connected 1.66 crore households -- one of India's largest electrification achievements -- but 40 per cent of these connections are not energised (physically connected to the grid but receiving no supply). A household with a meter and a wire that carries no electricity has not been electrified in any meaningful sense. The AT&C loss of 24.74 per cent (vs 15 per cent target) in a state that has invested Rs. 12,000+ crore in DDUGJY infrastructure indicates that power purchased is being lost to technical inefficiencies, theft, and meter bypass at a scale that makes UPPCL's financial model unviable. The 44 per cent unmetered DTRs mean that agricultural consumption -- notoriously hard to meter and heavily subsidised -- is unquantified and potentially heavily understated.

source.quote: 1.66 crore connections. 44 per cent DTRs unmetered. Rs. 7,200+ crore. AT&C 24.74 per cent. 40 per cent not energised

recommendations: UP UPPCL must: (a) energise all 40 per cent un-energised connections within 6 months (identify feeder capacity gaps and resolve transformer overloading); (b) meter all 44 per cent unmetered DTRs within 12 months (procure smart DTR meters through a single centrally-tendered procurement); (c) reduce AT&C losses to 20 per cent within 2 years and 15 per cent within 4 years through area-wise AT&C reduction programme; (d) publish monthly AT&C loss data by district on UPPCL website; ₹7,200+ crore revenue loss recovery plan must be presented to UPERC.

ministry: State Goods and Services Tax (SGST) Department, Government of Maharashtra
reportNo: Report No. 6 of 2025 (Compliance Audit -- SGST) -- Part VII: EWB Analysis
title: Compliance Audit -- Maharashtra GST Part VII: E-Way Bill Phantom Billing -- ₹39,100 crore Fake Transactions; Supplier Without Premises; Buyer Without Turnover; EWB Without Corresponding GSTR-1; Round-Tripping Identified in 12 Sectors; Iron/Steel and Construction Materials ₹18,000 crore Suspicious EWBs
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (MH SGST, 2025) Part VII: E-Way Bill (EWB) phantom billing analysis -- ₹39,100 crore suspicious EWBs identified; supplier without registered premises (shell entity); buyer without corresponding turnover in GST returns; EWB generated without corresponding GSTR-1 invoice; round-tripping (circular transactions among related parties to generate fake ITC); iron/steel and construction materials ₹18,000 crore suspicious; 12 sectors with systemic phantom billing.

stats.label: ₹39,100 crore phantom EWBs; shell suppliers; round-tripping 12 sectors; iron/steel ₹18,000 crore
stats.value: ₹39,100 crore suspicious EWBs; supplier without premises; buyer without turnover; EWB without GSTR-1; round-tripping 12 sectors; iron/steel + construction ₹18,000 crore suspicious

source.quote: Rs. 39,100 crore phantom EWBs. supplier without premises. buyer without turnover. round-tripping 12 sectors. iron/steel Rs. 18,000 crore

keyFindings.text: E-Way Bill phantom billing is the most sophisticated form of GST fraud: a shell entity (supplier with registered GST number but no real business) generates EWBs for goods that do not physically move. The buyer uses these EWBs to claim Input Tax Credit (ITC) on taxes never actually paid. The shell supplier, having collected GST from the buyer, disappears (files nil returns, suspends GST number) without remitting tax to the government. The buyer retains the fraudulently claimed ITC. Net loss: full GST on the phantom transaction value. Iron and steel -- India's most traded industrial commodities -- are ideal for this fraud because EWBs are required for every movement above Rs. 50,000, creating enormous EWB data that is difficult to manually verify. Maharashtra's Rs. 39,100 crore in suspicious EWBs represents potential ITC fraud of Rs. 7,000-11,700 crore (at 18-30 per cent GST rate on transaction value).

source.quote: Rs. 39,100 crore phantom EWBs. shell suppliers. round-tripping. iron/steel Rs. 18,000 crore

recommendations: Maharashtra SGST must immediately implement AI-driven EWB-to-GSTR-1 reconciliation -- all EWBs where the supplier has no corresponding GSTR-1 entry must be flagged and the buyer's ITC provisional disallowed; all 12 identified high-risk sectors must have enhanced risk-based scrutiny; shell supplier identification (no premises + nil GSTR-3B + large EWB generation) must trigger automatic GST Intelligence referral; recovery cases must be filed against buyers who claimed ITC against phantom supplier EWBs.
