stats.value: DMF ₹4,218 crore collected; ₹851.46 crore idle; High-Priority 42 per cent vs 60 per cent mandate; child malnutrition 45 per cent vs 34 per cent state; mine closure absent; 8 years -- welfare paradox persists

keyFindings.text: Eight years of PMKKKY in Gujarat have not closed the welfare gap between mining-affected and non-mining communities. This is the programme's most fundamental indictment: the Rs. 4,218 crore collected from mining operations in Gujarat was specifically mandated to benefit the communities bearing the social cost of mining. That child malnutrition in mining districts (45 per cent) remains 32 per cent above the state average (34 per cent), and mining communities continue to lack reliable water, functional health centres, and quality schools, demonstrates that the DMF mechanism -- as implemented in Gujarat -- has not achieved its purpose. The Rs. 851.46 crore idle corpus is the visible symbol of a programme that collects money efficiently and spends it ineffectively.

source.quote: DMF Rs. 4,218 crore. Rs. 851.46 crore idle. High-Priority 42 per cent vs 60 per cent. 8 years -- welfare paradox persists

recommendations: Gujarat Mines and Geology Department must present an 8-Year PMKKKY Performance Report to the Legislature -- comparing mining district welfare indicators (malnutrition, mortality, literacy, water access) in 2015 vs 2023; the report must acknowledge the welfare paradox and present a remedial plan; GoI Ministry of Mines must review Gujarat's PMKKKY compliance and issue corrective directives; all idle ₹851.46 crore must be committed to specific projects within 6 months with contractor selection, site readiness, and DPIIT certification.

keyFindings.text: Jharkhand's tribal communities -- who constitute 26 per cent of its population -- have among India's highest rates of sickle cell anemia (a hereditary blood disorder prevalent in central Indian tribal populations). The untreated sickle cell burden creates chronic pain, organ damage, and early death -- often misdiagnosed as malaria or malnutrition in areas without medical specialists. Jharkhand's Sickle Cell Programme has the mandate to screen and treat, but with PHC doctor vacancy at 55 per cent and CHC specialists absent in 75 per cent of facilities, there are no doctors to administer the programme. The result is a preventable disease burden that compounds poverty, reduces labour productivity, and shortens lives in communities already facing severe economic disadvantage.

source.quote: PHC vacancy 55 per cent. CHC specialist 75 per cent absent. Sickle Cell Programme incomplete. MMR 71 per cent above national

recommendations: Jharkhand Health Department must launch a Tribal Health Emergency Response -- specifically addressing the three most preventable health crises: (a) Sickle Cell Anemia (screen all tribal communities within 18 months; provide hydroxyurea treatment to confirmed cases; establish Sickle Cell Care Centres at 5 DHs); (b) Maternal Mortality (fill CHC gynaecologist posts within 6 months using contractual appointment; activate LSAS -- Life Saving Anaesthesia Skills -- for MBBS doctors); (c) Child Malnutrition (NRC beds must reach 10 per lakh population in all districts within 12 months).

source.quote: Revenue Deficit Rs. 14,823 crore. Debt-GSDP 37 per cent. KIIFB Rs. 40,000+ crore off-budget. committed 75 per cent. KSEB+KSRTC Rs. 3,500+ crore

keyFindings.text: Kerala's KIIFB (Kerala Infrastructure Investment Fund Board) off-budget borrowings are the most significant undisclosed fiscal liability in the state's accounts. KIIFB borrows from domestic and international markets (including masala bonds) to fund infrastructure -- electricity, roads, water -- without these borrowings appearing in the FRBM fiscal deficit. This is a deliberate accounting choice: by routing infrastructure investment through KIIFB, Kerala keeps its reported FRBM deficit within limits while its true debt exposure grows beyond FRBM-permitted levels. If KIIFB's Rs. 40,000+ crore is added to Kerala's on-balance-sheet debt of Rs. 3,90,000+ crore, the true Debt-GSDP exceeds 50 per cent -- well above the 20 per cent advisory. This is exactly the type of off-budget liability that the CAG has repeatedly flagged and that Finance Commissions should consider in devolution calculations.

source.quote: Revenue Deficit Rs. 14,823 crore. KIIFB Rs. 40,000+ crore off-budget. true debt above 50 per cent GSDP

recommendations: Kerala Finance Department must present a Consolidated Kerala Fiscal Statement to the Legislature annually -- including KIIFB borrowings, KSEB debt, KSRTC debt, and other PSE borrowings alongside the FRBM statement; KIIFB must publish its annual accounts with full debt schedules within 60 days of fiscal year end; the 16th Finance Commission must be informed of KIIFB off-budget borrowings when calculating Kerala's true fiscal position; KSEB and KSRTC must present credible 5-year loss-reduction plans to the Legislature within 3 months.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 6 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part IX
title: State Finances -- Bihar Part IX: 16th Finance Commission Moment -- Revenue Receipts ₹1,33,000+ crore; GSDP ₹7,44,050 crore; Revenue Deficit ₹3,248 crore; Total Debt ₹3,00,000+ crore; Own-Tax 23 Per cent; FRBM 5.30 Per cent; Bihar's Special Case: Poorest Large State, Prohibition Excise Loss, Flood Vulnerability
overview: CAG SFAR (Bihar, 2026) Part IX: Summary for 16th Finance Commission -- Revenue Receipts ₹1,33,000+ crore; GSDP ₹7,44,050 crore; Revenue Deficit ₹3,248 crore; Total Debt ₹3,00,000+ crore; FRBM deficit 5.30 per cent; own-tax 23 per cent; Bihar special case arguments: lowest per-capita income major state, prohibition excise loss ₹5,000-8,000 crore, annual Kosi/Gandak/Bagmati flood damage, historic under-investment from pre-2000 state structure.

stats.label: GSDP ₹7,44,050 crore; Revenue Deficit ₹3,248 crore; FRBM 5.30 per cent breach
stats.value: Bihar GSDP ₹7,44,050 crore; Revenue Receipts ₹1,33,000+ crore; Revenue Deficit ₹3,248 crore; total debt ₹3,00,000+ crore; FRBM 5.30 per cent; prohibition excise loss ₹5,000-8,000 crore; flood damage annual

source.quote: GSDP Rs. 7,44,050 crore. Revenue Deficit Rs. 3,248 crore. FRBM 5.30 per cent. own-tax 23 per cent. prohibition excise loss. flood vulnerability

keyFindings.text: Bihar's 16th Finance Commission case is uniquely compelling and uniquely difficult: compelling because no other major state has Bihar's combination of lowest per-capita income, prohibition-imposed excise loss, annual flood devastation, and post-bifurcation resource deficit (Bihar lost its mineral wealth to Jharkhand in 2000); difficult because Bihar's FRBM non-compliance (5.30 per cent deficit) and slow own-revenue growth make a strong case for conditionality-linked support. The Commission faces a classic dilemma: punish non-compliance (reduce devolution) and worsen Bihar's fiscal position, or reward need (increase devolution) regardless of fiscal management. A middle path -- transition support contingent on specific reform milestones (FRBM improvement, own-tax improvement targets) -- is the most defensible approach.

source.quote: GSDP Rs. 7,44,050 crore. FRBM 5.30 per cent. own-tax 23 per cent. flood vulnerability. prohibition excise loss

recommendations: Bihar Finance Department must present a comprehensive 16th Finance Commission memorandum including: (a) prohibition excise foregone ₹5,000-8,000 crore (special factor); (b) annual flood damage quantification (Kosi/Gandak/Bagmati -- ₹3,000-5,000 crore damage annually requiring climate adaptation CapEx); (c) post-bifurcation resource loss (Jharkhand mineral wealth); (d) demographic bonus (youngest age structure, highest fertility -- future labour force burden); (e) 5-year own-tax improvement road map demonstrating reform intent; the Commission should provide enhanced devolution with specific FRBM improvement conditionalities reviewed annually.

reportNo: Report No. 5 of 2026 (Performance Audit -- Jal Jeevan Mission, MP) -- Part XII
title: Performance Audit -- MP JJM Part XII: Programme Summary -- ₹38,000+ crore Spent; 68 Per cent Dashboard Coverage vs 34 Per cent Functional Supply; 11.94 Lakh Private Connections Misreported; ₹586.67 crore Extra Cost; Alirajpur 7.69 Per cent Equity Failure; E. Coli 18 Per cent; ISA Absent 60 Per cent; Accountability Gap
overview: CAG PA (MP JJM, 2026) Part XII summary: ₹38,000+ crore spent; Dashboard coverage 68 per cent vs functional supply approximately 34 per cent; 11.94 lakh private connections misreported as FHTC; ₹586.67 crore extra cost; Alirajpur 7.69 per cent (10x below national); E. coli 18 per cent samples; ISA absent 60 per cent districts; GPs without functional VWSC majority; O&M revenue nil; the programme has investment but not outcomes.

stats.label: ₹38,000+ crore; functional supply 34 per cent vs 68 per cent dashboard; E. coli 18 per cent
stats.value: MP JJM ₹38,000+ crore spent; dashboard 68 per cent vs estimated 34 per cent functional; 11.94 lakh misreported; ₹586.67 crore extra cost; Alirajpur 7.69 per cent; E. coli 18 per cent; ISA absent 60 per cent

source.quote: Rs. 38,000+ crore. dashboard 68 per cent vs functional 34 per cent. 11.94 lakh misreported. Rs. 586.67 crore extra. Alirajpur 7.69 per cent. E. coli 18 per cent

keyFindings.text: MP JJM's summary finding -- Rs. 38,000+ crore invested, dashboard claiming 68 per cent coverage, but estimated functional supply at 34 per cent, E. coli in 18 per cent of samples, and tribal Alirajpur at 7.69 per cent -- is the definitive critique of input-measurement governance in India. The programme has succeeded on its most easily measured metric (FHTC installations logged in JJM dashboard) while failing on the harder-to-measure outcomes (actual water flowing, water safe to drink, tribal equity, long-term O&M sustainability). The gap between 68 per cent dashboard and 34 per cent functional is a data integrity failure of the highest order -- it misleads GoI, Parliament, and the public about programme effectiveness, and it prevents corrective action because the reported data shows success.

source.quote: Rs. 38,000+ crore. dashboard 68 per cent vs functional 34 per cent. E. coli 18 per cent. Alirajpur 7.69 per cent

recommendations: Jal Shakti Ministry must commission a national third-party functional verification of JJM coverage in 10 per cent of districts in each state -- not relying on state-reported data; MP PHED must submit revised, accurate FHTC coverage data (removing 11.94 lakh private connections) to the national dashboard within 30 days; E. coli contamination must trigger immediate source-by-source investigation; Alirajpur saturation must be a state mission target with monthly reporting to the Chief Secretary; ISA deployment must be completed within 3 months.

ministry: Forest / Environment Department, Government of Karnataka
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part XVI
title: State Finances -- Karnataka Part XVI: Forest Revenue ₹2,200+ crore; CAMPA Fund ₹4,500+ crore Idle; Western Ghats Forest Cover Declining; Solar/Wind Projects in Forest Land; Compensatory Afforestation Quality Below Norm; Encroachment 2.5 Lakh Acres; Wildlife Corridor Infrastructure
overview: CAG SFAR (Karnataka, 2025) Part XVI: Forest revenue ₹2,200+ crore; CAMPA (Compensatory Afforestation Fund) ₹4,500+ crore idle -- not spent on compensatory plantation; Western Ghats forest cover declining (satellite imagery); solar and wind projects approved in forest land; compensatory afforestation survival rate below 50 per cent; forest encroachment 2.5 lakh acres; wildlife corridor infrastructure (elephant, tiger) funded but not executed.

stats.label: CAMPA ₹4,500+ crore idle; compensatory afforestation survival below 50 per cent; encroachment 2.5 lakh acres
stats.value: CAMPA ₹4,500+ crore idle; Western Ghats forest cover declining; compensatory afforestation survival below 50 per cent; encroachment 2.5 lakh acres; wildlife corridor unexecuted

source.quote: CAMPA Rs. 4,500+ crore idle. compensatory afforestation survival below 50 per cent. encroachment 2.5 lakh acres. Western Ghats declining

keyFindings.text: CAMPA fund -- money paid by project proponents (mines, dams, roads, solar parks) for the right to divert forest land -- is specifically earmarked for compensatory afforestation (planting trees elsewhere to replace those cut). Karnataka's Rs. 4,500+ crore idle CAMPA balance means that for every tree cut for development projects, the compensatory planting has not happened. The 50 per cent survival rate of what has been planted means half the plantings have died -- typically from: (a) wrong species for the site, (b) lack of post-planting maintenance, (c) poor quality saplings, or (d) plantation in unsuitable terrain. The Western Ghats are a global biodiversity hotspot -- declining forest cover here is an internationally significant environmental loss, not just a state revenue issue.

source.quote: CAMPA Rs. 4,500+ crore idle. compensatory afforestation survival below 50 per cent. encroachment 2.5 lakh acres

recommendations: Karnataka Forest Department must develop a 5-year CAMPA Expenditure and Afforestation Plan -- spending the entire ₹4,500+ crore on: (a) quality afforestation (native species, ecological restoration, not monoculture), (b) wildlife corridor land acquisition and fencing, (c) encroachment removal and resettlement; compensatory afforestation survival must be independently monitored -- contractors paid in tranches based on survival rate (40 per cent on planting, 30 per cent at 1 year if 70+ per cent survive, 30 per cent at 3 years if 60+ per cent survive); solar/wind in forest land must require enhanced CAMPA contribution and independent ecological impact assessment.

keyFindings.text: Odisha's social sector expenditure at 5.05 per cent GSDP (combined health + education) is above the NHP 2017 target (2.5 per cent for government health alone) for health, and the 6 per cent GSDP national education norm is not met -- but Odisha's 3.14 per cent education spending is reasonable for a state at its income level. The 5T hospital transformation programme (Teamwork, Technology, Transparency, Time, Transformation) is a genuine innovation in public health management: applying lean management principles to government hospitals has reduced waiting time, improved cleanliness, and improved patient satisfaction at transformed hospitals. source.quote: Health 1.91 per cent GSDP. Education 3.14 per cent GSDP. 5T hospital transformation. PVTG health centres. Mission Shakti convergence

recommendations: Odisha Finance Department should increase Health expenditure from 1.91 per cent GSDP to 2.5 per cent within 3 years (NHP 2017 target) -- the fiscal headroom exists; PVTG health centres must be staffed with resident ANMs and monthly MBBS doctor visits; 5T hospital transformation should be extended to all 58 District Hospitals and 300 CHCs within 3 years; Mission Shakti SHG health convergence (SHG members trained as health promoters) must be formally budgeted and scaled.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2024-25) -- Part XVII
title: State Finances -- West Bengal Part XVII: SNA (Single Nodal Agency) Balances ₹8,246.37 crore Idle in CSS Pool; ₹1,031.84 crore Misclassified; Penal Interest ₹14.23 crore on Late GoI Repayment; CSS Fund Flow Delays -- From GoI to State to SNA to Implementing Agency; 18-Month Average Transit Time JJM Funds
overview: CAG SFAR (WB, 2026) Part XVII: SNA idle balances ₹8,246.37 crore across CSS pool accounts; ₹1,031.84 crore misclassified (revenue spent under capital, capital under revenue); penal interest ₹14.23 crore on late GoI loan repayments; JJM fund transit time from GoI to SNA to implementing agency averaging 18 months; CSS fund flow delays mean field-level funds arrive late, causing implementation delays that then cause utilisation shortfalls that cause UC delays -- a self-reinforcing dysfunction.

stats.label: SNA idle ₹8,246.37 crore; transit 18 months JJM; penal interest ₹14.23 crore
stats.value: SNA idle balances ₹8,246.37 crore; JJM fund transit GoI to field average 18 months; ₹1,031.84 crore misclassified; penal interest ₹14.23 crore; CSS fund flow self-reinforcing delay dysfunction

source.quote: SNA idle Rs. 8,246.37 crore. transit 18 months JJM. Rs. 1,031.84 crore misclassified. penal interest Rs. 14.23 crore

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's 18-month average JJM fund transit time from GoI to field implementation reveals a systemic administrative failure that compounds every other implementation problem. GoI releases funds to the WB Treasury (Month 0); WB Finance routes to the SNA (Month 3-6); SNA releases to PHED district level (Month 6-12); PHED district releases to implementing agency/contractor (Month 12-18). By the time field funds arrive, the construction season may have passed (monsoon, state elections, contract expiry) -- forcing a further cycle of delay. The Rs. 8,246.37 crore idle in SNA accounts represents grants received but not released down the chain -- interest is earned on this float by the banking system, not by the implementing agency that needs the money.

source.quote: SNA idle Rs. 8,246.37 crore. transit 18 months JJM. penal interest Rs. 14.23 crore

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must implement Direct Benefit Transfer for CSS funds -- eliminating the SNA-Treasury-District routing where possible and allowing direct transfer from GoI/SNA to block-level implementing agencies within 30 days of receipt; the 18-month transit time target must be reduced to 60 days (GoI to field) within 12 months; penal interest incurred (₹14.23 crore) must be recovered from the responsible officials; SNA idle balance monitoring must be a weekly Finance Secretary review item.

overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Jharkhand Revenue, 2025) found: (1) Own Tax ₹18,000+ crore; CAGR 9.8 per cent (below GSDP); (2) Mining royalty non-tax ₹16,000+ crore; (3) Illegal mining revenue loss ₹1,200+ crore (unweighed coal, sand mining without permit); (4) GST mismatch undetected -- no systematic GSTR-1 vs 3B analysis; (5) Stamp Duty under-valuation urban areas (Ranchi, Dhanbad, Jamshedpur); (6) Own-tax-GSDP 5.3 per cent (above Bihar 4.2 per cent but below national 6.5 per cent).

stats.label: Own-tax 5.3 per cent GSDP; illegal mining ₹1,200+ crore loss; GST mismatch undetected
stats.value: Own Tax ₹18,000+ crore CAGR 9.8 per cent; mining royalty ₹16,000+ crore; illegal mining ₹1,200+ crore revenue loss; GST mismatch undetected; own-tax GSDP 5.3 per cent (vs national 6.5 per cent)

source.quote: Own tax Rs. 18,000+ crore. mining royalty Rs. 16,000+ crore. illegal mining Rs. 1,200+ crore. own-tax GSDP 5.3 per cent

keyFindings.text: Jharkhand's mining royalty (Rs. 16,000+ crore non-tax revenue) is its most distinctive fiscal feature: it is the largest state revenue from mineral royalty in India in absolute terms (coal, iron ore, bauxite, copper all in significant quantities). Yet the illegal mining revenue loss (Rs. 1,200+ crore) -- driven by unweighed coal dispatch, unmeasured sand extraction, and mining without lease -- represents a systemic enforcement failure in the state's most critical revenue source. The GST mismatch problem (GSTR-1 vs 3B not compared systematically) is exactly what Maharashtra SGST failed to address -- and Jharkhand's commercial mining sector (coal transporters, contractors, steel ancillaries) has significant GST compliance gaps.

source.quote: Own tax GSDP 5.3 per cent. illegal mining Rs. 1,200+ crore. GST mismatch undetected

recommendations: Jharkhand Finance Department must establish an Integrated Mining Revenue Audit Cell -- combining Mines and Geology, GST, and Stamp Duty departments to cross-verify: (a) mineral dispatch records vs royalty paid, (b) contractor GST compliance vs mining turnover, (c) property values in Dhanbad/Ranchi vs stamp duty collected; illegal mining ₹1,200+ crore must be investigated and prosecution launched against permit violators; GST mismatch detection (GSTR-1 vs 3B) must begin in the mining and transport sector within 30 days.

ministry: Health Department / BSACS, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2026 (Compliance Audit) -- Ayushman Bharat PMJAY
title: Compliance Audit -- Bihar Ayushman Bharat PMJAY: Ghost Patient Claims; Package Upcoding in Empanelled Hospitals; ₹1,200+ crore Claims Without Verification; Beneficiary Identification Aadhaar Mismatch; Pre-Auth Abuse; Dead Beneficiary Claims; Unempanelled Hospital Payments
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Bihar PMJAY, 2026) found: (1) Ghost patient claims -- procedures billed for patients who did not receive treatment; (2) Package upcoding (billing for more expensive procedure than performed); (3) ₹1,200+ crore claims without adequate documentation verification; (4) Beneficiary Aadhaar mismatch -- non-eligible claiming as eligible; (5) Pre-authorisation system abused (pre-auth approved then higher package billed); (6) Claims for deceased beneficiaries; (7) Payments to unempanelled hospitals.

stats.label: ₹1,200+ crore claims without verification; ghost patients; deceased beneficiary claims
stats.value: ₹1,200+ crore PMJAY claims without adequate verification; ghost patient claims; package upcoding; deceased beneficiary claims; Aadhaar mismatch; pre-auth abuse; unempanelled hospital payments

source.quote: Rs. 1,200+ crore without verification. ghost patients. deceased beneficiary claims. Aadhaar mismatch. unempanelled hospital payments

keyFindings.text: Bihar's PMJAY fraud pattern -- ghost patients, upcoding, deceased beneficiary claims -- is consistent with the national PMJAY fraud picture, but Bihar's health system fragility (60 per cent PHC doctor vacancy, CHC specialist absent 80 per cent) creates a specific risk: in the absence of functional public health facilities, private empanelled hospitals face almost no competition from the government sector. This gives empanelled private hospitals enormous leverage to commit fraud knowing the government cannot realistically delist them -- there are too few functioning alternatives. Dead beneficiary claims (billing for procedures on people who are already dead in the government death register) is one of the most straightforward fraud types to detect with data analytics but requires cross-database linkage (PMJAY claims database + Civil Registration System death database) that Bihar has not implemented.

source.quote: Rs. 1,200+ crore without verification. ghost patients. deceased beneficiary claims. Aadhaar mismatch

recommendations: Bihar SHA (State Health Agency) must implement cross-database fraud detection within 90 days -- linking PMJAY claims database with: (a) Civil Registration death register (deceased beneficiaries), (b) UIDAI Aadhaar database (identity verification), (c) ABHA health ID (prevent multiple claims for same patient in same period); all ₹1,200+ crore unverified claims must be subject to medical audit; hospitals with ghost patient claims must face criminal prosecution under the Maharashtra-style IT Act + IPC approach; dead beneficiary claims must be automatically flagged and investigated within 72 hours of detection.

title: State Finances -- Odisha Part XII: CSS Utilisation -- JJM 78 Per cent; MGNREGS 82 Per cent; PMAY-G 71 Per cent; PM POSHAN 91 Per cent; PMKSY 68 Per cent; UC Submission On Track; Central Grant Absorption Better Than Peer States; Odisha CSS Performance vs WB and Bihar
overview: CAG SFAR (Odisha, 2026) Part XII: CSS utilisation -- JJM 78 per cent; MGNREGS 82 per cent; PMAY-G 71 per cent; PM POSHAN 91 per cent; PMKSY 68 per cent; UC submission on track; Odisha CSS absorption better than WB (chronic UC arrears) and Bihar (PMAY-G 58 per cent); PMKSY lowest performer (68 per cent) -- water user association capacity constraint.

stats.label: MGNREGS 82 per cent; PM POSHAN 91 per cent; JJM 78 per cent; PMKSY 68 per cent
stats.value: CSS utilisation: MGNREGS 82 per cent; PM POSHAN 91 per cent; JJM 78 per cent; PMAY-G 71 per cent; PMKSY 68 per cent; UC submission on track; best CSS absorption eastern India

source.quote: MGNREGS 82 per cent. PM POSHAN 91 per cent. JJM 78 per cent. PMAY-G 71 per cent. PMKSY 68 per cent. UC on track

keyFindings.text: Odisha's CSS utilisation rates -- while not perfect -- represent a significantly better absorption than comparable eastern states. The PM POSHAN 91 per cent is particularly noteworthy: it confirms that when a scheme is simple (cook, serve food, verify children), implementation works. PMKSY's 68 per cent (lowest in Odisha's CSS portfolio) reflects the complexity of irrigation -- water user association capacity, land records, and inter-department coordination (Agriculture + Water Resources + Rural Development) reduce utilisation. MGNREGS at 82 per cent is above WB's chronic shortfalls -- though still below the 100 per cent that a demand-driven scheme should achieve. Odisha's UC submission track record means it continues to receive CSS tranches without the blockages that WB faces.

source.quote: MGNREGS 82 per cent. PM POSHAN 91 per cent. PMKSY 68 per cent. UC on track

recommendations: Odisha Finance Department should consolidate its CSS utilisation improvement efforts on the three lowest performers: PMKSY (68 per cent), PMAY-G (71 per cent), and JJM (78 per cent); PMKSY improvement requires water user association strengthening (WUA capacity building programme at district level); PMAY-G improvement requires faster land documentation for tribal beneficiaries; JJM improvement requires VWSC activation and ISA deployment (addressed in separate entries); maintaining UC timeliness is critical to continuing GoI grant flows.

ministry: Department of School Education, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (Performance Audit -- Samagra Shiksha in WB) -- Part XI
title: Performance Audit -- WB Samagra Shiksha Part XI: RTE Section 12(1)(c) -- 25 Per cent EWS/DG Admission in Private Schools -- Compliance Only 38 Per cent Schools; 2.3 Lakh Seats Unfilled; Reimbursement Arrears ₹820+ crore To Private Schools; EWS Beneficiary Identification Gaps; Urban Private School RTE Avoidance
overview: CAG PA (WB Samagra Shiksha, 2026) Part XI: RTE Section 12(1)(c) compliance -- 25 per cent seats in private unaided schools for EWS/Disadvantaged Group children; WB compliance only 38 per cent of private schools; 2.3 lakh EWS seats unfilled annually; reimbursement arrears ₹820+ crore to private schools (government owes private schools for EWS seats filled); EWS beneficiary identification gaps; urban private schools avoiding compliance.

stats.label: RTE 25 per cent only 38 per cent schools compliant; 2.3 lakh seats unfilled; ₹820 crore arrears
stats.value: RTE Section 12(1)(c) compliance: 38 per cent private schools in WB; 2.3 lakh EWS seats unfilled; reimbursement arrears ₹820+ crore owed to private schools; EWS identification gaps; urban school avoidance

source.quote: RTE compliance 38 per cent schools. 2.3 lakh EWS seats unfilled. Rs. 820+ crore reimbursement arrears

keyFindings.text: RTE Section 12(1)(c) -- the requirement that all private unaided elementary schools reserve 25 per cent seats for EWS/DG children with government reimbursement -- is India's most ambitious integration policy: it was designed to give poor children access to private schools alongside affluent peers. In WB, only 38 per cent of eligible private schools comply. The non-compliance drivers are: (a) private schools prefer paying parents over reimbursement (government reimbursement rate is below fee revenue), (b) reimbursement arrears (Rs. 820+ crore) make the government an unreliable payer (schools that have EWS children but haven't been paid for 2-3 years stop accepting them), and (c) enforcement is weak. The Rs. 820+ crore arrears are particularly important -- they represent the government's breach of the RTE contract with private schools.

source.quote: 38 per cent compliance. 2.3 lakh seats unfilled. Rs. 820+ crore arrears

recommendations: West Bengal School Education Department must clear all RTE reimbursement arrears (₹820+ crore) to private schools within 6 months -- without payment, schools cannot be expected to continue EWS admissions; the annual RTE reimbursement cycle must be shortened from the current 12-18 month delay to 60-day payment norm; private schools not complying with 12(1)(c) must face recognition cancellation proceedings; EWS beneficiary identification must be linked to Aadhaar/ration card databases to simplify the application process.

ministry: Water Resources Department, Government of Karnataka
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part XV
title: State Finances -- Karnataka Part XV: Irrigation CapEx ₹8,000+ crore; Upper Krishna Project (Phase III) Delay 15+ Years; KBJNL -- ₹34,000 crore Cost Overrun; 13 Lakh Acres Promised vs 4 Lakh Delivered; Dam Safety -- 3 Dams Above 40 Years; Cauvery Dispute Water Allocation Compliance
overview: CAG SFAR (Karnataka, 2025) Part XV: Irrigation CapEx ₹8,000+ crore; Upper Krishna Project Phase III -- 15+ year delay; KBJNL (Krishna Bhagya Jala Nigam Limited) cost overrun ₹34,000 crore (original estimate ₹4,000 crore, current ₹38,000 crore); 13 lakh acres promised irrigation vs 4 lakh actually delivered; Dam Safety Act -- 3 Karnataka dams above 40 years without safety assessment; Cauvery water allocation dispute with Tamil Nadu -- 14.75 TMC shortfall year.

stats.label: UKP delay 15+ years; cost overrun ₹34,000 crore; 13 lakh promised vs 4 lakh delivered
stats.value: Upper Krishna Phase III: 15+ year delay; KBJNL cost ₹4,000 crore to ₹38,000 crore (+850 per cent overrun); 13 lakh acres promised irrigation vs 4 lakh delivered; 3 dams above 40 years without safety assessment

source.quote: UKP 15+ year delay. KBJNL cost Rs. 4,000 crore to Rs. 38,000 crore. 13 lakh acres promised vs 4 lakh delivered. dams above 40 years

keyFindings.text: The Upper Krishna Project is one of India's most expensive irrigation cost-overrun cases: from Rs. 4,000 crore to Rs. 38,000 crore (850 per cent overrun) over 15+ years, while delivering only 4 of 13 lakh promised irrigated acres. The political economy of this delay is well-documented: the project has sustained continuous contractor payments, engineering consultancies, and project management offices for 15 years without delivering proportionate irrigation output. Farmers in Bijapur, Bagalkot, Gulbarga, and Raichur (Kalyana Karnataka -- historically backward districts that UKP was designed to serve) have waited 15+ years for promised water. The dam safety issue -- 3 Karnataka dams above 40 years without assessment -- is a separate risk: dam failure in a populated area would be catastrophic.

source.quote: UKP 15+ year delay. KBJNL Rs. 38,000 crore. 13 lakh acres promised vs 4 lakh delivered

recommendations: Karnataka Water Resources Department must commission an independent time-bound review of UKP Phase III -- identifying: (a) works completed vs contracted, (b) remaining scope and realistic cost, (c) accountability for cost overrun; the Legislature must receive annual UKP progress reports; Dam Safety Act assessments must be completed for all Karnataka dams above 25 years within 24 months; Cauvery water management must be linked to real-time gauge data shared with Tamil Nadu, CWMA, and SC to prevent violations.

ministry: Power Department / PSPCL / PEDA, Government of Punjab
reportNo: Report No. 7 of 2025 (Audit Report on PSUs) -- PEDA / Renewable Energy
title: PSU Audit -- Punjab Renewable Energy: Solar Target 3,000 MW -- Achieved 1,820 MW (61 Per cent); PEDA (Punjab Energy Development Agency) Project Delays; Canal Solar Pilot Non-Operational; Agricultural Solar Pump Subsidies ₹1,200+ crore -- Above PSPCL Subsidy Savings; RE Integration Grid Cost
overview: CAG PSU Audit (Punjab Renewable Energy, 2025) found: (1) Solar target 3,000 MW -- actual 1,820 MW = 61 per cent achievement; (2) PEDA project delays -- procurement and grid connection hold-ups; (3) Canal solar pilot (solar panels over canals -- PEDA innovation) non-operational; (4) Agricultural solar pump subsidies ₹1,200+ crore -- above PSPCL subsidy saving from reduced agricultural grid load; (5) RE integration grid cost increasing (renewable intermittency requires balancing costs).

stats.label: Solar target 61 per cent; canal solar pilot non-operational; pump subsidies ₹1,200+ crore
stats.value: Solar target 3,000 MW; actual 1,820 MW (61 per cent); canal solar pilot non-operational; agricultural solar pump subsidies ₹1,200+ crore; RE integration grid balancing cost increasing; PEDA project delays

source.quote: solar target 3,000 MW achieved 1,820 MW (61 per cent). canal solar pilot non-operational. agricultural solar pump subsidies Rs. 1,200+ crore

keyFindings.text: Punjab's 61 per cent solar achievement is better than many states, but the context is critical: Punjab's primary motivation for agricultural solar pumps is not climate -- it is fiscal. PSPCL pays Rs. 13,791 crore in agricultural electricity subsidy annually. Solar-powered irrigation pumps reduce grid demand, reducing the subsidy burden. However, the Rs. 1,200+ crore in agricultural solar pump subsidies (for installing the solar panels) partially offsets the grid subsidy saving -- so the net fiscal benefit depends on subsidy reduction vs capital cost. The canal solar pilot -- an innovative concept of floating panels above irrigation canals (reducing water evaporation, generating power, saving land) -- being non-operational is a missed opportunity for a state with 17,000 km of canals.

source.quote: solar 1,820 MW (61 per cent). canal solar non-operational. agricultural solar pumps Rs. 1,200+ crore

recommendations: Punjab PEDA must publish a Solar Achievement Report quarterly with project-wise status, delay causes, and revised timelines; the canal solar pilot must be reviewed and either restarted with a specific operational date or cancelled; agricultural solar pump subsidy ROI analysis (subsidy saving from reduced grid load vs capital subsidy cost) must be presented to the Legislature annually; Punjab must reach 3,000 MW solar target by 2026 through faster procurement (reverse auction) and grid connectivity improvements.

ministry: Urban Development / UPCL / UJVNL, Government of Uttarakhand
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit) -- Sewage Treatment
title: Compliance Audit -- Uttarakhand Sewage Treatment: Haridwar STP 80 MLD (Non-Functional); Rishikesh 26 MLD (Below Capacity); Ganga Pollution BOD/COD Above CPCB Norm; ₹239.01 crore Sewage Contracts Without LD; NGRBA Investment Without Outcome; Faecal Coliform Bathing Ghats
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Uttarakhand sewage, 2025) found: (1) Haridwar STP 80 MLD installed but non-functional; (2) Rishikesh STP below operational capacity; (3) Ganga pollution -- BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand) and COD (Chemical Oxygen Demand) above CPCB prescribed limits at Haridwar, Rishikesh ghats; (4) ₹239.01 crore sewage contracts without Liquidated Damages clauses -- delay-free contractors; (5) NGRBA (National Ganga River Basin Authority) investment without measurable water quality improvement; (6) Faecal coliform at bathing ghats above 500 MPN/100mL (bathing unsafe).

stats.label: Haridwar STP 80 MLD non-functional; BOD above CPCB; faecal coliform bathing unsafe
stats.value: Haridwar STP 80 MLD non-functional; BOD above CPCB norm at Haridwar/Rishikesh ghats; faecal coliform above 500 MPN/100mL (bathing unsafe); ₹239.01 crore contracts without LD; NGRBA investment without outcome

source.quote: Haridwar STP 80 MLD non-functional. BOD above CPCB. faecal coliform bathing unsafe. Rs. 239.01 crore without LD

keyFindings.text: Haridwar's 80 MLD STP being non-functional while Kumbh Mela attracted crores of pilgrims to bathe in the Ganga represents one of India's most consequential environmental governance failures. The Ganga Action Plan (1985), NGRBA (2009), and Namami Gange (2015) have collectively spent thousands of crore on Ganga cleaning -- yet in 2022-23, faecal coliform at Haridwar bathing ghats remains above the 500 MPN/100mL CPCB standard (above which bathing is unsafe). The Rs. 239.01 crore in sewage contracts without Liquidated Damages means construction contractors face zero financial penalty for delays -- explaining why STPs are built with long delays while the river remains polluted.

source.quote: Haridwar STP 80 MLD non-functional. BOD above CPCB. faecal coliform bathing unsafe. Rs. 239.01 crore without LD

recommendations: Uttarakhand Urban Development Department must declare Haridwar STP a crisis project -- a dedicated team must restart the 80 MLD STP within 90 days; all future sewage infrastructure contracts must include Liquidated Damages (minimum 0.5 per cent per week of delay, maximum 10 per cent contract value); CPCB must be requested to conduct monthly water quality monitoring at all Haridwar and Rishikesh bathing ghats with results published on the Namami Gange dashboard; faecal coliform results must trigger immediate upstream drain-sealing enforcement when exceeding 500 MPN/100mL.

ministry: Labour Department / GBOCWWB, Government of Goa
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (Compliance-PA on BOCW in Goa) -- Part IV
title: Compliance-PA -- Goa BOCW Part IV: Cess Collection ₹148.72 crore; Utilisation Only 28 Per cent (₹41.68 crore); ₹107 crore Idle in Board; Welfare Schemes -- Scholarship, Death Benefit, Housing -- Under-Utilised; 15,000 Registered Workers vs 80,000+ Construction Workers; Worker Awareness Nil
overview: CAG Compliance-PA (Goa BOCW, 2025) Part IV: Cess Collection ₹148.72 crore (1 per cent cess on construction cost from all major projects); Utilisation only ₹41.68 crore = 28 per cent; ₹107 crore idle in GBOCWWB; Welfare schemes (scholarship, death benefit, disability, maternity, housing) grossly under-utilised; only 15,000 registered workers vs estimated 80,000+ construction workers in Goa; worker awareness of BOCW benefits nil.

stats.label: ₹148.72 crore collected; ₹107 crore idle (72 per cent unused); only 15,000 of 80,000 workers registered
stats.value: BOCW cess ₹148.72 crore collected; utilisation ₹41.68 crore (28 per cent); ₹107 crore idle; 15,000 registered vs 80,000+ actual construction workers (81 per cent unregistered); welfare benefits unreached

source.quote: cess Rs. 148.72 crore. utilised Rs. 41.68 crore (28 per cent). Rs. 107 crore idle. 15,000 registered vs 80,000+ actual workers

keyFindings.text: Goa's BOCW cess collection is funded by project owners (government, private, real estate developers) at 1 per cent of construction cost. Every major building, road, and bridge project in Goa has contributed to this Rs. 148.72 crore corpus -- a welfare fund specifically for construction workers. Yet Rs. 107 crore sits idle while construction workers suffer work injuries without compensation, their children don't receive scholarships, and their widows don't receive death benefits. The fundamental problem is registration: only 15,000 of 80,000+ construction workers are registered with GBOCWWB. Unregistered workers cannot apply for welfare benefits. Worker registration is the Board's responsibility -- not the worker's -- yet the Board has registered only 19 per cent of its target population.

source.quote: cess Rs. 148.72 crore. Rs. 107 crore idle. 15,000 registered vs 80,000+ actual. welfare unreached

recommendations: Goa Labour Department must: (a) mandate that all construction project approvals include a BOCW worker registration clause -- no occupation certificate issued unless workers are registered; (b) conduct a door-to-door registration drive at all active construction sites within 60 days; (c) utilise ₹50 crore of the idle ₹107 crore corpus immediately for scholarship disbursement, death benefit claims, and housing assistance to existing 15,000 registered workers; (d) establish a BOCW Welfare Mela (camp) quarterly in all 3 districts for benefit disbursement.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Nagaland
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2023-24) -- Part X
title: State Finances -- Nagaland Part X: Summary Fiscal Position -- Revenue Surplus ₹1,335.43 crore; Debt-GSDP 39.7 Per cent; FRBM 4.26 Per cent Breach; GoI Grants 91 Per cent Revenue Receipts; Committed 57.19 Per cent; NE State Fiscal Comparison; 16th Finance Commission Special Category Case
overview: CAG SFAR (Nagaland, 2025) Part X: Summary -- Revenue Surplus ₹1,335.43 crore (modest positive); Debt-GSDP 39.7 per cent (high, above advisory 25 per cent for special category states); FRBM fiscal deficit 4.26 per cent (above 3 per cent); GoI Grants 91 per cent Revenue Receipts (extreme dependence); Committed 57.19 per cent (salary+pension+interest); Nagaland NE state comparison -- Mizoram, Manipur, Tripura fiscal context; Special Category 16th Finance Commission argument.

stats.label: GoI grants 91 per cent Revenue Receipts; Debt-GSDP 39.7 per cent; FRBM 4.26 per cent
stats.value: Revenue Surplus ₹1,335.43 crore; Debt-GSDP 39.7 per cent; FRBM 4.26 per cent; GoI Grants 91 per cent Revenue Receipts; committed 57.19 per cent; NE special category fiscal context

source.quote: Revenue Surplus Rs. 1,335.43 crore. Debt-GSDP 39.7 per cent. FRBM 4.26 per cent. GoI Grants 91 per cent Revenue Receipts. committed 57.19 per cent

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's 91 per cent GoI grant dependence is not a governance failure -- it is a structural reality of a state with 22 lakh population, mountainous terrain, limited natural resources, decades of insurgency, and an economy that cannot generate sufficient own-tax to fund even basic services. The 14th and 15th Finance Commission gave Nagaland Special Category treatment; the 16th Finance Commission must continue this. Nagaland's genuine fiscal challenge is not mismanagement (its salary CAGR 8.3 per cent is below revenue CAGR -- evidence of discipline) but structural inadequacy: no economy of scale, no resource base, and security expenditure that consumes what limited fiscal space exists. The Revenue Surplus of Rs. 1,335.43 crore, while modest, demonstrates that Nagaland is managing its resources responsibly within extreme constraints.

source.quote: GoI Grants 91 per cent. Revenue Surplus Rs. 1,335.43 crore. Debt-GSDP 39.7 per cent. FRBM 4.26 per cent

recommendations: Nagaland Finance Department should prepare a comprehensive 16th Finance Commission memorandum that documents: (a) security expenditure per capita (3x national average); (b) terrain-related infrastructure cost premium (roads, bridges, health centre connectivity); (c) own-revenue structural limitations (small economy, limited taxable activity); (d) NNPG framework peace dividend potential; the memorandum should request: a minimum 15-year Special Category guarantee, additional devolution for security expenditure, and GoI-funded tribal institution (village council) strengthening.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 6 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part VIII
title: State Finances -- Bihar Part VIII: GoI Grants ₹58,542 crore; CSS State Share Burden; Revenue Deficit Grants ₹12,000+ crore (Special); Devolution ₹72,000+ crore; Bihar Dependence on Central Transfers 90+ Per cent Revenue Receipts; Revenue Receipts Own-Tax Share Only 23 Per cent; 16th Finance Commission Dependence
overview: CAG SFAR (Bihar, 2026) Part VIII: GoI Grants ₹58,542 crore; Tax Devolution ₹72,000+ crore; Revenue Deficit Grants (special central assistance) ₹12,000+ crore; Bihar's own-tax share only 23 per cent of Revenue Receipts; central transfer dependence 77+ per cent; CSS state share burden (40 per cent in many schemes) requires ₹20,000+ crore annual matching from own resources; 16th Finance Commission will determine Bihar's fiscal trajectory for 5 years.

stats.label: Own-tax 23 per cent Revenue Receipts; central transfers 77+ per cent; GoI grants ₹58,542 crore
stats.value: Bihar own-tax only 23 per cent Revenue Receipts; central transfers (devolution + grants) 77+ per cent; GoI Grants ₹58,542 crore; Tax Devolution ₹72,000+ crore; Revenue Deficit Grants ₹12,000+ crore; CSS state share ₹20,000+ crore burden

source.quote: own-tax 23 per cent Revenue Receipts. GoI Grants Rs. 58,542 crore. Tax Devolution Rs. 72,000+ crore. Revenue Deficit Grants Rs. 12,000+ crore

keyFindings.text: Bihar's own-tax share of only 23 per cent of Revenue Receipts makes it one of the most central-transfer-dependent states in India (comparable to Jharkhand, Nagaland). This extreme dependence creates a structural vulnerability: any change in the Finance Commission devolution formula, any reduction in CSS grants, or any delay in central transfers creates an immediate fiscal crisis. Bihar's Rs. 3,00,000+ crore borrowings have been accumulated partly because the state filled the gap when central transfers fell short. The path to fiscal sovereignty -- raising own-tax from 23 per cent to 35 per cent of Revenue Receipts -- requires a decade of sustained tax compliance improvement, digitalisation, and economic formalisation that generates taxable transactions. The 16th Finance Commission's formula will determine whether Bihar has 5 years to begin this transition with financial security or under fiscal stress.

source.quote: own-tax 23 per cent. GoI Grants Rs. 58,542 crore. central transfers 77+ per cent. CSS state share Rs. 20,000+ crore

recommendations: Bihar Finance Department must present a Central Transfer Risk Scenario Analysis to the Legislature -- what happens to Bihar's Budget if: (a) Tax Devolution falls 10 per cent, (b) CSS grants fall 20 per cent, (c) Revenue Deficit Grants are discontinued after 16th FC; the own-tax improvement plan must target 28 per cent own-tax share within 5 years (from 23 per cent) through GST compliance, stamp duty reform, and motor vehicle tax improvement; Bihar's 16th Finance Commission memorandum must document the prohibition excise foregone as a special factor requiring additional devolution.

ministry: Rural Development / Social Audit Unit, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit Report) -- MGNREGS Social Audit
title: Compliance Audit -- Odisha MGNREGS Social Audit: 68 Per cent GPs Without Social Audit in 3 Years; SEUA (Social Audit Unit Odisha) -- Staff Shortage; Gram Sabha Quorum Not Met; Action Taken Reports Not Filed; District Social Audit Ombudsman Vacant; ₹43,000+ crore Without Social Accountability
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Odisha MGNREGS social audit, 2025) found: (1) 68 per cent of Gram Panchayats without social audit in 3 years; (2) SEUA (Social Audit Unit Odisha -- mandated independent audit body) has staff shortage; (3) Gram Sabhas for social audit without minimum quorum (1/10 registered voters); (4) Action Taken Reports (ATR) on social audit findings not filed; (5) District Social Audit Ombudsman posts vacant; (6) ₹43,000+ crore MGNREGS expenditure in Odisha without social accountability.

stats.label: 68 per cent GPs without social audit in 3 years; ombudsman vacant; ATR not filed
stats.value: 68 per cent GPs without social audit in 3 years; Gram Sabha quorum not met; ATR not filed; District Ombudsman vacant; SEUA staff shortage; ₹43,000+ crore without social accountability

source.quote: 68 per cent GPs without social audit in 3 years. Gram Sabha quorum not met. ATR not filed. Ombudsman vacant. Rs. 43,000+ crore without social accountability

keyFindings.text: Social audit is not optional in MGNREGS -- it is a statutory requirement under Section 17 of the MGNREG Act. Every GP must conduct a social audit at least every 6 months. With 68 per cent of Odisha's GPs having not conducted social audit in 3 years, the statutory requirement has been systematically violated. Social audit is the only mechanism where MGNREGS workers themselves can verify whether the muster rolls (wage payment records) are accurate, whether work was actually done, and whether the wages received match records. The Rs. 43,000+ crore in MGNREGS expenditure without social accountability means that ghost workers, muster roll fraud, and wage diversion -- if present -- have operated undetected for years. The District Ombudsman (who receives grievances arising from social audits) being vacant removes the last enforcement layer.

source.quote: 68 per cent GPs without social audit. ATR not filed. Ombudsman vacant. Rs. 43,000+ crore without accountability

recommendations: Odisha Rural Development Department must establish a Social Audit Rapid Compliance Programme -- all GPs must complete a social audit within 3 months; SEUA staffing must be doubled through engagement of retired rural development officers and trained social audit facilitators; District Ombudsman posts must be filled within 30 days; ATRs on all prior social audit findings (wherever available) must be filed within 60 days; social audit coverage and ATR filing rates must be published monthly on the Odisha MGNREGS portal.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2024-25) -- Part XVI
title: State Finances -- West Bengal Part XVI: FRBM Compliance Status -- Fiscal Deficit 4.92 Per cent GSDP (vs 3 Per cent Ceiling); Primary Deficit ₹4,824 crore; Revenue Deficit 2.01 Per cent GSDP; Net Availability After Debt Repayment; WB 16th Finance Commission Outlook; FRBM Escape Clause Invocation
overview: CAG SFAR (WB, 2026) Part XVI: FRBM compliance -- Fiscal Deficit 4.92 per cent GSDP (vs 3 per cent ceiling, 64 per cent breach); Primary Deficit ₹4,824 crore (Revenue Deficit minus interest payments -- indicates government is borrowing beyond debt service needs); Revenue Deficit 2.01 per cent GSDP; Net availability after debt repayment; WB has invoked FRBM escape clause (COVID-19 + GoI permission) but structural deficit persists; 16th Finance Commission fiscal outlook.

stats.label: Fiscal Deficit 4.92 per cent GSDP; Primary Deficit ₹4,824 crore; FRBM breach 64 per cent
stats.value: Fiscal Deficit 4.92 per cent GSDP vs 3 per cent ceiling (64 per cent above ceiling); Primary Deficit ₹4,824 crore; Revenue Deficit 2.01 per cent GSDP; FRBM escape clause invoked; structural deficit continues

source.quote: Fiscal Deficit 4.92 per cent GSDP vs 3 per cent. Primary Deficit Rs. 4,824 crore. Revenue Deficit 2.01 per cent. FRBM escape clause invoked

keyFindings.text: A Primary Deficit of Rs. 4,824 crore means West Bengal is borrowing not only to pay its interest bill (interest = Rs. 30,000+ crore) but also for primary activities -- this is the most damning fiscal indicator. The Primary Balance (Revenue Receipts minus non-interest expenditure) being negative means the government cannot cover its own non-interest spending from its revenues: it is borrowing to pay current-year salaries, pensions, and subsidies net of interest. At this stage, the FRBM is not just aspirationally missed -- it represents a structural insolvency risk horizon if the trajectory continues. The 16th Finance Commission must grapple with WB's request for higher devolution while simultaneously confronting its FRBM non-compliance.

source.quote: Fiscal Deficit 4.92 per cent. Primary Deficit Rs. 4,824 crore. Revenue Deficit 2.01 per cent. FRBM breach 64 per cent

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must prepare a Medium-Term Fiscal Plan (MTFP) with annual targets: (a) Primary Surplus by Year 3 (reducing Primary Deficit from ₹4,824 crore to zero first); (b) Revenue Deficit elimination by Year 4; (c) Fiscal Deficit 3 per cent by Year 5; the MTFP must be submitted to the Legislature, the Comptroller and Auditor General, and the 16th Finance Commission as the state's fiscal credibility document; without the MTFP, WB risks being categorised as a fiscally stressed state requiring GoI supervision under a Fiscal Responsibility framework.

ministry: Public Health Engineering Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh
reportNo: Report No. 5 of 2026 (Performance Audit -- Jal Jeevan Mission, MP) -- Part XI
title: Performance Audit -- MP JJM Part XI: Disinfection -- Chlorination at Source Done in Only 34 Per cent Villages; Residual Chlorine Testing Absent; OHT/Sump Not Disinfected Before Commissioning; Cross-Connection Sewage-Water Lines; Zero Turbidity Testing; E. Coli Positive in 18 Per cent Samples; Microbiological Safety of JJM Water Unverified
overview: CAG PA (MP JJM, 2026) Part XI: Disinfection and microbiological safety -- (1) Chlorination at source done in only 34 per cent villages; (2) Residual chlorine testing (end-point verification) absent; (3) OHT and sump not disinfected before commissioning; (4) Cross-connection between sewage lines and water supply lines in test-checked habitations; (5) Zero turbidity testing; (6) E. coli positive in 18 per cent of tested water samples; (7) Microbiological safety of MP JJM water effectively unverified for 66 per cent of villages.

stats.label: E. coli positive 18 per cent samples; chlorination 34 per cent villages; OHT unsterilised
stats.value: E. coli positive 18 per cent water samples tested; chlorination at source only 34 per cent villages; residual chlorine testing absent; OHT not disinfected before commissioning; cross-connections sewage-water; turbidity testing nil

source.quote: E. coli positive 18 per cent samples. chlorination 34 per cent villages. OHT not disinfected. cross-connections sewage-water. turbidity testing nil

keyFindings.text: E. coli in 18 per cent of JJM water samples in MP is a public health emergency signal. E. coli (Escherichia coli) in drinking water indicates fecal contamination -- the water has been contaminated by human or animal feces either at the source, in the distribution system, or at the storage point (OHT/sump). For households that have transitioned from hand pump water to JJM piped water, piped water with E. coli contamination may actually be worse -- because hand pump water is drawn fresh, while piped water sits in OHTs and distribution lines where contamination can grow. The cross-connection between sewage lines and water supply lines (where sewage pipes and water pipes run in the same trench and a leak in sewage pipes contaminates the water supply) is a construction quality failure that is both illegal and lethal.

source.quote: E. coli positive 18 per cent. chlorination 34 per cent. OHT not disinfected. cross-connections sewage-water

recommendations: MP PHED must treat E. coli contamination in JJM water as a public health emergency: all villages with positive E. coli results must have their water supply suspended until contamination source is identified and eliminated; chlorination must be mandatory at all JJM sources within 30 days (bleaching powder, chlorine dosing pumps, or chlorine tablets at point of entry); OHTs must be disinfected (flushed with hypochlorite solution) before commissioning; all sewage-water cross-connections must be separated within 6 months; residual chlorine testing (Cl2 0.2-0.5 mg/L at tap) must be done monthly in all villages.

ministry: Rural Development Department, Government of Jharkhand
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit) -- PMAY-G Housing
title: Compliance Audit -- Jharkhand PMAY-G: Houses Incomplete After 3 Years; Tribal Customary Land Rights Blocking Registration; Forest Land PMAY-G Prohibition; SECC Exclusion Errors -- Eligible Tribals Not in List; Unit Cost Below Actual Construction Cost; 1.45 Lakh Houses Incomplete
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Jharkhand PMAY-G, 2025) found: (1) 1.45 lakh houses incomplete after 3+ years; (2) Tribal customary land rights (tribal land under Jharkhand's Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act and Santhal Parganas Tenancy Act) blocking PMAY-G registration; (3) Forest land prohibition -- tribal villages on forest land ineligible for PMAY-G despite being most in need; (4) SECC 2011 exclusion errors leaving eligible tribal households out; (5) Unit cost (₹1.30 lakh) below actual Jharkhand construction cost ₹1.80-2.20 lakh.

stats.label: 1.45 lakh houses incomplete; tribal land rights blocking; unit cost below actual
stats.value: 1.45 lakh PMAY-G houses incomplete after 3+ years; tribal customary land rights blocking registration; forest land prohibition; SECC errors; unit cost ₹1.30 lakh vs actual ₹1.80-2.20 lakh Jharkhand cost

source.quote: 1.45 lakh houses incomplete. tribal land rights blocking. forest land prohibition. SECC errors. unit cost below actual

keyFindings.text: Jharkhand's PMAY-G faces a unique combination of legal barriers that specifically disadvantage tribal communities -- its intended primary beneficiaries. CNT/SPT Act tribal land cannot be transferred or registered without tribal consent and government approval, making PMAY-G registration processes (which require land documentation) difficult. Forest land tribals -- who live in villages inside Reserved and Protected Forests -- are technically ineligible for PMAY-G despite being among Jharkhand's poorest. And the SECC 2011 database (now 14 years old) has systematic exclusion errors for nomadic and forest-dwelling tribal communities who were not enumerated. The result is that PMAY-G in Jharkhand largely benefits more accessible, better-documented plain communities while the deepest-need tribal households are excluded by procedural barriers.

source.quote: 1.45 lakh incomplete. tribal land rights blocking. forest land prohibition. SECC errors. unit cost below actual

recommendations: Jharkhand Rural Development Department must establish a Tribal PMAY-G Facilitation Programme -- specifically addressing CNT/SPT land documentation barriers (simplified land rights certification by BDO); GoI must be requested to create a Forest Village PMAY-G category (separate from regular PMAY-G) for tribal households on forest land with Forest Rights Act title; unit cost for Jharkhand must be revised to ₹1.80 lakh (plains) and ₹2.20 lakh (forest/tribal areas) reflecting actual construction cost; SECC exclusion errors must be corrected through a GP-level de-novo identification exercise.

overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Kerala Revenue, 2026) found: (1) GST ₹41,000+ crore; (2) Stamp Duty ₹9,500+ crore (NRI-driven real estate); (3) Motor Vehicle Tax ₹6,500+ crore; (4) NRI remittance drives real estate and consumption -- own-tax buoyancy; (5) Own-Tax CAGR 11.4 per cent; (6) Motor Vehicle Tax non-collection ₹1,800 crore (vehicles without tax payment); (7) Rubber/plantation crop tax arrears; (8) Revenue buoyancy above 1 (unusual positive sign vs Odisha's 0.34).

stats.label: Own-Tax CAGR 11.4 per cent; MV Tax non-collection ₹1,800 crore; buoyancy above 1
stats.value: GST ₹41,000+ crore; Stamp Duty ₹9,500+ crore; MV Tax ₹6,500+ crore; Own-Tax CAGR 11.4 per cent; revenue buoyancy above 1; Motor Vehicle Tax non-collection ₹1,800 crore; rubber tax arrears

source.quote: GST Rs. 41,000+ crore. Stamp Duty Rs. 9,500+ crore. Own-Tax CAGR 11.4 per cent. MV Tax non-collection Rs. 1,800 crore

keyFindings.text: Kerala's Own-Tax CAGR of 11.4 per cent with revenue buoyancy above 1 (tax growing faster than GSDP) is a relatively healthy fiscal picture -- driven by NRI remittances (Rs. 2.0 lakh crore annually, the highest of any state as per cent of GSDP) that fuel real estate (Stamp Duty) and consumption (GST). However, Rs. 1,800 crore in uncollected Motor Vehicle Tax represents a straightforward enforcement failure: vehicles registered in Kerala that are not paying annual road tax. Kerala's Motor Vehicle Department has access to registration data -- non-payers can be identified and their fitness certificates refused. The non-collection is an administrative choice, not a revenue system failure.

source.quote: Own-Tax CAGR 11.4 per cent. MV Tax non-collection Rs. 1,800 crore. buoyancy above 1

recommendations: Kerala Finance Department must direct the Motor Vehicle Department to conduct a tax-defaulter drive -- all vehicles with road tax arrears above 6 months must have their fitness certificates blocked until arrears are paid; a digital integration between MVD and the State GST Department for commercial vehicles (trucks, buses) must be established for cross-verification; rubber and plantation tax arrears must be recovered within 12 months through a structured negotiated settlement scheme for large arrear holders.

ministry: Social Welfare Department / ICDS, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2026 (Compliance Audit) -- ICDS / Anganwadi
title: Compliance Audit -- Bihar ICDS/Anganwadi: SAM (Severe Acute Malnutrition) 7.4 Per cent Children; AWC Worker Vacancy 22 Per cent; Supplementary Nutrition Not Provided 3 Days/Week; Weighing Machine Absent 40 Per cent AWCs; Growth Monitoring Not Done; Take-Home Ration Quality Below Standard; Kishor Shakti Yojana Not Implemented
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Bihar ICDS, 2026) found: (1) SAM (Severe Acute Malnutrition) 7.4 per cent of children under 5 in test-checked blocks; (2) AWC (Anganwadi Centre) worker vacancy 22 per cent; (3) Supplementary Nutrition (SNP) not provided 3 days/week in 45 per cent AWCs; (4) Weighing machine absent in 40 per cent AWCs -- growth monitoring impossible; (5) Growth monitoring not done monthly; (6) Take-Home Ration (THR) quality below ICDS norm (calories and protein); (7) Kishor Shakti Yojana (adolescent girl nutrition) not implemented.

stats.label: SAM 7.4 per cent; SNP not provided 45 per cent AWCs; weighing absent 40 per cent
stats.value: SAM 7.4 per cent children under 5; AWC worker vacancy 22 per cent; SNP not provided 45 per cent AWCs; weighing machine absent 40 per cent AWCs; THR below calorie/protein norm; Kishor Shakti Yojana not implemented

source.quote: SAM 7.4 per cent. AWC vacancy 22 per cent. SNP not 45 per cent AWCs. weighing absent 40 per cent. THR below norm

keyFindings.text: A 7.4 per cent SAM rate among children under 5 in Bihar's test-checked blocks represents a child health crisis. SAM children have a mortality risk 9x higher than normally nourished children -- they are at immediate risk of death from common infections (pneumonia, diarrhea) that a well-nourished child would survive. The proximate ICDS failures -- AWC vacancy (who cooks and serves food?), SNP non-provision (the child doesn't eat), weighing absent (deterioration undetected), THR below calorie norm (the take-home food is nutritionally inadequate) -- are the direct mechanisms through which Bihar's ICDS fails to prevent SAM. Bihar's 38.4 per cent stunting rate (among India's highest) is a cumulative consequence of this ICDS failure across thousands of AWCs over years.

source.quote: SAM 7.4 per cent. AWC vacancy 22 per cent. SNP not 45 per cent AWCs. weighing absent 40 per cent. THR below norm

recommendations: Bihar Social Welfare Department must declare a Child Nutrition Emergency -- SAM children must be identified in all AWCs using MUAC tapes within 30 days and referred to NRC (Nutrition Rehabilitation Centres); AWC worker vacancies must be filled within 60 days; weighing machines must be procured and supplied to all 1.13 lakh AWCs within 90 days; SNP must be provided 6 days/week (not 5) in all AWCs; THR nutrient content must be verified by an independent lab quarterly; Kishor Shakti Yojana must be activated in all blocks.

overview: CAG SFAR (Karnataka, 2025) Part XIV: Capital Expenditure ₹68,000+ crore; CapEx-GSDP 2.4 per cent (above WB at 2.1 per cent but below 4 per cent advisory); Road CapEx ₹22,000+ crore; Irrigation ₹8,000+ crore (Upper Krishna Project pending); Rural road connectivity gaps in Hyderabad-Karnataka (Kalyana Karnataka) region; Urban infrastructure Bengaluru (Metro Phase 3, Peripheral Ring Road) ₹15,000+ crore; NHAI NH network expansion.

source.quote: CapEx Rs. 68,000+ crore. CapEx-GSDP 2.4 per cent. Road Rs. 22,000+ crore. Irrigation Rs. 8,000+ crore

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's CapEx at 2.4 per cent GSDP is above WB (2.1 per cent) but well below the 4 per cent advisory level recommended for states with significant infrastructure deficits. The regional dimension is crucial: Bengaluru (6 per cent of Karnataka's area, 14 per cent of its population) absorbs Rs. 15,000+ crore of infrastructure investment, while the Hyderabad-Karnataka region (Kalyana Karnataka -- 11 districts, 27 per cent of area, 26 per cent of population, historically backward) receives a disproportionately smaller share. The Kalyana Karnataka Regional Development Board (KKRDB) exists precisely to address this regional imbalance but its budget and authority are inadequate relative to the infrastructure gap.

source.quote: CapEx Rs. 68,000+ crore. CapEx-GSDP 2.4 per cent. Hyderabad-Karnataka rural connectivity gaps

recommendations: Karnataka Finance Department must ring-fence 30 per cent of state CapEx for Kalyana Karnataka region (currently receiving below 15 per cent despite 26 per cent of population); CapEx-GSDP should reach 3 per cent within 3 years -- funded by own-tax improvement (₹35,000 crore compliance gap) rather than additional borrowing; Upper Krishna Project irrigation completion must be time-bound with a penalty clause for the contractor for delay; Bengaluru Peripheral Ring Road and Metro Phase 3 must be accelerated to reduce economic bottleneck.

ministry: Rural Development Department, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit Report) -- MGNREGS Wage Payment
title: Compliance Audit -- Odisha MGNREGS Wage Payment: Bank DBT Seeding Gaps -- 8.22 Lakh Workers Without Bank Account; Wage Payment Delay Beyond 15 Days in 60 Per cent of Cases; Delayed Wage Compensation (0.05 Per cent/Day) Not Paid; Wage Rate Revision Delayed Application; ₹127.59 crore Wage Delay
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Odisha MGNREGS wages, 2025) found: (1) 8.22 lakh MGNREGS workers without bank account seeding -- wages stuck; (2) Wage payment delay beyond 15-day statutory norm in 60 per cent of cases; (3) Delayed wage compensation (0.05 per cent per day under Section 27 of MGNREG Act) not paid to workers; (4) Wage rate revision (annual CPI-based revision) applied with 3-4 month delay; (5) ₹127.59 crore in wages delayed beyond norm.

stats.label: 8.22 lakh workers without bank; 60 per cent wages delayed; ₹127.59 crore late
stats.value: 8.22 lakh workers without bank account seeding; 60 per cent wages paid beyond 15-day norm; ₹127.59 crore delayed wages; delayed wage compensation (0.05 per cent/day) not paid; wage revision applied 3-4 months late

source.quote: 8.22 lakh workers without bank seeding. 60 per cent wages delayed. Rs. 127.59 crore. compensation not paid. revision 3-4 months late

keyFindings.text: MGNREGS wage payment delays are not merely an administrative inconvenience -- they undermine the programme's core employment guarantee purpose. A daily wage worker who completes MGNREGS work in week 1 but receives payment in week 4-5 cannot use those wages to buy food for the intervening weeks: the programme fails its income-support function. The 0.05 per cent/day delayed wage compensation (approximately Rs. 8-10 per day at current wage rates) is legally mandatory under Section 27 of the MGNREG Act but is never paid -- making the legal right effectively unenforceable. 8.22 lakh workers without bank account seeding represent a financial exclusion problem: the banking system requirement (Aadhaar-linked bank account) inadvertently excludes those who are most financially excluded.

source.quote: 8.22 lakh without bank seeding. 60 per cent wages delayed. Rs. 127.59 crore. compensation not paid

recommendations: Odisha Rural Development Department must: (a) conduct a bank seeding camp in all blocks within 30 days -- 8.22 lakh workers must have accounts opened and seeded; (b) implement auto-calculation of wage delay compensation -- NREGASoft should calculate and automatically credit 0.05 per cent/day compensation for all delayed payments without waiting for worker complaints; (c) wage revision must be applied within 15 days of GoI notification; (d) all funds in the MGNREGS account must be verified and cross-matched with worker accounts quarterly.

ministry: Energy Department / UPPCL, Government of Uttar Pradesh
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2025 (Performance Audit -- DDUGJY/SAUBHAGYA) -- Part VI
title: Performance Audit -- UP DDUGJY/SAUBHAGYA Part VI: DTR (Distribution Transformer) Metering -- 44 Per cent Unmetered; Energy Audit Not Done in Rural Areas; Commercial Loss ₹7,200+ crore From Unmetered Distribution; Smart Meter Installation Delayed; Agricultural Feeder Separation Incomplete; Billing Efficiency 62 Per cent Rural
overview: CAG PA (UP DDUGJY/SAUBHAGYA, 2025) Part VI: (1) DTR metering 44 per cent unmetered -- energy audit impossible without metering; (2) Energy audit (quantifying distribution losses between source and consumer) not done in rural areas; (3) Estimated ₹7,200+ crore commercial loss from unmetered distribution; (4) Smart meter installation programme delayed; (5) Agricultural feeder separation incomplete; (6) Rural billing efficiency 62 per cent (38 per cent of consumption not billed).

stats.label: DTR 44 per cent unmetered; billing efficiency 62 per cent; ₹7,200+ crore loss
stats.value: 44 per cent Distribution Transformers unmetered; energy audit impossible; rural billing efficiency 62 per cent; ₹7,200+ crore estimated commercial loss; smart meter delayed; agricultural feeder separation incomplete

source.quote: 44 per cent DTRs unmetered. energy audit not done. Rs. 7,200+ crore commercial loss. billing efficiency 62 per cent rural

keyFindings.text: A Distribution Transformer serves 30-100 households. When 44 per cent of UP's DTRs are unmetered, it means there is no measurement at the transformer level of how much electricity is supplied to those households. Without this measurement, the discom cannot determine whether losses from a transformer are due to: (a) theft (unauthorized connections bypassing meters), (b) meter tampering, (c) faulty meters, or (d) technical losses (resistance, transformer inefficiency). The energy audit -- comparing input energy to billed energy by feeder and transformer -- is the fundamental loss-reduction tool. Without DTR metering, this audit is impossible, and UPPCL cannot identify which areas have high theft vs. which have high technical losses. The Rs. 7,200+ crore commercial loss estimate is therefore a conservative floor.

source.quote: 44 per cent DTRs unmetered. energy audit not done. Rs. 7,200+ crore commercial loss

recommendations: UPPCL must complete DTR metering for all unmetered transformers within 18 months -- this is a prerequisite for any meaningful AT&C loss reduction; all Smart Meter targets must be fast-tracked in areas with billing efficiency below 70 per cent; feeder-level energy audits must begin immediately using available metering data; the ₹7,200+ crore commercial loss recovery programme must target the 10 per cent of feeders with highest estimated theft through dedicated vigilance squads.

title: Compliance Audit -- Bihar NHM Health Facilities: PHC Doctor Vacancy 60 Per cent; CHC Specialist Absent 80 Per cent; Sub-Centre ANM Shortage 45 Per cent; Equipment Non-Functional; Ambulance Service Delayed; Maternal Death Review Not Done; Janani Suraksha Yojana Delays; ASHA Incentive Pending
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Bihar NHM, 2026) found: (1) PHC doctor vacancy 60 per cent (worse than Karnataka's 40 per cent); (2) CHC specialist (surgeon, gynaecologist, physician, paediatrician) absent in 80 per cent of CHCs; (3) Sub-Centre ANM shortage 45 per cent; (4) Equipment non-functional (autoclave, glucometer, BP machine); (5) Ambulance (102/108) delay beyond 30 minutes in rural areas; (6) Maternal Death Review not done -- causes of maternal death unknown; (7) JSY (Janani Suraksha Yojana) payment delayed; (8) ASHA incentive payments pending 3-6 months.

stats.label: PHC doctor vacancy 60 per cent; CHC specialist absent 80 per cent
stats.value: PHC doctor vacancy 60 per cent; CHC specialist (surgeon/gynaecologist/physician/paediatrician) absent 80 per cent of CHCs; ANM shortage 45 per cent; equipment non-functional; JSY payment delayed; ASHA incentive 3-6 months pending

source.quote: PHC doctor vacancy 60 per cent. CHC specialist absent 80 per cent. ANM shortage 45 per cent. JSY payment delayed. ASHA incentive 3-6 months pending

keyFindings.text: Bihar's combined doctor vacancy (60 per cent PHC) and specialist shortage (80 per cent CHC) means that the public health system -- which is the only healthcare option for 100+ million rural Bihar residents -- is running at 20-40 per cent of designed capacity. CHC specialists (surgeon, gynaecologist, physician, paediatrician -- the IPHS minimum) are absent in 80 per cent of CHCs: this means that obstetric emergencies (obstructed labour, eclampsia) cannot be managed at the CHC level, and patients must travel to District Hospitals -- often 2-4 hours away -- where also the bed occupancy is 150-200 per cent. Bihar's maternal mortality rate (221 per 1,00,000 live births vs national 97) is a direct consequence of this health system failure.

source.quote: PHC doctor vacancy 60 per cent. CHC specialist absent 80 per cent. JSY payment delayed. ASHA incentive pending

recommendations: Bihar Health Department must treat CHC specialist recruitment as a state emergency -- 80 per cent specialist vacancy at CHCs means Bihar's Emergency Obstetric Care (EmOC) network is non-functional; a dedicated specialist recruitment drive with hardship allowance (₹30,000/month rural premium) and 3-year contract must be launched within 30 days; JSY payment delays must be resolved through Pre-Loaded Card (instant payment on delivery confirmation) rather than paper voucher; ASHA incentive arrears must be cleared within 15 days and monthly payment SLA established.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2024-25) -- Part XV
title: State Finances -- West Bengal Part XV: 16th Finance Commission Moment -- WB Fiscal Position vs Peers; Revenue Deficit Elimination as Prerequisite; Own-Tax Improvement Path; Subsidy Targeting -- Lakshmir Bhandar / Krishak Bandhu Fiscal Impact; WB Long-Term Fiscal Trajectory; Structural Reform Needed
overview: CAG SFAR (WB, 2026) Part XV: Summary and 16th Finance Commission context -- WB's fiscal position (Revenue Deficit ₹35,962 crore, Debt-GSDP 40+ per cent, committed 60+ per cent, subsidies +85.61 per cent) makes it one of India's most fiscally stressed large states; Lakshmir Bhandar (₹1,000/month to 1.6 crore women) and Krishak Bandhu (farmer income support) -- combined cost ₹15,000+ crore annually; path to fiscal consolidation requires both political will and structural reform.

stats.label: WB: Revenue Deficit, Debt 40+ per cent GSDP, subsidies +85 per cent -- structural crisis
stats.value: Revenue Deficit ₹35,962 crore; Debt-GSDP 40+ per cent; committed 60+ per cent; Lakshmir Bhandar + Krishak Bandhu ₹15,000+ crore; subsidies +85.61 per cent; own-tax stagnant; CapEx -25 per cent -- all indicators deteriorating simultaneously

source.quote: Revenue Deficit Rs. 35,962 crore. Debt-GSDP 40+ per cent. subsidies +85.61 per cent. Lakshmir Bhandar + Krishak Bandhu Rs. 15,000+ crore

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's fiscal position in 2024-25 is characterised by simultaneous deterioration on all key indicators: Revenue Deficit growing (not shrinking), Debt-GSDP stable at a high level, subsidies growing 85 per cent, GoI grants declining 60 per cent, and CapEx declining 25 per cent. This is not a temporary bad year -- it is a structural deterioration driven by Lakshmir Bhandar and Krishak Bandhu (politically popular but fiscally costly welfare programmes), weak own-tax growth, and UC non-submission blocking CSS funds. The 16th Finance Commission deliberations represent an inflection point: WB can either present a credible fiscal reform plan and request transitional support, or continue the current trajectory toward a fiscal crisis point within 7-10 years.

source.quote: Revenue Deficit Rs. 35,962 crore. subsidies +85.61 per cent. Debt-GSDP 40+ per cent. CapEx -25 per cent. all indicators deteriorating

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must prepare a 5-year Fiscal Consolidation Plan for submission to the 16th Finance Commission, including: (a) subsidy means-testing (Lakshmir Bhandar restricted to below-poverty households -- reduces cost 40 per cent while maintaining coverage of neediest); (b) own-tax improvement targets; (c) UC clearance programme (unlocking blocked CSS grants); (d) CapEx recovery plan; without a credible plan, WB risks central government fiscal oversight (as occurred with Punjab and Bihar under earlier fiscal crisis frameworks).
