title: State Finances -- Odisha Part XI: Fiscal Position Summary -- Revenue Surplus ₹22,651 crore; CapEx 30.27 Per cent; Debt-GSDP 15.1 Per cent; Own-Tax CAGR 12.8 Per cent; Committed 37.19 Per cent; 16th Finance Commission Opportunity; Odisha as Investment Hub -- Infrastructure Readiness; Cyclone/Flood Vulnerability as CapEx Case
overview: CAG SFAR (Odisha, 2026) Part XI summary: Revenue Surplus ₹22,651 crore; CapEx 30.27 per cent; Debt-GSDP 15.1 per cent (best eastern state); committed 37.19 per cent (best); Own-Tax CAGR 12.8 per cent; Odisha fiscal position is the strongest in eastern India; 16th Finance Commission opportunity to leverage fiscal performance for higher untied grants; Odisha's cyclone/flood vulnerability as a legitimate case for GoI CapEx support; infrastructure investment opportunity.

stats.label: Revenue Surplus ₹22,651 crore; Debt-GSDP 15.1 per cent; best eastern state
stats.value: Odisha Revenue Surplus ₹22,651 crore; Debt-GSDP 15.1 per cent; CapEx 30.27 per cent; committed 37.19 per cent; own-tax CAGR 12.8 per cent; best fiscal position among eastern states; 16th FC opportunity

source.quote: Revenue Surplus Rs. 22,651 crore. Debt-GSDP 15.1 per cent. committed 37.19 per cent. Own-Tax CAGR 12.8 per cent. best eastern state

keyFindings.text: Odisha's fiscal position -- summarised as Revenue Surplus, moderate Debt-GSDP, low committed expenditure, strong own-tax growth -- is the most positive fiscal story in eastern India. The contrast with West Bengal (Revenue Deficit Rs. 35,962 crore, Debt-GSDP 40+ per cent, committed 60+ per cent) and Bihar (FRBM deficit 5.30 per cent, committed 74 per cent) is stark. Odisha's fiscal discipline has been achieved despite being a poorer state (per-capita income below India average), indicating that good fiscal management is a governance choice, not a wealth outcome. The 16th Finance Commission should treat Odisha's fiscal track record as evidence warranting higher untied grants -- rewarding fiscal discipline encourages other states toward similar management.

source.quote: Revenue Surplus Rs. 22,651 crore. Debt-GSDP 15.1 per cent. best eastern state. 16th FC opportunity

recommendations: Odisha Finance Department should: (a) present a comprehensive 16th Finance Commission memorandum highlighting fiscal performance metrics relative to peer states, cyclone/flood CapEx needs, and tribal welfare investment requirements; (b) issue Green Bonds for coastal resilience infrastructure (cyclone shelters, sea walls, mangrove restoration) -- a ring-fenced instrument that justifies above-FRBM borrowing for legitimate climate adaptation; (c) increase CapEx from 30.27 per cent to 35 per cent of total expenditure -- the fiscal headroom exists and Odisha's infrastructure needs (tribal roads, irrigation, port connectivity) justify it.

ministry: Health and Family Welfare / Aarogyasri, Government of Karnataka
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part XIII
title: State Finances -- Karnataka Part XIII: Ayushman Bharat / Arogya Karnataka -- ₹7,000+ crore Annual Expenditure; 5.5 Crore Beneficiaries; Empanelled Hospital Fraud; TPA Claim Settlement Delays; Package Rate Below Market; Government Hospital vs Private Hospital Benefit Distribution; Health Insurance Premium Burden
overview: CAG SFAR (Karnataka, 2025) Part XIII: Ayushman Bharat / Arogya Karnataka health insurance -- ₹7,000+ crore annual expenditure; 5.5 crore beneficiaries; empanelled private hospital fraud (ghost procedures, upcoding); TPA claim settlement delays beyond 30-day norm; package rates below market rates for procedures (leading hospitals to prefer non-AB patients); government hospital vs private hospital benefit distribution analysis.

stats.label: ₹7,000+ crore annual spend; empanelled hospital fraud; claim delay beyond norm
stats.value: Ayushman/Arogya Karnataka ₹7,000+ crore annual expenditure; 5.5 crore beneficiaries; empanelled hospital ghost procedure/upcoding fraud; TPA claim settlement beyond 30-day norm; package rate below market

source.quote: Rs. 7,000+ crore annual. 5.5 crore beneficiaries. empanelled hospital fraud. TPA claim delay beyond 30 days. package rate below market

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's Ayushman Bharat / Arogya Karnataka programme at Rs. 7,000+ crore is one of India's largest state health insurance programmes by absolute expenditure. The empanelled hospital fraud problem -- ghost procedures (billing for procedures not performed), upcoding (billing for a more expensive procedure than performed) -- is documented across PM-JAY nationally. Karnataka's scheme has implemented AI-based fraud detection (Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission analytics), but fraud continues because empanelled hospitals face minimal criminal risk for false billing: the enforcement mechanism (delisting + fine) is not sufficient deterrent. Package rates below market rates create perverse incentives: empanelled hospitals are financially better off treating non-AB (self-pay or private-insurance) patients than AB patients, leading to discriminatory admission practices.

source.quote: Rs. 7,000+ crore annual. empanelled hospital fraud. package rate below market. TPA claim delay

recommendations: Karnataka Health Department must implement a zero-tolerance fraud policy for empanelled hospitals: the first instance of ghost procedure/upcoding fraud must result in immediate delisting for 3 years and recovery of fraudulent claims; package rates must be revised every 3 years based on a market rate survey (Karnataka Medical Council and hospital cost data); TPA claim settlement must be monitored weekly -- hospitals not paid within 30 days must receive 12 per cent penal interest; a random 5 per cent audit of all AB/AK claims by independent clinical auditors must be institutionalised.

ministry: Mines and Geology Department, Government of Gujarat
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (Performance Audit -- PMKKKY) -- Part VIII
title: Performance Audit -- Gujarat PMKKKY Part VIII: Mine Closure Plans Absent; Progressive Rehabilitation Not Done; Mine Overburden Dumps -- Landslide Risk; Acid Mine Drainage Uncontrolled; DMF Funds Not Used for Environmental Rehabilitation; Mined-Out Land Not Reclaimed; Post-Closure Community Livelihood Absent
overview: CAG PA (Gujarat PMKKKY, 2025) Part VIII: Environmental mining rehabilitation findings -- (1) Mine closure plans absent for majority of Gujarat mines; (2) Progressive rehabilitation (restoring mined-out benches as mining progresses) not done; (3) Mine overburden dumps creating landslide risk in monsoon; (4) Acid mine drainage from lignite and salt mines uncontrolled; (5) DMF funds not allocated for environmental rehabilitation despite legal requirement; (6) Mined-out land not reclaimed for agriculture or forest; (7) Post-closure community livelihood planning absent.

stats.label: Mine closure plans absent; overburden dump landslide risk; DMF not for rehabilitation
stats.value: Mine closure plans absent majority Gujarat mines; progressive rehabilitation not done; overburden dumps -- monsoon landslide risk; acid mine drainage uncontrolled; DMF not used for environmental rehabilitation; mined-out land not reclaimed

source.quote: Mine closure plans absent. progressive rehabilitation not done. overburden dumps landslide risk. acid mine drainage uncontrolled. DMF not for rehabilitation

keyFindings.text: Mine closure planning is legally required under the Mineral Concession Rules and the Environment Impact Assessment notifications. A mine closure plan must describe how the mined-out area will be rehabilitated (slopes stabilised, vegetation restored, water bodies cleaned, overburden dumps regraded) and how communities dependent on the mine for employment will be supported post-closure. The absence of closure plans for the majority of Gujarat mines is not just a regulatory violation -- it means that when mines close (as all mines eventually do), the environmental liability (acid drainage, unstable dumps, contaminated groundwater) becomes the state's and the surrounding community's problem, not the mining company's. DMF, which collects royalty from these same mines, should logically fund post-closure rehabilitation -- but this linkage has not been made.

source.quote: Mine closure plans absent. overburden dumps landslide risk. acid mine drainage uncontrolled. DMF not for rehabilitation

recommendations: Gujarat Mines and Geology Department must: (a) require all mining lease holders to submit approved mine closure plans within 180 days as a condition for lease renewal; (b) allocate 5 per cent of each district's DMF corpus to Environmental Rehabilitation (overburden grading, vegetation, acid drainage treatment) as a mandatory High-Priority expenditure; (c) establish a Mine Environmental Monitoring Cell with quarterly field inspection of overburden dumps and drainage outlets; (d) post-closure livelihood plans must be prepared 5 years before anticipated mine closure for every major mine.

title: State Finances -- West Bengal Part XIV: Capital Expenditure ₹37,480 crore (-25 Per cent); CapEx-GSDP 2.1 Per cent (Below 4 Per cent Advisory); Road Works 63 Per cent Utilisation; Irrigation CapEx Minimal; CapEx Financed By GoI Grants + SNA Releases -- Not From Own Resources; Infrastructure Investment Decline
overview: CAG SFAR (WB, 2026) Part XIV: Capital Expenditure ₹37,480 crore (-25 per cent YoY); CapEx-GSDP 2.1 per cent (below 4 per cent advisory); Road works 63 per cent budget utilisation; Irrigation CapEx minimal; WB CapEx almost entirely from GoI grants (PMGSY, RRDA, AIBP) and SNA releases -- negligible own-state CapEx; Revenue Deficit means no own resources for investment; infrastructure investment in long-term decline relative to GSDP.

stats.label: CapEx ₹37,480 crore -25 per cent; CapEx-GSDP 2.1 per cent (below 4 per cent advisory)
stats.value: Capital Expenditure ₹37,480 crore, down 25 per cent YoY; CapEx-GSDP 2.1 per cent vs 4 per cent advisory; road works 63 per cent utilisation; irrigation minimal; own-state CapEx negligible -- funded by GoI grants only

source.quote: CapEx Rs. 37,480 crore -25 per cent. CapEx-GSDP 2.1 per cent. road works 63 per cent. own-state CapEx negligible

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's CapEx-GSDP ratio at 2.1 per cent (vs 4 per cent advisory) and declining is a structural consequence of its Revenue Deficit position. With a Revenue Deficit of Rs. 35,962 crore consuming all borrowing capacity, WB has no own-state resources for capital investment. Its CapEx (Rs. 37,480 crore) is therefore almost entirely funded by GoI grants (PMGSY roads, AIBP irrigation, AMRUT urban infrastructure) -- grants that are declining (-60 per cent cumulative). The 25 per cent YoY CapEx decline and the 63 per cent road works utilisation (not spending all even the grants available) indicate that WB cannot absorb available central investment funds, let alone generate its own. The long-term consequence is deteriorating infrastructure quality -- older roads, older bridges, older irrigation systems -- relative to GSDP growth.

source.quote: CapEx Rs. 37,480 crore -25 per cent. CapEx-GSDP 2.1 per cent. own-state CapEx negligible. revenue deficit consuming all borrowing

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must treat CapEx improvement as an emergency priority equal to Revenue Deficit elimination -- the two are linked: eliminating the Revenue Deficit creates borrowing capacity that can fund CapEx; road works budget utilisation must improve from 63 per cent to 90 per cent through better project preparation (DPR readiness), procurement, and contractor management; GoI must be requested to allow direct district-level fund release for PMGSY and AMRUT (bypassing state treasury) to improve utilisation in WB.

ministry: Rural Development Department, Government of Jharkhand
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit) -- MGNREGS Material Component
title: Compliance Audit -- Jharkhand MGNREGS Material Component: Material Ratio Exceeded 40 Per cent Cap in Test-Checked Works; Stone Quarrying Labour Not Counted Separately; Water Conservation Works Without Water Source Survey; Convergence With PMKSY Absent; Completed Ponds -- Silt Removal Not Done
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Jharkhand MGNREGS material, 2025) found: (1) Material component exceeding 40 per cent cap in test-checked works -- violating MGNREGS' labour-intensive programme character; (2) Stone quarrying treated as labour, not material -- artificially depressing material percentage; (3) Water conservation works (ponds, check dams) without prior water source survey; (4) PMKSY (agricultural water) convergence absent; (5) Completed ponds -- annual silt removal not done, reducing storage capacity.

stats.label: Material ratio exceeded 40 per cent; stone quarrying miscategorised; ponds without silt removal
stats.value: Material component exceeded 40 per cent MGNREGS cap in test-checked works; stone quarrying treated as labour (artificially depressing material ratio); water works without source survey; PMKSY convergence absent; completed pond silt removal not done

source.quote: Material component exceeded 40 per cent cap. stone quarrying miscategorised. water works without source survey. PMKSY convergence absent. silt removal not done

keyFindings.text: MGNREGS' 40 per cent material cap is not arbitrary -- it is designed to ensure that MGNREGS is primarily an employment programme, not a construction programme. When material exceeds 40 per cent, it means the work is capital-intensive (machine-excavated, material-heavy) rather than labour-intensive. The stone quarrying miscategorisation is a workaround: by treating stone quarrying (which requires blasting, machinery, and contractors) as "labour," the executing agency artificially reduces the reported material percentage while the actual work character remains contractor-driven. The result is works that generate fewer person-days of employment per rupee spent than MGNREGS standards require -- defeating the income-support purpose.

source.quote: Material component exceeded 40 per cent. stone quarrying miscategorised. silt removal not done. PMKSY convergence absent

recommendations: Jharkhand Rural Development Department must clarify that stone quarrying for MGNREGS works is classified as material (not labour) in all future work orders; all water conservation works (pond desilting, check dam, farm pond) must have a water source survey and water yield estimate before work approval; convergence with PMKSY must be activated through district convergence committees; all completed ponds must have annual silt removal scheduled in the MGNREGS annual work plan.

overview: CAG SFAR (Nagaland, 2025) Part IX: Fiscal governance context -- NNPG (Naga National Political Group) Framework Agreement uncertainty impacts long-term fiscal planning; Security expenditure ₹3,200+ crore (including CRPF, Assam Rifles, state police -- highest per-capita security expenditure of any state); Police-to-population ratio 3x national average; GoI peace package dependency; village council (customary tribal institution) role in local fiscal governance; 16th Finance Commission special category case.

stats.label: Security expenditure ₹3,200+ crore; police ratio 3x national; GoI peace package
stats.value: Security expenditure ₹3,200+ crore; police-to-population ratio 3x national average (highest in India); GoI peace package dependency; NNPG framework uncertainty; village council local fiscal governance; 16th FC special category claim

source.quote: Security expenditure Rs. 3,200+ crore. police ratio 3x national. GoI peace package. NNPG framework uncertainty. village council governance

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's security expenditure context -- Rs. 3,200+ crore annually for a state of 2 million people -- reflects the ongoing cost of 70 years of insurgency and the continuing NNPG Framework Agreement uncertainty. On a per-capita basis, Nagaland's security expenditure is among the highest of any state in the world relative to its economic size. Unlike Punjab's police expenditure (which is driven by district policing), Nagaland's security costs include CRPF and Assam Rifles central forces (funded by GoI) and state police (funded by state). If and when a final peace settlement is reached (Framework Agreement signed in 2015 but detailed agreement pending), the security expenditure reduction could be the most significant fiscal restructuring opportunity Nagaland has -- potentially freeing Rs. 1,000-1,500 crore annually for development.

source.quote: Security expenditure Rs. 3,200+ crore. police ratio 3x national. NNPG framework uncertainty

recommendations: Nagaland Finance Department must present a Peace Dividend Fiscal Plan to the Legislature -- modelling the impact of security expenditure reduction on development spending over 5-10 years; the 16th Finance Commission presentation must include the unique security expenditure burden as a special category argument for higher devolution; village councils (traditional tribal institutions) must be formally integrated into the local fiscal governance framework -- their role in MGNREGS, JJM, and PMAY-G implementation must be legally recognised and resourced.

ministry: Public Health Engineering Department, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (Compliance Audit -- HGNJ) -- Part VI
title: Compliance Audit -- Bihar HGNJ Part VI: Water Quality Testing -- Only 4.2 Per cent Samples Tested; Arsenic Exceedance in 8 Districts Undetected Due to Testing Gap; Fluoride Exceedance Purnia/Katihar; Nitrate Above Limit Vaishali/Muzaffarpur; NABL Lab Nil; PHE Sub-Division Lab Results Unreliable; ₹13,899 crore Programme Without Systematic Water Safety
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Bihar HGNJ, 2025) Part VI: Water quality testing gap -- only 4.2 per cent of functional FHTCs tested for water quality; arsenic exceedance in 8 Gangetic districts undetected; fluoride above limit in Purnia/Katihar; nitrate above WHO limit in Vaishali/Muzaffarpur; no NABL-accredited labs (vs 5 per cent BIS requirement); PHE sub-division lab results unreliable; 11 mandatory parameters not tested; heavy metal contamination unmonitored.

stats.label: Only 4.2 per cent samples tested; arsenic/fluoride/nitrate exceedance undetected
stats.value: Only 4.2 per cent of HGNJ FHTCs tested for water quality; arsenic exceedance 8 Gangetic districts undetected; fluoride above limit Purnia/Katihar; nitrate above limit Vaishali/Muzaffarpur; NABL labs nil; 11 parameters not tested

source.quote: only 4.2 per cent FHTCs tested. arsenic exceedance 8 districts undetected. fluoride Purnia/Katihar. nitrate Vaishali/Muzaffarpur. NABL labs nil

keyFindings.text: Bihar's water quality testing rate of 4.2 per cent means that 95.8 per cent of HGNJ-connected households are receiving water whose chemical quality has never been verified. This is not abstract risk: Bihar's Gangetic plain sits over one of the world's largest natural arsenic aquifer systems. Bhojpur, Buxar, Vaishali, Munger, Patna, Begusarai, Samastipur, and Khagaria districts have documented groundwater arsenic exceeding 0.05 mg/L (5x WHO limit). HGNJ sources in these districts include shallow tube wells -- which may draw from contaminated aquifers. If HGNJ water is delivered from arsenic-contaminated sources, it provides the false assurance of "piped water" while delivering water that causes arsenicosis, cancer, and birth defects. The testing gap makes this scenario invisible.

source.quote: only 4.2 per cent tested. arsenic 8 districts undetected. fluoride Purnia/Katihar. nitrate Vaishali/Muzaffarpur

recommendations: Bihar PHED must immediately: (a) test 100 per cent of FHTCs in 8 arsenic-affected Gangetic districts within 30 days using available field test kits (while NABL lab capacity is built); (b) any source testing above 0.01 mg/L arsenic must be taken offline immediately and an alternative safe source provided; (c) NABL-accredited water quality labs must be established in all 38 districts within 12 months (a central lab per 3-4 districts is feasible); (d) all 11 BIS/IS 10500 parameters must be tested annually for each HGNJ source.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part X
title: State Finances -- Odisha Part X: Total Debt ₹1,34,000+ crore; Debt-GSDP 15.1 Per cent (Well Below 20 Per cent Advisory); Market Borrowings ₹18,000+ crore; Debt Repayment On Track; Revenue Surplus Financing CapEx (Golden Rule Compliance); Best-in-Class Among Eastern States
overview: CAG SFAR (Odisha, 2026) Part X: Total Debt ₹1,34,000+ crore; Debt-GSDP 15.1 per cent (well below 20 per cent advisory limit); Market Borrowings ₹18,000+ crore; debt repayment on track -- no arrears; Revenue Surplus (₹22,651 crore) partially financing Capital Expenditure -- golden rule compliance; Odisha debt-GSDP is best among comparable eastern states (WB 40 per cent, Bihar 30+ per cent, Jharkhand 25 per cent).

stats.label: Debt-GSDP 15.1 per cent vs advisory 20 per cent; Revenue Surplus funds CapEx
stats.value: Odisha Debt-GSDP 15.1 per cent (well below 20 per cent advisory); Total Debt ₹1,34,000+ crore; Market Borrowings ₹18,000+ crore; Revenue Surplus ₹22,651 crore financing CapEx (golden rule compliance); best eastern state

source.quote: Debt-GSDP 15.1 per cent vs advisory 20 per cent. Revenue Surplus Rs. 22,651 crore. golden rule compliance. best eastern state

keyFindings.text: Odisha's Debt-GSDP at 15.1 per cent -- compared to West Bengal (40+ per cent), Bihar (30+ per cent), Jharkhand (25 per cent) -- makes it the only major eastern state with genuine fiscal headroom. This fiscal space, built over 15 years of disciplined FRBM compliance under successive governments, is Odisha's most important development asset: it means the state can borrow more to invest in infrastructure (roads, ports, irrigation, urban development) without fiscal risk. Revenue Surplus partially financing Capital Expenditure (the golden rule -- borrow only for investment, not consumption) is a sound fiscal architecture. The contrast with WB (where the entire borrowing covers revenue deficit, leaving zero for investment) is stark -- Odisha is a fiscal management success story in India's eastern region.

source.quote: Debt-GSDP 15.1 per cent. Revenue Surplus Rs. 22,651 crore financing CapEx. golden rule compliance

recommendations: Odisha Finance Department should leverage its fiscal headroom to accelerate infrastructure investment -- increasing CapEx from 30.27 per cent to 35 per cent of total expenditure; the 16th Finance Commission presentation must highlight Odisha's FRBM compliance and Debt-GSDP 15.1 per cent as evidence of fiscal responsibility deserving higher untied CapEx grants; Green Bonds (for coastal resilience, cyclone infrastructure) should be issued by Odisha to access additional lower-cost capital for climate-related infrastructure.

ministry: Department of School Education, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (Performance Audit -- Samagra Shiksha in WB) -- Part X
title: Performance Audit -- WB Samagra Shiksha Part X: Secondary Schools -- Science Lab Without Equipment; Library Without Books; Computer Lab 40 Per cent Non-Functional; Class XII Math/Science Pass Rate Below 50 Per cent; Teacher Deployment Imbalanced; Rural-Urban Learning Outcome Gap
overview: CAG PA (WB Samagra Shiksha, 2026) Part X: Secondary school infrastructure and outcome findings -- (1) Science laboratories without equipment in majority of test-checked schools (lab room exists, equipment absent); (2) Libraries without books or with outdated stock; (3) Computer labs 40 per cent non-functional; (4) Class XII Math and Science pass rate below 50 per cent in multiple districts; (5) Teacher deployment imbalanced (over-staffed in certain subjects, shortage in Maths/Science/English); (6) Rural vs urban learning outcome gap widening.

stats.label: Science lab without equipment; Class XII Math/Science below 50 per cent pass
stats.value: Science labs without equipment majority test-checked schools; computer labs 40 per cent non-functional; Class XII Math/Science pass rate below 50 per cent; library without books; teacher deployment imbalanced; rural-urban outcome gap widening

source.quote: Science lab without equipment. computer lab 40 per cent non-functional. Class XII Math/Science below 50 per cent. library without books

keyFindings.text: A science laboratory without equipment is a room, not a lab. Students who study Chemistry without ever performing a titration, Physics without observing a prism refraction, or Biology without examining a slide under a microscope are receiving a textbook education that is fundamentally inferior to what Indian public examination boards expect. Class XII Math and Science pass rates below 50 per cent in WB's rural districts directly translate to students being ineligible for engineering, medical, and science undergraduate admissions -- permanently closing those career pathways. The teacher imbalance (too many teachers in some subjects, acute shortage in Maths/Science/English) is partly a consequence of appointment politics and partly a reflection of the shortage of qualified Math/Science teachers willing to serve in rural WB schools.

source.quote: Science lab without equipment. Class XII Math/Science below 50 per cent. computer lab 40 per cent non-functional

recommendations: West Bengal School Education Department must fund science equipment procurement for all secondary school labs within 12 months -- a state-level bulk procurement (rather than district-level) will reduce cost by 30-40 per cent; computer lab non-functionality must be diagnosed (power, hardware, software, connectivity) and repaired; Math and Science teachers must be recruited on a priority basis in districts with Class XII pass rates below 60 per cent; bridge tutoring centres (evening classes by qualified teachers) must be established in rural Block headquarters for Class XI-XII Math/Science.

ministry: Transport Department / PUNBUS / PRTC, Government of Punjab
reportNo: Report No. 7 of 2025 (Audit Report on PSUs) -- PUNBUS / PRTC
title: PSU Audit -- Punjab PUNBUS/PRTC: Combined Losses ₹1,800+ crore; Fleet Utilisation 62 Per cent; Revenue Per Bus-km Below Cost; Private Operator Competition; Concessional Pass Burden ₹480+ crore; Route Rationalisation Not Done; Old Fleet -- Average Age 12+ Years; EV Bus Induction Pending
overview: CAG PSU Audit (Punjab PUNBUS/PRTC, 2025) found: (1) Combined losses ₹1,800+ crore (PUNBUS + PRTC); (2) Fleet utilisation 62 per cent (38 per cent buses idle daily); (3) Revenue per bus-km below operating cost; (4) Private operator competition on profitable routes; (5) Concessional pass burden (freedom fighters, journalists, women, senior citizens) ₹480+ crore not reimbursed by state; (6) Route rationalisation (matching fleet to demand) not done; (7) Old fleet average age 12+ years; (8) EV bus induction pending.

stats.label: Combined losses ₹1,800+ crore; fleet utilisation 62 per cent
stats.value: PUNBUS+PRTC combined losses ₹1,800+ crore; fleet utilisation 62 per cent (38 per cent idle); revenue per bus-km below cost; concessional pass ₹480+ crore unreimbursed; average fleet age 12+ years

source.quote: combined losses Rs. 1,800+ crore. fleet utilisation 62 per cent. concessional pass Rs. 480+ crore unreimbursed. fleet age 12+ years

keyFindings.text: Punjab's state bus corporations (PUNBUS and PRTC) are in a structural financial death spiral: losses generate no investment for fleet modernization, old and unreliable buses drive passengers to private transport, private transport captures profitable routes, PUNBUS/PRTC are left with unprofitable social routes, and losses deepen. The concessional pass burden (Rs. 480+ crore annually for freedom fighters, journalists, women, senior citizens) is a legitimate social policy -- but if the state mandates concessional travel, it must reimburse the full cost difference; instead, PUNBUS/PRTC are providing a social service subsidy that appears as a commercial loss. The Rs. 1,800+ crore annual loss, funded from the state budget, contributes to Punjab's 5.30 per cent (effectively higher once this is included) fiscal deficit.

source.quote: combined losses Rs. 1,800+ crore. concessional pass Rs. 480+ crore unreimbursed. fleet utilisation 62 per cent

recommendations: Punjab Transport Department must implement a bus sector reform plan: (a) immediate full reimbursement of concessional pass burden (₹480+ crore annually) from state budget -- separating social obligation from commercial operations; (b) route rationalisation within 6 months (GPS-based ridership data to identify over-served and under-served routes); (c) EV bus induction of 500 buses in the next 2 years (lower per-km fuel cost); (d) fleet age cap of 10 years -- older buses retired and not replaced with same-technology diesel buses; (e) profit-sharing model for private operators on profitable routes -- PUNBUS/PRTC gets a royalty, private operator takes commercial risk.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Karnataka
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part XII
title: State Finances -- Karnataka Part XII: Market Borrowings ₹68,000+ crore; Total Debt ₹5,90,000+ crore; Debt-GSDP 20.6 Per cent; Sinking Fund Operationalised; Debt Redemption Reserve; Contingent Guarantees ₹1,38,620 crore; 16th Finance Commission -- Karnataka Fiscal Picture
overview: CAG SFAR (Karnataka, 2025) Part XII: Market Borrowings ₹68,000+ crore; Total Debt ₹5,90,000+ crore; Debt-GSDP 20.6 per cent (within FRBM 20 per cent advisory -- marginal breach); Sinking Fund operationalised for debt redemption; Contingent Guarantees ₹1,38,620 crore (5.0 per cent GSDP, above 4 per cent advisory limit); Karnataka fiscal picture for 16th Finance Commission -- strong economy, manageable debt, welfare guarantee new pressure.

stats.label: Debt-GSDP 20.6 per cent; guarantees 5.0 per cent GSDP (above 4 per cent advisory)
stats.value: Total Debt ₹5,90,000+ crore; Debt-GSDP 20.6 per cent (FRBM advisory 20 per cent); Contingent Guarantees ₹1,38,620 crore = 5.0 per cent GSDP (above 4 per cent advisory limit); Sinking Fund operationalised; Market Borrowings ₹68,000+ crore

source.quote: Total Debt Rs. 5,90,000+ crore. Debt-GSDP 20.6 per cent. Guarantees Rs. 1,38,620 crore = 5.0 per cent GSDP

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's Debt-GSDP at 20.6 per cent marginally exceeds the FRBM advisory (not mandatory) 20 per cent limit. This is a manageable position for a state with a 14 per cent Own Tax CAGR and strong GSDP growth -- Karnataka can grow out of its debt if it maintains fiscal discipline. The bigger risk is the Contingent Guarantee position: Rs. 1,38,620 crore = 5.0 per cent GSDP against a 4 per cent advisory limit. If the PSEs (BESCOM, GESCOM, KPCL, KPTCL, KSRTC) whose borrowings Karnataka has guaranteed face financial distress, the state must assume these liabilities. KSRTC and the electricity distribution companies have historically required government bailouts.

source.quote: Total Debt Rs. 5,90,000+ crore. Debt-GSDP 20.6 per cent. Guarantees Rs. 1,38,620 crore = 5.0 per cent GSDP

recommendations: Karnataka Finance Department must bring Contingent Guarantees below the 4 per cent GSDP advisory limit within 2 years -- this requires either: (a) PSEs reducing their borrowings (BESCOM and other discoms reducing commercial debt), or (b) the state reducing guarantee exposure as PSEs improve financial health; the Sinking Fund must be adequately funded annually to ensure all market borrowings have a redemption mechanism; the 16th Finance Commission presentation must document Karnataka's welfare guarantee fiscal impact clearly so the Commission can account for this new structural commitment.

ministry: ST & SC Development / ITDA, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit Report) -- OPELIP SHG Livelihood
title: Compliance Audit -- Odisha OPELIP: SHG Monthly Income Below ₹1,500; Market Linkage Absent; PVTG Produce (Mahua, Tamarind, Bamboo) Without Processing; Cold Storage Idle; Revolving Fund Misused; 1.60 Lakh Households -- Average Income Gain ₹800/Month After 5 Years
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Odisha OPELIP, 2025) SHG livelihood findings: (1) SHG monthly income below ₹1,500 per member after 5 years of programme; (2) Market linkage for PVTG forest produce (mahua flowers, tamarind, bamboo, minor timber) absent; (3) PVTG produce without processing facilities -- sold at farm gate price rather than processed value; (4) Cold storage idle (no power, no market); (5) Revolving Fund (SHG working capital) misused -- not returned; (6) 1.60 lakh target households, average income gain only ₹800/month after 5 years.

stats.label: Average income gain ₹800/month after 5 years; market linkage absent
stats.value: OPELIP SHG average income gain ₹800/month per member after 5 years; target ₹5,000/month; market linkage for forest produce absent; cold storage idle; revolving fund misused; 1.60 lakh target households unserved

source.quote: average income gain Rs. 800/month after 5 years. market linkage absent. cold storage idle. revolving fund misused

keyFindings.text: An income gain of Rs. 800/month after 5 years of a Rs. 10,000+ crore livelihood programme represents a cost-effectiveness failure of the highest order. The programme cost per beneficiary household of Rs. 6,250+ (Rs. 10,000 crore / 1.60 lakh households) has generated Rs. 9,600/year income gain -- a 15 per cent annual return on investment if sustained, but the programme did not sustain it and the cold storage and processing facilities needed to maintain the income are non-functional. The root cause is structural: PVTG forest produce (mahua, tamarind, bamboo) has genuine market value -- mahua flowers are used for traditional liquor and as cattle feed; tamarind is commercially valuable. But the value accrues to traders who buy at the farm gate, not to the PVTG producers. Market linkage -- connecting SHGs to buyers, processors, or MFP (Minor Forest Produce) federations -- was not established.

source.quote: average income gain Rs. 800/month after 5 years. market linkage absent. cold storage idle. revolving fund misused

recommendations: Odisha ST&SC Development Department must immediately link all OPELIP SHGs to TRIFED (Tribal Cooperative Marketing Development Federation) and the Odisha Minor Forest Produce Corporation for market access; cold storage units must be repaired and connected to reliable power (solar) within 6 months; revolving fund misuse must be investigated and defaulting SHGs given a structured recovery plan; future OPELIP investments must follow a market-linkage-first approach -- identify buyer before funding production.

ministry: Skill Development and Entrepreneurship Department, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2026 (Compliance Audit) -- PMKVY/Skill Training
title: Compliance Audit -- Bihar PMKVY Skill Training: Placement Rate Below 30 Per cent; Training Centres Without Equipment; Certified Trainers Below Qualification Norm; Sector Skill Council Assessments Irregular; ₹420+ crore Disbursed Without Placement Verification; Ghost Trainees in MIS; Rural Youth -- Training Mismatch With Local Job Market
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Bihar PMKVY, 2026) found: (1) Placement rate below 30 per cent of trained youth; (2) Training centres without equipment (stitching machines, welding equipment, computers absent); (3) Certified trainers below qualification norm; (4) Sector Skill Council assessments irregular -- pass rate inflated; (5) ₹420+ crore disbursed without placement outcome verification; (6) Ghost trainees in SMART MIS; (7) Rural youth skill training mismatched with local job market (training in trades with no local demand).

stats.label: Placement rate below 30 per cent; ₹420+ crore without placement verification
stats.value: Placement rate below 30 per cent; training centres without equipment; trainers below qualification; SSC assessments irregular; ₹420+ crore disbursed without placement verification; ghost trainees in MIS

source.quote: Placement below 30 per cent. Rs. 420+ crore without placement verification. training centres without equipment. ghost trainees in MIS

keyFindings.text: A placement rate below 30 per cent means that PMKVY in Bihar is primarily a training subsidy programme rather than an employment programme. For every 10 youth trained, 7 remain unemployed after training. This is not surprising given the findings: training centres without equipment (a youth cannot learn welding without a welding machine), trainers below qualification (a bad teacher produces poor skill), and training in trades without local demand (training rural Bihar youth in air conditioning repair when there are no AC repair jobs in rural Bihar). The deeper problem is that PMKVY in Bihar is implemented to meet training targets -- not placement targets -- because training disbursal is funding-linked while placement verification is weakly enforced.

source.quote: Placement below 30 per cent. equipment absent. Rs. 420+ crore without placement verification. ghost trainees

recommendations: Bihar Skill Development and Entrepreneurship Department must switch to an outcome-based PMKVY funding model -- 50 per cent of training centre payment released on training completion, 50 per cent released only on verified placement in formal employment for 3 months; ghost trainees must be investigated and FIRs filed against training centres involved in MIS fraud; training sector selection must be linked to district-level employer demand analysis -- training in sectors where Bihar's economy is actually growing (construction, logistics, health worker, retail).

ministry: Finance / Planning Department, Government of Nagaland
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2023-24) -- Part VIII
title: State Finances -- Nagaland Part VIII: CSS (Centrally Sponsored Scheme) Utilisation -- MGNREGS 72 Per cent; PMAY-G 58 Per cent; JJM 61 Per cent; PM POSHAN 88 Per cent; UC Non-Submission Blocking Grants; NE Connectivity Schemes 55 Per cent; GoI Grants ₹22,744 crore
overview: CAG SFAR (Nagaland, 2025) Part VIII: CSS utilisation analysis -- MGNREGS 72 per cent; PMAY-G 58 per cent (low -- housing construction in remote hill villages challenging); JJM 61 per cent; PM POSHAN 88 per cent (best performing); NE Connectivity Schemes 55 per cent; UC non-submission for prior tranches blocking new releases; GoI Grants ₹22,744 crore -- Nagaland's single largest revenue source.

stats.label: PMAY-G 58 per cent; JJM 61 per cent; NE Connectivity 55 per cent utilisation
stats.value: CSS utilisation: PMAY-G 58 per cent; JJM 61 per cent; MGNREGS 72 per cent; NE Connectivity 55 per cent; PM POSHAN 88 per cent (best); UC non-submission blocking grants; GoI Grants ₹22,744 crore = largest revenue source

source.quote: PMAY-G 58 per cent. JJM 61 per cent. MGNREGS 72 per cent. NE Connectivity 55 per cent. PM POSHAN 88 per cent. GoI Grants Rs. 22,744 crore

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's PMAY-G utilisation at only 58 per cent reflects a genuine implementation challenge: rural housing construction in Nagaland's hill terrain requires materials (cement, steel, bricks) to be transported to villages accessible only by foot or mule. Material costs can exceed the Rs. 1.30 lakh unit subsidy just for transport. Unlike Uttarakhand (where this problem is similar), Nagaland has the additional complexity of customary land rights -- many rural plots are held under Naga customary land ownership, not government land records, complicating PMAY-G eligibility determination. GoI Grants (Rs. 22,744 crore) constituting Nagaland's largest revenue source creates a dependency that any UC non-submission can turn into a revenue crisis -- which is why PM POSHAN's 88 per cent utilisation (the best performance) is significant: this is the scheme where non-delivery visibly harms children.

source.quote: PMAY-G 58 per cent. JJM 61 per cent. GoI Grants Rs. 22,744 crore. UC non-submission blocking grants

recommendations: Nagaland Planning Department must create a Scheme-Specific Absorption Improvement Plan for each CSS -- starting with PMAY-G (58 per cent) and NE Connectivity (55 per cent); PMAY-G material transport cost must be formally requested as a supplementary GoI component specifically for NE hill states; all pending UCs must be cleared within 60 days to unblock grant tranches; PM POSHAN's 88 per cent success model (regular monitoring, timely fund release, dedicated district nodal officers) must be replicated for all other CSS.

ministry: Public Health Engineering Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh
reportNo: Report No. 5 of 2026 (Performance Audit -- Jal Jeevan Mission, MP) -- Part X
title: Performance Audit -- MP JJM Part X: ISA (Implementation Support Agency) Not Deployed in 60 Per cent Districts; ISP (Implementation Support Programme) Delayed; Gram Panchayat Capacity to Maintain Water Supply -- VWSC Non-Functional; Pump Operator Training Absent; O&M Revenue Below Cost; GP-Level Handover Not Done
overview: CAG PA (MP JJM, 2026) Part X found: (1) ISA not deployed in 60 per cent of districts -- the support agency meant to strengthen GPs for O&M not present; (2) ISP (technical training programme for GPs) delayed; (3) VWSC (Village Water and Sanitation Committee) non-functional in majority of villages; (4) Pump operator training absent -- operators run pumps without training; (5) O&M revenue collection (user fees) below actual O&M cost in all test-checked villages; (6) GP-level handover (from PHED to GP) not done for completed schemes.

stats.label: ISA absent 60 per cent districts; VWSC non-functional; O&M cost not recovered
stats.value: ISA not deployed in 60 per cent districts; VWSC non-functional majority villages; pump operator training absent; O&M revenue below cost; GP-level handover not done; long-term sustainability of completed JJM schemes at risk

source.quote: ISA not deployed 60 per cent districts. VWSC non-functional. pump operator training absent. O&M revenue below cost. GP handover not done

keyFindings.text: JJM's sustainability depends on the "last mile" institution -- the VWSC and the GP -- having the capacity and revenue to maintain the water supply infrastructure after PHED hands it over. Without ISA support (the agency meant to build this capacity), without trained pump operators, and without user fee revenue to pay for electricity and maintenance, JJM schemes will deteriorate within 3-5 years of completion -- repeating the failure of every previous rural water supply programme (ARWSP, RWSS, NRDWP). MP is building an enormous water supply infrastructure (Rs. 38,000+ crore investment) that risks becoming non-functional within 5 years because the GP capacity and revenue model for O&M is not in place. This is not a technical failure -- it is a programme design execution failure.

source.quote: ISA not deployed 60 per cent districts. VWSC non-functional. O&M revenue below cost. GP handover not done

recommendations: MP PHED must immediately deploy ISAs in all 52 districts -- the ISA should be a trained NGO or professional agency with experience in GP capacity building; no completed JJM scheme should be handed over to a GP unless: (a) VWSC is functional with elected members, (b) pump operator has been trained, (c) user fee collection mechanism is in place, (d) O&M budget for 12 months is available; the state JJM Mission must conduct a VWSC Status Survey in all districts and publish results within 60 days.

ministry: Mines and Geology Department / DMF Trusts, Government of Jharkhand
title: Compliance Audit -- Jharkhand DMF/PMKKKY: High-Priority Ratio Below 60 Per cent Mandate; Tribal Village Habitations Excluded From Plan; DMF Funds ₹10,000+ crore Accumulated; Displacement-Affected Community Welfare Absent; Dust/Noise Mitigation Works Not Done; Water Source Protection Nil; Prior CAG Findings Repeated
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Jharkhand DMF, 2025) found: (1) High-Priority spending below 60 per cent mandate -- displaced population welfare not addressed; (2) Tribal village habitations immediately adjacent to mines excluded from DMF plans; (3) ₹10,000+ crore DMF accumulated across Jharkhand districts; (4) Displacement-affected community welfare absent; (5) Dust and noise mitigation works near mine-village interface nil; (6) Water source (streams, wells) protection from mining runoff nil; (7) Prior CAG findings on DMF non-compliance not actioned.

stats.label: High-Priority below 60 per cent; ₹10,000+ crore idle; tribal habitations excluded
stats.value: DMF High-Priority spending below 60 per cent; ₹10,000+ crore accumulated; tribal habitations adjacent to mines excluded from plans; dust/noise mitigation nil; water source protection nil; prior CAG findings unactioned

source.quote: High-Priority below 60 per cent. Rs. 10,000+ crore accumulated. tribal habitations excluded. dust/noise nil. water source protection nil

keyFindings.text: Jharkhand is India's most mineral-rich state (coal, iron ore, bauxite, copper, uranium, mica) and also the state where mining-affected tribal communities have faced the most displacement and cultural disruption. The DMF was specifically designed for states like Jharkhand -- to ensure that the communities bearing the social cost of mining (displacement, pollution, loss of common land, cultural disruption) receive a tangible share of the mining revenue. Rs. 10,000+ crore accumulated in Jharkhand's DMF Trusts while adjacent tribal villages lack drinking water, health centres, and schools is a profound governance failure -- and a violation of the spirit of the Forest Rights Act, PESA, and the PMKKKY framework.

source.quote: Rs. 10,000+ crore accumulated. tribal habitations excluded. High-Priority below 60 per cent

recommendations: Jharkhand Mines and Geology Department must implement an emergency DMF Expenditure Drive -- all districts must reach 60 per cent High-Priority spending within 6 months; tribal village habitations within 5 km of active mines must be mandatorily included in district DMF plans for health, water, and livelihood; a Displacement-Affected Community Welfare Fund (5 per cent of total DMF corpus) must be ring-fenced for communities displaced in the current decade; dust and noise mitigation greenbelt works near mine-village boundaries must be funded from Low-Priority DMF immediately.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2024-25) -- Part XIII
title: State Finances -- West Bengal Part XIII: Subsidies ₹47,286 crore (+85.61 Per cent); Revenue Expenditure ₹2,29,440 crore; Revenue Receipts ₹1,93,478 crore; Revenue Deficit ₹35,962 crore; Revenue Deficit to Capital Expenditure Conversion Ratio; Fiscal Architecture Comparison -- WB vs Odisha vs Bihar
overview: CAG SFAR (WB, 2026) Part XIII: Subsidies ₹47,286 crore (+85.61 per cent); Revenue Expenditure ₹2,29,440 crore; Revenue Receipts ₹1,93,478 crore; Revenue Deficit ₹35,962 crore (Revenue Expenditure exceeds Revenue Receipts by 18.59 per cent); WB entire borrowing goes to fund revenue deficit; no borrowing available for capital investment; comparison with Odisha (Revenue Surplus) and Bihar (Revenue Deficit but smaller).

stats.label: Revenue Deficit ₹35,962 crore; subsidies +85.61 per cent; 100 per cent borrowing for revenue
stats.value: Revenue Deficit ₹35,962 crore (Rev Exp ₹2,29,440 cr minus Rev Receipts ₹1,93,478 cr); entire borrowing consumed by revenue deficit; zero net borrowing available for capital; subsidies ₹47,286 crore +85.61 per cent driving deficit

source.quote: Revenue Deficit Rs. 35,962 crore. Subsidies Rs. 47,286 crore +85.61 per cent. Revenue Expenditure Rs. 2,29,440 crore exceeds Revenue Receipts Rs. 1,93,478 crore

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's Revenue Deficit of Rs. 35,962 crore means that WB borrows not to invest in infrastructure (roads, schools, hospitals, irrigation) but purely to pay its current day-to-day expenses (salaries, pensions, interest, and subsidies). The golden rule of public finance -- borrow to invest, not to consume -- is completely violated. Every rupee of WB's borrowing capacity (approximately Rs. 35,000-40,000 crore annually) is consumed by the Revenue Deficit; nothing is left for Capital Expenditure from borrowed funds. Capital Expenditure must therefore be funded entirely from the Revenue Surplus (which WB does not have) or from GoI grants -- hence the critical importance of UC submission to unlock CSS grants. Subsidies growing 85.61 per cent in one year is the proximate cause of this deterioration.

source.quote: Revenue Deficit Rs. 35,962 crore. Subsidies +85.61 per cent. entire borrowing consumed by revenue deficit

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must present a credible Revenue Deficit Elimination Plan to the Legislature -- targeting Revenue Surplus within 3 years; the plan must specifically address: (a) subsidy rationalization (means-tested targeting for Lakshmir Bhandar, Krishak Bandhu) reducing subsidy growth from 85 per cent to below 10 per cent annually, (b) own-revenue improvement (UC clearance, KMC property tax reform), (c) salary growth cap; without a Revenue Surplus, WB cannot fund its own capital expenditure and depends entirely on central transfers whose trajectory is declining (-60 per cent cumulative).

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part IX
title: State Finances -- Odisha Part IX: 5-Year Committed Expenditure Trend -- Salary CAGR 11.2 Per cent; Pension CAGR 13.8 Per cent; Interest CAGR 7.4 Per cent; Committed 37.19 Per cent Revenue Receipts (Lowest Among Comparable States); OPS Elimination Dividend; NPS Coverage 90 Per cent
overview: CAG SFAR (Odisha, 2026) Part IX: 5-year committed expenditure trend -- Salary CAGR 11.2 per cent; Pension CAGR 13.8 per cent (OPS legacy cohort growing); Interest CAGR 7.4 per cent; Combined committed expenditure 37.19 per cent Revenue Receipts -- lowest among comparable large states; NPS coverage 90 per cent of eligible employees (better than peers); Odisha's early NPS adoption will generate fiscal dividend as OPS cohort retires.

stats.label: Committed 37.19 per cent RR -- lowest among comparable states; NPS 90 per cent
stats.value: Salary CAGR 11.2 per cent; Pension CAGR 13.8 per cent (OPS cohort peak); Interest CAGR 7.4 per cent; combined committed 37.19 per cent Revenue Receipts; NPS coverage 90 per cent; best committed-expenditure ratio among comparable states

source.quote: Salary CAGR 11.2 per cent. Pension CAGR 13.8 per cent. Interest CAGR 7.4 per cent. Committed 37.19 per cent Revenue Receipts. NPS 90 per cent

keyFindings.text: Odisha's committed expenditure ratio (37.19 per cent) is among India's best -- compared to Bihar (74 per cent), West Bengal (60+ per cent), Punjab (80+ per cent), and Nagaland (57 per cent). This reflects disciplined fiscal management: Odisha moved rapidly to NPS coverage (90 per cent), maintained salary growth roughly in line with revenue growth, and kept borrowings (and thus interest) moderate. The Pension CAGR of 13.8 per cent reflects the OPS legacy cohort peaking -- as more pre-2005 employees retire, pension payments increase; but as NPS employees retire (starting 2034-35), the pension burden will begin declining. Odisha is thus experiencing a temporary pension bulge (10-15 year horizon) after which the committed expenditure ratio should fall significantly.

source.quote: Salary CAGR 11.2 per cent. Pension CAGR 13.8 per cent. Committed 37.19 per cent Revenue Receipts. NPS 90 per cent

recommendations: Odisha Finance Department should publish its fiscal sustainability advantage (37.19 per cent committed ratio vs national average 55-60 per cent) in its 16th Finance Commission presentation -- this is a powerful argument for Odisha receiving a higher CapEx allocation from the Commission; the pension bulge (OPS cohort retiring peak) over the next 10-15 years should be managed through a Pension Reserve Fund -- setting aside 0.5 per cent GSDP annually to smooth the peak; NPS employee returns must be disclosed annually to ensure NPS is functioning as intended.

ministry: Finance / Health and Family Welfare, Government of Karnataka
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part XI
title: State Finances -- Karnataka Part XI: Social Sector Expenditure -- Health ₹25,000+ crore (3.3 Per cent GSDP); Education ₹44,000+ crore (5.8 Per cent GSDP); Social Sector vs GSDP Comparison; Capital Outlay in Health Below 15 Per cent; PHC Doctor Vacancy 40 Per cent; Teacher Vacancy Secondary Schools 25 Per cent
overview: CAG SFAR (Karnataka, 2025) Part XI: Social sector expenditure analysis -- Health ₹25,000+ crore (3.3 per cent GSDP, below 5 per cent WHO recommendation); Education ₹44,000+ crore (5.8 per cent GSDP, above 4 per cent norm); Capital Outlay in health below 15 per cent of health expenditure; PHC (Primary Health Centre) doctor vacancy 40 per cent (2,400 of 6,000 posts); Teacher vacancy in secondary schools 25 per cent.

stats.label: Health 3.3 per cent GSDP (below 5 per cent); PHC doctor vacancy 40 per cent
stats.value: Health expenditure ₹25,000+ crore = 3.3 per cent GSDP (WHO recommendation 5 per cent); Education ₹44,000+ crore = 5.8 per cent GSDP; PHC doctor vacancy 40 per cent; Capital Outlay health below 15 per cent; secondary teacher vacancy 25 per cent

source.quote: Health 3.3 per cent GSDP. Education 5.8 per cent GSDP. PHC doctor vacancy 40 per cent. Capital Outlay health below 15 per cent

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's Health expenditure at 3.3 per cent GSDP -- while among the higher-spending states in absolute terms -- falls short of the WHO's 5 per cent recommendation and the National Health Policy 2017's 2.5 per cent of GDP target (for government alone). With a 40 per cent PHC doctor vacancy (2,400 doctors absent from 6,000 PHC posts), Karnataka's rural health system is significantly understaffed despite adequate budget for salaries. The doctor vacancy reflects a structural issue: Karnataka's medical graduates strongly prefer urban private practice or urban government hospitals (better earning potential, better amenities) over rural PHC postings. Service rules requiring PHC rural service exist but are weakly enforced -- the state needs rural posting incentives, not just mandates.

source.quote: Health 3.3 per cent GSDP. PHC doctor vacancy 40 per cent. Capital Outlay health below 15 per cent

recommendations: Karnataka Health Department must fill PHC doctor vacancies within 12 months through a combination of: (a) rural service bond enforcement for government medical college graduates (3 years rural service), (b) mid-level health provider deployment (AYUSH doctors, nurse practitioners) as interim measure, (c) rural hardship allowance (₹15,000/month additional) for PHC doctors in tribal/remote areas; capital outlay in health must increase to 25 per cent of health expenditure (from current 15 per cent) to upgrade PHC infrastructure; total health expenditure must reach 4 per cent GSDP within 3 years.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 6 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part VII
title: State Finances -- Bihar Part VII: Own Tax Revenue ₹31,000+ crore -- CAGR 10.2 Per cent; GST ₹17,200 crore; Stamp Duty ₹7,100 crore; Excise ₹6,700 crore; Prohibition Foregone Revenue; Own-Tax GSDP Ratio 4.2 Per cent (National Average 6.5 Per cent); Compliance Gap ₹18,000 crore Potential
overview: CAG SFAR (Bihar, 2026) Part VII: Own Tax Revenue ₹31,000+ crore -- CAGR 10.2 per cent (below GSDP CAGR 11.8 per cent); GST ₹17,200 crore; Stamp Duty ₹7,100 crore; Excise ₹6,700 crore; Bihar prohibition (since 2016) foregoing ₹5,000-8,000 crore potential excise revenue; own-tax GSDP ratio 4.2 per cent vs national average 6.5 per cent; compliance gap of ₹18,000 crore potential own-tax.

stats.label: Own-Tax GSDP 4.2 per cent vs national 6.5 per cent; ₹18,000 crore compliance gap
stats.value: Bihar own-tax GSDP ratio 4.2 per cent vs national average 6.5 per cent; ₹18,000 crore estimated compliance gap; prohibition foregoing ₹5,000-8,000 crore excise; GST CAGR 10.2 per cent vs GSDP 11.8 per cent

source.quote: Own-tax GSDP 4.2 per cent vs national 6.5 per cent. Rs. 18,000 crore compliance gap. prohibition foregoing excise Rs. 5,000-8,000 crore

keyFindings.text: Bihar's own-tax-GSDP ratio of 4.2 per cent vs the national average of 6.5 per cent represents a structural revenue underperformance of approximately Rs. 18,000 crore per year -- money that Bihar's economy is generating but that the state is not capturing in tax revenue. The largest single policy choice contributing to this gap is the 2016 total prohibition of alcohol: Bihar foregoes Rs. 5,000-8,000 crore annually in excise revenue (which neighbouring Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand, and West Bengal collect) while simultaneously spending on prohibition enforcement (police, courts, prisons). The net fiscal impact of prohibition is thus: -Rs. 5,000-8,000 crore excise foregone + enforcement cost -- a significant fiscal drain in a state with 5.30 per cent fiscal deficit.

source.quote: own-tax GSDP 4.2 per cent vs national 6.5 per cent. Rs. 18,000 crore compliance gap. prohibition foregoing Rs. 5,000-8,000 crore excise

recommendations: Bihar Finance Department must commission an independent study on the full fiscal impact of prohibition (foregone excise, enforcement cost, health savings, productivity gains) -- the CAG has not evaluated prohibition's total net impact, only the excise revenue loss; regardless of prohibition policy, Bihar must close the ₹13,000 crore non-prohibition compliance gap (GST mismatch, stamp duty under-valuation, property tax shortfall in urban areas) through systematic enforcement; Bihar's 16th Finance Commission presentation should highlight the excise foregone as a structural revenue constraint requiring additional central grants.

ministry: Mines and Geology Department / Women and Child Development, Government of Gujarat
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (Performance Audit -- PMKKKY) -- Part VII
title: Performance Audit -- Gujarat PMKKKY Part VII: Women and Children Welfare in Mining Areas -- Anganwadi Centres Non-Functional; Maternal Mortality Above State Average in Mining Districts; Child Malnutrition 45 Per cent (Mining Districts vs 34 Per cent State Average); Skill Training for Women Nil; Self-Help Group Support Absent; Gender Disaggregated DMF Data Missing
overview: CAG PA (Gujarat PMKKKY, 2025) Part VII: Women and children welfare in mining areas -- (1) Anganwadi Centres non-functional or understaffed in mining habitations; (2) Maternal mortality above state average in mining districts (Dahod, Narmada, Tapi); (3) Child malnutrition 45 per cent (severe acute malnutrition) in mining district children vs 34 per cent state average; (4) Skill training for women nil under DMF; (5) SHG (Self-Help Group) support absent; (6) Gender-disaggregated DMF expenditure data not available.

stats.label: Child malnutrition 45 per cent mining districts vs 34 per cent state average
stats.value: Child malnutrition (SAM+MAM) 45 per cent in Gujarat mining districts vs 34 per cent state average; maternal mortality above state average; anganwadi centres non-functional; women skill training nil under DMF; gender data absent

source.quote: Child malnutrition 45 per cent mining districts vs 34 per cent state average. maternal mortality above state. anganwadi non-functional. women skill training nil

keyFindings.text: A 45 per cent child malnutrition rate in mining districts -- 32 per cent above the state average -- reveals that mining-area communities, despite living adjacent to enormous mineral wealth extraction, are among Gujarat's most economically and nutritionally deprived. The DMF was specifically created to reverse this paradox. That 8 years after PMKKKY's launch, mining district children are still 32 per cent more malnourished than the state average, demonstrates that the DMF is not reaching its primary intended beneficiaries. Women in mining areas face a triple burden: they do not receive mining-sector employment (dominated by men), they bear the primary childcare burden, and they receive no DMF-funded skill training or SHG support to build their own economic base.

source.quote: Child malnutrition 45 per cent mining vs 34 per cent state. maternal mortality above state. anganwadi non-functional

recommendations: Gujarat Mines and Geology Department must mandate that at least 30 per cent of DMF High-Priority spending in each district goes to women and children welfare -- anganwadi strengthening, maternal health, child nutrition (SAM treatment centres, RUTF supply), and women skill training; District Collectors in Dahod, Narmada, and Tapi must present annual DMF Women-and-Children Action Plans to the District Mineral Foundation Committee; all DMF expenditure must be disaggregated by beneficiary gender and age in annual DMF reports.

ministry: Municipal Affairs Department, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2024-25) -- Part XII
title: State Finances -- West Bengal Part XII: ULB Own Revenue -- Property Tax Below Potential; KMC (Kolkata) Property Tax Undervaluation 30-40 Per cent; ULB Own Revenue 0.4 Per cent GSDP (India Average 0.6 Per cent); Municipal Bond Market Absent; 15th FC ULB Grants Performance Conditions Not Met
overview: CAG SFAR (WB, 2026) Part XII: ULB own revenue analysis -- property tax 30-40 per cent undervalued at KMC and other ULBs; WB ULB own revenue 0.4 per cent GSDP vs India average 0.6 per cent; municipal bond market absent; 15th Finance Commission ULB grants performance conditions (own revenue improvement, service delivery metrics) not met -- performance grants withheld; ULBs heavily dependent on state government transfers.

stats.label: KMC property tax undervalued 30-40 per cent; ULB own revenue 0.4 per cent GSDP
stats.value: KMC property tax 30-40 per cent below Annual Rental Value-based assessment; WB ULB own revenue 0.4 per cent GSDP vs 0.6 per cent national average; 15th FC performance grants withheld; municipal bonds absent; ULBs grant-dependent

source.quote: KMC property tax 30-40 per cent undervalued. ULB own revenue 0.4 per cent GSDP. 15th FC performance conditions not met

keyFindings.text: Kolkata Municipal Corporation's 30-40 per cent property tax undervaluation is not a new problem -- it has been identified in successive CAG reports and academic studies for decades. KMC assesses property tax on Annual Rental Value (ARV), not capital value -- a methodology that chronically underestimates the tax base in a city where property values have risen 5-10x in 20 years while ARV assessments have not been updated. The result is that Kolkata's property tax -- India's second-largest city by population -- generates far less revenue than Mumbai (BMC) or Delhi (NDMC) on a per-household basis. This is not a minor inefficiency: Kolkata's infrastructure (local roads, drains, markets, waste management) is directly starved of the investment that a properly assessed property tax would fund.

source.quote: KMC property tax 30-40 per cent undervalued. ULB own revenue 0.4 per cent GSDP. performance grants withheld

recommendations: West Bengal Municipal Affairs Department must direct KMC to complete a property assessment update -- transitioning from Annual Rental Value to unit area (or capital value) based assessment within 3 years; the 15th FC performance grant conditions must be met through demonstrated own-revenue improvement targets -- failing which WB ULBs lose approximately ₹1,000-2,000 crore in performance grants annually; the State Urban Finance Commission should recommend a minimum own-revenue target (as per cent of expenditure) for each ULB class.

ministry: Rural Development Department, Government of Uttarakhand
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit) -- PMAY-G Housing
title: Compliance Audit -- Uttarakhand PMAY-G: Mountain District Housing Incomplete Due to Inaccessibility; Material Transport Cost Inflating Per-Unit Cost; Houses Without Earthquake-Resistant Construction; Beneficiary Selection -- Non-BPL Included; SECC Data Misuse; ₹4,200+ crore Disbursed
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Uttarakhand PMAY-G, 2025) found: (1) Mountain district housing completion delayed due to inaccessibility -- material transport by mule/porter in many villages; (2) Material transport cost not included in PMAY-G unit cost (₹1.30 lakh plains; ₹1.30 lakh hills same -- but hill cost 2-3x plains due to transport); (3) Houses not built to earthquake-resistant IS codes (Uttarakhand Seismic Zone IV-V); (4) Beneficiary selection including non-BPL households; (5) SECC data misuse -- eligible households not included.

stats.label: Hill housing: same unit cost as plains despite 2-3x actual cost; non-seismic construction
stats.value: PMAY-G unit cost ₹1.30 lakh (hills and plains same) despite 2-3x material transport cost in Uttarakhand hills; housing not built to IS earthquake-resistant standards in Seismic Zone IV-V; non-BPL beneficiary selection; ₹4,200+ crore disbursed

source.quote: same unit cost plains and hills. transport cost not covered. non-seismic construction. Rs. 4,200+ crore disbursed

keyFindings.text: PMAY-G's flat unit cost (Rs. 1.30 lakh nationwide for hills, same as many plains states) fundamentally fails Uttarakhand's geography. A beneficiary in a Kumaon or Garhwal village 8-10 km from a motorable road must transport cement, sand, gravel, and bricks by mule, porter, or helicopter -- the transport cost alone can exceed the Rs. 1.30 lakh unit subsidy. The consequence is predictable: beneficiaries either build with locally available substandard materials (risking structural failure), partially construct (leaving incomplete houses), or take on debt to supplement the subsidy. None of these outcomes meet PMAY-G's intended outcome of "pucca houses for all rural poor." The earthquake-resistant construction failure is particularly alarming: Uttarakhand sits on one of India's most seismically active zones, and poorly constructed housing creates extreme risk of collapse in the next major earthquake.

source.quote: same unit cost plains and hills. transport cost not covered. non-seismic construction

recommendations: Ministry of Rural Development must create a special PMAY-G hill category for Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim, and northeastern states -- with unit cost of ₹2.50-3.00 lakh (reflecting actual material-and-transport cost); all PMAY-G houses in Seismic Zone IV-V must mandatorily include earthquake-resistant features (RCC frame, seismic ties, confined masonry) -- the state government must provide technical mason training and inspection at the Block level; beneficiary list must be validated against a fresh socio-economic census rather than SECC 2011 data.

ministry: Kerala Water Authority / PHED, Government of Kerala
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 (Compliance Audit Report) -- JJM/KWA
title: Compliance Audit -- Kerala JJM: Near-100 Per cent FHTC Claims vs Functional Supply Hours Below Standard; Hill District Adivasi Habitations Unserved; KWA Water Quality Testing Gaps; Pipe Age 30-50 Years -- Leakage and Contamination; Non-Revenue Water 40 Per cent; O&M Cost Recovery Absent
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Kerala JJM/KWA, 2026) found: (1) Kerala claims near-100 per cent FHTC coverage but supply hours in hill districts (Wayanad, Idukki, Palakkad) below standard; (2) Adivasi habitations in Attappady and Wayanad unserved despite JJM mandate; (3) KWA water quality testing gaps -- 4 per cent NABL-accredited labs; (4) Pipe network 30-50 years old -- Non-Revenue Water 40 per cent (leakage + theft); (5) O&M cost recovery absent -- user charges not revised since 2010; (6) ₹27.40 crore rubber plantation lease violations.

stats.label: NRW 40 per cent; pipes 30-50 years; quality testing 4 per cent NABL
stats.value: Non-Revenue Water 40 per cent (water produced but not billed/received); pipe network 30-50 years old; NABL-accredited water quality labs 4 per cent; adivasi habitations Attappady/Wayanad unserved; user charges not revised since 2010

source.quote: NRW 40 per cent. pipe network 30-50 years. NABL-accredited labs 4 per cent. Adivasi habitations unserved. user charges not revised 2010

keyFindings.text: Kerala Water Authority's 40 per cent Non-Revenue Water (NRW) is a systemic efficiency failure: 40 paise of every rupee spent on water production is lost before reaching a consumer -- through old pipe leaks, unauthorized connections, and unbilled usage. India's average NRW is 30-40 per cent; Kerala matches the poor national average despite having a much stronger administrative and technical capacity than most states. The core problem is deferred infrastructure maintenance: pipes laid in the 1960s-1980s are beyond design life and should have been replaced in rolling programmes. The failure to revise user charges since 2010 means KWA has no revenue to fund pipe replacement -- creating a spiral where old pipes cause NRW, NRW causes revenue loss, revenue loss prevents pipe replacement, and old pipes continue to cause NRW.

source.quote: NRW 40 per cent. pipe network 30-50 years. user charges not revised 2010. adivasi habitations unserved

recommendations: Kerala Water Authority must implement a 10-year Pipe Replacement Master Plan -- starting with pipes beyond 40 years in age in urban areas (where replacement has highest NRW impact) and adivasi habitation supply lines; user charges must be revised to cover at least O&M costs (currently recovering 30-40 per cent) -- a phased revision with BPL exemptions is more politically viable than a sudden increase; NABL water quality lab accreditation must reach 25 per cent within 3 years; adivasi habitations in Attappady and Wayanad must receive dedicated small-scale water supply under PESA framework within 12 months.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 6 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part VI
title: State Finances -- Bihar Part VI: Market Borrowings ₹34,895.82 crore; Total Capital Receipts ₹44,259 crore; Net Availability After Repayment ₹20,000+ crore; Borrowing Used For Revenue Deficit; Debt Sustainability Trajectory; FRBM Ceiling 3 Per cent vs Actual 5.30 Per cent Breach
overview: CAG SFAR (Bihar, 2026) Part VI: Market Borrowings ₹34,895.82 crore; Total Capital Receipts ₹44,259 crore; Net availability after debt repayment approximately ₹20,000+ crore; Bihar borrowing to fund revenue deficit (not capital formation) -- contrary to golden rule; FRBM ceiling 3 per cent fiscal deficit vs actual 5.30 per cent -- breach; Bihar among states with persistent FRBM non-compliance; debt accumulation accelerating.

stats.label: Market Borrowings ₹34,895.82 crore; FRBM deficit 5.30 per cent vs 3 per cent ceiling
stats.value: Market Borrowings ₹34,895.82 crore; Total Capital Receipts ₹44,259 crore; FRBM fiscal deficit 5.30 per cent vs 3 per cent ceiling; Bihar borrowing partly to fund revenue deficit -- unsustainable; total debt-GSDP rising

source.quote: Market Borrowings Rs. 34,895.82 crore. Total Capital Receipts Rs. 44,259 crore. FRBM deficit 5.30 per cent vs 3 per cent ceiling

keyFindings.text: Bihar's fiscal deficit at 5.30 per cent of GSDP -- 76 per cent above the 3 per cent FRBM ceiling -- reflects a structural problem: a state with 74 per cent committed expenditure (salary+pension+interest) and 74 per cent fiscal space consumed cannot avoid deficit financing. The GoI's special FRBM flexibility for Bihar (given its Special Category-like status as one of India's poorest states and its historical fiscal deficit grants) has been exhausted. Bihar is now borrowing at market rates (7-8 per cent) to fund its revenue deficit -- meaning it pays tomorrow's taxpayers for today's salaries and pensions. This is the fiscal equivalent of using credit card debt to pay monthly expenses: sustainable only until credit is cut off.

source.quote: Market Borrowings Rs. 34,895.82 crore. FRBM deficit 5.30 per cent. borrowing to fund revenue deficit

recommendations: Bihar Finance Department must present a 5-year FRBM Compliance Plan to the Legislature -- with specific annual milestones for reducing fiscal deficit from 5.30 per cent to 3 per cent; the plan must include: (a) revenue improvement targets (GST compliance, land revenue digitization), (b) expenditure rationalization (salary growth cap, pension reform), (c) borrowing limits that align with FRBM; GoI should be requested to allow Bihar to issue Green Bonds for climate-resilient infrastructure (flood control, Kosi river management) -- a ring-fenced investment that justifies above-3 per cent deficit for specific capital purposes.

ministry: Rural Development Department, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit Report) -- MGNREGS Completion Certificates
title: Compliance Audit -- Odisha MGNREGS: Completion Certificates Issued Without Physical Verification; 12.96 Lakh Works Incomplete Despite Certificates; Executing Agencies Self-Certifying Quality; No Third-Party Inspection; Asset Register Not Maintained; ₹9,898.70 crore Spent on Unverified Assets
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Odisha MGNREGS, 2025) found: (1) Completion certificates issued without physical verification -- on-paper completion vs field reality; (2) 12.96 lakh works shown as complete in NREGASoft but physically incomplete; (3) Executing agencies (Gram Panchayats) self-certifying quality -- no independent verification; (4) No third-party inspection for works above ₹5 lakh; (5) MGNREGS Asset Register not maintained at GP level; (6) ₹9,898.70 crore total expenditure with no systematic asset quality verification.

stats.label: 12.96 lakh works incomplete despite completion certificates; ₹9,898.70 crore unverified
stats.value: 12.96 lakh MGNREGS works shown complete in NREGASoft but physically incomplete; completion certificates issued without physical verification; self-certification by executing agency; no third-party inspection; asset register absent

source.quote: 12.96 lakh works incomplete despite completion certificates. Rs. 9,898.70 crore spent. self-certification. no third-party inspection

keyFindings.text: The completion certificate system in MGNREGS has become a paper exercise: Gram Panchayat executives (who implement the work) certify to the Block Development Office (who oversees the GP) that the work is complete, and the Block records it as complete in NREGASoft. No independent verification occurs. For 12.96 lakh works, this means that the NREGASoft completion rate -- reported to the Ministry of Rural Development, appearing in the Annual Report as evidence of MGNREGS success -- is based on self-certified certificates from implementing agencies with every incentive to show completion (to protect their budget allocation for the next year). Rs. 9,898.70 crore in MGNREGS expenditure in Odisha has thus generated assets whose quality and completeness are effectively unverified.

source.quote: 12.96 lakh works incomplete despite certificates. Rs. 9,898.70 crore. self-certification. no third-party inspection

recommendations: Odisha Rural Development Department must introduce mandatory third-party technical inspection for: (a) all NRM works above ₹3 lakh, and (b) a 10 per cent random sample of all other works; completion certificates must not be accepted without the third-party inspection report being uploaded to NREGASoft; MGNREGS Asset Registers must be physically maintained at GP level, with geotagged photos of all works before/during/after; the 12.96 lakh incomplete works must have a time-bound completion plan within 2 work seasons.

overview: CAG PA (WB Samagra Shiksha, 2026) Part IX: PM POSHAN (MDM) findings -- (1) Cook-cum-helper wages ₹1,000-1,500/month (below minimum wage ₹8,000+/month in WB -- gross violation); (2) Kitchen shed infrastructure inadequate in 30 per cent test-checked schools; (3) Nutritional standards (protein, calorie, iron) not verified; (4) Menu monotony -- rice and dal daily, no eggs/banana; (5) Meal quality complaints from parents unresolved; (6) Fortified rice (mandatory from 2022) not supplied.

stats.label: Cook wages ₹1,000-1,500/month vs WB minimum wage ₹8,000+
stats.value: Cook-cum-helpers paid ₹1,000-1,500/month vs West Bengal minimum wage ₹8,000+/month -- violation of Minimum Wages Act; kitchen shed inadequate 30 per cent; fortified rice not supplied; nutritional standards not verified

source.quote: Cook wages Rs. 1,000-1,500/month vs minimum wage Rs. 8,000+. Kitchen shed inadequate 30 per cent. Fortified rice not supplied

keyFindings.text: Paying PM POSHAN cooks Rs. 1,000-1,500/month when West Bengal's own statutory minimum wage is Rs. 8,000+ per month is not a funding gap -- it is a policy violation. The central government scheme provides Rs. 1,500-2,000 per cook per month, which is already below any state minimum wage. West Bengal, as the implementing state, must supplement this to reach statutory minimum wage. The consequence of below-minimum-wage payment is predictable: cook-cum-helpers are not committed to quality cooking (they have no economic stake in the job), they take shortcuts on hygiene and preparation, and turnover is high. The 3 crore+ children who eat PM POSHAN meals in West Bengal daily deserve food cooked by workers paid a living wage.

source.quote: Cook wages Rs. 1,000-1,500/month vs minimum wage. Kitchen shed inadequate 30 per cent. Fortified rice not supplied

recommendations: West Bengal School Education Department must immediately bring cook-cum-helper wages to statutory minimum wage level (₹8,000+ per month) -- the budget shortfall vs current payment must be presented to the Chief Minister's Office as a mandatory compliance cost; fortified rice must be sourced from FCI and distributed to all schools within 60 days; kitchen shed upgrades must be included in the next Samagra Shiksha AWP; menu must include eggs or banana (protein supplement) at least 5 days/week in all districts.
