reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part X
title: State Finances -- Karnataka Part X: Own Tax Revenue 5-Year Growth 14.2 Per cent CAGR; GST ₹87,427 crore; Stamp Duty ₹22,000+ crore; Excise ₹34,000+ crore; IT Sector GST Compliance; Services Tax Growth 18 Per cent; Revenue From Gambling / Online Gaming Emerging; Potential Own-Tax 20 Per cent Higher
overview: CAG SFAR (Karnataka, 2025) Part X: Own Tax Revenue analysis -- CAGR 14.2 per cent (5 years) driven by GST ₹87,427 crore, Stamp Duty ₹22,000+ crore (Bengaluru real estate), Excise ₹34,000+ crore; IT sector GST compliance driven by reverse charge on exports; services tax growing 18 per cent (professional services, hospitality); online gaming / gambling tax emerging revenue source; CAG estimates potential own-tax 20 per cent higher if compliance improved.

stats.label: Own Tax CAGR 14.2 per cent; GST ₹87,427 crore; services tax +18 per cent
stats.value: Own Tax Revenue CAGR 14.2 per cent (5-year); GST ₹87,427 crore; Stamp Duty ₹22,000+ crore; Excise ₹34,000+ crore; services tax +18 per cent CAGR; potential 20 per cent higher with compliance improvement

source.quote: Own Tax CAGR 14.2 per cent. GST Rs. 87,427 crore. Stamp Duty Rs. 22,000+ crore. Excise Rs. 34,000+ crore. potential 20 per cent higher

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's 14.2 per cent Own Tax CAGR is among India's strongest state-level own-tax performances -- driven by Bengaluru's economic concentration (IT, real estate, hospitality), Karnataka's strong excise performance (Bengaluru is India's largest liquor market), and improving GST compliance. The CAG's estimate of 20 per cent higher potential own-tax with improved compliance suggests approximately Rs. 35,000-40,000 crore in uncollected potential own-tax annually. For a state running 5 welfare guarantees costing Rs. 50,000+ crore, finding Rs. 35,000 crore in untapped own-tax revenue through compliance improvement -- rather than borrowing -- would significantly change the fiscal sustainability equation.

source.quote: Own Tax CAGR 14.2 per cent. GST Rs. 87,427 crore. potential 20 per cent higher with compliance

recommendations: Karnataka Commercial Taxes Department must publish an annual Own-Tax Potential Study comparing actual collections against economic activity benchmarks by sector; the 20 per cent compliance gap (~₹35,000 crore) must be addressed through: (a) AI-driven GST mismatch detection (GSTR-1 vs 3B), (b) stamp duty under-valuation detection through circle rate vs transaction value comparison, (c) excise compliance raids in border areas with Maharashtra/Tamil Nadu; online gaming GST (28 per cent) must be enforced on all offshore platforms used by Karnataka residents.

ministry: Public Health Engineering Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh
reportNo: Report No. 5 of 2026 (Performance Audit -- Jal Jeevan Mission, MP) -- Part IX
title: Performance Audit -- MP JJM Part IX: MVS (Multi-Village Scheme) -- Awarded But Not Started; SVS Completion Below 60 Per cent; PFMS Fund Diversion Outside PFMS; Advance to Agencies Without Work; Cost Per FHTC ₹32,000-38,000 (Above Benchmark); Contractor Cartel in Districts; Ground-Level Reality vs Dashboard
overview: CAG PA (MP JJM, 2026) Part IX found: (1) MVS (Multi-Village Scheme) -- multiple schemes awarded years ago but not started; (2) SVS (Single Village Scheme) completion below 60 per cent; (3) JJM funds released outside PFMS (Public Financial Management System) -- fund diversion; (4) Advances to implementing agencies without work orders; (5) Cost per FHTC ₹32,000-38,000 (above ₹30,000 benchmark); (6) Contractor concentration -- few contractors capturing most JJM work creating cartel risk; (7) Dashboard shows high completion vs ground reality.

stats.label: MVS awarded not started; funds outside PFMS; cost per FHTC above benchmark
stats.value: MVS awarded but not started; SVS completion below 60 per cent; JJM funds outside PFMS; advances to agencies without work; cost per FHTC ₹32,000-38,000 vs ₹30,000 benchmark; contractor concentration risk

source.quote: MVS awarded not started. funds outside PFMS. cost per FHTC Rs. 32,000-38,000 vs benchmark. SVS completion below 60 per cent

keyFindings.text: JJM funds flowing outside PFMS is a serious control violation. PFMS (Public Financial Management System) is the central government's fund tracking system -- all JJM releases from Central and State governments are mandated to flow through PFMS to implementing agencies (PHED, GP implementing agencies, contractors). Fund diversion outside PFMS creates untracked cash flows that cannot be audited or monitored by PFMS-based reporting systems. The cost-per-FHTC exceeding the Rs. 30,000 benchmark, combined with contractor concentration, suggests that MP's JJM procurement is not competitive -- a few large contractors are winning most work at above-benchmark rates. MVS schemes awarded years ago but not started mean communities are waiting for water supply while funds are committed and idle.

source.quote: funds outside PFMS. MVS awarded not started. cost per FHTC Rs. 32,000-38,000 vs benchmark. contractor concentration

recommendations: MP PHED must mandate 100 per cent PFMS compliance for all JJM fund releases immediately -- any payment made outside PFMS must be investigated and the responsible officer held accountable; all MVS schemes awarded but not started must be reviewed within 30 days: contracts must be either activated (with a specific start date and milestone schedule) or rescinded and re-tendered; cost-per-FHTC must be benchmarked quarterly against state average -- works above ₹33,000 per FHTC must have technical justification reviewed by PHED headquarters.

ministry: Rural Development Department, Government of Jharkhand
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit) -- MGNREGS Employment
title: Compliance Audit -- Jharkhand MGNREGS Employment: Average 43 Days Per Household (vs 100 Days); Tribal Household Coverage; Women Workers 56 Per cent (Positive); Social Audit Not Done in 65 Per cent Blocks; Unemployment Allowance Nil; ₹20,098.82 crore AC Bills + MGNREGS Wage Diversion
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Jharkhand MGNREGS, 2025) found: (1) Average employment only 43 days/household vs 100-day guarantee; (2) Tribal household coverage -- Jharkhand with 26 per cent tribal population; MGNREGS should be highest impact here; (3) Women workers 56 per cent (above 33 per cent target -- positive); (4) Social audit not done in 65 per cent blocks; (5) Unemployment allowance: nil paid despite 100-day guarantee gap; (6) Wage diversion concerns linked to ₹20,098.82 crore AC bill system.

stats.label: Average 43 days employment; social audit absent 65 per cent blocks
stats.value: Average employment 43 days/household vs 100-day guarantee (57 per cent shortfall); social audit not done in 65 per cent blocks; unemployment allowance nil; women workers 56 per cent (positive); tribal areas underserved

source.quote: Average 43 days employment vs 100 days. Social audit 65 per cent blocks absent. Unemployment allowance nil. Women 56 per cent positive

keyFindings.text: Jharkhand's tribal communities -- Santals, Mundas, Oraons, Hos, Kharias -- depend heavily on MGNREGS as their primary source of income security during the agricultural off-season. The state's 26 per cent tribal population is concentrated in districts (Khunti, West Singhbhum, Simdega, Gumla, Dumka) where agricultural wages are low and alternative employment is scarce. MGNREGS's 100-day guarantee is designed precisely for this context. At 43 days average employment, Jharkhand's tribal households receive less than half the income security they are entitled to. Social audit absence in 65 per cent of blocks compounds this -- without social audits, the ghost workers, muster roll fraud, and wage diversion that reduce effective MGNREGS employment go undetected.

source.quote: Average 43 days employment vs 100 days. Social audit 65 per cent blocks absent. tribal areas underserved

recommendations: Jharkhand Rural Development Department must establish a MGNREGS Employment Guarantee Cell at the Block level -- each Block Development Officer must ensure that every registered Job Card holder who demands work receives it within 15 days; Block-level employment generation data must be published weekly; social audit must be conducted in all blocks within 3 months using SEUA facilitators independent of DRDA; unemployment allowance must be automatically calculated and paid for every instance of demand without work.

ministry: Local Government Department, Government of Punjab
reportNo: Report No. 5 of 2025 (Performance Audit -- SWM) -- Part IV
title: Performance Audit -- Punjab SWM Part IV: MRF (Material Recovery Facility) Non-Operational; Private Concession Agreements Without Output Guarantee; Tipping Fee Unpaid to Concessionaire; Wet/Dry Waste Segregation Below 20 Per cent; Extended Producer Responsibility Not Enforced; Urban SWM User Charges Not Collected
overview: CAG PA (Punjab SWM, 2025) Part IV found: (1) MRF (Material Recovery Facility) non-operational at multiple test-checked sites -- machinery installed but not running; (2) Private concession agreements for waste processing without guaranteed input volume -- concessionaires cannot plan capacity; (3) Tipping fee (payment to concessionaire for waste processing) unpaid -- concessionaires in financial distress; (4) Wet/dry waste segregation below 20 per cent (vs 100 per cent target); (5) EPR (Extended Producer Responsibility) for plastic/e-waste not enforced; (6) User charges not collected in most ULBs.

stats.label: MRF non-operational; segregation below 20 per cent; tipping fee unpaid
stats.value: MRF non-operational despite investment; wet/dry segregation below 20 per cent; tipping fee unpaid to concessionaire; private concession without input guarantee; user charges not collected; 68 per cent waste unprocessed

source.quote: MRF non-operational. Segregation below 20 per cent. Tipping fee unpaid. Concession without input guarantee. User charges not collected

keyFindings.text: Punjab's private concession model for solid waste processing has failed because the concessionaire -- responsible for running MRFs and waste-to-compost or waste-to-energy facilities -- is not paid the agreed tipping fee (the ULB's payment per tonne of waste delivered). Without tipping fee payment, the private concessionaire has no income -- the model assumes the concessionaire processes waste for a tipping fee, not for recyclable/compost revenue alone. Wet/dry segregation below 20 per cent means MRFs receive mixed waste, increasing sorting cost and reducing recycling yield. The combined effect is that private partners exit or stop operations while formal waste continues to go to open dumps, and 68 per cent remains unprocessed. This is a procurement-and-payment design failure, not a technology failure.

source.quote: MRF non-operational. Tipping fee unpaid. Segregation below 20 per cent. 68 per cent unprocessed

recommendations: Punjab Local Government Department must immediately pay all pending tipping fees to private concessionaires -- any concessionaire owed more than 3 months of tipping fee must receive payment within 15 days or the ULB must show cause; future SWM concession agreements must include: (a) guaranteed minimum waste volume delivery by ULB, (b) quarterly tipping fee payment schedule, (c) performance penalties for segregation failures on both ULB and concessionaire sides; household wet/dry segregation must be enforced through a graduated compliance programme (awareness + warning + fine) in all Class-I ULBs within 12 months.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part VIII
title: State Finances -- Odisha Part VIII: 5-Year Revenue Trend -- Own Tax CAGR 12.8 Per cent; Non-Tax CAGR 5.4 Per cent; GoI Grants CAGR 9.2 Per cent; Revenue Receipts CAGR 10.1 Per cent vs GSDP CAGR 11.1 Per cent; Revenue-GSDP Ratio Flat; Iron Ore Price Impact on Mineral Royalty
overview: CAG SFAR (Odisha, 2026) Part VIII: 5-year revenue trend analysis -- Own Tax CAGR 12.8 per cent (good, above GDP); Non-Tax CAGR 5.4 per cent (below GSDP -- mineral royalty volatility); GoI Grants CAGR 9.2 per cent (stable unlike WB); Revenue Receipts CAGR 10.1 per cent vs GSDP CAGR 11.1 per cent -- revenue lag of 1 per cent CAGR; iron ore price volatility (₹3,000-8,000/tonne range 2019-2024) creating mineral royalty instability.

stats.label: Own Tax CAGR 12.8 per cent; Revenue CAGR 10.1 per cent vs GSDP 11.1 per cent
stats.value: Own Tax CAGR 12.8 per cent (5-year) -- above GSDP; Non-Tax CAGR 5.4 per cent (below GSDP); GoI Grants CAGR 9.2 per cent; Revenue Receipts CAGR 10.1 per cent vs GSDP 11.1 per cent; 1 per cent CAGR revenue-GSDP lag

source.quote: Own Tax CAGR 12.8 per cent. Non-Tax CAGR 5.4 per cent. GoI Grants CAGR 9.2 per cent. Revenue Receipts CAGR 10.1 per cent vs GSDP 11.1 per cent

keyFindings.text: Odisha's Own Tax Revenue CAGR at 12.8 per cent (above GSDP growth) is the most positive long-term fiscal signal in this audit cycle. It means Odisha is expanding its tax base faster than the economy -- driven by GST compliance improvement, stamp duty digitization, and commercial activity growth. The Non-Tax Revenue CAGR at only 5.4 per cent (below GSDP) reflects iron ore price volatility: when iron ore prices fell (2019-2022), Odisha's royalty revenues fell sharply; when prices recovered (2022-2024), royalties recovered. The annual Rs. 1,790 crore decline in FY 2024-25 non-tax revenue likely reflects a moderate iron ore price correction from the 2022-23 peak. Odisha should treat mineral royalty as a non-recurrent windfall -- not as structural revenue -- and plan expenditure conservatively.

source.quote: Own Tax CAGR 12.8 per cent. Non-Tax CAGR 5.4 per cent. Revenue Receipts CAGR 10.1 per cent vs GSDP 11.1 per cent

recommendations: Odisha Finance Department should formalize a Mineral Revenue Stabilization Fund -- when iron ore / coal royalties exceed a 5-year moving average, the excess should be transferred to the Fund; in years of royalty shortfall (like FY 2024-25 with -₹1,790 crore), the Fund supplements the revenue gap; this smooths the fiscal planning cycle and prevents boom-bust dependency on commodity royalties; own tax revenue improvement should target CAGR above 13 per cent through GST compliance drives and property tax reform in ULBs.

ministry: Department of School Education, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (Performance Audit -- Samagra Shiksha in WB) -- Part VIII
title: Performance Audit -- WB Samagra Shiksha Part VIII: Financial Entitlements -- 22 Per cent Students Denied Uniforms/Books/Stipend; Scholarship Disbursement Delayed 6-18 Months; KGBV Residential Girls Below Target; Cycle Scheme Beneficiary Gaps; Aadhaar Seeding for Scholarship Blocking Access
overview: CAG PA (WB Samagra Shiksha, 2026) Part VIII: (1) 22 per cent students denied statutory financial entitlements (uniform, textbooks, stipend) -- RTE Act and scheme mandate; (2) Scholarship disbursement delayed 6-18 months -- effectively denial of financial support; (3) KGBV (Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya) residential schools for ST/SC/OBC/BPL girls -- below target occupancy; (4) Cycle scheme (cycle for girls in secondary schools) -- beneficiary gaps; (5) Aadhaar seeding mandatory for scholarship blocking access for students without Aadhaar.

stats.label: 22 per cent students denied entitlements; scholarship delayed 6-18 months
stats.value: 22 per cent of students not receiving statutory entitlements (uniform, textbooks, stipend); scholarship disbursement delayed 6-18 months; KGBV below target occupancy; cycle scheme gaps; Aadhaar-blocking scholarship access

source.quote: 22 per cent students denied entitlements. Scholarship delayed 6-18 months. KGBV below target occupancy

keyFindings.text: Scholarship delays of 6-18 months effectively negate the scholarship's purpose. A family too poor to afford secondary school fees or books cannot wait 18 months for the government scholarship to arrive -- the student is likely to drop out within 2-3 months of non-payment. The Aadhaar-mandatory scholarship requirement compounds the problem: in West Bengal's remoter areas (Sundarbans, tea garden estates, tribal villages), many students lack Aadhaar or have Aadhaar-bank account seeding errors. Blocking scholarships pending Aadhaar resolution -- without a paper-based interim mechanism -- means the poorest students (who are least likely to have Aadhaar) are most likely to lose scholarship access. The 22 per cent entitlement denial is directly linked to dropouts (35 per cent at secondary level).

source.quote: 22 per cent students denied entitlements. Scholarship delayed 6-18 months. Aadhaar blocking access

recommendations: West Bengal School Education Department must implement a 45-day scholarship disbursement SLA -- all scholarships must be credited within 45 days of application approval; Aadhaar-blocking cases must have an interim cash/cheque payment mechanism while Aadhaar seeding is resolved; the 22 per cent entitlement denial must be investigated district-by-district to identify whether the cause is: (a) fund shortage, (b) administrative lapse, or (c) exclusion criteria -- each cause requires a different fix; KGBV residential schools must conduct annual capacity improvement plans.

overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Bihar MGNREGS employment, 2026) found: (1) Average employment only 40-45 days/household vs 100-day guarantee -- MGNREGS right to work not fulfilled; (2) Women workers 53 per cent (positive -- above 33 per cent mandate); (3) Wage rate below current schedule in some test-checked districts; (4) Wage payment delay beyond 15-day statutory norm; (5) SC/ST share 45 per cent (slightly below 50 per cent target); (6) Aadhaar-DBT coverage gaps -- some wages not reaching workers' accounts.

stats.label: Average employment 40-45 days (vs 100-day guarantee); wages delayed
stats.value: Average employment 40-45 days/household vs 100-day statutory guarantee; 100-day guarantee not met for vast majority; wage rate below schedule; payment delay beyond 15 days; unemployment allowance not paid

source.quote: Average employment 40-45 days. 100-day guarantee not met. Wage below schedule. Payment delay. Unemployment allowance not paid

stats.label: Women workers 53 per cent (positive); SC/ST 45 per cent
stats.value: Women workers 53 per cent -- above 33 per cent mandate (positive outcome); SC/ST share 45 per cent (target 50 per cent -- slightly below); Aadhaar DBT gaps causing wage misdirection

source.quote: Women workers 53 per cent. SC/ST 45 per cent. Aadhaar DBT gaps

keyFindings.text: Bihar's average MGNREGS employment of 40-45 days/household (vs 100-day guarantee) is not primarily a budget constraint -- Bihar's MGNREGS allocation has generally been adequate. The shortfall is primarily a demand-side implementation failure: GPs not receiving and registering work demands, Rozgar Sewaks not creating enough work, and districts not generating adequate work orders to allow 100 days of employment. Bihar's active labour force has significant seasonal migration (to Gujarat, Punjab, Delhi for construction and agriculture) which means the 100-day MGNREGS demand may be partly met by migration rather than MGNREGS -- but this is not a reason to not provide work when demanded in the village. The 53 per cent women worker share is genuinely positive -- it suggests MGNREGS is providing women in Bihar with economic participation that they might not otherwise have.

source.quote: Average employment 40-45 days. Women workers 53 per cent. 100-day guarantee not met

recommendations: Bihar Rural Development Department must implement demand-driven work generation -- all work must start within 15 days of demand registration on NREGASoft; Block MGNREGS officers must be required to generate work orders equivalent to registered demand within 7 days; GP-level employment demand data must be published daily on the Bihar MGNREGS portal; wage delay compensation (0.05 per cent per day) must be automatically calculated and credited to all workers whose wages are delayed beyond 15 days.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Nagaland
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2023-24) -- Part VII
title: State Finances -- Nagaland Part VII: Budget Utilisation By Department -- Health 62 Per cent; Education 91 Per cent; Roads 55 Per cent; Water Supply 78 Per cent; 5-Year Range 55-91 Per cent; Savings Surrendered at Year-End; Re-Appropriation Not Used; Expenditure Front-Loading Absent
overview: CAG SFAR (Nagaland, 2025) Part VII: Department-wise budget utilisation analysis -- Health 62 per cent; Roads 55 per cent; Water Supply 78 per cent; Education 91 per cent; overall 5-year range 55-91 per cent; departments surrendering savings at year-end rather than re-appropriating to higher-absorbing departments; expenditure not front-loaded (concentrated in Q4); Nagaland's implementation capacity limits the impact of GoI special packages.

stats.label: Health 62 per cent utilisation; Roads 55 per cent; 5-year range 55-91 per cent
stats.value: Department-wise: Roads 55 per cent; Health 62 per cent; Water Supply 78 per cent; Education 91 per cent; overall 5-year range 55-91 per cent; savings surrendered at year-end; Q4 expenditure concentration; GoI package absorption limited

source.quote: Health 62 per cent. Roads 55 per cent. Water Supply 78 per cent. Education 91 per cent. 5-year range 55-91 per cent

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's Roads Department utilising only 55 per cent of its budget has compounding effects: unspent road funds mean GoI's NESIDS (North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme) investments are not fully absorbed, road quality improvements are delayed, and economic connectivity -- critical for Nagaland's isolated highland communities -- stagnates. The 55 per cent utilisation is not primarily a procurement issue (Nagaland has exemptions from standard procurement norms); it is primarily a contractor capacity issue (insufficient quality contractors for hill road construction) and a project preparation issue (DPRs not ready when budget is released). Surrendering the unspent 45 per cent at year-end means these roads do not get built at all -- and the following year's budget starts fresh rather than building on unspent carryover.

source.quote: Roads 55 per cent utilisation. Health 62 per cent. 5-year range 55-91 per cent

recommendations: Nagaland Finance Department must introduce a Budget Utilisation Improvement Programme -- departments below 75 per cent utilisation must prepare quarterly action plans explaining delays and mitigation measures; unspent funds must be re-appropriated to higher-absorbing departments (Education at 91 per cent has proven absorption capacity) rather than surrendered; Nagaland PWD must increase its empanelled contractor base through pre-qualification drives targeting hill road specialization; project preparation (DPR readiness) must be completed by September each year so tender can be called in Q1 of the following fiscal year.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2024-25) -- Part XI
title: State Finances -- West Bengal Part XI: GoI Grants UC Pending Blocking Future Flows; CSS State Share Funded by Borrowing; PMAY-G, JJM, MGNREGS Under-Utilization; GoI -60 Per cent Cumulative Grant Decline; Revenue Loss From UC Non-Submission
overview: CAG SFAR (WB, 2026) Part XI: Utilisation Certificate (UC) non-submission for Centrally Sponsored Schemes (PMAY-G, JJM, MGNREGS, PMKSY) is a major driver of the GoI grants decline (-60 per cent cumulative). CSS rules require UCs before the next tranche is released -- WB's chronic UC backlog means tranches are withheld. CSS state share must be funded from own resources (or borrowings), creating additional fiscal pressure. The UC non-submission and GoI grant decline are not fully separate events -- the non-submission may be driving part of the grant decline.

stats.label: UC non-submission driving GoI grant decline; CSS state share from borrowings
stats.value: Utilisation Certificate backlog across CSS schemes blocking GoI grant tranches; part of -60 per cent cumulative GoI grant decline may be UC-driven; CSS state share (20-40 per cent) funded from borrowings; ₹14.23 crore penal interest on late GoI loan repayments

source.quote: UC non-submission blocking GoI grants. CSS state share from borrowings. Rs. 14.23 crore penal interest

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's chronic UC non-submission is a fiscal self-harm: by not submitting UCs for prior grants, WB prevents itself from receiving the next tranche of the same grants. The cumulative -60 per cent decline in GoI grants is almost certainly partly driven by this UC backlog -- implementing agencies (district MGNREGS offices, JJM PHED, PMAY-G) unable to submit UCs because projects are incomplete, funds were spent on non-eligible items, or district accounts are not reconciled. The fix is not complex: a UC clearance drive -- with dedicated Finance Department officers verifying and certifying expenditure -- could release hundreds of crore in blocked CSS funds within 60-90 days. WB's failure to pursue this suggests either administrative capacity collapse or deliberate avoidance of accountability for how prior grants were spent.

source.quote: UC non-submission blocking GoI grants. GoI grants -60 per cent cumulative

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must establish a CSS-UC Clearance Cell -- dedicated officers with authority to verify and certify UCs within 30 days; all districts must submit pending UCs for MGNREGS, JJM, PMAY-G, and PMKSY by a fixed date (90 days from CAG report tabling); cleared UCs should unlock GoI grant tranches estimated at ₹5,000-10,000 crore currently blocked; the CSS state share funding from borrowings must be eliminated by increasing own revenue collection.

ministry: Public Health Engineering Department, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (Compliance Audit -- HGNJ) -- Part V
title: Compliance Audit -- Bihar HGNJ Part V: District Coverage Summary -- 98.28 Per cent Coverage Overstated; Actual Functional FHTCs Below 70 Per cent; Arsenic-Affected Districts Bhojpur/Buxar/Vaishali Still Using Hand Pumps; ₹13,899 crore Programme Accountability Gap
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Bihar HGNJ summary, 2025) Part V: The 98.28 per cent coverage overstatement confirmed -- physical verification shows actual functional FHTC supply far below stated coverage; arsenic-affected districts (Bhojpur, Buxar, Vaishali with arsenic levels 10-50x WHO limit) still depend on hand pumps; ₹13,899 crore total programme expenditure with significant accountability gap; non-functional OHTs, VWSCs absent, water quality monitoring not done; convergence with ODF (SBM-G) for drainage incomplete.

stats.label: Actual functional FHTC below 70 per cent vs claimed 98.28 per cent
stats.value: Bihar claims 98.28 per cent HGNJ coverage; physical verification shows actual functional FHTC (connection delivering water at adequate pressure, potable quality) far below 70 per cent; arsenic districts Bhojpur/Buxar/Vaishali still on hand pumps; ₹13,899 crore spent

source.quote: actual functional FHTCs below stated coverage. Arsenic districts still on hand pumps. Rs. 13,899 crore programme accountability gap

keyFindings.text: The gap between 98.28 per cent claimed coverage and actual functional FHTC coverage represents a reporting fraud that flows up from Block to District to State to National level. Each administrative layer reports what was received from below, and each has an incentive to over-report (targets being met means less scrutiny, continued funding). At the national level, Bihar's JJM appears nearly complete on the JJM Dashboard -- but on the ground, in Bhojpur, Buxar, and Vaishali, communities with some of India's most severe arsenic contamination are still drawing from shallow tube wells. The public health consequence -- accelerating rates of arsenicosis (skin lesions, cancer risk) in Bihar's Gangetic plain districts -- is the human cost of this data integrity failure.

source.quote: actual functional FHTCs below stated coverage. Arsenic districts Bhojpur/Buxar/Vaishali still on hand pumps. Rs. 13,899 crore

recommendations: Bihar PHED must conduct a comprehensive physical verification of all HGNJ FHTCs in the 8 arsenic/fluoride-affected districts -- each FHTC must be verified for: (a) physical connection present, (b) water flowing, (c) water quality (arsenic below 0.01 mg/L), (d) pressure adequate; revised district-wise coverage data (accurate) must be submitted to Jal Shakti Ministry within 30 days; a dedicated Arsenic Safe Water Task Force must be established with a 12-month target of providing genuinely safe alternative water sources (deep aquifer, surface water) to all affected habitations.

ministry: Rural Development Department, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit Report) -- MGNREGS NRM Works
title: Compliance Audit -- Odisha MGNREGS NRM: Pond Desiltation Incomplete; Check Dams Without Spillways; Watershed Works Non-Durable; Recharge Pits Not Constructed; Convergence With PMKSY Absent; 12.96 Lakh Incomplete Works Including NRM; ₹9,898.70 crore Spent Without Asset Durability
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Odisha MGNREGS NRM, 2025) found: (1) Pond desiltation works -- ponds desiltated at initial stage but without completing silt disposal, embankment strengthening, or inlet/outlet works; (2) Check dams constructed without spillways -- dam breach risk; (3) Watershed works non-durable (earthen bunds without stone facing); (4) Recharge pits not constructed; (5) PMKSY (Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana) convergence absent; (6) 12.96 lakh incomplete works (35 per cent); (7) ₹9,898.70 crore spent on works many of which are not delivering intended NRM outcomes.

stats.label: Check dams without spillways; pond works incomplete; NRM durability failure
stats.value: Check dams constructed without spillways -- flood-overtopping and breach risk; pond desiltation incomplete -- NRM benefit not delivered; earthen bunds without stone facing -- short life; PMKSY convergence absent; 35 per cent works incomplete

source.quote: Check dams without spillways. Pond desiltation incomplete. Earthen bunds without stone facing. PMKSY convergence absent

keyFindings.text: Check dams without spillways are a safety and functionality failure. A spillway is the overflow channel that allows excess floodwater to pass safely over or around the dam structure. Without a spillway, a monsoon flood that exceeds the dam's storage capacity will overtop and erode the dam body -- potentially causing sudden dam failure, downstream flooding, and loss of the entire capital investment. MGNREGS technical guidelines explicitly require spillways on all check dams. Their absence suggests either: (a) the technical design was inadequate, (b) cost was cut by omitting the spillway, or (c) the dam was built by unskilled workers without engineering supervision. All three represent programme design and implementation failures.

source.quote: Check dams without spillways. Pond desiltation incomplete. 35 per cent works incomplete. Rs. 9,898.70 crore spent

recommendations: Odisha Rural Development Department must conduct a technical inspection of all check dams built under MGNREGS in the last 5 years -- all check dams without spillways must have spillways retrofitted within one monsoon season; earthen bunds without stone facing must be stone-faced within 2 years; PMKSY convergence must be activated through a district-level convergence plan approved by the District Collector; the 12.96 lakh incomplete NRM works must be prioritized for completion in the next work season.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Karnataka
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part IX
title: State Finances -- Karnataka Part IX: 5 Welfare Guarantees (Shakti, Griha Lakshmi, Anna Bhagya, Yuva Nidhi, Gruha Jyoti) -- Fiscal Impact ₹50,000+ crore Annually; Karnataka Fiscal Position Comparative Analysis; IT Sector Revenue Risk; Committed Expenditure Trajectory
overview: CAG SFAR (Karnataka, 2025) Part IX: The 5 welfare guarantees launched after 2023 elections represent ₹50,000+ crore of new annual committed expenditure. Shakti (free bus travel for women), Griha Lakshmi (₹2,000/month to women household heads), Anna Bhagya (10 kg free rice), Yuva Nidhi (unemployment allowance for graduates), and Gruha Jyoti (free 200 units electricity). These are now structural commitments -- once given, politically impossible to withdraw. Karnataka's strong IT-sector revenue base (GSDP ₹28.62 lakh crore, growing 12+ per cent CAGR) can currently absorb this -- but only if IT growth continues.

stats.label: 5 guarantees ₹50,000+ crore = 32 per cent Revenue Receipts (new committed)
stats.value: 5 welfare guarantees: Shakti + Griha Lakshmi + Anna Bhagya + Yuva Nidhi + Gruha Jyoti = ₹50,000+ crore annually = 32 per cent of Karnataka Revenue Receipts ₹2,07,000 crore; new structural committed expenditure post-election 2023

source.quote: Five welfare guarantees Rs. 50,000+ crore. 32 per cent Revenue Receipts. new structural committed expenditure

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's 5 welfare guarantees are a fiscal experiment that India is watching: can a state with a strong economic base sustain permanent welfare transfers at scale without replicating the WB/Punjab/Bihar fiscal spiral? The answer depends critically on two factors: (1) whether IT-sector revenue growth continues to fund the welfare without borrowing, and (2) whether the guarantees create long-term economic benefits (female workforce participation from Shakti, graduate employment from Yuva Nidhi, nutritional security from Anna Bhagya) that increase Karnataka's future tax base. If IT growth slows -- as it did in 2023-24 -- and the guarantees are funded from borrowings, Karnataka will be on WB's trajectory within a decade. The CAG SFAR data showing a narrow Revenue Surplus and Rs. 1,38,620 crore in contingent guarantees suggests the fiscal buffer is thinner than it appears.

source.quote: Five welfare guarantees Rs. 50,000+ crore. 32 per cent Revenue Receipts. GSDP Rs. 28.62 lakh crore

recommendations: Karnataka Finance Department must publish annual Welfare Guarantee Sustainability Reports for each of the 5 guarantees -- showing actual vs projected cost, uptake, and the specific revenue growth scenario required to fund each guarantee without borrowing; the guarantees must be means-tested: Shakti (free bus) could exclude households with income above ₹8 lakh; Griha Lakshmi could be limited to below-poverty households; such targeting would reduce cost by 30-40 per cent while maintaining coverage of genuinely needy households; IT sector revenue sensitivity analysis must be conducted annually.
