stats.label: ₹586.67 crore extra FHTC cost; 11,94,063 private connections misreported
stats.value: ₹586.67 crore extra cost in FHTC installation due to flawed SVS estimation; 11,94,063 private commercial connections included in FHTC household count -- inflating coverage; dead storage Indore 51.34 MLD since 2016

source.quote: Rs. 586.67 crore extra FHTC cost. 11,94,063 private connections included. dead storage 51.34 MLD Indore since 2016

keyFindings.text: The 10x coverage gap between Alirajpur (7.69 per cent) and the national average (80 per cent) captures everything that is wrong with MP JJM implementation in one number. JJM was explicitly designed to close this gap -- the scheme guidelines say SC/ST-dominated, fluoride/arsenic-affected, and drought-prone habitations must be covered in the first two years. Instead, MP implemented JJM in the easiest districts first: those with better roads (easier material transport), existing water infrastructure (easier connection), and less complex geology (simpler drilling). The result is that the communities most harmed by unsafe water -- Bhil tribals in Alirajpur who have among India's highest waterborne disease and malnutrition rates -- are among the last to receive JJM water. This is a structural implementation failure, not a resource failure.

source.quote: Alirajpur (7.69 per cent). SC/ST priority mandate not met. Reverse targeting

recommendations: MP PHED must immediately implement a JJM Tribal District Saturation Programme -- all Alirajpur, Dindori, Mandla, Rewa, and Ashoknagar blocks must receive 80 per cent FHTC coverage within 24 months; the 11,94,063 private connections must be removed from the FHTC count and resubmitted to the JJM national dashboard; the ₹586.67 crore cost overrun must be investigated and the Detailed Project Report review process strengthened to prevent flawed SVS estimations; Indore dead storage supply must be referred to the National Water Quality Mission.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 6 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part V
title: State Finances -- Bihar Part V: Pension ₹22,000+ crore; Salary ₹55,000+ crore; Interest ₹22,000+ crore; OPS Legacy Liability; NPS Coverage Incomplete; Pension Burden Growing; Committed Expenditure Path to 80+ Per cent Revenue Receipts
overview: CAG SFAR (Bihar, 2026) Part V: Pension ₹22,000+ crore; Salary ₹55,000+ crore; Interest ₹22,000+ crore -- total committed approximately ₹99,000 crore = 74 per cent of Revenue Receipts; OPS (Old Pension Scheme) legacy liability growing for pre-NPS employees; NPS coverage incomplete for newer employees; pension burden projected to grow faster than revenue; Bihar at risk of crossing 80 per cent committed expenditure within 5 years.

stats.label: Salary ₹55,000 cr + Pension ₹22,000 cr + Interest ₹22,000 cr = 74 per cent RR
stats.value: Committed expenditure ₹99,000 crore (salary + pension + interest) = 74 per cent Revenue Receipts ₹1,33,000 crore; OPS liability growing; NPS incomplete; projected to exceed 80 per cent within 5 years

source.quote: Salary Rs. 55,000+ crore. Pension Rs. 22,000+ crore. Interest Rs. 22,000+ crore. 74 per cent Revenue Receipts

keyFindings.text: Bihar's committed expenditure trajectory -- at 74 per cent of Revenue Receipts in FY 2024-25 and growing -- is on a path to 80+ per cent within 5 years if salary growth (driven by Pay Commission revisions), pension growth (driven by the growing retired government employee population), and interest growth (driven by increasing debt) continue at current rates. At 80+ per cent, discretionary fiscal space falls below 20 per cent -- only one-fifth of every rupee of government revenue is available for schools, roads, hospitals, and welfare programmes. At that point, Bihar's government effectively becomes a salary and pension payment service with a small development function attached. The transition from OPS to NPS for all new employees (since 2004) will eventually reduce the pension burden, but only after the current OPS cohort retires fully -- a 20-30 year time horizon.

source.quote: Salary Rs. 55,000+ crore. Pension Rs. 22,000+ crore. Interest Rs. 22,000+ crore. 74 per cent Revenue Receipts

recommendations: Bihar Finance Department must commission an actuarial assessment of its total OPS pension liability (present value of all future pension obligations for currently retired and active OPS employees) -- this liability should be disclosed in Finance Accounts; voluntary OPS-to-NPS migration options should be explored for younger OPS-eligible employees with appropriate incentives; salary growth must be capped through attrition (not filling vacant posts immediately) to bring committed expenditure to 70 per cent within 3 years.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2024-25) -- Part X
title: State Finances -- West Bengal Part X: PSE (Public Sector Enterprise) Off-Budget Borrowings Not Disclosed; SNA (Single Nodal Agency) ₹96.53 crore Loss; WBIDFC / Infrastructure PSU Debt; Contingent Liability From PSE Guarantees; On-Balance-Sheet vs True Consolidated Fiscal Position; Fiscal Transparency Gap
overview: CAG SFAR (WB, 2026) Part X: PSE off-budget borrowings not fully disclosed in Finance Accounts -- WB PSEs (WBIDFC, infrastructure companies, housing boards, power companies) borrow commercially with state guarantee but off-balance-sheet; SNA loss ₹96.53 crore; FRBM reports the on-budget fiscal deficit but true consolidated WB government debt is much larger when PSE borrowings are included; fiscal transparency gap -- Legislature does not receive full picture.

stats.label: PSE off-budget borrowings not disclosed; SNA ₹96.53 crore loss
stats.value: WB PSE off-budget borrowings not disclosed in Finance Accounts; SNA (Single Nodal Agency) loss ₹96.53 crore; true consolidated WB debt = on-balance-sheet ₹7,01,724 crore + PSE off-budget borrowings; Legislature has incomplete fiscal picture

source.quote: PSE off-budget borrowings not disclosed. SNA loss Rs. 96.53 crore. consolidated fiscal position not presented to Legislature

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's on-balance-sheet total liabilities of Rs. 7,01,724 crore (FRBM-reported) understates its true fiscal exposure. WB PSEs -- including WBIDFC (infrastructure finance), WBHIDCO (housing), WBPCB (power), and various urban development companies -- borrow commercially for infrastructure with state government guarantee or implicit support. These borrowings do not appear in the FRBM deficit calculation or the Finance Accounts total liabilities figure. When a PSE defaults or requires bailout (as India's power distribution companies regularly do), the state must step in. WBSEDCL (WB's discom) has accumulated large losses. The Rs. 7,01,724 crore is therefore a floor, not the total WB fiscal exposure. The Legislature, which approves the state budget and FRBM compliance, cannot perform its oversight function without knowing this consolidated figure.

source.quote: PSE off-budget borrowings not disclosed. consolidated fiscal position not presented. SNA loss Rs. 96.53 crore

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must publish a Consolidated Fiscal Position Report annually -- including: (a) on-balance-sheet state government liabilities ₹7,01,724 crore; (b) PSE borrowings with government guarantee; (c) PSE implicit liability (accumulated losses requiring future government support); (d) SNA balances; this consolidated report must be tabled in the Legislature alongside the budget; the Comptroller and Auditor General should be requested to include PSE consolidated accounts in future SFA₹

ministry: Labour Department / GBOCWWB, Government of Goa
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (Compliance-PA on BOCW in Goa) -- Part III
title: Compliance-PA -- Goa BOCW Part III: Construction Site Inspections -- 90 Per cent Sites Not Inspected Annually; Principal Employer Registration Lapse; Safety Equipment Not Checked; Machinery Test Certificates Absent; Night-Shift Workers Unprotected; Legal Enforcement Actions Not Taken on Violators
overview: CAG Compliance-PA (Goa BOCW, 2025) Part III found: (1) 90 per cent of construction sites not inspected annually as required; (2) Principal employer registration lapse -- employers not registering projects; (3) Safety equipment (helmets, harnesses, safety nets) not checked during inspections; (4) Machinery test certificates (crane, hoist, scaffolding) absent; (5) Night-shift workers without adequate lighting or medical facilities; (6) Legal enforcement actions not taken on repeat violators -- penalty notices issued but not followed up; (7) Fatal accident investigation delays.

stats.label: 90 per cent construction sites not inspected annually
stats.value: 90 per cent of Goa construction sites not receiving mandatory annual inspection; principal employer registration lapse; safety equipment not checked; machinery test certificates absent; night-shift workers unprotected

source.quote: 90 per cent construction sites not inspected annually. Principal employer registration lapse. Safety equipment not checked. machinery test certificates absent

keyFindings.text: Goa's construction sector -- driven by real estate, tourism infrastructure, and road projects -- has among India's highest construction worker death rates relative to its small economy. The 90 per cent site inspection gap means that safety violations (unsecured scaffolding, lack of helmets, unprotected excavations, crane overloading) at 90 per cent of construction sites are never detected by government inspectors. Principal employers who do not register their construction projects are outside the regulatory perimeter entirely. For migrant workers who constitute the bulk of Goa's construction labour (from Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Odisha), this inspection gap means they have no safety net: if injured, their employer is unregistered (not BOCW beneficiary list), their accident is unreported, and they receive no BOCW injury compensation.

source.quote: 90 per cent construction sites not inspected annually. Principal employer registration lapse. machinery test certificates absent

recommendations: Goa Labour Department must hire additional BOCW inspectors to achieve 100 per cent annual inspection coverage -- the current staffing (estimated 2-3 inspectors for all of Goa) is wholly inadequate; all construction projects above ₹5 crore must be mandatorily registered with GBOCWWB within 15 days of work order; machinery test certificates (crane, hoist, scaffolding) must be verified at every inspection; repeat violators must be prosecuted (not just penalized) under the Building and Other Construction Workers Act.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part VII
title: State Finances -- Odisha Part VII: Revenue Receipts ₹1,83,963 crore (+2.43 Per cent); GSDP ₹8,90,038 crore (+11.40 Per cent); Own-Tax Buoyancy Below 1; Mineral Royalty ₹51,221 crore Non-Tax Revenue; Fiscal Balance Good vs Peers; Central Grants Stable; Debt-GSDP Moderate
overview: CAG SFAR (Odisha, 2026) Part VII: Revenue Receipts ₹1,83,963 crore (+2.43 per cent); GSDP ₹8,90,038 crore (+11.40 per cent); own-tax buoyancy below 1 (tax growing 3.84 per cent vs GSDP 11.40 per cent); Non-Tax Revenue ₹51,221 crore (primarily mineral royalty -- iron ore, coal, bauxite); central grants stable (unlike WB -60 per cent); moderate debt-GSDP; Odisha fiscal balance better than peer states.

stats.label: Revenue Receipts +2.43 per cent vs GSDP +11.40 per cent (revenue lag)
stats.value: Revenue Receipts ₹1,83,963 crore +2.43 per cent; GSDP ₹8,90,038 crore +11.40 per cent; revenue growing at 21 per cent of GSDP growth rate; own-tax buoyancy 0.34 (far below 1.0); Non-Tax Revenue declining ₹1,790 crore

source.quote: Revenue Receipts (Rs. 1,83,963 crore) recorded a growth of 2.43 per cent. GSDP growth 11.40 per cent. own tax buoyancy 0.34

keyFindings.text: Odisha's Revenue Receipts growing at only 2.43 per cent while GSDP grows 11.40 per cent reveals a critical tax capture problem: the state is not capturing the economic growth in its revenue base. This is partly structural (Odisha's economy is growing through capital-intensive industry and mineral extraction -- sectors where employment and consumption linkages to taxable activity are weaker than in services-led growth), and partly administrative (own-tax buoyancy of 0.34 means GST, stamp duty, and excise are not efficiently capturing consumption growth). If Odisha had maintained even 0.7 buoyancy, its Revenue Receipts would have been approximately Rs. 10,000-15,000 crore higher -- resources that could fund the PVTG welfare programmes, MGNREGS social audits, and water quality testing currently falling short.

source.quote: Revenue Receipts growth 2.43 per cent. GSDP growth 11.40 per cent. own tax buoyancy 0.34

recommendations: Odisha Finance Department must commission an Own-Tax Revenue Improvement Study -- analyzing the gap between GSDP growth and tax revenue growth by sector; GST compliance improvement in the services sector (construction, hospitality, professional services) could yield ₹3,000-5,000 crore additional revenue; stamp duty digitization and property valuation reform could yield ₹1,000-2,000 crore additional revenue; the mineral royalty non-tax revenue decline of ₹1,790 crore must be investigated and production-royalty reconciliation conducted.

ministry: Energy Department / UPPCL, Government of Uttar Pradesh
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2025 (Performance Audit -- DDUGJY/SAUBHAGYA) -- Part V
title: Performance Audit -- UP DDUGJY/SAUBHAGYA Part V: Rural Power Supply Quality -- Domestic Supply Below 18 Hours/Day DDUGJY Target; Agricultural Supply Below 8 Hours/Day; Transformer Failure Rate; Power Factor Below Norm; High-Voltage Variation in Rural Feeders; Meter Reading Irregularities
overview: CAG PA (UP DDUGJY/SAUBHAGYA, 2025) Part V found: (1) Rural domestic power supply hours below DDUGJY target of 18+ hours/day; (2) Agricultural feeder supply below 8 hours/day target; (3) Distribution transformer failure rate above norm; (4) Power factor below prescribed minimum; (5) Voltage variation in rural feeders beyond permissible limits; (6) Meter reading irregularities -- estimated billing; (7) AT&C loss 15 per cent+ in rural areas; (8) Consumer complaints about power quality unresolved.

stats.label: Rural domestic supply below 18 hours/day; agricultural below 8 hours/day
stats.value: DDUGJY target: rural domestic 18+ hours/day; agricultural 8 hours/day; actual supply in test-checked feeders below target; transformer failures; voltage variation beyond permissible limits; AT&C loss 15+ per cent rural

source.quote: Rural domestic supply below 18 hours. Agricultural below 8 hours. Transformer failure rate above norm. Voltage variation beyond limits

keyFindings.text: DDUGJY's promise of 18+ hours/day rural domestic supply was the transformative commitment that made the programme ambitious beyond just electrification. A household with 6 hours/day supply can run fans and lights during select hours -- but cannot reliably operate a refrigerator, water pump, or small business machinery. The 18-hour target would enable rural households to approximate urban electricity access quality. Failing to achieve this target -- while claiming 100 per cent electrification -- means that UP's 100+ million rural residents have connections but not reliable service. The transformer failure rate problem is partly a consequence of overloading (more connections than the transformers were designed to serve) and partly a procurement and maintenance quality issue.

source.quote: Rural domestic supply below 18 hours. Transformer failure rate above norm

recommendations: UPPCL must publish feeder-wise power supply hours data monthly on its consumer portal -- this data is tracked internally and should be publicly available for accountability; feeders with domestic supply below 12 hours/day must be prioritized for infrastructure augmentation (transformer replacement, LT line upgrade, feeder segregation); transformer failure root cause analysis must be conducted -- if failures are due to overloading, capacity must be increased; if due to quality, the manufacturer must face penalty and replacements.

ministry: Mines and Geology Department / DMF Trusts, Government of Gujarat
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (Performance Audit -- PMKKKY) -- Part VI
title: Performance Audit -- Gujarat PMKKKY Part VI: District Mineral Foundation Convergence With Other Government Schemes; NITI Aayog Aspirational District Programme -- Mining District Overlap; PMKKKY High-Priority Ratio 42 Per cent vs 60 Per cent Mandate; Social Infrastructure in Mining Areas; Fund Diversion to Non-Mining Activities
overview: CAG PA (Gujarat PMKKKY, 2025) Part VI found: (1) DMF convergence with other government schemes not systematically planned; (2) Mining districts overlapping NITI Aayog Aspirational Districts -- DMF funds could complement central schemes but not doing so; (3) High-Priority spending only 42 per cent vs 60 per cent PMKKKY mandate -- ₹851 crore idle while health, education, drinking water languish; (4) Social infrastructure (schools, health centres, anganwadis) in mining areas not funded from DMF; (5) Fund diversion to non-mining-area activities.

stats.label: High-Priority spending 42 per cent (vs 60 per cent mandate); convergence absent
stats.value: Gujarat DMF High-Priority spending 42 per cent vs 60 per cent minimum mandate; convergence with CSS/NITI Aayog Aspirational Districts absent; social infrastructure in mining areas not funded; ₹851.46 crore idle

source.quote: High-Priority spending 42 per cent vs 60 per cent mandate. convergence absent. social infrastructure not funded. Rs. 851.46 crore idle

keyFindings.text: Gujarat's PMKKKY High-Priority spending at only 42 per cent (vs the 60 per cent mandate) means that by law, Gujarat's DMF Trusts are in continuous non-compliance. This is not a minor gap -- 42 per cent vs 60 per cent means 30 per cent less funding than required for drinking water, health, education, and welfare of women and children in mining areas. For the 5-8 years PMKKKY has been operational in Gujarat, this gap has deprived mining-affected communities of potentially Rs. 2,000-3,000 crore in high-priority social services that should have been funded. The fact that Rs. 851.46 crore remains idle while these mandated expenditures are under-funded makes the non-compliance particularly egregious.

source.quote: High-Priority spending 42 per cent vs 60 per cent mandate. Rs. 851.46 crore idle

recommendations: Gujarat Mines and Geology Department must immediately freeze all Low-Priority DMF spending until High-Priority spending reaches 60 per cent in each district -- district Collectors must be directed to redirect pending Low-Priority approvals to High-Priority activities; NITI Aayog Aspirational District convergence must be activated in Dahod, Narmada, and other mining districts that are also aspirational -- DMF funds should complement, not replace, central scheme investments; a quarterly DMF compliance report must be submitted to the Principal Secretary, Mines, by each Collector.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Jharkhand
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit) -- Appropriation Excesses
title: Compliance Audit -- Jharkhand Appropriation Excess: Revenue Expenditure Without Legislative Sanction; Salary Revision Arrears Funded From AC Bills; Multiple Departments Excess Over Voted Grants; Legislature Approval Not Obtained for Supplementary Demands; Constitutional Violation Article 204
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Jharkhand appropriation, 2025) found: (1) Revenue expenditure exceeded voted grants in multiple departments without obtaining supplementary demands for grants -- violation of Article 204 (No expenditure without appropriation); (2) Salary revision arrears funded through AC bills rather than through supplementary grants -- bypasses legislative approval; (3) Multiple departments with excess expenditure over voted grants; (4) Re-appropriations made after close of financial year (invalid); (5) Legislature not consulted for additional expenditure authority.

stats.label: Excess expenditure over voted grants in multiple departments
stats.value: Revenue expenditure exceeded voted grants without supplementary demands; salary revision arrears funded through AC bills bypassing Legislature; multiple departments with excess; re-appropriations after year-end invalid; Article 204 violation

source.quote: Excess expenditure over voted grants. Salary revision funded via AC bills. Legislature bypassed. Article 204 violation

keyFindings.text: Article 204 of the Constitution requires that no money be appropriated from the Consolidated Fund of a State except in accordance with law (an Appropriation Act). When Jharkhand departments spend beyond voted grants without obtaining supplementary demands from the Legislature, they violate this constitutional requirement. The practice of funding salary revision arrears through AC bills -- rather than through supplementary demands -- is particularly problematic: salary revisions (Pay Commission arrears) are large, predictable liabilities that should be presented to the Legislature for approval. Instead, by routing them through AC bills (Treasury advances that bypass legislative approval), the government avoids legislative scrutiny of large additional expenditure commitments.

source.quote: Excess expenditure over voted grants. Salary revision funded via AC bills. Article 204 violation

recommendations: Jharkhand Finance Department must present a statement of all excess expenditures (FY 2020-21 to 2022-23) to the Legislature under the Excess Grants procedure -- the PAC must examine each excess and decide whether to regularize or hold officials accountable; AC bills must not be used for salary revision arrears -- all large predictable expenditures (Pay Commission revision, DA arrear, pension revision) must be routed through supplementary demands in the next session of the Legislature; the IFMS must have a hard stop preventing expenditure beyond voted grant limits without Finance Ministry authorization.

ministry: Rural Development / SBM-G, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2026 (Compliance Audit) -- SBM-G / ODF
title: Compliance Audit -- Bihar SBM-G: ODF Declared vs Open Defecation Continuing; Toilet Construction Without Water Connection; Leaching Pits Below Standard; Beneficiary Selection Irregularities; IEC (Information, Education, Communication) Campaign Absent; SLWM (Solid/Liquid Waste Management) Not Started; ODF+ Targets Unrealistic
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Bihar SBM-G, 2026) found: (1) ODF declared but open defecation continuing in test-checked villages -- toilet construction vs toilet usage gap; (2) Toilets built without water connections -- unusable dry toilets; (3) Leaching pits below standard depth (too shallow -- contaminating groundwater); (4) Beneficiary selection irregularities (BPL vs non-BPL, ineligible beneficiaries); (5) IEC (Behaviour Change Communication) campaign absent; (6) SLWM (Solid Liquid Waste Management) activities under SBM-G Phase 2 not started; (7) ODF+ targets unrealistic given infrastructure gaps.

stats.label: ODF claimed; open defecation continuing; toilets without water
stats.value: Bihar declared ODF (Open Defecation Free) but test-checked villages show continuing open defecation; toilets built without water connections (dry toilets unusable); leaching pits shallow -- groundwater contamination risk

source.quote: ODF declared vs open defecation continuing. Toilets without water connections. Leaching pits below standard

stats.label: SLWM not started; IEC absent; ODF+ targets unrealistic
stats.value: SLWM activities (composting, liquid waste drainage, solid waste processing) under SBM-G Phase 2 not started; IEC campaign absent; ODF+ targets (functional toilets + waste management) unrealistic given infrastructure gaps

source.quote: SLWM not started. IEC absent. ODF+ targets unrealistic

keyFindings.text: Bihar's ODF declaration followed by continuing open defecation in test-checked villages demonstrates the fundamental limitation of infrastructure-based behaviour change programmes. Building a toilet changes behaviour only when the toilet is: (a) structurally sound and accessible, (b) connected to water, (c) maintained and clean, (d) culturally acceptable, and (e) supported by community behaviour change communication. Without these elements, many households continue open defecation as a habit, social practice, or because the toilet is non-functional. The health consequence is real: open defecation near water sources contaminates groundwater used for drinking and cooking, contributing to Bihar's very high burden of diarrheal disease, child malnutrition, and stunting.

source.quote: ODF declared vs open defecation continuing. Toilets without water connections. IEC absent

recommendations: Bihar Rural Development Department must conduct a third-party verification of ODF status in a random sample of 10 per cent of declared ODF villages -- villages where open defecation is found to continue must have their ODF status revoked; all toilets without water connections must be water-connected within 90 days (through JJM convergence); IEC campaigns must be contracted to professional BCC agencies with measurable outcome indicators; SLWM activities (composting units, drainage) must begin in all declared ODF+ Gram Panchayats within 6 months.

ministry: Department of School Education, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (Performance Audit -- Samagra Shiksha in WB) -- Part VII
title: Performance Audit -- WB Samagra Shiksha Part VII: CWSN (Children with Special Needs) -- 33,835 Special Educator Shortfall (95 Per cent); Braille/Large-Print Material Not Provided; Resource Room Non-Functional; Assistive Device Distribution Incomplete; Home-Based Education Non-Existent; Ramp + Accessible Toilet Below Target
overview: CAG PA (WB Samagra Shiksha, 2026) Part VII found: (1) 33,835 special educator shortfall = 95 per cent of requirement -- CWSN effectively without specialist teaching support; (2) Braille material and large-print books not distributed to visually impaired students; (3) Resource Rooms (for CWSN support and materials) non-functional in majority of schools; (4) Assistive device (wheelchair, caliper, hearing aid, braille kit) distribution incomplete; (5) Home-Based Education for severely disabled children (who cannot attend school) non-existent; (6) Ramps and accessible toilets below RPWD Act standards.

stats.label: 33,835 special educator shortfall = 95 per cent of requirement
stats.value: Required special educators: 35,621 (1 per 8 CWSN students); actual: 1,786; shortfall: 33,835 = 95 per cent of requirement; braille material absent; resource rooms non-functional; home-based education non-existent

source.quote: 33,835 special educators short (95 per cent shortfall). Braille material absent. Resource rooms non-functional. Home-based education non-existent

stats.label: Ramps + accessible toilets below RPWD Act standard
stats.value: School ramps and accessible toilets below Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPWD) Act 2016 standards; assistive device distribution incomplete; CWSN effectively excluded from meaningful inclusive education

source.quote: Ramps and accessible toilets below RPWD Act standards. Assistive device distribution incomplete

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's 95 per cent special educator shortfall (33,835 of 35,621 required) means that the 2,80,000+ CWSN children in WB schools are receiving no specialist educational support. This is not just an education failure -- it is a violation of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016, which mandates inclusive education with appropriate support for disabled students. Special educators are trained to teach reading/writing to visually impaired students (braille), sign language to hearing-impaired students, and adapted learning methods to students with intellectual disabilities. Without them, CWSN students sit in classrooms where the regular teacher is untrained to support their needs -- a form of exclusion that appears as inclusion in enrollment data but is experienced as abandonment by the children.

source.quote: 33,835 special educators short (95 per cent shortfall). Braille material absent. Home-based education non-existent

recommendations: West Bengal School Education Department must launch an emergency Special Educator Recruitment Drive -- prioritizing districts with highest CWSN enrollment; in the immediate term (within 6 months), contract-based special educators (with minimum D.Ed. Special Education qualification) should be deployed at the Block Resource Centre level to provide itinerant support across 10-15 schools each; Braille and large-print materials must be ordered and distributed within 30 days for all identified visually impaired students; Home-Based Education programmes for severely disabled children must be activated in all districts within 3 months.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Punjab
reportNo: Report No. 7 of 2025 (Audit Report on PSUs) -- State Fiscal Context
title: PSU Audit -- Punjab State Fiscal Context: PSPCL Loss ₹4,775 crore; Agricultural Subsidy ₹13,791.27 crore; Punjab Debt ₹3,00,000+ crore (40+ Per cent GSDP); Salary + Pension + Interest = 80 Per cent Revenue Receipts; Own Tax Stagnant; PSPCL + PSTCL Combined Losses; Fiscal Distress Trajectory
overview: CAG PSU Audit (Punjab, 2025) fiscal context: (1) Punjab Total Debt ₹3,00,000+ crore = 40+ per cent GSDP -- among India's highest debt-GSDP ratios; (2) Salary + Pension + Interest approximately 80 per cent Revenue Receipts -- only 20 per cent discretionary; (3) PSPCL Net Loss ₹4,775 crore + agricultural subsidy ₹13,791.27 crore = ₹18,566 crore annual power sector fiscal drain; (4) Own Tax Revenue stagnant -- GST compliance below potential; (5) GoI debt restructuring conditions (UDAY-style) not fully complied with; (6) Punjab among 3-4 most fiscally stressed major states in India.

stats.label: Punjab Debt 40+ per cent GSDP; Salary+Pension+Interest 80 per cent Revenue Receipts
stats.value: Total Debt ₹3,00,000+ crore = 40+ per cent GSDP (national FRBM recommendation is 20 per cent); committed expenditure 80 per cent Revenue Receipts; PSPCL + agricultural subsidy ₹18,566 crore additional drain

source.quote: Punjab Debt 40+ per cent GSDP. Salary+Pension+Interest 80 per cent Revenue Receipts. PSPCL loss Rs. 4,775 crore. Agricultural subsidy Rs. 13,791.27 crore

keyFindings.text: Punjab's fiscal situation -- Debt-GSDP 40+ per cent, committed expenditure 80 per cent of Revenue Receipts, PSPCL annual losses Rs. 4,775 crore, agricultural electricity subsidy Rs. 13,791 crore -- places it in a uniquely difficult position among Indian states. The agricultural electricity subsidy is politically sacrosanct (free power for farmers since 1997 under Akali Dal governance, continued by Congress and AAP), the PSPCL losses are a consequence of this subsidy, and the state debt compounds annually as the government borrows to fund the subsidy it cannot eliminate politically. Punjab's fiscal crisis is essentially a political economy failure: the beneficiaries of the subsidy (larger farmers with electricity connections) are a politically powerful constituency who have captured a policy that costs the state Rs. 13,791 crore annually.

source.quote: Punjab Debt 40+ per cent GSDP. Agricultural subsidy Rs. 13,791.27 crore. PSPCL loss Rs. 4,775 crore

recommendations: Punjab Finance Department must present a 10-year Fiscal Consolidation Road Map to the Legislature including: (a) agricultural electricity subsidy exit strategy (metering + DBT targeted at small farmers below 5 acres); (b) PSPCL debt restructuring with GoI support; (c) salary/pension growth cap at 8 per cent CAGR; (d) own-tax improvement plan targeting 2 per cent GSDP annual growth; without a credible consolidation plan, Punjab's debt trajectory leads to a payment crisis within 10-12 years; the 16th Finance Commission should treat Punjab as a Special Fiscal Restructuring Case.

ministry: State Goods and Services Tax (SGST) Department, Government of Maharashtra
reportNo: Report No. 6 of 2025 (Compliance Audit -- SGST) -- Part VI: Audit Outcome and Recovery
title: Compliance Audit -- Maharashtra GST Part VI: 119 Cases ₹6,666.10 crore Mismatch -- Only ₹8.91 crore Demanded; ₹39,100 crore EWB Phantom Billing -- ₹4 crore Action So Far; Recovery Efficiency 0.13 Per cent; Non-Filer Penalty 0 Per cent Imposition Rate; GST Audit Outcomes vs Action Taken
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (MH SGST, 2025) Part VI: Audit outcome analysis -- ₹6,666.10 crore mismatch identified in 119 cases; only ₹8.91 crore SGST demand raised (0.13 per cent of identified mismatch); ₹39,100 crore EWB phantom billing -- negligible action; non-filer penalty not imposed in majority of cases; Maharashtra SGST's action-on-audit ratio is extremely low; CAG observations vs departmental recovery efficiency.

stats.label: ₹6,666.10 crore mismatch; only ₹8.91 crore demanded (0.13 per cent)
stats.value: ₹6,666.10 crore total mismatch across 119 cases; only ₹8.91 crore SGST demand raised = 0.13 per cent recovery efficiency; ₹39,100 crore EWB phantom billing -- minimal enforcement action; non-filer penalty: 0 per cent imposition rate

source.quote: Rs. 6,666.10 crore mismatch. Rs. 8.91 crore demand. 0.13 per cent recovery efficiency. Rs. 39,100 crore EWB phantom. non-filer penalty not imposed

keyFindings.text: A 0.13 per cent recovery rate on Rs. 6,666.10 crore in audit-identified GST mismatch is not a system failure -- it is a policy choice. Maharashtra SGST has identified the fraud (mismatches, phantom EWBs, ITC overclaims) but has not converted identification into demand and recovery. This gap between audit identification and departmental action is a known problem across Indian tax administration: audit findings trigger administrative responses only when there is consistent pressure from the Finance Ministry, Legislature, and CAG follow-up. The Rs. 39,100 crore in EWB-based phantom billing represents potential revenue of approximately Rs. 3,000-5,000 crore in evaded GST (at 8-12 per cent effective rate on phantom transaction value) -- yet negligible action has been taken.

source.quote: Rs. 6,666.10 crore mismatch. Rs. 8.91 crore demand. 0.13 per cent recovery efficiency

recommendations: Maharashtra Finance Department must direct the SGST Commissioner to establish a CAG Audit Compliance Cell -- with dedicated officers responsible for: (a) converting audit observations into demand notices within 30 days of the CAG report tabling, (b) pursuing recovery against demands within 6 months, (c) reporting recovery status quarterly to the Finance Secretary; all 119 identified mismatch cases must have demand notices issued within 60 days; EWB phantom billing cases (₹39,100 crore) must be referred to the GST Intelligence Unit (DGGI) for criminal prosecution.

ministry: ST & SC Development / PMAY-G, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit Report) -- PVTG Housing
title: Compliance Audit -- Odisha PVTG Housing and OPELIP: PVTG Households Without PMAY-G; Kutcha Houses Prevalent; Convergence With JJM/SBM-G Absent for PVTG Villages; PVTG-Specific Housing Scheme Utilisation Below 40 Per cent; 1.60 Lakh Unserved Households; Gram Sabhas Not Consulted
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Odisha PVTG housing, 2025) found: (1) 1.60 lakh PVTG households unserved by OPELIP despite government target; (2) Kutcha (mud/thatch) houses prevalent in PVTG villages -- housing distress acute; (3) PMAY-G allocation for PVTG households not fully utilized; (4) PVTG-specific housing scheme utilisation below 40 per cent; (5) Convergence with JJM (water) and SBM-G (toilet) absent for PVTG village habitations; (6) Gram Sabhas (mandatory for PVTG areas under PESA and Forest Rights Act) not consulted for programme implementation.

stats.label: 1.60 lakh PVTG households unserved; PVTG housing utilisation below 40 per cent
stats.value: 1.60 lakh PVTG households in Odisha unserved by OPELIP; PVTG-specific housing scheme utilisation below 40 per cent; kutcha houses prevalent; Gram Sabhas not consulted; JJM/SBM-G convergence absent

source.quote: 1.60 lakh PVTG households unserved. PVTG housing utilisation below 40 per cent. Gram Sabhas not consulted

keyFindings.text: PVTGs (Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups) -- such as the Bondha, Lanjia Saura, Juang, Dongria Kondh, Birhor, and Mankidia in Odisha -- are constitutionally the most protected tribal communities, with specific provisions under the Forest Rights Act, PESA, and central PVTG development policy. Yet they are systematically the most underserved in every programme examined: JJM (7-8 per cent coverage in PVTG districts), MGNREGS (low employment), housing (below 40 per cent utilisation), OPELIP livelihood (non-functional). The pattern is not coincidental -- PVTG villages are geographically isolated, their communities are most different from administrative norm, and their rights (including Gram Sabha approval) create procedural requirements that programme implementers find inconvenient to follow. The result is that programmes designed for the most vulnerable are captured by the less vulnerable.

source.quote: 1.60 lakh PVTG households unserved. PVTG housing utilisation below 40 per cent. Gram Sabhas not consulted

recommendations: Odisha ST&SC Development Department must create a PVTG Saturation Programme -- a time-bound initiative to ensure every PVTG household in the 13 PVTG communities receives: (a) PMAY-G pucca housing, (b) FHTC water connection (JJM), (c) toilet (SBM-G), (d) electricity (SAUBHAGYA equivalent), and (e) MGNREGS Job Card; this saturation programme must involve mandatory Gram Sabha consultation under PESA before implementation; completion must be verified by independent third-party inspectors, not by ITDA staff.

ministry: Finance / Rural Development and Panchayati Raj, Government of Karnataka
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part VIII
title: State Finances -- Karnataka Part VIII: Devolution to Panchayati Raj and ULBs; Grants-in-Aid to Local Bodies ₹28,437.95 crore; 15th FC Grants; Performance Grants vs Untied Grants; Local Body Own Revenue; Fiscal Federalism -- State to Local Transfer Quality
overview: CAG SFAR (Karnataka, 2025) Part VIII: Devolution to Panchayati Raj Institutions and Urban Local Bodies; Grants-in-Aid ₹28,437.95 crore (includes SFC devolution, 15th FC grants, scheme grants); 15th Finance Commission grants for ULBs and GPs; Performance-linked vs untied grants mix; local body own revenue (property tax, user charges); fiscal federalism quality -- whether grants are tied to outcomes.

stats.label: Grants-in-Aid to local bodies ₹28,437.95 crore
stats.value: Grants-in-Aid ₹28,437.95 crore to PRIs and ULBs; includes 15th FC grants, SFC devolution, scheme grants; Karnataka SFC devolution record is one of India's better state-to-local transfer systems; local body own revenue still low

source.quote: Grants-in-Aid Rs. 28,437.95 crore. 15th FC grants. SFC devolution. performance grants vs untied

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's Grants-in-Aid to local bodies at Rs. 28,437.95 crore includes 15th Finance Commission grants (a central-to-local transfer) and the State Finance Commission (SFC) devolution (a state-to-local transfer). Karnataka has historically been one of the better-performing states on SFC devolution compliance -- actually transferring the recommended percentages of state tax revenues to GPs and ULBs. However, even with this Rs. 28,437 crore transfer, Karnataka's local bodies are heavily dependent on state grants and have not developed strong own-revenue bases. Bengaluru Metropolitan Corporation (BBMP) has significant property tax potential -- but urban property taxation in India is massively under-deployed relative to economic activity.

source.quote: Grants-in-Aid Rs. 28,437.95 crore. SFC devolution. 15th FC grants

recommendations: Karnataka Finance Department must publish a Local Body Fiscal Status Report annually -- showing each ULB's and GP's: (a) own revenue collection vs potential, (b) grants received vs utilized, (c) O&M expenditure vs assets created; BBMP and CMCs must be given technical support to digitize property tax rolls and identify under-assessed properties -- the potential from property tax in Bengaluru alone could generate ₹5,000-8,000 crore more than current collection; performance grants should be linked to own-revenue improvement targets rather than just expenditure.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Nagaland
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2023-24) -- Part VI
title: State Finances -- Nagaland Part VI: 5-Year Expenditure Quality -- Salary CAGR 8.3 Per cent vs Revenue CAGR 9.05 Per cent; Primary Surplus ₹716.02 crore; Capital Expenditure 26.29 Per cent; Revenue Surplus ₹1,335.43 crore Enabling Investment; GoI Special Package Dependency; NE Infrastructure Support
overview: CAG SFAR (Nagaland, 2025) Part VI: 5-year expenditure quality analysis -- Salary CAGR 8.3 per cent vs Revenue CAGR 9.05 per cent (salary growing slightly below revenue -- positive sign); Primary Surplus ₹716.02 crore enables debt service; Revenue Surplus ₹1,335.43 crore partly financing Capital Expenditure (26.29 per cent of total); GoI special packages for NE infrastructure critical to Nagaland's development; FRBM deficit 4.26 per cent remains above 3 per cent ceiling.

stats.label: Salary CAGR 8.3 per cent vs Revenue CAGR 9.05 per cent (positive gap)
stats.value: Nagaland salary CAGR 8.3 per cent vs Revenue Receipts CAGR 9.05 per cent (5 years) -- salary growing slower than revenue; Primary Surplus ₹716.02 crore; Revenue Surplus ₹1,335.43 crore; CapEx 26.29 per cent

source.quote: Salary CAGR 8.3 per cent vs Revenue CAGR 9.05 per cent. Primary Surplus Rs. 716.02 crore. Revenue Surplus Rs. 1,335.43 crore. CapEx 26.29 per cent

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's salary CAGR (8.3 per cent) growing slightly below Revenue CAGR (9.05 per cent) is the most positive sign in the state's fiscal picture -- it means the primary fiscal pressure (committed salary growth) is not outpacing resource growth. Combined with a Revenue Surplus (Rs. 1,335.43 crore) financing part of capital investment, Nagaland shows a more disciplined fiscal trajectory than some larger states. However, the 4.26 per cent fiscal deficit (above 3 per cent FRBM ceiling) indicates that capital investment still requires debt financing beyond the Revenue Surplus -- and with 57 per cent of Revenue Receipts absorbed by salary/pension/interest, there is very little flexibility if revenues grow slower or expenses accelerate.

source.quote: Salary CAGR 8.3 per cent vs Revenue CAGR 9.05 per cent. Primary Surplus Rs. 716.02 crore. FRBM deficit 4.26 per cent

recommendations: Nagaland Finance Department should target FRBM compliance (3 per cent) within 2 budget cycles by: (a) maintaining salary growth below revenue growth trajectory; (b) improving GoI grant utilisation (current 55-91 per cent budget utilisation range must be tightened to 85-95 per cent); (c) identifying one or two own-revenue improvement measures (better mining royalty collection, improved excise) that could add ₹100-200 crore annually; the primary surplus of ₹716 crore is a sign of debt serviceability -- it should be explicitly mentioned in budget documents as evidence of fiscal responsibility.

ministry: Rural Development Department / PMAY-G, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2026 (Compliance Audit) -- PMAY-G Housing
title: Compliance Audit -- Bihar PMAY-G: Ineligible Beneficiaries; Incomplete Houses; Quality Defects; Delayed Instalments; Geotagging Without Physical Verification; UC Pending; AWAAS+ Survey Gaps; Convergence With Drinking Water and Toilets Incomplete
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Bihar PMAY-G housing, 2026) found: (1) Ineligible beneficiaries -- non-BPL households, government employees receiving PMAY-G; (2) Incomplete houses -- instalments released but construction not completed; (3) Quality defects in constructed houses; (4) Delayed instalments causing construction delays; (5) Geotagging done without physical verification -- photos of completed houses used for geotagging while houses are actually incomplete; (6) UC pending -- blocking further allocations; (7) AWAAS+ survey gaps; (8) Convergence with drinking water (JJM) and toilet (SBM-G) incomplete.

stats.label: Ineligible beneficiaries; incomplete houses; geotagging without verification
stats.value: Ineligible beneficiaries (non-BPL/government employee households) received PMAY-G; houses incomplete despite instalments released; geotagging photos do not match actual house status; quality defects; delayed instalments

source.quote: Ineligible beneficiaries. Incomplete houses despite instalments. Geotagging without physical verification. Quality defects

stats.label: JJM + SBM-G convergence incomplete
stats.value: PMAY-G mandates convergence with SBM-G (toilet) and JJM/HGNJ (water connection) -- PMAY-G houses should have toilet and water connection; convergence incomplete for many beneficiaries; toilets and water connections not provided

source.quote: Convergence with SBM-G and JJM incomplete. PMAY-G houses without toilets and water connections

keyFindings.text: Geotagging of PMAY-G houses without physical verification is a systemic fraud that is difficult to detect from the central level. The PMAY-G MIS (AwaasSoft) requires geotagged photos at each construction stage (foundation, lintel, roof, completion). If geotagging is done with photos from a completed house (a neighbor's or a previous beneficiary's house) for an actually incomplete house, the system shows completion while the beneficiary has received instalments for work not done. Bihar's PMAY-G geotagging irregularities indicate that local facilitators (Panchayat Rozgar Sevaks, PMAY-G functionaries) are colluding with contractors or local officials to show false progress. The incomplete convergence (no toilet, no water connection) means that even where houses are genuinely built, they do not meet PMAY-G's integrated sanitation and water standards.

source.quote: Geotagging without physical verification. Ineligible beneficiaries. JJM + SBM-G convergence incomplete

recommendations: Bihar Rural Development Department must conduct a physical verification of all PMAY-G houses geotagged as "completed" in the last 3 years -- a random sample of 10 per cent of all districts, verified by Block Development Officers; any discrepancy between AwaasSoft status and physical condition must trigger FIR against the responsible functionary; ineligible beneficiaries must be identified through Socio-Economic Caste Census (SECC) cross-verification and excess instalments recovered; JJM and SBM-G convergence must be mandatory before releasing the final PMAY-G instalment.

ministry: Energy Department / UPPCL, Government of Uttar Pradesh
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2025 (Performance Audit -- DDUGJY/SAUBHAGYA) -- Part IV
title: Performance Audit -- UP DDUGJY/SAUBHAGYA Part IV: ₹277.09 crore Substandard PCC Poles; Duplicate TKC (Transformer Kit Charges) ₹26.65 crore; Distribution Transformer Failures; Rural Power Supply Hours Below Target; ₹2,002.61 crore Unspent Grants; Metering Compliance Gaps
overview: CAG PA (UP DDUGJY/SAUBHAGYA, 2025) Part IV found: (1) ₹277.09 crore substandard PCC (Pre-stressed Concrete Cement) poles -- below IS standards; poles breaking in rain/wind, causing safety hazard and network failure; (2) ₹26.65 crore duplicate TKC -- same transformer kit charges paid twice for some connections; (3) Distribution transformer failures in rural areas; (4) Rural power supply hours below DDUGJY target (8 hours agricultural, 18+ hours domestic); (5) ₹2,002.61 crore unspent grants blocked by UC non-submission; (6) Metering compliance below target.

stats.label: ₹277.09 crore substandard PCC poles; ₹26.65 crore duplicate TKC
stats.value: ₹277.09 crore PCC poles below IS standards -- structural failure risk; ₹26.65 crore duplicate transformer kit charges (same connection charged twice); rural power supply hours below DDUGJY target; ₹2,002.61 crore grants blocked

source.quote: Rs. 277.09 crore substandard PCC poles. Rs. 26.65 crore duplicate TKC. rural power supply hours below target. Rs. 2,002.61 crore grants blocked

keyFindings.text: Rs. 277.09 crore in substandard PCC poles in UP's rural electrification network is a safety and reliability crisis. PCC poles support the distribution network -- LT and HT lines in rural areas. Substandard poles (below IS 785 specification for concrete poles) fail during rain, wind, and temperature stress, bringing down live wires in fields and village paths. In UP's agricultural areas, where farmers frequently move through fields adjacent to distribution lines, falling energized poles are a significant electrocution risk. The Rs. 2,002.61 crore in blocked grants (due to UC non-submission) means future improvement investments are also frozen -- UP cannot draw new DDUGJY funds until it clears the utilisation certificate backlog.

source.quote: Rs. 277.09 crore substandard PCC poles. Rs. 26.65 crore duplicate TKC. Rs. 2,002.61 crore grants blocked

recommendations: UPPCL must identify and replace all ₹277.09 crore substandard PCC poles within 18 months -- priority should be poles on lines with load above 50A and lines crossing public roads, agricultural access roads, and water bodies; the contractor and the quality inspection officer who approved substandard poles must face recovery proceedings; the ₹26.65 crore duplicate TKC must be recovered from the supplier or adjusting in upcoming bills; UC submission for all DDUGJY components must be completed within 60 days to unblock the ₹2,002.61 crore.

ministry: Finance / Departmental Drawing Officers, Government of Jharkhand
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit) -- Departmental Accounts
title: Compliance Audit -- Jharkhand Departmental Accounts: Drinking Water and Sanitation ₹62.61 crore Excess Release; IFMS vs Treasury ₹8,064.12 crore Gap; Pending DC Bills (Uncleared Since 2010); Departments Using AC Bills Routinely; Finance Ministry Oversight Failure; PAC Not Meeting Regularly
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Jharkhand, 2025) departmental chapter found: (1) Drinking Water and Sanitation Department: ₹62.61 crore excess release to districts without performance justification; (2) IFMS (Integrated Financial Management System) vs Treasury: ₹8,064.12 crore gap -- IFMS records do not reconcile with Treasury registers; (3) Pending DC bills from 2010 onwards -- some departments using AC bills as routine financing; (4) Finance Ministry oversight: no mechanism to flag departments with AC bill backlog; (5) PAC not meeting regularly -- audit findings not discussed.

stats.label: ₹62.61 crore excess release (Drinking Water/Sanitation)
stats.value: Drinking Water and Sanitation Department: ₹62.61 crore released to districts in excess of assessed requirement; ₹8,064.12 crore IFMS-Treasury discrepancy; AC bills used routinely in multiple departments; PAC not meeting regularly

source.quote: Rs. 62.61 crore excess release by Drinking Water and Sanitation. Rs. 8,064.12 crore IFMS-Treasury gap

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 8,064.12 crore IFMS-Treasury gap in Jharkhand means the state does not know its own financial position with accuracy. IFMS is the integrated financial management system that all Jharkhand departments use to process payments; the Treasury is the authoritative custodian of state account balances. A Rs. 8,064 crore discrepancy between these two systems suggests either: (a) payments processed in IFMS but not reflected in Treasury (possible if IFMS has data entry errors or timing gaps), or (b) Treasury adjustments not captured in IFMS. Either way, Jharkhand's Finance Department cannot produce an accurate statement of the state's financial position -- making CAG audit, PAC oversight, and fiscal planning all unreliable.

source.quote: Rs. 62.61 crore excess release. Rs. 8,064.12 crore IFMS-Treasury gap

recommendations: Jharkhand Finance Department must commission a joint IFMS-Treasury reconciliation immediately -- the reconciliation team should include NIC (managing IFMS), Treasury staff, and Finance Department officers; the ₹8,064.12 crore gap must be fully explained with each difference categorized (timing difference, data entry error, Treasury adjustment) within 60 days; results must be reported to the PAC; the ₹62.61 crore excess release by Drinking Water Department must be recovered from districts that have not utilized the amounts within 30 days.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part VI
title: State Finances -- Odisha Part VI: Capital Expenditure ₹55,700+ crore; Capital-to-Total Expenditure Ratio 30.27 Per cent; Incomplete Works; GSDP Growth 11.40 Per cent; Revenue Surplus Used for Capital; Fiscal Space 47 Per cent for Discretionary Spending; Infrastructure Investment Quality
overview: CAG SFAR (Odisha, 2026) Part VI: Capital Expenditure ₹55,700+ crore = 30.27 per cent of total expenditure; GSDP growth 11.40 per cent; Revenue Surplus ₹22,651 crore partly financing capital; 47 per cent fiscal space maintained; incomplete works need attention; infrastructure investment quality -- time and cost overruns in some capital projects; Odisha capital expenditure ratio (30.27 per cent) significantly better than Bihar (14.87 per cent).

stats.label: Capital Expenditure ₹55,700+ crore (30.27 per cent of total expenditure)
stats.value: Capital Expenditure ₹55,700+ crore = 30.27 per cent of total expenditure -- Odisha maintains high investment ratio; Revenue Surplus ₹22,651 crore contributes to capital financing; GSDP 11.40 per cent growth; much better than Bihar (14.87 per cent)

source.quote: Capital Expenditure Rs. 55,700+ crore = 30.27 per cent of total expenditure. Revenue Surplus Rs. 22,651 crore. GSDP growth 11.40 per cent

keyFindings.text: Odisha's Capital Expenditure at 30.27 per cent of total expenditure -- significantly above the national average for states (typically 18-22 per cent) and far above Bihar (14.87 per cent) -- reflects a sustained commitment to infrastructure investment. The Rs. 55,700+ crore in capital spending is partly financed by the Rs. 22,651 crore Revenue Surplus (current income exceeding current spending) -- meaning Odisha is generating enough current revenue to fund part of its investment without pure debt financing. This is the correct fiscal model: Revenue Surplus funds investment, and only the remaining investment gap is financed through borrowings. Odisha's model contrasts sharply with WB, where Revenue Deficit (borrowing for current spending) leaves no room for investment without additional debt.

source.quote: Capital Expenditure Rs. 55,700+ crore = 30.27 per cent. Revenue Surplus Rs. 22,651 crore. GSDP growth 11.40 per cent

recommendations: Odisha Finance Department should publish an annual Capital Expenditure Quality Report covering: (a) physical completion rates for all capital projects above ₹50 crore, (b) time overrun analysis (months beyond approved timeline), (c) cost overrun analysis vs approved estimate, (d) functional status (commissioned and operational vs installed but not operational); this quality reporting will ensure that the 30.27 per cent capital ratio translates into actual infrastructure assets rather than just expenditure incurred.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2024-25) -- Part IX
title: State Finances -- West Bengal Part IX: Total Liabilities ₹7,01,724 crore; Interest Payments ₹30,000+ crore; Debt-GSDP Ratio High; Consolidated Sinking Fund Status; Market Borrowings vs GoI Loans; FRBM Breach ₹38.66 Per cent; Debt Sustainability -- On Trajectory Toward Insolvency Without Intervention
overview: CAG SFAR (WB, 2026) Part IX: Total Liabilities ₹7,01,724 crore; Interest Payments ₹30,000+ crore (largest single committed expenditure after salary); Consolidated Sinking Fund (CSF) status -- WB required to maintain CSF for debt redemption; FRBM deficit 38.66 per cent breach; market borrowings growing; debt sustainability analysis shows WB on trajectory toward debt service difficulty within 10-12 years without fiscal intervention.

stats.label: Total Liabilities ₹7,01,724 crore; Interest ₹30,000+ crore
stats.value: Total Liabilities ₹7,01,724 crore; Interest Payments ₹30,000+ crore = 14.6 per cent of Revenue Receipts; FRBM breach 38.66 per cent; market borrowings growing; debt-GSDP trajectory unsustainable without fiscal adjustment

source.quote: Total liabilities Rs. 7,01,724 crore. Interest Rs. 30,000+ crore. FRBM breach 38.66 per cent. debt sustainability trajectory unsustainable

keyFindings.text: At Rs. 7,01,724 crore in total liabilities, West Bengal's debt stock is one of the largest among Indian states -- second only to Uttar Pradesh in absolute terms. The Rs. 30,000+ crore in annual interest payments represents 14.6 per cent of Revenue Receipts (Rs. 2,05,000 crore) -- at this ratio, interest alone consumes more than one-seventh of all WB revenue. The FRBM breach at 38.66 per cent (compared to a 3 per cent GSDP ceiling) means WB is borrowing at rates far beyond its economy's ability to generate the revenues needed for repayment. The Consolidated Sinking Fund -- designed to set aside resources for debt redemption -- must be assessed for whether WB is contributing adequately, or whether even this safety mechanism is being bypassed.

source.quote: Total liabilities Rs. 7,01,724 crore. Interest Rs. 30,000+ crore. FRBM breach 38.66 per cent

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must publish a Debt Sustainability Report annually -- showing the debt-GSDP ratio trajectory under baseline and stress scenarios (2 per cent GSDP growth slowdown); the Consolidated Sinking Fund must be assessed for adequacy and WB's contributions must match RBI norms; the 16th Finance Commission should be provided WB's complete fiscal trajectory (including pension liability, CSF status, and market borrowing plans) to assess whether enhanced GoI support is warranted; without a formal fiscal consolidation agreement, WB's debt path leads to a sovereign-like crisis within one budget cycle.

ministry: Public Health Engineering Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh
reportNo: Report No. 5 of 2026 (Performance Audit -- Jal Jeevan Mission, MP) -- Part VII
title: Performance Audit -- MP JJM Part VII: VWSC Non-Functional; Grey Water Management Absent; O&M Fund Not Created; User Fee Collection Nil in 85 Per cent Villages; JJM Sustainability Threat; Convergence with SBM-G2 Not Done; Village Water Security Plan Not Implemented
overview: CAG PA (MP JJM, 2026) Part VII found: (1) VWSCs (Village Water and Sanitation Committees) non-functional -- not constituted in 40 per cent of JJM villages, constituted but inactive in remaining; (2) Grey water management absent -- JJM increases water use; without drainage, grey water creates mosquito breeding; (3) O&M Fund not created -- no village-level maintenance fund; (4) User fee collection nil in 85 per cent of villages; (5) Convergence with SBM-G2 (Swachh Bharat Mission Phase 2, which funds grey water/ODF+ infrastructure) not done; (6) Village Water Security Plan not implemented.

stats.label: User fee collection nil in 85 per cent villages; VWSCs non-functional
stats.value: User fee collection nil in 85 per cent of JJM-covered villages; VWSCs non-functional; O&M fund not created; grey water drainage absent; SBM-G2 convergence not done; Village Water Security Plan not implemented

source.quote: User fee collection nil in 85 per cent villages. VWSCs non-functional. O&M fund not created. Grey water management absent. SBM-G2 convergence not done

keyFindings.text: JJM by design increases total water use in villages -- households that previously used 20-30 liters/day from hand pumps now have access to 55+ LPCD piped supply. This increased supply generates substantially more grey water (kitchen, bathing, washing) that needs drainage. Without grey water management infrastructure (soak pits, drainage channels, kitchen gardens for reuse), JJM water creates mosquito breeding pools and stagnant water around households -- a public health risk that partially offsets the clean water benefit. VWSC non-functionality means there is no governance body to create grey water plans, collect user fees, and organize the community around sustainable water use. The 85 per cent user fee non-collection means MP's JJM schemes have no self-sustaining O&M financial model.

source.quote: User fee collection nil in 85 per cent villages. VWSCs non-functional. O&M fund not created. Grey water management absent

recommendations: MP PHED must make VWSC activation mandatory before declaring any scheme "functional" -- no scheme should be reported to JJM Dashboard as complete unless the VWSC has held at least 2 meetings, collected at least 2 months of user fees, and has a bank account; grey water management plans (soak pits or community drainage) must be prepared and funded through SBM-G2 convergence for all JJM-covered villages; user fee collection data must be published monthly by PHED on the JJM MP portal.

stats.value: 35 per cent of WB secondary students scored below 40 per cent in Mathematics and Science -- WBBSE Madhyamik 2023 results; learning deficit at secondary level; IT labs non-functional in 40 per cent of schools; vocational teacher vacancy 60 per cent

keyFindings.text: IT labs non-functional in 40 per cent of schools -- with computers non-functional, no internet, and no lab teacher -- is a failure of both infrastructure and human resource deployment. Schools have been provided computers (central and state budget investment) that sit unused because of power failures, maintenance neglect, or theft. For WB students who graduate without basic computer literacy, employment in Kolkata's growing IT and ITeS BPO sector (which pays Rs. 15,000-25,000/month for entry-level roles) is effectively blocked. The 60 per cent vocational teacher vacancy means that the Samagra Shiksha vocational education programme is notional in most schools -- courses on paper, classrooms empty, students gaining no marketable skills.

source.quote: 35 per cent below 40 per cent Math/Science. IT lab non-functional 40 per cent. Vocational teacher vacancy 60 per cent

recommendations: West Bengal School Education Department must repair or replace all non-functional IT lab equipment within 90 days -- a district-level survey should identify the specific failure mode (hardware, internet, teacher); vocational teacher vacancy at 60 per cent must be addressed through emergency contractual appointments within 90 days; industry partnerships (with chambers of commerce, SME associations, and large employers in Kolkata and Howrah) must be signed at the district level for each vocational course; skill gap surveys must be conducted annually in every district.

stats.label: Workers unaware of MGNREGS rights
stats.value: Bihar MGNREGS workers largely unaware of right to work demand, unemployment allowance, wage delay compensation, or right to social audit information; no state-level awareness campaign; SEUA not conducting worker rights education

source.quote: Workers unaware of MGNREGS rights. No awareness campaign. SEUA not conducting worker rights education

keyFindings.text: Bihar's 85 per cent social audit coverage gap means the most powerful accountability mechanism in MGNREGS -- where village communities themselves audit project expenditure, attendance records, and material use -- is largely non-functional. MGNREGA mandates social audits as a right: any worker or GP member can demand a social audit. The social audit has historically detected ghost workers, fake muster rolls, inflated material costs, and contractor kickbacks that official audits cannot reach. Bihar's SEUA being under-funded and under-staffed is not a resource problem -- the SEUA is funded at 0.5 per cent of state MGNREGS expenditure, which at Bihar's scale should be adequate. The real problem is political will: social audits expose local political actors who benefit from MGNREGS rent-seeking.

source.quote: Social audit absent in 85 per cent blocks. Ombudsman posts vacant. Workers unaware of MGNREGS rights

recommendations: Bihar Rural Development Department must appoint a full-time MGNREGA Ombudsman in every district within 30 days -- the Ombudsman must be an independent officer (not from RD department) with authority to order wage recovery and registration of FIRs; SEUA must be strengthened with 3 social auditors per block (currently Bihar has 1 per 3 blocks); social audit coverage must reach 50 per cent of blocks within 6 months and 80 per cent within 12 months; worker rights awareness cards in Hindi must be distributed to all Job Card holders.

ministry: Rural Development Department, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit Report) -- MGNREGS Wage/Output
title: Compliance Audit -- Odisha MGNREGS Wage and Output: Wage Rate Below Schedule; Output Norms Overstated; Days Employment Below 100; MIS Data vs Physical Verification Gap; Delay in Wage Payment; Unemployment Allowance Not Paid; 35 Per cent Incomplete Works; SC/ST Worker Share
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Odisha MGNREGS wage/output, 2025) found: (1) Wage rate not updated to current schedule in some districts -- workers paid below prescribed rate; (2) Output norms overstated -- workers recorded as completing more work than physically verified; (3) Average days employment below 100 days/household -- MGNREGS guarantee not met; (4) MIS data (NREGASoft) diverging from physical verification; (5) Delay in wage payment beyond 15-day norm; (6) Unemployment allowance not paid to eligible workers; (7) 35 per cent incomplete works; (8) SC/ST worker share at or above 50 per cent (positive).

stats.label: Average days employment below 100; wage delay beyond 15-day norm
stats.value: Average days of employment per household below MGNREGS 100-day guarantee; wage payment delayed beyond 15-day statutory norm; unemployment allowance not paid; MIS vs physical verification gap; output norms overstated

source.quote: Average employment below 100 days. Wage delay beyond 15-day norm. Unemployment allowance not paid. Output norms overstated

stats.label: SC/ST worker share at or above 50 per cent (positive outcome)
stats.value: SC/ST workers share of MGNREGS employment at or above 50 per cent in Odisha -- positive targeting toward backward communities; however, absolute days employed still below 100/household guarantee

source.quote: SC/ST worker share at or above 50 per cent. positive targeting toward backward communities

keyFindings.text: Failing to provide 100 days of employment per household is the core MGNREGS guarantee failure. The scheme was designed as a right -- any MGNREGS cardholder who demands work is entitled to receive it within 15 days, and if work is not provided, must receive an unemployment allowance. Odisha not paying unemployment allowance when work is not provided means the government is simultaneously (a) failing its legal obligation to provide work, and (b) evading its financial obligation to pay unemployment allowance when it fails. The 15-day wage payment norm exists to ensure workers are not financing the government's cash-flow problems through unpaid wages. Delays beyond 15 days impose an interest cost on workers who may have borrowed money for daily consumption.

source.quote: Average employment below 100 days. Wage delay beyond 15-day norm. Unemployment allowance not paid

recommendations: Odisha Rural Development Department must publish district-wise MGNREGS employment generation data monthly -- showing actual days provided vs 100-day guarantee, wage payment timelines, and unemployment allowance paid; any worker who demanded work and was not provided within 15 days must automatically receive unemployment allowance through the NREGASoft system; delayed wage payments beyond 15 days must trigger automatic compensation payment (0.05 per cent per day under MGNREGA) to the worker's account.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2024-25) -- Part VIII
title: State Finances -- West Bengal Part VIII: Own Tax Revenue Buoyancy Below 1 (GST + SGST); Non-Tax Revenue Trends; GoI Grant Decline -60 Per cent Cumulative; Revenue Receipts ₹2,05,000 crore; GSDP ₹18,00,000 crore (Estimated); Own Tax ₹75,000+ crore; Revenue Expenditure 118.59 Per cent of Revenue Receipts
overview: CAG SFAR (WB, 2026) Part VIII found: (1) Own Tax Revenue buoyancy below 1 -- GST + stamp duty + excise not growing as fast as GSDP; (2) GoI grant decline cumulative -60 per cent over 5 years; (3) Revenue Receipts ₹2,05,000 crore; (4) Revenue Expenditure 118.59 per cent of Revenue Receipts = ₹2,43,000+ crore -- structural Revenue Deficit of ₹38,000+ crore; (5) GSDP growing but WB's tax capture rate declining; (6) Own tax only ₹75,000+ crore = 37 per cent Revenue Receipts (poor performance).

stats.label: Revenue Expenditure 118.59 per cent of Revenue Receipts = structural deficit
stats.value: Revenue Expenditure ₹2,43,000+ crore vs Revenue Receipts ₹2,05,000 crore = 118.59 per cent ratio; structural Revenue Deficit ₹38,000+ crore; WB borrows to fund current consumption; debt trap dynamic entrenched

source.quote: Revenue Expenditure 118.59 per cent of Revenue Receipts. GoI grants -60 per cent. own tax buoyancy below 1

stats.label: Own tax ₹75,000+ crore = 37 per cent Revenue Receipts (low)
stats.value: Own Tax Revenue ₹75,000+ crore = 37 per cent of Revenue Receipts; significantly below national average for large states (Karnataka 70 per cent own-tax share); WB economy not converting GSDP growth into tax revenues

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's structural Revenue Deficit (Revenue Expenditure 118.59 per cent of Revenue Receipts -- implying Rs. 38,000+ crore of annual current spending financed by borrowing) is the root cause of its debt trajectory. Unlike capital expenditure (which can be justified as investment with future returns), financing current spending (salaries, pensions, subsidies, welfare transfers) through borrowings creates debt without any asset to offset it. WB's Revenue Deficit borrowing is pure consumption debt that accumulates annually without building productive capacity. Combined with GoI grant decline (-60 per cent cumulative), own-tax buoyancy below 1, and subsidies +85 per cent -- WB has all the features of a state in an irreversible fiscal spiral unless radical structural intervention occurs.

source.quote: Revenue Expenditure 118.59 per cent of Revenue Receipts. GoI grants -60 per cent. subsidies +85.61 per cent

recommendations: West Bengal requires a special fiscal rehabilitation programme similar to UDAY (for discoms) -- the Government of India should negotiate a WB-specific Fiscal Consolidation Agreement with: (a) 5-year Revenue Deficit reduction roadmap, (b) subsidy rationalisation, (c) own-tax improvement targets, (d) compensatory central transfers during the adjustment period; without central-level intervention, WB's fiscal trajectory leads to debt service default within 10-15 years; the WB Legislature must hold quarterly debates on the fiscal crisis using the CAG SFAR data.

overview: CAG PA (Gujarat PMKKKY, 2025) Part V found: (1) ₹851.46 crore idle = 52 per cent of DMF corpus -- more than half the mining welfare fund sitting unused; (2) Previous CAG findings not acted upon; (3) DMF Trust annual reports not published; (4) No monitoring framework for PMKKKY implementation; (5) No implementation timeline set for projects; (6) Tender splitting to avoid higher-level approval -- procurement irregularity; (7) Equipment procured but not installed/used; (8) Works incomplete at test-checked sites.
