keyFindings.text: The 52 per cent idle rate (Rs. 851.46 crore of the DMF corpus) in Gujarat reveals that the problem is not lack of money -- it is lack of will and capability to deploy it. Gujarat is not a resource-constrained state. It has one of India's best administrative machinery, experienced IAS cadre, and functional district-level governance. The 52 per cent idle rate therefore reflects political decisions -- DMF Trusts are governed by Collectors and committee members with political appointments, and the choice of what to fund (and what not to fund) reflects priorities that serve the political economy rather than the mining-affected communities. Previous CAG findings not being acted upon shows these findings are viewed as manageable administrative inconveniences rather than serious accountability failures.

source.quote: Rs. 851.46 crore idle (52 per cent). Previous CAG findings not acted on

recommendations: Gujarat Mines and Geology Department must present a mandatory DMF Fund Utilisation Action Plan to the State Legislature within 30 days -- specifying project-by-project deployment targets for the ₹851.46 crore idle funds within 12 months; all identified procurement irregularities (tender splitting) must be investigated and show-cause notices issued to responsible Collectors; equipment procured but not installed must be accounted for and deployed within 30 days; previous CAG recommendations must be formally resolved through Action Taken Reports presented to the PAC.

ministry: Punjab State Power Corporation Limited (PSPCL) / Power Department
reportNo: Report No. 7 of 2025 (Audit Report on PSUs) -- PSPCL Part III
title: PSU Audit -- Punjab PSPCL Part III: AT&C Loss 15.48 Per cent (National Norm 12 Per cent); Consumer Tariff Below Cost of Supply; Transformer Failure Rate; Grid Tripping; Voltage Fluctuation in Rural Feeders; Metering Compliance; Smart Meter Rollout Delayed; Commercial Loss Recovery
overview: CAG PSU Audit (Punjab PSPCL, 2025) Part III found: (1) AT&C loss 15.48 per cent vs national norm 12 per cent -- 3.48 percentage point excess represents significant revenue leakage; (2) Consumer tariff below cost of supply -- cross-subsidy mechanism not covering full cost; (3) Distribution transformer failure rate above norm; (4) Grid tripping events causing supply interruptions; (5) Voltage fluctuation in rural feeders -- power quality below standard; (6) Smart meter rollout delayed; (7) Commercial loss recovery below target -- large consumers with arrears not disconnected.

stats.label: AT&C loss 15.48 per cent (3.48 pp above 12 per cent national norm)
stats.value: AT&C loss 15.48 per cent vs 12 per cent national norm -- 3.48 percentage point excess; at Punjab distribution network scale, 1 per cent AT&C = ₹300-400 crore revenue loss; total AT&C excess loss ₹1,000-1,400 crore annually

source.quote: AT&C loss 15.48 per cent. national norm 12 per cent. transformer failure rate above norm

keyFindings.text: PSPCL's AT&C loss at 15.48 per cent (3.48 percentage points above the 12 per cent national norm) represents an annual revenue leakage of Rs. 1,000-1,400 crore -- electricity distributed but not billed or collected. AT&C loss has two components: technical losses (heat loss in wires and transformers -- unavoidable but reducible through infrastructure upgrade) and commercial losses (theft, unbilled connections, collection inefficiency). Punjab's high agricultural connected load creates substantial technical losses through long rural feeder lines serving dispersed farms. However, the commercial loss component -- meters bypassed or tampered, connections not metered -- is a controllable factor. With PSPCL already losing Rs. 4,775 crore annually, the Rs. 1,000-1,400 crore AT&C excess loss is the one recoverable component that smart metering and enforcement could address.

source.quote: AT&C loss 15.48 per cent. national norm 12 per cent

recommendations: PSPCL must accelerate smart meter installation in all connections above 5 KW -- smart meters eliminate meter tampering, enable remote monitoring, and facilitate time-of-day tariffs; the AT&C loss reduction must be a KPI in PSPCL CMD's Annual Performance Review with a target of 13 per cent within 2 years and 12 per cent within 4 years; distribution transformer losses must be reduced through higher-efficiency transformer procurement in all new installations; large consumer arrears above ₹1 crore must be resolved within 30 days through a Consumer Arrears Resolution Programme.

ministry: Public Health Engineering Department / VWSC, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (Compliance Audit -- HGNJ) -- Part IV
title: Compliance Audit -- Bihar HGNJ Part IV: VWSC (Village Water and Sanitation Committees) Non-Functional; Operation and Maintenance Plan Absent; User Fee Collection Below Requirement; Chlorination Records Missing; Scheme-Level O&M Funding Gap; Community Training Absent; ₹13,899 crore Programme With Sustainability Gap
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Bihar HGNJ Part IV) found: (1) VWSCs (Village Water and Sanitation Committees) non-functional -- not constituted, or constituted but not meeting; (2) O&M plan absent -- no mechanism for maintaining pipes, pumps, OHTs after installation; (3) User fee collection far below what is required for O&M -- communities using water for free cannot fund maintenance; (4) Chlorination records missing; (5) Community training (for pump maintenance, basic chlorination, water quality testing) absent; (6) Sustainability gap: ₹13,899 crore installed but O&M funding ₹0 from structured community sources.

stats.label: VWSCs non-functional; O&M plan absent; user fees below O&M requirement
stats.value: VWSCs non-functional at test-checked sites; O&M plan absent; user fee collection far below O&M requirement; chlorination records missing; community training absent; ₹13,899 crore scheme with no sustainability framework

source.quote: VWSCs non-functional. O&M plan absent. User fee collection below requirement. Chlorination records missing. Community training absent

keyFindings.text: Bihar's Rs. 13,899 crore JJM/HGNJ investment is creating hardware (pipes, overhead tanks, pumps, connections) that will begin to deteriorate within 3-5 years without systematic O&M. Every piped water scheme in India -- from colonial-era Bombay waterworks to modern JJM schemes -- fails primarily due to O&M neglect: pipes corrode, pumps break, overhead tanks develop cracks, chlorinators stop working. VWSC non-functionality means no community ownership of the infrastructure. Without VWSCs collecting user fees (even Rs. 50-100/month per household), there is no local funding for repairs. Within 10 years of installation, a significant fraction of Bihar's Rs. 13,899 crore JJM investment will be non-functional -- a pattern already visible in older government water schemes across the state.

source.quote: VWSCs non-functional. O&M plan absent. Rs. 13,899 crore scheme with no sustainability framework

recommendations: Bihar PHED must mandate VWSC activation in all JJM-covered Gram Panchayats within 3 months -- each VWSC must have a bank account, meet monthly, collect user fees (minimum ₹100/month/FHTC), and maintain an O&M fund; the O&M fund must be ring-fenced and only usable for water scheme maintenance; annual O&M plans must be prepared by VWSC with technical support from Block PHED; chlorination records must be submitted to GP/VWSC monthly; community training on basic water system maintenance must be provided through JJM's capacity building allocation.

overview: CAG SFAR (Karnataka, 2025) Part VII: Revenue Receipts ₹2,07,000+ crore; Revenue Expenditure ₹2,05,000+ crore -- narrow Revenue Surplus (unlike WB's structural Revenue Deficit); Total Expenditure ₹3,19,000+ crore; Debt-GSDP manageable (2.42 per cent liabilities/GSDP ratio); GoI transfers 30 per cent Revenue Receipts -- much lower dependency than Bihar (62 per cent) or Nagaland (81 per cent); own-tax revenue buoyancy driven by IT/services sector.

stats.value: Revenue Receipts ₹2,07,000+ crore; Revenue Expenditure ₹2,05,000+ crore; narrow Revenue Surplus; debt-GSDP 2.42 per cent; GoI dependency 30 per cent (vs Bihar 62 per cent, Nagaland 81 per cent); IT-sector own-tax base strong

source.quote: Revenue Receipts Rs. 2,07,000+ crore. Revenue Expenditure Rs. 2,05,000+ crore. narrow Revenue Surplus. GoI transfers 30 per cent

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's 30 per cent GoI dependency (vs Bihar 62 per cent and Nagaland 81 per cent) means Karnataka finances 70 per cent of its needs from own revenue -- making it far more fiscally sovereign than North-East or BIMARU states. This fiscal sovereignty comes from Bengaluru's IT/ITeS sector generating high commercial tax, professional tax, stamp duty, and consumer spending (GST). However, the narrow Revenue Surplus (Revenue Receipts barely exceeding Revenue Expenditure) leaves little buffer -- if the welfare guarantees (Rs. 50,000+ crore annually) push Revenue Expenditure above Revenue Receipts, Karnataka will transition from a Revenue Surplus state to a Revenue Deficit state, triggering the same debt spiral visible in WB. The 2023-24 welfare guarantee launch is the critical inflection point to monitor.

source.quote: Revenue Receipts Rs. 2,07,000+ crore. Revenue Expenditure Rs. 2,05,000+ crore. GoI transfers 30 per cent. GSDP Rs. 28.62 lakh crore

recommendations: Karnataka Finance Department must publish a Welfare Guarantee Revenue Impact Report within 6 months of the 2023-24 fiscal close -- showing actual Revenue Surplus after full-year guarantee costs; if the Revenue Surplus has declined by more than 30 per cent from the pre-guarantee baseline, the government should begin guarantee cost-containment measures; IT sector revenue risk should be stress-tested annually -- the 2023-24 global tech layoff wave demonstrated that IT employment can contract rapidly; any contraction scenario should be reflected in the MTFP.

overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Odisha MGNREGS, 2025) found: (1) 0.82 lakh eligible households denied Job Cards -- denied MGNREGS right to work; (2) 4.17 lakh duplicate/ghost Job Cards -- multiple cards for same household or cards for deceased/migrated persons; (3) Aadhaar seeding incomplete -- wages going to wrong accounts; (4) Muster roll irregularities -- attendance over-recorded; (5) Wage diversion -- wages credited to accounts other than workers; (6) Social audit not done in 12 blocks (statutory requirement); (7) 12.96 lakh incomplete works (35 per cent).

stats.label: 0.82 lakh households denied Job Cards; 4.17 lakh duplicate/ghost cards

keyFindings.text: The simultaneous existence of 0.82 lakh eligible households denied Job Cards and 4.17 lakh duplicate/ghost Job Cards in Odisha's MGNREGS system reveals a corrupt registration process: genuine poor households are denied cards (often because they lack political connections or cannot pay facilitation fees to Gram Rozgar Sahayaks) while ghost cards are created to enable wage diversion. The ghost card holder's "wages" go to the account of whoever controls that card -- typically the local contractor, GRS, or elected representative. Social audit non-conduct in 12 blocks means this fraud remains undetected at the community level. Odisha's 35 per cent incomplete work rate (12.96 lakh works) amplifies the problem -- incomplete works are harder to audit physically.

source.quote: 0.82 lakh eligible households denied Job Cards. 4.17 lakh duplicate/ghost Job Cards. Social audit not done in 12 blocks

recommendations: Odisha Rural Development Department must conduct a biometric-verified Job Card cleaning drive in all blocks -- every active Job Card must be re-verified against Aadhaar biometric in the MGNREGS payment system; all 4.17 lakh identified duplicate/ghost cards must be deleted within 30 days; the 0.82 lakh denied households must be issued Job Cards within 15 days; wage diversion cases must be FIR-filed in all instances where there is documentary evidence of wage credit to non-worker accounts.

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's 26.29 per cent Capital Expenditure share is better than many richer states, reflecting the state's relative emphasis on infrastructure investment. However, this CapEx is predominantly GoI-funded through state-specific packages for NE infrastructure (NLCPR, North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme, NESIDS) rather than financed from Nagaland's own resources. The 4.26 per cent FRBM deficit (vs 3 per cent limit) means even with this GoI-funded CapEx, Nagaland borrows more than FRBM allows -- primarily to fund the committed expenditure gap (salary + pension + interest absorbing 57 per cent of Revenue Receipts). Nagaland's fiscal path requires both committed expenditure rationalisation and improved own revenue generation to be sustainable without perpetual GoI special packages.

recommendations: Nagaland Finance Department must develop a Capital Expenditure Quality Assessment -- tracking physical completion rates, cost overruns, and economic returns for all capital projects; CapEx financed through GoI-specific NE packages must have quarterly progress reporting; guarantees at 14.45 per cent of Net Revenue Receipts must be monitored against the FRBM guarantee ceiling and guaranteed entity financial health reviewed annually.

overview: CAG PA (MP JJM, 2026) Part VI found: (1) NABL-accredited laboratory testing -- target 5 per cent samples; only 1.60 per cent tested; (2) Fluoride above permissible limits: Narsimhapur 2.60 mg/L (vs 1.5 mg/L limit), Vidisha, Ratlam also above limits; (3) Chlorination not maintained at treatment plants and distribution networks; (4) Field test kits (procured) not used in villages; (5) Bacteriological testing (for E. coli and coliforms) absent from most test-checked schemes; (6) ODF villages receiving contaminated tap water -- public health risk.

stats.value: Narsimhapur JJM water: fluoride 2.60 mg/L -- 73 per cent above 1.5 mg/L permissible limit; Vidisha and Ratlam also above limit; NABL testing only 1.60 per cent vs 5 per cent target; chlorination not maintained

stats.value: Field test kits (for basic water quality parameters) procured but not deployed/used in villages; bacteriological testing (E. coli, coliforms) absent from most test-checked schemes; ODF villages receiving contaminated tap water

keyFindings.text: Fluoride at 2.60 mg/L (73 per cent above the 1.5 mg/L limit) in Narsimhapur's JJM water supply is a serious public health danger. Fluorosis -- caused by chronic high-fluoride water intake -- causes dental fluorosis (mottled, brown teeth), skeletal fluorosis (joint pain, bone deformity), and in severe cases neurological damage. These are irreversible conditions. Children are most vulnerable. If JJM's piped water in Narsimhapur is delivering 2.60 mg/L fluoride to households that previously used lower-fluoride sources, the scheme is actively harming the communities it was meant to help. JJM progress reports would claim these households now have "safe tap water" -- the fluoride testing data shows the water is unsafe.

source.quote: Narsimhapur: fluoride 2.60 mg/L vs 1.5 mg/L permissible. NABL testing 1.60 per cent vs 5 per cent target

recommendations: MP PHED must immediately suspend household connections in all JJM schemes where water quality testing shows fluoride above 1.5 mg/L or arsenic above 0.01 mg/L -- these connections must not be recorded as "functional FHTCs" until the source is changed to a compliant one; NABL testing must reach the 5 per cent target within 6 months; all field test kits must be distributed to Gram Panchayats with training for GP members on monthly testing; chlorination records must be maintained at all treatment plants and submitted to the district PHED monthly.

source.quote: Tea garden children in child labour. Seasonal migration disrupting schooling. Urban slum children unserved

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's 83 per cent failure rate in its OOSC enrolment drive reflects the gap between an administrative programme (identifying and enrolling out-of-school children) and a social intervention (addressing why children are out of school). Tea garden children in Darjeeling and the Dooars are not out of school because no school is nearby -- schools exist in tea garden areas. They are out of school because estate management allows or encourages child labour, families depend on child income, and there is no enforcement of child labour laws within private estate boundaries. An enrolment drive that does not address these structural factors will not enrol tea garden children regardless of how many block education officers conduct house-to-house visits.

source.quote: 83 per cent targeted out-of-school children not enrolled. Tea garden children in child labour

recommendations: West Bengal School Education Department must collaborate with the Labour Department and District Collectors in tea garden districts (Darjeeling, Jalpaiguri, Alipurduar) to enforce the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act on all tea estates -- estate managers must be served notice that employing children during school hours attracts prosecution; residential schools (like Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas) must be established in all tea garden blocks to provide children a school environment where estate social pressure does not reach; AECs in urban slums must be activated with full-time instructors.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 6 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part IV
title: State Finances -- Bihar Part IV: Capital Outlay ₹43,281 crore (14.87 Per cent); Capital Expenditure Quality; Infrastructure Projects; GoI Loans for Capital; CSS State Share Funded by Borrowing; Revenue Deficit at Margin; Own Capital Resources Thin
overview: CAG SFAR (Bihar, 2026) Part IV: Capital Outlay ₹43,281 crore = 14.87 per cent of total expenditure -- moderate but insufficient for Bihar's infrastructure deficit; CSS state share (20-40 per cent of scheme cost Bihar must contribute) funded through borrowings because own revenue insufficient; revenue deficit at margin (Revenue Expenditure close to or exceeding Revenue Receipts at times); own capital resources thin; GoI capital loans (PMGSY, JJM, PMAY) providing bulk of capital investment.

stats.label: Capital Outlay ₹43,281 crore (14.87 per cent of expenditure)
stats.value: Capital Outlay ₹43,281 crore = 14.87 per cent of total expenditure; Bihar infrastructure deficit requires 20+ per cent CapEx share; CSS state share 20-40 per cent funded by borrowings; own capital resources thin

source.quote: Capital Outlay Rs. 43,281 crore = 14.87 per cent of total expenditure

keyFindings.text: Bihar's Capital Outlay at 14.87 per cent of total expenditure is below the 18-20 per cent recommended for states with large infrastructure deficits. In absolute terms, Rs. 43,281 crore sounds large, but Bihar's infrastructure needs -- roads, schools, hospitals, irrigation, power, water supply -- are among the largest in India due to historical underinvestment and population density. The compounding problem is that Bihar must fund 20-40 per cent of CSS scheme costs (PMAY-G, JJM, MGNREGS material component) from its own resources -- and since its own revenue is thin (38 per cent of receipts), it funds this state share from borrowings. This means Bihar's borrowings partly finance current consumption (subsidies) and partly finance capital co-financing -- making it difficult to distinguish productive investment debt from consumptive debt.

source.quote: Capital Outlay Rs. 43,281 crore = 14.87 per cent. CSS state share funded by borrowings

recommendations: Bihar Finance Department must separate capital investment borrowing from consumption borrowing in its annual debt statement -- showing specifically which GoI loans fund capital formation and which borrowings fund revenue expenditure; CSS state share funding must be ring-fenced in the budget as a priority call on own-revenue (salary savings, tax growth); Capital Outlay should be increased to 18 per cent within 3 years through attrition-based salary savings and CSS state share utilisation improvement (full utilisation of GoI capital loans).

ministry: Mines and Geology Department / DMF, Government of Gujarat
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (Performance Audit -- PMKKKY) -- Part IV
title: Performance Audit -- Gujarat PMKKKY Part IV: Block Level Plans Not Prepared; District Level Plans Not Converging Village Needs; Environmental Mitigation Absent; Dust Control Measures Not Funded; Community Awareness About PMKKKY Rights Nil; Annual Reports Not Published; DMF Trust Website Inactive; Audit Findings Not Acted Upon
overview: CAG PA (Gujarat PMKKKY, 2025) Part IV found: (1) Block-level plans not prepared -- PMKKKY requires block-level granular planning; (2) District plans not aggregating village-level needs; (3) Environmental mitigation (dust suppression, green belts, water body restoration) not funded; (4) Community awareness about PMKKKY rights nil -- most mining-affected communities not aware they are entitled to DMF benefits; (5) Annual reports of DMF Trusts not published; (6) DMF Trust websites inactive; (7) CAG findings from earlier reviews not acted upon.

stats.label: Community awareness nil; environmental mitigation absent
stats.value: Mining-affected communities not aware of PMKKKY entitlements; DMF Trust websites inactive; annual reports not published; block-level plans not prepared; environmental mitigation (dust, water restoration) not funded

source.quote: Community awareness about PMKKKY rights nil. Annual reports not published. DMF Trust websites inactive. Block plans not prepared. Environmental mitigation absent

keyFindings.text: If mining-affected communities do not know they are entitled to DMF benefits, they cannot demand them, cannot identify misuse, and cannot participate in DMF Trust governance. This information asymmetry is exploited by contractors and local officials who divert DMF funds to non-PMKKKY activities or low-priority infrastructure. Transparency is the primary accountability mechanism: DMF Trust websites publishing annual plans, expenditures, and beneficiary lists would allow community members, journalists, and NGOs to identify misuse. Gujarat's DMF Trust websites being inactive and annual reports unpublished means Rs. 851.46 crore in idle funds and Rs. 5,000+ crore in prior disbursements are effectively unmonitored by the communities they were meant to serve.

source.quote: Community awareness about PMKKKY rights nil. Annual reports not published. DMF Trust websites inactive

recommendations: Gujarat Mines and Geology Department must mandate all DMF Trusts to publish: (a) annual plan (by November each year), (b) quarterly expenditure reports, (c) beneficiary lists for all direct welfare schemes, (d) project completion photos; these must be available on the DMF Trust website in Gujarati and English within 30 days; a community grievance hotline for PMKKKY complaints must be established; block-level plans must be prepared within 3 months by aggregating Gram Panchayat-level needs; environmental mitigation must be funded as High-Priority expenditure in all mining districts.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part V
title: State Finances -- Odisha Part V: Salary ₹35,000+ crore; Pension ₹14,000+ crore; Interest ₹14,500+ crore; Committed ₹63,500+ crore (37.19 Per cent Revenue Receipts); Subsidies ₹27,186 crore; Total Committed + Subsidies 52.96 Per cent; Fiscal Space 47 Per cent; Capital Expenditure Quality
overview: CAG SFAR (Odisha, 2026) Part V: Committed expenditure (salary + pension + interest) ₹63,500+ crore = 37.19 per cent Revenue Receipts; subsidies ₹27,186 crore = 15.94 per cent; combined 53.13 per cent -- better than WB (74 per cent) and Bihar (74 per cent); 47 per cent fiscal space for discretionary spending; Capital Expenditure maintained at healthy levels; Odisha's fiscal management better than stressed states.

stats.label: Committed + Subsidies 53.13 per cent Revenue Receipts (vs WB 74 per cent)
stats.value: Odisha committed expenditure 37.19 per cent + subsidies 15.94 per cent = 53.13 per cent Revenue Receipts; 47 per cent fiscal space -- significantly better than WB (74 per cent) and Bihar (74 per cent); Revenue Surplus ₹22,651 crore maintained

source.quote: committed expenditure constituting 37.19 per cent of Revenue Receipts. subsidies 15.94 per cent. Revenue Surplus Rs. 22,651 crore

keyFindings.text: Odisha's 47 per cent fiscal space (compared to WB's 26 per cent) reflects decades of relatively disciplined fiscal management. Odisha was itself a stressed state in the early 2000s, requiring significant central assistance and debt restructuring. Its subsequent turnaround was driven by: strong mineral royalty revenues (iron ore price boom 2003-2012), FRBM compliance, and continued GoI transfer inflows. The state maintained Capital Expenditure at healthy levels through this period, building schools, hospitals, and roads that improve long-term economic productivity. The lesson from Odisha vs WB is that fiscal discipline -- keeping subsidies below GSDP growth, maintaining CapEx, not running structural Revenue Deficits -- is achievable even for poorer states, but requires political will over multiple election cycles.

source.quote: committed expenditure constituting 37.19 per cent of Revenue Receipts. Revenue Surplus Rs. 22,651 crore. 47 per cent fiscal space

recommendations: Odisha Finance Department should formalize its fiscal management framework as an Odisha Fiscal Responsibility Framework (beyond the statutory FRBM) -- publishing quarterly fiscal bulletins showing actual vs projected salary, pension, interest, and subsidy growth; this framework should be presented to the Legislature and made publicly available as a model for other states; Capital Expenditure quality reporting (physical completion rates, time-and-cost overruns) should be included in the annual Finance Accounts.

ministry: Education Department / Samagra Shiksha, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2026 (Compliance Audit) -- School Education
title: Compliance Audit -- Bihar School Education: Mid-Day Meal (PM-POSHAN) -- Irregularities; Unspent Funds; Dropout Rate 40 Per cent (Secondary Level); Teacher Vacancy 50,000+; Infrastructure Gap (Toilets, Kitchens, Classrooms); SMS Alerts Fund Misuse; Cooking Cost Below Norm
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Bihar school education, 2026) found: (1) Mid-Day Meal (PM-POSHAN) irregularities -- unspent funds, cooking cost below prescribed norms, SMS-based attendance alerts misused; (2) Dropout rate 40 per cent at secondary level -- among India's highest; (3) Teacher vacancy 50,000+ -- single-teacher schools widespread; (4) Infrastructure gaps: inadequate toilets, kitchen sheds not constructed, classrooms insufficient; (5) Enrolment vs attendance gap -- enrolled students not attending; (6) CWSN (Children with Special Needs) facilities absent.

stats.label: Dropout 40 per cent (secondary); teacher vacancy 50,000+
stats.value: Bihar secondary school dropout rate approximately 40 per cent -- among India's highest; teacher vacancy 50,000+ across government schools; single-teacher schools in multiple districts; CWSN facilities absent

source.quote: dropout rate 40 per cent secondary level. teacher vacancy 50,000+. single-teacher schools widespread

stats.label: PM-POSHAN irregularities; cooking cost below norm
stats.value: PM-POSHAN (Mid-Day Meal) irregularities: cooking cost below prescribed norms (students receiving lower-quality meals); unspent funds not utilised; SMS attendance alert system misused; kitchen sheds not constructed

source.quote: PM-POSHAN irregularities. cooking cost below norm. unspent funds. SMS alerts misused. kitchen sheds not constructed

keyFindings.text: Bihar's 40 per cent secondary dropout rate is not primarily a supply-side failure (schools exist in most areas) -- it is a demand-side crisis driven by extreme poverty, child labour (brick kilns, agriculture, domestic work), early marriage, and the immediate income opportunity cost of education for poor families. PM-POSHAN (Mid-Day Meal) is one of the few demand-side incentives for school attendance -- when cooking costs are below norm, meal quality drops, and the meal's role as an attendance incentive weakens. A cooked meal that is nutritionally inadequate (thin dal, minimal vegetables) does not provide the same attendance pull as a full nutritious meal. The 50,000+ teacher vacancy compounds the supply-side failure: schools without adequate teachers push students away even when they do attend.

source.quote: dropout rate 40 per cent secondary level. teacher vacancy 50,000+. PM-POSHAN irregularities. cooking cost below norm

recommendations: Bihar Education Department must fill 50,000+ teacher vacancies within 18 months through an emergency recruitment process -- the Bihar Public Service Commission must be directed to conduct a Teacher Recruitment Drive; PM-POSHAN cooking cost compliance must be audited in all schools and the prescribed per-child cost (₹6.19 primary / ₹9.27 upper primary per day) must be fully disbursed; dropout rate reduction requires a convergence programme with Labour Department to identify and rescue child labourers from brick kilns and agricultural labour in Bihar's most affected districts (Gaya, Nawada, Araria, Kishanganj).

ministry: Tourism / Forest Department, Government of Uttarakhand
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit) -- Part III
title: Compliance Audit -- Uttarakhand Part III: Forest Land Diversion Violations; Tourism Infrastructure on Forest Land Without Permission; Mining Royalty Evasion; Royalty ₹59.45 crore Not Deducted; Works Abandoned After Expenditure; Idle Plant and Machinery at Construction Sites; Cost Escalations Without Sanction
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Uttarakhand, 2025) Part III found: (1) Tourism and other infrastructure constructed on forest land without obtaining FC Act permission -- violation of Forest Conservation Act 1980; (2) Mining royalty ₹59.45 crore not deducted from contractors (sand, stone, gravel used in government works); (3) Works abandoned mid-execution with significant expenditure incurred (including Ganga-related schemes); (4) Idle plant and machinery at project sites -- government equipment unutilized; (5) Cost escalations approved without government sanction.

stats.label: Forest land diversion without FC Act permission
stats.value: Tourism and infrastructure on forest land constructed without Forest Conservation Act permission; violation of FC Act 1980 (any non-forest use requires Central/State government approval); Ganga basin projects violating environmental norms

source.quote: Forest land diversion without FC Act permission. Tourism infrastructure on forest land

stats.label: ₹59.45 crore mining royalty not deducted; idle plant and machinery
stats.value: ₹59.45 crore mining royalty (on sand, stone, gravel used in government construction) not deducted from contractor bills; idle plant and machinery at project sites; abandoned works; cost escalations without sanction

source.quote: Rs. 59.45 crore royalty not deducted. Abandoned works. Idle machinery. Cost escalations without sanction

keyFindings.text: Forest land diversion without FC Act clearance is not just a revenue or administrative violation -- it is a criminal offense under the Forest Conservation Act 1980, which mandates prior Central Government approval for any non-forest use of classified forest land. Uttarakhand's forests form the watershed of the Ganga-Yamuna river system, and illegal diversion -- even for tourism infrastructure -- contributes to watershed degradation, increased flood risk (the 2013 Kedarnath disaster demonstrated this), and loss of biodiversity. The fact that government departments themselves are violating FC Act norms (rather than just private actors) makes enforcement particularly problematic -- it normalizes forest diversion and sends a signal to private developers that clearances are optional.

source.quote: Forest land diversion without FC Act permission. Tourism infrastructure on forest land

recommendations: Uttarakhand Forest Department must survey all tourism and infrastructure projects in forest areas -- each project must be checked for FC Act clearance; projects without clearance must be either regularized (if eligible) or demolished and the land restored; the ₹59.45 crore royalty from mining materials used in government contracts must be recovered from contractors within 30 days; idle plant and machinery must be inventoried and redistributed to active projects within 60 days.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2024-25) -- Part VII
title: State Finances -- West Bengal Part VII: Pension ₹34,000+ crore (Pay + Pension +25 Per cent 5-Year); GPF Liability Growing; OPS vs NPS for New Employees; Salary ₹60,000+ crore; Interest ₹30,000+ crore; Total Committed Expenditure ₹1,30,000+ crore; Revenue Receipts ₹2,05,000 crore
overview: CAG SFAR (WB, 2026) Part VII: Pension expenditure ₹34,000+ crore; Salary ₹60,000+ crore; Interest ₹30,000+ crore -- total committed expenditure ₹1,24,000+ crore out of Revenue Receipts ₹2,05,000 crore (60 per cent); WB still on Old Pension Scheme (OPS) for most employees -- pension liability growing as a stock; GPF (General Provident Fund) liability growing; Pay+Pension+Interest growing +25 per cent over 5 years vs Revenue Receipts growth; structural committed expenditure problem.

stats.label: Salary ₹60,000+ crore + Pension ₹34,000+ crore + Interest ₹30,000+ crore
stats.value: Committed expenditure: Salary ₹60,000+ crore + Pension ₹34,000+ crore + Interest ₹30,000+ crore = ₹1,24,000+ crore; 60 per cent Revenue Receipts ₹2,05,000 crore; Pay+Pension+Interest +25 per cent (5 years)

source.quote: Salary, pension and interest Rs. 1,24,000+ crore. 60 per cent Revenue Receipts. Pay+Pension+Interest +25 per cent over 5 years

stats.label: OPS pension stock liability growing (vs NPS defined contribution)
stats.value: WB on Old Pension Scheme -- defined benefit obligation growing as a stock liability; GPF liability growing; pension actuarial liability not disclosed; NPS migration for new employees not consistent; pension burden will compound

source.quote: OPS pension liability growing. GPF liability growing. pension burden compounding

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's committed expenditure consuming 60 per cent of Revenue Receipts (rising 25 per cent over 5 years) while Revenue Expenditure runs at 118.59 per cent of Revenue Receipts creates a simple arithmetic conclusion: WB is borrowing to pay salaries, pensions, and interest. This is the textbook definition of a debt trap. The Old Pension Scheme liability is a particular concern -- OPS promises a defined benefit (50 per cent of last drawn pay as pension, linked to dearness allowance) that compounds over the retiree's lifetime and passes to their spouse. As WB's large post-1970s government workforce reaches retirement age, pension expenditure will grow faster than the workforce itself. Unlike NPS (where the government contributes a fixed 14 per cent of salary into a fund), OPS pension is paid from current revenues -- an unfunded liability of potentially Rs. 2-3 lakh crore.

source.quote: Salary, pension and interest Rs. 1,24,000+ crore. 60 per cent Revenue Receipts. Pay+Pension+Interest +25 per cent over 5 years

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must commission an actuarial valuation of its OPS pension liability -- the total future obligation (discounted at 7 per cent) should be disclosed in the Finance Accounts as a note; migration to NPS for all new employees must be implemented uniformly; the Government should request the 16th Finance Commission to include WB's pension liability in the horizontal devolution formula; GPF liability must be matched against GPF fund assets and the deficit disclosed.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Karnataka
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part VI
title: State Finances -- Karnataka Part VI: Grants-in-Aid ₹28,437.95 crore; Subsidies ₹29,891.94 crore; Revenue vs Capital Grants; State PSU Off-Budget Borrowings; ₹6,92,115 crore Total Liabilities; Contingent Liabilities ₹1,38,620 crore; Off-Budget Risk from Infrastructure PSUs
overview: CAG SFAR (Karnataka, 2025) Part VI found: (1) Grants-in-Aid ₹28,437.95 crore -- funding local bodies, educational institutions, and NGOs; (2) Subsidies ₹29,891.94 crore -- power, agriculture, social welfare; (3) Total Liabilities ₹6,92,115 crore; (4) Off-budget borrowings by PSUs: Karnataka PSUs (KPCL, KPTCL, KRIDL, etc.) borrow commercially with government guarantee -- not on balance sheet but government-backed; (5) Contingent Liabilities ₹1,38,620 crore -- off-balance-sheet risk; (6) Infrastructure investments by BDA, BMRDA, BMRCL funded by PSU borrowings.

stats.label: Grants-in-Aid ₹28,437.95 crore; Subsidies ₹29,891.94 crore
stats.value: Grants-in-Aid ₹28,437.95 crore (local bodies, NGOs, educational institutions); Subsidies ₹29,891.94 crore (power, agriculture, welfare guarantees); Total ₹58,329 crore = 37 per cent Revenue Receipts

source.quote: Grants-in-Aid Rs. 28,437.95 crore. Subsidies Rs. 29,891.94 crore. Total Liabilities Rs. 6,92,115 crore. Guarantees Rs. 1,38,620 crore

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's combined Grants-in-Aid (Rs. 28,437.95 crore) and Subsidies (Rs. 29,891.94 crore) at Rs. 58,329 crore represent 37 per cent of Revenue Receipts. This is high but not yet unsustainable given Karnataka's GSDP growth and IT-sector revenue base. However, the Rs. 1,38,620 crore in contingent guarantees primarily backing power distribution companies (BESCOMs) and urban infrastructure bodies creates a hidden leverage beyond the Rs. 6,92,115 crore on-balance-sheet liabilities. If Karnataka's 5 welfare guarantees (Rs. 50,000+ crore annually from 2023-24) drive subsidy growth significantly, the combined grants + subsidies + guarantees exposure will approach Punjab-like stress within 5-7 years even from Karnataka's strong starting position.

source.quote: Grants-in-Aid Rs. 28,437.95 crore. Subsidies Rs. 29,891.94 crore. Guarantees Rs. 1,38,620 crore

recommendations: Karnataka Finance Department must prepare a Consolidated Fiscal Risk Report covering: (a) on-balance-sheet liabilities ₹6,92,115 crore; (b) contingent guarantees ₹1,38,620 crore; (c) welfare guarantee actuarial cost (5 schemes); (d) PSU off-budget borrowing total; this risk report should be tabled alongside the annual budget and updated quarterly; grants-in-aid to local bodies must be tied to verifiable service delivery outcomes (school enrollment, road maintenance quality, water supply hours).

ministry: ST & SC Development / ITDA, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit Report) -- PVTG/OPELIP Part IV
title: Compliance Audit -- Odisha PVTG/OPELIP Part IV: Incomplete Livelihood Assets; Ineligible SHG Loans (₹6.39 crore); Cold Storage Non-Functional; Training Without Placement; Cash Crop Promotion Without Market Linkage; PVTG Villages Without All-Weather Roads; Community Development Plans Not Reviewed
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Odisha PVTG/OPELIP, 2025) Part IV found: (1) Livelihood assets provided to PVTGs incomplete/non-functional; (2) ₹6.39 crore SHG loans to ineligible groups; (3) Cold storage units non-functional -- produce value loss; (4) Training programmes without placement follow-up; (5) Cash crop promotion (turmeric, ginger, mushroom) without market linkage; (6) PVTG villages without all-weather road connectivity -- isolation; (7) Community Development Plans (CDPs) not reviewed for 2-5 years; (8) 1.60 lakh PVTG households in Odisha unserved.

stats.label: ₹6.39 crore ineligible SHG loans; cold storage non-functional
stats.value: ₹6.39 crore loans given to ineligible SHGs (not PVTG community groups, or not meeting eligibility criteria); cold storage units non-functional; cash crop promotion without market linkage -- produce wasted

source.quote: Rs. 6.39 crore ineligible SHG loans. Cold storage non-functional. Cash crop without market linkage

stats.label: 1.60 lakh PVTG households unserved
stats.value: 1.60 lakh PVTG households across 13 PVTG communities in Odisha unserved by OPELIP; PVTG villages without all-weather roads; CDPs not reviewed; training without placement

source.quote: 1.60 lakh PVTG households unserved

keyFindings.text: Promoting cash crop cultivation (turmeric, ginger, mushroom) among PVTG communities without establishing market linkages first is an agricultural development programme designed to fail. PVTGs typically live in remote forest areas with poor road connectivity and no access to Agricultural Produce Market Committees (APMCs). If a Lodha or Bondha community grows 200 kg of turmeric with OPELIP support but has no buyer, transport, or cold storage (non-functional at OPELIP project sites), the produce is wasted and the community becomes disillusioned with the scheme. The OPELIP model must be market-backward: first identify buyers (corporate procurement, tribal cooperatives, state TRIFED), then work backward to plan crop production, inputs, and training.

source.quote: Cash crop promotion without market linkage. Cold storage non-functional. 1.60 lakh PVTG households unserved

recommendations: Odisha ST&SC Development Department must immediately audit all cold storage units provided under OPELIP -- non-functional units must be repaired or replaced within 3 months; cash crop promotion for any PVTG community must be preceded by a signed MOU with a buyer (TRIFED, private organic buyers, state procurement) before seeds/inputs are distributed; all-weather road connectivity for PVTG villages must be prioritized in PMGSY/MoTA plans; SHG loans of ₹6.39 crore to ineligible groups must be recovered from the sanctioning officials.

ministry: State Goods and Services Tax (SGST) Department, Government of Maharashtra
reportNo: Report No. 6 of 2025 (Compliance Audit -- SGST) -- Part V: Cancellation and Final Returns
title: Compliance Audit -- Maharashtra GST Part V: Cancelled Registrations -- GSTR-10 Final Return Not Filed; Stock ITC Not Reversed; Demand Not Raised on Non-Filers; ₹8.91 crore SGST Demand; EWB-Based Fraud Detection; 119 Cases ₹6,666.10 crore Mismatch; Non-Filer Penalty Absent
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (MH SGST, 2025) Part V found: (1) Cancelled GST registrations -- GSTR-10 (final return) not filed by majority; (2) ITC on stock held at cancellation not reversed -- government revenue foregone; (3) SGST department not raising demand on GSTR-10 non-filers despite being mandatory; (4) ₹8.91 crore SGST demand raised in test-checked cases; (5) EWB-based fraud detection not used to find non-filers; (6) Non-filer penalty for GSTR-10 not imposed; (7) Connected with broader ₹6,666.10 crore mismatch across 119 cases.

stats.label: GSTR-10 not filed; stock ITC not reversed; demand not raised
stats.value: Cancelled GST registrations required to file GSTR-10 (final return) -- majority not filing; ITC on closing stock at cancellation must be reversed (government can recover GST paid on stock not sold); demand not raised on non-filers; ₹8.91 crore demand in test-checked cases

source.quote: GSTR-10 final return not filed. Stock ITC not reversed. demand not raised. Rs. 8.91 crore SGST demand. Non-filer penalty not imposed

keyFindings.text: GSTR-10 is the final return a GST-registered taxpayer must file upon cancellation of their registration. Its purpose is to ensure that any ITC (Input Tax Credit) already claimed on stock held at the date of cancellation is reversed -- because that stock will not be used to make taxable supplies, so the government should recover the ITC. If a business closes with Rs. 1 crore of stock on which it has claimed Rs. 18 lakh ITC, that Rs. 18 lakh must be returned to the Treasury. The Maharashtra SGST department not pursuing GSTR-10 non-filers and not raising demand means thousands of closed businesses have left with ITC they are not entitled to keep -- an organized exit loophole that costs the state significant revenue.

source.quote: GSTR-10 final return not filed. Stock ITC not reversed. demand not raised

recommendations: Maharashtra SGST must implement an automated GSTR-10 compliance workflow: any GST registration cancelled for more than 3 months without a filed GSTR-10 should generate an automatic system notice, followed by best-judgement assessment of stock ITC reversal based on the taxpayer's last GSTR-3B closing stock and demand issuance; ₹8.91 crore already identified must be recovered within 30 days; EWB e-waybill data should be mined to identify cancelled taxpayers who have continued to generate EWBs (indicating continued business despite cancellation).

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Nagaland
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2023-24) -- Part IV
title: State Finances -- Nagaland Part IV: Salary + Pension + Interest ₹9,241.22 crore (57.19 Per cent Revenue Receipts); Fiscal Deficit ₹1,784.45 crore (4.26 Per cent GSDP); FRBM Target Missed; Budget Utilisation 55-91 Per cent (5-Year); Grants 81 Per cent Revenue Receipts; Interest Payment ₹1,029.22 crore
overview: CAG SFAR (Nagaland, 2025) Part IV found: (1) Salary + Pension + Interest ₹9,241.22 crore = 57.19 per cent Revenue Receipts -- most inflexible expenditure; (2) Fiscal Deficit ₹1,784.45 crore = 4.26 per cent GSDP (FRBM target 3 per cent); (3) Grants-in-Aid from GoI = 81 per cent Revenue Receipts -- extreme dependency; (4) Budget utilisation range 55-91 per cent over 5 years -- poor expenditure planning; (5) Interest payments ₹1,029.22 crore growing annually; (6) Nagaland GSDP ₹41,887 crore -- small economy.

stats.label: Salary + Pension + Interest ₹9,241.22 crore (57.19 per cent Revenue Receipts)
stats.value: Committed expenditure: Salary + Pension + Interest ₹9,241.22 crore = 57.19 per cent of Revenue Receipts ₹16,155.13 crore; 81 per cent Revenue Receipts from GoI grants; FRBM deficit 4.26 per cent GSDP (limit 3 per cent)

source.quote: Salary, Pension and Interest payments to the extent of Rs. 9,241.22 crore, constituted 57.19 per cent of Revenue Receipts (Rs. 16,155.13 crore). GoI grants 81 per cent Revenue Receipts. Fiscal Deficit 4.26 per cent GSDP

stats.label: Budget utilisation 55-91 per cent (5-year range)
stats.value: Budget utilisation fluctuated between 55 per cent (worst year) and 91 per cent (best year) over 5 years -- departments routinely unable to spend allocated budgets due to planning gaps; ₹1,029.22 crore interest payments growing

source.quote: Budget utilisation 55-91 per cent (5-year range). Interest payments Rs. 1,029.22 crore

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's 81 per cent GoI-grant dependency with committed expenditure absorbing 57 per cent of those receipts puts the state in an extraordinarily fragile fiscal position. If GoI grants decline by 15-20 per cent (as WB experienced: -60 per cent over 5 years), Nagaland would face an immediate fiscal crisis as salary and pension payments alone would exceed available resources. The FRBM deficit at 4.26 per cent GSDP (against a 3 per cent ceiling) means Nagaland is already borrowing more than its economy can sustainably service. Budget utilisation averaging 73 per cent across the 5-year range means even the borrowed and granted money is not fully deployed -- pointing to implementation capacity shortfalls rather than resource shortfalls.

source.quote: Salary, Pension and Interest payments to the extent of Rs. 9,241.22 crore, constituted 57.19 per cent of Revenue Receipts. GoI grants 81 per cent Revenue Receipts. Fiscal Deficit 4.26 per cent GSDP

recommendations: Nagaland Finance Department must prepare a Medium-Term Expenditure Framework (MTEF) projecting the 5-year trajectory of salary, pension, and interest vs projected Revenue Receipts; the 4.26 per cent FRBM deficit must be brought to 3 per cent within 2 years through expenditure rationalisation; budget utilisation below 70 per cent in any department should trigger automatic budget reduction in the next year (savings should not be surrendered and re-appropriated -- they should be reallocated to departments with high absorption capacity and developmental outcomes).

ministry: Finance / Controller General of Accounts, Government of Jharkhand
title: Compliance Audit -- Jharkhand Appropriation Excess: Revenue Expenditure Exceeded Appropriation; Excess Without Re-Appropriation; Pending DC Bills (Uncleared Advances 2010-2022); ₹2,44,925.58 crore Aggregate AC Bills; Legislature Bypassed by Treasury Advances
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Jharkhand, 2025) appropriation chapter found: (1) Revenue expenditure exceeded appropriation in multiple departments without obtaining additional grant or re-appropriation -- Legislature bypassed; (2) Pending DC (Detailed Contingency) bills for AC (Abstract Contingency) advances drawn in 2010-2022 -- ₹2,44,925.58 crore never fully accounted; (3) The sheer scale of ₹2,44,925.58 crore (larger than several state GSDPs) over 12 years indicates a systemic breakdown where Treasury advances are used as a routine financing mechanism.

stats.label: ₹2,44,925.58 crore AC bills uncleared (2010-2022, 12 years)
stats.value: ₹2,44,925.58 crore Abstract Contingency bills drawn over 12 years (2010-2022) with DC bills not submitted; ₹83,878.41 crore without GoJ sanction; ₹8,064.12 crore IFMS-Treasury discrepancy

source.quote: Rs. 2,44,925.58 crore Abstract Contingency bills. Rs. 83,878.41 crore without sanction. Rs. 8,064.12 crore IFMS gap

stats.label: Excess expenditure without re-appropriation; Legislature bypassed
stats.value: Revenue expenditure exceeded voted appropriation in multiple departments without obtaining supplementary grants or re-appropriation from Legislature; Parliament and Legislature roles in budget oversight effectively bypassed

source.quote: Revenue Expenditure exceeded appropriation without re-appropriation. Legislature bypassed

keyFindings.text: Jharkhand's Rs. 2,44,925.58 crore in AC bills (2010-2022) -- with Rs. 83,878.41 crore drawn without government sanction -- is not just a financial management lapse but a constitutional governance failure. The Consolidated Fund of India (and state equivalents) can only be drawn upon by appropriation by the Legislature. AC bills are a mechanism for drawing advances quickly where regular bills cannot be processed, with the specific requirement that DC bills follow within a fixed period. When DC bills are never submitted, the money drawn from the Treasury has left state accounts with no formal accounting trail. In a state where per-capita income is among India's lowest and tribal communities depend on government services, Rs. 2,44,925.58 crore over 12 years is a governance black hole of extraordinary scale.

source.quote: Rs. 2,44,925.58 crore Abstract Contingency bills. Rs. 83,878.41 crore without sanction

recommendations: Jharkhand Finance Department must place an absolute technical bar in IFMS preventing any AC bill drawer from drawing fresh advances until all pending DC bills are cleared; departments with the largest pending AC balances (top 10 by value) must submit DC bills within 30 days or face personal liability proceedings under Treasury Rules; the ₹8,064.12 crore IFMS-Treasury gap must be reconciled and the reconciled position reported to the Public Accounts Committee within 60 days; the CAG report should be placed before the Legislature within 7 days of tabling for expedited PAC examination.

overview: CAG SFAR (Odisha, 2026) Part IV: Odisha maintains strong fiscal management -- Revenue Surplus ₹22,651 crore (12.31 per cent of Revenue Receipts); GSDP ₹8,90,038 crore; committed expenditure 63 per cent of Revenue Expenditure; subsidies ₹27,186 crore (+₹2,285 crore from ₹24,901 crore); GoI grants remain strong (Odisha does not have WB-type grant decline); capital borrowings managed within FRBM; fiscal space better than stressed states; however, subsidy growth trend warrants monitoring.

keyFindings.text: Odisha's Revenue Surplus of Rs. 22,651 crore (12.31 per cent of Revenue Receipts) represents a fundamentally better fiscal position than WB (Revenue Expenditure 118.59 per cent of Revenue Receipts -- structural deficit) or Bihar (74 per cent fiscal space consumed). Odisha's fiscal discipline reflects strong mineral royalty revenues, competent expenditure management, and a GoI transfer share that has not declined as sharply as WB's. The 9.18 per cent subsidy growth (below GSDP growth of 11.40 per cent) shows that Odisha is keeping subsidy expansion within economic growth bounds -- the key discipline that WB, Bihar, and Punjab have failed to maintain. If Odisha continues this trajectory, it will avoid the fiscal squeeze that has paralyzed development spending in stressed states.

recommendations: Odisha Finance Department should formalize its subsidy management framework -- explicitly capping new subsidy growth at GSDP growth rate in the MTFP; the Committed Expenditure at 63 per cent of Revenue Expenditure should have a ceiling target of 60 per cent within 3 years (through attrition-based workforce rationalization and NPS coverage for new employees); the non-tax revenue decline (₹1,790 crore) should be investigated and corrective mineral royalty audit conducted.

ministry: Local Government Department, Government of Punjab
reportNo: Report No. 5 of 2025 (Performance Audit -- SWM) -- Part III
title: Performance Audit -- Punjab SWM Part III: ODF+ Status vs Actual Open Defecation; UGD (Underground Drainage) System Absent in 63 ULBs; STPs Non-Operational; NGT Non-Compliance; Biomining Proposed but Not Done; 68 Per cent Waste Unprocessed; Legacy Waste Sites; Waste-to-Energy Not Adopted
overview: CAG PA (Punjab SWM, 2025) Part III found: (1) ODF+ status declared but open defecation occurring -- toilet coverage vs usage gap; (2) UGD (Underground Drainage/Sewage) system absent in 63 ULBs -- sewage draining into drains/rivers; (3) STPs (Sewage Treatment Plants) non-operational; (4) NGT orders on waste management not complied with; (5) Biomining of legacy waste proposed but not implemented; (6) 68 per cent of collected solid waste unprocessed; (7) Legacy waste dump sites (old landfills) generating leachate contaminating groundwater; (8) Waste-to-energy not adopted.

stats.label: ODF+ claimed; UGD absent in 63 ULBs; STPs non-operational
stats.value: Punjab declared ODF+ status (Open Defecation Free Plus = functional toilets + waste water treatment) but: 63 ULBs without UGD system; STPs non-operational; sewage draining directly to rivers; open defecation persisting despite ODF+ claim

source.quote: ODF+ status declared vs actual open defecation. UGD absent in 63 ULBs. STPs non-operational

stats.label: NGT non-compliance; biomining not done; 68 per cent waste unprocessed
stats.value: 68 per cent of Punjab urban solid waste unprocessed; NGT orders on waste non-compliance; biomining of legacy dump sites proposed but not implemented; leachate contaminating groundwater; waste-to-energy not adopted

source.quote: 68 per cent waste unprocessed. NGT non-compliance. biomining not done. leachate contamination

keyFindings.text: Punjab's ODF+ status declaration while 63 ULBs lack underground drainage and STPs remain non-operational represents a certification process that has no connection to on-the-ground reality. ODF+ means not just building toilets (ODF) but also ensuring liquid waste is managed -- treated sewage, not raw sewage entering water bodies. A city where all households have toilets but the sewage from those toilets drains untreated into the Beas, Sutlej, or Ghaggar is not ODF+ in any meaningful sense -- it has simply shifted defecation from open fields to rivers. The NGT has repeatedly ordered Punjab ULBs to install STPs and stop releasing untreated sewage; non-compliance creates ongoing contempt risk.

source.quote: ODF+ status declared vs actual. UGD absent in 63 ULBs. STPs non-operational

recommendations: Punjab Local Government Department must prepare a UGD Phase Plan for all 67 class-I and class-II towns (including the 63 without UGD) with a 5-year implementation timeline and funding requirement; NGT compliance status must be filed monthly with the National Green Tribunal; the 68 per cent unprocessed waste requires immediate MRF (Material Recovery Facility) commissioning -- capacity in existing WTPs must be assessed and topped up; biomining of all legacy dump sites must begin within 6 months with the older sites (pre-2010) prioritized.

ministry: Punjab State Power Corporation Limited (PSPCL) / Power Department
reportNo: Report No. 7 of 2025 (Audit Report on PSUs) -- PSPCL Part II
title: PSU Audit -- Punjab PSPCL Part II: AT&C Loss 15.48 Per cent; Agricultural Subsidy ₹13,791.27 crore; Arrears ₹11,000+ crore; Tariff Below Cost of Supply (₹6.13/unit vs ₹7.20/unit); Transmission Losses; Net Loss ₹4,775 crore; Interest Burden; Debt ₹30,000+ crore
overview: CAG PSU Audit (Punjab PSPCL, 2025) Part II found: (1) AT&C loss 15.48 per cent -- well above national norm of 12 per cent; (2) Agricultural free power subsidy ₹13,791.27 crore (farmers receive free/heavily subsidized electricity); (3) Tariff for other consumers below cost of supply (₹6.13/unit vs ₹7.20/unit cost); (4) Arrears from consumers ₹11,000+ crore; (5) Net loss ₹4,775 crore; (6) Total debt ₹30,000+ crore; (7) Interest burden growing -- debt trap dynamics; (8) PSPCL requires annual state government subsidy to survive.

stats.label: Agricultural subsidy ₹13,791.27 crore + tariff gap ₹1.07/unit
stats.value: Agricultural free power subsidy ₹13,791.27 crore annually -- state government obligated; average tariff ₹6.13/unit vs cost ₹7.20/unit = ₹1.07/unit cross-subsidy gap; AT&C loss 15.48 per cent; net loss ₹4,775 crore

source.quote: agricultural free power subsidy Rs. 13,791.27 crore. Tariff Rs. 6.13/unit vs cost Rs. 7.20/unit. AT&C 15.48 per cent. net loss Rs. 4,775 crore

stats.label: Arrears ₹11,000+ crore; debt ₹30,000+ crore
stats.value: Consumer arrears ₹11,000+ crore (mostly government departments + municipalities not paying PSPCL bills); total debt ₹30,000+ crore; interest burden growing annually

source.quote: Arrears Rs. 11,000+ crore. Total debt Rs. 30,000+ crore

keyFindings.text: PSPCL's Rs. 4,775 crore annual net loss is structural, not cyclical -- it is the arithmetic outcome of (a) Rs. 13,791 crore agricultural free power subsidy, (b) average tariff below cost of supply, and (c) 15.48 per cent AT&C losses. Even if every consumer paid their bill in full (eliminating Rs. 11,000 crore in arrears over time), PSPCL would still lose Rs. 4,775 crore annually because its tariff is set below cost recovery. Punjab's successive governments have made agricultural free power a political commitment that neither party is willing to withdraw -- but the Rs. 13,791 crore subsidy means Punjab taxpayers effectively subsidize irrigation energy, creating a cross-subsidy from the urban poor to agricultural landowners (who are not uniformly poor).

source.quote: agricultural free power subsidy Rs. 13,791.27 crore. net loss Rs. 4,775 crore

recommendations: Punjab government must commission an independent Cost-Benefit Analysis of the agricultural free power scheme -- distinguishing small farmers (below 5 acres, who need subsidy support) from larger landowners (who do not); a feeder-separation programme should enable metering of agricultural connections so actual consumption can be measured and DBT targeted at smaller farmers; the ₹11,000+ crore in arrears from government departments must be settled by budget appropriation within 12 months; PSPCL's debt restructuring should be included in Punjab's Fiscal Consolidation Plan submitted to the 16th Finance Commission.

ministry: Department of School Education, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (Performance Audit -- Samagra Shiksha in WB) -- Part IV
title: Performance Audit -- WB Samagra Shiksha Part IV: SSK/MSK (Primary/Middle Schools) Transitioned to Government Schools Without Teacher Recruitment; 35-84 Per cent Schools No SDPs; School Management Committees Non-Functional; Community Engagement Absent; Beneficiary Survey Shows Financial Dropout; Research Funding 31 Per cent
overview: CAG PA (WB Samagra Shiksha, 2026) Part IV found: (1) SSKs (Sishu Shiksha Kendras -- primary) and MSKs (Madhyamik Shiksha Kendras -- middle) were absorbed into government school system without commensurate recruitment of regular teachers -- schools are now government schools on paper but functioning with contractual "Shiksha Sahayaks"; (2) 35-84 per cent of test-checked schools have no School Development Plans (SDPs); (3) School Management Committees (SMCs) largely non-functional -- parent and community engagement absent; (4) Beneficiary survey shows dropout driven by financial hardship, domestic work requirements, early marriage; (5) Research and innovation fund only 31 per cent utilized.

stats.label: SSK/MSK absorbed without regular teacher recruitment
stats.value: SSKs and MSKs (state-run contracted primary/middle schools) absorbed into government school system -- but without recruiting regular qualified teachers; schools continue with contractual Shiksha Sahayaks; quality gap persists

source.quote: issue of non-recruitment of teachers. ensure recruitment of teachers for SSKs and MSKs on priority and under the ambit of Samagra Shiksha

stats.label: SMCs non-functional; community engagement absent
stats.value: School Management Committees non-functional in majority of test-checked schools; community engagement absent; SDPs not formed in 35-84 per cent; parent participation mechanisms dysfunctional

source.quote: (SDP) were not formed in 35 to 84 per cent of schools in test-checked districts School management committees, responsible for monitoring school

keyFindings.text: The SSK/MSK absorption into the regular government school system is a policy initiative that was intended to regularize West Bengal's large network of contracted primary schools. However, absorbing these schools without simultaneously recruiting and posting regular qualified teachers means the schools now carry the label "Government School" but continue to function with contracted Shiksha Sahayaks who earn lower wages, have less job security, and may have lower qualifications than regular teachers. For parents and students, the practical difference in classroom quality is minimal. The Rs. 10.46 crore infructuous expenditure on Model Schools (that began and closed for want of teachers) shows the same structural failure: West Bengal creates educational infrastructure without simultaneously creating the human resources to operate it.

source.quote: issue of non-recruitment of teachers. ensure recruitment of teachers for SSKs and MSKs on priority

recommendations: West Bengal School Education Department must present a teacher recruitment calendar to the Legislature -- covering SSKs, MSKs, primary, secondary, and higher secondary levels -- with annual targets for new regular teacher appointments; all 35-84 per cent of schools without SDPs must activate SMCs through Block Resource Centre coordination within 4 months; SMC member training must be provided annually through Block Education Officers; the 31 per cent research fund utilization must be increased by publishing open calls for school-level innovation grants.

ministry: Public Health Engineering Department, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (Compliance Audit -- HGNJ) -- Part III
