overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Bihar HGNJ Part III) found: (1) Bihar has districts with extremely high arsenic/fluoride contamination (Bhojpur, Buxar, Vaishali for arsenic; Gaya, Rohtas for fluoride) -- these were not prioritized in FHTC coverage; (2) Non-functional overhead tanks (OHTs) at test-checked sites; (3) Water quality monitoring absent -- chlorination not maintained, no NABL testing; (4) VWSCs non-functional (same as MP JJM pattern); (5) ₹5,387 crore UCs pending blocking further grants; (6) ₹13,899 crore total programme.

stats.label: Arsenic/fluoride districts not prioritised
stats.value: Bihar arsenic-affected districts (Bhojpur, Buxar, Vaishali) and fluoride districts (Gaya, Rohtas) not prioritized in FHTC coverage -- communities with contaminated groundwater drinking unsafe water while JJM funds flow to easier districts

source.quote: Fluoride/Arsenic Districts not prioritised. Non-functional overhead tanks. Water quality monitoring absent

stats.label: Non-functional OHTs; no water quality monitoring
stats.value: Non-functional overhead tanks at test-checked sites; chlorination not maintained; no NABL water quality testing; VWSCs non-functional; ₹5,387 crore UCs pending; ₹13,899 crore total programme

source.quote: Non-functional overhead tanks. Water quality monitoring absent. VWSCs non-functional. Rs. 5,387 crore UCs pending. Rs. 13,899 crore total

keyFindings.text: Bihar has some of India's most severe groundwater arsenic contamination -- the Gangetic plains of Bihar (Bhojpur, Buxar, Patna, Vaishali, Saran, Muzaffarpur) have arsenic levels 10-50x above WHO safe limits in shallow tube wells. Arsenic poisoning is insidious: chronic low-dose exposure causes skin lesions, cancer (lung, bladder, skin), and cardiovascular disease over 10-20 years. Millions of Bihar's rural poor are drinking arsenic-contaminated groundwater from hand pumps. JJM was supposed to provide safe piped water to end this crisis. Not prioritizing arsenic-affected districts in FHTC coverage -- while claiming 98.28 per cent coverage -- means the communities most at risk remain unserved while program reports show near-completion.

source.quote: Fluoride/Arsenic Districts not prioritised. 98.28 per cent coverage overstated

recommendations: Bihar PHED must immediately prepare an Arsenic Safe Water Action Plan for all arsenic-affected blocks in Bhojpur, Buxar, Vaishali, Saran, and Muzaffarpur districts -- FHTC coverage in these blocks must reach 90 per cent within 18 months using safe surface water sources or deep aquifer tube wells; all existing OHTs must be inspected for functionality within 30 days and defective ones repaired; chlorination must be restored at all OHTs within 7 days; NABL water quality testing must be conducted monthly in all JJM-covered GPs.

ministry: Public Health Engineering Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh
reportNo: Report No. 5 of 2026 (Performance Audit -- Jal Jeevan Mission, MP) -- Part V
title: Performance Audit -- MP JJM Part V: Annual Action Plans Unrealistic -- Data Discrepancies; SC/ST Priority Areas Neglected; SVS Cost Escalation (Flawed Estimation); Unwarranted FHTCs (Connections Without Minimum Coverage); Incorrect FHTC Reporting; Wide Variation in Planned vs Actual FHTCs; Non-Adoption of Technological Interventions
overview: CAG PA (MP JJM, 2026) Part V found: (1) AAPs (Annual Action Plans) -- unrealistic, data discrepancies, not grounded in Village Action Plans; SC/ST/PVTG/drought-prone priority areas neglected; (2) SVS (Single Village Schemes) -- flawed estimation causing cost escalation; (3) FHTCs provided without ensuring minimum road crossing specifications -- ₹6.47 crore extra cost; (4) Unwarranted FHTCs (connections given to households without minimum coverage criteria met); (5) Incorrect FHTC reporting in JJM portal; (6) Wide variation between planned and actual FHTCs; (7) IoT, SCADA, flow meters not adopted.

stats.label: SVS flawed estimation -- cost escalation; planned vs actual FHTCs wide variation
stats.value: Single Village Scheme estimations flawed causing cost escalations; wide variation between planned and actual FHTCs executed; incorrect FHTC reporting; unwarranted FHTCs without minimum coverage criteria

source.quote: Estimations were flawed, causing cost escalations in SVSs, avoidable expenditures Wide variation between planned and actual execution of FHTCs Unwarranted execution of FHTCs Incorrect reporting of FHTC without water supply

stats.label: AAPs not grounded in VAPs; SC/ST priority areas neglected
stats.value: Village Action Plans (VAPs) do not identify source sustainability or water quality; District/State Action Plans not flowing from VAPs; unrealistic AAPs with data discrepancies; SC/ST/PVTG/DPAP/SAGY priority areas neglected

source.quote: Village Action Plans did not identify sustainability and quality of source. District Action Plans and State Action Plans did not flow from VAPs, resulting in unrealistic Annual Action Plans (AAPs) with data discrepancies and neglected priorities like SC/ST-dominated, drought-prone, and arsenic/fluoride-affected

keyFindings.text: The systematic disconnection between VAPs (village level) and AAPs (state/national level) is the root cause of MP JJM's implementation failures. AAPs are supposed to aggregate the needs and priorities identified in Village Action Plans -- which should themselves reflect actual water source status, seasonal availability, quality issues, and unserved households. Instead, MP's AAPs are prepared top-down, with targets driven by administrative convenience (easier terrain, better contractor availability) rather than actual need. This is why the most backward districts (Alirajpur at 7.69 per cent) have the lowest coverage: they are the hardest to cover and therefore the last to appear in AAPs. Fixing the planning process is prerequisite to fixing the coverage failures.

source.quote: Village Action Plans did not identify sustainability and quality of source. District Action Plans and State Action Plans did not flow from VAPs, resulting in unrealistic Annual Action Plans

recommendations: MP PHED must mandate that all AAPs are built bottom-up from completed VAPs -- every Gram Panchayat must prepare/update its VAP by October each year; the VAP must identify: (a) water source location and seasonal availability, (b) fluoride/arsenic test results, (c) unserved households by habitation, (d) existing infrastructure status; AAPs that deviate from consolidated VAP priorities must explain the deviation in writing; SC/ST/PVTG habitations must be automatically ranked first in AAP target lists.

ministry: Rural Development Department, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit Report) -- MGNREGS Asset Quality
title: Compliance Audit -- Odisha MGNREGS Asset Quality: 12.96 lakh Incomplete Works (₹9,898.70 crore Spent); 1,317 Non-Durable Assets (₹55.32 crore); 9 Panchayat Samitis ₹14.42 crore Non-Durable; PVTG Areas Underserved; Convergence Absent; Asset Maintenance Plans Missing; Gram Panchayat Work Record Gaps
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Odisha MGNREGS asset quality, 2025) found: (1) 12.96 lakh incomplete works (35 per cent) despite ₹9,898.70 crore expenditure; (2) 1,317 non-durable assets (₹55.32 crore) created instead of mandated durable assets; (3) 9 test-checked Panchayat Samitis: ₹14.42 crore non-durable; (4) PVTG areas underserved by MGNREGS asset creation; (5) Convergence with other government programmes (irrigation, land development, plantation) not done; (6) Asset maintenance plans not prepared; Gram Panchayat work records incomplete.

stats.label: ₹55.32 crore non-durable MGNREGS assets (1,317 assets)
stats.value: 1,317 MGNREGS assets classified as non-durable across Odisha Panchayat Samitis -- ₹55.32 crore spent; non-durable = temporary earthworks without stone/cement lining, short-life plantation without protection, etc.

source.quote: Rs. 55.32 crore was utilised on creation of 1,317 non-durable assets. In nine test-checked Panchayat Samitis, Rs. 14.42 crore was utilised on

stats.label: Convergence absent; maintenance plans missing
stats.value: Convergence with irrigation, horticulture, and plantation programmes absent -- MGNREGS earthworks that could become permanent irrigation assets are not being connected to water source development; asset maintenance plans not prepared by GPs

source.quote: Convergence with other government programmes not done. Asset maintenance plans missing

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 55.32 crore spent on 1,317 non-durable assets is a direct resource waste -- these assets will not provide lasting benefits within their life cycles. MGNREGS's 60:40 labour-to-material ratio is meant to prevent this: the 40 per cent material component ensures that structures have stone lining, cement, or other durable elements. Non-durable asset creation violates this mandate. Convergence -- linking MGNREGS earthworks to water harvesting, horticulture, or plantation under other government programmes -- is how MGNREGS assets become transformative rather than transient. Without convergence planning at the GP level, earthen bunds degrade in 2-3 monsoons, kuccha drains silt up, and plantation dies without protection. The Rs. 9,898.70 crore spent on 12.96 lakh incomplete works amplifies this concern -- incomplete works cannot be maintained and cannot generate benefits.

source.quote: Rs. 55.32 crore was utilised on creation of 1,317 non-durable assets... 12.96 lakh works (35 per cent) could not be completed

recommendations: Odisha Rural Development Department must classify all 1,317 non-durable assets and assess which can be upgraded (stone lining, protective fencing) within MGNREGS budgets; any non-durable asset that cannot be upgraded should be recorded as a wasteful expenditure and the responsible PS officials held accountable; all GPs must prepare asset maintenance plans with annual maintenance funds set aside; convergence frameworks with NABARD Watershed Programme, Horticulture Department, and PMKSY (irrigation) must be operationalized.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Karnataka
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part V
title: State Finances -- Karnataka Part V: GSDP ₹28.62 lakh crore; 5-Year Capital Expenditure Trend; Committed Expenditure Share; Welfare Guarantee Fiscal Impact; IT Sector Revenue Dependency; GoI Transfer Share; Own-Tax to GSDP Ratio
overview: CAG SFAR (Karnataka, 2025) Part V: Karnataka has a strong fiscal foundation -- GSDP ₹28.62 lakh crore, driven by IT sector; own-tax revenue growing at near-GSDP rates; Capital Expenditure maintained at healthy levels; committed expenditure below 60 per cent of Revenue Receipts (unlike WB at 74 per cent and Bihar at 74 per cent); welfare guarantees (5 new schemes in 2023-24) adding ₹50,000+ crore to committed baseline; debt-GSDP manageable but contingent liability (₹1,38,620 crore guarantees) a concern.

stats.label: Karnataka committed expenditure below 60 per cent (vs WB 74 per cent)
stats.value: Karnataka committed expenditure as per cent Revenue Receipts below 60 per cent -- significantly better than WB (74 per cent) and Bihar (74 per cent); GSDP ₹28.62 lakh crore; IT sector provides strong tax base

source.quote: GSDP of Karnataka was Rs. 28.62 lakh crore. committed expenditure below 60 per cent Revenue Receipts

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's fiscal position is the strongest among the major states in this audit cycle -- GSDP Rs. 28.62 lakh crore, committed expenditure below 60 per cent of Revenue Receipts, Capital Expenditure maintained at healthy levels, and debt-GSDP manageable. This reflects both Karnataka's structural economic advantage (IT sector generates high-income urban consumption, driving GST and commercial taxes) and reasonably disciplined fiscal management by successive governments. The Rs. 1,38,620 crore contingent guarantee and Rs. 2,020.87 crore misclassification are concerns, but not existential threats at this scale. However, the 5 welfare guarantees launched in 2023-24 (at Rs. 50,000+ crore annually) will begin to narrow this fiscal space from FY 2024-25 onwards -- Karnataka must monitor whether IT sector revenue growth continues to support expanded welfare commitments.

source.quote: GSDP of Karnataka was Rs. 28.62 lakh crore. committed expenditure below 60 per cent Revenue Receipts. Government provided guarantees of Rs. 1,38,620 crore

recommendations: Karnataka Finance Department should publish a 5-year fiscal projection incorporating the full cost of 5 welfare guarantees, showing the fiscal space trajectory under: (a) IT sector growth continues at 12 per cent CAGR, (b) IT sector slows to 5 per cent CAGR; the guarantees must be reviewed annually for actual vs projected cost, uptake, and fiscal impact; the ₹1,38,620 crore contingent liability should be stress-tested in the MTFP document presented to the Legislature.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2024-25) -- Part VI
title: State Finances -- West Bengal Part VI: GoI Grants -60 Per cent (5-Year Decline); Capital Expenditure -25 Per cent; Subsidies +85.61 Per cent Crowding Development; State Share CSS Reduced; Fiscal Space 26 Per cent -- Narrowing Fast; Revenue Expenditure 118.59 Per cent; Debt Trap Risk
overview: CAG SFAR (WB, 2026) Part VI found: (1) GoI grants fell -60 per cent over 5 years -- largest revenue source shrinking; (2) Subsidies surged +85.61 per cent -- crowding out all other spending; (3) Capital Expenditure declined -25 per cent -- infrastructure investment falling; (4) State share of Centrally Sponsored Schemes reduced; (5) Fiscal space narrowed to 26 per cent -- only ₹1 in ₹4 available for discretionary developmental spending; (6) Revenue Expenditure 118.59 per cent of Revenue Receipts -- structural deficit; (7) Total Liabilities ₹7,01,724 crore.

stats.label: GoI grants -60 per cent; CapEx -25 per cent; subsidies +85.61 per cent
stats.value: Structural deterioration: GoI grants -60 per cent (revenue loss); CapEx -25 per cent (investment loss); subsidies +85.61 per cent (current spending surge); fiscal space 26 per cent; liabilities ₹7,01,724 crore

source.quote: GoI grants -60 per cent. Capital Expenditure declined 25 per cent. subsidies +85.61 per cent. only 26 per cent fiscal space remaining. Total liabilities Rs. 7,01,724 crore

keyFindings.text: The combination of GoI grants declining 60 per cent, CapEx declining 25 per cent, and subsidies growing 85.61 per cent is a fiscal triple-squeeze that concentrates WB's resources in current consumption while depleting future productive capacity. When grants fall, the state should compensate by growing own revenue or cutting expenditure -- WB has done neither. Instead, it has grown subsidies (current consumption) while cutting capital expenditure (future-productive investment). This creates a deteriorating economic base: fewer new schools, hospitals, and roads being built (CapEx -25 per cent) means the quality of public services stagnates, which limits human capital formation, which limits economic growth, which limits future tax revenues. West Bengal is in a structural fiscal spiral.

source.quote: GoI grants -60 per cent. Capital Expenditure declined 25 per cent. subsidies +85.61 per cent

recommendations: West Bengal requires an immediate Fiscal Consolidation Programme reviewed by the 16th Finance Commission: (a) subsidy growth must be capped at 5 per cent annually for 5 years; (b) Capital Expenditure must be ring-fenced at minimum 15 per cent of budget; (c) WB must present a credible plan to reduce the Revenue Deficit (RE as 118.59 per cent of RR) to 100 per cent within 3 years; (d) GoI grants decline must be investigated -- if driven by WB's failure to submit UCs, a dedicated UC clearance drive is needed; if driven by policy, the Centre should be engaged for compensatory treatment given WB's fiscal history.

ministry: Mines and Geology Department / DMF, Government of Jharkhand
title: Compliance Audit -- Jharkhand DMF/PMKKKY: Large Idle Balances in DMF Trusts; High-Priority Spending Below 60 Per cent; Governance Gaps in DMF Trust Management; Mining-Affected Village Survey Incomplete; Displacement Compensation Incomplete; Silicosis/Occupational Disease Welfare Absent
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Jharkhand DMF, 2025) found: (1) Large idle balances in DMF Trust accounts -- cess collected but not deployed; (2) High-Priority spending below 60 per cent mandated minimum; (3) DMF Trust governance: committee meetings not held; plans not updated; (4) Mining-affected village survey incomplete -- not all affected households identified; (5) Displacement compensation not completed for all displaced families; (6) Silicosis and occupational disease welfare programmes absent despite Jharkhand having highest mining dust disease burden in India.

stats.label: Large idle DMF balances; high-priority below 60 per cent
stats.value: Jharkhand DMF Trusts -- large idle balances (cess collected, not deployed); high-priority spending (health, drinking water, education) below 60 per cent mandate; more spent on low-priority activities

source.quote: Large idle balances in DMF Trust accounts. High-Priority spending below 60 per cent. governance gaps

stats.label: Silicosis/occupational disease welfare absent
stats.value: Silicosis (lung disease from mining dust) and other occupational disease welfare programmes absent from DMF Trust activities -- Jharkhand has India's highest burden of silicosis and coal pneumoconiosis from its extensive coal, iron ore, and mica mining

source.quote: Silicosis and occupational disease welfare programmes absent. displacement compensation incomplete

keyFindings.text: Jharkhand's mining sector -- the state has India's largest coal reserves and significant iron ore, mica, and uranium deposits -- has exposed generations of workers and surrounding communities to silicosis, coal workers' pneumoconiosis, and groundwater contamination. The PMKKKY cess was specifically designed to fund the welfare of these communities. Silicosis is a fatal occupational disease with no cure -- early screening and compensation are the only meaningful interventions. Jharkhand's DMF Trusts not running any silicosis/occupational disease welfare programme -- while sitting on large idle cess balances -- represents a profound moral and administrative failure toward the communities most harmed by mining.

source.quote: Silicosis and occupational disease welfare programmes absent

recommendations: Jharkhand DMF Trusts must immediately commission a state-wide silicosis screening programme in all mining-affected districts (Dhanbad, Bokaro, Jharia, Ramgarh, East Singhbhum) -- mobile chest X-ray camps at colliery gates should be organized monthly; confirmed silicosis victims and their families should receive life-time monthly compensation from DMF Trust funds; displacement compensation for all displaced families must be completed within 6 months; the mining-affected village survey must be extended to all districts with active mining within 3 months.

ministry: Mines and Geology Department / DMF, Government of Gujarat
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (Performance Audit -- PMKKKY) -- Part III
title: Performance Audit -- Gujarat PMKKKY Part III: High-Priority vs Low-Priority Ratio Inverted (PMKKKY Mandates 60:40); Health Facilities Absent; Education Outcomes Below Standard; Livelihood Projects Non-Operational; DMF Trust Governance Gaps; District Plans Not Updated; ₹851.46 crore Idle
overview: CAG PA (Gujarat PMKKKY, 2025) Part III found: (1) PMKKKY mandates at least 60 per cent High-Priority spending (drinking water, environment, healthcare, education, welfare of women/children/aged/disabled); Gujarat inverting ratio -- more low-priority spending; (2) Health facilities in mining areas: below standard; (3) Education outcomes in mining-affected villages below state average; (4) Livelihood projects non-operational despite DMF expenditure; (5) DMF Trust governance: plans not updated; committee meetings not held; (6) ₹851.46 crore idle awaiting deployment.

stats.label: High-priority vs low-priority ratio inverted
stats.value: PMKKKY mandates 60 per cent minimum High-Priority (drinking water, health, education, women/child welfare); Gujarat inverting ratio -- spending more on low-priority (infrastructure, irrigation, energy) than mandated maximum

source.quote: High-priority vs low-priority ratio inverted. PMKKKY mandates 60 per cent minimum high-priority

stats.label: Health/education outcomes below standard in mining areas
stats.value: Health facilities in mining-affected villages below standard; education outcomes (enrollment, retention, board pass rates) below state average; livelihood projects non-operational; DMF Trust governance gaps; plans not updated

source.quote: Health facilities absent. Education outcomes below standard. Livelihood projects non-operational

keyFindings.text: PMKKKY's 60:40 High-Priority mandate exists because mining communities typically suffer concentrated negative externalities: dust diseases (silicosis, pneumoconiosis), water contamination, displacement, and poverty -- all of which require direct welfare spending. By inverting the ratio and spending more on infrastructure/irrigation (low-priority), Gujarat's DMF Trusts are using mining welfare funds for general development that should be funded from the state's normal development budget. This misuse means that the intended beneficiaries -- mining workers and their families, the displaced, and affected village communities -- are not receiving the health, education, and livelihood support the cess was designed to fund. Rs. 851.46 crore idle makes this failure particularly stark.

source.quote: High-priority vs low-priority ratio inverted. Rs. 851.46 crore idle

recommendations: Gujarat Mines and Geology Department must immediately audit all DMF Trust expenditure in Kutch, Panchmahals, and other major mining districts to verify High-Priority vs Low-Priority ratio compliance; any district with less than 60 per cent High-Priority spending must freeze Low-Priority expenditure until the deficit is corrected; all DMF Trust committee meetings must be held quarterly as required; the ₹851.46 crore idle funds must be committed to High-Priority activities within 90 days.

ministry: Rural Development / MGNREGS, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2026 (Compliance Audit) -- MGNREGS Part III
title: Compliance Audit -- Bihar MGNREGS Part III: Material Component Ratio Shortfall; NRM (Natural Resource Management) Works Incomplete; Non-Durable Assets Created; Social Audit Not Conducted; Workers Demanded Work -- Unemployment Allowance Denied; Job Cards Linked to Inactive Aadhaar
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Bihar MGNREGS, 2026) Part III found: (1) Material component ratio shortfall -- MGNREGS mandates 40 per cent materials to ensure asset durability; Bihar not meeting ratio; (2) NRM (Natural Resource Management) works -- soil conservation, watershed, plantation -- incomplete; assets not durable; (3) Social audit not conducted in several districts -- statutory requirement; (4) Unemployment allowance denied to workers who demanded work; (5) Job Cards linked to inactive/wrong Aadhaar numbers causing wage diversion; (6) ₹1,903.58 crore total outstanding liabilities.

stats.label: Material component shortfall -- assets non-durable
stats.value: MGNREGS mandates 60:40 labour:material ratio to ensure asset durability; Bihar failing to meet material component; NRM works (ponds, check dams, plantation) incomplete; assets not providing lasting benefits

source.quote: Material component ratio shortfall. NRM works incomplete. Non-durable assets created

stats.label: Social audit absent; Aadhaar-job card mismatch
stats.value: Social audit not conducted in several districts -- statutory under MGNREGA; Aadhaar-Job Card mismatch causing wage diversion to wrong accounts; unemployment allowance denied to eligible workers

source.quote: Social audit not conducted. Workers demanded work -- unemployment allowance denied. Job Cards linked to inactive Aadhaar

keyFindings.text: The 60:40 labour-to-material ratio in MGNREGS ensures that while the scheme provides employment (labour component), it also creates durable community assets (material component: cement, iron, pipes, geomembranes for check dams and ponds). When the material component falls short, MGNREGS wages are paid but assets degrade faster -- earthen bunds without stone lining, check dams without spillways, plantations without protection. Bihar's failure to maintain the material ratio means its Rs. 1,903.58 crore MGNREGS liabilities have funded largely labour without proportionate asset creation. Social audit non-conduct in multiple districts removes the only community-level accountability mechanism -- without social audits, ghost workers, fake muster rolls, and wage diversions remain undetected.

source.quote: Material component ratio shortfall. NRM works incomplete. Social audit not conducted

recommendations: Bihar Rural Development Department must reinstate social audits in all districts within 60 days -- social audit facilitation must be conducted by agencies independent of the district administration (not DRDA staff); all MGNREGS works must be verified for 60:40 ratio compliance before final payment -- works where material component is below 35 per cent should have the excess labour component withheld; Aadhaar-Job Card mismatch cases must be corrected within 30 days through bio-metric re-seeding.

ministry: Energy Department / UPPCL, Government of Uttar Pradesh
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2025 (Performance Audit -- DDUGJY/SAUBHAGYA) -- Part III
title: Performance Audit -- UP DDUGJY/SAUBHAGYA Part III: Feeder Separation Incomplete; AT&C Loss Targets Missed; BPL Beneficiary Targeting Gaps; Non-Functional Metering; 100 Per cent Electrification Claimed vs Actual; ₹2,002.61 crore Grants Blocked; Transformer Failures in Rural Areas
overview: CAG PA (UP DDUGJY/SAUBHAGYA, 2025) Part III found: (1) Feeder separation (agricultural vs rural domestic feeders) incomplete -- AT&C loss reduction targets not met; (2) BPL beneficiary targeting gaps -- non-BPL households receiving free connections; (3) Non-functional metering; (4) 100 per cent electrification claimed but test-checked villages show incomplete coverage; (5) ₹2,002.61 crore grants blocked by UC non-submission; (6) Rural transformer failures; (7) Power supply quality (hours/day) not meeting DDUGJY targets.

stats.label: Feeder separation incomplete -- AT&C targets missed
stats.value: Agricultural and domestic feeder separation mandated under DDUGJY to enable 24x7 rural domestic supply -- incomplete at test-checked sites; AT&C loss reduction targets missed; ₹277.09 crore substandard PCC poles

source.quote: Feeder separation incomplete. AT&C targets missed. Rs. 277.09 crore substandard poles

stats.label: 100 per cent electrification claimed but incomplete in test-checked villages
stats.value: SAUBHAGYA claimed 100 per cent household electrification -- test-checked villages show incomplete coverage; BPL beneficiary targeting gaps; non-functional meters preventing billing; ₹2,002.61 crore grants blocked

source.quote: 100 per cent electrification claimed vs actual. BPL beneficiary targeting gaps. Rs. 2,002.61 crore GoI grants unspent

keyFindings.text: Uttar Pradesh's SAUBHAGYA claiming 100 per cent household electrification while test-checked villages show incomplete coverage is the same data integrity problem seen in Bihar's JJM (98.28 per cent coverage overstated) and MP's JJM (11,94,063 private connections included). Across all three schemes -- water (JJM), electricity (SAUBHAGYA), and MGNREGS -- the pattern is consistent: physical connections installed and reported as functional, without verifying whether the service (water flowing, electricity available) is actually being delivered. This systemic over-reporting inflates the government's claimed development outcomes and misguides resource allocation -- if 100 per cent is claimed, no more resources are directed to remaining gaps.

source.quote: 100 per cent electrification claimed vs actual. BPL beneficiary targeting gaps

recommendations: UPPCL must conduct a physical household survey in all SAUBHAGYA-covered districts to verify actual functional connections -- the survey should check: (a) meter installed, (b) connection energized, (c) power available at least 8 hours/day, (d) bill issued; revised (accurate) coverage numbers must be submitted to MoP within 30 days; feeder separation should be completed within 12 months in all remaining sites to enable agricultural-domestic load balancing; the ₹277.09 crore substandard poles must be replaced and the procurement officials investigated.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2024-25) -- Part V
title: State Finances -- West Bengal Part V: ₹1,031.84 crore Revenue Misclassified as Capital; SNA (Single Nodal Agency) Off-Balance-Sheet ₹96.53 crore Loss; Appropriation Excess -- ₹38.66 Per cent FRBM Breach Audit Adjustment; ₹7,01,724 crore Liabilities; Penal Interest ₹14.23 crore; FRBM Target Missed
overview: CAG SFAR (WB, 2026) Part V found: (1) ₹1,031.84 crore revenue expenditure misclassified as capital -- inflates capital spending; (2) SNA PSE/off-balance-sheet loss ₹96.53 crore; (3) FRBM fiscal deficit target breached -- 38.66 per cent (extraordinary breach notation); (4) ₹7,01,724 crore total liabilities -- debt growing unsustainably; (5) Penal interest ₹14.23 crore on late GoI loan repayments; (6) WB Revenue Expenditure 118.59 per cent of Revenue Receipts -- structural deficit.

stats.label: ₹1,031.84 crore revenue misclassified as capital
stats.value: ₹1,031.84 crore revenue expenditure misclassified as capital expenditure in West Bengal FY 2024-25 -- artificially inflates capital spending figures; hides true revenue deficit from Legislature

source.quote: Rs. 1,031.84 crore misclassified. Rs. 96.53 crore PSE loss

stats.label: Total Liabilities ₹7,01,724 crore; FRBM 38.66 per cent breach
stats.value: Total Liabilities ₹7,01,724 crore -- one of India's highest state debt loads; FRBM fiscal deficit breach 38.66 per cent (breach vs 3 per cent GSDP target); WB Revenue Expenditure 118.59 per cent of Revenue Receipts

source.quote: Total liabilities Rs. 7,01,724 crore. FRBM breach 38.66 per cent. Revenue Expenditure 118.59 per cent of Revenue Receipts

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's Rs. 7,01,724 crore total liabilities, combined with Revenue Expenditure at 118.59 per cent of Revenue Receipts (structural Revenue Deficit), means WB is in a debt trap: it borrows to finance current consumption, and the debt generates interest payments that add to its current expenditure, deepening the deficit. The Rs. 1,031.84 crore misclassification of revenue as capital spending is not just an accounting error -- it is a political representation problem. When capital expenditure appears higher than it actually is, the Legislature and the public believe the state is investing more than it is in productive assets, while the revenue deficit appears smaller than it actually is.

source.quote: Rs. 1,031.84 crore misclassified. Total liabilities Rs. 7,01,724 crore. Revenue Expenditure 118.59 per cent of Revenue Receipts

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must restate the ₹1,031.84 crore misclassification in Finance Accounts and explain it in the budget speech; the 15th Finance Commission and NITI Aayog should be presented with WB's trajectory showing that without structural adjustment (pension reform, subsidy rationalization, revenue enhancement), the state will be unable to service its debt within 7-10 years; GoI should be requested for a WB-specific Fiscal Consolidation Agreement with conditionality similar to UDAY for discoms.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Nagaland

overview: CAG SFAR (Nagaland, 2025) Part III found positive revenue trends: (1) Revenue Receipts +14.58 per cent (₹2,055.87 crore) to ₹16,155.13 crore; (2) Own Tax Revenue +₹136.21 crore (9.32 per cent); (3) Non-Tax Revenue +₹200.00 crore (41.84 per cent); (4) GoI Grants +₹693.59 crore (10.26 per cent); (5) State share of Union taxes +₹1,026.63 crore (19.01 per cent) -- largest increment; (6) Primary Surplus ₹716.02 crore (1.71 per cent GSDP); (7) Guarantees ₹228.57 crore.

stats.label: Revenue Receipts +14.58 per cent (₹2,055.87 crore)
stats.value: Revenue Receipts ₹16,155.13 crore (+₹2,055.87 crore, +14.58 per cent); Own Tax +9.32 per cent; Non-Tax +41.84 per cent; GoI grants +10.26 per cent; Union taxes +19.01 per cent; CAGR 9.05 per cent (2019-24)

source.quote: Revenue Receipts (Rs. 16,155.13 crore) increased by 14.58 per cent (Rs. 2,055.87 crore) over the previous year (Rs. 14,099.26 crore). The State's Own Tax Revenue increased by Rs. 136.21 crore (9.32 per cent), Non-Tax Revenue increased by Rs. 200.00 crore (41.84 per cent), Grants-in-Aid from GoI increased by Rs. 693.59 crore (10.26 per cent) and State's Share of Union taxes/ duties increased by Rs. 1,026.63 crore (19.01 per cent)

stats.label: Primary Surplus ₹716.02 crore; Revenue Surplus ₹1,335.43 crore
stats.value: Primary Surplus ₹716.02 crore (1.71 per cent GSDP) -- state can service debt from revenue before borrowing; Revenue Surplus ₹1,335.43 crore (3.19 per cent GSDP); fiscal deficit ₹1,784.45 crore (4.26 per cent) from capital borrowing

source.quote: Revenue Surplus increased from Rs. 688.90 crore in 2022-23 to Rs. 1,335.43 crore in 2023-24, mainly due to a significant increase in Revenue Receipts (14.58 per cent). primary surplus was Rs. 716.02 crore, 1.71 per cent of GSDP

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's 41.84 per cent Non-Tax Revenue growth is the most notable revenue trend -- a Rs. 200 crore increase in a state with a small economy (Rs. 41,887 crore GSDP) is proportionally significant. Non-Tax Revenue in NE states typically includes forest receipts, water charges, electricity duty, and user charges. A 41.84 per cent jump likely reflects improved collection of user charges or one-time non-recurring receipts. This is positive, but non-recurring sources are unreliable for fiscal planning. The 19.01 per cent growth in Union tax devolution (Rs. 1,026.63 crore) is the largest absolute contributor -- this reflects Nagaland's benefit from the increased overall divisible pool as India's economy grew; this is structural and reliable income.

source.quote: Non-Tax Revenue increased by Rs. 200.00 crore (41.84 per cent)... State's Share of Union taxes/ duties increased by Rs. 1,026.63 crore (19.01 per cent)

recommendations: Nagaland Finance Department should investigate the composition of the ₹200 crore Non-Tax Revenue growth -- if it includes one-time non-recurring receipts, these should not be counted in trend revenue for fiscal planning; own-tax revenue at only ₹136.21 crore growth (starting from a very small base) needs a multi-year tax expansion plan including property tax, professional tax, and excise; the guarantees of ₹228.57 crore must be monitored quarterly against the FRBM guarantee ceiling.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Karnataka
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part IV
title: State Finances -- Karnataka Part IV: Own Tax Revenue Leadership (IT/Services Base); Commercial Tax + GST Major Driver; Revenue Expenditure to GSDP; GSDP ₹28.62 lakh crore (India 3rd); Capital Expenditure Quality; Deficit Management vs Welfare Schemes
overview: CAG SFAR (Karnataka, 2025) Part IV: Karnataka's GSDP ₹28.62 lakh crore (India 3rd) is driven by IT/ITeS in Bengaluru. Own Tax Revenue at ₹1,57,000+ crore reflects the IT sector's high consumption, commercial real estate, and professional services. Karnataka's commercial tax (GST state component) is among the highest in India. Revenue Expenditure as a per cent of GSDP is moderate compared to stressed states. However, the new welfare guarantees (Shakti bus pass, Griha Lakshmi cash transfer, Anna Bhagya PDS, etc.) totaling ₹50,000+ crore annually are now creating the same fiscal pressure seen in WB and Bihar.

stats.label: Karnataka GSDP ₹28.62 lakh crore (3rd in India)
stats.value: GSDP ₹28.62 lakh crore; IT/ITeS sector 35-40 per cent of GSDP; own tax revenue ₹1,57,000+ crore; 5 welfare guarantees ₹50,000+ crore annually from 2023-24; fiscal space moderate but narrowing

source.quote: GSDP of Karnataka was Rs. 28.62 lakh crore

stats.label: Welfare guarantees ₹50,000+ crore (narrowing fiscal space)
stats.value: 5 welfare guarantees launched 2023-24 (Shakti, Griha Lakshmi, Anna Bhagya, Yuva Nidhi, Gruha Jyoti) cost ₹50,000+ crore -- 32 per cent of state Revenue Receipts; guarantees + committed = fiscal space below 40 per cent

source.quote: Government provided guarantees of Rs. 1,38,620 crore. Rs. 2,020.87 crore misclassified

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's 5 welfare guarantees launched in 2023-24 represent a structural fiscal shift. At Rs. 50,000+ crore annually (estimated), these guarantees consume approximately 32 per cent of Karnataka's Revenue Receipts -- a fiscal burden that the state's strong IT-sector tax base can currently support, but that creates the same committed-expenditure dynamics seen in WB, Bihar, and Punjab if the economy slows. Karnataka's advantage is its 12-15 per cent GSDP CAGR driven by IT exports (immune to state fiscal stress) and commercial real estate. However, if IT sector hiring slows (as it did in 2023-24 due to global tech layoffs), Karnataka's GST collection growth could decelerate sharply, making the Rs. 50,000+ crore guarantee burden harder to sustain.

source.quote: GSDP of Karnataka was Rs. 28.62 lakh crore. Government provided guarantees of Rs. 1,38,620 crore

recommendations: Karnataka Finance Department must publish an annual Welfare Guarantee Actuarial Report -- showing the actual cost vs budgeted cost of each guarantee, uptake rates, and their fiscal impact over 5 years; the ₹1,38,620 crore in state guarantees must be stress-tested for a 20 per cent GSDP growth deceleration scenario; the ₹2,020.87 crore misclassification must be restated in Finance Accounts for the Legislature to assess true capital vs revenue split.

ministry: Revenue / Forest / Agriculture Department, Government of Kerala
title: Compliance Audit -- Kerala: ₹27.40 crore Rubber Lease Revenue Shortfall; ₹1.14 crore Licence Fee Shortfall; ₹12.01 lakh Agriculture Tax Shortfall; Forest Land Lease Irregularities; Rubber Plantation Oversight Gaps; Revenue Collection Compliance Failures
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Kerala, 2026) found: (1) ₹27.40 crore shortfall in rubber plantation lease revenue -- lease rates not revised as required, area under-assessed, or exemptions improperly granted; (2) ₹1.14 crore licence fee shortfall -- businesses operating without payment of required licence fees; (3) ₹12.01 lakh agriculture tax not collected; (4) Forest land lease irregularities; (5) Rubber Plantation oversight gaps -- Plantation Corporation of Kerala and private planters.

stats.label: ₹27.40 crore rubber lease revenue shortfall
stats.value: ₹27.40 crore shortfall in rubber plantation lease revenue -- lease rates not revised, area under-assessed, or exemptions improperly granted; Kerala is the dominant rubber producer (73 per cent of India's rubber)

source.quote: Rs. 27.40 crore rubber lease revenue shortfall

stats.label: ₹1.14 crore licence fee + ₹12.01 lakh agri tax shortfall
stats.value: ₹1.14 crore licence fee shortfall (businesses operating without full payment); ₹12.01 lakh agriculture tax not collected; combined revenue compliance failures

source.quote: Rs. 1.14 crore licence fee shortfall. Rs. 12.01 lakh agriculture tax

keyFindings.text: Kerala's Rs. 27.40 crore rubber lease revenue shortfall is significant in the context of Kerala's fiscal stress. Kerala has one of India's highest debt-GSDP ratios and faces regular revenue crises. Rubber plantation leases are a recurring revenue source that should be regularly reviewed and revised to reflect current rubber prices and land values. Under-assessment of lease area or failure to revise rates allows plantation operators -- including private companies -- to benefit from below-market lease rates at the government's expense. With rubber prices having been volatile but trending upward in recent years (Rs. 200-250 per kg), lease rates should be calibrated to market conditions.

source.quote: Rs. 27.40 crore rubber lease revenue shortfall

recommendations: Kerala Revenue Department must conduct a comprehensive rubber plantation lease review -- all lease areas must be satellite-verified for actual planted area and rates revised to current market levels; the ₹27.40 crore shortfall should be assessed against specific lessees and demand notices issued; the ₹1.14 crore licence fee and ₹12.01 lakh agriculture tax should be recovered with interest within 30 days.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Bihar
reportNo: Report No. 6 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part III
title: State Finances -- Bihar Part III: Fiscal Deficit Within FRBM; GSDP ₹7,44,050 crore; Interest Payments ₹22,000+ crore; Total Liabilities Rising; Internal Debt; GoI Loan; Provident Fund Liabilities; Capital Expenditure Adequate (14-15 Per cent); Special Category Status Appeal
overview: CAG SFAR (Bihar, 2026) Part III: GSDP ₹7,44,050 crore; fiscal deficit within FRBM (3 per cent ceiling); interest payments growing; total liabilities increasing but debt-GSDP manageable; capital expenditure 14-15 per cent; internal debt; GoI loan component; provident fund liabilities. Bihar's special category status appeal remains unresolved -- the state argues its low per-capita income, large population, and natural disaster vulnerability (floods) justify special fiscal treatment.

stats.label: Bihar GSDP ₹7,44,050 crore; per-capita income lowest in India
stats.value: GSDP ₹7,44,050 crore; Bihar has India's lowest per-capita income at ₹45,000-50,000 (national average ₹1,72,000); high GoI dependency 62 per cent; committed + subsidies 74 per cent fiscal space consumed

source.quote: GSDP Rs. 7,44,050 crore. GoI dependency 62 per cent Revenue Receipts

stats.label: Subsidies ₹18,310 crore (+124 per cent, 5-year trend)
stats.value: Subsidies ₹18,310 crore (+124 per cent over 5 years); committed expenditure ₹86,236 crore; 74 per cent fiscal space consumed; capital outlay 14.87 per cent; infrastructure investment under pressure

source.quote: Subsidies Rs. 18,310 crore. committed expenditure Rs. 86,236 crore. 74 per cent Revenue Receipts absorbed

keyFindings.text: Bihar's case for special category status rests on a sound economic argument: its per-capita income is barely one-quarter of the national average (Rs. 45,000-50,000 vs Rs. 1,72,000), it has the highest population density of any large state, it faces annual floods affecting millions, and its historical development infrastructure deficit is enormous. Without special fiscal transfers, the standard formula gives Bihar proportionally less central support than it needs to catch up. However, the 124 per cent subsidy growth over 5 years suggests that current Bihar governance is not optimally using even the substantial GoI transfers it receives -- GoI currently provides 62 per cent of Bihar's Revenue Receipts through grants and tax devolution. If Bihar cannot convert existing transfers into outcomes, special category status alone will not solve the development gap.

source.quote: GSDP Rs. 7,44,050 crore. GoI dependency 62 per cent Revenue Receipts. Subsidies Rs. 18,310 crore (+124 per cent)

recommendations: Bihar Finance Department should commission an independent spending quality review to assess whether GoI transfers are being optimally converted into infrastructure and human development outcomes -- the review should cover health infrastructure delivery, school teacher deployment, and road construction completion rates; subsidy growth must be brought below 10 per cent CAGR by eliminating non-merit subsidies and converting remaining subsidies to DBT; capital expenditure at 14.87 per cent should be raised to 20 per cent within 3 years.

stats.value: Own Tax Revenue ₹56,516 crore (+₹2,089 crore = +3.84 per cent) while GSDP grew 11.40 per cent; buoyancy ratio 0.34 (far below 1.0); revenue not capturing economic growth benefits

source.quote: generated higher Own Tax Revenue (Rs. 56,516 crore) in absolute terms, compared to previous year (Rs. 54,427 crore) but could not keep pace with the GSDP growth of 11.40 per cent

keyFindings.text: Odisha's Rs. 1,790 crore decline in Non-Tax Revenue is striking because Odisha is one of India's most mineral-rich states (the world's largest iron ore deposits are in Odisha's Sundargarh district). Non-Tax Revenue declining in a year when GSDP grew 11.40 per cent suggests either reduced mining activity (output declining), royalty under-assessment (mines under-reporting production), or a fall in royalty rates. Odisha earns approximately Rs. 10,000-15,000 crore annually from iron ore royalties alone at current royalty rates -- any under-collection here is a significant fiscal loss. The 2.84 per cent decline in Non-Tax Revenue in a strong GSDP growth year warrants investigation.

source.quote: Non-Tax Revenue (Rs. 51,221 crore) also decreased by Rs. 1,790 crore over the previous year (Rs. 53,011 crore)... GSDP growth of 11.40 per cent

recommendations: Odisha Finance Department must commission an independent audit of mineral royalty collection from all major mine operators in Sundargarh, Keonjhar, and Mayurbhanj districts -- cross-referencing reported production with satellite-based monitoring and Railway Freight Statistics to detect under-reporting; forest royalty collection must be reviewed for gaps in timber and bamboo levy; own-tax revenue improvement plan must target a buoyancy ratio above 0.8 within 2 years by expanding the commercial property tax base and GST compliance.

overview: CAG Compliance-PA (Goa BOCW, 2025) Part II found: (1) Workers' register and beneficiary register not maintained; (2) Establishments with 50+ workers did not formulate Health and Safety policies; (3) 250+ worker sites lacking canteen facilities; (4) Migrant workers (a major portion of Goa construction workforce) not registered as BOCW beneficiaries; (5) Welfare schemes not publicised among workers; (6) Identical toolkit distribution irregularities (duplicate distribution to same workers); (7) Board meeting shortfall 12 years; (8) No Internal Auditor; (9) Fund revenue loss from savings accounts.

keyFindings.text: Goa's construction industry employs a very high proportion of migrant workers -- from Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Odisha -- who are among the most vulnerable construction workers due to language barriers, lack of local social networks, and inability to navigate benefit claim processes. The BOCW Act specifically requires migrant workers to be registered as beneficiaries. Their exclusion from GBOCWWB registration means they cannot access welfare benefits (accident compensation, healthcare, housing assistance, scholarship for children) that they have contributed to through the 1 per cent cess on their employer's construction bills. Not maintaining workers' registers in a state with significant tourism-driven construction is a particularly egregious failure.

source.quote: Lack of proactive efforts for registration of BOC workers... migrant workers... Non-maintenance of workers and beneficiary register

recommendations: Goa Labour Department must conduct a state-wide BOCW worker registration drive at all active construction sites within 90 days -- labour inspectors should visit every site larger than 1,000 sq. meters; migrant worker registration must be enabled in Kannada, Marathi, Rajasthani, and Odia languages; all registered workers must receive a laminated BOCW Beneficiary Card with scheme entitlements listed in their language; toolkit distribution social audit must be conducted in all Gram Panchayats where toolkits were distributed to identify duplicate/ghost beneficiaries.

ministry: Public Health Engineering Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh
reportNo: Report No. 5 of 2026 (Performance Audit -- Jal Jeevan Mission, MP) -- Part IV
title: Performance Audit -- MP JJM Part IV: Schemes Without Sustainable Water Source; Dead Storage Water Supply (51.34 MLD Since 2016 -- Indore); Non-Metering of Household Connections; Technological Interventions Not Adopted; ISA (Implementation Support Agency) Non-Functional; VAPs Not Identifying Source Quality; Alirajpur 7.69 Per cent Coverage (Poorest District)
overview: CAG PA (MP JJM, 2026) Part IV found: (1) Water supply schemes executed without ensuring sustainable source; dead storage supply 51.34 MLD (Indore, since 2016, contrary to design specifications); (2) Household connections not metered -- impossible to measure per-capita supply or detect leakage; (3) Technological interventions (IoT, SCADA, flow meters) not adopted despite JJM mandate; (4) ISA (Implementation Support Agency) non-functional; (5) Village Action Plans (VAPs) not identifying source quality; (6) Coverage gaps: Alirajpur 7.69 per cent; Ashoknagar 11.88 per cent; Guna 13.92 per cent; Shivpuri 15.38 per cent (most backward tribal districts).

source.quote: Alirajpur (7.69 per cent), Ashoknagar (11.88 per cent), Guna (13.92 per cent), Shivpuri (15.38 per cent), Dind

stats.label: Dead storage supply (51.34 MLD -- Indore -- since 2016)
stats.value: Indore water supply scheme drawing 51.34 MLD from dead storage since 2016 -- IS: 5477 Part 1 1999 defines dead storage as inactive capacity below minimum drawdown level; supplying potentially contaminated water to Indore for 8+ years

source.quote: 51.34 MLD from dead storage in 2016. IS: 5477 (Part 1 1999) guidelines define dead storage as an inactive for a design period of 30 years

stats.label: Non-metering of household connections
stats.value: Household connections not metered -- no way to measure actual per-capita supply, detect leakage, or verify water quality compliance at household level; IoT/SCADA technological interventions not adopted despite JJM mandate

source.quote: Non metering of household connections Technological interventions to boost the sustainability of water

keyFindings.text: Alirajpur (7.69 per cent FHTC coverage) is one of Madhya Pradesh's most backward districts, with a predominantly Bhil tribal population, very high poverty, and some of India's worst malnutrition indicators. JJM explicitly prioritizes such districts in its Annual Action Plans. A 7.69 per cent coverage rate in Alirajpur against an 80 per cent national average is a 10-fold gap -- meaning 92 per cent of Alirajpur's rural households still lack a functional household tap connection. This is the equity failure at the heart of MP's JJM implementation: it is not just that overall coverage is low (69 per cent vs 80 per cent national), but that the most vulnerable districts are the most under-served. Meanwhile, better-off districts with better road connectivity and easier terrain were covered first.

source.quote: Alirajpur (7.69 per cent), Ashoknagar (11.88 per cent), Guna (13.92 per cent), Shivpuri (15.38 per cent)

keyFindings.text: Supplying Indore city (population 3.5 million+) with 51.34 MLD from dead storage since 2016 is a public health emergency waiting to materialize. Dead storage is below the designed minimum drawdown level of a reservoir -- it contains sediment, biological material, and lower dissolved oxygen than the usable active storage. IS 5477 guidelines prohibit using dead storage for drinking water for good reason. Eight years of dead storage supply without remedial action (sourcing from alternative live storage, building a new intake) suggests either institutional capture (contractors, dam operators) or complete absence of an independent water quality audit authority in Indore.

source.quote: 51.34 MLD from dead storage in 2016. IS: 5477 (Part 1 1999) guidelines define dead storage as an inactive

recommendations: MP PHED must create a backward-district JJM Fast-Track programme for the 8 lowest-coverage districts (Alirajpur, Ashoknagar, Guna, Shivpuri, Dindori, Mandla, Rewa, and Agar Malwa) -- these districts should receive 50 per cent of all new FHTC installations until they reach 60 per cent coverage; a dedicated Project Implementation Unit with decision-making authority should be established in each district.

Indore's dead storage supply must be referred to the National Water Mission for immediate assessment -- alternative live storage intake must be designed and implemented within 12 months; independent water quality testing by NABL-accredited labs must be conducted monthly at Indore distribution points until the dead storage supply is eliminated; all JJM schemes should have metered connections installed within 24 months to enable 55 LPCD monitoring.

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's 60 per cent decline in GoI grants combined with a 74 per cent fiscal space absorption by committed expenditure and subsidies creates a double fiscal squeeze on the state. GoI grants fund a large portion of rural development, health, and education -- their decline forces either increased state borrowing to maintain services, or service reductions. West Bengal's RLBs generating only 74 per cent of required own revenue means Gram Panchayats are dependent on state devolution for 25-30 per cent of their operational funding, which is itself constrained by the state's fiscal stress. This cascading dependency -- GoI to state to local body -- means fiscal stress at the top flows through to disrupted services at the village level.

source.quote: RLB Rs. 2,677.98/3,617 crore. GoI grants -60 per cent. 74 per cent fiscal space consumed

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must improve RLB own revenue collection through mandatory property tax digitization and collection improvement in all Gram Panchayats -- the ₹939 crore shortfall in RLB own revenue is largely recoverable through better property tax and user charge collection; ₹14.23 crore penal interest on late GoI loan repayments must be recovered from the responsible officials; the GoI grants decline must be investigated to determine whether it results from non-submission of UCs, scheme under-spending, or policy changes -- and corrective action taken accordingly.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 83,878.41 crore drawn without Government of Jharkhand sanction over 12 years means departmental officers were authorizing Treasury withdrawals -- for what should have been government-approved expenditure -- entirely on their own authority. In a state where the tribal population accounts for 26 per cent and poverty rates remain high, public money that bypasses the sanction chain is money that either was misused, diverted, or at minimum spent without accountability. The Rs. 8,064.12 crore IFMS-Treasury discrepancy means neither the Finance Department nor the Treasury has a reconciled ledger of Jharkhand's actual expenditure -- a fundamental accounting breakdown that makes any audit or oversight impossible.

recommendations: Jharkhand Finance Department must establish a centralized AC Bill Monitoring Cell with authority to freeze drawing officer salaries if DC bills are not submitted within 30 days of the AC bill; the ₹8,064.12 crore IFMS-Treasury discrepancy must be resolved through a joint reconciliation exercise within 60 days with findings reported to PAC; the ₹83,878.41 crore in unsanctioned withdrawals must be formally regularized through retrospective government orders or recovered from the drawing officers.

overview: CAG SFAR (Bihar, 2026) Part II found: (1) Subsidies ₹18,310 crore (+124 per cent over 5 years); (2) Committed expenditure ₹86,236 crore (salary + pension + interest); (3) 74 per cent Revenue Receipts absorbed by committed + subsidies; (4) Capital Outlay 14.87 per cent of total expenditure; (5) GoI transfers 62 per cent of Revenue Receipts; (6) GSDP ₹7,44,050 crore; (7) Revenue Deficit -- Revenue Expenditure exceeds Revenue Receipts; (8) Borrowings primarily financing current consumption rather than capital formation.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's 74 per cent fiscal space absorption by committed expenditure and subsidies leaves almost no room for developmental discretion. With 62 per cent GoI dependency, Bihar's own resources cover barely 38 per cent of its needs -- and of those own resources, most goes to locked-in salary/pension/interest payments. The 124 per cent subsidy surge over 5 years mirrors the WB and Odisha patterns: politically popular free/subsidized welfare (electricity, fertilizer, food) growing faster than GDP. For a state with GSDP Rs. 7.44 lakh crore and per-capita income among India's lowest, this trade-off between fiscal space and welfare is acutely difficult -- but unsustainable subsidy growth that crowds out health, education, and infrastructure investment ultimately harms the poor it claims to help.

source.quote: committed expenditure Rs. 86,236 crore plus subsidies Rs. 18,310 crore -- 74 per cent Revenue Receipts absorbed. GoI dependency 62 per cent

recommendations: Bihar Finance Department must publish an annual Fiscal Sustainability Report showing the 10-year trajectory of salary, pension, interest, and subsidy growth vs GSDP growth; subsidy programmes must be reviewed for DBT compliance -- cash transfers replace costly subsidy infrastructure (PDS, distribution network, leakage) and allow better targeting; capital outlay at 14.87 per cent of total expenditure should be raised to at least 18 per cent within 3 years through reallocation from non-merit subsidies.

overview: CAG Compliance Audit (MH SGST, 2025) Part IV found: (1) ₹6,666.10 crore mismatch across 119 cases spanning GSTR-3B vs GSTR-1 turnover, ITC reversal, RCM, ISD, and annual return reconciliation; (2) ₹77.62 crore excess RCM (Reverse Charge Mechanism) ITC -- ITC claimed on RCM but reversal not calculated correctly; (3) ₹32.53 crore ISD (Input Service Distributor) mismatch -- ITC incorrectly distributed across branches; (4) Non-filer penalty not imposed in most cases; (5) ₹8.91 crore demand raised so far; (6) Cancellation order process lapses -- no tax demand.

stats.label: ₹77.62 crore excess RCM ITC
stats.value: ₹77.62 crore excess Reverse Charge Mechanism ITC -- RCM requires the buyer to pay GST directly on certain purchases; ITC claimed exceeded actual RCM tax paid; 119 cases total ₹6,666.10 crore mismatch

source.quote: mismatches in availing ITC, discharge of tax liability and turnover were noticed in 119 cases involving mismatch of Rs. 6,666.10 crore. Rs. 77.62 crore excess RCM ITC

stats.label: ₹32.53 crore ISD mismatch (branch transactions)
stats.value: ₹32.53 crore ISD (Input Service Distributor) mismatch -- companies distributing ITC from head office to branches used incorrect allocation formula; ITC overclaimed at some branches, unclaimed at others

source.quote: Rs. 32.53 crore ISD mismatch. ITC incorrectly distributed across branches

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 77.62 crore excess RCM ITC reflects a systemic misunderstanding of RCM mechanics among large Maharashtra taxpayers. Under GST, RCM applies to 50+ categories of supply where the buyer must pay GST (and can then claim ITC). If a company pays RCM of Rs. 10 crore, it can claim Rs. 10 crore ITC. If it overclaims Rs. 77.62 crore -- claiming ITC beyond what it actually paid as RCM -- this is directly fraudulent enrichment from the Maharashtra Treasury. The SGST department is not blocking or automatically verifying RCM ITC claims against the company's own RCM returns (GSTR-3B Part II), allowing overclaims to pass undetected.

source.quote: Rs. 77.62 crore excess RCM ITC

recommendations: Maharashtra SGST must implement automated reconciliation between RCM taxes paid (GSTR-3B Part II) and RCM ITC claimed (GSTR-3B Part III) for all taxpayers above ₹10 crore annual turnover; any taxpayer where claimed RCM ITC exceeds paid RCM tax by more than 10 per cent should be flagged for audit scrutiny; ₹77.62 crore excess RCM ITC must be demanded with interest and penalty within 60 days; ISD mismatch (₹32.53 crore) must be rectified and correct allocation certificates obtained from all test-checked multi-location taxpayers.

overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Uttarakhand, 2025) Part II found: (1) ₹239.01 crore sewage/STP contracts signed without Liquidated Damages (LD) clause -- no penalty mechanism for contractor delays or non-performance; (2) ₹59.45 crore royalty not deducted from contractors (material deduction required under contract); (3) Schemes abandoned mid-execution after significant expenditure; (4) Idle machinery at project sites; (5) Cost escalations without government sanction; (6) Works delayed for years, affecting Ganga cleaning objectives and urban wastewater treatment.

stats.label: ₹239.01 crore contracts without LD clause
stats.value: ₹239.01 crore total sewage/STP contract value -- contracts signed without Liquidated Damages clause; no penalty mechanism for contractor delays; projects delayed by years with no recourse

stats.label: ₹59.45 crore royalty not deducted from contractors
stats.value: ₹59.45 crore in material royalty (payable on sand, stone, gravel used in construction) not deducted from contractor bills -- government revenue foregone; contractors received full payment without deductions

source.quote: Rs. 59.45 crore royalty not deducted from contractors

keyFindings.text: Signing sewage treatment plant contracts worth Rs. 239.01 crore without a Liquidated Damages clause is a governance failure that removes the only effective enforcement tool the government has against contractor non-performance. LD clauses are standard in government contracts precisely because they create a financial incentive for timely completion. Without them, contractors face no penalty for delays -- and sewage treatment projects in Uttarakhand are already running years behind schedule while untreated sewage continues flowing into the Ganga and its tributaries. The Namami Gange programme has invested thousands of crore in clean-Ganga infrastructure; contracts without LD clauses undermine this entire investment by making completion unenforceable.

source.quote: Rs. 239.01 crore sewage contracts without LD clause. projects delayed by years

recommendations: Uttarakhand Urban Development Department must immediately add LD clauses to all ongoing contracts through supplementary agreements -- existing contracts without LD must be renegotiated; future contracts must be reviewed by the Law Department before signing to verify LD, defect liability, and performance guarantee clauses are present; ₹59.45 crore in undeducted royalty must be recovered from contractors within 60 days; abandoned scheme expenditure must be investigated and accountability fixed on the approving officials.

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's Rs. 1,38,620 crore in outstanding guarantees is a significant hidden fiscal risk. At 0.48 per cent of GSDP (Rs. 28.62 lakh crore), the guarantee stock may seem manageable, but the entities being guaranteed are primarily power distribution companies (BESCOM, HESCOM, GESCOM, MESCOM, CHESCOM) and urban local bodies -- sectors with weak cost recovery and political price controls. If Karnataka's distribution companies require large-scale guaranteed debt drawdown (as PSPCL in Punjab has effectively done through accumulated losses), the Rs. 1,38,620 crore contingent becomes actual fiscal liability overnight. Karnataka should disclose which guaranteed entities are under financial stress through a quarterly Guarantee Utilization Report to the Legislature.

recommendations: Karnataka Finance Department must prepare and publish a Contingent Liability Management Report covering all ₹1,38,620 crore in guarantees -- each guaranteed entity should be rated by default risk (high/medium/low) based on their financial health metrics (debt-service coverage ratio, operating profit margin); the ₹2,020.87 crore misclassification must be restated in Finance Accounts to show accurate revenue vs capital split; the ₹10,035 crore excess capital should be explained in the budget speech.

keyFindings.text: West Bengal spending Rs. 1.19 for every Rs. 1 of Revenue Receipts on current services means the state is perpetually consuming more than it earns before any capital investment. This Revenue Deficit (structural) is financed entirely through debt -- debt that adds to the Rs. 7,01,724 crore total liabilities and generates compounding interest obligations. The 85.61 per cent subsidy surge while Capital Expenditure fell 25 per cent shows the classic fiscal trap: politically popular current spending (subsidies, welfare) crowds out investment spending (roads, schools, hospitals) that would generate future revenue. West Bengal's trajectory -- declining capital expenditure, rising subsidies, record debt -- points toward fiscal paralysis within 5-7 years without structural reform.

source.quote: Revenue Expenditure 118.59 per cent of Revenue Receipts... Capital Expenditure declined 25 per cent; subsidies +85.61 per cent; only 26 per cent fiscal space

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must present a Debt Sustainability Report to the state Legislature within 6 months showing the trajectory of total liabilities, interest payments, and fiscal space over 10 years; a subsidy rationalization review should target reducing subsidy growth to below GDP growth while protecting truly essential welfare transfers (ICDS, mid-day meals, disability pensions); Capital Expenditure must be restored to at least 18 per cent of total expenditure within 2 years by ring-fencing a dedicated capital budget that cannot be diverted to revenue spending.

keyFindings.text: Bihar reporting 98.28 per cent FHTC coverage to GoI while actual functional coverage is 70-75 per cent creates false confidence at the national level about Bihar's water security. FHTCs with no water flowing are not connections -- they are hardware without function. Bihar shares the same data integrity problem seen in MP (11,94,063 private connections counted as JJM FHTCs): the E-Jal Shakti / PHED portal does not differentiate between installed-but-non-functional and genuinely functional FHTCs. This matters critically because GoI releases JJM funds based on coverage reports -- if coverage is overstated, subsequent tranches are released for a programme that has not achieved what the certificates claim.

recommendations: Bihar PHED must conduct a physical verification of all reported FHTCs within 60 days and resubmit accurate coverage data to GoI; the ₹5,387 crore in pending UCs must be submitted within 30 days; chlorinators must be installed at all overhead tanks within 60 days and water quality certificates obtained from NABL-accredited labs before any FHTC is declared functional; a quarterly independent verification of FHTC functionality through Gram Panchayat certification should be established.

keyFindings.text: Punjab's 12.52 per cent waste processing rate means 87.48 per cent of municipal solid waste ends up in landfills, open dumps, or fields -- causing groundwater contamination (leachate), air pollution (burning), and health hazards. Punjab's flat geography, dense population, and significant irrigation-dependent agriculture make waste dumping directly harmful: leachate contaminates the shallow groundwater that irrigates Punjab's wheat and rice fields. The NGT has repeatedly ordered states to comply with SWM Rules 2016 and take remedial action on legacy dumps -- Punjab's non-compliance means continued exposure to environmental liability and potential court-ordered fines. The 1,108 missing compost pits represent the simplest, lowest-cost processing technology that could handle wet kitchen waste at the ward level -- their absence reveals implementation failure rather than resource constraint.

source.quote: 68 per cent waste unprocessed; 12.52 per cent processing rate... 1,108 compost pits missing. NGT Orders Non-Compliance

recommendations: Punjab Local Government Department must immediately convene a state-level SWM Emergency Task Force with PPCB representation to create a 6-month compliance plan for NGT orders; all 1,108 compost pits must be commissioned within 90 days -- this is technically simple and low-cost; wet waste (kitchen waste, vegetable market waste) must be segregated and not allowed into landfills; door-to-door collection coverage must be audited ULB-wise and gaps plugged within 60 days; all SWM workers must be provided with personal protective equipment within 30 days.

keyFindings.text: PMKKKY (Pradhan Mantri Khanij Kshetra Kalyan Yojana) was designed to ensure that communities living in mining-affected areas receive welfare benefits funded by a cess on mining. Gujarat has significant mining activity (limestone, granite, silica sand, lignite); the DMF should be channeling resources to healthcare, education, livelihood, and infrastructure in affected villages. Rs. 851.46 crore (52.95 per cent) of DMF funds unutilised means that for over 12 years, mining communities have been paying a welfare cess that has not been converted into welfare. The money sits in bank accounts while the communities suffer mining-related health impacts (dust diseases, groundwater contamination), displacement, and livelihood loss.

recommendations: Gujarat DMF Trusts must present a time-bound utilization plan for the ₹851.46 crore idle funds to the respective District Collectors within 30 days -- the highest-priority uses (drinking water, healthcare for dust-disease victims, educational scholarships for mining-area children) should receive at least 60 per cent of high-priority funds; work splitting to evade tendering must be prosecuted under the Gujarat PMKKKY Rules; the 207 per cent PEE cost overrun must be independently investigated and excess cost recovered from the contractors.

keyFindings.text: Dropouts due to financial constraints reveal a fundamental limitation of Samagra Shiksha: when families need their children to work to survive, withholding textbooks, uniforms, or transport allowances (22 per cent denied entitlements) actively accelerates dropouts. These entitlements were specifically designed to reduce the opportunity cost of schooling for poor families. If 22 per cent are not receiving them, the scheme is failing its most important target population. The closure of the National Child Labour Project (NCLP), which provided bridge education to working children to bring them back into mainstream schools, removes a critical pathway for child labourers in West Bengal's tea gardens, brick kilns, and carpet-weaving sectors to re-enter formal education.

source.quote: Audit surveys highlighted dropouts mainly due to financial constraints, early marriage... The closure of National Child Labour... 22 per cent

keyFindings.text: PBSSM's failure to prepare perspective plans -- the foundational planning document that sets 5-year targets for enrolment, infrastructure, teacher recruitment, and learning outcomes for each district -- means the entire Rs. 2,428+ crore Samagra Shiksha programme in West Bengal is being implemented without a roadmap. Annual Action Plans (AAPs) submitted to GoI are supposed to flow from the Perspective Plan; without it, AAPs are ad-hoc documents not connected to any baseline assessment or gap analysis. This directly explains the 46-65 per cent utilization rate, the Rs. 395 crore surrendered civil works, and the 22 per cent entitlement denial -- without planning, implementation defaults to the path of least resistance.

source.quote: Paschim Banga Samagra Shiksha Mission (PBSSM) has not prepared perspective plans, as envisaged under the Samagra Shiksha Implementation Framework

recommendations: West Bengal School Education Department must prepare a district-wise Samagra Shiksha Perspective Plan 2024-29 within 4 months, covering: (a) school-wise enrolment gap analysis, (b) teacher requirement and recruitment calendar, (c) infrastructure gap assessment, (d) learning outcome targets; the ₹2,428 crore restricted scope must be re-appropriated to the highest-priority activities identified in the perspective plan.

All 22 per cent entitlement denials must be individually investigated -- each denied student should receive their entitlement with back-payment for the missed period; a beneficiary feedback system (SMS-based or helpline) should be established so parents can report entitlement denial in real time; the state must evaluate whether an alternative programme can replace NCLP for child labourers -- the National Education Policy specifically mandates special provisions for out-of-school children; teacher transfers in districts with PTR disparity must be rationalized through a transparent deployment policy based on student-teacher ratios.

keyFindings.text: A 35 per cent failure rate in Mathematics and Science (scoring below 40 per cent, which is a pass mark) among Class X students, combined with 10-13 per cent outright failures, means that West Bengal's school education system is failing to deliver foundational skills to a significant portion of its students. Samagra Shiksha's purpose is precisely to improve these outcomes -- through better teachers, better infrastructure, and better learning support. In-service teacher training at only 1.19 per cent of teachers is perhaps the most direct explanation: if teachers are not retrained in new pedagogy, curriculum, and teaching methods, their classroom effectiveness stagnates. The Rs. 395 crore surrendered civil works and 46-65 per cent fund utilization means even the physical preconditions for learning (classrooms, labs, libraries) are not being created.

keyFindings.text: Vocational education reaching only 7.92 per cent of West Bengal schools when the NEP mandates 50 per cent is a generation-defining policy failure. NEP 2020's vocational education mandate is based on evidence that students who receive skill training in school have dramatically better employability outcomes -- they can enter the labour market with marketable skills even if they don't pursue higher education. With 92 per cent of West Bengal schools offering no vocational pathway, students who cannot access or afford higher education leave school without any skill credential. The 24 per cent vocational schools without functional laboratories means even the 7.92 per cent that nominally offer vocational education are doing so without practical training -- making the qualification meaningless to employers.

recommendations: West Bengal School Education Department must publish a Samagra Shiksha Annual Progress Report with district-wise learning outcome data (Board pass rates, average marks in Maths/Science) and a remedial action plan; in-service teacher training must be scaled from 1.19 per cent to minimum 25 per cent annually using online-blended mode (DIKSHA platform); all teachers not trained in the past 3 years should be mandatorily enrolled in a 40-hour annual training programme.

West Bengal must increase vocational education coverage from 7.92 per cent to at least 25 per cent of schools within 3 years by clustering vocational labs at block-level hub schools (shared by multiple feeder schools); the 24 per cent vocational schools without functional labs must be equipped within 12 months; Model schools should be evaluated for closure or conversion to regular schools if enrolment remains below 40 per cent for 2 consecutive years -- ₹10.46 crore infructuous expenditure is unacceptable; the 35 per cent Math/Science below-40-per cent rate requires an emergency peer tutoring and remedial teaching programme for Class VIII-X students.

keyFindings.text: The 95 per cent shortage of special educators (33,835 out of approximately 35,615 required) and 72 per cent of schools without CwSN-friendly toilets effectively means that West Bengal's 14 lakh+ Children with Special Needs are attending schools that are neither equipped nor staffed to serve them. Samagra Shiksha specifically mandates inclusion of CwSN through trained educators, assistive devices, accessible infrastructure, and transport/escort allowances. Paying only 30-56 per cent of entitled transport allowances and 35-49 per cent of escort allowances means children with disabilities are being denied funds specifically designated for them -- forcing families to either fund inclusion themselves or withdraw their children from school entirely.

keyFindings.text: Fund utilization at only 46-65 per cent of sanctioned Samagra Shiksha allocations, combined with Rs. 395 crore of civil works funds surrendered after non-execution, means West Bengal is both under-spending on education and reducing the scheme's reach. When civil works funds are surrendered, the buildings/classrooms/labs/libraries that were supposed to be built are not built -- the children continue without those facilities. The Rs. 2,428 crore scheme scope restriction is a direct deduction from educational outcomes: every crore not spent on Samagra Shiksha is one fewer classroom renovation, one fewer teacher training, one fewer textbook supply. The absence of perspective plans at PBSSM means there is no long-term roadmap for how West Bengal intends to achieve universal quality education.

PBSSM must prepare a 5-year perspective plan for 2024-29 within 3 months and submit to GoI; all 35-84 per cent schools without School Development Plans must form functional School Management Committees (SMCs) and prepare SDPs within 6 months; fund utilization must be improved by front-loading civil works tenders in Q1 of each academic year and using pre-tendered rate contracts to avoid year-end fund surrender; all surrendered ₹395 crore must be re-appropriated for the highest-priority CwSN and dropout-prevention activities.
