reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit) -- AC Bills and IFMS
title: Compliance Audit -- Jharkhand AC Bills: ₹20,098.82 crore Abstract Contingency Bills Outstanding; ₹2,44,925.58 crore AC Bills (2010-2022); ₹83,878.41 crore Without GoJ Sanction; ₹8,064.12 crore IFMS/Treasury Gap; ₹62.61 crore Excess Release
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Jharkhand, 2025) found: (1) Abstract Contingency (AC) bills -- ₹20,098.82 crore outstanding (unrendered accounts for advances drawn from Treasury); (2) Long-period AC bills -- ₹2,44,925.58 crore (2010-2022), of which ₹83,878.41 crore drawn without GoJ sanction; (3) IFMS gap -- ₹8,064.12 crore discrepancy between IFMS and Treasury; (4) ₹62.61 crore excess release from State Government to implementing agencies (Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation).

stats.label: ₹20,098.82 crore outstanding AC bills
stats.value: ₹20,098.82 crore Abstract Contingency bills outstanding -- advances drawn from Treasury for which Detailed Contingency bills (actual expenditure accounts) not yet submitted; some years-old

source.quote: Rs. 20,098.82 crore Abstract Contingency bills outstanding. Rs. 8,064.12 crore IFMS gap

stats.label: ₹2,44,925.58 crore AC bills (2010-2022) -- ₹83,878 crore unsanctioned
stats.value: ₹2,44,925.58 crore total AC bills 2010-2022; ₹83,878.41 crore drawn without GoJ sanction -- funds released to implementing agencies without government authorization; ₹62.61 crore excess release

source.quote: Rs. 2,44,925.58 crore AC bills (2010-22); Rs. 83,878.41 crore without sanction. Rs. 62.61 crore excess release

keyFindings.text: Jharkhand's Rs. 2,44,925.58 crore in un-adjusted Abstract Contingency bills (2010-2022) represents 12 years of advances drawn from the Treasury for which the state has never rendered final accounts to the Legislature. This means the Legislature approved budgets and the Finance Department released funds, but neither the departments nor the Treasury can confirm what the money was actually spent on. Rs. 83,878.41 crore of this -- nearly Rs. 84,000 crore -- was drawn without even the government's own sanction, meaning middle-level officials took Treasury withdrawals without authorization. This is the most fundamental financial control failure possible: it means Jharkhand has been operating without meaningful public financial accountability for over a decade.

source.quote: Rs. 2,44,925.58 crore AC bills (2010-22); Rs. 83,878.41 crore without sanction

recommendations: Jharkhand Finance Department must immediately stop all new AC bill withdrawals above ₹1 lakh without DC bill submission within 3 months; all ₹20,098.82 crore outstanding AC bills must be either converted to DC bills within 90 days or recovered from the drawing officers; the ₹8,064.12 crore IFMS/Treasury discrepancy must be reconciled within 30 days and the sources of variance identified; any AC bill beyond 3 years without DC bill submission must trigger automatic salary attachment of the drawing officer.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Karnataka
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report) -- Part II
title: State Finances -- Karnataka Part II: GSDP ₹28.62 lakh crore; Total Liabilities ₹6,92,115 crore; Revenue Deficit ₹2,020.87 crore Misclassified; ₹10,035 crore Excess Capital Expenditure; Guarantees ₹1,38,620 crore; Own-Tax Revenue + GoI Transfers; Committed Expenditure Ratio
overview: CAG SFAR (Karnataka, 2025) Part II -- Karnataka is India's third-largest state economy (GSDP ₹28.62 lakh crore). Key fiscal metrics: Total Liabilities ₹6,92,115 crore; ₹2,020.87 crore revenue expenditure misclassified as capital; ₹10,035 crore excess capital (beyond what Maharashtra or national norms permit); guarantees ₹1,38,620 crore (large contingent liability); committed expenditure consuming significant share of Revenue Receipts. Karnataka's rapid IT sector growth (Bengaluru) and robust own-tax revenue base provide resilience, but the misclassification and guarantee load are material risks.

stats.label: Guarantees ₹1,38,620 crore (contingent liability)
stats.value: Outstanding government guarantees ₹1,38,620 crore -- contingent liability that could crystallize into actual debt if guaranteed entities default; GSDP ₹28.62 lakh crore; liabilities ₹6,92,115 crore

source.quote: Government provided guarantees of Rs. 1,38,620 crore GSDP of Karnataka was Rs. 28.62 lakh crore... Total liabilities stood at Rs. 6,92,115 crore

stats.label: ₹2,020.87 crore revenue misclassified as capital
stats.value: ₹2,020.87 crore revenue expenditure misclassified as capital expenditure; ₹10,035 crore excess capital expenditure beyond prescribed norms

source.quote: Rs. 2,020.87 crore revenue expenditure misclassified as capital... Rs. 10,035 crore excess capital expenditure

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's guarantee load of Rs. 1,38,620 crore represents a contingent fiscal liability that is typically off-balance-sheet but can materialize suddenly. Most Karnataka state guarantees back borrowings by state PSUs in power, water, and urban infrastructure -- all sectors where cost recovery has historically been poor. If KPTCL (Karnataka Power Transmission), BESCOM, or Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike default on guaranteed debt, Karnataka's fiscal deficit could spike sharply. The Rs. 2,020.87 crore misclassification (revenue as capital) makes Karnataka's capital spending appear higher and current spending appear lower -- overstating the quality of the state's fiscal management.

source.quote: Government provided guarantees of Rs. 1,38,620 crore... Rs. 2,020.87 crore revenue expenditure misclassified as capital

recommendations: Karnataka Finance Department must publish a quarterly guarantee utilization report to the Legislature showing each guaranteed entity, the amount guaranteed, and whether any drawdowns/defaults occurred; the ₹2,020.87 crore misclassification must be rectified in the Finance Accounts; the ₹1,38,620 crore contingent liability must be stress-tested for default scenarios in the MTFP.

overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Bihar MGNREGS, 2026) Part II found: (1) Outstanding liabilities ₹1,903.58 crore -- wages ₹735.10 crore delayed; (2) Compensation -- ₹31.78 crore due for delayed wages; only ₹1.33 crore paid (4.19 per cent); (3) Material component shortfall -- 60:40 labour:material ratio not maintained; (4) NRM (Natural Resource Management) works incomplete; non-durable assets created; (5) Job Cards not updated; (6) Workers demanded work but no unemployment allowance.

stats.value: ₹1,903.58 crore total outstanding MGNREGS liabilities in Bihar; ₹735.10 crore specifically for delayed wage payments; workers waiting months/years for earned wages

source.quote: Rs. 1,903.58 crore outstanding MGNREGS liabilities of Bihar. Delayed wage payment of Rs. 735.10 crore

stats.value: ₹31.78 crore delayed-wage compensation due to MGNREGS workers; only ₹1.33 crore paid (4.19 per cent); ₹30.45 crore (95.81 per cent) withheld from workers who earned it under MGNREGA Section 3(3)

keyFindings.text: Bihar's Rs. 1,903.58 crore outstanding MGNREGS liability is a debt owed to some of India's poorest workers. MGNREGS wages in Bihar are typically Rs. 228-246 per day (2024-25 rate); Rs. 1,903.58 crore represents approximately 8 crore person-days of work already completed by workers who have not been paid. These are daily-wage workers with no savings buffer -- delayed wages create immediate food insecurity. The 4.19 per cent compensation rate (Rs. 1.33 crore of Rs. 31.78 crore) is even more troubling: the statutory right to delayed-wage compensation is being denied at a 95.81 per cent rate in Bihar, suggesting the compensation mechanism has been administratively disabled rather than functioning as designed.

source.quote: Rs. 1,903.58 crore outstanding MGNREGS liabilities of Bihar... compensation Rs. 31.78 crore due for delayed wages; only Rs. 1.33 crore paid (4.19 per cent)

recommendations: Bihar Rural Development Department must publish a monthly dashboard of MGNREGS pending wage liabilities by district, showing age of each outstanding payment (15-30 days, 30-60 days, 60+ days) -- this is a statutory obligation under MGNREGA Rule 29; all wages overdue beyond 15 days must automatically trigger compensation computation and payment without requiring worker applications; the ₹30.45 crore unpaid compensation must be released immediately from state funds pending GoI settlement; the MGNREGS Commissioner must personally explain to the Legislature why compensation was rejected at 95.81 per cent rate.

ministry: State Goods and Services Tax (SGST) Department, Government of Maharashtra
reportNo: Report No. 6 of 2025 (Compliance Audit -- SGST) -- Part III: E-Way Bill and Non-Filer ITC
title: Compliance Audit -- Maharashtra GST Part III: E-Way Bills ₹39,100 crore Phantom Firm Transactions; ₹4.90 crore Non-Filer ITC Availed After Cancellation; ₹12.02 crore ITC by Cancelled-Ab-Initio Registrants; 13 Bogus Firms (14 Buyers -- 184 EWBs -- ₹39,100 crore); No System Block for Non-Filers Availing ITC (FY 2019-23)
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (MH SGST, 2025) Part III found: (1) Phantom firms -- 13 bogus firms used 184 EWBs (₹39,100 crore) -- 14 buyers availed ITC; ₹9.26 crore SGST demand raised; (2) Non-filer ITC -- ₹4.90 crore ITC availed after GSTIN cancellation by non-filers who had not filed returns for 6+ months before cancellation; system did not block ITC on purchases from non-filers; (3) Cancelled-ab-initio ITC -- ₹12.02 crore ITC availed from cancelled-ab-initio (retrospectively cancelled) suppliers; (4) No reconciliation between EWB data and GSTR to identify phantom transactions; (5) ₹4.90 crore + ₹12.02 crore = ₹16.92 crore combined ITC leakage.

stats.label: Phantom firm EWBs ₹39,100 crore (13 firms -- 14 buyers)
stats.value: 13 bogus firms issued 184 E-Way Bills (₹39,100 crore) -- used to justify fraudulent ITC claims by 14 buying firms; ₹9.26 crore SGST demand raised; ITC on phantom goods

source.quote: E-Way Bills issued by 13 non-existent bogus firms, involving 184 EWBs of value Rs. 39,100 crore used by 14 buyers to avail ITC. Rs. 9.26 crore was raised as demand

stats.label: ₹4.90 crore ITC -- non-filer suppliers after cancellation
stats.value: ₹4.90 crore ITC availed by buyers from non-filer suppliers after GSTIN cancellation (non-filers had not filed returns for 6+ months before cancellation); GST system did not block ITC claims on purchases from non-filer/cancelled suppliers

source.quote: Rs. 4.90 crore non-filer ITC availed after cancellation by 26 of 33 cancellation GSTR 10

stats.label: ₹12.02 crore ITC from cancelled-ab-initio registrants
stats.value: ₹12.02 crore ITC availed from suppliers whose GST registration was subsequently cancelled ab-initio (retroactively cancelled from inception) -- ITC from registrations that never legally existed

source.quote: Rs. 12.02 crore cancelled-ab-initio ITC availed from suppliers whose registration was subsequently cancelled ab-initio

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 39,100 crore phantom EWB scheme -- 13 bogus firms issuing 184 E-Way Bills to enable 14 buyers to fraudulently claim ITC -- is one of the largest input-tax-credit fraud cases highlighted in Maharashtra's CAG audit. The scale is extraordinary: Rs. 39,100 crore in fake goods supposedly transported represents transactions larger than the annual GSDP of a small state. This is made possible by the disconnect between EWB issuance (which requires only a GSTIN and a vehicle number) and actual physical goods movement. EWBs can be issued for non-existent goods by non-existent firms if GSTIN verification fails. The Rs. 9.26 crore demand against 14 buyers is a tiny fraction of the ITC that may have been fraudulently claimed -- the actual ITC at stake at 18 per cent GST rate on Rs. 39,100 crore could be Rs. 7,000+ crore.

source.quote: E-Way Bills issued by 13 non-existent bogus firms, involving 184 EWBs of value Rs. 39,100 crore used by 14 buyers to avail ITC. Rs. 9.26 crore was raised as demand

keyFindings.text: The twin ITC leakages from non-filer suppliers (Rs. 4.90 crore) and cancelled-ab-initio suppliers (Rs. 12.02 crore) expose a fundamental GST system design gap: the GSTN (GST Network) allows buyers to avail ITC from suppliers who are non-compliant (have not filed returns for months), cancelled (registration cancelled but GSTR 10 not filed), or retroactively cancelled. A properly designed GST system should automatically block ITC claims on purchases from suppliers who are non-filers or cancelled. The absence of this system-level control means the entire burden of detecting fraudulent ITC falls on manual audit -- which can only cover a small fraction of the 1.3 crore registered taxpayers.

source.quote: Rs. 4.90 crore non-filer ITC availed after cancellation... Rs. 12.02 crore cancelled-ab-initio ITC availed

recommendations: Maharashtra SGST must immediately pursue full adjudication of all 14 buyers who used the 13 phantom firms' EWBs (₹39,100 crore) -- the demand of ₹9.26 crore must be supplemented by a comprehensive ITC audit covering all purchases from the 13 bogus firms; a cross-state alert should be sent to GSTN to flag all 14 buyer GSTINs for enhanced scrutiny; physical verification should be conducted at the buyers' declared premises.

GSTN must be requested by Maharashtra SGST to implement system-level ITC blocks: (a) no ITC should be auto-credited to a buyer if the supplier is a non-filer (returns not filed for 3+ months), (b) ITC from cancelled-ab-initio suppliers must be automatically reversed, (c) EWB generation should require physical vehicle GPS verification for invoices above ₹50 lakh; the ₹12.02 crore cancelled-ab-initio ITC must be recovered with interest and penalty within 60 days.

ministry: ST & SC Development Department, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2025 (Compliance Audit Report) -- PVTG Empowerment Fund
title: Compliance Audit -- Odisha PVTG Empowerment Fund: ₹6.39 crore Irregular Loans to Ineligible SHGs; ₹12.95 crore Loans (₹7.10 crore Outstanding -- 45 Per cent Repayment); ₹1.91 crore Cold Storage Defunct; ₹4 crore Sanctioned (2018-19) Not Implemented (January 2025); 69 Drinking Water Projects -- 38 (55 Per cent) Non-Functional; 40 Irrigation Projects -- 23 (58 Per cent) Non-Functional
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Odisha PVTG, 2025) found systemic failures in the OPELIP Empowerment Fund -- designed to provide livelihood support to India's most vulnerable tribal groups: (1) ₹6.39 crore irregular loans to ineligible SHGs (from ₹12.95 crore total); (2) repayment only 45 per cent (₹7.10 crore outstanding of ₹12.95 crore); (3) ₹1.91 crore cold storage facility defunct; (4) ₹4 crore sanctioned in 2018-19 not implemented as of January 2025 (7 years); (5) Infrastructure -- 38 of 69 drinking water projects (55 per cent) non-functional; 23 of 40 irrigation projects (58 per cent) non-functional; ₹3.59 crore sunk in non-operational assets.

stats.label: ₹6.39 crore irregular loans to ineligible SHGs
stats.value: ₹6.39 crore out of ₹12.95 crore PVTG Empowerment Fund loans paid to ineligible SHGs -- funds meant for the most marginalized tribal women's groups diverted to non-PVTG beneficiaries

source.quote: irregular payment of loan to ineligible SHGs (Rs. 6.39 crore) were noticed. Repayment rate was low (45 per cent), as out of Rs. 12.95 crore loan provided to 1,437 PVTG SHGs, Rs. 7.10 crore was outstanding for recovery

stats.label: Cold storage ₹1.91 crore defunct; ₹4 crore (2018-19) unimplemented
stats.value: ₹1.91 crore cold storage facility defunct -- no benefit to PVTG agricultural produce; ₹4 crore sanctioned in 2018-19 for PVTG livelihoods not implemented as of January 2025 (7 years)

source.quote: Cold storage Rs. 1.91 crore defunct (January 2025), despite sanction of funds (Rs. 4 crore) in 2018-19

stats.label: PVTG non-functional infrastructure (55-58 per cent)
stats.value: 38 of 69 drinking water projects (55 per cent) non-functional; 23 of 40 irrigation projects (58 per cent) non-functional; ₹3.59 crore sunk in non-operational infrastructure; 1.60 lakh PVTG (54 per cent) unserved by OPELIP

source.quote: 23 (58 per cent) out of 40 irrigation projects and 38 (55 per cent) out of 69 drinking water projects were expenditure of Rs. 3.59 crore, were lying non-operational

keyFindings.text: The PVTG Empowerment Fund's purpose is to help Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups -- India's most marginalized communities, legally recognized as requiring special protection -- build sustainable livelihoods through microfinance to SHGs. Lending 49 per cent of this fund (Rs. 6.39 crore) to ineligible SHGs completely defeats this purpose. The 45 per cent repayment rate (Rs. 7.10 crore outstanding) suggests even legitimate PVTG SHGs are struggling to repay -- which may reflect the vulnerability of the borrowers, the quality of livelihoods supported, or the absence of adequate handholding support. A defunct cold storage facility (Rs. 1.91 crore) and Rs. 4 crore of fund sanctioned in 2018-19 but still not deployed in 2025 (7 years) show that the empowerment programme is failing at every stage: targeting, disbursement, asset creation, and repayment.

source.quote: irregular payment of loan to ineligible SHGs (Rs. 6.39 crore)... Repayment rate was low (45 per cent)... Cold storage Rs. 1.91 crore defunct... despite sanction of funds (Rs. 4 crore) in 2018-19

recommendations: Odisha ST & SC Development Department must immediately recover the ₹6.39 crore from ineligible SHGs and redirect it to verified PVTG SHGs; an independent beneficiary audit should be conducted for all 1,437 SHGs that received PVTG Empowerment Fund loans to verify PVTG status; the ₹7.10 crore outstanding from legitimate PVTG SHGs should be reviewed -- for PVTG borrowers facing genuine hardship (drought, disability, widowhood), a structured repayment rescheduling should be offered; the ₹4 crore sanctioned 7 years ago should either be implemented within 30 days or surrendered; the cold storage facility should be repaired or handed to an NGO for operation.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Odisha
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2024-25) -- Part II
title: State Finances -- Odisha Part II: Committed + Subsidies 37 Per cent of Revenue Receipts; Fiscal Space 63 Per cent; BC Welfare ₹586.62 crore Capital Transferred to Revenue; Own-Tax Buoyancy Below 1 (GSDP +11.40 Per cent vs Tax Shortfall); Revenue Surplus Adjusted ₹22,651 crore; GSDP CAGR 13.30 Per cent from ₹5,40,185 crore (2020-21)
overview: CAG SFAR (Odisha, 2026) Part II found: (1) Committed expenditure + subsidies = 37 per cent Revenue Receipts -- 63 per cent fiscal space; the best fiscal space among most Indian states; (2) BC Welfare Department -- ₹586.62 crore of capital nature expenditure misclassified as revenue; (3) Own-tax buoyancy below 1: GSDP grew 11.40 per cent but own-tax growth lagged; Non-Tax Revenue -₹1,790 crore; (4) GSDP CAGR 13.30 per cent (₹5,40,185 crore 2020-21 to ₹8,90,038 crore 2024-25); (5) Revenue Receipts ₹1,83,963 crore (+2.43 per cent); own tax ₹56,516 crore; non-tax ₹51,221 crore.

stats.label: Committed + subsidies 37 per cent -- 63 per cent fiscal space
stats.value: Committed expenditure + subsidies ₹9,134 crore = 37 per cent of Revenue Receipts ₹1,83,963 crore; 63 per cent fiscal space for developmental priorities -- one of India's best fiscal positions

source.quote: nearly 37 per cent of Revenue Receipts were absorbed by committed expenditure and subsidies, leaving only 63 per cent fiscal space

stats.label: GSDP CAGR 13.30 per cent (₹5.40 lakh crore to ₹8.90 lakh crore)
stats.value: GSDP ₹8,90,038 crore (2024-25); CAGR 13.30 per cent from ₹5,40,185 crore (2020-21); Revenue Receipts +2.43 per cent ₹1,83,963 crore; own-tax buoyancy below 1 vs GSDP growth 11.40 per cent

source.quote: Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) grew at a CAGR of 13.30 per cent from Rs. 5,40,185 crore in 2020-21 to Rs. 8,90,038 crore in 2024-25. GSDP increased by 11.40 per cent Revenue Receipts (Rs. 1,83,963 crore) increased by 2.43 per cent

stats.value: ₹586.62 crore of capital nature expenditure (Backward Classes Welfare Department) misclassified as revenue expenditure -- inflating Revenue Expenditure and understating Capital Expenditure

source.quote: the State Government misclassified, Rs. 721 crore of expenditure Rs. 586.62 crore capital transferred

keyFindings.text: Odisha's 63 per cent fiscal space is exceptional by Indian state standards -- most large states have 20-40 per cent fiscal space after committed expenditure and subsidies. This gives Odisha the ability to respond to shocks (floods, crop failures, pandemics) without fiscal crisis, and to invest in long-term infrastructure without immediate borrowing constraints. GSDP CAGR of 13.30 per cent (Rs. 5.40 lakh crore to Rs. 8.90 lakh crore in 4 years) reflects Odisha's industrialization story -- steel, aluminum, ports -- combined with mining revenue from iron ore and coal. However, own-tax buoyancy below 1 (tax growing slower than GSDP) suggests the formal economy is not fully captured in the tax base; the Rs. 1,790 crore decline in Non-Tax Revenue (mineral royalties, forest receipts) is worth investigating.

source.quote: nearly 37 per cent of Revenue Receipts were absorbed by committed expenditure and subsidies, leaving only 63 per cent fiscal space. GSDP grew at a CAGR of 13.30 per cent

recommendations: Odisha Finance Department should leverage its 63 per cent fiscal space by directing at least 30 per cent of Revenue Receipts to non-committed developmental expenditure -- tribal welfare, health, education -- while the ₹586.62 crore BC Welfare misclassification must be rectified in the next Finance Accounts; an own-tax buoyancy improvement plan should target bringing the buoyancy ratio above 1.1 by expanding GST compliance and improving stamp duty collection in Odisha's rapidly urbanizing areas.

reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2025 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2023-24) -- Part II
title: State Finances -- Nagaland Part II: Budget Utilization 55.55-91.29 Per cent Range (5-Year Trend); Revenue Expenditure 35.38 Per cent of GSDP; Committed Expenditure CAGR 8.40 Per cent (Outpacing GSDP CAGR 8.96 Per cent); GoI Grants Down 60.04 Per cent to 46.13 Per cent; Own Tax Revenue ₹136.21 crore (+9.32 Per cent); ₹228.57 crore Guarantees (2023-24)
overview: CAG SFAR (Nagaland, 2025) Part II found: (1) Budget utilization ranged 55.55-91.29 per cent over 5 years -- wide variance suggesting unrealistic budgeting; (2) Revenue Expenditure 35.38 per cent of GSDP (82.60 per cent of total); (3) Committed expenditure CAGR 8.40 per cent (₹7,874.46 crore to ₹10,873.14 crore) approaching GSDP CAGR 8.96 per cent -- fiscal risk if trend continues; (4) GoI grants declining (60.04 per cent to 46.13 per cent of Revenue Receipts) while own-tax growing from small base; (5) Capital Expenditure ₹3,122.52 crore (+15.47 per cent, 17.41 per cent of total); (6) Inflexible expenditure ₹1,186.01 crore (-11.14 per cent); (7) Guarantees ₹228.57 crore.

At the end of 2023-24, the Government provided guarantees of Rs. 228.57 crore

stats.label: Committed expenditure 67.30 per cent of Revenue Receipts (CAGR 8.40 per cent)
stats.value: ₹10,873.14 crore committed expenditure (CAGR 8.40 per cent, 2019-24); 67.30 per cent Revenue Receipts; 73.37 per cent Revenue Expenditure; inflexible expenditure ₹1,186.01 crore (-11.14 per cent vs previous year)

source.quote: Committed expenditure steadily increased by Rs. 2,998.68 crore at a CAGR of 8.40 per cent from Rs. 7,874.46 crore in 2019-20 to Rs. 10,873.14 crore in 2023-24. The Committed Expenditure during the year 2023-24 was 67.30 per cent of the Revenue Receipts and 73.37 per cent of the Revenue Expenditure. Further, the inflexible expenditure (Rs. 1,186.01 crore) decreased by 11.14 per cent during 2023-24 over the previous year (Rs. 1,334.71 crore)

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's committed expenditure CAGR of 8.40 per cent is almost at parity with GSDP CAGR of 8.96 per cent. This is a critical warning sign: if committed expenditure grows at the same rate as GSDP, it consumes the same share of GDP every year and never leaves room for new developmental spending without additional debt. The 67.30 per cent of Revenue Receipts absorbed by committed expenditure means only Rs. 1 in every Rs. 3 of state revenue is available for discretionary developmental priorities (health, education, infrastructure beyond salary/pension). For a state managing a post-conflict peace process and needing to demonstrate economic dividends to its population, this fiscal rigidity directly constrains the government's ability to deliver visible development.

source.quote: Committed expenditure steadily increased by Rs. 2,998.68 crore at a CAGR of 8.40 per cent... 67.30 per cent of the Revenue Receipts

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's budget utilization dropping to 55.55 per cent (2023-24) from 91.29 per cent (2021-22) is a 36-percentage-point collapse in absorption capacity in two years. This matters because capital expenditure is the productive part of the budget -- building roads, schools, hospitals. A state that budgets Rs. 3,000 crore but only spends Rs. 1,666 crore is either (a) unable to execute projects for want of contractors, materials, or technical staff, or (b) budgeting unrealistically high to show intent rather than commitment. The fiscal deficit at 4.26 per cent GSDP becomes harder to justify if the capital expenditure it is financing is only 55 per cent utilized -- borrowing more than you can spend inflates debt without delivering equivalent infrastructure.

source.quote: ranged between 55.55 per cent (2023-24) and 91.29 per cent (2021-22)

recommendations: Nagaland Finance Department must investigate why capital expenditure utilization fell to 55.55 per cent in 2023-24 -- if the bottleneck is contractor availability or terrain/weather, the budget should be realistically adjusted; if the bottleneck is administrative approval, the delegation of financial powers to district-level officers should be enhanced; a surplus-fund management policy should ensure GoI grants not spent in the year are parked in FDs rather than idle bank accounts.

Nagaland must initiate a committed expenditure rationalization review -- pension liabilities (a major driver of committed expenditure in NE states) should be assessed for migration to the National Pension System (NPS) for new employees; the falling inflexible expenditure (₹1,186.01 crore, -11.14 per cent) is a positive sign that should be continued; guarantees of ₹228.57 crore must be monitored against the FRBM guarantee ceiling and the contingent liability must be disclosed in the state budget speech.

ministry: Public Health Engineering Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh
reportNo: Report No. 5 of 2026 (Performance Audit -- Jal Jeevan Mission, MP) -- Part III
title: Performance Audit -- MP JJM Part III: Non-Prioritization of SC/ST PVTG Villages; Flawed SVS Estimations Causing Cost Escalation; Non-Utilization of Funds -- Central Grants Not Released; JJM Funds Diverted on Inadmissible Activities; Sustainability -- No Greywater Management; Irregular FHTCs Without Water Supply; Non-Functional VWSCs (2019-24)

keyFindings.text: JJM fund diversion to inadmissible construction activities combined with parking funds outside PFMS creates a dual accountability failure: (1) money meant for safe water delivery is being spent on construction unrelated to JJM objectives, and (2) PFMS-bypassed funds are invisible to GoI monitoring systems, making it impossible for central officials to track expenditure against targets. The non-release of Central grants due to fund non-utilization is a counterintuitive self-harm: MP is not spending the money it has, so the Centre withholds additional tranches, further slowing scheme completion. The root cause appears to be weak contract management -- delayed work awards and unrealistic site assessments mean works start late, utilization falls short, and the Centre's release conditions go unmet.

keyFindings.text: The absence of greywater management in JJM schemes is a medium-term environmental and public health risk. JJM is connecting lakhs of rural households to piped water for the first time -- this is generating significant new volumes of greywater (wastewater from kitchens and bathrooms) that previously did not exist because households had no running water. Without drainage infrastructure or greywater recycling, this water accumulates near homes, creating stagnant pools that breed mosquitoes (malaria, dengue risk) and contaminate the shallow groundwater that many villages also use for drinking and irrigation. The non-functional VWSCs mean there is no community-level maintenance capacity; once the PHED construction teams leave, there is no one to operate and maintain chlorinators, water quality test kits, or minor scheme repairs.

recommendations: MP PHED must bring all JJM funds within PFMS within 30 days and stop all expenditure on inadmissible activities immediately -- any expenditure already incurred on inadmissible activities must be quantified and referred to the state Finance Department for recovery; a quarterly JJM Utilization Certificate must be submitted to GoI to ensure Central grant releases are not blocked; the 27 per cent MVS completion rate requires accelerating contract awards for all incomplete schemes with a hard December 2025 deadline.

MP must develop and implement a Greywater Action Plan for all JJM-covered Gram Panchayats -- soak pits, low-cost drainage, or constructed wetlands should be provided for every cluster of 50+ FHTCs; all 6,000+ VWSCs in JJM-covered villages should be activated through Gram Panchayat standing resolutions with at least one trained VWSC operator per village; JJM AAPs must be revised to ensure all 59,288 SC/ST-dominated habitations are covered in the next 2 years.

keyFindings.text: JJM's Rs. 25,000 per FHTC norm exists specifically to ensure cost discipline -- if the actual cost exceeds this, the excess must be justified and the variance explained to GoI. Rs. 586.67 crore of extra FHTC costs in MP suggest that the state either (a) procured supplies at inflated rates, (b) used non-standard pipe materials or laying methods, or (c) approved cost revisions without GoI concurrence. This is a direct diversion of national programme funds to cover cost overruns that the state should have managed through better contract management. Combined with Rs. 9.38 crore avoidable SQC (Supervisory/Quality Control agency) expenditure and Rs. 6.47 crore road-crossing extra cost, the total avoidable/extra expenditure exceeds Rs. 600 crore on this scheme alone.

keyFindings.text: JJM's operational guidelines explicitly prioritize SC/ST-dominated habitations, PVTG villages, aspirational districts, and fluoride/arsenic-affected areas. Deprioritizing 59,288 SC/ST habitations in Annual Action Plans -- leaving them for later rounds when the easiest (least expensive, least complex) habitations have already been covered -- is a systematic equity failure. These communities have historically had the worst water access; JJM was supposed to be corrective. With NABL lab accreditation expired for 13-18 months in 4 districts, there is no legally valid water quality certificate for FHTCs in those districts -- meaning households may be receiving piped water of unknown quality. For SC/ST and PVTG communities often located in groundwater-stressed zones with higher fluoride/arsenic risk, this combination of deprioritization and quality-testing failure is deeply concerning.

MP must revise JJM Annual Action Plans to front-load all 59,288 SC/ST-dominated habitations in the next 2 years; NABL accreditation for all 4 expired district labs must be renewed within 30 days; arsenic testing instruments and centrifuges must be procured and installed; the Indore scheme supplying 51.34 MLD from dead storage since 2016 must be immediately referred to the dam operator for a corrective drawdown strategy or alternative source development to avoid supplying sub-standard water to Indore city households.

keyFindings.text: The inclusion of 11,94,063 private/own source connections in the JJM FHTC count is a significant data integrity failure. JJM's core mandate is to provide NEW government-funded tap connections to households that previously had none. Including private connections inflates the reported FHTC count by approximately 2 lakh, making MP's JJM progress appear better than it actually is. Compounding this, E-Jal Shakti portal shows FHTCs for villages where water supply has not commenced or schemes are incomplete -- these are "paper connections" (physically installed taps with no water flowing). When the GoI and Parliament review JJM progress, they are looking at numbers that are systematically overstated. MP's actual FHTC coverage (excluding private connections and non-functional schemes) would be significantly below the reported 69 per cent.

source.quote: 11,94,063 private/own source tap connections were not the actual beneficiaries of JJM tap connections, same were also included in the JJM FHTCs in the JJM portal... E-Jal shakti portal displayed FHTCs provided to the households of those villages in the test checked districts wherein water supply had not commenced

keyFindings.text: Diverting 1.62 per cent of JJM funds from water quality monitoring to construction -- while only spending 0.38 per cent on the mandated 2 per cent water quality allocation -- means that even where water connections are functional, water safety is not being verified. JJM's goal is "safe and adequate drinking water" -- not just any piped water. In rural Madhya Pradesh, groundwater in many areas contains fluoride, arsenic, iron, and nitrates above safe limits. The NGT's 2020 directive to cover all arsenic/fluoride-affected areas was missed; Electrolytic Defluorination Units installed in only 18 of 33 fluoride-affected villages in Dindori means 15 villages continue receiving fluoride-contaminated water through the very taps that JJM installed. Fluoride poisoning causes skeletal fluorosis -- an irreversible crippling disease.

source.quote: Government spent only 0.38 per cent and diverted 1.62 per cent for construction... Electrolytic Defluorination Unit were installed in only 18 villages out of 33 fluoride-affected villages in Dindori

recommendations: MP PHED must immediately audit the E-Jal Shakti portal data -- all 11,94,063 private/own source connections included as JJM FHTCs must be excluded from the official count; villages shown with FHTCs where water supply has not commenced must be flagged as "non-functional" in the portal; the revised (accurate) FHTC count should be submitted to GoI within 30 days; LDs must be imposed on all contractors responsible for non-functional FHTCs at 28 inspected sites and recovered from pending bills.

MP must immediately deploy water quality testing kits in all 33 fluoride-affected villages in Dindori and complete Electrolytic Defluorination Unit installation in the 15 pending villages within 60 days; the ₹1.62 per cent diverted DWQM&S funds must be restored to water quality activities and a quarterly water quality testing programme launched in all JJM-covered GPs; JJM funds parked outside PFMS must be brought into PFMS within 30 days; VWSCs must be activated through Gram Panchayat resolutions with trained operators for scheme maintenance.

keyFindings.text: Building and Other Construction Workers (BOCW) are among India's most vulnerable labour force: employed informally, often on daily wages, with no fixed employer, no ESI or PF coverage, and high risk of work-related injury. The BOCW Act and Cess exist precisely to create a welfare fund for them. Goa's GBOCWWB failing to: (a) hold Board meetings (12 years of shortfall), (b) register establishments with 500+ workers, (c) pay wage loss compensation, (d) publicise welfare schemes to workers, and (e) register migrant workers -- means the welfare apparatus exists on paper but provides no real benefit to the construction workers it was designed to serve. Without worker registration, workers cannot access any scheme. Without scheme publicity, even registered workers don't claim benefits.

source.quote: registration of establishments employing more than 500 workers was not of 12 years. Substantial shortfall in conducting Board meetings... Non-payment of wage loss compensation to BOC Workers... Lack of proactive efforts for registration of BOC workers

keyFindings.text: Parking the BOCW Welfare Fund in savings bank accounts instead of time deposits, debt funds, or other instruments available to statutory bodies represents a foreseeable and avoidable revenue loss. BOCW Boards across India hold substantial surplus funds (collected from cess but not yet distributed as welfare); parking these in savings accounts earning 3-4 per cent instead of fixed deposits earning 7-7.5 per cent (FY 2023) causes meaningful interest losses that reduce the fund available for workers' welfare. The absence of an Internal Auditor means there is no independent check on financial management, cess collection accuracy, or expense claims -- creating conditions where financial irregularities can persist undetected.

source.quote: Board incurred financial loss due to parking of funds in savings accounts which indicated ineffective financial management... No Internal Auditor was appointed

recommendations: Goa Labour Department must appoint a full-time Internal Auditor for GBOCWWB within 30 days -- recruitment rules for vacant posts should be finalized immediately; BOCW Welfare Fund corpus should be invested in fixed deposits/government securities to maximize returns for workers' welfare; the ₹4.79 crore delayed cess should be recovered with penal interest from the defaulting establishments; BOCW Welfare Fund annual accounts must be audited and published on the Board website.

GBOCWWB must conduct a state-wide BOC worker registration drive -- every construction site in Goa should be surveyed and all workers (including migrant workers) registered as BOCW beneficiaries; wage loss compensation claims must be activated immediately with a 30-day processing SLA; all establishments with 250+ workers must be inspected for canteen provision within 60 days; non-compliant establishments should be prosecuted under BOCW Act; welfare scheme awareness camps must be held at all major construction sites quarterly.

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's fiscal deficit at 4.26 per cent of GSDP -- exceeding the FRBM 3 per cent ceiling by 1.26 percentage points -- is concerning for a small state with a Rs. 41,887 crore economy. However, Nagaland has a Revenue Surplus (Rs. 1,335.43 crore = 3.19 per cent GSDP), meaning the deficit is driven by capital borrowing for investment, not current consumption. This is the textbook "good deficit" -- borrowing to invest -- but the fiscal deficit ceiling exists to prevent over-borrowing even for capital purposes. The committed expenditure at 67.30 per cent of Revenue Receipts (Rs. 10,873.14 crore) leaves only 32.70 per cent for developmental and capital spending from revenue, requiring significant capital borrowing for infrastructure investment.

source.quote: Fiscal deficit was Rs. 1,784.45 crore during 2023-24 which was 4.26 per cent of GSDP... the State had a Revenue surplus of Rs. 1,335.43 crore which was 3.19 per cent of GSDP... Committed Expenditure during the year 2023-24 was 67.30 per cent of the Revenue Receipts

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's dependence on GoI Grants-in-Aid declining from 60.04 per cent to 46.13 per cent of Revenue Receipts over 5 years is a structural fiscal transition. Nagaland has historically been one of the most GoI-dependent states (the Naga peace process era saw special grants); as the grant component normalizes, Nagaland must grow its own tax revenue to maintain fiscal balance. Own Tax Revenue growth of 9.32 per cent in a single year is positive, but starting from a small base, own tax revenue remains a small fraction of total receipts. The 15.47 per cent growth in capital expenditure (Rs. 3,122.52 crore) and 17.41 per cent share of total expenditure shows Nagaland is investing, but the fiscal deficit ceiling requires managing the pace of capital borrowing.

source.quote: the share of Grants-in-aid in Revenue Receipts decreased from 60.04 per cent in 2019-20 to 46.13 per cent in 2023-24. Capital Expenditure (Rs. 3,122.52 crore) increased by Rs. 418.30 crore (15.47 per cent)

recommendations: Nagaland Finance Department must present a FRBM compliance path to the state legislature -- bringing fiscal deficit from 4.26 per cent to below 3 per cent of GSDP within 2 years requires either increasing revenue receipts or containing capital expenditure growth; a mid-year fiscal review should be institutionalized; any excess borrowing above the 3 per cent GSDP ceiling must be reported to GoI immediately as required under FRBM.

Nagaland must accelerate Own Tax Revenue growth to offset declining GoI grants -- the 9.32 per cent own tax growth is a good start, but the base must be expanded by bringing informal businesses into the GST net, improving property tax collection in municipalities, and rationalising excise and vehicle tax administration; committed expenditure CAGR of 8.40 per cent growing faster than GSDP CAGR (8.96 per cent) suggests the state is at fiscal risk of crowding out development spending within 5 years if the trend continues.

keyFindings.text: The MGNREGS Ombudsman -- an independent grievance mechanism with legal authority to recommend recovery from erring officials -- found Rs. 1.61 crore recoverable from officials who made irregular wage payments. Yet only Rs. 14.54 lakh (9 per cent) was actually recovered. This 91 per cent non-enforcement of the Ombudsman's recovery directions fundamentally undermines the accountability architecture of MGNREGS. If officials can make irregular payments and face no financial consequence even after the Ombudsman recommends recovery, the deterrence against future irregularities collapses. The 99 per cent rejection rate for delayed-wage compensation claims (Rs. 1.02 crore of Rs. 1.03 crore rejected) is similarly alarming -- either Odisha has a systematic process of denying workers their statutory compensation rights, or the rejection criteria are being applied incorrectly.

source.quote: Out of Rs. 1.61 crore recommended for recovery by the MGNREGS Ombudsman from the erring officials, only Rs. 14.54 lakh was recovered... Rs. 1.02 crore was rejected

keyFindings.text: 1.22 lakh Odisha households demanded MGNREGS work, received neither work nor unemployment allowance -- a double statutory violation. MGNREGS guarantees 100 days of employment on demand; if work is not provided within 15 days, the household is entitled to unemployment allowance (25-50 per cent of minimum wage). Zero unemployment allowance paid to 1.22 lakh eligible households is a direct denial of a constitutional-legislative guarantee. In a state where 32.59 per cent of the population (2011-12) lives below the poverty line, MGNREGS employment and unemployment allowance are critical income floors -- their denial directly translates to deprivation and hunger.

source.quote: 1.22 lakh HHs demanded work. This figure ranged between 0.20 and 16.18 per cent in Despite demand for work, 1.22 lakh HHs unemployment allowance was paid to these 1.22 lakh HHs, as envisaged

recommendations: Odisha Rural Development Department must immediately process unemployment allowance for all 1.22 lakh HHs who demanded work and received neither work nor allowance -- this is a statutory obligation under Section 7 of the MGNREGA; a time-bound clearance (30 days) should be directed by the state; a complaint mechanism allowing HHs to claim unpaid unemployment allowance online should be launched; all 0.82 lakh rejected Job Card applications must be reviewed with each rejection individually justified and communicated to the applicant.

Odisha must enforce Ombudsman recovery directions -- the ₹1.465 crore outstanding recovery from erring officials must be recovered within 90 days through salary deduction or bank account attachment; the MGNREGS Commissioner must personally review all 119 delayed-wage compensation rejections (₹1.02 crore) and determine whether rejections were legally valid; if not, compensation must be paid within 30 days; going forward, rejected compensation claims must be publicly listed on the MGNREGS state portal with stated legal reasons.

overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2025 (MH SGST) Part II found: (1) ITC mismatches -- ₹6,666.10 crore mismatch (119 cases) across ITC reversal, RCM ITC, ISD distribution, annual return, and financial statement reconciliation; (2) Large ITC case -- ₹4,359.78 crore ITC available; taxpayer claims ₹4,278.13 crore reversed, ₹81.66 crore rightly availed -- audit could not verify (supporting documents not provided); (3) Revenue -- ₹154.64 crore interest + misclassification (20 cases); ₹8.91 crore SGST demand with interest+penalty; (4) Cancellation failures -- 26 of 33 taxpayers did not file GSTR 10 after cancellation; no tax demand in cancellation orders; multiple delayed cancellations (9 months); 4 charge offices did not issue GSTR 3A notices.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 6,666.10 crore in ITC mismatches across 119 Maharashtra GST cases -- involving ITC reversal (Rs. 4,359.78 crore), RCM ITC (Rs. 77.62 crore), ISD distribution (Rs. 32.53 crore), annual return, and financial statement reconciliation -- shows that Maharashtra's GST ITC scrutiny system is systematically failing to detect overused ITC. The Rs. 4,359.78 crore ITC case is particularly concerning: this is the single largest ITC mismatch in the report. The taxpayer claims Rs. 4,278.13 crore was reversed (only Rs. 81.66 crore net ITC claimed), but the SGST department could not verify this because supporting documents were not provided. A DRC-07 demand of Rs. 8.91 crore was issued -- but this is only 0.2 per cent of the Rs. 4,359.78 crore ITC pool; the Rs. 81.66 crore disputed ITC itself deserves full adjudication with document verification.

source.quote: mismatches in availing ITC, discharge of tax liability and turnover were noticed in 119 cases involving mismatch of Rs. 6,666.10 crore... out of the total ITC available of Rs. 4,359.78 crore, taxpayer had reversed ITC of Rs. 4,278.13 crore and remaining credit of Rs. 81.66 crore was rightly availed. The reply could not be verified as supporting

keyFindings.text: GSTR 10 (final return after GST cancellation) non-filing by 26 of 33 cancelled taxpayers means Maharashtra SGST has no record of the closing stock position of these businesses -- and therefore cannot calculate the ITC that should have been reversed on that stock. When a business closes/cancels its GST registration, it must reverse ITC on unsold stock; if GSTR 10 is not filed, this reversal is not made, allowing the business to effectively pocket the ITC on unsold inventory. Issuing cancellation orders without demanding tax arrears (found in all cancellation orders examined) means the department is administratively cancelling registrations but leaving tax recovery undone -- allowing cancelled taxpayers to escape their GST liabilities.

source.quote: 26 cancellation GSTR 10 till January 2024... tax arrears were not demanded in any of the cancellation orders

recommendations: Maharashtra SGST Department must implement automated GSTR 10 follow-up -- when a taxpayer's GST registration is cancelled, the system should automatically generate a GSTR 3A notice after 3 months if GSTR 10 is not filed; the 26 non-filing cancellation cases should be served demand notices within 30 days requiring GSTR 10 filing or best-judgment assessment of closing stock ITC; all future cancellation orders must include a statement of assessed tax arrears based on the taxpayer's last filed returns.

Maharashtra SGST must conduct a comprehensive ITC reversal audit for all taxpayers with ITC available above ₹10 crore (the 119-case ₹6,666.10 crore mismatch suggests the issue is systemic, not isolated) -- GSTR 9 (annual return) data should be cross-validated with GSTR 3B monthly returns and audited financial statements for all large taxpayers; the ₹4,359.78 crore ITC case must be specifically adjudicated with mandatory documentary verification of every ITC reversal claimed by the taxpayer; the ₹77.62 crore excess RCM ITC must be recovered with interest.

keyFindings.text: PSPCL's swing from profit Rs. 1,069.21 crore (2021-22) to loss Rs. 4,775.93 crore (2022-23) -- a Rs. 5,845.14 crore reversal in a single year -- is catastrophic for Punjab's fiscal position. PSPCL's accumulated losses require state government bailouts, which add to Punjab's already-stressed fiscal position (Punjab is among India's most fiscally stressed states, with one of the highest debt-GSDP ratios). The primary driver cited is "substantial increase in power purchase costs" -- this reflects Punjab's inability to match power purchase costs with consumer tariffs, because free power to farmers (and heavily subsidised power to domestic consumers) prevents PSPCL from recovering costs. AT&C losses of 14.08-82.53 per cent (93 towns) mean that in the worst-performing towns, for every unit of power purchased, 82.53 per cent is not billed or not recovered.

source.quote: The overall profits of Rs. 1,269.90 crore earned by the working SPSEs in 2021-22 has turned into losses of Rs. 4,809.76 crore in 2022-23... remaining 93 towns, the losses ranged between 14.08 and 82.53 per cent

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 94.79 crore avoidable deduction from GoI subsidy claims -- which cost PSPCL Rs. 8.05 crore in interest -- illustrates how internal process failures compound PSPCL's financial distress. This is not a market or policy problem; it is a self-inflicted financial injury from administrative error in filing subsidy claims. The Rs. 64.37 crore in unmetered agricultural energy consumption means PSPCL has no record of how much electricity was actually consumed by farmers -- preventing any accurate loss calculation or targeted efficiency improvement. This is a fundamental metering gap that makes AT&C loss reduction impossible to achieve systematically.

source.quote: resulted in avoidable deduction of Rs. 94.79 crore from the provisional subsidy claims by the GoI and consequential interest loss of Rs. 8.05 crore... energy consumption valuing Rs. 64.37 crore in respect of Agricultural meter readings. The Company was unable to compute distribution losses of AP feeders

recommendations: Punjab government must require PSPCL to publish a 3-year Turnaround Plan (TAP) with specific quarterly targets for: (a) AT&C loss reduction to below 14 per cent across all towns; (b) power purchase cost renegotiation; (c) metering of all agricultural feeders (the ₹64.37 crore unmetered consumption must be fully metered within 12 months to enable accurate loss calculation); (d) revenue collection improvement from commercial consumers; the ₹94.79 crore GoI subsidy claim error must be corrected in the next claim cycle.

Punjab must implement a hard ceiling on PSPCL state government guarantee -- any new guarantee or bailout above ₹500 crore should require cabinet approval and an independent assessment of PSPCL's repayment capacity; towns with AT&C losses above 50 per cent (82.53 per cent highest) should be placed under emergency metering programs -- all distribution transformers and feeders must be energy-metered within 6 months to identify loss sources; PSPCL board must report quarterly AT&C loss data by town to the Legislature.

Repayment rate was low (45 per cent), as out of Rs. 12.95 crore loan provided to 1,437 PVTG SHGs, Rs. 7.10 crore was outstanding for recovery

keyFindings.text: Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs) are India's most marginalized communities -- constitutionally and legally recognized as requiring special protection. 1.60 lakh of Odisha's 2.94 lakh PVTG population (54 per cent) being left completely unserved by OPELIP (Odisha PVTG Empowerment and Livelihoods Improvement Programme) -- simply because their 1,138 villages were identified after the programme started in 2020 -- is an administrative failure with profound human consequences. These are communities with no other safety net. The Rs. 594.78 crore invested so far also delivered poor quality outcomes: 55-58 per cent of drinking water and irrigation projects are non-functional; Rs. 4 crore sanctioned in 2018-19 was not implemented even by January 2025 (7 years later).

source.quote: 1.60 lakh (54 per cent) PVTG implemented only in 541 villages having 1.34 lakh PVTG population... 38 (55 per cent) out of 69 drinking water projects were... non-operational. (January 2025), despite sanction of funds (Rs. 4 crore) in 2018-19

keyFindings.text: Rs. 9,898.70 crore spent on 12.96 lakh MGNREGS works that remain incomplete is a massive inefficiency. MGNREGS is supposed to create durable community assets (bunds, ponds, roads, plantations) while providing wage employment. Incomplete works deliver neither -- workers are paid for labor, but the community asset is not created. Rs. 55.32 crore additionally spent on non-durable assets means that even completed works failed to create lasting benefits. The Rs. 1.02 crore in delayed wage compensation claims being rejected is particularly concerning -- MGNREGS compensation is a legal entitlement that cannot simply be "rejected" without the process being independently reviewable; the rejection rate suggests systemic denial of workers' statutory rights.

source.quote: 12.96 lakh works (35 per cent) could not be completed even after incurring an expenditure of Rs. 9,898.70 crore... Rs. 55.32 crore was utilised on creation of 1,317 non-durable assets... Rs. 1.02 crore was rejected

recommendations: Odisha ST & SC Development Department must extend OPELIP to all 1,138 newly identified villages with 1.60 lakh PVTG population within 2 years -- a supplementary action plan with time-bound coverage targets should be submitted to GoI; the 55-58 per cent non-functional drinking water/irrigation infrastructure must be repaired within 6 months; the ₹3.59 crore in non-functional assets should be investigated for contractor quality failures; the ₹4 crore sanctioned 7 years ago and not implemented should be allocated to a specific agency with 90-day implementation mandate.

Odisha Rural Development Department must publish the MGNREGS Ombudsman's rejected compensation claims for public review -- ₹1.02 crore in claims cannot be rejected without transparent, individually stated reasons accessible to the workers; the 12.96 lakh incomplete works should be prioritised for completion with a ₹2,000 crore dedicated annual allocation; ₹55.32 crore in non-durable asset creation should be audited and the responsible Panchayat Samiti officials penalized; the ₹6.39 crore loans to ineligible SHGs must be recovered immediately.

title: State Finances -- Odisha: Revenue Surplus ₹22,651 crore (2.54 Per cent GSDP); GSDP ₹8,90,038 crore; Total Liabilities 15.48 Per cent GSDP (Well Below 25 Per cent FRBM); Subsidies +₹5,011 crore (121.54 Per cent) to ₹9,134 crore; Capital Expenditure ₹45,481 crore (22 Per cent); ₹721 crore Revenue Misclassified as Capital; Non-Tax Revenue -₹1,790 crore (FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 3 of 2026 (Odisha SFAR FY 2024-25) found: (1) Fiscal strength -- GSDP ₹8,90,038 crore (CAGR 13.30 per cent); Revenue Surplus ₹22,651 crore (2.54 per cent GSDP); Fiscal Deficit ₹25,042 crore (2.81 per cent, within 3 per cent FRBM); Total liabilities ₹1,37,784 crore (15.48 per cent GSDP) -- well below 25 per cent ceiling; (2) Revenue -- Own Tax Revenue ₹56,516 crore; Non-Tax Revenue ₹51,221 crore (-₹1,790 crore); Revenue buoyancy below 1 vs GSDP growth 11.40 per cent; (3) Subsidies -- surged ₹5,011 crore (121.54 per cent) to ₹9,134 crore -- mainly input assistance ₹5,848.70 crore; (4) Committed + subsidies = 37 per cent Revenue Receipts; 63 per cent fiscal space; Capital Expenditure ₹45,481 crore (22 per cent); (5) Misclassification ₹721 crore revenue as capital.

stats.label: Revenue Surplus ₹22,651 crore (rare among Indian states)
stats.value: Revenue Surplus ₹22,651 crore (2.54 per cent GSDP); Fiscal Deficit ₹25,042 crore (2.81 per cent GSDP) -- within FRBM 3 per cent; total liabilities 15.48 per cent GSDP vs 25 per cent ceiling

source.quote: During the year 2024-25, the State recorded a Revenue Surplus of Rs. 22,651 crore (2.54 per cent of GSDP). The Fiscal Deficit of the State was Rs. 25,042 crore (2.81 per cent of GSDP), which was well within the stipulated ceiling of 3 per cent of GSDP. Total liabilities stood at 15.48 per cent of GSDP in 2024-25, significantly below the prescribed limit of 25 per cent

stats.label: Subsidies surged 121.54 per cent (₹5,011 crore)
stats.value: Subsidies ₹9,134 crore (2024-25) -- +₹5,011 crore (+121.54 per cent) from previous year; mainly input assistance ₹5,848.70 crore; exceeded original budget ₹8,068 crore

source.quote: The total Subsidy expenditure of Odisha in 2024-25 rose sharply to Rs. 9,134 crore, exceeding the original budget of Rs. 8,068 crore and increasing by Rs. 5,011 crore (121.54 per cent) compared to the previous year. This was mainly due to grant of Rs. 5,848.70 crore as input assistance

stats.label: Capital Expenditure ₹45,481 crore (22 per cent of total)
stats.value: Capital Expenditure ₹45,481 crore (22 per cent of total expenditure) -- improved from 16 per cent (2020-21) to 22 per cent (2024-25); ₹721 crore revenue misclassified as capital

source.quote: developmental spending from 16 per cent of Total Expenditure in 2020-21 to 22 per cent in 2024-25. The Capital Expenditure as per the Accounts of the State was Rs. 45,481 crore. Audit found that, during 2024-25, the State Government misclassified, Rs. 721 crore of expenditure

stats.label: Revenue buoyancy below 1 (own-tax underperforming)
stats.value: GSDP growth 11.40 per cent vs Own Tax Revenue growth (₹54,427 crore to ₹56,516 crore = 3.8 per cent); revenue buoyancy well below 1; Non-Tax Revenue -₹1,790 crore

source.quote: generated higher Own Tax Revenue (Rs. 56,516 crore) in absolute terms, compared to previous year (Rs. 54,427 crore) but could not keep pace with the GSDP growth of 11.40 per cent. Further, Non-Tax Revenue (Rs. 51,221 crore) also decreased by Rs. 1,790 crore over the previous year (Rs. 53,011 crore)

keyFindings.text: Odisha is one of India's rare Revenue Surplus states -- Rs. 22,651 crore revenue surplus (2.54 per cent GSDP) -- meaning it earns more from revenues than it spends on current expenditure before debt servicing. This is a strong fiscal foundation. Total liabilities at 15.48 per cent GSDP are exceptionally low (national average 27.63 per cent) -- Odisha has significant debt capacity. However, the 121.54 per cent surge in subsidies (primarily input assistance Rs. 5,848.70 crore, a one-time agricultural support payment that exceeded the original budget) shows that fiscal discipline can be tested by political decisions. The committed + subsidy burden at only 37 per cent of Revenue Receipts leaves 63 per cent fiscal space -- far better than heavily indebted states like West Bengal (26 per cent fiscal space) and Bihar.

source.quote: Revenue Surplus of Rs. 22,651 crore (2.54 per cent of GSDP)... Total liabilities stood at 15.48 per cent of GSDP... nearly 37 per cent of Revenue Receipts were absorbed by committed expenditure and subsidies, leaving only 63 per cent fiscal space

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 721 crore misclassification of Revenue Expenditure as Capital (plus Rs. 586.62 crore of capital nature transferred from Backward Classes Welfare Department) is the key area of concern in an otherwise strong fiscal picture. Odisha's own-tax revenue growing only 3.8 per cent while GSDP grew 11.40 per cent suggests that the state is not fully capturing the benefit of rapid economic growth in its tax base -- own-tax buoyancy well below 1. Non-Tax revenue declining Rs. 1,790 crore is also concerning since Odisha's mineral royalties and forest receipts are major non-tax revenue sources; declining non-tax revenue may indicate lower mining activity or under-collection.

source.quote: could not keep pace with the GSDP growth of 11.40 per cent. Non-Tax Revenue (Rs. 51,221 crore) also decreased by Rs. 1,790 crore... misclassified, Rs. 721 crore of expenditure

recommendations: Odisha Finance Department should leverage its strong fiscal position (15.48 per cent GSDP debt, 63 per cent fiscal space) to accelerate Capital Expenditure above 25 per cent of total expenditure -- the transition from 16 per cent (2020-21) to 22 per cent (2024-25) is positive but can be accelerated with infrastructure investment in roads, irrigation, and urban services; the ₹721 crore misclassification must be corrected in Finance Accounts.

Odisha must investigate the ₹1,790 crore decline in Non-Tax Revenue -- a revenue stream that should be growing with mining and forest resource activity; district-wise mineral royalty collection data should be audited to identify whether royalty under-assessment or under-collection is occurring; the 121.54 per cent subsidy surge (₹5,011 crore input assistance) must be evaluated for effectiveness -- whether input assistance reached intended farmers through DBT mechanisms and what crop yield/income improvements resulted.

ministry: Urban Development Department / UJN, Government of Uttarakhand
title: Compliance Audit -- Uttarakhand Sewage/UJN: ₹239.01 crore Contracts (No LD/Cost Escalation); ₹205.88 crore Sewage Projects; ₹59.45 crore Royalty/DMF Not Deducted from Contractor Bills; ₹7.87 crore Missing Performance Security; ₹4.76 crore + ₹3.10 crore Short Security; Multiple Sewage Schemes Abandoned After Partial Expenditure (₹9.57 to ₹9.61 crore per Scheme)
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Uttarakhand, July 2025) found: (1) Sewage contracts ₹239.01 crore (9 agreements across UJN Rishikesh, Gopeshwar, Haridwar, Srinagar) -- no liquidated damages/cost escalation provisions; ₹205.88 crore appended for additional work; (2) Royalty/DMF -- ₹59.45 crore payments to contractors without deducting royalty and DMF (8 forest divisions + UJN); ₹0.59 crore labour cess not deducted; (3) Performance security -- ₹2.18 crore bank guarantees deficient; ₹4.76 crore + ₹3.10 crore short security; (4) Multiple sewage schemes abandoned after partial expenditure (₹9.57 crore of ₹9.61 crore; ₹12.62 crore STP ₹0.71 crore done; ₹22.51 crore no household connections); (5) SWM and 27 MLD STP tertiary treatment irregular.

stats.label: ₹239.01 crore contracts without LD provisions
stats.value: ₹239.01 crore across 9 sewage/UJN contracts (Rishikesh, Gopeshwar, Haridwar, Srinagar) without liquidated damages provisions; land sliding/excess rainfall cited as justification but not accepted by audit

source.quote: Additionally, the cited reasons land sliding and excess rainfall do not justify delays of Rs. 239.01 crore. It was not only against the general conditions of contract provisions but resulting in cost escalation on this count. UJN, Rishikesh: (1) 18/GM/2017-18 (Rs. 4.12 crore), (2) 20/GM/2017-18 (Rs. 67.02 crore), (3) 01/GM/2021-22 (Rs. 6.38 crore)

stats.value: ₹59.45 crore paid to contractors (8 forest divisions + UJN) without deducting royalty and DMF contributions; ₹0.59 crore labour cess also not deducted

source.quote: deduction of royalty as well as DMF from the contractor's bills was irregular, and the divisions Rs. 59.45 crore against the bills submitted by contractors without deducting the labour cess of Rs. 0.59 crore. Alaknanda Soil Conservation Forest Division, Gopeshwar - Rs. 3.35 crore

stats.label: Performance security shortfall (₹7.87 crore)
stats.value: ₹2.18 crore bank guarantees deficient (3 agreements); ₹4.76 crore short (contract ₹135.96 crore); ₹3.10 crore short (contract ₹62.07 crore); total ₹7.87 crore performance security missing

source.quote: agreements amounting to Rs. 2.18 crore submitted for performance security had been government order, amount of Rs. 4.76 crore and Rs. 3.10 crore should have been taken Agreement No.-02/GM/2018-19 estimated cost - Rs. 135.96 crore... Agreement No.-11/GM/2017-18 estimated cost - Rs. 62.07 crore

stats.label: Sewage schemes abandoned after partial expenditure
stats.value: Multiple sewage schemes abandoned: ₹9.57 crore spent of ₹9.61 crore (Rudraprayag STP damage); ₹12.62 crore only ₹0.71 crore I&D work done; ₹22.51 crore no household connections; ₹61.83 crore with no household connections

source.quote: at a cost of ₹ 9.61 crore. Work closed in March 2017 after spending Rs. 9.57 crore. at a cost of Rs. 12.62 crore... Only partial I&D work got done worth 0.71 crore and project abandoned. sanctioned (March 2017) at a cost of Rs. 22.51 crore. No household sewer connections at a cost of Rs. 61.83 crore. No household sewer connections

keyFindings.text: Uttarakhand's UJN sewage contracts totalling Rs. 239.01 crore without liquidated damages provisions mean that contractors face no financial penalty for delays. Construction delays in Uttarakhand's hilly terrain are common (landslides, monsoon disruptions), but the absence of LD clauses in contract agreements transfers 100 per cent of delay cost to the public exchequer -- the contractor gets full payment regardless of when they complete. The Rs. 205.88 crore in additional works appended to these contracts suggests scope creep that further inflates costs. When Rs. 59.45 crore in royalty and DMF contributions are also not deducted from contractor bills, the government is paying contractors for materials (sand, stone, gravel) without collecting the state's entitlement from those minerals.

source.quote: Rs. 239.01 crore. It was not only against the general conditions of contract provisions... Rs. 59.45 crore against the bills submitted by contractors without deducting the labour cess

keyFindings.text: Multiple Uttarakhand sewage schemes abandoned after partial expenditure -- Rs. 9.57 crore spent of Rs. 9.61 crore (Rudraprayag STP, damaged in disaster), Rs. 12.62 crore project with only Rs. 0.71 crore I&D work done (abandoned), Rs. 22.51 crore and Rs. 61.83 crore with no household sewer connections -- represent failed public health investments in Uttarakhand's holy cities (Rishikesh, Haridwar, Srinagar, Gopeshwar) that discharge untreated sewage into the Ganga system. Untreated sewage from Uttarakhand's pilgrimage towns is a major Ganga pollution source. The Rs. 2.18 crore performance security gap means contractors can abandon projects without financial consequence -- the performance security is the government's only financial protection against contractor default.

source.quote: Work closed in March 2017 after spending Rs. 9.57 crore... Only partial I&D work got done worth 0.71 crore and project abandoned... No household sewer connections

recommendations: Uttarakhand Urban Development Department must amend all active UJN contract agreements to include LD (liquidated damages) clauses at 0.5 per cent of contract value per week of delay, capped at 10 per cent -- going forward, no contract should be awarded without LD provisions; the ₹59.45 crore in royalty/DMF not deducted from contractor bills must be recovered immediately by demanding royalty certificates from the contractors and setting off the shortfall against pending bills or invoking recovery proceedings.

Uttarakhand must commission a post-completion audit of all abandoned sewage schemes -- for each scheme above ₹5 crore that was abandoned, the responsible engineer and contractor should be identified; where contractor default caused abandonment, the performance security must be encashed and contractors blacklisted; the ₹9.57 crore Rudraprayag STP loss should be claimed under State Disaster Relief Fund provisions; the ₹7.87 crore performance security shortfall must be demanded from the respective contractors within 30 days.

ministry: Department of Local Government, Government of Punjab
reportNo: Report No. 5 of 2025 (Performance Audit -- Solid Waste Management, Punjab)
title: Performance Audit -- Punjab SWM: 68 Per cent Waste Unprocessed (54.32 lakh MT of 80.20 lakh MT Collected, Jan 2017-Dec 2021); Test-Checked ULBs 66 Per cent Unprocessed; Compost Pit Shortage 1,108 Pits (5 ULBs); Processed Waste Fell from 50.44 Per cent (2019) to 12.52 Per cent (2021); Amritsar Zero Composting Despite Concessionaire; ULBs Claimed Processing Without Facilities
overview: CAG Performance Audit on SWM in Punjab found: (1) State-level -- 80.20 lakh MT waste collected (Jan 2017-Dec 2021); only 25.88 lakh MT (32 per cent) processed; 54.32 lakh MT (68 per cent) unprocessed; processing rate ranged 15.48-47.86 per cent; (2) Test-checked ULBs (19 selected, 116 ULBs) -- 36.19 lakh MT collected; only 12.31 lakh MT processed; 23.88 lakh MT (66 per cent) unprocessed; processed share fell from 50.44 per cent (2019) to 12.52 per cent (2021); (3) Compost pits -- 2,239 required (17 ULBs); 1,310 constructed; 5 ULBs short by 1,108 pits of 1,607 required; ULB Rajpura: 80 of 150 pits not in use; (4) Amritsar -- despite concessionaire responsible for composting, no composting done; (5) ULBs claimed 13,663 MT processed in 2017-18 without any facilities (compost pits constructed only from 2018-19 onwards).

stats.label: State-wide unprocessed waste (68 per cent)
stats.value: 80.20 lakh MT waste collected (Jan 2017-Dec 2021); 54.32 lakh MT (68 per cent) left unprocessed; processed ranged 15.48-47.86 per cent; only 25.88 lakh MT (32 per cent) actually processed

source.quote: During January 2017 to December 2021, 80.20 lakh MT of waste was collected in the State. Of this, 25.88 lakh MT (32 per cent) was processed and 54.32 lakh MT (68 per cent) left unprocessed. The percentage of processed waste ranged from 15.48 per cent to 47.86 per cent

stats.label: Test-checked ULBs processing collapsed to 12.52 per cent
stats.value: In 19 selected 116 ULBs: 36.19 lakh MT collected; only 12.31 lakh MT processed; 23.88 lakh MT (66 per cent) unprocessed; processed share fell from 50.44 per cent (2019) to 12.52 per cent (2021)

source.quote: In 19 selected 116 ULBs, of 36.19 lakh MT of waste collected, only 12.31 lakh MT was processed and the remaining 23.88 lakh MT of waste i.e. 66 per cent was left unprocessed. The percentage of total waste processed to waste collected came down from 50.44 in 2019 to 12.52 in 2021

stats.label: Compost pit shortage (1,108 pits unbuilt)
stats.value: 2,239 compost pits required (17 ULBs); only 1,310 constructed; 5 ULBs short 1,108 pits of 1,607 required; Rajpura: 80 of 150 pits not in use; ULBs cited concessionaire planning issue

source.quote: In 17 ULBs, a total of 2,239 compost pits were required, of which only 1,310 compost pits were constructed. In five ULBs, against the requirement of 1,607 compost pits, only 499 compost pits were constructed, a shortage of 1,108 compost pits. In ULB Rajpura, out of 150 constructed compost pits, 80 were not used

stats.label: ULBs claimed processing without having facilities
stats.value: ULBs claimed 13,663 MT processed in 2017-18 -- but compost pits only constructed from 2018-19; no processing facilities in 2017-18; claims unverified/false; Amritsar zero composting despite concessionaire

source.quote: it was claimed that 13,663 MT of waste was processed during 2017-18 though no facilities for composting were available with the ULBs during this period, as the compost pits were constructed during 2018-19. Thus, claims of ULBs in respect of processing of waste were not in ULB Amritsar, no composting

keyFindings.text: Punjab's 68 per cent unprocessed waste ratio -- 54.32 lakh MT left unprocessed over 5 years -- represents a massive accumulated environmental and public health burden. Under SWM Rules 2016 (Rule 15), local authorities must process waste. The collapse from 50.44 per cent processing rate in 2019 to 12.52 per cent in 2021 in test-checked ULBs is a 75 per cent decline in processing effectiveness in two years -- the direction of travel is wrong. This waste is either being openly dumped (generating methane, a potent greenhouse gas), burned (generating dioxins and particulate matter), or accumulated at unsanitary dumping grounds (contaminating groundwater). Punjab's rivers, including the Sutlej and Beas, are already severely polluted; unprocessed municipal waste is a major contributor.

source.quote: 54.32 lakh MT (68 per cent) left unprocessed... percentage of total waste processed to waste collected came down from 50.44 in 2019 to 12.52 in 2021

keyFindings.text: The finding that 17 ULBs claimed to have processed 13,663 MT of waste in 2017-18 when they had no processing facilities (compost pits were only built from 2018-19 onwards) is a falsification of official records. These claims were reported upward to the state government and likely to GoI in compliance reports -- they are fraudulent claims that inflate apparent scheme performance. Amritsar -- Punjab's largest city -- achieving zero composting despite having a concessionaire contractually responsible for composting is a contract monitoring failure: the concessionaire is not performing, and the ULB is not enforcing or penalising the non-performance.

source.quote: it was claimed that 13,663 MT of waste was processed during 2017-18 though no facilities for composting were available... in ULB Amritsar, no composting

recommendations: Punjab Department of Local Government must implement a real-time waste processing tracking system -- each ULB must daily report waste collected and processed (by category: composting, RDF, bio-methanation, landfill) through a state-level dashboard linked to GoI SWM portal; the 1,108-compost-pit shortfall (5 ULBs) must be completed within 6 months with budget allocated from SWM cess collections; Amritsar's concessionaire must be given a 30-day cure notice and if composting is not commenced, the contract must be terminated and composting handed to an emergency contractor.

Punjab government must initiate disciplinary action against ULB officials who falsified 2017-18 waste processing records (claimed 13,663 MT processed without facilities) -- fabricating compliance records for GoI-funded schemes is a serious misconduct; going forward, processing claims must be backed by weighbridge records and end-product (compost/RDF) offtake receipts; the 80 unused compost pits at Rajpura (built at ₹8 lakh) should be made operational within 30 days or the assets transferred to neighboring panchayats for farm use.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 (State Finances Audit Report, FY 2024-25) -- Part III
title: State Finances -- West Bengal: Total Liabilities ₹7,01,724 crore (38.66 Per cent GSDP) BREACHES FRBM 38 Per cent Ceiling; ₹1,87,547 crore (30.66 Per cent) Debt Due in 7 Years; Misclassification ₹1,031.84 crore Revenue as Capital; ₹2,395.67 crore Under Minor Head 800; ₹2,863.57 crore Payment Failures; ₹33.76 crore Bank Balance Discrepancy; Excess Expenditure ₹13,486.92 crore; Misappropriation ₹3.56 crore + Loss ₹96.53 crore (FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 2 of 2026 (WB SFAR FY 2024-25) Part III found: (1) FRBM breach -- Total liabilities ₹7,01,724 crore (38.66 per cent GSDP) exceeding FRBM ceiling 38 per cent; public debt ₹6,11,645 crore; ₹1,87,547 crore (30.66 per cent) due in next 7 years; (2) Misclassification -- ₹1,031.84 crore revenue as capital; ₹2,395.67 crore under minor head 800 (61 Major Heads, 0.87 per cent); ₹707.55 crore (4,976 cases) under MH 800; (3) Payment failures -- ₹2,863.57 crore failed; ₹2,662.03 crore paid again; ₹201.54 crore under Suspense; (4) Bank discrepancy ₹33.76 crore (WB ₹28.52 crore vs RBI ₹5.24 crore); (5) Excess expenditure ₹13,486.92 crore (7 grants); misappropriation ₹3.56 crore; loss ₹96.53 crore.

stats.label: FRBM breach -- total liabilities 38.66 per cent GSDP
stats.value: Total liabilities ₹7,01,724 crore (38.66 per cent GSDP) -- breaches WBFRBM ceiling 38 per cent; public debt ₹6,11,645 crore; ₹1,87,547 crore (30.66 per cent) due in next 7 years

source.quote: As of March 2025, overall outstanding liability of the State stood at Rs. 7,01,724 crore. There was decline in the Debt-GSDP ratio from 42.60 per cent in FY 2020-21 to 38.66 per cent in FY 2024-25. Total liabilities stood at 38.66 per cent of GSDP in 2024-25, breaching the FRBM target of 38.00 per cent. Of the total outstanding public debt (Rs. 6,11,645 crore), more than 30 per cent will become payable in the ensuing seven years {Rs. 1,87,547 crore (30.66 per cent)}
