stats.value: ₹1,031.84 crore Revenue Expenditure classified as Capital; ₹2,395.67 crore under Minor Head 800 (61 Major Heads, 0.87 per cent total); ₹707.55 crore (4,976 cases, 27 heads); ₹1,104.80 crore receipts under MH 800

source.quote: Rs. 1031.84 crore of expenditure of Revenue nature as Capital Expenditure Rs. 2,395.67 crore under 61 Major Heads of account, constituting 0.87 per cent of the total Revenue and Capital expenditure Rs. 707.55 crore in 4976 cases under 27 Rs. 1,104.80 crore under 47 Major Heads of Account, constituting 0.52 per cent of the total Revenue (Rs. 2,13,699.56 crore)

stats.label: Payment failures (₹2,863.57 crore) and Suspense
stats.value: ₹2,863.57 crore payment failures; ₹2,662.03 crore paid again; ₹201.54 crore under Suspense Head; bank balance discrepancy ₹33.76 crore (WB ₹28.52 crore vs RBI ₹5.24 crore)

source.quote: Rs. 2,863.57 crore failed, out of which payments worth Rs. 2,662.03 crore were paid again leaving a balance of Rs. 201.54 crore under the Suspense Head. Government of West Bengal (Rs. 1,703.41 crore) is not at par with that depicted in the Accounts (Rs. 425.30 crore). Rs. 28.52 crore (Credit) while the same was reported as Rs. 5.24 crore (Debit) by the Reserve Bank of India. As such, there was an unreconciled difference of Rs. 33.76 crore

stats.label: Excess expenditure and misconduct cases
stats.value: ₹13,486.92 crore excess expenditure (7 grants, 1 appropriation); ₹57,263.62 crore additional; misappropriation ₹3.56 crore + loss ₹96.53 crore + theft ₹0.29 crore; departmental action ₹411.25 crore pending

source.quote: Rs. 13,486.92 crore was incurred under seven grants and one appropriation which Rs. 57,263.62 crore. misappropriation cases (Rs. 3.56 crore), eight cases of loss (Rs. 96.53 crore) and 17 cases of theft (Rs. 0.29 crore). Rs. 411.25 crore were pending initiation/completion of departmental

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's total liabilities breaching the FRBM 38 per cent GSDP ceiling -- even marginally at 38.66 per cent -- is a significant milestone because FRBM ceilings exist precisely as early warning limits. The state is not in a debt crisis, but the trajectory is concerning: debt-GSDP was 42.60 per cent in FY 2020-21 and has declined to 38.66 per cent (due to GSDP growth), but Rs. 1,87,547 crore (30.66 per cent of total debt) becoming due in the next 7 years means annual repayment obligations will be very high. With interest payments already forming a large share of committed expenditure and Revenue Expenditure at 118.59 per cent of Revenue Receipts, West Bengal has very limited capacity to service this debt from revenue surpluses.

source.quote: Total liabilities stood at 38.66 per cent of GSDP in 2024-25, breaching the FRBM target of 38.00 per cent... Rs. 1,87,547 crore (30.66 per cent) will become payable in the ensuing seven years

keyFindings.text: Rs. 2,863.57 crore in payment failures with Rs. 201.54 crore still stuck in Suspense indicates a broken payment reconciliation system. When a government payment fails (treasury system does not receive confirmation of bank credit), the correct procedure is to cancel the payment and re-issue -- not to leave it in suspense. Rs. 201.54 crore of unresolved failed payments may represent cases where: (a) the payee was paid twice; (b) the payee was not paid at all; or (c) the payment was redirected to wrong accounts. The Rs. 33.76 crore discrepancy between WB Treasury accounts and RBI records (different sign -- WB shows Rs. 28.52 crore credit; RBI shows Rs. 5.24 crore debit) is particularly serious as it means the two authoritative books cannot agree on even whether the account is in surplus or deficit.

source.quote: Rs. 2,863.57 crore failed, out of which payments worth Rs. 2,662.03 crore were paid again leaving a balance of Rs. 201.54 crore under the Suspense Head... Rs. 28.52 crore (Credit) while the same was reported as Rs. 5.24 crore (Debit) by the Reserve Bank of India. As such, there was an unreconciled difference of Rs. 33.76 crore

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must table a FRBM compliance restoration plan in the next budget session -- with specific year-wise targets to bring total liabilities below 38 per cent of GSDP within 3 years; the ₹1,87,547 crore debt due in 7 years must be mapped to a debt redemption calendar published annually; any new borrowing above the approved fiscal deficit ceiling must require prior Finance Department and cabinet approval; the ₹1,031.84 crore revenue-as-capital misclassification must be corrected before Finance Accounts are finalised.

West Bengal must resolve the ₹201.54 crore in Suspense (failed payments) within 30 days -- each case must be traced to determine whether double-payment occurred; the ₹33.76 crore bank balance discrepancy with RBI must be reconciled urgently since different signs (credit vs debit) suggest a systemic accounting error; the ₹13,486.92 crore excess expenditure across 7 grants must be brought before the Public Accounts Committee for regularisation; the ₹96.53 crore in identified losses and ₹3.56 crore in misappropriation must be reported to police with FIR filed where prima facie evidence of criminal misappropriation exists.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of West Bengal

title: State Finances -- West Bengal: Revenue Expenditure 118.59 Per cent of Revenue Receipts (5 Years Consecutive 112 Per cent+); Capital Expenditure Collapsed ₹21,622 crore (-25 Per cent, ₹7,341 crore Fall); Subsidies +₹8,968 crore (85.61 Per cent); Committed Exp + Subsidies = 74 Per cent Revenue Receipts; Revenue Deficit ₹39,727 crore; GSDP ₹18.15 lakh crore (FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 2 of 2026 (WB SFAR FY 2024-25) Part II found: (1) Revenue performance -- GSDP ₹18.15 lakh crore (2024-25); CAGR 9.57 per cent (2015-16 to 2024-25); Revenue Deficit ₹39,727 crore (2.19 per cent GSDP); Revenue Expenditure 118.59 per cent of Revenue Receipts (112 per cent+ for 5 consecutive years); (2) Capital collapse -- Capital Expenditure ₹21,622 crore (1.19 per cent GSDP) -- fell ₹7,341 crore (-25 per cent) from ₹28,963 crore; (3) Subsidies -- increased ₹8,968 crore (85.61 per cent) in FY 2024-25; PDS rice subsidy +₹5,858 crore; (4) Fiscal squeeze -- committed expenditure ₹1,39,202 crore + subsidies ₹19,444 crore = 74 per cent of Revenue Receipts; only 26 per cent fiscal space; (5) Budget savings ₹70,662.25 crore (18.09 per cent) of ₹3,90,638.04 crore budget.

stats.value: Revenue Expenditure consistently above 112 per cent of Revenue Receipts for 5 years; 118.59 per cent in FY 2024-25 -- state spending ₹1.19 on revenue for every ₹1 earned; persistent deficit spending

keyFindings.text: West Bengal spending Rs. 1.19 in revenue for every Rs. 1 of revenue receipts -- for 5 consecutive years -- is the definition of structural fiscal unsustainability. Revenue Expenditure above 100 per cent of Revenue Receipts means the state is borrowing to pay for current consumption (salaries, pensions, interest, subsidies), not just capital investment. This is the opposite of sound fiscal management. The 85.61 per cent surge in subsidies (Rs. 8,968 crore) -- largely driven by PDS rice -- in a single year brings total subsidies to Rs. 19,444 crore, which combined with committed expenditure (Rs. 1,39,202 crore) consumes 74 per cent of all revenue receipts. The FRBM principle of "revenue surplus to fund capital expenditure" is the exact opposite of West Bengal's trajectory.

source.quote: Revenue Expenditure consistently accounted for over 112 per cent of Revenue Receipts during FYs 2020-25 and stood at 118.59 per cent in FY 2024-25... The committed expenditure (Rs. 1,39,202 crore) coupled with Subsidy expenditure (Rs. 19,444 crore) absorbed nearly 74 per cent of Revenue Receipts

keyFindings.text: The 25 per cent collapse in Capital Expenditure (from Rs. 28,963 crore to Rs. 21,622 crore) is the most alarming single-year finding. Capital expenditure is the investment that creates productive assets -- roads, bridges, hospitals, schools, irrigation -- that generate economic returns and future revenues. A 25 per cent decline in one year (Rs. 7,341 crore less) while subsidies increased Rs. 8,968 crore in the same year is a direct trade-off: West Bengal chose to spend Rs. 8,968 crore more on food subsidies and Rs. 7,341 crore less on infrastructure. At 1.19 per cent of GSDP, West Bengal's capital expenditure is below the national average (states typically target 3-4 per cent GSDP) and represents inadequate investment in the state's economic future.

source.quote: Capital expenditure (Rs. 21,622 crore) during FY 2024-25 constituted only 1.19 per cent the GSDP of the State. In FY 2024-25, it fell by 25 per cent (Rs. 7,341 crore) vis-a-vis the previous financial year (Rs. 28,963 crore)

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must publish a multi-year Fiscal Consolidation Roadmap -- with specific annual targets to bring Revenue Expenditure below 100 per cent of Revenue Receipts within 5 years; the PDS rice subsidy (the largest single driver of the ₹8,968 crore surge) should be rationalized through better beneficiary targeting using Aadhaar/DBT; the subsidy budget should have a hard annual ceiling approved by the cabinet, with any excess requiring a supplementary demand.

West Bengal must set a Capital Expenditure floor of 2.5 per cent of GSDP (₹45,375 crore based on FY 2024-25 GSDP) -- the ₹21,622 crore (1.19 per cent) is critically inadequate; capital expenditure savings (₹70,662 crore overall) should be analysed to identify which capital projects were not executed and why; the 18.09 per cent budget savings rate suggests systematic over-budgeting or under-execution; project-wise budget utilisation should be published quarterly.

keyFindings.text: Jharkhand's IFMS data showing Rs. 4,222.50 crore for loans and advances when the actual Finance Accounts figure is Rs. 12,286.62 crore means that IFMS is missing 65.6 per cent of all loan and advance transaction data. This is not a minor technical error -- it means that 12 years of financial decisions about loans, advances, and fund releases have been made using a system that was missing two-thirds of the relevant data. Budget planning, expenditure monitoring, and cash management all depend on accurate IFMS data. With Rs. 83,878.41 crore released under 10,060 heads of accounts without matching sanction records, the IFMS release workflow is also bypassed at massive scale -- this represents either system configuration failures or deliberate process circumvention.

source.quote: amount of Rs. 4,222.50 crore was captured was Rs. 12,286.62 crore... amount of Rs. 8,064.12 crore could not be captured in IFMS... Rs. 83,878.41 crore was shown released under 10,060 heads of accounts against

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 2,44,925.58 crore in AC bills drawn between April 2010 and November 2022 without full DC bill reconciliation represents 12 years of a broken accountability chain. AC bills are legitimate for field officers who need advance cash, but the reconciliation requirement (DC bills within a defined period) is the control that prevents embezzlement. With Rs. 1,013.69 crore drawn in new AC bills by DDOs who had not adjusted their previous AC bills, these officers were issued additional advances without clearing previous ones -- a control violation that the IFMS should have blocked automatically. The 344 excess pension payment cases (of which 198 were found on validation to be not actual excess) suggests pension payment data quality issues in IFMS that could affect thousands of pensioners.

source.quote: Rs. 2,44,925.58 crore were drawn between April 2010 and November 2022... AC bills without adjustment of previous AC bills of Rs. 1,013.69 crore drawn

recommendations: Jharkhand Finance Department must commission a complete IFMS data reconciliation exercise -- the ₹8,064.12 crore in loan/advance transactions not captured in IFMS must be traced to source documents (manual registers, subsidiary accounts) and entered into IFMS; the gap represents 12 years of missing data that cannot be reconstructed from IFMS alone; the AG should be requested to share subsidiary ledger data for reconciliation; results must be published in the next Finance Accounts.

Jharkhand must implement IFMS-level controls: (a) block new AC bill drawings by DDOs with unadjusted AC bills older than 6 months; (b) require a matching sanction record before any fund release can be processed in IFMS (the ₹83,878.41 crore without sanction records must be reviewed within 90 days); (c) implement real-time duplicate checks in the pension module to prevent double payments; the IFMS revenue validation module must be strengthened to prevent the ₹4.40 crore-type revenue pilferage where collection is recorded but remittance is not enforced.

keyFindings.text: PMKKKY exists precisely to ensure that mining royalties are re-invested in the welfare of communities whose land and lives are disrupted by mining. Gujarat's 32 DMFs sitting on Rs. 851.46 crore (52.95 per cent) of unutilised funds while mining continues to impact Directly Affected Villages is a direct policy failure: the money exists, the mandate exists, but the institutional capacity to plan and spend it effectively does not. The utilisation gap is increasing year-on-year, meaning the problem is getting worse, not better. EC (Executive Committee) meetings are the primary decision-making mechanism for DMF spending -- with 29-85 per cent shortfall in meetings across 5 DMFs, the governance mechanism that approves spending is itself not functioning.

source.quote: Rs. 1,608.08 crore, the expenditure incurred for projects under PMKKKY was Rs. 756.62 crore (47.05 per cent) and unutilized DMF contribution was Rs. 851.46 crore (52.95 per cent)... The shortfall in the EC meetings for the five DMFs ranged from 29 to 85 per cent

keyFindings.text: The procurement findings -- Rs. 1.06 crore work artificially split below the Rs. 5 lakh open tender threshold, PEE work expanded from Rs. 75.15 lakh to Rs. 155.79 lakh (207 per cent) on nomination basis without competitive bidding, and ECC units paid at double the contracted rate -- show a pattern of deliberate tender avoidance in DMF procurements. These are not isolated errors; they reflect the absence of a functional procurement oversight mechanism. DMF expenditure is meant to benefit mining-affected communities -- when procurement is manipulated, the benefit reaches contractors instead of communities. The Rs. 39.53 lakh healthcare expenditure delivering no functional services is the ultimate consequence: money spent, communities unserved.

source.quote: total value of the work was Rs. 1.06 crore, the L-1 in each case remained below Rs. 5 lakh... Rs. 155.79 lakh for PEE at seven villages on nomination basis... was more than 207 per cent of the original contract value of Rs. 75.15 lakh

recommendations: Gujarat Mines & Geology Department must set a utilisation target of 70 per cent of DMF funds per year for all 32 DMFs -- DMFs unable to reach 70 per cent should have their Annual Plans reviewed by the DMF-SNU with a mandatory top-up list of pre-approved high-priority projects ready for immediate sanction; EC meetings must be held quarterly as required by GDMF Rules -- any DMF where EC meetings are pending should have the District Collector issue notices within 7 days; ₹851.46 crore of unutilised funds should be deployed urgently with priority to drinking water, healthcare, and education in Directly Affected Villages.

Gujarat must implement mandatory open tender for all DMF procurements above ₹2 lakh (the current ₹5 lakh threshold that is being gamed should be lowered) -- all nomination-basis awards above ₹50,000 should require written justification approved by the Governing Council; an IT-based procurement portal (similar to GeM) should be mandatory for all DMF purchases; the ₹63 lakh ECC excess payment should be recovered from the agency and the DMF officer who approved the double-rate payment should face disciplinary action; Annual Accounts and Annual Plans should be published on each DMF's website within 30 days of approval.

keyFindings.text: Jharkhand's AC (Abstract Contingent) bill system -- where Rs. 20,098.82 crore was drawn without full DC (Detailed Contingent) bill submission -- is a massive unaccountable cash pool. AC bills are advance drawings; DC bills are the reconciliation mechanism that shows what the money was spent on. With 4,979 bills (Rs. 9,078.19 crore) only partially adjusted and Rs. 1,013.69 crore drawn without adjusting previous AC bills, a substantial fraction of Rs. 20,098.82 crore exists in a state where the state treasury has released money but has no verified end-use records. The Rs. 2,44,925.58 crore drawn between April 2010 and November 2022 (12+ years of data) suggests this has been an ongoing systemic weakness -- every year, more AC bills are drawn than are adjusted, creating a growing pile of unreconciled public funds.

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 8,064.12 crore discrepancy between IFMS-captured data (Rs. 4,222.50 crore) and actual Finance Account data (Rs. 12,286.62 crore) is a critical IT governance failure. IFMS (Integrated Financial Management System) is supposed to be the single source of financial truth for Jharkhand's government -- if Rs. 8,064.12 crore of transactions are not captured in IFMS, the system's reports are systematically misleading. Policy-makers, the Finance Department, and legislators are making budget decisions based on IFMS reports that are missing 65 per cent of the actual loan/advance transaction data. The Rs. 83,878.41 crore released under 10,060 heads without matching sanction records means that a massive volume of fund releases happened outside the normal sanction-and-release workflow, bypassing the primary control against unauthorized expenditure.

recommendations: Jharkhand Finance Department must immediately halt new AC bill drawings by any DDO with pending unadjusted AC bills older than 3 months -- the Finance Rules should be amended to make IFMS blocking of new AC bills mandatory until all previous AC bills are fully adjusted; all 287 DDOs with partially adjusted bills (₹9,078.19 crore) should submit DC bills within 30 days or face suspension of their drawing powers; ₹1,013.69 crore drawn without previous adjustment should be investigated for potential misappropriation.

Jharkhand must commission an IT audit of IFMS to identify why ₹8,064.12 crore of loan/advance transactions are not being captured -- the system needs to be patched to ensure 100 per cent capture of all treasury transactions; the AG should reconcile the 10,060 heads with missing sanction data (₹83,878.41 crore) against manual sanction records and publish findings within 6 months; all IFMS-based budget reports should carry a caveat disclosing known data gaps until the reconciliation is complete.

keyFindings.text: MGNREGA compensation for delayed wages is a statutory right of workers under Section 3(4) of the MGNREGA Act -- if wages are not paid within 15 days of work completion, workers are entitled to compensation at 0.05 per cent per day of delay. Bihar approved compensation for only 4.19 per cent of claims (0.42 crore of 10 crore person-days), meaning 95.81 per cent of workers who should have received compensation did not. This is not administrative negligence -- it is a denial of statutory rights to India's most vulnerable daily-wage workers. The Rs. 735.10 crore in delayed wages itself represents the scale of the problem: at MGNREGA's minimum wage of Rs. 221-294 per day (Bihar FY 2023-24), this represents approximately 2.5-3 crore person-days of work for which workers waited beyond the statutory 15-day period.

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 28.97 crore in flood protection works that failed to protect 5.26 lakh population and 17,400 ha agricultural land is a catastrophic implementation failure for one of Bihar's most flood-prone states. Bihar experiences annual flooding affecting 76 per cent of its North Bihar region; MGNREGA-funded embankment and flood protection works are meant to be the frontline defence for rural communities. The fact that Rs. 6.09 crore in additional flood protection expenditure also failed, and that Rs. 1,903.58 crore in outstanding liabilities includes pre-2019-20 arrears, suggests systemic contractor payment delays that may be discouraging quality work completion.

recommendations: Bihar Rural Development Department must immediately clear ₹302.24 crore in pre-2019-20 MGNREGA wage and material arrears -- these are the oldest outstanding liabilities and represent workers who have waited 5+ years for payment; a time-bound payment schedule (30 days per tranche) should be published; the compensation module should be activated for all 9.58 crore approved-but-uncompensated person-days and compensation calculated and paid within 90 days; ₹6.95 crore in deducted royalties/taxes that were not remitted must be transferred to the appropriate government accounts immediately.

Bihar must commission a flood protection works post-completion assessment -- all MGNREGA-funded embankments and drainage works should be independently verified for functional effectiveness within 90 days of completion; the ₹28.97 crore in non-functional flood protection should be investigated and the responsible contractors blacklisted if quality failures are established; Mithila University must recover ₹5.37 crore in inadmissible IGST from the printing agency and the IGST payment should not have been made on an intra-state supply (which attracts CGST+SGST, not IGST) -- the accounts officer who approved this should be proceeded against.

keyFindings.text: The gap between Rs. 13,899.14 crore transferred and only Rs. 5,387.24 crore in UCs (38.8 per cent) means that Bihar's PHED cannot demonstrate what happened to Rs. 8,511.90 crore of Har Ghar Nal Ka Jal funds. UCs are the primary accountability mechanism for public funds -- their absence does not necessarily mean the money was stolen, but it means there is no verified confirmation of end use. The Rs. 3,405.40 crore surrendered suggests that a substantial portion was simply not used -- returned to the state treasury without being deployed for water supply. The 98.28 per cent household coverage reported to GoI is likely overstated (audit found it overstated in test-checked GPs), meaning Bihar may have claimed near-complete coverage of Nal Ka Jal while hundreds of thousands of households remain without functional tap connections.

source.quote: out of the total allocation of Rs. 13,899.13 crore for HGNJ, utilisation certificates showing an expenditure of Rs. 5,387.24 crore... 98.28 per cent HHs were covered by piped water supply scheme, however, this coverage was found overstated in test-checked

keyFindings.text: Omitting chlorinators from HGNJ water supply schemes is a public health failure. Chlorination is the most basic and cost-effective water disinfection method, mandated by BIS standards for piped water supply. A water supply scheme without chlorination means households are receiving piped water but not necessarily safe water -- in many cases, piped water from hand-pumped or surface sources without treatment can carry higher microbial loads than the wells it replaces. Bihar has historically high rates of waterborne disease; the HGNJ investment of Rs. 13,899 crore would be far more valuable if it included functional chlorination in every scheme. The 150 scheme agreements without OHT (Overhead Tank) specification further compromise continuous supply, as OHTs provide the pressure head needed for 24x7 tap flow.

source.quote: components like chlorinators and ground water recharge were omitted in model estimates, affecting water safety and scheme sustainability. agreements for 150 water supply schemes were executed by ULBs, without the OHT was specified for uninterrupted water supply

recommendations: Bihar PHED must conduct a state-wide physical verification of all 186.13 lakh reported FHTC (Functional Household Tap Connections) within 6 months -- geo-tagged photographs and water pressure tests should be conducted for a 10 per cent random sample in each district; findings should be reported to GoI under Jal Jeevan Mission; UCs for ₹8,511.90 crore (the gap between transfer and furnished UCs) must be collected within 3 months or fund recovery proceedings initiated against responsible DDOs.

Bihar PHED must retrofit chlorination systems in all HGNJ schemes identified as lacking them -- chlorinator installation costs are minimal (₹15,000-50,000 per scheme) relative to the health benefits; scheme-wise operational status (functional/non-functional) should be published monthly on the JJM dashboard; the ₹6.37 crore non-functional schemes should be activated within 60 days or reported to NITI Aayog JJM review committee; WIMCs holding ₹1.92 crore unspent must refund these amounts within 30 days.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's power subsidy growing 127 per cent (Rs. 8,583 crore) over 5 years while GSDP grew only 75 per cent means energy subsidisation is outpacing economic growth by 1.7x. This is a classic fiscal trap: as subsidies grow, the budget for productive investment shrinks; as productive investment shrinks, economic growth slows; as economic growth slows, the political pressure to maintain subsidies grows. The power subsidy reaching Rs. 14,600+ crore (80 per cent of Rs. 18,310 crore total subsidy) represents annual payment to energy companies on behalf of consumers who pay low or zero tariffs. Bihar's electricity distribution losses (AT&C losses typically 30-40 per cent for poorly managed distribution networks) mean that a significant portion of this subsidy is covering distribution inefficiency, not genuine affordability support to the poor.

source.quote: total subsidies increased sharply from Rs. 8,167 crore in 2020-21 to Rs. 18,310 crore in 2024-25, marking an overall rise of 124 per cent... The energy subsidy rose by Rs. 8,583 crore (127 per cent) in the last five years

keyFindings.text: Committed expenditure (Rs. 86,236 crore = salaries + pensions + interest) at 39.44 per cent of total expenditure, combined with 83 per cent revenue expenditure share, means Bihar has very limited fiscal flexibility. Every additional borrowing to fund capital expenditure adds to interest (currently Rs. 19,678.14 crore), further crowding out productive spending. Bihar's internal debt growing 54.61 per cent in a single year -- faster than GSDP (75 per cent over 5 years) -- signals accelerating debt accumulation. When interest payments (Rs. 19,678.14 crore) are growing faster than revenue receipts, the state's debt becomes self-reinforcing: more debt → more interest → less surplus to reduce debt → need for more debt.

recommendations: Bihar Finance Department must publish an annual Subsidy Review Report with department-wise subsidy data, targeting, leakage estimates, and 3-year projections -- the power subsidy (₹8,583 crore increase in 5 years) should be subjected to a DBT (Direct Benefit Transfer) conversion feasibility study to target only Below Poverty Line and agricultural households while removing cross-subsidies to commercial/industrial consumers; subsidy growth above 10 per cent per year should require cabinet approval with fiscal impact assessment.

Bihar must implement a Pension Liability Management Strategy -- pensions at ₹26,139.61 crore (2024-25) growing alongside a still-large government workforce means future pension liabilities will be substantially larger; NPS implementation quality should be audited to ensure all new government employees are on NPS (reducing future defined-benefit pension obligations); the 54.61 per cent internal debt growth should be reported to the Bihar State Finance Commission with a proposed trajectory to bring annual debt growth below GSDP growth within 3 years.

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's Rs. 2,020.87 crore of Revenue Expenditure misclassified as Capital Expenditure understates the revenue deficit by Rs. 1,948.41 crore (net of the Rs. 72.46 crore going the other way). This is not a new CAG finding -- misclassification has been a recurring issue -- but at Rs. 2,020.87 crore, the scale is significant. When revenue expenditure (office expenses, administrative salaries, maintenance, grants to non-capital entities) is booked as capital, it: (a) makes the revenue deficit appear smaller than it actually is; (b) makes capital expenditure appear larger, suggesting more productive investment than is actually occurring; (c) violates the FRBM's intent of distinguishing productive capital creation from current consumption. For Karnataka's legislative oversight to be effective, these misclassifications should be corrected in the Finance Accounts.

source.quote: Misclassification of Rs. 2,020.87 crore Revenue Expenditure as Capital Expenditure and Rs. 72.46 crore of Capital Expenditure as Revenue Expenditure Deficit to the tune of Rs. 1,948.41 crore

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's own-tax buoyancy ratio of 0.75 -- where every 1 per cent GDP growth generates only 0.75 per cent own-tax revenue growth -- is a structural warning. A buoyancy above 1 is the norm for a growing economy because formalization, urbanisation, and consumption growth should generate more than proportionate tax revenue. Karnataka's buoyancy below 1 could reflect: (a) large exempt sectors growing faster than taxed sectors; (b) tax administration capacity not keeping pace with economic growth; (c) the VAT-to-GST transition continuing to compress state tax revenue (VAT share declining from 55 per cent to 43 per cent); (d) large informal sectors. With Rs. 24,917.22 crore in revenue arrears, Karnataka is also not collecting what it is legally owed, compounding the revenue underperformance.

recommendations: Karnataka Finance Department must correct the ₹2,020.87 crore misclassification through journal entries before the Finance Accounts are finalised -- each misclassified head should be identified and re-booked to the correct Major/Sub-Major/Minor head; the AG should not certify the Finance Accounts as final until misclassifications are corrected; a one-time full review of all Major Head 4000-series (capital expenditure) entries should be conducted to identify systematic misclassification patterns.

Karnataka must launch a revenue arrears recovery campaign targeting the ₹24,917.22 crore outstanding -- a department-wise recovery plan should be submitted to the Finance Department within 30 days; arrears above ₹10 crore should be personally monitored by the respective Secretary; the ₹10,035.13 crore excess expenditure across 21 grants must be regularised through the next budget session's supplementary demands; excess expenditure accumulated since 2020-21 (₹5,175.21 crore) must be regularised in the next session to avoid constitutional violation.

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's GoI grants collapsing from Rs. 38,172 crore (2020-21) to Rs. 15,205 crore (2024-25) -- a Rs. 22,967 crore reduction -- is a fiscal shock equivalent to losing 60 per cent of one of its largest revenue streams. The 2020-21 peak was elevated due to COVID-19 relief grants and GST compensation; the normalisation was expected. However, the specific declines in PMAY-Urban (-45.96 per cent, fewer houses being built), IGNOAPS/IGNWPS (social pension -18.78 per cent/-20.45 per cent, fewer elderly/widows supported), and "other transfers" (-83.7 per cent, from Rs. 8,217 crore to Rs. 1,342 crore) have direct social welfare consequences -- fewer houses, fewer pension beneficiaries. Despite receiving Rs. 45,128 crore in PDRD grants over the 15th FC period, CAG notes that even these grants did not mitigate West Bengal's revenue deficit, indicating structural expenditure-revenue imbalance.

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 26.65 crore in excess payments for duplicate connections under SAUBHAGYA represents a classic contractor fraud pattern in electrification schemes: TKCs (Turnkey Contractors) claim payment for connections they released twice or connections that were never released. Rs. 5.79 crore recovered after CAG pointed it out means the fraud was only uncovered through audit -- internal monitoring by DISCOMs completely missed the duplication. The Rs. 277.09 crore PCC pole investment under SAUBHAGYA in waterlogged areas without cement-concrete grouting is a safety and durability risk -- PCC poles without proper grouting in waterlogged soil are prone to tilting, collapse, and electrocution risks; this is Rs. 402.44 crore combined (DDUGJY + SAUBHAGYA) of electrification infrastructure that may require costly retrofitting or replacement within a few years.

keyFindings.text: That 55.84 per cent of surveyed beneficiaries reported stable power supply (implying 44.16 per cent face unstable supply) after a multi-thousand-crore rural electrification investment shows that getting a connection is not the same as getting reliable electricity. SAUBHAGYA's success metric was "households electrified" -- but having an electric meter without reliable power provides limited economic benefit. The AT&C (Aggregate Technical and Commercial) loss reduction targets not being met means the fundamental economic viability of rural distribution (collecting revenue from rural consumers to pay for power purchased from generators) has not improved, so DISCOMs continue to incur losses that require state subsidies. The 49-month delays in project execution mean the investments were made in a slower-growing infrastructure environment than anticipated.

recommendations: UP Energy Department must deploy an automated SAUBHAGYA connection verification system -- every new connection must be geo-tagged and photographed at the time of installation; TKC bills should not be processed unless GPS coordinates and photographs are uploaded to the DISCOM portal; the ₹3.37 crore excess payments still outstanding from duplicate connections should be recovered by deduction from current TKC bills; ₹26.65 crore total excess should be investigated for intent-to-defraud and FIR filed if supported by evidence.

PCC poles in waterlogged areas (24.41 lakh total, ₹402.44 crore) must be assessed within 6 months for structural integrity -- poles showing tilting or ground exposure should be re-grouted with cement concrete immediately; future works must include soil surveys before PCC pole selection, with H-Beam or Tubular poles mandatory in waterlogged zones; the off-grid connections omitted from DPRs should be added in revised DPRs and funded from scheme balance amounts; AT&C loss reduction targets should be tied to future DISCOM subsidy releases.

keyFindings.text: A single taxpayer generating Rs. 39,100.10 crore in E-Way Bills in a single month (November 2020) against GSTR-1 declared sales of Rs. 119.10 crore -- a 328-fold discrepancy -- is a textbook GST fraud indicator. E-Way Bills are used to create a paper trail for goods movement, and the fake EWB is used to pass Input Tax Credit (ITC) fraudulently to recipient businesses, who then offset this ITC against their real GST liability, reducing their tax payments. The November 2020 timing (during COVID, when physical inspections were reduced) is significant. Rs. 39,100.10 crore in fraudulent EWBs -- if even 18 per cent of this was used to claim fraudulent ITC -- represents Rs. 7,038 crore in potential ITC fraud in a single month from a single taxpayer. This must be investigated as an organised crime case.

source.quote: generated high value EWB for an amount of Rs. 39100.10 crore during November 2020, whereas, as per GSTR 1, sales during the month of November 2020 was only Rs. 119.10 crore

keyFindings.text: The GST system's failure to block EWBs by: (a) taxpayers who have not filed returns for 2 consecutive periods, (b) taxpayers whose registration was cancelled ab initio, and (c) taxpayers generating EWBs far in excess of their reported sales -- shows that Rule 138E (which is supposed to block EWBs for non-filers) was either not implemented or not effective in Maharashtra. The ITC passed to recipients from a cancelled-ab-initio GSTIN (Rs. 12.02 crore) is especially serious because a cancelled-ab-initio registration means the taxpayer was never legally registered -- the supplies are fictitious -- and any ITC claimed by recipients on those supplies is fraudulent. Yet the SGST department had not taken action to reverse this ITC as of the audit period.

source.quote: As per the taxpayer's profile on GST portal, the taxpayer as per GSTR 1 for the period April to August 2020... prevent flow of ITC to the recipients and the Department needs to take action to recover ITC from the recipients of supplies from the taxpayer

recommendations: Maharashtra SGST Department must file a complaint with the GST Intelligence (DGGI) for the ₹39,100.10 crore EWB anomaly (Bandra-West taxpayer) -- this is a potential organised ITC fraud requiring investigation of all recipients of ITC downstream from this taxpayer; a real-time EWB analytics system should be deployed that flags any EWB exceeding 5x the taxpayer's average monthly turnover for immediate scrutiny; all 97 EWBs by non-filers (₹4.90 crore) must have downstream ITC blocked and recovered from recipients.

SGST must implement automated EWB blocking for: (i) taxpayers with 2+ consecutive quarters of non-filing; (ii) taxpayers with cancelled/suspended registrations; (iii) any single EWB exceeding the taxpayer's total GSTR-1 supply for that month by more than 50 per cent -- these are system-level controls that can be implemented in the GST portal within 30 days; the ₹12.02 crore ITC passed from the cancelled-ab-initio taxpayer must be reversed from all identified recipients through DRC-07 demand notices within 90 days.

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 27.40 crore rubber lease short collection is a 12-year-plus receivable (the lease rent is accruing continuously) where the Collector's failure to realise dues has allowed interest to compound to Rs. 5.95 crore -- 27.7 per cent of the principal. Section 79 of the relevant law treats arrears of public revenue on land as recoverable with 12 per cent interest, but the statutory recovery mechanism has not been invoked. Kerala's rubber sector is one of the state's largest agricultural revenue sources -- lease rent collection integrity is essential to ensure that state land granted to rubber companies generates the contracted revenue. The Collector holding jurisdiction must issue a certificate of demand and proceed to attachment of the company's property.

keyFindings.text: Using land revenue rates frozen since 1998 to calculate licence fees for 25 years (2012-2024) has cost the state Rs. 1.14 crore in this audit period alone -- but the longer-term impact is significantly larger because all the years before 2012-13 (since 1998) are not captured in this audit. Land revenue rates in Kerala have been revised multiple times since 1998, but the licence fee calculation formula was not correspondingly updated. This is a standard bureaucratic inertia failure where no department takes ownership of updating a cross-departmental formula. The fix is simple -- a one-time government order updating the formula -- but it has not happened for 25+ years.

recommendations: Kerala Revenue Department must invoke Section 79 of the Revenue Recovery Act for the rubber lease short collection of ₹27.40 crore -- the Collector should issue a demand certificate and, if the company does not pay within 30 days, proceed to attachment of the company's movable and immovable property; the ₹5.95 crore interest already due should continue to accrue until payment is made; all rubber and plantation leases with arrears above ₹1 crore should be audited by the Revenue Department and recovery proceedings initiated within 90 days.

Kerala Government must issue an updated Government Order immediately revising the licence fee formula to use current land revenue rates -- the 1998 freeze on rates has caused progressive undercharging for 25+ years; the updated formula should also provide for automatic annual revisions linked to land revenue rate notifications; the ₹12.01 lakh Agricultural Income Tax with irregular exemption should be assessed under Section 148 of the ITA (income escaping assessment) and demand issued with interest.

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 196.66 crore underestimation of utility shifting costs (Rs. 29.19 crore DPR vs Rs. 225.85 crore actual -- a 673 per cent shortfall) is a DPR quality crisis. HAM projects are structured around a Bid Project Cost (BPC) -- the concessionaire bids based on the DPR cost estimate. If utilities shifting is underestimated by 6.7x, the concessionaire faces a cost structure that is fundamentally different from what they bid for, leading to disputes, delays, and either contractor default or GoM having to bear the excess cost. Across 140 packages with BPC Rs. 28,593.28 crore, if utility shifting is systematically underestimated, the actual total cost could be significantly higher than the BPC. The Rs. 43.40 crore land acquisition fees paid to consultants for work that produced no actual land acquisition adds to the DPR process failure.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 297.97 crore interest paid to HAM contractors in 18 packages due to GoM's delayed fund releases is an entirely avoidable cost. HAM (Hybrid Annuity Model) requires GoM to release its equity share (60 per cent) on a milestone basis -- delays in releasing this equity trigger contractual interest obligations. The interest liability is thus a direct cost of GoM's own cash flow management failures, not any contractor wrongdoing. Rs. 297.97 crore in interest across 18 packages averages Rs. 16.55 crore per package -- substantial money that could fund additional road infrastructure. The Rs. 891.29 crore revenue deficiency observations (2,119 cases in a single year) across PWD show that beyond road construction itself, the revenue recovery from road-related activities (tolls, mining royalties on road materials, contractor penalties) is severely under-enforced.

recommendations: Maharashtra PWD must reform its DPR preparation process for HAM projects -- a pre-DPR utility survey (telecom, electricity, water, gas) must be mandatory for all packages, with actual utility-shifting costs obtained from BSNL/MSEB/MSEDCL/municipal corporations before DPR finalisation; DPR consultants must be held to performance bonds linked to cost estimate accuracy (within plus or minus 20 per cent of final utility shifting cost); the ₹43.40 crore land acquisition consultancy should be investigated to determine whether land was not acquired due to consultant failure or project design changes.

Maharashtra Finance Department must establish an HAM equity release calendar -- GoM's 60 per cent equity (₹18,000 crore) must be released in tranches aligned with construction milestones, not when convenient; delayed releases trigger contractual interest (₹297.97 crore across 18 packages) which is money diverted from road construction to interest payments; a real-time HAM payment dashboard should be created visible to PWD, Finance, and ADB/World Bank monitoring teams; the ₹891.29 crore revenue deficiencies (2,119 cases) should be followed up with a mass recovery drive targeting the ₹188.45 crore in 89 observations already confirmed by audit.

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's Rs. 682 crore in unadjusted advances under Samagra Shiksha (since scheme inception) is both a financial accountability failure and a governance risk. Advances are given to executing agencies for specific works -- when they are not adjusted (i.e., expenditure vouchers not submitted), there is no verification that the money was used for its intended purpose. The Rs. 195.14 crore in just test-checked districts (implying the full state total is larger still) means that a significant portion of Samagra Shiksha spending in West Bengal cannot be fully verified. Combined with Rs. 6.53 crore diverted to salary/office expenses (an explicit misuse of scheme funds), the evidence suggests that financial controls over Samagra Shiksha at district and block level are seriously deficient.

recommendations: West Bengal Education Department must clear the ₹682 crore unadjusted advances within 6 months -- district-wise adjustment targets should be set with fortnightly review by PBSSM; for the ₹195.14 crore in test-checked districts, physical verification of completed works should be conducted before adjustment is accepted; the ₹6.53 crore diverted to salary/office should be recovered from the diverted heads and restored to the scheme account; the KGBV hostels (₹12.10 crore) must be operationalised with warden recruitment, kitchen facilities, and security arrangements within 3 months -- girls' residential hostels are the single most impactful intervention for reducing female dropout.

keyFindings.text: 55 per cent of Delhi's groundwater samples failing BIS norms means that more than half the groundwater Delhi is using (either directly via borewells or blended with surface water in WTPs) is not safe for drinking without adequate treatment. Using banned chemicals in WTPs -- despite an internal memorandum prohibiting them -- shows that operational staff are either unaware of or ignoring safety protocols. The combined effect: Delhi residents may be receiving water that was contaminated at source (groundwater) and inadequately treated (banned chemicals used instead of approved alternatives). With 127 MGD of water lost between production and distribution (371 MGD produced, 244 MGD distributed), the water that does reach taps may be further contaminated by leakage into old pipes from surrounding soil.

keyFindings.text: DJB's 29.17 per cent grievance resolution rate means that 7 in 10 complaints about water supply (no water, contamination, billing errors, leakage) are never formally addressed. For a utility serving 20 million people, unresolved water complaints translate directly into public health risks -- contamination complaints that go unaddressed can cause waterborne disease outbreaks. The billing database integrity issue (16.48 lakh records without meter serial numbers = 37.2 per cent of records) means DJB's revenue collection is built on a fundamentally flawed database -- meters without serial numbers cannot be physically identified for meter reading, leading to estimated billing, disputes, and revenue loss. Combined with the 20 KL free water scheme irregularities (824 consumers with 4+ connections), DJB is simultaneously under-collecting legitimate revenue and over-subsidising ineligible consumers.

recommendations: DJB must immediately stop using banned chemicals in all WTPs and recycling plants -- a complete audit of all WTP chemical procurement and usage for 2017-22 should be conducted to determine whether banned chemicals were purchased through DJB's procurement system (which would indicate systemic procurement failure) or smuggled in; the groundwater quality failures (55 per cent) should be reported to CPCB and Delhi Pollution Control Committee with a remediation plan; all borewells supplying contaminated water should be identified, tagged, and taken out of the potable water supply until remediated.

DJB must overhaul its grievance management system -- all 9.52 lakh pending grievances should be reviewed, categorised by type (contamination, no supply, billing, leakage), and assigned to accountable engineers with a 30-day resolution deadline; the billing database should be cleaned by deploying meter verification teams to physically verify all 16.48 lakh records with blank meter serial numbers; DJB should implement a public-facing grievance tracker (like CPGRAMS) showing real-time status of every complaint.

keyFindings.text: Awarding 15 contracts worth Rs. 255.75 crore without verifying contractor documents -- with the subsequent cancellation of contracts due to suspected fake documents -- is a procurement failure of the first order. UPSIDA is awarding public contracts (infrastructure development, road construction, drainage) without basic document verification. The range Rs. 1.01 crore to Rs. 63.41 crore (27 contract bonds) suggests this was not a one-time lapse but a systemic verification failure. When contracts are cancelled after award due to fraud, UPSIDA faces: (a) project delays as re-tender takes 6-12 months; (b) mobilization advances already paid that may be unrecoverable; (c) contractor blacklisting disputes. The Rs. 13.71 crore LD not recovered and Rs. 1.63 crore quality fee not recovered from the same contracts further show that even where UPSIDA knows it is owed money, it does not collect it.

keyFindings.text: UPSIDA's GoUP loan outstanding of Rs. 132.49 crore on a Rs. 41 crore principal is a striking example of compound interest compounding inaction -- Rs. 91.49 crore in interest has accrued on a Rs. 41 crore loan because neither UPSIDA nor the state government has resolved it, a 223 per cent interest accumulation. Simultaneously, Rs. 57.23 crore was invested in FDs with banks that had 3 consecutive years of losses -- this violates the investment guidelines which prohibit FDs in loss-making institutions because the risk of bank failure could mean the FD is not returned. The Rs. 184.43 crore income tax liability (failure to obtain a tax exemption that UPSIDA was legally entitled to) is the single largest financial loss in this audit and was entirely avoidable through a one-time application to the IT department.

keyFindings.text: NRW of 51-53 per cent means DJB is producing water for Delhi -- at enormous cost -- and losing more than half of it before it reaches paying customers. At a cost of Rs. 4,988 crore, this is not a minor technical issue: it is a catastrophic waste of financial, energy, and water resources. Delhi is classified as a water-scarce city, drawing from the Yamuna (severely polluted), the Ganga canal, and groundwater (55.1 per cent of 16,234 groundwater samples already failed). Every litre lost to NRW is a litre that required treatment energy (electricity), treatment chemicals (alum, chlorine), pumping energy, and capital infrastructure -- all of which DJB paid for and received zero revenue from. International benchmarks for well-managed utilities are 15-25 per cent NRW; at 51-53 per cent, DJB is among the worst-performing large water utilities globally.

keyFindings.text: 212.59 MGD of untreated sewage flowing from 1080 unauthorised colonies directly into storm drains (and from there into the Yamuna) is the single largest source of Yamuna pollution in Delhi. Delhi generates approximately 720 MGD of sewage; 212.59 MGD (29.5 per cent) from unauthorised colonies alone is entirely untreated. The STPs that do exist are not performing -- 25 of 35 STPs released effluent that failed to meet CPCB norms, meaning even the "treated" sewage is inadequately treated. DJB's Rs. 66,595 crore debt (accumulated despite the ADB walking away from Rs. 2,243 crore) has not translated into either adequate sewage treatment or adequate water supply -- it has translated primarily into contractor payments, debt service, and subsidies.

recommendations: Delhi Jal Board must immediately commission a full NRW reduction programme -- a District Metering Area (DMA) approach should be implemented across Delhi, where the city is divided into ~500 supply zones with bulk meters at inlet and individual meters at exit, enabling precise leak detection; the international standard for reducing NRW is 1 percentage point per year through active leakage control; reducing NRW from 52 per cent to 30 per cent over 10 years would save approximately ₹2,000 crore per year and improve per capita availability significantly.

DJB must present a time-bound sewage treatment gap closure plan to the NGT -- the 212.59 MGD untreated sewage from 1080 unauthorised colonies should be addressed through decentralised STPs (DEWATS technology is suitable for smaller catchments); the 25 non-compliant STPs should be upgraded with fixed 12-month deadlines and daily effluent monitoring data published online; the ₹66,595 crore debt portfolio should be reviewed by an independent financial restructuring consultant with a target of reducing interest costs by ₹1,000 crore per year through debt renegotiation.

keyFindings.text: The 95 per cent shortfall in community involvement under PMAY-G is significant because the community-led construction (Mazdoor Mahila Aapno Swarojgar) model was designed to reduce contractor dependence, create local employment, and ensure owner-driven construction -- all of which improve quality and reduce leakage. The Rs. 30.96 crore (62 per cent of Rs. 50 crore) BSS bathroom grant stuck at the state level shows that even when Central funds arrive, state administrative bottlenecks prevent them from reaching the ground.

keyFindings.text: The EWDS failure is especially troubling given Karnataka's escalating disaster exposure (Rs. 65,594 crore crop loss in 2023 alone). An Early Warning System is the single highest-impact investment a disaster-prone state can make -- warnings of 30-60 minutes can allow evacuation of flood plains, crop harvesting before storms, and livestock movement. Karnataka allocated Rs. 24.97 crore for EWDS, then cut it to Rs. 11.51 crore, then spent only Rs. 1.55 crore -- 6.2 per cent of the original allocation. Equipment worth Rs. 2.20 crore was not even supplied. The result: Rs. 65,594 crore in crop losses without any functional early warning infrastructure. The cost-benefit ratio of a functional EWDS (Rs. 11.51 crore would save even 1 per cent of Rs. 65,594 crore = Rs. 655 crore) is overwhelmingly positive -- the failure to deploy it is a governance catastrophe.

source.quote: EWDS was reduced from Rs. 24.97 crore to Rs. 11.51 crore... only Rs. 1.55 crore (as against the revised contractual amount of Rs. 11.51 crore)... In 2023, all the 31 districts were declared drought affected causing an estimated crop loss of Rs. 65,594 crore

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's SDMP 2018-19 mandated every hospital and school to have a Disaster Management Plan -- a requirement that has existed since the SDMP was published in 2018-19 (i.e., 5+ years before the audit) and that none of the public hospitals or educational institutions have implemented. In a major earthquake, flood, or fire event, hospital DM plans determine whether patients can be evacuated, whether medical supplies are accessible, and whether staff know their roles. Karnataka has 8,000+ government schools and 5,000+ government health centres -- none with DM plans means that an event like the 2019 Coorg floods (which destroyed roads and cut off Kodagu district for days) would find healthcare and education infrastructure without any preparation protocol.

recommendations: Karnataka Revenue Department must revive the EWDS project immediately -- the ₹11.51 crore revised contract (of which ₹9.96 crore remains unspent) should be executed with a hard deadline of March 2026; the supplier who failed to deliver ₹2.20 crore of equipment should face liquidated damages as per contract terms; KSNDMC's ₹27.04 crore bank balance (accumulated but unspent) should be deployed on district-level rain gauge networks and mobile weather stations within 12 months.

Karnataka DDMA (District Disaster Management Authority) in all 31 districts must implement the SDMP hospital and school DM plan requirement within 6 months -- a simple 2-page template DM plan should be developed for government hospitals and schools with standardised evacuation routes, emergency contact lists, and supply inventories; compliance should be verified by KSNDMC and reported to the state government quarterly; private hospitals that already have DM plans (Bengaluru Urban) should be engaged as trainers to accelerate public institution compliance.

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's Rs. 65,594.92 crore estimated crop loss in 2023 with all 31 districts drought-declared represents a state-wide agricultural crisis. To put this in context, Karnataka's GDP from agriculture is approximately Rs. 1.2 lakh crore -- a Rs. 65,594 crore crop loss equals approximately 55 per cent of one year's agricultural output wiped out in a single year. The multi-year trend from the audit (2023: Rs. 65,594 crore; earlier year with Rs. 35,160.81 crore; Rs. 28,046.95 crore; Rs. 23,481.63 crore) shows an escalating pattern of climate-driven agricultural losses. Despite this trend, the audit found that the flood forecasting investment of Rs. 2.45 crore was rendered ineffective, and capacity building funds (Rs. 1.33 crore released, only Rs. 38.54 lakh spent from a prior period) were not being deployed.

source.quote: Total loss estimated - Rs. 65,594.92 crore (crop loss). In 2023, all the 31 districts were declared drought affected... for flood forecasting in the State/region, rendering the investment of Rs. 2.45 crore

keyFindings.text: Retaining the entire Rs. 210.80 crore NDRF corpus at state HQ (2021-22) when disaster-affected districts urgently need funds is a textbook administrative failure. NDRF disbursements to districts are the primary mechanism for immediate relief -- compensating crop losses, providing emergency rations, restoring minimal housing. When state HQ sits on the full corpus and releases only Rs. 184.50 crore (87.6 per cent), the Rs. 26.30 crore retained represents relief that never reached its intended recipients. Combined with the Rs. 213.94 crore in irregular compensation payments (20 per cent of sampled cases), the aggregate amount reaching genuine disaster victims may be significantly lower than disbursement figures suggest. The Rs. 18.59 lakh misappropriation at Chintamani taluk and the cashbook irregularities show that even the funds released to districts are not fully accountable.

recommendations: Karnataka Revenue Department must automate NDRF fund release to districts within 5 working days of GoI credit -- holding the entire corpus at state HQ violates NDRF guidelines; funds should be pre-allocated to district DM accounts based on vulnerability rankings; the 22,496 irregular compensation cases (₹213.94 crore) should be re-verified through Bhoomi land records integration and Aadhaar-linked bank accounts; the ₹18.59 lakh misappropriation (Chintamani) and ₹1.81 crore (Haveri) must be investigated and prosecution initiated.

Karnataka must operationalise its ₹2.45 crore flood forecasting system immediately -- if the technology is defective, replacement should be procured through CWC (Central Water Commission) framework contracts; the insecure ₹6.25 crore vulnerable-site infrastructure must be assessed for relocation; the ₹12.00 crore fund lapse (2022-23) must be investigated to determine whether it reflected inadequate absorption capacity or administrative failure; absent UCs must be collected from all district offices within 60 days under threat of fund freeze.

keyFindings.text: 6.06 lakh fraudulent/irregular ration cards that allowed 5.15 lakh MT (approximately Rs. 2,500 crore worth at market rates) of foodgrains to reach ineligibles over 23 months represents a major PDS (Public Distribution System) corruption case. The fact that this was eventually detected and 6.06 lakh cards cancelled shows the system does have self-correction mechanisms -- but the 23-month detection lag means years of subsidised grain went to income-tax-paying households (the list includes people with annual income above Rs. 1.80 lakh, auto-rickshaw/taxi owners). keyFindings.text: The SNA (State Nodal Account) interest issue is a systemic Central Government scheme problem visible across multiple states in this audit cycle -- Gujarat earned Rs. 51.86 crore in interest on PMAY-G funds between 2017 and 2022, but only returned Rs. 15.02 crore, keeping Rs. 36.84 crore. The Ministry of Rural Development's instructions are clear: interest earned on scheme funds must be credited back to the SNA and used only for scheme purposes. Using scheme interest as a general revenue is both a violation of the scheme guidelines and a diversion of resources meant for housing. The Rs. 112.99 crore in undisbursed installments to eligible beneficiaries -- who may be living without a pucca house waiting for their second or third installment -- is the direct human cost of this financial mismanagement.

recommendations: Gujarat Civil Supplies must conduct a fresh biometric seeding and Aadhaar deduplication exercise to identify remaining fraudulent ration cards -- despite the 2016-18 cancellation drive, the 3.47 lakh MT distribution-record mismatch suggests ongoing leakage; all Fair Price Shop owners with systematic stock discrepancies should be investigated by the Vigilance Commissioner; GPS-tagged monthly inspections of FPS should be made mandatory with results published on the state food portal.

Gujarat Rural Development must release the ₹112.99 crore PMAY-G installments to pending beneficiaries immediately -- each installment corresponds to a construction milestone (foundation, roof level, completion); delaying installments stalls construction and forces poor households to borrow at high interest; the ₹36.84 crore undeposited SNA interest must be credited back within 30 days as per MoRD guidelines; recovery of ₹17.10 lakh excess payment from 57 beneficiaries should be completed before any new installments are released.

keyFindings.text: The inflation of mineable quantity in mining plans (98.37 lakh cum shown vs correct 86.15 lakh cum across 7 cases) is both a governance and revenue loss issue. Mining plans set the legal quantity a lessee can extract -- if the plan shows a larger quantity than geologically available, the lessee can remove more minerals while appearing to comply with the approved plan. The 12.22 lakh cum excess shown in plans creates a regulatory cover for excess extraction. In the context of the IISc finding that 25.73 lakh MT was actually extracted in excess of permitted quantities, inflated mining plans may be one of the mechanisms enabling this -- the lessee over-states plans, gets official approval, and then extracts beyond even the inflated plan.

keyFindings.text: The black vs colour granite misclassification has significant revenue implications because the two are regulated differently: black granite is a major mineral (regulated by the central MMDR Act, higher royalty rates, central-state shared oversight), while colour granite has historically been a minor mineral in AP (regulated by state rules, lower royalty rates). Misclassifying black granite as colour granite deflates royalty payments. Given that granite comprises 95.30 per cent (Rs. 1,780.88 crore) of AP's total mineral royalty, even a small misclassification percentage represents large absolute revenue losses. IISc has been engaged to assess the extent -- the final findings from IISc will determine the full demand.

recommendations: AP Mines Department must review all 7 inflated mining plan cases -- the excess 12.22 lakh cum shown in plans should be corrected with revised plan approvals; if excess extraction occurred under cover of the inflated plans, demand notices for royalty and penalty should be issued; all mining plan approvals should be subjected to independent geological verification before sign-off, rather than relying on lessee-submitted plans.

The ₹14.88 crore for minor mineral exploration (already approved from NMET and MERIT funds) must be deployed immediately -- exploration reports should be commissioned from state geological survey agencies and completed within 12 months; the DGPS survey backlog for composite lease areas must be completed as a precondition for any future lease renewal; dead rent arrears (₹1.09 crore) should be recovered with interest; non-working leases that have not operated for more than 2 years should be served termination notices.

keyFindings.text: SBS claiming Rs. 32.81 crore in excess agency commission by applying 2001 RBI rates in 2017-23 (when RBI had revised rates multiple times) is a straightforward overcharging of the state government -- the agreement governing agency commission explicitly requires using "rates made applicable from time to time by the RBI for nationalised banks." SBS ignored 20+ years of RBI rate revisions to maximise its commission. The failure of Government of Sikkim's Finance Department to vet commission claims before payment shows that GoS was paying excessive amounts without any checking -- a basic oversight failure. The Rs. 32.81 crore excess must be recovered from SBS and credited back to the state exchequer.

keyFindings.text: SBS's inability to use SARFAESI Act to enforce security interests on NPAs is a fundamental handicap in recovering the Rs. 1,682.04 crore NPA. SARFAESI allows banks to seize and sell mortgaged assets without going to court -- it is the primary reason why NPA resolution accelerated after 2002 for scheduled commercial banks. Without it, SBS must use Civil Courts for recovery, which typically takes 5-15 years per case. With 3,664 NPA cases, SBS cannot litigate its way to recovery. The state government's liability exposure is real: with GoS holding the entire Rs. 0.53 crore paid-up capital, any bank failure or depositor run would require an immediate GoS bailout far exceeding the nominal share capital. Depositors have no DICGC protection -- a bank failure could wipe out millions in uninsured Sikkim depositor savings.

keyFindings.text: The CBS misuse finding -- bank statements issued without staff consent -- reveals that SBS's Core Banking System lacks basic access controls. In a well-governed bank, every sensitive action (issuing statements, modifying accounts, accessing account history) requires dual authentication and leaves an audit trail. The ability to issue statements without staff consent suggests that account history can be accessed and potentially manipulated without detection. Combined with the temporary misappropriation of cash at Namchi Branch (a physical fraud) and the Rs. 3.65 crore suspected borrower-to-employee transfers (a digital fraud), SBS faces simultaneous fraud vectors in both its physical and digital operations -- indicating a deeply compromised internal control environment.

recommendations: Government of Sikkim must engage with Ministry of Finance and RBI to convert SBS to a cooperative bank licensed under Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act -- this conversion would bring SBS under RBI supervision, make it eligible for SARFAESI enforcement, provide its depositors with DICGC insurance, and give it access to RBI's Liquidity Adjustment Facility; the conversion requires meeting RBI's capital adequacy and NPA resolution conditions, which itself will force a long-overdue cleanup of the ₹1,682.04 crore NPA.

Pending regulatory conversion, GoS must mandate an independent bank turnaround specialist firm to take over day-to-day management of SBS -- the turnaround team should: (a) close or stabilise the CBS security vulnerabilities within 30 days; (b) implement mandatory 10-day annual leave and 3-year rotation for all accounts staff; (c) investigate the ₹3.65 crore borrower-to-employee transfers and Namchi Branch misappropriation; (d) establish an NPA Recovery Cell targeting ₹200 crore in recoveries within 12 months through property attachment and settlement negotiations; (e) submit monthly governance reports to GoS Finance Secretary.

keyFindings.text: A bank with 52.23 per cent Gross NPA ratio -- where over half of all loans are not being repaid -- is technically a zombie bank. For context, the RBI's worst-performing regulated commercial banks have NPAs of 5-8 per cent; even the most troubled PSU banks during the 2015-2018 NPA crisis had NPAs of 15-20 per cent. SBS at 52.23 per cent (Rs. 1,682.04 crore reported; Rs. 1,798.62 crore actual per audit) has a lending portfolio that is more bad loan than good loan. This is not a bank performing lending intermediation -- it is a state government subsidy vehicle that has deployed Rs. 1,698+ crore of public and depositor funds that are unlikely to be fully recovered. The Rs. 116.58 crore underreporting of NPAs further shows that SBS management has been presenting an artificially flattering picture of the bank's health.

source.quote: existing high level of Gross Non-Performing Assets (GNPA) aggregating Rs. 1,682.04 crore (52.23 per cent) of its total advance as on 31 March 2023. gross NPAs reported by SBS was Rs. 1,682.04 crore whereas the gross NPAs as worked out by audit was Rs. 1,798.62 crore

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 3.65 crore in suspected fraudulent transactions -- where borrower accounts directly funded bank employees' personal accounts, with Rs. 1.29 crore corresponding exactly in timing to loan disbursals -- is a classic kick-back fraud pattern: a borrower receives a loan and immediately transfers a portion to the approving bank official as a kickback. SBS's failure to implement mandatory staff rotation and leave (despite RBI's explicit directive following similar fraud patterns across Indian banks) means the same employees who may have approved or processed these loans continued to have access to the accounts. Combined with the CBS (Core Banking System) weakness (bank statements issued without staff consent), the fraud detection environment at SBS is severely inadequate for a bank managing Rs. 3,000+ crore in deposits.

recommendations: Government of Sikkim must initiate an immediate forensic audit of SBS by a RBI-empanelled forensic auditor covering all NPA accounts above ₹1 crore and all transactions between borrower accounts and employee accounts from 2017-23 -- the ₹3.65 crore suspected fraud and the ₹116.58 crore NPA underreporting require investigation to determine whether there was intentional misreporting; if fraud is confirmed, FIR under IPC Section 420 and Prevention of Corruption Act should be filed against responsible officers; SBS management should be placed under administrative oversight.

Government of Sikkim must urgently explore getting SBS regulated under the Banking Regulation Act by converting it to a cooperative bank licensed under the BR Act, or by merging it with a scheduled commercial bank -- the absence of RBI supervision, DICGC deposit insurance, and lender-of-last-resort access leaves Sikkim depositors with no protection if the bank fails; the 52.23 per cent NPA ratio is already a de facto bank failure signal; the state government should also implement all RBI's staff rotation, mandatory leave, and CBS security requirements immediately to contain further fraud.

keyFindings.text: Arunachal Pradesh's BOCW Board achieving 94.55 per cent welfare expenditure (Rs. 164.62 crore of Rs. 174.12 crore) with only 5.45 per cent on administration is actually a positive finding relative to many states where administrative costs consume 10-20 per cent of welfare budgets. However, the absolute reach is limited -- only 695 children received educational benefits, 102 families received normal death benefit. Given Arunachal's large construction workforce (involved in roads, dams, tunnels, military construction), these beneficiary numbers suggest either significant under-registration of workers or weak outreach. BOCW Board membership and Aadhaar-linked registration should be a priority to expand coverage.

keyFindings.text: The failure to disclose maximum guarantees outstanding in Finance Accounts -- a mandatory requirement under CAG's Guidelines for Annual Accounts -- means the Legislature and public cannot assess the contingent liability borne by the state. Guarantees that are not disclosed are also not budgeted for potential default. Given that Arunachal's SPSEs include entities with accumulated losses exceeding their capital (negative net worth), the guarantees extended to these entities are at high risk of being called -- and an undisclosed guarantee called unexpectedly creates a sudden fiscal shock. The CAMPA arrears issue further compounds this: CAMPA funds for compensatory afforestation are a Central mandate, and uncleared arrears risk GoI stopping future forest diversions for infrastructure projects.

recommendations: Arunachal Pradesh BOCW Board must expand worker registration by partnering with major construction project managers (NHIDCL, NHPC, BRO, CPWD) operating in the state -- every major infrastructure project should provide worker registration facilitation to BOCW Board as a contractual condition; the Board should set a target of tripling registered membership in 2 years and increase educational benefit disbursements proportionally; biometric verification of beneficiaries should be enabled to prevent duplication and fraud.

Arunachal Pradesh Finance Department must disclose all outstanding guarantees in the Finance Accounts as a mandatory schedule -- a Guarantee Register should be maintained and the Accountant General should be provided the register annually before Finance Accounts finalisation; CAMPA arrears must be cleared with a specific timeline provided to the Supreme Court-appointed CAMPA National Authority; unclearcd CAMPA arrears risk a stop-work order on forest diversions which would halt all infrastructure development.

keyFindings.text: Arunachal Pradesh's capital expenditure growing at 23.1 per cent CAGR over 5 years (from Rs. 3,693 crore to Rs. 8,466 crore) is positive for a frontier state that is heavily dependent on Central funds and is building out its physical infrastructure. However, the 1,061.81 per cent surge in Minor Irrigation capital outlay (Rs. 22.39 crore to Rs. 260.16 crore in a single year) should be scrutinised for absorption capacity -- can the Irrigation Department, with its existing engineering and administrative strength, absorb 10x more capital in one year without quality and execution compromises? keyFindings.text: Three working SPSEs with accumulated losses (Rs. 36.57 crore) that have completely eroded their paid-up capital (Rs. 7.68 crore) are technically insolvent -- they have negative net worth. Despite this, they continue operating ("working SPSEs"), which means the state government is either funding their losses through grants or allowing them to accumulate payables they cannot repay. SPSEs with negative net worth typically cannot borrow commercially (no assets to pledge) and depend entirely on government support -- the government should either: (a) recapitalise them with a clear turnaround plan; (b) merge them into viable entities; or (c) wind them up. The 39 accounts in arrears (some going back 9 years) means even the basic accountability mechanism (audited accounts) is not functioning for these SPSEs.

recommendations: Arunachal Pradesh Finance Department must conduct a SPSE viability review for all 6 working SPSEs -- the 3 with negative net worth (accumulated losses ₹36.57 crore > capital ₹7.68 crore) should be assessed for whether their mandate remains relevant; if the mandate is relevant, a time-bound turnaround plan with specific milestones should be prepared and placed before the state cabinet within 6 months; if the mandate has been superseded or duplicated, dissolution should be recommended; all 39 accounts in arrears should be cleared within 12 months with CAMPA and Forest Corporation as priority cases.

For the 1,061.81 per cent surge in Minor Irrigation capital outlay, the Finance Department should conduct a mid-year review to ensure (a) the ₹260.16 crore was actually spent on sanctioned works (not diverted), (b) the works are physically executing on time, and (c) water user associations are being formed for O&M sustainability; a surge of this magnitude in a single year from a low base typically indicates a budget utilisation drive rather than genuine absorption, which risks quality compromises; third-party quality checks are essential.

keyFindings.text: Assam's Ways and Means Advances (WMA) usage of Rs. 16,242.25 crore in FY 2023-24 is exceptionally large for a state of Assam's GSDP size. WMA is a short-term overdraft facility from RBI to help states manage temporary cash mismatches between receipts and payments -- it is meant to be used occasionally for a few days, not structurally throughout the year. Rs. 16,242.25 crore in WMA (nearly 2.53 per cent of Assam's GSDP) indicates that the state was chronically cash-deficient -- spending money before it received corresponding revenue. This reliance on WMA also means Assam is paying RBI's repo rate plus 100 basis points as interest on these short-term borrowings, adding to the fiscal cost. FY 2024-25's Rs. 9,819.70 crore is a partial improvement but still very high.

keyFindings.text: 86.08 per cent of Assam's borrowings going to capital expenditure (Rs. 26,404.20 crore) would normally be positive -- it means borrowings are funding investment rather than consumption. However, in the context of Assam's Rs. 28,529.52 crore fiscal deficit and Rs. 3,090.85 crore revenue deficit, this ratio requires scrutiny: are the items booked as Capital Expenditure genuinely productive investment, or do they include the Rs. 40.02 crore office expenditure misclassified as Capital (as CAG found in Chapter II)? If Capital Expenditure is inflated by misclassification, the 86.08 per cent figure overstates the productive use of borrowings.

recommendations: Assam Finance Department must address the structural cash flow deficit that drives large WMA usage -- the transition from ₹4,608 crore WMA (2022-23) to ₹16,242 crore (2023-24) suggests that either revenue receipts are becoming more back-loaded (concentrated in March) or expenditure is front-loaded; a Cash Flow Forecasting System should be implemented to predict weekly cash positions 8 weeks ahead; surplus receipts in early-year should be invested in short-term government securities rather than sitting in the Consolidated Fund at zero yield.

Assam should accelerate repayment of the ₹2,767.87 crore GST back-to-back loan -- this is a Central Government loan carrying specific repayment terms; partial repayment (₹753.62 crore in 2024-25) is happening but the balance ₹2,014.25 crore should be cleared within 2 years; the state should explore using 15th Finance Commission grants or PDRD grants for this prepayment to reduce the interest burden and clean up the balance sheet.

keyFindings.text: Assam's Rs. 93.77 crore misclassification is a structural accounting discipline failure that has direct consequences for fiscal reporting. Rs. 40.02 crore in office expenditure (a Revenue item by nature) booked under Capital inflates the Capital Expenditure figure, making it appear that more productive investment is happening than is actually the case. Conversely, Rs. 22.24 crore of construction (Capital) booked as Revenue understates Capital Expenditure and overstates Revenue Expenditure. These misclassifications distort the Revenue/Capital split used by the Finance Commission and FRBM assessments -- Assam's official fiscal deficit number may already partially reflect these classification errors.

keyFindings.text: Assam's SNA-SPARSH transition (24 CSS schemes onboarded May 2024) is a positive reform step, but unreconciled balances in earlier SNA accounts represent a systemic risk: if unspent funds in pre-SPARSH SNA accounts are not refunded to the Consolidated Fund correctly, they remain off-budget. CAG notes that the unspent fund was refunded to CFI in July 2025 -- but only after the audit period ended. The NPS contribution data (due Rs. 956.14 crore, actual Rs. 1,060.34 crore, plus Rs. 193.95 crore transfer anomaly) suggests that Assam's NPS accounting has complex transfer mechanisms that may not accurately reflect the state's actual pension liability accrual.
