recommendations: Assam Finance Department must implement a mandatory pre-audit classification check for all expenditure vouchers above ₹10 lakh -- the check should verify whether the expenditure is revenue or capital in nature using CPWA Code definitions before payment is processed in PFMS; the ₹93.77 crore in misclassified expenditure should be rectified through journal entries with concurrence from the Accountant General; going forward, departmental accounts officers should be trained annually on Revenue vs Capital classification rules.

For SNA reconciliation, Assam Finance Department should complete the reconciliation of all pre-SPARSH SNA accounts by December 2025 and submit a reconciliation certificate to the Accountant General -- any unrecovered interest from SNA holding accounts (including the ₹0.22 lakh noted still to be refunded) should be systematically recovered; the NPS contribution mechanism should be reviewed to ensure the ₹193.95 crore transfer anomaly under MH-8342-117 is fully explained and accounted for in the state's pension liability computation.

keyFindings.text: Assam's internal debt doubling in 5 years (Rs. 67,014 crore to Rs. 1,27,718 crore, a Rs. 60,703.95 crore increase or 90.58 per cent) represents one of the fastest debt accumulation rates among Indian states. For context, this is a Rs. 60,703 crore increase in 5 years -- averaging Rs. 12,140 crore per year in new borrowings. The interest burden has grown correspondingly: Rs. 8,406.08 crore in interest on internal debt alone in FY 2024-25, which is almost the entirety of the Revenue Deficit (Rs. 3,090.85 crore) plus a significant portion of primary expenditure. With 53 per cent of the debt maturing in the near term, Assam faces significant rollover risk -- if market conditions tighten, the cost of refinancing this debt could further worsen the fiscal deficit.

keyFindings.text: A Primary Deficit of Rs. 19,061.77 crore (2.96 per cent of GSDP) means that even before paying interest, Assam's expenditure exceeds its revenues by nearly 3 per cent of GSDP. This is a fundamental fiscal sustainability problem: primary deficit = revenue + capital receipts (excluding borrowings) minus revenue + capital expenditure (excluding interest payments). A positive primary deficit means the state is borrowing not just to pay for past debt service, but to finance current operations and capital investment. The FRBM ceiling breach for the fiscal deficit (4.43 per cent vs the ceiling) confirms that Assam has not been able to bring its borrowing within statutory limits.

source.quote: Primary Deficit was Rs. 19,061.77 crore (2.96 per cent of GSDP)... Fiscal Deficit stood at Rs. 28,529.52 crore (4.43 per cent of GSDP), breached... Revenue Deficit of Rs. 3,090.85 crore (0.48 per cent)

recommendations: Assam Finance Department must prepare a 5-year Medium Term Fiscal Consolidation Plan (MTFCP) -- the plan should target: (a) reducing fiscal deficit from 4.43 per cent to below 3.5 per cent by FY 2027-28 and 3 per cent by FY 2029-30; (b) eliminating Revenue Deficit by FY 2028-29 (currently ₹3,090.85 crore); (c) extending the average maturity of new borrowings to reduce the 53 per cent near-term concentration risk; the plan should be laid before the Assam Legislative Assembly for transparency.

The ₹8,406.08 crore annual interest payment on internal debt demands a Debt Management Strategy -- Assam should explore: (a) swapping high-interest state borrowings for lower-rate Central Government loans through MSME/infrastructure financing windows; (b) issuing longer-duration bonds (15-20 year) to reduce rollover risk; (c) renegotiating financial institution loans (₹2,650.32 crore) for extended repayment; simultaneously, every new capital expenditure scheme should be subject to a fiscal impact assessment to prevent further fiscal deficit expansion.

keyFindings.text: Himachal Pradesh's non-tax revenue (Rs. 1,236.66 crore over 5 years, rising to 9.97 per cent of total non-tax receipts) is primarily driven by royalties, user charges, and fees from natural resource sectors -- mining, water, and forests. The finding of Rs. 1.81 crore shortfall across 27 mineral leases (dead rent + surface rent not collected) shows that even as revenues grow, the collection mechanism has systematic gaps. Dead rent is payable annually for the right to hold a mineral lease even without extraction -- it ensures the state is compensated for the exclusive right granted to the lessee; non-collection means lessees receive this exclusivity free of charge.

source.quote: non-tax revenues, rising from Rs. 221.04 crore (7.81 per cent of non-tax receipts) in 2018-19 to Rs. 286.34 crore (9.97 per cent) in 2022-23... discovered a shortfall of Rs. 1.81 crore across 27 leases

keyFindings.text: The Compensatory Afforestation Fund (CAF) short realisation is particularly significant in a state like Himachal Pradesh where forest coverage (about 27 per cent of state area) is both ecologically critical and economically linked to tourism, watershed services, and hydropower. CAF amounts are levied on project proponents who divert forest land -- they fund compensatory plantation. Short realisation means either fewer trees are planted, or the state government must subsidise plantations that should have been paid for by the diverting entity. Given Himachal's climate vulnerability (glacier retreat, forest fires), every lakh of CAF short-collected is a direct deficit in ecological restoration funding.

source.quote: Short realisation of Compensatory Afforestation Fund

recommendations: Himachal Pradesh Mines and Geology Department must automate dead rent demand generation -- a software trigger should auto-generate demand notices on all active and renewal-pending mineral leases on their anniversary dates; manual demand-and-collection processes are prone to exactly the ₹74.81 lakh (dead rent) and ₹7.27 lakh (surface rent) gaps found; the department should also reconcile the 27-lease shortfall (₹1.81 crore) and issue recovery notices within 30 days.

HP Forest Department should audit all forest diversion cases from 2017-23 against CAF deposits to identify and recover short-levied amounts -- for each case where CAF was levied at a lower rate or on a smaller area than the actual diversion, supplementary demand should be raised on the project proponent; going forward, CAF calculations should be verified by the Deputy Conservator of Forests before work orders are issued, preventing under-levy at source.

keyFindings.text: A 53.50 per cent shortfall in quality control inspections of HAM road construction sites means approximately half of the planned inspections are not happening. In a HAM model where the private concessionaire does the construction and is supposed to be held accountable through third-party and government inspections, the absence of half the inspections fundamentally undermines the accountability mechanism. Roads built without adequate QC inspections are at higher risk of early-life pavement failures, which then require expensive rehabilitation within the concession period at government cost (since HAM annuity contracts typically make the government responsible for any major structural failure beyond what the concessionaire's maintenance obligation covers).

keyFindings.text: MPCB's shortfall in visiting highly polluting industries in HAM road corridors (stone crushers, hot mix plants, batching plants, and other construction-linked industries) allows polluters to operate without oversight during the high-intensity construction phase. HAM road corridors in Maharashtra often run through agricultural and residential areas where dust, noise, and water pollution from construction sites are major concerns. CAG's finding that MPCB inspections are significantly behind schedule confirms that the environmental compliance monitoring system is not keeping pace with the Rs. 30,000 crore construction programme.

recommendations: Maharashtra PWD must establish a real-time digital QC inspection tracking system for all 140 HAM packages -- each package should have a monthly inspection schedule; deviations of more than 20 per cent from the schedule should automatically alert the Chief Engineer; the shortfall finding (53.50 per cent) in QC inspections should be treated as a systemic failure requiring immediate deployment of additional Quality Control Engineers from the PWD quality assurance cadre; all HAM packages should undergo a comprehensive catch-up inspection in the next 90 days with results uploaded to the MahaRail/MahaHAM portal.

Maharashtra Pollution Control Board must prioritise inspection of all industrial units (stone crushers, hot mix plants, batching plants) operating within 5 km of HAM road construction corridors -- a HAM Environmental Monitoring Cell should be established within MPCB with dedicated inspectors for the 140-package programme; real-time air quality monitoring should be mandated at construction sites above 20 km length; DPR insurance provisions should be standardised using IRDAI benchmark rates rather than lumpsum estimates to prevent the ₹34.56 crore overestimation pattern.

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 6,666.10 crore GST ITC mismatch across 119 cases -- where the ITC claimed in GSTR-3B does not match what is reflected in GSTR-2A (the auto-populated supplier-side data) -- represents the most significant systemic tax enforcement gap in Maharashtra GST. GSTR-2A is a supplier-verified credit; where a buyer claims more than GSTR-2A shows, the excess is either fraud (claiming fake credit) or an administrative discrepancy. At Rs. 6,666.10 crore across 119 cases, even if a portion is ultimately reconciled, the revenue risk is enormous. The Rs. 154.64 crore confirmed implication in 20 cases is likely the conservative floor, not the ceiling. Maharashtra is the largest GST-contributing state -- weaknesses in its ITC verification directly affect national GST revenue.

source.quote: noticed in 119 cases involving mismatch of Rs. 6,666.10 crore. 20 cases with a revenue implication of Rs. 154.64 crore

keyFindings.text: The Mumbai stamp duty short levy of Rs. 10.50 crore arose because the Collector of Stamps valued a property at Rs. 62.28 crore when its market value was Rs. 100.11 crore -- a Rs. 37.83 crore undervaluation (61 per cent of true value). Stamp duty fraud through deliberate undervaluation of property in registration documents is a pervasive problem; CAG's finding that the Collector accepted a grossly under-market valuation without reference to Ready Reckoner rates (which are mandatory in Maharashtra for property registration) suggests either inadequate use of Ready Reckoner tools or institutional capture by vested interests. The Pune irregular concession of 1 per cent (short levy Rs. 1.50 crore) represents a different abuse: applying a concession not authorised in law.

source.quote: The Collector of Stamps, Mumbai, valued a property at Rs. 62.28 crore and levied Stamp Duty of Rs. 3.11 crore... Audit assessed the market value at Rs. 100.11 crore, calculating the Stamp Duty payable as Rs. 5.00 crore. This led to a short levy of Rs. 1.89 crore State, Pune allowed irregular concession of one per cent, which led to short levy of Stamp Duty of Rs. 1.50 crore

recommendations: Maharashtra State Tax Department must implement automated ITC mismatch notices for all 119 cases (₹6,666.10 crore) -- the department's GST audit system should flag GSTR-3B vs GSTR-2A mismatches above ₹1 lakh automatically and generate System Generated Discrepancy Reports (SGDRs) for each such case; the ₹96.85 crore tax non-recovery should be pursued through attachment proceedings and tax recovery certificates; for the 3 taxpayers with 340-813 day filing delays, penalty assessment under Section 125 CGST Act should be initiated along with interest under Section 50.

Maharashtra Registration and Stamps Department must mandate Ready Reckoner cross-check for all commercial properties above ₹5 crore -- every registration above this threshold should require a mandatory Ready Reckoner verification and a certified valuation report from a IBBI-registered valuer before the Sub-Registrar stamps the document; the ₹10.50 crore Mumbai short levy should be raised as a demand notice on the party; the Pune concession case (₹1.50 crore) should be investigated for whether the concession was granted illegally and whether an officer is accountable.

keyFindings.text: Maharashtra's HAM (Hybrid Annuity Model) road programme is one of India's largest state-level road investment portfolios (Rs. 30,000 crore, 6,000 km, 140 packages). Finding Rs. 34.56 crore in excess insurance charges inflated into DPRs of 17 of 42 packages -- i.e. 40 per cent of selected packages -- suggests a systemic overestimation of O&M costs at DPR stage, not isolated errors. Inflated DPRs inflate the annuity the government must pay over 15+ years, creating a compounding financial liability. The Rs. 297.97 crore in interest costs from delayed GoM fund releases in 18 packages shows that the state's own payment delays are a significant source of project cost escalation in HAM models where interest is a primary cost driver.

source.quote: inclusion of excess insurance charges in O&M cost to the tune of Rs. 34.56 crore in respect of 17 out of selected 42 packages... short/delay in release of funds by GoM. As a result Rs. 297.97 crore in 18 packages

keyFindings.text: Rs. 9.64 crore idle expenditure (construction done before land acquisition was completed) and Rs. 17.80 crore unfruitful underground construction represent preventable losses from starting work before the enabling conditions are in place. In infrastructure projects, the sequence is: land acquisition → forest clearance → utility shifting → then civil work. Reversing this sequence -- doing civil work while land acquisition is incomplete -- creates idle assets (built but inaccessible), claims, and rework costs. The Rs. 891.29 crore revenue observation backlog (only Rs. 25.58 crore collected of Rs. 891.29 crore pointed) indicates that Maharashtra's tax enforcement apparatus is not translating audit findings into actual revenue recovery.

source.quote: of the required land resulted expenditure of Rs. 9.64 crore Unfruitful expenditure of Rs. 17.80 crore on construction of underground... Rs. 891.29 crore in 2119 observations... The departments collected Rs. 25.58 crore

recommendations: Maharashtra PWD must revise the DPR preparation guidelines for HAM packages to require that insurance cost estimates use actual market quotations (not lump sum approximations) from at least three insurers -- the ₹34.56 crore overestimation in 17 packages indicates that current DPR standards are inadequate; for new HAM packages, a DPR Quality Assurance cell under the Chief Engineer (Projects) should cross-check O&M cost assumptions including insurance, maintenance, and toll-related costs against NHAI benchmarks before sanction.

Maharashtra Finance Department must enforce timely GoM equity releases for HAM projects -- the ₹297.97 crore in interest costs from fund release delays is avoidable; a dedicated HAM Equity Release Calendar should be prepared for each package with releases scheduled 45 days before contractual due dates; any delay in equity release should be flagged to the Chief Secretary within 7 days; land acquisition for all remaining HAM stretches must be completed before any further construction award in that stretch to prevent repeat idle expenditure.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 10.12 crore unfruitful expenditure in Kullu district on PMKSY irrigation schemes -- rendered useless by floods, land disputes, and forest clearance failures -- represents the systemic consequence of implementing infrastructure projects without resolving preconditions (land, forest clearance, flood risk assessment) before tendering. The PMKSY guidelines require site feasibility and land-owner consent before sanction; schemes in Kullu that were sanctioned without resolving forest clearance or land disputes were always at risk of becoming unfruitful. The 12-48 month time overruns in 13 of 24 test-checked schemes and Rs. 4.41 crore in unrecovered contractor delay compensation confirm that the department does not enforce its own contract conditions.

keyFindings.text: Himachal Pradesh's 96.22 per cent shortfall in mason training for disaster management (only 3.78 per cent trained) represents a critical preparedness gap for a state that is among the most vulnerable to landslides, cloud bursts, and flash floods in India. The Joshimath land subsidence, the 2023 Himachal Pradesh floods, and recurring NDMA alerts all highlight the state's exposure. Trained masons who can apply earthquake-resistant and flood-resilient construction techniques are the front line of community-level disaster risk reduction. With Rs. 2.37 crore sitting unutilised in the disaster management training budget, the failure to train 5,307 masons is not a resource problem -- it is an execution failure.

source.quote: Training targets for youth volunteers (shortfall: 8,566; 51.77 per cent) and masons (shortfall: 5,307; 96.22 per cent) were not met during 2019-23 and Rs. 2.37 crore remained unutilised as of October 2023

recommendations: HP Irrigation and Public Health Department must make pre-construction verification of forest clearance, land acquisition completion, and flood risk zone status mandatory before tendering any PMKSY scheme -- a "Start of Work" compliance checklist should be signed by the divisional engineer and submitted to the Chief Engineer before any expenditure; schemes in Kullu and other high-risk districts should additionally require a geo-technical survey certificate before sanction; the ₹4.41 crore in unrecovered contractor delay compensation should be deducted from the contractors' security deposits or pending bills within 30 days.

Himachal Pradesh Disaster Management Authority (HSDMA) must urgently utilize the ₹2.37 crore training budget -- mason training is especially critical and the 96.22 per cent shortfall should be addressed by partnering with ITIs (Industrial Training Institutes) and polytechnics to run compressed disaster-resilient construction modules; HSDMA should set a binding target of training 3,000 masons and 4,000 youth volunteers in FY 2025-26; the SDRF excess sanctions (43 per cent above norms) should be reviewed and clawback orders issued for the ₹12.79 crore overdrawn.

keyFindings.text: Keeping Rs. 122.27 crore in SDRF savings bank accounts (at ~3.5 per cent interest) instead of permitted instruments like FDs (at 6-7 per cent) costs HP approximately Rs. 3-4 crore per year in foregone returns. Simultaneously, MHA deducted Rs. 61.02 crore from HP's SDRF allocation because HP submitted inaccurate data -- meaning HP lost Rs. 61.02 crore in Central grants while keeping Rs. 122.27 crore idle in low-yield accounts. This twin failure (cash management failure + data reporting failure) in the SDRF is compounded by Rs. 11.76 crore in inadmissible works -- routine maintenance and new construction funded through disaster relief money -- which directly reduces the funds available for actual disaster victims.

keyFindings.text: The ERP system that HP procured for Rs. 11.19 crore to modernise its administration has 30 of 37 modules (81 per cent) non-functional, with hardware worth Rs. 1.99 crore sitting non-functional since 2015, 2017, and 2021 -- meaning some equipment has been non-functional for up to 9 years. This is not a technical failure; it is an administrative failure to commission, maintain, and demand contractual performance from the ERP vendor. A government that spent Rs. 11.19 crore on an ERP that operates at 19 per cent capacity (7 of 37 modules) has essentially written off the investment -- the opportunity cost is enormous given what functional ERP would enable in fiscal management, including better SDRF data to avoid MHA deductions.

recommendations: Himachal Pradesh Finance Department must immediately invest the ₹122.27 crore SDRF balance in permitted instruments (Fixed Deposits with nationalised banks or Government securities as specified by the Finance Commission guidelines) -- the interest rate differential between savings accounts and FDs (~2-3 per cent) can recover ₹2-4 crore annually for the SDRF; simultaneously, the state should submit a corrected account of SDRF utilisation to MHA to seek restoration of the ₹61.02 crore deduction; inadmissible SDRF expenditure of ₹11.76 crore should be refunded to the SDRF from the concerned departments' budgets.

Himachal Pradesh must convene an emergency review of its ₹11.19 crore ERP system -- 30 of 37 modules non-functional is an implementation failure requiring vendor accountability; the state should: (a) invoke contractual SLA clauses and demand operationalisation of all 30 modules within 6 months with penalty for delay; (b) procure replacement hardware for the 3 units non-functional since 2015-2021; (c) designate a Chief Information Officer (CIO) at Additional Secretary level responsible for ERP performance; if the vendor is unresponsive, explore migration to a functional NIC or NeST solution rather than continuing to carry dead IT infrastructure.

keyFindings.text: DMFT funds are collected from mining companies specifically to benefit the communities and areas affected by mining -- the Pradhan Mantri Khanij Kshetra Kalyan Yojana (PMKKKY) guidelines mandate that 60 per cent of DMFT funds go to High Priority areas (drinking water, environment, healthcare, education). Finding only 41 per cent in High Priority and 59 per cent in Other Priority inverts the statutory priority framework. More fundamentally, spending only Rs. 47.03 crore of Rs. 239.21 crore received (19.66 per cent utilisation) means Rs. 192.18 crore earmarked for mining-affected communities is sitting idle in DMFT accounts -- these communities (often tribal or forest-dwelling) are bearing the environmental and social costs of mining while their compensation fund accumulates unspent.

source.quote: Out of Rs. 239.21 crore received for DMFTs in the four test-checked districts, only Rs. 86.56 crore (36.18 per cent) was sanctioned for projects, and merely Rs. 47.03 crore... 59 projects valued at Rs. 26.48 crore (41 per cent) were allocated to High-Priority Areas

keyFindings.text: The splitting of 18 schemes worth Rs. 48.25 crore into sub-Rs. 5 lakh components to avoid competitive bidding is a classic public procurement integrity failure. By staying below the threshold for open tendering, the department denies the state government the benefit of competitive pricing and enables work to be assigned to favoured contractors without scrutiny. At Rs. 48.25 crore across 8 divisions, this is a systemic pattern rather than isolated incidents. Combined with the Rs. 61.07 crore withheld by GoI because HP failed to submit accurate utilisation data, the pattern suggests systemic financial reporting and governance failures in the Irrigation and Public Health Department.

recommendations: Himachal Pradesh Mining Department must convene DMFT Trust meetings in all four audited districts within 60 days to sanction projects in the 60 per cent High Priority category -- until DMFT spending reaches 60 per cent High Priority, no new Other Priority sanctions should be approved; the ₹192.18 crore unspent DMFT balance should be invested in fixed deposits with scheduled commercial banks (earning interest for future use) rather than sitting in zero-interest accounts; monthly utilisation reports should be made public on the DMFT portal.

The Irrigation and Public Health Department must immediately stop splitting works to evade tender thresholds -- the Principal Secretary should issue a circular making work splitting a punishable misconduct; any officer found to have split contracts to avoid procurement rules should face departmental action; for user charge recovery, HP should implement property-linked billing (water charges embedded in property records) with automatic demand generation to move from ₹0.37 crore to ₹9.79 crore potential collections; data systems for PMKSY must be strengthened to prevent further GoI grant withholdings.

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 9.69 crore petroleum lease non-recovery traces to a structural problem in the Petroleum and Natural Gas (Production and Exploration) rules: once a PEL (Petroleum Exploration Licence) expires or is due for PML (Petroleum Mining Lease) conversion, the holder is liable for dead rent on the entire licence area until formal surrender. Delays in conversion processing (within the department) and non-surrender by lessees create a window during which dead rent and royalty accrue but are not demanded. At Rs. 9.69 crore across multiple leases, this represents systematic lax enforcement of India's petroleum revenue rules in Gujarat. This revenue belongs to the state and can fund public services; its non-recovery subsidises petroleum companies at taxpayer expense.

source.quote: non-recovery of Rs. 9.69 crore on account of dead rent and royalty from PEL/PML holders

keyFindings.text: The failure to recover Rs. 83.05 lakh in electricity charges from the Airports Authority of India (AAI) -- a central government entity -- highlights the problem of inter-governmental receivables where state governments are reluctant to pursue recovery from Central PSUs or ministries. The Rs. 62.39 lakh in solar PV irregularities and Rs. 9.18 lakh in NPV short-levies, while individually smaller, collectively represent revenue leakage that, if replicated across all divisions and departments, would aggregate to a significant annual loss. CAG audits consistently find that small individual amounts in each department collectively represent hundreds of crores at the state level.

recommendations: Gujarat Energy and Petrochemicals Department should issue demand notices for ₹9.69 crore dead rent and royalty to all PEL/PML holders with arrears within 30 days -- a register of all active and expired PEL/PML licenses with due-date tracking and automated demand generation should be maintained; for each lapsed/surrendered area, final accounts should be settled within 60 days of surrender date; the department should explore online real-time tracking of PEL/PML status linked to the revenue accounting system to prevent future accumulation.

Gujarat Forest Department should recalculate NPV in the two flagged cases and issue supplementary demand notices for the ₹9.19 lakh (₹2.76 lakh + ₹6.43 lakh) shortfall; for AAI electricity arrears of ₹83.05 lakh, Gujarat Power Distribution Company should write to AAI's regional head with a 30-day payment notice and, if unresolved, escalate to the Ministry of Civil Aviation through the state government's Chief Secretary.

keyFindings.text: Punjab collected Rs. 1.06 crore in user charges against a projected Rs. 204.84 crore over 3 years -- a 99.48 per cent shortfall. User charges are the financial backbone of sustainable SWM because they make the service self-funding and create a direct incentive for households to engage with the system. At Rs. 1.06 crore for 20 ULBs over 3 years, the average per-ULB collection is Rs. 5.30 lakh/year -- negligible. This has two consequences: (a) ULBs are entirely dependent on government grants for SWM funding, and (b) Rs. 319.01 crore in allocated grants went unspent while 65 per cent of waste went untreated -- meaning Punjab simultaneously failed to spend available money and failed to collect money it should have raised itself.

source.quote: Of Rs. 1,011.33 crore allocated for SWM between 2017 and 2022, only Rs. 692.32 crore was spent. collected only Rs. 1.06 crore (0.52 per cent) as user charges, falling short of the projected Rs. 204.84 crore

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 100 crore NGT penalty on Ludhiana Corporation (associated with the dumpsite where 7 people died) is more than 11.8x the cost of the Rs. 8.48 crore Waste Processing Plant that sits idle due to public protests at the same site. This is the core irony of Punjab's SWM failure: the plant built to process waste and eliminate the dumpsite's hazards is not operational because of community opposition -- opposition that may itself stem from inadequate public consultation -- while the dumpsite that should have been closed continues to operate unsafely, resulting in deaths and a Rs. 100 crore penalty. The Rs. 20.57 crore spent on slaughterhouses that still do not follow scientific waste management practices is another instance of capital spending without operational follow-through.

recommendations: Punjab State Government must make user charge collection mandatory for all ULBs with a staggered but binding rollout -- the ₹204.84 crore target was set by the state itself; ULBs collecting below 10 per cent of their target should have their SWM grants reduced proportionally to create an incentive for collection; user charges can be embedded in property tax bills (a proven method in Bengaluru and Chennai); the Local Government Department should issue a Government Order mandating door-to-door user charge collection by April 2026 with monthly monitoring.

The Ludhiana Waste Processing Plant (₹8.48 crore, idle due to protests) must be made operational through a structured community engagement process -- the state should commission an independent social impact assessment, hold public hearings in affected wards, and offer visible odour/vector control measures to address the public's concerns; operating the plant is the only path to closing the Ludhiana dumpsite, eliminating ongoing safety hazards, and complying with the NGT's conditions for the ₹100 crore penalty waiver/reduction; inaction perpetuates both the safety risk and the penalty liability.

UPSIDA must engage tax consultants to immediately apply for income tax exemption under the applicable provisions of the Income Tax Act, 1961 and settle the ₹184.43 crore tax liability -- the delay itself creates interest/penalty; simultaneously, the ₹52.84 crore unsecured loans should be secured (call for security or pledge) or converted to grants-in-aid with board approval; the ₹57.23 crore FD in loss-making banks should be moved at maturity to scheduled commercial banks with healthy balance sheets per RBI guidelines.

keyFindings.text: Punjab's SWM failure is a governance compliance gap sustained over 6+ years after its own SWM Policy was notified. The finding that bio-remediation and C&D waste machinery is lying idle at multiple ULBs while 17,000 MT + 6,000 MT of legacy waste sits unprocessed at dumpsites shows that equipment procurement happened without operational planning. The MSWM Manual 2016 requires waste composition assessment as the foundation for infrastructure sizing -- 17 of 20 ULBs instead borrowed figures from a PMIDC template, meaning their DPRs, equipment selection, and capacity planning are all built on fabricated baselines. This explains why machinery procured for those ULBs sits idle: it may be sized or specified for the wrong waste fractions.

keyFindings.text: 711 ragpickers and 2,682 waste collectors have been identified in the system but denied integration -- no identity cards, no social security benefits, no formal role in the SWM chain despite the SWM Rules 2016 and Punjab State SWM Policy explicitly requiring their integration. These are workers who already handle waste for a living, but without formal integration they are denied accident insurance, health care, EPFO coverage, and child schooling benefits. Their exclusion is not a capacity problem -- it is an administrative choice to identify but not integrate 3,393 informal workers.

recommendations: Punjab Local Government Department must deploy the idle bio-remediation and C&D machinery to the 17,000 MT and 6,000 MT legacy waste dumpsites immediately -- an operational timeline with monthly milestones should be fixed and the District Commissioner should review progress monthly; for the 17 ULBs with incorrect waste composition baselines, a state-level SWM technical cell should conduct rapid waste composition surveys within 6 months and revise DPRs accordingly; future equipment procurement must be refused until accurate waste composition data is verified by the technical cell.

Punjab Urban Local Bodies must issue identity cards to all 711 ragpickers and 2,682 waste collectors within 60 days -- this is a non-discretionary requirement under SWM Rules 2016 Rule 15; identity card issuance unlocks EPFO, ESIC, and PMSBY coverage; ULBs citing "lack of interest" from informal collectors should be directed by the state government to conduct awareness camps through ULB Commissioners; the State SWM Policy's commitment to ragpicker mainstreaming should be operationalised with a quarterly integration target reported to the State Urban Development Authority.

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 61.08 crore RDSS performance grant forfeiture because AT&C targets were not met is a direct financial consequence of the same systemic failure: Punjab power utilities cannot reduce AT&C losses (ranging 14.08 per cent to 82.53 per cent across 93 towns) because agricultural energy (Rs. 64.37 crore) is unmetered and unrecorded, consumers in high-loss areas are not metered accurately (Smart Meter shortfall of 11,193 meters despite Rs. 13.75 crore expenditure), and the free power scheme for farmers removes the revenue incentive for the utility to recover consumption. The RDSS scheme's 15 per cent additional performance grant (Rs. 61.08 crore) is specifically designed to incentivise AT&C loss reduction -- Punjab's failure to earn it confirms that the structural incentives for efficient operation have been distorted by the agricultural free power scheme.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 64.37 crore in Agricultural Power (AP) feeder energy consumption that is not recorded in billing -- despite incurring Rs. 2.88 crore to install monitoring equipment on those feeders -- means the utility knows energy is flowing but chooses not to bill it (due to the free power scheme) or fails to record it in its consumption accounts. This creates a systemic distortion in the utility's energy balance and AT&C loss computation: AT&C losses are calculated as (energy input - energy billed) / energy input; if Rs. 64.37 crore of agricultural consumption is unrecorded, it inflates the apparent AT&C loss, making even efficient urban circuits look worse and preventing accurate policy design.

recommendations: Punjab State Power Corporation should immediately install prepaid smart meters on all agricultural connections to measure consumption -- even if electricity remains subsidised/free, accurate metering eliminates the ₹64.37 crore in unrecorded consumption and enables proper accounting of the subsidy cost; accurate agricultural consumption data is essential for subsidy DBT (Direct Benefit Transfer) reform which requires knowing how much each farmer actually uses; the 11,193 Smart Meter shortfall in RDSS should be completed urgently to earn the ₹61.08 crore forfeited performance grant in the next assessment cycle.

The ₹94.79 crore avoidable GoI deduction from RDSS grants must be reviewed by a high-level state committee -- if the deduction was due to avoidable actions (procurement irregularities, milestone delays, improper claims), the responsible officers should be identified and the loss recovered; for the ₹3.82 crore irregular grant claim on 318 sites, full refund to GoI should be made along with a rectification plan; the Company should engage with MoP to seek restoration of the ₹61.08 crore forfeited grant once AT&C milestones are demonstrably achieved.

keyFindings.text: Polavaram Irrigation Project is one of India's most contentious infrastructure projects -- a national project on the Godavari river with a 17-year construction history and Rs. 19,346.49 crore in R&R cost overrun alone. The fact that only 14,500 of 1,06,006 displaced families (13.67 per cent) have received R&R cash benefits -- with Rs. 6,429.07 crore in target expenditure still unspent -- while 67 per cent of R&R colonies lack free ration access shows that the project's most vulnerable dimension (displacement rehabilitation) has been systematically underprioritised relative to civil construction. Displacing families and failing to rehabilitate them while completing 77.57 per cent of headwork expenditure is a reversal of the mandatory sequencing in the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013.

source.quote: Against the targeted expenditure of Rs. 7,270.41 crore for payment of R&R cash benefits to 1,06,006 PDFs, only Rs. 841.34 crore was paid to 14,500 PDFs... free ration to PDFs was not available in 67 per cent of R&R colonies

keyFindings.text: Rs. 619.83 crore in avoidable financial burden to the government and Rs. 15.74 crore in excess payments to contract agencies on a project with a 17-year history of contract management issues reflects chronic procurement governance failure. The "loss of interest to Department" from delayed Bank Guarantee enforcement and excess payments to contractors on a project of this scale and national importance is compounded by the Rs. 19,346.49 crore R&R cost overrun -- which was foreseeable given the project's geographical scope (2.91 lakh hectares irrigation potential, 80 TMC diversion, 540 villages, 28.50 lakh population) and the 2013 LARR Act's enhanced compensation framework. The estimated cost revisions (Rs. 10,151.05 crore at 2003-04 prices → Rs. 16,010.45 crore at 2010-11 prices → much higher now) represent catastrophic project cost estimation failures at appraisal.

source.quote: This led to an avoidable financial burden of Rs. 619.83 crore to the Government... excess payment to contract agency by Rs. 15.74 crore

recommendations: Ministry of Jal Shakti and GoAP must immediately release the R&R cash benefits to the remaining 91,506 PDFs (₹6,429.07 crore target minus ₹841.34 crore paid) as a non-negotiable precondition for further civil construction funding -- the LARR Act, 2013 requires R&R to be completed before the affected families are asked to vacate; continuing headworks construction while 86.33 per cent of displaced families remain uncompensated violates the Act and creates legal challenges that will further delay project completion; a dedicated R&R Project Management Unit (PMU) with monthly review by the Chief Secretary should be constituted immediately.

Free ration access for PDFs in all 26 R&R colonies must be ensured within 30 days -- GoAP should authorise emergency ration supply through the Civil Supplies Corporation to all R&R colonies; the state government should audit why 67 per cent of colonies lack this basic entitlement and fix the supply chain failure; additionally, the project authority should recover the ₹15.74 crore excess payment from contract agencies and submit a time-bound recovery plan for the ₹619.83 crore avoidable burden to the project oversight committee.

keyFindings.text: Punjab's power SPSE (most likely PSPCL -- Punjab State Power Corporation Limited) swinging from Rs. 1,069.21 crore profit (2021-22) to Rs. 4,775.93 crore loss (2022-23) is a Rs. 5,845.14 crore deterioration in a single year, attributed to "substantial increase in power purchase costs." This is the direct financial consequence of the free electricity scheme for farmers in Punjab (approximately 8,000 MW of agricultural consumption) -- when market power purchase costs rise, the gap between subsidised tariff and procurement cost is borne by the DISCOM, manifesting as operating losses. PSPCL's Rs. 4,775.93 crore loss is not an operational failure; it is the unbooked fiscal cost of the free power scheme, transferred from the state budget to the DISCOM's balance sheet.

source.quote: incurred loss of Rs. 4,775.93 crore in 2022-23 as compared to profit of Rs. 1,069.21 crore in 2021-22 on account of substantial increase in power purchase costs

keyFindings.text: Rs. 3.88 crore dividend on Rs. 68,938.97 crore in SPSE investment is a 0.006 per cent return -- functionally zero. For context, even a savings bank account at 3.5 per cent per annum would yield Rs. 2,413 crore on this corpus. The fact that 17 SPSEs are in loss for two consecutive years (same count, dramatically higher losses) suggests the loss-making set is chronic rather than cyclical -- the same entities failing year after year. The AT&C loss of up to 82.53 per cent in some distribution towns is extreme -- it implies that for every 100 units distributed, 82.53 units are either unbilled or uncollected. Even towns at 40-50 per cent AT&C loss represent a catastrophic commercial failure of the distribution franchise.

source.quote: dividend of Rs. 3.88 crore. working SPSEs was Rs. 68,938.97 crore... remaining 93 towns, the losses ranged between 14.08 and 82.53 per cent

recommendations: Government of Punjab must operationalise the power subsidy through direct DBT (Direct Benefit Transfer) to farmers rather than routing it through PSPCL -- the current model (free power to farmers, PSPCL absorbs the revenue gap) creates ₹4,775.93 crore in DISCOM losses and distorts the utility's financial health; under DBT, the government pays farmers a cash transfer equal to the electricity cost, farmers pay market tariff to PSPCL, and PSPCL is financially healthy; the state should phase in this transition over 2 years with a simultaneous metering programme for agricultural connections to enable accurate subsidy calculation.

Punjab Finance Department must implement a SPSE dividend policy and PSU performance accountability framework -- ₹3.88 crore dividend on ₹68,938.97 crore is unacceptable; the framework should require all SPSEs reporting net profit to pay 25 per cent as dividend and should tie new equity/grant releases to demonstrable improvements in AT&C losses (specific target: bring all towns to below 20 per cent AT&C within 3 years); towns with AT&C losses above 50 per cent should be audited for energy theft and billing irregularities within 60 days.

keyFindings.text: The failure to pay unemployment allowances to 18.26 lakh households denied employment is a clear statutory violation. Under MGNREGS, if the state fails to provide employment within 15 days of demand, it must pay unemployment allowance at a rate not less than 1/4th of the wage rate for the first 30 days and half the wage rate thereafter (Section 7 of the MGNREGA). Chhattisgarh not only failed to employ 18.26 lakh HHs but also failed to pay the mandatory compensation -- effectively denying both the job and the legal remedy for its absence. The Rs. 2.22 crore budget provision was not disbursed at all. This is a violation of a justiciable entitlement -- each affected household has a legal right to unemployment allowance enforceable in court.

source.quote: shortfall of 18.26 lakh (12 per cent) in providing employment. However, no unemployment allowances were paid to these HHs... budgetary provisions of Rs. 2.22 crore for unemployment allowances during

keyFindings.text: The 2023-24 Person Day (PD) budget cut from 1,700 lakh to 700 lakh (59 per cent reduction) is a supply-side throttle on a demand-driven scheme. MGNREGS is explicitly designed to be driven by demand (any household applying must be given work within 15 days) -- a government that pre-determines a lower PD ceiling than projected demand is systematically preventing workers from exercising their statutory right. The "significant cut" of 1,000 lakh PDs in the initial approval means hundreds of thousands of households were administratively denied the right to work before they even applied, and the subsequent revision to 1,250 lakh PDs was still below the 1,700 lakh projected need.

source.quote: significant cut was observed in 2023-24, where only 700 lakh PDs were initially approved against the 1,700 lakh PDs projected... highest shortfall recorded in 2023-24 (423.36 lakh PDs or 25 per cent)

recommendations: Chhattisgarh MGNREGS Commissioner must immediately compute and disburse outstanding unemployment allowances to all 18.26 lakh households denied employment during 2019-24 -- the statutory rate is 25 per cent of wage for days 1-30 and 50 per cent thereafter; even at minimum computation, this liability should be estimated and placed before the State Employment Guarantee Council (SEGC) for immediate budgetary provision; failure to pay is a justiciable violation and affected households can approach courts for mandamus.

Social audit fund utilisation of ₹42.55 crore vs ₹58.68 crore earmarked must improve -- the ₹16.13 crore lapse is particularly problematic because social audits are the primary accountability mechanism for MGNREGS; 45 per cent of sanctioned social audits not held means half the scheme expenditure is operating without the community oversight layer; State Audit Authority for MGNREGS should conduct a root cause analysis of what prevents social audit organisation and address the specific blockers (venue, quorum, facilitator availability) rather than simply under-spending the fund.

keyFindings.text: Chhattisgarh MGNREGS's EPF failure illustrates the cumulative cost of ignoring a small recurring obligation: Rs. 29.62 crore in unpaid contributions over 8 years (April 2015 to March 2023) has snowballed into Rs. 84.59 crore total liability (penalty + interest Rs. 54.96 crore = 185 per cent of the original obligation). The state government sanctioned Rs. 40 crore for clearance -- not even enough to cover the penalty, let alone the principal. MGNREGS workers are among the most vulnerable -- their EPF contributions are a statutory right and a form of social security; non-deposit of their contributions for 8 years means their EPF accounts did not accrue returns for nearly a decade.

source.quote: Rs. 29.62 crore for the period April 2015 to March 2023 remained unpaid which resulted in accumulation of liabilities of Rs. 84.59 crore... Rs. 54.96 crore was on account of penalty, interest and damages under the EPF Act

keyFindings.text: The 97 per cent training shortfall for Gram Rozgar Sahayaks is functionally a complete absence of capacity building for the field-level implementers of MGNREGS. With 21 per cent of posts vacant (3,218 vacancies) and shortfalls of 25 to 54 per cent in test-checked districts, the scheme is being implemented by an understaffed and undertrained workforce. The result is visible in the output: 4.32 lakh works never started (21 per cent of approved works) and 83 per cent of workers receiving less than 100 days -- less than the scheme's own guaranteed minimum. CAG notes only 1.23 lakh of 134.10 lakh HHs (0.92 per cent) received the promised 100 days, making the 100-day employment guarantee nearly fictional in Chhattisgarh for the 2019-24 period.

source.quote: Out of 134.10 lakh HHs that were provided employment, 111.31 lakh HHs (83 per cent) were provided employment for less than 100 days, 1.23 lakh HHs (0.92 per cent) were provided full 100 days employment... 3,218 posts (21 per cent) were lying vacant

recommendations: Chhattisgarh Rural Development Department must immediately clear all EPF arrears for MGNREGS workers -- the full ₹84.59 crore (principal + penalty) should be deposited to EPFO within 90 days; the sanctioned ₹40 crore is insufficient; the balance ₹44.59 crore should be sought from the MGNREGS Administrative Expenses head (2 per cent of total programme expenditure which amounts to ₹369.15 crore for the 5-year period -- adequate for full clearance); going forward, EPF contributions must be remitted monthly to EPFO within the statutory 15-day window with automatic internal audit verification.

The State MGNREGS Commissioner must prepare a district-wise employment guarantee fulfilment plan -- with only 0.92 per cent of registered households receiving the statutory 100 days, the guarantee is effectively non-existent; the plan should: (a) fill all 3,218 vacancies within 6 months; (b) mandate district-level Labour Budget preparation with realistic 100-day targets; (c) penalise District Programme Coordinators where the district delivery rate falls below 40 per cent for two consecutive years; (d) make GRS training (97 per cent unmet target) mandatory before deployment of new GRS with training completion tracked in MIS.

title: Compliance Audit -- Uttarakhand: Namami Gange STPs Non-Functional Despite ₹873.17 crore Expenditure; ₹4.93 crore Paid for STP Not Treating Sewage; Joshimath ₹42.73 crore Project Has No Household Connections; Safety Audits Not Conducted; Excess Sewage Bypassed Into Ganga
overview: CAG Report No. 1 of 2025 (Uttarakhand Compliance Audit, Namami Gange) found: (1) Of ₹873.17 crore total sewage infrastructure expenditure, ₹680.79 crore (77.96 per cent) spent on infrastructure that is not achieving treatment targets -- timely safety audits of STPs not conducted; human lives lost due to STP failures; (2) Joshimath -- three successive projects (₹9.57 crore 2010, ₹33.16 crore 2017, ₹42.73 crore 2019) on Namami Gange Ganga; STPs built but no house connections; 2019 project (₹42.73 crore) a drain-catching project with zero household sewage connections; (3) ₹4.93 crore STP payment made in full despite the STP not treating sewage from intended nalla (flow diverted elsewhere); (4) STP operators bypassing excess sewage directly into Ganga on UJN instructions; (5) GoI released ₹1,149 crore to Uttarakhand out of ₹14,260 crore national NMCG release (2014-23); Namami Gange Mission-II ₹22,500 crore approved.

keyFindings.text: The Joshimath Namami Gange story is a case study in repeated public expenditure without accountability: three separate projects (2010: Rs. 9.57 crore, 2017: Rs. 33.16 crore, 2022: Rs. 42.73 crore) were sanctioned and executed over 13 years, each time with similar mandates for sewage treatment -- and each project was completed without providing household sewage connections. A Sewage Treatment Plant (STP) that receives no household sewage can only treat runoff and nalla (drain) water. CAG found the 2022 project (Rs. 42.73 crore) to be "essentially a drain catching project" -- Rs. 85.46 crore spent over 13 years on Joshimath sewage without resolving the fundamental problem of connecting households to the sewer network. Additionally, a Rs. 202 crore proposal for household connections was pending NMCG approval, suggesting the executing agency knew connections were the missing link but did not make it a prerequisite for the earlier projects.

source.quote: Rs. 42.73 crore did not include sewage connection to any household... essentially a drain catching project wherein drains were intercepted and diverted... connections at a cost of Rs. 202 crore as per instructions given by NMCG team

keyFindings.text: Full payment of Rs. 4.93 crore to a contractor for an STP that treats no sewage -- because the nalla its inlet was designed to receive had been diverted elsewhere, meaning the STP sits empty -- is a textbook avoidable loss. The executing agency (UJN) paid the contractor in full despite the STP's inlet being empty, without verifying that the STP was actually receiving and treating sewage before making final payment. UJN also instructed STP operators to bypass excess sewage directly into the Ganga -- the very river Namami Gange is designed to clean -- because the DPR capacity was underestimated relative to actual sewage load. The combination of empty STPs (no flow) and overloaded STPs (bypassing flow) illustrates both undersizing and misallocation of the Rs. 873.17 crore Namami Gange investment in Uttarakhand.

source.quote: receiving full payment of Rs. 4.93 crore for construction despite an expenditure of Rs. 4.93 crore... that he was bypassing the excess sewage as per instructions of UJN i.e. the discharging excess sewage into river without treatment

recommendations: Uttarakhand Jal Sansthan must implement a mandatory Performance Certificate requirement before any final payment to STP contractors -- the Performance Certificate should be issued only after the STP has operated for 90 continuous days with actual sewage flow meeting the designed treatment capacity (BOD/TSS removal rates) as verified by an accredited independent laboratory; full payment should not precede Performance Certificate issuance regardless of project completion date.

NMCG should commission immediate safety audits of all STPs in Uttarakhand and make safety audit compliance a condition for continued funding -- the loss of human lives due to absent safety audits is unacceptable; NMCG should constitute a state-level STP Safety Inspection Committee (SSIC) with semi-annual mandatory inspections of all STPs; bypass of untreated sewage into the Ganga should be reported to the National Green Tribunal as a violation of the Environment Protection Act with personal accountability for UJN officers who instructed bypass operations.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 5,735.58 crore classified under Minor Head 800 catch-all across 53 major heads (expenditure + receipts combined) -- representing 2.22 per cent of Revenue Receipts and a significant portion of expenditure -- severely limits legislative oversight of what is being spent on and what is being collected. Rs. 3,203.05 crore under "800-Other Receipts" specifically means 1.24 per cent of revenue receipts are of unknown origin or type within the formal accounting system. For a state where the Finance Commission assesses own-revenue performance, unclassified receipts distort the baseline used for devolution calculations.

source.quote: Rs. 2,532.53 crore under four Major Heads Rs. 3,203.05 crore under 49 Major Heads of Account, constituting 1.24 per cent of the total Revenue Receipts (Rs. 2,58,152.52 crore) was classified under 800-Other Receipts

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 1,443.23 crore discrepancy between Karnataka's own accounts and RBI records is a banking reconciliation failure that directly affects confidence in the state's financial statements. The Finance Accounts are certified as reflecting the true position of the state's finances -- a Rs. 1,443.23 crore discrepancy with the banker (RBI) means neither the state nor the RBI has a clean view of the actual cash position. This is not a trivial difference -- at Rs. 1,443 crore, it exceeds the annual budget of multiple departments. The Rs. 2,409.53 crore in excess expenditure pending regularisation (from earlier years) represents spending that exceeded legislative appropriation and has not been formally authorised retroactively.

source.quote: State Government as on 31 March 2025 was Rs. 1,445.62 crore (Debit) while the same was reported as Rs. 2.39 crore (Credit) by the Reserve Bank of Rs. 1,443.23 crore (Debit) mainly due to non-receipt of bank scrolls

recommendations: Karnataka Finance Department must constitute a Bank Scroll Reconciliation Cell to clear the ₹1,443.23 crore RBI discrepancy within 90 days -- the reconciliation cell should have daily access to RBI's State accounts system and be empowered to trace and clear each unreconciled transaction; unreconciled bank scrolls often represent payments that have been made but not accounted for (or vice versa) -- the Accountant General should sign off on a zero-discrepancy statement before the Finance Accounts are finalised next year.

The excess expenditure of ₹2,409.53 crore should be brought before the Legislature for formal regularisation in the current Budget Session -- spending in excess of appropriation is constitutionally impermissible under Article 204 of the Constitution; presenting it for regularisation is not just a procedural step, it is an accountability mechanism that requires the government to explain why controls failed; the PAC should examine each case of excess before recommending regularisation.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 24,917.22 crore in revenue arrears -- approximately 14 per cent of Karnataka's GSDP of Rs. 28,61,929 crore -- represents a massive uncollected revenue backlog. While some arrears are genuinely contested and require litigation, the scale suggests systemic weaknesses in tax enforcement, demand notice follow-up, and enforcement officer accountability. Karnataka simultaneously has a Revenue Deficit (driven by guarantee schemes) and Rs. 24,917 crore in uncollected taxes -- even partial recovery would significantly reduce the deficit. CAG's characterisation of "high risk in taxation" suggests the arrears may not ultimately be recoverable at face value, making these a contingent fiscal loss as much as a collection challenge.

source.quote: as on 31 March 2025, the State had Rs. 24,917.22 crore as risks in taxation

keyFindings.text: The SDRMF (State Disaster Response and Mitigation Fund) being 20 per cent short of GoI's allocation -- while Karnataka's own accounts show a Revenue Deficit and insufficient fiscal space for emergency response -- means the state's disaster response capacity is under-funded from both sides. The energy sector loan concentration (Rs. 4,117 crore, 62 per cent of PSU disbursements) reflects Karnataka's DISCOM debt problem -- the government is essentially lending to its electricity utilities (likely BESCOM, MESCOM, etc.) to cover their operational losses, which are partly driven by the Rs. 9,157.66 crore power subsidy under the guarantee schemes -- the subsidy creates losses in the DISCOM, the DISCOM borrows from the state, and the state borrows from the market, completing the fiscal loop.

source.quote: Rs. 4,117 crore (62 per cent) was towards Energy... Rs. 50,077 crore, subsidy, Rs. 22,631 crore (45 per cent) constituted the three out of five guarantee schemes

recommendations: Karnataka Commercial Tax and Revenue Departments should implement a joint revenue arrear resolution task force -- the task force should triage the ₹24,917.22 crore into (a) legally contested (stay/appeal); (b) undisputed but unpaid; and (c) potentially unrecoverable; for category (b), attachment of bank accounts, property, and TDS diversion should be activated within 60 days for cases over ₹1 crore; for category (c), write-off proposals should go to the Revenue Secretary; the task force should target a 10 per cent reduction (₹2,491 crore) in arrears in FY 2025-26.

Karnataka Energy Department should prepare a DISCOM Financial Restructuring Plan that addresses the circular subsidy-loan-deficit loop -- the five guarantee schemes create power losses in DISCOMs (₹9,157.66 crore power subsidy, then ₹4,117 crore loans to energy PSUs); a restructuring plan should: (a) ring-fence guarantee scheme subsidy flows through direct-to-DISCOM transfers rather than market loans; (b) benchmark DISCOM recovery efficiency to eliminate distribution losses above the national average; (c) stop new state loans to energy PSUs until existing loans generate audited returns.

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's fiscal governance failure is most visible in one number: only 2.77 per cent of savings were surrendered in FY 2024-25, leaving Rs. 45,072.68 crore in unspent funds unreturned to the Finance Department. At the same time, Capital Expenditure fell 25 per cent from Rs. 28,963 crore to Rs. 21,622 crore -- meaning the state spent less on infrastructure while also retaining Rs. 45,072 crore that it could have used for capital works. The 16 schemes with persistent savings for 3 consecutive years (2022-23 to 2024-25) are schemes whose budgets are not based on realistic implementation capacity -- they are paper allocations that inflate the total budget while creating no productive output.

source.quote: savings under 40 Grants and 16 Appropriations amounting to Rs. 45,072.68 crore were not surrendered at all. Analysis revealed that only 2.77 per cent of the savings were surrendered... Capital expenditure (Rs. 21,622 crore) in the year 2024-25 fell by 25 per cent

keyFindings.text: Rs. 17,546 crore in outstanding loans to public entities earning 0.25 per cent interest (Rs. 44 crore on Rs. 17,546 crore) is a fiscal subsidy of extraordinary magnitude. The state borrows at 7-8 per cent per annum and lends at an effective 0.25 per cent -- the net annual subsidy is approximately Rs. 1,300 crore in foregone interest income. The 91.2 per cent collapse in loan recovery (from Rs. 1,456 crore to Rs. 128 crore) in a single year is alarming -- it suggests either a specific large repayment in 2023-24 that was one-time, or a systemic breakdown in recovery discipline. Combined with Rs. 10,355.68 crore in outstanding loanee principal with near-zero interest receipts (Rs. 366 crore vs Rs. 3,557 crore BE), West Bengal's asset side of the balance sheet earns almost nothing.

recommendations: Finance Department, West Bengal should implement automatic savings surrender -- any savings above ₹10 crore in any grant as of 1 March should be automatically identified by IFMS and surrender notices issued to DDOs with a 7-day response period; the Finance Secretary should personally review all grants with persistent savings (3+ years) and either reduce the budget provision to reflect actual absorption capacity or transfer the programme to a capable implementing agency; the 2.77 per cent surrender rate (one of the lowest among major states) is a systemic control failure that undermines the entire appropriation process.

West Bengal must immediately implement a dividend policy for profit-making PSUs -- the Finance Department should issue a circular requiring all PSUs reporting net profit to remit a minimum 25 per cent of PAT as dividend within 90 days of account closure; the 1.09 per cent return on ₹22,086 crore in PSU investment is unacceptable; the loan recovery collapse from ₹1,456 crore to ₹128 crore must be investigated and the finding reported to the PAC within 60 days.

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's receipt of Rs. 45,128 crore in Post Devolution Revenue Deficit (PDRD) grants over five years (2020-21 to 2024-25) is the most revealing indicator of its fiscal position. PDRD grants are paid only to states where even after receiving their share of Central taxes, total revenue receipts fall short of revenue expenditure -- they are grants for states that cannot break even. Receiving Rs. 45,128 crore over 5 years -- approximately Rs. 9,026 crore per year -- while simultaneously having outstanding liabilities at 38.66 per cent of GSDP means West Bengal has both a chronic revenue gap and a large accumulated debt stock. The GoI grants (now declining from Rs. 38,172 crore to Rs. 15,205 crore) were partly propping up this revenue position.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 7,873 crore in revenue arrears with Rs. 1,285 crore undisputed (including Rs. 167 crore over 10 years old) shows a failure of enforcement rather than legal dispute. Undisputed arrears are amounts where the state government knows the money is owed, there is no legal challenge, and yet collection has not happened. Rs. 167 crore sitting in "undisputed, over 10 years" is a permanent write-off in practice even if not in accounting. The Rs. 2,498 crore Consolidated Sinking Fund withdrawal is a fiscal warning sign -- the CSF is designed to provide a buffer for debt redemption; drawing it down means the state lacks sufficient current-year surplus to meet debt repayments without dipping into its accumulated reserve.

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department should prepare a 3-year revenue arrears resolution plan with a dedicated Revenue Recovery Unit -- the ₹1,285 crore in undisputed arrears should be prioritised for immediate collection through engagement of recovery officers and OTS (One Time Settlement) schemes for long-outstanding cases; ₹167 crore in arrears over 10 years should be referred to the Revenue Board for a formal write-off decision with accountability for why each case was allowed to age beyond 10 years without action.

The Finance Department should establish a Consolidated Sinking Fund replenishment plan to restore the CSF balance withdrawn -- ₹2,498 crore drawn down for debt repayment weakens the state's buffer for future debt maturities; the FRBM Act requires systematic CSF contributions; the Finance Department should schedule quarterly CSF contributions from the Cash Balance Investment Account to restore the withdrawn amount within 2 years; the Investment Division should also optimise CSF investment returns by shifting from overnight deposits to slightly longer-duration instruments.

keyFindings.text: CAG explicitly diagnoses Karnataka as trapped in a "loop of indebtedness": the five guarantee schemes create a Revenue Deficit (Rs. 20,834 crore), the Revenue Deficit is financed by borrowings (net Rs. 71,525.15 crore), the borrowings increase the debt stock and future interest obligations, which further reduces fiscal space for development spending, which makes the state more dependent on the guarantee schemes for political legitimacy. The guarantee scheme cost trajectory confirms this -- from Rs. 36,538 crore (2023-24 budgeted) to Rs. 51,646 crore (2024-25 actual) in one year is a 41.3 per cent jump, driven by scheme universality and growing enrollment. If this CAGR continues, the five schemes alone will cost Rs. 72,937 crore by FY 2026-27 -- approximately 20 per cent of a higher revenue expenditure base.

source.quote: State availed net market borrowing of Rs. 71,525.15 crore... To finance the guarantee schemes and the deficits arising thereof... The State had budgeted Rs. 36,538 crore for these schemes in 2023-24 which have increased to Rs. 51,646 crore in 2024-25

keyFindings.text: Rs. 26,904.16 crore in savings with only 73.22 per cent surrendered and Rs. 10,448 crore surrendered on the last day of March are tell-tale signs of budgetary management failure. Rs. 10,448 crore surrendered on a single day at year-end means these appropriations were never genuinely intended to be spent -- they were parking reserves. The Rs. 7,979.13 crore in supplementary provisions across 17 cases proved excessive (Rs. 1,353.31 crore unutilised) means even the supplementary budget process is not based on realistic demand assessment. When Karnataka simultaneously has Rs. 71,525 crore in market borrowings and Rs. 26,904 crore in savings, it is borrowing unnecessarily -- the excess borrowing adds to debt and interest costs.

source.quote: only 73.22 per cent of the savings were surrendered. Out of surrendered amount of Rs. 16,547 crore, Rs. 10,448 crore... supplementary provisions of Rs. 7,979.13 crore in 17 cases... proved excessive... Rs. 1,353.31 crore remained unutilised

recommendations: Karnataka Finance Department must immediately suspend borrowing in any quarter where: (a) quarterly surrenders are below 5 per cent of total savings for that quarter; or (b) cumulative year-to-date savings exceed 15 per cent of total grant authorisation -- the simultaneous existence of ₹71,525 crore in borrowings and ₹26,904 crore in savings (of which ₹10,448 crore surrendered in a single day) is proof that borrowing decisions are not being calibrated to actual cash needs; the Finance Department must implement monthly cash flow planning that reduces market borrowings to actual net cash requirement.

Government of Karnataka should wind up the 16 defunct PSU entities and recover ₹67.63 crore in investments -- even ₹67.63 crore, though small relative to the ₹74,325 crore PSU portfolio, demonstrates that public funds remain locked in entities with no operational existence; the Chief Minister's office should receive a quarterly report on PSU revival, merger, or liquidation progress; for the energy sector PSU loans (₹4,117 crore, 62 per cent of ₹6,631 crore disbursed), dividend and interest recovery should be reviewed against actual DISCOM financial performance.

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's Grants-in-Aid from GoI declining 60.2 per cent from Rs. 38,172 crore (2020-21) to Rs. 15,205 crore (2024-25) is one of the most dramatic reductions in state-central fiscal relations in recent years. A significant part of this decline reflects the cessation of GST compensation grants (the back-to-back bonds ended) and the transition from 14th FC to 15th FC with different grant structures. However, even within 15th FC allocations, Rs. 2,893.51 crore in grants recommended but not released in FY 2024-25 (Rs. 8,132.02 crore allocated vs Rs. 5,238.51 crore released) means West Bengal lost specific-purpose infrastructure and service delivery funding. The PDRD grants (Rs. 568 crore vs expected higher allocation) reflect GoI's assessment of WB's own revenue performance -- states with stronger own revenue growth receive less revenue deficit support.

source.quote: Rs. 38,172 crore in 2020-21 to Rs. 15,205 crore in 2024-25... GoI released Fifteenth Finance Commission (15th FC) grants of Rs. 5,238.51 crore, against the allocation of Rs. 8,132.02 crore

keyFindings.text: Interest Receipts of Rs. 366 crore against a Budget Estimate of Rs. 3,557 crore -- a 89.7 per cent miss -- reveals that West Bengal budgeted interest recovery from loans given to public entities but collected only 10.3 per cent of what it projected. With Rs. 10,355.68 crore in outstanding loans to loanees, the state is effectively providing nearly Rs. 10,356 crore in interest-free loans (since interest recovery is near-zero) to entities while simultaneously borrowing at 7-8 per cent per annum for its own needs. The Rs. 452.20 crore misclassification of mineral royalties as land revenue overstates Own Tax Revenue -- a metric closely watched by credit rating agencies and the Finance Commission for assessing fiscal capacity.

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must initiate a structured loan recovery drive for the ₹10,355.68 crore in outstanding principal -- the starting point should be identifying the 10 largest loanee entities by outstanding amount, computing interest due, and sending formal demand notices; for entities that cannot repay, a formal rescheduling agreement should be executed with specific interest rates and timelines; the Budget Estimate for interest receipts should be reduced to reflect realistic recovery rates until the recovery programme yields results.

The ₹452.20 crore mineral royalty misclassification must be corrected by booking royalty receipts under the correct non-tax revenue head (Mining Receipts) and the FY 2024-25 Finance Accounts should carry a disclosure note -- Own Tax Revenue as a percentage of GSDP is a key indicator used by the Finance Commission for future devolution shares; inflating it by ₹452.20 crore distorts WB's own-revenue assessment; the Finance Department should implement a Treasury system control that prevents royalty receipts from being booked under land revenue heads without Finance Secretary approval.

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's five guarantee schemes (Gruha Jyoti, Gruha Lakshmi, Shakti, Anna Bhagya, Yuva Nidhi) consuming Rs. 52,525.60 crore -- 19 per cent of Revenue Expenditure -- have fundamentally altered the state's fiscal composition. CAG notes this creates a "loop of indebtedness": the guarantee schemes increase the Revenue Deficit, which is then financed by debt, which increases future interest burden, which further crowds out productive expenditure. The state was forced to "apply a squeeze" on other budget heads -- irrigation (Rs. 19,000 crore), transport (Rs. 8,236 crore) and special area programmes (Rs. 3,600 crore) received allocations despite the subsidy squeeze, but Capital Expenditure at Rs. 57,906 crore (approximately 19 per cent of total) competes directly with the guarantee scheme expenditure of the same percentage.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 2,020.87 crore misclassified from Revenue to Capital Expenditure understates the Revenue Deficit and overstates Capital Expenditure in Karnataka's Finance Accounts. The net impact is a Rs. 1,948.41 crore Fiscal Deficit understatement -- meaning Karnataka's true Fiscal Deficit is larger than officially reported. Combined with Rs. 10,035.13 crore in supplementary provisions covering 21 grants that lack legislative approval (36 per cent of total Supplementary), the picture is of a state where significant spending decisions are being taken outside the formal legislative appropriation process.

The ₹2,020.87 crore misclassification and ₹10,035.13 crore in supplementary grants without legislative approval should be brought to the Public Accounts Committee immediately -- misclassifying revenue as capital expenditure materially misstates the fiscal deficit; the State Legislature should pass a resolution acknowledging the misclassification, direct the Finance Department to implement an independent line-item validation step before Finance Account finalisation, and the ₹10,035.13 crore in unapproved supplementary grants should be regularised in the current session.

keyFindings.text: Mizoram's fiscal structure is fundamentally different from major states: 80.02 per cent of Revenue Receipts come from the Central Government (80 per cent Central transfers vs. 20 per cent own revenue). This is a function of geography, population, and the special category status -- but it creates an acute vulnerability to any reduction in devolution or grants. The shift from grants (55.78 per cent in 2019-20) to tax devolution (growing share) is a structural change in the composition of Central transfers that matters: grants are programme-specific and release-conditional, while tax devolution is unconditional -- the shift gives Mizoram more flexibility but also means more spending decisions depend on the state's own fiscal discipline, which is tested by the 69.98 per cent committed expenditure ratio.

source.quote: constituted 80.02 per cent of the Revenue Receipts... share of Grants-in-aid in revenue receipts fell from 55.78 per cent in 2019-20 to 30.54 per cent

keyFindings.text: Committed + inflexible expenditure at 69.98 per cent of Revenue Expenditure (Rs. 7,584.04 crore of Rs. 10,836.96 crore) means Mizoram's state government has only Rs. 3,252.92 crore -- approximately 30 per cent of revenue spending -- available for discretionary development expenditure in any given year. With Capital Expenditure of only Rs. 1,253.78 crore, the state's total development headroom is constrained to roughly Rs. 4,506 crore. Subsidies growing at compound rate from Rs. 52.09 crore (2019-20) to Rs. 142.61 crore (2023-24) -- a 173.8 per cent increase -- will further compress this space, particularly because Power subsidies (Rs. 116 crore) reflect a systemic cost of an underdeveloped transmission infrastructure rather than a policy choice easily reversed.

source.quote: committed and inflexible expenditure in 2023-24 was Rs. 7,584.04 crore, 69.98 per cent of the revenue expenditure

recommendations: Government of Mizoram should develop a 5-year Own Revenue Enhancement Plan to reduce Central transfer dependency from 80 per cent to below 70 per cent -- the plan should include: (a) property tax reform in Aizawl Municipal Corporation; (b) professional tax expansion to informal sector; (c) tourism fee rationalisation; (d) mining and bamboo resource royalty revision; and (e) recovery of ₹52.92 crore in outstanding revenue arrears (including ₹13.77 crore over 5 years old) through an OTS scheme; this is not just fiscal prudence -- a state that is 80 per cent Central-funded cannot develop local administrative accountability.

Mizoram Finance Department must prepare a committed expenditure rationalisation plan to bring the committed + inflexible ratio below 65 per cent within 3 years -- the immediate levers are: (a) NPS transition (already on track) which limits pension growth for new recruits; (b) salary grade rationalisation for contractual and daily-wage employees; (c) power subsidy reduction through DISCOMS efficiency improvement; current trajectory at 69.98 per cent with growing subsidy CAGR will crowd out all development spending by FY 2026-27.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 2,574.45 crore classified under Minor Head 800 "Other Expenditure" across 83 major heads is a fiscal opacity problem of the first order in a small state like Mizoram. Minor Head 800 is a residual classification used when expenditure does not fit any of the prescribed minor heads -- it is supposed to be exceptional. When Rs. 1,633.42 crore (38 major heads) and Rs. 941.03 crore (45 major heads) land under MH-800, it means these expenditures are being accounted at a level that makes scheme-wise, programme-wise, and purpose-wise analysis impossible. In a state like Mizoram, with small absolute revenue receipts, Rs. 2,574 crore under a catch-all head is a significant portion of total spending that has escaped programmatic classification.

source.quote: Rs. 1,633.42 crore under 38 Major Heads, constituting Minor Head 800 Other Expenditure. Similarly, Rs. 941.03 crore under 45 Major Heads

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 235.62 crore in grants to three Autonomous District Councils (Chakma, Lai, Mara Autonomous District Councils) with outstanding UCs is structurally different from ordinary UC pendency -- Autonomous District Councils in Mizoram operate under the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution with separate legislative and administrative authority; the state government's ability to enforce UC submission is limited compared to ordinary grant recipients. Yet the grants are made from the state's Consolidated Fund and CAG's audit jurisdiction covers them. The failure to receive UCs for Rs. 472.19 crore in total grants means a substantial share of scheme implementation in Mizoram is happening without accountability.

source.quote: As on 31 March 2024, 32 Utilisation Certificates (UCs) in respect of grants aggregating Rs. 235.62 crore given to the three Autonomous District Councils were outstanding. amounting to Rs. 472.19 crore were not received

recommendations: Finance Department, Mizoram should identify the specific programmes hidden under MH-800 and reclassify them under appropriate minor heads -- the state's Finance Department should prepare a scheme-specific list of all expenditures under MH-800 across the 83 major heads and submit a reclassification proposal to the Principal Accountant General within 3 months; going forward, no expenditure exceeding ₹10 lakh should be booked under MH-800 without a specific sanction from the Finance Secretary explaining why no appropriate minor head exists.

Grant releases to the three Autonomous District Councils should be conditioned on UC submission for previous grants -- the state should formally notify the three ADCs that new grants under any scheme will be withheld until outstanding UCs totalling ₹235.62 crore are submitted and verified; the Planning and Finance Departments should jointly maintain a UC compliance register for ADC grants updated quarterly.
