keyFindings.text: The Rs. 8,064.12 crore discrepancy between IFMS and Finance Accounts for internal debt (Rs. 4,222.50 crore in IFMS vs Rs. 12,286.62 crore in Finance Accounts) reveals that Jharkhand's IFMS cannot capture Central Government loan transactions -- specifically, Central Government loans to the state under MH 6003 (Rs. 59,500.24 crore) and MH 6004 (Rs. 5,642.34 crore) were processed outside IFMS, making it impossible for the Treasury system to show the true state of government finances. An IFMS where Rs. 8,064 crore in government borrowings are invisible is not a financial management system -- it is a partial record that creates a false picture of fiscal health for anyone relying on IFMS data.

source.quote: a discrepancy of Rs. 8,064.12 crore in the figures (Rs. 4,222.50 crore) and Finance Accounts (Rs. 12,286.62 crore) arose... amount of Rs. 8,064.12 crore could not be captured in IFMS as the records of

keyFindings.text: Rs. 20,098.82 crore in AC bills drawn and Rs. 9,078.19 crore only partially adjusted reflects a core fiscal control failure: Abstract Contingency (AC) bills are supposed to be drawn for short-term advances requiring adjustment within one month through Detailed Contingency (DC) bills. When 4,979 bills worth Rs. 9,078.19 crore are "partially adjusted", it means cash has left the treasury but the expenditure accounting is incomplete -- who received the money, under what head, for what purpose. Rs. 1,013.69 crore was drawn as new AC bills without adjusting previous outstanding AC bills, a direct violation of financial rules that IFMS should have prevented. The historical backlog (April 2010 to November 2022: Rs. 2,44,925.58 crore) shows this has been systemic for over a decade.

source.quote: 12,217 AC bills amounting to Rs. 20,098.82 crore were drawn... 4,979 bills of Rs. 9,078.19 crore drawn by 287 DDOs had only been partially adjusted... AC bills without adjustment of previous AC bills of Rs. 1,013.69 crore drawn

recommendations: Jharkhand Finance Department must integrate IFMS with the RBI/Controller of Aid, Accounts and Audit (CAAA) data feed for Central Government loan disbursements -- the ₹8,064.12 crore discrepancy stems specifically from Central Government loans (MH 6003/6004) not being auto-captured in IFMS; until this integration is live, a manual reconciliation cell should update IFMS with every Central loan receipt within 48 hours; the Finance Accounts should not be finalised until IFMS and Accountant General records reconcile.

IFMS must be enhanced with hard application controls on AC bill issuance -- specifically: (a) block new AC bill issuance to any DDO with outstanding AC bills not adjusted within 60 days; (b) trigger automatic audit alerts for AC bills exceeding ₹1 crore outstanding for over 30 days; (c) prevent partial adjustment submission -- require DDOs to either fully adjust or provide a formal extension request approved by the Treasury Officer; the ₹9,078.19 crore in partially adjusted bills represents accountability gaps that cannot be closed without system-enforced controls.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 6,239.92 crore sitting unspent in SNA bank accounts while the state has a Fiscal Deficit of Rs. 25,042 crore is a fundamental contradiction. Rs. 2,499.76 crore of that idle money relates specifically to 19 schemes on-boarded on SNA-SPARSH -- funds that should have been remitted back to GoI (the whole point of SNA-SPARSH "Just-in-Time" releases is that states should not park Central funds). The failure to remit means Odisha is holding GoI money interest-free, while GoI may not re-release until the balance is cleared -- effectively blocking future scheme funding.

It suggests either transfers are being entered in VLC (the state's accounting system) that have not been matched in PFMS (the Centre's tracking system), or payments shown in PFMS have not been entered in VLC. The March rush (18.83 per cent of all expenditure in one month) is a known driver of such discrepancies -- hurried month-end entries create errors. recommendations: Odisha Finance Department should remit the ₹2,499.76 crore in SNA accounts of the 19 SNA-SPARSH on-boarded schemes within 30 days -- this is a compliance requirement under DoE circular of July 2023; failure to remit risks GoI withholding future releases under those schemes; the Finance Department should designate a nodal officer for SNA-SPARSH compliance with weekly reporting on balance remittance status.

The ₹509.30 crore + ₹815.37 crore VLC-PFMS discrepancy should be reconciled by a joint team of the Finance Department VLC cell and State NIC PFMS team within 60 days -- each line-item discrepancy should be traced to the actual bank transaction and corrected in the appropriate system; the March rush expenditure pattern (18.83 per cent in single month) should be capped at 15 per cent through a Treasury circular requiring monthly expenditure plans, and the Contingency Fund advance of ₹117.73 crore should be recouped within the first quarter of FY 2025-26.

The ₹721 crore revenue-to-capital misclassification and ₹586.62 crore PLAs transfer should be corrected in the Finance Accounts and future accounts should implement PFMS-level controls -- specifically, the Backward Classes Welfare Department's PLA transfers of capital nature must be tracked through the Treasury Single Account (TSA) system to ensure the funds are recorded in the Capital section and utilisation is verified before further releases; the misclassification must be brought to the PAC's attention.

keyFindings.text: Bihar extended Rs. 31,036.15 crore in guarantees during FY 2024-25, exceeding the Bihar FRBM Act's prescribed ceiling of Rs. 25,256.75 crore by Rs. 5,779.40 crore -- a 22.8 per cent overshoot. This is not a marginal exceedance; it represents extending nearly Rs. 5,780 crore more in contingent liability than the legislature authorised. Guarantees extended by the state government are off-balance-sheet obligations -- if the guaranteed entities default, the state is liable to pay. Power sector guarantees alone account for Rs. 15,606 crore of outstanding exposure, with state finance companies adding another Rs. 7,104 crore. The Guarantee Redemption Fund has only Rs. 1,000 crore -- covering 4.1 per cent of outstanding exposure.

source.quote: Government extended guarantees of Rs. 31,036.15 crore, which were above the limits (Rs. 25,256.75 crore) prescribed in the BFRBM Act... The larger the stock, the larger the fiscal shock that would be arising on default

keyFindings.text: Outstanding liabilities growing from Rs. 1,16,578 crore (2015-16) to Rs. 3,74,134 crore (2024-25) -- a 220.9 per cent increase in 10 years -- combined with persistent BFRBM violations across fiscal deficit (4.16 per cent vs 3.50 per cent cap), outstanding liabilities/GSDP, and now guarantee ceiling, shows that Bihar's FRBM Act is not a binding constraint. Fiscal rules that are violated across multiple dimensions simultaneously without enforcement consequences stop being rules and become aspirational targets. The CAG's 10-year trend analysis underscores that the direction of fiscal parameters is consistently negative: outstanding liabilities up, deficit above target, debt-to-GSDP rising marginally.

source.quote: Outstanding liabilities of Rs. 1,16,578 crore in 2015-16 increased to Rs. 3,74,134 crore in 2024-25. Thus, the Outstanding to GSDP ratio remained persistently above the limit prescribed in BFRBM continued dependence on borrowings for financing fiscal gaps

recommendations: Bihar Finance Department must seek ex-post legislative sanction for the ₹5,779.40 crore guarantee overshoot in FY 2024-25 -- the BFRBM Act ceiling is statutory; extending guarantees above it without legislative amendment is a violation of the Act; the government should present a supplementary resolution in the Assembly authorising the excess and explaining which specific guarantees it covers.

The Guarantee Redemption Fund of ₹1,000 crore covers only 4.1 per cent of ₹24,370.83 crore in outstanding guarantees -- this is dangerously low; the Finance Department should build the GRF to at least 2.5 per cent of the outstanding guarantee stock annually until it reaches 15 per cent; given the concentration of power sector guarantees (₹15,606 crore), a stress test should be conducted on the DISCOMs' ability to service their guaranteed loans, and the results presented to the PAC.

stats.value: ₹13,925 crore -- Companies ₹10,992 crore, Co-ops ₹1,570 crore, Corporations ₹805 crore

source.quote: and other bodies stood at Rs. 13,925 crore, comprising Government Companies (Rs. 10,992 crore), Co-operative Societies (Rs. 1,570 crore), Statutory Corporations (Rs. 805 crore), Other Joint Stock Companies and Partnerships (Rs. 539 crore) and Rural Banks (Rs. 19 crore)

keyFindings.text: The Odisha PSU dividend picture illustrates a classic asymmetry in state-PSU accountability: Odisha Mining Corporation (OMC), a highly profitable mining PSU with a windfall in FY 2024-25 (Rs. 4,223 crore dividend), dominates the headline dividend number, masking the fact that 27 other profitable PSUs have collectively accumulated Rs. 5,146.76 crore in unpaid dividends. The Finance Department, knowing these PSUs are profitable (they filed accounts showing PAT), has neither raised demand notices nor maintained a centralised dividend tracking system. This is not a legal ambiguity -- the Finance Department itself has a policy mandating 30 per cent of PAT as dividend; the failure to enforce its own policy for 27 entities simultaneously is a financial governance failure.

source.quote: 27 SPSUs, despite reporting PAT, did not remit the required dividends to the State Government as mandated by the Finance Department... Rs. 5,146.76 crore remained unpaid... Finance Department also failed to raise the necessary demand for these dividends... had not maintained any centralised system to track collection of outstanding dividends

keyFindings.text: The decision to not collect dividends from Odisha Power (OPGC), reportedly to allow retention for expansion, is precisely the kind of individually-made exception that, when replicated across 27 PSUs, amounts to Rs. 5,146.76 crore in foregone state revenue. OPGC paid Rs. 111.82 crore but the broader pattern of ad hoc exceptions -- individual entities negotiating non-payment -- is the mechanism through which the dividend policy collapses. The state borrows at 7-8 per cent per annum; allowing profitable PSUs to retain surpluses interest-free (instead of paying them as dividends and having the state borrow less) is a subsidy to PSU management at taxpayer cost.

source.quote: it had been decided not to collect dividends from Odisha Power their surpluses for expansion activities. However, the reply is not acceptable, since the existing dividend guidelines which prescribe payment of annual dividend to the State

recommendations: Finance Department, Odisha should establish a centralised SPSU Dividend Compliance Portal -- the portal should automatically pull PAT data from annual accounts submitted to the Registrar of Companies, calculate mandatory dividend (30 per cent of PAT), and generate demand notices to each SPSU within 60 days of annual account submission; any SPSU unable to pay within 6 months of demand should be required to provide a Board resolution with a specific payment plan.

The ₹5,146.76 crore in outstanding dividends should be pursued through a time-bound recovery plan -- the Finance Secretary should meet with the CEOs of the 27 defaulting PSUs within 30 days, obtain committed payment schedules, and report the outstanding position to the Finance Minister quarterly; PSUs whose annual budget proposals include capex or equity support requests should be required to first clear 50 per cent of outstanding dividends as a precondition for Finance Department approval.

While the state borrows at 7-8 per cent per annum for its market loans, its PSU equity earns 0.0082 per cent. keyFindings.text: Bihar's subsidy expenditure at CAGR 20.61 per cent, simultaneous FRBM breach, and 50.18 per cent of outstanding debt maturing within 7 years creates a fiscal triple-squeeze. Subsidies at 20.61 per cent CAGR outpace GSDP growth of 13.09 per cent by 7.52 percentage points -- meaning subsidies consume a growing share of output every year. The Rs. 1,57,322 crore of debt maturing in 0-7 years will require refinancing at then-prevailing interest rates; if rates rise, debt servicing costs rise. A state with growing committed expenditure (subsidies, pension, salaries), declining PSU returns, and a concentrated debt maturity wall is exposed to fiscal shock from any combination of revenue miss, interest rate increase, or central transfer reduction.

recommendations: Bihar Finance Department must prepare a time-bound PSU rationalisation plan -- ₹3,991.60 crore invested in three loss-making PSUs with zero commercial viability should either receive a funded turnaround plan with specific milestones (break-even within 3 years, dividend by year 4) or be liquidated/merged with commercial entities; continuing equity infusions without performance accountability is a perpetual subsidy disguised as investment.

Finance Department should institute a dividend policy requiring all state PSUs with net profit to transfer a minimum 30 per cent of profit to the state as dividend, with the Finance Secretary personally reviewing PSU annual results within 30 days of filing -- the lack of a dividend collection mechanism despite ₹45,665 crore in PSU equity is a governance failure; ₹3.34 crore in dividends when profitable PSUs exist means money is being retained by PSUs for internal use without state authorisation.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's Fiscal Deficit of 4.16 per cent of GSDP breaching the 3.50 per cent FRBM ceiling is doubly significant because the state recorded Revenue Receipts growth of 13.09 per cent -- the same rate as GSDP growth -- meaning the breach was not driven by revenue shortfall but by expenditure expansion beyond its fiscal rule. Bihar has a large capital expenditure programme (Rs. 45,665 crore) and growing subsidies (CAGR 20.61 per cent). When Rs. 66,952 crore in savings are not surrendered (indicating 21.22 per cent of the budget was unused) simultaneously with a fiscal deficit breach, it suggests the government borrowed against an overstated expenditure plan -- taking on Rs. 41,222 crore in deficit financing while leaving Rs. 66,952 crore unspent.

keyFindings.text: Bihar's UC pendency of Rs. 92,132.75 crore (62,632 cases) growing 26.15 per cent in a single year is one of the largest UC outstanding figures in the country. Rs. 92,132 crore is approximately 42.2 per cent of Bihar's total revenue receipts for FY 2024-25 (Rs. 2,18,658 crore) -- nearly half the year's revenue has been given to grant recipients without verified utilisation. The Rs. 1,478.41 crore discrepancy between PFMS and SNA records means even the digital tracking of centrally-sponsored scheme funds cannot be reconciled -- either funds are being double-counted, misreported, or PFMS entries are being made that do not match actual bank transactions.

source.quote: As of March 2025, 62,632 Utilisation Certificates (UCs) amounting to Rs. 92,132.75 crore were outstanding. During 2024-25, outstanding UCs increased by 26.15 per cent

recommendations: Bihar Finance Department must cap next year's deficit borrowing by reducing the approved supplementary estimate ceiling -- ₹6,225.58 crore in unnecessary supplementary provisions and ₹66,952 crore in unsurrendered savings from the same fiscal year are proof that the budget was over-estimated; over-estimation enables higher deficit financing than the state actually needs; the Finance Department should reduce the supplementary estimate ceiling for FY 2025-26 by ₹10,000 crore and model the actual savings rate from FY 2024-25 to compute a realistic Budget Estimate.

Bihar must implement a real-time UC compliance dashboard linked to the grant-release system -- ₹92,132.75 crore growing at 26.15 per cent per year is an accountability emergency; the Finance Department should block new grant releases to any department or agency whose UC pendency has grown more than 10 per cent year-over-year, and the ₹1,478.41 crore PFMS-SNA discrepancy should be investigated and resolved within 60 days through a joint task force of the Finance Department, PFMS cell, and State NIC team.

title: State Revenues -- Kerala: ₹27.40 crore Forest Land Lease Rent Uncollected from Rubber Company (2009 Rate Used Since 2018); ₹111.28 crore Stamp Duty Irregularities (Sub-Registrar Offices); ₹1.14 crore Parambikkulam Aliyar Forest Shortfall (FY 2023-24)
overview: CAG Report No. 2 of 2026 (Kerala State Revenues, Chapters IV-V) found: (1) Forest land lease -- 356.1232 hectares of forest land in Thrissur leased to a Rubber Company at a 2009 rate (₹1,300 per hectare for one section); despite the lease rent ceiling being removed with effect from 7 November 2018, neither the Forest Department nor District Collector Thrissur revised the rate; lease rent shortfall + interest (12 per cent per annum) = ₹27.40 crore (principal ₹21.45 crore + interest ₹5.95 crore) as of March 2024; (2) Parambikkulam Aliyar Project (PAP) forest land -- 2,455.23 hectares leased to Tamil Nadu for PAP; licence fee not revised in line with land tax rate increases; shortfall ₹1.14 crore (2012-13 to 2023-24); (3) Stamp duty irregularities -- ₹111.28 crore in irregularities detected across Sub-Registrar offices including misclassification of land, application of incorrect fair values, and splitting of deeds to reduce stamp duty.

keyFindings.text: The Rubber Company lease case is a 15-year revenue failure: the lease runs since 1917, the Forest Rights Act rules were framed in 1990, the District Collector revised the rent in 2009 -- and then did nothing when the rate ceiling was removed in 2018, which would have allowed lease rent to be revised upward to Rs. 86,048 per hectare (3 per cent of land value Rs. 7,035 per cent). The Forest Department, as the primary custodian of the lease, allowed Rs. 21.45 crore in principal shortfall to accumulate over 5 years of non-revision (2018-2024). Adding 12 per cent interest brings the total to Rs. 27.40 crore owed by a single corporate lessee for a commercial rubber cultivation operation on government forest land.

source.quote: Due to non-revision of lease rent, the short collection of lease rent, along with interest up to March 2024, in respect of the 356.1232 hectares of land leased to the company, was calculated at Rs. 27.40 crore

keyFindings.text: Rs. 111.28 crore in stamp duty irregularities -- primarily from Sub-Registrar offices misclassifying land (residential vs. agricultural vs. commercial), applying pre-revision fair values, and allowing deed splitting to reduce document value below thresholds -- represents a structural failure in property transaction taxation. Fair value-based stamp duty is Kenya's primary revenue from property transfers; when sub-registrars apply incorrect classifications or allow obvious tax avoidance through deed fragmentation, the revenue loss is invisible unless audited. The pattern of multiple small cases (Rs. 0.04 crore to Rs. 64.16 lakh per case) across dozens of sub-registrar offices suggests either systemic skill gaps in fair value computation or deliberate collusion with transacting parties.

source.quote: number and other irregularities amounting to Rs. 111.28 crore were detected in Table 4.2: Details of non/short levy of Stamp Duty and Registration Fees

recommendations: Forest Department, Kerala should send a demand notice to the Rubber Company lessee within 30 days for the revised lease rent from 7 November 2018 and pursue recovery through the District Collector, Thrissur -- the legal ground is clear (the ceiling was removed by amendment, the rate revision formula is prescribed) and the ₹27.40 crore demand is fully calculable; continued non-collection will increase the interest liability at ₹2.57 crore per year.

Inspector General of Registration, Kerala should implement a real-time KAVERI portal integration with e-Jantri (fair value registers) to automatically compute and validate stamp duty at the time of document upload -- the ₹111.28 crore in Sub-Registrar irregularities are largely preventable through system-level checks; specifically, the portal should flag and require supervisor override whenever a deed involves land that was fragmented from a larger survey number in the preceding 12 months (to prevent deed splitting).

overview: CAG Report No. 2 of 2026 (Kerala State Revenues, Chapter III) found systemic excise oversight failures: (1) TSCL Distillery, Thiruvalla -- 4,60,659 BL of ENA found missing on 7 September 2021 (quarterly stock verifications not conducted); Department levied fine of ₹1,54,41,293; but audit found a stock certificate issued by Excise officials showed no discrepancy, making the regularisation irregular; revised unaccounted shortage 1,48,050.384 BL (equivalent to 2,43,542.882 PL); estimated 1,14,048 cases of IMFL could have been produced from the missing ENA; (2) Transit theft -- 20,386 BL stolen in transit (two tanker lorries; drivers admitted diversion); (3) IMFL diversion -- 12,302 cases involving 1,10,720 BL had no exit records from transit permits, indicating possible diversion; estimated revenue loss ₹5.10 crore (excise duty ₹0.90 crore + sales tax ₹4.20 crore); (4) Tax defaulters retain Abkari licences -- no mechanism in Foreign Liquor Rules to demand sales tax arrears from licensees; (5) Excise irregularities total ₹75.21 crore (transfer of licences and other cases).

keyFindings.text: The TSCL distillery case illustrates the failure of Excise oversight in full: quarterly stock verifications of ENA were not conducted (a mandatory requirement), which allowed 4,60,659 BL to go missing without timely detection; when finally detected in September 2021, the department levied a fine but then regularised the shortage using a stock certificate issued by the same Excise officials -- a case of the regulator certifying away a shortage it was responsible for detecting earlier. The revised unaccounted shortage of 1,48,050 BL, if converted to IMFL at production efficiency, represents 1,14,048 cases of liquor that should have been produced, bottled, and taxes paid on -- instead they went unaccounted. The estimated tax loss is not fully quantified in the audit but clearly exceeds the Rs. 1.54 crore fine levied.

source.quote: On 07 September 2021, the shortage was determined to be 4,60,659.1 BL... the revised shortage was computed as 1,48,050.384 BL (equivalent to 2,43,542.882 PL)

keyFindings.text: 12,302 IMFL cases (1,10,720 BL) transported with transit permits had no corresponding exit records -- the permits show the liquor left its origin but there is no record of it arriving at its permitted destination in Kerala. CAG notes "possible diversion" -- the liquor may have been illegally sold in Kerala without payment of Kerala excise duty and sales tax, representing Rs. 5.10 crore in estimated revenue loss. The inability to demand sales tax arrears from liquor licence holders (because the Foreign Liquor Rules do not provide for it) means tax defaulters can continue to hold licences and conduct business while evading tax -- a fundamental regulatory design flaw that the Kerala government has not corrected despite repeated audit findings.

source.quote: permits, involving 1,10,720 BL of IMFL, had no corresponding records of exit... indicating possible diversion to Kerala... diversion of 12,302 cases of IMFL amounts to Rs. 5.10 crore

recommendations: Kerala Excise Department must immediately implement mandatory bimonthly (not quarterly) ENA stock verification at all distilleries with CCTV coverage of tank gauging -- quarterly verifications at TSCL allowed a 4,60,659 BL shortage to accumulate undetected; the verification protocol must require a Gazetted Officer's counter-signature on stock certificates and a real-time entry into the Excise department's central monitoring system, making it impossible for a "no discrepancy" certificate to co-exist with a subsequently discovered shortage.

Government of Kerala should amend the Foreign Liquor Rules to expressly include sales tax arrears as a ground for cancellation or non-renewal of liquor licences -- the current legal gap that prevents the Excise department from treating tax defaulters as Abkari defaulters is a legislative loophole exploited by distilleries and bar licensees to continue operations while evading state revenue; the amendment should be introduced in the next legislative session with retrospective application to pending tax arrears.

(-) 149.96 crore and had availed Rs. 8,918.31 crore in Ways and Means Advances (short-term RBI overdrafts) for 69 days during the year. Rs. 8,918.31 crore in WMAs against total revenue receipts of Rs. 15,893.15 crore means Manipur borrowed 56.12 per cent of its annual revenue as temporary overdraft at some point in the year. Simultaneously, committed expenditure (salaries, pensions, interest) consumed 64.17 per cent of all revenue spending, leaving only 35.83 per cent for programmes and capital.

keyFindings.text: NPS shortfall of Rs. 210.85 crore -- with Rs. 191.94 crore still due to NSDL -- is a recurring pattern across northeastern states where committed expenditure (including pension-equivalent NPS contributions) competes with routine government operations for available cash. When the state borrows Rs. 8,918.31 crore in WMAs while simultaneously failing to remit Rs. 191.94 crore in NPS contributions to employee retirement accounts, the fiscal priority is clear: current operations run on borrowed money while employee retirement entitlements are deferred. This is inter-temporal financial mismanagement -- trading current cash flow for future pension liability.

recommendations: Manipur Finance Department must treat NPS remittances to NSDL as non-deferrable, legally-mandated cash outflows on par with salary payments -- the ₹191.94 crore outstanding to NSDL should be cleared in a maximum of 4 quarterly instalments; going forward, NPS transfers should be built into the monthly treasury release schedule as a standing instruction, not a discretionary item competed against other departments.

The Finance Department must prepare and publish a monthly cash-flow management plan for each quarter of the financial year -- given the pattern of 69 days of WMAs in FY 2022-23, the state clearly cannot sustain its expenditure level from its own revenues during certain periods; a visible, publicly disclosed cash plan that identifies which months will require WMAs and which Central transfer receipts are expected allows better advance planning and reduces dependence on RBI overdrafts.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 1,584.52 crore disbursed to Autonomous and Development Councils over 5 years with no audited accounts of recipient councils is a black hole in Assam's tribal development expenditure. The money leaves the state treasury and enters an administrative structure -- the autonomous district councils -- that has no annual audit, no verified utilisation certification, and no mechanism for the state legislature to determine whether the funds reached intended beneficiaries. When a state simultaneously: (a) disburses Rs. 1,584 crore to unaudited entities, (b) submits inflated UCs for the same heads (Para 2.7.1.7), and (c) books 67.82 per cent of the grant under Minor Head 800 (obscuring the nature of spending) -- the combination represents a near-total opacity in tribal welfare expenditure.

source.quote: Rs. 1,584.52 crore on Autonomous/Development Councils from 2020-21 to 2024-25 annual accounts and their audit, proper utilisation of the funds disbursed cannot be ascertained

keyFindings.text: Booking 67.82 per cent (Rs. 556.19 crore) of Tribal Affairs (Plain) grant expenditure under Minor Head 800-Other Expenditure is not a technical classification error -- it is a deliberate or systemic choice to use a catch-all minor head to hide the programmatic purpose of spending. CAG notes that specific Minor Heads were available for this expenditure. When over two-thirds of an entire grant's spending is booked as "Other", it becomes impossible for the legislature, finance department, or civil society to analyse what the money was actually spent on. The 88 per cent March rush compounding the MH-800 overuse confirms a pattern of booking money in the last month of the year into a catch-all head -- the standard mechanism for accounting for funds that were not spent as planned.

source.quote: out of the total expenditure of Rs. 820.13 crore under Grant No. 38, expenditure amounting to Rs. 556.19 crore (67.82 per cent) was booked under the Minor Head 800

recommendations: Assam Finance Department must mandate annual audits of all Autonomous and Development Councils receiving state funds above ₹10 crore per year -- the CAG's inability to verify utilisation of ₹1,584.52 crore should be treated as an emergency accountability gap; the state should assign audit responsibility explicitly (CAG, State Finance Audit, or a qualified external auditor under the CAG's supervision) and make audit completion a precondition for next-year disbursements.

Tribal Affairs (Plain) Department must reduce Minor Head 800 booking to below 5 per cent of grant expenditure within 2 years -- a structured mapping exercise should be conducted to identify, for each sub-type of District Council grant, which specific minor head applies; the PFMS/iFMS system should be configured to require a supervisor override for any booking under MH-800 above ₹1 crore, with a mandatory reason code recorded.

title: MGNREGA -- Madhya Pradesh: ₹1.46 crore Wages on 2,426 Fake/Duplicate Job Cards; Only 2 Per cent Households Got Full 100 Days; Women Quota Missed in 3 Districts; Demand Declined from 36 Lakh to 2.29 Crore HH; No District Ombudsman (Lokpal) Appointed (2019-24)
overview: CAG Report No. 4 of 2026 (MP MGNREGA, Chapters II-III) found: (1) Fake/duplicate job cards -- ₹1.46 crore in wages paid on 2,426 duplicate, fake or incorrectly maintained job cards during 2019-24; (2) 100-day employment -- only approximately 2 per cent of households received the full 100 days' employment entitlement under the Act; (3) Women participation -- the one-third women employment norm was not achieved in 3 districts, 7 Janpad Panchayats, and 16 Gram Panchayats in the test-checked area; (4) No Ombudsman (Lokpal) appointed in any district -- the MGNREGA mandate for a Lokpal in every district for independent grievance redressal was not fulfilled; (5) Employment demand fell from 36 lakh households (2020-21) to 2.29 crore in 2024, with job demand declining from 70.32 per cent to 64.72 per cent in 8 test-checked districts (2019-24, excluding COVID period).

keyFindings.text: Only 2 per cent of MGNREGA-registered households in MP received their full statutory entitlement of 100 days' employment -- meaning 98 per cent of households who exercised their right under a Parliamentary Act that guarantees employment on demand did not receive what the law promises. MGNREGA is unique in Indian social policy: it is a legal guarantee, not a welfare scheme. A state that registers households, issues job cards, and then provides employment to only 2 per cent of them for the full 100 days is not administering a scheme; it is managing paperwork for an unfulfilled legal entitlement. The decline in demand from 70.32 per cent to 64.72 per cent of job card households suggests that workers have stopped even asking, knowing they will not get 100 days.

source.quote: Only around two per cent of households have been provided the full 100 days' employment

keyFindings.text: No district in MP has an MGNREGA Lokpal (Ombudsman) -- this is a statutory requirement under the 2011 MGNREGA Ombudsman Rules, not a discretionary governance mechanism. The Lokpal is the primary accountability layer between the scheme administration and citizens: workers can complain to the Lokpal about non-payment, non-provision of employment, and fake job cards. When no Lokpal exists, Rs. 1.46 crore in wages going to 2,426 fake job cards becomes very easy -- there is no independent authority to receive complaints from workers who know their name was used to draw wages they never received. The absence of the Lokpal and the presence of fake job card payments are directly connected.

source.quote: appointment of an Ombudsman (Lokpal) in every district resulted in the department appointment of an Ombudsman in each district, strengthening the grievance redressal

recommendations: Government of Madhya Pradesh must appoint Ombudsman (Lokpal) in all 52 districts within 3 months -- this is a mandatory statutory obligation under the MGNREGA Ombudsman Rules 2011, not a recommendation; the Secretary, Rural Development must be personally accountable to the Chief Secretary for compliance; Lokpal appointments should be published in district-level public notices and on the MGNREGS state portal so workers know how to file complaints.

The 2,426 fake/duplicate job cards with ₹1.46 crore in wages should be investigated by district vigilance committees within 60 days with specific identification of beneficiary accounts that received wages against these cards; NREGASoft should be cross-referenced with Aadhaar-seeded bank accounts to identify individuals who received wages against multiple job cards for the same work period, and First Information Reports filed where the amounts exceed ₹10,000 per card.

title: MGNREGA -- Madhya Pradesh: 31.75 Per cent Material Ratio (₹350.73 crore); Skilled Labour Cap Breach Caused 3.93 Lakh Person-Day Shortfall; ₹30.00 crore Social Audit Fund Blocked as FDR; ₹3.24 crore Misappropriation Cases; ₹0.33 crore Pending Recovery (2019-24)
overview: CAG Report No. 4 of 2026 (MP MGNREGA, Chapters VI and VII) found: (1) Material ratio violation -- ₹350.73 crore (31.75 per cent) of ₹1,104.66 crore total expenditure was on materials; expenditure on labour in Jabalpur works was ₹114.58 crore (56.33 per cent) of a ₹203.40 crore work cluster, against the 60 per cent minimum labour norm, causing a shortfall of 3.93 lakh person-days; (2) Social Audit fund blockage -- ₹30.00 crore transferred from State Audit Unit account was parked in an FDR and unavailable for social audit activities; ₹2.84 crore in interest also not usable; (3) Financial misappropriation -- ₹3.24 crore misappropriation cases; ₹2.91 crore recovered in 4,450 cases; ₹0.33 crore pending recovery in 71 cases; (4) Worksite facilities missing across test-checked sites -- no first aid, drinking water, shade -- reducing women's workforce participation; (5) 736 works (23 per cent of total costing ₹80 crore) in 2 JPs not completed within one year.

keyFindings.text: MGNREGA's 60:40 labour-to-material ratio is non-negotiable because the scheme's purpose is wage employment -- if material costs crowd out labour, fewer person-days are generated per rupee spent, defeating the scheme's primary objective. In Jabalpur, material expenditure resulted in only 56.33 per cent going to labour instead of 60 per cent minimum, causing 3.93 lakh person-days that should have been generated to disappear. At the prevailing wage of Rs. 190 per day (FY 2020-21), this means approximately 20,700 workers who should have received 19 days of work each did not -- a direct denial of employment entitlement to rural households caused by administrative material-cost overrun.

source.quote: of Rs. 203.40 crore. Of this, only Rs. 114.58 crore (56.33 per cent) was spent on labour... deviation led to a shortfall in employment generation, amounting to Rs. 3.93 lakh person-days

keyFindings.text: Rs. 30.00 crore of social audit funds parked in an FDR -- a fixed deposit earning interest instead of funding oversight activity -- is a striking example of how the institutional architecture for MGNREGA accountability was hollowed out in MP. Social audits are the scheme's primary citizen-accountability mechanism: workers, Gram Sabhas, and external auditors jointly verify whether works were actually done and wages actually paid. When the State Audit Unit cannot fund social audit activities because its operational funds have been converted into a bank deposit, the entire oversight ecosystem collapses. This explains why, despite Rs. 3.24 crore in detected misappropriation, recovery processes are slow and the pattern likely continues.

source.quote: an amount of Rs. 30.00 crore was transferred from the account of the SAU at unavailable for social audit activities. It was also observed that the interest of Rs. 2.84 crore

recommendations: GoMP must immediately release the ₹30.00 crore from the FDR and transfer it to the operational account of the State Audit Unit for social audit activities -- the Ministry of Rural Development guidelines require 0.5 per cent of MGNREGS expenditure to be allocated to social audit; in MP, the funds exist but are immobilised; unblocking them and providing a clear annual social audit calendar to cover all GPs on a 2-year rotation is the immediate fix.

The 71 pending misappropriation recovery cases (₹0.33 crore) must be referred to Revenue Recovery within 30 days -- while the amount is small, the pattern of 4,450 detected cases shows that misappropriation is systemic and the recovery rate indicates willingness to act; the 71 pending cases must not be left as open items to expire by limitation; recovery should be pursued through Gram Panchayat sarpanch personal liability where the GP was the disbursing unit.

overview: CAG Report No. 4 of 2026 (MP MGNREGA, Chapter VI -- Works) found: (1) Incomplete old works + new approvals -- 189 community works started before 2019-20 remained incomplete; despite this, 1,131 new community works (₹32.86 crore) were approved for same Gram Panchayats during 2019-22; as of 31 March 2024, 189 old + 206 new works (₹5.60 crore expended) remained incomplete, violating MGNREGA requirement that no work remain incomplete beyond one fiscal year; (2) Micro-irrigation without convergence -- 309 micro-irrigation works (₹21.90 crore out of ₹34.98 crore sanctioned) in selected zones executed without mandatory convergence with PMKSY/IWMP/other NRM schemes, missing material cost-sharing; (3) Physical verification found works incomplete or not in accordance with specifications; (4) Livelihood works -- 2 livelihood-related works in JP Kurwai and JP Vidisha remained incomplete after 24-48 months despite incurring ₹3.76 lakh and ₹4.44 lakh respectively; 85 and 6 additional new works approved for same GPs.

keyFindings.text: Approving 1,131 new community works (Rs. 32.86 crore) for Gram Panchayats that already had 189 incomplete works is the most fundamental governance failure in MGNREGA work planning. The MGNREGA Annual Master Circular explicitly prohibits new work sanctioning for GPs with incomplete old works. Yet the pattern repeated year after year in MP -- GPs with years-old incomplete works continued to receive fresh sanctions. The result as of March 2024 is 395 incomplete works, many half-built rural assets (wells, ponds, earthworks) that deliver no benefit to the community but are fully recorded in the system as expenditure. Rs. 5.60 crore of public money is sunk in assets that were never completed.

source.quote: 189 community works started before 2019-20 and undertook 1131 new community works costing Rs. 32.86 crore during 2019-22... 189 works initiated prior to 2019-20 and 206 works initiated during 2019-22 with expenditure of Rs. 5.60 crore remained incomplete as of 31 March 2024

keyFindings.text: MGNREGA NRM (Natural Resource Management) works like micro-irrigation are required to be executed in convergence with PMKSY, IWMP, and similar schemes so that the material component (pump sets, piping, structures) is funded by the NRM scheme while MGNREGA funds the labour. Bypassing convergence means MGNREGA bears both labour and material costs (up to 40 per cent permitted for materials), reducing the wage component that goes to workers. 309 micro-irrigation works executed without convergence in MP spent Rs. 21.90 crore that included material costs which PMKSY should have shared -- this is a missed convergence opportunity worth tens of crores in redirected public money.

source.quote: 309 micro irrigation works convergence. An expenditure of Rs. 21.90 crore was incurred on these micro irrigation works against sanctioned cost Rs. 34.98 crore... The fact remains that executing minor irrigation works under MGNREGA without opportunity to share material costs through related schemes like PMKSY, IWMP

recommendations: NREGASoft should be configured to prevent any new work sanction for a GP that has more than 10 per cent of its active works incomplete beyond the approved time limit -- the ability to continuously sanction new works despite an accumulation of incomplete works is a system design failure; the software gatekeeping mechanism must enforce the Annual Master Circular prohibition on new work approval for GPs with outstanding incomplete works.

For the 309 micro-irrigation works executed without convergence, GoMP Rural Development Department should prepare a convergence facilitation plan with PMKSY and IWMP State Programme Management Units to fund future NRM works under the required multi-scheme arrangement; the Department of Agriculture and Department of Water Resources must be made joint signatories on MGNREGA work orders for micro-irrigation so that PMKSY material component approval is a prerequisite, not an afterthought.

keyFindings.text: The simultaneity of Rs. 295.59 crore in excess payments (above GoI-approved PDs) and Rs. 1,703.80 crore in unutilised funds reveals a structural disconnect in MP MGNREGA: the state made payments beyond sanctioned limits (which could be irregular/unlawful) while also leaving massive funds unspent. Excess PD generation is a compliance failure -- GoI approves a specific Person Day target; any payment beyond this requires fresh approval. Generating Rs. 295.59 crore in payments without that approval means workers were employed and paid with money that was never properly sanctioned for that purpose. Meanwhile, the Rs. 1,703.80 crore sitting unused in 2021-22 was available for lawful employment generation but went undisbursed.

source.quote: payments of Rs. 295.59 crore beyond the approval of GoI were made during 2020-23... amounts unutilized during 2019-2024, with a peak of Rs. 1703.80 crore in 2021-22

keyFindings.text: Rs. 2,061.49 crore (15.14 per cent of total releases) deposited late into worker/Gram Panchayat accounts is significant because MGNREGA mandates a strict payment timeline -- wages must be paid within 15 days of work completion, and the penal interest of 12 per cent per annum applies to the government's delay. The Rs. 10.36 crore in penal interest not paid to affected workers is both a legal violation and a direct financial loss to rural workers who are the scheme's intended beneficiaries. The fact that Rs. 35.13 lakh in delayed wage compensation was levied but only Rs. 9.07 lakh paid confirms that GoMP treats penal interest as an accounting entry rather than an obligation to workers.

source.quote: Rs. 2061.49 crore out of Rs. 13,615.31 crore (Central and State share) released by GoMP was deposited in the bank accounts after the specified period... Penal interest of Rs. 10.36 crore remained unpaid due to delays in fund transfer

recommendations: GoMP Rural Development Department must set up automated PD tracking with a hard system-level block in NREGASoft preventing work generation once approved PDs are exhausted for the fiscal year -- ₹295.59 crore in unauthorised excess payments show that the current NREGASoft configuration allows payment generation beyond GoI-sanctioned limits; this must be fixed before the next approval cycle.

MGNREGS penal interest of ₹10.36 crore owed to workers must be paid directly to affected worker accounts within 90 days -- the compensation for delayed payment is a right under the Act, not a discretionary payment; GoMP should also designate a Senior Officer as the Penal Interest Compliance Officer with quarterly reporting to the State Employment Guarantee Council on all delays and payments made.

title: Performance Audit -- State Bank of Sikkim: ₹863.73 crore (32.1 Per cent) of Loans Turned NPA; Profits Overstated (No Mandatory Provisions); No RBI Licence; No CAR Norms; KYC Deficiencies in 3,969 Accounts; Fresh Loans Given to Existing NPAs
overview: CAG Report No. 2 of 2025 (Performance Audit on State Bank of Sikkim, 2017-23) found: (1) NPA -- of ₹2,773.80 crore in loans sanctioned, ₹863.73 crore (32.1 per cent) turned NPA; 17 specific loan accounts (₹109.69 crore outstanding against ₹88.37 crore sanctioned) became NPAs due to poor due diligence; (2) Fresh loans and enhancements given to 10 existing NPA accounts (₹17.56 crore outstanding) which subsequently became NPAs with ₹25.52 crore outstanding; (3) Profits of ₹17.13 crore to ₹44.56 crore declared without creating mandatory provisions -- had provisions been created, profits would turn into losses; (4) No Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) norms framed by Government of Sikkim; no Basel-I compliance; capital base only ₹0.53 crore paid-up; (5) No RBI banking licence (SBS operates outside RBI regulation); (6) KYC deficiencies -- 3,969 accounts without uploaded signatures; PAN details not available in 1,39,357 accounts; no CKYC arrangement.

keyFindings.text: The State Bank of Sikkim operates outside RBI's banking regulatory framework -- it does not hold a banking licence from RBI, has no Capital Adequacy Ratio norms, and is not subject to Basel-I requirements. This regulatory gap means that the usual safety net for depositors -- mandatory provisioning for bad loans, capital buffer, CKYC compliance, RBI inspection -- does not apply. When 31.1 per cent of all loans sanctioned (Rs. 863.73 crore) become NPA over a 6-year period, and mandatory provisions for these NPAs are not created, the bank's reported profits are fictional -- a bank that books Rs. 44.56 crore profit while sitting on Rs. 863.73 crore of bad loans without adequate provisioning is not profitable; it is insolvent on a risk-adjusted basis.

source.quote: SBS had sanctioned 10,166 loans amounting to Rs. 2,773.80 crore... 890 loans worth Rs. 863.73 crore had turned into NPA... profit had been arrived at without creating mandatory provisions... profits during the period under review would turn into losses

keyFindings.text: Giving fresh loans to existing NPA accounts (the 10 cases of Rs. 25.52 crore) is the textbook definition of loan evergreening -- extending new credit to prevent the borrower from being formally classified as defaulted, artificially reducing reported NPAs while compounding the actual loss. In regulated banks, this practice is specifically prohibited by RBI. Since SBS has no RBI oversight, there is no mechanism to detect or prevent evergreening. Combined with no due diligence on 224 random accounts scrutinised and 32.1 per cent NPA rate, the SBS loan book cannot be considered reliable without an independent forensic review.

source.quote: 10 out of 224 NPA accounts which had become NPA with outstanding balance of Rs. 17.56 crore were given fresh loans/enhancements under Construction loan, subsequently turned NPAs with an outstanding balance of Rs. 25.52 crore. This indicates

recommendations: Government of Sikkim must immediately bring the State Bank of Sikkim under a regulatory framework modelled on RBI norms -- at minimum, GoS should enact a State Bank of Sikkim Regulation Act requiring: (a) CAR of at least 9 per cent on Basel-I norms, (b) mandatory NPA classification and provisioning, (c) prohibition on lending to NPA accounts without documented restructuring, and (d) annual inspection by an independent statutory body; until these are enacted, GoS should publish annual audited accounts showing the position after full provisioning.

The 31.1 per cent NPA rate requires an immediate independent loan review committee comprising RBI-empanelled bank auditors to examine all NPA accounts above ₹1 crore -- the finding that loan appraisals were not based on standard criteria is a systemic failure, not an isolated lapse; the committee should within 6 months recommend write-offs, restructuring, or recovery action for each material NPA and the GoS should inject capital commensurate with the provisioning requirement.

keyFindings.text: Nagaland's capital expenditure exceeding Budget Estimate by 73.21 per cent (Rs. 1,319.78 crore more than voted) is a significant parliamentary/legislative control failure. Budget authorisation means nothing if actual spending exceeds it by three-quarters. In Nagaland's case, the CE overrun was concentrated in Urban Development (Rs. 274.09 crore for slum improvement and other urban schemes) -- large transfers that moved quickly at year-end. When CE is simultaneously 73 per cent above BE and 220.34 per cent increase in financial assistance (essentially grants transferred to local bodies/agencies), the pattern suggests funds being rapidly disbursed without matching absorptive capacity, explaining the 333 unadjusted AC Bills worth Rs. 613.29 crore.

source.quote: Capital Expenditure increased... to Rs. 3,122.52 crore (17.41 per cent of TE) in 2023-24... Rs. 1,319.78 crore (73.21 per cent) more than the Budget Estimates (Rs. 1,802.74 crore)

keyFindings.text: Five Nagaland PSUs with negative net worth (Rs. 83.42 crore negative) against State equity investment of Rs. 40.66 crore means the state has already lost more than twice what it invested -- and returns ranged from Rs. 0.49 crore to Rs. 4.94 crore per year against a borrowing cost that is always higher than a 1-2 per cent return on equity. CAG explicitly notes that "returns are far below borrowing costs, exacerbating financial inefficiencies." These PSUs should be either closed, restructured with time-bound turnaround plans, or their loss-making activities transferred to line departments -- continuing equity infusions into loss-making entities with no viable commercial future is a subsidy by another name.

source.quote: Five State PSUs, in which the State Government held investment of Rs. 15.87 crore had aggregated accumulated losses of Rs. 114.26 crore... returns on these investments are far below borrowing costs, exacerbating financial inefficiencies

recommendations: Nagaland Finance Department must institute a strict quarterly capital expenditure monitoring system with BE vs. actual reports presented to the PAC -- a 73 per cent exceedance over BE is not a rounding error; it reflects either gross under-budgeting of capital needs or unplanned year-end fund releases; either way, the legislature's authorization is being bypassed and the Appropriation Act is rendered meaningless.

The 333 unadjusted AC Bills of ₹613.29 crore must be adjusted within 3 months of the CAG report -- the Finance Department should issue a circular that AC Bill drawals above ₹1 crore by any official will be blocked at source unless prior DCC Bills for all previous AC drawals are cleared; the accumulation of ₹613.29 crore in unjustified AC Bills is a direct risk of public money being misappropriated with no recourse.

keyFindings.text: Kerala's revenue arrears of Rs. 30,308.52 crore (24.35 per cent of revenue) represents systemic non-collection across principal heads -- nearly a quarter of the state's annual revenues are recorded in accounts but never actually flow into the treasury. This is a persistent structural problem in Kerala that compounds the fiscal crisis: the state has a large government apparatus (high salary/pension committed expenditure) funded by borrowings and GoI grants, both of which are declining (GoI grants fell 55.92 per cent in FY 2023-24). The Finance Commission grant reduction of Rs. 8,136.62 crore in a single year, combined with Rs. 30,308 crore stuck in arrears and a revenue gap of Rs. 603.53 crore in unresolved audit findings, means Kerala's fiscal space is narrowing from all three directions simultaneously.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 37.48 crore was spent on vehicle tracking technology by Kerala, but enforcement wings neither issued notices nor initiated action against defaulters -- an almost perfect example of technology expenditure without behavioural change. The Enforcement Wing had data identifying vehicles that changed classification (and therefore owed different tax rates) but did not use it to raise demand. This pattern -- expenditure on detection systems paired with non-enforcement -- creates a perverse outcome: the government invests in catching evasion and then does not act on what it finds, making the investment a pure sunk cost while the evasion continues.

recommendations: Kerala Finance Department should publish an annual Revenue Arrears Reduction Plan targeting reduction of ₹30,308 crore arrears to below 15 per cent of revenues within 3 years -- the plan must identify the top 20 arrear heads by amount, set department-wise collection targets, and make Collector-level performance reviews quarterly; the current system where arrears grow unchecked each year does not create any accountability for non-collection.

Motor Vehicles Department, Kerala must configure VAHAN to automatically block vehicles from registration renewal if vehicle tax or compounding fees have been outstanding for more than 90 days -- the ₹37.48 crore spent on vehicle tracking should produce enforcement action, not just data; integrate VAHAN tax payment status into the fitness certificate and permit renewal workflow so every interaction at the RTO is a collection opportunity.

ministry: Roads and Buildings Department, Government of Gujarat
title: Compliance Audit -- Gujarat R&B: ₹4.74 crore Irregular/Excess Price Variation (PV) Payments in 5 R&B Divisions; PV Paid for Labour/POL on Works Below Threshold; ₹55.70 lakh Overpaid Instead of ₹15.57 lakh Recovered; Wrong Steel Index Applied (2017-24)
overview: CAG Report No. 1 of 2026 (Gujarat, Para 3.6) found ₹4.74 crore in irregular/excess Price Variation (PV) payments in five R&B Divisions over April 2017 to March 2024: (1) A Division paid PV of ₹40.13 lakh against a case where recovery of ₹15.57 lakh was due from the contractor (wrong Steel index applied -- used index 122.5 vs correct formula), resulting in an overpayment of ₹55.70 lakh instead of recovering money; (2) R&B Division Godhra paid PV of ₹71.02 lakh including PV for labour, POL, and other materials -- but a March 2022 GR provided PV only for materials used; actual PV admissible was ₹4.57 lakh for material only, making ₹56.75 lakh irregular; (3) Ten works in divisions paid PV of ₹3.40 crore in overpayment; (4) Two works suffered cost overrun of ₹2.21 crore due to incorrect adoption of bid validity period.

keyFindings.text: The Steel index PV error illustrates how accounting inversion leads to double loss: the Division calculated PV incorrectly, arriving at a number that was negative -- the steel price had moved in the contractor's favour meaning the Division should have recovered Rs. 15.57 lakh -- but instead applied the formula wrong, showing positive PV, and paid Rs. 40.13 lakh. The result was Rs. 55.70 lakh in net loss (a payment error of Rs. 40.13 lakh plus a recovery foregone of Rs. 15.57 lakh). This type of error in PV calculation is hard to detect without cross-checking the commodity price indices at the time of payment against the payment vouchers -- which only audit can do systematically across multiple divisions.

source.quote: instead of recovery of Rs. 15.57 lakh from the Contractor, the Division paid PV of Rs. 40.13 lakh. Thus, there was overpayment of Rs. 55.70 lakh due to incorrect calculation of PV

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 2.21 crore cost overrun from expired bid validity reveals a process failure: when the competent authority's approval took longer than the bid validity period (the Circle communicated approval on 27 October 2021 after the validity lapsed on 17 October 2021), the L1 bidder used the opportunity to decline -- knowing material prices had risen. The work was then re-tendered and awarded to another contractor at higher rates. This is a common pattern in public works that adds avoidable cost: approval processes within government should match the bid validity period guaranteed to external bidders, or the bid validity should be set conservatively long.

source.quote: Circle office communicated the approval to the Division only on 27 October 2021 i.e. after the lapse of the bid validity period on 17 October 2021... L1 bidder declined (22 November 2021) to accept the tender, citing expiry of the bid validity period

recommendations: R&B Department, Gujarat should deploy a PV calculation verification module in the contract management system -- PV claims above ₹5 lakh should be auto-calculated by the system using official commodity indices (IOCL HSD price, WPI Steel) at the correct quarter, and payment should be blocked unless the system-calculated PV matches the claimed amount within 1 per cent; the Godhra case and the steel index error would both have been caught and prevented by such a module.

The Department should establish an internal audit function that specifically reviews PV calculations for all contracts with PV clauses, at least annually -- five R&B Divisions spanning seven years of PV errors suggests there is no ongoing check; the present system relies entirely on CAG external audit to detect these errors, by which time recovery from contractors requires legal proceedings.

overview: CAG Report No. 1 of 2026 (Gujarat, Para 3.4 and 3.5) found two related revenue shortfalls from property transactions: (1) Stamp Duty -- ₹12.18 crore short-levied across 126 documents at multiple Sub-Registrar offices due to use of old Jantri rates (pre-April 2023 rates applied to documents that should have used the revised Jantri effective April 2023), incorrect determination of property value, and non-compliance with Jantri guidelines; (2) Land Premium / NA Permission -- ₹55.16 crore in premium and differential premium short-levied in 173 cases due to: (a) adoption of incorrect Jantri rates in 21 cases (₹16.22 crore short premium), (b) use of pre-revised Jantri rates for premium payments made after 14 April 2023 (₹26.55 crore), (c) non-recovery of differential premium where NA permission obtained after 1 year (₹3.74 crore), (d) other valuation errors. keyFindings.text: Rs. 67.34 crore in combined stamp duty and premium shortfalls stems entirely from the transition to revised Jantri rates effective April 2023 -- registrars and Collectors across the state applied old rates to documents that qualified for the revised rates, creating a systematic revenue undercount. The Jantri revision is a significant administrative event; the fact that multiple offices across Gujarat (12 offices for stamp duty, 13 Collector offices for premium) all made the same error suggests the guidance from the Revenue Department on when to apply revised vs. old rates was inadequate, and the VAHAN/STAMPS portal was not updated to enforce the correct rate schedule automatically.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 26.55 crore in premium shortfall from extension cases -- where applicants obtained extensions to pay premium but paid at old rates after the April 2023 revision -- reflects a procedural gap: the rules explicitly required revised rates for extension payments made after 14 April 2023, but Collectors continued applying old rates. This is not a one-off error but a consistent pattern across multiple Collector offices, suggesting either the GR clarification of April 2023 was not disseminated to field offices or the field offices chose to continue with old rates to reduce burden on applicants.

source.quote: premium had been paid during period of extension for payment of premium and therefore, revised Jantri rates were required to be adopted. This resulted in short levy of premium price of Rs. 26.55 crore

recommendations: Revenue Department, Gujarat should program a mandatory rate-effective-date check in the STAMPS portal and land revenue management system -- any document dated after 15 April 2023 must automatically apply Jantri 2023 rates; manual rate selection by the sub-registrar or Collector should be blocked in favour of system-computed duty/premium based on the document execution date.

All 126 short-duty documents and 173 short-premium cases should be referred to the respective District Collectors for demand notices and recovery within 6 months -- the Audit has identified the specific documents; failure to initiate recovery within a prescribed time frame should be treated as a dereliction of duty by the Superintendent of Stamps and Deputy Collectors concerned.

ministry: Transport Department / Commissioner of Transport, Government of Gujarat
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2026 -- Chapter II, Motor Vehicles
title: Compliance Audit -- Gujarat Motor Vehicles: ₹178.36 crore in Challan Recovery Pending >1 Year (65.67 Per cent of Outstanding); ₹284.38 crore Recurring Vehicle Tax Unpaid >1 Year (23,066 Vehicles); Old Vehicles Issued AITP Against Rules; Fitness to Tax Defaulters (2019-24)
overview: CAG Report No. 1 of 2026 (Gujarat Compliance Audit, Chapter II) found systematic failures in motor vehicle tax and enforcement: (1) E-Challan recovery -- 19.01 lakh challans worth ₹878.77 crore were issued during April 2019 to March 2024, of which only 14.04 lakh (₹607.18 crore) were paid; ₹271.59 crore remained unpaid, of which ₹178.36 crore (65.67 per cent) was pending for more than one year; (2) Vehicle tax default -- 23,066 vehicles at nine selected RTOs/ARTOs had tax of ₹284.38 crore pending recovery for more than one year despite prolonged default; (3) Old vehicles given AITP against rules -- 158 vehicles older than the maximum age limit received All India Tourist Permits, posing road safety hazards; (4) Fitness certificates issued to tax defaulters; (5) Short levy of fees of ₹41.87 lakh due to delayed update of revised fee schedule in VAHAN portal.

stats.label: E-Challan outstanding recovery (pending >1 year)
stats.value: ₹178.36 crore -- 65.67 per cent of ₹271.59 crore total unpaid challans

source.quote: As per e-Challan portal, during the period from April 2019 to March 2024, total 19.01 lakh challans amounting to Rs. 878.77 crore were issued, of which 14.04 lakh challans amounting to Rs. 607.18 crore were paid. Out of the total outstanding amount of Rs. 271.59 crore, an amount of Rs. 178.36 crore was pending for more than one year which constitutes 65.67 per cent of total unpaid amount

stats.label: Vehicle tax default pending >1 year (selected RTOs)
stats.value: ₹284.38 crore (23,066 vehicles at 9 RTOs/ARTOs) -- no RRC proceedings initiated

source.quote: 23,066 vehicles where tax of Rs. 284.38 crore was pending for recovery for more than one year. In spite of the prolonged default

stats.label: Old vehicles issued AITP against age limit rules
stats.value: 158 vehicles older than 8/9-year maximum age limit given All India Tourist Permits

source.quote: before 01 May 2023 AITPs were issued to 158 vehicles older than eight/nine years... The issue of permits to old vehicles was not only against the rules but also posed road safety hazard

keyFindings.text: Two-thirds (65.67 per cent) of outstanding challan recovery in Gujarat has been pending for more than one year -- meaning enforcement action was issued but revenue was not collected. A challan that is issued but unpaid for over a year represents a complete breakdown of the enforcement loop: the violation was detected, recorded, and notified, but the money was never recovered. The 19.01 lakh challans (Rs. 878.77 crore) issued over 5 years with Rs. 271.59 crore unpaid (31 per cent collection failure) means nearly one in three challans is effectively unenforceable in practice.

source.quote: total 19.01 lakh challans amounting to Rs. 878.77 crore were issued... Rs. 271.59 crore, an amount of Rs. 178.36 crore was pending for more than one year

keyFindings.text: Issuing fitness certificates to vehicles that are tax defaulters creates a perverse incentive structure: a vehicle owner who owes Rs. 284.38 crore in collective tax (23,066 vehicles) can keep their vehicle on the road with a valid fitness certificate despite non-payment. The fitness certificate is the gatekeeping mechanism that should deny roadworthiness certification to non-compliant vehicles; when RTOs issue fitness certificates without checking tax payment status, the enforcement system's choke point is bypassed. This is not an isolated error but a systemic oversight failure.

source.quote: 23,066 vehicles where tax of Rs. 284.38 crore was pending for recovery for more than one year. In spite of the prolonged default

recommendations: Commissioner of Transport, Gujarat should configure VAHAN to block fitness certificate renewal for any vehicle with tax outstanding for more than 90 days -- the link between tax compliance and fitness certificate is the most effective enforcement choke point; RRC (Revenue Recovery Certificate) proceedings for all 23,066 tax-defaulting vehicles should be initiated within 60 days with a monthly progress report to the Transport Secretary.

The e-challan system should implement an automatic escalation to RRC after 60 days of unpaid challan -- the ₹178.36 crore pending for more than one year shows the current soft-follow-up mechanism fails; challans that are unpaid after 60 days must be automatically converted into revenue recovery demands with the same legal force as tax arrears, removing the option for indefinite non-payment without consequence.

ministry: Finance Department / Tribal Affairs / Multiple Departments, Government of Assam
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 -- Chapter III Financial Reporting
title: Financial Reporting -- Assam: ₹508.88 crore NPS Contribution Shortfall; ₹20,736.09 crore UCs (6,545 Outstanding); ₹1,050.73 crore Under Minor Head 800 Despite Specific Heads; Tribal Affairs Inflated UCs; Contingency Fund ₹6,050.04 crore Withdrawn (FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 2 of 2026 (Assam SFAR, Chapter III) found multiple financial reporting and compliance failures: (1) NPS Shortfall -- Assam short-contributed ₹508.88 crore to the National Pension System; as of 1 April 2024, ₹318.65 crore remained in Public Account instead of being transferred to NPS, on which ₹17.05 crore interest was payable in FY 2024-25; (2) Outstanding UCs -- 6,545 UCs aggregating ₹20,736.09 crore due up to 31 March 2025 were not submitted; (3) Tribal Affairs submitted inflated UCs -- showing utilisation in excess of actual expenditure under two heads; (4) Minor Head 800 overuse -- ₹1,050.73 crore under 9 Major Heads booked under MH-800 despite specific minor heads being available; total ₹15,195.07 crore under MH-800 (out of ₹1,43,330 crore total expenditure); (5) Contingency Fund extended to ₹6,000 crore (from ₹2,000 crore), with ₹6,050.04 crore withdrawn, of which ₹691.82 crore (11.44 per cent) was used for committed expenditure (salary/wages).

keyFindings.text: Rs. 508.88 crore in NPS contributions that the Assam government deducted from employees' salaries but did not transfer to the National Pension System represents a breach of the state's fiduciary duty to government employees. The employee already bore the deduction from salary; the government holding the employer and employee contributions in the Public Account instead of investing them in NPS means the retirement corpus of Assam government employees has not grown at market rates for the duration of the delay. Rs. 318.65 crore sitting in Public Account as of April 2024 was earning government account rates instead of the NPS fund returns that employees are entitled to.

source.quote: The State Government short contributed Rs. 508.88 crore to National Pension System... As on 01 April 2024, an amount of Rs. 318.65 crore remained in the Public Account on which interest of Rs. 17.05 crore was payable

keyFindings.text: Tribal Affairs (Plain) submitting inflated UCs -- showing more utilisation than actually incurred -- is a qualitatively different problem from merely not submitting UCs. Non-submission creates an accountability gap; inflated submission is an active misrepresentation to the sanctioning authority. Given that Tribal Affairs received Rs. 1,584.52 crore from Autonomous/Development Councils over 2020-21 to 2024-25, and annual accounts of District Councils have not been audited, the inflated UC submission prevents detection of actual vs. reported utilisation -- a precondition for misappropriation.

source.quote: Tribal Affairs (Plain) submitted UCs showing utilisation of funds in excess of the actual utilisation under two Heads of Account

recommendations: Assam Finance Department must remit the entire ₹318.65 crore of NPS contributions sitting in Public Account to the NPS Trust within 30 days and establish an automated monthly sweep -- every rupee of NPS employer + employee contribution deducted must be transferred to NSDL/PFRDA within 7 working days of payroll processing; the ₹17.05 crore interest payable must be separately charged to the Finance Department as a penalty, not buried in general accounts.

Tribal Affairs (Plain) must be required to resubmit corrected UCs for the two inflated submissions, with detailed expenditure statements reconciled to the Financial Accounts, and the matter should be referred to the Assam Vigilance Commission for investigation into why utilisation was overstated -- submitting inflated UCs to avoid triggering UC-non-submission consequences is a possible fraud and must be treated as such, not as a routine accounting correction.

ministry: Finance Department / Multiple Departments, Government of Assam
title: Appropriation Audit -- Assam: ₹18,438.29 crore Savings Not Surrendered (99.37 Per cent of Savings); ₹329.95 crore Misclassification (Grants-in-Aid as Capital); 33.61 Per cent of Expenditure in Last Quarter; Real Capex ₹26,074.25 crore Not ₹26,404.20 crore (FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 2 of 2026 (Assam SFAR, Para 2.5.5 and 2.5.6) found: (1) Non-surrender -- of total savings of ₹23,126.06 crore, only ₹145.31 crore (0.63 per cent) was surrendered; ₹18,438.29 crore under 31 Grants and 1 Appropriation was not surrendered at all; even Tribal Affairs (Grant No. 38 with ₹145.06 crore savings and Grant No. 51 with ₹141.28 crore savings) surrendered virtually nothing (₹0.03 crore and ₹0 respectively); (2) Misclassification -- ₹329.95 crore misclassified, of which Grants-in-Aid of ₹30.96 crore was booked under Capital section (down from ₹5,640.47 crore in 2020-21, a reduction), office expenses ₹40.02 crore under Capital, minor works ₹22.24 crore under Capital; (3) Actual capex after audit = ₹26,074.25 crore (not ₹26,404.20 crore); (4) March rush -- 33.61 per cent of total expenditure incurred in Q4; in 13 sub-heads ₹616.14 crore (75.13 per cent of ₹820.13 crore) spent entirely in March.

stats.value: ₹329.95 crore total misclassification; real capex = ₹26,074.25 crore

keyFindings.text: Rs. 18,438.29 crore unsurrendered -- 99.37 per cent of savings -- in Assam in FY 2024-25 means that a quantum equivalent to 12.5 per cent of the state's total annual budget (Rs. 1,47,855 crore in liabilities) was sitting unused in grant heads but was not returned to the Finance Department. The state borrowed Rs. 30,673.01 crore in FY 2024-25 to fund its fiscal deficit -- if even a fraction of the Rs. 18,438 crore unsurrendered savings had been surrendered timely, the borrowing requirement could have been reduced. Tribal Affairs, with Rs. 286 crore in combined savings under two grants, surrendered Rs. 0.03 crore -- a non-compliance so total it can only reflect institutional indifference to the surrender rule.

source.quote: savings (more than Rs. 100 crore) under 31 Grants and one Appropriation amounting to Rs. 18,438.29 crore were not surrendered at all... only 0.63 per cent (amounting to Rs. 145.31 crore) of the overall savings of Rs. 23,126.06 crore were surrendered

keyFindings.text: The long-term trend of Grants-in-Aid booked as Capital shows a partial improvement: GIA misclassified under capital dropped from Rs. 5,640.47 crore in FY 2020-21 to Rs. 30.96 crore in FY 2024-25 -- an 8-year reduction that CAG acknowledges. But the residual Rs. 329.95 crore in other misclassifications (office expenses, minor works, maintenance booked as capital) suggests the classification discipline has not fully embedded. Year-end rush spending with 75.13 per cent of certain heads spent in March is a parallel pattern -- the two together (late spending, misclassification) are common indicators that spending is being managed against optics rather than programme delivery.

source.quote: there was an overall misclassification of Rs. 329.95 crore... Grants-in-Aid of Rs. 30.96 crore were booked under Capital Section instead of Revenue... from Rs. 5,640.47 crore in 2020-21 to Rs. 30.96 crore in 2024-25

recommendations: Finance Department of Assam should implement a quarterly savings forecast system -- each department should submit a projected savings/expenditure statement by 31 December of the fiscal year, enabling Finance to compute likely year-end surplus and adjust borrowings or reallocate funds before the surrender deadline; the 0.63 per cent surrender rate is not a capacity problem but an incentive problem -- departments must face consequences for non-surrender.

The 33.61 per cent Q4 expenditure concentration must be reduced by introducing a Q3 expenditure floor -- any department with less than 20 per cent of annual budget spent by end of December should be required to explain to the Finance Secretary or face a proportionate withholding of Q4 release, forcing earlier programme execution rather than last-minute payment bunching.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Assam
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 -- Chapter I, Debt Analysis
title: State Finances -- Assam: Internal Debt Up 90.58 Per cent in 5 Years (₹1,27,718 crore); Fiscal Deficit Widened 36.80 Per cent to ₹28,529.52 crore (4.43 Per cent of GSDP); Off-Budget Borrowings Rose to ₹2,639.20 crore; Total Liabilities ₹1,47,855.85 crore (FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 2 of 2026 (Assam SFAR, Chapter I) found significant debt escalation: (1) Internal debt grew 90.58 per cent in five years, from ₹67,014.07 crore in FY 2020-21 to ₹1,27,718.02 crore in FY 2024-25 -- nearly doubling; (2) Total outstanding liabilities rose 18.88 per cent to ₹1,47,855.85 crore in FY 2024-25 (up from ₹1,24,376.09 crore in FY 2023-24); (3) Fiscal deficit widened 36.80 per cent from ₹20,854.69 crore to ₹28,529.52 crore (4.43 per cent of GSDP), breaching FRBM targets; (4) Off-budget borrowings rose from ₹2,193.13 crore to ₹2,639.20 crore; (5) Of FY 2024-25 total borrowings (₹30,673.01 crore), ₹7,193.25 crore (23.45 per cent) was used to repay earlier borrowings (rollover pattern); (6) Post-audit, revenue deficit was revised up to ₹3,090.85 crore (from reported ₹3,000.05 crore) due to misclassification of ₹329.95 crore.

source.quote: The fiscal deficit of the State widened from Rs. 20,854.69 crore in 2023-24 to Rs. 28,529.52 crore in 2024-25, reflecting an increase of 36.80 per cent
outstanding Off-budget borrowings also rose from last year's Rs. 2,193.13 crore to Rs. 2,639.20 crore this year, indicating continued use of contingent financing
