stats.value: ₹1,47,855.85 crore -- 18.88 per cent increase from ₹1,24,376.09 crore

source.quote: outstanding total liabilities 18.88 per cent--from Rs. 1,24,376.09 crore in 2023-24 to Rs. 1,47,855.85 crore

stats.label: FY 2024-25 borrowings used to repay earlier debt (rollover)
stats.value: ₹7,193.25 crore of ₹30,673.01 crore total borrowings (23.45 per cent) for debt repayment

source.quote: Rs. 7,193.25 crore (23.45 per cent) was utilised for repayment of earlier borrowings, Rs. 26,404.20 crore (86.08 per cent) was applied towards capital expenditure

keyFindings.text: Assam's internal debt nearly doubled in five years (90.58 per cent growth) while GSDP grew at 18 per cent CAGR -- meaning debt grew five times faster than the economy. Total liabilities of Rs. 1,47,855.85 crore against GSDP of Rs. 6,43,667 crore implies a debt-to-GSDP ratio of approximately 22.97 per cent for internal debt alone, with total liabilities at 22.97+ per cent. When a fiscal deficit of 4.43 per cent of GSDP is added -- which FRBM rules typically cap at 3-3.5 per cent -- the trajectory is structurally unsustainable without either rapid GSDP growth or significant fiscal consolidation.

source.quote: Internal debt of the State Government increased by Rs. 60,703.95 crore (90.58 per cent) from Rs. 67,014.07 crore in 2020-21 to Rs. 1,27,718.02 crore in 2024-25

keyFindings.text: Off-budget borrowings of Rs. 2,639.20 crore are separately concerning because they are not captured in the fiscal deficit figure reported by the state. CAG explicitly notes their "continued use of contingent financing." These borrowings -- typically taken through state-owned entities -- create debt obligations that will eventually come back to the state budget as either equity infusions, guarantees called, or loan repayments. The true fiscal deficit, including off-budget obligations, is higher than the reported 4.43 per cent. Cash balance discrepancy of Rs. 247.16 crore between state accounts and RBI adds another layer of concern about financial reporting accuracy.

source.quote: outstanding Off-budget borrowings also rose from last year's Rs. 2,193.13 crore to Rs. 2,639.20 crore this year, indicating continued use of contingent financing

recommendations: Assam Finance Department must publish a consolidated debt disclosure that includes off-budget borrowings alongside on-budget public debt -- the FRBM Act fiscal deficit ceiling of 3.50 per cent of GSDP is meaningless as a fiscal discipline tool if it excludes ₹2,639 crore of off-budget obligations; the legislature should amend the Assam Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act to include off-budget borrowings within the defined fiscal deficit.

The state should set a 5-year internal debt reduction path targeting debt-to-GSDP ratio below 20 per cent by FY 2029-30, with annual milestones -- the 90.58 per cent internal debt growth in 5 years cannot continue at the same rate or the interest-to-revenue ratio will crowd out development spending entirely; the first step is publishing the plan so the PAC can hold the government accountable for adherence.

ministry: Gujarat State Tax Department / Transport Department, Government of Gujarat
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2026 (Compliance Audit -- Civil, Period Ended March 2024)
title: Compliance Audit -- Gujarat: ₹2,606.62 crore GST Deviations (291 Cases); 63 of 65 Taxpayers Refused to Produce Records (₹1,234.71 crore Risk Unexamined); 1,91,977 Vehicles Without State Permit; ₹88.58 crore Renewal Fees Not Recovered
overview: CAG Report No. 1 of 2026 (Gujarat Compliance Audit for period ended March 2024) covers two Subject Specific Compliance Audits: (1) GST Oversight (Phase II) -- out of 65 high-risk taxpayers selected for detailed audit, 63 (96.9 per cent) failed to produce granular records to the department, representing ₹1,234.71 crore in unexamined risk exposure; in the remaining cases, deviations of ₹2,606.62 crore were found in 291 cases across ITC mismatches, undischarged tax liability, e-Way Bill mismatch; (2) Motor Vehicles (Tax and Permit) -- 1,91,977 new vehicles were issued without any State permit as of March 2024; permits had delays of 31 to 1,808 days in issuance (4,839 permits delayed >500 days); 98,619 vehicles had expired permits with neither owner renewal nor RTO action; renewal registration certificate fees of ₹88.58 crore had not been recovered; additionally, certain taxpayers declared taxable turnover of ₹0.03 crore in returns while their financial statements showed ₹137.53 crore (a ₹137.50 crore mismatch).

source.quote: There were delays ranging between 31 days to 1,808 days in issuance of Contract Carriage Permits, and Goods Carriage Permits. These included 4,839 permits where delay was more than 500 days

keyFindings.text: GST self-assessment works only if the tax authority can verify compliance when returns raise red flags. In Gujarat, 63 of the 65 highest-risk taxpayers selected for detailed audit refused to produce their records to the department -- an effective non-cooperation rate of 96.9 per cent among the audit sample. This means that Rs. 1,234.71 crore of identified high-risk exposure went unexamined because the department has no effective enforcement mechanism to compel record production. The fact that recovery of only Rs. 1.50 lakh was made in the 291 deviation cases (against Rs. 2,606.62 crore in deviations) confirms that the audit finding translates into virtually zero actual tax recovery.

source.quote: Out of 65 taxpayers selected for detailed audit, in 63 cases the granular records of the taxpayers were not forthcoming... potential risk exposure of Rs. 1,234.71 crore... 291 cases turned out to be deviations, with a revenue implication of Rs. 2,606.62 crore

keyFindings.text: 1,91,977 vehicles on Gujarat's roads without State permits -- combined with 98,619 vehicles with expired permits that neither owners renewed nor RTOs acted on -- means that roughly 2.9 lakh commercial vehicles are operating in a regulatory grey zone. These vehicles likely lack insurance cover, fitness certificates, and pollution control compliance that the permit process enforces. The Rs. 88.58 crore in uncollected renewal fees is the revenue consequence; the safety and consumer-protection consequence is a fleet of commercial transport vehicles whose roadworthiness has never been assessed or re-assessed.

source.quote: 1,91,977 new vehicles were not issued any State permit... delays ranging between 31 days to 1,808 days... 4,839 permits where delay was more than 500 days... renewal fees of Rs. 88.58 crore (as of March 2024)

recommendations: Gujarat State Tax Department must invoke compulsory record production under Section 71 of the GGST Act for all 63 taxpayers who refused to provide records -- failure to produce records to an authorised officer is itself a violation under the Act and cannot be treated as a scope limitation that closes the audit; the department should initiate proceedings against these 63 taxpayers and recover the ₹1,234.71 crore risk exposure through best-judgment assessment where records are withheld.

The Gujarat Transport Department should conduct a one-time clearing exercise for the 1,91,977 un-permitted vehicles: each RTO should issue show-cause notices within 30 days and revoke registrations of vehicles that fail to obtain permits within 90 days -- the 1,808-day maximum permit delay (nearly 5 years) shows that the current system has no escalation mechanism; vehicles operating for years without permits must be brought into compliance or de-registered.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Assam
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 -- State Finances Audit Report FY 2024-25
title: State Finances -- Assam: Finance Commission Grants Collapsed 75.8 Per cent (₹5,599 crore to ₹1,355 crore); Revenue Receipts Fell to 15.06 Per cent of GSDP (from 19.10 per cent); Fiscal Deficit ₹28,529.52 crore; Off-Budget Borrowings Growing (FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 2 of 2026 (Assam State Finances Audit Report FY 2024-25) found significant fiscal deterioration: (1) Finance Commission Grants collapsed from ₹5,599.23 crore in FY 2023-24 to ₹1,355.73 crore in FY 2024-25 -- a 75.8 per cent drop -- substantially constraining state finances; (2) Revenue receipts as a percentage of GSDP declined from 19.10 per cent in FY 2020-21 to 15.06 per cent in FY 2024-25, a 4-percentage-point weakening in the state's revenue effort; (3) Fiscal Deficit stood at ₹28,529.52 crore in FY 2024-25; (4) Committed expenditure and subsidies absorbed 64.93 per cent of revenue spending; (5) Off-budget borrowings were growing and their impact was identified by CAG as a concern for transparency; (6) Cash balance discrepancy of ₹247.16 crore between state accounts (₹223.00 crore) and RBI (₹24.16 crore); (7) Own Tax Revenue ₹30,052.36 crore was ₹4,006 crore (11.99 per cent) below Budget Estimate; (8) Excess expenditure of ₹604.40 crore requires legislative regularisation.

keyFindings.text: The 75.8 per cent collapse in Finance Commission grants -- from Rs. 5,599 crore to Rs. 1,355 crore -- in a single year is a fiscal shock for a state that is structurally dependent on central transfers. Assam's own tax revenue is only 15.06 per cent of GSDP and declining as a share of the economy; the state covers one-third of its expenses from GoI grants. When FC grants fall by Rs. 4,243 crore in one year while the state's own revenue misses target by Rs. 4,006 crore, the combined fiscal squeeze is Rs. 8,249 crore -- roughly equivalent to Assam's entire health expenditure for the year (Rs. 6,399.23 crore).

source.quote: Commission Grants, which dropped sharply from Rs. 5,599.23 crore to Rs. 1,355.73 crore

keyFindings.text: Revenue receipts declining from 19.10 per cent to 15.06 per cent of GSDP over five years, while GSDP itself grew at 18 per cent CAGR from Rs. 3,39,803 crore to Rs. 6,43,667 crore, means the state is capturing a shrinking share of a fast-growing economy. CAG explicitly notes this as "a weakening revenue effort." Combined with growing off-budget borrowings and committed expenditure at 64.93 per cent of revenue spending, Assam is running a fiscal structure where the expenditure base is increasingly inflexible while the revenue base is increasingly inadequate.

source.quote: declining trend of revenue receipts as a percentage of GSDP--from 19.10 per cent in 2020-21 to 15.06 per cent in 2024-25--indicates a weakening revenue effort

recommendations: Assam Finance Department should publish a medium-term fiscal strategy explicitly modelling the reduction in Finance Commission grants over the remaining FC-XVI award period, with specific revenue augmentation targets for SGST, excise, and stamps -- the state cannot plan spending without acknowledging that FC grants are structurally lower than they were in 2023-24, and that the ₹4,006 crore own tax revenue miss is a baseline risk.

Off-budget borrowings in Assam should be disclosed in a separately published annual statement -- CAG has flagged their growing scale as a transparency concern; these borrowings affect the true fiscal deficit and debt-to-GSDP ratio, and the legislature cannot perform meaningful financial oversight without knowing their full extent.

ministry: Finance Department / Multiple Departments, Government of West Bengal
title: Financial Reporting -- West Bengal: Cess Proceeds Not Transferred to Reserve Fund; ₹535.59 crore Parked in PD Accounts (Extent of Overstatement Not Determinable); ₹26,876.61 crore Spent Without Budget Provision (FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 2 of 2026 (West Bengal SFAR, Para 3.2 and 3.7) found three related financial management concerns: (1) Cess proceeds -- certain cess revenues collected by the state were not transferred to their designated Reserve Funds; (2) PD Account parking -- ₹535.59 crore was transferred from the Consolidated Fund to Personal Deposit (PD) accounts during FY 2024-25; since PD accounts show only cumulative balances, the extent to which expenditure from the Consolidated Fund is overstated (by amounts sitting unused in PD accounts) could not be determined by audit; amounts exceeding 2 years in PD accounts were also identified; (3) Budget-less spending -- the state government expended ₹26,876.61 crore without any budget provision or re-appropriation order, constituting spending outside the legislative financial framework. Additionally, the Contingency Fund advance of ₹26.95 crore (11 departments, 21 schemes) had ₹4.71 crore unrecouped at year-end.

However, the quantum of funds remaining unutilised in these PD accounts at the end of the year... was not discernible, as the PD accounts only depicted cumulative balances. keyFindings.text: Rs. 26,876.61 crore spent without any budget provision -- not even through a re-appropriation order -- means that a sum larger than West Bengal's entire capital expenditure (Rs. 21,622 crore) was spent in FY 2024-25 outside the legislative appropriation framework. This is not a supplementary grant situation (which at least has legislative sanction) -- it is executive spending that Parliament never authorised. Combined with Rs. 70,750 crore of un-regularised excess expenditure, the picture is of a state whose spending routinely exceeds or bypasses what the legislature has approved.

source.quote: Government expended Rs. 26,876.61 crore, without any provision in the

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 535.59 crore transferred to PD accounts creates an audit blind spot: once money moves from the Consolidated Fund to a PD account, the Finance Accounts show it as "expenditure" even though it may still be sitting unspent. Since PD accounts only show cumulative balances (not the FY 2024-25 inflow and outflow separately), neither audit nor legislature can determine how much of that Rs. 535.59 crore actually reached its intended purpose. PD account parking is a well-documented technique for inflating expenditure figures while retaining control of the funds.

source.quote: an amount of Rs. 535.59 crore was transferred from the Consolidated Fund of the State to PD Accounts... the extent of overstatement of expenditure from the Consolidated Fund, if any, could not be determined

recommendations: The West Bengal Finance Department should configure IFMS to track PD account sub-balances by source transaction -- every transfer from the Consolidated Fund to a PD account should be linked to a specific scheme, so that at year-end the unspent balance can be identified precisely and either returned to the Consolidated Fund or correctly reported as outstanding in the Finance Accounts.

Budget-less spending of ₹26,876.61 crore must be explained transaction by transaction in the next Excess Grant presented to the legislature -- the state cannot normalise the practice of spending tens of thousands of crore outside approved appropriations; each such transaction should be investigated and responsible officers held accountable for bypassing the appropriation process.

ministry: Finance Department / Multiple Departments, Government of West Bengal
title: Financial Reporting -- West Bengal: ₹707.55 crore Expenditure (4,976 Cases) and ₹1,104.80 crore Receipts Under "Other Expenditure" Minor Head 800 Despite Specific Minor Heads Existing; Total ₹2,75,048.44 crore Under MH-800 in Accounts (FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 2 of 2026 (West Bengal SFAR, Para 3.8) found that despite the availability of appropriate Minor Heads, West Bengal classified ₹707.55 crore of expenditure under 4,976 cases across 27 Major Heads as Minor Head-800 (Other Expenditure), and ₹1,104.80 crore of receipts under 47 Major Heads as Minor Head-800 (Other Receipts). Total expenditure classified under Minor Head-800 in WB accounts reached ₹2,75,048.44 crore in FY 2024-25, of which the ₹707.55 crore represents identifiable misclassifications where specific Minor Heads did exist and should have been used. Minor Head 800 is an accounting catch-all that is supposed to be used only when no specific minor head exists for a transaction; using it as a default prevents meaningful analysis of what the government spent money on and makes it impossible to track spending by specific activity or scheme.

stats.label: Expenditure misclassified under Minor Head 800 despite specific heads available

stats.label: Receipts misclassified under Minor Head 800
stats.value: ₹1,104.80 crore (0.52 per cent of total revenue) under 47 Major Heads

source.quote: in case of receipts, Rs. 1,104.80 crore under 47 Major Heads of Account, constituting 0.52 per cent of the total Revenue (Rs. 2,13,699.56 crore)

keyFindings.text: Rs. 2,75,048.44 crore -- more than the entire state's annual budget provision of Rs. 3,90,638 crore -- classified under Minor Head 800 (Other Expenditure) makes West Bengal's Finance Accounts essentially unreadable at the minor-head level. Minor Head 800 is supposed to be the last resort classification when no specific head exists; instead it has become the default for the vast majority of state expenditure. This prevents legislators, auditors, and citizens from understanding what the government actually spent money on -- only that it was spent under "other expenditure" within each major head.

source.quote: (Rs. 2,75,048.44 crore) was classified under the Minor Head-800-Other Expenditure in the accounts

keyFindings.text: The 4,976 specific cases where Rs. 707.55 crore was booked under Minor Head 800 despite specific minor heads being available are directly traceable misclassifications -- not edge cases. These represent transactions where the accounting officer knew (or should have known) the correct minor head and chose the catch-all instead. At Rs. 1,104.80 crore on the receipts side under 47 major heads, the same pattern holds for revenue collections. Taken together, Rs. 1,812.35 crore in specifically identifiable misclassifications adds to the fiscal picture opacity in an already complex state budget.

source.quote: Rs. 707.55 crore in 4976 cases under 27 Major Heads was classified under Minor Head-800-Other Expenditure... despite availability of appropriate Minor Heads... Rs. 1,104.80 crore under 47 Major Heads of Account

recommendations: The West Bengal Accountant General should work with IFMS to configure the payment portal to reject any transaction coded to Minor Head 800 under Major Heads where specific minor heads exist -- the list of 27 Major Heads with ₹707.55 crore misclassification provides a starting point for which heads need enforced minor-head coding at source rather than after-the-fact correction.

Finance Department should publish a revised Chart of Accounts circular clarifying that Minor Head 800 is a last-resort classification that requires approval from the departmental Finance Officer -- the current practice of routinely using 800 as a default contributes to the ₹2.75 lakh crore opacity in accounts; transparency in government accounts requires specificity, not aggregate buckets.

ministry: Multiple Departments (Health, Rural Development, Urban Affairs, etc.), Government of West Bengal
title: Budgetary Management -- West Bengal: ₹8,296.51 crore Unspent in SNA Accounts; 17 CSS Schemes Delayed >30 Days in SNA Transfer; ₹3,855.82 crore (289 Sub-heads) Spent Entirely in March; ₹93.89 crore Stranded in Old SNA Accounts (FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 2 of 2026 (West Bengal SFAR, Para 2.6 and 2.7) found two related spending quality problems: (1) Centrally Sponsored Scheme SNA management -- ₹8,296.51 crore was lying unspent in SNA (Single Nodal Agency) bank accounts as of 31 March 2025; 17 schemes under 8 departments had delays beyond 30 days in transferring Central share to SNA accounts (attracting 7 per cent interest liability on the state); only 14 out of 67 CSS schemes had migrated to the new JIT-SPARSH platform; ₹93.89 crore was stranded in old SNA accounts of those 14 migrated schemes that should have been refunded before migration; (2) March rush spending -- ₹3,855.82 crore was spent in March 2025 alone, spread across 289 sub-heads under 42 grants, including 12 sub-heads in 6 grants with 100 per cent of their full-year expenditure booked in a single month (March). Concentrated year-end spending increases the risk of payment without proper delivery verification.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 8,296.51 crore sitting unspent in SNA accounts at year-end is money that the Government of India released for specific schemes like Swachh Bharat, PMGSY, or PMAY -- it did reach the state's designated SNA account, but was not transferred to implementing agencies or spent on the ground. This is a second layer of fund blockage: GoI's transfer reached the state but the state's internal plumbing stopped it there. Citizens who should have received benefits under these schemes did not, while the funds sat idle earning no interest (or below-market interest) in SNA accounts.

source.quote: Rs. 8,296.51 crore were lying unspent in the bank accounts of SNAs as on 31 March 2025

keyFindings.text: 100 per cent of full-year expenditure under 12 sub-heads in 6 grants spent in March -- a single month -- is a spending pattern that makes quality assurance impossible. When a department spends its entire annual allocation in March, it is not implementing a programme over the year; it is making bulk payments at the deadline to avoid lapsing funds. The likelihood that Rs. 3,855.82 crore of March spending produced commensurate outputs is low -- payments at year-end frequently precede physical delivery verification.

source.quote: in six grants, under 12 sub-heads (Rs. 100 crore and above), 100 per cent expenditure... incurred in the month of March 2025

recommendations: West Bengal should set a hard cap of 25 per cent of annual allocation as the maximum allowed in any single month for all non-salary, non-interest heads -- exceptions require Finance Secretary approval with written justification; the current system where 100 per cent of a sub-head's annual allocation can be booked in March has no mechanism to ensure the spending represents genuine delivery.

The ₹93.89 crore stranded in old SNA accounts of migrated JIT-SPARSH CSSs must be refunded to GoI or the new JIT accounts within 30 days -- allowing old SNA accounts to carry unspent CSS balances after the scheme has migrated to a new platform creates duplicate account structures that are outside the audit trail of PFMS, increasing the risk of funds being misused without detection.

ministry: School Education / Panchayats & Rural Development / Health & Family Welfare / Multiple Departments, Government of West Bengal
title: Financial Reporting -- West Bengal: ₹2,56,106 crore Utilisation Certificates Outstanding as of 1 April 2024; School Education, Panchayats & RD, Minority Affairs, Urban Development, Health Among Top 5 Departments (FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 2 of 2026 (West Bengal SFAR, Para 3.4) found that as of 1 April 2024, outstanding Utilisation Certificates (UCs) in West Bengal stood at ₹2,56,106 crore. A UC is the only mechanism by which the state can confirm that grants-in-aid disbursed to schools, hospitals, panchayats, NGOs, and other grantees were actually used for the intended purpose. The five departments with the highest outstanding UCs as of 31 March 2025 were: School Education (largest share), Panchayats & Rural Development, Minority Affairs & Madrasah Education, Urban Development & Municipal Affairs, and Health & Family Welfare. Under WB Treasury Rules Rule 330A, grantees must submit a UC within one year of receiving the grant or before applying for a further grant. The chronic non-submission of UCs, combined with grants continuing to be released to the same grantees without prior-year UCs, means the state has no accountability trail for more than ₹2.5 lakh crore in historical grants.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 2,56,106 crore in outstanding UCs in West Bengal -- against a state GSDP of Rs. 18.15 lakh crore -- means that more than 14 per cent of the state's entire annual GDP worth of grants-in-aid has no confirmed utilisation trail. School Education is the top category: the state is releasing grants to schools, colleges, and universities for which it has no confirmation that the money was spent as intended. The scale makes this a systemic governance failure, not a compliance gap in a few departments. WBTR Rule 330A requires UCs within one year; the Rs. 2.56 lakh crore backlog proves the rule has been structurally ignored for years.

source.quote: As of 1 April 2024, UCs amounting to Rs. 2,56,106 crore were outstanding in the... Rule 330A of the West Bengal Treasury Rules... within one year from the date of receipt of grant

keyFindings.text: The combination of School Education, Panchayats & Rural Development, Health & Family Welfare, and Urban Development & Municipal Affairs as the top UC-delinquent departments means the accountability gap is concentrated precisely in the sectors with the highest direct citizen impact -- schools, village-level schemes, hospitals, and urban infrastructure. When a school receives a grant and does not submit a UC, neither the state government nor CAG knows whether the grant funded the intended construction, equipment, or salaries, or was diverted or simply unspent.

source.quote: Chart 3.1: Outstanding UCs in respect of five major Departments as on 31 March 2025... School Education, Panchayats & Rural Development, Minority Affairs & Madrasah Education, Urban Development & Municipal Affairs, Health & Family Welfare

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must implement a mandatory IFMS block on all grants-in-aid release orders for any grantee with an outstanding UC older than one year -- the WBTR Rule 330A already requires this; the government should enforce it at the payment processing level, not as a post-facto audit observation. PFMS-linked UC tracking with a visible dashboard should be made a public reporting obligation.

The state government should conduct a time-bound UC recovery drive for School Education and Health & Family Welfare departments -- these are the highest-impact sectors where unaccounted grants could represent diverted funds affecting children's education and patient healthcare; each department should set a 3-year timeline to clear its UC backlog with annual targets reported to the Public Accounts Committee.

title: Financial Audit -- West Bengal: 224 Cases of Misappropriation, Loss and Theft Worth ₹411.25 crore Pending Resolution; 39 Misappropriation Cases Pending Over 10 Years; ₹96.53 crore Loss Cases Uninvestigated for Decade+ (FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 2 of 2026 (West Bengal SFAR, Para 3.10) found that as of 31 March 2025, 224 cases of misappropriation, loss, and theft involving ₹411.25 crore were pending initiation or completion of departmental proceedings. Age-profile breakdown of cases pending over 10 years: 39 misappropriation cases (₹3.56 crore), 8 cases of loss (₹96.53 crore), and 17 cases of theft (₹0.29 crore). For 145.02 crore of these cases, departmental and criminal proceedings had been initiated but were still pending -- predominantly in Irrigation & Waterways (16 cases) and Public Works departments. Separately, audit test-checked 8 DDOs (Drawing and Disbursing Officers) and found ₹33.56 crore in advances outstanding in personal deposit accounts with risk of misappropriation; 421 annual accounts were due but pending.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 96.53 crore in loss cases sitting uninvestigated for more than 10 years in West Bengal government is not a legacy problem -- it is a current accountability failure. Every year that passes without departmental action makes recovery more difficult, witnesses less accessible, evidence harder to reconstruct, and personnel harder to hold responsible. Eight loss cases totalling Rs. 96.53 crore have been pending for a decade or more; none has been resolved. The applicable rules (WBFR Rule 39) explicitly require every employee to be held personally responsible for losses through fraud or negligence -- that rule is not being applied.

source.quote: cases pending for more than ten years involved... eight cases of loss (Rs. 96.53 crore)... Rule 39 of WBFR any loss of public money... every Government employee would be held personally responsible for any loss sustained by Government through fraud or negligence

keyFindings.text: The pattern of 224 open misappropriation/loss/theft cases at any given year-end is a signal about the accountability culture of the government, not just about specific bad actors. When departmental proceedings are initiated but remain pending for years -- in Rs. 145.02 crore of cases across Irrigation & Waterways and Public Works -- the implicit message is that the inquiry process is used as a way to formally acknowledge an incident without actually resolving it. This signals to current employees that the consequences of misappropriation are indefinitely deferred.

source.quote: 224 cases of misappropriation, loss, theft, etc., involving Rs. 411.25 crore were pending... involving Rs. 145.02 crore, departmental and criminal proceedings were pending

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must issue a 90-day deadline to all departments to submit a status report on all 224 pending cases -- each case should have a named inquiry officer, a current status (inquiry stage), and a projected resolution date; cases where no inquiry officer exists after 10+ years should be treated as constructive closure of inquiry and referred to the AG (Audit) for reporting to the Public Accounts Committee.

The 8 loss cases pending over 10 years involving ₹96.53 crore should be referred to the Vigilance Commission for independent review of why departmental proceedings have not concluded -- in cases this old, the normal departmental inquiry process has demonstrably failed, and an independent body needs to determine whether there has been a deliberate delay to protect the responsible officials.

ministry: Finance Department / Legislature Secretariat, Government of West Bengal
title: Appropriation Audit -- West Bengal: ₹70,750.54 crore Excess Expenditure Un-regularised; ₹57,263.62 crore Pending from FY 2023-24 and Earlier; ₹13,486.92 crore New Excess in FY 2024-25 Under 7 Grants (Persistent Breach of Article 205)
overview: CAG Report No. 2 of 2026 (West Bengal SFAR, Para 2.5.1) found that as of FY 2024-25, ₹70,750.54 crore of excess expenditure remained un-regularised -- comprising ₹57,263.62 crore from previous years (up to FY 2023-24) and ₹13,486.92 crore from FY 2024-25 itself (incurred under seven grants and one appropriation). Under Article 205 of the Constitution, excess expenditure beyond Parliament-approved grants must be regularised by presenting an Excess Grant to the state legislature. West Bengal has a persistent multi-year backlog of such regularisations. Additionally, excess expenditure exceeding ₹10 crore in each case was noted for multiple years. Separately, additional provision of ₹4,489.31 crore in 16 grants proved unnecessary (expenditure did not utilise the supplementary provision) and ₹5,119.18 crore of supplementary provisions proved excessive.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 70,750.54 crore of un-regularised excess expenditure means West Bengal's legislature has not approved spending of that magnitude -- it was done without constitutional authority. Article 205 requires the government to present an Excess Grant to the legislature; the accumulation of Rs. 57,263.62 crore from previous years shows that this constitutional obligation has been ignored for multiple consecutive years. Un-regularised excess is not a minor procedural gap: it means the legislature's financial control over the executive is effectively non-functional for thousands of crore in actual spending.

source.quote: expenditure of Rs. 70,750.54 crore remained un-regularised indicating excess expenditure of more than Rs. 10 crore in each case during the last five years

keyFindings.text: Rs. 4,489.31 crore in unnecessary supplementary provisions (funds sought but not needed) combined with Rs. 5,119.18 crore in excessive supplementary provisions (funds sought but unable to be spent) in the same year reveals a supplementary demand process that is systematically inaccurate. The government cannot predict its own spending needs within the supplementary window (October-February), which means supplementary grants are being sought on the basis of aspirational rather than evidence-based requirements. These are public funds committed from the Consolidated Fund on the basis of inaccurate projections.

source.quote: provisions of Rs. 4,489.31 crore in 16 grants proved unnecessary... Rs. 5,119.18 crore proved excessive as full amount of this provision could not be utilised

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department must present an Excess Grant to the legislature covering all un-regularised excess expenditure from FY 2020-21 onwards -- the ₹57,263.62 crore prior-year backlog cannot be allowed to grow further; the Public Accounts Committee should be given a year-by-year breakdown with the departments responsible and an explanation for why each excess occurred.

The West Bengal legislature should amend the WBFRBM to require that any supplementary demand for a grant that had actual savings exceeding 10 per cent in the previous year must be accompanied by a written justification from the Administrative Secretary and Finance Secretary countersignature -- the current system allows departments to routinely seek supplementary funds they do not use, inflating the apparent scale of government commitment.

keyFindings.text: Booking Rs. 1,031.84 crore of maintenance and stores expenditure as capital understates revenue expenditure and overstates the state's capital asset creation. This is not a trivial accounting technicality -- West Bengal's capital expenditure trajectory is already alarming (fell 25 per cent to Rs. 21,622 crore); the real figure is Rs. 20,594.56 crore, meaning the collapse was even steeper than the reported numbers show. Policy decisions about whether the state is investing adequately in physical assets are made on the reported capex figure; systematic misclassification corrupts that decision base.

source.quote: Rs. 1,031.84 crore of expenditure of Revenue nature as Capital Expenditure... overstatement of Capital Expenditure... Expenditure, after Audit, for FY 2024-25, was Rs. 20,594.56 crore

keyFindings.text: A 1.09 per cent return on Rs. 22,086 crore of PSU investment -- with no dividend policy enforced until FY 2024-25 -- means the state is subsidising PSU operations at a hidden cost equal to the difference between the return on government securities (typically 7-8 per cent) and 1.09 per cent, on Rs. 22,000+ crore of capital. This implicit subsidy to loss-making or low-dividend PSUs does not appear in the subsidy line of the budget (which showed Rs. 19,444 crore) -- it is carried as foregone return, invisible in the accounts, adding to fiscal stress without any legislative appropriation.

source.quote: return on investment from PSUs was Rs. 240 crore (1.09 per cent of the average investment of Rs. 22,086 crore)... West Bengal had not enforced a dividend policy for its PSUs till 2024-25

recommendations: West Bengal must implement a Finance Department circular requiring all spending units to classify maintenance, stores, and equipment expenditure under the correct revenue object heads before processing payment in IFMS -- the ₹1,031.84 crore misclassification was detectable at transaction level; a pre-payment classification check in the payments portal would prevent it from entering the accounts at all.

The state should issue a formal dividend policy for all state PSUs specifying a minimum annual dividend as a percentage of paid-up capital -- the absence of such a policy for decades has resulted in persistent 1 per cent returns on ₹22,000 crore; PSUs that cannot pay a modest dividend should be referred for restructuring or disinvestment rather than continuing to absorb capital without financial return.

ministry: Finance Department / Multiple Departments, Government of West Bengal
title: Appropriation Audit -- West Bengal: ₹45,072.68 crore Savings Not Surrendered (97.23 Per cent of Total Savings); Only 2.77 Per cent Surrendered; 49 Cases of Persistent Savings >₹100 crore for 3 Consecutive Years (FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 2 of 2026 (West Bengal SFAR, Para 2.5.5) found that in FY 2024-25, West Bengal spent ₹3,19,975.79 crore against a budget of ₹3,90,638.04 crore, producing overall savings of ₹70,662.25 crore (18.09 per cent). However, of these savings, only ₹2,326.98 crore (2.77 per cent) was surrendered, while ₹45,072.68 crore (64 per cent of savings) was not surrendered at all. The balance (₹23,262.59 crore) represents savings that lapsed without surrender. Additionally: (i) ₹11.76 crore (0.51 per cent of surrendered amount) was surrendered on the very last working day of March 2025; (ii) 49 cases under 33 grants had persistent savings exceeding ₹100 crore in each case for three consecutive years (FY 2022-23 to FY 2024-25); (iii) re-appropriation proved injudicious in cases where excess expenditure resulted; (iv) three grants recorded zero expenditure against a total grant of ₹12.29 crore. The non-surrender of savings prevents the Finance Department from reallocating funds to better-performing departments mid-year or reducing market borrowings.

keyFindings.text: Rs. 45,072.68 crore not surrendered -- combined with 18.09 per cent overall savings -- means West Bengal went into the capital and debt markets to borrow (its fiscal deficit was Rs. 61,924 crore) while simultaneously sitting on Rs. 45,072 crore of unspent funds it chose not to return. Every rupee borrowed has interest cost; every rupee not surrendered prevented the Finance Department from reducing borrowings or redirecting spending. The 2.77 per cent surrender rate is functionally close to zero and indicates that the expenditure and surrender cycle is broken at department level.

source.quote: Rs. 45,072.68 crore (Appendix 2.10) were not surrendered at all. Analysis revealed that only 2.77 per cent of the savings were surrendered

keyFindings.text: 49 persistent savings cases under 33 grants for three consecutive years point to systemic over-budgeting rather than one-time implementation delays. When the same grant records Rs. 100+ crore savings every year for three years, the budget provision is no longer a realistic estimate of expected spending -- it is a notional figure. Carrying inflated provisions year after year produces two harms: the government appears to be committing more to a sector than it actually is, and the persistent underspend builds a false baseline for the next year's budget.

source.quote: in 49 cases under 33 grants there was persistent savings exceeding Rs. 100 crore in each case during 2022-23 to 2024-25

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department should mandate that any Department with savings exceeding ₹50 crore as of 31 December of the fiscal year must submit a surrender proposal or an explanation of planned utilisation to the Finance Secretary by 15 January -- the current deadline of 21 February allows too little time for the finance department to act; 0.51 per cent last-day surrenders are proof the current system is ignored.

The 49 persistent-savings cases under 33 grants must be reviewed in the next budget cycle with explicit downward revisions to provisions for those heads -- Parliament's Budget approval is meaningful only if it is based on realistic absorption capacity; grants that have had ₹100+ crore savings for three consecutive years should be provisioned at actual absorption levels, not aspirational ones.

ministry: Panchayat and Rural Development Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh
title: Performance Audit -- MGNREGA Madhya Pradesh: ₹1,217.05 crore Wages and Material Costs Unpaid; ₹54.79 crore (4.7 lakh Transactions) Blocked Due to Aadhaar Mismatch; Only 2 Per cent of Households Got Full 100-Day Employment (2019-24)
overview: CAG Report No. 4 of 2026 (Madhya Pradesh) is a performance audit of MGNREGS for FY 2019-20 to 2023-24. Key findings: (1) ₹1,217.05 crore in wages and material costs had become a pending liability by 31 March 2024, including ₹54.79 crore (4.7 lakh transactions) blocked specifically because beneficiary bank accounts were not mapped to Aadhaar -- meaning workers completed the work and were not paid due to a database linkage failure; (2) Only approximately 2 per cent of households were provided the full 100 days of guaranteed employment; (3) MGNREGA wage rates in MP were consistently lower than prevailing market wages throughout 2019-24, which CAG identifies as a probable cause of low labour participation; (4) ₹1.46 crore was paid on 2,426 duplicate, fake, or incorrect job cards; (5) Persistent discrepancies in fund data between different databases (PFMS vs. MIS); (6) ₹1,703.80 crore was the expenditure figure for 2021-22, indicating scale; (7) Mandatory registers were not maintained at Gram Panchayat level; (8) Staff shortages at all four levels (State, District, Block, GP).

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 54.79 crore Aadhaar-blocked wage liability (4.7 lakh transactions) represents some of the most egregious MGNREGA failures: workers did the physical work, the government acknowledged the work was done, but did not pay because the department failed to complete a database task (Aadhaar seeding). The government is simultaneously denying the legal entitlement (full payment for completed work) and penalising the worker for an administrative failure that is entirely within the government's control to fix. At an average daily wage of ~Rs. 221 in MP, 4.7 lakh transactions represents roughly 2.5 lakh person-days of completed unpaid work.

source.quote: a liability of Rs. 54.79 crore (4.7 lakh transactions) towards wages, which was attributable to the non-mapping of beneficiary accounts with Aadhaar

keyFindings.text: Wage rates consistently below market rates in MP for five consecutive years is not a data anomaly -- it is a structural feature that makes MGNREGA an unattractive option for rural workers with any alternatives. CAG identifies this as the probable cause of low labour participation. A guaranteed employment scheme whose wage is set below the market rate creates a self-defeating guarantee: the workers most in need of the guarantee are the ones who cannot afford to take it up. The political cost of raising MGNREGA wages to market rate falls on the Centre (which sets notified wages); the political cost of low participation falls on no one.

source.quote: MGNREGS wage rates were consistently lower than the prevailing wage rates during 2019-24, which is attributed to be the reason for the shortfall

recommendations: All 4.7 lakh Aadhaar-blocked transactions (₹54.79 crore) must be resolved within 90 days through an emergency seeding drive by the MP Department of Panchayat & Rural Development -- no worker who has completed verified MGNREGA work should wait more than one fiscal year for payment due to an Aadhaar linkage failure; after the drive, a monthly dashboard must track blocked transactions so no new backlog accumulates.

The Government of India should commission a state-level market wage survey for MP and compare notified MGNREGA wage rates against those findings, with a commitment to revise the MP MGNREGA wage schedule if it is found to be below market rate for unskilled agricultural labour -- the persistent sub-market wage is the root cause of scheme under-utilisation and cannot be addressed by improving implementation without first addressing the wage gap.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of West Bengal
reportNo: Report No. 2 of 2026 -- State Finances Audit Report FY 2024-25
title: State Finances -- West Bengal: Revenue Deficit ₹39,727 crore; Committed Expenditure + Subsidy = 74 Per cent of Revenue Receipts; Subsidy Spiked 85.61 Per cent; Capital Expenditure Fell 25 Per cent to ₹21,622 crore (FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 2 of 2026 (West Bengal State Finances Audit Report FY 2024-25) found that WB's finances showed deepening structural stress: (1) Revenue Deficit ₹39,727 crore (2.19 per cent of GSDP) despite GSDP growing 9.91 per cent; (2) Fiscal Deficit ₹61,924 crore (3.41 per cent of GSDP) -- within FRBM limit but against a backdrop of revenue deficit financing; (3) Committed expenditure (salary ₹67,937 crore + pension ₹25,859 crore + interest ₹45,406 crore = ₹1,39,202 crore) plus subsidies (₹19,444 crore) together consumed 74 per cent of revenue receipts (₹2,13,700 crore), leaving only 26 per cent for developmental spending; (4) Subsidies jumped 85.61 per cent (₹8,968 crore) -- mainly food PDS (₹5,858 crore), largely due to State-funded free rice distribution; (5) Capital expenditure fell 25 per cent (₹7,341 crore) to ₹21,622 crore (1.19 per cent of GSDP); (6) ₹1,031.84 crore of revenue expenditure was misclassified as capital expenditure; (7) Excess expenditure ₹13,486.92 crore under 7 grants without parliamentary sanction; (8) ₹8,296.51 crore unspent in SNA bank accounts; (9) GoI subsidy share of ₹997.25 crore still receivable from GoI (FY 2020-25).

keyFindings.text: West Bengal's fiscal structure in FY 2024-25 shows the hallmark of a state trapped in a subsidy-salary-interest spiral: 74 per cent of every rupee of revenue goes to committed costs (salary, pension, interest) and subsidies before a single rupee reaches infrastructure or development. When the state also borrows (fiscal deficit Rs. 61,924 crore), those borrowings finance current consumption rather than asset creation -- CAG explicitly notes that "a large portion of revenue expenditure was met from net borrowings adding to future liabilities." The 85.61 per cent subsidy spike (mostly free rice distribution) locked in more future commitments that will prevent fiscal space recovery.

source.quote: committed expenditure (Rs. 1,39,202 crore) coupled with Subsidy expenditure (Rs. 19,444 crore) absorbed nearly 74 per cent... leaving only 26 per cent fiscal space for developmental and capital spending

keyFindings.text: Capital expenditure fell 25 per cent -- Rs. 7,341 crore -- in a single year, to just 1.19 per cent of GSDP. For a state that is 5th largest by population and contains Kolkata (a major urban centre with infrastructure backlogs), a capex of 1.19 per cent of GSDP is inadequate for maintaining, let alone expanding, public assets. The compression of capex while simultaneously growing subsidies by Rs. 8,968 crore reveals the choice being made: current political transfers (food subsidies, salaries) are being funded at the expense of future-serving investments (roads, hospitals, schools).

source.quote: Capital expenditure (Rs. 21,622 crore) during FY 2024-25 constituted only 1.19 per cent the GSDP of the State... it fell by 25 per cent (Rs. 7,341 crore)

recommendations: West Bengal Finance Department should publish a multi-year subsidy rationalisation roadmap -- the 85.61 per cent single-year spike in subsidies (mainly free rice) reflects a discretionary political choice being made without a corresponding fiscal adjustment; the FRBM amendment that set the 3.50 per cent fiscal deficit target must also mandate a revenue deficit elimination timeline as a complement to the deficit ceiling.

The ₹13,486.92 crore excess expenditure under 7 grants must be regularised through Excess Grant in the next Legislative session with detailed explanations -- excess expenditure without parliamentary sanction violates Article 205 of the Constitution; regularisation, not just reporting, must be tracked by the Public Accounts Committee as a mandatory follow-up item.

ministry: Panchayat and Rural Development Department, Government of Chhattisgarh
title: Performance Audit -- MGNREGA Chhattisgarh: 18.26 lakh Households Denied Guaranteed Employment; ₹84.59 crore Statutory Dues Accumulated; 86 Per cent Works Without Gram Sabha Approval; Only ₹7,677 of ₹24.97 crore Compensation Actually Paid (2019-24)
overview: CAG Report No. 3 of 2026 (Chhattisgarh) is a performance audit of MGNREGS covering FY 2019-20 to 2023-24. Key findings: (1) Employment Shortfall -- 152.36 lakh households demanded work; only 134.10 lakh received it, a shortfall of 18.26 lakh households (12 per cent). Of those who did get work, 83 per cent (111.31 lakh) were given less than 100 days -- only 1.23 lakh HHs (0.92 per cent) got the full legally guaranteed 100 days; (2) No unemployment allowance paid -- ₹2.22 crore was budgeted for unemployment allowances across 2019-24 but none was spent; (3) Gram Sabha bypassed -- 86 per cent (10,997 of 12,714) of works in test-checked Gram Panchayats were undertaken without Gram Sabha approval; (4) Compensation for delayed wages nearly entirely unpaid -- out of ₹24.97 crore payable for delayed wages, only ₹7,677 was actually disbursed; 66 to 91 per cent of compensation claims were rejected; (5) Statutory dues accumulated -- ₹29.62 crore employee contributions unpaid (April 2015 to March 2023) leading to ₹84.59 crore total liability including penalty and interest; (6) Only 61 per cent of works completed.

keyFindings.text: MGNREGA's three core guarantees were all broken simultaneously in Chhattisgarh during 2019-24: (i) the right to work guarantee -- 18.26 lakh HHs denied employment; (ii) the 100-day guarantee -- only 0.92 per cent of employed HHs got 100 days; (iii) the unemployment allowance guarantee -- zero paid despite 18.26 lakh eligible HHs and Rs. 2.22 crore budget. A scheme whose entire legal basis rests on three guarantees violated all three at scale for five years while the state's implementing apparatus prepared Labour Budgets "without household surveys" and held only one Gram Sabha meeting per year against the required ten.

source.quote: During 2019-24, 152.36 lakh HHs demanded employment... shortfall of 18.26 lakh (12 per cent)... no unemployment allowances were paid... 111.31 lakh HHs (83 per cent) were provided employment for less than 100 days... 1.23 lakh HHs (0.92 per cent) were provided full 100 days employment

keyFindings.text: The near-total rejection (66-91 per cent) of compensation claims for delayed wage payments -- under a system that should disburse automatically through MIS -- and the disbursement of just Rs. 7,677 against Rs. 24.97 crore owed, represents a systematic denial of a legal entitlement. Workers who were already paid late (the trigger for compensation) were then told via MIS rejection that their delay was due to "natural calamities" or "compensation not applicable." Meanwhile, accumulated statutory dues on employee contributions rose to Rs. 84.59 crore because the state failed to remit contributions for 8 years (April 2015 to March 2023).

source.quote: out of a total payable compensation of Rs. 24.97 crore, only Rs. 7,677 was disbursed... 66 to 91 per cent compensation claims... rejected... Rs. 84.59 crore including penalty and interest

recommendations: Chhattisgarh must automate unemployment allowance payment through MIS -- any job card holder who demanded work and was not provided employment within 15 days must receive a system-generated allowance payment without requiring manual application, as the law requires. The fact that ₹2.22 crore was budgeted and zero was paid for five years proves the manual process does not work.

All 10,997 works executed in test-checked GPs without Gram Sabha approval should be reviewed for asset quality and utilisation -- works without community approval are structurally at risk of being unwanted, poorly maintained, and non-functional. State government should institute a mandatory real-time lock in the MIS that prevents work order generation without a recorded GS resolution.

ministry: Department of Economic Affairs / Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs / Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation, Government of India
title: Appropriation Audit -- Six Grants with Savings Over ₹30,000 crore Each: DEA ₹62,586 crore, Drinking Water ₹51,132 crore, Interest Payments ₹44,570 crore, Transfers to States ₹36,219 crore, HUA ₹32,660 crore, Food ₹30,934 crore (Union Government FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2026 (Para 4.2.2.1-4.2.2.2) found that six Union Government Grants/Appropriations each had savings exceeding ₹30,000 crore in FY 2024-25, together accounting for ₹2,58,103.26 crore (52.54 per cent) of the total ₹4,91,302.81 crore in savings across all 102 grants. keyFindings.text: Jal Jeevan Mission's 66.07 per cent underspend (Rs. 51,132 crore of Rs. 77,395 crore+ unspent) in a programme explicitly committed to providing safe drinking water to every rural household by FY 2024-25 -- the original target year -- represents one of the largest single-scheme delivery failures in the Budget. The savings mean that connection targets, water quality testing, and distribution infrastructure funded in Parliament's approved budget simply did not happen. The government met its commitment to Parliament financially (budget was passed) while failing its commitment to citizens (water connections not delivered).

Jal Jeevan Mission's ₹51,132 crore underspend should be reported to Parliament with a reconciled household-connection target vs. achievement figure -- each crore unspent under this scheme represents specific villages that did not get water connections that were budgeted, and citizens are entitled to know which districts and States drove the shortfall.

ministry: Department of Telecommunications, Government of India
title: Appropriation Audit -- DoT Took ₹23,476.69 crore in Supplementary Grants Despite 3 Consecutive Years of ₹5,000+ crore Savings; FY 2024-25 Final Savings ₹23,245.20 crore (14.99%); ₹11,898.55 crore Not Surrendered (Union Government)
overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2026 (Para 4.2.2.2 and 4.2.2.3) found that the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) ran a persistent savings-while-seeking-supplementary pattern for at least three consecutive years. In FY 2024-25, DoT had savings of ₹23,245.20 crore (14.99 per cent) against its total sanctioned provision -- yet in the same year it sought and received ₹23,476.69 crore in Supplementary Provisions. DoT was also in the persistent savings category for FY 2022-23 to FY 2024-25 with savings exceeding ₹5,000 crore every year (savings in the Transfers to States and DoT grants exceeded ₹10,000 crore each year across all three years). Additionally, ₹11,898.55 crore of DoT savings -- more than ₹10,000 crore -- was not surrendered to the Consolidated Fund at year-end, allowing funds to lapse rather than be available for reallocation. DoT replied that supplementary demand was raised based on RE proposals from DoT units with "proper reasoning," and that ₹3,655 crore under three Capital-Voted sub-heads could not be surrendered.

keyFindings.text: The combination of Rs. 23,476.69 crore in supplementary grants sought and Rs. 23,245.20 crore in final savings in the same year -- while also carrying a three-year track record of Rs. 5,000+ crore persistent savings -- is a textbook case of what CAG calls "injudicious supplementary demand." DoT was, in effect, telling Parliament via its supplementary demand that it needed more money while simultaneously failing to spend what it already had. Rs. 11,898.55 crore was then allowed to lapse rather than surrendered in time for the government to reallocate it to better-absorbing programmes.

source.quote: savings of Rs. 23,245.20 crore (14.99%)... Supplementary provisions of Rs. 23,476.69 crore

keyFindings.text: Rs. 11,898.55 crore not surrendered is the largest single non-surrender in the Union Government's FY 2024-25 appropriation cycle. Timely surrender of savings is constitutionally required -- funds that are not needed must be returned to the Consolidated Fund so Parliament's financial oversight applies to the full budget, not just what Ministries choose to spend or lapse. The Consolidated Fund receives back less, Parliament's ability to redirect resources is curtailed, and the illusion of a higher spending commitment in telecom is maintained in Budget documents.

source.quote: Savings not surrendered in respect of Department of Telecommunications was more than Rs. 10,000 crore, i.e. Rs. 11,898.55 crore

recommendations: Finance Ministry should impose a rule that any Ministry with persistent savings exceeding ₹5,000 crore for two consecutive years is ineligible to seek supplementary grants in the third year without written approval from the Finance Secretary documenting why the structural underspend will not recur -- DoT's pattern of seeking ₹23,476 crore supplementary while sitting on ₹23,245 crore savings must not be possible without explicit scrutiny.

The ₹3,655 crore claimed by DoT as incapable of surrender (Capital-Voted sub-heads) should be examined by the Public Accounts Committee -- if Capital-Voted funds genuinely cannot be used in the fiscal year for which they were sanctioned, the Budget provision for those heads should be reduced, not carried as a permanent overhang that nominally inflates DoT's capital commitment every year.

ministry: Department of Space / IN-SPACe, Government of India
title: Financial Audit -- Department of Space: ₹86.88 crore Satellite Expenditure Booked as Revenue Instead of Capital; ₹40.16 crore IN-SPACe Grants Misclassified; Canteen Expenditure Under Space Technology Head (Union Government FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2026 (Para 3.5.2) found multiple accounting misclassifications in the Department of Space and IN-SPACe grants: (1) ₹86.88 crore spent on "Satellite and Launch Vehicles" was booked under the revenue section when it should have been under the capital section -- satellite hardware is a capital asset; (2) ₹40.16 crore in grants to IN-SPACe (Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre) were booked under the wrong object heads -- ₹24.79 crore under object head 31 (Grants-in-Aid General) and ₹15.37 crore under object head 35 (Grants for creation of Capital Assets) instead of object head 36 (Grants-in-Aid Salaries), because IN-SPACe is a statutory body where contributions should be classified as salary-related grants; (3) ₹9.33 crore of canteen-related expenditure was booked under Minor Head 101 "Space Technology" under Major Head 3402 instead of the correct head; (4) Multiple IT equipment items (firewall management devices, rack module servers, workstations) were booked under "Machinery & Equipment" instead of the correct "ICT Equipment" object head 71.

stats.label: Satellite and Launch Vehicle capital expenditure misbooked as revenue
stats.value: ₹86.88 crore (should be capital section, booked as revenue)

source.quote: Expenditure of Rs. 86.88 crore over Satellite and Launch Vehicles is booked under revenue section, while it should have been booked in capital section. Reply is awaited from DoS

stats.label: IN-SPACe grants misclassified across wrong object heads
stats.value: ₹40.16 crore (₹24.79 crore + ₹15.37 crore booked under wrong heads)

source.quote: funds aggregating to Rs. 5,456.84 crore were booked under heads for release of grants-in-aid to IN-SPACe - Rs. 24.79 crore under revenue section and Rs. 15.37 crore under capital section. IN-SPACe being... booked under object head 31-Grants-in-aid-General and 36-Grants-in-aid-Salaries and Rs. 15.37 crore under object head 35-Grants for creation of Capital Assets

source.quote: Department of Space incorrectly booked Canteen related expenditure of Rs. 9.33 crore in Minor Head 101-Space Technology under Major head 3402 instead

keyFindings.text: Booking Rs. 86.88 crore of satellite and launch vehicle spending as revenue expenditure instead of capital expenditure distorts two key figures simultaneously: (a) it understates capital asset creation by the government, and (b) it overstates revenue expenditure. For a programme like the space department whose capital asset base (satellites, launch infrastructure) is what Parliament should be tracking, misrouting nearly Rs. 87 crore of hardware procurement into the revenue head makes the department appear to be spending more on operations and less on assets than it actually is.

source.quote: Expenditure of Rs. 86.88 crore over Satellite and Launch Vehicles is booked under revenue section, while it should have been booked in capital section

keyFindings.text: IN-SPACe -- the new autonomous body that authorises private space activities in India -- had Rs. 40.16 crore of grants to it misclassified between object heads. Correct classification matters for accountability: object head 36 (Grants-in-Aid Salaries) tracks salary support to statutory bodies separately from general grants (head 31) and capital asset creation (head 35). Mixing these makes it impossible to determine from the accounts what share of IN-SPACe's funding went to salaries vs. operations vs. capital, which is the baseline data needed to assess whether the new regulator is being adequately staffed.

source.quote: funds aggregating... to IN-SPACe - Rs. 24.79 crore under revenue section and Rs. 15.37 crore under capital section... IN-SPACe being... booked under object head 31-Grants-in-aid-General and 36-Grants-in-aid-Salaries

recommendations: Department of Space should implement a transaction-type classification checklist in its internal finance system -- any expenditure tagged with "satellite", "launch vehicle", "spacecraft", or "orbital" keywords should be flagged for mandatory capital-section review before booking, preventing the ₹86.88 crore revenue-misclassification from recurring.

CGA should issue a specific clarification for grants to IN-SPACe and similar new statutory bodies on the correct object head split between salaries (head 36), general operations (head 31), and capital creation (head 35) -- the classification confusion arises from ambiguity in how new-age regulatory bodies fit existing grant-in-aid categories.

ministry: Multiple Ministries / Departments, Government of India
title: Appropriation Audit -- 33,973 Utilisation Certificates Worth ₹54,282.32 crore Outstanding as of 31 March 2025; Oldest Pending Since FY 1985-86; ₹38,287.52 crore from Last 3 Years (Union Government)
overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2026 (Para 4.5) found that as of 31 March 2025, 15 Ministries/Departments had 33,973 Utilisation Certificates (UCs) worth ₹54,282.32 crore outstanding. A Utilisation Certificate is the only mechanism through which the Union Government can confirm that grants-in-aid released to grantee institutions, NGOs, and implementing agencies were actually used for their intended purpose. Without a UC, there is no assurance that the money reached the target beneficiaries. Key metrics: (1) ₹38,287.52 crore (13,926 UCs) is from grants released in the last 3 years (FY 2021-22 to FY 2023-24) -- indicating that current-year grant releases are not being followed up; (2) The oldest outstanding UCs date back to FY 1985-86 -- meaning some grants from 40 years ago have never been confirmed as utilised; (3) Rules require UCs within 12 months and block fresh grants until previous UCs are submitted. These rules are routinely flouted. CAG has raised UC non-submission repeatedly in prior reports and found no systemic improvement.

stats.label: Total outstanding utilisation certificates as of 31 March 2025

source.quote: we noted that 33,973 UCs, aggregating to Rs. 54,282.32 crore, were outstanding as on 31st March 2025, as detailed in Annexure 4.12

stats.label: Recent-year UCs outstanding (FY 2021-22 to FY 2023-24)
stats.value: 13,926 UCs worth ₹38,287.52 crore from the last 3 years

source.quote: Of these, 13,926 UCs amounting to Rs. 38,287.52 crore pertain to the last three years (2021-22 to 2023-24)

stats.label: Oldest outstanding UC
stats.value: FY 1985-86 -- grants from 40 years ago never confirmed utilised

source.quote: The earliest grants for which UCs remained outstanding date back to FY 1985-86. This indicates that the Departments/Ministries were not adequately addressing the issues of outstanding UCs

keyFindings.text: Rs. 54,282.32 crore in unconfirmed grant utilisation means the government has no assurance whether that money reached intended beneficiaries -- schools, hospitals, NGOs, research institutions, local bodies -- or was diverted, spent on ineligible items, or simply sits unspent in grantee accounts. The UC is the last accountability checkpoint between Treasury and actual delivery; 33,973 missing UCs is 33,973 gaps in the audit trail for public funds. The rule that blocks fresh grants until prior-year UCs are submitted exists precisely to prevent this accumulation -- yet 13,926 UCs from the past three years show it is not enforced.

source.quote: 33,973 UCs, aggregating to Rs. 54,282.32 crore, were outstanding as on 31st March 2025... The earliest grants for which UCs remained outstanding date back to FY 1985-86

keyFindings.text: CAG explicitly notes that "the issue of non-submission of UCs has been repeatedly highlighted in previous Audit Reports." Persistent non-enforcement of the UC rule over decades -- to the point where 40-year-old grants remain unconfirmed -- suggests that the oversight gap has been normalised. Ministries that release fresh grants to the same grantees without insisting on prior-year UCs are effectively signalling that the rule has no teeth. Until UC non-submission carries a consequence (grant suspension actually executed, not just threatened), the backlog will continue growing.

source.quote: The issue of non-submission of UCs, which has been repeatedly highlighted in previous Audit Reports

recommendations: Ministry of Finance should hard-code UC compliance into PFMS -- any Ministry attempting to release a grant to a grantee with an overdue UC should face a system block, not a soft warning. The current system allows Ministries to override the rule; that override capability should be removed or require Finance Secretary approval with an audit log.

A one-time resolution campaign for the ₹15,994.80 crore in pre-2021-22 UCs (the difference between ₹54,282.32 crore total and ₹38,287.52 crore recent) should be undertaken -- grants from FY 1985-86 to FY 2020-21 cannot realistically produce UCs 5 to 40 years later and should be referred to the Public Accounts Committee for write-off proceedings with full accountability for the responsible officials.

ministry: Ministry of Finance / Controller General of Accounts (PAO-IDA), Government of India
title: Financial Audit -- CGEGIS Savings Fund Overstated: Ministry of Railways Figures Double-Counted for FY 2022-23 (₹43.99 crore) and FY 2023-24 (₹43.66 crore); ₹134.72 crore Net Receipts Discrepancy Over Audit Period (Union Government)
overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2026 (Para 3.1.1.3) found that PAO-IDA (the accounting unit for CGEGIS -- the Central Government Employees Group Insurance Scheme) double-counted Ministry of Railways CGEGIS contribution figures for two consecutive financial years. From FY 2022-23, the CGDA (Controller of Defence Accounts) started consolidating CGEGIS data for all Ministries including Railways and forwarding it to PAO-IDA. However, PAO-IDA continued receiving separate figures from the Ministry of Railways directly, without stopping the duplicate feed. For FY 2022-23 and FY 2023-24, Railways data was included twice -- ₹43.99 crore and ₹43.66 crore respectively -- resulting in excess crediting of CGEGIS interest on the Savings Fund and overstatement of Savings Fund and Insurance Fund balances for both years. Separately, there was a net difference of ₹134.72 crore in receipts and ₹321.23 crore in payments between CGEGIS figures in the UGFA and those maintained by PAO-IDA over the audit period. Additionally, interest calculations were based on provisional figures rather than final figures, causing ₹9.10 crore of excess interest to be reversed via a Journal Entry pertaining to 2016-17 to 2022-23.

keyFindings.text: The CGEGIS Savings Fund -- into which government employees contribute a share of their salary every month against a guaranteed lump-sum payout on retirement -- had its balance overstated for two years because no one on either side of the data handoff (CGDA or PAO-IDA) verified that the Ministry of Railways data was being submitted once, not twice. CGEGIS is a defined-benefit scheme for 50+ lakh central government employees; accurate fund balances are not a bookkeeping technicality but a fiduciary obligation to employees who will claim this benefit on retirement.

source.quote: receipt figures pertaining to Ministry of Railways were included twice... This resulted in excess crediting of CGEGIS interest on the Savings Fund for FY 2022-23 and FY 2023-24 and overstatement of balances under Savings Fund and Insurance Fund

keyFindings.text: The broader pattern -- Rs. 134.72 crore receipts and Rs. 321.23 crore payments difference between UGFA and PAO-IDA records, interest calculated on provisional not final figures, and now a two-year double-count of a major Ministry -- points to a CGEGIS data reconciliation process that has systemic control gaps. CAG has raised CGEGIS accounting issues in prior reports; the recurrence indicates that point-in-time corrections (like JE no. 28 reversing 6 years of excess interest) are substituting for process-level fixes.

source.quote: There was a net difference Rs. 134.72 crore in receipts and Rs. 321.23 crore in payments between CGEGIS figures appearing in the UGFA and those maintained by PAO-IDA

recommendations: CGA should implement an automated deduplication check in PFMS for CGEGIS data submissions -- any Ministry whose data is already included in a consolidated CGDA submission should be flagged if it also submits directly, preventing a repeat of the Railways double-count without relying on manual vigilance.

CGEGIS interest calculations must be performed on final confirmed figures only, with a hard system lock preventing interest posting until the final Supplementary-II reconciliation is complete -- the ₹9.10 crore retroactive Journal Entry adjustment for 6 years of provisional-figure interest is exactly the kind of late correction that erodes the reliability of the Finance Accounts.

ministry: Ministry of Labour and Employment / Ministry of MSME, Government of India
title: Appropriation Audit -- Ministry of Labour ₹11,078.45 crore Savings (49.28 per cent of Grant); MSME ₹12,437.47 crore Savings (57.71 per cent); PMEGP Employment Scheme ₹6,358.77 crore Unspent (Union Government FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2026 (Para 4.2.2.2) found two major labour and enterprise schemes significantly under-executed in FY 2024-25: (1) Ministry of Labour and Employment -- savings of ₹11,078.45 crore (49.28 per cent) against sanctioned Revenue-Voted provision of ₹22,481.88 crore. The bulk of savings occurred under four sub-heads: New Employment Generation Scheme (₹6,479.84 crore), SC Sub-Plan -- New Employment Generation (₹1,660 crore), Tribal Area Sub-Plan -- New Employment Generation (₹860 crore), and Social Security (₹144.32 crore). Nearly half the employment-generation budget lapsed unused; (2) Ministry of MSME -- savings of ₹12,437.47 crore (57.71 per cent) against sanctioned Revenue-Voted provision of ₹21,549.89 crore. Sub-head breakdowns show ₹6,358.77 crore under PMEGP (Prime Ministers Employment Generation Programme), ₹2,168.20 crore under PMEGP-SC Sub-Plan, and ₹1,065.65 crore under PMEGP-Tribal Sub-Plan. Together, two Ministries with explicit mandates to create employment and support micro-enterprises failed to deploy ₹23,515.92 crore of their combined Revenue-Voted budgets.

keyFindings.text: Ministry of Labour left Rs. 11,078 crore (nearly half its employment budget) unspent in a year when India's official unemployment rate remains elevated and scheme-related wage employment demand persists. The Rs. 6,479.84 crore unspent under "New Employment Generation Scheme" alone represents foregone wages, livelihoods, and skill-development investments for workers who were budgeted for but never reached. Nearly Rs. 2,520 crore of SC and ST sub-plan employment allocations (Rs. 1,660 crore + Rs. 860 crore) also lapsed -- these ring-fenced sub-plan amounts are mandated specifically to reach the most marginalised workers.

source.quote: savings of Rs. 11,078.45 crore (49.28 per cent) under Revenue-Voted segment... 2230.01.789.29 (Rs. 1,660 crore), 2230.01.796.29 (Rs. 860 crore) - New Employment Generation Scheme

keyFindings.text: PMEGP -- the flagship self-employment scheme for micro-enterprises -- left Rs. 6,358.77 crore unspent against its main sub-head, plus Rs. 2,168.20 crore of SC sub-plan and Rs. 1,065.65 crore of Tribal sub-plan amounts. Together Rs. 9,592.62 crore of PMEGP allocations went unused while MSME sector job creation and first-generation entrepreneurship remained stated national priorities. Ministry of MSME's aggregate 57.71 per cent underspend suggests systemic capacity or demand constraints that are not being resolved year to year.

source.quote: 2851.00.102.96 (Rs. 6,358.77 crore), 2851.00.789.64 (Rs. 2,168.20 crore), 2851.00.796.63 (Rs. 1,065.65 crore) - Prime Ministers Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP)

recommendations: Ministry of Labour must publish a utilisation-vs-target dashboard for the New Employment Generation Scheme on a quarterly basis -- 49 per cent savings at year-end after ₹22,481 crore in Budget provision means either the scheme's disbursement pipeline is structurally broken or the budget is inflated; both possibilities require public-facing accountability.

PMEGP should move to a demand-side budgeting model backed by quarterly loan sanction and disbursement data from KVIC and banks -- ₹9,592 crore of PMEGP allocations lapsing in a single year while micro-entrepreneurs face credit gaps is a policy contradiction that cannot be resolved by simply re-budgeting the same amount next year.

ministry: Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region / Ministry of Rural Development, Government of India
title: Appropriation Audit -- ₹11,232.08 crore NER Fund (MH 2552) Re-appropriated Late; PMAY-Rural Persistent Savings ₹2,455 to ₹14,226 crore for 3 Years Attributed to Same Vague Reason Every Year (Union Government FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2026 (Para 4.2.2.4) found that Major Head 2552 -- the dedicated budget head for North Eastern Region spending -- had ₹11,232.08 crore re-appropriated to functional heads during FY 2024-25 (with the remainder surrendered), as mandated by DoNER guidelines. However, the re-appropriation itself signals implementation failure: the schemes under MH 2552 (covering NER-specific allocations for agriculture, employment, etc.) could not absorb their allocations -- reasons cited include non-finalization of proposals, PMFBY fund-sharing unviable in NER, no proposals received from NER States for PM AASHA, and capacity constraints. Separately (Para 4.2.2.5), PMAY-Rural (Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana-Rural) showed persistent savings of ₹2,455.51 crore to ₹14,226.98 crore over FY 2022-23 to FY 2024-25 -- with the same generic reason cited every year: "due to receipt of less proposals from State Governments." CAG found this indicates injudicious budget formulation, as persistent large savings with the same generic reason year-after-year means the budget is not being set on the basis of realistic demand projections.

keyFindings.text: PMAY-Rural citing "less proposals from State Governments" for Rs. 2,455 to Rs. 14,226 crore in savings every year for three consecutive years is precisely what CAG identifies as injudicious budgeting -- if the government knows demand will be below allocation, the budget should reflect that. Overstating PMAY-Rural in the Union Budget by Rs. 2,455 to Rs. 14,226 crore annually gives a misleadingly ambitious housing-spend figure, and the explanatory notes submitted to the Public Accounts Committee add no analytical value.

recommendations: DoNER should commission a scheme-by-scheme feasibility review for all programmes that have failed to absorb NER allocations under MH 2552 for more than two consecutive years -- schemes like PMFBY and PM AASHA whose design parameters are structurally incompatible with NER conditions should either be redesigned for NER or their NER sub-allocations should be redirected to programmes that actually reach the region.

Ministry of Rural Development must break its PMAY-Rural budget methodology's dependence on State proposal intake as the sole demand signal -- if States consistently under-propose, the central budget should model actual historical absorption, not aspirational allocations that lap every year with the same explanation.
