source.quote: there was a difference of Rs. 16,250.64 crore between two set of figures

keyFindings.text: NBCC's August 2024 bonus share allotment changed the GoI's equity position in a government-owned company but is not reflected in UGFA 2024-25 Statement 11. This means Parliament's approved Finance Accounts do not accurately reflect the government's ownership position in one of its own public sector enterprises -- a disclosure gap that investors, ratings agencies, and the Public Accounts Committee rely on Statement 11 to fill.

source.quote: UGFA 2024-25 does not include any disclosure regarding allotment of bonus shares by NBCC

recommendations: Department of Financial Services and O/o CGA should establish a quarterly reconciliation protocol between Statement 11 investment figures and MCA-21 paid-up capital data for all banks/PSUs -- the ₹16,250.64 crore gap would have been detected and corrected before Parliament received the Finance Accounts if even a basic annual reconciliation existed.

UGFA should include a mandatory section for "Material Corporate Events" covering bonus issues, rights issues, buybacks, and mergers affecting government equity stakes -- NBCC's bonus share allotment in August 2024 should have triggered a Statement 11 update before the accounts were certified in December 2025.

ministry: Ministry of Finance / Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, Government of India
title: Financial Audit -- ₹3,880.67 crore Total Cash Balance Unreconciled Between RBI and UGFA; ₹2,070.03 crore CBIC Non-Tax Receipts Misclassified as Tax Revenue (Union Government FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2026 identified two separate accounting accuracy failures: (1) RBI Cash Balance Unreconciled -- Statement 13 of UGFA 2024-25 shows a net cumulative difference of ₹1,961.75 crore (credit) between RBI Reserve Bank Deposits and the Finance Accounts, comprising ₹2,921.21 crore credit less ₹959.46 crore debit. The total cash balance requiring reconciliation with RBI at year-end is ₹3,880.67 crore. Specifically, the Ministry of External Affairs showed an adverse balance of ₹44,714.77 crore that was inadvertently shifted to the wrong head -- MEA subsequently confirmed the error was rectified via a Transfer Entry. O/o CGA directed reconciliation efforts; (2) CBIC Receipt Misclassification -- ₹2,070.03 crore in non-tax revenue receipts at Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) was misclassified: ₹1,011.71 crore in CBIC and ₹930.17 crore in CBDT were receipts of non-tax nature booked under tax receipt heads, distorting the tax-vs-non-tax revenue split in the Finance Accounts.

stats.label: Total cash balance to be reconciled with RBI at 31 March 2025

source.quote: total cash balance to be reconciled with RBI at the end of the FY 2024-25 was Rs. 3,880.67 crore

stats.label: Net cumulative difference between RBI deposits and UGFA Statement 13
stats.value: ₹1,961.75 crore (credit net) -- ₹2,921.21 crore credit less ₹959.46 crore debit

source.quote: Scrutiny of Statement 13 revealed a net cumulative difference of Rs. 1,961.75 crore (credit) -- {Civil Ministries Rs. 1,240.41 crore (credit), Union Territories Rs. 287.04 crore (credit) and Non-Civil Ministries Rs. 434.30 crore (credit)} between the cash balance of the Reserve Bank Deposits and Union Government Finance Accounts

stats.label: CBIC non-tax receipts misclassified as tax revenue

source.quote: Receipts of non-tax revenue nature amounting to Rs. 930.17 crore in Central Board for Direct Taxes (CBDT) and Rs. 1,011.71 crore in Central Board of Indirect Taxes... Rs. 2,070.03 crore in CBIC

stats.label: MEA adverse balance -- subsequently corrected via Transfer Entry
stats.value: ₹44,714.77 crore adverse balance under MH 8670.103 (inadvertent error, TE issued)

source.quote: For adverse balance of Rs. 44,714.77 crore in Ministry of External Affairs, the Ministry replied (October 2025) that the debit balance under Head 8670.103- Cheques and Bills for the FY 2024-25 had been inadvertently shifted... rectification has since been carried out through a TE

keyFindings.text: CBIC and CBDT collected Rs. 2,070.03 crore in non-tax receipts (penalties, fees, interest, etc.) but booked them under tax receipt major heads -- making the government's Gross Tax Revenue (GTR) figure appear larger than the actual tax collections. Since fiscal deficit calculations, tax buoyancy analysis, and Goods and Services Tax Council compensation calculations all depend on accurate GTR, this Rs. 2,070.03 crore misclassification distorts multiple downstream fiscal metrics.

source.quote: Receipts of non-tax revenue nature amounting to Rs. 930.17 crore in Central Board for Direct Taxes (CBDT) and Rs. 1,011.71 crore in Central Board of Indirect Taxes

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 3,880.67 crore in unreconciled cash balances with RBI at year-end means the government cannot confirm whether its Consolidated Fund cash position matches the RBI's records. While the net difference (Rs. 1,961.75 crore) is small relative to the government's total cash, the gross unreconciled amounts (Rs. 2,921.21 crore credit and Rs. 959.46 crore debit) reflect a book-keeping backlog that grows each year without a time-bound resolution mandate.

source.quote: total cash balance to be reconciled with RBI at the end of the FY 2024-25 was Rs. 3,880.67 crore

recommendations: CGA should establish a rule in PFMS that blocks booking of receipts under Customs/Excise/Income Tax receipt major heads if the challan description contains keywords indicating non-tax nature (penalty, fee, interest, forfeiture, fine) -- this would catch the ₹2,070.03 crore CBIC/CBDT misclassification at entry point rather than detecting it at annual audit.

RBI and CGA should implement a monthly automated reconciliation of Statement 13 (cash with RBI) using PFMS and RBI's Core Banking Solution -- the ₹3,880.67 crore year-end unreconciled amount results from a process that only reconciles annually; monthly reconciliation would limit the maximum unresolved balance to one month's difference rather than an annual accumulation.

ministry: Ministry of Jal Shakti / Ministry of Defence / Department of Atomic Energy, Government of India
title: Financial Audit -- ₹9,045.01 crore Booked Under Omnibus Minor Head 800 (81.79 per cent Expenditure, 75.39 per cent Receipts in Respective Major Heads); DoAE Heavy Water ₹2,000 crore Regular Expenditure Misrouted (Union Government FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2026 (Para 3.3.3) found that Minor Head 800 -- an omnibus "Other Expenditure / Other Receipts" catch-all -- is being used as the primary booking head under multiple Major Heads, defeating the purpose of a detailed chart of accounts. Under three Major Heads, ₹4,957.58 crore (81.79 per cent of total expenditure of ₹6,061.58 crore under these heads) was classified under Minor Head 800. Under six Major Heads, ₹4,087.43 crore (75.39 per cent of ₹5,421.99 crore in receipts) was similarly classified under Minor Head 800 -- including defence services receipts for Navy (MH 0077) and Air Force (MH 0078) for which CGDA only stated that a "review is under process." Additionally, DoAE books Heavy Water Pool Management expenditure (₹2,000 crore in FY 2024-25, ranging ₹1,300--2,000 crore over five years) under MH 2801.03.800 (Minor Head 800) rather than under a specific program minor head -- a recurring booking that is regular in nature and should have its own classified head.

stats.label: Expenditure under Minor Head 800 across 3 Major Heads (>50% of each head)

source.quote: under three Major Heads of accounts, more than 50 per cent of expenditure under each Head, amounting to Rs. 4,957.58 crore (81.79 per cent of total expenditure of Rs. 6,061.58 crore under these Major Heads), was classified under Minor Head 800- Other Expenditure

stats.label: Receipts under Minor Head 800 across 6 Major Heads (>50% of each head)

source.quote: under six Major Heads of accounts, more than 50 per cent of the receipts under each Head, amounting to Rs. 4,087.43 crore (75.39 per cent of the total receipts of Rs. 5,421.99 crore under these Major Heads), was classified under Minor Head 800-Other Receipts

stats.label: DoAE Heavy Water Pool Management -- regular expenditure under Minor Head 800
stats.value: ₹2,000 crore in FY 2024-25 (₹1,300 to ₹2,000 crore per year over last 5 years)

source.quote: expenditure relating to Heavy Water Pool Management (HWPM) was being booked under minor head 800-Other Expenditure of Major Head 2801. During FY 2024-25, the amount booked was Rs. 2,000 crore... During last five FYs (2020-21 to 2024-25), amount booked under MH: 2801.03.800 ranged between Rs. 1,300 crore to Rs. 2,000 crore

keyFindings.text: When 81.79 per cent of expenditure under a Major Head is classified under Minor Head 800 (Other Expenditure), the government's Appropriation Accounts provide no information about what the money was actually spent on. Minor Head 800 is an accounting residual designed for genuinely uncategorised items -- using it as the primary head for Rs. 4,957.58 crore is a transparency failure that makes it impossible for Parliament or the public to understand spending composition.

source.quote: under three Major Heads of accounts, more than 50 per cent of expenditure under each Head, amounting to Rs. 4,957.58 crore (81.79 per cent of total expenditure of Rs. 6,061.58 crore under these Major Heads), was classified under Minor Head 800-Other Expenditure

keyFindings.text: DoAE's Heavy Water Pool Management is a recurring, predictable programme -- Rs. 1,300 to Rs. 2,000 crore per year over five years. Booking it under Minor Head 800 (Other Expenditure) for five consecutive years suggests either that the correct specific minor head does not exist and has never been created, or that it exists but DoAE does not use it. Five years of HWPM expenditure under "Other Expenditure" means the government's accounts show no separately visible line for nuclear fuel management costs over half a decade.

source.quote: During last five FYs (2020-21 to 2024-25), amount booked under MH: 2801.03.800 ranged between Rs. 1,300 crore to Rs. 2,000 crore. In this case, significant amount of expenditure, though below 50 per cent of total expenditure under concerned Major Head, was booked under minor head 800

recommendations: CGA should publish a mandatory "Minor Head 800 Reduction Plan" requiring every Ministry/Department where more than 30 per cent of any Major Head is classified under Minor Head 800 to submit a new minor head proposal to CGA within 120 days -- continuing to add up ₹9,045 crore per year to the omnibus head while defence and nuclear spending details remain invisible is incompatible with fiscal transparency.

For DoAE Heavy Water Pool Management, a dedicated minor head under MH 2801 should be created before FY 2025-26 -- 5 years of recurring ₹1,300-2,000 crore expenditure booked as "Other Expenditure" is ample evidence that this is a permanent programme needing its own classification.

ministry: Ministry of Finance, Government of India
title: State Finances Audit -- Fixed Revenue Expenditure Components (Interest, Salary, Pension) Rose to 46.07 per cent of Revenue Expenditure in FY 2024-25; Pension Up 12.30 per cent; Interest Payments ₹11,52,514 crore (Union Government)
overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2026 (Para 2.7.3) presents data showing that the Union Government's three committed/fixed revenue expenditure components -- interest payments, salaries, and pension -- collectively rose from 44.18 per cent of total revenue expenditure in FY 2023-24 to 46.07 per cent in FY 2024-25. This increase leaves a shrinking share of revenue expenditure for discretionary spending on welfare schemes, infrastructure grants, and other programmes. Key metrics: (1) Interest payments -- Internal Debt interest grew 5.62 per cent to ₹10,67,443 crore; External Debt interest grew 15.35 per cent to ₹34,162 crore; Small Savings interest ₹49,679 crore; total interest outgo ₹11,52,514 crore -- accounting for 29.20 per cent of revenue expenditure and the single largest fixed component; (2) Pension -- total pension and retirement benefits grew 12.30 per cent to ₹3,45,942 crore, with Defence pensions at 45.57 per cent of total (₹1,57,650 crore) and Civil pensions at 33.57 per cent; (3) Capital expenditure -- ₹8,58,256 crore (2.70 per cent of GDP), slightly lower than FY 2023-24's 2.78 per cent, with transport as the dominant driver (Railways capex up 743 per cent over 5 years).

stats.label: Fixed expenditure (interest + salary + pension) as share of revenue expenditure

source.quote: Three components of revenue expenditure viz. interest payments, salary and pension payments constitute committed expenditure... fixed components of revenue expenditure, namely salary, pension, and interest payments, increased as a share of total revenue expenditure from 44.18 per cent in FY 2023-24 to 46.07 per cent in FY 2024-25

stats.label: Total interest payments (FY 2024-25)
stats.value: ₹11,52,514 crore (29.20 per cent of revenue expenditure)

source.quote: Interest on Internal Debt grew by 5.62 per cent (from Rs. 10,10,671 crore in FY 2023-24 to Rs. 10,67,443 crore in FY 2024-25)... interest payments account for the largest share, comprising 29.20 per cent of revenue expenditure in FY 2024-25

the total expenditure incurred on pensions and other retirement benefits increased by 12.30 per cent to Rs. 3,45,942 crore from Rs. 3,08,040 crore in FY 2023-24. Defence pensions account for 45.57 per cent of the total pension outgo of the Union Government in FY 2024-25, followed by civil pension (33.57 per cent)

stats.label: Capital expenditure (FY 2024-25)
stats.value: ₹8,58,256 crore (2.70 per cent of GDP, up 6.33 per cent from FY 2023-24)

source.quote: the capital expenditure (capex) of the Union Government was Rs. 8,58,256 crore. We observed that capex increased by 6.33 per cent as compared to last year. As a percentage of GDP, capex stood at 2.70 per cent in FY 2024-25

stats.label: Railways capital expenditure growth (5-year trend)
stats.value: Up 743.51 per cent -- from ₹29,910 crore (FY 2020-21) to ₹2,52,293 crore (FY 2024-25)

source.quote: capital outlay on Indian Railways-Commercial Lines by 743.51 per cent (from Rs. 29,910 crore in FY 2020-21 to Rs. 2,52,293 crore in FY 2024-25) and capital outlay on Roads and Bridges by 216.05 per cent (from Rs. 92,524 crore in FY 2020-21 to Rs. 2,92,424 crore in FY 2024-25)

keyFindings.text: The Union Government's revenue expenditure discretion is shrinking: 46.07 per cent of every rupee of revenue spending now goes to three committed items -- interest, salaries, and pensions -- before any welfare scheme, grant, or service delivery expenditure. The trend from 44.18 per cent in FY 2023-24 to 46.07 per cent in FY 2024-25 (a 1.89 percentage point shift in one year) means discretionary revenue spending fell correspondingly. At this rate, within a decade, more than half of revenue expenditure will be committed to interest, salaries, and pensions.

source.quote: fixed components of revenue expenditure, namely salary, pension, and interest payments, increased as a share of total revenue expenditure from 44.18 per cent in FY 2023-24 to 46.07 per cent in FY 2024-25

keyFindings.text: Pension expenditure is growing at 12.30 per cent per year while GDP grew at 9.74 per cent in nominal terms -- pension outlays are growing faster than the economy. Defence pensions alone account for 45.57 per cent of all government pension spending (Rs. 1,57,650 crore), a share that will continue rising as the Agnipath scheme transition (which reduces permanent recruiting) has not yet materialized in pension outflow reduction.

source.quote: the total expenditure incurred on pensions and other retirement benefits increased by 12.30 per cent to Rs. 3,45,942 crore... Defence pensions account for 45.57 per cent of the total pension outgo

recommendations: Finance Commission and Budget Division should publish an annual "Fiscal Flexibility Index" tracking the share of total government expenditure that is discretionary vs. committed, so Parliament can see the structural narrowing of fiscal space over time -- the present Appropriation Accounts format does not highlight the committed-vs-discretionary split in a way that triggers corrective policy consideration.

The Ministry of Defence should accelerate publication of projections for the Defence pension tail as Agnipath inductees begin replacing permanent cadres -- without a credible pension outflow trajectory, Budget planning for Defence pension provisions is flying blind on the single largest component of Union Government pension spending.

ministry: National CAMPA / Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Government of India
title: Financial Audit -- ₹10,380.36 crore CAMPA Forest Levy Pending Disbursement to States; ₹2,184.78 crore Not Transferred to Public Account; Accounting Not in Accordance with 2016 CAMPA Act (Union Government FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2026 found that National CAMPA (Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority) is not accounting for or distributing forest compensatory levies in accordance with the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016 and Rules 2018. The 2016 Act requires user agencies to deposit compensatory levies directly in State-specific accounts and distribute them 90:10 to States and Centre -- but CAMPA continues using a pre-2016 procedure routing money through MH-8336 Civil Deposits. At end of FY 2024-25, ₹10,380.36 crore was lying in MH-8336 pending disbursement to States/UTs -- a ₹599.53 crore discrepancy exists between UGFA figures and CAMPA's own records indicating potential understatement of Public Account. Additionally, ₹2,184.78 crore that should have been transferred to the Public Account of India by 31 March 2025 was still lying in Union Bank of India bank accounts and was only transferred in April 2025. CAG noted the accounting procedure is not in accordance with the 2016 Act; CAMPA's response that it is still developing a streamlined mechanism (as of August 2025 meeting) was not accepted as convincing.

stats.label: CAMPA compensatory levy pending disbursement to States/UTs (MH-8336)

source.quote: at the end of FY 2024-25, Rs. 10,380.36 crore was lying under MH-8336-102-National Compensation Afforestation Deposits pending disbursement to respective States/Union territories

stats.label: CAMPA levy not transferred to Public Account -- lying in Union Bank of India accounts
stats.value: ₹2,184.78 crore (transferred only in April 2025, one month late)

source.quote: Out of total amount of Rs. 2,192.95 crore, Rs. 2,184.78 crore should have been transferred to the Public Account of India by the end of FY 2024-25... receipts for February 2025 of Rs. 1,095.21 crore... it could only be transferred to Public Account in April 2025

stats.label: Discrepancy between UGFA and CAMPA records (potential Public Account understatement)

source.quote: the amount reflected in HoA 8336.00.102 was lower than the figures of the National CAMPA by Rs. 599.53 crore as of 31 March 2025, indicating a potential understatement of Public Account by the same amount

keyFindings.text: The Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016 was specifically enacted to replace the pre-2016 ad hoc CAMPA arrangement with a statutory framework -- including a precise accounting path for levies that bypasses the MH-8336 Civil Deposits route. Eight years after the Act, and seven years after the 2018 Rules, National CAMPA still operates on the pre-Act procedure, with the Governing Body formally approving continuation of the old route in December 2023. The States' forest development funds are being held in an accounting limbo that does not comply with the legislation Parliament enacted to govern them.

source.quote: we found that in contravention of the accounting procedure, the collected levy was initially transferred to the Public Account of India under Major Head- 8336 Civil Deposits... The National CAMPA replied (December 2025) that the Governing Body of the Authority, in its meeting (December 2023), had approved continuation of the existing procedure

keyFindings.text: Rs. 10,380.36 crore in forest compensatory levies collected from industries and infrastructure project developers has been sitting in the Public Account pending disbursement to States at year-end -- these are funds meant for afforestation activities in the States where forest land was diverted. The delay in releasing these funds to State CAMPAs directly delays the planting of compensatory trees for forests already destroyed.

source.quote: Rs. 10,380.36 crore was lying under MH-8336-102-National Compensation Afforestation Deposits pending disbursement to respective States/Union territories

recommendations: Ministry of Environment should mandate that National CAMPA migrate to the Bharat Kosh platform for real-time bifurcation of CAMPA levies between State and National accounts by 31 March 2026 -- the August 2025 meeting that discussed Bharat Kosh integration must be given a binding timeline, not an open-ended feasibility discussion.

A monthly reconciliation between CAMPA's own records and the UGFA head MH-8336.00.102 should be mandated with a maximum tolerance of zero -- the ₹599.53 crore discrepancy at year-end cannot persist when a reconciliation committee was only constituted in October 2025 to address it.

ministry: Ministry of Finance / Controller General of Accounts, Government of India
title: Financial Audit -- ₹91,534 crore Loans to States/Entities in Arrears; ₹22,242.67 crore Suspense Head Balances Awaiting Clearance; Some Outstanding from FY 2002-03 (Union Government FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2026 found two large unresolved balance categories in Union Government accounts: (1) Loans and Advances Arrears -- Against total outstanding loans of ₹9,94,278.08 crore to State/UT Governments and other entities as on 31 March 2025, there were arrears in recovery of ₹91,534 crore including interest. CAG noted that given the age of pendency, some of these loans may not be recoverable; (2) Suspense Head Balances -- ₹22,242.67 crore in Suspense Heads under MH 8658 were awaiting clearance, of which ₹16,964.02 crore was debit balance and ₹5,278.65 crore credit balance. These suspense balances arise when transactions cannot be booked to final heads for want of information -- their persistence means at least one financial head of account is understated by the suspense amount. CAG separately found 18 dormant Reserve Fund/Deposit accounts with accumulated net credit balance of ₹844.93 crore, some dormant since FY 2002-03.

stats.label: Arrears in recovery of loans (States/UTs and other entities) as on 31 March 2025
stats.value: ₹91,534 crore including interest (against total loans of ₹9,94,278.08 crore)

source.quote: Against the total loans of Rs. 9,94,278.08 crore outstanding against State/UT Governments and other entities as on 31 March 2025, there were arrears in recovery amounting to Rs. 91,534 crore including interest... Given the age of pendency, some of these loans may not be recoverable
Suspense heads with significant balances in FY 2024-25... These balances aggregate to Rs. 22,242.67 crore (Rs. 16,964.02 crore Debit and Rs. 5,278.65 crore Credit)

stats.label: Dormant Reserve Fund/Deposit accounts (18 accounts, credit balance)

source.quote: three financial years or more with an accumulated net credit balance of Rs. 844.93 crore. The oldest Reserve Fund or Deposits account was dormant since FY 2002-03

keyFindings.text: Rs. 91,534 crore in loan recoveries outstanding from States, UTs and entities is 9.2 per cent of total loans outstanding -- and CAG explicitly flagged that "given the age of pendency, some of these loans may not be recoverable." This is an implicit write-off signal: the Union Government's Rs. 9,94,278 crore loan portfolio contains a tail of unrecoverable loans that are still carried at face value without provisions or impairment disclosure.

source.quote: there were arrears in recovery amounting to Rs. 91,534 crore including interest. Given the age of pendency, some of these loans may not be recoverable

keyFindings.text: Rs. 22,242.67 crore in suspense head balances means that at least one final head of account is understated by this amount in the Union Government Finance Accounts -- the Government's own accounts acknowledge that Rs. 22,242 crore in transactions have been parked in suspense without being assigned to their correct final head. CGA's response was that reconciliation is in progress, but the pattern of significant suspense balances is recurring year after year in CAG reports.

source.quote: Balance in a Suspense Account implies that at least one financial Head of Account is understated... These balances aggregate to Rs. 22,242.67 crore

recommendations: For the ₹91,534 crore in loan arrears, Ministry of Finance must publish an age-wise recovery schedule distinguishing performing loans from effectively unrecoverable ones -- continuing to carry all loan arrears at face value without impairment disclosure misrepresents the Union Government's actual financial position to Parliament.

CGA should set a 90-day maximum age for any single Suspense Head balance above ₹100 crore in PFMS -- after 90 days, the balance should be automatically escalated to the Financial Adviser of the relevant Ministry for resolution, replacing the current unlimited-duration accumulation that has allowed some balances to persist for years.

ministry: Ministry of Finance / Department of Telecommunications / Multiple Ministries, Government of India
title: Financial Audit -- ₹36,766.60 crore Savings Not Surrendered (64 Grants); ₹38,287.52 crore Utilisation Certificates Outstanding for 3+ Years; Earliest Pending Since FY 1985-86 (Union Government FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2026 found two systemic failures in Union Government expenditure tracking for FY 2024-25: (1) Savings Not Surrendered -- of ₹4,91,302.81 crore total savings, ₹36,766.60 crore (7.48 per cent) was not surrendered back to the Consolidated Fund under 64 Grants/Appropriations where amounts above ₹1 crore were involved. The Department of Telecommunications alone did not surrender ₹11,898.55 crore. Excess surrender (more than available savings) of ₹622.55 crore was also found under 3 grants; (2) Outstanding Utilisation Certificates (UCs) -- ₹54,282.32 crore in UCs were outstanding as on 31 March 2025 across multiple Ministries. Of these, 13,926 UCs worth ₹38,287.52 crore relate to the last three years (FY 2021-22 to 2023-24). The earliest uncleared UC dates to FY 1985-86 -- 40 years of pending accountability. UCs are the only mechanism to verify that government grants have been used for their intended purpose; their non-submission means the government cannot confirm how ₹38,287.52 crore was spent.

stats.label: Savings not surrendered -- 64 Grants/Appropriations (amounts above ₹1 crore)
stats.value: ₹36,766.60 crore (7.48 per cent of total savings of ₹4,91,302.81 crore)

stats.value: ₹54,282.32 crore (13,926 UCs for last 3 years: ₹38,287.52 crore)

source.quote: aggregating to Rs. 54,282.32 crore, were outstanding as on 31st March 2025... Of these, 13,926 UCs amounting to Rs. 38,287.52 crore pertain to the last three years (2021-22 to 2023-24)
The earliest grants for which UCs remained outstanding date back to FY 1985-86. This indicates that the Departments/Ministries were not adequately addressing the issues of outstanding UCs

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 36,766.60 crore in unsurrendered savings is distinct from the money that was spent -- it represents funds that were budgeted, not spent, and then neither returned to the Consolidated Fund nor redeployed. This money effectively disappeared from accountability at year-end without Parliament being informed of its reabsorption. The Government's response was simply to confirm the figures are correct, without explaining why 64 Grants failed to surrender their unspent balances as required.

source.quote: Rs. 36,766.60 crore (7.48 per cent of total savings) was not surrendered and was allowed to lapse under 64 Grants/Appropriations... Department of Expenditure (O/o CGA) replied (February 2026) that figures with respect to Annexure 4.6A in respect of Civil Grants have been verified and found correct

keyFindings.text: A Utilisation Certificate is the single document that certifies whether a government grant was used for its intended purpose -- without a UC, neither the Ministry nor Parliament knows if Rs. 38,287.52 crore in FY 2021-24 grants actually reached the intended beneficiaries or was diverted. The existence of UCs outstanding since FY 1985-86 proves that this is not a new problem: the government has never built a system that forces grantee bodies to account for grants before receiving the next one.

source.quote: Since the receipt of UCs is the only mechanism to confirm that funds have been utilised for their intended purpose, the Departments should establish a robust system to ensure the timely submission of UCs by grantee bodies. The earliest grants for which UCs remained outstanding date back to FY 1985-86

recommendations: PFMS should block grant release to any grantee body with overdue UCs beyond 12 months -- the current pattern of releasing subsequent grants regardless of UC status enables the 40-year accumulation of unverified grant utilisation; a system-enforced freeze is the only remedy that has not been tried.

The Ministry of Finance should mandate that any savings above ₹1 crore that remain unsurrendered 15 days before year-end be automatically credited back to the CFI by PFMS without requiring a surrender order -- the ₹36,766.60 crore lapse results from a manual surrender process that 64 grant managers failed to complete.

ministry: Ministry of Micro Small and Medium Enterprises / Multiple Ministries, Government of India
title: Financial Audit -- ₹3,035.37 crore Unnecessary Supplementary Provisions; ₹457.17 crore SC/ST Sub-Plan Funds Re-appropriated to Other Heads in Violation of Budget Circular (Union Government FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2026 found two distinct violations of Union Government budgetary discipline in FY 2024-25: (1) Unnecessary Supplementary Provisions -- in 26 minor/sub-heads under 16 Grants/Appropriations, Supplementary Demands amounting to ₹3,035.37 crore were obtained from Parliament mid-year, but final expenditure of ₹54,544.46 crore was lower than even the original provision of ₹56,535.81 crore -- making the entire supplementary grant unnecessary. Obtaining Parliamentary approval for additional funds that are never needed distorts fiscal accountability and wastes legislative time; (2) SC/ST Sub-Plan Fund Diversion -- Budget Circular 2024-25 (Para 13.3) explicitly prohibits re-appropriation of funds from Minor Head 789 (Scheduled Castes Sub-Plan) and Minor Head 796 (Tribal Area Sub-Plan) to other heads. Despite this, the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises issued 7 re-appropriation orders diverting ₹457.17 crore from SCSP and TASP funds to other minor heads, directly contrary to the NITI Aayog guidelines and the Budget Circular.

stats.label: Unnecessary supplementary provisions obtained -- 26 minor heads, 16 grants
stats.value: ₹3,035.37 crore supplementary grants obtained but final expenditure below original provision

source.quote: supplementary provisions amounting to Rs. 3,035.37 crore were obtained during FY 2024-25 in anticipation of higher expenditure, but final expenditure of Rs. 54,544.46 crore was lower than even the original provision of Rs. 56,535.81 crore, making the supplementary grant unnecessary

stats.value: Original provision ₹56,535.81 crore; Final expenditure ₹54,544.46 crore

keyFindings.text: When a Ministry obtains a Supplementary Demand, it presents to Parliament that its original budget is insufficient -- this is a constitutional process for urgent mid-year funding. But in 26 minor heads across 16 grants, the Ministries ultimately spent less than their original budget, not less than their supplementary budget. The Rs. 3,035.37 crore in Supplementary Demands obtained was entirely unnecessary because even without them, actual spending fell short of the original grants. Parliament was asked to approve additional spending that was never going to happen.

source.quote: supplementary provisions amounting to Rs. 3,035.37 crore were obtained during FY 2024-25 in anticipation of higher expenditure, but final expenditure of Rs. 54,544.46 crore was lower than even the original provision of Rs. 56,535.81 crore, making the supplementary grant unnecessary

keyFindings.text: Budget Circular 2024-25 Para 13.3 is unambiguous: funds earmarked for SCSP (SC welfare) and TASP (Tribal welfare) under Minor Heads 789 and 796 cannot be re-appropriated to other heads. The Ministry of MSME issued 7 re-appropriation orders transferring Rs. 457.17 crore out of SC/ST welfare funds. These funds were supposed to be ring-fenced for Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe programme delivery; their diversion to other heads removes them from any accountability framework for SC/ST development outcomes.

source.quote: As per para 13.3 of the Budget Circular 2024-25, the provisions made under these Minor Heads will not be allowed to be re-appropriated, except to the same Minor heads in other schemes... re-appropriation orders had been issued on seven instances from Minor Heads 789 and 796 to other minor heads, amounting to Rs. 457.17 crore, in contravention of the above-cited guidelines

recommendations: PFMS should add a validation rule that rejects any re-appropriation order from Minor Head 789 or 796 to any other minor/sub-head -- the Budget Circular prohibition has existed for years but is ignored by Ministries because the PFMS re-appropriation module does not enforce it; a system block would make human override impossible.

Before the Supplementary Demands are tabled in Parliament, the Budget Division must verify via PFMS data that the grants requesting supplementary provisions are actually on track to exhaust their original grants -- the 16-grant pattern of unnecessary supplementary demands suggests no such pre-tabling verification exists.

ministry: DIPAM / Department of Pharmaceuticals / Department of Telecommunications, Government of India
title: Financial Audit -- ₹842.82 crore CPSE Dividend Short Receipt (7 Entities), ₹322.13 crore Sovereign Guarantee Fee Not Recovered from MTNL, BSNL, and IDPL (Union Government FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2026 found two categories of uncollected government dues from Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs): (1) Dividend Short Receipt -- DIPAM guidelines (May 2016) require every CPSE to pay a minimum annual dividend of 30 per cent of Profit After Tax (PAT) or 5 per cent of net worth, whichever is higher. Audit test check found that of ₹1,814.59 crore receivable from 7 entities under 6 Ministries, only ₹971.77 crore was received -- a shortfall of ₹842.82 crore; (2) Guarantee Fee Non-Recovery -- the Union Government extends sovereign guarantees (outstanding total ₹3,33,454.63 crore at end of FY 2024-25) and charges a guarantee fee. Audit found ₹322.13 crore in guarantee fee not recovered from three CPSEs: IDPL (sick PSU, never paid from start), MTNL (not paid since FY 2022-23 due to financial distress), and BSNL (DoT seeking waiver from DEA). IDPL's non-payment has been ongoing since its guarantee was first issued; MTNL has not paid for at least 3 consecutive years.

source.quote: against receivable dividend amounting to Rs. 1,814.59 crore, dividend amounting only to Rs. 971.77 crore was received, resulting in short receipt of dividend of Rs. 842.82 crore, in respect of seven entities functioning under six Ministries/Departments

source.quote: DoT replied (October 2025) that MTNL has not paid guarantee fee since FY 2022-23, due to financial distress

keyFindings.text: IDPL (under Department of Pharmaceuticals) has never paid guarantee fee from the first day the guarantee was issued -- the Department replied that IDPL could not pay due to shortage of funds and its closure is under process per a Union Cabinet decision of December 2016. The Cabinet decision to close IDPL is 9 years old; the PSU continues to hold sovereign guarantees it cannot service, and the guarantee fee liability compounds annually. This is a known fiscal risk that has been unresolved for nearly a decade.

source.quote: Department of Pharmaceuticals replied (August 2025) that IDPL could not pay the guarantee fees from the very beginning due to shortage of funds as IDPL is a sick PSU and its closure is under progress in terms of Union Cabinet decision dated 28 December 2016

keyFindings.text: The 7-entity CPSE dividend shortfall (Rs. 842.82 crore of Rs. 1,814.59 crore receivable) represents a 46 per cent collection failure against a DIPAM-mandated minimum dividend policy -- a policy intended to ensure that taxpayer-owned enterprises remit a share of profits to the public exchequer. The total GoI dividend received in FY 2024-25 was Rs. 3,08,435.86 crore, which means the shortfall (Rs. 842.82 crore) is 0.27 per cent of total dividends -- but this figure reflects only the 7 test-checked entities; the actual underpayment across all CPSEs may be higher.

source.quote: Total dividend received by the GoI during FY 2024-25 was Rs. 3,08,435.86 crore. On test check of records relating to dividend received from the CPSEs, we observed that against receivable dividend amounting to Rs. 1,814.59 crore, dividend amounting only to Rs. 971.77 crore was received

recommendations: PFMS / DIPAM should automate dividend receivable tracking against CPSE PAT/net-worth data from MCA21: if a CPSE files audited accounts showing PAT or net worth above the minimum threshold, a dividend demand should auto-generate with a mandatory payment deadline, replacing the current manual follow-up.

For MTNL, BSNL, and IDPL, the guarantee fee write-off or restructuring must be formally approved by Parliament as a budget line -- the current practice of indefinitely deferring guarantee fee without Parliamentary authorisation is off-balance-sheet quasi-debt that is not reflected in the government's reported fiscal deficit.

ministry: Department of Space / Department of Atomic Energy / Ministry of Finance, Government of India
title: Financial Audit -- ₹12,754.47 crore Classification Errors in Union Government Accounts: Department of Atomic Energy ₹3,089.97 crore Capital Expenditure Under Revenue Heads, DoSpace ₹40.16 crore Wrong Object Heads (FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2026 (Para 3.5) identified ₹12,754.47 crore in classification errors across Union Government accounts in FY 2024-25: ₹8,742.56 crore in expenditure misclassifications (predominantly wrong object heads: ₹8,723.83 crore) and ₹4,011.91 crore in receipt misclassifications. Key cases: (1) Department of Atomic Energy -- ₹3,089.97 crore of operational expenditure under Heavy Water Board booked under Capital Major Head 4861 using revenue object heads, contrary to accounting principles. CGA refused the Department's request to shift it to revenue section. (2) Department of Space/IN-SPACe -- ₹24.79 crore released to IN-SPACe under wrong object heads (not under grants-in-aid codes 31/36); ₹15.37 crore capital grants also misclassified; ₹9.33 crore canteen expenditure booked under Space Technology (Minor Head 101) instead of Other Expenditure (Minor Head 800); ₹86.88 crore satellite/launch expenditure booked under revenue instead of capital. The IN-SPACe misclassification persisted from FY 2023-24 without correction. (3) 21 cases across 6 grants: ₹5,456.84 crore booked under wrong object heads within grants.

This is a deliberate accounting practice that inflates the capital section and suppresses the revenue section of the Department's accounts, distorting the capital-to-revenue expenditure ratio for nuclear programmes by a significant margin.

keyFindings.text: The IN-SPACe grants-in-aid misclassification (Rs. 40.16 crore in wrong object heads) was reported by CAG in FY 2023-24 accounts and remained uncorrected in FY 2024-25. The Department of Space did not reply to the current year's audit observation either. A repeat misclassification with no reply and no correction across two consecutive audit years indicates that the accounting authority does not consider this a priority -- despite the error distorting grants-in-aid reporting for an autonomous body under a strategically sensitive department.

source.quote: This issue was also raised in IN-SPACe's accounts of FY 2023-24. Reply of DoS was awaited

recommendations: CGA should implement a hard-coded object-head validation in PFMS that rejects bookings where revenue object heads (11-30 series) are used under Capital Major Heads -- this would have prevented the ₹3,089.97 crore DoAE misclassification at the time of payment.

IN-SPACe grant-release codes should be pre-mapped in PFMS by the DoS PAO so that the correct object heads (31/35/36) are the only available options for IN-SPACe payment transactions -- eliminating the discretionary booking that created the repeat misclassification across two financial years.

ministry: Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Government of India
title: Financial Audit -- ₹2,94,150 crore Oil Industry Cess Retained in CFI Without Transfer to OIDB: 50 Years of Non-Compliance (Union Government FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2026 (Financial Audit of Union Government for FY 2024-25) found that since FY 1974-75, the Union Government has collected ₹3,12,782 crore as cess on crude oil under the Oil Industry (Development) Act, 1974 -- but transferred only ₹902 crore to the Oil Industry Development Board (OIDB) during FY 1974-75 to 1991-92. After that, for 32 years (FY 1992-93 to FY 2023-24), no transfer was made to OIDB despite continuous cess collection. As on 31 March 2025, ₹2,94,150 crore of cess collected for oil industry development was retained in the Consolidated Fund of India (CFI) instead of being transferred to its designated fund. Only in FY 2024-25 did the Government operationalise the Oil Industry Development Fund (OIDF) for the first time in Union Government Finance Accounts -- and transferred ₹17,730 crore of the ₹17,931 crore collected that year. CAG also found that ₹9,222 crore in total was short-transferred to four Reserve Funds during FY 2024-25, and at least ₹100 crore in the Income Tax Welfare Fund (ITWF) has been lying idle since FY 2008-09 -- 16 years.

The Department replied (October 2025) that they are of the view to not liquidate the ITWF fund. The fact remains that fund is lying idle since last 16 years

keyFindings.text: The Oil Industry (Development) Act, 1974 created a cess on crude oil specifically to fund the Oil Industry Development Board (OIDB). Yet from 1992-93 to 2023-24 -- 32 consecutive fiscal years -- no cess transfer was made to OIDB. The Government collected Rs. 17,931 crore in cess in FY 2024-25 alone, suggesting that over the 32-year blackout the annual collection would have been in the tens of thousands of crores, all retained in the Consolidated Fund. Only CAG scrutiny in FY 2024-25 prompted the Government to operationalise the OIDF for the first time and begin transfers.

source.quote: Thereafter, no transfer of cess proceeds to the OIDB was made during FY 1992-93 to FY 2023-24, despite continued collection of the cess. The Oil Industry Development Fund (OIDF) has been operationalised for the first time in the Union Government Finance Accounts (UGFA) during current FY 2024-25

keyFindings.text: The broader pattern of FY 2024-25 is Rs. 9,222 crore short-transferred to four Reserve Funds -- every fund designed to receive ring-fenced cess money received less than it was entitled to, while the Consolidated Fund of India retained the difference. This is the structural mechanism by which the Union Government has effectively used purpose-specific cess collections as general revenue, circumventing the designated-fund architecture established by Parliament.

source.quote: Test check of cess and levies collected during FY 2024-25 revealed cases of short/non-transfer of collected amounts... Details of short transfer of Rs. 9,222 crore to four Reserve Funds during FY 2024-25

recommendations: Parliament should mandate that all cess/levy transfers to designated Reserve Funds be automated at the CFI level within 30 days of collection -- the present system where Ministries initiate transfers manually enables the 32-year OIDB blackout to recur for any other cess whenever a Ministry finds it convenient to delay or omit transfers.

For the ₹2,94,150 crore of cumulative oil cess retained in CFI, Parliament should direct the Ministry of Petroleum to table a reconciliation plan specifying how the diverted amount will be credited to OIDF over a defined schedule, and the use to which it will be put for oil industry development -- simply activating the fund for future transfers while silently absorbing past retentions is insufficient accountability.

ministry: Ministry of Finance / Multiple Central Ministries, Government of India
title: Financial Audit -- ₹8,637.23 crore Excess Expenditure at Minor Head Level Without Authorisation; ₹4,91,302.81 crore Savings Including DoT ₹23,245.20 crore Underspend Despite Supplementary Demands (Union Government FY 2024-25)
overview: CAG Report No. 6 of 2026 (Chapter 4, Budgetary Management) found two structural failures in Union Government expenditure management for FY 2024-25: (1) Excess Expenditure Without Authorisation -- ₹8,637.23 crore of excess expenditure at minor/sub-head level was incurred across 16 minor/sub-heads without approval through re-appropriation or Supplementary Demands, violating GFR Rule 61 of 2017 which prohibits payment beyond budget provisions without Chief Accounting Authority approval; (2) Massive Unexplained Savings -- ₹4,91,302.81 crore in savings under 102 Grants/Appropriations (3.33 per cent of total provision), including ₹23,245.20 crore (14.99 per cent) under the Department of Telecommunications Grant alone -- despite DoT having obtained Supplementary Demands of ₹23,476.69 crore specifically for additional needs that year. Four grants each saw savings exceeding ₹30,000 crore, suggesting systemic budgetary unrealism rather than prudent spending management.

source.quote: We found excess expenditure of Rs. 25 crore or more aggregating to Rs. 8,637.23 crore in FY 2024-25 under 16 minor/sub-heads relating to nine Grants and two Appropriations, attributable to inadequate provisioning of funds through re-appropriations/Supplementary Demands

source.quote: We observed savings of Rs. 5,000 crore or more at Grant/Appropriation level in 19 Grants/Appropriations during FY 2024-25, aggregating to Rs. 4,17,825.75 crore and constituting 85.04 per cent of the total savings of Rs. 4,91,302.81 crore under 102 Grants/Appropriations

keyFindings.text: A Department of Telecommunications obtained Supplementary Demands of Rs. 23,476.69 crore mid-year -- Parliament's emergency budget approval mechanism -- and then underspent by Rs. 23,245.20 crore (99.02 per cent of what it sought in Supplementary Demands). Obtaining Supplementary Demands for amounts that are never spent is a misuse of Parliament's approval process: it creates a false picture of spending urgency and, once approved, diverts parliamentary attention away from the original budget grants.

source.quote: Audit observed that there were savings of Rs. 23,245.20 crore (14.99%) under Grant no. 13-Department of Telecommunications... including Supplementary provisions of Rs. 23,476.69 crore

keyFindings.text: Rs. 8,637.23 crore in excess expenditure was incurred across 16 minor heads without any of the required re-appropriation or Supplementary Demand approvals. GFR Rule 61 prohibits payments beyond budget provisions without Chief Accounting Authority sign-off. The Government's own response to CAG was that figures had been "verified and found correct" -- confirming the excess rather than explaining how it was authorised.

source.quote: We found excess expenditure of Rs. 25 crore or more aggregating to Rs. 8,637.23 crore in FY 2024-25 under 16 minor/sub-heads... attributable to inadequate provisioning of funds through re-appropriations/Supplementary Demands

recommendations: PFMS should block expenditure processing at minor-head level once 100 per cent of sanctioned provision is consumed -- the ₹8,637.23 crore excess would not have been possible if the payment system enforced the budget ceiling automatically rather than relying on officer compliance.

Parliament's Public Accounts Committee should review all Supplementary Demand grants where savings exceed 50 per cent of the Supplementary Demand obtained -- DoT's pattern (99 per cent underspent) suggests either false urgency in seeking Supplementary Demands or expenditure planning failure, and both require correction before the next budget.

ministry: Commercial Taxes Department, Government of Karnataka
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (Chapter II -- SSCA Construction Services Major Cases)
title: Compliance Audit -- ₹21.82 crore GST Short Levy in 5 Construction Services Cases: JDA Taxable Value Depressed ₹111.59 crore, Wrong Time-of-Supply Rate, Advance Accounting Gap
overview: CAG audit of Karnataka's SSCA on Works Contract and Construction Services (Report No. 3 of 2026) found ₹21.82 crore in GST short levy across 5 major cases: (1) JDA apartment handover undervaluation -- ₹20.09 crore: a works contractor handed over apartments to a landowner under a JDA at a notional ₹1,000 per sq. ft., while simultaneously selling identical apartments to third parties at ₹4,840 per sq. ft. in the same project. By applying ₹1,000 instead of Open Market Value ₹4,840 per sq. ft. to 2,90,610 sq. ft. of taxable area, the taxpayer suppressed taxable value by ₹111.59 crore and underpaid GST by ₹20.09 crore (18 per cent); (2) Time-of-supply wrong rate -- ₹86.90 lakh: the departmental audit used an outdated 2018 property rate (₹3,079/sq. ft.) instead of the prevailing 2021 market rate (₹4,500/sq. ft.) for valuing construction services rendered to the landowner, leaving ₹4.83 crore undervalued and ₹86.90 lakh GST unpaid; (3) Advance accounting short declaration -- ₹65.31 lakh: a taxpayer's financial statements showed ₹13.54 crore in advances received but only ₹7.45 crore was declared in GST returns, leaving ₹5.44 crore in advances (net of tax) undeclared and ₹65.31 lakh in GST unpaid.

The GST law requires valuation at Open Market Value for non-monetary consideration -- but the contractor used the 1/5th notional price, suppressing taxable value by Rs. 111.59 crore and underpaying Rs. 20.09 crore in GST. recommendations: For JDA transactions with non-monetary consideration (land share for flat share), mandate that LGSTO officers obtain comparables of third-party apartment sales by the same developer in the same project from the sub-registrar database before accepting any valuation -- the ₹111.59 crore under-valuation would have been immediately visible from the same project's registered sale deeds.

Add a mandatory field in the ASMT-02 audit order template requiring the ACCT to certify the date of the OMV reference and confirm that the reference matches the time-of-supply date -- using a 3-year-old rate as OMV for a 2021 transaction should fail this certification.

ministry: Commercial Taxes Department, Government of Karnataka
title: Compliance Audit -- 19 of 34 GST Taxpayers Using Legacy Service Tax Codes (00440XXX) Instead of GST SAC-9954; ₹97.34 lakh Compliance Deficiencies (Karnataka)
overview: CAG audit (Chapter II Para 2.4.8, Report No. 3 of 2026) found that 19 of 34 sampled works contract/construction services taxpayers in Karnataka were still declaring their GST services using outdated legacy service tax codes (00440XXX) from the pre-GST era instead of the correct GST Service Accounting Codes (SAC 9954XX). This code mismatch prevents the GSTN system from correctly identifying and monitoring works contract taxpayers -- DGARM risk analytics and LGSTO scrutiny functions depend on SAC-code-based filtering, and returns filed with legacy codes fall outside these monitoring mechanisms. As a result, 29 cases from the 34-taxpayer sample generated ₹97.34 lakh in compliance deficiencies that went undetected: ₹86.55 lakh in ITC mismatches and service code issues, ₹5.92 lakh in additional lapses, ₹3.40 lakh in penalty non-levy, and ₹1.46 lakh in interest short-demand. LGSTOs were updating codes only after CAG notification -- 16 cases still awaited final reply as of September 2025.

keyFindings.text: Over 55 per cent of sampled works contract taxpayers in Karnataka were still using legacy pre-GST service tax codes (00440XXX) to declare their GST transactions -- 7+ years after GST launched in 2017. This is not a taxpayer error but a systemic failure: the GSTN provisional registration process migrated many pre-GST assesses without updating their SAC codes, and LGSTOs never corrected them. DGARM risk analytics and LGSTO scrutiny systems use SAC code as the primary filter for monitoring construction services compliance, meaning these 19+ taxpayers were effectively invisible to automated monitoring.

source.quote: in 19 out of the sample of 34 taxpayers continued to declare their services using outdated service tax codes relating to legacy tax regime (00440XXX) rather than the correct SAC codes related to works contract or construction services (9954XX) in GST regime

keyFindings.text: Karnataka LGSTOs acted on SAC code correction only after CAG notification -- even then, 16 of 19 notified cases had no final resolution by September 2025. The Department's inability to pro-actively update its own registration database means that a systemic data quality issue that corrupts DGARM analytics and compliance monitoring continues to exist without a correction timeline.

source.quote: updated the new SAC-9954 code in the Registration certificate in one case, endorsements were issued for non-core amendment for updating of SAC codes in two cases and final reply was awaited in the remaining 16 cases

recommendations: GSTN should run a one-time mass migration query to identify all active registered taxpayers whose SAC codes begin with 00440XXX (legacy service tax codes) and auto-flag them for LGSTO correction with a system-imposed 30-day deadline -- the data cleanup is a one-time technical operation, not a case-by-case manual process.

DGARM risk reports and LGSTO scrutiny workflows must add a legacy-code filter: any GSTR return filed with SAC codes beginning 00440XXX should auto-generate a data quality alert to the LGSTO to update registration before processing scrutiny.

ministry: Commercial Taxes Department, Government of Karnataka
title: Compliance Audit -- ₹1.60 crore GST Interest Not Demanded from Late Filers (97 of 400 Sampled Cases), LGSTOs Failing to Follow Up on ASMT-13 Interest (Karnataka)
overview: CAG audit of Karnataka GST enforcement for works contract/construction services taxpayers (Chapter II Para 2.4.10, Report No. 3 of 2026) found systematic failure to levy and collect interest on late GST filers: Audit selected the top 20 cases of late filers from 5 LGSTOs for each year from 2020-21 to 2023-24 (400 cases total) under SAC-9954. In 97 of the 400 cases, LGSTOs levied no interest despite delayed GSTR-3B filing and late payment -- ₹1.60 crore in interest was not demanded. Additionally, Audit examined 67 taxpayers to whom Best Judgment Assessment Orders (ASMT-13) were issued (272 tax periods) -- 15 taxpayers across 43 GSTR-3B returns (September 2020 to January 2024) had not paid or short-paid interest on delayed tax due to late filing, totalling ₹7.06 lakh in non-payment not followed up. The systemic cause: GSTN's Demand, Collection and Balance (DCB) statement does not capture Section 50 interest demand notices, preventing LGSTOs from tracking whether demanded interest was actually paid.

stats.label: Interest not demanded from late GST filers (97 of 400 cases, 5 LGSTOs)

source.section: Chapter II Para 2.4.10.1 -- Late Filer Interest
source.quote: Audit noticed that in 97 of the 400 cases, no interest was levied despite delayed filing and payment in GSTR-3B returns. The total interest not demanded was Rs. 1.60 crore

stats.label: Interest not paid post ASMT-13 (15 taxpayers, 43 returns, Sep 2020-Jan 2024)

source.quote: Fifteen taxpayers, across 43 monthly GSTR-3B returns for the tax periods from September 2020 to January 2024, had not paid or short paid interest on delayed payment of tax, due to late filing of returns. The total interest not paid amounted to Rs. 7.06 lakh

stats.label: Interest collected post-audit intervention (38 of 97 non-demand cases)
stats.value: ₹0.43 crore collected; 27 cases with recovery action initiated

stats.label: Systemic gap -- GSTN DCB not capturing Section 50 interest demands
stats.value: No system-based module to track demand from notice to recovery

source.quote: When a notice is issued demanding interest under Section 50, it does not get reflected in the taxpayer's Electronic Balance (DCB) statement at the field level. In the absence of a system-based module to capture Demand, Collection and Balance (DCB) statement

keyFindings.text: Karnataka LGSTOs failed to levy interest in 97 of 400 sampled late-filer cases (24.25 per cent) despite GST Prime generating monthly Late Filer Analytic Reports specifically to prompt this action. The LGSTOs received the data -- they were subscribed to GST Prime reports -- but did not act on it. Rs. 1.60 crore in mandatory interest was foregone because officers received the information and did nothing with it.

source.quote: To assist in monitoring of late filers, GST Prime generates an Analytic Report Late Filers each month... Audit noticed that in 97 of the 400 cases, no interest was levied despite delayed filing and payment in GSTR-3B returns. The total interest not demanded was Rs. 1.60 crore

keyFindings.text: GSTN's Section 50 interest demand notices do not appear in the taxpayer's DCB (Demand, Collection and Balance) statement -- creating a structural tracking gap where LGSTOs cannot see whether demanded interest was actually paid without manually checking each case. This design flaw means that even when LGSTOs do issue interest demands, there is no automatic follow-up trigger if payment is not received.

source.quote: When a notice is issued demanding interest under Section 50, it does not get reflected in the taxpayer's Electronic Balance (DCB) statement at the field level. In the absence of a system-based module to capture Demand, Collection and Balance (DCB) statement

recommendations: GSTN must integrate Section 50 interest demand notices into the taxpayer's DCB statement -- this is a system design change that would make interest recovery automatically trackable by LGSTOs without manual case-by-case follow-up.

Karnataka should activate an automated Section 50 interest assessment for all late GSTR-3B filings where the delay is system-detected -- the GSTN already knows which returns are late; auto-assessment notices for interest should be generated within 7 days of late filing without requiring officer action.

ministry: Commercial Taxes Department, Government of Karnataka
title: Compliance Audit -- ₹1.60 crore from Deficient GST Return Scrutiny: ₹71.27 lakh Excess ITC, ₹45.77 lakh Non-realised Revenue, Incomplete ASMT-10 Notices (Karnataka)
overview: CAG audit of Karnataka GST scrutiny operations for works contract taxpayers (Chapter II Para 2.4.9, Report No. 3 of 2026) found ₹1.60 crore in revenue at risk or foregone due to deficient return scrutiny. Under Section 61 of the KGST Act, LGSTOs must scrutinise GSTR returns and issue notices (ASMT-10) for discrepancies. Audit found that in 12 cases, scrutiny was incomplete -- ASMT-10 notices were issued but discrepancies identified in those notices were not captured in the scrutiny notices, meaning the discrepancies went unaddressed. Specific findings from scrutiny: (1) Excess ITC claims of ₹71.27 lakh in six cases; (2) Under-declaration of tax liability of ₹40.67 lakh in one case; (3) Non-levy of penalty/interest of ₹2.25 lakh in two cases; (4) Non-realisation of revenue of ₹45.77 lakh due to lack of follow-up on underpaid tax. Total from scrutiny deficiencies: ₹1.60 crore. Only ₹2.99 lakh was collected in three cases after audit intervention.

keyFindings.text: LGSTOs in Karnataka issued ASMT-10 notices for GST return discrepancies but then failed to capture those discrepancies in the scrutiny notices themselves -- meaning the notices were effectively blank on the specific violations. In 12 cases, the discrepancies were identified but the notices issued did not contain them, rendering the scrutiny process procedurally complete but substantively empty.

source.quote: in 12 cases, scrutiny of Returns was incomplete. Although ASMT-10 had... discrepancies were not captured in the scrutiny notices

keyFindings.text: Only Rs. 2.99 lakh of the Rs. 1.60 crore at risk from scrutiny deficiencies was collected before CAG intervened -- a 1.9 per cent recovery rate from a process specifically designed to identify and recover under-paid tax. The scrutiny function consumed officer time and generated paperwork but produced virtually no revenue, reflecting a compliance exercise done for form rather than substance.

source.quote: underpaid tax, amounted to Rs. 1.60 crore... Rs. 2.99 lakh was collected in three cases

recommendations: GSTN should be requested to make ASMT-10 a structured form with mandatory fields for each discrepancy type (excess ITC, under-declaration, etc.) -- officers should be unable to submit an ASMT-10 without specifying the discrepancy and the amount; free-form blank notices should be rejected by the system.

Mandate that all scrutiny cases with identified revenue implications above ₹1 lakh must be escalated to adjudication within 45 days of ASMT-10 issuance; the current pattern of non-realisation (₹45.77 lakh) after notice issuance shows that notice without time-bound adjudication is meaningless.

ministry: Stamps and Registration Department, Government of Karnataka
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (Chapter III Para 3.4 -- Special Instructions Undervaluation)
title: Compliance Audit -- ₹4.05 crore Stamp Duty Short Levy: Enhancement Factors Not Applied (Highway Proximity, Commercial Conversion, Residential Conversion, Sital Rates)
overview: CAG audit of Karnataka Sub-Registrar Offices (Chapter III, Report No. 3 of 2026) found ₹4.05 crore in Stamp Duty and Registration Fee short levy from systematic non-application of enhancement factors prescribed in the Market Value Guidelines Special Instructions. Four distinct sub-categories were identified: (1) Highway/road proximity enhancement not applied -- 11 cases in 8 SROs where properties abutting National Highways, Ring Roads, State Highways, and 100-foot roads were not given the prescribed 50 per cent, 35 per cent, or 30 per cent enhancement, causing ₹0.84 crore short levy; (2) Commercial conversion enhancement not applied -- 8 cases where converted commercial lands used residential rates, causing ₹1.42 crore short levy; (3) Residential conversion enhancement not applied -- 8 cases where unconverted residential land rates were used for developed parcels, causing ₹0.78 crore short levy; (4) Sital rates not applied/incorrect sital rates -- 5 cases where specific approved site rates were available but general agricultural rates were used, causing ₹0.65 crore short levy. Government confirmed ₹38.47 lakh was recovered in 3 cases after audit notice.

stats.label: Total undervaluation from non-adherence to Special Instructions

source.quote: The overall short levy in Stamp Duty and Registration Fees in all the above cases was Rs. 4.05 crore. The lapses primarily arose from non-application or incorrect application of enhancement factors, incorrect categorization of land use, and failure to adopt prescribed sital or specific rates

stats.label: Highway/road proximity enhancement not applied (11 cases, 8 SROs)
stats.value: ₹0.84 crore (National Highways 8 cases, State Highway 1, 100-foot road 2)

source.quote: In 11 cases in eight SROs, prescribed enhancements were not applied though the properties were abutting National Highways/Ring Roads (eight cases), State Highway (one case), and 100 feet Road (two cases) leading to short levy of SD and RF of Rs. 0.84 crore

stats.label: Commercial conversion enhancement not applied (8 cases, 5 SROs)

source.quote: In six cases in five SROs, enhancement for commercial purpose was omitted though the properties were converted for commercial purposes... These cases resulted in a short levy of SD and RF of Rs. 1.42 crore

stats.label: Residential conversion enhancement not applied (8 cases, 5 SROs)

source.quote: In eight cases across five SROs, residential site rates as prescribed were not considered for valuation resulting in short levy of SD and RF of Rs. 0.78 crore

The Government replied that Rs. 38.47 lakh was recovered in three cases and in the remaining cases the District Registrars have issued notices to the parties concerned under Section 46A

keyFindings.text: The Karnataka Market Value Guidelines contain explicit enhancement tables for road proximity, land-use conversion, and site classification -- these are not discretionary, they are prescribed percentages that must be applied by SROs. Yet across 32 cases and multiple SROs, enhancement factors prescribed as mandatory by the Special Instructions were simply ignored. The systematic nature across different categories (highways, commercial, residential, sital) and different SROs indicates institutional ignorance of the enhancement rules, not individual error.

source.quote: The lapses primarily arose from non-application or incorrect application of enhancement factors, incorrect categorization of land use, and failure to adopt prescribed sital or specific rates. These not only resulted in revenue loss to the Government but also point to weaknesses in oversight mechanisms in the registration process

keyFindings.text: KAVERI registration software does not auto-apply road proximity, land-use conversion, or sital enhancements -- Sub-Registrars must manually calculate and apply them. This human-in-the-loop design is the structural root of these valuation failures. Automating enhancement application in KAVERI based on property coordinates, road proximity data from BBMP/BDA, and land use from Bhoomi would eliminate all four sub-categories of undervaluation in this finding.

source.quote: Automate valuation processes within the KAVERI software to minimise human discretion and prevent revenue leakage. Generate alerts where multiple instruments involving the same property or parties are registered, to flag potential undervaluation or duty evasion

recommendations: Integrate KAVERI with BBMP/BMRDA/BDA road network GIS data: when a property address is entered, the system should automatically compute proximity to National Highways, Ring Roads, State Highways, and 80-foot roads, and apply the applicable enhancement percentage without Sub-Registrar input.

Integrate KAVERI with Bhoomi land-use conversion records: when a survey number is entered, the system should auto-fetch conversion status (agricultural, residential, commercial, industrial) from Bhoomi and apply the applicable enhancement rate, flagging any manual override for District Registrar review.

ministry: State Excise and Transport Departments, Government of Karnataka
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (Chapter IV Para 4.1, Chapter V Para 5.1)
title: Compliance Audit -- Internal Audit Wings Collapsed: State Excise Zero Audits Since 2017-18 (480 Cases ₹16.39 crore Pending), Transport No Audits in 2022-23/2023-24 (540 Observations ₹36.76 crore Unsettled)
overview: CAG Report No. 3 of 2026 found that internal audit functions in two major Karnataka revenue departments have completely collapsed: (1) State Excise Internal Audit Wing (IAW) -- has conducted zero audits since 2017-18 (more than 7 years). Of the 471 offices due for audit in 2023-24, not a single one was audited, attributed to staff shortage. As of 2017-18, 480 cases involving ₹16.39 crore were pending; no data exists for the years since because no audits were conducted; (2) Transport Department IAW -- conducted no internal audits in 2022-23 or 2023-24. As of 31 March 2022, 540 observations involving ₹36.76 crore remained unsettled, and this position continued unchanged through 31 March 2024 because no new audits added to or resolved the backlog. Both IAWs represent the first line of departmental self-correction; their effective non-existence means all compliance failures in these departments escape detection until CAG audit -- a cycle that guarantees annual revenue leakage.

stats.label: State Excise offices due for IAW audit in 2023-24 (audited: zero)

source.section: Chapter IV Para 4.1 -- State Excise IAW
source.quote: none of the 471 offices due for audit in 2023-24 were audited due to the shortage of staff in the Wing

stats.label: State Excise IAW pending cases (last recorded -- 2017-18)

keyFindings.text: Karnataka's State Excise IAW has conducted zero audits for over 7 years (2017-18 to 2024-25) -- the entire department operates with no first-line financial oversight. The CAG discovered Rs. 27.48 crore in deficiencies in a test-check of just 8 offices in 2023-24; the IAW would have detected these deficiencies before revenue was lost, but it does not function. The Government's explanation of staff shortage is a systemic excuse that has been accepted for 7+ years without resolution.

source.quote: the activities of IAW in the Department are almost nil in the last five years... none of the 471 offices due for audit in 2023-24 were audited due to the shortage of staff in the Wing

keyFindings.text: The Transport Department's 540 unsettled IAW observations representing Rs. 36.76 crore have been pending since 2022 -- two years later, the exact same number of observations at the exact same money value remain outstanding, because no internal audit activity has occurred to either add new observations or settle existing ones. This is a complete institutional paralysis: money owed to the State that nobody is pursuing.

source.quote: As of 31 March 2022, 540 observations involving Rs. 36.76 crore remained unsettled, and position continued to be the same at the end of 2023-24. The non-conduct of internal audit in the recent years indicates that the Department has not accorded due importance to this function

recommendations: Treat IAW non-functioning as a governance failure reportable to the Finance Minister and Chief Secretary -- staff shortage cannot be the perpetual excuse for a function that has produced zero output for 7 years in Excise. Immediate secondment from other departments or outsourced internal audit must be arranged within 90 days.

The 540 Transport Department IAW observations worth ₹36.76 crore should be transferred to a special recovery cell under the Transport Commissioner with monthly settlement targets; the fact that this backlog is unchanged across two complete financial years indicates that no official has accountability for its clearance.

ministry: Department of Labour, Government of Karnataka (ESIS)

title: Compliance Audit -- ESIS: ₹4.03 crore Suspected Misappropriation (Sanction Order Manipulation), ₹7.74 crore Medical Equipment Idle in 7 Hospitals (Karnataka)
overview: CAG audit of Employee State Insurance Scheme (ESIS) implementation in Karnataka (Chapter II, Report No. 1 of 2026) found two categories of serious financial failure: (1) Suspected misappropriation of ₹4.03 crore -- manipulation of sanction orders for medical reimbursement claims under ESIS. Sanction orders were altered to enable payment to different amounts and payees than authorised; (2) Idle investment of ₹7.74 crore -- the Director, ESIS, Bengaluru procured lab equipment (June 2021) and medical equipment (February 2023) including Digital Radiography Systems and Mammograph X-ray machines costing ₹7.74 crore. As of March 2024, these machines remained uninstalled in all seven ESIS hospitals because the required infrastructure was not provided. Additionally, ₹5.30 crore was spent on a project taken up without any need assessment, rendering the expenditure unfruitful. The audit found ESIS Karnataka plagued by low bed occupancy rates, ICU unavailability, NSQ drug distribution, and a telemedicine portal that remained underutilized -- systemic failures that increased patient referrals to expensive tie-up hospitals.

Medical reimbursement manipulation is a well-documented fraud pattern in ESI; Karnataka's internal audit and the ESIC's own vigilance mechanisms failed to detect it before CAG intervention.

keyFindings.text: ESIS Karnataka spent Rs. 7.74 crore on diagnostic equipment for its hospitals -- equipment that sat in boxes or open yards for up to 3 years while the hospitals continued referring patients to costly tie-up private hospitals for diagnostic tests. The procurement was completed without ensuring installation infrastructure (civil works, power supply, AC systems) was ready -- a basic project management failure that completely negated the purpose of the purchase.

source.quote: these machines remained uninstalled in all seven ESIS hospitals as the infrastructure required for installation was not provided... Digital Mammography equipment worth Rs. 3.27 crore pending installation in ESI Hospital, Indiranagar

recommendations: Conduct a forensic audit of all medical reimbursement sanction orders above ₹1 lakh for the last 5 years; implement digital sanction orders with immutable audit trails (preventing post-signature modification) and dual-authorization for all disbursements above ₹10,000.

Before procurement of any capital medical equipment above ₹25 lakh, the ESIS must obtain a signed infrastructure readiness certificate from the hospital superintendent confirming civil works, electrical supply, and dedicated room are complete -- no purchase order should be issued without it.

Recover the ₹4.03 crore suspected misappropriation amount through departmental proceedings; file FIR if sanction order manipulation is confirmed by a forensic examination of original versus altered documents.

ministry: Departments of Higher Education and Revenue, Government of Karnataka
title: Compliance Audit -- ₹5.72 crore Interest Liability from Delayed Polytechnic Takeover, ₹2.96 crore Avoidable Interest from Land Acquisition Delay (Karnataka)
overview: CAG audit of Karnataka (Chapter II, Report No. 1 of 2026) found two separate interest liability failures: (1) Increased interest liability ₹5.72 crore from delay in taking over SGES Rural Polytechnic, Hubballi -- the Government issued formal takeover orders in December 2010 converting the institution to Government Polytechnic, Tarihal, acknowledging outstanding dues; however, the outstanding liabilities were not settled promptly after takeover, and the delay in settlement caused ₹5.72 crore in accumulated interest; (2) Avoidable interest ₹2.96 crore from DC Hassan land acquisition delays -- the District Collector, Hassan failed to promptly initiate payment of court-enhanced compensation from the dates of applications under Section 28(A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Court-enhanced compensation carries mandatory interest from the date of the Section 28(A) application; the DC's delay in processing these applications caused ₹2.96 crore in avoidable interest to accrue on compensation that the Government was ultimately liable to pay anyway.

stats.label: Increased interest liability from delayed polytechnic takeover (SGES/Tarihal)

source.quote: Increased interest liability due to delay in taking over Polytechnic - outstanding dues - 5.72 crore

stats.label: Avoidable interest from DC Hassan land acquisition delay (Section 28A applications)

source.section: Chapter II Para 2.8 -- Land Acquisition Interest
source.quote: The inability of DC Hassan in promptly initiating the payment of court-enhanced compensation from the dates of applications under Section 28(A) of Land Acquisition Act, 1894 resulted in avoidable interest to the extent of Rs. 2.96
