keyFindings.text: The Government formally acknowledged the outstanding liability of the SGES Rural Polytechnic when it issued takeover orders in December 2010 -- the liability was not a surprise. Yet the dues remained unsettled for years after the formal government takeover, during which interest on the outstanding principal compounded to Rs. 5.72 crore. The interest was entirely avoidable: had the Government settled the acknowledged dues at the time of takeover, no interest would have accrued.

source.quote: a committee was formed by DTE... Based on the Committee's recommendations, the DTE submitted a proposal to the Government... while acknowledging a liability of crore to be settled. Subsequently, the Government issued orders... to take over the college as Government Polytechnic, Tarihal officially

keyFindings.text: Land acquisition claimants who successfully obtain court-enhanced compensation under Section 28(A) of the Land Acquisition Act are entitled to interest from the date of their application -- not from when the government chooses to process it. DC Hassan's failure to initiate payment promptly after court orders meant the interest clock kept running on public funds, resulting in Rs. 2.96 crore of avoidable expenditure that benefited neither the State nor the claimants.

source.quote: The inability of DC Hassan in promptly initiating the payment of court-enhanced compensation from the dates of applications under Section 28(A) of Land Acquisition Act, 1894 resulted in avoidable interest to the extent of Rs. 2.96

recommendations: All acknowledged liabilities at the time of institutional takeover must be settled within 90 days of the Government takeover order -- establish this as a standard condition in all future institution-takeover orders and monitor compliance through the Education Department Finance Wing.

KAVERI/Revenue portal should auto-generate a 30-day escalation alert to DC/Collector when a court-enhanced compensation order under Section 28(A) is received but payment has not been initiated -- the current process relies entirely on manual follow-up by the office, creating the conditions for delay.

ministry: Commercial Taxes Department, Government of Karnataka
title: Compliance Audit -- ₹7.28 crore GST Short Levy: KREIS TDS Cross-verification Reveals Turnover Under-reporting and Wrong Rate Post-January 2022 Revision
overview: CAG used Karnataka Residential Educational Institutions Society (KREIS) TDS data (filed as GSTR-7) as a third-party benchmark to verify GST compliance of 28 works contractors. Cross-verification uncovered ₹7.28 crore in short tax collection that the Department had not detected through routine processing: (1) Turnover under-reporting -- 8 taxpayers (10 cases) declared construction services taxable value lower than payments received from KREIS per GSTR-7, with ₹7.37 crore total mismatch indicating ₹90.34 lakh potential tax shortfall; (2) Incorrect tax rate post-GST revision -- GST on works contract services to Government Authorities was revised from 12 per cent to 18 per cent effective 1 January 2022, but 9 contractors continued to discharge tax at 12 per cent. A single LGSTO-LTU Bengaluru taxpayer supplied ₹87.07 crore to Government entities in February-March 2022 at the pre-revised 12 per cent rate, resulting in ₹5.22 crore short payment. In aggregate, incorrect rate application caused ₹6.38 crore in short tax. The discrepancy between KREIS-disbursed amounts and taxpayer GSTR-3B filings was not detected in real time because the Department had no mechanism to cross-reference TDS filers' GSTR-7 data against their suppliers' GST returns.

This was not a sampling anomaly: it represents a structural blind spot in the Department's compliance monitoring system.

source.quote: The discrepancy between actual payments disbursed by KREIS and the turnover filed by the taxpayers went undetected in real time by the tax Authorities

keyFindings.text: Nine contractors continued to pay GST at 12 per cent on works contracts with Government Authorities well after the January 2022 upward revision to 18 per cent -- earning Rs. 6.38 crore in effective tax savings by not updating their rate. LGSTOs had access to these GSTR-3B filings but did not flag the continued application of the pre-revised rate, which was identifiable from the service codes alone.

source.quote: nine contractors continued to pay tax at the pre-revised rate of 12 per cent instead of the applicable 18 per cent. This application of incorrect rate resulted in short payment of tax of Rs. 6.38 crore

recommendations: Automate monthly cross-matching of GSTR-7 TDS filers' payment data against the corresponding suppliers' GSTR-1/3B turnover in the GST portal -- any month where a supplier's declared turnover is less than GSTR-7 amounts received should auto-generate a system alert to the LGSTO.

Build a rate-change compliance check into the GSTR-3B filing portal: when a taxpayer applies a rate that was revised after the filing period, the system should flag it with a warning popup citing the effective date and revised rate; adjudication action on any such flagged returns should complete within 60 days.

ministry: Department of Higher Education, Government of Karnataka
reportNo: Report No. 1 of 2026 (Chapter II -- Irregular GIA to Private Universities)
title: Compliance Audit -- ₹146.23 crore Irregular Grants-in-Aid Released to Two Ineligible Private Universities (Constituent Colleges Post-University Act Conversion)
overview: CAG found that two Grants-in-Aid (GIA) colleges in Karnataka, which had been constituent colleges receiving Government financial assistance, became part of two Private Universities during 2015-16 under their respective University Act provisions. Under the University Acts, constituent colleges absorbed into a private university are no longer eligible for Government Grants-in-Aid -- they become part of a private entity and the Government's GIA obligation ceases. However, the Department of Higher Education continued to release GIA to these two institutions even after they ceased to be GIA-eligible institutions, disbursing ₹146.23 crore in irregular financial assistance after their conversion. The continued disbursement indicates that neither the Department nor the Finance Department cross-checked university conversion status against the active GIA beneficiary list before releasing funds -- a compliance failure that persisted across multiple budget cycles and annual GIA releases.

stats.label: Irregular GIA released to two ineligible private universities post-conversion

source.section: Chapter II -- Irregular GIA to Private Universities

keyFindings.text: Rs. 146.23 crore in taxpayer money flowed to two private universities as Grants-in-Aid after those universities' constituent colleges became part of a private university -- a status change that, per the applicable University Act, disqualified them from GIA. The Department continued releasing funds across multiple financial years without verifying whether the receiving institutions remained GIA-eligible, a failure that no annual audit check or inter-departmental verification caught until CAG intervention.

source.quote: Two Grants-in-Aid (GIA) colleges became part of two Private Universities during 2015-16 and they were not eligible to receive GIA from the Government as per provisions of the University Act. However, the Government continued to release GIA amounting to Rs. 146.23 crore

keyFindings.text: The Rs. 146.23 crore was released in the form of GIA -- salary grants and non-salary grants to the teaching and non-teaching staff of these colleges. While the individual beneficiary teachers and staff may not have been aware of the legal ineligibility, the bulk financial transfer from the State exchequer to private university accounts was an avoidable subsidy to private entities that had voluntarily exited the GIA framework through their choice to join a private university.

source.quote: Two Grants-in-Aid (GIA) colleges became part of two Private Universities during 2015-16 and they were not eligible to receive GIA from the Government as per provisions of the University Act. However, the Government continued to release GIA amounting to Rs. 146.23 crore

recommendations: Create a mandatory annual reconciliation between the active GIA beneficiary list and the University Grants Commission / State University list: any college that becomes a constituent of a private university must be automatically removed from GIA rolls in the same financial year as conversion.

Recover ₹146.23 crore from the two private universities under the applicable provisions of the GIA conditions -- private universities that received ineligible government grants are financially enriched institutions that can be required to return the ineligible disbursements.

Institute a Finance Department pre-release check: before GIA disbursement to any college above ₹10 crore, confirm with the Higher Education Department that the institution still holds GIA-eligible status under the current University Act.

ministry: Stamps and Registration Department, Government of Karnataka
reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (Chapter III -- Sale Agreement/POA Misclassification)
title: Compliance Audit -- ₹18.84 crore Stamp Duty Short Levy: Sale Deeds Misclassified as Agreements, POA Misclassification, MoU Used to Avoid Duty (Karnataka)
overview: CAG audit of Karnataka Sub-Registrar Offices (Chapter III, Report No. 3 of 2026) found ₹18.84 crore in Stamp Duty and Registration Fee short levy across three categories of document misclassification: (1) Sale deeds executed with Power of Attorney were presented as mere agreements and charged at lower rates under Article 5(e)(ii) -- the POA coupled with possession delivery and covering the same property triggered Article 5(e)(i) (conveyance rate of five per cent) but SROs missed the Explanation-I deemed possession clause, causing ₹16.19 crore in short levy in two cases; (2) Further incorrect sub-article classification of sale agreements with POAs caused ₹2.52 crore short levy; (3) A high-value Sale Agreement of land was registered as a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), attracting only ₹1,000 nominal duty instead of ad valorem stamp duty on the full property value, causing ₹0.13 crore short levy. All three categories reflect systematic inadequacy of SRO document scrutiny beyond the face title.

source.quote: duty was charged at lower rates under Article 5(e)(ii) leading to short levy of stamp and Registration Fee of Rs. 2.52 crore... The correct levy of duty including Registration Fee works out to Rs. 16.19 crore whereas only Rs. 20,000 was levied for each document. The short levy of stamp duty and Registration Fee on the two documents works out to Rs. 16.19 crore

stats.label: Sale Agreement with POA sub-article short levy (Article 5(e)(i) vs 5(e)(ii) misclassification)

source.quote: Powers of Attorney were executed by the same parties for same properties mentioned in the corresponding Sale Agreements... duty was charged at lower rates under Article 5(e)(ii) leading to short levy of stamp and Registration Fee of Rs. 2.52 crore

stats.label: Sale Agreement of land registered as MoU (₹1,000 duty instead of ad valorem)

source.quote: Sale Agreement misclassified as MoU leading to short levy of Stamp and Registration Fee... it was charged a nominal duty of Rs. 1,000, resulting in short levy of stamp duty and Registration Fee of Rs. 0.13 crore

stats.label: Total Sale Agreement/POA misclassification short levy

source.quote: Total Short levy of Stamp Duty and Registration Fee in all the cases works out to Rs. 18.84 crore

keyFindings.text: Two high-value sale deed transactions in Karnataka were charged maximum Rs. 20,000 in stamp duty (the cap for agreements) instead of five per cent on the full property value (conveyance rate) -- losing Rs. 16.19 crore on just two documents. The documents included Power of Attorney executed by the same parties for the same property, triggering the deemed-possession clause of Explanation-I under Article 5(e), which mandates conveyance-rate stamp duty. SROs missed this mandatory legal linkage between the sale agreement and the POA.

source.quote: The correct levy of duty including Registration Fee works out to Rs. 16.19 crore whereas only Rs. 20,000 was levied for each document. The short levy of stamp duty and Registration Fee on the two documents works out to Rs. 16.19 crore

keyFindings.text: A high-value land Sale Agreement was registered as a Memorandum of Understanding, paying just Rs. 1,000 in nominal stamp duty. MoUs are not conveyances and are not subject to ad valorem stamp duty under KSA -- but this document, when examined beyond its title, clearly constituted a Sale Agreement for land transfer that requires ad valorem treatment. SROs registering documents by title alone rather than examining their substance enable this form of stamp duty evasion.

source.quote: Sale Agreement misclassified as MoU leading to short levy of Stamp and Registration Fee... it was charged a nominal duty of Rs. 1,000, resulting in short levy of stamp duty and Registration Fee of Rs. 0.13 crore

recommendations: Mandate that KAVERI flag any document presented as an Agreement or MoU where the same parties have simultaneously presented a Power of Attorney for the same property -- the co-registration pattern is the triggering condition for Explanation-I deemed-possession, and the system can detect it automatically.

Require Sub-Registrar signature on a checklist confirming: (a) Article classification verified beyond document title, (b) Explanation-I deemed-possession check completed, (c) co-registered POA reviewed before charging Agreement-rate duty.

All cases with total short levy above ₹1 crore must be reviewed by the District Registrar before registration is completed -- the two ₹16.19 crore cases are exactly the scenario that a secondary review gate would catch.

title: Compliance Audit -- ₹14.10 crore Stamp Duty Short Levy by Suppression of Land Status, Mislabelled Agreements to Sell, and Misreported Survey Numbers (Karnataka)
overview: CAG audit of Karnataka Stamps and Registration (Chapter III, Report No. 3 of 2026) found ₹14.10 crore in Stamp Duty and Registration Fee short levy through suppression of material facts in documents: (1) Land status suppression -- ₹11.22 crore: documents registered as agricultural land or general plots when the khata and revenue records clearly showed them to be converted/approved sites, which attract higher guidance rates; SROs did not cross-check the actual status in revenue records; (2) Agreement to Sell used to avoid conveyance stamp duty -- ₹2.18 crore: parties executed formal "Agreement to Sell" documents for fully completed transactions (possession transferred, full consideration paid) and paid capped ₹20,000 instead of five per cent ad valorem conveyance duty; (3) Misreported survey numbers, missing sital rates, and non-adherence to road-proximity enhancements -- ₹0.70 crore. keyFindings.text: Rs. 11.22 crore in stamp duty was lost because documents presented land as agricultural/general when VAHAN and revenue records (khata) showed it had already been converted and approved by development authorities. SROs registered documents based on what was written rather than cross-referencing the actual status in the online Revenue portal (Bhoomi/KAVERI integration) -- a verification that takes minutes but was systematically skipped.

source.quote: Short levy due to suppression of the actual status of the land Rs. 11.22 crore... All the above omissions resulted in the short levy of SD and RF of Rs. 11.22 crore

keyFindings.text: Rs. 2.18 crore was lost through parties executing formal "Agreement to Sell" documents on properties where possession had already transferred and full consideration was paid -- the classic stamp duty evasion mechanism. A completed transaction structured as an Agreement avoids ad valorem conveyance duty by paying only Rs. 20,000 maximum. SROs did not examine possession and consideration clauses to detect completed conveyance disguised as agreement.

source.quote: Agreement to avoid higher duty. This led to short levy in SD and RF of Rs. 2.18 crore

recommendations: Integrate KAVERI with Bhoomi (land records) and BBMP/BDA/Panchayat conversion records so that when a property survey number is entered, its actual status (agricultural, converted, layout, approved site) auto-populates and the applicable guidance rate is selected without SRO discretion.

Flag any Agreement to Sell document where (a) consideration exceeds ₹50 lakh, (b) possession is stated as delivered, or (c) the same parties appear in a prior Occupancy Certificate -- these three conditions together constitute the profile of a completed conveyance structured as an agreement.

Require District Registrar review of all land status suppression cases found by Audit; issue demand notices under Section 46A of the Karnataka Stamp Act for the ₹14.10 crore; currently only ₹7.57 lakh (0.5 per cent) has been recovered despite the audit observations being reported.

reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (Chapter III -- Joint Development Agreements)
title: Compliance Audit -- Joint Development Agreements: ₹32.82 crore Stamp Duty Short Levy (99 Cases, 29 SROs) -- Layouts ₹5.27 crore, Apartments ₹27.55 crore (Karnataka)
overview: CAG audit of Joint Development Agreements (JDAs) registered under the Karnataka Stamp Act, 1957 found ₹32.82 crore in Stamp Duty and Registration Fee short levy across 99 cases in 29 Sub-Registrar Offices (SROs) -- out of 2,066 JDAs audited (from 5,168 registered). Under Article 5(f) and 41(ea) of the KSA, JDA Stamp Duty is payable at two per cent on the market value of the developer's share in land or the owner's share in the developed property, whichever is higher. Two broad categories of under-levy were found: (1) Layout development -- 43 cases in 17 SROs where incorrect guideline rates (village panchayat rates instead of higher authority-approved rates) were applied for site valuation, causing ₹5.27 crore short levy; (2) Apartment development -- 56 cases in 20 SROs where the Floor Area Ratio (FAR, needed to compute total built-up area for valuation) was mentioned in only 33 of 56 documents, and SROs failed to requisition FAR data from the developer or approving authority before computing stamp duty, causing ₹27.55 crore in short levy.

keyFindings.text: Karnataka SROs consistently applied lower village panchayat guidance rates for layout sites approved by BDA/BMRDA/BIAAPA -- even though the Market Value Guidelines explicitly prescribe higher values for authority-approved sites. 43 cases across 17 SROs show this is a systemic misapplication, not an individual error, pointing to either inadequate SRO training or deliberate under-assessment.

source.quote: incorrect guideline rates were applied for valuing such sites resulting in short levy in SD and RF of Rs. 5.27 crore

keyFindings.text: In 23 of 56 apartment JDA cases, the Floor Area Ratio was not mentioned in the document -- the single figure needed to compute the developer's share and thus the correct stamp duty base. SROs registered and stamped these documents without requisitioning FAR data from approving authorities, leaving Rs. 27.55 crore in stamp duty un-levied. The KAVERI registration software did not flag the missing data field.

source.quote: the FAR to determine the total built-up area was mentioned only in 33 cases... Rs. 27.55 crore

keyFindings.text: Audit sampled only 40 per cent of registered JDAs (2,066 of 5,168) and found Rs. 32.82 crore in short levy. Extrapolating to all 5,168 JDAs, the systemic under-levy could be Rs. 80+ crore -- representing one of the largest single categories of stamp duty leakage in Karnataka's rapidly growing real estate sector.

source.quote: An Audit of 2,066 JDAs (out of 5,168 JDAs registered) across 29 Sub-Registrar Offices (SRO) upto March 2023, revealed 99 instances of short levy of Stamp Duty and Registration Fee aggregating to Rs. 32.82 crore

recommendations: Update KAVERI software to flag JDA registrations where FAR is blank or zero -- the system should refuse to complete registration unless FAR is entered or an override note is recorded by the Sub-Registrar with documentary justification.

Publish and enforce a circular distinguishing BDA/BMRDA/authority-approved site rates from village panchayat rates in the Market Value Guidelines; train SROs to cross-reference the type of approval authority before selecting the applicable guideline rate.

Conduct a full audit of the remaining 3,102 JDAs not covered in this report; given the 4.8 per cent deficiency rate found, even a conservative extrapolation suggests ₹50+ crore in additional recoverable short levy.

reportNo: Report No. 3 of 2026 (Chapter III -- Mortgage and UDS Undervaluation)
title: Compliance Audit -- Mortgage Deed Misclassification ₹6.69 crore, UDS Undervaluation ₹9.00 crore, Commercial Enhancement Non-application ₹6.42 crore (Karnataka Stamps)
overview: CAG audit of Sub-Registrar Offices in Karnataka (Chapter III, Report No. 3 of 2026) identified three distinct categories of stamp duty undervaluation: (1) Mortgage by Deposit of Title Deeds misclassified as Agreements to Deposit -- 12 cases in 6 SROs where documents clearly recording actual deposit of title deeds with sale-on-default covenants were wrongly assessed under Article 6 (0.2 per cent) instead of Article 34(b) (0.5 per cent), causing ₹6.69 crore short levy; (2) Undivided Share (UDS) undervaluation in conveyance deeds -- cases where commercial usage enhancement (40 per cent prescribed) was not applied, causing ₹9.00 crore in short levy across two Bengaluru SROs; (3) Non-application of commercial usage enhancement to one sale deed -- property valued at ₹243.39 crore instead of ₹340.68 crore (₹97.30 crore undervaluation) causing ₹6.42 crore Stamp Duty short levy. Following KSA amendments aligning Article 6 rates with Article 34(b), future mortgage misclassification revenue risk has been eliminated -- but the ₹6.69 crore from past cases remains recoverable.

Consequently, the scope for loss of revenue due to such misclassification in the future has been eliminated

keyFindings.text: In 12 mortgage cases, the deposited title deeds contained explicit default-sale covenants -- the defining feature of a mortgage under Section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act. SROs classified them as agreements instead of mortgages despite this explicit language, halving the applicable stamp duty. All 12 documents clearly satisfied every legal criterion for mortgage classification; the misclassification reflects either SRO ignorance of the legal distinction or deliberate under-assessment.

source.quote: documents explicitly recorded the deposit of original Title Deeds... included covenants enabling the lender to initiate recovery, including sale of the mortgaged property, upon default... Despite fulfilling all legal criteria for classification under Article 34(b), these documents were wrongly assessed under Article 6

keyFindings.text: A single Banasawadi sale deed for a commercial property was stamped on a market value of Rs. 243.39 crore -- Rs. 97.30 crore below the correct value after mandatory 40 per cent commercial enhancement. The Special Instruction No. 05 enhancement is prescribed in the Market Value Guidelines and leaves no discretion; the SRO's failure to apply it resulted in Rs. 6.42 crore in lost stamp duty on one transaction.

source.quote: The document was valued at Rs. 243.39 crore, instead of the correct enhanced value of Rs. 340.68 crore. This resulted in undervaluation of Rs. 97.30 crore and consequent short levy of Stamp Duty and Registration Fee of Rs. 6.42 crore

recommendations: Update KAVERI to flag documents containing terms "deposit", "security", "title deed", "default" and "sale on default" as potential Mortgages by Deposit -- requiring Sub-Registrar confirmation of classification before stamp duty computation proceeds.

Automate commercial enhancement application in KAVERI: when a sale deed involves property zoned commercial in SRO records, the 40 per cent enhancement must be applied automatically and require explicit override with reasoning if a lower value is submitted.

Issue demand notices under Section 46A of the Karnataka Stamp Act for all 12 mortgage misclassification cases and UDS undervaluation cases; the Government has acknowledged the findings and notices have been issued -- ensure recovery is monitored quarterly.

ministry: Transport Department, Government of Karnataka
title: Compliance Audit -- 75 Per Cent DSA Cases Pending Over a Year, Offenders Freely Renewing FC and Permits, ₹46.61 lakh Overloading Fine Non-levy (Karnataka)
overview: CAG audit of Karnataka Transport Department enforcement activities (Chapter V paras 5.4.7.2-5.4.7.3, Report No. 3 of 2026) found that Departmental Statutory Action (DSA) cases -- booked for MV Act violations including overloading, expired permits, and FC violations -- are systematically not being disposed of: 75 per cent of pending DSA cases are over a year old and more than 40 per cent are over three years old. In a sample of 356 DSA cases across 9 RTOs, 218 (61 per cent) were still pending disposal. Of these, 254 booked vehicles (71 per cent) continued to pay quarterly tax -- indicating active road operation -- while their cases were undisposed. 192 vehicles (53.9 per cent) even renewed their Fitness Certificates or permits after the DSA case was booked. RTOs failed to levy overloading compounding fines on 26 occasions, resulting in non-collection of ₹46.61 lakh. Second Karnataka Administrative Reforms Commission (June 2021) recommendations on enforcement technology remain unimplemented as of August 2025.

Set a 90-day maximum DSA disposal deadline with automatic escalation to Joint Commissioner after 30 days of non-response; the current situation where 40 per cent of cases are over 3 years old represents complete enforcement failure.

Enable VAHAN to automatically generate overloading compounding fine demand notices at the time of challan entry -- the non-levy of ₹46.61 lakh in compounding fines was caused by RTOs not following through, which a system-generated demand would eliminate.

ministry: Transport Department, Government of Karnataka
title: Compliance Audit -- Karnataka RTOs Process Only 3.5 Per Cent of Applications Online, 37.9 Per Cent Fees in Cash, 28.38 Per Cent SAKALA Violations
overview: CAG audit of Karnataka Transport Department service delivery (Chapter V para 5.4.8, Report No. 3 of 2026) found that despite the rollout of VAHAN 4.0 and SARATHI digital platforms, RTO services remain largely manual: only 3.5 per cent of applications were processed online, and 37.9 per cent of fees were still collected in cash. Service delivery timelines under SAKALA (Karnataka guarantee of services to citizens) were breached in 28.38 per cent of applications when measured from the date of fee receipt to approval -- far exceeding the 4.71 per cent officially reported by the Department. The discrepancy arose because the Department measured SAKALA timelines from a later "date of application" rather than from when fees were actually received. Audit reviewed 12 services across 9 RTOs and found systematic delays, with age-wise analysis showing a significant backlog.

The Department was timing SAKALA from the "date of application" (which can be backdated or delayed) rather than "date of fee receipt" (the actual service trigger), systematically masking a six-times-higher real delay rate from citizens and oversight bodies.

recommendations: The Transport Commissioner must restate SAKALA compliance metrics using "date of fee receipt" as the start time, not "date of application" -- the current method produces a fictitiously low delay rate that masks 6x the actual service failures from public disclosure.

title: Compliance Audit -- 3.88 lakh Transport Vehicles with Expired Fitness Certificates, 4.70 lakh Without Valid Permits, 9.32 lakh Without Speed Governors (Karnataka)
overview: CAG audit of Karnataka's Transport Department (Chapter V, paras 5.4.4-5.4.5, Report No. 3 of 2026) found systemic road safety and regulatory enforcement failures: 3,87,831 transport vehicles had Fitness Certificates expire between April 2019 and March 2024 without renewal -- of which 20,557 vehicles (5.3 per cent) continued to pay quarterly tax even after FC expiry, implying active on-road operation. None of the 9 sampled RTOs had Automated Testing Stations (ATS); 6 had no testing facility at all; FCs were being issued by manual inspection alone. 9,32,012 transport vehicles manufactured before 1 October 2015 had no Speed Limiting Device UIN recorded in VAHAN -- meaning Fitness Certificates were issued without verifying mandatory speed governor installation. One-third of all transport vehicles requiring a permit (4,70,028 of 14,01,202) had no valid permit as of 31 March 2024.

keyFindings.text: 20,557 transport vehicles with expired Fitness Certificates continued to pay quarterly tax -- strong evidence they were actively on the road while legally unfit for operation. recommendations: Block quarterly tax acceptance in VAHAN for any transport vehicle with an expired FC -- if a vehicle cannot legally operate, it should not be able to pay road tax. This single system change would expose 20,000+ illegally operating vehicles.

Make speed governor UIN a mandatory field in VAHAN's FC renewal workflow for all pre-2015 transport vehicles -- the FC issuance screen must fail validation if no UIN is entered, ensuring manual inspectors cannot bypass the requirement.

Mandate ATS installation at all 67 RTOs within 18 months, with phased timelines and funding; FC issuance from RTOs without ATS should trigger automatic review by the Joint Commissioner to prevent manual inspection subjectivity.

Of 24 taxpayers sampled by CAG for audit, 19 (79 per cent) did not produce records to Audit despite statutory provisions mandating their availability; data analysis of these 19 cases revealed potential revenue risks of ₹1.75 crore even without physical records. A systemic deficiency in the GSTN auto-interest computation system allowed 21 taxpayers across 97 cases to modify auto-populated interest figures, resulting in ₹33.81 lakh in interest non-payment that no LGSTO flagged for rectification. The low 8.2 per cent departmental audit recovery rate indicates either inadequate follow-up by adjudicating authorities or poor acceptance of observations.

The 91.8 per cent non-recovery is not just an administrative failure: it represents Rs. 102.98 crore in acknowledged tax dues that the State has failed to collect.

The fact that even without documents, data analysis found Rs. 1.75 crore in risks suggests the actual non-compliance would be far higher with complete records.

keyFindings.text: GSTN auto-populated interest computation -- introduced in February 2022 to reduce manual evasion of interest liability -- was being defeated: 21 taxpayers across 97 cases modified the auto-computed figures or made other payments to bypass interest. LGSTOs took no action to report the GSTN system bug to NIC or GSTN; the issue remains unaddressed.

recommendations: Mandate that all Section 65 departmental audit demand notices above ₹1 crore be escalated to adjudication within 90 days of issue -- the current backlog with 8.2 per cent recovery proves that observation issuance without time-bound follow-up is ineffective.
Invoke Section 70 of the KGST Act (power to summon) for taxpayers who deny records to Audit -- failure to produce statutory records is an offence and cannot be permitted to nullify audit proceedings.

Report the GSTN interest auto-computation bypass vulnerability to CBIC/NIC immediately; implement a system lock that prevents filing unless interest liability is cleared, or auto-debit the interest from the next refund claim.

ministry: Transport Department, Government of Karnataka
title: Compliance Audit -- Green Tax Short Collection ₹9.80 crore, Quarterly Tax Penalty Non-levy ₹4.45 crore, PSV Lease Tax ₹82.63 lakh (Karnataka Transport)
overview: CAG audit of Karnataka Transport Department (Chapter V paras 5.4.6.1-5.4.6.3, Report No. 3 of 2026) found: (1) Green Tax of ₹9.80 crore was short-collected from transport vehicles renewing Fitness Certificates between April 2019 and March 2024 -- RTOs computed arrears incorrectly, applying reduced rates instead of the arrears method specified under the KMVT Act; additionally ₹3.80 lakh in Green Tax was not levied at all on 1,901 vehicles; (2) Quarterly tax penalty of ₹4.45 crore was not demanded or collected by RTOs from transport vehicles that paid quarterly tax late -- VAHAN flagged the defaults but RTOs took no collection action; (3) 76 PSVs (32 per cent of 238 checked) at 4 RTOs were held under company lease agreements but taxed at lower Item 8 rates instead of higher Item 8-A rates, causing short collection of ₹82.63 lakh; and (4) RTOs allowed unauthorized tax breaks of ₹16.80 lakh from transport vehicles without the mandatory prior approval under Section 16/Rule 34.

keyFindings.text: Karnataka RTOs were computing Green Tax arrears incorrectly -- instead of applying the flat Rs. 200 per annum cess on vehicles that failed to pay during FC renewal, RTOs applied concessional rates, causing Rs. 9.80 crore in systematic under-collection across the State over five years (2019-24). The same deficiency was systemic across multiple RTOs, suggesting either a VAHAN configuration error or deliberate leniency.

source.quote: as against Green Tax... Rs. 9.80 crore. The RTO wise details of the number of vehicles for which Green Tax was not levied/collected are given in Appendix-5.15

keyFindings.text: VAHAN automatically flags transport vehicles with delayed quarterly tax payments and calculates the 20 per cent penalty due -- yet RTOs across Karnataka collected none of the Rs. 4.45 crore in penalties that their own system had already computed and flagged. The data was in the system; the enforcement decision was deliberate inaction.

source.quote: penalty at the rate of 20 per cent... was not levied and collected by the RTOs. The total amount of penalty applicable in these cases amounted to Rs. 4.45 crore

keyFindings.text: Karnataka has two different quarterly tax rates for PSVs -- higher rates (Item 8-A) for vehicles leased to companies for employee transport vs. lower rates (Item 8) for other PSVs -- but GoK never prescribed a form for documenting these lease agreements. Without a dedicated form, VAHAN cannot distinguish Item 8 from Item 8-A vehicles, and RTOs are taxing company-leased PSVs at the lower public rate, losing Rs. 82.63 lakh.

source.quote: GoK did not prescribe any specific form or return for reporting vehicle lease agreements with industrial undertakings or companies... This resulted in short collection of quarterly tax including cess, amounting to Rs. 82.63 lakh

recommendations: Fix the VAHAN Green Tax computation module to apply ₹200 per annum per vehicle as a mandatory arrear during all FC renewals -- the current incorrect formula has caused ₹9.80 crore in under-collection over 5 years and will continue to compound until corrected.

Enable VAHAN to automatically generate penalty demand notices when a transport vehicle's quarterly tax goes unpaid beyond the first month of a tax period -- the current system flags defaults but takes no action; add an auto-notice trigger.

Prescribe a mandatory Form 34-A (or equivalent) for recording PSV operational lease agreements with companies; update VAHAN to capture Item 8-A categorization at registration for leased fleet vehicles.

ministry: Transport Department, Government of Karnataka
title: Compliance Audit -- Quarterly Tax Arrears, Road Safety Cess Non-collection and Lifetime Tax Short-levy, Karnataka Transport Department
overview: CAG audit of Karnataka's Transport Department (Chapter V, Report No. 3 of 2026, paras 5.4.6.4-5.4.6.6) found accumulated quarterly tax arrears of ₹258.96 crore from 40,171 transport vehicles in default across 9 sampled RTOs -- default periods ranging from 1 quarter to 10 years, with 7,833 vehicles over 20 years old. Road Safety Cess of ₹4.68 crore was not collected from 73,290 vehicles statewide, including 16,355 Electric Vehicles (22 per cent) incorrectly exempt from RSC. Additionally, short collection of Lifetime Tax of ₹50.49 lakh was identified due to incorrect vehicle age and undervalued sale price. Despite accumulated arrears, no systematic Revenue Recovery Certificate proceedings were initiated; of 40,171 defaulters, RRC was initiated only for 5,065 vehicles and ₹7.62 lakh was recovered in 11 cases.

stats.note: Default periods range from 1 quarter to 10 years; 7,833 vehicles over 20 years old still in arrears

initiated RRC proceedings against 5,065 vehicles only and recovered an amount of Rs. 7.62 lakh in case of 11 vehicles till the date of audit

keyFindings.text: Karnataka Transport Dept allowed Rs. 258.96 crore in quarterly vehicle tax to accumulate over decades across 9 RTOs without systematic Revenue Recovery Certificate enforcement: only 5,065 of 40,171 defaulters had RRC initiated, and only Rs. 7.62 lakh was actually recovered in 11 cases -- a recovery rate of 0.003 per cent of arrears.

source.quote: initiated RRC proceedings against 5,065 vehicles only and recovered an amount of Rs. 7.62 lakh in case of 11 vehicles till the date of audit

keyFindings.text: Karnataka was not collecting Road Safety Cess from Electric Vehicles on the mistaken premise that the MV Tax exemption for EVs also covers RSC -- but RSC and MV Tax are levied under separate Acts and the RSC exemption notification does not cover EVs. This error alone costs Rs. 83.07 lakh per year in the 9 sampled RTOs.

source.quote: Exemption from Motor Vehicle Tax and levy of Road Safety Cess are governed by separate Acts. Hence, RSC is applicable to electric vehicles as well, similar to other types of vehicles

keyFindings.text: Vehicles detained by RTOs for compliance violations were physically deteriorating in RTO compounds for years -- out of a backlog of hundreds of detained vehicles, only 129 were auctioned across 8 RTOs as a result of a November 2024 drive, with "work in progress" at the remaining offices.

source.quote: detained vehicles were not being maintained properly resulting in deterioration of their condition day-by-day... prolonged non-disposal of these vehicles reflects inadequate enforcement of statutory provisions and weak monitoring by the taxation authorities

recommendations: Automate RRC initiation in VAHAN for any transport vehicle with more than two quarters of unpaid tax -- the 0.003 per cent recovery rate on ₹258.96 crore arrears demonstrates that the manual RRC process is effectively non-functional.

Issue an immediate circular clarifying that Road Safety Cess applies to all EVs regardless of MV Tax exemption; enable VAHAN to generate RSC demand notices automatically for all eligible vehicle classes at time of registration and renewal.

Set a 90-day maximum holding period for detained vehicles and require RTOs to auction or dispose of vehicles beyond that period -- the current open-ended detention converts enforcement into a liability for the State.

ministry: Public Health Engineering Department / Jal Nigam, Government of Madhya Pradesh
reportNo: Report No. 5 of 2026 (Chapters III-IV Execution Compliance)
title: JJM Execution Irregularities -- Liquidated Damages, Royalty, Cost Inflation, and Community Contribution Failures, Madhya Pradesh
overview: CAG Performance Audit on JJM in Madhya Pradesh (Report No. 5 of 2026, Chapters III-IV) uncovered systemic execution compliance failures: only ₹8.46 crore of ₹95.92 crore leviable Liquidated Damages (LD) was withheld, leaving ₹87.46 crore unrecovered from contractors who delayed delivery of water supply schemes. FHTC excess cost over original estimates reached ₹586.67 crore across 8 test-checked districts. Royalty on sand and metal was not deducted from contractor bills -- ₹3 crore undue benefit to Jal Nigam contractors and ₹12.90 lakh short-deducted by PHED. Community contributions of ₹241.74 crore were collectable but only ₹27 lakh (0.01 per cent) was actually collected from beneficiaries. SQC firm paid avoidable ₹9.38 crore for extended project period attributable to contractor delays. Estimates were inflated by ₹3.75 crore (wrong cement grade) and ₹5.41 crore in other items.

stats.label: Liquidated Damages not imposed on delayed contractors
stats.note: Only ₹8.46 crore (8.8%) of ₹95.92 crore leviable LD actually withheld; contractors delayed schemes by up to 1,971 days without consequence

source.quote: Against the total leviable LD of Rs. 95.92 crore, only Rs. 8.46 crore was withheld (against Rs. 64.54 crore). This resulted in non/short imposition of LD of Rs. 87.46 crore

stats.note: Per-FHTC cost exceeded ₹1 lakh in 106 SVSs; highest ₹3.28 lakh per connection -- far beyond national JJM benchmarks

source.quote: resulted in undue financial benefit amounting to Rs. three crore to the contractors

stats.label: Avoidable SQC expenditure due to contractor delays
stats.note: Jal Nigam paid SQC firm for extended project supervision period caused by contractor delays -- LD not enforced while supervisory costs escalated

source.quote: Nigam has paid avoidable expenditure amounting to Rs. 9.38 crore to SQC for the extended

stats.label: Estimate inflation (incorrect cement grade M-30 used for CC road work)
stats.note: PHED used higher M-30 concrete grade instead of the specified standard in estimates, artificially inflating project costs

source.quote: M-30 for CC road work, resulted in inflated estimation amounting to Rs. 3.75 crore

keyFindings.text: LD enforcement in JJM-MP collapsed: contractors delayed schemes by up to 1,971 days and only 8.8 per cent of leviable penalties were withheld. Jal Nigam simultaneously paid Rs. 9.38 crore to a supervision quality consultant for the same extended period -- the cost of contractor failure fell on taxpayers, not contractors.

source.quote: Against the total leviable LD of Rs. 95.92 crore, only Rs. 8.46 crore was withheld (against Rs. 64.54 crore). This resulted in non/short imposition of LD of Rs. 87.46 crore

keyFindings.text: JJM community sustainability was hollow in MP: the scheme mandates beneficiaries contribute to ensure local ownership of water schemes, but only Rs. 27 lakh of Rs. 241.74 crore (0.01 per cent) was collected -- meaning 99.99 per cent of expected beneficiary contribution was never recovered and the state bore the full cost.

source.quote: GPs/VWSCs/PHED had collected only Rs. 27 lakh against the recoverable amount of Rs. 241.74 crore towards community contribution

keyFindings.text: Royalty on sand and metal -- a mandatory deduction from contractor bills under MP rules -- was systematically not deducted by Jal Nigam, providing Rs. 3 crore in undue financial benefit to contractors at the cost of state mining revenues.

source.quote: resulted in undue financial benefit amounting to Rs. three crore to the contractors

recommendations: Mandate automatic LD deduction from every running account bill for any scheme running beyond deadline -- manual approval for LD waiver defeats the penalty mechanism entirely.

Community contribution collection must be a pre-condition for scheme commissioning -- schemes must not be handed over to VWSCs unless at least 50 per cent of the mandatory contribution is collected, with the balance secured by a bank guarantee.
Royalty deduction should be built into the ERP/billing system as a mandatory line item -- the No-Royalty-Due Certificate must be a system-verified gateway, not a paper formality.

ministry: Commercial Taxes Department, Government of Karnataka
title: Subject Specific Compliance Audit -- Works Contract and Construction Services under GST, Karnataka (CAG Report No. 3 of 2026)
overview: CAG Subject Specific Compliance Audit of Works Contract/Construction Services under GST in Karnataka (Chapter II, Report No. 3 of 2026) covering 34 taxpayers, 24 under Detailed Audit, 5 LGSTOs and 10 departmentally audited. Audit found 205 compliance deficiencies with a revenue implication of ₹33.34 crore -- 187 deficiencies (₹32.85 crore) were accepted by the Department. Nine contractors of Karnataka Residential Educational Institutions Society (KREIS) continued paying GST at the old 12 per cent rate after the Government revised the rate to 18 per cent from 01 January 2022, resulting in short payment of ₹6.38 crore. Eight contractors mis-declared taxable turnover against KREIS payments, causing a potential tax shortfall of ₹90.34 lakh. Audit further found five cases with ₹21.82 crore undervaluation of construction services. Departmental audit formations failed to maintain mandatory Assessee Master Files, Audit Plans, and Verification Reports as required by the GST Audit Manual.

source.quote: audit findings emanating from this SSCA on Works Contract and Construction services comprised 205 compliance deficiencies involving an amount of Rs. 33.34 crore
Out of these compliance deviations the department accepted 187 deficiencies with revenue implication of Rs. 32.85 crore

stats.label: Short payment of GST -- KREIS contractors used pre-revised 12% rate after GoI revised to 18%

source.quote: nine contractors of KREIS continued to pay tax at older rates despite revision of tax rates for Government Authorities, resulting in short payment of tax of Rs. 6.38 crore

stats.label: Turnover mismatch (KREIS GSTR-7 vs contractors GSTR returns, 8 cases)
stats.value: ₹90.34 lakh potential shortfall (₹7.37 crore turnover mismatch)

source.quote: the taxable value declared by the contractors was less than the consideration reported by KREIS, indicating short declaration of turnover. The total mismatch amounted Rs. 7.37 crore, leading to a potential tax shortfall of Rs. 90.34 lakh

stats.label: Works contract service undervaluation (5 cases, departmental audit sample)

source.quote: Audit observed five cases of compliance deficiencies specifically related with the works contract services, with a revenue implication of Rs. 21.82 crore due to undervaluation of construction services, under declaration of construction services, short accounting of Advances

stats.label: GST Audit Manual compliance -- Assessee Master Files / Audit Plans maintained

source.quote: GST Audit Manual as Assessee Master Files, Audit Plan and Verification Report were not maintained

keyFindings.text: Nine KREIS contractors continued to remit GST at 12 per cent on Government-authority construction services for at least two billing cycles after the GoI revised the applicable rate to 18 per cent from 01 January 2022 -- one contractor alone short-paid Rs. 5.22 crore on Rs. 87.07 crore worth of services; Karnataka Commercial Taxes detected none of these failures without CAG prompting.

source.quote: nine contractors of KREIS continued to pay tax at older rates despite revision of tax rates for Government Authorities, resulting in short payment of tax of Rs. 6.38 crore

keyFindings.text: 205 compliance deficiencies across just 34 taxpayers -- an average of 6 deficiencies per taxpayer -- indicates that the Karnataka GST audit framework for works contractors is systematically ineffective. The department accepted 187 of the 205 findings (91 per cent), confirming these were not contested.

source.quote: audit findings emanating from this SSCA on Works Contract and Construction services comprised 205 compliance deficiencies involving an amount of Rs. 33.34 crore. Out of these compliance deviations the department accepted 187 deficiencies with revenue implication of Rs. 32.85 crore

keyFindings.text: Departmental GST audit formations in Karnataka did not maintain Assessee Master Files, Audit Plans, or Verification Reports -- the basic documentation required by the GST Audit Manual -- meaning audit coverage of works contractors was conducted without evidence trails and accountability mechanisms.

source.quote: GST Audit Manual as Assessee Master Files, Audit Plan and Verification Report were not maintained

recommendations: The Commercial Taxes Department must build automatic GST rate-revision alerts into the GSTN reconciliation system -- any taxpayer still remitting at a superseded rate after 60 days of the revision date should trigger a compliance notice without requiring manual audit.

Cross-verification of contractor turnover with KREIS/government-authority GSTR-7 data must become a standard monthly reconciliation, not an ad hoc audit exercise -- the ₹7.37 crore turnover mismatch found by CAG was visible in publicly available GST data.

Departmental audit formations must mandatorily complete Assessee Master Files before beginning any Section 65 audit -- the absence of these records makes findings unenforceable and damages revenue recovery prospects in adjudication proceedings.

ministry: Roads and Buildings Department, Government of Gujarat
title: Compliance Audit -- Roads and Buildings Department, Gujarat (Paras 3.6-3.10, CAG Report No. 1 of 2026)
overview: CAG Compliance Audit of Gujarat's Roads and Buildings Department (April 2017 -- March 2024) found irregular/excess payment of Price Variation of ₹4.74 crore across 11 R&B works (incorrect indices, ineligible items, period and ceiling violations); ₹2.40 crore bonus paid to a contractor for early completion after the Division itself extended the project deadline; ₹2.21 crore cost overrun due to non-finalisation of tenders within bid validity period; ₹1.62 crore avoidable expenditure from road widening at 99 curves beyond IRC norms; and ₹83.05 lakh electricity charges not recovered from Airport Authority of India Surat plus ₹62.39 lakh in avoidable electricity payments.

keyFindings.text: Gujarat R&B Division paid Rs. 2.40 crore in "early completion" bonus to a contractor -- after the Division itself proposed and extended the project completion deadline, making the "early completion" premise factually incorrect.

source.quote: The R&B Division proposed and extended the project completion timeline after the date of completion of the work and paid bonus of 2.40 crore to the contractor for early completion

keyFindings.text: Five R&B Divisions paid Price Variation to contractors using incorrect indices (interchanging cement and steel indices), ineligible items (labour and POL not permitted under 2022 GR), periods before the 12-month lock-in, and without capping at 5% ceiling -- total irregular/excess payment Rs. 4.74 crore.

source.quote: overpayment of PV of 3.40 crore to the Contractor in 10 works... PV paid for Labour and POL... 2022 Resolution, which permitted for payment of PV for material only

keyFindings.text: Road widening at 99 horizontal curves was designed beyond the extra widening permitted by IRC:38-1988 -- the Division spent Rs. 1.62 crore widening roads more than mandated technical standards required, with the excess neither justified by IRC:SP:73-2018 as claimed.

source.quote: the Division incurred an avoidable excess expenditure of 1.62 crore

recommendations: Mandate independent PV computation verification by the Circle/SE office before payment is released for any work above ₹1 crore -- the current Division-level calculation has produced systematic errors in ceiling, indices, and eligible period.

Remove "early completion bonus" authority from Division level; all such bonuses must be reviewed by a superintending engineer to confirm the contractor actually completed early relative to an unextended schedule.

Install a bid validity calendar alert in GISS/CPMS that flags expiry 45 days before deadline and escalates non-finalized tenders to SE level automatically -- the cost overruns from expired validity are preventable administrative failures.

ministry: Home Department, Government of Gujarat
title: Compliance Audit -- Storage and Disposal of Seized Narcotic Drugs, Gujarat (Para 3.14)
overview: CAG Compliance Audit (Para 3.14 of Gujarat CA Report No. 1 of 2026) found that Gujarat's Home Department failed to establish secure storage facilities for seized narcotic drugs, resulting in theft of 144.18 kg of Cannabis from evidence stores, destruction of drugs by rats and moisture loss, and a 35 per cent shortfall between seized (6,510.54 kg, 848 bottles in 17 cases) and actually disposed drugs (4,177.86 kg). Some drug lots were retained for up to three decades before disposal, directly contravening Supreme Court orders and Ministry of Finance instructions. Drug disposal percentages across cases ranged from 11.99 per cent to 93.21 per cent of seized quantities.

source.quote: various drug enforcement agencies had seized 6,510.54 kg and 848 bottles of narcotic drugs and controlled substances in 17 cases between August 2010 and November 2022

stats.label: Shortfall in drugs disposed vs seized
stats.value: 35 per cent (4,177.86 kg of 6,510.54 kg disposed)

source.quote: significant variation (35 per cent) in the actual quantity disposed (4,177.86 kg) between October 2022 and July 2023 vis-a-vis quantity of the drugs seized (6,510.54 kg)

stats.label: Cannabis stolen from government evidence stores

source.quote: Theft of nearly 144.180 kg of Cannabis (Ganja)
the drugs seized and the drugs disposed which ranged between 11.99 per cent to 93.21 per cent
prolonged retention of drugs for periods extending up to three decades and significant shortfall in quantities ultimately disposed

keyFindings.text: Gujarat's ADGP (CID Crime and Railways) office admitted that 144.18 kg of Cannabis was stolen from government evidence storage -- a catastrophic chain-of-custody failure that violates NDPS Act provisions and directly contradicts Supreme Court orders on narcotic drug storage and disposal.

source.quote: Theft of nearly 144.180 kg of Cannabis (Ganja), Destruction by rats due to lack of proper storage facilities, and Drying out of the green plants of Cannabis (Ganja) and Opium, and loss of moisture in Poppy Straw

keyFindings.text: Narcotic drug lots seized as early as 2010 were retained for up to three decades before disposal -- Supreme Court orders require timely disposal of seized drugs to prevent deterioration, theft, and diversion; Gujarat ignored this for 30 years in some cases.

source.quote: prolonged retention of drugs for periods extending up to three decades... persistent and widespread non-compliance with instructions Ministry of Finance and the directions of the Honble Supreme Court for storage and disposal of seized narcotic drugs

keyFindings.text: Gujarat attributed the 35 per cent shortfall in drug disposal (2,332 kg unaccounted) to moisture loss and rat destruction -- but in the absence of specific guidelines for acceptable weight loss limits, CAG noted these losses lacked justification.

source.quote: In the absence of specific guidelines regarding acceptable limits of weight loss due to evaporation and weather factors, the loss attributed to such reasons lacked justification

recommendations: Establish dedicated, secure, CCTV-monitored narcotic evidence stores in all district offices -- rat and moisture destruction of 2+ tonnes of evidence is a systemic storage failure, not acceptable force majeure.
Implement a 90-day mandatory disposal protocol for all NDPS seizures pending court order, as per Supreme Court directions; 30-year retention of narcotic evidence is inexcusable.
Conduct an independent CBI/SIT investigation into the 144.18 kg Cannabis theft from ADGP's evidence stores; theft of scheduled narcotic substances from government custody is a criminal matter.

ministry: Forest and Environment Department, Government of Gujarat
title: Compliance Audit -- Forest Diversion and NPV Levies in Gujarat (Paras 3.11-3.13, CAG Report No. 1 of 2026)
overview: CAG Compliance Audit of Gujarat's Forest Department (April 2015 -- March 2024) found road widening projects executed inside Wildlife Sanctuaries and National Parks without mandatory NBWL approval; 21.43 hectares of forest land diverted in Reserved and Protected Forests without MoEFCC prior permission; Non-Agricultural activity permissions granted inside Eco-Sensitive Zones in violation of PA Zone Notifications; and ₹1.16 crore short levy of Net Present Value plus ₹2.94 crore short levy of Compensatory Afforestation across four DCF offices due to incorrect application of NPV multipliers and rates.

stats.label: Forest land diverted without MoEFCC permission (RF/PF projects)

source.quote: 21.43 Ha of Forest land was diverted without taking prior permission of MoEF&CC

stats.label: NPV short levy -- incorrect categorisation/rates (4 DCF offices)

source.quote: short levy of Net Present Value of 1.16 crore due to incorrect categorization of forest or adoption of incorrect rates

stats.label: Compensatory Afforestation short levy (incorrect Right of Way)

source.quote: short levy of Compensatory Afforestation amount of 2.94 crore due to adoption of incorrect Right of Way for the afforestation

stats.label: NPV short levy -- GETCO Navsari (incorrect Eco-Class)

source.quote: application of NPV rate for Open Forest instead of Dense Forest for the land diverted in Dang South Division was incorrect, resulting in short levy of NPV of 2.76 lakh

stats.label: NPV short levy -- Marine National Park Jamnagar (incorrect NPV multiplier)

source.quote: incorrect application of NPV MF resulted in short levy of 9.13 lakh

keyFindings.text: Road widening projects were executed inside Wildlife Sanctuaries and National Parks without prior approval of the National Board for Wildlife (NBWL) -- a mandatory requirement under Sections 29 and 35 of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 -- and 21.43 ha of Reserved/Protected Forest was diverted without MoEFCC permission.

source.quote: 21.43 Ha of Forest land was diverted without taking prior permission of MoEF&CC

keyFindings.text: GETCO Navsari applied the NPV rate for "Open Forest" for land that audit confirmed was "Dense Forest" (152 trees/ha vs 58 trees/ha threshold) -- a typology error causing Rs. 2.76 lakh short levy; the Marine National Park DCF applied NPV multiplier 5 instead of mandatory multiplier 10 for Protected Forest within a National Park.

source.quote: the number of trees required to be cut per hectare in the forest under Dang North Division was 152 while that in the Dang South Division was 58. As such, both these areas fell under the category of Dense Forest

keyFindings.text: Non-Agricultural activity permissions were granted inside Eco-Sensitive Zones of Protected Areas in violation of PA Zone Notifications, with some District Collectors granting NA permissions without NOC from the Forest Department or granting permissions exceeding the scope of the NOC.

source.quote: certain cases the District Collector had either granted NA permission without NOC from the Forests Department, or the NA permissions were not commensurate with the NOCs granted

recommendations: Mandate NBWL clearance as a hard pre-condition in VAHAN/GIMS before any road project is registered in Wildlife Sanctuary or National Park boundaries.
Audit all 48+ identified cases of NA permissions in ESZs and PA peripheries for compliance with Zone Notification distance restrictions; initiate recovery of irregularly-granted permissions.

Standardise NPV computation: require DCFs to run a second-check on Eco-Class categorisation against the Tree Density Register before issuing demand notes, to prevent NPV multiplier errors like GETCO Navsari.

ministry: Energy and Petrochemicals Department (Directorate of Petroleum), Government of Gujarat
title: Compliance Audit -- Petroleum Royalty, Mining Receipts and Police Escort Charges, Gujarat (Paras 3.15-3.16)
overview: CAG Compliance Audit of Gujarat's Directorate of Petroleum (DoP) found ₹1.54 crore in royalty short payments by nine Petroleum Mining Lease (PML) holders who computed royalty using crude prices below the mandatory Indian Basket benchmark; ₹0.67 crore in interest not levied on royalties paid late by five PML holders (delays up to 264 days); ₹0.89 crore in dead rent not recovered from 10 PML holders; and ₹2.51 crore in short levied Bandobast/escort charges across 590 cases from incorrect rates.

stats.label: Royalty short payment -- 9 PML holders used sub-benchmark crude price

source.quote: in case of nine PML holders the Crude price considered for Royalty calculation was less than the Price of Indian Basket of Crude Oil notified by PPAC in certain months which resulted in short payment of royalty amounting to 1.54 crore

stats.label: Interest non-levy on late royalty payments (5 lease holders, 29 PML, delays up to 264 days)

source.quote: five lease holders in cases of 29 PML paid royalty with delay ranging from five days to 264 days. However, due to lack of verification controls, the DoP did not levy interest on the late payment amounting to 0.67 crore
Non-recovery/ short recovery of dead rent and non-levy of interest on delayed payments from ten PML holders amounting to 0.89 crore

stats.label: Bandobast/escort charges short levy (590 cases, incorrect rates)

source.quote: In 590 cases, Bandobast/escort charges were levied at incorrect rates resulting in short levy of 2.51 crore
Non-raising of demand for Dead Rent and Royalty, and non-realisation of Royalty and Interest, resulted in loss of revenue of 12.92 crore

keyFindings.text: Nine Gujarat PML holders calculated petroleum royalty using crude prices below the mandatory Indian Basket benchmark set by PPAC -- a regulatory floor price specifically introduced to prevent royalty under-payment -- resulting in Rs. 1.54 crore in short-paid royalty pending recovery as of November 2025.

source.quote: in case of nine PML holders the Crude price considered for Royalty calculation was less than the Price of Indian Basket of Crude Oil notified by PPAC in certain months which resulted in short payment of royalty amounting to 1.54 crore. However, recovery of royalty of 1.54 crore and interest on its delayed payment was pending (November 2025)

keyFindings.text: Five PML holders paid royalties late (5 to 264 days) but the DoP's own records showed no reason for waiving the mandatory 200 bps penal interest over SBI PLR -- DoP replied only that "the matter has been taken up" with the lease holders, not that interest had been recovered.

source.quote: due to lack of verification controls, the DoP did not levy interest on the late payment amounting to 0.67 crore... Reason for non-levy of interest by DoP was not found on record

keyFindings.text: HDCPL (Sanganpur Mining Lease) went into liquidation in 2017 with its PSC cancelled by MoPNG -- but DoP failed to timely reconcile production/sales figures for recovery of statutory dues, exemplifying systemic monitoring gaps that persist to date.

source.quote: DoP did not timely take up reconciliation of production and sales figures for recovery of Statutory dues from HDCPL

recommendations: Automate royalty computation in DoP's system by pulling PPAC Indian Basket price directly as the floor: if a leaseholder submits ARS using a lower crude price, the system should auto-generate a differential demand.

Implement automated interest calculation on every delayed royalty payment -- the DoP currently relies on manual detection, which is why 29 cases of late payment across five leaseholders escaped interest levy.
Set a mandatory 30-day reconciliation window after PSC cancellation or leaseholder default; the HDCPL liquidation case shows that without this, years pass without recovery action.

ministry: Transport Department (Motor Vehicles), Government of Karnataka

keyFindings.text: Karnataka Government claimed 31 transport services were being provided faceless since November 2021 -- but the Parivahan national portal MIS showed only 4 faceless services active, and audit confirmed under 1 per cent of sampled RTO applications were actually processed faceless.

source.quote: While the GoK claimed that 31 services were being provided faceless since November 2021, Parivahan website MIS report only four faceless services... less than one per cent of the applications were processed faceless in VAHAN during November 2021 to March 2024

recommendations: Mandate VAHAN system blocks on FC renewal for vehicles missing Speed Limiting Device UIN -- currently the system allows renewal without this safety check.

Activate all VAHAN faceless-service modules and publish monthly RTO-wise dashboards comparing GoK claims against Parivahan MIS data.
Set a 90-day deadline for all nine sampled RTOs to migrate to cashless, online-first fee collection; 37.9 per cent cash prevalence is unacceptable five years after the digital mandate.

title: Performance Audit on ICDS and Integrated Child Protection Scheme -- Madhya Pradesh (2019-24)

AWC construction: 202 AWCs delayed; cost increase ₹6.18 crore. Interest ₹2.32 crore earned on AWC construction funds (utilisation questioned). Women Working Houses (WWHs): 9 of 13 functional at 40-50% occupancy. Child Care Institutions (CCIs): 126 CCIs; 39 audited -- staff vacancies 47-54% in 14 CCIs; 47-54% at SCPS; 29-38% at DCPU; 75% at SARA. Street children: survey in only 9 districts in 2021-22. Funds unspent 17-61%. Excess grant of ₹1.11 crore to Open Shelter; excess maintenance payment ₹1.29 crore.

keyFindings.text: 8,842 villages and urban wards in Madhya Pradesh have no Anganwadi Centre -- 16% of all habitations left without ICDS coverage. This means children under 6 in these villages receive no supplementary nutrition, no health check-up, and no early childhood education through the government system. In one of India's largest states by tribal population, this gap is especially damaging for ST communities in remote blocks.

source.quote: 8,842 villages/wards (16 per cent) out of a total 54,903 in the state lacked AWCs. This led to inadequate monitoring of scheme implementation

keyFindings.text: With 55% of DPO posts vacant and 40% CDPO posts unfilled, MP's ICDS has no functional supervision structure across a major share of its districts. AWWs -- who receive training (90.75%) but work without oversight -- cannot substitute for a monitoring system. Funds are unspent at 17-61% per year not because of complex barriers, but because supervisors to plan and authorise expenditure are absent.

source.quote: District Project Officers (55 per cent), Child Development Project Officers (40 per cent), and Supervisors (17 per cent). This led to inadequate monitoring. Funds remained unspent in range of 17 to 61 per cent

keyFindings.text: 2,819 children living in 126 MP Child Care Institutions face chronic understaffing: 47-54% staff vacancies in audited CCIs, 75% vacancy at SARA (State Adoption Resource Agency). These children -- already separated from families due to abandonment, trafficking, or abuse -- are housed in institutions that lack the human capacity to provide care, protection, or the path to adoption/reintegration that the ICPS promises.

source.quote: significant staff shortages ranging from 47 per cent to 54 per cent in 14 CCIs. 53 per cent to 69 per cent at State Child Protection Society (SCPS) level. 75 per cent at State Adoption Resource Agency (SARA) level. 2,819 children have been accommodated as of

keyFindings.text: Women Working Houses in MP (day-care shelters for working poor women) ran at only 40-50% occupancy in 9 of 13 functional WWHs -- indicating either poor targeting, poor awareness, or services not meeting user needs. Meanwhile the state carries out a street children survey in only 9 of 55 districts, leaving most of MP's street child population unmapped and unassisted.

source.quote: Nine out of 13 functional WWHs showed occupancy rate ranged between 40 per cent and 50 per cent during the audit period (2019-20 to 2023-24). While a survey of street children was carried out in nine districts in 2021-22

recommendations: Fill all 8,842 AWC gaps within 2 years: complete construction of delayed AWCs and open makeshift centres in underserved villages within 6 months; link DPO performance to AWC coverage targets.
Declare ICDS staffing an emergency: fill DPO, CDPO, and Supervisor posts within 6 months via special recruitment drive; link fund release to district-level staffing compliance.
Conduct a comprehensive safety audit of all 126 CCIs: independent inspectors to assess child protection protocols in each; suspend CCIs with below-minimum staffing until corrective action is taken.

Mandate full ICDS fund utilisation: any district surrendering more than 5% of ICDS allocation faces a mandatory Secretary-level review; district officers cannot surrender AWC construction funds without written justification.

Mental Health: 13.90% of MP population has mental illness (vs national average 10.70%); only 82 of 163 MHEs (50%) provisionally registered; SMHA received ₹2.40 crore -- no expenditure in 2020-22, 46-89% funds unspent annually; manpower shortages 13-67% in MHEs; IEC funds ₹43.89 lakh entirely unspent; 105 recovered patients forced to stay with mentally ill patients; 409 LAMA and absconding cases; 16% iCall calls unanswered. University governance (Gwalior region): 2.43 lakh pass-out students but degrees issued to only 14,870 (2021-24); 72% teaching vacancies; ₹306.31 crore investments in 29 FDs without proper mandate.

ministry: Panchayat and Rural Development Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh
title: Performance Audit on Implementation of MGNREGS -- Madhya Pradesh (2019-24)
overview: CAG Performance Audit Report No. 4 of 2026 on MGNREGS (MGNREGA) implementation in Madhya Pradesh (period 2019-24). Outstanding liability for unpaid wages and material costs: ₹1,217.05 crore (as of 31 March 2024) including ₹54.79 crore in 4.7 lakh Aadhaar-based transactions. Only 2% of registered households received full 100 days' employment; 31.21-46.60% received fewer than 40 days. 2.29 crore households registered in MP. ₹1.46 crore spent on 2,426 duplicate/fake/incorrect job cards (2019-24). Delayed payment of wages: ₹35.13 lakh compensation due, ₹9.07 lakh unpaid. Peak funds available 2021-22: ₹1,703.80 crore.

keyFindings.text: ₹1,217.05 crore in unpaid MGNREGA wages and material costs are outstanding in Madhya Pradesh as of March 2024. This is money legally owed to rural workers who completed government-mandated work but were not paid. In a state where 31-47% of MGNREGA workers get fewer than 40 days' work and only 2% get the full 100-day guarantee, the combination of work shortage and unpaid wages is a systemic failure of the rural employment safety net.

source.quote: a liability of Rs.1217.05 crore towards unpaid wages and material costs as of 31 March 2024. Only around two per cent of households have been provided the full 100 days' employment

keyFindings.text: 2,426 duplicate, fake, or incorrect job cards were used to draw ₹1.46 crore in MGNREGA wages (2019-24) in MP. MGNREGA job card fraud diverts funds meant for the poorest rural households into fictitious accounts. While the absolute amount appears modest, the signal is that MP's job card verification systems are porous -- the actual scale of fraud is likely larger than what audit samples can detect.

source.quote: Rs. 1.46 crore on 2,426 duplicate, fake/incorrect job cards during 2019-24

keyFindings.text: Even when wages are delayed, MP fails to pay the mandatory delay compensation: ₹9.07 lakh of ₹35.13 lakh due remains unpaid. Workers who are denied timely payment under MGNREGA are entitled to compensation -- denying even this remedy, while simultaneously carrying ₹1,217.05 crore in unpaid wage liability, illustrates the complete breakdown of MGNREGA financial accountability in MP.

source.quote: against Rs.35.13 lakh compensation towards delayed payment of wages, Rs.9.07 lakh remained unpaid. a liability of Rs.1217.05 crore towards unpaid wages and material costs

keyFindings.text: With 2.29 crore registered MGNREGA households in Madhya Pradesh but only 2% receiving the full 100-day guarantee, the state's rural employment system is delivering a fraction of its statutory promise. The combination of under-employment (47% getting fewer than 40 days), unpaid wages (₹1,217 crore liability), and Aadhaar-based payment failures (₹54.79 crore in 4.7 lakh transactions) indicates structural system failure across registration, work provision, and payment.

source.quote: 2.29 crore. Only around two per cent of households have been provided the full 100 days' employment. 31.21 per cent to 46.60 per cent were provided less than 40 days. a liability of Rs.54.79 crore (4.7 lakh transactions) towards Aadhaar

recommendations: Discharge ₹1,217.05 crore wage and material liability within 6 months; set monthly targets for clearing all pending MGNREGA wage arrears under supervision of the Chief Secretary.
Resolve all 4.7 lakh Aadhaar-linked payment failures (₹54.79 crore) within 90 days: NIC to diagnose each failed transaction and release payment through alternate verified channels.
Pay all ₹9.07 lakh outstanding wage delay compensation within 30 days; implement automatic compensation payment whenever wages are delayed by more than 15 days.

Conduct a State-wide job card de-duplication drive using Aadhaar seeding; prosecute individuals responsible for ₹1.46 crore fraudulent job card expenditure; cancel all 2,426 identified fake/duplicate cards.

ministry: Panchayat and Rural Development Department, Government of Chhattisgarh
title: Performance Audit on Implementation of MGNREGS -- Chhattisgarh (2019-24)
overview: CAG Performance Audit Report No. 3 of 2026 on MGNREGS in Chhattisgarh (period 2019-24). 152.36 lakh HHs demanded employment; 134.10 lakh provided (18.26 lakh shortfall, 12%). 83% of employed HHs got fewer than 100 days; only 1.23 lakh (0.92%) got full 100 days. 16% more than 100 days. Unpaid wages: ₹29.62 crore (April 2015-March 2023); liability ₹84.59 crore including penalty. 86% works undertaken without Gram Sabha approval in 48 test-checked GPs. Social Audit: ₹58.68 crore earmarked; only ₹42.55 crore utilised; 45% of sanctioned works pending Social Audit; 53%+ Social Audit observations unresolved; 99.97% GPs left unaudited in some years. 21% vacancy among technical assistants. Women participation: 43-59% (exceeds mandated 33%). ₹29.62 crore in arrears not paid; liabilities accumulated to ₹84.59 crore with penalty. ₹2.22 crore for unemployment allowances not budgeted.

Meanwhile 18.26 lakh households who applied for work were outright denied, and no unemployment allowance (₹2.22 crore) was even budgeted for them. MGNREGA in CG is delivering 0.92% of its core promise while violating the legal rights of 12% of applicants.

The accumulation of penalty on top of principal shows the state has been aware of the arrears for years without resolving them.

PVTGs are India's most marginalised tribal communities -- identified for special protection precisely because mainstream development bypasses them. When the programme specifically designed for their welfare itself bypasses 54% of them, the failure is complete.

source.quote: 1.60 lakh (54 per cent) PVTG implemented only in 541 villages having 1.34 lakh PVTG population

overview: CAG Performance Audit Report No. 2 of 2025 on State Bank of Sikkim (SBS) (period ended March 2023). SBS was established under the Proclamation 1968 of the Chogyal of Sikkim and is not regulated under the Banking Regulation Act 1949 -- making it the only bank in India without a central bank lender of last resort. Gross NPA: ₹1,682.04 crore (52.23% of total advances of ₹3,220.67 crore). Capital Adequacy Ratio: 4.35-6.72% against required 9%. 34 term loans to 6 GoS departments: ₹913.37 crore; 25 of 34 (₹555.93 crore) turned NPA. Excess agency commission claimed from GoS: ₹32.81 crore. Under-provisioning for NPAs: ₹225.28 crore. Total paid-up capital: ₹0.53 crore -- critically thin.

ministry: Finance and Commercial Taxes Department, Government of Tamil Nadu
title: Compliance Audit Report on State Revenues -- Tamil Nadu (year ended March 2022)

Under-assessments, short levy, and revenue loss: ₹149.08 crore (GST and other taxes). Irregularities in 436 test-checked taxpayers: ₹992.38 crore (GST); only ₹5.46 crore recovered and 103 demand notices issued. Stamp duty and registration: ₹2,978.46 crore in draft paragraphs. Undischarged tax liability (56 cases): ₹22.68 crore. Unpaid differential excise duty (revision): ₹30.50 crore. GST compliance deficiencies: cancelled taxpayers not filing GSTR-10; undischarged liabilities through systemic audit gaps.

Demand notices for 103 cases represent only partial follow-through on a substantially larger problem.

source.quote: pointed out irregularities amounting to Rs.992.38 crore. Department recovered Rs.5.46 crore and also issued notices in 103 cases

keyFindings.text: ₹2,978.46 crore in draft audit paragraphs on stamp duty and registration represents a massive property transaction revenue gap. source.quote: Draft Paragraphs in Stamp Duty and Registration, involving Rs.2,978.46 crore

keyFindings.text: Cancelled GST taxpayers in Tamil Nadu did not file their mandatory GSTR-10 final return -- meaning their unsettled tax liabilities were not formally closed. keyFindings.text: Tamil Nadu raised only 65% of total revenue receipts from its own sources in 2021-22 (down from 67% in 2020-21) -- despite being one of India's highest-GDP states. recommendations: Escalate all ₹992.38 crore GST irregularity cases to district-level adjudicating authorities; mandate demand recovery within 90 days for each of the 436 identified cases.

Mandate GSTR-10 filing before cancellation is marked final in the GST portal; send system-generated notices with penalty escalation to all cancelled taxpayers who have not filed.
Commission a third-party audit of all excise duty assessment processes; recover ₹30.50 crore differential excise with interest from non-compliant manufacturers.

ministry: Energy Department (DISCOM), Government of Rajasthan
title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Ujwal DISCOM Assurance Yojana (UDAY) in Rajasthan (2015-21)
overview: CAG Performance Audit Report No. 1 of 2024 on UDAY in Rajasthan (period 2015-21). UDAY was launched in 2015 to turnaround financially stressed DISCOMs. Rajasthan DISCOMs (JVVNL, JDVVNL) had revenue deficit of ₹12,474 crore and accumulated losses of ₹81,411 crore in 2014-15; debts of ₹80,529.90 crore as on 30 September 2015. GoR took over ₹62,422.88 crore (75%) of DISCOM debts under UDAY. UDAY targets: AT&C loss reduction to 15% by 2018-19 and reduction in gap between Average Cost of Supply (ACoS) and Average Revenue Realised (ARR). Monthly DISCOM losses grew from ₹15.83 crore (April 2015) to ₹17,458.79 crore. GoR subsidy grew from initial levels to ₹1,831.76 crore in 2020-21. DISCOMs could not turnaround financially despite UDAY debt restructuring.

title: Performance Audit on Development and Allotment of Plots by Ghaziabad Development Authority (2017-22)

ministry: Lucknow Metro Rail Corporation (LMRCL), Government of Uttar Pradesh
title: Performance Audit on Construction and Operation of Lucknow Metro Rail Project (Phase-1A)

Revenue grew from ₹5.55 crore (2017-18) to ₹99.35 crore (2023-24) -- a 1,690.10% increase; operating expenses grew from ₹16.17 crore to ₹76.11 crore. LKCC-07 contract: ₹51.40 crore billed against bonded cost of ₹15.75 crore (226% overrun). 1.98 hectares (7.67%) of metro land not used for metro purposes. ₹3.16 crore royalty/mineral charges not recovered from contractor.

ministry: Health and Family Welfare Department, Government of Chhattisgarh
title: Performance Audit on Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services -- Chhattisgarh
