Overall staff shortage: 34% (25,793 vacant posts). In 172 CHCs: Specialist Doctor shortage 72%; Doctor shortage 15%. In 776 PHCs: MO shortage 32%; Staff Nurse shortage 32%; Paramedic shortage 36%. Drug procurement irregularities: ₹13.14 crore at higher rates; ₹31.83 crore equipment procurement issues; ₹9.53 crore expired drugs; ₹22.98 crore from blacklisted firms; ₹3.27 crore reagent kits expired; ₹4.62 crore penalty not recovered. Institutional MMR (Maternal Mortality Rate) at 85.8% -- in context of India's ongoing MMR reduction efforts. Procurement system failures across drugs, equipment, and consumables indicate systemic procurement governance deficit.

Total plantation expenditure: ₹3,459.69 crore (including ₹1,216.79 crore from State CAMPA Fund) during 2016-17 to 2021-22. Target of 101.35 crore saplings was met with 103.78 crore planted -- but forest cover still decreased inside recorded forests. ₹88.77 crore plantation expenditure by Rural Development Department found irregular. ministry: Department for Empowerment of Differently Abled and Senior Citizens, Government of Karnataka
title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPWD) -- Karnataka
overview: CAG Performance Audit Report No. 2 of 2024 on Implementation of RPWD Act 2016 in Karnataka (period 2017-22). Karnataka has 13.24 lakh PwDs (Census 2011) -- 4.94% of India's 2.68 crore PwDs. RPWD Act 2016 covers 21 disabilities (vs 7 under old PWD Act 1995) and mandates free education for all children with benchmark disability (6-18 years), reservation in employment, accessible infrastructure, and legal safeguards. Only 46% of differently abled persons were issued Unique Disability ID (UDID). ₹5 crore sanctioned for survey covering all 21 disabilities but survey outcomes were inadequate. Key gaps: hearing aids and audio aids unavailable for eligible PwDs; accessibility standards not met across public buildings; scheme coverage far below eligible population.

ministry: Water Resources Department, Government of Andhra Pradesh
title: Performance Audit on Polavaram Irrigation Project, Andhra Pradesh (2007-23)
overview: CAG Performance Audit Report No. 4 of 2025 on Polavaram Irrigation Project, AP (period 2007-23). Polavaram was declared a National Project in 2014 and aims to provide irrigation potential to 2.91 lakh hectares and water to 28.50 lakh people in 540 villages via diversion of 80 TMC of Krishna river. As of March 2023, headworks costing ₹7,422.69 crore were awarded and ₹5,757.48 crore was spent. Despite 17+ years since commencement, even major irrigation canals -- Left Main Canal (LMC) and Right Main Canal (RMC) -- were only 12% and 17% constructed. Land acquisition: only 67.43% (1,13,119 acres) of required land acquired. R&R: only 0.67% of Project Displaced Families (PDFs) rehabilitated; only 11% relocated to R&R colonies. Avoidable financial burden of ₹619.83 crore due to land acquisition delays. R&R cost escalated by ₹19,346.49 crore due to revisions. Only ₹841.34 crore paid to 14,500 of 1,06,006 PDFs for cash benefits.

ministry: Public Health Engineering Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh
title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Jal Jeevan Mission in Madhya Pradesh (2019-24)
overview: CAG Performance Audit Report No. 5 of 2026 on Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) in Madhya Pradesh covering period 2019-24. JJM targeted 1.12 crore Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTCs) for MP; at launch only 13.53 lakh rural HHs (12.10%) had tap connections. By December 2024, only 60.90 lakh HHs were covered -- state coverage 69% against revised 80% target. Execution was sluggish: only 27% of Multi-Village Schemes and 58% of Single-Village Schemes completed as of September 2024. Water quality monitoring funds severely misused: Government spent only 0.38% of earmarked funds on testing and diverted 1.62% for construction. District and sub-divisional water quality labs conducted only 11-19% of prescribed tests. Skill development for barefoot mechanics achieved only 23% of target (₹402.10 lakh of ₹1,712.62 lakh approved). Liquidated damages not recovered from non-functional sites.

ministry: Panchayat and Rural Development Department, Government of Chhattisgarh
title: Performance Audit on Implementation of MGNREGS in Chhattisgarh (2019-24)
overview: CAG Performance Audit Report No. 3 of 2026 on MGNREGS in Chhattisgarh (period 2019-24). During 2019-24, 152.36 lakh households demanded employment; 134.10 lakh (88%) were provided work -- but 18.26 lakh (12%) received no employment and no unemployment allowances were paid despite ₹2.22 crore budgetary provision (entirely surrendered). Of households provided employment, 83% received fewer than 100 days; only 0.92% received the full 100-day entitlement. EPF contributions amounting to ₹29.62 crore for April 2015-March 2023 remained unpaid, accumulating liabilities of ₹84.59 crore including penalty and interest. 86% of works were undertaken without mandatory Gram Sabha approvals in test-checked 48 GPs. Women participation ranged 43-59%, exceeding the 33% mandate. Social Audit earmark of ₹58.68 crore had only ₹42.55 crore utilised; 45% of SAU posts vacant; 99.97% of GPs left unaudited in some years.

recommendations: Halt all new FHTC sanctioning until the 24.52 lakh pending HH backlog is cleared; create a district-wise completion calendar with monthly milestones published on the JJM Karnataka portal.

Establish an O&M user-charge collection target of at least ₹100/month per FHTC; link GP grant releases to verified community contribution collections.
Make land availability a mandatory pre-condition for any FHTC contract award; require certificate from District Collector before tendering commences.

ministry: School Education Department, Government of West Bengal
title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Samagra Shiksha — West Bengal (2019–24)
overview: CAG Performance Audit on Implementation of Samagra Shiksha in West Bengal (R3/2026, period 2019-20 to 2023-24) assessed planning, financial management, access, inclusive education, teacher management and infrastructure. Paschim Banga Samagra Shiksha Mission (PBSSM) did not prepare perspective plans; fund utilisation ranged 46-65%, causing unspent balances. Non-execution of sanctioned civil works led to surrender of ₹395 crore and short receipt of ₹2,428 crore scheme funds, restricting scope. A shortage of 33,835 special educators (95%) denied quality education to children with special needs; 30-56% of CwSN were deprived of transport allowance and 35-49% of escort allowance. Only 7.92% of schools introduced vocational education against NEP target of 50%. Poor Board outcomes persisted with 10-13% of Class X and 12-17% of Class XII students failing. Infructuous expenditure of ₹10.46 crore on Model Schools was noticed. In-service teacher training was virtually non-existent at 1.19%.

Require every state-funded Civil Work to be completed or its grant cancelled within 24 months — introduce a penalty clause on unspent balances returned to the Centre.
Audit Model School viability before construction; shut-down schools with infructuous expenditure should trigger government accountability proceedings against district officials.

ministry: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Development Department, Government of Odisha

Processing units costing ₹48.29 crore were established under MPAs — 46% (105 units) reported as non-functional and during Joint Physical Inspection (Aug-Dec 2024) of 50 units, 96% (48) were found defunct. Cold storage establishments (₹1.91 crore, 12 units) were entirely unfruitful. RO plants (₹77.36 lakh) and eco-cottage complexes were mostly defunct. As of 2024, 288 PVTG villages lacked motorable roads, 231 had no electricity, 297 had no drinking water source, and 773 had no telecom. Under MGNREGS convergence, only 45% of 11,493 approved projects (₹267.79 crore) were taken up and only 35% (₹93.64 crore) expended.

Despite the high expenditure, only 8.70% of households that demanded employment received the full 100-day entitlement; 31.21-46.60% received fewer than 40 days. ministry: Finance, Stamps and Registration, Excise Departments, Government of Maharashtra
title: Compliance Audit on State Revenues — Maharashtra (period ended March 2023)
overview: CAG Compliance Audit Report No. 6 of 2025 for Maharashtra (Nagpur jurisdiction, period ended March 2023) covers Stamps and Registration, Goods and Services Tax and State Excise Departments. Audit tested 217 units and identified major failures: GST EWB audit found ₹96.85 crore non-recovery from 43 taxpayers whose registrations were cancelled (32 classified as non-genuine); nil-return taxpayers made taxable supplies worth ₹3.53 crore; no-return EWB users moved goods of ₹4.90 crore with tax effect ₹0.72 crore. Stamp duty shortcomings included: ₹10.50 crore short levy from document misclassification, ₹1.89 crore from property undervaluation (₹62.28 cr assessed at ₹100.11 cr), ₹1.50 crore from irregular 1% concession, and ₹76.18 lakh from incomplete plot area valuation. 21 explanatory memoranda on prior Audit Reports were outstanding.

recommendations: Require tax clearance certificate (covering all EWB-period liabilities) as mandatory input to registration cancellation proceedings — no cancellation without prior demand verification.
Dedicate EWB interception teams with GPS-tracked vehicles in all Joint Commissioner zones; set monthly interception targets linked to NIC analytical risk scores.
Standardise market value assessment: require two independent valuations for all commercial properties above ₹10 crore; Collector cannot rely solely on self-declaration.
Issue a state circular revoking Pune IGRS 1% concession retroactively; initiate recovery from affected transactions in the audit period.

ministry: Agriculture and Local Government Departments, Government of Punjab
title: Performance Audit — Punjab: Punjab Agricultural University & Solid Waste Management (2017–22)
overview: CAG Performance Audit Report No. 5 of 2025 for Punjab contains two PAs: Punjab Agricultural University (PAU) for 2017-22, and Solid Waste Management by Urban Local Bodies for 2017-22. PAU was established in 1962, played a key role in the Green Revolution and won ICAR's Best Institution Award in 1995 and 2017 — but its NIRF ranking declined from 24 (2017) to 51 (2019). PAU spent 71-86% of available funds; unadjusted advances of ₹64.61 crore remained (₹13.42 crore for >5 years). Teaching vacancies ranged 22-44% and non-teaching vacancies 34-51%. Enrolment remained at 14-31% of intake capacity. Only 193 of 616 research projects proposed (31.33%) were sanctioned. SWM by ULBs showed widespread failures in waste segregation, processing and landfill management.

ministry: Delhi Jal Board, Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi
title: Performance Audit on Functioning of Delhi Jal Board (year ended March 2022)
overview: CAG Performance Audit Report No. 3 of 2025 on the Delhi Jal Board (DJB) for the year ended March 2022 assessed water supply, sewerage, financial management and governance. Delhi requires 1,260 MGD per CPHEEO norms; DJB supplies only 935 MGD — a 26% shortfall increasing year-on-year (deficit grew from 283 MGD in 2017-18 to 325 MGD in 2021-22). Non-Revenue Water (NRW) was 51-53% of supply — worth ₹4,988 crore annually. Of 935 MGD produced, only 371 MGD (40%) was billed; of 371 billed, only 244 MGD (66%) collected — revenue collection rate just 26%. 25 STPs released treated effluent not meeting prescribed standards into Yamuna; 212.59 MGD of untreated sewage reaches the river. Asian Development Bank withdrew ₹2,243 crore financing citing DJB performance failures.

ministry: Commercial Taxes, Motor Vehicles, Registration, Excise and Forest Departments, Government of Kerala
title: Compliance Audit on State Revenues — Kerala (2023–24)
overview: CAG Revenue Compliance Audit of Kerala (period ended March 2024) covers Motor Vehicles, Excise, Registration, Forest and GST departments. Total state revenue was ₹1,24,486.15 crore (own: ₹90,674.97 crore; GoI: ₹33,811.18 crore). Revenue arrears stood at ₹30,308.52 crore — 24.35% of total revenue. The 11 paragraphs including two SSCAs identified aggregate revenue impact of ₹603.53 crore. The SSCA on Motor Vehicles found that despite ₹37.48 crore spent on nine Automated Driving Test Tracks and nine Automated Testing Stations, only two ADTTs became functional and none of the nine ATSs were operational, perpetuating manual licensing. Non-collection of Green Tax, expired-CF penalties and expired-RC fees cost the exchequer ₹50.26 crore; 197 vehicles with expired certificates met accidents causing 19 fatalities.

ministry: Department of Youth Empowerment and Sports, Government of Karnataka
title: Compliance Audit — Karnataka: Sports Authority, ESIS & Autonomous Bodies (2019–24)
overview: CAG Compliance Audit of Karnataka for the period ending March 2024 (R1/2026, 155 pages) covers the Department of Youth Empowerment and Sports (DYES) and nine Autonomous Bodies under the State Legislature. A SSCA on the Karnataka Sports Policy 2018 found the Sports Authority of Karnataka (SAK) released ₹7.94 crore beyond its annual financial ceiling of ₹25 lakh. SAK and GETHNAA failed to submit Utilisation Certificates for ₹94.40 crore of grants-in-aid received during 2019–24. Cash award distribution records worth ₹8.46 crore were not produced to audit. District Stadium Management Committees (DSMCs) held ₹30.79 crore in bank accounts unutilised. Ineligible sportsperson incentives of ₹4.54 crore were paid under various policy heads.

keyFindings.text: The Karnataka Sports Authority operated beyond its delegated financial powers: ₹7.94 crore released by the Chairman exceeded the ₹25 lakh annual GIA ceiling — including a single ₹1 crore grant to a film cricket association — without Cabinet approval, in violation of SAK's GIA Code and Sports Policy 2018.

source.quote: the expenditure of ₹7.94 crore released by the Chairman was beyond the annual financial ceiling of ₹25 lakh

keyFindings.text: Grants totalling ₹94.40 crore disbursed to SAK and GETHNAA over five years without any Utilisation Certificates — a systemic accountability failure enabling unverified expenditure across the Karnataka sports ecosystem.

Enforce GIA Code financial delegation strictly: release exceeding the annual ceiling should require prior Cabinet/Government sanction with public disclosure.
Require DSMCs to maintain stadium infrastructure through a dedicated maintenance reserve funded by user fees, not left idle in bank accounts.
Conduct a forensic reconciliation of the ₹8.46 crore in undocumented cash award payments to verify beneficiary eligibility under Karnataka Sports Policy 2018.

ministry: Rural Development and Water Resources Departments, Government of Bihar
title: Performance and Compliance Audit — Bihar: MGNREGS & Embankment Construction (2019–24)
overview: CAG Audit Report No. 1 of 2026 for Bihar covers a Performance Audit on MGNREGS (2019–24), a Subject Specific Compliance Audit on embankment construction under the Water Resources Department, and individual compliance audit paragraphs. Bihar utilised ₹30,615.93 crore (96%) of ₹31,730.69 crore available under MGNREGS but left ₹36.22 crore unadjusted. Outstanding liabilities of ₹1,903.58 crore remained, with ₹302.24 crore pending since before 2019. ₹735.10 crore (3.61%) of ₹20,374.91 crore in wages were paid with delays. Of 1.21 crore works taken up, only 37% were completed. The embankment SSCA found ₹247.80 crore spent without achieving flood protection for 5.26 lakh people and 17,400 ha of farmland — ₹28.97 crore declared unfruitful.

ministry: Higher Education, Mines and Irrigation Departments, Government of Himachal Pradesh
title: Compliance Audit — HP: University Gaps, Mines & Minor Irrigation (period ended March 2023)
overview: CAG Compliance Audit Report No. 4 of 2025 for Himachal Pradesh (172 pages) covers three major audits: a SSCA on institutional gaps at Himachal Pradesh University (HPU), a SSCA on regulation of mines and minerals, and a SSCA on execution of minor irrigation schemes under PMKSY. HPU carried a 27–37% faculty shortage; its ₹11.19 crore ERP system had 30 of 37 modules non-functional and lab equipment worth ₹1.99 crore was non-functional since 2015. Of ₹7,602.95 crore planned under PMKSY, only ₹804.51 crore was sanctioned (129 of 6,478 planned schemes); DMFT funds of ₹239.21 crore received but only ₹47.03 crore spent. Work-splitting of ₹48.25 crore across 18 schemes avoided mandatory e-tendering.

ministry: Commercial Taxes, Stamps and Registration, Excise and Transport Departments, Government of Karnataka
title: Compliance Audit on State Revenues — Karnataka (2023–24)
overview: CAG Revenue Compliance Audit of Karnataka (R3/2026, 231 pages) covers Commercial Taxes (GST), Stamps and Registration, State Excise, and Transport departments for the period ending March 2024. Total state revenue was ₹2,33,342.93 crore (tax: ₹1,63,505.04 crore; non-tax: ₹13,117.41 crore). The 11 audit paragraphs including two SSCAs found short/non-levy of tax and revenue foregone totalling ₹169.18 crore. A critical GST Section 65 departmental audit found ₹112.16 crore in additional revenue for 2020–21 but recovered only ₹9.18 crore — a recovery rate below 10%. Joint Development Agreement (JDA) under-valuation led to ₹118.06 crore undervaluation and ₹21.26 crore short levy. Stamp duty short levies across nine paragraphs totalled over ₹100 crore.

title: Performance Audit on Namami Gange Programme — Uttarakhand (2018–23)
overview: CAG Performance Audit on implementation of the Namami Gange Programme by Uttarakhand (R2/2025, 96 pages) assessed 23 of 42 projects carried out during 2018–23. The National Mission for Clean Ganga released ₹14,260 crore to states (₹1,149 crore to Uttarakhand) under the ₹20,000 crore Namami Gange outlay; Mission II added ₹22,500 crore. Crematoria constructed without demand analysis remain unutilised; forestry interventions achieved only 16% of planned spend.

Appoint a dedicated Joshimath Sewage Task Force with a fixed 12-month completion mandate; recover costs from the original contractors who abandoned ₹9.57 crore and ₹33.16 crore worth of works.
Re-design crematoria adoption through community co-planning, not post-construction IEC — involve local Panchayats in location selection and management from the outset.

ministry: Mines and Geology Department, Government of Jharkhand
title: Performance Audit on Management of Minor Minerals — Jharkhand (2017–22)
overview: CAG Performance Audit on Management of Minor Minerals in Jharkhand (R4/2025, 152 pages) covered six district mining offices and JSMDC for the period 2017–22. State minor mineral revenue declined from ₹1,082.44 crore (2017–18) to ₹697.73 crore (2021–22). Unauthorised extraction of 33.21 lakh m³ beyond Environmental Clearance limits attracted ₹205.21 crore in unrecovered penalties. Stone extraction of 93.53 lakh m³ across 13 of 63 test-checked leases was estimated at ₹292.75 crore. Non-mineable coal reserves of 30.66 lakh tonnes were irregularly accounted as mineable, worth ₹34.96 crore. Only 3.77% (11 of 292 blocks) of planned mineral block auctions were completed during 2018–23, blocking State revenue. DMFT funds of ₹7.53 crore were irregularly used in 30 cases.

ministry: Finance Department, Government of Jharkhand
title: IT Audit: Integrated Financial Management System — Jharkhand (2011–22)
overview: CAG IT Audit Report No. 1 of 2025 for Jharkhand (100 pages) assessed the Integrated Financial Management System (IFMS) implemented over 2011–22 at a cost of ₹21.65 crore. IFMS was designed to automate budget management, treasury, and accounts across Jharkhand Government. Audit found a ₹8,064.12 crore discrepancy between BEAMS (₹4,222.50 crore) and Finance Accounts (₹12,286.62 crore) — a fundamental data integrity failure. Deficient validation controls allowed ₹4.40 crore revenue short-realisation and ₹11 crore in over-payments against authorised amounts. DCRG/CVP overpayments of ₹2.03 crore were made in 47 cases due to weak application controls. Thirteen DDOs incurred ₹34.33 crore expenditure without any allotment, and six DDOs exceeded allotment by ₹1.24 crore.

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Yettinahole Integrated Drinking Water Project in Karnataka
ministry: Karnataka Urban Water Supply and Sewerage Board / VJNL
overview: The Yettinahole Integrated Drinking Water Project was conceived in 2012 to divert surplus water from the Western Ghats to the water-scarce districts of Kolar, Chikkaballapura, Tumkur and Ramanagara in Karnataka. Originally estimated at ₹8,323.50 crore, the project cost has already been revised twice to ₹23,251.66 crore — a 2.8x overrun — and is still incomplete after 10 years. CAG found: design changes added ₹621.45 crore avoidable cost; only 25-54% of annual budget requirements were provided; ₹7,954.63 crore still needed to complete works; and the projected water yield was overestimated from private gauge station data.

stats.label: Project cost escalated 2.8× — ₹8,323 Cr to ₹23,251 Cr
stats.value: Two DPR revisions; still incomplete after 10 years
stats.note: The Yettinahole project's Detailed Project Report has been revised twice since original approval in July 2012: from ₹8,323.50 crore to ₹12,912.36 crore in February 2014, and again to ₹23,251.66 crore in January 2023. Despite 10 years of execution since March 2014, the project remains far from complete. None of the DPRs envisaged a credible completion schedule for benefit delivery. CAG noted that the design did not account for downstream demand or system integration, and that continuous supply during summer months was never part of the original design scope.

source.quote: ₹8,323.50 crore to ₹12,912.36 crore in February 2014 and again to ₹23,251.66 crore in January 2023. The works were taken up since March 2014 in various packages to be executed in two phases. However, Project works are still under progress and far from completion and intended benefit delivery.

stats.label: Only 25–54% of annual budget provided — chronic underfunding
stats.value: VJNL faces ₹7,954.63 Cr funding uncertainty for balance works
stats.note: The project suffered from severe financial constraints throughout 2018-19 to 2022-23. The Government provided only 25 to 54 per cent of the budget requirements each year. As of June 2023, the project authority VJNL applied for fresh loans to complete remaining works — but approval was still pending in March 2024. The water yield projection used in the DPR was based on data from private gauge stations and found to be "on the higher side," meaning the actual water available may be less than designed for. Audit found the available water yield may be as low as 24.70 TMC versus the DPR's estimated 32.15 TMC.

source.quote: The Project suffered from financial constraints as the Government provided only 25 to 54 per cent of the budget requirements for the Project during the period 2018-19 to 2022-23.

stats.label: ₹621 Cr extra cost from avoidable design change; ₹7,954 Cr still needed
stats.value: Changed from 10 TMC to 2 TMC storage — requiring more monsoon pumping
stats.note: When the project design was revised, the storage reservoir component was reduced from a proposed 10 TMC to 2 TMC. This required compensatory increased pumping during monsoon months to make up the storage deficit, and the consequent design changes resulted in additional cost of ₹621.45 crore to the project — avoidable expenditure if the original design had been properly validated. As of March 2024, ₹7,954.63 crore is still required for completing the project and approval for fresh loans is pending. Benefit delivery to Kolar, Chikkaballapura and other dry districts — the core purpose of the scheme — remains deferred indefinitely.

source.quote: the consequent design changes resulted in additional cost of ₹621.45 crore to the Project. Resultantly, as of March 2024, VJNL faces financial uncertainty regarding the ₹7,954.63 crore required for completing the Project.

keyFindings.text: Yettinahole project cost escalated 2.8× from ₹8,323.50 crore to ₹23,251.66 crore after two DPR revisions — still incomplete after 10 years with no water delivered to target districts.

source.quote: ₹8,323.50 crore to ₹12,912.36 crore in February 2014 and again to ₹23,251.66 crore in January 2023. Project works are still under progress and far from completion and intended benefit delivery.

keyFindings.text: Government provided only 25–54% of annual budget; ₹7,954.63 crore still needed; water yield overestimated at 32.15 TMC vs actual 24.70 TMC — the project's viability is in question.

source.quote: The Project suffered from financial constraints as the Government provided only 25 to 54 per cent of the budget requirements for the Project during the period 2018-19 to 2022-23. VJNL faces financial uncertainty regarding the ₹7,954.63 crore required for completing the Project.

recommendations: State Government should ensure full annual budget allocation to VJNL to prevent further cost escalation from delayed execution.
Water yield projections must be verified using official gauge station data and revised in DPR if the 32.15 TMC figure is overstated.
A credible time-bound completion plan with accountability for project management must be developed.

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme in Kerala
ministry: Local Self Government Department, Government of Kerala
overview: Kerala MGNREGS covers 77.21 lakh households with ₹18,806.62 crore released over 2019-24. Despite being a comparatively better-managed state than many others, CAG found: 88.73% of individual projects in Annual Plans were not implemented; wage payment delays affected ₹269.27 crore (paid 16–90 days late) and ₹39.24 crore (paid after 3 months); demand for work fell 13.77%; and 44.01% of surveyed beneficiaries were not enrolled in any insurance scheme despite being entitled.

stats.label: 88.73% of individual MGNREGS projects in Annual Plans — never implemented
stats.value: GPs bypassed Grama Sabha; projects selected without ground identification
stats.note: Kerala's MGNREGS requires Gram Panchayats to identify individual beneficiaries through the Grama Sabha. CAG found that this participatory process was systematically bypassed — GPs identified beneficiaries directly without Grama Sabha approval, thereby infringing on the democratic right of the Grama Sabha. The consequence: non-identification of beneficiaries by GPs and non-implementation of 88.73 per cent of individual projects included in their Annual Plans. These are projects that were officially approved on paper, allocated to specific households, but never executed. Person-days of employment generated declined by 6% as a result of the declining demand.

source.quote: non-identification of beneficiaries by GPs and non-implementation of 88.73 per cent of individual projects included in their Annual Plan. We found that demand for work declined by 13.77 per cent during the period 2020-21 to 2023-24.

stats.label: ₹269.27 Cr wages paid 16–90 days late; ₹39.24 Cr after 3 months
stats.note: MGNREGS mandates payment of wages within 15 days of closure of each Muster Roll. In Kerala, wages amounting to ₹269.27 crore were paid after 16 to 90 days, and ₹39.24 crore was paid after three months from the date of muster roll closure. As of December 2024, ₹43.59 crore was still outstanding in unpaid wages, semi-skilled wages, material costs, and taxes. Workers — mostly daily wage labourers — were denied their earnings for months. There was also delay of 8 or more days in fund transfers between accounts, adding to the payment chain delay. ₹2.54 crore was paid as interest/penalty for these wage payment delays.

source.quote: wages amounting to ₹269.27 crore was paid after 16 to 90 days and ₹39.24 crore was paid after three months from the date of closure of muster rolls.

stats.label: 44% of MGNREGS workers not enrolled in insurance schemes they're entitled to
stats.value: State failed to sensitise/enrol job card holders in PMSBY/PMJJBY
stats.note: MGNREGS workers are entitled to enrolment in social insurance schemes including Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY). The State Government is responsible for sensitising workers about these entitlements and facilitating their enrolment. CAG's beneficiary survey found that 44.01 per cent of beneficiaries surveyed were not enrolled in any of the insurance schemes — meaning nearly half the workforce is unprotected against accidental death and disability. This is not a resource constraint but a failure of outreach and sensitisation by state authorities.

source.quote: 44.01 per cent of beneficiaries surveyed were not enrolled in any of the insurance schemes, indicating that the State has not fulfilled its responsibilities regarding sensitising and enrolling job card holders in insurance schemes.

keyFindings.text: 88.73% of individual MGNREGS projects in Annual Plans were never implemented — Gram Panchayats bypassed Grama Sabha, leaving workers without work despite formal allocations.

source.quote: non-implementation of 88.73 per cent of individual projects included in their Annual Plan.

keyFindings.text: ₹269.27 crore in wages paid 16–90 days late; ₹43.59 crore still outstanding — workers went unpaid for months despite a 15-day statutory deadline.

source.quote: wages amounting to ₹269.27 crore was paid after 16 to 90 days and ₹39.24 crore was paid after three months from the date of closure of muster rolls.

recommendations: Grama Sabha participation must be enforced for all individual project identification — GPs cannot bypass this statutory requirement.
Wage payment pipeline must be audited and delays reduced to the 15-day statutory limit; compensation for delays must be automatically triggered.
State must conduct drives to enrol all MGNREGS workers in PMSBY and PMJJBY insurance schemes.

title: Performance Audit on Functioning of District Transport Offices in Bihar
ministry: Transport Department, Government of Bihar
overview: Bihar's District Transport Offices (DTOs) are responsible for issuing driving licenses, registering vehicles, collecting taxes and enforcing the Motor Vehicles Act. CAG found pervasive systemic failure: during joint physical verification, only 21 of 789 applicants had physically appeared for the Learner's Licence test — yet 766 (97%) were marked successful in the system. 73 Heavy Motor Vehicle licenses were granted to applicants who never appeared for their driving skill test. Revenue losses of ₹4.35 crore and uncollected fines of ₹18.11 crore were found due to inadequate document verification at vehicle registration.

stats.label: Learner's Licence test fraud — only 2.66% of applicants physically appeared
stats.value: 21 of 789 applicants appeared; 766 (97%) shown as "passed" in system
stats.note: During a Joint Physical Verification (JPV) conducted with departmental officials, CAG auditors checked actual test attendance against SARATHI database records. They found that only 21 applicants (2.66 per cent) out of a total 789 applicants had actually appeared for the Learner's Licence (LL) test for Light Motor Vehicle. Of these 21, only 7 completed the test successfully. Yet the SARATHI database showed 766 applicants (97.08 per cent) as having passed the test. This means 759 licenses were issued to people who never sat for the test — a systemic fraud enabling unqualified drivers onto public roads, posing direct road safety risks.

source.quote: Audit noted that only 21 applicants (2.66 per cent) out of total 789 applicants, appeared for Learners' Licence (LL) test for Light Motor Vehicle (LMV). Of this, seven applicants completed this test successfully but as per 'SARATHI' database 766 applicants (97.08 per cent) were found successful in the test.

stats.label: 73 Heavy Motor Vehicle licenses granted without driving skill test
stats.value: HMV drivers — trucks, buses — licensed without physical verification
stats.note: Heavy Motor Vehicles — trucks and buses — pose the greatest danger on roads when operated by unqualified drivers. Despite the statutory requirement for a driving skill test, 73 HMV licenses were granted to applicants who did not appear for the skill test on the given date. DTOs and Motor Vehicle Inspectors did not exercise due diligence in these cases. The SARATHI software itself had inadequate input controls — it accepted test-pass records for applicants who had never presented themselves, indicating a broken link between physical attendance and database entry.

source.quote: Despite this, 73 licenses related to HMV were granted. This shows DTOs and Motor Vehicle Inspectors (MVIs), did not exercise due diligence.

stats.label: ₹4.35 Cr revenue lost; ₹18.11 Cr fines not levied on 18,851 vehicles
stats.value: Authorised dealers submitted false vehicle documents; VAHAN had no controls
stats.note: DTOs and Motor Vehicle Inspectors failed to verify documents and information furnished by 861 authorised dealers at the time of registration of 18,851 vehicles. This resulted in short realisation of revenue of ₹4.35 crore and non-levy of fines amounting to ₹18.11 crore. The VAHAN software also showed critical deficiencies — it accepted a date of purchase of a vehicle that was later than the date of insurance for that vehicle, a logically impossible sequence that should have been rejected by the system. These weaknesses in software controls enabled dealers to submit inconsistent data without detection.

source.quote: verification of documents/information related to vehicles furnished by 861 authorised dealers at the time of registration of 18,851 vehicles which resulted into short realisation of revenue of ₹ 4.35 crore and non-levy of fine amounting to ₹ 18.11 crore.

keyFindings.text: Only 2.66% of Learner's Licence applicants physically appeared for tests — yet 97% were marked as passing in SARATHI. 73 HMV licenses granted without skill test: systemic fraud enabling unqualified drivers onto roads.

source.quote: only 21 applicants (2.66 per cent) out of total 789 applicants, appeared for Learners' Licence (LL) test. 766 applicants (97.08 per cent) were found successful in the test.

keyFindings.text: ₹4.35 crore revenue short-collected and ₹18.11 crore fines uncollected from 18,851 vehicles registered on false dealer documents — VAHAN software lacked basic input validation.

source.quote: short realisation of revenue of ₹ 4.35 crore and non-levy of fine amounting to ₹ 18.11 crore.

recommendations: Physical attendance for Learner's Licence and driving skill tests must be verified biometrically; SARATHI must reject records without verified attendance.
VAHAN software must be strengthened with mandatory input validation to reject logically inconsistent registration data.
Revenue recovery proceedings should be initiated for the ₹4.35 crore shortfall; fine liability of ₹18.11 crore should be enforced against dealers.

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (Ayushman Bharat) in Bihar
ministry: State Health Agency, Government of Bihar
overview: PMJAY (Ayushman Bharat) provides ₹5 lakh health cover per family per year to 1.21 crore poor Bihar households (6.18 crore beneficiaries). CAG found: only 41% of targeted beneficiaries verified as of March 2024; 22% of empanelled hospitals inactive; ₹33.44 crore in inadmissible claim payments; payments of ₹2.31 crore on disabled Ayushman cards; closing balances ranging ₹53.58–₹159.53 crore indicating chronic fund underutilisation; and claim processing taking up to 1,821 days in same-state cases.

stats.label: Only 41% of targeted Ayushman Bharat beneficiaries verified in Bihar
stats.value: 2.56 cr of 6.18 cr beneficiaries verified; 1.21 cr families at risk
stats.note: Bihar was supposed to cover 1.21 crore poor and vulnerable households (6.18 crore beneficiaries) under PMJAY. As of March 2024, only 2.56 crore beneficiaries (41%) were verified in the state. The primary reason: the State Health Agency (SHA) failed to execute a contract with an Implementation Support Agency (ISA) to cover all targeted beneficiaries. Inadequate IEC activities and poor outreach left most eligible households unaware of their entitlement. The unverified 59% cannot receive cashless treatment at empanelled hospitals — effectively locked out of a scheme meant for them.

source.quote: only 2.56 crore beneficiaries (41 per cent) were verified in the State (March 2024). This was mainly attributable to non-execution of a contract by the State Health Agency (SHA) with the Implementation Support Agency (ISA), to cover all targeted beneficiaries of PMJAY.

stats.label: 226 hospitals (22%) empanelled but inactive — no pre-authorisations started
stats.value: 17 hospitals had zero pre-authorisations since empanelment
stats.note: Of 1,005 hospitals empanelled under PMJAY in Bihar, 226 hospitals (22%) were shown as inactive — they had not initiated any pre-authorisations for treatment of scheme beneficiaries during the last three months of the audit period. Of these 226 inactive hospitals, 17 had never initiated a single pre-authorisation since the day they were empanelled. PMAM (Pradhan Mantri Aarogya Mitras) kiosks were absent in many of these hospitals. Empanelment without follow-through creates a false sense of scheme coverage: Bihar looks fully covered on paper but large areas are effectively unserved.

source.quote: 226 hospitals (22 per cent) were shown as inactive, as they did not start pre-authorisations for treatment of the Scheme beneficiaries, during the last three months. Of these 226, 17 hospitals had not initiated any pre-authorisations since their empanelment.

stats.label: ₹33.44 Cr in inadmissible claim payments; ₹2.31 Cr on disabled cards
stats.value: SHA admitted time-barred claims; paid on 2,186 disabled Ayushman cards
stats.note: Bihar's State Health Agency committed multiple financial control failures. SHA admitted 19,917 time-barred claims from empanelled hospitals and made inadmissible payments of ₹33.44 crore. SHA also processed 2,186 claims amounting to ₹2.31 crore on disabled Ayushman cards — cards that had been deactivated or blocked but remained payable in the system. Additionally, 139 Ayushman cards in the Transaction Management System (against which ₹25.25 lakh was paid) did not exist in the beneficiary identification database at all. Claim processing ranged from 1 day to 1,821 days — over 5 years — for same-state cases, a failure of basic insurance administration.

source.quote: SHA admitted time barred 19,917 claims received from claimant empanelled hospitals and made inadmissible payments amounting to ₹ 33.44 crore. SHA made claim payments in 2,186 cases amounting to ₹ 2.31 crore on disabled Ayushman cards.

keyFindings.text: Only 41% of Bihar's targeted PMJAY beneficiaries verified — SHA never executed contract with ISA; 59% of intended households lack access to cashless treatment they're entitled to.

source.quote: only 2.56 crore beneficiaries (41 per cent) were verified in the State (March 2024).

keyFindings.text: ₹33.44 crore paid on time-barred claims; ₹2.31 crore on disabled cards; 226 empanelled hospitals inactive — Ayushman Bharat in Bihar is failing both beneficiary access and financial control.

source.quote: inadmissible payments amounting to ₹ 33.44 crore. SHA made claim payments in 2,186 cases amounting to ₹ 2.31 crore on disabled Ayushman cards.

recommendations: SHA must immediately execute an ISA contract and complete beneficiary verification for all 6.18 crore targeted beneficiaries.
Disabled Ayushman cards must be purged from the payment system; controls must prevent payments on deactivated cards.
Inactive empanelled hospitals must be issued notices; empanelment must be cancelled if no pre-authorisation activity begins within 3 months.

title: Performance Audit on Functioning of Micro Project Agencies for Development of Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups in Odisha
ministry: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Development Department, Government of Odisha
overview: Odisha's 13 Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs) — 2.94 lakh people — are among India's most marginalized communities. The state runs 20 Micro Project Agencies (MPAs) to deliver welfare. CAG found that the SSD department ignored 1,138 newly notified PVTG villages (June 2020), leaving 54% of the PVTG population entirely unserved. Infrastructure built with public money — irrigation channels, drinking water projects, Nutrition Resource Centres — was overwhelmingly non-functional. Loan repayment from PVTG SHGs was only 45%, with ₹7.10 crore outstanding.

stats.label: 54% of PVTG population excluded from welfare programs
stats.value: 1.60 lakh out of 2.94 lakh PVTGs unserved
stats.note: In June 2020, the state notified 1,138 new villages as PVTG habitations — but the SSD Department and its field formations adopted an apathetic approach and simply didn't extend welfare to those villages. As a result, 1.60 lakh (54%) of Odisha's PVTG population remained excluded from all welfare programmes and schemes. PVTG-specific programmes operated in only 541 villages covering 1.34 lakh population — the same villages that had been covered for decades. The newly notified villages, where tribal communities are often most vulnerable and isolated, saw no action for years after official notification.

source.quote: 1.60 lakh (54 per cent) PVTG population remained excluded from the coverage of welfare programmes/ schemes. The PVTG specific programmes had been implemented only in 541 villages having 1.34 lakh PVTG population.

stats.label: PVTG Empowerment Fund — 45% repayment, ₹7.10 Cr outstanding
stats.value: ₹6.39 Cr irregular loans; ₹7.10 Cr of ₹12.95 Cr unrecovered
stats.note: The PVTG Empowerment Fund was designed to provide microloans to PVTG Self Help Groups for income-generating activities. CAG found ₹6.39 crore was paid to ineligible SHGs (irregular sanction). Loan recovery was only 45%: out of ₹12.95 crore disbursed to 1,437 PVTG SHGs, ₹7.10 crore was outstanding for recovery as of March 2024. The late marriage incentive programme to prevent child marriage reached only 43% of villages during 2019-24 — a programme meant to benefit every PVTG girl in every village.

source.quote: instances of irregular payment of loan to ineligible SHGs (₹6.39 crore) were noticed. Repayment rate was low (45 per cent), as out of ₹12.95 crore loan provided to 1,437 PVTG SHGs, ₹7.10 crore was outstanding for recovery, as of March 2024.

stats.label: Infrastructure non-operational — 58% irrigation, 55% drinking water
stats.note: Physical inspections conducted jointly with state officials found: 23 (58%) of 40 irrigation projects non-operational; 38 (55%) of 69 drinking water projects non-operational. People in these PVTG areas resorted to fetching water from rivers, springs, and canals — water sources that carry waterborne disease risk. Additionally, 55 Nutrition Resource Centres (NRCs), built to provide nutrition support to PVTG children and women at ₹3.59 crore, were lying non-operational due to lack of maintenance arrangements.

source.quote: During joint physical inspection, 23 (58 per cent) out of 40 irrigation projects and 38 (55 per cent) out of 69 drinking water projects were found non-operational. The people of these areas resorted to the old practice of fetching water from river, springs, canals/ channels, etc., which was unhygienic, with possible risk of water borne diseases.

keyFindings.text: 54% of Odisha's PVTG population (1.60 lakh) remained excluded from welfare because the SSD Department ignored 1,138 newly notified villages for years after June 2020 notification.

source.quote: 1.60 lakh (54 per cent) PVTG population remained excluded from the coverage of welfare programmes/ schemes.

keyFindings.text: Physical inspections found 58% of irrigation projects and 55% of drinking water projects non-operational in PVTG villages — residents using rivers and springs with disease risk.

source.quote: During joint physical inspection, 23 (58 per cent) out of 40 irrigation projects and 38 (55 per cent) out of 69 drinking water projects were found non-operational.

recommendations: State Government should extend all welfare schemes to all 1,138 newly notified PVTG villages without further delay.
All non-operational irrigation, drinking water, and Nutrition Resource Centres should be repaired under a time-bound plan.
PVTG Empowerment Fund administration should be overhauled to prevent irregular sanctions and improve recovery mechanisms.

title: Performance Audit on Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme in Uttarakhand
ministry: Rural Development Department, Government of Uttarakhand
overview: MGNREGS guarantees 100 days of employment to every rural household. In Uttarakhand, where 66% of the population is rural and hilly districts face geographic isolation, the scheme is critical. CAG found that 2019-24 outcomes were dismal: only 1-4% of households received the full 100-day entitlement; social audits had a 79-99% shortfall in selected districts; 33% of wage payments were delayed; vigilance cells at state, district, and village levels were all absent; and complaint registers were not maintained.

stats.label: Only 1–4% of households got full 100-day entitlement
stats.value: Average 21 days/year; 4.72–6.54 lakh of 10–11 lakh HHs employed
stats.note: MGNREGS guarantees 100 days of wage employment per household per year. In Uttarakhand, the average employment delivered was just 21 days per household — 21% of the statutory entitlement. Only 1 to 4 per cent of households received the full 100-day entitlement. Labour Budgets were approved without grassroots consultation or baseline surveys, resulting in inaccurate demand estimation. Many job card holders were denied employment even after making formal requests. Unemployment allowances — the statutory fallback when work is not provided — were not paid, despite being required by law.

source.quote: only one to four per cent of households received the full entitlement of 100 days of work, and average financial benefits were significantly below targets.

stats.label: Social audit shortfall — 79–99% in selected districts
stats.value: Social audits nearly absent in test-checked GPs
stats.note: Social audits are MGNREGA's primary accountability mechanism — mandated to catch wage theft, ghost workers, and asset fraud at the village level. In the selected districts, the shortfall in conducting social audits ranged between 79% and 99%. Even where social audits were conducted statewide (88,915 observations raised during 2019-24), corrective measures were taken in only 59% of cases. Vigilance cells — required at state, district, and village levels — were entirely absent at all three levels. The State Employment Guarantee Council did not function effectively.

source.quote: the shortfall in conducting of social audit was ranging between 79 per cent and 99 per cent. Thus, the Department missed an opportunity to utilize the social audit mechanism to strengthen the implementation of the scheme for the benefit of the intended beneficiaries.

stats.label: Wage payment delays — 33% of Muster Rolls delayed 4–157 days
stats.note: CAG examined 1,232 Muster Rolls (MRs) across 160 selected works and found 411 MRs (33%) had wage payments delayed by 4 to 157 days, affecting 2,946 labourers. Despite statutory provisions, compensation for delays was rarely approved and no unemployment allowances were paid. Job Card quality was also poor: 78 of 200 JCs (39%) had no photographs; 50 JCs (25%) had no updated work information. Original MRs were often unavailable post-work initiation — raising concerns about wage disbursement accuracy and enabling fraud.

source.quote: 1,232 MRs across 160 selected works revealed that payments for 411 MRs (33 per cent), involving 2,946 laborers, were delayed by four to 157 days.

keyFindings.text: Only 1–4% of Uttarakhand MGNREGS households received the full 100-day entitlement; average delivery was 21 days/year despite 100-day legal guarantee.

source.quote: only one to four per cent of households received the full entitlement of 100 days of work, and average financial benefits were significantly below targets.

keyFindings.text: Social audits had a 79–99% shortfall in selected districts; vigilance cells absent at state, district, and village levels — the core accountability mechanism was completely non-functional.

source.quote: the shortfall in conducting of social audit was ranging between 79 per cent and 99 per cent.

recommendations: State Government must ensure 100-day entitlement is delivered and unemployment allowances paid when work is not provided.
Social Audit Units should conduct mandatory audits and the State Government must ensure corrective action on observations.
Vigilance cells at state, district, and village level must be constituted as required under MGNREGA.

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Smart Cities Mission in Dehradun
ministry: Urban Development Department, Government of Uttarakhand
overview: Dehradun was the only Uttarakhand city selected under the Smart Cities Mission (2017) with a ₹1,000 crore budget. CAG found that Dehradun Smart City Limited (DSCL) failed on every front: ₹4.55 crore SWM module unutilised since March 2022; ₹5.91 crore Smart Schools equipment non-functional; 8 projects delayed 19–38 months; ₹19.06 crore not recovered from implementing agency; ₹6.20 crore interest lost; ₹5.19 crore in PMC payment irregularities. Smart City objectives — core infrastructure, quality of life, smart solutions — only partially achieved.

stats.label: Smart Cities Mission spend — ₹634 Cr of ₹737 Cr released
stats.note: The total budget for Dehradun Smart City Mission was ₹1,000 crore in equal sharing between Central and State governments. By 2022-23, ₹737.50 crore had been released and ₹634.11 crore spent. However, utilization of the money — what was actually delivered on the ground — was deeply deficient. Numerous Smart Solutions outlined in Detailed Project Reports were dropped during execution or remained non-functional. DSCL did not appoint a full-time CEO, Additional CEO, or Finance Controller — making the SPV structure ineffective in spirit and in law.

source.quote: An expenditure of ` 634.11 crore was incurred during the period 2016-17 to 2022-23 against the funds of ` 737.50 crore released during the said period.

stats.label: Smart Solutions non-functional — ₹4.55 Cr SWM module unused
stats.value: Biometric SWM module idle since March 2022; e-rickshaws non-operational
stats.note: A biometric and sensor-based Solid Waste Management module developed in March 2022 under the Doon ICCC (Integrated Command and Control Centre) to monitor real-time waste collection remained completely unutilised till February 2025 — over two years after deployment — rendering ₹4.55 crore unfruitful. E-rickshaws procured at ₹0.90 crore under the Smart Waste Vehicles project were non-operational for almost two years. Smart Schools equipment (interactive boards, CCTVs, biometric attendance) installed in three government schools at ₹5.91 crore became non-functional because schools couldn't afford electricity bills.

source.quote: remained unutilised till February 2025, rendering expenditure of ` 4.55 crore unfruitful.

stats.label: DSCL failed to recover ₹19.06 Cr from implementing agency
stats.value: Unutilised funds not returned; ₹1.41 Cr penalties not enforced
stats.note: Dehradun Smart City Limited could not provide hindrance-free work fronts to implementing agencies, leading to 19–38 month delays in 8 projects. DSCL failed to enforce penalties of ₹1.41 crore for project delays and failed to recover the unutilised amount of ₹19.06 crore from the implementing agency. Financial mismanagement caused ₹6.20 crore in interest loss. PMC payments had ₹5.19 crore in irregularities including procurement violations and reimbursement without documentation. Cost escalation of ₹10.34 crore and works worth ₹2.93 crore executed without tenders were also found.

source.quote: DSCL failed to recover unutilised amount of ` 19.06 crore from the implementing agency.

keyFindings.text: ₹4.55 crore SWM module and ₹5.91 crore Smart Schools equipment were non-functional; e-rickshaws non-operational for 2 years — Smart Solutions failed to deliver after deployment.

source.quote: remained unutilised till February 2025, rendering expenditure of ` 4.55 crore unfruitful.

keyFindings.text: DSCL failed to recover ₹19.06 crore; lost ₹6.20 crore interest; PMC payments had ₹5.19 crore irregularities — financial control failures across the board.

source.quote: DSCL failed to recover unutilised amount of ` 19.06 crore from the implementing agency.

recommendations: State Government should address operational shortcomings and ensure functioning of all non-operational Smart Cities infrastructure.
Full-time CEO, ACEO, and Finance Controller must be appointed in DSCL to ensure governance effectiveness.
Milestone-based payment structures should be mandated in future contracts to prevent payments for incomplete work.

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Namami Gange Programme in Uttarakhand
ministry: State Mission for Clean Ganga, Government of Uttarakhand
overview: Namami Gange is India's integrated Ganga conservation mission (2014). CAG found that in Uttarakhand, Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) were either unconnected to household sewers or barely operating. Uttarakhand Jal Sansthan declined to take over 18 STPs due to construction deficiencies. Forestry interventions achieved only 16% of planned expenditure. Ganga water quality in Rishikesh and Haridwar remained in category B (fit for bathing, not drinking) throughout 2019-2023, unchanged from pre-programme levels. NMCG released ₹20,000 crore nationally for the programme.

stats.label: Jal Sansthan refused 18 STPs — defective construction
stats.value: 18 Sewage Treatment Plants not handed over due to deficiencies
stats.note: Uttarakhand's implementation of Namami Gange built multiple Sewage Treatment Plants as the core anti-pollution infrastructure. However, Uttarakhand Jal Sansthan (UJS) — the agency responsible for operating and maintaining the STPs — declined to take over 18 STPs due to deficiencies in their construction and operation. Many remaining STPs were either unconnected to household sewer networks or only partially connected. Existing STPs lacked sufficient treatment capacity for the sewage volume, resulting in significant discharge of untreated sewage directly into the Ganga.

source.quote: Uttarakhand Jal Sansthan declined to take over 18 STPs due to deficiencies in their construction and operation.

stats.label: Forestry interventions — only 16% of planned expenditure implemented
stats.value: Crematoria unutilized; garbage dumped on river slopes
stats.note: One of Namami Gange's key supplementary interventions was ecological restoration — afforestation and biodiversity conservation along the Ganga banks. CAG found the progress was minimal: only 16 per cent of the planned expenditure was implemented on forestry interventions. Crematoria constructed by State Mission for Clean Ganga remained largely unutilised due to insufficient public awareness activities. Solid waste management in Ganga Towns was critically deficient — garbage was primarily dumped on river slopes or burned instead of being processed, causing it to flow back into the river.

source.quote: The progress of forestry interventions was minimal, with only 16 per cent of the planned expenditure implemented.

stats.label: Ganga water quality — B category in Haridwar/Rishikesh 2019–23
stats.value: River water not clean despite ₹20,000 Cr national spend
stats.note: The ultimate measure of Namami Gange's success is whether the Ganga became cleaner. CAG found that water quality in Haridwar remained consistently in category B (suitable for bathing, not drinking) throughout the audit period 2019-2023. In Rishikesh, the water was in category B from 2019 to 2023 — with only a temporary improvement to category A during the COVID-19 lockdown years (2020-21) when industrial and human activity stopped. STPs that were operating frequently failed to meet NGT treatment norms. NMCG launched Namami Gange with a ₹20,000 crore budget (extended to ₹22,500 crore in Mission-II to 2026).

source.quote: In Rishikesh, the water quality of river Ganga remained in B category from 2019 to 2023, with the exception of COVID-19 period (2020 & 2021), when it improved to A category. The river water quality in Haridwar remained consistently in B category throughout the audit period.

keyFindings.text: Uttarakhand Jal Sansthan declined to take over 18 STPs due to construction deficiencies — the core Namami Gange infrastructure was not operationally handed over.

source.quote: Uttarakhand Jal Sansthan declined to take over 18 STPs due to deficiencies in their construction and operation.

keyFindings.text: Ganga water quality in Haridwar and Rishikesh remained in category B throughout 2019-2023 — no measurable improvement in the river's condition despite the mission.

source.quote: The river water quality in Haridwar remained consistently in B category throughout the audit period.

recommendations: State Government should conduct comprehensive safety audits of STPs and address deficiencies before transfer to maintenance agencies.
House sewer network connectivity must be ensured for all STPs — unconnected STPs cannot treat sewage that never reaches them.
Solid waste management in Ganga Towns must be enforced to prevent riverbank dumping and burning.

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation in Kerala
ministry: Local Self Government Department, Government of Kerala
overview: AMRUT was launched in 2015 to provide tap water, sewerage, parks, and urban transport in 9 Kerala cities. GoI released ₹1,161.17 crore over 2015-2024. After 9 years, CAG found: no city achieved universal 135 lpcd water supply; 27 projects (₹233.55 crore) were abandoned; a ₹40.62 crore water treatment plant was idling; 4 overhead reservoirs (₹31.51 crore) idle; water coverage ranging from 9.39% (Guruvayur) to 89.16% (Kochi); and most cities unable to establish any sewage treatment at all.

stats.label: 27 AMRUT projects abandoned — ₹233.55 Cr wasted
stats.value: DPRs prepared without surveys; cost overruns; abandoned mid-way
stats.note: Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) were prepared by empanelled agencies without proper site investigation or public consultation — a fundamental planning failure. The result: DPRs required extensive revision, costs escalated beyond estimates, and ultimately 27 projects with a total project cost of ₹233.55 crore had to be abandoned. Funds released by GoI were delayed by 43 days to 15 months (average 5.9 months) due to State-level processing failures. KWA parked funds in violation of GoI instructions. The State Level Technical Committee (SLTC) didn't meet for 29 months (Sep 2018–Jan 2021) — failing to appraise 38 projects.

source.quote: Preparation of Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) by empanelled agencies without proper site investigation, public consultation etc., resulted in extensive revision of estimates, cost overrun and abandoning of 27 projects with project cost of ₹233.55 crore.

stats.label: ₹40.62 Cr water treatment plant idling at Vasoorichira
stats.value: Also: 4 OHSRs (₹31.51 Cr) idle in Kochi, Thrissur, Palakkad
stats.note: A 100 MLD Water Treatment Plant was constructed at Vasoorichira, Kollam at ₹40.62 crore — but lay completely idle because the raw water pumping main was never laid. The plant cannot treat water that never arrives. Four Overhead Service Reservoirs constructed at ₹31.51 crore across Kochi and Thrissur Corporations and Palakkad Municipality were also idle due to unfinished pumping mains, distribution lines, or leakages. The AMRUT mission's primary goal — universal tap water — was not achieved in any of the nine mission cities even after 9 years.

source.quote: 100 MLD Water Treatment Plant constructed expending ₹40.62 crore at Vasoorichira in Kollam was idling due to non-completion of laying of raw water pumping main.

stats.label: Tap water coverage: 9.39% (Guruvayur) to 89.16% (Kochi)
stats.value: Zero cities achieved 135 lpcd universal coverage target
stats.note: AMRUT's core objective was universal 135 litres per capita per day (lpcd) tap water supply for all households in mission cities. After 9 years and ₹1,161 crore released, zero of the nine Kerala mission cities achieved this target. Coverage ranged from 9.39% in Guruvayur Municipality (only 1 in 10 households have tap connections) to 89.16% in Kochi Corporation. In sewerage — even more critical for public health — only Thiruvananthapuram, Kochi, and Kannur had any sewage collection and treatment. Kochi (3%) and Kannur (1%) had negligible sewage network coverage.

source.quote: Coverage of household water supply among the nine mission cities ranged from 9.39 per cent (Guruvayur Municipality) to 89.16 per cent (Kochi Corporation).

keyFindings.text: 27 AMRUT projects (₹233.55 crore) abandoned after DPRs were prepared without site surveys — a planning failure that wasted crores before construction even started.

source.quote: abandoning of 27 projects with project cost of ₹233.55 crore.

keyFindings.text: Zero of nine Kerala AMRUT cities achieved universal 135 lpcd tap water coverage after 9 years; ₹40.62 crore WTP and ₹31.51 crore OHSRs idle due to incomplete supporting infrastructure.

source.quote: 100 MLD Water Treatment Plant constructed expending ₹40.62 crore at Vasoorichira in Kollam was idling due to non-completion of laying of raw water pumping main.

recommendations: DPRs must be based on proper site investigations, public consultations, and field surveys before approval.
Incomplete water supply infrastructure (pumping mains, distribution networks) must be expedited to make idle treatment plants operational.
SLTC must meet regularly and provide mandatory technical appraisal for all projects per AMRUT guidelines.

title: Performance Audit on Solid Waste Management in Urban Local Bodies in Rajasthan
ministry: Local Self Government Department, Government of Rajasthan
overview: Rajasthan's urban areas face a solid waste management crisis. CAG audited 18 Urban Local Bodies and found: waste processing at only 11-25% of generation at state level; direct dumping at 63-79%; 15 of 18 ULBs lacking sanitary landfills; 12 ULBs with no health and sanitation committees; ₹11.99 crore in IEC funds allocated but 12 ULBs conducted zero awareness activities. DPRs were based on incorrect data, weigh-bridges absent in 14 ULBs, and compost machines in four ULBs unused since installation in 2019.

stats.label: Waste processing — only 11–25% processed at state level
stats.note: Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 and Swachh Bharat Mission mandate scientific processing of waste (composting, recycling, waste-to-energy) before disposal. In Rajasthan, processing of waste was only 11 to 25 per cent at the state level and 29 to 35 per cent in the 18 test-checked ULBs. The gap between collection and processing means that 63 to 79 per cent of waste at the state level was directly dumped — raw, mixed, unprocessed — in open dump sites. The remaining unprocessed waste at the state level was not being dumped at designated dumping sites either, indicating uncontrolled open dumping.

source.quote: Processing of waste was only 11 per cent to 25 per cent at State level and 29 per cent to 35 per cent in test checked ULBs. Direct dumping of solid waste ranged between 63 per cent to 79 per cent at the State level and 65 per cent to 71 per cent in test checked ULBs.

stats.label: Direct dumping — 63–79% of state waste, 65–71% in test ULBs
stats.value: Raw MSW dumped in open sites; not in sanitary landfills
stats.note: The flip side of near-zero processing is near-total dumping. In 15 of 18 test-checked ULBs, sanitary landfill sites were not constructed — meaning all dumping was in open sites without scientific treatment. Weigh-bridges for measuring waste were not installed in 14 of 18 ULBs, making it impossible to measure or monitor waste collection. Compost machines procured in six ULBs between Feb-Dec 2019 were not in use in four of them from the day of installation — treating ₹11.99 crore in IEC funds for 12 ULBs went entirely unspent.

source.quote: Direct dumping of solid waste ranged between 63 per cent to 79 per cent at the State level and 65 per cent to 71 per cent in test checked ULBs.

stats.label: 15 of 18 ULBs have no sanitary landfill — open dumping only
stats.value: Jaipur landfill (₹12.06 Cr, 2012) and Baran (2016) also unused
stats.note: 15 of 18 test-checked Urban Local Bodies had not constructed sanitary landfill sites — dumping all municipal solid waste in open sites in violation of law. Even the two ULBs that did build landfills wasted the investment: Jaipur (MC) and Baran (Municipal Council) constructed landfill sites in 2012 and 2016 respectively at ₹12.06 crore, but both remained completely unused since construction because no waste processing plants were set up alongside them. The Solid Waste Management Rules require processing before landfilling — without a processing plant, the landfill couldn't be used, so waste was dumped openly instead.

source.quote: Out of 18 test checked Urban Local Bodies, 15 ULBs did not construct sanitary landfill sites and dumped the municipal solid waste in open dumping sites.

keyFindings.text: Only 11–25% of Rajasthan's urban waste is processed; 63–79% is directly dumped raw — open dumping is not the exception but the norm across the state.

source.quote: Processing of waste was only 11 per cent to 25 per cent at State level. Direct dumping of solid waste ranged between 63 per cent to 79 per cent at the State level.

keyFindings.text: 15 of 18 ULBs had no sanitary landfill; two that built landfills (₹12.06 crore) left them unused since 2012/2016 because no processing plants were built alongside.

source.quote: Out of 18 test checked Urban Local Bodies, 15 ULBs did not construct sanitary landfill sites and dumped the municipal solid waste in open dumping sites.

recommendations: State Government must establish waste processing plants (composting, recycling, waste-to-energy) in all ULBs before setting up landfills.
Weigh-bridges should be installed in all ULBs and waste tracking data should be monitored by the State Government.
Health and Sanitation Committees must be constituted in all ULBs and IEC funds deployed for public awareness.

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Har Ghar Nal Ka Jal Yojana in Bihar
ministry: Public Health Engineering Department & Panchayati Raj Department, Government of Bihar
overview: Bihar launched Har Ghar Nal Ka Jal (HGNJ) in December 2015 to provide piped water to every household by 2020. CAG found: ₹30,500.92 crore allocated over 2017-23; reported 98.70% rural coverage was inflated vs 95.71% actual; 11.22 lakh households missed in 46,633 rural wards; ₹2.31 crore paid for unexecuted works; Fluoride Removal Plants installed in habitations without fluoride; 28 of 38 districts had contaminated water; chlorinators absent in most schemes; and monitoring platforms unreliable or non-functional.

stats.label: HGNJ Bihar — ₹30,500.92 Cr allocated, coverage inflated
stats.value: Reported 98.70% rural coverage vs actual 95.71% on JJM dashboard
stats.note: Bihar allocated ₹30,500.92 crore to three departments (PRD, PHED, UD&HD) for HGNJ Yojana over 2017-23. The State reported 98.70% coverage of targeted rural households as of March 2023 — but the JJM-Har Ghar Jal dashboard showed only 95.71% as of November 2025. The reported urban coverage was 94% as of March 2023, showing non-achievement of the 100% target that was originally due in March 2020. In 2011, only 2.60% of rural Bihar households had tap water; 28 of 38 districts had groundwater contaminated with arsenic, fluoride, or iron.

source.quote: During the period 2017-18 to 2022-23, the PRD, PHED and the UD&HD allocated ₹ 30,500.92 crore to their implementing units for HGNJ yojana.

stats.label: 11.22 lakh households missed — including 8.07 lakh in water-quality wards
stats.value: PHED failed to cover 46,633 rural wards; 77 quality wards without WTPs
stats.note: Inadequate baseline surveys led to unreliable targeting. PHED could not cover 11.22 lakh households under 46,633 rural wards — including 8.07 lakh households in quality-affected wards where contaminated groundwater poses direct health risks. 77 quality-affected wards were covered without Water Treatment Plants, meaning these households received contaminated water through new pipes. 41 wards had schemes implemented without any water treatment infrastructure at all. In 1,000 fluoride-affected habitations, Fluoride Removal Plants worth ₹2.77 crore were installed in places where water wasn't even fluoride-affected.

source.quote: PHED could not cover 11.22 lakh households under 46,633 rural wards including 8.07 lakh households in quality affected wards.

stats.label: ₹2.31 Cr paid to contractors for unexecuted works
stats.value: Five PH divisions; ghost works; IoT devices non-standardised
stats.note: In five test-checked Public Health divisions, ₹2.31 crore was paid to contractors for works that had actually not been executed — direct financial fraud or gross oversight failure. IoT devices for real-time scheme monitoring suffered from non-standardised procurement, cost inconsistencies, and poor follow-up after installation. NischaySoft and Nagarsewa (monitoring platforms) were either unreliable or non-functional. Community engagement through Lavuk Committees, Jal Choupals, and health camps was minimal. Most beneficiaries were unaware of complaint mechanisms.

source.quote: In five test-checked PH divisions, ₹ 2.31 crore was paid to contractors for works that had actually not been executed.

keyFindings.text: PHED missed 11.22 lakh households in 46,633 rural wards — including 8.07 lakh in quality-affected areas where contaminated groundwater makes safe supply critical.

source.quote: PHED could not cover 11.22 lakh households under 46,633 rural wards including 8.07 lakh households in quality affected wards.

keyFindings.text: ₹2.31 crore paid in five PH divisions for unexecuted works; ₹2.77 crore Fluoride Removal Plants installed where there was no fluoride problem — misallocation at scale.

source.quote: In five test-checked PH divisions, ₹ 2.31 crore was paid to contractors for works that had actually not been executed.

recommendations: Detailed baseline surveys and ward-level identification must be completed before scheme implementation to ensure no household is missed.
All quality-affected wards must be provided functional Water Treatment Plants — covering these wards without treatment is worse than not covering them.
Responsibility must be fixed for ₹2.31 crore payments made for unexecuted works, and recovery initiated.

title: Report No. 03 of 2025-Performance Audit on Effectiveness of measures taken by the Government of West Bengal for containing water pollution.
overview:
This Performance Audit examines the effectiveness of measures implemented by the Government of West Bengal to contain water pollution, with a focus on the adequacy, efficiency, and impact of these interventions. The audit highlights significant shortcomings in program execution, regulatory compliance, and inter-departmental coordination that have undermined pollution control efforts.

Critical findings include poor utilisation of funds earmarked for mitigating water pollution, inadequate monitoring mechanisms, and failure to meet key targets in sanitation infrastructure. The report also identifies multiple instances where water bodies remained polluted despite official interventions, due to systemic lapses in governance and enforcement.

The audit underscores the lack of robust deterrence against polluters and calls attention to the insufficient staffing and weak institutional capacity of State Pollution Control entities. These shortcomings have collectively resulted in persistent water quality violations and limited public health gains, highlighting the urgent need for course correction.

title: Report of the C&AG of India on Compliance and Performance Audit of State Public Sector Enterprises for the period ended March 2023 (Report No.6 of 2025)
overview:
This report presents the results of compliance and performance audit of State Public Sector Enterprises (SPSEs) in Odisha for the period up to March 2023. Of the 76 SPSEs under the CAG’s audit jurisdiction, 42 are covered in detail; they registered a turnover of ₹47,902.01 crore in 2022-23, making up 6.18% of Odisha's GSDP, with the turnover increase at 24.41% over the previous year. Despite this overall growth, financial stress persists: 8 SPSEs reported total accumulated losses of ₹9,449.38 crore, and 4 have fully eroded net worth, now negative by ₹5,735.80 crore as against paid-up capital.

The report highlights significant lapses in operational and financial efficiency. Odisha Mining Corporation (OMC), the state’s largest mining PSU, continues to incur avoidable expenditure due to inoperative mines (₹163.36 crore over 2018–23), unpaid royalty on excess/extralegal mining (₹3,761.88 crore), and additional costs from poor grade segregation and planning. Notably, targeted mineral production at OMC’s mines was missed by 15%–88% for various ores, causing steep revenue loss, including a shortfall of one million tonnes iron ore (₹606.43 crore revenue loss).

Audit also exposes weaknesses in compliance and internal controls. Corporate governance compliance is lacking — in 2022-23, 5 out of the 27 required PSUs did not appoint the mandated independent directors, and 20 out of 51 working SPSEs skipped the minimal four Board meetings. Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) requirements were only partially implemented, and several PSUs failed to have policies and budgets.

Additional compliance audits disclose avoidable expenditures (interest-free advances, overheads, GST), revenue losses from mismanaged projects, and undue benefits extended to contractors or beneficiaries. The CAG underscores persistent bottlenecks in internal accountability, violation of statutory regulations, and delays in account finalization, all of which elevate the risk of fraud and impede public sector value generation.

title: Performance Audit Report on E-Way Bill System under GST, Union Government (Department of Revenue – Indirect Taxes -Goods and Services Tax)
overview:
This Performance Audit assessed the effectiveness of the E-Way Bill (EWB) system under GST in protecting revenue interests and the efficiency of preventive activities by the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC). Covering transactions from April 2018 to March 2022, the audit used a risk-based methodology and data analytics, examining 2,244 EWBs related to 956 taxpayers. The audit revealed systemic issues such as significant non/short discharge of tax liability (e.g., 103 taxpayers failed to report turnover worth ₹2,285.23 crore, leading to a tax loss estimate of ₹307.37 crore with ₹3.25 crore interest). There were also violations of composition scheme conditions, cases of cancelled registrations continuing to generate EWBs, and instances of nil filers carrying on outward supplies undetected by the system.

Audit found that 108 taxpayers did not produce any records, and only partial records were produced for 334, affecting the assurance on compliance and correctness of department action on booked cases. Analytical discrepancies, such as mismatch in ITC claims (₹155.41 crore) and wilful suppression of turnover totalling ₹168.21 crore across 18 taxpayers, indicate weaknesses in interoperability, validation, and enforcement.

Operationally, while NIC generates 97 analytical reports for enforcement, 46 of 58 commissionerates admitted not using these for vehicle interception planning. Audit also found demands of ₹2.60 crore not raised in 200 cases where vehicles were released after EWB verification, and unregistered persons generated EWBs exceeding registration thresholds.

Constraints in access to taxpayer records and follow-up documentation, in part due to non-production by the department or taxpayer, further limit corrective action. The report concludes with recommendations focusing on automating validations, directing enforcement efforts, and ensuring timely audit access to records.

title: Performance Audit on “Welfare of Building and other construction workers”
overview:
This Performance Audit, conducted by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, assesses the effectiveness of the welfare measures for building and other construction workers (BOCW) in the National Capital Territory of Delhi. The audit examined registration, cess collection, fund utilisation, and implementation of welfare schemes by the Delhi Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Board over the four-year period 2019–20 to 2022–23.

The CAG identified serious shortcomings, notably the lack of reliable data for BOCW population in Delhi and major deficiencies in the identification and registration of establishments and workers. Out of the reported 6.96 lakh registered workers, only 1.98 lakh had complete database entries, with issues such as duplicate or missing images and multiple registrations for the same beneficiary. In terms of renewals, Delhi’s performance lagged far behind the national average, with only 7.3% of registrations renewed compared to the all-India figure of 74%.

On the financial side, the Board accumulated Rs 3579.05 crore in funds as of March 2023 but failed to reconcile cess collections; discrepancies totaling Rs 204.95 crore between District records and Board records were identified and not addressed. Expenditure on welfare schemes was low, ranging from 9.53% to 11.33% of receipts (with the exception of Covid-period ex-gratia), and several mandated schemes saw zero spend throughout the audit period.

Operational gaps included failure to conduct required inspections and no proactive measures for worker identification, despite Supreme Court directives and central government advisories. Benefits under critical health and safety schemes remain inadequate, and systematic delays up to 1423 days were noted in processing applications. No social audit had been conducted despite a Supreme Court directive five and a half years earlier.
