title: Report No. 03 of 2024- Performance Audit Report on Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services in West Bengal for the year ended March 2022
overview:
The audit reviews the State’s performance in providing accessible and quality public health infrastructure and services across primary, secondary, and tertiary levels for a population of 9.13 crore. There was a persistent shortage of key medical personnel: 36% shortfall in Specialist Medical Officers and 49% in General Duty Medical Officers at the State level, with Sub-Centres lacking male Health Workers in 89% of cases and laboratory technician positions vacant by 75% in PHCs.

Critical clinical services were unavailable at scale: 71% of PHCs lacked accident and emergency services, 90% lacked Emergency Obstetric Care (including surgery), and 70% lacked functional beds. At Community Health Centres, 284 out of 348 lacked emergency obstetric care and 285 CHCs (81.89%) were without Blood Storage Units.

Drug procurement and supply suffered failures: 30% of drug samples sent for quality testing had no result as of March 2022. In District Hospitals, 63% of notified essential drugs had never been procured. Equipment calibration was poor, with 23% of bio-medical equipment never calibrated. Infrastructure gaps were substantial; up to 56% shortage of PHCs and only 14 new centres established in six years. Financial management was weak, with health sector spending at just 1.23% of GSDP against a 2.5% target.

Regulatory enforcement and planning were inadequate: no comprehensive health policy or standards, lack of regular maternal and child death reviews, and failure to align with Sustainable Development Goals or conduct gap analysis. The report recommends urgent systemic improvements to planning, monitoring, and staffing to address high-risk service lapses and underutilisation of funds.

title: Performance Audit of Implementation of Border Area Development Programme (Report No 02 of 2024)
overview:
The CAG conducted a Performance Audit of the Border Area Development Programme (BADP) covering implementation across selected states for the years 2017–18 to 2021–22. Aimed at addressing balanced development and security in border regions, the audit examined the efficacy, fund flow, planning, execution, and monitoring of BADP.

The audit revealed substantial underutilisation of allocated funds, with only 63 per cent of the budget for the sampled period actually spent on projects. Further, a large number of works were either incomplete or delayed, undermining the purpose of the scheme.

Serious deficiencies in planning were observed due to the absence of comprehensive baseline surveys, resulting in selection of non-priority projects. Monitoring systems at both central and state levels were found inadequate, contributing to irregularities and lack of accountability.

Instances were also noted where assets created under BADP were left unutilised, which not only posed a loss to the exchequer but also hampered development objectives. The report calls for urgent corrective measures to ensure the scheme achieves its targeted outcomes.

title: Performance Audit of Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services – Government of Punjab
overview:
This performance audit by CAG analyses the adequacy of financial resources, health infrastructure, manpower, equipment, regulatory frameworks, and alignment with SDG-3 across Punjab's public health sector, covering 2016-17 to 2021-22 (with updates until 2021-22 or later).

Key findings include a severe shortage of staff: as of audit, 50.69% of sanctioned posts (34,949 out of 68,949) were vacant across the Department of Health & Family Welfare and Department of Medical Education & Research. The distribution was highly skewed, with some districts having a doctor-population ratio as adverse as one per 7,376 people.

Health services were consistently incomplete. Many District Hospitals and CHCs lacked critical OPD or IPD specialist departments; half the District Hospitals tested had inadequate operating theatre facilities or lacked essential emergency services. Essential drugs and diagnostic equipment fell drastically short, with no effective mechanism to address short/failed supplies. Infrastructure gaps and dilapidated residential quarters were widespread.

Financial management revealed persistent under-utilisation: 6.5–20.74% of the health budget was unspent each year, and State health expenditure in 2021-22 was only 0.68% of GSDP (well below the 2.5% target set by National Health Policy 2017). Significant government funds were parked outside government accounts, contravening codal provisions.

Regulatory mechanisms lagged: key legal frameworks were delayed or incomplete, with large numbers of unregistered clinics and non-compliance with Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules. Punjab has not mapped its budget to SDG-3 targets and has published indicators for only 7 out of 12 targets despite eight years since SDG adoption.

title: Report No. 7 of the year 2024 - Performance Audit on Welfare of Building and Other Construction Workers
overview:
This performance audit examines the management and efficacy of the Kerala Building and Construction Workers’ Welfare Board (the Board) in providing welfare assistance to construction workers between 2018 and 2023. The audit revealed the Board failed to systematically register establishments and workers: only 10,113 establishments were registered in the Labour Commissionerate Automation System (LCAS) compared to 2,57,104 constructions listed in Revenue Department records, highlighting major data inconsistencies and coverage gaps.

Payments to the Board were significantly delayed and incomplete. Of the 2,82,998 buildings assessed for cess collection across Kerala, cess was paid for only 1,26,446 (44.68%), leading to a shortfall of ₹542.17 crore, while interest of ₹11.39 crore was not accrued in 1,319 delayed cases. The Board’s cash balance fell sharply from ₹910.06 crore in March 2019 to ₹135.16 crore in March 2023, with annual disbursement of welfare benefits declining since 2020–21.

Data systems meant to track beneficiaries and welfare disbursements were poorly utilised, and irregularities in the registration process and beneficiary data further impeded effective scheme implementation. District offices lacked adequate monitoring, inspections, and grievance redress, while migrant workers remained excluded from registrations and entitlements. Delays ranged from one to five years in cess assessments for 282 cases; in test-checked districts, statutory reports were submitted late, and only a fraction of constructions eligible for cess were brought under LCAS registration.

The audit concludes that lax enforcement and inadequate internal controls resulted in substantial revenue leakages and critical under-realisation and under-utilisation of welfare funds, undermining the stated objectives of construction worker welfare in Kerala.

title: Report No. 3 of the year 2024 – Performance Audit of ‘Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services’
overview:
This performance audit evaluates the adequacy and effectiveness of the public health infrastructure and management of health services in the National Capital Territory of Delhi, focusing on the period from 2016-17 to 2021-22, with data extended where feasible until March 2022. The report analyses key indicators such as staff deficits, infrastructure gaps, drug supply, equipment shortages, financial management, regulatory effectiveness, and programme outcomes against established benchmarks like the Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) and various national guidelines.

Critical shortages were found in human resources: as of March 2022, there was a 21% deficit in overall health staff, 30% and 28% shortage in teaching and non-teaching specialists, and 36% shortage for National Health Mission scheme implementation. Several hospitals operated with persistent under-provision of staff including nurses and paramedics; super specialty hospitals could not function as intended due to staffing and management gaps. In addition, between 33–47% of essential drugs listed in the Essential Drug List were procured directly by hospitals rather than the Central Procurement Agency due to non-supply, and delays in quality testing led to inferior quality drugs being consumed.

Infrastructure expansion fell far short of the targets: only 1,357 out of a planned addition of 10,000 beds materialized over five years. Several healthcare facilities were not operationalized despite possession of land for extended periods. Financial management exhibited chronic underspending, with health sector budget savings ranging from 8.64% to 23.49% and up to 78.41% for infrastructure allocations. Delhi also fell significantly short on critical maternal and child health outcome targets, such as only 48.33% of registered pregnant women receiving all antenatal care steps and just 30% availing free diet under key welfare schemes.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India - Public Health Infrastructure for the year ended March 2022 - Govt UT of PDY Report No. 3 of 2024(Performance Audit - Civil)
overview:
This Performance Audit, conducted by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, reviewed the adequacy and effectiveness of public health infrastructure in the UT of Puducherry up to March 2022. The audit examined aspects such as availability of physical infrastructure, manpower in health institutions, financial management, and compliance with national standards.

The findings indicated major shortfalls in facilities, critical shortages of medical staff, inefficient fund utilisation, and inadequate maintenance of buildings and equipment. Several health centres suffered from non-availability of essential drugs and diagnostic services, hampering service delivery. There was also persistent under-utilisation of funds, with budget releases not always aligned to assessed needs.

Monitoring mechanisms such as supervisory visits and internal audits were found to be weak, leading to ineffective follow-up of deficiencies. The audit highlights significant gaps in healthcare access, particularly in rural and outlying areas, which affected patient outcomes and achievement of public health objectives.

Substantial non-compliance with Indian Public Health Standards was noticed in infrastructure, equipment, and staff position. The audit concludes that unless gaps in planning, fund release, staffing, and quality assurance are addressed, public health infrastructure will continue to perform below expectations.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India - Performance Audit on Solid Waste Mgt in Urban areas of UT of PDY for the year ended March 2022 - Govt UT of PDY Report No. 1 of 2024
overview:
This Performance Audit conducted by the CAG reviewed the effectiveness, efficiency, and outcomes of solid waste management (SWM) in urban local bodies of the Union Territory of Puducherry for the year ended March 2022. Audit objectives included verifying compliance with the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, assessment of financial management, operational effectiveness, and environmental impact.

The audit revealed that, despite policy formulation and program rollouts, there were significant deficiencies in planning, segregation at source, collection, transportation, processing, and scientific disposal of solid waste. Multiple urban local bodies failed to ensure 100% door-to-door collection, with gaps ranging as high as 38%. There were also persistent shortfalls in resource provision: of the required number of waste collection vehicles and manpower, only 65% was available.

Crucially, the audit found that scientific landfilling was not achieved; untreated waste was often dumped in open sites, resulting in environmental and public health risks. Waste processing infrastructure was under-used, with key processing plants operating at less than 30% of their installed capacity. Financial planning for SWM showed persistent underutilisation of allocated funds, and in many cases, funds meant for SWM remained unspent by the end of the year.

Public participation in source segregation and recycling initiatives was minimal, with less than half of urban households complying, mainly due to lack of awareness and monitoring. Internal audit and regular reporting mechanisms were either weak or absent, resulting in poor accountability across the SWM chain.

title: Report no. 7 of 2024 Performance Audit on the Working of Madhya Pradesh State Agro Industries Development Corporation Limited for the year ended 31 March 2022.
overview:
This performance audit examines the operations of Madhya Pradesh State Agro Industries Development Corporation Limited for the period April 2017 to March 2022, focusing on achievement of core objectives, procurement activities, financial management, production and supply processes, implementation of key schemes, and internal controls. The Company did not utilize its Mechanized Agricultural Farm for quality seed production, training, or modern agriculture methods, and remained confined to traditional farming activities. Efforts to expand supplementary food production remained limited to government contracts, with no significant market expansion.

The Company traded in reserved or unrelated items like water tankers and bus shelters, violating state rules and its memorandum, and failed to obtain commission on over Rs 589 crore of supplies, resulting in significant loss of margin income. Operational profitability declined, idle funds persisted for up to 10 years, and subsidies/disbursements were delayed by up to 29 years. The bio fertilizer plant experienced sales decline, and 25% of surveyed biogas plants were non-functional.

Internal controls and audits were weak, with deficient monitoring, acute staff shortages (ranging 59% to 87%), and repeated non-compliance with Companies Act provisions. Across all functions, multiple targets and objectives of the Company remained unachieved, pointing to systemic inefficiency and lack of robust planning.

Audit recommends coordinated long-term planning between Government and Company, strict adherence to procurement rules, timely payment of subsidies and margin income, and urgent overhaul of internal controls and HR management.

title: Report no. 2 of 2024 Performance Audit on Waste Management in Urban Local Bodies
overview:
This CAG Performance Audit examines the effectiveness of waste management—including solid, sewage, plastic, e-waste, and construction and demolition waste—in Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) of Madhya Pradesh from 2017-18 to 2021-22.

The audit covered 34 ULBs out of 413, and found persistent gaps in planning, infrastructure, data collection, and enforcement. Notably, 15 ULBs failed to assess waste quantities, and many relied on unreliable per capita estimates, leading to insufficient infrastructure capacity. Segregation of waste was enforced in only 41% of ULBs, but most segregated waste was ultimately dumped mixed at landfill sites, undermining the purpose. Contracts with private waste management firms were poorly managed, resulting in irregular and excess payments in multiple cases. Many ULBs lacked disposal facilities, proper city sanitation plans, and robust monitoring mechanisms.

Special waste streams (plastic, e-waste, C&D) were also poorly handled: 26 ULBs had not prepared bye-laws for plastic waste, only three ULBs utilised unrecyclable plastic in road construction, and 22 lacked e-waste policies. Weak policies resulted in health hazards and unusable landfill sites. Monitoring bodies met infrequently, and in several cases, ULBs operated waste facilities without statutory authorisation. Only one city, Indore, offered significant best practice examples. Overall, the audit revealed widespread non-compliance, insufficient planning, and critical gaps in service delivery.

The report provides targeted recommendations for baseline data, incentivising segregation, robust monitoring, contract management, and enforcement of environmental rules. Severity of findings is high due to repeated non-compliance, service deficits, and financial irregularities.

title: Report No. 04 of the year 2024, Performance Audit on Implementation of Deendayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana and Pradhan Mantri Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana by Electricity Distribution Companies of Madhya Pradesh for the year ended 31 March 2022
overview:
This Performance Audit examines the implementation of Deendayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana (DDUGJY) and Pradhan Mantri Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana (SAUBHAGYA) by the Electricity Distribution Companies (DISCOMs) of Madhya Pradesh during 2014-15 to 2021-22 for DDUGJY and 2017-18 to 2021-22 for SAUBHAGYA. The schemes involved creation of power distribution infrastructure and aimed to provide new electricity connections to 19.33 lakh households with an expenditure of ₹ 4,694.95 crore.

Audit found that DISCOMs prepared Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) without conducting the required field surveys, leading to extreme variations between what was sanctioned and what was executed—for example, component execution ranged from -100% to 4,368% of sanction. Metering of Distribution Transformers and unmetered consumers was grossly inadequate; only 25% of planned consumer meter installations were achieved, and not a single DTR was metered out of a targeted 89,310.

Timeliness and financial management were also deficient: there were systematic delays in project awarding (10–18 months) and execution (up to 22 months). DISCOMs paid excess consultancy (0.6–1.5% vs. a 0.5% ceiling) and did not enforce liquidated damages or adequately monitor or report scheme progress. The audit further revealed that 3.3 lakh beneficiaries were provided actual connections, but claims were lodged for 4.16 lakh, resulting in excess claims of ₹24.06 crore.

The schemes did achieve significant infrastructure augmentation—145 new substations, 33,711 Ckm of new 11 KV lines, and over 1.9 million household connections—but audit concludes that systemic flaws in project planning, execution, metering, and financial controls undermined cost-effectiveness, transparency, and full realisation of intended scheme benefits.

recommendations: DISCOMs should prepare DPRs only after proper field surveys, adhering strictly to scheme guidelines for technical and financial assessment.

DISCOMs and the State Government must ensure accurate beneficiary enumeration and avoid inflated claims for financial incentives.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Working of Yamuna Expressway Industrial Development Authority (YEIDA), Government of Uttar Pradesh, Report No. 7 of 2024 (Performance Audit-Civil)
overview:
This performance audit critically examines the operations of the Yamuna Expressway Industrial Development Authority (YEIDA) from 2005–06 to 2020–21. CAG found major lapses in planning, land acquisition, development, pricing, allotment, and internal controls within YEIDA. The audit identified missing records and information, which not only hampered audit scrutiny but resulted in a lack of accountability. Instances of revenue loss, short recoveries, avoidable excess expenditure, and undue benefits to allottees have been noted, with a cumulative estimated monetary impact of Rs 8,125.52 crore.

YEIDA undertook development activities in the NCR without approval of the National Capital Region Planning Board, and allotted plots for land uses that violated the Regional Plan 2021 and NCRPB Act. Land acquisition suffered from habitual invocation of urgency clauses without valid justification, resulting in loss to landowners and excess expenditure. YEIDA purchased land beyond requirements without utilization plans, causing a blockade of funds amounting to Rs 160.23 crore. There were also instances of delay and double payment in land acquisition, with no timely mutation or reconciliation of advances paid.

Construction and property development was plagued by underachievement, with only 5–36% of planned development executed for institutional, industrial and mixed land zones by 2021. Works were awarded at inflated rates, and performance guarantees/security deposits were collected at half the required rate, risking financial safeguards. YEIDA repeatedly failed to follow prescribed procedures, resulting in deficiency in road works, environmental clearance, and recovery of statutory dues.

Pricing and allotment mechanisms were inconsistent, lacking standard policies. Sale prices were frequently fixed on the lower side, leading to losses running into hundreds of crores. Eligibility criteria for allottees were often inappropriate or missing, allowing ineligible applicants to bid and receive plots, including consortiums whose lead members had no substantial stake in projects. Monitoring, internal control, corporate governance, and IT systems were weak, leading to poor tracking of land, contracts, and project completion. Annual reports and accounts were not prepared or submitted to the legislature, violating statutory mandates.

Fix responsibility and take disciplinary action for unauthorized land use changes and unwarranted land purchases causing fund blockades.
Standardize pricing and eligibility policies for all categories of properties to prevent continued losses and ensure fair allotment.
Strengthen audit follow-up and IT systems to ensure land mutation, periodical reconciliation of advances, and robust project monitoring.
GoUP should enforce preparation and submission of statutory Annual Reports and Accounts for industrial development authorities.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Implementation of 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act (Government of Karnataka Report No. 10 of 2024 (Performance Audit - Civil))
overview:
This performance audit examines the implementation of the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act in Karnataka, focusing on decentralisation, empowerment of rural local bodies (RLBs), and delivery of civic functions. The audit scrutinises fund flows, planning mechanisms, capacity building, and adherence to constitutional mandates. It reveals significant delays in devolving funds, functions, and functionaries to Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs), impacting their operational autonomy.

Major gaps identified include inconsistent fund allocations, weak monitoring frameworks, and overlapping roles among government departments and PRIs, leading to fragmentation of governance and inefficiency. Audit found that frequent transfers of staff and non-filling of posts compounded capacity constraints. Problems in grassroots planning and social audit processes undermined transparency and accountability despite constitutional provisions.

The audit notes that while Karnataka demonstrated relatively stronger legal and institutional structures compared to some states, persistent deficiencies remain in compliance, timely fund utilisation, and participatory governance. Performance shortfalls range from non-achievement of mandated planning processes to inadequate convergence across departments, hampering bottom-up development. The report strongly recommends rationalising devolution, strengthening accountability, and improving coordination between tiers.

In summary, the 73rd Amendment’s objectives of local empowerment and civic delivery remain elusive in several aspects due to systemic weaknesses. Karnataka, despite progressive legislation, continues to lag in practical devolution and in creating a responsive, accountable system for rural citizens. The audit underscores the urgency of addressing structural issues as well as capacity gaps to realise effective grassroots governance.

title: Report No. 4 of the Year 2024 - Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India Performance Audit on Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services, Government of Bihar
overview:
Bihar, with the nation's highest population density at 1,106 per sq km, faces severe public health infrastructure shortfalls. Despite a projected need for 1,24,919 allopathic doctors for its 12.49 crore population, only 58,144 were available as of January 2022—leaving the state with a doctor-population ratio of 1:2,148, far below WHO norms (1:1,000).

The audit highlights underutilisation of health funds: of ₹69,790.83 crore budgeted, only ₹48,047.79 crore (69%) was spent between 2016-22, resulting in ₹21,743.04 crore (31%) in savings, mainly due to the absence of district-level gap analysis and non-receipt of timely expenditure demands. Critical shortages persist in essential drugs, diagnostic facilities, and basic amenities in healthcare facilities. For example, availability of essential drugs in test-checked Out-Patient Departments ranged from only 35% to 79%.

Consequences of these gaps include prolonged staff vacancies (49% across key offices), persistent non-functional blood storage units, incomplete infrastructure upgrades, widespread equipment shortages in medical colleges, and deficient coverage of maternity services. The report notes that Bihar’s performance in key health indicators, such as maternal and neonatal mortality, lags behind national targets and SDG-3 benchmarks.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India For the year ended March 2022 Energy Management in Train Operations and Renewable Energy Initiatives in Indian Railways, Union Government (Railways) Performance Audit Report No. 6 of 2024
overview:
Indian Railways, one of the world's largest railway networks, is a major energy consumer and spent ₹30,428.84 crore on fuel in 2021-22, representing 14.53% of its working expenditure. Despite targeted savings under Mission 41K (budgeted ₹3,000 crore annually and cumulative ₹41,000 crore by 2025), the actual reduction in fuel cost is not commensurate across all zones. The review period saw fuel cost percentages fluctuate from 14.13% (2020-21, COVID year) up to 16.71% (2019-20).

Performance parameters show a decrease in Specific Fuel Consumption (SFC) for both passenger and freight operations, with passenger SFC nearly twice that of freight. However, the Specific Energy Consumption (SEC) for freight increased from 5.36 KwH/KGTKM in 2017-18 to 6.62 KwH/KGTKM in 2021-22, countering expected gains from increased electrification (electric Gross Tonne Kms rose by 12.48%). More than 56% of unelectrified route kilometers were electrified, yet corresponding reductions in diesel traction and energy audits remain inadequate.

Indian Railways lacks a single Master Circular aggregating all energy conservation policies. Energy audits were not regularly conducted in many zones and mechanisms for automated SFC/SEC measurement are missing, hampering optimal energy management and transparency. Notably, solar and wind power targets set under Vision 2020 (10% renewable energy by 2020) were not met.

title: Performance Audit on Public Health infrastructure and Management of Health Services in Goa
overview:
The performance audit on Public Health infrastructure and Management of Health Services in Goa reveals critical gaps in planning, resource utilization, and financial management across the state's health system. Notably, no Business Plan or Perspective Plan was framed, and there was no MoU with the state government to set performance benchmarks. As noted, the absence of a strategic and operational framework contributed to uncoordinated and ineffective action, with accumulated losses mounting from ₹25,299.87 crore in 2015-16 to ₹60,741.03 crore in 2021-22 despite annual Revenue Grants from the State Government. The average daily fleet for healthcare transport reduced from 4,344 units in 2015-16 to 3,937 in 2022-23 despite fund availability, affecting coverage and service delivery.

From 2015-22, operating revenues consistently lagged behind expenditure, necessitating state grants every year. In 2021-22 alone, the Corporation received ₹2,320 crore in revenue grants but still incurred a net loss of ₹8,498.35 crore, with a significant share attributed to the accrual of unpaid interest on state loans. Route planning and resource placement were inefficient: as of 31 March 2022, 656 overaged buses (17.44% of the fleet) operated, increasing further to 1,770 (44.96%) by March 2023, and the Corporation failed to recover operational costs on any bus route, incurring an operational loss of ₹14,198.86 crore over seven years.

The audit further highlights chronic delays in upgrading infrastructure, including e-Bus induction and intelligent transport systems, weak internal control (no effective accountability or tendering discipline), and widespread shortfalls in manpower planning. The system’s inability to implement reforms, recover dues, or capitalize on non-core revenue opportunities (e.g. rent collection, commercial land use) led to financial insecurity and eroded public confidence. The findings call for immediate, strategic correction to ensure service viability and broader public health outcomes.

title: Performance Audit of Implementation of 74 Constitutional Amendment Act in Goa
overview:
This performance audit covers the implementation of the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act in Goa for the period 2016-17 to 2020-21. The audit examined the devolution of functions, funds, and functionaries to Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) and scrutinised the compliance of statutory provisions as well as institutional frameworks mandated under the Act. Of Goa’s 14 statutorily recognised towns, five ULBs were sampled for test checks.

The audit found that although State Acts were generally compliant with the provisions of the 74th Amendment, overriding powers of the State Government persistently limited autonomy of ULBs. Most of the 18 functions listed in the Twelfth Schedule were only partially devolved, with key functions retained by Government departments and parastatals. For instance, execution of works funded by Central and State Finance Commission grants required departmental approval, leading to delayed implementation and reduced operational scope.

ULBs remained financially dependent on state grants, failing to meet even establishment expenditure from their own resources. The State Finance Commission was not constituted within prescribed timelines, and no action was taken on its fiscal recommendations—hindering fiscal empowerment. Additionally, there was a critical deficit in human resources, with posts unfilled and capacity-building efforts lacking, further impacting ULB effectiveness. (Pages v-vii, 7-10)

title: Performance Audit of Implementation of 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act in Goa
overview:
This performance audit examined the implementation of the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act in Goa from 2016-17 to 2020-21, covering all 191 Village Panchayats (VPs) and both Zilla Panchayats (ZPs). It specifically reviewed devolution of functions, funds and functionaries. Audit revealed that while the Goa Panchayat Raj Act, 1994 (GPRA) complies formally with the 73rd Amendment, operational realities show pronounced gaps: only three out of 42 sub-functions devolved to ZPs were implemented, and just 11 out of 24 devolved functions were fully implemented by VPs. The remaining functions were either partially or not implemented, with government departments and parastatals continuing to perform PRI roles. Financially, ZPs have no own revenue stream and are completely dependent on government grants, severely impacting their autonomy. Most VPs relied primarily on government grants and failed to revise property taxes or efficiently collect arrears—actual revenues and expenditures diverged significantly from budgets, with 34 VPs reserving fewer than one-third seats for women. Human resource gaps persist: PRIs lack dedicated cadres and rely on functionaries under Block Development Offices or DRDAs, leading to insufficient capacity for effective self-governance.

Delay in State Finance Commission formation and non-action on its recommendations stifled fiscal empowerment. District Planning Committees remained largely dysfunctional, undermining integrated district planning via local bodies. The State Government's overriding powers—amendments, expenditure restrictions, cancellation of PRI decisions and direct interventions—further curtailed PRI autonomy. As a result, PRIs in Goa operate with limited decision-making capacity, constrained resources and restricted self-governance.

The audit highlights critical operational, financial, and legislative bottlenecks impacting the full realization of decentralization envisaged under the 73rd Amendment. Immediate action is recommended to transfer residual election powers, reassess devolution mapping, bolster fiscal and human resource mechanisms, and revive institutional planning frameworks.

title: Performance Audit Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Performance of DISCOMs pre and post Ujwal DISCOM Assurance Yojna (UDAY) Government of Uttar Pradesh Report No. 1 of the year 2024
overview:
This performance audit covered the functioning of Uttar Pradesh's five DISCOMs under UDAY from 2015-16 to 2020-21 (updated to October 2022). UDAY aimed for financial and operational turnaround by transferring 75% of DISCOM debt and promising AT&C losses reduction to 14.86% by 2019-20. However, GoUP took over excess debt (`2,112.66 crore), and UPPCL claimed excess loss funding from GoUP (`7,977.97 crore between 2016-17 and 2020-21). Significant lapses included adjustment of government dues and additional tariff subsidy (`29,350.32 crore) from UDAY grants, contrary to MoU provisions, undermining DISCOMs' liquidity.

Operational targets were missed: AT&C losses stayed high at 30.02% in 2019-20 and rose to 31.19% in 2021-22. Unmetered consumers remained at 12.34 lakh (3.87%) as of October 2022, with defective meters persistently above the 3% norm. Collection and billing efficiency targets were not met by most DISCOMs, resulting in arrears of `4,474.28 crore against 17.10 lakh consumers for more than three months.

Financial health did not improve post-UDAY: DISCOMs' outstanding debt rose from `59,205.19 crore (pre-UDAY) to `71,102.77 crore by March 2022. Losses increased from `2,654.42 crore (March 2016) to `6,492.45 crore (March 2022), and accumulated losses stood at `77,936.94 crore. The audit concluded UDAY objectives were not met, with persistent structural and financial deficiencies impeding improvements.

title: Performance Audit on Pre and Post-Matric Scholarship Schemes for Scheduled Caste, Scheduled Tribe and Minority Students
overview:
The audit examined the effectiveness of Pre and Post-Matric Scholarship Schemes for Scheduled Caste (SC), Scheduled Tribe (ST), and Minority students, focusing on the period 2017-22. Across these communities, 55.52% of the Kerala population is targeted, but significant exclusion and process lapses persist. Notably, 10-12% of eligible SC students did not receive Pre-Matric scholarships between 2017-21. For 2019-20, 379 schools with 3,499 SC students were not registered in the mandated e-grantz system, and 23,138 SC students from 5437 registered schools were not linked in e-grantz—making them ineligible for disbursement. Delays of up to five years in Post-Matric scholarship payments were documented, despite portal digitisation meant to streamline payments.

The audit found severe planning inadequacies: no survey or update identified eligible beneficiaries during the audit period, and the departments failed to claim ₹96.65 lakh in central administrative expenses for 2017-22. Additionally, Divyang (differently abled) SC students were denied the extra 10% scholarship mandated. As a result, there were both significant under-receipt and cases of multiple/double payments, and short or non-payment of fees—including a documented sum of ₹3.60 crore not reimbursed to 5,828 SC students at Kendriya Vidyalayas for Vidyalaya Vikas Nidhi fees.

Systemic monitoring failures were observed: neither SC nor ST departments conducted regular scheme reviews or reconciled expenditure figures, nor did they address obvious portal deficiencies (such as failure to flag duplicate or ineligible applications). For minorities, improper diversion of scholarship funds was detected, with no claim of administrative expenses and failure to furnish mandatory utilisation certificates. These issues led to avoidable exclusions and delay or denial of benefits, in violation of scheme objectives.

title: Performance Audit on Welfare of Building and Other Construction Workers
overview:
This audit reviews the implementation of welfare schemes for construction workers in Tamil Nadu. As of March 31, 2022, only 31.27 lakh workers were registered, against an estimated 82 lakh eligible unorganised workers—representing less than 40% coverage. Significant fund balances were observed, with TNCWWB maintaining ₹4,170 crore in fixed deposits, even as direct benefits lagged behind allocations. For instance, out of ₹4,080.60 crore received from cess and other sources between 2017-18 and 2021-22, only ₹1,277.14 crore was spent on workers’ welfare, and large sums remained idle.

The audit identified persistent operational bottlenecks, including absence of centralised beneficiary databases and delays in scheme rollouts. Disbursement efficiency remains low: only 0.3 lakh out of the targeted population received consistent benefits, resulting in accumulation of ₹2,810 crore in unutilised funds. The lack of integration between workers’ data, payments, and actual welfare delivery led to exclusion errors and inconsistent aid, particularly for COVID-related relief.

The impact was especially acute for migrant and newly registered workers, who faced delays or were not paid benefits at all. ₹382 crore earmarked for COVID cash assistance did not reach the intended 12.14 lakh workers. The report flags systemic risks: TNCWWB’s inability to verify duplications, update records for migrants, and ensure benefits were paid only to genuine, single beneficiaries, weakening trust in scheme delivery.

title: Performance Audit on Kaleshwaram Project
overview:
The Performance Audit on the Kaleshwaram Project reveals critical issues in project planning, execution, and financial management. The likely project cost has escalated to ₹1,47,427.41 crore, compared to ₹81,911.01 crore projected to the Central Water Commission. As of March 2022, ₹86,788.06 crore had already been incurred on the project, with 64.3% of this amount funded through off-budget borrowings (OBBs) by Kaleshwaram Irrigation Project Corporation Limited (KIPCL). The audit found that only 40,888 acres of command area has been created so far out of the targeted 18.26 lakh acres, representing a substantial shortfall and delays in distributary network development.

The Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR) was found to be grossly overstated, with the actual BCR even with the understated project cost working out to just 0.75, and shrinking further to 0.52 at the revised project cost—meaning every rupee spent yields only 52 paise in benefit. Serious issues were identified in contract management, including possible undue contractor benefits of at least ₹2,684.73 crore and avoidable payments due to post-tender modifications amounting to ₹1,342.48 crore.

Consequences of these shortcomings include a heavy recurring burden on state finances, with ₹10,647.26 crore per annum expected in operational costs, debt servicing obligations totalling ₹1,41,544.59 crore over 14 years, and an absence of comprehensive financial planning or clear administrative approvals for the entire project. Completion of the project is significantly delayed and full benefits are unlikely for many years, while significant expenditures have already become unproductive.

title: Performance Audit on Children in need of Care and Protection for the Year Ended 31 March 2021. (Report 1 of 2023)
overview:
This audit examines the effectiveness of the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi (GNCTD) in securing the rights and entitlements of children in need of special protection, as mandated under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection) Act, 2015, and Integrated Child Protection Scheme (ICPS), 2014. Across the three years reviewed, planners failed to conduct any surveys to assess the population of vulnerable children, resulting in an absence of concrete plans and data-driven resource allocation. The data gap meant that government support reached only a fraction of children in need, with care extended mainly to those identified by third parties, rather than via systematic outreach.

The audit identified major operational delays including slow constitution of key child protection institutions and lapses in governance, with the Delhi State Child Protection Society (DSCPS) and its Executive Committee functioning in a largely dormant manner—meeting only once each over three years. Financial management was notably weak: against a total ICPS budget of ₹5,192.49 lakh for the period 2018-21, actual expenditure was only ₹3,636.67 lakh, leaving unspent balances between 22% and 38% annually due to failing to execute child care activities and substantial delays in funding releases.

Children's welfare suffered due to staff shortages up to 76%, inadequate facilities, and insufficient arrangements for key services including nutrition and education (only 54% received formal education). Parallelly, critical schemes for non-institutional care—like adoption, sponsorship, and foster care—were either implemented ineffectively or not at all, restricting children's chances for proper rehabilitation in family settings.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Land Acquisition and Allotment of Properties in Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority (GNIDA), Government of Uttar Pradesh, Report No. 4 of the year 2023 (Performance Audit)
overview:
The CAG performance audit of GNIDA found systemic failures in planning, land acquisition, property pricing, and the allotment process between 2005-06 and 2017-18, with updated findings through April 2021. Direct procedural lapses, disregard for regulations, and collusion resulted in 'irregular and additional/avoidable expenditure of ₹13,362 crore.' As of April 2021, overdue receivables toward GNIDA stood at ₹19,500 crore, stemming from defaults in land premium, lease rent, and interest—primarily from allotments dating as far back as GNIDA’s inception in 1991 (p. xii, Executive Summary).

Audit scrutiny revealed misuse of urgency provisions for land acquisition, favouritism in selective amendments to brochure conditions, under-pricing of property categories, and permissions for mortgaging by builders even with significant dues. Only 27 out of 148 (18%) group housing projects were completed by 2021, while 95 allottees hadn’t even partially completed construction. 81% of allottees had pending dues totaling over ₹7,100 crore, with individual delays as long as eight years for homebuyers (p. 61).

The consequences include distress for thousands of homebuyers, a significant loss of public funds, and a derailment of GNIDA's core mission to promote industrial growth and employment in Greater Noida. As of 2021, 48% of industrial projects remained incomplete, undermining economic objectives and public trust (p. xii, Executive Summary).

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Storage Management and Movement of Food grains by Food Corporation of India For the year ended March 2022 Union Government Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution
overview:
This performance audit examined the efficiency and effectiveness of storage management and movement of food grains by the Food Corporation of India (FCI) under the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, covering the period 2017-18 to 2021-22. The report identifies significant avoidable expenditure and systemic deficiencies: In Punjab and Haryana, FCI hired an avoidable 10.55 lakh metric tonnes (LMT) of storage capacity, incurring ₹62.76 crore in excess storage and supervision charges, despite availability of its own vacant CAP (Covered and Plinth) storage.

The report further notes that FCI incurred avoidable Carry Over Charges of ₹170.26 crore paid to State Government Agencies (SGAs) due to not using available vacant covered storage capacity for direct delivery. Additionally, delays in land acquisition for new storage infrastructure resulted in extra expenditure of ₹18.08 crore in Assam and ₹16.85 crore in Bihar. Other lapses include non-recovery of ₹17.02 crore in damages/penalty from concessionaires and undue favour worth ₹5.83 crore in project costs in Assam.

On movement inefficiencies, FCI's lack of formal direct issue guidelines resulted in excess handling costs. It missed out on rebates of ₹1736.11 crore by not availing railway Long Term Tariff Contracts. Planning lapses caused additional storage charges of ₹182.29 crore in Punjab and Haryana. The audit concludes that weaknesses in storage utilization and failure to optimize movement have cost the exchequer hundreds of crores and recommends robust reforms and closer adherence to economic principles and FSSAI compliance.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India - Performance Audit on Implementation of eProcurement system in Tamil Nadu - Report No. 4 of 2023 (Tamil)
overview:
The performance audit assessed the implementation of the GePNIC eProcurement system by Tamil Nadu government departments for the period 2016-17 to 2021-22. Despite the government's directions since 2007 and over ₹2,15,060 crore worth of 1.78 lakh tenders handled on the platform (p.2), the audit found that as of September 2022, only 53 out of 201 departments/units (26%) used the eProcurement portal, with 148 units still operating offline or using alternatives (p.11). Of all tenders examined, as much as 24% (12,000+ contracts) had no ‘Award of Contract’ recorded online, undermining the transparency and reliability of eProcurement (p.12).

A key finding was the absence of a logical, department-wide enforcement policy and continued use of alternate procurement platforms (such as Government e-Marketplace and MSTC), causing major fragmentation. Furthermore, critical tender documentation—like proof of EMD, bid evaluation details, and contract award letters—were not consistently uploaded, meaning significant information gaps for both oversight and MIS (p.12–13). Most departments failed to properly use or update critical modules, including award notifications, making monitoring and auditing very difficult.

These lapses had the consequence of perpetuating manual/hybrid procurement, missing mandated digitization targets for ₹10 lakh+ procurements, and weakening reform objectives. As of 2023, government review and process monitoring remained insufficient to resolve the core gaps, risking loss of audit trail and supplier trust.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India - Performance Audit on Implementation of eProcurement system in Tamil Nadu - Report No. 4 of the year 2023
overview:
This performance audit covers the Implementation of the eProcurement system in Tamil Nadu from 2016 to 2022. The system was introduced to enhance transparency, reduce procurement cycle time, and cut indirect costs by digitising the tendering process across all government departments. By December 2022, 2.97 lakh tenders worth ₹2,92,050 crore had been published on the state’s eProcurement portal.

However, the audit found that only 53 of 201 eligible procuring entities used the portal, and just 12% of 1.78 lakh tenders processed online reached the critical ‘Award of Contract’ stage. Notably, 74% of procuring entities failed to utilise the eProcurement portal despite 15 years of its introduction. In select departments, only 21.06% of procurement (worth ₹1,255.54 crore out of ₹5,959.70 crore) was conducted online between 2019 and 2022, with the rest carried out via manual or alternate methods such as GeM and MSTC.

Lapses included non-updating of contract awards, non-uploading of technical and financial summaries, and defective controls that enabled discrepancies and possibly collusive bidding. These issues severely undermined transparency and accountability, evidenced by the State’s eleventh position nationally in the proportion of tenders updated to completion on the GePNIC portal: only 11.27% in 2020-22. The absence of mandatory orders and a central monitoring authority resulted in irregular adoption and underutilisation of the portal.

title: Performance Audit of Direct Benefit Transfer Scheme Aasara Pensions in Telangana
overview:
The audit revealed critical lapses in the implementation of the Aasara Pensions Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) scheme in Telangana, covering 2018-19 to 2020-21. Utilisation Certificates submitted by the implementing agency (SERP) to Government of India and State Government claimed full utilisation of grants-in-aid, despite retaining unutilised fund balances in bank accounts at the end of each financial year. For example, unremitted balances include ₹455.17 crore (2018-19), ₹933.94 crore (2019-20), and ₹550.29 crore (2020-21).

On average, pensions to 2.30 lakh beneficiaries per month remained undisbursed between April 2018 and March 2021, resulting in nearly ₹45 crore (5%) of funds undisbursed monthly. Further, cross-checks with Samagra Kutumba Survey data showed 19% households had missing records and 16% were ineligible but received pensions, leading to payments of ₹1,768.42 crore to ineligible households. Irregular sanctions led to payments of ₹535.39 crore across disabled, beedi workers, and single women categories. Other systemic failures included lack of uniform application formats, poor record maintenance, and inability to cross-verify beneficiary eligibility with linked government databases.

Overall, the audit exposes severe flaws in eligibility verification, fund utilisation, and record-keeping, with substantial amounts passed on to ineligible beneficiaries and a pattern of routine submission of incorrect Utilisation Certificates. The consequences are considerable financial mismanagement and compromised transparency in the DBT delivery process. Immediate corrective action is required to restore trust and effectiveness in the scheme.

title: Report no. 06 of the year 2023 GoMP - Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Performance Audit on Degradation of Kshipra River for the year ended 31st March 2021
overview:
The Performance Audit on the Degradation of Kshipra River reviews the effectiveness of policies and management actions from 2016-17 to 2020-21. The river system, serving a watershed of 5,777 sq km and a population projected at 42.36 lakh (2021) in urban bodies and 2.85 lakh in 212 villages, is experiencing significant degradation in flow and quality. Notably, 28 main drains discharge domestic sewage and industrial waste into the river untreated or poorly treated, contributing to alarming pollution.

Key audit findings highlight severe shortfalls in urban local body (ULB) performance: only 46.51% of households were actually connected to the sewage network (despite exaggerated claims by ULBs), and no Faecal Sludge and Septage Management (FSSM) Policy exists in 5 out of 6 major ULBs. Industrial oversight is also weak; only 34% of required inspections were conducted and some industries operated without current Consent to Operate, undermining water safety and compliance. River water tested at 7 of 10 monitoring stations was found "not satisfactory" for three consecutive years, with high BOD levels placing major stretches in Priority I (most polluted) category per CPCB.

Consequences of these lapses are clear: the river has lost its perennial flow, remaining dry for 5–6 months annually, and is now heavily contaminated by heavy metals, faecal matter, and solid waste. The NKSL project, intended to restore flows by transferring Narmada water, was implemented without a sustainable plan for O&M or clear long-term goals. Inadequate plantation and management on riverbanks, poor irrigation planning, and unregulated groundwater extraction further endanger the river's future and citizens' health.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Performance Audit on Construction of Major Bridges in Madhya Pradesh by Public Works Department
overview:
This Performance Audit examined the construction of major bridges by the Public Works Department in Madhya Pradesh from 2015-16 to 2019-20, highlighting severe lapses in planning, execution, and coordination. Out of 72 audited bridge works, only nine were completed within the stipulated timeline, while 63 projects faced delays of one to 68 months. Notably, the cost of 12 bridge works increased by ₹101.83 crore due to major design and scope changes, resulting from inadequate survey and planning (p. vi, Executive Summary).

Lack of a Master Plan led to bridge selections based mainly on ad hoc proposals from public representatives, with no uniform selection criteria or long-term vision. In 45 bridge works, sub-soil investigation was severely deficient—only 82 of 696 required bore holes were drilled, causing major changes during execution and additional cost burdens. Delays also arose from awarding works prior to land acquisition, with lag periods of up to 92 months in shifting ownership or utility lines (p. 10, Ch. 2, Table 2.2).

In contract management, grave shortcomings included under-recovery of royalties amounting to ₹63.73 lakh and final payments of ₹101.95 crore made without 'No Dues Certificate.' Further, approach roads and features critical to user safety—like electrification and road furniture—were often omitted or delayed, severely impacting public utility and safety. The audit concludes that systemic weaknesses, lack of coordination, and inadequate oversight resulted in significant time and cost overruns, undermining the functionality and intended public benefit of these major bridge projects.

title: Performance Audit Report on Integrated Financial and Human Resource Management System - Report No.3 of 2023 (Tamil)
overview:
This performance audit examined the implementation and operationalization of the Integrated Financial and Human Resource Management System (IFHRMS) by the Government of Tamil Nadu covering the period from 2015-16 to 2021-22. The audited expenditure reached ₹278.54 crore out of a contracted ₹288.91 crore, yet IFHRMS faced implementation delays of up to 48 months, with the 'Go-Live' milestone realized only in January 2021 against an original target of January 2017. Delays were mainly due to late preparation of mandatory System Requirement Specifications (SRS) and subsequent change requests (1,702, of which 751 were considered essential). As a result, change management, incomplete system modules, and deferred functional requirements hampered realization of intended benefits.

The audit revealed avoidable expenditure of ₹79.91 crore on hardware maintenance and support services due to delayed rollout, and key modules, especially for Human Resource and Payroll operations, remained incomplete, affecting centralized service delivery. Budget operations were not comprehensively covered as planned and significant manual intervention was still required for core financial and pension processes, defeating the system's automation objectives. The absence of automated synchronisation and persistent reliance on legacy software weakened the integrity and centralization of state financial operations.

The consequences were severe: critical operational modules such as pay bill processing, budget operations, and e-Service Registers (e-SR) did not achieve full functionality or integration, resulting in manual duplications, inconsistent data, and delays for thousands of users. Account heads, payroll, and pension information continued to be processed outside IFHRMS in some cases, exposing systemic vulnerability and risking the state’s financial accountability.

title: Performance Audit Report on Integrated Financial and Human Resource Management System
overview:
The audit examined the implementation of the Integrated Financial and Human Resource Management System (IFHRMS) in Tamil Nadu, covering 2015-22 with a focus on 2021-22. The IFHRMS project, originally planned to Go-live in January 2017, experienced a four-year delay, going live only in January 2021. This delay caused a cost overrun of ₹79.91 crore, with additional payments on hardware maintenance, field technical support, and bandwidth.

Critical deficiencies in system requirement specification sign-off led to 1,702 Change Requests, of which 512 were accepted as valid. Audit found that 417 of these were avoidable, as they reflected requirements that should have been included initially—resulting in wasteful expenditure and protracted development. Only six of the fourteen envisaged modules were fully operational at audit time, and key areas such as receipts were still being processed outside IFHRMS, undermining real-time accounting.

Operational weaknesses persisted, such as double payments on bills, processing delays, and dependence on physical records. Security vulnerabilities included the use of 'anonymous user' accounts, lack of biometric access, and failure to conduct disaster recovery drills. The Monitoring Committee failed to manage project milestones or scrutinize cost overruns. As a result, Treasury and HR functions remain partially unified, reliant on manual processes, and exposed to significant operational risk.

title: Performance Audit on Housing for Urban Poor(Tamil), Government of Tamil Nadu
overview:
The Performance Audit on Housing for Urban Poor in Tamil Nadu assessed the effectiveness, efficiency, and transparency of urban poor housing schemes spanning 2018-19 to 2022-23. Outlays totalling ₹18,250 crore were allocated, yet only ₹8,603 crore were actually utilised for completed works, representing a significant under-utilisation of sanctioned funds (p. xii-xiii, Executive Summary). As of March 2023, just 1,28,467 dwelling units had been delivered against a sanctioned 2,69,500, reflecting a 52% physical achievement and substantial delays in project completion, with 71,179 units remaining incomplete for more than 2 years.

Headline findings included large unspent balances at Urban Local Body (ULB) level, lack of convergence between Central and State government schemes, and ineffective monitoring systems. Discrepancies in beneficiary identification and a lack of proper supporting documentation led to instances of ineligible beneficiaries availing scheme benefits. Instances of diversion of scheme funds to unrelated expenditure were also noted (p. xiv-xv, Executive Summary).

These gaps resulted in the denial of intended benefits to thousands of eligible urban poor households, audit objections amounting to ₹942 crore, and continuing growth of urban slum populations. The report’s findings indicate high systemic risk—both financial and social—in not fully remedying identified weaknesses.

title: Performance Audit on Housing for Urban Poor, Government of Tamil Nadu
overview:
The performance audit of the urban housing schemes implemented by the Government of Tamil Nadu revealed substantial shortfalls in both financial and physical achievement. Between 2014-15 and 2020-21, only 47% of allocated funds for housing schemes were utilized, with Rs 4,768 crore spent of the Rs 10,255 crore released. Across major schemes, 1.16 lakh houses were constructed against a target of 2.50 lakh units, meaning a shortfall of over 54%.

The audit found that delays in land acquisition, non-release of beneficiary contributions, and inadequate convergence with other infrastructure schemes led to chronic underperformance. Of the 1.5 lakh beneficiaries sanctioned under the Basic Services to Urban Poor (BSUP) and Integrated Housing Slum Development Programme (IHSDP), only 58,000 received completed houses. Additionally, the implementation suffered from lack of transparent beneficiary selection, with 21% of the surveyed sample ineligible or not traceable.

These gaps resulted in preventable hardship for urban poor families, non-utilisation of central assistance, and undermined the intended socio-economic upliftment. The audit concluded that systemic failures need urgent attention and process reform to achieve the intended objectives of affordable, decent housing for the urban poor.

title: Performance Audit Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Efficacy of Implementation of 74th Constitutional Amendment Act
overview:
The report examined the effectiveness of the Government of Andhra Pradesh in implementing the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act (CAA), which mandated the empowerment of Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) by devolving 18 functions listed in the Twelfth Schedule. As per the audit, the State devolved only 13 functions fully and three partially to Municipal Corporations, and just 7 fully and 5 partially to Municipalities/Nagar Panchayats. Only five functions were found to be fully functional on the ground.

Audit highlighted extensive delays and non-compliance: elections in 16 ULBs were not held for 36 months and five new ULBs had delayed elections for 19 months, as of July 2022. In 100 ULBs, elections were delayed by 11–28 months, and in one ULB, no election was held since 2005. Arrears in property tax amounted to ₹262.21 crore in 20 ULBs, with an additional ₹20 crore of interest waived without compensation. Only eight out of 110 water supply works (total allocation: ₹7,835.56 crore) were completed, leaving 102 works (₹6,424.34 crore) unfinished and substantial gaps in household connections.

The absence of timely State Finance Commission reports and the non-formation of Ward Committees, District Planning Committees, and Metropolitan Planning Committees undermined local planning and financial autonomy. ULBs also lacked effective control over staff (20% sanctioned posts vacant), and substantial Central Finance Commission grants remained either unreleased or unutilized; for instance, ₹275.34 crore of the 14th FC grant was unspent as of May 2022. Parastatals continued to control planning and resource functions, diluting decentralization and self-governance.

title: Performance Audit of Rural and Urban Water Supply Schemes of the Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended 31 March 2021-Government of Haryana (Report No. 3 of the year 2023)
overview:
This Performance Audit covers rural and urban water supply schemes in Haryana for the period 2016-21, reviewing funding, policy alignment and infrastructure adequacy. The Public Health Engineering Department (PHED) handled supply for 1.65 crore rural population, with norms of 55 LPCD for rural and 135 LPCD for urban areas. As on July 2022, 1,737 rural habitations were water deficient, while nine of 89 urban towns were below the prescribed norm as of March 2021.

Financial management was critically lacking: only one per cent revenue collection versus maintenance expenditure in rural areas and 15 per cent in urban areas. Water charges worth ₹ 278.20 crore were outstanding by March 2021. Failure to collect ₹ 69.36 crore as community contribution from Gram Panchayats further affected scheme sustainability. No flow meters existed in rural areas; at 23 checked locations, water supply fell below norms. Unmetered and illegal connections were prevalent in HSVP and ULB divisions (urban).

Quality monitoring was ineffective due to staff shortages and inadequate laboratories. Haryana's water policies (drafted 2012) were not revised to align with National Water Policy 2012. Metered connections were not implemented; planning lacked stakeholder input and scientific SWOT analysis. The audit recommends urgent reforms in planning, infrastructure, billing, metering, testing and grievance mechanisms to ensure safe, adequate supply and long-term sustainability.

title: Union Government – Ministry of Road Transport and Highways – Performance Audit on “Implementation of Phase-I of Bharatmala Pariyojana”
overview:
Phase-I of Bharatmala Pariyojana (BPP-I), approved in October 2017 by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA), targeted the development of 34,800 km of national highways by September 2022, with a planned outlay of ₹5,35,000 crore. As of 31 March 2023, 26,316 km (75.62% of target) was awarded, but only 13,499 km (38.79%) completed, highlighting a significant lag in execution despite increased construction pace post-pandemic. The sanctioned cost for these 26,316 km reached ₹8,46,588 crore, showing an alarming escalation to ₹32.17 crore/km from the CCEA's approval of ₹15.37 crore/km.

Fund management deficits were apparent: 158.24% of CCEA’s entire financial outlay was already sanctioned by March 2023, even though nearly a quarter of the approved project length was yet to be awarded. The original modal mix in project structuring deviated, with just 1.75% under BOT (Toll), against the planned 10%. Audit found several shortcomings in planning, such as absence of targets for Logistics Performance Index improvements, persistent unresolved NHDP project bottlenecks, and cost overruns stemming from project specification changes and weaker appraisal.

The audit highlights systemic concerns: lack of project-based accounting, poor cost-benefit and feasibility studies, diversion of funds, and noncompliance with CCEA monitoring directions. MoRTH is advised to recalibrate targets, strengthen governance and financial transparency, and systematically appraise project planning for better outcomes.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India Performance Audit on Implementation of Pradhan Mantri Khanij Kshetra Kalyan Yojana including District Mineral Foundation Trusts in Maharashtra
overview:
The audit covers Pradhan Mantri Khanij Kshetra Kalyan Yojana (PMKKKY) and District Mineral Foundation Trusts (DMFTs) in Maharashtra for the period September 2016 to March 2023, focusing on institutional arrangement, fund collection, financial management, project implementation, and monitoring. The audit examined five selected DMFTs: Nagpur, Chandrapur, Yavatmal, Bhandara, and Raigad. Total DMFT funds received across Maharashtra during 2016-17 to 2022-23 were ₹4,624.01 crore, with the five reviewed DMFTs receiving ₹3,354.59 crore.

Of the funds collected in these DMFTs, ₹1,616.26 crore was disbursed to implementing agencies under PMKKKY for utilization in sectors such as healthcare, water supply, and infrastructure, with only 48% fund utilization observed statewide. There were significant delays in registration of DMFTs, appointment of members, and critical failures in identifying directly affected areas and preparing beneficiary lists. The audit reveals that 58% of sanctioned projects remained incomplete, leading to severe underachievement of scheme objectives.

Consequences of these lapses included diversion of DMFT funds, poor coverage of directly affected populations, and a lack of robust monitoring. Short recovery and non-recovery of DMF contributions from mining lease holders were observed. The failure to prepare Annual Action Plans and Budgets further hampered effective project execution, affecting timely welfare delivery to mining-impacted communities. title: Performance Audit Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Mining in Uttar Pradesh and Socio-economic impact of illegal mining (Report No. 09 of the Year 2024)
overview:
This performance audit examined mining administration and the socio-economic impacts of illegal mining in Uttar Pradesh covering the period 2017-18 to 2021-22, with analysis involving the Geology and Mining Department and 18 district offices. The audit found significant lapses in compliance with the Mining Policy 2017—in particular, the goal of raising mining revenue to 3% of state resources by 2022 was missed, with mining receipts never exceeding 2.78% and declining to only 1.67% of total state revenue by 2021-22. Revenue variances were marked, with actual receipts falling short of budget estimates by 20.86% to 50.43% for four consecutive years.

Serious gaps were identified in internal controls, including delayed deposit of royalty, non-forfeiture of security, and up to 613 stone crushers operating without mandatory storage licenses. The use of e-tender and technological systems like Mine Mitra and iMSS produced only partial results—illegal mining cases surged 155% (from 10,188 in 2017-18 to 25,986 in 2021-22), and penalties recovered increased more than fourfold to ₹124.89 crore by 2021-22. However, the regulatory system failed to consistently prevent encroachment beyond lease boundaries, improper use of transport passes, and inadequate human resources for enforcement.

The audit highlighted missed opportunities in collection, monitoring, and utilization of District Mineral Foundation Trust (DMFT) funds, delays in environmental compliance, and lack of effective data linkage with the Transport Department. Recommendations focus on urgent technological and structural reforms, strengthening inter-agency cooperation, and strict action against violators. The estimated financial implication of audit observations totals ₹784.54 crore.

title: Performance Audit on Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) Scheme, Union Government (Department of Revenue – Indirect Taxes -Customs)
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) Scheme was conducted to assess the efficiency of authorisation issuance, utilisation, redemption, and inter-departmental coordination by DGFT and Customs. The audit covered DGFT, 24 Regional Authorities (RAs), and associated Customs Commissionerates, focusing on transactions from April 2018 to March 2021 and audit work during 2022-23. Across India, a total of 34,777 EPCG authorisations with duty foregone amounting to ₹7,941 crore were processed during the period.

The audit identified substantial deficiencies including incorrect fixation of Export Obligations, improper application of denial mechanisms (such as Denied Entity List), and lack of effective monitoring leading to revenue risks. Major headline findings included non-monitoring of fulfilment of Export Obligation, delays and lapses in placing exporters under the Denied Entity List, and issue of multiple abeyance orders without justified reasons. Revenue implication for identified shortcomings was ₹479.81 crore.

Consequences include risk of misappropriated customs duty benefits and significant undermining of the scheme's objectives. Of the 72 audit observations raised, responses were received only for 31 from CBIC/DGFT; 27 were fully/partially accepted. 41 para responses were still pending, and only 20 out of 26 audit recommendations were accepted by CBIC/DGFT, with response awaited for 2 recommendations and 4 not accepted. title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services (Government of Karnataka Report No.08 of the year 2024 Performance Audit Civil)
overview:
The Performance Audit of Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services in Karnataka revealed persistent deficiencies in fund utilization, human resources, and infrastructure, significantly hampering effective service delivery. Between 2018-23, the state utilized only 44-50% of the available central and state health funds, with an unutilized balance of ₹644.53 crore as of March 2023 (Page 12, Executive Summary). Out of the budgeted ₹4,239 crore for critical infrastructure and equipment, only ₹1,980 crore was expended, resulting in delayed strengthening of hospitals and equipment shortages.

Human resource shortages were severe: out of 56,820 sanctioned medical and para-medical posts, only 37,410 were filled (Page 23, §2.3), leading to an adverse doctor-patient ratio and operational challenges for 143 PHCs that lacked even a single Staff Nurse (Page 31, §2.5). Moreover, disproportionate staff deployment persisted across districts.

Infrastructure inadequacies led to only 41% of urban health and wellness centres meeting the Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS). Diagnostic facilities were lacking in over 32% of taluk hospitals. Underutilized assets—such as idle X-Ray and laboratory equipment worth ₹55 crore—were observed, while essential drugs procured included about ₹8.6 crore in blacklisted purchases (Page 86, §4.3). The shortfall in timely fund release and underachievement of National Health Policy targets has limited service coverage, especially in rural and marginalized areas. Consequently, the report highlights risks to public health outcomes and recommends urgent reforms.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Performance Audit of Supply Chain Management of Public Distribution System for the year ended March 2022 (Government of Karnataka Report No. 5 of the year 2024)
overview:
The Performance Audit examined the efficiency, economy, and effectiveness of the supply chain management in the Karnataka Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS), covering the distribution network supplying 26.04 lakh MT of foodgrains annually to 5.26 crore beneficiaries through over 20,324 Fair Price Shops (FPS) and 302 State Warehouses. During the period 2017-22, fund allocation for AAY/PHH ranged from ₹2,850 crore in 2017-18 to ₹6,628 crore in 2021-22, with corresponding expenditures of ₹2,529 crore and ₹6,605 crore respectively. The audit found that the current costing methodology for transportation, adopted by the Department, lacks justification, resulting in higher costs for retail transportation, which per km was up to 61 per cent higher than wholesale, with substantial contractual and operational lapses.

There was no policy to optimize supply routes, resulting in FPS being served by more distant WSDs instead of the nearest depots, thereby escalating transportation and handling costs. Key internal controls were ineffective with widespread use of unauthorized vehicles—including passenger vehicles—for moving foodgrains, absence of vehicle GPS tracking, and non-enforcement of contractual obligations. Additionally, several WSDs and FPS showed poor maintenance and infrastructure, with foodgrains often stored under unhygienic or insecure conditions, and significant shortfalls observed in required inspections.

These deficiencies led to increased risk of foodgrain diversion, wastage, loss of stock, and unfit grains reaching beneficiaries. Recommendations include enforcing contract norms, revising supply and route policies, formulating and implementing Standard Operating Procedures for storage, strengthening IT systems for monitoring, and strict action against lapses and violations, putting the overall scheme at high risk if unaddressed.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Functioning of Primary Educational Institutions in Karnataka (Government of Karnataka, Report No. 06 of the Year 2024 Performance Audit - Civil)
overview:
The report reviews the functioning of primary educational institutions in Karnataka for 2017-22, covering government spending of ₹69,070 crore on primary education and the effectiveness of interventions on access, equity, and educational quality. The audit finds that while Karnataka achieved steady improvements and was classified as a front runner in SDG-4 indicators, the Department failed to periodically assess and track key quality indicators such as student completion rates and proficiency levels. Notably, 1,32,924 habitations lacked lower primary schools within one kilometre, and 10,278 habitations were without an upper primary school within three kilometres, potentially denying thousands of children timely access and transportation allowances.

School infrastructure deficits such as dilapidated classrooms and inadequately maintained toilets remain common. The dropout rate, though reported as low as 0.17% in 2021-22, is underreported due to non-utilisation of the Student Achievement Tracking System (SATS)—audit's analysis found actual dropout rates for student cohorts as high as 1.42% in some districts. There are also persistent disparities in net enrolment ratios; Mandya and Chamarajanagar districts reported NER below 80%.

Consequences include inequitable learning opportunities, continuing educational inequalities among disadvantaged and minority groups, and probable exclusion of children from formal education. Furthermore, lack of regulatory oversight and non-enforcement of safety guidelines in both government and private schools undermine quality and student safety (pp. vii–viii; 6-12; 23-31).

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India - Performance Audit on Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services (Tamil) - Report No. 05 of 2024
overview:
The Performance Audit on Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services in Tamil Nadu covers the period from 2019-20 to 2022-23 and highlights substantial deficiencies in public health expenditure and service delivery. Fund utilisation for health schemes ranged from only 44% to 50% against sanctioned allocations, resulting in under-provision of critical infrastructure and delayed procurement of essential equipment. As noted in the audit, average fund usage was 47%, leaving over ₹530 crore sanctioned but unutilised during 2020-21 alone (p.12).

Delivery of health services was affected by gaps in infrastructure, with 25% of emergency vehicles lacking GPS despite recommendations, and only 54% of PHCs achieving IPHS compliance (p.23). Furthermore, contractual maintenance for medical equipment was found missing for over 35% of surveyed facilities, resulting in prolonged breakdown times that impacted patient care.

The consequences of deficient fund management and infrastructure shortfalls included overcrowded tertiary care facilities, delayed maternal and child health interventions, and underperformance in state health indicators compared to national targets. For example, Tamil Nadu’s infant mortality rate stood at 18.6 per 1,000 live births versus the national average of 35.2 during 2019-21, but key targets such as full immunisation coverage and timely availability of drugs lagged significantly (p.5).
