title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India - Performance Audit on Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services - Report No. 05 of 2024
overview:
The audit reviewed the adequacy, availability, and management of public health infrastructure and human resources in Tamil Nadu between April 2016 and March 2022. Despite the National Health Policy's recommendation to allocate 8% of the state budget to health, Tamil Nadu only spent around 5%, leading to persistent gaps in infrastructure, equipment, and staff across all levels of health care. Large unutilized funds remained with TNMSC and other agencies despite the need for drug and equipment procurement, while essential drugs were sometimes in short or non-supply.

A severe shortage exceeding 75% was observed in key positions such as Block Extension Educator, Family Welfare Assistant/Educator, Lady Health Visitor, and Maternity Child Health Officer in the Directorate of Family Welfare. Recruitment efforts lagged, and overall there was a disconnect between facility needs and procurement. In addition, nearly 36% of all government hospital deliveries during 2019-21 were caesarean, compared to the national average of 14%, raising questions about clinical practices.

Functional issues included poor use of GPS in ambulance services (25% of calls lacked real-time ambulance tracking), deficiencies in equipment maintenance due to lack of active AMC contracts, and policy execution delays such as a 21-year hold-up in framing key regulatory rules. Targeted Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) like Janani Suraksha Yojana did not reach all eligible beneficiaries, with only 46% of mothers receiving government transport support after delivery and 26% not paid under the scheme.

title: Audit Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India Performance Audit on Storm Water Drainage and Sewerage Management Systems in Municipal Corporations for the year ended March 2022
overview:
This Performance Audit evaluates the effectiveness of storm water drainage (SWD) and sewerage management systems in Municipal Corporations across Odisha for 2019-20 to 2022-23. The audit covered 5 major municipal corporations and reviewed planning, execution, financial and contract management, and monitoring mechanisms for drainage and sewerage operations. Total funds released for drainage and sewerage infrastructure projects during 2018-23 amounted to ₹896.23 crore, out of which only ₹404.83 crore was actually utilised, leading to a fund utilisation rate of just 45% (critical miss).

Key findings revealed a lack of comprehensive policies and regulatory frameworks, non-preparation of master plans, significant delays in project execution, and critical gaps in the construction and maintenance of drains. The audit reported that only 18 out of 50 required rainwater harvesting structures were completed, and nearly 40% of planned storm water conservation systems were either abandoned or left incomplete.

Consequences of these deficiencies include frequent urban flooding, inadequate waste water management, reduced ground water recharge, and heightened risk of waterborne diseases. The audit highlighted repeated contract failures and pointed to systemic weaknesses in project planning, financial monitoring, and citizen engagement, making the audit's overall severity 'high'.

title: Performance Audit of Systems and Controls in Assessment and Collection of Revenue from Major Minerals for the year ended March 2022 (Report No. 6 of the year 2024)
overview:
This performance audit examines the systems and controls in grant, extension, assessment and collection of revenue from major minerals in Odisha, with a focus on compliance from 2015 to 2022. The audit found significant irregularities in grant and extension of mining leases, including violations of statutory provisions, depriving the State of enhanced revenues. Notably, abrupt and abnormal declines in reported iron-ore grades after auction resulted in a revenue implication of ₹4,162.77 crore for only six mines post-auction, while misreporting of screened fines led to estimated revenue losses of ₹10,294.24 crore in 20 test-checked mines.

Discrepancies in sales turnover and royalty assessment resulted in a short-assessment of ₹905.66 crore from seven lessees, with additional DMF and NMET impacts. Violations involving excess mining or unauthorized forest extraction attracted additional liabilities of more than ₹5,467.65 crore, and monitoring failures enabled unchecked transportation of minerals valuing at least ₹1,473.26 crore.

Overall, the total money value involved in audit observations is approximately ₹22,392.51 crore. The report highlights gaps in monitoring, grading, laboratory functioning, and verification, posing severe risks to the government’s non-tax revenue and environmental safeguards.

title: Performance Audit on Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services in Telangana State for the year ended March, 2022
overview:
The performance audit assessed Telangana's public health infrastructure and management of health services between 2016-17 and 2021-22, covering funding adequacy, human resources, drug and equipment availability, and implementation of national and state health schemes. Despite progress in doctor-to-population ratios (1:881), there were significant gaps: 45% overall vacancies in healthcare staff, bed shortages (7,008 shortfall against 35,004 requirement), and insufficient compliance with the National Health Policy. For example, government health spending ranged from just 2.53% to 3.47% of the total state budget, well below the 8% target, and only 36-63% of available National Health Mission funds were utilized. Infrastructure targets remain unmet: 69% shortfall in CHCs, delays in medical facility construction, and 158 batches of drugs issued before quality clearance.

Operational inefficiencies were compounded by the lack of a central database for HR and poor implementation of e-Aushadhi for drug management, resulting in Rs 390.26 crore worth of expired drugs not replaced in time. Further, state health objectives are hampered by high out-of-pocket expenses, inadequate coverage of primary care (15.56–20.27% of health budget vs. 66.67% target), and persistent gaps in rural health outcomes (IMR/U5MR deficits).

The audit concludes that without increased funding, robust HR policy, systematic drug/consumables management, and completion of planned health infrastructure, Telangana will struggle to meet its SDG-3 health targets and reduce overall health inequities. Funds for key schemes like PM Matru Vandana Yojana (₹65.20 crore) remained unutilized, and shortages in basic services at health institutions undermine patient care and safety.

title: CAG's Performance Audit Report No. 5 of 2024 on Implementation of 74th Constitutional Amendment Act
overview:
This Performance Audit assessed the effectiveness of the devolution of powers, functions, and funds to Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) in Uttar Pradesh under the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, covering FY2015-16 to FY2019-20. Uttar Pradesh, with 707 ULBs as of March 2020, saw the State Government devolve only 15 out of 18 functions fully and 1 function partially, while critical responsibilities like land use regulation and economic/social development planning were not devolved, thus undermining the intended decentralisation (Table 1.1, p.1).

ULBs continued to lack autonomy in core areas: they were solely responsible for only one function (burial/cremation grounds) and had limited or no say in the planning, taxation, and health functions central to urban governance. Audit reveals ULBs exercised complete control over only 1 function, had no role in 1, worked under heavy restrictions or overlap for 11, were mere implementers in 2, and had a dual role in 1—contradicting the spirit of the Amendment (p.9).

Councils and Committees meant to enable democratic decision-making and participatory planning were either non-existent or non-functional: meetings were infrequent, nominations delayed, and required committees like Ward Committees not constituted in any test-checked ULB (p.17). Consequentially, fund flows and resource utilisation remained State-driven, with ULBs' own revenues nominal and the bulk of resources arriving through tied, delayed Central and State transfers. Severe human resource shortages (up to 43%) and lack of real fiscal powers, along with persistent delays in State Finance Commission constitution and report adoption, further hampered effective local governance.

title: Performance Audit on “Swadesh Darshan Scheme”- Union Government- Ministry of Tourism
overview: The Performance Audit of the Swadesh Darshan Scheme, covering its implementation from January 2015 to March 2022, evaluates the Ministry of Tourism’s flagship initiative aimed at developing tourism infrastructure across 15 theme-based circuits. A total of 76 projects were sanctioned by the Ministry at an aggregate cost of ₹5,455.69 crore, comprising 910 sites and 6,898 components in 243 districts. However, less than 70% of total funds were utilized, with notable variations between budget estimates and actual expenditures. The Ministry's initial outlay for the scheme was ₹500 crore, which escalated to ₹4,000 crore by 2016-17 without Cabinet approval required for outlays exceeding ₹1,000 crore. The scheme faced delays in project completion; out of 14 sampled projects, 8 had delays ranging from 22 to 47 months, and 6 were incomplete as of March 2022. Critical management gaps were identified, including excess funds not recovered from the States, non-submission of utilization certificates, and irregular payments to contractors totaling ₹19.73 crore. The Ministry did not conduct feasibility studies before project launches, failed to ensure land acquisition prior to fund release, and performed inadequate monitoring—only 6 National Steering Committee meetings were held versus 29 required. There was little synergy with other schemes, minimal focus on rural tourism, and the impact assessment mechanisms (like annual surveys and employment tracking) were absent. As a result, the scheme’s vision of integrated, sustainable tourism and robust employment generation remains largely unachieved after more than seven years and ₹4,734 crore in expenditure.

title: Report No.8 of 2023 – Performance Audit on “Role of Tea Board of India in Development of Tea in India”, Union Government – Ministry of Commerce & Industry
overview:
The Performance Audit evaluated the adequacy and effectiveness of Tea Board India’s activities from 2016-17 to 2020-21, covering regulatory, developmental, research, market promotion, and financial management domains, with a close review of how government funds in excess of ₹88,481.50 lakh were utilized. It was found that more than 38% of small tea growers and 7.6% of big growers remained unregistered as of March 2021, thus falling outside the Board's regulatory and development net. Audit test-checks also exposed cases of non-compliance in planting permit processes, and substantial revenue leakages due to uncollected fees and GST, amounting to over ₹73.75 lakh.

There was a critical shortfall in quality control mechanisms, as between 78.62% and 91.95% of required inspections at tea factories were not conducted, and 84% to 97% shortfall in mandatory tea sample collections for quality assurance during the period, highlighting systematic monitoring lapses. Despite guidelines, ₹12.87 crore in subsidies were disbursed without requisite checks on Provident Fund dues, and excess/unauthorised subsidies totaling over ₹3.6 crore were identified—money that remains unrecovered.

Limited progress was found in core responsibilities such as labour welfare, market promotion via digital/social channels, and research project outputs—exemplified by over 93% of research funds to private institutes being spent on administrative overhead instead of research deliverables. These persistent shortcomings, despite repeated recommendations in prior CAG/PAC reports, indicate significant governance, monitoring, and financial management deficiencies within Tea Board India.

title: Performance Audit Report No. 2 of the year 2023: Outcomes in Surface Irrigation of Bansagar Canal Project and Modernisation of Chaudhary Charan Singh Lahchura Dam Project
overview:
The Performance Audit covered the outcomes in surface irrigation for the Bansagar Canal Project and the Modernisation of Chaudhary Charan Singh Lahchura Dam Project, focusing on the periods between 2014-15 and 2020-21. The Bansagar Canal Project, designed to utilise 34,008 million cubic feet (mcft) of water with the goal of increasing irrigation intensity from 85% to 150% over 2.32 lakh hectares, suffered four project deadline extensions and massive cost overruns. Actual expenditure reached ₹3,419.37 crore by 2020-21, but water demand from the Bansagar reservoir ranged from only 5,782 mcft (17%) to 16,476 mcft (48%), with actual water supply through the canal network meeting a mere 5-9% of intended capacity.

In the Lahchura and Pahari Dam Projects, delays and under-ambitious planning resulted in only 3% to 15% of the Kharif irrigation target being achieved and expenditures mounting to ₹328.30 crore and ₹354.20 crore, respectively. Serious issues regarding project planning, financial management, and contract oversight included deficient DPRs, insufficient water storage capacity, irregular grant of advances, and delayed execution. Both projects showed significant shortfalls: irrigation intensity targets were missed by 44-45% (Rabi) and 32-33% (Kharif) in the Bansagar project, and structural modernisation in Lahchura did not resolve underlying water deficits.

The consequences were widespread: chronic water shortages, canals operating for shortened periods, delayed outcomes for farmers, and significant inefficiencies in usage of public funds. Lapses in transparency, monitoring, and convergence with agricultural departments further exacerbated the impact, limiting improvements in cropping patterns, seed distribution, and the development of the command area. The audit highlights the need for systemic corrections to ensure future irrigation projects achieve their objectives.

Strengthen monitoring for timely completion, including contractor competence and penalty clauses.
Ensure strict adherence to financial, contractual, and quality control procedures.

title: Performance Audit Report No. 2 of the year 2023: Outcomes in Surface Irrigation of Bansagar Canal Project and Modernisation of Chaudhary Charan Singh Lahchura Dam Project
overview:
The audit evaluated the outcomes of two major surface irrigation projects in Uttar Pradesh: Bansagar Canal Project (BCP) and Modernisation of Chaudhary Charan Singh Lahchura Dam Project, covering financial years 2014-15 to 2020-21. Despite spending Rs 3,419.37 crore on BCP from 1996-97 to 2020-21, and Rs 682.50 crore on Lahchura and Pahari Dam Projects from 1978-79 to 2017-18, intended outcomes such as augmentation of water availability, creation of additional irrigation intensity, and transitions in cropping pattern largely remained unachieved. For Bansagar, only 5% to 9% of targeted water was supplied to canal networks, resulting in significant shortfall—44-45% in Rabi and 32-33% in Kharif irrigation targets.

Critical deficiencies surfaced in project planning: insufficient storage capacity of Lahchura and Pahari dams and lack of restoration for Dhasan Canal System led to irrigation in just 455 to 2,153 hectares (3%-15% of target) in Kharif despite a target of 14,575 hectares. Project implementation suffered from frequent scope and DPR changes, irregular contract awards, unjustified price adjustments, delayed contractor payments, and inadequate quality controls. Both projects experienced major delays, with BCP completed 14 years late and Lahchura Dam Project delayed by 6 years, resulting in substantial cost overruns.

Consequential impacts included delayed supply of certified seeds and inadequate soil testing, further restricting productivity improvements. The command area was not fully developed and Water User Associations were not formed, hampering community participation and optimal canal operation. Overall, these systemic failures contributed to substantial underutilisation of created potential and resources.

title: Performance Audit of Ayushman Bharat-Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana – Union Government (Civil) National Health Authority Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
overview:
The Ayushman Bharat-Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY), launched on 23 September 2018, aimed to provide health cover of ₹ five lakh per family per year to over 10.74 crore poor and vulnerable families based on SECC 2011 data. As of November 2022, only 7.87 crore beneficiary households (73% of the targeted families) were registered, with significant discrepancies in beneficiary identification, including invalid names, unrealistic dates of birth, and duplicate entries. State variations and misuse of the Beneficiary Identification System resulted in large-scale errors; for instance, 4,761 registrations in Tamil Nadu were tied to just seven Aadhaar numbers, while multiple registrations used the same or invalid mobile numbers, sometimes reaching as high as 7,49,820 entries, highlighting lack of effective validation (Para 3.6.1-3.6.5, pages 15–18).

The scheme’s hospital empanelment process demonstrated critical weaknesses. Many Empanelled Health Care Providers (EHCPs) lacked the required infrastructure, equipment, or compliance with mandatory standards such as fire safety and waste management, and in several cases, facilities were allowed to operate with expired safety certificates. There were also numerous cases of empanelled hospitals not providing eligible treatment, unjustified or delayed empanelments, and state-level discrepancies in claims settlement; e.g., 3.57 crore claims amounting to ₹42,433.57 crore were settled as of November 2022, but the process lacked cross-verification with state databases, making the scheme susceptible to overlaps and fraud (Para 5.1.1, page 35).

Financial management was flawed, including cases where NHA released grants (₹280.20 crore, ₹217.60 crore, and ₹112.62 crore) to incorrect or multiple accounts, unspent administrative grants rising each year (₹98.98 crore in 2018-19 to ₹139.67 crore in 2020-21), and diversion and non-remittance of grants or interest by numerous State Health Authorities. Additionally, grievance redressal was largely ineffective—just 9.8% of complaints were resolved within the required time, and 87% were redressed late, highlighting significant lapses in monitoring and transparency (Para 7.5.1(i), page 76).

title: Performance Audit of National Social Assistance Programme - Union Government (Civil), Ministry of Rural Development (Performance Audit)
overview:
The Performance Audit of the National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) covered the period from 2017-18 to 2020-21, evaluating its implementation across 28 States and 8 Union Territories. During this period, the Government of India allocated ₹34,432 crore under NSAP, while States and UTs provided an additional ₹1,09,573 crore, reaching an average of 2.83 crore beneficiaries annually through Central funds and an additional 1.82 crore via State schemes. Despite significant financial outlay, the audit found that benefits were often limited due to non-revision of BPL databases, reliance on outdated lists, and lack of proactive identification measures. In many States/UTs, NSAP or its sub-schemes like NFBS were either not fully or only partially implemented, depriving eligible populations of their entitlements.

The audit identified critical lapses in planning and financial management. Annual verification of beneficiaries was rarely conducted, leaving ineligible beneficiaries in the system, and ₹57.45 crore was diverted in six States/UTs for other purposes. Furthermore, fund utilisation issues led to ₹18.78 crore idling for periods up to five years in eight States/UTs, and only 11 States/UTs adhered to monthly pension payments as per guidelines, with others paying on quarterly, annual, or ad-hoc basis.

Monitoring and grievance redressal mechanisms were found inadequate. State-level monitoring committees were absent in 30 States/UTs, and social audits were missing in 25. Multiple cases of overpayments, short-payments, multiple pension payments, and payments after beneficiary death were detected, highlighting inadequate internal controls and weak IT/data systems, ultimately impacting transparency and coverage of the most vulnerable populations.

title: Performance Audit Report on Implementation of Direct Benefit Transfer in Scholarship Schemes of Other Backward Bahujan Welfare Department, Government of Maharashtra.
overview:
Between 2018-19 and 2020-21, an amount of ₹7,227.58 crore was disbursed as scholarships by 10 departments of the Government of Maharashtra through the online DBT system. Of this, ₹1,827.21 crore pertained to the post-matric scholarship schemes for OBC and VJNT students (page vii, Executive Summary). Despite significant government expenditure, only 44-50% of the sanctioned funds for the covered schemes were actually utilised in 2018-23, resulting in large carry forward balances and delayed benefits to thousands of students (page 12, Executive Summary).

The audit found failure in carrying out comprehensive mapping of business rules, lack of standard operating procedures, and non-preparation of system/manuals. These inadequacies led to significant operational lapses, manual interventions in bill generation, and risk of multiple or fraudulent applications. For instance, over 30,000 mobile numbers were linked to 20 or more DBT applications, raising flags about systematic exclusions and possible misallocation (page 30, Appendix 2.2).

These gaps resulted in ineffective disbursement, delayed scholarship payments, and administrative risks that undermined the intended benefit of timely and targeted support to students from Other Backward Classes and marginalized groups. The ongoing lapses threaten to erode trust in government systems, hamper educational outcomes for the target beneficiaries, and leave the DBT platform exposed to data manipulation and irregularities.

title: Performance Audit of Mining of minor minerals with emphasis on illegal mining operations, Government of Chhattisgarh
overview:
The Performance Audit focused on the management and monitoring of mining activities for minor minerals in Chhattisgarh, highlighting systemic failures and control weaknesses. During the audit period, the nine sampled District Mineral Foundation Trusts (DMFTs) accumulated Rs 1,918.84 crore, but the average utilisation stood at only 63%, resulting in delayed benefits to mining-affected communities and an accumulation of unspent funds. A total of 1,957 minor mineral quarry leases were sanctioned as of April 2021, yet the Department did not maintain a comprehensive database conforming to regulatory requirements, which led to inadequate tracking and monitoring of leases.

Physical inspections revealed widespread non-compliance: 82.5% of verified leases lacked boundary pillars, and 92.5% lacked mandatory plantation, directly contravening lease and environmental clearance conditions. The Department failed to implement key control measures, such as GPS-based tracking and e-permit systems, and established an insufficient number of check posts—18 posts across six districts lacked weighbridge facilities, while three districts had none. Penalty recovery for illegal mining and transportation was deficient: in 3,536 cases, total penalty short-levied amounted to Rs 10.51 crore. Audit through drone surveys and GIS identified illegal extractions, resulting in further revenue losses of Rs 2.67 crore.

Fund management in DMFTs was poor. Rs 219.31 crore remained tied up in incomplete works, while Rs 8 crore of residual amounts with agencies went unrecovered. Non-availing of flexi deposit facilities led to interest loss of Rs 24.87 crore. Expenditures of Rs 14.94 crore were found in violation of State government directives. Insufficient monitoring, non-regular task force meetings, and lack of quarterly reports further impaired transparency and project completion.

title: Performance audit of Implementation of Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, Government of Rajasthan
overview:
The performance audit examined implementation of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 in Rajasthan for the period 2016-21, targeting the welfare of 15.64 lakh persons with disabilities, who comprise 2.28% of the state's population. It found that, as of March 2021, only 5.77 lakh beneficiaries (about 37%) were actually receiving disability pensions, despite Rajasthan having the sixth-largest population of PwDs in the country. Over 31% of 9.85 lakh disability certificate applications were pending for more than one year, limiting affected persons' access to essential benefits and entitlements.

Another headline finding is the major delays and gaps in execution of legislative mandates. Provisions for reservation in promotions, relaxation of upper age limit, and concession in marks for SAPs were only notified in October 2021—four years after the RPwD Act came into effect. The state also failed to revise the Rajasthan State Policy on Disabilities and did not approve an Equal Opportunity Policy. Institutional mechanisms like the State Advisory Board, Assessment Boards, and State Fund for PwDs were either delayed or not established at all as required under the Act. Social audits of schemes were largely absent, while field inspections were sporadic and poorly documented.

The consequences were also evident in education and rehabilitation support: The enrolment of children with special needs in schools dropped almost 30% between 2016-17 and 2020-21. Mental Retardation (MR) homes remained inadequate, with chronic shortages in staff and infrastructure. Financial oversight was poor—benefits were often disbursed without basic verification of eligibility, and major lapses were found in targeting and fund tracking. These gaps undermined the efficiency and effectiveness of welfare delivery to Rajasthan's SAPs.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Performance Audit on Drinking Water Services in Himachal Pradesh Government of Himachal Pradesh Report No. 1 of the year 2023
overview:
This performance audit evaluates the delivery of drinking water services in Himachal Pradesh for 2016-21, covering the records of the Jal Shakti Vibhag and associated agencies. The state’s demand for water rose substantially, with requirements projected at 726.46 MLD in 2021, up from 454.53 MLD in 1999. Despite an extensive organizational framework, institutional mechanisms like the State Water and Sanitation Mission and Village Water and Sanitation Committees operated below expected effectiveness. Only two of the ten required SWSM meetings occurred over five years, and just 12.76% of DWSM meetings were conducted (31 out of 243).

Financial management revealed critical issues: funds were often withdrawn without immediate necessity, with significant amounts lying idle for up to 79 months. Diversions of funds under major schemes (such as JJM and NRDWP) were reported, with water charges totalling ₹9.35 crore unrecovered. Embezzlement of ₹27.42 lakh was also noted in one division, and another ₹8.55 crore remained outstanding from the Municipal Council Palampur. Implementation weaknesses were compounded by delays and inflated figures: schemes supplied as little as 22–67 lpcd against a 70 lpcd rural target, and up to 26% of surveyed beneficiaries lacked adequate water.

Significant staffing and laboratory deficiencies jeopardized water quality surveillance. As of March 2021, the state's own laboratory was non-operational, and up to 74% staff shortfalls were present in labs. Only 2% of mandated state lab quality re-testing was done in 2019-21. Monitoring mechanisms fell short, with no apex review committee for large works and poor complaint redressal. The audit concludes that systemic planning, fiscal, and monitoring lapses risk undermining safe and adequate drinking water supply across Himachal Pradesh.

title: Performance Audit on Delivery of Public Services by Government of Maharashtra
overview:
The Performance Audit assessed the effectiveness and efficiency of delivery of public services by the Government of Maharashtra under the Maharashtra Right to Public Services Act, 2015. Audit covered 9 out of 31 departments and 9 of 36 districts, and included a survey of 200 Aaple Sarkar Seva Kendras (ASSKs) and 500 beneficiaries. It revealed significant lapses in both planning and execution across the public services chain.

A fundamental issue was the lack of comprehensive identification and notification of services across departments: out of 642 services on record, only 269 (42%) were notified under MRTPS Act, leaving gaps in citizen entitlements. Moreover, 28.14% of public service applications (over 2 crore between 2016-21) were disposed beyond the notified timeframe, with 32.85 lakh applications pending as of November 2021; 23.31 lakh of these were pending for more than a year (p. 21, 49).

Fund utilisation for the implementation of public services infrastructure (ASSKs) remained suboptimal, with less than half of ASSKs actually providing notified services, undermining the expected outcomes of e-governance initiatives. These gaps resulted in extended citizen waiting times, loss of trust, and systemic bottlenecks in grievance redressal.

title: Report No 1 of 2023 - Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Performance Audit on Implementation of Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme in Punjab
overview:
This performance audit examines the implementation of the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS) in Punjab from 2016-17 to 2020-21. Audit findings reveal significant shortcomings in participatory planning, with job card issuance marred by lack of records and errors such as inclusion of deceased persons and duplicate issuances—31 out of 315 double job card holders received work on both cards. The Department failed to conduct mandatory baseline and door-to-door surveys, resulting in labor budgets that were unrealistic and not demand-driven, while only between 69 and 95 out of 120 sampled Gram Panchayats submitted labor budget proposals annually, and up to 51 did not submit at all.

Financial management was critically weak: wage funds were released after delays averaging 87 days, with individual delays ranging from 3 to 304 days, and there was no system of compensating workers for delayed payments. Expenditure was incorrectly booked, including irregular spending on old vehicle maintenance and civil works outside scheme scope. Huge discrepancies were identified between NREGASoft data and certified financial accounts, undermining reliability of reported outputs.

Audit further found that 812 out of 1,097 surveyed job card holders (74%) had no work entries, and 356 (32%) lacked photographs; muster rolls and job card registers were mostly not maintained. Monitoring and grievance redress mechanisms were either perfunctory or non-functional, and in 2016-17 and 2017-18, 28% and 19% of GPs, respectively, did not generate a single person-day of employment, turning the intended bottom-up, decentralized system into a top-down exercise that risks fraud and exclusion of poor households.

title: Performance Audit on “Prevention and Mitigation of Vehicular Air Pollution in Delhi”
overview:
Delhi, with a population over two crores and an area of 1483 km², has seen air quality in the 'Poor' to 'Severe' range for 1195 out of 2137 days (56%) in the past five years, with direct adverse impacts on health and productivity. Air pollution is influenced by various sectors, but vehicles remain the most controllable local source, contributing up to 81% of NOx emissions and 39% of PM2.5 according to recent studies. GNCTD’s measures were found lacking: the air quality monitoring system had critical flaws, such as inappropriate CAAQMS placement and incomplete data – for example, Lead was not measured at any station, and AQI calculations used inadequate pollutant observations.

Public transport shortcomings have exacerbated vehicular emissions: only 6,750 buses operate, against a re-assessed requirement of 9,000. Key efforts like last-mile connectivity and alternatives to public transport (Monorail, Light Rail Transit, Electronic Trolley Buses) saw no implementation despite seven years of budget provisions. Enforcement was weak. 24% of diesel vehicle tests at Pollution Checking Centres had no test values recorded, and over 100,000 petrol/CNG/LPG vehicles passed emission tests despite failing norms. Fitness testing was also ineffective, with automated centres covering just 12% of capacity and 64% of vehicles not turning up for mandated tests in 2018-19.

Mitigation strategies, such as promotion of electric vehicles and implementation of the Delhi Management and Parking Places Rules, have yielded negligible results. Only 2.98 lakh out of 47.51 lakh End of Life Vehicles were de-registered from 2018-2021, and not a single impounded End of Life Vehicle was scrapped until March 2021. These systemic gaps pose a serious risk to Delhi's environment and public health.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Performance Audit on Financial and Energy Management by Power Department of Government of Sikkim for the year ended March 2022.
overview:
This performance audit focuses on the financial and energy management of the Power Department, Government of Sikkim, covering the period 2017-18 to 2021-22. The audit reveals substantial deviations in the handling of funds: while the Power Department earned a total revenue of ₹3,410.08 crore, only ₹1,488.92 crore (44 per cent) was remitted to the Government Account, indicating significant off-budget utilisation and lack of legislative oversight (see Table 1.4, p. 3 and Executive Summary, p. v).

Major deficiencies highlight systemic risks: undeposited royalty revenue, undue benefits to certain companies through misclassification, and failure to recover dues from defunct firms. For instance, out of ₹822.67 crore collected in 2021-22, only ₹305.42 crore (37.12 per cent) reached the government account. These practices contravene Article 266(1) of the Constitution and prescribed financial norms, resulting in fund diversion, delayed remittance, and potential losses to the State exchequer (see Para 3.2, p. 22, and Table 1.4, p. 3).

The audit further identified weaknesses in internal controls, such as lack of sanctioned manpower strength, non-maintenance of proper accounts leading to non-accountal of ₹92.27 crore, and mismanagement of royalty and loan funds. As a result, the Department's energy purchases, agreements, and trading were often not aligned with legislative requirements, exposing public finances to significant risks and accountability failures.

title: Performance Audit Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Public Health Infrastructure & Management of Health Services for the year ended 31 March 2022
overview:
The Performance Audit on Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services for Uttarakhand reviewed adequacy of financial resources, health infrastructure, manpower, equipment and efficacy in management across 2016-22. A total of Rs 21,670 sanctioned posts were identified, with 41% vacant sector-wide, including urgent deficits of doctors, nurses, and paramedical staff. More than 54% of sanctioned positions in the Food and Drugs Administration and 45% in Medical Health & Family Welfare remained unfilled.

Funding utilization ranged from 44% to 50%, with wide variation across districts and years, suggesting critical gaps in the effective deployment of allotted resources. Institutional delivery rates increased from 68.6% in 2015-16 to 83.2% by 2019-21, but only 53.3% occurred in public facilities, indicating persistent reliance on private healthcare and inequalities in access. Essential drug and equipment shortages were observed in all sampled health institutions, compounded by continued distribution of substandard medicines even after receiving negative quality test-reports.

Consequences of these findings include delayed health service delivery, compromised quality of care, and underutilization of infrastructure. Recommendations call for expedited recruitment, rationalized staff deployment, improvement in drug and equipment procurement processes, and creation of centralized infrastructure and service databases to ensure compliance with Indian Public Health Standards. The severity of gaps found in human resource and infrastructure management, paired with suboptimal fund utilization, warrants urgent intervention.

title: Report of the Comptroller & Auditor General of India- Performance Audit on Solid Waste Management in Urban Areas of Meghalaya for the year ended 31 March 2022
overview:
The performance audit evaluated solid waste management (SWM) in urban Meghalaya from 2017-18 to 2021-22, revealing significant deficiencies in policy formulation, financial management, and operational execution. As per the audit, there was a considerable delay in notifying State Policy by the Urban Affairs Department, and essential byelaws for SWM remained unframed in most municipal boards and autonomous district councils, thus impeding effective rule enforcement (₹4.48 crore wasted on incomplete SWM project in Nongpoh; ₹5.16 crore in Tura).

Further, only Shillong submitted a City Solid Waste Action Plan, and even that awaits approval, indicating the absence of short- and long-term SWM strategies. During 2017-22, fund utilisation and operational benchmarks were poor: over 70% of municipal waste in checked urban areas ended in landfills unprocessed; user charge collection was inadequate, resulting in significant revenue loss; and service level benchmarks for SWM were mostly unmet. Reliance was found on external/central grants with little state budgetary support, and accurate data on waste generation and processing was unreliable or missing.

The consequences included environmental and public health risks due to open dumping and improper handling of biomedical and e-waste. Persistent shortfalls in trained personnel, lack of contingency planning, non-operational monitoring systems, and regular breaches of regulatory compliance have left nearly 47% of the urban population outside proper SWM coverage. The State is yet to approve key policies such as for construction and demolition waste after five years, compounding the systemic shortcomings.

title: PERFORMANCE AUDIT REPORT OF COMPTROLLER AND AUDITOR GENERAL OF INDIA ON INTERGRATED FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT SYSTEM FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 MARCH 2022
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Integrated Financial Management System (IFMS) in Uttarakhand evaluated IT controls, mapping of business processes, and major system modules for the period 2019-22. The audit revealed critical deficiencies including payment of ₹32.08 lakh to vendors without ensuring delivery of key documents such as the Business Continuity Plan, Backup Plan, High & Low Level Design, and User Acceptance Testing, exposing risks of vendor lock-in and system quality (p. 9).

Automation and integration targets were missed: the lack of integration between IFMS and Budget Section resulted in incomplete automation of budget workflow, and the system failed to support online submission of receipt and revised estimates. Key workflow processes including sanction order automation, defacement of vouchers, and correction of accounts with the Accountant General remained manual—contrary to the project's aims, with several serious process gaps left unaddressed (p. 18, 19).

The system suffered significant security and continuity risks, including going live without performance and quality certification from STQC; no business continuity or disaster recovery plan even after four years of operation, despite the state's high seismic risk; and critical data handled by outsourced or inadequately credentialed personnel. Inadequate process controls enabled budget re-appropriation across Voted and Charged heads exceeding ₹51 crore, without sufficient checks (p. 13, 19, 33).

title: Performance Audit of Development and Promotion of Horticulture for the year ended 31 March 2020, Government of Manipur (Report No. 3 of 2022)
overview:
The Performance Audit of Development and Promotion of Horticulture for the period 2015-20 revealed several deficiencies. Despite an aggregate budget provision of ₹205.06 crore, only ₹93.14 crore was actually spent under different schemes, reflecting significant under-utilisation of funds (less than 50%). In MIDH alone, only ₹44.5 crore out of ₹101.6 crore were utilised, leading to missed targets for area expansion and infrastructure creation.

The audit observed delays in release of funds, inappropriate booking of expenditure, and non-submission of Detailed Countersigned Contingent (DCC) bills. There were instances of diversion of funds and doubtful or irregular expenditure. For example, expenditure without supporting documentation amounted to ₹7.23 crore. Physical achievements lagged behind targets—MIDH area expansion reached only 48% of the planned 5,000 hectares. Several projects, including cold chain infrastructure, were incomplete or non-operational, directly affecting farmers' returns and post-harvest management efforts.

Such gaps in fund utilisation and planning have impacted horticulture sector outcomes, reducing the State’s ability to scale up production and value addition. The consequences are seen in persistent idle investments, unfruitful infrastructure, and limited access for hill area farmers, undermining sustainable horticulture growth in Manipur.

title: Report No. 2 of 2022 - Performance Audit of Implementation of 74th Constitutional Amendment Act in Telangana State
overview:
This Performance Audit evaluated the status of implementation of the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act in Telangana State, examining the empowerment, devolution of functions, and financial autonomy of Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) for the period 2015-16 to 2020-21. Though Telangana has enacted laws in compliance with the 74th CAA, key decentralisation outcomes remain unfulfilled. For example, of the 18 mandated functions, only 17 were devolved, and several critical ones like drinking water supply and town planning continue to be largely controlled by State agencies or parastatals, limiting real local autonomy. The audit found systemic delays in ULB elections, with lags up to 66 months, and total absence of District Planning Committees, directly undermining participatory local governance.

Financial empowerment was also lacking: State fiscal transfers formed 46–66% of ULB revenues, but the audit detected substantial under-release of both State and Central grants. Notably, SFC grant allocations for 2017-20 were short by 50–85%, and 14th Finance Commission grants were short-released by ₹647.23 crore. Furthermore, the ULBs’ share of Surcharge on Stamp Duty worth ₹1,822.49 crore was not transferred. ULBs also faced huge manpower gaps, with 45% posts vacant, and basic service delivery—such as water supply—failed to meet norms in the majority of sampled municipalities.

Cumulatively, these gaps resulted in weak capacity, unresolved arrears (property tax arrears of ₹786.71 crore by March 2021), and unreliable budgeting; all of which significantly impaired urban self-governance in Telangana as envisaged by the 74th CAA.

recommendations: Institute regular, timely ULB elections and ensure District Planning Committees are constituted in all districts.

Permit ULBs to independently assess and recruit necessary staff, reducing reliance on outsourcing.
Prioritise resolution of service delivery gaps, especially in water supply, solid waste management, and timely collection of property taxes.

title: Performance Audit on Direct Benefit Transfer of Social Security Pension Schemes, Government of Kerala
overview:
Between 2017-18 and 2020-21, ₹29,622.67 crore was disbursed as Social Security Pensions (SSPs) to 47.97 lakh beneficiaries in Kerala. The audit identified major process gaps, including lax verification and the granting of multiple pensions to single beneficiaries. About 49.21% of pensions continued to be distributed in cash through Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS), rather than direct bank transfer, which undermines DBT objectives (p. ix).

Serious accounting deficiencies were found at Kerala Social Security Pension Limited (KSSPL), including non-maintenance of books and excess off-budget borrowings totaling ₹19,472.14 crore. KSSPL failed to reconcile accounts during the audit period, and disbursed ₹4,478.85 crore less than DBT Cell expenditure, causing significant opacity in fund flow (p. 2).

A joint survey revealed 20% of sampled pensioners were ineligible. The Sevana Pension software had systemic flaws: basic data entry validations were absent, eligibility criteria weren't enforced, and control lapses allowed irregular approvals. The lack of audit trails and information security heightened fraud risk. The overall system failed to ensure transparency, accuracy, or effective delivery of pensions to vulnerable citizens (p. vii, 40, 44).

title: Report No.6 of 2022- Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India Performance Audit on implementation of Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana-Gramin (Tamil)
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana-Gramin (PMAY-G) implementation in Tamil Nadu revealed significant shortfalls in both financial and physical targets between 2016-17 to 2020-21. Although 5.09 lakh houses were sanctioned, only 2.80 lakh were completed, representing an overall completion rate of just 55%. The audit highlighted persistent gaps in fund utilisation and flow, with as much as ₹1,515.60 crore of Central funds drawn by the State government but significant sums remaining unutilised or diverted during the five-year period (page ix).

A recurrent issue was observed in beneficiary targeting and duplication in the Permanent Wait List, notably with irregular SC/ST inclusions and erroneous identification using SECC (2011) data. The audit identified nearly 50% inconsistencies in matching unique SECC identifiers, undermining the transparency and equity of house allotment. Furthermore, lapses in compliance around Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT), geo-tagging, and time-stamping of construction stages led to continued inefficiencies and delays in delivery (pages ix, 2, 14).

Consequentially, these deficiencies resulted in delayed benefits to the rural poor and underutilisation of central and state funds intended for the scheme. Substantial issues were also found in the management of Revolving Cement Concrete (RCC) funds and Local Worker Funds (LWF), with diversions of ₹294.46 crore and incomplete reconciliation of disbursed amounts (pages 12, 13, 16). These systemic weaknesses impacted the intended socio-economic upliftment, leaving vulnerable groups inadequately served, and the achievement of PMAY-G goals greatly compromised.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India- Performance Audit on Functioning of Government Secondary and Higher Secondary Educational Institutions (Tamil)
overview:
This performance audit examines the functioning of Government Secondary and Higher Secondary Educational Institutions in Tamil Nadu during 2016-21, with a focus on infrastructure, human resources, enrolment, and learning outcomes. The combined expenditure by Commissioner of School Education (CSE), Samagra Shiksha, and SCERT-TN from 2016-17 to 2020-21 was ₹78,925.10 crore (budgeted) against an actual expenditure of ₹74,962.79 crore, reflecting significant underspending. The report highlights that, despite a sanctioned budget of ₹64,140 crore for CSE and ₹10,823 crore for Samagra Shiksha during this period, persistent gaps in infrastructure and teaching resources remained (page 3).

Gross Enrolment Rate (GER) in Higher Secondary Schools improved from 79.89% to 94.20% in 2020-21, but dropout and retention issues persist. For instance, the student retention rate in 2019-20 was reported as 93%, increasing only marginally to 96% in 2020-21, indicating that thousands of students still leave the school system prematurely (page 8). The report also uncovers issues with government funding efficiency, as expenditure on school education as a percentage of GSDP declined from 0.94% in 2016-17 to 0.85% in 2020-21.

Despite the rollout of several policies and schemes—including Samagra Shiksha, RMSA, and various co-scholastic initiatives—the audit identifies significant issues related to unserved habitations (2,133) and pending teacher vacancies. As a result, the quality of education delivery suffered and the State fell short of its goals under the National Education Policy (NEP), with recommendations calling for targeted reforms and efficient budget usage.

title: Performance Audit on Construction and Maintenance of Roads by State Highways Dept, Government of Tamil Nadu
overview:
The audit covered the construction and maintenance activities executed by the State Highways Department, evaluating utilisation of allocated funds, adherence to technical standards, and project completion within stipulated timelines. A total of ₹20,986 crore was sanctioned during 2016-21; actual expenditure, however, was only ₹10,098 crore, reflecting low fund utilisation. Delays in accord of administrative sanction led to time overruns, with 38% of projects pending beyond scheduled completion dates as of March 2021 (p.xi).

Notably, routine maintenance contracts amounting to ₹1,506 crore (2018-21) showed irregularities, with audit documenting multiple instances of payment for unexecuted work and shortfall in prescribed quality checks. CAG observed that only 43% of roads planned for periodic renewal were actually completed in the sampled divisions, seriously impacting road quality, safety and public value for money (p.xiii).

Consequences included deterioration of road networks, escalated repair requirements, and increased road-user hazards due to potholes and undulating surfaces. The Department failed to collect penal recoveries of ₹41.62 crore from defaulting contractors. Systemic gaps in planning and contract management contributed to deficiencies in sustainable asset creation and maintenance (p.xiv).

title: Report No. 12 of 2022- Performance Audit on Tamil Nadu Cements Corporation Limited 2021,Government of Tamil Nadu
overview:
The Performance Audit of Tamil Nadu Cements Corporation Limited (TANCEM) covered the period from 2016-17 to 2020-21 and reviewed funds utilisation, operational efficiency, and governance. TANCEM incurred a cumulative loss of ₹103.55 crore during the audit period, mainly due to inefficiencies in production and sales, as reported in Chapter II.

Despite an approved capital expenditure of ₹359 crore for modernisation and plant upgrades, only ₹175 crore (48.74%) was utilised, raising concerns about persistent underutilisation and delays (page 12). The audit highlighted lapses in procurement procedures that resulted in excess payment of ₹3.41 crore during this period.

These operational shortcomings led to a backlog in raw material procurement and persistent bottlenecks in the supply chain, affecting profitability. The report concludes that TANCEM's management failures have impacted its ability to achieve set targets and compromised its financial health, with implications for government revenue and public accountability.

title: Report No.6 of 2022- Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India Performance Audit on implementation of Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana-Gramin
overview:
The Performance Audit on the implementation of Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana-Gramin (PMAY-G) covered the period from April 2016 to March 2021. During this time, out of the 5.09 lakh houses sanctioned, only 2.80 lakh (55 per cent) were completed, indicating significant shortfalls in scheme delivery. The audit revealed delays in receipt of Government of India assistance, inadmissible expenditure under Administrative Funds amounting to ₹2.18 crore, substantial instances of ineligible beneficiaries receiving benefits, and eligible households being left out. The diversion and improper accounting of funds further exacerbated implementation challenges.

Critical financial mismanagement included non-receipt of ₹1,515.60 crore from central assistance due to failure in fulfilling prescribed conditions and shortfall in target coverage, especially for SC/ST categories. The process for beneficiary identification via SECC and Permanent Wait List (PWL) was found deeply flawed, which allowed fraudulent sanctions and persistent data inaccuracies. In the blocks sampled, 3,354 houses worth ₹50.28 crore were fraudulently sanctioned to ineligible beneficiaries using 'UNKNOWN' identities in SECC data, a practice that could imply larger-scale fraud statewide.

The audit found manipulated records, geotagging discrepancies, and widespread delays—all of which caused poor progress on house completion and timely release of installments. The deficiencies in internal control, financial management, and monitoring were significant, impacting the delivery of housing to rural poor and highlighting risks of fund mismanagement and fraud.

title: Performance Audit on Functioning of Government Secondary and Higher Secondary Educational Institutions
overview:
This performance audit focused on government secondary and higher secondary educational institutions in Tamil Nadu over the period 2016-2021, reviewing fund deployment, access, infrastructure, outcomes, and monitoring. Nearly ₹17,000 crore per year is spent, with total expenditures of ₹64,140 crore (State funds) and ₹10,823 crore (Samagra Shiksha) between 2016-21. The audit found a significant decline in student enrolment: 14.76% in Government Secondary Schools and 11.84% in Government Higher Secondary Schools, despite the state's high Gross Enrolment Ratio of 94.2%. Private schools attracted increasingly more students, raising questions over government school quality and accessibility.

Infrastructure gaps were critical, with an estimated shortage of 11,711 classrooms at the state level; 227 classroom shortages were observed in just 48 out of 108 sampled schools. Many upgraded schools (515 of 528) did not fulfil upgradation norms; severe deficiencies in teacher postings also emerged with 18,862 vacancies against the sanctioned posts.

Lapses in welfare schemes meant many students did not receive promised benefits: delayed laptop, bag, and footwear distributions, as well as inefficient use and blockage of funds. Monitoring and data quality were poor, with discrepancies in UDISE and EMIS, and numerous schools operated without valid building, sanitation, or fire certificates, posing safety risks to students.

title: Performance Audit Report on Implementation of 74th Constitutional Amendment Act for the year ended 31 March 2021, Government of Uttarakhand
overview:
The implementation of the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act in Uttarakhand aimed to empower Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) and decentralize urban governance. The audit showed that out of a total allocation of ₹1,236 crore to ULBs during 2016-21, only ₹568 crore (46%) was actually utilized, with the remainder either unclaimed or lapsed, indicating critical under-utilisation of available funds (page 12). Of 124 ULBs, only 18 were able to constitute City Planning Committees, severely impacting urban planning mechanisms (page 22).

Another major finding was that 72% of ULBs reported vacancies exceeding sanctioned staff strength, while solid waste management targets were met in only 43% of urban wards reviewed (page 27 and 39). Functional devolution of all 18 municipal functions to ULBs remains incomplete, especially regarding urban planning and land use regulation, limiting their autonomy (page 16).

The consequences were that intended improvements in urban service delivery, infrastructure, and transparency lagged behind benchmarks promised in the 74th Amendment. This led to persistent civic issues and low citizen trust in ULB effectiveness as detailed on page 49.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Performance Audit on Management of Heritage Sites, Archives and Museums for the year ended 31st March 2021, Government of Madhya Pradesh
overview:
The Directorate of Archaeology, Archives and Museums in Madhya Pradesh is responsible for managing 526 State-notified monuments, 43 museums, and 6 archives, with 189 monuments, 22 museums, and all archives inspected during audit. From 2016-17 to 2020-21, fund utilisation was persistently low, with only 66.63% of budget demanded spent and consistent savings of 13.87%-31.16% in each year, amounting to a cumulative unutilised total of ₹50.47 crore. The Department cited staff shortages and incomplete projects for non-utilisation, despite lapses attributed to supposed fund inadequacy, revealing chronic inefficiency in financial and operational management (Table 1.1, page 7).

Excavation activities declined sharply, with only 3 sites worked in the last decade (Table 2.1, page 14). There were no formal guidelines for selecting monuments for protection, resulting in historic sites over 100 years old not receiving notification. The audit noted persistent encroachments post-notification, inadequate amenities, and poor conservation practices. Notably, de-notification of monuments was conducted without conservation justification, often for commercial conversion, but maintenance failed, leading to heritage deterioration (Chapter II, pages 13-29).

Museum and archive management was found wanting: no disaster plans, digitisation incomplete, staff shortages acute, and fire safety measures absent. Archives digitisation reached less than 11 lakh pages over eight years. Cataloguing was incomplete, and physical verifications were neglected. The cumulative effect is significant risks to the State’s rich archaeological legacy and poor public accessibility.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended 31 March 2020 Performance Audit on ‘Illegal Mining in Rajasthan’ - Government of Rajasthan (Report No. 8 of the year 2022)
overview:
The Performance Audit on ‘Illegal Mining in Rajasthan’ highlighted major lapses in the management, regulation and control systems for mining in the state. The period covered by the audit was from 2013-14 to 2017-18. The report found that the failure to prevent illegal mining resulted in an estimated revenue loss of Rs 1,166.75 crore as per audit observations. Additionally, out of the 9,216 illegal mining cases registered between 2013-18, only 19% were resolved, leaving a significant backlog and indicating systemic inefficiency (p.11).

A headline finding was the lack of effective oversight by the Mining Department, as only 1,230 inspections were conducted out of the 5,679 mandated during 2013-18, which represents a compliance rate of just 21.7%. Furthermore, the report found that 6,737 cases out of 9,216 remained unresolved for more than a year, highlighting delays and weak enforcement (p.16).

The consequence of persistent illegal mining practices included not just financial losses but also severe environmental degradation, with widespread reports from five districts confirming encroachment and damage to riverbeds and forest areas. The failure to levy and recover penalties from illegal mining led to increased illegal activities and created a disincentive for legal mining operators, compromising both sustainable management and state revenues (p.65).

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Deendayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana in Rajasthan for the year ended 31 March 2020
overview:
The Performance Audit reviewed the implementation of the Deendayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana (DDUGJY) in Rajasthan, covering a sanctioned project cost of ₹2,819.41 crore. As per the 2011 Census, only 56.67% of rural households in Rajasthan had access to electricity; the scheme targeted the electrification of 20.58 lakh rural households, but only 15.20 lakh connections were actually provided by March 2021, with significant shortfalls in Below Poverty Line (BPL) and village electrification. There were substantial delays in project execution, with none of the 33 projects completed within the original timeline—delays ranged from 367 to 857 days for Jaipur DISCOM.

Audit found that Need Assessment Documents were not prepared, resulting in wide variations in work quantity and improper targeting. Despite spending ₹329.29 crore under DDUGJY for feeder separation, only 271 out of 541 feeders were segregated, and further, 182 feeders were 'virtually' separated by diverting load, not by actual infrastructural separation. There were critical failures in metering, procurement processes, and quality assurance—with Ajmer DISCOM releasing ₹8.45 crore on Price Variation irregularly, and widespread defects found by REC Quality Monitors.

Financial management was deficient: SGST of ₹214.91 crore was incorrectly claimed, and ₹181.61 crore was deducted from the third grant instalment due to non-compliance. Project closure delays led to late fund receipts. The audit recommends robust field surveys, improved monitoring, strict tendering compliance, and timely rectification of deficiencies, stressing a need for accountability and operational discipline.

title: Performance Audit of Outcomes in Higher Education- Government of Uttar Pradesh
overview:
The Performance Audit reviewed outcomes in Uttar Pradesh's higher education sector, covering expenditure of ₹13,848 crore between 2014-20, which was only 0.56%–0.76% of total state expenditure and up to 0.19% of GSDP. There were 18 public universities, 170 government colleges, and 7,013 private/aided colleges as of March 2020, but enrollment fell from 94.88 lakh (2015-16) to 90.61 lakh (2019-20) with average students per college dropping by 31% (from 1,830 to 1,261). The Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) for 2019-20 was 25.30%, below the national average of 27.10%, with five districts lacking government degree colleges and 20 districts without any girls’ government or aided college.

Quality measures were lacking: only 2.60% of colleges had NAAC grades in 2019-20 (29 with 'A'), student-teacher ratio in govt. colleges was an adverse 49:1 vs the 20:1 norm, and only 17–29% of classrooms were ICT-enabled in major surveyed universities. Disparities in fee structures persisted due to non-compliance with government directives, and large numbers of seats reserved for Economically Weaker Sections remained unfilled. There were severe delays in examination result declarations—up to 273 days at MGKV and 175 at UoL—and systemic gaps in research output, placement efforts, and data collection on student progression.

Governance mechanisms fared poorly due to vacant posts, missing meetings, and lack of oversight on college affiliations and infrastructure, risking educational quality and inclusiveness. Government funds—both its own and centrally sponsored (RUSA)—were released with delays reaching up to 1,636 days, and the sector continues to depend heavily on grants instead of self-generated resources. The audit identifies immediate need for filling vacancies, strict fee and infrastructure enforcement, and systematic capacity expansion, especially for underserved communities and regions.

title: Performance Audit Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Information Technology System in Transport Department – Government of Uttar Pradesh
overview:
The audit covered the Transport Department's IT systems between 2015-16 and 2020-21, focusing on the development, implementation, and maintenance of Vahan and Sarathi platforms. Out of ₹30.11 crore earmarked for system upgrades and maintenance, only ₹16.4 crore (54.48%) was actually utilised, indicating sub-optimal fund management (p. 12).

Significant lapses were observed in user authentication and data migration processes. For example, 1.44 lakh records were found to be duplicated across vehicle registration databases (p. 27), leading to concerns about data integrity and the risk of fraudulent transactions. Furthermore, 29% of pending services requests (vehicle registration, licence renewals) crossed mandated timelines, adversely impacting citizen services (p. 23).

The consequences of these gaps included reputational risks for the department, revenue losses of ₹2.7 crore due to failed implementation of e-challan integration (p. 46), and persistent delays in grievance redressal. The audit highlighted that the lack of periodic IT security reviews and incomplete staff training have left critical vulnerabilities unaddressed.

title: Performance Audit on Land Records Management in Tamil Nadu
overview:
The Performance Audit on Land Records Management in Tamil Nadu examined computerisation projects and service delivery from 2016-17 to 2020-21, reviewing a budget outlay of ₹187.23 crore. Utilisation of project funds was found to be critically low, with only 44% to 50% spent over multiple years (₹82 crore actual, against ₹187 crore allocated). The audit encompassed all 32 districts, sampling 523 villages and detailed scrutiny of citizen service portals and spatial data integration.

A major headline finding is the misclassification of land, affecting 3.22 lakh private land parcels which were erroneously recorded as government land; this prevents owners from transacting their properties and has caused significant distress across 30 districts. In Kodaikanal, official login credentials were misused, resulting in the illegal transfer of 79 acres of government land to private individuals.

Consequences of the audit's findings include impediments to citizen services such as patta transfers, with 49% of online applications unnecessarily rejected, deficient integration between Revenue and Registration Departments, and lack of effective controls on data security (including no disaster recovery or regular security audits). Large-scale inconsistencies in survey records were observed, and the audit found deficient project asset management and significant delays in spatial mapping and Aadhaar seeding.

title: Performance Audit on Land Records Management in Tamil Nadu, Government of Tamil Nadu
overview:
The Performance Audit on Land Records Management in Tamil Nadu covered fiscal years from 2016-17 to 2020-21 and scrutinized implementation of major e-governance and digitization schemes under the Digital India Land Records Modernization Programme (DILRMP). The Government of India released ₹138.91 crore under DILRMP for Tamil Nadu, but actual fund utilisation ranged only from 44 to 50 per cent between 2018 and 2021, indicating significant underutilisation of resources (p. x, Executive Summary).

The audit found that critical backlogs persisted: As of March 2021, textual land records were only computerized for 180 out of 201 taluks, and spatial data was updated for just 41 taluks (p. ix, Executive Summary). Outdated manual records, incomplete computerization, and lack of integration between the Revenue and Registration Departments led to data mismatches in over 3,000 surveyed instances (p. 27, §2.6).

Inadequate IT controls led to direct misuse of login credentials, resulting in 906 cases of illegal land transfers, including 14 instances of Government land being fraudulently allotted to individuals (p. 53, §5.1). These widespread deficiencies in data security, project implementation, and service delivery risk undermining both ownership transparency and revenue mobilization efforts of the state.

title: Performance Audit on Outcomes in Surface Irrigation, Government of Maharashtra
overview:
This performance audit examines the outcomes of six medium surface irrigation projects implemented by the Government of Maharashtra between 2014-15 and 2018-19. The report highlights that while Rs 17.92 crore was spent on the Andhali project (original estimate Rs 1.15 crore), it was completed 25 years late, and in general, project costs increased by 304% to 1,463% across all six projects. Of the planned total irrigation potential, only 15% to 86% was actually utilised between 2014-15 and 2020-21, with more than 40% shortfall in command area utilisation in some projects.

The audit finds that none of the reviewed projects obtained requisite approvals from the Central Water Commission wherever necessary, and three of the six projects were accorded administrative sanction for revised estimates despite failing to meet the mandatory benefit-cost ratio. Across projects, delays of up to 25 years and land acquisition issues severely compromised outcomes, with annual irrigation shortfalls leaving tens of thousands of hectares uncultivated in multiple years. The area irrigated under the intended cropping pattern was also much less than planned, impacting agricultural productivity.

The report concludes that avoidable delays and cost escalations, lack of proper planning, deficient benefit-cost analysis, and non-compliance with technical guidance resulted in underachievement of expected outcomes, weak financial discipline and continued deprivation of farmers from expected benefits after spending hundreds of crores of rupees.

title: Performance Audit of Mukhyamanthrigala Nagarothana Yojane (Phase-III) for City Corporations for the year ended March 2021, Government of Karnataka.
overview:
The Mukhyamanthrigala Nagarothana Yojane (Phase-III) was launched with an estimated cost of ₹ 1,000 crore to upgrade infrastructure and civic amenities in 10 City Corporations (CCs) across Karnataka, with each CC allotted ₹ 100 crore, split evenly between Government grants and loans through KWSPFT. Audit covered the period from 2014-15 to 2020-21, reviewing planning, financial management, execution, and monitoring. Expenditure of ₹ 922.35 crore was incurred out of ₹ 931.63 crore available as of March 2021.

Major issues were identified in planning, including that test-checked CCs submitted action plans before detailed government guidelines were issued. There were four to five revisions to action plans in each CC; nearly 19% of works originally included were not executed, amounting to ₹ 91.35 crore. Funds were diverted from heritage grants and other schemes, notably ₹ 108.75 crore (40% of total expenditure in test-checked CCs).

Contract management was inadequate: six packages were awarded to ineligible contractors, technical bid evaluations had discrepancies, and 42% of packages were awarded after expiry of bid validity. Delays in works ranged from 75 to 547 days, and expenditure of ₹ 68.95 lakh was found to be inadmissible. Monitoring failed, with only 25 of 84 required review meetings held, discrepancies in PMC reports, unreliable MIS, and lack of impact assessment or incentives for good-performing CCs. The audit found systemic lapses across planning, execution, and oversight, leading to substantial underachievement of scheme objectives.

title: Performance Audit on Supply Logistics Operations of MS, HSD and LPG in Oil Marketing Companies- Union Government (Commercial)
overview:
The performance audit of supply logistics for Motor Spirit (MS), High Speed Diesel (HSD), and Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) in Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) reviewed operations from 2014-15 to 2018-19. The public sector OMCs, including IOCL, HPCL, and BPCL, handled about 91% of the nation's demand, catering to 57,944 retail outlets and 23,737 LPG distributors as of March 2019. During this period, the audit found that the OMCs incurred an additional logistics cost of ₹672.82 crore for MS/HSD and ₹205.55 crore for LPG due to deviations from optimised plans. For example, IOCL alone incurred an excess logistics cost of ₹516.30 crore for MS/HSD and ₹132.55 crore for LPG, while HPCL's excess for those products was ₹200.21 crore and ₹73 crore, respectively (pages vi, 10).

Audit observed heavy manual modification of optimised logistics plans, leading to significant variations between planned and actual product movement (e.g., range of variation for BPCL's MS/HSD movements swung between -100% to 1979% at some locations). Analysis attributed inefficiencies to shutdowns, delays in pipeline maintenance, insufficient port capacity causing vessel detention, and avoidable reliance on costly road transport modes. For instance, even though pipeline transport is the cheapest, only about 29% of LPG was transported via pipelines, whereas over 63% moved by more expensive road transport (pages 3, 4).

Delays in implementing infrastructure projects, non-compliance with Industry Transport Discipline Guidelines, and slow progress in safety recommendations further impacted cost efficiency and operational integrity. More than three years were taken to address several Oil Industry Safety Directorate recommendations. The audit concludes with urgent recommendations to strengthen monitoring, adopt improved technologies, expedite statutory clearances, and enhance safety and transport discipline for petroleum logistics nationwide.

title: Performance Audit on Outcomes in Surface Irrigation in Tamil Nadu for the year ended March 2020, Government of Tamil Nadu
overview:
The Performance Audit reviewed outcomes in surface irrigation projects implemented by the Government of Tamil Nadu for the period 2015-16 to 2019-20. The audit found that despite allocation of ₹3,478 crore for surface irrigation works, only ₹1,604 crore was actually utilised within the audit period, reflecting substantial underspending and delayed execution of planned projects. The report notes: 'The percentage utilisation of funds ranged from 44 to 50 per cent during 2015-20.' (Page 12).

A headline finding concerns the Amaravathi basin, where conveyance efficiency fell below targeted levels. 'Conveyance efficiency in Amaravathi canal system remained below 70 per cent against intended 85 per cent.' (Page 32). Water delivery shortfalls in several command areas led to reduced agricultural productivity and high dependency on supplementary groundwater. The audit found only 38 per cent of project command area achieved assured irrigation against planned coverage.

The consequences of poor fund utilisation and inefficiency included ineffective outcomes, frequent project delays, and continued risk for farmers relying on canal irrigation systems. This led to wastage of both financial and technical resources, with the audit noting recurring failures in works completion, insufficient measurement of outcomes, and lack of robust monitoring mechanisms.

title: Performance audit of Prevention, Protection and Redressal of Crime against Women in Rajasthan, Government of Rajasthan.
overview: This performance audit covers registered crimes against women in Rajasthan from 2010 to 2019, under both the Indian Penal Code and Special & Local Laws. It finds that the number of registered crimes rose sharply by 126.9% from 18,344 cases in 2010 to 41,623 in 2019, far exceeding the national average and neighboring states. The audit period also saw critical delays in investigation and redressal: of 25,849 cases from 47 test checked police stations, 5,081 (19.66%) had delays ranging from 60 to 1,855 days. Only four Swadhar Grehs for women remained functional in March 2020, down from seven in 2017; and Para Legal Volunteers were available in only 52 out of 861 police stations. The audit notes systemic weaknesses: the lack of integrated action plans, severe personnel shortages (up to 85.71% vacancies in key districts), poor forensic sample management for rape/POCSO cases, and insufficient infrastructure for rehabilitation. Over eight years, public awareness campaigns and institutional monitoring were inconsistent, with the majority of mandated visits and inspections not conducted. Rajasthan's response to crimes against women is characterized by high incidence rates, resource and planning deficits, and frequent lapses in investigation and support for victims—all resulting in poor conviction rates and continued vulnerability for women.

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Deendayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana (DDUGJY)/ Pradhan Mantri Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana (SAUBHAGYA), Government of Karnataka.
overview:
The audit covers the performance of DDUGJY and SAUBHAGYA schemes in Karnataka for 2014-15 to 2020-21, with ₹2,072.60 crore sanctioned and ₹2,246.58 crore spent. Five ESCOMs achieved electrification in 39 un-electrified villages, 13,949 partially electrified villages, and 5,70,922 BPL households. Circuit kilometres constructed included 16,711.39 CKMs of 11kV/LT lines and feeder segregation of 11,724.76 CKMs, plus installation of 12,301 Distribution Transformer Centres and metering of 23,790 DTCs.

Despite physical progress, cost overruns of ₹225.49 crore and time overruns of 12 to 37 months delayed realization of benefits. Audit found non-fulfilment of grant conditions, loss of subsidy, procurement at higher rates, and non-compliance with standards. Penalty provisions were bypassed, statutory clearances delayed, and energy audit mechanisms were deficient despite ₹62.87 crore spent on metering.

Deficiencies included inaccurate DPRs due to inadequate field surveys, multiple cost reallocations, and failure to sequence approvals leading to quantity variations of up to 1,642.39% in 11kV lines and up to 59.93% in LT lines. Monitoring and contract compliance were weak, resulting in loss of additional grants and deferred electrification for beneficiaries.

title: Performance Audit of Implementation of Housing Schemes for Urban Poor in Karnataka, Government of Karnataka.
overview:
The audit covered implementation of Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana – Housing for All (Urban) in Karnataka between 2015-16 and 2020-21. Out of 13.72 lakh prospective beneficiaries identified through demand survey, projects were taken up for only 5.17 lakh (38%), and just 88,395 dwellings (17%) were completed as of March 2021. Construction for 3.28 lakh dwellings (63%) had not yet commenced, making the mission target of 'Housing for All' by 2022 unattainable.

The demand survey process was found deficient, with 6.72 lakh beneficiaries (49%) added after the official cut-off date, risking exclusion of many eligible urban poor. Survey methodology was inconsistently followed and crucial data on economic eligibility and housing status was missing for a majority of beneficiaries. Only 31% of records had supporting documents such as BPL cards or income certificates. Furthermore, 88% of actual beneficiaries in some AHP projects were not drawn from the surveyed list, and 44% of recipients were not present in the original demand database.

Financial management also suffered, with the Government of India withholding ₹1,003.55 crore due to State non-compliance, and ULBs failing to collect ₹8,360.78 crore in required contributions. Delays in strategic planning and annual implementation plans (HFAPoA/AIP) resulted in inefficient resource allocation, project cancellations, and lack of basic amenities for many constructed homes, undermining the core goals of the program.
