title: Performance Audit on Achievement of objectives of Sindh Project Phase-II for the year ended 31 March 2019, Government of Madhya Pradesh.
overview:
The Performance Audit on the Sindh Project Phase-II reviewed outcomes over 2014-15 to 2018-19, covering key investments in irrigational infrastructure across Gwalior, Shivpuri, Bhind and Datia districts. The total project expenditure reached Rs 1,973.70 crore as of 2019-20, with significant central (NABARD and AIBP) and state contributions (Rs 814.91 crore and Rs 509.94 crore respectively).

The audit found notable shortfalls: while the project aimed to create irrigation potential for 1.62 lakh hectares, utilisation never exceeded 64 per cent, with 2019-20 showing a 36.1% gap (58,525 hectares). The primary shortfall was worsened by delays in the completion of Harsi High Level Canal, design flaws, and disproportionate water distribution upstream. Foodgrain production increased by only 2,45,205 MT against the targeted 5,76,860 MT, and irrigation intensity was restricted to 105% versus a planned 165%.

These shortcomings have resulted in partial achievement of objectives, ongoing water scarcity in lower reaches, and crops in upstream areas shifting to more water-intensive varieties (wheat and sugarcane) threatening equitable access. Furthermore, secondary objectives like providing drinking water to Shivpuri town and ecological benefits were also delayed or fell short.

title: Performance Audit of Implementation of 74th Constitutional Amendment Act in Madhya Pradesh, Government of Madhya Pradesh
overview:
The Performance Audit examines the effectiveness of implementing the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act in Madhya Pradesh, covering 407 Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) with a population of 2.01 crore urban residents. Only 60 ULBs had democratically elected city governments during the audit period, while 347 ULBs operated under State Government administrators, highlighting major gaps in democratic decentralisation. Over 24,437 audit paras were pending in 30 out of 33 sampled ULBs, reflecting deep operational weaknesses.

Key findings include acute staff shortages: the ULBs lacked authority to assess and recruit permanent staff, remaining dependent on state appointments and outsourced personnel. The report points to significant delays in the constitution and functioning of State Finance Commissions (Third to Fifth), resulting in continued fund devolution based on outdated recommendations despite the sixth Commission being due. The financial position of ULBs is further hampered by low own-source revenue — with property tax GIS surveys conducted in only 123 ULBs (30%), and arrears in property tax and water charges.

Other major deficiencies documented include the absence of Metropolitan Planning Committees in all cities, irregular meetings of elected Councils, failure to constitute Ward and Mohalla Committees, and lack of consolidated District Development Plans in 25 districts. Weak budget formulation was evident, with large variations between estimates and actuals and delays in budget approval ranging from 4 to 707 days. These systemic issues critically undermine urban governance and grassroots democracy in Madhya Pradesh.

title: Performance Audit of DISCOMs pre and post Ujwal DISCOM Assurance Yojana (UDAY), Government of Madhya Pradesh.
overview:
The performance audit assesses the financial and operational outcomes of Madhya Pradesh DISCOMs before and after the implementation of the Ujwal DISCOM Assurance Yojana (UDAY), covering 2016-17 to 2020-21. Key objectives of UDAY included reducing outstanding debts and accumulated losses of DISCOMs and improving operational indicators such as Aggregate Technical and Commercial (AT&C) losses and bridging the Average Cost of Supply and Average Realisable Revenue (ACS-ARR) gap. However, significant lapses were observed in implementation and target achievement.

The report highlights that the Government of Madhya Pradesh (GoMP) only managed to take over ₹12,690 crore out of the targeted ₹26,055 crore of DISCOM debt (48.7%), failing to meet the commitment set in the Memorandum of Understanding, and resulting in a negligible reduction in overall outstanding debt (from ₹34,739 crore pre-UDAY to ₹34,727.04 crore post-UDAY). Accumulated losses increased sharply, reaching ₹52,978.39 crore by March 2020, well above the target of ₹38,479.36 crore. In addition, the GoMP was irregular in paying its own electricity dues and subsidies, with claims amounting to ₹2,453.85 crore remaining unrecovered, affecting DISCOM liquidity and leading to fresh borrowing of ₹11,200 crore during the scheme period.

The operational goals also remained largely unmet. Instead of bringing AT&C losses down to the targeted 15% by 2019-20, losses worsened from 23.45% in 2015-16 to 33.08% in 2019-20. Billing efficiency remained stagnant at about 80%, and collection efficiency dropped from 97% to 86%. The crucial ACS-ARR gap, which should have been eliminated, persisted at ₹(0.83) per unit in 2019-20, indicating DISCOMs' continued commercial unviability. These failures resulted in increased costs, impaired revenue realisation, and threat to infrastructure investment, undermining the twin objectives of UDAY.

title: Report No. 1 of 2022 - Performance Audit on Wildlife Conservation and Sustainable Management of Wildlife Habitats in Madhya Pradesh, Government of Madhya Pradesh
overview:
The performance audit covers wildlife conservation and sustainable management of habitats in Madhya Pradesh from 2014-15 to 2018-19. The audit found that while the number of tigers increased in the state during the period (with Madhya Pradesh holding the largest national population), financial management and planning were critically deficient. The State spent ₹633.32 crore under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme and ₹1,265.92 crore under four State Schemes, but fund utilisation for core conservation and habitat management was below national standards. Only 44% to 50% of allotted funds were used for key activities in tiger reserves and protected areas.

Long-term plans such as Management Plans and Tiger Conservation Plans were lacking in most sampled areas—only three of six Tiger Reserves and one of three National Parks had plans in place. The absence of strategic planning and approved Zonal Master Plans led to risks related to rising tiger population density (potentially over 10 per 100 sq km), inbreeding, territorial conflicts, and disease outbreaks. Nearly 73% rise in documented human-wildlife conflicts was observed over the audit period. The Department failed to establish institutional research linkages or properly identify and monitor research topics relevant to conservation, with only 2 out of 206 proposed themes actioned.

Furthermore, important habitat consolidation and protection actions were not completed. No comprehensive plans were in place for disease surveillance, corridor development, encroachment removal, or mitigation of impacts from major infrastructure projects like the Ken-Betwa River Linking Project. The Special Tiger Protection Force was not constituted, and significant gaps in equipment, welfare provisions, and administrative coordination persisted, risking sustainability of wildlife populations.

title: Performance Audit of Direct Benefit Transfer
overview:
The audit assessed the effectiveness and adequacy of the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) system in Karnataka across 2018-20, focusing on process re-engineering, infrastructure, and management. Out of 239 schemes identified for onboarding onto the Core DBT Portal, only 83 (35%) had been successfully integrated as of April 2021, resulting in the disbursement of ₹2,829.02 crore outside the DBT system across 168 schemes from 22 departments (Page vii). The audit revealed critical delays at approval transaction points: 75% of delayed transactions occurred at the Scroll/final approval stage in Khajane 2 (K2), and 13% at DDO approval, with the average time for transaction completion being 45 days, much above recommended benchmarks (Page 8). Moreover, 6.67 lakh beneficiaries were deprived of financial benefits totaling ₹153.30 crore due to prolonged pendency (Page 11), and 91,283 failed transactions awaited re-initiation due to poor monitoring and technical gaps (Page 10).

Technical deficiencies included insufficient validation checks, lack of timely response from departments for rectification of failed or rejected transactions, and storing of Aadhaar information in departmental databases against regulatory guidelines (Page 16). The audit also uncovered cases of incorrect credits due to name mismatch, with ₹97.14 lakh miscredited across 523 transactions (Page 9). Furthermore, the monitoring mechanism by DBT Cell was found inadequate, with no centralized grievance redressal system or fixed timelines for resolving transactional issues, leading to inconsistent delivery of benefits, ineffective oversight, and the inability to ensure corrective actions (Page 34).

Overall, the audit concluded that the DBT framework’s implementation was slow, with high rejection rates (up to 42% in test-checked schemes), technical lapses, and ineffective monitoring that undermined the intended objectives of minimizing intermediaries, delays, pilferage, and duplication. Evaluation and impact assessment of the Core DBT portal and major schemes had not been conducted, further calling into question the ability to measure the true effectiveness of DBT in Karnataka (Page x).

title: Performance Audit Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Systems and controls in assessment and collection of mineral receipts for the year ended 31st March 2021.
overview:
Receipts from Mines and Minerals in Bihar, administered by the Mines and Geology Department (MGD), formed 28% of the State's total non-tax revenue in 2020-21, totaling ₹1,708.93 crore. The audit found the department failed to ensure accurate reconciliation of mineral revenues, and vital District Survey Reports remained incomplete due to a lackadaisical approach by MGD. As much as ₹94.97 crore in security deposits for extended lease periods went unrealized, and ₹97.41 crore in Stamp Duty and Registration Fee was not collected due to non-execution of registered deeds, reflecting significant lapses in revenue collection oversight.

Serious deficiencies included non-auction of declared minor minerals, loss of revenue from surrendered leases, and widespread illegal mining, as evidenced by satellite imagery and the generation of fake or unrealistic e-challans. Notably, 2,43,811 e-challans were generated using 46,935 vehicles, including ambulances and motorcycles, purportedly to transport minerals, raising concerns about proper IT controls. Audit also highlighted poor fund utilization, with just ₹9.56 crore of the ₹91.86 crore District Mineral Foundation (DMF) Fund spent during 2014–21, leaving ₹82.30 crore unutilized and the Fund's objectives unachieved.

These failures resulted in revenue losses, non-levy of mandatory interest and penalties, inadequate monitoring, and rampant illegal mining. With a total of 4,608 FIRs registered and recoveries amounting to ₹113.30 crore from penalty on illegal mining, the audit exposes a high risk and ongoing systemic weaknesses that require urgent remediation.

title: Performance Audit Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Systems and Controls in assessment and collection of mineral receipt for the year ended 31st March 2021.
overview:
This Performance Audit examines the efficacy and adequacy of systems and controls implemented by Central Government agencies in the assessment and collection of mineral receipts from 2015-16 to 2020-21, covering more than ₹10,345 crore in mineral revenue collections. It highlights substantial shortfalls and structural weaknesses in verification of royalty payments, delayed reconciliations, lack of electronic monitoring, and under-assessment causing significant revenue loss.

The Audit revealed systemic lapses such as incorrect computation of dues in 37 percent of sampled cases, resulting in a short recovery of ₹894 crore. Monitoring and enforcement were found to be inadequate, as seen in non-recovery actions in over 1,200 defaulting leases, further exacerbated by absence of cross-verification with transport and export data. These issues led to critical slippage in revenue realization, undermining the intended use of mining royalties for local area development and environmental safeguards.

Delays and gaps in enforcement negatively affect government funds available for health, education, and infrastructure, as mining receipts constitute a major non-tax resource. The report recommends robust IT interventions, timely reconciliations, routine audits, and strict penalty collections to ensure accountability and full realization of revenue due to the state, with mechanisms to plug leakage and ensure transparent fund flow.

title: The performance audit on “the Efficacy of Implementation of Seventy-fourth Constitutional Amendment Act in Maharashtra”
overview:
This performance audit focused on evaluating the efficacy of the Seventy-fourth Constitutional Amendment Act's implementation in Maharashtra from 2015-16 to 2020-21. The audit covered 44 out of 396 Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), including Municipal Corporations, Municipal Councils, and Nagar Panchayats, with a particular emphasis on water supply, sanitation, and fire services. Significant shortfalls were observed in fund devolution, resource allocation, and the empowerment of ULBs, which undermined the intended decentralization of urban governance.

During the audit period, the average property tax collection efficiency in test-checked ULBs was only 53%, and the Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai achieved merely 28%. Critical delays and inadequacies in the constitution and operationalization of local governance institutions, such as Ward Committees and Metropolitan Planning Committees, further hindered effective administration. Additionally, a shortfall in disbursement of ₹1,220.22 crore in Additional Stamp Duty and ₹2,679.15 crore in assigned grants such as Nagarpalika Sahayak Anudan, Pilgrim Tax, and Road Grant were reported.

The consequences were visible across essential civic services: 83% of test-checked ULBs did not provide 100% water supply coverage; 69% failed to supply the required 135 litres per capita per day; 61% shortage in fire stations; and only one ULB achieved 100% sewage network coverage. Such deficiencies contributed to compromised service delivery, inequitable resource allocation, and a persistent gap in ULBs' capacities to address rapid urbanization and citizen needs.

title: Performance Audit on Functioning of Transport Department (Government Of Haryana)
overview:
The audit revealed significant operational and fund management deficiencies in the Transport Department, Haryana, over the period 2015-16 to 2019-20. Actual receipts declined from ₹1,254.01 crore to ₹1,105.77 crore, with the shortfall between budget estimates and actual receipts increasing from 14% to 45% during this period. Revenue from operations also dropped from ₹1,152.96 crore to ₹998.84 crore, and cumulative losses mounted from ₹3,767.02 crore to ₹6,762.29 crore, primarily due to declining vehicle productivity, underutilization of fleet, and high manpower costs.

Substantial funds were diverted: out of ₹32.02 crore received for specific schemes between 2008 and 2014, ₹21.97 crore was used for purposes other than intended by May 2019-June 2020. Moreover, there was delayed procurement and deployment of new buses; only 450 ordinary bus chassis, 150 mini-buses, and 18 super luxury buses were acquired against a target of 995, while 1,613 buses were scrapped. This led to a decreasing and ageing fleet, resulting in greater breakdowns and service interruptions.

Further, budget utilization for crucial components such as chassis purchase, major works, and machinery was poor, with 48% of allotted funds remaining unspent. Inefficiencies in fare policy, excess staff deployment, and inadequate internal controls in non-traffic receipts—as well as irregularities in Motor Vehicle Tax collection—worsened the Department's financial and operational health.

title: Performance Audit on Direct Benefit Transfer (Report No. 2 of the year 2022)
overview:
The CAG Performance Audit evaluates the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) mechanism in Haryana for social security pension schemes, covering nearly ₹37,736 crore transferred across 143.83 lakh beneficiaries in 2018-19 alone. The audit identified that only ₹16,695.71 crore out of ₹19,803.12 crore were successfully credited as per database status, with over ₹3,025.61 crore in ambiguous or untraced payment status, raising concerns over reconciliation and tracking (Page viii).

Critical systemic issues resulted in delays ranging from 1 to 963 days in beneficiary enrolment, violating Haryana Right to Service Act and compromising the schemes’ income support objectives. Payments totaling ₹98.96 crore were transferred to deceased beneficiaries’ accounts, revealing poor data validation and weak IT controls (Page viii).

Further observations included double payments, transfer to incorrect accounts, and disbursement of ₹64.13 crore to untraceable beneficiaries. The lack of audit trails and incomplete legacy data increased systemic vulnerability, risking pilferage and duplication. Recommendations focus on authentication, real-time monitoring, and rigorous recovery mechanisms (Pages vii–x, 13–14, 20–23).

title: Performance Audit on Exemptions to Charitable Trusts and Institutions, Union Government Department of Revenue - Direct Taxes
overview:
This performance audit examined the assessment process for exemptions granted to charitable trusts and institutions under the Income Tax Act, covering over 6.89 lakh entities from AY 2014-15 to 2017-18. A sample of 7,026 cases was scrutinized, with departmental records produced for 6,260 cases, while 766 records were not presented for audit. The audit identified 1,580 errors with a total tax effect of ₹1,983.34 crore, highlighting significant compliance, systemic, and procedural deficiencies.

One headline finding was that 91.4% of returns were processed in summary manner by the ITD, and only 3.7% of cases underwent scrutiny, which resulted in multiple instances of incorrect exemptions, lack of verification of registration, and the possibility of revenue leakage. Audit noted that exemptions totaling ₹1.31 lakh crore (50.8%) were granted to government entities and ₹1.27 lakh crore (49.2%) to private entities among high-value cases. In over 0.21 lakh cases, exemption was allowed without valid section 12AA registration.

Consequently, critical areas such as monitoring of income accumulation, identity of donors, registration verification, and application of income were found to be weak, resulting in significant risks of ineligible claims and potential revenue loss. Key recommendations include tighter monitoring, clarifying provisions, strengthening IT inputs and internal controls, and more detailed data capture and audit coverage. The audit further observed gaps in addressing previous CAG and PAC recommendations.

title: Performance Audit on Conservation of Coastal Ecosystems, Union Government (Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change)
overview:
The CAG performance audit examined institutional, regulatory, and project-level effectiveness in the conservation of India’s 7,516 km coastline—covering the period from 2015 to 2020. The report highlights India’s critical coastal resources and population pressures, noting, for example, that coastal regions support 13.36% of the country's population while providing for diverse and vulnerable ecosystems such as mangroves, coral reefs, estuaries, and turtle nesting sites. Despite Rs 6.23 crore spent on specific conservation and monitoring initiatives, multiple systemic, procedural, and monitoring failures were found.

There were persistent institutional weaknesses, such as NCZMA and SCZMA functioning as ad-hoc bodies lacking permanent members and even sufficient manpower (58 out of 73 posts vacant in Goa's SCZMA/DLCs), leading to critical regulatory gaps. The audit also found that nearly all coastal states failed to comply with mandatory management plan timelines, with delays in demarcating high tide lines and preparing Coastal Zone Management Plans (CZMPs). Said plans—crucial for environmental clearance—remained unapproved or outdated in several states into 2020, causing clearances to proceed on the basis of 1991 maps, in many cases not reflecting current conditions.

Further, project clearance processes were undermined by outdated or inadequate Environment Impact Assessments, lack of domain expertise on appraisal committees, non-compliance with monitoring requirements by project proponents, and weak enforcement of CRZ norms. As a result, critical conservation outcomes were compromised: for example, invasive species in the Gulf of Mannar coral reefs and prohibited construction in sand dunes were left unchecked. Only one coastal state, Gujarat, localized SDG-14 indicator frameworks below the state level, highlighting both implementation and planning gaps.

title: Performance Audit on Waste Management in Indian Railways, Union Government (Railways)
overview:
This Performance Audit evaluated the management, assessment, and disposal of waste across Indian Railways from 2015-16 to 2019-20, focusing on stations, coaching depots, workshops, production units, hospitals, and e-waste centers. Indian Railways operates over 720 major stations and generates approximately 670 tonnes per day (TPD) of solid waste, with budget allocations rising from ₹1,751 crore in 2016-17 to ₹2,796 crore in 2019-20, and ₹2,081 crore in 2020-21. While over 90% of allocated funds were utilised annually, the absence of dedicated fund allocation and lack of single authority resulted in significant gaps in the waste management mechanism. EnHM wings—the designated environment units—were not established in 11 divisions, and 59 stations had not complied with regulatory requirements for obtaining Consent to Establish (CTE) from State Pollution Control Boards as of July 2021.

Further, basic conditions for waste segregation were not met at 70% of audited stations, and there was incomplete compliance with National Green Tribunal orders requiring action plans based on 24 verifiable indicators at major stations. The audit also found that assessment of plastic waste was not done at 71 stations and 26 depots, and most stations lacked plastic-only bins. Storage, segregation, and disposal of hazardous, plastic, bio-medical, and e-waste were poorly tracked, posing significant environmental and health risks. Records show persistent non-compliance, delayed implementation, and weak monitoring mechanisms for waste management activities.

The consequences of these lapses are serious: poor waste handling can endanger public health, decrease environmental quality, and undermine flagship government initiatives like Swachh Bharat Abhiyan. The audit calls for immediate reforms, including exclusive funding, robust monitoring, and strict regulatory compliance to address the acute shortcomings in India's railway waste management systems.

title: Performance Audit on Assessment of Assessees of Gems and Jewellery Sector, Union Government Department of Revenue - Direct Taxes
overview:
India's Gems and Jewellery sector, contributing 6–7% of GDP and employing over 2.5 million, was subject to significant audit review due to risks of misuse, including money laundering and round tripping. The sector handles high-value transactions, making it prone to systemic risks and regulatory challenges, as highlighted by previous audits and ongoing enforcement investigations. For this audit, 2,593 out of a planned sample of 3,232 assessments completed from 2015-16 to 2018-19 were scrutinised, representing over ₹30,000 crore in transactions.

Key findings included irregular trends in imports/exports: 76% of diamond imports and 80% of exports concentrated in the UAE, Belgium, and Hong Kong, despite negligible mining in those regions; pearl imports between 2013-18 were 3-10 times above global production, indicating potential mis-invoicing and round-tripping. Assessment procedures were found lacking: deductions of ₹115.45 crore allowed under section 10AA despite export proceeds of ₹3,878.95 crore being outstanding for over six months, risking a ₹28.57 crore revenue loss. There was no standardised verification of inventory valuations, business codes, or related-party transactions, and the absence of guidelines for sector-specific scrutiny increased the risk of tax evasion and errors.

Systemic issues included mismatch in assessment data, inadequate mechanisms for validating share premium and application money, and inconsistent disallowance of bogus purchases. The lack of inter-departmental coordination and weak monitoring compounded the risks, particularly regarding large and suspicious transactions. The report concludes that high-value, high-risk practices continue to expose significant vulnerabilities, underlining the urgent need for regulatory and procedural reforms.

title: Performance Audit of Procurement and Supply of Drugs in CGHS of Union Government(Civil), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
overview:
This Performance Audit examined the efficiency, effectiveness, and integrity of the procurement and supply of drugs in the Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS). During 2016-17 to 2020-21, CGHS served 38.50 lakh beneficiaries across 74 cities with a medical procurement budget rising from ₹1,515 crore in 2016-17 to ₹3,435 crore in 2020-21. However, only ₹6,623 crore out of ₹12,534 crore budgeted funds were utilised for procurement, highlighting persistent shortfalls in fund and drug utilisation.

A critical gap was the delayed revision of the drug formulary, which was updated only once after a 7-year hiatus in February 2022; as a result, newer essential drugs were not included in procurement, impacting service quality. Of the 2030 drugs listed, rate contracts were finalised for only 220-641 drugs yearly, leading to severe shortages: wellness centres often had only 6 to 290 drugs available out of an annual requirement of 1169.

Heavy dependence on Authorised Local Chemists (ALC) resulted, with Delhi centres procuring up to 93.61% of drugs from ALCs at higher branded rates rather than generic. CGHS also faced persistent issues in supply delays, expired drug deliveries, and systemically weak quality assurance and monitoring processes. Meanwhile, large sums (₹484.66 crore) remained outstanding in payments from CGHS to drug depots, and claims amounting to ₹527.62 crore were pending for settlement.

title: Follow-up on the Performance Audit of Preservation and Conservation of Monuments and Antiquities of Union Government, Ministry of Culture
overview:
India possesses an immense archaeological heritage, with more than 4 lakh heritage structures and 58 lakh antiquities, primarily under the protection of Central and State authorities, museums, and religious bodies. The Ministry of Culture, via the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), is mandated to preserve national monuments, excavate historic sites, and manage artefact collections. Between 2013-14 and 2020-21, ASI expenditure on heritage protection moderately increased, but only 40% of its total budget was allocated to preservation tasks. PAC recommendations led to some reforms, but several fundamental gaps persist. Notably, ASI documentation remains incomplete, with only 1.84 lakh monuments and 16.83 lakh antiquities mapped, well below government targets. Over 31% of ASI staff positions were vacant, affecting field operations and museum management, and National Culture Fund utilisation stayed below 14% of corpus, reflecting weak inter-agency coordination.

Critical policy measures, including updated Act amendments and comprehensive museum procedures, remain incomplete after decades. The National Monument Authority has prepared heritage bye-laws for just 31 out of 3693 monuments, a severe lag in regulatory implementation. Joint field inspections exposed severe deficiencies: public amenities like toilets, water, ramps, and guides are often absent at many central monuments. Numerous heritage sites continue to suffer from encroachments and unsatisfactory conservation work. Museums under ASI face weak accession, verification, and display systems, with artefacts in storage conditions often below standard, raising concerns about artefact security and preservation.

Consequences of these deficiencies include continued risk of heritage erosion, unmanaged visitor impacts, and inefficient use of public funds. Despite promise of improvements, ASI’s follow-up actions on PAC and audit findings remain slow, leaving most recommendations pending. The Ministry/ASI has pledged further corrective steps, but holistic change is urgently required to safeguard India's cultural legacy and meet national and international standards.

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of 74th Constitutional Amendment Act in Chhattisgarh, Government of Chhattisgarh for the year ended 31 March 2020
overview:
This performance audit reviewed the implementation of the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act in Chhattisgarh, specifically the devolution of functions, funds, and functionaries to Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) for the period 2015-16 to 2019-20. Chhattisgarh has 169 ULBs, comprising 14 Nagar Nigams, 43 Nagar Palika Parishads, and 112 Nagar Panchayats, with a combined urban population of 59.37 lakh as per Census 2011 (page 1).

Significant deficiencies were observed in the institutional empowerment and financial devolution mandated by the amendment. Notably, elections in 15 ULBs were delayed by one year, and three ULBs remained under administrator-ship with no elected councils (page v). 10 test-checked ULBs lacked Advisory Committees, while Ward and Mohalla Committees were instituted in only one ULB out of 27 checked. The State Finance Commission (SFC) was constituted late and its recommendations implemented with delay, resulting in funds being devolved as per the outdated Second SFC even though the Fifth SFC was due (page vi).

Revenue mobilisation remained weak, with significant arrears in property tax and water tax collections. Only fixed water charges were levied from most connections, insufficient to cover operational costs, and only one ULB installed water meters (Korba). Acute staffing shortages persisted: ULBs could only appoint contractual staff, not permanent, as most powers were retained by the State Government (page vi). These gaps adversely affected service delivery, compliance with constitutional mandates, and the financial stability of ULBs.

title: Union Government (Ministry of Communications Department of Telecommunications), Performance Audit of Management of Spectrum assigned on the Administrative basis to Government Departments/ Agencies.
overview:
The CAG performance audit examined the management of spectrum administratively assigned to government departments and agencies, covering Rs 1.82 lakh crore worth of nationally critical radio frequencies. Major audit attention centred on ineffective spectrum utilization across ministries like Defence, Railways, Department of Space, and Home Affairs, with the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) failing to periodically review allocations or update pricing since 2012, despite annual revenue from spectrum amounting to thousands of crores.

The audit uncovered suboptimal and idle use of high-value spectrum bands—including 470–646 MHz, 700 MHz, 900 MHz, 1800 MHz, 2100 MHz, 2300–2400 MHz, 2500–2690 MHz and 3.3–3.6 GHz—where several agencies had not deployed networks for years after administrative assignment. For example, Railways commissioned equipment in just 57.9% of planned routes for the GSM-R system despite pan-India spectrum allocation, while Ministry of Information & Broadcasting’s 470–698 MHz was described as "very suboptimal due to obsolete technology".

Further, spectrum monitoring remains weak due to outdated databases, lack of a permanent policy framework, and under-resourced enforcement. Many agencies operated wireless services without valid licenses, risking interference and loss of public revenue. The audit concludes with high-severity risks and calls for urgent reforms: spectrum pricing overhaul, stricter oversight, and accelerated harmonization for commercial and 5G use—warning that continued inefficiencies could cost the exchequer and public services dearly.

title: Performance Audit Report on Outcomes of Surface Irrigation Projects in Bihar, Government of Bihar
overview:
This Performance Audit covers the period 2015-21, focusing on five major and medium surface irrigation projects in Bihar, including the Extension, Renovation, and Modernization (ERM) of the Eastern Gandak Canal System (EGCS). Despite a project expenditure of ₹723 crore for EGCS, audit findings reveal that out of a targeted 39.80 lakh hectares for irrigation during the review period, only 28.09 lakh hectares were reportedly covered (71%), but actual possible irrigation based on water availability was only 11.85 lakh hectares (30%). The gap was primarily due to siltation, non-functional outlets, and poor maintenance.

Agricultural production attributable to the project ranged from just 11% to 76% of envisaged output, with post-project cropping patterns often diverging sharply from what was projected in the DPR. Notably, only 33% of field channels constructed were pucca (concrete), and functional coverage dropped to less than 2% of the command area. Participatory Irrigation Management was ineffective, with most Water User Associations either non-existent or non-functional.

Serious fund mismanagement was detected, including instances of double payments (₹1.93 crore), excess payments (₹14.57 crore), contractual failures causing direct loss (₹15.66 crore), and improper liquidation of guarantees. Revenue realization for water charges was also abysmal—out of a possible ₹111.38 crore, only ₹1.73 crore was collected. Acute shortages of technical staff (46-83%) further impaired planning, execution, and monitoring of the projects.

title: Performance Audit Report on Outcomes of Higher Education in Punjab, Government of Punjab
overview: The Performance Audit covers April 2015 to March 2020, examining higher education delivery in Punjab, including fund utilisation, access, equity, quality, and governance across 32 universities and 1079 colleges. Despite a 45% increase in Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) from 2010-11 to 2019-20, Punjab's GER ranking improved only marginally (from 19th to 18th) nationwide (page 2). Regional imbalances persist: seven sub-divisions lack any government, constituent, or aided college; only 32.56% to 34.78% of government colleges operate in rural areas meant to serve 62.52% of the target 18–23 age population (pages vii, 12-18). Infrastructure gaps are evident: twelve of 27 planned colleges' construction was incomplete due to lack of funds, causing overcrowding in hostels (PU Patiala: 12.63% over capacity; GNDU Amritsar: 18.16% students deprived) and poor facilities for differently abled students (pages viii, 23-27). Faculty shortages plague colleges, with an average Student-Teacher Ratio of 49:1—more than twice the prescribed 20:1—and up to 70% contractual staff in government colleges (pages ix, 33-49). Only 30.23% of eligible colleges are NAAC accredited, with a mere 1.74% graded A++/A+ statewide (page x, 79-81). Lack of job placement, career counseling, and alumni outreach undermines employability and career progression outcomes. Substantial vacancies (27.94%-54.35% in universities; 48% in government colleges) in non-teaching staff further hinder administration (page xi, 81-82). The audit concludes the state is far from ready for NEP-2020 implementation, risking key objectives, and urges coordinated reforms.

title: Performance Audit Report on Direct Benefit Transfer, Government of Punjab
overview:
This performance audit reviews the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) implementation in Punjab for the period April 2017 to July 2020, covering Rs 14,432.79 crore transferred through 94 schemes across 13 departments. Of this, 60% of the amount was transferred under just 18 schemes in the Department of Social Security and Women and Child Development. The audit finds only partial process re-engineering: more than three years after the government's decision (March 2017), only one intermediary level (Gram Panchayat) was removed, with transfer still not fully direct to beneficiary accounts, contrary to central guidelines.

Serious data validation issues were identified: 8,256 duplicate records were weeded out, yet Rs 9.89 crore in excess payments was not recovered. There were 941 duplicate/ineligible records, paying a further Rs 1.82 crore in error, and Rs 0.72 crore paid to 651 children above eligibility. Likewise, 213 beneficiaries received aid under two schemes (OAP, FAWDW) violating rules, resulting in Rs 0.37 crore excess payment. Meanwhile, Rs 277.96 crore in financial assistance was denied in the three selected schemes during the period; 8,371 cases experienced payment delays up to 1,432 days beyond the 30-day norm.

Organisational gaps are severe: the State Advisory Board for DBT Cell never met during the audit period, essential technical and governance layers were not fully constituted, and no recovery mechanism is in place for excess payments. Portal management lacks quality checks and reconciliation, with unresolved data mismatches up to Rs 4,555.58 crore between DBT Portal and department records. There is still no disaster recovery or password policy for the State DBT Portal.

title: Audit Report on Performance Audit of Surface Irrigation for the year ended March 2020, Government of Odisha
overview:
The Performance Audit of Surface Irrigation in Odisha examined project implementation and financial management between 2014-2020. Odisha’s Department of Water Resources (DoWR) was allotted ₹30,366.51 crore for surface irrigation, of which only ₹25,153.35 crore (83%) was utilised; a significant ₹842.98 crore (14%) was surrendered due to delays in land acquisition, forest clearances and site readiness. Cost escalation in major projects ranged from 182% to an alarming 4,596%, with only one major project (UIIP extension) completed and four others remaining ongoing as of March 2021.

Despite incurring ₹12,742.11 crore across test checked projects, irrigation potential achieved was just 1,22,418 ha against a proposed 5,02,842 ha (24% achievement). Delays in completion ranged up to 43 years and financial irregularities included non-receipt of central assistance (₹311.60 crore), non-remittance of revenue (₹66.94 crore), parking funds in bank accounts (₹334.64 crore), and inadmissible payment of GST (₹10.23 crore). Audit also found incomplete land acquisition, deficient works management, and lack of stakeholder coordination lead to substantial shortfall in ayacut and risks to economic viability.

Defective DPR preparation, monitoring failures, and non-clearance of forest land led to deprival of intended benefits for farmers, with only paddy cropping practiced instead of proposed multi-cropping. Stakeholders did not provide adequate handholding, with only ₹70.93 crore of ₹282.93 crore deposited for afforestation actually utilised. Overall, the audit reveals persistent weaknesses and underscores the need for strategic, timely action by government departments.

title: Performance Audit of Efficacy of Implementation of 74th Constitutional Amendment Act
overview:
This performance audit examined whether the Government of Haryana empowered Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) in line with the intent of the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act. Covering 2015-16 to 2019-20, the audit sampled 15 ULBs across all tiers and found significant delays in implementation, ineffective transfer of functions, and lack of autonomy for ULBs. For example, only 4 out of 18 functions have been fully devolved to ULBs, with significant overlaps and limited jurisdiction, while 5 functions remain under other departments (page 9).

The audit found ULBs heavily dependent on fiscal transfers (50.22% of total revenue). There was a short release of ₹102.53 crore of basic grants from GoI due to delayed formation of elected bodies, and ULBs forgone ₹14.64 crore in property tax rebates in 2019-20 (page ix). Significant vacancies persisted (21.79% to 93.54%) in crucial technical posts, directly hampering service delivery.

Further, flawed budget exercises and insufficient technical autonomy resulted in unrealistic budgeting and low fund utilization (average 57%). Delays in elections, ward delimitation (50 municipalities, delayed 7–29 months), and only 226 house meetings against 710 stipulated undermined local democracy (page vii-viii). The audit recommends critical changes to institutional rules, fiscal practices, and human resource policies to achieve the decentralisation envisioned by the 74th CAA.

title: Performance Audit Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Implementation of 74th Constitutional Amendment Act for the year ended 31 March 2021
overview:
This audit report critically examines the implementation status of the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act in Uttarakhand for the five-year period ending 31 March 2021. Financial devolution to Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) remained suboptimal, with only 47 per cent of the recommended grant being actually transferred between 2018-23, amounting to significant unutilised allocations.

The audit also recorded considerable delays in conducting ULB elections. Statutory committees—like the Ward Committees and District Planning Committees—were either not constituted or non-functional in most cities, undermining decentralised governance.

These governance lapses contributed directly to impaired service delivery, with crucial urban schemes facing interruptions. The non-utilisation and delayed release of funds hindered urban infrastructure expansion, impacting more than 60% of eligible urban residents. The report concludes with a high severity rating due to persistent fund underutilisation, weakened urban planning mechanisms, and non-compliance with mandatory provisions.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Performance Audit of Select District Hospitals in Manipur for the year ended 31 March 2019 (2018-19) Government of Manipur
overview:
The Performance Audit of Select District Hospitals in Manipur covers patient care at secondary and tertiary care levels for the period 2014-19. The Health and Family Welfare Department received a budget allotment of ₹3,282.62 crore, representing 4.8% of the overall State Budget, but only spent ₹2,740.71 crore (4.7%). This is well below the National Health Policy benchmark of 8% for health sector allocation. Savings ranged from ₹46.46 crore (7%) in 2014-15 to ₹197.50 crore (29%) in 2016-17 and ₹159.68 crore (20.63%) in 2018-19, indicating consistent underutilisation of allocated funds.

There was a critical shortage of healthcare infrastructure, with 255 vacant doctor posts out of 355 sanctioned in seven District Hospitals, and an overall shortfall of 72 nurses (27.17%). The State also had a deficit of 150 Sub-Centres and 71 Community Health Centres, comprising shortfalls of 26.27% and 29.17% respectively. Essential equipment and drugs were often missing, with drugs procurement receiving only 3% of revenue expenditure and equipment just 1%, far below recommended levels.

Delivery of healthcare services was compromised. For example, OPD registration counter patient load was nearly double the prescribed norm, basic facilities were lacking, and diagnostic services were missing in many hospitals. Additionally, gaps were found in maternal and child health, cancer care, and HIV/AIDS treatment, including mismatches in data reporting and irregular drug supplies to ART centres. The overall conclusion highlights the urgent need for improved fund utilisation, human resource incentives, infrastructure upgrades, and rigorous monitoring in Manipur’s public health sector.

title: Performance Audit Report on Integrated Financial Management System - Khajane-II, Government of Karnataka.
overview:
The audit assessed the implementation of Khajane-II (K2), an Integrated Financial Management System meant to enhance transparency and accountability in Karnataka’s financial administration. The Performance Audit covered the period from 2014-15 to 2020-21 and scrutinized critical aspects such as project management, compliance with timelines, contract and financial management, security, and effectiveness of monitoring and evaluation mechanisms.

The report found significant lapses: project milestones were repeatedly missed, resulting in delays. Several modules envisaged in Stage-II were not operational till at least March 2021, and declaration of 'Go-live' was not possible due to incomplete roll-out. The Operation & Maintenance phase commenced without fulfilling contract conditions, leading to an additional financial commitment of ₹38.75 crore and loss of at least two years of O&M utility by the Department [Executive Summary, pg vii; Ch. II §2.6.5, p. 17].

Crucial failures included lack of business process reengineering, non-revision of Financial Codes, limited capability for Government Accounting Standards, and inadequate integration with stakeholders. These issues compromise transparency, timely accounting, and real-time budget control—undermining public finance management and the realization of Government’s stated objectives for K2. Risks to control and data integrity were also increased due to delay in securing the application’s source code and documentation [Executive Summary, pg vii-x].

title: Report No. 3 of the year 2021 - Performance Audit on Outcomes in Higher Education in the State for the period 2014-2019, Government of Odisha
overview:
The Performance Audit examines outcomes in higher education across Odisha between 2014 and 2019, focusing on employability, research, governance, and equity. Out of nine general stream State Universities, Utkal University and North Odisha University (22%) were selected along with 32 out of 299 affiliated colleges for detailed scrutiny. The findings reveal critical gaps in data management, placement support, and infrastructure: only 26.10% of UU students and 3.79% of NOU students secured placements, with placement cells either underfunctioning or absent.

Curriculum revision lagged, with 15 out of 18 subjects not updated, and only a quarter of courses in NOU focused on employability, while no value-added courses were introduced. ICT-enabled classrooms ranged from 8% to 58%, faculty vacancies persisted at 38% (UU) and 34% (NOU), and Student-Teacher Ratio norms (20:1) were not met. Research completion rates at UU were just 16%, with zero patents and industry MoUs at both universities.

College density stagnated at 23, with 19 blocks lacking any HEI; 12% of govt colleges were rural. Only 8 test-checked colleges had ramps, but none offered Braille, sign language, or accessible websites. Only 20.50% of colleges were NAAC-accredited; just 8 of 181 had ‘A’ grade. Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) rose slightly by 4.4, remaining well below the national average, and GER for SC/ST groups lagged further (22.1).

title: Performance Audit on 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, Government of Punjab
overview:
This performance audit evaluated the efficacy of implementation of the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act (CAA) in Punjab, covering 167 Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) from 2015 to 2020. The report found that Fiscal transfers constituted only about 18% of ULB revenues for the period, far below adequate levels. Out of a mandated devolution of ₹3,287 crore, only ₹7 crore (0.21%) was actually released to ULBs during 2015–20. Punjab received ₹1,902.65 crore as Basic Grant and ₹200.15 crore as Performance Grant out of the Central Finance Commission's recommended ₹1,962.36 crore and ₹490.59 crore, resulting in a shortfall of ₹350.15 crore. There were major outstanding dues for property tax and service charges from various bodies, and user charges collected covered only 18% of O&M expenditure instead of 90% recommended.

Institutional empowerment was weak: functions actually devolved were few, with significant overlap, and Ward Committees or District Planning Committees were not constituted in any ULB. State Government retains overriding powers in rules, dissolution, and financial approvals, undermining ULB autonomy. Elections were delayed up to two years in 130 ULBs due to delayed delimitation, and ULBs had minimal control over staff with shortages ranging 29.08%–36.48%.

Consequences include severely hampered service delivery, poor financial viability, deficient staff capacity building (training for only 0.75% to 1.44% of staff), and failure to realise local self-governance, restricting ULBs’ effectiveness as foreseen in the 74th CAA.

title: Performance Audit Report on ‘Pre and Post Ujwal Discom Assurance Yojna in Punjab State Power Corporation Limited’ for the year ended 31 March 2020 - Government of Punjab
overview:
The Performance Audit assessed the implementation and outcomes of the Ujwal Discom Assurance Yojana (UDAY) Scheme in Punjab State Power Corporation Limited (PSPCL) over the period 2015-16 to 2019-20. The Government of Punjab (GoP) was required by the UDAY Scheme and Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to take over 75% of PSPCL’s debt, amounting to ₹15,628.26 crore, to be converted into a mix of grant and equity by 2019-20. Contrary to the MoU, the entire debt was converted to equity, breaching scheme provisions and impacting PSPCL's capital structure. Additionally, PSPCL was meant to convert ₹5,209.42 crore in remaining debt to bonds or loans at concessional rates, but neither bonds were issued nor concessional rates achieved, leading to excess interest payments of ₹261.09 crore during 2016-17 to 2019-20.

Outstanding government dues grew alarmingly, with departmental electricity dues rising from ₹524.78 crore in March 2016 to ₹2,183.49 crore in 2019-20. Similarly, subsidy arrears owed by GoP increased from ₹1,603.17 crore at the end of 2015-16 to ₹5,598.60 crore at the end of 2019-20. Tariff revision and fee recovery mechanisms were not adhered to as scheduled, resulting in substantial irrecoverable losses; PSPCL lost ₹85.08 crore in interest due to delayed Fuel Cost Adjustment (FCA) recoveries, and ₹45.44 crore due to delayed tariff orders from 2017-18 to 2020-21.

Operational targets under UDAY, such as reduction in AT&C losses to 14% by 2018-19, were missed comprehensively, with the number of divisions failing targets ranging from 52 to 62 annually and maximum losses ranging between 42.84% and 57.65%. Smart meter implementation proved almost nonexistent, with only 335 meters installed versus thousands required. Failure to segregate feeders and incomplete monitoring also resulted in financial and operational setbacks. Overall, PSPCL failed to achieve UDAY objectives, resulting in increased debt, subsidy arrears, operational inefficiencies, and loss to the exchequer.

title: Union Government (Civil) Ministry of Education, Performance Audit of Setting up of new Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs)
overview:
The performance audit evaluated the establishment of eight new IITs between 2008-09, covering the five-year period 2014-19 and a capital outlay escalated from ₹6,080 crore to ₹14,332 crore—a 135% increase due to infrastructure delays and cost overruns. Significant land acquisition issues persisted for four of the IITs, restricting the planned campus size and contributing to delays of up to 56 months in crucial construction.

Envisaged student intake for 2008-14 was 18,880 but only 6,224 (33%) could be enrolled, severely missing targets. Vacancies in faculty ranged from 5% to 36% in seven of the eight IITs, and shortfall in reserved category student intake went up to 75% for certain categories. These factors reduced educational and research opportunities and impacted student and faculty experience.

The report finds that ongoing dependence on government grants due to low internal receipts, faulty contract practices, delayed equipment procurement, and weak governing oversight have collectively undermined timely, cost-effective campus and academic development. The deficits directly impacted research outcomes, evident from low non-government research funding (as little as 0.35% of total projects), and further compounded the growth challenges for these premier institutions.

title: Performance Audit of Select District Hospitals in Mizoram for the year ended 31 March 2019
overview:
The performance audit covered the functioning, resources, and delivery of patient care at three district hospitals in Mizoram (Aizawl, Champhai, and Lawngtlai) between 2014-15 and 2018-19. The State's total health expenditure increased from ₹331.53 crore in 2014-15 to ₹576.85 crore in 2018-19, but at just 5.38% of total State expenditure, falling short of the 8% target under the National Health Policy 2017. Capital outlay constituted only 9.2% of the total, with most funds directed towards salaries.

Resource gaps were acute: essential drug shortages ranged from 50% to 81% in test-checked hospitals, specialist doctor posts went vacant—e.g., both Lawngtlai and Champhai lacked orthopaedics, radiology, and other critical specialists—and no hospital possessed the full set of essential equipment as per IPHS norms. Key diagnostics and high-dependency care services were also lacking.

Consequences included high neonatal mortality (up to 85.71% in Lawngtlai, 2018-19), rising cancer (cases grew from 1,581 in 2013 to 1,731 in 2017), more than doubling of HIV/AIDS cases over five years, and evidence of critical medicine stock-outs. Systemic weaknesses in procurement, HR policy, and essential record-keeping led to poor quality and accessibility of healthcare for Mizoram’s population.

title: Performance Audit of Select District Hospitals in Tripura, Government of Tripura
overview:
The Performance Audit of Select District Hospitals in Tripura reviewed health services at primary, secondary, and tertiary levels for the years 2014-2019. The audit revealed substantial under-utilisation of funds: average health sector budget allocation was 6.07%, while actual expenditure was 5.91%. Notably, in 2018-19, of ₹1,117.99 crore allocated (6.22% of total State budget), only ₹929.81 crore (6.66% of expenditure) was used, with annual savings ranging from ₹316.23 crore (33%) in 2015-16 to ₹188.18 crore (17%) in 2018-19.

There were acute resource shortages, including 53% shortfall in Medical Officers as per IPHS norms, and vacancies of 33% Medical Officers, 71% Dental Surgeons, and 46% paramedical staff relative to sanctioned strength. Essential equipment availability in two audited district hospitals was just 65-66%, and up to 91% of essential drugs were absent throughout the year. Patient service delivery suffered, with increased OPD cases per doctor, missing OPD facilities, and persistent stock-outs forcing patients to purchase medicines out of pocket. Maternal and child care indicators showed fluctuating trends, with only 62.6% pregnant women registering for ANC and declining tablets distribution.

Support services lagged with poor drug storage, deficient dietary and laundry services, non-functional fire safety measures, and open hospital waste disposal. Intensive care and trauma centre infrastructure remained underutilised, further burdening state-level hospitals. Serious gaps in cancer and AIDS programmes were identified, with low screening target achievement, poor IEC activities, and increasing HIV cases among non-high risk populations. Overall, the audit underscored critical gaps in resources, fund utilisation, and quality healthcare outcomes, with recommendations for urgent systemic reforms.

title: Union Government (Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology), Performance Audit on Functioning of Unique Identification Authority of India
overview:
The Performance Audit examined the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) from 2014-15 to 2018-19, with updated statistics through March 2021. UIDAI has generated over 129 crore Aadhaar numbers by the end of March 2021 and managed a budget of ₹613 crore in 2020-21, though actual expenditure was ₹892.67 crore due to carry forward of unspent balances from previous years. UIDAI earned ₹322.40 crore in revenue during that period.

However, significant system defects were identified: Over 4.75 lakh Aadhaars were cancelled in November 2019 due to duplication, with ongoing flaws in the de-duplication process. Of the 3.04 crore biometric updates in 2018-19, more than 73% were voluntary (fee-based) updates by residents correcting faulty biometrics, signaling poor initial data capture. The audit also highlighted excess and avoidable expenditure, such as ₹310 crore spent on Bal Aadhaars for children below five using parents’ biometrics, plus a further ₹288.11 crore in ICT assistance released to states and schools up to 2020-21 predominately for this purpose.

The absence of robust residency verification, lack of a data archival policy, failure to charge user entities for authentication services until March 2019, and ineffective redressal of grievances further compromised scheme efficiency. Additionally, UIDAI did not adequately penalize vendors or enforce quality parameters on service providers, resulting in financial and operational risks that require urgent systemic improvements.

title: Union Government (Civil) Ministry of Home Affairs, Performance Audit of Indo-Nepal Border Road Project
overview:
The Indo-Nepal Border Road Project (INBRP) was approved in November 2010 by the Government of India for the construction and upgradation of 1377 km of strategic border roads in Bihar (564 km), Uttar Pradesh (640 km), and Uttarakhand (173 km), at an estimated cost of ₹ 3853 crore. The timeline set for completion was five years from 2011-12 (i.e., March 2016), but delays in land acquisition and obtaining environment, forest, and wildlife clearances caused extensions up to December 2022.

From 2011 to 2020, only 27 DPRs covering 842.86 km (67% of the target) were approved. By March 2021, only 367.48 km (29%) of targeted roads had surfacing completed, and 81% of Border Out Posts (BOPs) remained unconnected to the main alignment, severely impacting troop mobility. Furthermore, ₹ 1709.17 crore was released but fund utilization was weak, as MHA released funds despite unutilised balances, resulting in blocked funds between 2013-16, inadmissible spending of ₹ 13.41 crore, and unrecovered advances totaling ₹ 136.60 crore.

Contract management was poor, with 408.98 km (49% of approved DPRs) experiencing stoppage of work due to encumbrances and land acquisition delays. Quality assurance was also neglected—mandated third-party inspections were not ensured, and in Uttar Pradesh shortfalls in sample testing ranged from 28-91%. These failures resulted in time and cost overruns, non-achievement of objectives, and strategic voids for border management.

title: Government of Tamil Nadu- Report No.8 of 2021 - Performance Audit on the Implementation of 74th Constitutional Amendement- Report for the year ended March 2020
overview:
The audit identified that the implementation of devolved functions under the 74th Constitutional Amendment in Tamil Nadu was partial and fragmented. As per the report, out of the 18 functions listed in the XII Schedule, only four had been fully devolved to Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), while the remaining functions continued to be managed by State line departments, thus undermining the Amendment's intent to empower ULBs (page 11).

Financial analysis revealed significant underutilisation of Central and State funds earmarked for municipal governance. Of the Rs 10,986.83 crore allocated to ULBs during 2015-20, nearly 53% remained unutilised as of March 2020, leading to suboptimal delivery of basic civic services (page 12). The audit further noted delays in fund release, diversion of grants, and weak accounting procedures at the ULB level.

As a result, there was poor service delivery in critical areas such as water supply, solid waste management, and urban planning. Citizens in 71% of the test-checked ULBs reported unsatisfactory access to municipal amenities, indicating the direct social consequences of poor fund usage and incomplete devolution (page 35).

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on ‘Performance Audit of Outcomes in Surface Irrigation in Rajasthan’ (Report No. 6 of the year 2021)
overview:
Rajasthan, with only 2% of India’s surface water but 10% of its land area and 5% of its population, faces severe water constraints. During 2014-15 to 2019-20 the audit examined outcomes of surface irrigation projects and found critical deficiencies: Only 31% of total gross irrigated area is serviced by surface irrigation, highlighting over-reliance on groundwater (69%). Rs 33.62 crore was incurred in avoidable land acquisition expenditure due to delays of 3 to 19 years, and cost overruns ranged from 2% to 3,536% with project delays up to 39 years. Of projects scrutinised, four failed to create any irrigation potential despite an investment of Rs 455.76 crore.

The audit found poor project planning (inaccurate pre-construction surveys, insufficient design) requiring mid-execution changes and large cost escalations. In two projects, water was released in excess, causing risk of waterlogging and salinity, while in five others actual irrigation water releases were far below design. Coordination between departments was absent—no formal mechanism existed for regular inter-agency monitoring, and critical usage data were not compiled. Surface irrigation targets for cropping pattern were largely unmet and only 65% of plantation targets were achieved.

Unauthorised canal water lifting, poor Water Users Associations (WUA) functioning, silted canals, dam seepages, and unaddressed defects further reduced beneficial outcomes. Data on groundwater, revenue before DPR, and project-specific crop yields were unavailable, making project-level assessment difficult. Many administrative lapses, including non-mutation of acquired land and delayed clearances, show systemic weaknesses. title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on ‘Performance Audit of Efficacy of implementation of 74th Constitutional Amendment Act’
overview:
The Performance Audit reviewed implementation of the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, focusing on the period 2015-16 to 2019-20. Statutory amendments to empower Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) were enacted, but not fully implemented; only 17% of ULB revenue came from their own sources, with significant reliance on state grants (₹17,059.77 crore disbursed) and notable fiscal transfer shortfalls (₹52.58 crore). Out of 18 functions mandated for ULBs, only two were fully devolved, four were handled as implementing agencies, while 11 overlapped with state departments and parastatals, affecting effective decentralization.

Key institutional mechanisms were weak; Ward Committees were not constituted, District Planning Committees did not prepare comprehensive development plans, and there was no Metropolitan Planning Committee. The State Government deducted ₹726.74 crore from SFC grants between 2017-20, diverting funds meant for ULBs, impacting their financial autonomy and resource mobilization.

Human resource constraints prevailed, as ULBs lacked full powers over recruitment and assessment of staff; only population criteria were used to determine staffing, resulting in up to 61% vacancies in critical posts. Poor budget planning, absence of reliable tax databases, and lack of surveys for potential revenue sources further crippled financial management and delivery of urban services.

title: Performance Audit of Select District Hospitals for the year ended 31 March 2019, Government of Assam.
overview:
This CAG performance audit reviews seven district hospitals and broad secondary-level health infrastructure in Assam over FY2014-15 to FY2018-19. The audit finds that the State's total health sector expenditure was ₹17,065 crore out of ₹2,70,636 crore (just 6%), with capital expenditure on infrastructure at only 3.95%. Health sector allocation ranged from 4.9% to 6.7% of the state budget, falling short of the National Health Policy’s 8% target. Alarmingly, the Department failed to utilize the full budget in every year, leaving between 22% (₹1,267 crore) and 40% (₹1,299 crore) unspent. The NHM also saw delays in State matching share and fund releases.

Crucial health resources showed systemic shortages: doctors by 15%, nurses by 6%, paramedics by 55% (against bed-based IPHS norms). If population-based norms are used, shortfall balloons to 45% for doctors, 50% nurses, and 74% paramedics. Of 4,274 equipment required, only 2,267 (53%) were available. Six newly created districts (as of 2016) lacked any District Hospital, and there was a state-wide shortage of 98 PHCs, 239 CHCs, and 3,234 sub-centres. Essential drug stockouts were persistent—up to 51 out of 65 key drugs were out of stock for 23 to 1,770 days at a time in test-checked hospitals.

Service delivery struggles included long wait times (often exceeding one hour for OPD), lack of ICU or Trauma Care at most hospitals, widespread deficiencies in infection control and bio-medical waste management, and high maternal and infant mortality rates—MMR at 229 versus the national average of 122. Patient satisfaction levels were middling, with 76% rating DH services as merely average.

title: Union Government, Performance Audit on Advance Authorisation Scheme (Department of Revenue – Indirect Taxes -Customs)
overview:
The Advance Authorisation Scheme (AAS) was designed to allow exporters duty-free imports of basic inputs, promoting exports by enabling procurement at international prices. Between 2015-16 and 2018-19, a total of 88,157 Advance Authorisations were issued by 38 Regional Authorities, covering CIF imports worth ₹7,58,141 crores. Audit examined a significant sample—4,048 authorisation files (4.96%), accounting for ₹2,08,126 crores (29.56%) of CIF imports. Notably, 405 AA files worth ₹9,906.73 crores from key regions like Mumbai, Ahmedabad, and Delhi were not produced for audit, despite repeated requests.

Key findings included systemic delays, with a backlog of unprocessed applications rising from 5,606 on 31 March 2019 to 6,044 by 31 March 2020, and delays in norm fixation stretching up to 16 years. Staff shortages and partial automation in the DGFT processes undermined both efficiency and oversight. The scheme exhibited significant risks of revenue loss and noncompliance, with revenue implications of ₹1,386.80 crore identified. Of this, recoveries accepted by authorities amounted to ₹1,291.93 crore, but only ₹0.70 crore was actually recovered by the time of reporting.

Audit observed weak inter-departmental coordination, ineffective online systems, absence of timely internal control measures, and inadequate monitoring of exporters and defaulters. Recommendations emphasize urgent system reforms, timely action, and better internal controls to reduce leakage, ensure accountability, and strengthen safeguards, given the scheme’s critical role in India’s export sector.

title: Performance Audit Report on “Land Acquisition and Allotment of Properties in NOIDA” in Uttar Pradesh
overview:
This performance audit reviews the process and propriety of land acquisition and property allotment in NOIDA over 2005-2018, covering an area of 1,237.58 lakh sqm acquired and 188.34 lakh sqm allotted for non-residential purposes. The report highlights that only 23% of developed land was allocated to industrial use, far below the Authority’s primary mandate. Conversely, residential allocations dominated, consuming 52% of land as of March 2020, with group housing plots alone making up 71.03 lakh sqm (37.72%) of total allotments.

Audit found severe governance and probity failures: ‘urgency’ clauses were improperly used in nearly 80% of land acquisitions, bypassing farmers' rights of objection despite overwhelming evidence that urgent industrial need did not exist. Administrative delays of up to 46 months in 'urgent' cases were common, and Supreme Court criticism on this front was unheeded. Allotments were rife with favoritism, violation of prescribed eligibility, arbitrary waivers, and even allocation to companies not yet incorporated, resulting in a huge backlog of incomplete projects and outstanding payments to NOIDA. Commercial activities were permitted on industrial use plots by manipulating regulations, causing loss to the exchequer.

NOIDA’s management and Board selectively diluted Master Plan regulations, creating loopholes for under-priced, discretionary assignments across property categories. Key internal controls, such as systematic internal audit, Board approval of terms, reconciliation of major payments, and oversight on sub-division, transfer, and mortgaging permissions, were either diluted or absent. The ethos of transparency and planned development was persistently undermined, seriously impacting both local farmers and thousands of home buyers.

title: Performance Audit Report No. 3 of 2021 on “Centralised Information Technology Billing System Being Operated by State Power Utilities” in Uttar Pradesh
overview:
Para 1: The Centralised Information Technology Billing System (CITBS) was implemented across 33 towns under the R-APDRP (Restructured Accelerated Power Development and Reforms Programme) in Uttar Pradesh, covering a total of 66,86,222 consumers. Out of these, only 41,80,837 consumers were mapped in the GIS system, indicating significant shortfalls in coverage. The audit found that substantial portions of the allocated funds, amounting to ₹189.75 crore, remained unutilised as of March 2020, resulting in delays and incomplete project outcomes (p. 5).

Para 2: Despite centralisation, the audit highlighted multiple deficiencies in system integration and functioning of the Meter Data Acquisition System (MDAS), GIS mapping, and Meter, Billing and Collection (MBC) modules. Poor consumer indexing and asset mapping led to inaccurate billing and misreporting of energy losses. The audit also observed cases where the Network Analysis Module failed to provide reliable load flow reports due to incomplete data inputs (p. 7).

Para 3: These failures had consequences such as persistent AT&C losses, unresolved billing disputes, and inaccurate energy auditing. Delayed project completion and shortfalls in intended coverage have undermined consumer trust and opportunities for more efficient utility operations. Persistent deficiencies in IT implementation contributed to inefficiencies and financial shortfalls within power utilities of Uttar Pradesh.

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Phase-III, Delhi Mass Rapid Transit System by DMRC, Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs
overview:
Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) implemented Phase-III of the Mass Rapid Transit System covering 160.75 km (107.27 elevated, 53.48 underground), with a sanctioned cost of ₹48,565.12 crore and actual expenditure of ₹45,468.89 crore as of March 2020. The audit covered 93 out of 259 contracts (valued above ₹5 crore), totaling ₹25,616 crore, amounting to a 36% contract coverage and 53% coverage by monetary value. The audit period spans April 2011 to March 2020.

A major finding was persistent underperformance in ridership: as against projected ridership of 20.89 lakh in 2019-20, actual was only 4.38 lakh—a shortfall of 79%. Across the network (Phase-I, II, III), projected ridership was 53.47 lakh but actual was 27.79 lakh (2019-20), only 51.97% of projections. Further, significant gaps were identified in contract and project management, such as advance payments beyond contractual provision (₹555.69 crore) and excess expenditure for station design and construction (e.g. extra ₹72.73 crore at Majlis Park).

Deficiencies in planning were noted, including no minimum Financial Internal Rate of Return for corridor approvals until 2013, lack of land acquisition for property development targets, and inadequate procedures for cost estimation and technology selection. On revenue, DMRC generated ₹657.13 crore (26.23%) from property development against a target of ₹2,505 crore (Phase-II & III), with 40,071 sqm property area remaining idle. Overall, the audit highlights critical lapses in planning, financial management, contract execution, project monitoring, and revenue realisation, resulting in substantial missed targets and operating inefficiency.

title: Government of Karnataka Report No.2 of the year 2021 - Performance Audit of Management of Storm Water in Bengaluru Urban area, Audit Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India
overview:
Bengaluru has experienced a rapid rise in urban flooding, with urbanization causing a loss of 1,258 water bodies since the early 1800s—dropping from 1,452 to just 194 by 2016 and reducing water storage capacity from 35 TMC to a mere 1.2 TMC (2016) due to siltation and encroachment (p. v). The audit tested records from BBMP, BDA, and BWSSB, revealing drastic lapses in stormwater management, including large-scale encroachment of lakes/drains, lack of interconnectivity, and failure to treat urban runoff as a water resource despite average annual rainfall of 969 mm (p. v).

Over 40% of properties failed to install mandatory rainwater harvesting structures, and BBMP did not maintain a comprehensive inventory of drains—hampering planning, buffer zone enforcement, and maintenance, with the result that utility lines often obstruct stormwater flow (p. vi). Works were incomplete or abandoned, leading to a loss of ₹83.59 crore in central assistance under JnNURM and improper payments made totaling ₹35.31 crore to contractors, with financial controls described as weak due to missing records such as completion plans and grants register (p. vii).

Frequent flooding, sewage discharge (780 MLD) into stormwater drains, partial removal of 714 out of 2,626 encroachments, and no boundary markings or inspection regime were cited (pp. v-vii). The audit concludes that deficiencies in planning, coordination, and documentation led to environmental, public health, and financial risks. The report recommends urgent policy and management reform to address persistent flooding, ground water depletion, and systemic governance failures.

title: Government of Rajasthan Report No. 1 of 2021- Performance Audit of Outcomes of Higher Education, Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the period 2014-2019
overview:
The Performance Audit assessed outcomes of higher education in Rajasthan, covering three state universities (UoR Jaipur, JNVU Jodhpur, GGTU Banswara) and 69 constituent/affiliated government and private colleges for 2014-2019. The audit focused on student employability, academic quality, access, and governance. Rajasthan's Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) ranking for higher education dropped from 20 (2010-11) to 23 (2018-19), with state run HEIs not featuring in the top 100 in India (NIRF 2019).

Job facilitating mechanisms were dysfunctional or non-existent; employability programmes were not organised in 99% of test-checked HEIs and none of the students undertook internships or field projects in 2018-19. Over 77% of students graduated below first division/grade B*, indicating weak academic outcomes. Feedback was not collected before curriculum design. Choice Based Credit System (CBCS) and semester system implementation was limited—mainly in select postgraduate programmes—restricting academic flexibility. ICT infrastructure and teaching tool adoption was found inadequate in multiple institutions.

Faculty quality was a major concern: 45.71% teachers in 19 out of 30 test-checked private colleges lacked necessary NET qualification. Professional development was irregular and insufficient. No test-checked HEI had revised curriculum since establishment (GGTU, since 2012) or in the last decade. Consequently, the state's higher education system failed to deliver expected employability, academic quality, and social contribution [Executive Summary p. vii; Chapter VI p. 95; Chapter II p. 12; Appendices p. 102].

title: Report No. 3 of 2020 - Performance Audit of Select District Hospitals in Nagaland for the year ended 31 March 2019
overview:
This report covers a performance audit of select district hospitals in Nagaland for the period 2014-15 to 2018-19. The audit assessed the adequacy and quality of health care services, focusing on financial resources, infrastructure, human resources, drugs and equipment, and delivery of critical medical services. The total expenditure on health during the five-year period amounted to ₹2,649.93 crore, with revenue expenditure comprising 94.10% and capital outlay only 5.90%. Notably, the Department failed to utilize allocated funds, with savings ranging from ₹103 crore (19.77%) in 2014-15 to ₹166.07 crore (20.82%) in 2018-19.

Nearly 61% of required positions for doctors in test-checked hospitals were vacant, and only 19% of essential equipment was available in the main referral hospital. Blood Banks, critical for emergency care, were non-functional in three of four test-checked hospitals, and only 33% of essential drugs were available in sub-centres. Emergency services, fire safety, infection control, and ambulance services showed severe deficiencies, posing risks to patient care and safety.

The consequences included insufficient service delivery, additional burdens on patients, and ineffective implementation of national health programs. The audit highlights the need for significant enhancements in budget allocation, fund utilization, infrastructure, staff deployment, and compliance with safety and quality standards.

title: Performance Audit of Select District Hospitals in Meghalaya
overview:
The Performance Audit covers select district hospitals and primary health units in Meghalaya for 2014-19, examining fund management, resources, and delivery of patient services. The Health and Family Welfare Department spent only 7.51% of the state budget on health, consistently below the 8% national target until FY 2018-19, with unspent funds ranging from ₹41.56 crore to ₹172.24 crore in various years, indicating ineffective fund utilization (see Table 2.1, p. 7).

Critical shortages were observed across manpower and essential resources: 24% shortage of doctors state-wide, and up to 65% shortfall in certain test-checked hospitals. There were also persistent deficits of 54% in Sub-Centres (SCs), 24% in Primary Health Centres (PHCs), and 23% in Community Health Centres (CHCs), leading to underserved populations in multiple districts (p. viii-ix).

Other severe gaps included a lack of fully functional blood banks in most hospitals, non-availability of critical equipment, and frequent drug stock-outs—up to 53% of 60 audited essential drugs were never supplied. These failures not only force patients to out-of-pocket payments but undermine the state's free drugs policy. There were also deficiencies in support services like cleaning, waste management, and infection control, directly impacting patient safety and quality of care (p. x-xiii).
