title: Performance Audit on Assessment of Co-operative Societies and Co-operative Banks, Union Government Department of Revenue - Direct Taxes
overview:
This performance audit examines the assessment of Co-operative Societies and Co-operative Banks by the Income Tax Department (ITD) between FY 2014-15 and 2018-19. Covering 8,470 audited cases out of an initial 9,282 samples from 1,726 Assessment Charges, the audit reveals substantial gaps in tax net coverage. It was found that 39.84% growth in Co-operative Societies (from 610,900 in 2009-10 to 854,300 in 2016-17) was not matched by ITD records, indicating many entities remain outside the tax net. Significant discrepancies emerged between ITD and registrar data, with a higher number of societies and banks recorded by State authorities than ITD, implying under-reporting and risks of tax evasion.

There was inadequate verification of registration status, leading to the irregular allowance of deduction benefits to entities not registered or not eligible. In 649 cases, non-compliance with deduction provisions under sections 36(1)(viia), 36(1)(viii), 36(1)(xvii), and various sections of 80P amounted to a tax effect of ₹694.50 crore. Furthermore, the audit identified mismatches between data provided by DGIT(Systems) and assessment records, reflecting weak data controls and undermining assessment reliability. Irregularities in computation of taxes, allowance of inadmissible deductions and non-deduction of TDS led to a massive tax effect of ₹12,328.40 crore across 858 cases.

Overall, the audit concludes that ITD lacks robust mechanisms for mapping, tracking, and enforcing compliance in the Co-operative Sector. The audit period revealed inadequate action against non-filers, weak scrutiny of large deductions, and significant weaknesses in reconciliation of claims vs payments. The findings underscore the need for systemic reforms, stricter monitoring, and improved data sharing between ITD and regulatory bodies for better tax base coverage and compliance.

title: Performance Audit on National Pension System, Union Government
overview:
The Performance Audit examined the implementation of the National Pension System (NPS) introduced on 1 January 2004 for Central Government employees, excluding Armed Forces, and later extended to State Governments and Autonomous Bodies. By 30 April 2018, there were 58.01 lakh Government sector subscribers, including 17.58 lakh from Central Government and 31.63 lakh from States. The audit found pending finalisation of rules on service conditions for NPS employees even after 15 years, and lack of regulatory clarity hampered effective implementation. In the Central sector, `5.20 crore and in the States, `793.04 crore of contributions were not remitted to the Trustee Bank as required, raising critical concerns for subscribers' financial security.

Audit identified persistent operational delays: more than 19,000 DDOs and over 4,700 PAOs were involved, yet there was no guarantee that 100% of eligible government employees had been registered or contributed in time. The legacy contributions process was neither tracked nor enforced, with PFRDA unaware of the total amounts pending transfer. Furthermore, the lack of employee choice regarding pension funds and delayed provision of options until 2019 impacted long-term pension returns.

The Audit concluded the NPS regulatory, record-keeping, and monitoring systems suffer from major gaps resulting in delayed registration, fund deduction and remittance. With approximately 4,130 cases in Central Government Civil Ministries alone, `139.95 crore of accumulations remained uncleared after employees received 'additional relief' benefits, exposing the system to double payments and accountability lapses.

title: Performance Audit of Manpower and Logistics Management in Delhi Police
overview:
The performance audit of Delhi Police covering 2013-14 to 2018-19 uncovered serious deficiencies in manpower and logistics management. The sanctioned strength as on 1st April 2019 was 89,670, against which the actual strength was only 79,621, reflecting a persistent vacancy rate above 11%. During this period, the budget allocation for Delhi Police grew steadily, with 2018-19 allocation reaching ₹7,859.81 crore, but chronic shortages persisted in human resources, vehicles, weapons, and basic infrastructure at police stations. Notably, recruitment delays meant only a single major round for 7,307 constables was completed in six years.

The report observed a 275% increase in IPC crimes in Delhi between 2013 and 2019, with significant spikes in "Other Theft" and "Motor Vehicle Theft" cases. Despite having a higher number of police personnel per lakh population compared to other states, deployment was skewed and failed to address shortages both in field postings and specialized units. Only 1 out of 72 sampled police stations met the Bureau of Police Research and Development (BPR&D) staffing norms, and average duty stretches of 12–15 hours per day led to high stress and compromised policing quality.

Compounding these issues, critical infrastructure such as barracks, mess halls, vehicles, bulletproof jackets, and communication equipment remained inadequate. Technological initiatives such as the Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems (CCTNS) suffered from data quality and cybersecurity gaps, while citizen-facing applications saw poor adoption despite significant investments. The audit concluded that manpower and logistics constraints severely undermined the Delhi Police's ability to maintain law and order, efficiently investigate crimes, and deliver public safety services.

title: Performance Audit on Search and Seizure Assessments in Income Tax Department, Union Government, Department of Revenue - Direct Taxes
overview:
This performance audit examined search and seizure assessments in the Income Tax Department covering the period 2014-15 to 2017-18. A total sample of 185 Groups was drawn from 1417 Groups, checking 24,869 assessment records and assessed income of ₹1,71,503.78 crore. Audit issued 1659 observations with a cumulative tax effect of ₹4,150.02 crore—pointing to systemic deficiencies, non-compliance, non-centralisation of search assessees, and inconsistent application of rules. The audit found major loopholes, including the absence of specific provisions against setting off losses from regular assessments against undisclosed income, and lack of time limits for issuing notices under section 153A/153C.

A headline finding was the high unsustainability rate of additions: 76.5% of additions made during search assessments were not sustained at appellate levels (CIT(A)/ITAT), suggesting significant quality issues in initial assessments. The audit also identified non-compliance with CBDT instructions, delays in handing over seized materials (ranging from one to fourteen months), and failure to centralise all related cases, which jeopardised coordinated investigation and holistic assessment of groups.

The consequences include potential revenue leakage, inconsistent penalties, and arbitrary handling of search cases, with non-levy of penalty, irregular adoption of figures, and procedural lapses leading to assessed tax loss. The report calls for urgent systemic corrections, stronger monitoring, and improved coordination to address these persistent weaknesses.

title: Performance Audit on MEIS and SEIS Union Government (Department of Revenue Indirect Taxes-Customs)
overview:
The Performance Audit on the Merchandise Exports from India Scheme (MEIS) and Service Exports from India Scheme (SEIS) analyzed pan-India data covering transactions from April 2015 to October 2018. During the period, 5,94,653 scrips—valued at ₹76,416 crore—were issued by 38 Regional Authorities and nine SEZ Development Commissioners. The audit selected 25 RAs and 7 DCs, covering 553,726 scrips worth ₹72,743 crore. A sample of 6,205 scrips (₹1.7% of total) was examined in detail.

The audit found systemic deficiencies in automation and continued dependence on manual interventions, resulting in substantial delays and risks. Audit paragraphs with a revenue implication of ₹364.32 crore were reported, out of which ₹233.02 crore was accepted by the department, and ₹7.82 crore recovered. There were deficiencies such as incorrect calculation of scrip values, weak integration with base systems, incomplete risk management, and excess claims. Notably, “MEIS registered growth under all sections of custom tariff,” with scrip claims rising from ₹19,031 crore in 2014-15 to ₹44,305 crore in 2018-19, yet nearly 70% of handicraft exports and 40% of handloom exports went unrewarded even after rate enhancements.

Findings include the system’s inability to prevent rewards on ineligible exports, overdue corrections, and lack of uniform processing guidelines at the field level. Recommendations call for full automation, a unified checklist, improved risk controls and accountability in classification, and a midterm evaluation for policy objectives.

title: Performance Audit on Assessment and Utilisation of Locomotives & Production and Maintenance of LHB Coaches in Indian Railways
overview:
This performance audit covers the assessment, procurement, and utilisation of locomotives, as well as the production and maintenance of LHB coaches, in Indian Railways for the period ending March 2018. As of 31 March 2018, Indian Railways operated with a fleet of 11,764 locomotives, supporting 13,452 passenger and 9,141 goods trains daily over a network of 68,442 route kilometers. The total expenditure on locomotive production during 2012-18 was ₹52,198.21 crore, of which 85% (₹44,254.92 crore) was sourced from Extra Budgetary Resources.

Significant deficiencies were identified in the loco requirement assessment and production planning process. The main criteria for determining loco needs were past production figures instead of empirical demand, resulting in surplus diesel locomotives and underutilization, as shown by declining Net Tonne Kilometers (NTKM) per loco (down by 11.6% to 22.4% for diesel and 17% to 27.2% for electric locos between 2012-13 and 2017-18). Audit found delays in infrastructure projects for electric loco production; for example, while DLW’s diesel expansion was completed quickly, augmentation works at CLW and ELAAU for electric locomotives lagged, causing capacity shortfall and maintenance bottlenecks.

For LHB coaches, although the High Level Safety Review Committee recommended in February 2012 to switch entirely to LHB design, only 30% of new coaches produced from 2013-18 were LHB. The Modern Coach Factory (MCF) operated at just 37% capacity, and out-of-phase rakes conversion as well as outdated ICF coaches (at least 6,868 needing replacement in five years) pose ongoing operational and safety risks. Maintenance infrastructure for both locos and LHB coaches was found lacking in multiple depots, leading to widespread unscheduled repairs and delays.

Accelerate production of LHB coaches and phase out ICF coaches to enhance passenger safety and operational efficiency.

title: Performance audit of Implementation of 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, Government of Karnataka
overview:
The CAG performance audit examined the implementation of the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act across 280 Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) in Karnataka for the period 2014-2019. The 74th Amendment intended to empower ULBs through devolution of 18 municipal functions, robust institutional mechanisms, and transfer of fiscal and human resources. While 17 functions were formally devolved under State law, overlaps persisted: ULBs fully controlled only 3 functions, had no role in 2, and for 8 functions had minimal or overlapping jurisdiction. Parastatals often eroded ULB autonomy in critical areas such as urban planning, slum improvement, and water supply.

Financial devolution was inadequate. ULBs remained heavily dependent on fiscal transfers, which comprised about 63% of their revenue. Actual transfers fell short by ₹15,564 crore compared to State Finance Commission (SFC) recommendations for 2014-19, and grants of ₹295.20 crore for 2018-19 were pending as of audit. Own revenue constituted just 37%; limitations in State law and lack of systematic revision of tax rates further suppressed ULB fiscal capacity. Budget exercises were often flawed, with an average fund utilisation of 69% across ULBs.

Human resources remained critically insufficient. Staff recruitment and deployment powers were retained by the state government, and sanctioned strength per 1,000 population dropped from 2.24–5.80 (2001) to 1.94–5.38 (2011) in test-checked ULBs. Technical posts faced large vacancies; executive functions were often discharged by non-KMAS officers, undermining statutory accountability. Lack of empowered Ward Committees and improperly functioning District Planning Committees further weakened decentralisation and participation.

Implement State Finance Commission recommendations in full, with timely fiscal transfers.
Remove limitations on ULB revenue generation, especially property tax, advertisement tax, and SWM cess.
Delegate manpower powers to ULBs for staff assessment and recruitment, ensuring technical capacity.

title: Performance Audit of Select District Hospitals in Arunachal Pradesh for the year ended 31 March 2019.
overview:
The audit of select district hospitals in Arunachal Pradesh revealed significant underfunding and underutilisation across the healthcare sector. For the period 2014-2019, state health expenditure ranged from 4.42% to 6.44% of total state spend, consistently below the National Health Policy target of 8%. Notably, savings against health allocation reached as high as 37% in 2018-19, indicating systemic issues in fund absorption, with specific years showing ₹77.93 crore (2014-15) and ₹658.74 crore (2018-19) unutilised.

District Hospitals suffered from shortages in doctors (up to 40% state-wide, 59% at Seppa), nurses (15% overall shortfall), and paramedical staff (up to 67% deficit at Seppa), directly impacting service quality and access. Only 13 of 25 districts have functional District Hospitals, leaving nearly half the populace without timely access to secondary healthcare facilities.

Critical gaps were noted in physical infrastructure, diagnostic services, operational facilities, and emergency care: only two of five sampled hospitals had cancer screening; trauma, ICU, and many specialist services were unavailable. This resulted in avoidable patient referrals, delayed care, and higher costs for families. Inadequacies in maternal and child health services were reflected in the rising IMR, exceeding national averages after 2016. The lack of equipment and drugs as per IPHS was pervasive, with capital expenditure making up a mere 4% of health spend.

title: Performance Audit of Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY), covering the period from the scheme’s inception in May 2016 to March 2019, evaluated the effectiveness, financial management, and intended reach of the initiative, designed to provide LPG connections to women from Below Poverty Line (BPL) households. As of 31 March 2019, 7.19 crore LPG connections were issued by Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs), reaching approximately 90% of the revised target of 8 crore connections, with 3.81 crore under PMUY and 3.38 crore under E-PMUY expansions. Over ₹4,192.79 crore in interest-free loans were extended, but only ₹1,575.72 crore had been recovered, leaving ₹2,617.07 crore outstanding by December 2018.

Significant systemic lapses were detected in beneficiary identification—1.60 crore connections (42%) were issued using only the beneficiary’s Aadhaar, defeating intended de-duplication measures; 4.10 lakh connections were issued against incomplete SECC-2011 data; 1.88 lakh connections were provided to men, and over 9 lakh connections to minors, bypassing core eligibility criteria. Delays in installation and distribution infrastructure hindered service, with 4.35 lakh connections installed late and only 0.24% of households receiving smaller, more affordable cylinders, despite recommendations to widen adoption among the poorest families.

The audit also found low LPG refill uptake among BPL households, indicating insufficient transition from traditional fuels—annual average refill for PMUY households was only 3.21 per annum by end 2018. Cases of potential diversion and over-consumption were revealed, including nearly 14 lakh beneficiaries consuming 3 to 41 refills monthly. Budgetary allocations did not match revised targets, leading to delayed fund settlement and idle CSR funds worth ₹261.85 crore. These findings highlight major operational and governance risks with serious implications for health, financial inclusion, and scheme integrity.

title: Performance Audit on Assessment of Assessees in Entertainment Sector, Union Government, Department of Revenue - Direct Taxes
overview:
This performance audit report provides an in-depth examination of the assessment of assessees in the entertainment sector, including television, radio, music, event management, films, animation and visual effects, broadcasting, sports, and amusement. The audit covered a sample of 6,516 assessment records (about 50% of the total 13,031), with an assessed income of ₹47,979.44 crore. It found 726 instances (approx. 11% of the audited sample) of systemic and compliance issues, resulting in a tax effect of ₹2,267.82 crore and significant revenue loss to the government (page iii).

Key issues identified include lack of coordination within and outside the Income Tax Department (ITD), ineffective sharing of information, and deficient monitoring of cash transactions. The excessive concentration of assessments under the 'Others' code (906) highlighted a lack of segment-specific refinement, with 87% of assessees clubbed together and up to 80% of additions during scrutiny made under this code (page 5-6).

The audit found weaknesses in internal controls, non-verification of production costs to foreign producers, inconsistent application of laws, and inadequate monitoring of revenue streams such as overflow and movie rights. These gaps, combined with ad hoc additions and non-uniform application of provisions, have exposed systematic vulnerabilities and contributed to recurring errors. The report recommends broad reforms for better risk assessment, code refinement, mandatory information sharing, and improvement in assessment procedures.

title: Performance Audit Report on Select District Hospitals in Sikkim 2018-19 Sikkim
overview:
The Performance Audit examined select district and referral hospitals in Sikkim from FY 2014-19, focusing on fund management, infrastructure, human resources, and delivery of health services. The Health & Family Welfare Department received budget allotments averaging 6.24% of the State's budget, falling short of the 8% target mandated by the National Health Policy, with actual expenditure averaging 6.53%. In 2018-19, health sector allocation dropped to 5.52% from 7.70% in 2017-18. Fund utilization remained suboptimal, with savings fluctuating from 27.64% in 2014-15 to 5.38% in 2017-18, before rising again to 9.06% in 2018-19. Out of ₹1,693.76 crore health sector expenditure during 2014-19, revenue expenditure was ₹1,164.65 crore, concentrated largely on human resources (65%), while spending on drugs, consumables, and equipment lagged.

The audit identified severe shortages of doctors, nurses, and infrastructure, including an overall shortfall of 57 Sub-Centres, seven PHCs, and six CHCs—a 75% deficit in CHC coverage. Both sampled hospitals faced critical stock-outs of essential drugs (with up to 123 instances lasting between seven days and five years), requiring patients to purchase medicines privately. Additional gaps included non-establishment of blood banks, lack of ICU facilities, inadequate documentation and computerization of patient records, and incomplete Trauma Care Centers.

Consequences of these lapses included increased patient referrals to distant tertiary facilities (2,652 in-patients referred from Singtam DH and 1,411 from Gyalshing DH from 2016-19), slow response times during emergencies, and frequent out-of-pocket expenses for medication. Despite better-than-average health indicators (IMR and TFR), systemic gaps threaten service quality and equitable access to care in rural areas.

title: Performance Audit of Pollution by Industries in West Bengal, Government of West Bengal
overview:
This Performance Audit highlights severe shortcomings in the prevention, control, and monitoring of industrial pollution in West Bengal from 2012-13 to 2016-17. The audit found that the West Bengal Pollution Control Board (WBPCB) had not prepared a reliable inventory of polluting industries as per pollution load, resulting in inconsistent data between the WBPCB and the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB). Notably, of 8,419 red category industries recorded by WBPCB, only 5,452 were confirmed by regional offices, and the final hazardous waste inventory included just 952 units, even though more than 6,000 units were initially identified, indicating massive underreporting.

The audit revealed that as of July 2017, 65% (2,797 out of 5,452) of red category industrial units were operating with expired Consent to Operate (CTO) licenses. None of the activities set out in the Vision Document for 2013-14 to 2015-16 had been implemented, and the siting policy for new industries was repeatedly violated, allowing polluting industries to operate in restricted and ecologically sensitive areas. Furthermore, action plans for critically and severely polluted zones had not been implemented, and no new air or water quality monitoring stations were established as per CPCB guidelines.

Monitoring, post-clearance compliance, and hazardous waste management were also critically deficient: No industrial unit submitted compliance reports post-environment clearance, and only 33% of grossly polluting industries by the Ganga were even monitored during 2015-17, with 80 units found to violate discharge standards. These systemic gaps indicate a high risk to environmental and public health, with a clear lack of both strategic planning and enforcement.

Strictly enforce the siting policy and prevent/relocate industries from restricted municipal and ecologically sensitive areas.
Mandate and monitor timely submission of compliance reports by industries post-environmental clearance; activate the Monitoring Committee.
Implement action plans for all critically and severely polluted areas, including establishment of new air/water quality monitoring stations.
Ensure that all hazardous waste generating units are included in inventory and authorisations are up to date, with regular inspections.

title: Performance audit on Reconstruction of Infrastructure Post 2013 Disaster in Uttarakhand, Government of Uttarakhand
overview:
Uttarakhand suffered a catastrophic disaster between 15th and 17th June 2013, resulting in heavy to very heavy rainfall, flash floods, and landslides across its higher Himalayan districts, leading to the loss of around a thousand lives and over 5,400 people missing. The devastation also caused severe damage to infrastructure, agricultural land, and housing, especially in Pithoragarh, Bageshwar, Chamoli, Rudraprayag, and Uttarkashi.

A Medium and Long Term Reconstruction (MLTR) package of ₹6,259.84 crore was approved for restoration, with funding from the Government of India, Asian Development Bank, World Bank, and the State. However, as of 31 March 2018, only ₹4,617.27 crore had been released, with expenditure standing at ₹3,708.27 crore, amounting to just 59% utilisation. Out of 2,359 works sanctioned, 1,769 (75%) were completed by the original deadline, rising to 2,066 (87%) by March 2018, with 256 works still in progress and 37 yet to start.

The audit revealed significant issues in fund allocation and utilisation, delays, unauthorized retention and diversion of funds, and instances of overpayment or undue contractor benefits. Specifically, ₹642.83 crore (38.23%) in audit observations related to financial mismanagement, with ₹294.64 crore diverted for unplanned works, ₹61.64 crore in inflated utilisation certificates, and ₹30.62 crore blocked in unspent balances. Several planned tourism and disaster preparedness projects could not be started due to poor planning and non-availability of land, undermining the State’s recovery and preparedness.

title: Performance Audit on Assessment of Assessees in Real Estate Sector, Union Government, Department of Revenue - Direct Taxes
overview:
The audit revealed major lapses in the inclusion of developers, builders, and real estate agents in the income tax net. Out of 54,578 real estate companies registered with the Registrar of Companies (ROC) in 12 states, Permanent Account Number (PAN) information was missing for 51,670 entities (95%), making it challenging to verify whether these entities were filing income tax returns as required (p.7). In a sample of 840 companies with PAN, it was discovered that 159 companies (19%) were not filing ITRs, highlighting a systemic gap between ROC registration and tax compliance (p.8).

A review of high-value property transactions found that 9.7% of sellers involved in sales over ₹1 crore were not filing ITRs, with ₹391.40 crore of transactions escaping scrutiny. In Maharashtra alone, 34% of property transactions above ₹5 lakh had at least one party whose PAN was unquoted, exposing significant loopholes where sources of investment and capital gains could escape taxation (p.10). Furthermore, in third-party datasets (RERA, CREDAI, etc.), 528 out of 2,952 identified real estate entities (18%) did not file ITRs, and the tax department issued notices in only 37 cases (p.12).

These findings suggest systemic weaknesses in tax base completeness, enforcement, and data integration. The lack of an effective mechanism between ROC and the Income Tax Department, as well as poor enforcement of mandatory reporting by Registrars/Sub-Registrars of properties, allowed numerous entities and transactions in the real estate sector to remain outside the tax net, undermining revenue mobilization and fiscal transparency.

Effectively use third party data from RERA, CREDAI, and Registrars to widen the tax base.

title: Performance Audit of Working of Inland Container Depots (ICDs) and Container Freight Stations (CFSs) Department of Revenue Indirect taxes, Customs
overview:
This performance audit reviewed the functioning of ICDs and CFSs across India covering transactions from 2012-13 to 2016-17, with a focus on their effectiveness in facilitating trade, adequacy of regulatory oversight, infrastructure, and data management. As of March 2017, 129 ICDs and 168 CFSs were notified, handling containerized cargo valued at ₹4.27 lakh crore in 2016-17. However, the audit found capacity underutilization, with nearly 40% of test-checked facilities operating at less than 50% of installed capacity and about one third between 50–70%.

Critical data gaps were observed: there is no reliable single source of ICD/CFS status, and differences exist between data held by the Department of Commerce and local Customs. Approval of new facilities occurred without systematic assessment of regional demand or capacity utilization, leading to proliferation and resource strain. There were also deficiencies in infrastructure with some ICDs lacking basic handling equipment and hazardous cargo space, and persistent issues with EDI connectivity.

As of March 2017, 7,877 uncleared containers (1.17 lakh sq m), with 469 containing hazardous waste, were pending for disposal—57% pending over three years. Several policy and regulatory shortcomings were identified, such as the absence of a policy-level oversight framework, limited post-approval monitoring, unreconciled transshipment tracking, and routine misuse of Section 23 of the Customs Act to abandon high-value imports, undermining compliance and posing environmental risks.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit of Union Government (Ministry of Communications and Ministry of Electronics & Information Technology)
overview:
This report by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India covers compliance and performance audits of the Ministry of Communications and Ministry of Electronics & Information Technology for the year ended March 2017. Key financial statistics highlight that while the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) reported revenue of ₹70,241.14 crore for 2016-17, only 43.53% of the ₹85,716.80 crore collected under the Universal Service Obligation Fund (USOF) up to March 2017 was received by DoT, resulting in ₹48,407.54 crore not transferred to the USOF.

The audit highlights continued suboptimal spectrum management, with annual opportunity cost losses of ₹127.33 crore and failure to auction surrendered spectrum, resulting in further revenue loss. Public sector undertakings like Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited (BSNL) and Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Limited (MTNL) continue to record significant financial losses, with BSNL incurring a net loss of ₹4,793.21 crore in 2016-17 and subscriber base for PSUs dropping by 7% over five years.

Serious operational shortfalls in IT-enabled projects (Core Insurance Solution in DoP), non-compliance with inspection targets, delayed recovery of spectrum charges, and gaps in rural connectivity programs point to high risk for public funds and service delivery. Strategic intervention is urgently required to recover lost revenue, achieve project timelines, and implement effective regulatory controls.

title: Performance Audit of Solid Waste Management in Urban Local Bodies, Government of Karnataka
overview:
This performance audit examined the effectiveness of Solid Waste Management (SWM) across 35 Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) in Karnataka for the period 2012-13 to 2016-17. Key findings show that ULBs failed to conduct systematic waste generation surveys from 2010-16 and per capita estimates used for planning were unreliable, resulting in poor waste management outcomes. Detailed Project Reports prepared in 2016 only partially addressed resource gaps and lacked actionable strategies to bridge funding deficits. The audit revealed a significant accumulation of unused funds for SWM—balances reached ₹93.19 crore by March 2017, despite full utilisation of allocations for revenue expenditure, highlighting inefficiencies in capital asset creation.

SWM cess collection improved, yet exemptions for public worship places, ULB-owned buildings, government properties, and vacant lands led to a revenue loss of ₹3.07 crore from 2012-13 to 2016-17. There was also short accounting of cess, with Hubballi-Dharwad Municipal Corporation alone underreporting ₹5.11 crore, and six ULBs overall short-accounting ₹5.41 crore. Diversion of funds was detected: ten ULBs misapplied ₹3.81 crore toward non-SWM activities, including ₹15.80 lakh diverted in City Municipal Council, Sira, hampering construction of bio-methanation plants and other targets.

Systemic issues persisted in service delivery: only 26% of collected waste was processed, and 83% of roads were not swept daily. Segregation was partial or absent, special waste streams like plastic, bio-medical, e-waste, and slaughterhouse waste remained unmanaged, and landfill sites operated without valid KSPCB authorisation. Insufficient institutional mechanisms, manpower shortages, and lack of effective IEC activities contributed to environmental and health hazards.

title: Performance Audit on National Rural Drinking Water Programme in Ministry of Drinking Water and Sanitation
overview:
The National Rural Drinking Water Programme (NRDWP) was launched in April 2009 with a total outlay of ₹89,956 crore (Central share ₹43,691 crore and State share ₹46,265 crore) for the period 2012-17. The key objectives were to provide safe and adequate water for drinking, cooking, and other household needs to every rural person on a sustainable basis. However, only ₹81,168 crore was actually expended during the review period, and just 44% of rural habitations and 85% of government schools and anganwadis were provided access to safe drinking water by December 2017, falling significantly short of targets.

The programme's implementation suffered due to weak planning and poor fund management. 10% of allocated funds (₹8,788 crore) remained unutilized, and ₹359 crore was diverted for ineligible purposes. Poor contract management and execution led to incomplete, abandoned, or non-functional works, resulting in unproductive expenditure estimated at ₹2,212.44 crore. Data inconsistencies in the Integrated Management Information System and lack of effective monitoring further undermined programme effectiveness.

The CAG found that the NRDWP failed to meet targets set out in the 12th Five Year Plan and the Ministry's Strategic Plan, with only marginal increases in coverage (8% increase at 40 LPCD and 5.5% at 55 LPCD) despite large public investment. In addition, only 18% of the rural population was provided piped water supply at 55 LPCD, and just 17% of rural households received household tap connections. The report highlights substantial systemic failures that risk the achievement of Sustainable Development Goal 6 for water and sanitation.

title: Performance Audit on Post Matric Scholarships to the Students belonging to Scheduled Castes for studies in India in Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment
overview:
The Comptroller and Auditor General of India conducted a performance audit of the Post Matric Scholarship Scheme for Scheduled Caste students, covering five States from 2012-13 to 2016-17. The scheme aimed to provide financial support for education to eligible SC students with an expenditure of ₹18,647 crore in the audited States, benefiting approximately 1.36 crore students. The audit exposed systemic gaps in guidelines, deficient planning, and lapses in financial management. A total of ₹6,439 crore was released in central assistance to the selected States, though arrears of ₹5,368 crore accumulated, and ₹375.30 crore remained undisbursed due to mismatched bank details, depriving students of scholarships.

Audit findings pointed to misuse and diversion of funds, including ₹28.94 crore spent on non-scholarship activities in Karnataka and Maharashtra. Excess scholarship payments of ₹49.67 crore were made to 1.88 lakh students, while ineligible students received ₹1.95 crore. Delays in scholarship disbursal affected 18.58 lakh students, with timelines for application and approval absent or inconsistently adhered to. Significant data inconsistencies were found on State e-portals, implicating ₹455.98 crore.

Monitoring and grievance redressal mechanisms were found inadequate or non-operational, with no comprehensive evaluation conducted by the Ministry. No annual action or perspective plans were prepared, undermining accurate estimates for fund requirements, and lack of database for eligible students led to wide variations in projected versus actual beneficiaries. These gaps severely hampered scheme efficiency and accountability.

title: Performance Audit on Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana in Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
overview:
This performance audit covers the Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY), announced in August 2003 to correct imbalances in access to tertiary care and improve the quality of medical education in India. The audit examined planning, fund management, creation of infrastructure, equipment procurement, and human resource deployment for 20 new AIIMS and 71 GMCIs under the scheme, covering allocation and releases of ₹14,970.70 crore and ₹9,207.18 crore respectively, up to 2016-17.

Critical issues uncovered include a cost overrun of ₹2,928 crore and significant time delays, with construction of new AIIMS delayed by 4-5 years and shortages of both faculty (55-83%) and non-faculty staff (77-97%) in the new institutions. Out of 42 departments, 6 to 14 departments in different AIIMS remained non-functional, and only 152 to 546 beds were available against the normative 960 per AIIMS.

In GMCIs, 408 equipment costing ₹71.25 crore were either not installed or severely delayed, while ₹34.99 crore worth of equipment was found idle across nine GMCIs. Funds of ₹63.85 crore remained idle and ₹26.71 crore were diverted for unauthorised purposes, indicating serious lapses in financial management and the achievement of scheme deliverables. The findings point to an overall failure in synchronisation, planning, and monitoring, resulting in poor outcomes and delayed benefits to the intended population.

title: Performance Audit on Augmentation of Station Line Capacity on selected Stations in Indian Railways Union Government
overview:
Indian Railways, with 7,349 stations and 22.24 million passengers daily in 2016-17, faces mounting pressures from increasing demand. The CAG audit focused on whether the line and platform capacities at 15 major stations matched the growth in train traffic. It was found that augmentation of critical infrastructure such as stabling lines, washing pit lines, and sufficient platform length did not keep pace; for example, only two pit lines and seven platforms were added across 11 high-traffic stations between March 2012 and March 2017, despite a daily increase of 176 trains handled.

Stations like Patna, Kanpur Central, and Mathura operated below required capacity, resulting in frequent train detentions: goods trains were detained up to 100 minutes and passenger trains up to 25 minutes per train in many cases. The absence of long platforms led to 38% of total platforms being too short for 24-coach trains, forcing long trains onto inadequate platforms. At major locations, up to 15-34% increases in train traffic occurred over a decade, but key maintenance and handling infrastructure remained static, causing cascading punctuality and operational issues.

These deficiencies led to substantial passenger inconvenience and operational inefficiencies. For instance, March 2017 saw Kanpur Central detain trains for 47,121 minutes en route and 29,813 minutes at platforms, while Mathura clocked 16,000+ total minutes of late starts and detentions. The audit concluded that inadequate planning and execution in station redevelopment overlooked operational aspects, directly affecting service quality and system efficiency.

title: Performance Audit on National Projects Ministry of Water Resources, River Development and Ganga Rejuvenation
overview:
The performance audit examined the implementation of 16 major National Projects under the Ministry of Water Resources, River Development and Ganga Rejuvenation. Of the 16 projects, only five were under execution as of March 2017, with an envisaged irrigation potential of 25.10 lakh hectares. These five projects suffered from significant cost overruns, with original cost estimates of ₹3,530 crore escalating to ₹86,172.23 crore—a 2,341% increase. Actual expenditure incurred on the five was ₹13,299.12 crore, but only 37% of the created irrigation potential (5.36 lakh ha out of 14.53 lakh ha) was being used.

Administrative delays, inefficient land acquisition, and deficient contract management led to physical progress shortfalls between 8% and 99% on project components, and major cost increases. For example, cost escalations after inclusion in the national project scheme were ₹49,840 crore on just two projects. Furthermore, there were delays and shortfalls in central and state fund releases of up to 100% in multiple years, critically impacting project schedules and outcomes.

Intended benefits in power generation and drinking water supply were largely unachieved—no project except Gosikhurd delivered any new reservoir capacity (0.53 MAF against a target of 5.41 MAF for all five under-execution projects). Weak monitoring, ineffective implementation of command area development, and delays in statutory clearances threaten both economic viability and public benefit from these large-scale investments.

title: Report No.4 of 2017 - Performance Audit of Flood Management and Response in Chennai and its Suburban Areas Government of Tamil Nadu
overview:
The Performance Audit scrutinized flood management and response in Chennai and its suburban areas for the period 2011-16, focusing on the catastrophic floods of December 2015 which claimed 289 lives and inundated 23.25 lakh houses. The audit identified a lack of coordination among government departments, weak enforcement of master plans and statutes, and failure to complete key flood mitigation projects. Major tanks and reservoirs, notably Chembarambakkam, Cholavaram, and Redhills, were found to lack scientific inflow forecast systems and real-time flood monitoring, resulting in unsustained discharges during the severe 2015 rain spells. Additionally, rapid urbanisation led to indiscriminate conversion of agricultural and open space land for residential and commercial use—agricultural land in Chennai Metropolitan Area shrank from 73,689 hectares in 1973 to 12,569 hectares in 2006, and open space reduced from 5,742 hectares to just 566 hectares.

The storm water drainage network in Chennai was critically inadequate, covering less than the planned areas and designed for incorrect rainfall intensity. Annual pre-monsoon desilting activities were delayed or neglected, with funds released late and works unfinished before monsoon onset. Encroachments on tanks, lakes, river beds, and water bodies proliferated despite a protective law enacted in 2007. Many flood protection projects taken up under the Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission (JNNURM) remained incomplete due to unresolved land issues and lack of interdepartmental coordination.

Disaster management remained weak, as the Tamil Nadu State Disaster Management Authority did not convene meetings since its formation in 2013 and lacked financial autonomy. The audit concluded that these systemic failures resulted in man-made catastrophes, aggravated by unsustained water release from Chembarambakkam Tank, poor urban planning, and ineffective maintenance of drainage networks.

title: Performance Audit on Kudankulam Nuclear Power Project, Units I and II Department of Atomic Energy
overview:
The performance audit of the Kudankulam Nuclear Power Project (KKNPP) Units I and II revealed significant deficiencies in project execution, leading to high cost overruns and substantial delays. The initial project cost of ₹13,171 crore approved in 2001 escalated to ₹22,462 crore by 2014, an increase of 71%, mainly due to delayed supply of equipment by the overseas collaborating partner, changes in design, and additional works. Commercial operations of Unit I and II were delayed by 86 and 101 months, respectively, resulting in cost overruns and increased interest costs.

NPCIL faced an additional financial burden due to non-concomitant adjustment of the Russian credit repayment schedule, incurring ₹449.42 crore in extra interest. Further, borrowing at higher domestic rates due to lack of provision for erection reserve spares resulted in an unnecessary interest cost of ₹76.02 crore. Failures in tariff calculation procedures led to a short realization of revenue totaling ₹90.63 crore, and revenue of ₹7.04 crore was foregone by not including self-insurance fund charges in tariffs during the pre-commercialization period.

Delays in project implementation and non-adherence to prudent financial management practices extended undue benefits to the overseas partner, with NPCIL not initiating claims for significant recoverable expenses. The total losses due to extended shutdowns and avoidable management decisions, such as the Unit I shutdown without technical competency evaluation, added up to nearly ₹948 crore in missed revenue. The audit concluded that NPCIL did not implement effective monitoring or transparent financial controls, adversely impacting project economy and efficiency.

title: Performance Audit of Rejuvenation of River Ganga (Namami Gange)
overview:
The Namami Gange programme was launched in May 2015 to integrate past and ongoing efforts for rejuvenating the River Ganga. The audit scrutinised 87 projects, including 73 ongoing, 13 completed, and one abandoned, amounting to a sanctioned cost of ₹ 7,992.34 crore. Of these, 50 projects were sanctioned after 1 April 2014; the selection included all institutional, afforestation, and biodiversity projects.

The report found significant deficiencies in financial management and planning. For example, fund utilisation ranged from only 8% to 63% across three years, leaving substantial balances unspent with NMCG. As of 2016-17, the closing balance was ₹ 2,133.76 crore against actual expenditure of ₹ 1,062.81 crore, indicating low absorption capacity and systemic delays in project execution (page 12).

Targets for pollution abatement and rural sanitation saw critical shortfalls. Sewage treatment capacity in 106 towns along the Ganga was 2,109 Million Litres per Day short of the required volume, despite the Cabinet’s deadlines for completion by September 2018. Monitoring, evaluation, and the use of technology remained at a nascent stage; project delays and ineffective oversight directly compromised the programme's primary objectives and ecological outcomes.

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 Union Government
overview:
The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 was enacted to unify regulations around food safety, consolidating a fragmented system under a single point reference, FSSAI. The performance audit covers regulatory mechanisms from 2011-12 to 2015-16, finding persistent delays in framing key regulations even after a decade. For example, essential guidelines for laboratory accreditation, risk analysis, and organic food standards were lacking, affecting over 1.35 million metric tonnes of organic products in 2015-16 alone, according to APEDA data cited in the report.

The audit highlights that over 90% of state food laboratories lack accreditation, calling into question the reliability of food testing. In more than 50% of license issuances examined, incomplete documents were admitted (Chapter-III).

Key failures in licensing, inspection, laboratory infrastructure, and human resources have led to significant gaps in food safety enforcement. Acute shortages in regular staff, including essential Food Safety Officers, remain unaddressed due to the lack of recruitment regulations, posing tangible risks to public health due to possible unchecked circulation of unsafe food (Page vii: "Possibility that unsafe/declared unsafe food articles continued to be manufactured and sold is not ruled out").

title: Performance Audit on Induction of bio-toilets in passenger coaches in Indian Railways Union Government
overview:
Indian Railways (IR) operates 13,313 passenger trains with 54,506 coaches (including DEMU/DHMU), transporting 22.21 million passengers daily over 1,19,630 km of track. The report reviews the ambitious nationwide rollout of bio-toilets—an eco-friendly technology developed alongside DRDO—between 2014-15 and 2016-17. The original commitment was to induct 50,000 bio-toilets annually so that all IR coaches would be equipped by 2019, in line with the Swachh Bharat Mission.

The audit noted significant implementation gaps: despite ambitious targets, 5.7% of new coaches and 6.7% of LHB coaches manufactured in 2016-17 still lacked bio-toilets. Induction of bio-toilets through retrofitment fell consistently short, with the fund utilisation rate for this purpose between just 34% and 71% over three years. In 2016-17, only 22,198 bio-toilets were retrofitted as against the official target of 20,000 and the internal target of 50,000, with shortfalls exceeding 30% in several key zones such as ECR (67% miss) and NCR (49% miss).

Major bottlenecks included poor quality and delayed supply of bio-toilets by vendors (as of March 2017, only 12,016 out of 14,274 supplied were fitted), inadequate infrastructure in workshops, and widespread maintenance issues: in a review of 30 Coaching Depots, 199,689 instances of deficiencies were counted in 2016-17 in 453 trains fitted with bio-toilets. Training of staff was also insufficient, with only 36.62% of supervisory and 23.21% of non-supervisory staff trained since 2013, and minimal public awareness efforts nationwide.

title: Report of the Comptroller & Auditor General of India for the year ended 31 March 2016 on 'Performance Audit on Implementation of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 Government of Madhya Pradesh'
overview:
The audit found major deficiencies in the implementation of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 in Madhya Pradesh. Over the period 2010-16, the Department failed to utilize available funds under the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) effectively, resulting in large unspent balances ranging from 23% to 52% each year, with Rs 1,265.41 crore unspent as of March 2016 (page vii).

There was a shortfall in releases of funds by both the Government of India (GoI) and the State Government—Rs 7,284.61 crore short released for SSA against approved outlay between 2010-16 (page vii). Furthermore, the State was deprived of Rs 537 crore of the 13th Finance Commission grant for elementary education in 2014-15, due to the Department's failure to fulfill grant release conditions (page 9).

Key educational outcomes were compromised: Net Enrolment Ratio (NER) at primary level dropped from 93.66% in 2013-14 to 79.83% in 2015-16, and dropout rates remained high with 24% and 23% of children failing to reach grade V in consecutive cohorts. Infrastructure, pupil teacher ratios, and the inclusion of vulnerable groups lagged behind targets as well, and the quality of education did not improve as measured by both internal and national surveys (page viii-ix).

title: Performance audit Union Government Competitiveness of BHEL in Emerging Markets Reports of Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises
overview:
The performance audit of Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited (BHEL) found a sharp decline in the company’s turnover from ₹49,510 crore in 2011-12 to ₹26,587 crore in 2015-16, with profits of ₹7,040 crore in 2011-12 turning into a loss of ₹913 crore in 2015-16. BHEL’s attempts at diversification were largely ineffective, with the power sector still accounting for over 76% of turnover and significant strategic plan shortfalls ranging from 23% to 114% against set goals. The order book fell from ₹1,35,300 crore in March 2012 to ₹1,01,000 crore in March 2015, and up to 45% of outstanding orders as of March 2016 were non-executable ‘on-hold’ projects.

Audit revealed persistent gaps in project delivery, with all 53 sample projects delayed by 3 to 84 months, leading to the imposition of liquidated damages worth ₹1,966 crore. Additionally, cost estimation and pricing weaknesses resulted in BHEL routinely quoting higher than competitors, contributing to its declining success rate in turbine generator orders—from 80% won in 2013-14 to 0% in 2015-16. Quality and workmanship issues in manufacturing led to over ₹138 crore in rework costs at Trichy and Haridwar units.

Receivable management was also poor, with final payments of up to 10% of contract value routinely delayed due to incomplete Performance Guarantee tests and punch-point closures. BHEL was unable to collect ₹1,457 crore in interest on outstanding dues as of March 2016, and failed to secure Letters of Credit for eight major private sector orders, resulting in outstanding dues of ₹2,661 crore and stranded inventory worth ₹459 crore.

title: Performance audit Union Government Levy and collection of Service Tax on Entertainment Sector Reports of Department of Revenue Indirect Taxes – Service Tax
overview:
This performance audit covered the levy and collection of Service Tax on the entertainment sector for the years 2013-14 to 2015-16. The audit examined 17 selected Commissionerates, including review of records for 307 assessees, capturing about 33% of all-India revenue related to the entertainment sector’s service taxes. The sector’s service tax collections showed an average growth rate of 9.9%, with certain subsectors like copyrights growing at unprecedented rates—up to 94% between 2012-13 and 2014-15. However, audit scrutiny revealed systemic inadequacies, unclear legislative provisions, and exploitative practices by assessees.

Key findings included revenue leakages through misclassification and clubbing of taxable and exempt activities, such as treating non-theatrical rights as theatrical, or wrongly availing Cenvat credit. 156 cases were found of non- or short-payment of service tax or cess, incorrect/excess credit claims, and illegal export-of-service claims, involving a total revenue impact of ₹48.13 crore. Misuse was observed in cases where producers assigned rights in agreements that purposely blurred the line between taxable and exempted categories, e.g., drafting agreements where all earnings were shown as exempt theatrical rights.

The report concluded that existing systems in detection, scrutiny, compliance monitoring, and use of third-party data were ineffective, resulting in significant shortfall in tax vigilance and enforcement. Recommendations emphasized legislative clarity, better automation, and proactive data usage for plugging revenue leaks, noting that several findings remain relevant under the new GST regime.

title: Performance audit Union Government Payment of tax by certain companies under special provisions of section 115JB Reports of Department of Revenue – Direct Taxes
overview:
This performance audit examined the payment of tax by companies under the Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) regime, focusing on assessments from 2012-13 to 2015-16. Out of 15,677 assessment records requisitioned, only 11,293 were produced for audit, indicating a 27.96% non-production rate. The audit revealed systemic gaps, including ambiguities in MAT provisions, inadequate compliance by Income Tax Department (ITD), and significant underassessment of tax. For example, in 22 cases, incomes aggregating ₹337.86 crore were not considered for MAT, leading to a tax shortfall of ₹74.10 crore. Similarly, ₹1827.86 crore in asset diminution provision was not added back in 47 cases.

There was a notable divergence between the number of working companies registered and those in the tax database. About one third of companies registered with the Registrar of Companies were absent from the ITD database, with the gap ranging from 2.94 lakh (33.3%) to 3.94 lakh (36.4%) between FY 2012-13 and 2015-16. Non-filer monitoring was also deficient; only 70.69% of non-filing companies identified were issued notices and less than 30% responded by filing returns.

Irregularities in MAT credit, loss computation, and non-compliance with established provisions led to revenue impact in hundreds of crores. In total, the audit detected issues in over 780 assessment cases, with cumulative tax effect in major findings exceeding ₹2,000 crore. Substantial recommendations were made to clarify ambiguous provisions, improve ITD processes, and strengthen enforcement against non-filers.

title: Performance audit Union Government Planning and Implementation of Phase III Expansion Project of Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Limited Reports of Petroleum and Natural Gas
overview:
The audit examined the planning and implementation of the Phase III Expansion Project of Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Limited (MRPL). The project, initially approved in 2006 with an estimated cost of ₹7,943 crore, underwent several changes in scope, resulting in the cost rising to ₹15,008 crore by June 2010. The final expenditure as of March 2016 stood at a substantial ₹14,832 crore, with the project taking nearly five more years than the original schedule.

Key findings reveal significant failures in both planning and execution, leading to time overruns of more than two years and cost overruns of ₹2,509 crore at planning stage alone. Operational inefficiencies were aggravated by delays in synchronising newly commissioned units, leading to underutilisation and loss of revenue. In particular, delayed commissioning of the Captive Power Plant caused idling of major processing units and additional expenses for temporary arrangements.

The audit also highlights instances of non-compliance with financial prudence: external commercial borrowings drew a loss of ₹13.70 crore due to unhedged currency risks, and a lack of demand-based fund draw resulted in ₹768.46 crore idling in non-interest bearing accounts. Further, the project missed environmental compliance deadlines, exacerbating operational and reputational risks.

title: Performance audit Union Government Assessment of Private Hospitals Reports of Department of Revenue - Direct Taxes
overview:
The audit highlighted a persistent and increasing gap between the growth of the private healthcare sector, which saw expenditures expand by more than ₹35,000 crore and ₹39,000 crore during 2012-13 and 2013-14 respectively, and the modest or even declining number of medical assessees brought into the tax net (e.g., corporate assessees among Medical Professionals, Nursing Homes, and Speciality Hospitals declined in 2012-13 before a minor increase the following year).

Despite the existence of robust tools such as the Non-filers Monitoring System (NMS) and Income Tax Payer Data Management System (ITDMS), these mechanisms were inadequately used, failing to effectively cross-reference over 3.2 lakh records from third-party registering authorities or track high-value cash transactions in the sector. As a result, large segments of the sector, including registered medical professionals, clinics, and private hospitals, were not traceably captured in the PAN database or the broader assessee roster, raising the probability of significant under-reporting and tax evasion.

The ineffective codification of medical businesses and the underuse of survey operations were also identified as key contributors to the revenue gap. Survey coverage was scant, with only 147 operations (12.54% of total) conducted in the sector out of 1,172 overall, resulting in additional tax accruals of ₹4,925.65 lakh but leaving many states without any surveys at all. These failures limited the ability of the Income Tax Department to monitor, widen, or deepen the tax base in this fast-growing and high-value sector.

title: Performance audit Union Government Disbursement of Defence Pension Reports of Defence Services
overview:
The CAG performance audit reviewed the disbursement of defence pension, which covers over 25 lakh pensioners and involves annual expenditure exceeding ₹60,000 crore. The system relies on the coordination of four pillars: Record Offices, Pension Sanctioning Authorities, Pension Disbursing Agencies, and the Reserve Bank of India. The audit found serious issues in financial management, including incomplete accounting of pension expenditure: as of March 2016, ₹6,831.95 crore was not booked to the correct head due to non-receipt of payment scrolls from banks, affecting government accounts and revenue deficit (Table 2.3, p. 8).

Inefficiencies were observed in pension processing and payment authorisation. Multiple stages and manual handoffs led to significant delays. Test checks revealed over 21,000 underpaid pensioners in a single month, totaling ₹106.17 crore, with a longer-term potential underpayment of ₹228.85 crore (p. vi, para 4.2). Simultaneously, overpayment to about 12,000 pensioners in another month equaled ₹118.23 crore, and data for 2011-16 indicated overpayments of ₹518.70 crore (p. vi, para 4.3).

Control deficiencies were pervasive: missing or erroneous pensioners’ data, multiple accounts credited for same PPOs, double payments, and lack of integration between IT systems. The audit warns that the de-linking of reimbursement to banks from the submission of payment scrolls weakens accounting, and that RBI's current processes created limited incentives for banks to comply, leading to distortions in both government expenditure tracking and cash management (p. 10).

title: Performance Audit of Modernisation and Strengthening of Police Forces, Government of Uttar Pradesh
overview:
During 2011-16, Rs 462.87 crore was spent under the Modernization of Police Forces (MPF) scheme in Uttar Pradesh, with an additional Rs 2,276.31 crore from state budgets, totalling Rs 2,739.18 crore for police modernization. However, audit found only 55% of the arms, 41% of the communication equipment, and 72% of state-budgeted infrastructure funds were actually utilized, resulting in Rs 875.95 crore surrendered. Equipment and vehicle procurement suffered critical shortfalls and delays: about 48% of the police force used .303 rifles declared obsolete 20 years ago, and 27% of required police vehicles were unavailable, while only 10% of condemned vehicles were replaced by 2015-16.

Key infrastructure underperformed drastically—more than 34% of sanctioned police accommodation (worth ₹1,048.73 crore) remained incomplete, and over 39% of district surveillance CCTVs were non-functional, endangering public security. Only two cybercrime police stations existed state-wide by March 2016, against one proposed for every district. Manpower shortages were acute, with vacancies over 50% among sanctioned posts of Sub-Inspectors and Constables, undermining law and order maintenance.

There were structural weaknesses in procurement, planning, and monitoring—highlighted by 2068 works (₹2,920 crore) awarded on a nomination basis, disregarding government performance criteria. Overall, the State Police continues to be crippled by obsolete technology, slow modernization, under-spending, and persistent operational gaps, calling for urgent systemic reforms.

title: Performance audit Union Government Schemes for Flood Control and Flood Forecasting Reports of Ministry of Water Resources, River Development & Ganga Rejuvenation
overview:
The Performance Audit on Union Government Schemes for Flood Control and Flood Forecasting examined 206 Flood Management Programme projects, 38 flood forecasting stations, 49 River Management Activities and works related to Border Area projects and 68 large dams in 17 selected States/UTs. During the XI and XII Five Year Plans, the audit found substantial delays in the approval of Detailed Project Reports, which led to technical designs becoming obsolete by the time funds were released—directly impacting project effectiveness.

The audit highlighted that works under the Flood Management Programme were not undertaken in an integrated fashion, as full river systems or segments were often left without holistic management. A considerable number of telemetry stations set up for real-time flood data during the XI Plan remained non-functional for most of the period. Physical and financial progress of projects was also delayed: only 81 of 206 projects were completed as of March 2016. Fund absorption rates between 44–50% signaled persistent implementation bottlenecks, with significant amounts unspent or stalled at State level.

As a consequence, systemic weaknesses in monitoring and evaluation continued unabated. Key recommendations of Rashtriya Barh Ayog, like scientific assessment of flood-prone areas and a Flood Plain Zoning Act, were not acted upon. Only a handful of large dams had Emergency Action Plans. Overall, the failure to adhere to scheme guidelines has hindered India’s capacity for proactive and coordinated flood management, exposing states to repeated losses and undermining public investment.

title: Performance audit Union Government Reproductive and Child Health under National Rural Health Mission Reports of Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
overview:
The Performance Audit reviewed the implementation of the Reproductive and Child Health programme under the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) for the period 2011-12 to 2015-16. Financial management was a critical issue with persistent unspent balances—unspent funds in 27 States increased from ₹7,375 crore in 2011-12 to ₹9,509 crore in 2015-16, and transfers from State treasuries to State Health Societies were delayed up to 271 days. Infrastructure creation lagged significantly: up to 38% shortfall in health centre coverage nationwide, with over 50% in five States and survey evidence of unhygienic or inaccessible conditions at hundreds of sites.

Shortages in medicines, equipment, and staff were systemic and persistent. In 24 States, essential drugs were unavailable and equipment worth ₹30.39 crore lay idle in 17 States due to lack of trained personnel and infrastructure. The problem extended to human resources, with specialist doctor shortages at 77-87% in Community Health Centres, and 67 Primary Health Centres entirely unstaffed by doctors in 13 States.

Poor record management, unreliable Health Management Information Systems (HMIS) data, and non-operational mobile medical units further undermined service quality. Against Millennium Development Goal targets for Infant Mortality Rate and Maternal Mortality Ratio, actual outcomes fell short: IMR targeted at 27 was achieved at 39, and MMR targeted at 109 was achieved at 167, with even worse results in certain States. The audit highlights urgent need for improvements in fund utilization, infrastructure, staffing, data management, and programme monitoring.

title: Performance audit Union Government Agriculture Crop Insurance Schemes Reports of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
overview:
The CAG audit of the Union Government’s agricultural crop insurance schemes revealed significant weaknesses in financial management, implementation, and oversight for the period 2011-12 to 2015-16. Despite an expenditure of ₹32,606.65 crore towards premium subsidy and claim liabilities by the Centre and States, fund releases from several State governments were frequently delayed, impacting timely compensation to affected farmers and undermining the schemes' objectives (p. vi). For example, the Government of India released its share promptly, but delays by States like Andhra Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Maharashtra, and others led to deferred reimbursements (p. 9).

Coverage of intended beneficiaries remained low, with only 9.41 crore farmers insured and 2.96 crore receiving claims under NAIS in this five-year period. Notably, 97% of loanee farmers insured only up to their loan amount, indicating a lack of awareness or proper communication about full scheme benefits. The audit also found that databases of insured farmers were not maintained by central or state authorities, resulting in significant data integrity issues (p. vii).

Oversight and monitoring were significantly lacking. Technical Support Units were not established, periodic appraisals were not performed, and mandatory government audit over funds given to private insurance companies was lacking. Two-thirds of the farmers surveyed were unaware of the schemes, pointing to poor awareness. The cumulative effect of these shortcomings jeopardized both the efficacy and the credibility of India’s crop insurance initiatives (p. viii-ix).

title: Performance audit Union Government Electrification Projects Reports of Indian Railways
overview:
Indian Railways operates over a vast 66,687 Route Kilometers (RKM) network, carrying 22 million passengers daily and transporting over 1,000 million tonnes of freight annually. As of March 2016, 27,999 RKMs (42.4%) were electrified, with IR spending ₹23,699 crore on energy/fuel in 2015-16, of which 56% was on diesel and 44% on electricity. From 2011-12 to 2015-16, annual electrification ranged from 1,165 to 1,730 RKMs with annual expenditure rising from ₹678 crore to ₹1,668 crore.

Despite an improvement in the pace of electrification—1730 RKMs electrified in 2015-16 vs. 1165 in 2011-12—serious shortcomings were found. Delays were observed at every project stage: sending of abstract estimates to Railway Board took up to 59 months in 24 projects, whilst tender processing periods extended to a maximum of 3,177 days in some cases. There was no prioritisation of projects by expected financial or operational benefit, and cost overruns were common, with 14 projects seeing overruns between 2.02% and 76.62%. In 21 projects, ₹3,006 crore projected savings were not realised due to delays.

Further, utilitisation of electrified sections was sub-optimal, with 345 trains run using diesel traction on 15,286 RKM of electrified routes due to infrastructure and coordination issues. Mechanisms to penalise contractors for delays, such as levy of liquidated damages, were not effectively used: against leviable LD of ₹250.28 crore, only ₹0.93 crore was recovered in CORE projects. The report concludes that project execution, monitoring, and prioritisation need urgent strengthening to derive expected financial and social benefits.

title: Performance audit Union Government Credit Risk Management in IFCI Limited Reports of Ministry of Finance
overview:
The audit found sharp deterioration in IFCI Limited’s asset quality compared to the NBFC-ND-SI industry, with NPAs reaching ₹3544.54 crore (13.05% of total loans) as on 31 March 2016, significantly higher than the industry average of 3%. From 2012-13 to 2015-16, unrealized interest mounted by ₹40,638.98 crore, and principal written-off during the period was ₹1637.87 crore. Across 128 reviewed loan sanctions, 69 cases (54%) involved deviations from IFCI’s General Lending Policy, especially concerning minimum financial ratios, security cover, net worth requirements, and credit ratings.

The audit observed major non-compliance with RBI guidelines: asset classification errors resulted in overstated profits by ₹297.60 crore (2013-14 to 2015-16), and non-provisioning/short-provisioning against investments amounted to ₹734.31 crore (2014-15) and ₹706.17 crore (2015-16) despite clear signs of financial stress. In 11 NPA cases, loans worth ₹1235.65 crore were written off, including ₹674.51 crore of unrealized interest.

Deficient credit appraisal, acceptance of unenforceable security, and routine relaxation of laid-down lending criteria led to significant losses and doubtful recoveries, with Audit highlighting that 18 cases involved potentially unrecoverable exposure of ₹3799.33 crore. Equity investments in unquoted entities further compounded risk, with ₹1136.28 crore becoming non-performing due to buyback defaults. The audit concludes IFCI needs urgent improvements in appraisal, compliance, and recovery processes.

title: Performance audit on Catering Services Reports in Indian Railways, Union Government, Railways
overview:
The CAG's performance audit examines the adequacy and quality of catering services on Indian Railways, which carries about 22.21 million passengers per day and operates 7,216 stations across 66,687 route kilometers. Audit was conducted for 2013-14 to 2015-16, covering both departmental and IRCTC-managed units. Audit observed a persistent state of uncertainty and lack of accountability due to frequent policy changes, leading to gaps in catering infrastructure, notably in base kitchens, static catering units, and vending arrangements (page iii-iv).

Of 131 base kitchens audited, only 16 were located within railway premises, leaving 115 outside the premises and unsupervised. In joint inspections of 74 stations, Janta meals were missing at 46, highlighting poor coverage of affordable food for passengers. Furthermore, in 128 trains across seven Zonal Railways, meals were supplied from outside base kitchens, raising major quality and hygiene concerns (page vi).

The audit further uncovered issues in contract licensing, with a majority of the contract value paid as license fees to railways, leaving limited margin for service providers and risking quality compromises. Unauthorized vendors persisted, with 2,39,096 cases prosecuted in 2013-16, and reports of overcharging and substandard food continued despite complaint mechanisms. Audit recommends clear lines of accountability and effective enforcement to ensure affordable, quality food, and systematic policy implementation (pages v-vii).

title: Union Government Defence Performance Audit
overview:
The CAG Performance Audit of the Union Government Defence sector (Report No. 5 of 2017) evaluated procurement, inventory management, and fund utilisation for the period 2012-13 to 2015-16. The audit revealed critical lapses in timely procurement, with only 44 per cent of planned acquisitions executed within stipulated timelines, leading to persistent shortages of crucial military equipment. Significant under-utilisation and misallocation of budgeted funds were observed, with ₹22,023 crore pertaining to capital acquisitions unutilised as at March 2016 (page 12), severely impacting operational readiness.

The audit found recurring inefficiencies in the Inventory Management System. Of the 135 major contracts reviewed, 37 contracts worth ₹9,745 crore witnessed delays of over 24 months, affecting deployment schedules and operational preparedness. The audit further highlighted that 11 out of 24 procurement cases were processed without adequate threat assessment, resulting in mismatched prioritisation (page 23).

Overall, the Department of Defence failed to meet 39 per cent of its Modernisation Plan targets, with adverse consequences for force effectiveness, capacity building, and national security (page 28). The audit also observed poor documentation and lack of regular monitoring, leading to excessive inventory buildup valued at ₹13,215 crore that remained unused for over 30 months (page 33).

title: Performance Audit of Disaster Management in the State of Jammu and Kashmir Government of Jammu and Kashmir
overview:
The audit assessed disaster management activities in Jammu and Kashmir for the period 2010-11 to 2014-15, including the major events of the 2009 drought, 2010 Leh cloudburst, and 2014 floods. Audit revealed severe institutional gaps, notably that the State Disaster Management Authority, constituted in 2007, held only one meeting in six years and was not fully operational as of July 2016. The State Advisory Committee was never established, and no divisional authorities existed.

Financial management was poor, with Rs 1,571.35 crore available in the State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF), but substantial misuse, such as Rs 26.52 crore released for restoration without an official disaster declaration, and Rs 47.88 crore in the old Calamity Relief Fund lying idle resulting in a Rs 55.49 crore interest loss. Of the Rs 1,369.16 crore spent from the SDRF, significant amounts were disbursed without following eligibility norms and guidelines, leading to ineligible beneficiaries and delays of up to 60 months for drought relief.

Many disaster preparedness and risk reduction initiatives under government schemes were only partially executed. Only 68-81% of flood channel works were completed; major allocations like the Rs 20 lakh for risk mapping and Rs 2 crore for emergency operation centres remained unused or were diverted. 69% of trained rescue personnel were deployed to non-disaster administrative duties, compromising emergency response. Relief material worth crores was unutilized, and procurement bypassed established procedures. The audit underscores urgent institutional and operational reforms to ensure transparent, accountable disaster management.

title: Performance Audit Uttarakhand
overview:
The Performance Audit of Uttarakhand under the Rashtriya Madhyamik Shiksha Abhiyan (RMSA) highlighted major deficiencies in planning, fund utilisation, and achievement of core objectives aimed at enhancing access and quality in secondary education. Out of the total funds released (`167.14 crore), 53% (`88.33 crore) remained unutilised since the scheme’s inception, leading to the completion of only 25% of planned construction works in the state. This significant underutilisation deprived children of necessary infrastructure and directly impacted educational outcomes.

Additionally, the audit found that key basic amenities were missing from the majority of schools: 83% lacked activity rooms, 76% were without libraries, and 55% did not have a playground. Other severe gaps included the absence of computer rooms in 50% of schools, integrated science labs in 48%, and even classrooms and electricity in 14% of the surveyed institutions.

The audit concluded that the bottom-up planning approach was not followed, school-level planning was neglected, and funds provided for critical interventions such as vocational education and ICT remained unused. These findings indicate a high severity in lapses, resulting in serious consequences for universal access and retention targets set under RMSA, and undermining the scheme’s objectives of providing quality secondary education statewide.

title: Union Government (Defence Services–Army): Performance Audit on Working of Army Base Workshops
overview:
The audit reviewed Army Base Workshops (ABWs) responsible for overhauling essential equipment to maintain the operational readiness of the Indian Army. During 2010-11 to 2015-16, significant backlog in the overhaul of critical Class 'A' vehicles such as BMPs, ARV WZT-2, and Tank T-72 was observed. For instance, only 802 BMPs out of the total holding (2,412) were overhauled by 2015-16, keeping the backlog at 33% (802 units), and only 22 ARV WZT-2s overhauled out of 222, leaving 90% backlog. Tank T-72 backlog reduced from 713 to 479 units but still accounted for 20% of the fleet (page vi).

There were substantial delays in the overhaul process. The overhaul of BMPs, required to be completed in 153 days, took up to 1,512 days, while Tank T-72 overhauls extended up to 836 days against a norm of 144 days. On average, overhaul of each BMP engine took 308 days instead of the stipulated 30 days. Delays extended to signal equipment, with Radar overhauls taking up to 921 days (page vii).

Quality standards suffered, with the Quality Index (QI) for overhauled BMPs far below the prescribed 95: the highest QI recorded was between 70.28 and 77.4 in 2015-16. Additionally, many overhauled vehicles were issued to units without mandatory proof firing and amphibious testing due to lack of facilities. Cost accounting systems were absent, raising concerns about repair effectiveness and resource utilization. Non-availability of critical spares led to deviation sanctions impacting combat readiness (pages vii–viii).
