title: Commercial Civil Aviation Performance Audit
overview:
This Performance Audit reviewed the Turnaround Plan (TAP) and Financial Restructuring Plan (FRP) of Air India Limited for the period 2010-11 to 2015-16. The Government committed to infuse equity of ₹42,182 crore between 2011-12 and 2031-32, restructuring working capital loans of ₹22,157 crore, and targeted ₹5,000 crore from asset monetisation over ten years. However, actual equity releases were short in the initial years and monetisation of assets fell substantially short, leading to the working capital requirement exceeding approved limits and an increasing dependence on short term loans, further eroding financial stability. Operational performance of Air India lagged, with targets for aircraft utilisation, on-time performance, and employee rationalisation missed. For example, only two of six properties put for e-auction were sold, and narrow body aircraft leasing lagged behind requirements, compounding operational inefficiencies. Despite recovering fuel costs and achieving surplus over variable cost, the company consistently failed to recover total operational costs, recording a deficit of ₹5,514 crore in 2015-16. Challenges also included delays in technology integration and ongoing issues in human resources management. The audit concludes that without fast-tracked asset monetisation, cost rationalisation, and enhanced fleet, the turnaround goals remain unachieved.

Critically, the company incurred additional losses from uncompetitive aircraft sales, inefficient maintenance, underutilised rights in bilateral agreements, and poor slot management. Furthermore, promised equity infusions were not aligned to debt repayments, resulting in additional finance costs. Management’s slow implementation of HR reforms and IT systems contributed to excess staff costs and hindered operational efficiencies.

Overall, the audit found that AIL’s financial situation continued to be precarious. Major restructuring benefits were eroded, key milestones of TAP were not met, and significant government support was rendered less effective due to weak execution and persistent operational and financial inefficiencies.

title: Performance Audit Customs on Project Imports
overview:
The Performance Audit on Project Imports covered the period FY 2011-12 to FY 2015-16, examining 2,904 contracts across 24 Commissionerates, representing 24.58% of all project import contracts during this timeframe. There was a steep 49% decline in the number of registered contracts, from 264 in FY12 to 134 in FY16, and a corresponding revenue decrease by 40% over the same period, underlining waning industry interest and effectiveness of the scheme (Table 1, Figure 2, p.3).

Project Imports contributed less than 3% to total customs revenue during the audit period, with duty foregone amounting to ₹10,545.30 crore and the scheme's revenue implication identified at ₹1,822 crore, in addition to ₹203 crore in systemic losses due to regulatory ambiguities and weak controls (Figure 3, p.4; Executive Summary, p.vi).

Major deficiencies were found: ambiguous statutory provisions led to inconsistent application, under/over-assessments, and systemic risks, while 41% of selected files in key Commissionerates were not produced for audit (p.8). Delays up to 297 days in cargo clearance, significant transaction costs (5–14% of imports), lack of time-bound completion, absence of automated monitoring, and multiple sponsoring authorities allowed prolonged project finalisation or misuse of concessions (Executive Summary, pp.v-viii; Chapter 3, p.11).

title: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Performance Audit on Environmental Clearance and Post Clearance Monitoring
auditPeriod: 2011 to July 2015 (EC Grant Processes); 2008 to 2012 (Post Clearance Monitoring)
overview:
This performance audit examined the effectiveness, transparency, and procedural adherence in the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change's processes for granting Environmental Clearance (EC) and for monitoring compliance post-clearance between 2008 and 2015. The audit sampled 216 projects (2011–2015) for clearance processes and 352 projects (2008–2012) for compliance, revealing delays, data inconsistencies, and numerous instances of non-compliance. Delays in the grant of EC were observed in 89% of cases, with only 14% of projects receiving Terms of Reference (ToR) within the prescribed 60 days. For the actual EC grant, just 11% met the 105-day timeline mandated by procedure.

Furthermore, 25% of Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) reports did not comply with the prescribed ToR, and 23% failed the generic report structure, while cumulative impact assessment—a crucial ecological measure—was generally omitted. Non-compliance with general and specific EC conditions was widespread, impacting effectiveness of mitigation and rehabilitation measures for affected communities and the environment. Post-clearance monitoring was undermined by lack of manpower, procedural ambiguities, and gaps in data management across central, state, and regional bodies.

The consequences are significant: non-compliance in fulfilling Environment Management Plan activities occurred in up to 26% of projects, green belt development in 47%, and there were frequent unauthorized changes in project scope. Ministry, regional, and state pollution control authorities struggled with inadequate resources, poor data integrity, and absence of delegated enforcement powers, leaving environmental protections insufficient and undermining the legislative intent of India's foundational environmental laws.

title: Performance Audit Mizoram
overview:
The performance audit of Mizoram State Lotteries, covering 2010-11 to 2014-15, found significant procedural and financial lapses. Despite ₹11,834.22 crore of total sale proceeds from 2012-13 to 2014-15, only ₹25.45 crore (0.22%) was credited to the Consolidated Fund of the State, with the remaining ₹11,808.77 crore unaccounted for due to failure to demand and collect the face value of tickets as required by law. This led to immense revenue leakage.

The selection process for distributors ignored competitive bidding norms, leading to cartel formation, sub-letting of draws, and lack of real marketing activities by some appointed distributors. For instance, M/s N.V. International earned ₹4.57 crore by only subletting draws instead of actual operations. Further, online ticket sales had no effective control or verification; central computational servers were not under state oversight, risking manipulation and fraud.

Internal controls were weak and statutory records were not maintained. There was no verifiable evidence that lottery revenues were used for mandated social sector purposes like health and education. Additionally, printers were selected without tenders and security features on tickets were inadequate, further undermining accountability and transparency.

title: Union Performance Audit of Land Management in DDA
overview:
This performance audit covers the land management activities of the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) between 2010-11 and 2014-15. DDA is responsible for acquiring, developing, disposing, and protecting land for Delhi as per the Master Plan. The audit highlights severe lapses in planning and execution, citing delays of more than two years in finalizing zonal development plans, lack of consolidated land databases, and significant mismatches in records of acquired, utilized, and available land. Budget estimates for both receipts and expenditure were found unrealistic, with discrepancies of hundreds of crores in actuals versus projections.

In land acquisition, DDA received only 486 out of 2052 acres awarded in seven cases, risking lapse of 1566 acres under the 2013 Act. Delays ranged from 7 months to 8+ years for compensation, and even longer for transferring land to user departments. Land development activities were hampered by non-availability of clear sites and deficiency in project planning, resulting in delays of up to 17 years in commencement and up to 55 months in handing over completed projects.

On land disposal, DDA lacked any documented policy or centralized database. Institutional allotment processes were irregular, and in multiple cases land was allotted violating Nazul rules or at below-market prices. Post-allotment monitoring and protection of DDA land suffered from up to 31.77% shortfall in demolition programs and unreported encroachments. These systemic failures risk loss of public resources, revenue leakages, and leave large swathes of public land underutilized or encroached.

title: Union Performance Audit on ‘Fuel Management of Coal Based Power Stations of NTPC Ltd
overview:
This performance audit examines fuel management practices in 13 out of 26 coal-based power stations of NTPC Limited and its Joint Ventures for the period April 2010 to March 2016. Coal cost makes up 60-70% of the total generation tariff and is a major determinant of consumer power prices. The audit identified that NTPC faced critical fuel linkage gaps in certain stations, incurring extra costs of Rs 2,483.39 crore at three plants due to having to buy coal from more expensive sources. NTPC also entered into costlier Memoranda of Understanding and paid high premiums, with one agreement resulting in costs Rs 1,600.64 crore higher than FSA rates. Failures in timely signing of Fuel Supply Agreements (FSAs) led to significant extra expenditures (Rs 323.37 crore in 5 stations), and performance incentive payments that were above required levels by Rs 558 crore at 10 stations. Additionally, an absence of consistent import policy caused 75% of import contracts (over Rs 22,796.91 crore) to be awarded to a single vendor, Adani Enterprises Ltd.

Audit detected systemic weaknesses in measurement and billing of coal quality, wrongly indexed import pricing, inaccuracy in stock verification—some stations reported coal stock figures exceeding storage capacity by up to 114%. Inefficiencies in logistics led to heavy demurrage charges (Rs 129.67 crore), and shortages and quality measurement errors resulted in generation losses totalling 19,546.26 million units and potential revenue loss of Rs 4,299.80 crore between 2010-11 and 2015-16.

The report recommends urgent improvements in policy, procurement and inventory controls, and standardization of coal quality and billing measures to ensure affordable power and transparent accounting.

title: Performance Audit Power Union Govt
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Restructured Accelerated Power Development and Reforms Programme (R-APDRP) under the Union Government's Ministry of Power highlights chronic underutilisation of funds, delays in project completion, and inefficiencies in planning and monitoring. Out of an envisaged Gross Budgetary Support (GBS) of ₹28,424 crore for the XI and XII Plan periods (2008–17), only ₹12,415.04 crore was budgeted (43.68%) from 2008-09 to 2014-15, with actual releases amounting to just ₹8,175.45 crore, reflecting a slow pace of implementation and significant fund shortfall (Executive Summary, p. v; Chapter 3.1, p. 9).

Instances were noted of diversion of R-APDRP funds and overlapping with other schemes at State level, along with absence of evidence that counterpart funding was tied up in several States, further hampering progress. The audit flagged substantial mismatches where Utilisation Certificates indicated only ₹4,155.88 crore (49.29% of released funds) was actually utilised by March 2016, despite Power Finance Corporation reporting a disbursement of ₹8,606.62 crore (Executive Summary, p. vi).

Persistent lapses in programme implementation include only the first installment being released for hundreds of projects, repeated delays in baseline activity execution, and most States failing to complete the metering and baseline data collection required for effective loss reduction tracking. Failure to convert loans to grants was universal, as no projects met completion criteria. Weak monitoring and unreliable loss data raise serious questions about R-APDRP's actual impact.

title: Performance Audit on Allowance of deduction to the assessees Direct Tax Union Government
overview:
This performance audit covers the allowance of deduction to assessees engaged in infrastructure development under Section 80IA of the Income Tax Act, for financial years 2012-13 to 2014-15. The Comptroller and Auditor General found that the Income Tax Department (ITD) irregularly allowed deductions in 229 cases due to systemic deficiencies and lack of internal controls, leading to significant underassessment of income and revenue loss. For instance, unintended benefits of ₹2,716.79 crore in tax effect were noted, with deductions wrongly allowed to ineligible assessees (₹205.84 crore, 33 cases), businesses not specified under the Act (₹174.35 crore, 16 cases), and on infrastructure facilities developed for captive/private use (₹2,066.70 crore, 8 cases).

ITD failed to properly restrict deductions in cases where assessees did not meet eligibility criteria such as direct agreements with the government, being only contractors, or operating activities outside the scope of eligible infrastructure. The audit also found numerous instances of poor control over supporting documentation and the absence of systematic review by Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT), as 65 cases allowed deductions without verifying Form 10CCB. Additionally, 1,709 cases claimed ₹32,220 crore in deductions in FY 2012-13 alone, and up to 20.55% of audit-requested records were not produced, compromising transparency.

No mechanism exists in CBDT to assess the impact of revenue forgone on industrial growth, and there is a lack of analytical information to ensure tax holidays are cost-effective. The audit’s findings suggest these systemic weaknesses contribute to persistent gaps, revenue leakage, and ambiguities that encourage litigation, undermining the intended benefits of the tax incentives.

title: Performance Audit Government of Manipur – Functioning of Industrial Training Institutes
overview:
This Performance Audit reviews the functioning of 11 Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) in Manipur between 2010-11 and 2014-15, highlighting major lapses in infrastructure, planning, financial management, and training outcomes. The audit reveals that only 63% of targeted road length and 71% of targeted habitations were covered, while the ITIs themselves suffered from significant shortfalls in infrastructure, tools, equipment, and skilled instructors, leading to high dropout rates and declining enrolment.

Serious financial management weaknesses were identified, including funds idling in civil deposits, poor utilisation of maintenance grants, and documented misappropriation and leakage of funds. Rural and Social Sector schemes were often underperforming, as seen by unutilized programme fund balances ranging from ₹0.68 crore to ₹176.37 crore during 2010-15, as well as 39% of routine road maintenance works left unattended despite available maintenance funds of ₹4.79 crore.

At the institutional level, lack of basic amenities (such as drinking water, toilets, hostels, and library facilities), outdated or missing equipment, and poor record-keeping adversely affected training quality and job prospects for trainees. Many trades could not achieve National Council of Vocational Training (NCVT) affiliation, and dropout rates rose from 24.75% to 29.40% over the audit period. There was little evidence of effective monitoring or corrective action taken by authorities.

title: Report of 2016 - Performance Audit Government of Goa
overview:
This Performance Audit of the Government of Goa covers significant findings in Social, General, Economic, and Revenue Sectors, as well as State Public Sector Undertakings for the period 2012-13 to 2014-15. The report highlights that the State’s total expenditure increased from ₹7,347 crore in 2012-13 to ₹9,013 crore in 2014-15, with revenue expenditure constituting 82% of total expenditure and capital expenditure at 18%. Annual average growth was 11% for revenue expenditure compared to 16% for revenue receipts. Major findings include delays in procurement across hospitals leading to excess expenditure of ₹1.30 crore, unutilised equipment valued at ₹4.35 crore and ₹2.59 crore, and large-scale local purchases of medicines entailing extra expenditure of ₹16.22 crore due to delays and non-tendering.

The audit found persistent staff shortages in Goa Medical College, with a patient-nurse ratio of 5.6:1 compared to the required 3:1. In the Revenue sector, short recovery of mining revenue, stamp duty, VAT, and other taxes amounted to hundreds of crores, including a loss of ₹173.56 crore due to non-collection of Goa Rural Improvement and Welfare Cess on iron ore. Public investments were found to be idle or ineffective, with instances such as ₹8.10 crore spent on unused bus stand construction and ₹0.63 crore on an unapproachable foot-bridge.

The consequences include significant loss of public funds, unutilised infrastructure, inability to deliver public services efficiently, and failure to adhere to basic procurement and audit response procedures. The delays and inefficiencies also prevented the realisation of intended benefits from modernisation and capital investments in health, transport, and industrial projects.

title: Performance Audit on Empowerment of Women Government of Uttar Pradesh
overview:
This performance audit reviewed 11 major government schemes aimed at empowering women in Uttar Pradesh between 2010-11 and 2014-15. The State lagged significantly in gender equality indicators: sex ratio stood at 908 females per 1,000 males (Census 2011), and maternal mortality was 292 per one lakh live births, almost three times the UN Millennium Development Goal (109).

Fund utilisation remained low across schemes: only 54% of allocated funds for Pre-Conception and Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques Act implementation were spent, and just 11% of MTP funds were used. In supplementary nutrition programs, 22-32% of eligible pregnant women and children were excluded from benefits, and in vocational training for adolescent girls, achievements fell short by 87%.

These gaps resulted in persistent high rates of undernutrition (42% of children underweight) and rising crime against women (61% increase from 2010-11 to 2014-15). Poor infrastructure, lack of data, and ineffective monitoring compounded the issue; 76% fewer inspections of ultrasound centres than required were conducted, leaving 58% of such centres breaching mandatory provisions unpunished.

title: Performance Audit of Environmental Degradation Government of Assam
overview:
The Performance Audit focused on environmental degradation in greater Guwahati, covering pollution control, waste management, and the oversight role of the Pollution Control Board, Assam (PCBA). The audit period was 2010-2015. PCBA received total funds of ₹107.81 crore but spent only ₹70.60 crore during 2010-15, leaving consistently high unspent balances rising from ₹35.89 crore to ₹61.80 crore, even while critical environmental monitoring and enforcement remained weak. Administrative spending made up 80.38% to 94.38%, while direct pollution control expenditure never exceeded 5% annually, and technical manpower was disproportionally low compared to non-technical staff: 88 technical versus 130 non-technical (Appendix I).

The audit found that 68-84% of mandatory industry inspections were not conducted. Only 24 of 55 water polluting parameters were monitored, and station classification required for water quality management under NWMP was neglected. Key water bodies showed extreme pollution, e.g., Bharalu river's Dissolved Oxygen, BOD and Coliform levels were far beyond criteria: 'no aquatic organism can survive' (page vii). There was no sewage treatment plant statewide, resulting in untreated effluent release. 76% of hazardous waste-generating industries lacked PCBA authorization, while major lapses in air, solid waste, biomedical waste, plastic, battery, and e-waste regulations persisted.

Consequences include risk to drinking water and public health, unchecked industrial pollution, hazardous waste mismanagement, and threats to eco-sensitive sites such as Deepor Beel. The audit concluded high risk of environmental crisis due to regulatory gaps, poor enforcement, and unutilized resources.

title: Report 23 of 2016 - Performance Audit on Ministry of Rural Development Union Civil
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) evaluated 4,417 packages in 176 districts across 29 states involving expenditure of ₹7,734.93 crore between April 2010 and March 2015. The audit assessed rural road connectivity improvement, fund management, implementation, and quality control mechanisms.

Up to March 2015, out of 1.78 lakh eligible habitations, 1.09 lakh were provided all-weather connectivity, leaving 0.69 lakh habitations pending. In 26 states, 4,496 works were delayed by periods ranging from one to 129 months, largely due to land disputes, lack of clearances, and material shortages. Instances of inefficient contract management, misallocation and diversion of funds, and inadequate maintenance were widespread. Notably, ₹280.01 crore was spent on 372 works that were abandoned or proposed to be abandoned mid-way.

Quality and monitoring mechanisms were found deficient; in 12 states, irregularities in field laboratories, manpower deployment, and testing were observed. The Online Management, Monitoring and Accounting System (OMMAS) remained unreliable, with basic data updating requirements unmet and lack of validation controls leading to incorrect entries. The audit stresses systemic issues in planning, execution, financial management, and oversight, risking achievement of the scheme’s rural connectivity goals.

title: Union Railways Performance Audit Suburban Train Services
overview:
This performance audit of suburban train services in Indian Railways found that approximately 40 lakh passengers travelled without tickets during 2012-15, resulting in total fines of ₹127 crore being imposed (Table 25, p.36). Despite transporting over 450 crore passengers annually in suburban sections, significant deficiencies in passenger amenities and cleanliness were observed across the network. Contracts for mechanized cleaning were awarded to only 95 out of 578 suburban stations (16%), and it was noted that platforms, coaches, and station areas often remained dirty, with some cleaning being conducted manually in violation of contracted terms. There was inadequate provision of booking counters, with shortfalls at 51 inspected stations, and lack of access to Automatic Ticket Vending Machines (ATVMs) at 13 key locations. At 112 of 153 checked stations, platform shelters were not fully compliant, leaving substantial areas uncovered and causing passenger discomfort.

The absence of efficient ticketing and basic infrastructure, including insufficient toilets (with gents’ toilets missing at 5 stations and ladies’ at 32 stations, as per prescribed norms), continues to hinder passenger satisfaction. These operational and amenity deficits are especially concerning given the Public Accounts Committee's prior recommendations and the commitment made by the Ministry to upgrade 'Adarsh' suburban stations. Poor execution of mechanized cleaning contributed to unsanitary conditions, and, in cases where contracts were in place, non-enforcement of penalty clauses allowed quality issues to persist.

Consequently, the audit concludes that the Ministry of Railways' measures have been neither effective nor adequate to address operational losses, improve cleanliness and amenities, or enhance the overall suburban train passenger experience. The mounting losses (exacerbated by heavily subsidized season tickets and operational inefficiencies) remain a critical concern affecting the financial health and service quality of Indian Railways’ suburban segment.

title: Performance Audit on Voluntary Compliance Encouragement Scheme 2013-Union Indirect Taxes–Service Tax
overview:
The Performance Audit reviewed the implementation of the Voluntary Compliance Encouragement Scheme (VCES) 2013, which targeted the substantial gap between registered service tax assessees (17 lakh) and those filing returns (about 7 lakh). Despite aiming to capture up to 10 lakh non/stop filers, only 66,072 declarations totaling ₹7,750 crore were received, far short of projections. Just 22% of declarations were from new registrations, indicating limited success in broadening the tax base.

Significant design deficiencies and non-compliance were observed. Basic checks on the veracity of self-declared tax arrears were not performed and Board clarifications diluted eligibility criteria, leading to unintended benefits of at least ₹129.84 crore in 332 cases. In 444 cases, eligibility criteria were not properly verified, involving tax dues of ₹85.97 crore.

Post-VCES monitoring was weak: in 15 commissionerates, only 62% of required returns were filed after the scheme, with little departmental action against non-filers. Payments in 78 rejected cases (₹23.02 crore) were unrecovered, and the Ministry often cited 'lack of time' for procedural gaps. Amnesty granted without adequate documentation or validation undermined policy intent and future deterrence.

title: Union Ministry of Finance Public Debt Management Performance Audit
overview:
This report examines the management of public debt by the Ministry of Finance during 2009-10 to 2014-15. As on 31 March 2015, India's total outstanding public debt was ₹51,04,675 crore, of which 92.82% was internal debt and 7.18% was external debt. Notably, in 2014-15, 77% of long-term internal borrowings and 73% of external borrowings were utilized for debt servicing, leaving a diminished share for developmental expenditure—a core reason for incurring debt in the first place (p. iii).

The audit highlights shortcomings in strategic and organizational frameworks. There was no legal definition of 'Public Debt', nor were objectives, purposes, or mandatory strategies for public debt stipulated by law. The recommended Public Debt Management Agency (PDMA) was not set up, and the Middle Office (MO), which was to formulate strategy and conduct risk analysis, did not fulfill these roles. For external debt, no entity undertook risk analysis or monitoring of strategic targets (p. iv, v).

Significant variations were found between budgeted and actual external borrowings (ranging from -33% to 225%, p. vi), and the absence of a centralized debt database along with inconsistent debt figures in official reports point to systemic issues in debt reporting and transparency. The audit concludes the legal framework and information systems require urgent strengthening to ensure a robust, accountable public debt management system.

title: Union Civil Performance Audit: Implementation of Passport Seva Project
overview:
This performance audit critically examines the implementation of the Passport Seva Project (PSP) of the Ministry of External Affairs, covering the period from its inception in June 2012 to August 2015. Despite technological upgrades and service reforms, delivery of passport services remained delayed across multiple stages. The average police verification time at the national level in 2014 stood at 42 days against the prescribed 21 days limit, and only 21% of normal passports were issued within the intended three-day window. In RPO Delhi, total issuance time, including appointment and police processes, averaged 52 days, much higher than the target of 24 days.

Critical operational hurdles were observed: 48% of pending police verification reports exceeded the mandated 21 days, and in seven states pendency exceeded 100 days. There was lack of data transparency regarding dispatched passports, with the status of 27.38 lakh passports unaccounted for post-dispatch. The Ministry also left 25% of citizen grievances unaddressed by year-end, with 41% pending over 60 days.

In addition to operational deficiencies, governance weaknesses and inconsistencies in the Master Service Agreement (MSA) were noted. Payments to the Service Provider based on outdated Service Level metrics were unjustified post-system changes; key project oversight committees were often dormant, allowing deviation without documentation or approval. Financially, the project collected Rs 78.46 crore in appointment fees from applicants who never appeared, with no refund system in place.

title: Union Revenue Performance Audit Indirect Taxes Customs
overview:
The Performance Audit on Gems and Jewellery (G&J) sector (Chapter 71 of CTH) covered the period 2010-11 to 2014-15, examining imports and exports valued at ₹3,50,396 crore in 2010-11 rising to ₹3,81,515 crore in 2014-15 (9% growth). The export of similar goods rose by 28% to ₹2,53,940 crore in 2014-15. The audit scrutinised 21,245 bills of entry and 13,143 shipping bills selected from 3,26,012 and 11,55,362 transactions, respectively, and reviewed policies such as the 20:80 gold import scheme, its impact on trade, and control measures.

The report found a persistent trade deficit in the G&J sector: from 43% in FY11 to 34% in FY15, but with the share of customs duties foregone increasing from 14% to 20% of the value of imports. In 2014-15, G&J's share in total imports was 13.93% and in exports 13.39%. Despite large values, export growth at 0.7% in 2014-15 was far below the targeted 25%, and the DoC had to revise targets downward by 30%.

Major systemic lapses included lack of robust outcome analysis for schemes, insufficient coordination across agencies, poor data quality, an increase in trade mis-invoicing leading to illicit outflows (estimated at $83 billion USD in 2013), and incomplete implementation of recommended IT systems. The audit has a direct revenue implication of ₹1,003.37 crore in addition to systemic and internal control lapses potentially affecting ₹19,522.67 crore.

title: Performance Audit Report on Sikkim State Lotteries 2015-16
overview:
The Sikkim State Lotteries audit covered operations between 2010-2016, revealing significant lapses in transparency, revenue management, and compliance. During this period, the state organised 44,834 draws through three Marketing Agents (MAs), but appointment practices lacked consistency, often bypassing competitive tendering. The report notes that against a total sale proceeds of Rs 44,834.87 crore, only Rs 628.74 crore (1.40%) was deposited into the government account, with the state retaining a mere 0.40% of revenues.

Numerous procedural gaps were found, including the use of non-transparent methods (Random Number Generators) for online draws, failure to independently verify ticket sales, delayed deposits of prize money, and repeated litigations due to extension of contracts and failure to issue mandatory notifications. These led to a financial loss of Rs 13.52 crore due to suspension of paper lotteries between July 2015 and June 2016.

Internal controls were weak, with the Directorate lacking ICT expertise and relying entirely on MAs for scheme design, software, and server location (servers were operated outside Sikkim, violating statutory requirements). Annual financial and systems audits mandated by the Lottery Rules, 2010 were not conducted. The audit concludes that the MAs were the main beneficiaries, with minimal benefit accruing to the state and its stated welfare objectives.

Establish robust internal controls and independent verification systems for ticket sales and prize payments.

title: Report No. 52 of 2015-Performance Audit on Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme, Union Government-Ministy of Textiles
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) under the Ministry of Textiles critically assessed the planning, implementation, and monitoring of the scheme, which disbursed a substantial subsidy amounting to ₹18,580.45 crore from April 1999 to March 2014. Despite an enhanced plan allocation of ₹15,404 crore during the XI Five Year Plan, the scheme fell short of its investment target by ₹19,372 crore, with only ₹1,31,228 crore invested against a target of ₹1,50,600 crore (p.15).

There were critical lapses in the management of baseline data and beneficiary records, with the Ministry lacking segment-wise data of committed liabilities and modernization benchmarks. Audit found unreliable estimates for committed liabilities, resulting in scheme suspension between June 2010 and April 2011 due to budget exhaustion. Significant implementation failures included extending subsidy to ineligible beneficiaries (₹46.96 crore in 129 cases, six states), ineligible investments (₹52.87 crore in 193 cases, seven states), and excess payments (₹6.42 crore in 40 cases) (p.vi). Additionally, delayed subsidy credits affected 172 beneficiaries, with delays spanning from 1 to 1,509 days (p.vi).

Monitoring mechanisms were found insufficient, with minimal oversight of FI claim scrutiny, lapses by the Inter-Ministerial Steering Committee and Technical Advisory cum Monitoring Committee, and instances where projects sanctioned during the Black Out period were incorrectly included for subsidy. The audit emphasizes the need for segment-wise monitoring, robust due diligence, and improved data management to ensure efficient scheme delivery and accountability.

title: Performance Audit on Tribal Sub-Plan, Ministry of Human Resource Development, Ministry of Health & Family Welfare and Ministry of AYUSH
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Tribal Sub-Plan (TSP) covers financial and implementation aspects related to education and health sector schemes run by the Ministry of Human Resource Development, Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, and Ministry of AYUSH. The audit found that a total of ₹64,399.73 crore was allocated by 28 central ministries and departments for TSP from 2011-12 to 2013-14. However, funds earmarked at the central level were not appropriately channeled or utilized at the state or district level, leading to severe gaps in delivery and support for tribal beneficiaries.

Specifically, there was a short release of TSP funds of ₹13,138.05 crore across major schemes, with utilization certificates received for consolidated amounts rather than component-wise detail, making actual fund use unascertainable. The audit also identified improper earmarking and cases where TSP funds were released to states without Scheduled Tribe population, totaling ₹326.21 crore, and to tribal-majority states where TSP was not applicable, amounting to ₹706.87 crore.

Implementation issues included deficient infrastructure in sample districts, lack of basic amenities for health care and education, non-functioning or non-establishment of model schools, and inadequate monitoring. Only two out of 28 ministries/departments furnished quarterly progress reports, highlighting poor oversight and evaluation. The audit concludes the overall effectiveness of TSP was significantly weakened due to governance, planning, and financial management deficiencies and recommends a restructured framework to ensure tribal communities receive their entitled benefits. title: Performance Audit on Procurement and Milling of Paddy for the Central Pool Union Government, Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution
overview:
The Government of India’s food subsidy for rice procurement under TPDS has increased continuously, standing at ₹89,740 crore as on 31 March 2014. Despite rice millers carrying out operations at milling charges fixed in 2005, the realization value of by-products saw substantial growth, resulting in excess net realization of ₹3,743 crore by millers in Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Telangana, and Uttar Pradesh, which represented only 15.81% of total procurement; national figures are likely much higher. Audit revealed widespread irregularities in procurement incidentals, such as ₹194.23 crore undue benefit given to millers via unjustified Mandi Labour Charges (MLC) reimbursement, particularly in Bihar, Odisha, and Andhra Pradesh. An additional driage allowance of 1% for moisture, originally demanded only by Punjab millers, resulted in further avoidable subsidy outgo of ₹952.37 crore to millers between 2009-10 and 2013-14.

Serious lapses were found regarding authentication of farmers' identities and MSP payments: payments totaling ₹17,985.49 crore lacked assurance on reaching legitimate farmers, raising risks of diversion. Quality standards were also not enforced effectively—82.46 LMT of substandard paddy worth ₹9,788.50 crore was procured in Punjab, yet full payment was made. There were significant losses due to non-delivery of paddy or rice: 39.23 LMT (valuing ₹7,570.78 crore) was not delivered by millers across six states, with no collateral security to recover losses. Irregularities in transportation and allocation of charges were noted, with ₹163.72 crore paid to Punjab millers for transport wrongly, and 5,744.09 MT falsely depicted as transported via doubtful means in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Chhattisgarh, indicating fraudulent claims.

The audit calls for urgent intervention on fixing incidentals, strengthening verification, enforcing collateral security, and updating procedures to safeguard public funds and ensure benefits reach intended stakeholders. These deficiencies contribute to avoidable food subsidy expenditure and benefit intermediaries over genuine farmers or consumers.

title: Performance Audit on Sanitation Campaign /Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan for the year ended March 2014 Union Government, Ministry of Drinking Water and Sanitation
overview:
This performance audit covers Total Sanitation Campaign (TSC) and Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan (NBA) in rural India for the period 2009-10 to 2013-14. Despite over ₹13,494.63 crore available for sanitation schemes, only ₹10,157.93 crore (between 44% and 59% annually) was spent, leaving substantial amounts unutilized—ranging from ₹918.18 crore in 2009-10 to ₹2,450.52 crore in 2013-14. Approximately 52% coverage of household toilets for Below Poverty Line (BPL) families and 44% for Above Poverty Line (APL) was achieved, against targets of 426.32 lakh and 469.76 lakh, respectively.

The audit found that planning failures were critical: in 73 districts (49% sample), Gram Panchayat plans were not consolidated to block/district level and Annual Implementation Plans lacked GP-wise allocations and a community saturation approach. Over-reporting and inflated achievement data are significant, with actual toilets functional far less than claimed; in 53 districts across eight States, more than 33% of toilets (24.03 lakh of 71.86 lakh surveyed households) were defunct due to poor construction, incomplete structures, and lack of maintenance.

Serious financial irregularities were noted: fund diversion totaling ₹283.12 crore, suspected misappropriation in Andhra Pradesh, Jharkhand, and Manipur, advances worth ₹48.97 crore outstanding up to 120 months, and parked scheme funds of ₹212.14 crore remaining unutilized for months at state, district, block, or GP levels. A lack of effective monitoring and failure to cross-check Integrated Management Information System data led to over-reporting and ineffective programme oversight. The audit concludes that without realistic planning, effective IEC and convergence, and improved governance, resources alone will not yield desired sanitation outcomes.

title: Performance Audit on Medical Education Projects of Employees State Insurance Corporation Union Government, Ministry of Labour and Employment
overview:
The Performance Audit covered ESIC's Medical Education Projects between 2008-09 and 2014-15, examining a sanctioned expenditure of ₹1021.72 crore across 17 of 21 medical education projects prior to legal amendment—this comprised over 10% of total programme value and was spent without explicit administrative or financial approval from the Ministry of Labour and Employment, violating financial prudence (p. v, 6).

Site selection was arbitrary, with feasibility studies lacking consideration of costs, staffing needs, and future requirements. Of 21 projects, 6 were constructed where the minimum norm of insured persons was not met, directly contradicting Standing Committee recommendations. Cost overruns were significant, with total project costs rising from ₹8611.94 crore to ₹11997.15 crore—a 39% increase, resulting in an excess of ₹3385.21 crore (p. vi, 11).

As of 2015, only 14% of Post Graduate Institute graduates joined ESIC hospitals, indicating that the primary objective of filling vacancies was not met. Extensive delays plagued almost all projects except two. In December 2014, the Corporation decided to exit the medical education sector, declaring its efforts 'ineffective' (p. vi).

title: Performance Audit on Status of Ongoing Projects Union Government, Railways
overview:
This performance audit examined the status of 442 ongoing projects in Indian Railways as of March 2014, comprising New Lines, Doubling, and Gauge Conversion works. As per the report, the revised estimated cost of these projects soared to ₹2,62,478 crore, marking a significant 68.72% increase from the initial estimation of ₹1,55,570 crore. The anticipated amount required to complete the balance works, or throw-forward, stood at ₹1,85,559 crore.

A critical finding was that targets for completion were set for only 156 projects (35%), and even among these, there were time overruns of up to 16 years, resulting in a cost overrun of ₹1.07 lakh crore. Alarmingly, 75 projects had been ongoing for more than 15 years, while 82 projects claimed 100% physical progress but still required ₹10,832 crore for completion. Only 236 projects achieved the required 14% benchmark rate of return, with 126 posting negative returns, further questioning the viability of such investments.

The audit highlighted systemic deficiencies such as poor planning, inadequate fund allocation, and major delays in both physical and financial execution. These inefficiencies resulted in huge financial commitments and blocked resources, hampering the timely delivery of critical railway infrastructure across the country, and indicating a high risk level for the sector's current project management practices.

title: Performance Audit on Crew Management System Union Government, Railways
overview:
The Crew Management System (CMS) was introduced in Indian Railways to manage assignments and ensure efficiency in crew operations, with a targeted implementation across 747 lobbies/locations by 2010 at a cost of ₹80 crore. However, by 31st March 2015, it was operational in only 372 lobbies, indicating incomplete rollout and significant delays. The audit found that non-updation and improper feeding of crew master data, family details, routes, and railway assets led to unreliable inventory and ineffective monitoring, defeating the purpose of CMS (paras 2.1.1-2.1.8, p. viii).

Major issues include the use of manual parallel records due to incorrect CMS reports, 21,136,799 kms of wrong mileage allowance computation, and non-implementation of crucial security devices like Biometric and Breath Analyser at most locations (paras 2.2.1, 2.5.1, and 2.4.10, p. ix). Weak application controls resulted in payment of allowances for zero duty hours and other irregularities. Delayed project implementation was attributed to poor planning, lack of trained personnel, and failure to integrate CMS effectively with other applications such as COA and FOIS (para 5.1, p. ix-x).

As a result, CMS failed to achieve its original objectives of paperless working, improved crew deployment, and robust financial controls. Persistent deficiencies in IT security, backup policies, and absence of formal change management procedures further compromised the effectiveness and reliability of the system across Indian Railways.

title: Performance Audit on Public Private Partnership Projects in Major Ports, Union Government, Ministry of Shipping
overview:
The audit reviewed Public Private Partnership (PPP) projects in India's 12 Major Ports, as these ports, transacting over 95% of India's international trade, were in urgent need of modernization and private investment. Out of 91 PPP projects with a planned capacity addition of 751.71 MMTPA and an estimated cost of ₹63,712.95 crore approved by March 2014, only 35 projects (38%) were completed by the cutoff, contributing 264.69 MMTPA. This represented just 33% of total major port capacity. Additionally, 27 projects were under construction, and 27 were still in the pipeline or bidding stage, while two were terminated or dropped (p. v, Executive Summary).

Implementation issues plagued the sector. For example, in the flagship Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust project, flaws in the royalty structure left the operator with diminishing net revenue—royalty per TEU rose from ₹47 in 1999-2000 to ₹2670 by 2014-15, making the project unviable and prompting a shift toward revenue sharing after 18 years. Audit also found ₹467.95 crore in port revenues not shared due to poor contract structuring and lack of standardization in the pre-MCA concession agreements (p. v-vi, Executive Summary; p. 9, Chapter 2).

Overall, significant delays characterized 35 of 39 projects in tendering, mainly due to protracted tender finalizations, security clearances, and legal disputes. Further, ports often failed to fulfill their committed actions (handing over sites, providing draught facilities), resulting in additional complications and delays. Even after project completion, at least four projects with a total capacity of 25.7 MMTPA were not yet operational as of June 2015 (p. 6-7, Chapter 2). The audit concluded that the PPP implementation failed to deliver the planned improvements and benefits, and that revenue realization and monitoring mechanisms remain considerably weak.

title: Performance Audit on Capacity Utilisation, Electricity Generation, Sale and Collection of Revenue including Disaster Management by Hydro Power CPSEs, Union Government, Ministry of Power
overview:
This performance audit reviewed the operational efficiency, revenue management, and disaster preparedness of four major hydro power Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs)—NHPC, SJVN, THDC, and NHDC—which together accounted for a 23.72% share of national hydro generation capacity. The audit, covering FY 2009-10 to FY 2013-14, highlighted significant underutilization of design capacities, systemic delays in reservoir management, and shortfalls in compliance with disaster management protocols. Outstanding revenue collections were high, with Rs 4,112.49 crore remaining unrecovered from five major beneficiaries as of March 2015, and NHPC allowed Rs 60.48 crore in rebates to entities not eligible per the prescribed policy.

Technical inefficiencies included capacity utilization factor (CUF) shortfalls at multiple NHPC stations, including a 44.65 percentage point deficit at Chutak and persistent forced outages adding up to 9,871 hours during the monsoon. Reservoir desilting practices and maintenance of adequate reservoir levels did not align with CWC guidelines, resulting in reduced gross and live capacities at several stations, with direct repercussions for flood and sedimentation management. Revenue concerns were compounded by poor compliance in the opening and maintenance of Letters of Credit (LCs) by power purchasers and the absence of effective recovery mechanisms for recurring dues.

Disaster management preparedness was also inadequate: audit found most stations' disaster plans out of sync with updated CWC directives, lack of dam break Emergency Action Plans, and insufficient frequency of plan reviews or mock drills. Severe damages at Dhauliganga and Tanakpur stations during the 2013 Uttarakhand floods were attributed to failures in operational and warning protocols. The audit recommends both ministerial and CPSE-specific reforms for operational, financial, and disaster risk improvements.

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Ex-servicemen Contributory Health Scheme, Union Government, Defence Services - Army
overview:
The audit analyzed the implementation of the Ex-servicemen Contributory Health Scheme (ECHS) covering over 47.24 lakh beneficiaries (ex-servicemen and their dependents) as of April 2015. The CAG reviewed funding, enrollment, medicine procurement, empanelled facility management, bill processing, and other vital operations for the period 2012-13 to 2014-15.

Substantial deficiencies were observed in critical areas. Notably, `47.84 crore was irregularly collected from beneficiaries for smart cards, contrary to MoD's set guidelines. Medicine shortages were rampant, with non-issue rates from Mumbai AFMSD ranging from 63% to 76%. There was also substantial diversion of ECHS funds and medical stores, amounting to `40.78 crore, for the treatment of regular service personnel rather than ECHS beneficiaries.

These deficiencies resulted in inflated healthcare costs, increased risk of fraud, and compromised service delivery. Overpayments such as `3.51 crore for inflated bills, inadequate monitoring of emergency referrals, and lack of post-audit controls weakened scheme oversight, leaving many ex-servicemen underserved or financially disadvantaged.

title: Report No. 46 of 2015 - Performance Audit on Working of Automation of Central Excise and Service Tax Union Government, Department of Revenue - Indirect Taxes
overview: The Performance Audit assessed the effectiveness and utilisation of the Automation of Central Excise and Service Tax (ACES) as launched by the Central Board of Excise and Customs. Covering 40 selected Commissionerates and over 740 field divisions, the audit analysed system design, module utilisation, compliance, and resultant impact on taxpayer services and internal processes. ACES aimed to streamline indirect tax administration, reduce manual interventions, and facilitate prompt, transparent taxpayer interaction through web-based modules. However, significant gaps were found: only 11.1 lakh Registration Certificates were issued out of 14.3 lakh online applications till June 2014, marking a persistent backlog. Audit highlighted that only three of ten modules—Access Control, Registration, and Return—were being regularly used, with low/partial uptake of Refund, Export, Provisional Assessment, and Dispute Resolution modules. Lapses included the inability to upload/attach documents digitally, absence of digital signature, incomplete mapping of user roles (especially for legal and adjudication functions), and lack of Inspector-level access, all undermining the stated goals of automation. The audit concluded that full business process re-engineering remained unachieved due to design and implementation challenges, directly affecting accountability and efficiency in central excise and service tax management.

title: Performance Audit on Mid Day Meal Union Government, Ministry of Human Resource Development
overview:
The audit revealed that despite significant budget allocations, the implementation of the Mid Day Meal Scheme (MDM) suffered persistent issues across 27 states and 7 UTs. Total budgeted expenditure over five years was ₹47,721.01 crore, with actual expenditure only ₹43,714.78 crore, leaving ₹4,006.23 crore unspent. Enrolment in MDM covered schools dropped from 14.69 crore children in 2009-10 to 13.87 crore in 2013-14, while private school enrolment rose by 38%, indicating the scheme's limited impact on retention. Widespread financial indiscipline and leakage were identified, with inflated reporting of beneficiaries, diversion and theft of foodgrains, and submission of exaggerated transportation and utilization claims. Fund utilization delays, absence of regular health checks, and insufficient infrastructure such as kitchen sheds were highlighted, exposing children to health hazards and often resulting in substandard meals.

Key monitoring and evaluation mechanisms remained weak, with Steering and Monitoring Committees seldom meeting and Management, Monitoring and Evaluation (MME) funds underutilized. In Delhi alone, 89% of meal samples failed nutritional standards. Critically, actions on Public Accounts Committee recommendations were found to be largely unaddressed by both the Ministry and States, perpetuating audit findings from previous cycles and undermining the scheme's intended impact both nutritionally and educationally.

As a result, the Audit recommends urgent strengthening of the data collection, inspection, infrastructure provisioning, and governance mechanisms—in addition to a periodic revision of cooking costs and more flexible, locally-adapted nutritional models. Serious attention to transparency and accountability remains vital for any meaningful improvement in outcomes and the safeguarding of public resources.

title: Performance Audit on Construction activities in Central Armed Police Forces Union Government, Ministry of Home Affairs
overview: The performance audit covers construction activities for office and residential infrastructure in Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) under the Ministry of Home Affairs, evaluating budget utilization, land acquisition, transparency of agency selection, cost overruns, and asset maintenance. Against an authorised requirement of 2.99 lakh dwelling units, only 1.54 lakh units were available for personnel, and for 5113 office buildings, merely 2041 existed by March 2014 (Executive Summary, p. vi). Budget allocation between 2008-09 and 2013-14 was ₹12483.7 crore, with ₹12043.90 crore incurred, but significant delays and inefficiencies persisted, including land acquisition delays of up to 9.7 years in 56 out of 132 cases, and inflated preliminary estimates by ₹14.22 crore (p. vi-vii). Satisfaction levels for residential accommodation remained critically low, between 2.96% and 22.48% against a 25% target (p. vi). Financial irregularities were recorded, with mobilisation advances totalling ₹87.64 crore lacking proper accounts, and excess payments of ₹6.42 crore. Construction project delays resulted in total cost overruns of ₹148.05 crore with savings miscalculated at ₹289.08 crore due to errors in plinth area calculations, modification of drawings, and other planning lapses (p. vii-viii). Asset quality assurance and monitoring were inadequate, with no formal mechanisms established for most works and poor quality observed at physical sites.

title: Performance Audit on Levy and Collection of Service Tax on Works Contract Union Government, Department of Revenue - Indirect Taxes, Service Tax
overview:
This performance audit evaluated the effectiveness of the indirect tax administration in safeguarding revenue interests concerning Works Contract Services, covering the years 2010-11 to 2013-14. The audit examined 33 selected Commissionerates, reviewing records for 237 assessees, revealing important systemic and compliance gaps.

Key findings include discovery of 425 works contractors who were neither registered nor paid service tax, resulting in an uncollected revenue of ₹447.76 crore. There were delays in filing returns across 1857 cases under 17 Commissionerates, with late fees amounting to ₹1.70 crore. Additionally, 145 cases of non/short-payment of service tax totaling ₹44.74 crore and 34 instances of irregular Cenvat credit utilization (₹22.59 crore) were noted.

The audit further identified incorrect exemptions, improper application of service tax rates, and inadequate monitoring mechanisms, exposing total compliance/collection failures amounting to ₹543.46 crore. Consequences include substantial revenue leakage, weak enforcement against defaulters, and recommendation for mandatory inter-department data sharing and stricter compliance monitoring.

title: Performance Audit on Union Government, Railways
overview:
The CAG audit of Union Government (Railways) covers Fire Accidents in Passenger Coaches and the Distribution and Utilization of safety items over Indian Railways for the years 2011-12 to 2013-14. Indian Railways aimed at an 80% reduction in fire accidents by 2013 as per its Corporate Safety Plan, but instead the number of accidents actually increased by 160% from 5 in 2001-02 to 8 each in 2012-13 and 2013-14. The loss of human lives in fire accidents escalated from 3 in 2001-02 to 35 in 2013-14, highlighting a serious failure in safety measures (Page 1).

Audit found significant deficiencies in the adoption and upgrading of fire retardant materials; RDSO lacked modern testing facilities and delayed implementing new international safety standards (EN-45545). Procurement bottlenecks persisted as only 2-4 sources for critical materials were approved and production units faced delays, affecting coach maintenance and safety. Extensive survey and joint inspections in 1280 coaches across multiple depots and stations revealed persistent non-compliance with Railway Board instructions: junction boxes in SLRs were not shifted, bottom latches on doors remained, and emergency equipment like glass breaking hammers was missing in several coaches (Pages 6-12).

Fire-prone activities remained unchecked at stations and in trains. Inadequate monitoring led to cigarette sales, cooking on platforms, carriage of inflammables, and faulty exhaust systems, increasing fire risk. Audit detected insufficient passenger awareness programs, absence of fire safety notices, and lack of emergency contact lists at stations. Furthermore, communication gaps persisted; fire stations were unavailable in the neighborhood of 16 stations, and direct train crew communications were lacking at six Metro stations. Overall, the audit concludes that Indian Railways failed to achieve zero tolerance goals and urgent steps are needed to address the gaps in fire safety (Page 1-3).

title: Performance Audit on Hydrocarbon Exploration Efforts of Oil India Limited, Union Government, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas
overview:
This performance audit by the CAG scrutinizes Oil India Limited's (OIL) exploration efforts vis-à-vis the national Hydrocarbon Vision 2025. The audit covers 2009-10 to 2013-14 and found several systemic and operational shortcomings. For instance, OIL's accretion of hydrocarbon reserves lagged significantly—oil reserves under the highest confidence category (1P, proved) decreased, and gas reserves in all categories fell. OIL failed to meet reserve accretion targets in Rajasthan, achieving only 59% of its target.

OIL's survey and drilling operations were marked by inefficiencies: 75% of examined outsourced survey contracts overran schedule by 1 to 20 months, and the company consistently failed to meet its own drilling and survey goals. Drilling rig utilization suffered due to aged equipment, with Non-Productive Time (NPT) hitting 39% for own rigs by 2013-14—well above the ONGC benchmark of <10%. The audit also highlights organizational issues including delays in contract award, weak internal audit independence, and underinvestment in R&D.

The consequences are declining Reserve Replacement Ratio (from 1.84 in 2009-10 to 1.31 in 2013-14), unexplored or underutilized blocks, and foregone revenues. These gaps threaten both OIL's and the country's long-term energy security, necessitating urgent structural and policy action to align exploration activities with strategic national goals.

title: Performance Audit on Utilisation of Rigs in Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited, Union Government, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas
overview:
This performance audit examined ONGC's planning, acquisition, deployment, and maintenance of rigs from 2010-11 to 2013-14, encompassing both onland and offshore operations. Drilling activities made up between 42.92% and 58.40% of ONGC's total expenditure during this period, with total outlay rising from ₹28,275.54 crore in 2010-11 to ₹32,470 crore in 2013-14. Despite these significant investments, the audit uncovered that planned targets for exploratory drilling fell consistently short: only 674 exploratory wells were drilled versus 620 planned in four years, while actual rig months achieved were also typically below plan.

Critical inefficiencies were built into planning processes, as Rig Requirement Plans (RRPs) included up to 28% non-productive time (NPT) — much above the global norm of 12%. Of this NPT, between 86.26% and 93.89% in western offshore areas was controllable but went unaddressed, resulting in high opportunity costs. Acquisition and hiring of rigs suffered severe delays (up to 508 days in tender finalisation), leading to the loss of 391 rig-months, and in offshore areas, ₹517 crore was charged off for rigs being out of cycle, of which ₹403 crore pertained to owned rigs alone.

The audit found major governance and operational lapses, including: (i) relaxation of bid evaluation criteria post-bidding, leading to acceptance of non-compliant rigs and further rig month losses; (ii) inadequate long-term acquisition planning, with four of six owned offshore rigs surpassing their economic lives while major new procurements remained pending over a decade; and (iii) persistent issues of rigs and facilities idling, causing deferred production estimated at ₹4,003 crore for oil and ₹1,174 crore for gas. Ineffective maintenance and outdated equipment, with repair delays of up to 48 months and post-repair performance not improving, further aggravated operational inefficiency.

Set separate cycle and commercial speed targets for onland and offshore rigs, and monitor performance against appropriate benchmarks.
Ensure maintenance policies and cost-benefit analyses for old rigs are based on realistic efficiency assumptions and prior experience.

title: Performance Audit on Land Management in Major Ports, Union Government, Ministry of Shipping
overview:
This performance audit assessed clarity and implementation of land management guidelines in 12 major ports under the Ministry of Shipping, covering land holdings totalling 77,191.14 acres as of March 2014. A critical finding was that out of the total, title deeds were not available for 34,943.41 acres, representing 45.27% of port land, and six ports lacked title deeds for their entire holdings. Revenue impacts included delayed lease rent revisions and approvals, with Kandla Port Trust unable to recover ₹132.55 crore of ₹192.09 crore due to deferred SoR approvals, leading to significant financial losses to the exchequer.

Audit also revealed inconsistent application and ambiguity in policy updates, especially with legacy cases involving permanent structures and lack of definitions for 'unauthorized occupancy' or 'end use'. The absence of regular updates and digitization of land records resulted in discrepancies with state records and under-reporting of encroachments: 396.44 acres vs just 273.98 acres officially reported.

In terms of compliance and operational effectiveness, most ports failed to update land use plans every five years as required; only Cochin Port Trust initiated GIS-based land management, while others have not computerized land administration. Recommendations urge the Ministry to clarify and consolidate policies, define all critical terms, and institutionalize regular reviews for effective land governance.

title: Report No. 34 of 2015 - Performance Audit on Renewable Energy Sector in India Union Government, Ministry of New and Renewable Energy
overview: India's renewable energy (RE) sector saw installed capacity rise from 3,475 MW in April 2002 to 31,719 MW by March 2014, but this represented only a fraction of the sector's potential—0.35% of solar and 21% of wind by 2014. Significant underutilization was seen in high-potential states, with sectoral exploitation rates ranging from 0% to 68%, and some projects not being commissioned after public resources were allocated. Financial bottlenecks, lack of robust monitoring, policy inconsistencies, and insufficient transmission and maintenance infrastructure constrained rollout and impact. As of March 2014, against the National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) RE target of eight-nine percent for 2012-13/2013-14, only 4.28% and 4.51% achievement was recorded nationally. Over 93 lakh Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs), each valued at minimum ₹1,500, were lying unredeemed by August 2014, affecting generator cash flow. Across off-grid programmes, physical audit revealed 47% of systems were non-functional. The Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh initiatives faced implementation delays and planning flaws, with sanctioned hydel and off-grid projects often incomplete or wrongly targeted despite ₹358.46 crore spend in Arunachal alone. The CAG noted systemic weaknesses in project selection, land allotment, and post-commissioning maintenance, resulting in decades-long schedule overruns, idle assets, and unfulfilled rural electrification objectives.

title: Performance Audit on Functioning of Internal Audit in Income Tax Department Union Government, Department of Revenue - Direct Tax
overview: This performance audit reviewed the Internal Audit functioning within the Income Tax Department (ITD), covering assessment and accounting activities from 2010 to 2014. The audit evaluated effectiveness, compliance, and adequacy of follow-up mechanisms for audit findings. Key observations include substantial shortfall in cases covered: Internal Audit examined only 5,73,457 out of 7,00,398 cases assigned—a deficit of 1,26,941 cases. Delays in remedial action initiation were found in 6,172 cases, and completion delays in 1,640 cases, spanning across 13 and 10 regions, respectively. There were instances where audit objections—73 cases involving a tax effect of ₹134.10 crore—were settled without proper reply or remedial action. Poor follow-up led to time bar of 1,553 cases, worth ₹392.65 crore, resulting in unrecovered or misaddressed tax. Furthermore, as of March 2014, 24,313 audit objections (10,960 major and 13,353 minor) remained unsettled, with significant manpower shortages hampering audit effectiveness. Audit also highlighted that only 24.65% of required units under Pr. CCA, CBDT were actually audited, with 75.35% left unaudited and settlement rates for audit paras remained low. Revisions and new ITD technologies were introduced post-audit, but gaps in planning, risk targeting, and resource deployment persisted. The report calls for urgent improvements to planning, risk-based selection, manpower allocation, and centralised monitoring to enhance effectiveness and prevent loss to the exchequer.

title: Performance Audit on Modernisation and Expansion Plan in Steel Authority of India Limited Union Government, Commercial
overview:
The Performance Audit assessed the Modernisation and Expansion Plan in Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL), with a planned investment of ₹61,870 crore across five integrated steel plants. As of March 2014, ₹55,952 crore had been expended, representing 90.5% of the sanctioned estimate, yet only partial completion was achieved, with several units facing significant delays, cost overruns, and non-achievement of capacity. The Bokaro and Rourkela plants, for instance, were delayed by 36 and 32 months, respectively, leading to cumulative interest during construction of ₹8,077 crore.

The audit revealed serious deficiencies in project planning and execution. Delays in land acquisition and environmental clearances, as well as tardy performance by contractors, led to incremental costs and target shortfalls. Many units did not achieve designed capacity utilisation; the overall crude steel capacity rose by only 32% against the planned 65%. Procurement issues and non-integrated project sequencing also directly impacted outcomes, with the Durgapur and Burnpur units operating below 50% of new capacities post-commissioning.

The consequences are significant on financial and operational fronts. The delays and cost escalations contributed to SAIL's profit falling from ₹6,754 crore in 2008-09 to ₹2,616 crore in 2013-14. The company's failure to realise expected returns on investment and efficiency gains has undermined its competitive positioning. The audit concludes there were systemic weaknesses in internal controls, monitoring, and strategic project management.

title: Performance Audit on Union Government, Ministry of Power
overview:
Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) aimed to add 6250 MW capacity during the XI Plan, with a specific target of 4700 MW via its own projects and 1550 MW through joint ventures. However, up to March 2014, only 1025 MW was commissioned, resulting in a significant shortfall of 5225 MW against the original target. The audit covers all DVC activities, including X Plan spillover and XI Plan projects, examining all major contracts, performance, and coal linkage issues.

Key findings reveal substantial delays (up to 58 months) in commissioning multiple units due to inadequate project preparation, failure to secure land and infrastructure before contract award, and poor coal block development. Cost overruns were considerable, with five completed units and one unit in advanced stage costing ₹4615 crore (35%) above estimates, and three units under execution costing ₹2696 crore (42%) higher than approved cost. Furthermore, the Corporation lost the opportunity to earn additional return on equity amounting to ₹1011.73 crore.

Due to these inefficiencies, significant capacity (39% of new units, 33% of upcoming units) was left unallocated, leading to surplus power. There were also avoidable losses—non-recovery of fixed costs of ₹476.66 crore from underperformance and excess auxiliary/oil consumption losses totaling ₹108.94 crore—stemming from forced outages and inefficient unit operation.

title: Performance Audit on PSUs of Government of Uttar Pradesh
overview:
This audit report details the performance and financial standing of 126 Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) in Uttar Pradesh as of 31 March 2014, including 87 working PSUs and 39 non-working PSUs. The working PSUs registered a turnover of ₹65,683.38 crore but incurred an overall aggregate loss of ₹12,223.08 crore. Government investment in these PSUs swelled to ₹1,56,906.28 crore—a 296.53% increase since 2008-09—with 95.76% directed towards the power sector alone.

The performance of the PSUs is alarming: only 28 working PSUs posted profits totaling ₹1,315.03 crore, while 27 recorded losses amounting to ₹13,538.11 crore. Major losses stemmed from power distribution companies such as Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited (₹3,479.32 crore) and Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited (₹3,364.06 crore). Furthermore, the audit points out significant operational inefficiencies, including excess and avoidable expenditure, huge arrears in finalisation of accounts (83 PSUs had 274 accounts pending as of September 2014), and substantial shortfalls in collection, billing, and internal controls.

The consequences of inefficiencies and prolonged delays in settlements include controllable losses of ₹339.80 crore and infructuous investments of ₹47 lakh. The audit also highlights instances of undue favor to contractors (₹21.60 crore), violation of statutory obligations (₹21.93 crore), and short payment/retention of government dues. The report calls for urgent corrective action to improve governance, accounting quality, and strategic oversight of state PSUs.

title: Report No. 2 of 2015 - Performance Audit on Public Sector Undertakings of Government of Madhya Pradesh
overview:
The Performance Audit examines the financial management, operational efficiency, and compliance issues among Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) in Madhya Pradesh. The consolidated investments in 51 PSUs amounted to ₹14,581 crore while State government loans amounted to ₹2,879 crore as on March 2014. During the period 2010-11 to 2013-14, income from these PSUs totalled ₹16,499 crore, but net profits were only ₹349 crore, indicating poor financial returns.

Out of the 51 PSUs, only 19 achieved profit, while 26 reported losses. The accumulated losses reached ₹8,243 crore (over 56% of capital), negatively impacting State finances. For example, the AKVN (AKVN Indore) failed to collect a transfer fee of ₹1.08 crore and exceeded estimated civil works costs by ₹62.90 crore, raising concerns about mismanagement.

Overall, the Audit found lapses in fund utilization, planning, and transparency. Delays in project completion and non-realization of revenue directly reduced State returns and hindered effective management of public resources.

title: Performance Audit on Economic (Non-PSUs) Sector of Government of Madhya Pradesh
overview:
This report details significant findings from four performance audits and 11 transaction audits across Madhya Pradesh's Economic (Non-PSUs) sector for the year ended 31 March 2014. During 2013-14, the state incurred a total expenditure of ₹85,762 crore, up from ₹79,920 crore the previous year, with revenue expenditure constituting 81% and a marked 10.96% rise over 2012-13, indicating heavy reliance on revenue spending. However, key resource planning failures and lapses are observed: for instance, poor survey and investigation standards resulted in a 19.54% to 486.54% spike in project volumes and a cost escalation of ₹52.36 crore for medium irrigation projects.

Critical inefficiencies in wildlife conservation planning led to delays in buffer area notification and insufficient protection, with commercial activities in core areas negatively impacting wildlife and habitat, and Tiger Conservation Plans were not prepared. In the Public Works Department, road renewals suffered from costlier specifications, improper bitumen accounting, and missing technical oversight, causing an extra cost of ₹29.77 crore and ₹105.26 crore paid for bituminous works without proper vouchers.

Subsidy distribution under the Animal Husbandry Department was mismanaged, with 4,672 beneficiaries not receiving animals despite ₹6.53 crore released, and 456 beneficiaries withdrawing funds without purchases. Persistent and pervasive irregularities, embezzlement, non-compliance, and delays in liquidated damages and compensation imposition highlighted a systemic erosion of accountability and oversight, emphasizing the need for corrective action.

title: Performance Audit on Public Sector Undertakings of Government of Bihar
overview:
The Performance Audit examines the functioning of 71 State Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) in Bihar, assessing their financial management, profitability, and governance for the period 2009-14. During this period, the invested capital increased from ₹9,279.85 crore as on 31 March 2010 to ₹18,303.62 crore as on 31 March 2014, but overall returns remained well below expectations, with several units incurring persistent losses.

Notably, out of 26 working PSUs, 17 incurred cumulative losses amounting to ₹2,367.22 crore as of March 2014, severely affecting state finances and raising concerns of sustainability. The report highlights deficiencies in statutory compliance, lack of timely finalisation of accounts, and weak internal controls, resulting in delays and unauthorised expenditures.

The consequences of these inefficiencies impact public accountability and undermine the effectiveness of PSUs in leveraging public investments for social and economic development. The audit flags urgent need for strategic interventions to strengthen institutional controls and enhance financial discipline.

title: Performance Audit on Social Sector (Non PSUs) of Government of Delhi
overview:
This CAG report provides a comprehensive performance audit of social, general and economic sectors (excluding PSUs) under the Government of NCT of Delhi for the year ending 31 March 2014. Total state expenditure increased from ₹24,319.45 crore in 2009-10 to ₹32,726.31 crore in 2013-14, while revenue expenditure rose by 60.9% over the same period. However, capital expenditure remained stagnant, and there were persistent savings of up to 20% in key welfare-related grants.

Major findings include underperformance in critical schemes such as the Mid-Day Meal Scheme, where only 1,154 out of 18,000 eligible children in EGS/AIE centres were covered in 2013-14. Test results revealed that 89% of sampled meals failed nutritional guidelines. In welfare schemes for persons with disabilities, Asha Kiran Complex was severely overcrowded, accommodating 970 inmates against a capacity of 350, while academic staff shortages exceeded 50% in special schools.

Additionally, there was evidence of delayed fund releases from both the Centre and State Government, with substantial portions not reaching implementing agencies in a timely fashion, undermining service delivery in sanitation, MLALADS, and infrastructure development. This has resulted in inefficient fund utilization, asset creation backlogs, and avoidable/costly delays to the detriment of Delhi citizens.

title: Performance Audit on Revenue Sector and Social, General and Economic Sector (PSUs) of Government of Delhi
overview:
The audit of Revenue Sector and Social, General and Economic Sector (PSUs) of Government of Delhi for the year 2013-14 unveiled significant shortfalls in tax collection and systemic lapses in revenue administration, as well as underperformance in utilisation of allocated funds. Total revenue receipts during the year amounted to ₹31,139 crore, against the budget estimates of ₹34,716 crore, thus showing a shortfall of ₹3,577 crore (10%) [Page 2].

The audit observed widespread deficiencies in internal controls, assessment, and realisation of tax revenue in the departments of Trade and Taxes, State Excise, Stamps and Registration Fees, and Transport. Specific examples included non-levy of penalty in 126 cases resulting in loss of revenue of ₹26.92 crore, and non/short demand of stamp duty and registration fee amounting to ₹23.89 crore [Page 6, 61]. There was also significant unutilised grants amounting to ₹1,379 crore as of March 2014, indicating inefficiency in implementation of budgeted schemes [Page 9].

Such gaps have had direct consequences on Delhi's ability to provide timely public services and infrastructure. Persistent deficiencies led to revenue leakage, delayed development projects, and lower than anticipated returns from public sector undertakings. The report concludes that unless prompt corrective action is taken, public confidence and delivery of key government programmes will continue to suffer.
