title: Performance Audit on Social, Economic, Revenue and Economic (SPSUs) Sectors of Government of Arunachal Pradesh
overview:
The Performance Audit covers the implementation of key social sector schemes in Arunachal Pradesh during 2009-14, with a primary focus on Total Sanitation Campaign (TSC)/Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan (NBA) and the Mid-Day Meal (MDM) Scheme. Significant underutilisation and mismanagement of funds were observed across sectors. For the TSC/NBA, persistent underutilisation of funds was detected, with diversion and delays in fund transfer, non-existent revolving funds, and Rs 293.13 lakh imposed as additional financial burden because targets were not met on time. In the sample districts alone, Rs 183.76 lakh worth of sanitary materials lay idle and unused.

The audit also noted that critical infrastructure like individual household latrines (IHHLs) became defunct shortly after construction, and coverage targets remained unachieved in all eight sampled districts. Key project components—such as production centres, solid and liquid waste management, and information-education-communication (IEC) outreach—were either delayed or poorly executed. Additionally, state-level monitoring and cross-verification by officials was almost absent through the period, compounding implementation shortcomings.

In the MDM scheme, while all government schools were covered, there were substantial gaps: food grain allocations were short-lifted by 785.35 MT, leading to a shortfall of over 47,000 meals. Infrastructure for meal preparation and safe water access lagged severely behind targets—87% of test-checked schools lacked pucca kitchen sheds and 99% were without gas-based chullahs. Delays in fund release and non-contribution of the state share also hampered effectiveness, further evidencing systemic issues within the social sector programme execution.

title: Performance audit on Conservation and Ecological restoration of Lakes under the jurisdiction of Lake Development, Government of Karnataka
overview:
The Performance Audit evaluated the conservation and ecological restoration of 56 lakes under the jurisdiction of the Lake Development Authority (LDA), Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), and associated departments in Karnataka. The audit covered activities between 2009 and 2014 and revealed major weaknesses in institutional mechanisms, planning, and coordination. Key findings included the LDA's inactivity due to lack of statutory powers and skeletal staffing, with no region-wise branches or effective environmental planning executed by the authority. Financial management was fragmented and uncoordinated among entities, resulting in ad hoc restoration works and poor prioritization or impact assessment. Of note, BBMP, BDA, LDA, and two City Corporations collectively spent ₹234.87 crore on 238 lakes as of March 2014, with no comprehensive budget or utilization plan.

Survey and demarcation of the test-checked lakes remained incomplete, leading to encroachments, loss of lake area, and discrepancies in official records. The KSPCB monitored pollution in only 120 out of 36,568 lakes statewide and did not have complete water quality data or levy penalties effectively on polluters. Restoration efforts were undermined by untreated sewage inflow, construction of sewage diversion channels lacking coordination, and excessive de-silting without justification. The water quality in none of the selected lakes met prescribed standards as of the audit.

Community participation and transparency were minimal: no lake management committees existed for any test-checked lakes, and grievance redressal mechanisms were absent. Only partial information on lake works and custodians was available to the public. Damage to biodiversity, loss of water spread area, and lack of buffer zones were reported in the majority of lakes. The overall severity of findings was rated 'high' due to critical institutional, financial, and ecological lapses.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on General and Social Sector of Government of Rajasthan
overview:
The audit covered the performance and compliance of various sectors, examining fund utilization, targeting and delivery of benefits, and systemic efficiency across flagship programmes and general administration. For instance, the audit noted that out of ₹2,624.13 crore of central funds released for key social sector schemes, only ₹1,168.15 crore (44.54 per cent) was utilized, reflecting serious lapses in implementation and financial management (p.12, Executive Summary).

Key headline findings include significant backlog in construction works sanctioned under various schemes, lack of proper identification and selection of beneficiaries, and prolonged retention of unspent balances. Moreover, the report highlighted that more than 1.25 lakh intended beneficiaries remained unreached due to implementation gaps and poor monitoring frameworks (p.23, Chapter II §2.3).

These systemic weaknesses had compounding consequences, such as delayed project completion, undermined public trust, persistent social deprivation, and compromised fiscal discipline. The persistent under-utilization and misallocation of resources adversely affected the state’s ability to deliver critical social services, especially to the most vulnerable communities.

title: Report No. 1 of 2015 - Compliance and Performance Audit of Government of Pondicherry
overview:
Paragraph 1: The audit covered compliance and performance of the Pondicherry government for the period 2013-14 to 2014-15, highlighting significant lapses in implementation of schemes and utilization of public funds. Out of the total available grants of ₹3,292 crore, only ₹1,534 crore was actually utilized during the audit period, reflecting a marked underutilization of resources. The report pinpointed that, of ₹538 crore allocated for specific central sector schemes, nearly ₹222 crore remained unspent by the close of the review period (page 5).

Paragraph 2: Key audit findings noted major procedural lapses, frequent delays in project execution, and systemic non-compliance with statutory guidelines. For example, 38% of sampled beneficiary records lacked proper documentation or supporting evidence (page 24). Delays in tendering processes contributed to cost overruns amounting to ₹54 crore (page 27). Additionally, physical verification of assets funded by the government revealed that 17% of claimed assets did not exist or were incomplete at site inspection (page 31).

Paragraph 3: The consequences of these failures included idling of funds, incomplete infrastructure projects, and compromised public services, particularly in health and education sectors. The performance shortfall not only impeded intended outcomes but also reduced the credibility of central assistance programmes. The audit strongly advised institution of robust monitoring mechanisms and accountability frameworks to rectify and prevent recurrence of such lapses.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Social, Economic, Revenue and General Sectors of Government of Nagaland
overview:
This comprehensive performance audit highlights major shortfalls and financial irregularities across multiple social sector schemes in Nagaland. For the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM), there was chronic underutilisation and delay in fund releases, with only ₹53.20 crore released against committed financial assurances of ₹61.65 crore from 2009-14. Facility and household surveys were not properly conducted, compromising needs assessment and planning for health infrastructure. Essential activities such as community participation and baseline surveys were either incomplete or not undertaken, affecting targeted service delivery.

Audit found misuse and diversion of funds in several cases. The Health Department provided undue benefit of ₹10.25 crore to a local contractor for MRI setup, and diverted ₹8.76 crore meant for infrastructure to recurring salary expenditure and other unvouched spending, with supporting documentation missing. There were also major procurement irregularities—₹1.03 crore was spent by bypassing approved suppliers, and there was a shortfall of medicines and equipment worth ₹1.53 crore in district hospitals and subordinate health units. Central Store, NRHM, Kohima also recorded equipment shortfall worth ₹1.66 crore.

Similar structural deficiencies marred the Total Sanitation Campaign, with continued open defecation even in awardee villages, poor maintenance and non-functional toilets in schools and Anganwadis, and widespread lack of awareness and community engagement. Departmental monitoring and follow-up on audit recommendations remained weak, and social audits were not held in any test-checked villages. The overall impact was significant loss of efficiency and intended benefit delivery for key rural welfare schemes.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Revenue Sector of Government of Odisha
overview:
This report covers significant performance and compliance audits for the year ended March 2014 on the Revenue Sector of the Government of Odisha, comprising Commercial Tax, Excise, Revenue and Disaster Management, Transport, and Steel and Mines Departments. During 2013-14, Government of Odisha's total revenue receipts reached ₹48,946.85 crore, up from ₹43,936.91 crore the previous year. Of this, ₹16,891.59 crore (51.63%) was tax revenue and ₹8,378.60 crore (17.12%) was non-tax revenue, with the balance received from the Government of India. Major audit findings highlight a cumulative under-assessment and short levy amounting to ₹4,713.63 crore in 5,10,147 cases, alongside two performance audits on VAT regime and e-registration system.

Key financial lapses included unverified input tax credits of ₹2,247.38 crore by 26,511 dealers under the Odisha VAT Act, non-levy of mandatory penalties totaling ₹11.76 crore under CST Act, and delayed action on penalty and interest provisions for Entry Tax. The mining sector, excise duty, and motor vehicle revenue categories revealed unrealised dues exceeding ₹33 crore, systematic short-levies of royalties, and inefficiencies in tax assessments. Notably, delays and irregularities in e-registration subjected citizens to undue user charges, and critical system gaps risked fraudulent property registration.

These deficiencies reflect persistent operational and compliance issues in tax administration, road safety enforcement, and mining receipt collection—resulting in substantial revenue loss and increased risks of evasion, misappropriation, and public inconvenience. Recommendations include rigorous scrutiny to prevent fraud, timely penalty imposition, and adopting robust process mapping and IT controls.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on General and Social Sector of Government of Maharashtra
overview:
The audit report for General and Social Sector of Maharashtra highlights significant deficiencies in implementation across various departments. It notes a decline in child sex ratio from 913 in 2001 to 894 in 2011 and reveals that the Maharashtra State Child Protection Society (MSCPS) did not formulate state child protection plans for 2012-13 and 2013-14, despite a recorded fall in child sex ratio in 31 out of 35 districts. The audit detected major gaps in nutritional schemes, with 34% underweight girls in the tribal district of Nandurbar and 79% malnourished girl deaths between 2010-14. Financial assistance for victims of rape and acid attack under the Manodhairya Scheme was delayed due to lack of funds, and biometric attendance systems in children homes—despite `1.97 crore investment—were not operational, risking bogus reporting and fund leakage.

SARVA SHIKSHA ABHIYAN implementation suffered institutional shortcomings. Although the RTE Act came into effect in April 2010, rules for seat reservations in private schools were notified only in May 2012. Shortfalls in teacher numbers persisted, with a 63% vacancy rate under SSA at March 2014. A gap in tracking out-of-school children was evident: Women & Child Development Department identified 2.30 lakh, while School Education & Sports Department reported only 0.20 lakh. Delays in textbook and uniform distribution, deficiencies in school infrastructure, and poor reservation seat admissions were also noted.

Transaction audits highlighted improper contract awards (Rs 18.47 crore to Maharashtra Knowledge Corporation Ltd without tenders, p.99), avoidable hospital expenses due to non-installation of capacitors (Rs 85.12 lakh, p.98), and infrastructure failures like Maharashtra Jeevan Pradhikaran’s water supply scheme: 13 years’ delay and Rs 25.39 crore spent with zero benefit to villages (p.105). As of June 2014, 7722 Inspection Reports remained outstanding, and delays in Action Taken Notes on PAC recommendations (340/378 outstanding, see p.9) pointed to low departmental responsiveness.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Economic Sector of Government of Maharashtra
overview:
This performance audit report covers the economic sector departments of the Government of Maharashtra for the year ended March 2014. Major risks and compliance failures were examined in 226 units, with findings based on a test audit consuming 1,880 party-days. The audit investigated fund flows, project execution, and management controls in large infrastructure programmes, particularly Public Works Department (PWD), Water Resources, Industries, Energy, and Labour.

Significant findings include suspected misappropriation of government money and fictitious payments, notably in PWD Nagpur, where Rs 42 lakh was booked without supporting vouchers and Rs 1.41 lakh paid in advance as fictitious wages. In addition, delays in project completion, inadequate feasibility studies, and severe deficiencies in quality control plagued five PPP road and bridge projects, affecting both economic viability and public infrastructure outcomes.

The Maharashtra Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Board failed to register and cover its target population, disbursing only a fraction of cess receipts for workers’ welfare. Meanwhile, the Water Resources Department’s Mechanical Organisation was found ineffective, with poor internal controls, old machinery, and extensive outsourcing defeating the agency's purpose. Overall, Rs 1.39 crore in unwarranted insurance payments and Rs 10.15 crore in overpayments highlight substantial financial mismanagement in multiple departments.

title: Performance Audit on Public Sector Undertakings of Government of Maharashtra
overview:
The audit covered 87 State Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs), including 83 Government companies and four Statutory corporations operating in key sectors such as power, finance, infrastructure, manufacturing, and agriculture. As of 31 March 2014, total investments in these PSUs amounted to ₹97,137.39 crore—a substantial 105.5% growth from ₹47,268.03 crore in 2008-09, primarily driven by power sector investments (accounting for 88.53% of total PSU investment).

Despite a turnover of ₹77,462.56 crore in 2013-14—representing 5.25% of the State's GDP—these PSUs continued to struggle with profitability and operational inefficiencies. Overall, working PSUs earned an aggregate profit of ₹1,973.15 crore in 2013-14, but accumulated losses stood at ₹8,665.45 crore. Notably, 51 working PSUs were in arrears with 116 sets of accounts as of September 2014, and 22 non-working companies saw minimal progress, with two under liquidation and several years of unfinalized accounts.

Audit findings revealed critical governance gaps, delays in project implementation, and inadequacies in toll collection and monitoring, leading to significant revenue shortfalls. Losses due to non-commencement or premature closure of toll stations, deficient IT systems in statutory bodies, and recurring procurement issues further hampered financial and operational performance. These lapses resulted in avoidable costs, uncollected revenues, and unsafeguarded interests, indicating high-severity challenges that risk public resources and transparency.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Revenue Sector of Government of Meghalaya
overview:
This CAG report covers the audit of the Revenue Sector in Meghalaya for the year ending March 2014, highlighting significant deficiencies and irregularities across tax and non-tax revenue administration. The total money value of issues documented in the audit is ₹165.82 crore. During 2013-14, state-raised revenue was ₹1,547.44 crore, which comprised 24.69% of the state’s total revenue receipts, showing a significant reliance on central devolutions. Test checks in multiple revenue departments revealed under-assessments, short/non-levies, and other revenue losses totaling ₹598.25 crore across 283 cases. Departments accepted under-assessed or unrealized revenue totaling ₹439.19 crore but managed to recover only ₹0.34 crore.

The audit found substantial weaknesses in key processes. Arrears of revenue as of March 2014 stood at ₹98.16 crore, with ₹54.67 crore pending for more than five years—56% of the arrears—signaling systemic issues in revenue recovery. Large numbers of sales tax assessment cases remain unresolved, with only 18% of 51,626 cases disposed of in 2013-14, resulting in persistent backlogs and possible future revenue losses. There is also evidence of tax evasion, non-registration, improper claims, and a lack of timely departmental response to audit observations.

Other highlights include non-realisation and short-levy of various duties and taxes, such as unregistered mining leases leading to forfeited stamp duty (₹0.09 crore), loss of state excise revenue due to production norm violations (₹10.15 crore), and uncollected cess on mineral exports (₹0.78 crore). The audit's overarching conclusion is a need for robust internal controls, more responsive departmental action, and focused follow-up on outstanding audit issues to safeguard and enhance state revenues.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Revenue Sector of Government of Himachal Pradesh
overview:
The audit focused on the Revenue Sector covering taxes on sales, trade, goods, and stamp duties for Himachal Pradesh. The report highlighted substantial shortfalls in revenue collection, with ₹91.95 crore not realised due to non-levy and short levy of taxes as noted across various departments (page 3).

A major finding was underutilisation and poor monitoring of collection mechanisms, leading to delays and irregularities in the assessment and recovery processes. Recoveries observed during audit were only ₹23.56 crore, representing just 25% of identified dues (page 6). Additionally, there were widespread procedural lapses including irregular grant of exemptions, incorrect application of rates, and lack of system integration between collection agencies (page 9).

These deficiencies led to loss of government revenue, impeded effective tax administration, and created systemic risks by enabling avenues for evasion. The absence of robust internal controls and periodic review further compounded the consequences for fiscal management. The report recommends urgent remedial actions to address policy, procedural, and oversight weaknesses to safeguard state revenue.

title: Report No. 2 of 2015 - Compliance and Performance Audit on General and Social Sector of Government of Kerala
overview:
This report presents the results of performance and compliance audit conducted by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on the General and Social Sector of the Government of Kerala, covering key departments including General Education, Health and Family Welfare, and more, for the year ended March 2014. It identifies critical shortcomings such as non-utilisation of funds, ineffective project implementation, misappropriation, and lack of proper risk assessment and monitoring. For example, failure to furnish Utilisation Certificates to Government of India caused the State to lose GOI assistance of ₹12.75 crore between 2012-14, and project delays in Kerala Emergency Medical Services led to over 28,100 unattended calls and response times exceeding stipulated norms in over 54% of cases.

The audit also highlights inaccurate reckoning and incomplete support for Children With Special Needs (CWSN), resulting in disproportional allocation and ineffective utilisation of resource teachers, and insufficient enrolment under health insurance schemes (only 42% for Scheduled Tribe beneficiaries state-wise and 29% in Wayanad during 2013-14). Instances of unfruitful or blocked expenditure, such as ₹59.5 lakh spent on idle zoo infrastructure and ₹4.67 crore on a water supply scheme, further show administrative gaps.

Major consequences include public service gaps, wastage of taxpayer money, and compromised outcomes for vulnerable groups. The lack of responsiveness from the executive, incomplete compliance with audit recommendations, and absent follow-up actions are ongoing issues, as indicated by hundreds of Inspection Reports and Action Taken Notes pending across departments.

title: Report No. 1 of 2015 - Performance Audit on Public Sector Undertakings of Government of Kerala
overview:
The performance audit assessed the functioning of 42 Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) in Kerala for the period 2010-11 to 2013-14. The audit identified that out of total government investment of ₹5667.23 crore in PSUs, only 20 PSUs posted profits, while 17 PSUs incurred cumulative losses of ₹2824.42 crore, indicating a loss percentage of nearly 50%. Further, fund utilisation was found to be sub-optimal, with an average of only 47% usage across major schemes.

A key headline finding is that several PSUs were unable to meet mandated output targets: for example, production units achieved only 38% of planned output due to management inefficiencies and procurement delays (pg 23). Audit also noted frequent shortfalls in statutory compliance, with delays in annual report submission and non-adherence to prescribed accounting standards.

Consequences include continued erosion of government investment, increased dependency on loans, and persistent delays in dividend declarations. Subsequent accountability gaps led to missed opportunities for revitalisation and systemic risks to state finances, underscoring the urgency for stronger financial management and oversight mechanisms.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Social, General Economic (Non-PSUs) Sectors of Government of Jammu Kashmir
overview:
This audit report covers performance and compliance audits across five key sectors in the Government of Jammu & Kashmir, including Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme, Police Station Infrastructure, Skill Development for Youth, Forest Management, and the Energy Development Agency. The audit identified ₹795 crore in excess/wasteful/unfruitful/infructuous/avoidable unproductive expenditure, fraudulent drawals, idle investment, and fund blockages. For example, the total expenditure of the State increased from ₹21,607 crore to ₹31,686 crore during 2009-14. Revenue expenditure rose by 77% from ₹15,324 crore in 2009-10 to ₹27,058 crore in 2013-14, while capital expenditure decreased by 28% from ₹6,234 crore to ₹4,507 crore.

Headline findings include that funds utilization across programmes ranged from 62% to 77%, resulting in annual unspent balances between ₹66.62 crore and ₹133.34 crore. Of 770 irrigation schemes under execution, only 407 schemes (62%) were completed, with time overruns and irregularities in execution. Skill development initiatives suffered weak implementation with low employment generation. Infrastructure gaps were noted in police stations, forests, and energy.

The consequences of these lapses are significant, including the blocking of public funds on incomplete or poorly managed projects, reduced public benefit from social and economic schemes, and persistent inefficiencies that hamper service delivery to citizens. Unutilised funds, idle assets, and overlooked opportunities for employment generation have dealt a blow to public trust and state development.

title: Financial and Performance Audit on Revenue and Public Sector Undertakings of Government of Jammu Kashmir
overview:
The audit covers the financial management and performance of revenue administration and public sector undertakings in Jammu & Kashmir. Gross collection of taxes and non-tax revenue during 2013-14 was ₹7,244 crore, which indicated a shortfall of ₹2,200 crore (23%) against budget estimates (p.4). Value Added Tax (VAT) contributed the largest share, amounting to ₹3,207 crore, but arrears of revenue were ₹870 crore as of March 2014, and only 21% of this was likely recoverable (p.9).

PSU performance was marked by persistent losses and poor return on investment. Out of 23 government companies and statutory corporations, 15 had not finalized their accounts for 2013-14, and 12 PSUs incurred accumulated losses of ₹2,350 crore as of March 2014 (p.13). Delays in account finalization and lack of timely audit compromised transparency and effective oversight.

Such lapses in revenue collection and PSU governance result in significant fiscal stress. Delayed account finalization hampers government’s ability to detect financial irregularities on time, thereby increasing the risk of fraud and misappropriation. title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Local Bodies of Government of Andhra Pradesh
overview:
This report reviews the finances and performance of Local Bodies in Andhra Pradesh for the year ended March 2014, covering both Panchayat Raj Institutions (PRIs) and Urban Local Bodies (ULBs). The audit found total receipts of PRIs during 2013-14 to be ₹2,875.19 crore, with own revenue declining to ₹736.50 crore and Finance Commission grants increasing substantially. For ULBs, total receipts reached ₹5,513.29 crore in 2013-14, with a notable increase in capital expenditure by 35% over the previous year (₹1,573.30 crore).

Significant deficiencies emerged in both assessment and collection of taxes, non-tax revenues, and accounting practices. For example, audit of 100 Gram Panchayats revealed lack of systematic mechanisms for assessing and accounting tax revenues, resulting in substantial arrears and unverified collections. Urban bodies like the Greater Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation (GVMC) and Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation (GHMC) suffered from improper/non-assessment of property tax, delayed remittances, and revenue losses from unauthorised structures and advertisements.

Additional issues included arrears in audit (audit of 220 ULBs and 5,613 GPs outstanding), failure to create ePanchayat financial database despite receipt of ₹67.37 crore in grants, misappropriation cases amounting to ₹669.39 lakh in 2013-14, and unadjusted advances totaling ₹47.66 lakh. These gaps affect the integrity and transparency of local body finances, hindering delivery of civic services and accountability.

title: Report 1 of 2015 - Compliance and Performance Audit on Revenue Sectors of Government of Andhra Pradesh
overview:
This report audits the revenue sector of Andhra Pradesh for the year ended March 2014 and details significant findings across tax domains, including Commercial Taxes, Prohibition and Excise, Transport, Roads & Buildings, and Registration and Stamps. A total of 34 audit paragraphs and a major performance audit reveal revenue implications of ₹1,236.88 crore due to non/short levy of taxes, interest, and penalty, along with a performance audit observation of ₹749.52 crore related to deficiencies in public service delivery and IT services (CFST) in the Transport Department, totaling a financial impact of ₹1,986.40 crore.

Noteworthy findings include test checks at 279 units uncovering preliminary audit findings involving non-levy/short levy of taxes amounting to ₹2,314.38 crore in 1,784 cases. Major lapses were identified in VAT/Sales Tax, such as incorrect exemptions, excess claims of input tax credit, and non-levy of penalties. Misclassification and non-registration of leasing agreements resulted in substantial losses in Stamp Duty and Registration Fee collections, highlighted by the non-levy on 18 PPP lease agreements worth ₹665.38 crore, and on 33 BOT agreements amounting to ₹43.77 crore.

Serious governance issues persist in arrear recovery, with ₹2,337.06 crore pending for more than five years out of a total ₹7,326.52 crore in arrears. Additionally, persistent lapses in responding to audit observations and audit committee meetings, and non-production of records for audit, were flagged as ongoing systemic weaknesses.

title: Performance Audit on Assessment of Assessees in Pharmaceuticals Sector Union Government, Department of Revenue - Direct Taxes
overview:
The Comptroller and Auditor General's performance audit scrutinized 2,868 assessment records (representing 83.57% of records requested) in the Pharmaceuticals sector for the assessment period 2010-11 to 2013-14, revealing systemic deficiencies in oversight, compliance, and data management by the Income Tax Department (ITD). The audit identified 246 cases with deficiencies involving a total tax effect of ₹1,348.44 crore, stemming from both non-compliance with statutory requirements and control failures. The ITD failed to maintain sector-wise data on tax incentives given to the pharmaceuticals sector, precluding proper assessment of the fiscal impact as well as limiting policy analysis and planning.

The audit recorded specific instances where weighted deductions on R&D expenditure amounting to ₹570.59 crore were allowed without mandatory verification from the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR), as well as failure to cross-verify turnover figures between Income Tax and Excise returns. Cases of allowing inadmissible expenditure—especially regarding gifts and freebies to medical professionals, which totaled a tax effect of ₹55.10 crore in 36 cases—were also documented, indicating improper interpretation or implementation of prohibitory provisions.

Systemic issues included the lack of a mechanism to correlate data across departments, inconsistent handling of R&D expenditure approvals, and ambiguous application of relevant legal provisions such as Section 80IC and Section 194C. These lapses increased the risk of revenue leakage, unduly benefitting some assessees while reducing the overall transparency and integrity of tax assessments in this vital economic sector.

title: Performance Audit on Import and Export Trade Facilitation through Customs Ports Union Government, Department of Revenue-Indirect Taxes, Customs
overview:
This performance audit examines the effectiveness of import and export trade facilitation measures across customs ports in India, covering the period from 2010-11 to 2013-14. The report identifies high transaction costs, estimating a total impact of Rs 42,000 crore (US$ 6-7 billion) due to poor facilitation as per the Department of Commerce's Strategic Plan. A key finding is a decrease in average dwell time for imports from 13.94 days in 2010-11 to 10.95 days in 2013-14, yet 65% of this time is consumed in the filing of Bills of Entry (BEs) and payment of duty.

Various initiatives such as the ICEGATE e-filing system, Risk Management System (RMS), 24x7 customs clearance, ACP, AEO, and factory premises examinations were rolled out, but significant systemic bottlenecks remain. Delays were observed at multiple stages: port berth allocations, importer clearance, error correction in Import General Manifests (IGMs), and manual registration of licenses. The audit also notes that less than half of recommendations from previous task forces (2005, 2009, 2013) have been fully implemented, with particular gaps in interdepartmental coordination and monitoring.

The consequences of these delays and inefficiencies include increased transaction, compliance, and logistics costs for Indian exporters and importers, adversely affecting India’s competitiveness in global trade. The report concludes that targeted improvements across governance, automation, agency coordination, and infrastructure are needed to achieve the envisaged benefits and international obligations under the WTO trade facilitation agreement.

title: Performance Audit on Dual Freight Policy for Transportation of Iron Ore Traffic in Indian Railways Union Government, Railways
overview:
This performance audit examined the implementation of the Dual Freight Policy (DFP) for the transportation of iron ore by Indian Railways between May 2008 and September 2013, covering 83 major loading points and 180 unloading points spanning 15 Zonal Railways. The report exposed large-scale non-compliance by railway officials in verifying documentation, improper allocation of rakes, and misapplication of concessional domestic freight rates for iron ore, resulting in massive revenue losses. Specifically, freight evasion and non-imposition of penalty reached Rs 29,236.78 crore (including evasion of Rs 12,722.65 crore and unlevied penalty of Rs 11,418.16 crore, with an additional imposable penalty of Rs 5,095.97 crore for diversion of iron ore booked at domestic rates for trading or export).

Key findings included railway acceptance of incomplete or false documentation for rakes granted at domestic rates, significant shortfalls in internal controls and lack of effective field inspections, and widespread misuse of domestic rate iron ore for non-domestic purposes. Cases included 225 consignees with 2,079 rakes and 218 consignees with 5,083 rakes booked at concessional rates without adequate documentation; a single case of SAIL led to short charging of Rs 4,838.80 crore. Auditors also observed that variations in iron ore removals exceeded allowed thresholds by up to 100% in certain cases.

The audit concludes that critical gaps in monitoring, policy enforcement, and documentation checks allowed systemic leakage and misuse, resulting in substantial financial loss. The recommendations call for stricter compliance, improved inspection, better use of data from excise returns, and remedial policy guidance to curb revenue loss and malpractice.

title: Performance Audit on Export Oriented Unit scheme Union Government, Department of Revenue-Indirect Taxes, Customs
overview:
The Performance Audit reviews the functioning of the 100% Export Oriented Unit (EOU) Scheme from 2009-10 to 2013-14, highlighting significant decline in the number of EOUs from 3,109 in 2009-10 to 2,608 in 2013-14, with functional units also dropping from 2,279 to 2,095. Custom revenue forgone under EOU, EHTP and STP schemes during this period stood at ₹32,932 crore, while the share of EOUs in India’s total exports shrank substantially, falling from over 21% in 2008-09 to just 4.3% by 2013-14, failing to meet government strategic export goals.

The report establishes that no impact or midterm evaluation was conducted before the scheme’s implementation nor during competition with the SEZ scheme. There was absence of a structured internal audit mechanism in the Ministry of Commerce & Industry, with significant gaps in monitoring and regular data capture, increasing risks of undetected non-compliance and policy misrepresentation.

Operational deficiencies identified included non/delayed filing of Annual Progress Reports (APRs), misreporting of key data, short/non-levy of duties totaling ₹317.06 crore, and ambiguity in relevant provisions, leading to ambiguity in DTA sales and central excise exemptions. As a result, the scheme failed to attract entrepreneurs or contribute as envisaged, despite substantial revenue forgone.

title: Union Government (Defence Services) Army and Ordnance Factories (Performance Audit of Ammunition Management in Army)
overview:
The report presents a detailed performance audit of ammunition management in the Indian Army, covering the period from 2008-09 to 2012-13. The audit scrutinized the procurement, storage, and availability of war wastage reserves (WWR) and ensures the readiness of forces for wartime requirements.

One of the headline findings is that the Army was holding only 50% of the WWR against the authorization as of March 2013, with persistent shortfalls in key ammunition types. The audit also highlights underutilisation of procurement funds, significant delays in induction, and recurring stockouts for critical ammunition categories.

Consequences identified include a direct impact on operational preparedness, with units compelled to scale down training activities due to non-availability of ammunition, and an increased risk to national security from deficient reserves. The report calls for strategic improvements to ammunition planning, procurement processes, and oversight mechanisms.

title: Performance Audit of Financing of Renewable Energy Projects, Union Government, Ministry of New and Renewable Energy
overview:
This performance audit of the Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency (IREDA) examined loan sanctions, disbursements, recoveries, and subsidy administration from 2008-09 to 2012-13. IREDA’s share in the country’s commissioned renewable capacity fell sharply, dropping from 52.83% at the start of the Tenth Plan to 7.66% at the end of the Eleventh Plan, indicating a significant decline in market position. During the review period, 219 projects worth ₹13,593.58 crore were sanctioned, with ₹6,865.68 crore disbursed, but only 34.79% of loan applications were sanctioned.

Operational inefficiencies were evident: 39.34% of projects were sanctioned with an average delay of 66 days, and 65.21% of loan applications were dropped at various stages. The audit found deviations in 40% of selected cases, including excess credit exposure and bypassed norms. An ongoing One Time Settlement (OTS) scheme led to a sacrifice of ₹237.85 crore (53.25%) on outstanding dues, unlike peer institutions. Out of 17 OTS cases reviewed, 14 showed guideline violations, including non-verification of projects and lending to wilful defaulters.

Subsidy management was lax; in 5 of 12 sampled cases, continued payout to ineligible borrowers and weak monitoring threatened scheme objectives. The PIDMOS loan database had completeness and reliability issues. The audit concluded that targets were often understated, controls were weak, and the internal monitoring system did not prevent irregular sanctions or recoveries, undermining the sector’s growth and financial integrity.

title: Performance Audit of Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana RKVY, Union Government, Ministry of Agriculture
overview:
The Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY) was launched in the XIth Five Year Plan to rejuvenate faltering agricultural growth, with an aim to achieve a 4% annual growth rate in agriculture and allied sectors. During 2007-08 to 2012-13, a total of ₹32,460.45 crore was allocated and ₹30,873.38 crore was released to 28 States and 7 Union Territories. Out of 4,061 projects sanctioned in 19 selected sectors, only 2,506 projects were completed by March 2014, while 370 projects (worth over ₹1,500 crore) were either abandoned, dropped, or not implemented, highlighting serious operational challenges.

Fund utilisation presented a mixed picture, with around ₹2,800 crore remaining unspent at the end of the audit period. There were also systemic lapses in planning, monitoring, and fund flow, as almost 24 out of 27 audited States showed deficiencies in project planning and lack of grassroot-level participation, leading to inclusion of 143 projects (worth ₹1,962.29 crore) in State Agriculture Plans without bottom-up validation.

Irregularities surfaced in at least 38% of examined projects, including misallocation, diversion of ₹91.24 crore from RKVY for unrelated purposes, and serious delays. These led to large blocks of funds lying idle and compromised intended outcomes. The report concludes that expected benefits of RKVY did not adequately reach farmers, with identified gaps in effective oversight by the Ministry of Agriculture, insufficient convergence with other schemes, and inconsistent achievement of sectoral and regional targets.

title: Performance Audit Report on District Hospital Outcomes (Government of Uttarakhand) for the year 2014-2019
overview:
The performance audit of district hospitals in Uttarakhand, covering the years 2014-19, highlights systemic issues in healthcare delivery, resource management, and patient outcomes. The State ranked only 17th out of 21 in the NITI Aayog Health Index, underscoring substantial gaps in public healthcare. Key findings include significant shortfalls in state budget utilization for district hospitals, ineffective adoption of standards, and lack of linkages between patient volumes and allocation of medical staff. For example, against a backdrop of growing healthcare needs, the audit found the sanctioned strength of doctors and nurses often bore little relation to actual patient load or number of beds, impacting quality and timeliness of care (p. xii).

The increase or decrease in outpatient load was not matched with doctor staffing, resulting in some districts handling disproportionately higher OPD cases per doctor. Crucially, specialist coverage in hill regions lagged behind the plains; some posts in critical specialties like ENT and orthopaedics were left unfilled in the hills, while plains had either full or excess staff (p. xii-xiii).

Diagnostic and maternity facilities suffered further: 59% of OPD patients had to purchase drugs out-of-pocket, and essential equipment shortages ranged from 41% to 78% across sampled hospitals. ICU and trauma center facilities remained mostly non-functional due to lack of personnel and equipment. The consequences are stark, with high rates of patient referrals, inadequate emergency surgery capability, and poor quality metrics such as abnormally high bed turnover and absconding rates, especially in the hill districts. Financial rules were often ignored, with little to no alignment of resources to actual hospital performance (p. xiv-xv).

title: Report of 2014 - Performance Audit on Urban Local Bodies of Government of West Bengal
overview:
The audit covering 54 Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) of West Bengal revealed significant issues in fund management, execution of developmental schemes, and maintenance of accounts. Fund utilisation in selected municipalities was critically low, with utilisation ranging from only 44% to 50% of allocated resources (Rs 3,672.50 crore released; only Rs 1,679.18 crore utilised, leaving a balance of Rs 1,993.32 crore unutilised as of March 2013).

The audit further found diversion of scheme funds totalling Rs 24.87 crore meant for specific development and welfare projects, violating guidelines and depriving intended beneficiaries. Excess revenue expenditure of Rs 56.63 crore and excess capital expenditure of Rs 40.52 crore over budget provisions were also reported. Similarly, cases of deferred or incomplete developmental work were highlighted, showing deficiencies in internal controls and accountability.

Such lapses have led to a persistent backlog in civic amenities, sub-optimal delivery of basic services, and mounting liabilities. Key recommendations call for stricter monitoring of fund flows, transparent budgeting, timely completion of schemes, and improved records management to address systemic failures and improve public service delivery.

title: Report of 2014 - Performance Audit on Panchayati Raj Institutions of Government of West Bengal
overview:
This Performance Audit examines the financial management and scheme implementation by Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) in West Bengal for the year ending 31 March 2013. Major issues include a short release of ₹1261.35 crore against budget provisions during 2008-09, 2010-11, and 2011-12, which ranged from 7% to 22% shortfall. Own Source Revenue constituted only 1% to 4% of total receipts between 2008 and 2011, indicating low fiscal autonomy for PRIs.

Scheme utilization showed critical lapses. PRIs spent just 6% of the Thirteenth Finance Commission grant earmarked for safe drinking water, with only ₹2.55 crore out of ₹40.90 crore spent; furthermore, no fund was specifically earmarked for e-governance maintenance, despite ₹5.48 crore being spent under that sector. In implementation of major schemes like MGNREGS and IAY, issues included failure to provide 100 days employment, delayed wage payments, unauthorized beneficiary selection, diversion of funds, and low creation of durable assets.

Financial management weaknesses were clearly evident: audit found ₹37.37 crore expended by 25 PRIs without budget estimates, and ₹98.27 crore spent in excess of budget in 243 PRIs during 2010-12. Advances of ₹14.62 crore remained unadjusted in 23 PRIs and diversion of ₹20.65 crore from scheme funds was noted. These gaps resulted in unaddressed beneficiary needs, inefficient fund utilization, idle grants, and avoidable expenditures.

title: Performance Audit on Revenue Sector of Government of Madhya Pradesh
overview:
This performance audit examines the revenue receipts of Madhya Pradesh for the year ended 31 March 2014, covering commercial tax, state excise, taxes on vehicles, land revenue, stamps and registration fees, and mining receipts. The State’s total receipts for the year amounted to ₹74,539.01 crore, with 54% raised through state taxes (₹32,342.12 crore) and non-tax revenue (₹7,704.93 crore); the remainder came from the central government as share of union taxes and grants-in-aid. Test checks of 376 units revealed under-assessments and short levies amounting to ₹1,267.93 crore across 5,64,313 cases. Departments accepted audit observations worth ₹54.64 crore; only ₹5.94 lakh was recovered at audit time.

Major findings include irregular allowance and inadmissible Input Tax Rebate (ITR) under MP VAT Act totaling ₹16.97 crore, short realisation of excise duty of ₹39.83 crore by 709 foreign liquor shops, undue benefit to retail licensees, and short/non-levy of taxes/fees in vehicles, registration, and mining. For example, the state excise section found that retail licensees were given undue benefits leading to a short realisation of ₹39.83 crore, and the mining section uncovered non/short realisation of dead rent and contract money together exceeding ₹6 crore.

Systemic issues such as weak internal controls, insufficient departmental inspections, non-compliance with registration duties, and inordinate delays in revenue realisation and recovery were widespread. Departments failed to implement recommendations, ensure timely recovery, and coordinate with relevant public bodies, resulting in significant losses and revenue leakage.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Panchayat Raj Institutions and Urban Local Bodies of Government of Karnataka
overview:
This report assesses the compliance and performance of Panchayat Raj Institutions (PRIs) and Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) in Karnataka for the year ended March 2013. Audit found that only 3.43 lakh houses were completed against a target of 6.64 lakh under Indira Awaas Yojana, and only 88% of available funds (`2,457.12 crore) were spent, reflecting significant underutilisation and deficient financial management. The Backward Regions Grant Fund Programme suffered from lack of Perspective Plans, non-preparation of district-specific allocation guidelines, and delays in fund release, causing loss of central assistance and weak transparency in contract management.

Audit highlighted unproductive and wasteful expenditure across various schemes, such as a non-functional water supply project resulting in `6.14 crore wasted in Bellary, and solid waste management failures in Bruhat Bangalore Mahanagara Palike (BBMP) where a delay resulted in loss of `280.17 crore. The Urban Local Bodies underutilised 13th Finance Commission grants, maintained deficient accounts, and failed to collect property tax efficiently due to the absence of a GIS-based system.

Overall, the report uncovers systematic weaknesses in planning, fund management, monitoring, and transparency. These resulted in missed targets, direct financial losses, and lack of service delivery to beneficiaries, indicating high risk and impact for the state’s rural and urban local bodies.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Economic Sector of Government of West Bengal
overview:
Audit of West Bengal’s Economic Sector covering 26 departments highlights significant shortcomings in fund allocation, utilisation, and policy effectiveness between 2010-13. Total expenditure rose from ₹9,001.97 crore in 2010-11 to ₹13,267.43 crore in 2012-13, with Public Works, Power, and Irrigation accounting for the bulk of outlay. However, the efficiency of outcomes and accountability mechanisms displays systemic gaps: for instance, only 47% of planned forest management works were completed, and delays persisted in fund disbursement for developmental schemes.

Serious compliance issues were found. Major instances included diversion and mismanagement of grants, unauthorised retention of government receipts, and poor recovery of arrears by several departments. In Chapter 2, the performance audit of Forest Department found that expenditure under ‘compensatory afforestation’ underutilised funds by over ₹114 crore, affecting planned targets (p. 23).

Consequences of these audit findings included delayed developmental impact, loss to public exchequer, and compromised service delivery, particularly in infrastructure, rural development, and conservation schemes. The report underscores the need for robust internal controls and stronger project monitoring mechanisms as continued lapses threaten to erode the value of public investment and trust.

title: Report No. 3 of 2014 – Performance Audit on Public Sector Undertakings of Government of West Bengal
overview:
The CAG audit covers 91 Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) in West Bengal as of 31 March 2013, including 81 Government companies and 10 Statutory corporations. Only 31 working PSUs had finalized their 2012-13 accounts by September 2013. Their combined turnover was ₹36,755.18 crore, equaling 6.37% of West Bengal’s GSDP for 2012-13. The overall working results of all 91 PSUs showed a total turnover of ₹39,118.49 crore (6.78% of GSDP) and an aggregate net loss of ₹882.45 crore for their latest finalized accounts.

Critical audit findings revealed sustained underperformance, with the number of loss-incurring PSUs increasing from 32 (2010-11) to 37 (2012-13). Aggregate losses of these PSUs increased significantly from ₹1,181.40 crore in 2010-11 to ₹2,267.85 crore in 2012-13. The Audit also noted poor return on State investments and delay in finalization of accounts for non-working PSUs, increasing the risk of fraud and financial mismanagement.

Consequences include persistent erosion of public resources, lack of accountability for large government investments, and the risk of continued loss accumulation undermining State finances. The CAG explicitly notes systemic weaknesses in financial management and internal controls, with 30 out of 81 Government companies and 5 out of 10 Statutory corporations in default regarding finalization of accounts as of September 2013.

title: Performance Audit on Public Sector Undertakings of Government of Tamilnadu
overview:
As of 31 March 2013, Tamil Nadu had 64 working Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) and 13 non-working PSUs, employing around 2.80 lakh personnel. The State PSUs' combined turnover was ₹70,673.64 crore—equivalent to 9.49% of the State's Gross Domestic Product. Cumulative investment in 77 PSUs stood at ₹83,235.55 crore, of which the power sector accounted for 92.23%. The Government contributed ₹13,917.89 crore towards equity, loans, and subsidies during 2012-13. However, PSUs reported accumulated losses of ₹38,233.61 crore, indicating significant fiscal stress and inefficiencies in operations.

The State PSUs' performance showed that only 43 out of 64 working PSUs earned a profit of ₹615.29 crore, while 19 incurred substantial losses totalling ₹14,232.03 crore. Particularly notable was Tamil Nadu Generation and Distribution Corporation Ltd, with a loss of ₹13,321.33 crore, and State Transport Corporations with a loss of ₹856.52 crore. Audit reviews over the preceding three years (2010-2013) exposed controllable losses of ₹3,282.85 crore and infructuous investments of ₹216.96 crore, signifying a persistent issue with management, oversight, and operational efficiency.

Other critical findings included delays in finalisation of accounts—21 working PSUs had arrears in 25 accounts—and recurring deficiencies in internal controls, monitoring, and recovery of dues. The report highlights that only increased professionalism and accountability would enable PSUs to discharge their mandate better, with many units depending on state budgetary support to compensate for ongoing deficits. The consequences of inaction are mounting public sector losses and rising public financial risk to the state exchequer. [Overview, p.viii-xi of full report]

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on General and Social Sector of Government of West Bengal
overview: This performance audit examines the Government of West Bengal's disaster management from 2008-09 to 2012-13, covering institutional arrangements, planning, preparedness, fund utilisation, and relief distribution. The Disaster Management Department coordinated activities among 33 departments and 2258 units, managing a five-year expenditure rising from ₹52,096.74 crore in 2008-09 to ₹97,251.93 crore in 2012-13. Despite the presence of dedicated structures such as the SDMA and District DDMAs, key gaps were found: the State Disaster Management Authority met only once since inception, and advisory committees were dormant. The disaster preparedness was hampered by partial vulnerability assessments, non-functioning warning systems in critical districts, and significant delays or non-distribution of relief to communities. Construction of shelters and godowns lagged behind targets. Post-disaster relief showed cases of non-distribution and delays in both rice and cash assistance, depriving intended beneficiaries. There were also notable shortfalls in implementing centrally sponsored Disaster Risk Management Programme-II and National School Safety Programme. Furthermore, many key posts for disaster management officers remained vacant, potentially compromising future disaster readiness and response effectiveness.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Revenue Sector of Government of West Bengal
overview:
The Performance and Compliance Audit on the Revenue Sector of the Government of West Bengal highlights a persistent gap between revenue assessments and actual collections, with a recurring shortfall in realisation. The audit observed that out of the total revenue receipts of Rs 33,108 crore during 2012-13, revenue collected was significantly lower than estimated targets, and a considerable amount related to taxes on sales, trade, and professional taxes remained unrealised (Rs 2,087.23 crore).

Audit found inadequacies in controls across revenue departments. For example, test checks revealed deficiencies in the system of assessment and monitoring of professional tax, with more than 1.97 lakh certificates of enrollment pending issue and 1.04 lakh returns pending scrutiny. There were 42 cases of short levy of tax, non/short realisation, and various irregularities, resulting in an estimated revenue loss of Rs 24.71 crore.

These continued lapses have led to significant arrears and risk of further leakage, directly impacting the State’s fiscal health. The report underscores the need for urgent systemic reforms in revenue administration, including better coordination between assessing and enforcing authorities, and stronger oversight on tax arrears and compliance (para 1.3.2, p.7; para 2.3, pp.22-24).

title: Financial and Performance Audit on Forests, Ecology, Environment and Wildlife Department of Government of Nagaland
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Forests, Ecology, Environment and Wildlife Department in Nagaland for the period 2008-13 revealed persistent underutilisation of funds released under various forestry and environmental schemes. Out of the total provision of ₹246.96 crore, only ₹111.37 crore (45 percent) was utilised, leaving a balance of ₹135.59 crore unutilised as of March 2013 (p.11). This substantial underutilisation was coupled with delays in release and transfer of funds, adversely impacting implementation timelines.

Notably, there was widespread shortfall in achievement of afforestation targets. Against a physical target of 48,145 ha under various schemes, only 24,040 ha (50 percent) was achieved, with significant discrepancies across divisions (p.41). The department also failed to prepare annual administration reports for five years and did not maintain reliable records on wildlife conservation activities (p.69).

These shortcomings contributed to ineffective forest cover management and poor conservation outcomes. The lack of timely and comprehensive monitoring exacerbated these issues, resulting in significant gaps in meeting environmental protection goals and judicious public fund utilisation.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit of Government of Pondicherry
overview:
The CAG audit of the Government of Puducherry for the year 2012-13 highlights persistent under-utilisation of budget provisions and widespread instances of irregular expenditure. As per the audit, actual expenditure was consistently less than the budgeted amounts, with funds worth ₹802.85 crore remaining unutilised (16.75 per cent of total provision) during the year. Lapses in financial discipline, including savings in multiple grants and large-scale re-appropriations, were flagged, pointing towards weak planning and budgeting.

Instances of irregular release of funds, diversion, and misutilisation of resources were uncovered. The report notes, specifically, irregular expenditure of ₹13.90 crore in the implementation of infrastructure projects. Low fund absorption, delays in project execution, and lack of monitoring mechanisms hampered the intended outcomes for several developmental schemes.

The consequences of these lapses include delays in the completion of public works, ineffective service delivery, and a cumulative impact on socio-economic objectives of the Union Territory. The report calls for strengthened internal controls, enhanced monitoring, and prompt corrective actions to ensure prudent and timely utilisation of public funds.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Economic Sector of Government of Odisha
overview:
This report presents significant audit findings on the Economic Sector of Government of Odisha, focusing on the period ending March 2014. The CAG conducted a performance audit on the Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme (AIBP) and compliance audits of multiple departments, including projects funded under AIBP and the status of major and minor irrigation efforts. Key findings revealed project completion delays, cost overruns, and serious underachievement of irrigation targets: despite Rs 3,157.97 crore financial implication due to cost escalation and deficiencies, only 0.66 lakh hectares—40% of the 1.65 lakh hectare target—received irrigation during 2009-14, with some years as low as 11% achievement.

Notably, major projects such as Subarnarekha Irrigation Project, Lower Indra Project, and Lower Suktel Project suffered due to improper planning, land acquisition issues, and design delays, leading to staggering cost increases of more than 400-700% over original estimates. Instances of undue contractor benefits, inflated estimation rates, and idle investments were recorded, including a single excess payment of Rs 1.79 crore and an idle investment of Rs 5.50 crore. Monitoring and controls were consistently found lacking, resulting in persistent gaps and failures highlighted in earlier audits repeating in this period.

These issues led to tangible losses for the State, depriving intended beneficiaries of critical assured irrigation facilities and causing significant wastage of public funds. Serious irregularities in audit compliance, such as 18,940 outstanding audit paragraphs across 5,471 Inspection Reports, were unresolved as of June 2014, some pending for over a decade, raising issues of governance and accountability.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Economic Sector of Government of Odisha
overview:
The CAG Performance Audit of the Economic Sector in Odisha for the period 2008-13 highlighted critical deficiencies in planning, execution, and financial management across departments such as Works, Water Resources, and Agriculture. Out of a total budget provision of ₹2128.94 crore made for construction and maintenance, only ₹1501.13 crore, representing 71% utilisation, was actually spent due to delays in site selection, administrative approvals, and slow work progress (p. 13). The Works Department faced incomplete projects, cost overruns, and unwarranted supplementary provisions, with project completion rates declining from 95% in 2009-10 to 58% in 2012-13 (p. 9).

Significant irregularities include non-recovery of water rates amounting to ₹9503.31 crore due to failure to enforce Odisha Irrigation Act provisions (p. 3), and losses driven by the non-recovery of royalty and inflated estimates, resulting in undue benefit to contractors. Major implementation gaps persisted in central/state schemes, such as a loss of central assistance worth ₹82.54 crore in Watershed Development due to poor progress (p. 4).

Overall, the audit underscores the need for improved monitoring, better coordination with user departments, and effective budgetary controls. Weaknesses in internal controls led to idle investments and unfruitful expenditures, such as a ₹3.65 crore underpass that was not put to use. The report calls for systematic action to address avoidable delays, wastage, and lapses in transparency, impacting public service delivery and financial discipline across the audited sectors.

title: Performance Audit on Public Sector Undertakings of Government of Odisha
overview:
This Performance Audit examines Odisha’s Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) as of 31 March 2013, covering 37 working and 28 non-working PSUs, with a reported turnover of ₹11,294.70 crore—4.37% of State GDP. Aggregate profit for 2012-13 was ₹890 crore, yet losses remain significant, with GRIDCO Ltd. alone accounting for ₹936.81 crore loss. The state's cumulative investment in PSUs reached ₹10,471.51 crore, an increase of 26.69% over five years, mainly concentrated in the power sector (81.18%).

The report spotlights persistent issues: All 35 accounts finalized between Oct 2012 and Sept 2013 were qualified by auditors; 44 instances of non-compliance with Accounting Standards were found. The performance of PSU management is weakened by high arrears: 47 accounts were overdue, and liquidation of 17 PSUs remains incomplete. Key compliance lapses resulted in an identified loss of ₹3,142.41 crore across just six cases.

Critical operational deficiencies include non-collection of dues (GRIDCO: ₹3,372.29 crore outstanding), unwarranted procurement costs, and penalties exceeding ₹2,833 crore on Odisha Mining Corporation for unapproved mining. Shortfalls in planning, deficient internal controls, and lack of timely account finalization pose risks to transparency and governance.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Economic Sector of Government of Karnataka
overview:
The CAG's Performance Audit on the Economic Sector of Karnataka for the year ended March 2014 revealed widespread deficiencies in implementing Command Area Development activities. Despite allocation of ₹2,037.99 crore during 2009-14, only ₹831.47 crore (41%) was utilized for On Farm Development works such as construction of field irrigation channels, field drains, and other extension services. A persistent gap of 4.10 lakh hectares existed between irrigation potential created and potential actually utilized, primarily due to shortfall in construction of field irrigation channels – just 2.25 lakh hectares (30% of target 7.48 lakh hectares) was achieved.

Furthermore, financial management was poor: ₹1,206.52 crore (59% of allocation) lapsed or was surrendered during 2009-14, with fund allocation often exceeding what was requested by the implementing agencies. In 16 projects, even after channel construction, 2.71 lakh hectares remained unirrigated, resulting in estimated crop losses of ₹915 crore. The State also failed to secure central assistance, with ₹130 crore not reimbursed and ₹733 crore unutilized due to missing performance targets.

The audit identifies that the goals of Participatory Irrigation Management were unmet—water management was not handed over to water users’ co-operative societies as mandated. These shortcomings reflect critically on planning, execution, and fund management in a vital sector impacting millions in the state.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on General, Social, Revenue and Economic Sectors of Government of Mizoram
overview: This CAG report examines the functioning of the General, Social, Revenue, and Economic Sectors in Mizoram, covering the period ending 31 March 2013. The audit scrutinized fund flow and performance against targets across key departments. For the Home (Police) Department, it was found that the average crime rate remained significantly lower than the all-India average, indicating effective law and order maintenance. However, major lapses were observed in financial management. Out of the Central assistance released for modernization, only ₹183.17 crore was spent out of ₹199.98 crore received (91.6%), and ₹36.51 crore was irregularly parked in Civil Deposits with retention of ₹13.04 crore in cash, obstructing smooth implementation. Further, procurement practices showed violations: ₹1.72 crore in stationery and ₹1.54 crore for vehicle repairs occurred beyond delegated powers. Delays in submission of Annual Action Plans led to withholding and deduction of ₹1.05 crore by the Government of India. Additionally, compliance audit revealed that ₹1 crore spent by the Lai Autonomous District Council on potato seed procurement remained largely unfruitful, as distribution occurred after the sowing season. These issues collectively highlight systemic weaknesses in project planning, fund utilization, and internal controls, impacting intended benefits and outcomes for Mizoram's population.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Revenue Sector of Government of Karnataka
overview:
The CAG report for the year ended March 2014 examines significant shortcomings in Karnataka's revenue sector. The total revenue receipts of the State Government for 2013-14 stood at ₹89,542.53 crore, up from ₹78,176.22 crore in 2012-13, with 74% raised by the State and the remaining 26% being transfers from the Government of India (page 1, Paragraph 1.1). Audits revealed extensive under-assessment, short levy, and revenue loss totaling ₹380.22 crore documented in 1,425 cases during inspection of 439 departmental units (page 10, Paragraph 1.8). Further, a total of 4,114 pending Inspection Reports containing 8,753 audit observations, involving ₹1,851.83 crore, remained unsettled at the close of the audit period (page 4, Paragraph 1.5).

Major systemic and compliance failures include lapses in VAT and entry tax administration, undervaluation in stamp duty, and weaknesses in internal audit functions and information systems, notably the Mojini application for land records. These gaps fostered both revenue losses and opportunities for compliance breaches. Noteworthy was the identification of ₹941.14 crore discrepancy between TDS claimed by works contractors and actual TDS collected by the authorities (page vii, Overview).

Consequences for Karnataka include large arrears (₹4,945.97 crore outstanding, especially in commercial taxes), inadequacies in audit response and settlement, as well as recurring shortfalls in the settlement of previously identified revenue leaks. The Government’s own audit committees and follow-ups remain sporadic, impeding timely rectification and limiting revenue collection potential.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Local Bodies of Government of Karnataka
overview:
This report presents the audit findings for compliance and performance audits of Local Bodies in Karnataka, covering the period 2008-13. There was a significant increase in fund allocation to Panchayat Raj Institutions (PRIs), with total resources rising from ₹13,592 crore in 2008-09 to ₹17,405 crore in 2012-13. However, fund utilisation was suboptimal; for example, only 3.43 lakh houses were completed against the target of 6.64 lakh under Indira Awaas Yojana, with only 88% of available funds utilised and deficiencies in financial management, including unreconciled accounts and delays in certifications. In the Backward Regions Grant Fund Programme, perspective planning was lacking, and centrally funded schemes suffered from delays and omitted guidelines, resulting in loss of central assistance.

Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) faced deficiencies as the State had not devolved all mandated functions; Property Tax base mapping was incomplete, leading to revenue losses. In solid waste management, Bruhat Bangalore Mahanagara Palike lost assistance worth ₹280 crore due to delays in master planning and incurred wasteful expenditure of ₹630 crore on contractor payments for unscientific disposal of waste. Compliance audits noted unproductive investments, such as a water supply scheme in Bellary that failed, resulting in a loss of ₹6.14 crore.

Overall, deficient financial management, lack of planning, and failure to monitor and evaluate programme outcomes led to significant shortfalls in achievement and ineffective delivery of public services, with instances of wasteful and unfruitful expenditure noted across both rural and urban schemes.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Public Sector Undertakings of Government of Karnataka
overview:
As on 31 March 2013, the State of Karnataka had 79 working PSUs and 14 non-working PSUs, employing a total of 1.87 lakh staff and posting a combined turnover of ₹37,867.13 crore, amounting to 7.21% of the State’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP). The Comptroller and Auditor General noted controllable losses of ₹1,075.66 crore and infructuous investments of ₹524.48 crore across the PSUs as per their latest audited accounts. The aggregate profit among working PSUs was ₹1,144.33 crore while losses totaled ₹549.04 crore, with major contributors to profit being The Hutti Gold Mines Company Limited (₹257.13 crore) and Karnataka Power Corporation Limited (₹171.20 crore), but substantial losses incurred by Karnataka Neeravari Nigama Limited (₹235.37 crore) and Chamundeshwari Electricity Supply Corporation Limited (₹116.27 crore).

The audit observed significant deficiencies in project management and contract execution. Only 86.47 km out of 404.67 km of major roads targeted for completion in 2008-13 were achieved within the scheduled time. Out of nine major bridges, only four were completed as planned. PPP projects faced delays, design changes, and poor monitoring; critical elements such as appropriate concession periods, accurate estimation, and robust performance controls were often neglected. There were marked failures in levy rice procurement, leading to excess dependence on the Central Pool and unnecessary extra costs of ₹948.61 crore for two years alone.

The report highlights widespread issues of non-compliance with accounting standards (98 instances in 34 companies), high costs in transport and storage, poor internal controls, and unutilised funds. Misappropriations, shortages, and procurement of substandard grains were attributed to deficient monitoring and institutional weaknesses. The severity of findings is high, given major fund misutilisation, project delays, and procurement inefficiencies impacting supply to vulnerable populations.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on General and Social Sector of Government of Karnataka
overview:
This report covers the compliance and performance audit of selected programmes and activities of the Government of Karnataka for the year 2012-13. The CAG audit revealed serious shortcomings in multiple social sector schemes, most notably the functioning of the Karnataka Residential Educational Institutions Society. Out of 542 institutions, only 43% had their own buildings by April 2013, with the rest operating in substandard or rented premises lacking basic facilities. Land for 108 schools and colleges was not identified even though 47 of these existed from before 2008-09.

Financial mismanagement was substantial, as funds remained unused at the end of each year from 2008-13, due to 33-100% of allocations being released only in the last quarter, severely undermining operational effectiveness. For example, the society failed to optimize returns on surplus funds and also acquired private land worth ₹1.2 crore despite government land being available. Delays in tendering, frequent violations of the Karnataka Transparency in Public Procurement Act, and awarding contracts to ineligible agencies plagued infrastructure development and resulted in significant inefficiencies.

Further, the coverage of targeted beneficiaries was inadequate: 46% of schools served less than 75% of their primary target group, and 18% served less than 50%. The report documented multiple instances of wasteful expenditure, including ₹7.73 crore on surplus teachers, and highlighted irregularities in absorption of staff, excessive grants, and failure to ensure proper asset creation, ultimately citing a lack of effective monitoring and response systems.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Economic Sector of Government of Karnataka
overview:
This CAG report examines the performance and compliance audit of various economic service departments in Karnataka for the fiscal year ending March 2013. An expenditure of ₹381.30 crore was incurred between 2008 and 2013 under the sericulture sector, with fund utilisation and scheme implementation showing critical lapses. The report highlights persistent savings under plan expenditure at 39.10% of total grants and unutilised balances, including a ₹127.46 crore surplus in the Price Stabilisation Fund.

Non-plan expenditure exceeded plan expenditure, and many departmentally owned units ran into heavy losses. The audit reveals irregularities such as incorrect identification of schemes for gender budgeting and subsidies/incentives disbursed violating scheme guidelines. The mulberry cultivation area shrank from 91,434 hectares to 74,128 hectares, and raw silk production stagnated despite increased subsidies.

Moreover, major financial mismanagement was observed in contract management, release of grants without necessity, irregular payments, adoption of overestimated construction standards leading to avoidable extra costs, and losses due to illegal mining and improper scrutiny. The audit finds that responsiveness from departments to audit recommendations remains low, with six departments failing to submit Action Taken Notes for previous years.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Local Bodies of Government of Maharashtra
overview:
This report reviews the accounts and performance of Local Bodies in Maharashtra, including both Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) and Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) for the year ending 31 March 2013. Allocation to PRIs from State revenue fell from 16.99% in 2008-09 to 14.50% in 2012-13, versus the 40% recommended by the Second State Finance Commission, leaving PRIs significantly underfunded. Actual allocation to both PRIs and ULBs together was only 18.38% of state total revenue in 2012-13. Of the 33 Zilla Parishads, accounts for 2011-12 and 2012-13 were finalized but remained uncertified and unpublished as of December 2013.

The audit observes that the statutory format for accounts prescribed by the CAG was not adopted across the state, and only 11 out of 29 functions under the XI Schedule of the Constitution had actually been devolved to PRIs. For ULBs, receipts of 26 Municipal Corporations increased by 14.92% to Rs 37,046 crore in 2012-13, but audit completion rates lagged, with 10 corporations having arrears of 2–10 years. Delays in project implementation and significant cost overruns were seen in major urban development projects such as the Brihanmumbai Storm Water Drain Project, which saw expenditure of Rs 1,764.55 crore versus an approved cost of Rs 1,175.72 crore and only 27.6% completion as of September 2013.

Lack of clear criteria for consultant payments, non-compliance in tender processes, and widespread failure to hold mandated social audits in ULB housing projects were also observed. Weak internal controls are evidenced by 3,842 outstanding inspection reports (over 12,000 audit paras) still pending settlement across PRIs, despite repeated instructions.

title: Performance Audit on Social, General and Economic Sectors and Public Sector Undertakings of Government of Meghalaya
overview:
Paragraph 1: The CAG's performance audit of Social, General and Economic Sectors and Public Sector Undertakings in Meghalaya found significant deficiencies in fund utilisation. Out of the total allocation of Rs 3,140 crore during 2008-13, only Rs 1,480 crore (47%) was actually utilised, leaving Rs 1,660 crore unspent. On page 12 under the Executive Summary, it is noted: 'Only 47 per cent of allocated funds were utilised during 2008-13.'

Paragraph 2: Audit findings revealed incomplete implementation of schemes, resulting in only 36% of projects reaching the intended beneficiaries. In Chapter II §2.3 (page 23), the report states: 'Out of 254 sanctioned works, only 92 were completed.' Delays in project execution, poor monitoring, and lack of accountability were cited as major causes.

Paragraph 3: Consequences of these deficiencies include persistent gaps in healthcare delivery, education infrastructure, and welfare schemes. The report highlights that these gaps contributed to low literacy and high dropout rates. As noted on page 29: 'Dropout rates in primary education remained at 41 per cent in audited districts.' Overall, the audit emphasises the need for robust systems to ensure effective fund utilisation and timely completion of projects.
