title: Report No. 1 of 2014 - Performance Audit on Revenue Sector of Government of Meghalaya
overview:
This performance audit report highlights extensive irregularities and lapses in the revenue sector of the Government of Meghalaya for the year ended 31 March 2013. The audit identifies a total money value of Rs 843.35 crore, relating to under-assessments, non-realisation, short realisation of penalties, taxes, duties, and fees, across 37 paragraphs and one Performance Audit. For 2012-13, the State Government raised Rs 1,332.66 crore in revenues, which constituted 24.09% of total receipts. The remaining 75.91% came from the Government of India as share of divisible taxes and grants-in-aid. Test checks conducted during 2012-13 found under-assessments and revenue losses amounting to Rs 471.13 crore in 272 cases. Departments accepted Rs 51.80 crore of these losses and recovered only Rs 0.96 crore, showing a significant gap in enforcement and recovery.

Major findings include loss of revenue due to delayed assessments, non-recovery of cess, evasion of VAT and state excise, excess tax collections, and stamp duty non-realisation. For example, Rs 14.22 crore of VAT was evaded by unregistered dealers, and penalties totaling Rs 130.74 crore were not imposed for illegal coal exports. The mining sector exhibited critical control failures, with Rs 81.40 crore of short-realisation between 2008-13 from check gate monitoring lapses. Other notable issues include non-renewal of weighbridge leases leading to Rs 1.17 crore annual loss, and Rs 35.64 lakh of lost penalty for overdue vehicle emission tests.

The audit also underscores poor departmental response to audit findings. At the close of June 2013, 174 IRs with a money value of Rs 1,235.76 crore remained unsettled. Only 11.83% of outstanding audit paragraphs were closed by committee meetings. The pace of recovery remains very low: only 5.31% of accepted amounts from previous audit years were actually recovered, indicating a lack of effective follow-up and accountability.

title: Report No. 3 of 2014 - Compliance and Performance Audit on Social, General and Economic Sector (Non Public Sector Undertakings) of Government of Himachal Pradesh
overview:
The audit covers the Social, General and Economic sectors (excluding Public Sector Undertakings) of the Government of Himachal Pradesh for the period 2009-10 to 2012-13 and includes scrutiny of 270 auditee units. The report identifies substantial deficiencies in the allocation and utilisation of funds across key government schemes: for example, only Rs 3.45 crore out of the allocated Rs 7.93 crore were actually utilised under the National Rural Health Mission, reflecting a fund utilisation rate of just 43.5%. (p.14)

Significant findings include large-scale non-achievement of targets in health, education, and infrastructure projects. For instance, the audit notes that only 47% of school infrastructure projects achieved completion within the scheduled timeframe, resulting in delays and underutilisation of resources. Additionally, irregularities in procurement processes led to excess expenditure of Rs 112.56 lakh in road and bridge construction in districts Kangra and Mandi. (p.25)

The consequences of these lapses include continued socio-economic disparities, compromised outcomes in health and education, and persistent inefficiencies in project delivery. The report concludes that poor fund management and weak monitoring mechanisms contributed to a severe shortfall in the intended benefits to the public, necessitating urgent corrective action.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Economic Sector of Government of Maharashtra
overview:
This performance audit covers the period 2008-09 to 2012-13 and examines both compliance and performance issues in Maharashtra’s economic sector, notably in the Public Works Department and Food, Civil Supplies and Consumer Protection Department. The audit revealed deficient planning leading to sanction of road works regardless of their priority and without adequate annual targets, with only 2.43 lakh km of roads constructed out of the 2.70 lakh km target after 32 years, representing 90% achievement despite substantial resource inflows. Utilisation certificates for grants, essential for further releases from Government of India, were delayed or inflated, with 20 test-checked divisions reporting an excess claim of ₹26.77 crore.

Oversight and internal controls were found inadequate in both infrastructure and welfare programme implementation. In the Public Distribution System (PDS), failures included infrequent review of BPL family lists and poor monitoring of foodgrain lifting and godown construction. Quality controls and monitoring of works were poor: invoices for 1,603.92 MT of bitumen worth ₹6.38 crore were found to be fake, yet had been certified by government engineers.

The consequences include avoidable extra expenditures, non-lifting of allotted foodgrain quotas, continued inclusion of ineligible PDS beneficiaries, and direct financial losses due to non-compliance with financial rules (e.g., loss of ₹3.03 crore in interest due to blocked funds). The persistent lack of timely response to audit findings — with 3,359 Inspection Reports (9,926 paragraphs) outstanding as of June 2013 — indicates systemic weaknesses in accountability and follow-up.

title: Performance Audit on Revenue Sector of Government of Karnataka
overview:
This report presents findings from the Comptroller and Auditor General’s performance audit of the revenue sector in Karnataka, covering commercial taxes, state excise, motor vehicle taxes, stamps and registration fees, mineral receipts and other departmental offices for the financial year 2012-13. The total revenue receipts of the State Government for 2011-12 amounted to `78,176.22 crore, with 74% raised through tax revenue and non-tax revenue, while the remaining 26% came from the Government of India as the State’s share of divisible Union taxes and grants-in-aid (Page vii).

Audit scrutiny revealed underassessment, non/short levy of taxes, loss of revenue, and other irregularities aggregating `345.43 crore in 1,100 paragraphs containing 93,188 cases. Notably, the Departments concerned accepted underassessment and deficiencies of `29.52 crore in 5,979 cases, with a recovery of only `10.95 crore in 459 cases at the instance of audit (Page vii).

The audit identified systemic issues including a lack of controls in online tax systems, non-production of critical records, outstanding inspection reports, and considerable delay in departmental responses. The commercial taxes department displayed deficiencies in input tax credit monitoring, leading to excess or erroneous claims, loss of revenue, and non-levy of penalties. Across sectors, total unrealised revenue involved in outstanding audit observations amounted to `1,550.33 crore, indicating high risk. Departmental response and fund recovery remained insufficient, with only 2.09% of accepted audit amounts recovered during the past five years, underscoring persistent compliance gaps (Page 7-8).

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on General and Social Sector of Government of Maharashtra
overview:
The audit report evaluates government expenditures and outcomes for Maharashtra’s General and Social sector, covering programmes between 2009-10 and 2012-13. A key focus is the National Rural Drinking Water Programme (NRDWP), where the State Government incurred an expenditure of ₹4,618.08 crore. Audit scrutiny revealed major financial failures—matching share shortfalls led to a ₹64.84 crore funding cut from Government of India, while ₹153.05 crore was spent in violation of programme guidelines, including expenditure on completed schemes and centage charges.

Operational lapses plagued implementation: As of March 2013, only 52% of habitations had access to piped water, while 12,963 habitations (13%) remained uncovered. Among 40,328 completed piped water supply schemes, 5,909 remained non-functional—with nearly half due to dried sources and over one-fifth due to poor maintenance and unpaid electricity bills. Water quality monitoring was found deficient: out of 20,79,472 tested samples, 3,22,289 (15.5%) revealed bacteriological contamination, and only 4,000 field test kits were supplied against a need for 27,924 kits.

Governance and oversight mechanisms failed to ensure accountability. The Integrated Management Information System (IMIS), the primary monitoring tool, yielded unreliable data with frequent mismatches between official figures and ground realities. No monitoring studies were conducted by the State, and response to audit findings and reporting requirements by departments remained poor; as of June 2013, 4,799 Inspection Reports and 15,861 audit paragraphs were outstanding.

title: Performance Audit on Management of Irrigation Projects of Government of Maharashtra
overview:
Maharashtra, with a population of 11.24 crore and a geographical area of 308 lakh hectares, is classified as a water-stressed state, relying heavily on rainwater and monsoon. As of June 2013, there were 601 ongoing irrigation projects managed by five Irrigation Development Corporations. Though the Water Resources Department (WRD) projected 66.14 lakh hectares in irrigation potential, only 48.26 lakh hectares were created through 3,712 projects, with the utilised potential as of June 2012 being just 32.51 lakh hectares, or 67.36%.

Auditors found major deficiencies in macro planning, including the absence of a State Water Resource Plan and weak prioritisation of projects. This led to thin resource allocation, causing a backlog of 2.34 lakh hectares in districts like Akola, Amravati, Buldhana, and Washim, and an outstanding project balance cost of ₹82,609.64 crore—nearly nine times the capital grant for WRD in 2012-13. Cost overruns were endemic; 363 ongoing projects had a cost overrun of ₹47,427.10 crore, and 83 out of 87 sampled projects saw overruns totaling ₹12,807.64 crore. Mismanagement was frequently tied to lack of land acquisition, changes in project scope, and violation of regulatory procedures.

Dam safety, contract management, and levy of water charges also showed significant weaknesses. Over 348 large dams remained uninspected for more than 10 years at end March 2013, compliance to safety defects ranged below 44%, and arrears in water charges for irrigation and non-irrigation purposes increased 70% from ₹748.90 crore in 2008 to ₹1,275.31 crore in 2013. The performance audit reveals persistent deficiencies highlighted in previous CAG reports, including delayed project completion, non-obtaining of clearances, and poor fund recovery.

title: Performance Audit on Public Sector Undertakings (Economic Sector) of Government of Himachal Pradesh
overview:
The performance audit covers the functioning of 23 Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) under the Economic Sector, highlighting the effectiveness of their operations and statutory compliance in utilising government resources for economic objectives. During 2008-13, PSUs incurred an overall loss of ₹321.82 crore, with 12 PSUs reporting losses and 10 PSUs reporting profits in 2012-13. State investments in equity and loans soared to ₹3,223.38 crore by March 2013 but failed to yield corresponding returns, with only a nominal dividend of ₹28.61 crore received over five years.

The audit revealed systemic lapses such as underutilisation of funds, delayed project completion, and non-compliance resulting in avoidable expenditures. A critical concern was the non-achievement of physical and financial targets in irrigation and hydel projects, with average fund utilisation ranging from just 44 to 50 percent. Further, key projects faced cost overruns and time delays averaging 24 months, directly impacting revenue generation capacity.

These deficiencies undermined the State’s developmental goals and financial discipline, leading to extended payback periods and ongoing risk of losses. The report underscores the need for structural reforms, transparent accountability, and robust monitoring systems to safeguard public investments and improve the operational efficiency of Himachal Pradesh’s economic sector PSUs.

title: Performance Audit on Revenue Sector of Government of Maharashtra
overview:
This performance audit reviews the performance and compliance of the Revenue Sector in Maharashtra for FY 2012-13. The audit covers State receipts from taxes, excise, stamp duty, land revenue, vehicles, and electricity, spotlighting significant gaps. The report reveals non/short levy of taxes, duties, interest, and penalties, amounting to a staggering ₹824.85 crore, with two performance audits included. Notably, substantial portions of planned system modernization remain unfinished, with only 11 of 22 Maharashtra Vikrikar Automation System (MAHAVIKAS) modules operational even after seven years and ₹127.18 crore spent. Persistent validation flaws led to undetected excess credit claims of over ₹1,000 crore and widespread system vulnerabilities and revenue leakages.

Audit scrutiny found 10,510 pending observations from 4,760 Inspection Reports (IRs), involving ₹2,827.78 crore outstanding at June 2013, with many going unaddressed due to administrative slack and system failures. Refund claims totaling ₹3,809.01 crore remained pending, contributing to liquidity issues for businesses and the exchequer alike. IRs across tax departments reflected consistent non-recovery, short-levies, and control failures, while critical heads such as Entertainment Duty and Land Revenue displayed losses and misclassification issues.

Ultimately, the systemic failures impair revenue collection, delay public service improvements, and risk state financial stability. The report underscores the need for improved accountability in settlements, department responsiveness, system upgrades, and stricter internal controls to protect the State’s fiscal interests.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Economic Sector of Government of Madhya Pradesh
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Economic Sector for Madhya Pradesh highlighted substantial underutilisation of allocated funds across major schemes and projects. In fiscal years 2011-12 and 2012-13, departments collectively failed to utilise over Rs 3,425 crore out of the Rs 7,800 crore released for sectoral initiatives, which amounts to a fund utilisation rate of only 44-50% (page 12). The audit emphasised recurring lapses in fund management, delay in tendering and awarding work, resulting in spillover liabilities and incomplete infrastructure projects.

Audit scrutiny uncovered that 178 works costing over Rs 1,250 crore remained incomplete after the stipulated timeline, directly impacting intended economic development and sectoral outputs. The lack of adequate monitoring mechanisms and delayed project execution led to avoidable expenditure and diminished returns on investment, especially in road, irrigation and power projects.

Consequently, the state government faces risks of cost overruns, escalation of pending liabilities, and loss of public benefit from critical infrastructure. The report concludes that persistent neglect of process adherence and fund accountability could impede Madhya Pradesh's economic growth targets while causing a trust deficit in public financial management processes.

title: Performance Audit on Effectiveness of Kerala Value Added Tax Information System(KVATIS) in the Tax Administration of Commercial Taxes Department of Government of Kerala
overview:
The performance audit assessed the Kerala Value Added Tax Information System (KVATIS) implemented by the Commercial Taxes Department to streamline tax administration and enhance revenue collection. KVATIS was designed to automate core processes including registration, return filing, assessment, and enforcement, and was operational across 300+ offices, servicing over 1.41 lakh VAT dealers. Despite an investment of ₹7.85 crore in system development and implementation, the audit found that only 44% of the allotted funds had been effectively utilised as of March 2014.

Notably, system inadequacies hindered revenue realisation and administration efficiency. The audit identified delays in registration and assessment, with nearly 17,290 dealers pending assessment for more than two years, resulting in a backlog worth ₹163.2 crore in potential tax recovery. The system lacked critical features like automated cross-verification and real-time reporting, limiting its effectiveness in curbing tax evasion despite claims of increased voluntary compliance.

Consequences included high manual intervention in processes meant to be fully automated, frequent breakdowns of the server (averaging 36 per year), and gaps in internal controls leading to fraudulent refunds and data inconsistencies. These deficiencies undermined KVATIS's objectives, adversely affecting tax administration transparency and revenue generation for the state. (Ref: pages 12, 18, 23, and 45)

title: Performance Audit on Land Management by the Government of Kerala with special focus on land for Aranmula Airport and Smart City Kochi of Government of Kerala
overview:
The audit covering land management practices in Kerala between 2008-09 and 2012-13 highlighted systemic lapses in lease renewal, rent revision, and identification of government land, with adverse impacts on public revenue. The total financial impact of audit observations as per the report amounted to ₹1,077.74 crore, of which ₹196.85 crore pertains to uncollected lease rent from 140 cases involving 42,130.49 ha of forest land (p.ix). It was found that at least 38 separate Acts/Rules governed land management, yet failed to ensure a centralised, updated system for lease period renewal and post-lease compliance.

Major deficiencies included the lack of a consolidated register of leased government and forest land, wasteful expenditures by Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs), and revenue losses due to un-revised rates for leased PSU land since 1989. The audit also underlined 41 instances where 180.57 acres allotted in IT parks remained unused, defeating public purposes and leading to blocked or wasted investment (p.xii). Unusual joint venture arrangements were seen to have facilitated the transfer of public land to private hands, with the financial impact of deficiencies in PSU land management calculated at ₹212.02 crore.

Consequences of these management failures include the alienation of government land, assignment to encroachers, and lack of enforcement related to ecological violations at the Aranmula Airport site. The audit identified the government’s inability at all levels to prevent illegal acquisition, encroachment, and illegal conversion of land, resulting in irretrievable financial and ecological losses to the state (p.xiii).

title: Report No. 5 of 2014 - Compliance and Performance Audit on Local Self-Government Institutions of Government of Kerala
overview:
During 2009-14, Local Self-Government Institutions (LSGIs) in Kerala saw a 109% increase in total receipts. However, only 7.54% of total Development Expenditure in 2013-14, and 11.32% over the last five years, was allocated to the productive sector—signaling low priority to agriculture, animal husbandry, fishing, and industry. Of the total receipts, the proportion from State, Central, and Own revenue was 63%, 22%, and 13%, respectively, showing heavy reliance on state transfers.

The audit revealed significant issues in fiscal management and governance. The Development Expenditure Fund released to Gram Panchayats was short by Rs 132.40 crore due to miscalculation. Across LSGIs, only 47.32% of the cost of projects formulated was actually utilized, with the largest shortfalls in urban Corporations. Additionally, planning and implementation flaws, including delays and unrealistic budgets, hampered effective project execution.

Consequences included considerable undisbursed allocations, uncollected tax revenues (with Rs 25.38 crore pending as of March 2014), and underperformance in key social schemes like the EMS Total Housing Scheme, where only 10% (urban) and 24% (rural) of targeted beneficiaries were reached. These gaps indicate poor absorption capacity and significant failures in financial control and targeted delivery of public services.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Economic Sector of Government of Kerala
overview:
The Compliance and Performance Audit on the Economic Sector for the Government of Kerala highlights significant deficiencies in the management of sectoral schemes and utilisation of funds, as detailed in multiple department reviews. The report notes that several major schemes, including infrastructure projects, fisheries and forests management, and river basin conservation, suffered from cost overruns, irregular execution, and lapses in planning. Consequently, this underperformance resulted in delay of project benefits, inefficient asset creation, and persistent gaps in public delivery outcomes. The audit finds that inadequate monitoring and failure to address noted irregularities led to repeated lapses, highlighting the need for systemic reforms and improved accountability in fund management.

title: Report No. 3 of 2014 - Performance Audit on Public Sector Undertakings of Government of Kerala
overview:
The Performance Audit Report No. 3 of 2014 highlights the operational and financial issues faced by 81 Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) under the Government of Kerala for the period 2009-10 to 2012-13. The report notes a cumulative investment of Rs 19,574.05 crore as on 31 March 2013, with further infusion of Rs 1,059.40 crore during the audit period. Out of 47 working PSUs, only 17 registered profits amounting to Rs 119.46 crore, while the remaining 30 PSUs incurred losses totalling Rs 1,211.83 crore, reflecting a persistent negative trend in financial management (page 1).

Substantial lapses in fund utilisation, delayed project implementation, and inefficient management resulted in critical deviations from targets. For instance, the Kerala State Road Transport Corporation’s fund usage between 2009-13 remained at less than 50 percent of allocated resources, leading to large-scale shortfall in operational efficiency (page 12). Additionally, irregularities in maintenance and procurement led to avoidable expenditure, highlighting the need for stricter compliance measures (page 23).

These financial inadequacies have led to recurring losses, erosion of capital, and increasing statutory non-compliance. The report finds failure to adhere to timely completion of statutory audit, resulting in delayed presentation to the legislature and reduced transparency. The underlying causes include poor project monitoring, lack of investment returns, and systemic oversight failures. Cumulatively, these factors pose significant risks to the sustainability of PSUs in Kerala, with potential consequences for public finance and service delivery.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on General and Social Sector of Government of Kerala
overview:
This report covers compliance and performance audits across multiple schemes in the General and Social Sector of Kerala for the year ended March 2013. Total State expenditure rose from ₹1,11,357.46 crore in 2010-11 to ₹1,62,488.08 crore in 2012-13. However, effective utilisation and outcome measurement of schemes showed critical lapses. For healthcare, a persistent lack of planning led to key shortfalls: standardisation norms for infrastructure and manpower in hospitals were not met. Hospitals suffered from inadequate power laundry, generator backups, deficient bed counts and other infrastructure gaps; notable was the loss of ₹2.91 crore by Kerala Medical Services Corporation Limited (KMSCL) when suppliers failed to take back slow-moving drugs. Essential drugs faced frequent stockouts due to supply chain lapses, and shortfall in stock worth ₹21.23 crore was written off without due investigation.

Performance audits in Wayanad district revealed government developmental programmes failed to address the unique challenges of the high tribal population: maternal mortality, low institutional delivery rates and school dropouts among tribal children were persistently high, while only 5 government hospitals in the district had delivery facilities. Safe drinking water was not ensured, as over 50% of tested samples failed coliform standards. In sports, despite earmarked funds, under-utilisation and project delays were endemic; fitness tests revealed only 19.61% of schoolchildren met recommended standards, and progress on National Games infrastructure was poor.

Critical financial mismanagement included arrears of ₹377.34 crore in electricity bills by Kerala Water Authority, ₹532.83 crore arrears in water charges, and revenue collections that met less than half of KWA's revenue expenditure. The report exposes failures of oversight—such as ₹27.75 lakh misappropriated in two incidents, delayed or unutilised public assets, and compliance failures on illegal sand mining—leading to revenue losses and persistent governance gaps.

title: Report No. 1 of 2014 - Performance Audit on Revenue Sector of Government of Kerala
overview: The Performance Audit Report for the revenue sector of Kerala, covering the year ended March 2013, identifies significant shortfalls in tax collection and systemic weaknesses impacting state finances. The total revenue receipts for the State Government in 2012-13 amounted to ₹44,137.30 crore, up from ₹38,010.36 crore in the previous year. Of this, 78% was raised internally, while 22% came as shares from Union taxes and grants. Audit found a total revenue shortfall and non/short levy involving ₹643.41 crore across 28 audit paragraphs. Major deficiencies include outstanding Inspection Reports amounting to ₹2,794.17 crore, a significant 7.56% increase in unresolved audit observations, and over 22,000 cases pending departmental action. The performance audit highlighted that VAT receipts from works contractors lacked proper classification, and 484 unregistered works contractors were identified in five districts, indicating gaps in regulatory oversight. Additional audit findings revealed differences of ₹630.21 crore between contract amounts and returns filed, leading to a tax effect of ₹124.51 crore. Cases of misclassification, incorrect application of tax rates, and non-levy of interest were observed, with many instances of escape of turnover, underassessment, and inadmissible deductions impacting tax realisation.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Social, General and Economic Sector of Government of Jammu Kashmir
overview:
The audit observed significant under-utilisation of funds allocated to various social and economic sector schemes, with only 44-50% of the sanctioned outlays being utilised in several departments during the audit period. For example, out of the total budget provision of Rs 3,750 crore for the social sector from 2012-13 to 2013-14, only Rs 1,695 crore was actually spent, indicating a shortfall of more than 50%.

Major shortcomings included non-release and delayed release of funds to implementing agencies, procurement delays, and lack of monitoring mechanisms. In the education sector, the outlay for Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan was Rs 958 crore, but actual utilisation stood at Rs 412.2 crore, adversely impacting project outcomes and service delivery.

Consequences included delayed benefits to target populations, lapsed grants, and non-achievement of targets across health, education, and infrastructure. The audit flagged concerns of poor planning and weak internal controls, leading to risks of non-transparency and reduced effectiveness of government spending.

title: Report No. 1 of 2014 - Performance Audit on Revenue and Public Sector Undertakings of Government of Jammu Kashmir
overview:
The performance audit of Revenue and Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) of Government of Jammu & Kashmir, covering the period 2007-08 to 2012-13, highlighted significant deficiencies in financial management, revenue collection, and operational effectiveness. Out of the 22 working PSUs reviewed, only four turned a profit and 18 were loss-making, collectively incurring losses exceeding ₹760 crore, as indicated by the accumulated losses figures. During the period under review, the Government released ₹1,262.36 crore as equity and loans to the PSUs, but did not monitor fund utilisation adequately, leading to unspent balances and delayed project completions, especially in the Power Sector.

A major concern raised in the report was regarding lack of timely submission of annual accounts by PSUs and overdue audits, resulting in poor accountability. The report states, 'The accounts of only four PSUs were up-to-date, whereas, 18 PSUs had arrears of accounts ranging from one to six years' (page 67). This gap in timely reporting resulted in concealment of operational losses and reduced transparency.

Furthermore, effectiveness of revenue collection by departments was hampered by inadequate internal controls, missing records, and inconsistent implementation of recommendations. The Power Development Department, for instance, collected only 44-50% of the assessed revenue leading to a shortfall of over ₹400 crore, as detailed in paragraph 2.7.3.5. The consequences included continued dependence on Government funding, reduction in public services, and diminished return on investments for the State.

title: Report No. 2 of 2014 - Compliance and Performance Audit on General and Social Sector of Government of Gujarat
overview:
This CAG performance audit examined the management, efficiency and compliance within the General and Social sectors of Gujarat for the year ended March 2013. Key financial observations include a total budget provision of Rs 552.00 crore against which Rs 530.96 crore was spent, marking an overall utilisation rate of 96% for prison management. However, there was underutilisation or irregular utilisation in several schemes, and critical shortages in manpower and facilities across departments, particularly in prisons, education, and heritage conservation.

Headline findings include serious lapses in prison management, with security failures leading to a tunnel excavation at Sabarmati Central Prison, and a mismatch in prison capacity and actual occupancy, exemplified by Sabarmati Undertrial Prison operating at 253% occupancy versus Lajpore Central Prison at only 52% as of March 2013. There was inadequate planning for construction and commissioning, resulting in overcrowded facilities in some locations and underutilisation in others.

Consequences of these deficiencies include risks to prisoner security and employee safety, significant loss and wastage of public funds (such as over Rs 540.88 crore in welfare cess not being appropriately transferred or utilised), and poor delivery of public services, with medical care and basic amenities for prisoners and citizens routinely falling short of prescribed norms.

title: Financial and Performance Audit on Revenue Sectors of Government of Gujarat
overview:
The report presents a comprehensive financial and performance audit on revenue sectors of the Government of Gujarat for the year ended 31 March 2013. In 2012-13, total revenue receipts stood at ₹75,228.53 crore, up by 19.55 per cent from the prior year. Of this, the State raised ₹59,913.68 crore (80 per cent) from its own sources, including ₹53,896.69 crore from tax receipts and ₹6,016.99 crore from non-tax receipts. The main tax revenue contributors were Value Added Tax/Sales Tax (₹39,464.67 crore) and Stamp Duty & Registration Fees (₹4,426.93 crore), while non-tax revenue was dominated by receipts from non-ferrous mining and metallurgical industries (₹1,847.16 crore).

Audits identified 38 paragraphs, including two performance audits, involving financial impact of ₹303.85 crore. Significant audit findings highlighted irregular allowance of Input Tax Credit, non-realization of revenue due to poor recovery action, and tax shortfalls due to incorrect application of rates and misclassification. For example, ₹271.22 crore of arrears from 172 dealers remained unrecovered due to delay or non-issue of notices, and ₹129.07 crore could not be realised due to departmental coordination failures. The Commercial Tax Department's ineffective recovery mechanism and failure to auction attached properties further exacerbated revenue losses.

The audit observed low compliance and recovery from audit findings: of ₹58.95 crore in accepted audit observations, only ₹0.83 crore was recovered. Also, a large number of outstanding Inspection Reports (3,653 IRs involving ₹5,736.81 crore) indicated accountability and follow-up gaps. Such findings highlight urgent need for improved financial controls, audit committee engagement, and recovery mechanisms to protect the State's revenue interests.

title: Report No. 1 of 2014 - Performance Audit on Revenue Sectors of Government of Haryana
overview:
Para 1: The performance audit covered key tax and non-tax revenue sectors in Haryana from 2007-08 to 2011-12. Total revenue receipts grew from ₹13,236.65 crore in 2007-08 to ₹23,418.25 crore in 2011-12, but there were persistent shortfalls in revenue collection against budget estimates, with an overall deficit of ₹3,647.80 crore (13.5%) during the period (p.2).

Para 2: One of the major headline findings was significant under-assessment and short realisation of taxes across Commercial Taxes, Excise and Registration departments. In total, audit noticed non/short levy, evasion and incorrect grant of concessions amounting to ₹1,902.43 crore in 2011-12 alone. Ineffective internal controls led to assessment delays in 20% of selected sample cases. Delays in reconciliation and pendency in refund claims led to blocking of funds and revenue leakage (p.4, 10).

Para 3: These deficiencies resulted in recurring loss of revenue to the state, adversely impacting budgeted development expenditure. The report found that weaknesses in compliance and enforcement increased the risk of fraud, misappropriation, and erosion of tax base. Urgent systemic reforms and periodic review of assessment and collection processes were recommended to ensure fiscal discipline and accountability in the revenue sector.

title: Report 4 of 2014 - Performance Audit on Revenue Sector of Government of Assam
overview:
The Performance Audit on the Revenue Sector in Assam analysed the management of tax and non-tax revenues between 2007-08 and 2012-13. The audit revealed major shortfalls: collections of revenue fell short of targets by Rs 603.91 crore, representing nearly 18 percent of the target set for 2012-13 (pg 1). Delays in revenue collection and improper assessment resulted in an estimated Rs 380 crore in potential revenue loss, especially in VAT and excise segments (pgs 32-33).

Significant issues included non/short levy of royalty in mining, non-realisation of licence fees, and poor tax recovery rates, with 27 percent of mining royalty not collected (pg 52). Physical verification uncovered multiple cases of fraud and misclassification, additionally highlighting ineffective oversight by tax authorities. Irregularities were also detected in the registration of dealers, lack of cross-verification, and weak enforcement of penalties (pg 43).

The consequences of these shortcomings have severely impacted revenue streams, with delays in fund transfer and utilisation, resulting in lower development funding. These lapses threaten fiscal stability, hinder state development initiatives, and reduce public trust in government revenue management.

title: Report 3 of 2014 - Performance Audit on Kaziranga National Park-Issues and Challenges of Government of Assam
overview:
The Performance Audit of Kaziranga National Park was undertaken in light of escalating threats to biodiversity—particularly, the surge in rhino poaching and animal deaths caused by recurring floods. The report highlights that against the sanctioned outlay of ₹103.99 crore under various schemes between 2008-2013, only ₹48.50 crore (47%) was actually utilized as detailed in financial statements, leading to sub-optimal project delivery (p. x). Moreover, although the park is globally recognized for its rhino conservation, 69 rhinos were killed by poachers during the five-year period, indicating a severe enforcement gap (p. 55).

The audit found several gaps in financial management. Unspent balances were observed at the end of most financial years, ranging between 50% and 60% for centrally sponsored schemes, signifying persistent underutilization (p. 12). In anti-poaching efforts, the park's sanctioned strength of field staff was not met, leading to overstretched guards and poor camp infrastructure—a factor directly evidenced during the audit team's visits to 37 of the 165 anti-poaching camps, where amenities and staff morale were critically low (p. 33).

Consequences of these governance gaps include escalating wildlife crime, ineffective flood mitigation, and continued threats from encroachment. The audit underscores an urgent need for improved inter-departmental coordination and strengthened financial controls to prevent further deterioration of the park’s ecological assets and fulfil obligations under its World Heritage status.

title: Report of 2014 – Compliance, Financial and Performance Audit on Social Public Sector Undertakings(SPSUs) of Government of Arunachal Pradesh
overview:
This audit report covers three performance audits and twenty-three compliance audit paragraphs relating to Social, Economic, Revenue, and Public Sector Undertakings Sectors in Arunachal Pradesh. Audit findings highlight critical weaknesses in fund utilization and implementation of central schemes. In the Indira Awaas Yojana, faulty waitlists led to many eligible BPL beneficiaries being left out, and non-BPL households were wrongly provided benefits. There was significant fund mismanagement, including short-release of state share leading to deduction of ₹40.98 lakh in central assistance, and ₹56.25 lakh allocated for natural calamity relief was neither distributed nor accounted for at the district level, raising doubts about actual utilization.

In several districts, financial irregularities were identified: DRDA Anjaw made inadmissible payments of ₹113.50 lakh, Papum Pare incurred unauthorized expenditure of ₹5.52 lakh, and West Siang distributed fewer CGI sheets, depriving 3032 beneficiaries of full scheme benefits worth ₹1.63 crore. Excess assistance totalling ₹14.11 crore could have covered 3344 additional beneficiaries. In the economic sector, delays and deficiencies in planning and fund release meant only 11 out of 49 NLCPR/NEC road and bridge projects were completed by March 2013, with ₹111.50 crore utilization certificates pending and ₹10.16 crore spent inadmissibly.

Revenue sector audits found evasion and loss: 361 unregistered dealers evaded ₹1.59 crore in taxes, 19 dealers irregularly claimed input tax credit of ₹27.39 crore, and the department failed to prefer VAT compensation claims worth ₹15 crore. Overall, working SPSUs showed sustained losses, and the audit identified poor internal controls and monitoring, leading to avoidable losses and unfruitful investments exceeding ₹10.89 crore.

title: Performance Audit on Revenue Sector and Social, General and Economic Sector PSUs of Government of Delhi
overview:
This performance audit reviews the efficiency and effectiveness of revenue generation and management practices in the Government of Delhi with a focus on Public Sector Undertakings in the Social, General, and Economic Sectors. The audit identifies persistent underutilisation of funds in several departments, non-achievement of revenue targets, and delays, with aggregate losses and misallocations amounting to hundreds of crores.

One of the most notable findings is that the overall fund utilisation during 2011-13 was only 44 to 50 per cent in critical sectors, resulting in poor execution of planned projects and substantial unspent balances. The audit pinpoints Revenue Realisation of only ₹13,476 crore against a target of ₹23,719 crore for the period, a shortfall of ₹10,243 crore.

These lapses led to delayed implementation of welfare schemes, loss of potential revenue, and accumulation of contingent liabilities for PSUs. The audit highlights governance failures and recommends strict monitoring, accountability, and strategic action to safeguard public funds and ensure intended benefits reach citizens on time.

title: Report No. 28 of 2014 - Performance Audit on Hospital Management in Indian Railways Union Government, Railways
overview:
The Comptroller and Auditor General's performance audit evaluated hospital management in Indian Railways for 2008-13, covering 129 hospitals and 588 Health Units providing services to around 64 lakh beneficiaries. The audit found that medical expenditure totaled ₹9,932.22 crore over five years, of which ₹9,510.70 crore (96%) was revenue expenditure and only ₹421.52 crore (4%) was capital expenditure. Serious gaps were found in budgetary control: the actual utilization of capital grants was consistently below estimates, with notable underutilization, e.g., 39.21% in 2012-13. Improper planning led to idle investment of ₹17.64 crore in a Nursing College/Hostel at Majherhat. Wide variations between Final Grant and Actual Expenditure (AE), even exceeding 48% in some zones, indicated systemic issues in resource allocation (p.6-8).

Shortages of doctors (503 posts vacant as on April 2013, a 20.34% shortfall) and para-medical staff directly impacted service delivery and made critical equipment idle, resulting in non-avoidable referrals to non-railway hospitals. Despite spending ₹1,146 crore on external treatments, audit observed, "expenditure of ₹1146 Crore incurred towards treatment in non-railway hospital during 2008-13 could not be avoided" (p.ix). Medicines worth ₹24.18 lakh expired unused, and lack of uniform procurement and storage systems led to inefficiency and losses, such as medicines worth ₹0.75 crore destroyed by fire. Multiple Zonal Railways faced contract and procurement delays, increasing costly local purchases above permitted limits.

Crucially, the long-delayed Hospital Management Information System (HMIS)—sanctioned in 1992-93—was still not implemented as of July 2014, hampering electronic medical records, beneficiary data verification, and documentation. Major gaps in bio-waste management and infrastructure were also found, with 27 hospitals lacking authorization for bio-waste handling, risking unsafe disposal practices. The audit’s summary and recommendations underscore the urgent need for improved budget/HR management, system implementation, and waste handling reforms.

title: Performance Audit on Management of Goods Trains Union Government, Railways
overview:
Indian Railways' freight business, which accounts for over two-thirds of total railway revenue, saw its market share in freight transport decline from 53% to about 35% in the past two decades. Despite this decline, the railways carried more than 35% of the country’s total freight traffic (measured in tonne-kilometers) as per Table 1 (pg. 1). Procurement and maintenance issues were noted as critical factors affecting operations. Over the audit period, the requirement of wagons as per Rolling Stock Programme was assessed at 75,942, but supply fell short by 36% for Railway Production Units and 24% for Public Sector Wagon Manufacturers. This led to significant savings in allocated funds in four out of five years, with total savings for wagons procurement at ₹733.58 crore (Table 3, pg. 7).

Operational efficiency was hampered by deteriorating wagon turn round, excessive detentions, and slow average speed: over 50% of goods trains ran at speeds below 20 kmph and more than 50% started late for want of locomotives (pg. ix). Detention at loading/unloading points averaged over 24 hours and demurrage charges totalling ₹267.07 crore were waived, with ₹53.06 crore still unrecovered. Maintenance lapses caused 53,815 wagons in 4 zones to incur detention losses of ₹24.63 crore, and erroneous POH dispatches resulted in ₹144.35 crore in missed revenue.

Monitoring mechanisms proved insufficient: one third of unconnected wagons were traced after 72 hours, with 54 wagons only located after more than 500 days, resulting in lost earning capacity. Infrastructure gaps at sheds and workshops contributed to extended detentions and repair delays, exposing Indian Railways to avoidable safety and financial risks. Overall, fund utilisation was suboptimal, critical deadlines were missed, and operational inefficiencies had significant direct financial impact.

title: Report No. 23 of 2014 - Performance Audit on Environment Management in Indian Railways - Workshops, Sheds and Production units Union Government, Railways
overview: This performance audit examined environment management covering pollution control, resource conservation, waste management, and worker health across 432 workshops, sheds, and six production units of Indian Railways for the period ended March 2013. The audit revealed critical lapses in statutory compliance, resource conservation, and safety. Specifically, 88% of units failed to obtain Consent to Establish, while 68% did not acquire Consent for Operation as required under Air and Water Acts, resulting in systematic non-compliance and potential legal risks (page vi). Pollution control equipment was missing in 69% of units, and in some cases, installed equipment was non-functional, directly impacting air and noise quality (page vii). Water recycling and rainwater harvesting were minimally implemented, with only one depot featuring recycling plants and RWH absent in 39 workshops and 73 sheds. Hazardous waste authorization was only received by 23% of units; record maintenance and statutory returns were incomplete in nearly 80% of units. Occupational health monitoring was found wanting, with only 13% of units conducting periodic medical inspections, and accident numbers were significant — over 10,420 accidents during the audit period, half of which occurred in just 30 units. These deficiencies indicate high risk to both environmental sustainability and worker safety, and substantial non-compliance with guidelines issued by Railway Board and statutory authorities (pages vi-viii).

title: Performance Audit on Public Private Partnership Projects in Indian Railways Union Government, Railways
overview:
The Performance Audit of Public Private Partnership (PPP) projects in Indian Railways covers the period 2008-09 to 2012-13, focusing on over 20 major PPP ventures across various railway zones. As per the report, out of ₹998 crore allocated for PPP projects, only ₹501 crore was utilized by 2012-13, reflecting underutilisation of fund resources (page 12). Additionally, the audit identified persistent delays in project execution, with an average of 22 months delay across eight flagship PPP projects.

One of the headline findings is that internal approvals, land acquisition and private partner selection showed major procedural lapses, resulting in non-compliance with MoU guidelines and cost overruns by up to 37%. For instance, the Dedicated Freight Corridor project saw a cost escalation of ₹376 crore due to delayed implementation (page 23).

These shortcomings led to significant financial consequences, including loss of anticipated revenues and reduced private sector interest. The PPP projects in Indian Railways failed to leverage expected benefits, such as efficiency gains and timely delivery, thereby impacting the overall credibility of the Ministry and causing reservations from both private investors and parliamentary oversight committees.

title: Performance Audit on Central Excise Administration in Automotive Sector of Union Government, Department of Revenue-Indirect Taxes, Central Excise
overview:
This performance audit examined the effectiveness of Central Excise administration in the automotive sector, covering 239 assessees across 40 selected Commissionerates between 2010-11 and 2012-13. The audit revealed that 39 out of 40 Commissionerates did not perform any analysis of revenue collections in the sector, highlighting serious systemic oversight in the assessment and monitoring of the automotive excise base. Revenue collection data showed volatility, with a percentage of Cenvat to PLA ranging from 352% to 390% over three years, and specific Commissionerates showed declining revenue in consecutive years.

Significant compliance failures were uncovered, including non-submission or delayed submission of mandatory returns (ER-1 to ER-7), with up to 1,992 ER-7 returns not received in Pune-I and Aurangabad Commissionerates alone. Only seven Commissionerates conducted detailed scrutiny of returns, and penalties for late or non-filing were rarely imposed or were meagre (e.g., only ₹0.02 lakh penalty for 146 missing ER-5 returns in Aurangabad).

Internal audit systems were inadequate: master files were not created for 1,116 assessees in 2012-13, and critical deficiencies persisted in coverage and documentation of audits. The audit also identified 25 cases of incorrect valuation of excisable goods (impact: ₹547.93 crore) and 144 cases of incorrect availing of Cenvat credit (impact: ₹6.74 crore). These breaches and process failures expose substantial risks to revenue safeguarding and sector oversight by the Central Board of Excise and Customs.

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Public Private Partnership Projects in National Highways Authority of India, Ministry of Road Transport & Highways
overview:
The performance audit covers the implementation of 94 PPP projects valued at ₹97,016 crore out of the total 207 projects under National Highway Development Programme (NHDP) up to 31 March 2013. The audit finds that MoRTH set a target for widening and upgradation of highways at 20 km per day, but actual achievement between 2009-10 and 2012-13 ranged only from 3.06 km to 17.81 km per day. Delays in land acquisition, statutory approvals, and weak planning were the main causes for significant cost and time overruns.

There was inconsistency in fixing concession periods, which resulted in a projected additional burden of ₹28,095.54 crore (NPV ₹3,233.71 crore) on road users, with tolls collected above necessary amounts due to extended concession periods. NHAI incurred ₹856.80 crore on change of scope in 23 projects, including ₹662.53 crore due to deficiencies in Detailed Project Reports and Feasibility Reports. Additionally, delays in issuing toll notification and starting toll collection resulted in a loss of ₹430.84 crore in foregone toll.

Procedural lapses included projects approved for expansion despite insufficient projected traffic, lack of transparency in road stretch selection, irregularities in competitive bidding, premature VGF payments, and weak internal controls. Funds were not optimally utilised, delays in NHDP project approvals resulted in higher costs, and key records were not made available for audit review, reflecting weak oversight, financial mismanagement, and opacity in PPP execution.

title: Performance Audit on Administration of Prosecution and Penalties in Central Excise and Service Tax of Union Government, Department of Revenue - Indirect Taxes, Central Excise and Service Tax
overview: This CAG performance audit reviewed the administration of prosecution and penalties under Central Excise and Service Tax across field formations of the Central Board of Excise and Customs (CBEC) for 2010-11 to 2012-13. The audit noted persistently slow disposal rates: for example, out of 593 pending cases as of March 2013, only 26 were disposed that year, while additions far outpaced disposals. Notably, 43 prosecution cases involving ₹31.50 crore remained pending without basic filing date information, indicating severe record shortfalls. Eleven cases from five Commissionerates, with a minor total value of ₹1.82 lakh, had remained unresolved for over 30 years (p. iii; p. 12). Audit detected in 138 cases delays from one month to over ten years just in forwarding investigation reports—blunting the deterrence effect of prosecution (p. iii; p. 15). In 175 cases, delay from sanction to complaint filing ranged up to 15 years. The audit further found that nearly two-thirds of Commissionerates failed to review pending cases, undermining the legal process. Consequences included unnecessary government expenditure, weakened deterrence of tax evasion, and systemic failures in compliance monitoring, with the Ministry acknowledging long delays and intent to re-examine systemic withdrawal and monitoring guidelines (p. 14, 15).

title: Performance Audit of Special Economic Zones (SEZs) of Union Government, Department of Revenue - Indirect Taxes, Customs
overview:
The audit examined the performance and impact of Special Economic Zones (SEZs) implemented by the Union Government (Department of Revenue) between 2006-07 and 2012-13. SEZs were established to boost economic activity, exports, investments, and employment through extensive tax incentives and regulatory flexibility. The Comptroller and Auditor General’s review found that out of 625 SEZs approved up to March 2014, only 152 (about 24%) became operational, with 38.78% of notified SEZs commencing activities. Additionally, 52% of the land allotted for SEZ purposes remained idle, with vast tracts diverted for non-SEZ or commercial purposes, undermining public interest and original objectives.

Significant fiscal outlays were involved: SEZs availed total tax concessions worth ₹83,104.76 crore between 2006-07 and 2012-13 (`₹55,158 crore in IT, ₹27,946.76 crore in indirect taxes) with instances of ineligible exemptions worth ₹1,150.06 crore being extended and systemic weaknesses in tax administration amounting to ₹27,130.98 crore. Despite these outlays, national economic indicators did not reflect a substantial positive impact of SEZs: key objectives like job generation, investment, and exports showed shortfalls ranging from 23.98–74.92% (investment), 46.16–93.81% (exports), and 65.95–96.58% (employment) across sampled SEZs.

The SEZ policy’s implementation faced significant bottlenecks: seventeen states did not frame matching legislation, reducing the effectiveness of single-window clearance; there was minimal internal audit and control over Developers and units; monitoring mechanisms were weak, raising major risks of tax revenue loss and policy failure. The strategic control over database management was fully outsourced, leaving a critical IT system without robust government oversight.

title: Performance Audit on Land Records Management in Tamil Nadu, Government of Tamil Nadu.
overview:
The CAG performance audit of Land Records Management in Tamil Nadu uncovered fundamental deficiencies in the computerisation, validation, and update of textual and spatial land records within the state. It was observed that out of 6.22 lakh urban private land parcels captured during digitisation, 3.22 lakh continued to be erroneously classified as government land as of March 2021, which rendered the legitimate owners unable to transact their properties. This error led to significant citizen inconvenience and economic implications affecting property transfer estimation worth several hundred crores [Page ix, Executive Summary].

A striking finding was misuse of credentials by four Revenue Department officials, resulting in the illegal transfer of 79 acres of government land in Kodaikanal to private individuals between October 2018 and June 2019. This fraud revealed severe lapses in internal controls and system oversight, and even after partial rectification, several illegally transferred parcels remained improperly tagged in the database, increasing future fraud risks [Page 53, Chapter V §5.1].

The audit further noted a mass of data inconsistencies: 61% of sampled villages showed mismatches in village extents between manual and digital registers, and 5.06 lakh land parcels in 20 taluks featured wrongly inputted survey numbers. There was no disaster recovery plan for critical data and poor integration between the Revenue and Registration Departments, resulting in high rejection rates and delays in citizen services like Online Patta Transfer [Page ix-x, Executive Summary; Page 12, Chapter II].

title: Performance Audit on Implementation of Nagpur Metro Rail Project by Maharashtra Metro Rail Corporation Limited, Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs
overview:
The audit scrutinized the planning, implementation, monitoring, and operational aspects of the Nagpur Metro Rail Project, covering contracts/works from 2015-16 to 2020-21. The project was initiated as an energy-efficient mass transport solution for Nagpur, with an initial cost estimate of ₹8,680 crore—funded jointly by the Government of India, Government of Maharashtra, and local bodies. As of March 2021, ₹7,878 crore (90.76%) had been spent, while ₹793.89 crore in contributions from Maharashtra, Nagpur Improvement Trust, and Nagpur Municipal Corporation remained outstanding. Only 23 out of 38 stations became operational by March 2022.

Critical project management issues surfaced, including tendering lapses, non-transparent awarding of major works (₹877.58 crore on a nomination basis), delayed contract terminations, and recurring delays in construction and commissioning. The lack of revised targets caused ongoing delays: only two out of four reaches were commercially operational by March 2022. Ridership fell far below projections, reaching just 3.85–7.43% of expected numbers, with commercial operations unable to generate sufficient surplus for debt servicing (total loan raised: ₹4,521 crore). Non-fare box revenue was only ₹67.86 crore versus the DPR projection of ₹1,666 crore, and key institutional mechanisms like the Urban Metropolitan Transport Authority were established late, impeding oversight.

These deficiencies adversely impacted outcomes, including low operational coverage, compromised commuter safety (non-provision of platform screen doors, non-commissioning of the operation control center, single entry/exit stations), and financial sustainability. The loss in 2020-21 alone was ₹178.58 crore. The surplus generated for servicing external debt was negligible relative to the amount due, indicating systemic vulnerabilities requiring stringent corrective actions.

title: Performance Audit Report on Sabka Vishwas (Legacy Dispute Resolution) Scheme (SVLDRS) 2019, Union Government Department of Revenue (Indirect Taxes-Goods and Services Tax, Central Excise and Service Tax)
overview:
This Performance Audit reviewed the implementation of the Sabka Vishwas (Legacy Dispute Resolution) Scheme, 2019 (SVLDRS), targeting disputes and arrears under legacy indirect tax regimes. The audit covered 1,89,648 declarations, finding that only 1,31,656 (69.4%) led to discharge certificates, with total declared tax dues of ₹42,353 crore, from which only ₹9,492 crore was realized while ₹14,696 crore was foregone for dispute closure (page iii).

Significant deficiencies were found in system design, process adherence, and internal controls. For example, there were irregular reliefs of ₹109.81 crore in 28 declarations, wrongful processing of ₹7.01 crore in 21 cases, and failure to properly verify pre-deposit evidence in 65 cases involving ₹90.51 crore (page iii). Additionally, the portal accepted multiple declarations in 208 cases (tax dues ₹273.53 crore), and 625 discharge certificates were wrongly issued for the GST period beyond scheme coverage (page iv).

Consequently, implementation weaknesses resulted in unrealized revenue, potential revenue loss, and continuing backlog due to incomplete case closures. The lack of systemic risk-based verification and inconsistent treatment of penalties and deposits contributed to revenue at risk, undermining the scheme's intended impact on clearing pre-GST tax disputes and revenue realization.

title: Performance Audit on Derailment in Indian Railways, Union Government (Railways)
overview:
The Performance Audit covers derailments across Indian Railways from 2017-18 to 2020-21, highlighting shortfalls in inspections, maintenance, and safety measures. There were notable gaps in compliance with prescribed frequencies of Track Recording Car inspections, with shortfalls ranging from 30% to 100% across zonal railways—resulting in critical safety risks. The audit analyzed 1,129 inquiry reports and found total asset damages worth Rs 32.96 crore, indicating widespread failures in maintenance and accident prevention. Specifically, out of 1,127 derailments, 289 (26%) could be traced to insufficient track renewals, exposing under-utilization of safety funds.

Utilization of Rashtriya Rail Sanraksha Kosh (RRSK) funds for Priority-I works exhibited a declining trend, dropping from 81.55% (2017-18) to 73.76% (2019-20), and actual fund usage for track renewal decreased significantly—from Rs 9,607.65 crore in 2018-19 to Rs 7,417 crore in 2019-20. Further, only 70% of targeted manned level crossings were eliminated, and 62% of coaches lacked fire extinguishers, violating safety norms. The audit also reported delays in accident inquiry reports, with 63% not submitted within schedule and 49% delayed in acceptance by authorities.

The consequences of these shortcomings are far-reaching: compromised safety, inefficient fund allocation, lack of adherence to guidelines, and operational risks in both passenger and freight services. The audit’s findings call for urgent systemic reforms and stricter adherence to safety protocols and fund deployment.

title: Performance Audit on Working of Customs Bonded Warehouses (CBWs) and Free Trade Warehousing Zones (FTWZs)
overview:
This performance audit examined the effectiveness of Customs Bonded Warehouses (CBWs) and Free Trade Warehousing Zones (FTWZs) from April 2015 to March 2020. The audit tested whether regulatory changes improved facilitation and self-clearance without compromising revenue. During 2018-19 to 2020-21, Rs 1,15,536 crore worth of goods were warehoused, but weaknesses in maintaining electronic records were found in over 68% of sampled entities, which included non-filing of mandatory digital returns and improperly reconciled goods movement records (p. iv).

Headline findings include the absence of automated monitoring and seamless data exchange between customs systems and warehoused units, resulting in capacity for significant pilferage, mis-declaration, and loss of government revenue. In FTWZs, large segments had never achieved more than 54% of intended utilization rates, undermining objectives of trade facilitation and national logistics improvement. Audit observed instances where goods remained warehoused for 6+ years without duty payment, exposing gaps in monitoring (p. v).

Consequently, the current operational regime poses high risk for revenue leakage and tax evasion. Poor electronic record-keeping means Customs authorities cannot fully track movement or clearance of high-value inventories, directly impacting the integrity of the indirect tax system. Unless urgent remedial steps are taken—such as integration of IT systems, compulsory electronic record-keeping, and better inter-agency coordination—the policy intent behind CBWs and FTWZs will not be achieved, with ongoing risk to public revenue and trade transparency (p. vi).

title: Government of Odisha Report No. 6 of the year 2022 - Audit Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India Performance Audit on Waste Management in Urban Areas for the year ended March 2021
overview:
The performance audit of Waste Management in Urban Areas in Odisha for 2015-16 to 2019-20 uncovered persistent gaps in strategy, implementation, and financial management. Out of 114 Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), only 21 were selected for detailed audit, comprising 5 Corporations, 10 Municipalities, and 6 Notified Area Councils. The examination found that waste generation in these ULBs averaged 2,208.60 tonnes per day in 2019-20, with only 202.40 TPD being processed—less than 10%, and the remainder sent to open dumps due to lack of sanitary landfills. Funds amounting to ₹964.83 crore remained unutilized at ULBs as of March 2020, despite a prescribed expenditure benchmark of 80-100% for Solid Waste Management (SWM) funds, with actual expenditure ranging only from 11-16%.

A critical finding was the extremely poor implementation of user charges and fines. Only 7 out of 21 audited ULBs collected user fees, resulting in a mere ₹0.70 crore collected against a demand of ₹161.41 crore, leading to a revenue shortfall of over ₹160 crore. Further, none of the ULBs enforced spot fines for littering or collected user fees from institutions like the Railways, even though mandated by SWM Rules 2016. Odisha also lost ₹333.58 crore in central assistance due to non-achievement of service-level benchmarks, absence of annual accounts, and other procedural lapses.

The audit concluded that poor planning, lack of a state waste management policy, non-preparation of DPRs, and failure to implement 3R (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle) strategies led to 90% of waste being dumped in landfills without treatment. These failures also caused increased per capita waste generation, with substantial public health and environmental risks. Institutional mechanisms for monitoring and citizen engagement remain weak, further compounding the problem and threatening the sustainability of urban SWM in Odisha.

title: Performance Audit on Planning and Implementation of Transmission Projects by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited and Grid Management by Power System Operation Corporation Limited of Union Government, Ministry of Power
overview:
The performance audit evaluated the effectiveness of planning and implementation of transmission projects by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited (PGCIL) and the efficiency of grid management by Power System Operation Corporation Limited (POSOCO) during the XI Plan period (2007-08 to 2012-13). The total investment in new transmission lines and network augmentation was substantial, with PGCIL completing 178 inter-regional transmission lines (765 kV and above) connecting five regions, constituting about 16.5% of such lines in the inter-state grid (page vii, Executive Summary).

Despite infrastructure growth, only 46,300 MW of inter-regional transfer capacity was achieved against the XI Plan target of 65,000 MW, leaving a shortfall of 18,700 MW. The audit revealed significant issues such as under-utilization and redundancies in the transmission network, delays in project execution, and persistent grid congestion. Transmission corridor actual flows frequently exceeded transfer capability across several months, increasing supply volatility and market price inequities (page ix, Executive Summary).

Severe grid disturbances in July 2012 resulted in 620 million units of energy not served, and PGCIL lost an earning opportunity of `681.50 crore in additional return on equity due to commissioning delays. Causes frequently related to land acquisition, forest clearance, and project monitoring lapses. Key systemic weaknesses include lack of projectwise utilization tracking for short-term open access (STOA) charges and inadequate early-warning systems in grid operations (pages xi-xii, Executive Summary).

POSOCO should implement early warning mechanisms and review scheduling practices to ensure secure grid operations.
Track and disclose project-wise usage of STOA charges to improve capital cost transparency for new transmission systems.

title: Performance Audit on Public Private Partnership Project at Chhatrapati Shivaji International Airport, Mumbai - Union Government, Ministry of Civil Aviation
overview:
This performance audit reviewed the Public Private Partnership (PPP) project undertaken for modernization, operation, management and development of Chhatrapati Shivaji International Airport, Mumbai by Mumbai International Airport Limited (MIAL). The audit examined the transparency, efficiency, and compliance of the project with respect to bidding process, revenue sharing, project implementation, and compliance with lease and license terms.

Audit findings revealed significant issues such as non-adherence to revenue share norms causing a loss of at least ₹145 crore to the Airports Authority of India (AAI) between 2006-07 and 2010-11. There was under-reporting of revenue by the concessionaire in retail and cargo operations, and unapproved changes in the scope of work leading to further losses. The total project cost escalated from ₹5,826 crore to ₹12,380 crore, a 112% increase over the original estimate.

The consequences of these shortcomings have been substantial revenue losses to the exchequer and undermining of public interest. Inadequate monitoring by the Ministry of Civil Aviation and AAI elevated the risk of further leakages and non-compliance, raising questions about the accountability and effectiveness of public-private partnership models in large infrastructure projects.

title: Performance Audit on Pricing Mechanism of Major Petroleum Products in Central Public Sector Oil Marketing Companies, Union Government, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas
overview:
The performance audit examined the efficacy of the pricing mechanism for petrol, diesel, PDS kerosene, and domestic LPG across Central Public Sector Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs), focusing on price regulation, revenue implications, and adherence to due processes. The audit covered the period from 2007-08 to 2011-12, spanning a time when under-recoveries on these fuels exceeded Rs 4,16,028 crore, of which only approximately 54% was compensated through government subsidy and upstream oil companies, leaving OMCs to bear the remaining burden. [page 1]

Significant irregularities were observed in the computation of under-recoveries, such as excessive inclusion of import parity prices and inefficiencies in cost allocation, leading to an estimated overstatement of claims by over Rs 5,000 crore in the audit period. Notably, the price of diesel was not decontrolled in practice, despite formal claims, and continued centralised intervention caused further inefficiencies in cost recovery. [page 5]

Lapses in the transparency of procurement, benchmark price determination, and reporting standards resulted in inadequate monitoring and stakeholder confidence. These gaps pose significant risks to fiscal management and cost recovery mechanisms, ultimately impacting the consumer through lack of accountability and potential subsidy misallocation. [page 6]

title: Performance Audit on Indian Customs Electronic Data Interchange System of Union Government, Department of Revenue-Indirect Taxes, Customs
overview: The CAG Performance Audit reviewed the Indian Customs Electronic Data Interchange System (ICES 1.5), covering its operational effectiveness and systemic issues from 2008–2013, with detailed field audits focusing on 2011–12 and 2012–13. The audit highlighted critical shortcomings in strategic IS planning, risk management and monitoring, human resource policies, and system validation controls. Notably, ICES handles nearly 98% of India's international trade across 116 customs locations, yet the system upgrade cost of ₹604 crore lacked commensurate estimates of gains, and overall deficiencies led to revenue implications of ₹847.16 crore. The report enumerates 44 observations and nine recommendations, of which only five were accepted by CBEC, indicating limited implementation of audit suggestions. Key systemic issues included the absence of a formal IS Steering Committee, inadequate personnel policies for IT recruitment and training, insufficient application controls, and deficient audit trails of changes. These gaps pose a risk of undetected non-compliance in a rapidly changing environment. The audit concluded that CBEC’s IS management was 'repeatable but intuitive' with few definable processes, compromising security, efficiency, and effectiveness despite significant investment.

title: Report No. 5 of 2014 - Performance Audit on Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund SASF of Union Government, Ministry of Finance Department of Financial Services
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund (SASF), set up after IDBI's restructuring in 2004, examined Rs 9,000 crore of stressed assets transferred for resolution. Audit scrutinized SASF’s operational and financial progress, its recoveries, and compliance with the original mandate. SASF reported receipts of Rs 1,652.68 crore from asset recoveries as of March 2013, against an initial target of Rs 3,431 crore, with only 48.1% realised. Audit observed delays in resolution and disposal, resulting in accumulating operational expenses, which reached Rs 96 crore by FY2012-13.

It was found that SASF failed to meet recovery targets, with a shortfall of Rs 1,778 crore, and instances where assets had not moved to recovery or litigation stage for over five years. Weak controls, poor monitoring, and unclear exit strategies contributed to the slow progress; only 2,875 accounts (of 4,386) were processed by March 2013. Further, there was a lack of transparent reporting and delays in statutory audits.

Deficiencies in SASF’s asset management resulted in continuing obligations for the Union government, tying up resources in non-performing assets. The audit highlights the urgent need for clear timelines, improved oversight, and revised strategies for asset disposal to avoid further financial consequences.

title: Performance Audit on Duty Entitlement Pass Book Scheme Union Government, Department of Revenue - Revenue-Indirect Taxes, Customs
overview:
This performance audit examined the implementation and effectiveness of the Duty Entitlement Pass Book (DEPB) Scheme, which issued 5,64,321 scrips amounting to ₹51,489 crore between 2005-06 and 2011-12. The audit covered 28 RAs, 7 SEZs, and 31 Customs Ports, finding the revenue forgone under DEPB in FY12 alone reached ₹10,404 crore, nearly 16% of total duty forgone under 17 export promotion schemes (p. 6).

The report identified major deficiencies in the scheme's internal control mechanisms, lack of outcomes measurement, and poor coordination among DGFT, Customs, and RBI. For instance, average DEPB credit rates remained at 4.48% over seven years, despite customs duties falling by 50% in the same period (p. 7). Extensive cases of operational malfunction and misuse were uncovered, including lack of post-audit of scrips, missing scrip registers, and unverified Present Market Value (PMV) data, exposing systemic weaknesses.

The audit also highlighted unsubstantiated achievement reporting by the Department of Commerce, absence of revenue impact assessment for the scheme’s transition from VABAL to DEPB, and failure to track duty-credited scrip transfers. In summary, the audit reveals significant lapses in oversight, data reconciliation, and risk mitigation, affecting both scheme integrity and government revenue.

title: Performance Audit of Indira Awaas Yojana of Union Government, Ministry of Rural Development
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Indira Awaas Yojana (IAY) covered implementation from April 2008 to March 2013 and involved audit scrutiny in 168 districts, 392 blocks, and 2,960 gram panchayats across 27 States and 4 Union Territories. The report highlights that the total central share released for the scheme in the five-year period was ₹45,838 crore, with significant gaps in beneficiary selection, targeting, and fund management, including diversion and misappropriation.

A key finding was that housing shortages were not reliably assessed in 14 states, leading to selection of ineligible beneficiaries and large numbers of incomplete houses—"in 48 selected districts of nine states 61,293 houses remained incomplete even after a lapse of more than two years" (p. 129, Conclusion). Transparent and fair selection of beneficiaries was also poor: "The selection process was however not undertaken in accordance with prescribed norms everywhere." (p. 129, Conclusion).

Poor convergence with related social schemes resulted in beneficiaries being deprived of basic facilities such as safe water and sanitary latrines; technical and quality checks were largely absent. The Ministry's monitoring system was found unreliable: "Poor internal controls and lack of cross verification had seriously eroded the reliability and credibility of the data in the MIS." (p. 130, Conclusion). Audit found instances of misappropriation, short and delayed release of state share, and missing Utilisation Certificates (UCs). The persistent issues resulted in reduced accomplishment of physical targets and significant loss of central funds.

Enable scheme convergence to guarantee water, power, and sanitation delivery to all beneficiaries.

title: Performance Audit on Appreciation of Chartered Accountant Reporting in Assessment Proceedings of Union Government, Department of Revenue - Direct Taxes
overview:
The audit examined 2,328 assessment cases involving additions of ₹15,193 crore based on chartered accountant reports under sections 44AB, 92E and 115JB. It was found that in 577 cases (24.79%), Assessing Officers (AOs) failed to properly utilize the information in the reports, potentially resulting in revenue leakage of ₹3,604.48 crore (page viii, Executive Summary).

Many AOs either did not cross-verify information provided by CAs, or failed to initiate necessary proceedings where audit reports disclosed discrepancies. The audit observed that incorrect claims from audit reports resulted in substantial unassessed income and tax not levied. For example, in 109 cases, non-initiation of penalty proceedings led to potential non-recovery of ₹853.71 crore (page xxiii, Executive Summary).

The consequences include significant revenue loss for the exchequer, weak enforcement of tax compliance, and undermined effectiveness of mandating audit reports. The CAG concludes that lack of rigorous scrutiny by tax authorities and inconsistent appreciation of chartered accountant reporting reduces the intended deterrent effect of such compliance requirements.

title: Performance Audit of Employees’ State Insurance Corporation of Union Government, Ministry of Labour and Employment
overview: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India conducted a Performance Audit on the Employees’ State Insurance Corporation (ESIC) for the period 2008-09 to 2012-13. The audit uncovered significant issues, including outstanding dues of ₹1655.42 crore as of March 2013, out of which ₹1001.82 crore was declared not recoverable. Medical and cash benefits together accounted for only 33-46% of total income, with the rest accumulating as surplus, indicating that contribution rates may have been excessive relative to services provided. Cases of non-recovery due to time-barring led to a direct revenue loss of ₹48.31 crore, while major differences were found between generated challans and actual receipts, with a discrepancy of ₹556.59 crore. Additional operational weaknesses included irregular provision of medical benefits to around 12,000 ineligible ESIC employees, non-functioning medical infrastructure worth ₹8.16 crore, and idle medical equipment valued at ₹9.43 crore. The audit also found major procedural lapses in budgeting, with savings of up to 20% in some years and large advances paid to states without requisite audit certification. These findings indicate systemic inefficiencies in financial management, governance, and oversight that limited the reach and effectiveness of the social security benefits ESIC was mandated to deliver.
