title: Performance Audit on Global Estate Management by Ministry of External Affairs
overview:
The Performance Audit on Global Estate Management by the Ministry of External Affairs covered the audit period from 2009-10 to 2012-13 and assessed the ministry’s management of its global assets, including 174 properties over 104 missions worldwide. An expenditure of Rs 424 crore was incurred on acquisition, construction, renovation, maintenance and other works relating to these estates, but several critical lapses in documentation and financial oversight were found.

The Ministry failed to establish a comprehensive estate management system, resulting in the absence of consolidated and updated records for properties and their valuations. The audit highlighted that many of the properties lacked clear ownership documents, and there were delays ranging from 6 months to 2 years in project completion. Further, it was observed that almost 34% of the sanctioned works were not completed within the targeted timelines. Financial mismanagement was also observed, where Rs 87 crore was spent without adequate justification.

The consequences of these lapses included increased costs due to escalation, unutilized properties, risk of losing strategic holdings, and weakened institutional control over valuable assets abroad. The audit called attention to systemic deficiencies that could impact India’s diplomatic presence and operational efficiency.

title: Performance Audit on Allowance of Depreciation and Amortisation
overview:
The performance audit covering assessment years 2007-08 to 2011-12 revealed systemic irregularities in the allowance of depreciation and amortisation, impacting both government revenues and taxpayer compliance. The audit examined 11,634 assessment records across 14 states and flagged significant lapses where Rs 4,723.12 crore was either short assessed or incorrectly allowed.

Key issues involved admission of depreciation beyond entitled limits, wrongful carry forward, and incorrect application of Section 32 of the Income Tax Act. For instance, 169 cases in the sampled States involved undercharge of tax aggregating to Rs 1,339.79 crore. The report also highlighted that 1,561 cases involved direct loss to exchequer due to irregular depreciation claims.

The consequences include substantial revenue loss, non-enforcement of prescribed standards, and continued risk of future revenue leakage if systemic corrections are not implemented. The findings underscore the urgent need for improved scrutiny, technology integration, and standardized interpretation of depreciation rules across tax jurisdictions.

title: Performance Audit on Assessment of Firms Union Government, Department of Revenue - Direct Taxes
overview:
The audit focused on the assessment of partnership firms under the Income Tax Act, examining nearly 26,328 records out of 27,944 requisitioned. The aggregate returned income of firms increased from ₹36,942 crore in AY 2009-10 to ₹51,482 crore in AY 2012-13, yet the effective tax rate paid by these firms was only 23.80%, significantly lower than the statutory rate of 30.90% due to numerous exemptions and deductions.

CAG highlighted 1,497 cases with a total tax effect of ₹328.04 crore evidencing systemic, compliance, and internal control issues, including short levy of taxes, inconsistent application of law, and lapses in allowing exemptions and inadmissible remuneration to partners. Notably, in 937 cases with a tax effect of ₹16.95 crore, assessing officers failed to cross-verify partner returns with those of the firms, and often allowed deductions for salary and interest without proper partnership deed verification.

The consequences include potential misuse of exemptions, excess partner income exemptions (especially under Section 10(2A)), and lack of clarity in rules leading to incorrect assessments. These systemic flaws highlighted need for improved database management, interlinking partner and firm returns, and clarified guidance for assessment and exemption provisions.

title: Performance Audit on Acquisition and Development of land and Allotment of Karnataka Housing Board of Government of Karnataka
overview:
The Comptroller and Auditor General of India conducted a performance audit covering the Karnataka Housing Board’s acquisition, development, and allotment of land between 2008 and 2013. The audit found that the Board selected project locations arbitrarily without conducting demand surveys, leading to projects being delayed, shifted, or not executed at all. For example, only 8 out of 21 projects under the Suvarna Karnataka Housing Scheme were formed at approved locations; the rest were shifted due to lack of land or demand (pg 8). Land acquisition often ignored Master Plan prescriptions, with Rs 6.89 crore extra spent acquiring land reserved for a ring road at Bidadi (pg 12).

Direct purchase of fragmented land by KHB facilitated middlemen who bought from farmers at low prices and sold to KHB at high rates, leading to excessive payouts. Special Land Acquisition Officers paid Rs 8.52 crore in compensation without verifying ownership documents (pg v). Deficiencies were also recorded in project execution: tenders ignored transparency norms and costing for allotment rates lacked guidelines, resulting in a loss of Rs 146.26 crore across three projects (pg vi).

In allotment, the absence of rules for Discretionary Quota and Civic Amenity sites resulted in inconsistent and opaque allocations—239 houses in Suryanagar Phase III were allotted without public notification (pg vi). Many civic amenity sites and KHB properties remained encroached, with ineffective eviction actions. The audit concludes that KHB’s handling of acquisition, development, and allotment lacked transparency, resulting in substantial financial losses, procedural violations, and poor asset management.

title: Performance Audit on Social, Economic, Revenue sector of Government of Tripura
overview:
The CAG Performance Audit on the Social, Economic, and Revenue sectors of Tripura for 2012-13 covered 23 audit paragraphs and four Performance Audits across six chapters. Audit scrutiny revealed major lapses in important welfare and development schemes, under-utilisation of central funds, incomplete infrastructure projects, and extensive delays leading to financial losses. For example, the Information and Communication Technology in Schools scheme, with an expenditure of ₹21.90 crore up to March 2013, was affected by non-achievement of targets and failure to provide adequate training for teachers, ultimately stalling computer education after the contract period (page ix).

Multiple departments exhibited weak planning and monitoring. The Rural Development Department failed to complete nine staff quarters in Mungiakami RD Block despite five years of delay, rendering ₹61.69 lakh wasteful (page ix). Another case involved unverified sapling plantations costing ₹45.91 lakh under MGNREGA in Jampui Hill RD Block due to lack of documentation and monitoring (page ix).

The audit also found mixed results in the implementation of the Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY), with absence of state-level planning, poor fund utilisation (as low as 44% in several years), unspent balances, delayed projects, and frequent non-achievement of expected outcomes, which undermined overall sectoral progress and led to significant wastage of public funds (pages x-xi).

title: Performance Audit of Functioning of the Directorate of Mines & Geology in Andhra Pradesh
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Directorate of Mines & Geology in Andhra Pradesh identified severe lapses in the approval and renewal of mineral concessions as well as the enforcement of provisions for assessment and collection of mineral receipts. The Audit found that out of the total ₹5,691 crore of mineral revenue assessed, ₹710 crore remained uncollected as of March 2013, reflecting a persistent weakness in revenue realization and monitoring (p.vii).

Deficient regulatory control resulted in loss of revenue. Delays were noted in the disposal of 3,687 mineral concession applications, with 82 per cent pending for more than one year, hindering efficient administration of leases and promoting an environment where unauthorized mining could take place. Short levy of royalty, seigniorage fees and other statutory dues amounted to a loss of ₹105.37 crore during audit, while unauthorized mining/irregular transfer of leases led to additional losses exceeding ₹200 crore (p.22).

Consequences of these systemic failures include significant foregone revenue for the State, inadequate environmental safeguards, and continued legal disputes and irregularities. The lack of effective internal controls, unaddressed lapses in security deposit management, and irregular extensions of leases further contributed to revenue leakage and undue advantage to private parties at the expense of the public exchequer (p.12-13, 25-27).

title: Performance Audit on Social, Economic, Revenue sector of Government of Uttarakhand
overview:
The performance audit covers the implementation and utilisation of funds and schemes in the social, economic, and revenue sectors for the Government of Uttarakhand for the year ending March 2013. During the audit period, significant shortfalls in fund utilisation were observed. For instance, the audit notes that departmental utilisation of allocated funds ranged between 44% and 50%, indicating underutilisation and poor management of state resources (p. 12). Delays in release of funds further contributed to slow project execution, affecting scheme delivery and output.

The report also highlights structural deficiencies such as inadequate planning and lack of proper monitoring, with several large works experiencing delays or cost overruns. For example, development project completions lagged by an average of 12-18 months, and the stated revenue generation targets were not met, leading to substantial shortfall in receipt realisation for the state (p. 25). Both social welfare and infrastructure projects experienced fragmented execution and poor convergence due to interdepartmental coordination issues.

These systemic gaps resulted in direct consequences for beneficiaries, including incomplete benefits disbursement and delayed infrastructure provisioning. The audit thus flags urgent need for accountability reforms and improvements in project implementation for ensuring effectiveness of government interventions in Uttarakhand.

title: Financial and Performance Audit on Panchayat Raj Institutions and Urban Local Bodies of Government of Karnataka
overview:
The CAG audit of Panchayat Raj Institutions (PRIs) and Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) in Karnataka for the year ended March 2012 revealed substantial issues in fund devolution, utilisation, and accountability. The State’s allocation to PRIs amounted to `15,122.83 crore, which fell short of the stipulated 32% share from the Non-Loan Net Own Revenue Receipts (NLNORR), as only 30% was released, resulting in a shortfall of `1,057 crore. Decentralised planning was marred by significant procedural lapses: Comprehensive District Development Plans (CDDPs) were delayed by more than two years and not effectively utilised for annual plan preparation, and District Planning Committees (DPCs) did not meet as required, with only 4 meetings held against 20 mandated in Hassan from 2007-12.

The audit noted inefficiencies in the application of resources, with large shortfalls and savings; for example, under major schemes like the Indira Awas Yojana and Total Sanitation Campaign, less than 60% of available funds were utilized, with 45.22% and 43.18% shortfalls, respectively. Furthermore, critical asset-creating sectors, such as agriculture and soil conservation, suffered from poor devolution of functions and functionaries, with technical post vacancies at 56% and 34% in agriculture and soil conservation, respectively. This contributed to patchy implementation of state and centrally sponsored schemes.

These findings highlight ongoing weaknesses in fiscal decentralisation, planning, and public accountability systems at the PRI/ULB level in Karnataka. This poses risks to efficient delivery of rural and urban development outcomes, and reduces the effectiveness of central and state-funded social sector schemes.

Adverse consequences included higher dropout rates in schools and poor access to essential health services. The magnitude of resource wastage, with nearly Rs 1,648 crore remaining unutilized, underscores the critical need for systemic reforms. (Page 12, Executive Summary)

title: Performance Audit on MNREGA of Government of Uttar Pradesh
overview:
The audit reviewed implementation of MGNREGA in Uttar Pradesh from 2007-08 to 2011-12, covering 18 districts, 46 blocks, and 460 Gram Panchayats. A cumulative expenditure of ₹22,174 crore was incurred under the scheme during the period, yet several systemic weaknesses were observed. The audit noted delayed constitution and ineffective functioning of the State Employment Guarantee Council (SEGC) which met only once or twice a year instead of as required, leaving overall scheme oversight inadequate. Out of the total works examined, 4,453 were test-checked and 4,600 beneficiaries were interviewed across the state.

Critical gaps were found in planning and management: annual development plans and labour budgets were not timely prepared or followed at most levels. As a result, many works were undertaken without proper administrative or technical sanction, and SEGC/planning meetings were frequently skipped or lacked quorum. There were significant shortfalls in staff at Gram Panchayat, block, and district levels, hampering the scheme’s effective implementation and field-level monitoring.

Substantial lapses were detected in fund management and outcome delivery. The audit noted irregularities such as execution of unapproved works (e.g., 237 works worth ₹13.25 crore across 7 districts lacked sanction), excess rural connectivity works totaling ₹404.77 crore, and widespread delays in wage payments. These administrative and financial weaknesses led to unfruitful expenditure and compromised employment generation objectives, with long-term consequences for rural asset creation and public trust in the scheme.

title: Performance Audit on District Malda of Government of West Bengal
overview:
The District-centric Performance Audit of Malda evaluates implementation and impact of socio-economic development programmes between 2007-12. During this period, the district received significant allocations, with funds placed both through State budget and directly with district agencies. For major schemes, the audit found wide variation in fund utilisation: while schemes like Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, Indira Awaas Yojana, and MG National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme reported utilisation rates above 90%, flagship programmes like National Rural Health Mission, Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY), National Food Security Mission (NFSM), and Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY) spent less than 70% of available funds.

Notably, funds amounting to Rs 32.50 crore remained unutilised as parked balances across district/block/PRI/division levels, with considerable amounts incorrectly booked as spent by district authorities. Serious administrative deficiencies were identified, such as multiple unauthorised bank accounts for individual schemes without departmental approval, loss of bank interest (Rs 9.47 lakh) due to late account switching, and Rs 2.22 crore in unauthorised expenditure for non-permissible items.

Social sector schemes (health, education, nutrition, water supply) resulted in some positive impacts, but persistent planning gaps and shortages were observed. For instance, health infrastructure lacked sufficient CHCs and PHCs for the rural population, and high shortfalls in institutional deliveries (50–66%) left goals unachieved. Education sector planning relied on outdated census data, while employment generation schemes failed to reach intended targets, with only 0.6% SHGs credit-linked under SGSY and MGNREGS not ensuring 100 days of work for the majority. Lax monitoring, poor inter-departmental coordination, and irregular district plan preparation undermined development outcomes.

title: Performance Audit on Public Sector Undertakings of Government of Tamilnadu
overview:
The performance audit covered 65 public sector undertakings (PSUs) under the control of the Government of Tamil Nadu, with a total investment of `1,24,359 crore as of 31 March 2012. Audit observed that several PSUs accumulated losses of over `13,012 crore and 21 PSUs had not finalized their accounts for periods ranging from one to 15 years (Page 1: 'Investment in State PSUs increased from `77,443 crore in 2007-08 to `1,24,359 crore in 2011-12. As per their latest finalised accounts, 33 PSUs had incurred aggregate losses of `13,012 crore.')

A significant portion of budgetary support and government guarantees was mismanaged or remained unutilized, with only 44-50% of planned funds being actually utilised by many major companies. Also, delay in project execution led to cost overruns and suboptimal service delivery in sectors such as power, transport, and textiles. For example, TANGEDCO reported losses of `5,792 crore in 2011-12 with delays in major power projects (Page 16: 'TANGEDCO incurred losses of `5,792 crore in 2011-12 due to poor project implementation and cost overruns.').

The consequences include growing fiscal risk to the State, persistent underperformance of key infrastructure sectors, and long-pending audit observations leading to governance deficits. The audit called for urgent reforms in PSUs’ financial management, accountability, and timely completion of projects to prevent further erosion of public resources and service quality.

title: Report of 2013 - Performance Audit on Social, Economic, Revenue and General Sectors of Government of Tripura
overview: This audit report covers Social, Economic, Revenue, General, and Public Sector Undertakings of the Government of Tripura for the year ended 31 March 2012. For Social Sector, the Comptroller and Auditor General audited departments with total budget allocations of ₹3,873.07 crore, of which only ₹3,191.80 crore was spent. Key performance audits, including the Integrated Audit of the Education (Social Welfare and Social Education) Department, revealed significant mismanagement and inefficiencies, such as the short release and non-utilization of funds (impacting multiple schemes), persistent infrastructure gaps at Anganwadi Centres (AWCs), and non-achievement of targets, with 31% AWCs lacking drinking water, 49% without toilets, and 54% without kitchen sheds. In the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS), there were short-payments of wages by ₹34.50 lakh and diversion of funds of ₹16.60 crore to unrelated schemes. A large number of beneficiaries were found dead, ineligible, or non-existent, with pensions misapplied (21,288 cases, ₹21.05 crore liability). The Edusat Network was underutilized, failing to deliver educational benefits. Economic Sector audits highlighted unfruitful expenditures, delays in projects, and loss of interest totalling ₹2.46 crore due to improper advances. The governance and monitoring mechanisms were found lacking, and several departments failed to respond to audit queries. Overall, the severity is high due to large-scale financial and operational lapses, delayed project completions, undetected fraud, and persistent lack of controls.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit of Government of Pondicherry
overview:
This CAG report covers the compliance and performance audit of the Government of Pondicherry for 2011-12, identifying significant deficiencies in programme execution, financial management, and regulatory compliance across departments. For instance, the revenue receipts for 2011-12 stood at ₹2,771 crore, while revenue expenditure reached ₹3,222 crore, reflecting suboptimal fiscal management and a revenue deficit of ₹451 crore (page 1).

Key findings include failure to utilise ₹15.15 crore in grants for infrastructure development by the Pondicherry Engineering College, delays and avoidable overruns in Public Works projects amounting to over ₹3 crore, and idling of assets such as bridges due to non-completion of linked works (page 40). The education and local administration sectors were found to be blocking government funds, leading to inefficient use of scarce resources (page 42).

Consequences of these findings are seen in persistent gaps between budgeted and actual receipts, excess committed expenditure (salaries, pension, interest payments constitute over 60% of revenue expenditure), and avoidable financial cost overruns. The report underscores urgent need for improved planning, execution, and monitoring mechanisms, citing issues which, if unaddressed, could erode fiscal stability and service delivery quality.

title: Performance Audit on General and Social Sector Volume 3 of Government of Odisha
overview:
This Performance Audit examines the acquisition and allotment of land for industrial purposes by the Odisha Industrial Infrastructure Development Corporation (IDCO) and the planning and regulation of buildings by the Bhubaneswar and Cuttack Development Authorities during 2001-12. During the audit period, IDCO allotted 29,769.482 acres of private land and 16,963.412 acres of government land for 52 of 89 MoU industries and for 54 of 113 Non-MoU industries. In 86 Industrial Estates, 4,426.380 acres were allotted to small industries, and as of March 2012, 1,894.571 acres remained unallotted.

The audit found significant systemic deficiencies including the widespread and incorrect use of the 'public purpose' clause for land acquisition, arbitrary application of emergency provisions, and the bypassing of statutory land owner protections. Instances were also observed where land acquisition was made for locations identified by industry promoters without due consideration for agriculture, irrigation, and environmental impact. In many cases, the process for identifying suitable land (the Land Bank Scheme) was ineffective, and there was no documented due diligence or oversight regarding the selection of industrial sites.

There were delays of up to 430 days in allotting land—far exceeding the mandated 30 days as per the Odisha Industries (Facilitation) Rules 2005. The absence of transparent criteria, short or incorrect assessment of compensation, and ineffective enforcement of lease terms led to significant non-utilisation and diversion of acquired land. Despite statutory provisions for resuming unutilised land, no action was taken on land remaining unused for over three years. The audit highlights serious lapses in fund management, regulatory enforcement, and transparency, with negative consequences for land owners and the state's industrialisation efforts.

title: Report No. 1 of 2013 - Performance Audit of Government of Nagaland
overview:
The Performance Audit focuses on the implementation of MGNREGS and Watershed Development Programmes in Nagaland from 2007-08 to 2011-12. The audit revealed systemic failures in fund utilization, proper planning, project execution, and statutory oversight, with significant shortfalls and suspected misappropriations. There was a release shortfall of ₹113.17 crore in State share, which impacted scheme reach and efficiency. Additionally, suspected financial leakage amounting to ₹84.35 crore was observed during fund transmission from project offices to Village Development Boards (VDBs) in sampled districts.

The review found widespread tampering of muster rolls leading to wage payments of ₹10.31 lakh, and non-existent projects totaling ₹10.84 crore––indicating possible misappropriation. Moreover, 57 works worth ₹10.32 crore were only partly executed or diverted to non-permissible activities. State-level inspections, a mandated monitoring tool, covered less than one-third of targeted works, rendering oversight ineffective. Social audit meetings were also insufficient, with only 57% conducted in sampled VDBs instead of the required number.

The audit further highlighted extremely poor asset maintenance and ineffective convergence of programmes, with assets becoming defunct due to lack of operational and maintenance focus, inappropriate use of funds, and persistent arrears in finalisation of accounts by State PSUs. The consequences are a high risk of recurring misappropriation, loss of public trust, and failure to achieve primary and auxiliary scheme objectives. (Pages vii-x, 3-13)

title: Performance Audit on General and Social Sector Volume 2 of Government of Odisha
overview:
This Performance Audit report covers critical aspects of the General and Social Sector in Odisha for the year ended March 31, 2013. Notably, the General Administration Department allotted 1,977.94 acres of government land in 1,662 cases during 2001-2012 to individuals, government offices, undertakings, private bodies, and NGOs for purposes such as hotels, hospitals, educational institutions, and more. Of this, 751.77 acres (38%) were allocated to entities other than government institutions, raising concerns about equity and transparency.

Audit findings indicate the lack of a comprehensive database on land availability, allotment, and encroachment in Bhubaneswar, compounded by the absence of defined rules or criteria governing the process. This resulted in arbitrary land allotments and significant delays, with 43% of checked cases disposed within a year, but the remainder experiencing delays up to 17 years. Notably, there was a loss of ₹58.14 crore to the government between 2003-2010 due to non-revision of premium and failure to consider prevailing market values.

Other major schemes also suffered: Indira Awas Yojana implementation saw curtailment of central assistance and fraudulent payments of ₹14.13 crore to 1,888 beneficiaries without construction of houses. Duplicate allotments further burdened resources, as 246 fake BPL beneficiaries received ₹1.91 lakh in excess payments. Monitoring and inspection mechanisms across the schemes remained weak, contributing to ineffective outcomes and persistent risks to government revenue.

title: Performance Audit on Revenue Sector of Government of Meghalaya
overview: This Performance Audit of the Revenue Sector in Meghalaya for the year ended 31 March 2012 reveals significant deficiencies in revenue collection, assessment, and compliance across multiple departments. During 2011-12, the State Government raised ₹1,065.78 crore, accounting for only 22.90% of total revenue receipts of ₹4,654.47 crore. The audit identified under-assessment, non-realisation and short realisation of penalties, taxes and duties totalling ₹444.93 crore in 31 audit paragraphs and one Performance Audit chapter. Major findings include a 22.06% increase in revenue compared to the previous year but persistent gaps in recovery: departments accepted under-assessments of ₹187.59 crore but recovered only ₹0.62 crore. Audit scrutiny highlighted repeated omissions and systemic failures; for example, a single case of deficient assessment led to a revenue loss of ₹9.53 crore due to non-inclusion of royalty in coal sales. The audit also found that enforcement activities were often lacking—no audit assessments or investigations were carried out by enforcement branches and internal audit was neglected. Departments frequently failed to respond to audit observations and settle pending recovery cases. The consequences of these failures include high revenue leakage, weak internal controls, and significant amounts of government funds not collected, all exacerbated by gaps in departmental accountability and policy enforcement. (Pages iv–vi, 1–3)

title: Performance Audit on Social, General and Economic Sectors and Public Sector Undertakings of Government of Meghalaya
overview:
The Performance Audit of Social, General, and Economic Sectors and Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) in Meghalaya revealed significant underutilisation of allocated funds and persistent gaps in both infrastructure and delivery of public services. Total receipts during 2011-12 were ₹6,002 crore against an expenditure of ₹5,928 crore, with revenue surplus, yet there were notable lapses in expenditure and service realisation (p.7).

The audit highlighted that several departments failed to use between 44 to 50 per cent of allocated funds, leading to non-completion of planned schemes. Audit found that the Planning Department could not furnish Utilisation Certificates for ₹286.99 crore, reflecting poor financial oversight (p.12). Additionally, 16 out of 33 PSUs incurred losses and several had negative net worth, impacting state financial health (p.73).

Consequentially, delays in project completion, persistent shortfalls in achievement of intended benefits, and risk of mis-utilisation of public funds were observed. The CAG flagged numerous cases of unauthorized or inadmissible expenditure, lack of monitoring, and continued existence of idle assets, adversely affecting public welfare.

title: Performance Audit on Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme of Government of Karnataka
overview:
The performance audit of the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS) in Karnataka covered a five-year period from 2007-08 to 2011-12, assessing financial management, implementation, and outcomes. During this period, a total of ₹7,068.37 crore was made available under the Scheme, but only 54.51% (₹3,851.04 crore) was utilised (page 5). This significant underutilisation resulted in many planned works not being executed, and funds remaining unproductive.

Review of financial and administrative controls highlighted serious systemic deficiencies, including delays in the release of State share, shortcomings in work selection, and poor asset creation. Only 7.19 crore persondays were generated against a demand of over 12 crore, indicating shortfall in employment generation (page 8). Moreover, monitoring was weak and there were irregularities in wage payment, including instances of delayed or non-payment observed in multiple blocks.

The audit concluded that the objectives of providing livelihood security and the creation of durable rural assets through MGNREGS were not fully realised. The failure to achieve key outputs resulted in rural households not benefiting as intended, undermining public confidence in the Scheme’s effectiveness, and calling for urgent improvements in planning, financial discipline, and oversight.

title: Performance Audit on Government Land given on lease of Government of Maharashtra
overview:
This performance audit examines the management, allotment, renewal, and monitoring of government land leased to individuals, societies, and institutions in Maharashtra. Of 1,766 lease cases reviewed in three major collectorates (Mumbai City, Mumbai Suburban, Pune), 757 leases expired between 1940 and 2008, yet no renewal or eviction action was taken. Further, serious discrepancies were observed in lease record maintenance: data mismatches were identified in lessee names (12 cases), lease durations (10 cases), and land area (30 cases) in Mumbai City alone, while Pune's reported lease cases shifted from 214 to 258 during the audit.

Lack of transparency pervaded the grant process, as mandated newspaper advertisement for lease allotments was not followed in any of 319 checked cases. Procedures and norms for land leasing were found non-uniform across different authorities, with differing methods for levy/collection, period, and agreement format, raising potential issues for state revenue and property safeguards. Audit also found breaches of lease conditions (e.g., unauthorised sub-letting, encroachment, unutilised plots) with no resumption of land or penal action, and several cases of incorrect application of premium and lease rate calculation, resulting in large financial losses to the exchequer.

Consequences include substantial foregone revenue, extended unauthorised occupation of valuable urban government land, and systemic weaknesses in monitoring and internal control. The absence of record completeness, standardisation, monitoring, and enforcement has adversely impacted the effective and transparent management of government property assets, as highlighted by major findings and appendices in the report.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Social,General and Economic Sector (Non Public Sector Undertakings) of Government of Himachal Pradesh
overview:
This report presents findings from the Performance and Compliance Audit of select Social, General and Economic Sectors in Himachal Pradesh, featuring three major performance audits—covering Himachal Pradesh State Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (CAMPA), Medical Education and Research, and the Public Works Department. The audit highlights significant lapses in proper fund utilization, with ₹21.51 crore in catchment area treatment (CAT) funds not credited into the Ad hoc CAMPA corpus, and ₹25.85 crore in Net Present Value (NPV) for diverted forest land between 2002 to 2008 not realised by the Department. Out of ₹188.38 crore available between 2009–13 in CAMPA funds, only ₹127.09 crore (between 4% and 48% utilization per year) was put to use.

The report reveals that out of a required target of 8160.46 hectares, only 2789.51 hectares (a 66% shortfall) were afforested between 2006–2012. The Public Works Department also demonstrated systemic issues with excess, avoidable, and wasteful expenditures, including undue favour to contractors and cost escalation in outsourced works, such as ₹18.63 crore wasted in Kol Dam and Larji projects. The State’s monitoring and audit mechanisms in these departments were found to be ineffective, lacking the concurrent evaluation that could address leakages or enforce accountability.

Consequences of these critical lapses include blocked and diverted funds, missed afforestation targets contributing to long-term ecological risks, and ongoing inefficiencies that erode public trust in state financial management. The cumulative excess, wasteful and infructuous expenditure or blocked investment across 22 paragraphs totalled ₹1258.95 crore, affecting the State’s developmental capacity and environmental security.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Economic Sector of Government of Maharashtra
overview:
This audit report reviews the expenditure and implementation of economic sector schemes in Maharashtra from 2007-08 to 2011-12. It covered compliance and performance audits of key government departments and autonomous bodies. Major findings indicate inadequate planning and failures in implementation, as well as significant financial lapses.

A substantial ₹1,116.44 crore was spent in Washim district alone over five years, yet the District Planning Committee failed to consolidate an integrated district plan. Key social infrastructure projects costing ₹6.52 crore remained idle, and only 3% of Swarnajayanti Gram Swarojgar Yojana beneficiaries graduated above the BPL line despite ₹24.49 crore spent on the scheme. Health infrastructure was also critically short, with essential facilities missing in several centres.

Further, fraud and regulatory violations led to losses and avoidable expenditures, for instance, fraudulent bitumen payment of ₹57.30 lakh (detected after invoice forgery), and wrongful excise duty estimates benefitting contractors by ₹9.44 crore. Systemic shortcomings in monitoring, delayed Action Taken Notes, and poor response to audit letters undermine governance and accountability.

title: Performance Audit on General and Social Sector of Government of Maharashtra
overview:
This Performance Audit covers the General and Social Sector in Maharashtra, focusing on the period 2007-12. The audited entities include 19 government departments and 8 autonomous bodies, with the report analyzing both compliance and performance across key programmes. The state reported revenue receipts of ₹1,21,286.14 crore in 2011-12, with total government disbursements reaching ₹2,33,163.24 crore (Table 1, p.2). Major issues highlighted include critical deficiencies in the implementation of schemes, significant underachievement in infrastructure projects, shortfall in planned inspections and weak internal controls, resulting in unutilized funds and delays in asset creation.

The Maharashtra Maritime Board failed to formulate a master plan for port development, with only 2 of 6 expected ports operational by December 2012—achieving just 10.8 million tonnes capacity out of the 100.23 million tonnes initially planned (p. 4). Additionally, the Mumbai Building Repairs and Reconstruction Board reconstructed or redeveloped only 1,482 out of 19,642 cessed buildings, and significant numbers of tenants (7,872) remained in transit accommodation for periods from 1 to over 25 years due to project delays (p. 5).

These failures directly led to considerable unspent government grants and persistent outstanding inspection reports (4,407 IRs, 14,922 paras as of Dec 2012, p.7), impacting effective delivery of public services and violating mandated timelines and financial discipline. Procedural lapses resulted in losses—such as non-application of proper land rates causing a loss of ₹31.76 crore, and avoidable liabilities like recurring expenditure due to failed contracts.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on Economic & Revenue Services Sector of Government of Karnataka
overview:
This Performance Audit report, presented under Article 151 of the Constitution, examines the compliance and performance of major departments and autonomous bodies in Karnataka's Economic & Revenue Sector. For the year 2011-12, the audit focused on issues ranging from resource mismanagement, lack of budgetary control, and significant lapses in scheme implementation. Notably, improper budgetary control resulted in a clear liability of Rs 1,509 crore on the Government due to pending work bills, with expenditures frequently exceeding planned allocations and legislative approvals. In the Forest Department, underutilization of the Karnataka Forest Development Fund, unremitted taxes amounting to Rs 32.41 crore, and delay in staff postings critically undermined both funds management and forest conservation objectives.

The audit uncovered extensive cases of non-compliance with established rules—such as the diversion of Rs 61.51 crore for non-sanctioned works, irregular splitting of contracts, and the abandonment of Rs 27.29 crore worth of works with no value addition. Monitoring and internal controls were found seriously wanting, highlighted by non-existent committees for scheme oversight and persistent vacancies in front-line staff, leaving Rs 379.23 crore in liabilities for unfinished road works. The social and financial repercussions included failure to achieve targeted afforestation, inefficiency in wildlife management, and an unaddressed encroachment of 67,096 hectares as of March 2012.

Consequently, critical audits point towards systematic gaps in policy follow-through and financial discipline. The absence of prompt responses and action-taken notes by administrative departments further exacerbates these weaknesses, undermining public trust and impeding governance reforms across economic and resource-intensive sectors.

This significant underutilisation led to delays and incomplete projects in sectors such as power and transport.

Para 2: The audit found recurring financial losses among the PSUs. Specifically, six PSUs incurred losses of Rs 116.36 crore during 2011-12, while accumulated losses stood at Rs 1,077.92 crore. Himachal Pradesh Power Corporation alone reported a loss of Rs 20.97 crore for the year (Page 23). The report attributes poor performance to inadequate project management, delays in execution, and improper monitoring.

Para 3: Consequences include stalled infrastructure growth, reduced public service quality, and increase in contingent liabilities for the state. The report highlights that delayed completion of projects has adversely affected economic growth and public welfare, especially in rural areas dependent on power and transport connectivity. Audit recommends robust monitoring and accountability measures to address these issues.

title: Performance Audit on Revenue Receipts of Government of Maharashtra
overview:
This Performance Audit examines the revenue receipts of the Government of Maharashtra for the period 2007-08 to 2011-12. The total receipts of the State during 2011-12 were ₹1,21,268.54 crore, comprising ₹95,758.56 crore raised by the State and ₹25,509.98 crore received from the Government of India. Revenue raised constituted nearly 79 per cent of total net receipts. The audit highlights ₹233.59 crore relating to non/short levy of taxes, duties, interest, and penalties.

Major findings include persistent under-assessment and short recovery of taxes. Over 10,860 inspection report paragraphs involving ₹2,667.74 crore remained outstanding as of June 2012. Audit observations amounting to ₹3,536.21 crore were accepted by the Government between 2001-02 and 2010-11, out of which only ₹1,135.72 crore was recovered by March 2012.

The consequences of these gaps include loss of potential revenue, ineffective follow-up on outstanding cases, and systemic deficiencies in monitoring and compliance. Despite increases in VAT and State Excise collection (96% and 117% respectively over five years), significant audit evidence suggests that validation checks, recovery mechanisms, and oversight remain insufficient, leading to persistent revenue leakage and shortfalls.

title: Performance Audit on Public Sector Undertakings of Government of Karnataka
overview: As of 31 March 2012, Karnataka had 76 working Public Sector Undertakings (70 Companies and 6 Statutory Corporations) and 14 non-working PSUs, employing approximately 1.86 lakh employees and registering a turnover of ₹34,490.58 crore (7.94% of State GDP), with accumulated profits of ₹1,368.93 crore. Government investment in PSUs stood at ₹66,712.87 crore, with infrastructure and power sectors comprising 52.41% and 35.55% of total investments respectively. The State infused ₹11,853.81 crore towards equity, loans, grants, and subsidies in 2011-12 (page vii, Overview). Despite the significant financial input, audit found ₹1,890.63 crore in controllable losses, ₹112.95 crore in infructuous investments, and low quality of accounts: 45 of 58 finalized accounts had qualified reports and 2 had adverse reports (page vii). Additionally, 37 working PSUs had arrears of 42 accounts, and 14 non-working PSUs were pending government decision (page vii). Major losses were incurred by Karnataka Neeravari Nigam Limited (₹264.4 crore), The Mysore Paper Mills Limited (₹84.78 crore), and The Mysore Sugar Company Limited (₹70.21 crore), outweighing the profits of Hutti Gold Mines, Karnataka Power Corporation, and Mysore Minerals (page vii). Substantial deficiencies in project management, contract award procedures, material procurement, and water management were observed, resulting in avoidable and unfruitful expenditures exceeding ₹165.66 crore and ongoing delays in critical infrastructure projects (pages ix-xi).

title: Performance Audit on District Nainital of Government of Uttarakhand
overview:
The performance audit for District Nainital evaluated the effectiveness of district and sectoral planning, financial management, and implementation of social, economic, and general sector schemes. Total funds available in PRIs and ULBs during 2007-08 to 2011-12 amounted to ₹224.86 crore, of which only ₹117.91 crore (52 per cent) was utilized, indicating significant underutilization and unspent balances affecting scheme delivery. (p. xii).

Serious lapses were noted: only 65 per cent of targeted households received benefit under the Indira Awas Yojana, with cost escalation of ₹45.59 lakh due to delays; under the National Rural Health Mission, ₹9.16 crore was unutilized in 2011-12. Medical officer posts had a 31 per cent vacancy rate, which impeded service delivery. (pp. 19, 25, 79).

The audit also highlighted weak monitoring and reporting mechanisms, incomplete works, and diversion of funds. These deficiencies in planning, execution, and financial controls have adversely impacted developmental outcomes, with only 54 per cent of district plan funds being released and numerous projects delayed or abandoned, causing direct harm to local populations. (pp. 1, 11, 43).

title: Performance Audit on Revenue Receipts of Government of Karnataka
overview:
The Performance Audit on Revenue Receipts of the Government of Karnataka presents comprehensive findings from audit examinations conducted during 2011-12, covering major revenue heads such as taxes on sales, state excise, stamps and registration fees, motor vehicles tax, and electricity tax. The State collected total revenue receipts of ₹69,806.27 crore, a significant increase over the previous year, with tax revenue comprising ₹46,475.96 crore and non-tax revenue ₹4,086.86 crore. Despite this, the audit highlighted persistent issues of underassessment, non/short levy of taxes, revenue loss, and failure to raise demands, aggregating ₹211.00 crore as found in 2,360 cases.

The audit observed that 3,115 Inspection Reports with 6,668 pending audit observations involving ₹1,589.45 crore were outstanding at the end of June 2012, and several instances of non-compliance and delays in recovery were noted. Notably, cases of missing assessment files, non-preparation of key recovery statements, and weak IT audit procedures in critical departments curtailed effective monitoring and collection.

Consequences of these lapses include considerable unrealised State revenue, weaknesses in internal controls, and continuing risks of recurring deficiencies. The report urges the Government to address audit observations promptly and strengthen systems to safeguard State finances.

title: Performance Audit on Social and Public Sectors of Government of Uttarakhand
overview:
The CAG Performance Audit reviewed key programmes in Uttarakhand’s social and public sectors from 2009-12, covering schemes like Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS), Integrated Child Development Services, and the functioning of various welfare boards. The report highlights serious deficiencies in planning, fund utilization, and implementation, with the total State revenue expenditure rising by 22% over three years to ₹12,975.19 crore, while capital outlay increased by 41% to ₹2,316.94 crore.

Specific audit findings reveal under-utilisation of central funds, delay in release of State share, irregularities and inactive councils, asset non-maintenance, and compromised objectives of welfare schemes. In MGNREGS alone, of the ₹1,335.80 crore funds available during 2007-12, only 98% was utilized (₹1312.88 crore), with significant portions delayed or mismanaged, directly affecting employment guarantees promised to rural households. Only 2-4% of registered households received the legislated 100 days of employment in 2008-12, while delays in wage payments averaged 74 days per case.

The report also found that welfare boards like the Uttarakhand Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Board suffered delayed establishment, weak beneficiary enrollment (only 44 workers benefitting since inception), and lack of planning. Major audit recommendations urge the State to strengthen monitoring, ensure timely release and targeted utilization of funds, improve workforce capacity, and conduct periodic surveys for better coverage.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on General and Social Sector of Government of Karnataka
overview:
The CAG performance audit of the Karnataka State Drugs Logistics and Warehousing Society revealed serious systemic failures in procurement and distribution of drugs across the health sector in Karnataka. During 2008-12, direct procurements from KAPL, using government procurement exemptions, resulted in drugs being sourced at costs between 31 to 67 percent higher than comparable rates paid by other States, with Rs 55.44 crore (50 percent of Rs 111.14 crore purchases) identified as excess expenditure (p.13). Audit observed chronic delays in finalisation of drug rate contracts: contracts for 2008-09 were finalised only in March 2009 and for 2009-10, only in October 2010, causing major interruptions in drug supplies between March and October 2010 (p.13).

Inadequate planning led to repeated over-procurement of drugs, particularly IV fluids, causing storages to overflow with stocks dumped in unsuitable locations such as garages and toilets. Further, ineffective demand estimation and lack of quality control meant that 7223 drugs valued at Rs 15.82 crore had less than 80 percent shelf life on delivery, and 1024 had below 50 percent, while 87 drugs worth Rs 35.30 lakh arrived with less than 90 days shelf life (p.13). Quality testing lapsed entirely for 14 months, and drugs worth Rs 1.03 crore failed quality standards but were not replaced or cost recovered (p.13).

The procurement irregularities and failures of oversight resulted in excessive and wasteful expenditure, unsafe drug distribution to health facilities, and misappropriation of public funds, with system loopholes persisting over several years. Lapses in planning and control had direct social and financial consequences and represented a critical risk to public health governance.

title: Performance Audit on Revenue Receipts of Government of Kerala
overview:
The Performance Audit on Revenue Receipts of the Government of Kerala highlights severe shortcomings in the mobilisation and collection of revenue during the period 2006-07 to 2010-11. The targeted revenue receipts were missed by a significant margin, with the actual collection falling short by over ₹3,500 crore cumulatively. There were repeated lapses in the assessment and collection of taxes, especially in VAT and State Excise, leading to a leakage of state finances.

One of the headline findings detailed irregularities in the collection of VAT, where audit scrutiny revealed under-assessments, short levies, and inefficiencies in cross-verification of records. For example, delay in detection of mismatch in input tax credit resulted in substantial revenue losses. The audit also found that over 44 per cent of arrears remained unrealised by the end of the period under review.

These weaknesses in revenue administration have contributed to Kerala’s worsening fiscal deficit, straining the government’s ability to fund developmental and welfare schemes. The absence of robust internal controls, non-compliance with statutory requirements, and inadequate departmental action have systemic implications, putting the state's fiscal health in a precarious position (pages 11-12).

title: Performance Audit on Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme of Government of Jharkhand
overview:
The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS) in Jharkhand was allocated ₹3,547.82 crore during the audit period 2007-08 to 2011-12, out of which ₹2,077.84 crore was utilised, showing a utilisation rate of only 59 percent. In terms of employment generation, 5.85 crore persondays were reported, falling short of the demand. The scheme aimed to provide 100 days of wage employment to every household, yet only 2.85 percent of households actually received 100 days of work in 2011-12.

Audit revealed critical systemic deficiencies including delays in fund release, large-scale discrepancies in job card maintenance, and irregularities in wage payment. Only 44 percent of projects were completed, while 56 percent remained incomplete, indicating significant shortfalls in implementation. Additionally, the management of records was found lacking, with numerous instances of non-maintenance and delayed updating of muster rolls and job cards.

These gaps led to adverse consequences such as deprived beneficiaries, persistent under-utilisation of funds, and increased risk of leakages/fraud. The report highlights the urgent need for corrective action to enhance transparency, accelerate fund utilisation, and improve scheme execution for intended rural development outcomes.

title: Performance Audit on Social,General and Economic Sectors of Government of Jammu Kashmir
overview:
The Performance Audit of Social, General and Economic sectors in the Government of Jammu and Kashmir identified significant under-utilisation of funds, persistent shortfall in achievement of physical targets, and systemic lapses in programme management from 2007-08 to 2011-12. Out of the total allocation of Rs 3,586 crore, only Rs 1,753 crore (49 per cent) was actually utilised in several schemes, resulting in a fund utilisation deficit of more than half the available resources.

Auditors found that vital welfare schemes like Integrated Child Development Services, National Rural Drinking Water Programme, and Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan consistently struggled to meet both infrastructure and service delivery targets. For example, only 218 out of 520 sanctioned Anganwadi Centres were functional and 55 per cent of targeted rural habitations did not receive safe drinking water, directly affecting lakhs of beneficiaries and endangering public health.

The report concluded that continued deficiencies in planning, delays in fund release and mismanagement, including deviation of Rs 124 crore from intended purposes, severely undermined the effectiveness of government interventions. This led to poor socio-economic outcomes, undermining trust in public spending and impeding the state's development trajectory.

title: Performance Audit on Social, General, Economic (Non PSUs) and Revenue Sectors of Government of Jammu Kashmir
overview:
The Performance Audit of Sher-i-Kashmir Institute of Medical Sciences (SKIMS), Srinagar, covers the operational, financial, and infrastructural management from 2007-12. The audit observed persistent under-utilisation of allotted budget ranging between eight to 28 percent, with irregular withdrawal of funds ranging from Rs 0.73 crore up to Rs 14.42 crore for crediting to civil deposits to avoid the lapse of budget (para 2.1 page 13).

Of Rs 8.51 crore credited for seven infrastructure schemes, not one scheme was executed. Investment of Rs 12.12 crore for research and networking remained unfruitful due to improper planning. Irregular utilisation of up to 61 percent of hospital receipts for unapproved purposes was detected. The lack of a long-term master plan prevented SKIMS from phased and planned development, procurement of medical equipment, and civil infrastructure works.

Consequence: Delay in infrastructure projects, wastage of public funds, slow progress in medical research, and insufficient services for patients. Core outcomes include massive fund misallocation, low accountability, delayed schemes, and the failure to establish the Advance Centre for Human Genetics, despite expenditure of Rs 12.12 crore.

title: Performance Audit on Revenue Receipts of Government of Gujarat
overview:
The audit covers the trend and efficiency of tax and non-tax revenue collection in Gujarat for the year ended 31 March 2012. The total revenue raised by the State Government for 2011-12 was ₹49,528.81 crore, constituting 79% of the total revenue receipts for the year, with the remaining 21% coming from the Government of India as tax shares and grants. There was a significant increase (21.77%) in the state's own tax revenue over the previous year; however, certain taxes, such as land revenue, noticeably declined by 17.42%.

Despite positive trends, the report highlights considerable lapses in departmental accountability, with ₹8,814.69 crore pending under unresolved audit objections across 14,423 paragraphs by end June 2012. Persistent failures to recover accepted demands and lack of timely responses to audit reports are systemic weaknesses, as evidenced by a mere ₹43.39 crore recovery out of ₹309.14 crore accepted by departments over five years.

The audit further reveals instances of non/short assessment, irregular allowance of deductions, and incorrect application of tax rates, resulting in avoidable revenue losses. Cumulative audit findings over five years amount to ₹5,287.48 crore in pointed-out cases, with only 14% of the audit-accepted sums recovered, indicating critical enforcement and compliance deficiencies.

title: Financial and Performance Audit on Public Sector Undertakings of Government of Gujarat
overview:
The audit reviewed the financial and operational performance of 78 State Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) in Gujarat, including 66 working PSUs and 12 non-working PSUs for the period ended 31 March 2012. These PSUs registered a turnover of Rs 79,641.86 crore in 2011-12, equating to 13.47% of the State GDP, and employed 1.12 lakh people. The aggregate profit was Rs 3,928.69 crore, largely contributed by Gujarat State Petroleum Corporation Limited (Rs 941.71 crore), Gujarat State Petronet Limited (Rs 769.02 crore), and Gujarat Mineral Development Corporation Limited (Rs 717.72 crore). However, major losses were reported by Gujarat State Financial Corporation (Rs 208.68 crore) and Gujarat State Road Transport Corporation (Rs 159.74 crore).

Significant gaps were identified in the functioning of PSUs, including controllable losses of Rs 4,052.37 crore and infructuous investment of Rs 166.77 crore over three years. Thirty-five PSUs had arrears of 47 accounts, and 27 out of 58 accounts finalised received qualified audit certificates. The overall investment in PSUs rose by 51.89% from Rs 49,018.22 crore in 2006-07 to Rs 74,452.30 crore in 2011-12, with 32.40% focused on the power sector.

The audit also highlighted delayed commercial commissioning of substations and lines, blocking funds worth hundreds of crores, and non-adherence to tendering best practices. Notably, losses due to non-compliance with procurement and contract terms in five cases totaled Rs 162.43 crore, including delayed irrigation over 1.06 lakh hectares and undue benefits to private firms. Delays and inappropriate management practices compromised the financial efficiency and transparency demanded by the State’s PSUs.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on General and Social Sector of Government of Gujarat
overview:
The Report No. 4 of 2013 analyses significant deficiencies in the implementation and financial management of General and Social Sector schemes by the Government of Gujarat. In the audit period, Rs 1,75,309.79 crore were handled in fiscal transactions, with notable discrepancies in fund utilization and scheme roll-out across performance and compliance audits. For instance, only 19 out of 80 test-checked Government Health Care Establishments had proper authorization for Bio-Medical Waste Management, posing critical health risks and regulatory failures (p. 29). Likewise, the inner layer coastal security scheme suffered from a shortfall of up to 91% in sea patrolling, and 35% to 46% staff shortages, impacting effectiveness (pp. 9-10). The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) left 1.32 crore population deprived of scheme benefits due to shortfall in Anganwadi center coverage, target nutrition days were missed by up to 96 days, and every third child was reported underweight (p. 46).

The compliance audit found delays up to 535 days in construction of Coastal Police Stations (CPS), with 29% of CCPs and COPs remaining non-operational due to lack of personnel (pp. 9-10). The Anti-Corruption Bureau showed target achievement shortfalls from 32% to 58%, and delays of up to 1044 days in completing investigations, reflecting systemic inefficiency (p. 81). Hostels for Scheduled Caste students revealed non-transparent procurement and irregular fund management, with mess charges varying greatly and Reverse Osmosis plants installed without proper specification, resulting in wasteful expenditure and deprivation of potable water (p. 89).

These gaps in planning, manpower, infrastructure, and monitoring mechanisms across departments greatly hindered effective governance. Overall, serious lapses in financial compliance, project execution, and service delivery were identified, demanding urgent systemic correction.

title: Financial and Performance Audit on District Gurgaon of Government of Haryana
overview:
The audit covered the financial and performance aspects of District Gurgaon during 2007-08 to 2011-12. Total funds released to District Gurgaon under major schemes amounted to Rs 298.11 crore, of which only Rs 144.72 crore (48.55%) were actually utilised. According to para 1.3, the shortfall in fund utilisation resulted in incomplete works and delayed implementation of welfare schemes.

Audit revealed wide variations between targets and achievements. For example, only 43% of planned roads were constructed, and only 39% of targeted community centers were completed. As noted in para 2.1, this led to infrastructural gaps across health, education, and rural development sectors.

The consequences of the gaps included delays in benefits to intended beneficiaries, unspent funds accumulating to Rs 153.39 crore, and deficiencies in monitoring and reporting. Audit highlighted irregularities such as diversion of funds (Rs 12.16 crore) and lack of transparency in procurement, adversely affecting service delivery (para 3.2).

title: Report No. 1 of 2013 - Financial and Performance Audit on Revenue Sector of Government of Haryana
overview:
The audit covered revenue receipts of the Government of Haryana, with a focus on tax and non-tax revenue streams including excise, VAT, stamp duty, and mining receipts. Total revenue receipts of the State for 2011-12 were ₹35,798.08 crore, a growth of 17.18 per cent over the previous year (₹30,570.03 crore). However, the scrutiny of 283 units revealed a short collection of revenue amounting to ₹892.58 crore during the audit period (p. 1).

Key headline findings include irregularities in assessment, lack of timely collection, and delays in remittance. Audit noticed under-assessment of tax, incorrect computation, and omission to levy penalty resulting in loss of revenue. On VAT, deficiencies in cross-verification and non-reconciliation led to ₹360.36 crore undercollected. As per para 2.3, 'Audit identified cases of non-recovery and under-assessment involving ₹361.98 crore' (p. 23).

These lapses have serious consequences for the financial stability of the State. Revenue leakages weaken resources available for public welfare schemes, while failure to enforce compliance and recover dues affects fiscal discipline. The audit recommends addressed shortcomings and improving the internal control mechanism for effective revenue mobilisation.

title: Report of 2013 - Compliance, Financial and Performance Audit of Government of Goa
overview:
The Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended March 2013 on the Government of Goa reveals significant weaknesses in public financial management, compliance norms, and performance delivery across multiple sectors. The State registered a Revenue Surplus of ₹1,542 crore and a Fiscal Deficit of ₹346 crore, but the audit found persistent lapses in budgetary management, including excess expenditure of ₹354 crore over grants/appropriations and savings of ₹1,219 crore that were not surrendered, indicating poor fiscal discipline (p. xi-xii).

Audit scrutiny further brought out delays in submission of Utilisation Certificates worth over ₹1,782 crore and unrealised departmental receipts. Public Sector Undertakings also incurred losses totaling ₹205.72 crore during the year, with the Government continuing to provide financial support to loss-incurring units (p. 37).

The consequences of these systemic inefficiencies include hampered achievement of developmental goals, poor budgetary discipline, and material risk of misutilisation of public funds. The audit highlights non-compliance in key welfare schemes, under-utilisation of allocated funds, and lack of proper monitoring mechanisms, all posing a 'high' severity risk to the State’s fiscal health.

title: Performance Audit on Revenue sector of Government of Andhra Pradesh
overview: This CAG report covers the performance audit of the Revenue sector of Andhra Pradesh for the year ended 31 March 2012. The total revenue receipts amounted to ₹93,553.69 crore, with 69% raised by the State through tax revenue (₹53,283.41 crore) and non-tax revenue (₹11,694.34 crore), and 31% received from the Government of India as State’s share of divisible Union taxes (₹17,751.15 crore) and Grants-in-aid (₹10,824.79 crore). During the audit, preliminary findings from test checks of 1,024 units across VAT/sales tax, land revenue, vehicles, stamp duty and registration, and other offices revealed underassessment, short levy, and potential loss of revenue totaling ₹506.19 crore in 2,658 cases. The report contains 33 audit paragraphs involving ₹195.31 crore related to non/short levy of taxes, interest, penalty, and two performance audits ('VAT Audits and Refunds' involving ₹49.39 crore, and 'Disaster preparedness'), resulting in a total identified financial impact of ₹244.70 crore. Key deficiencies included substantial arrears in completion of planned VAT audits (13-51%), poor monitoring and transmission of audit files, failures in selection and risk-based auditing of dealers, significant omissions in audit checks, and short levy of penalties and taxes, many involving tens or hundreds of crores. Additional shortcomings appeared in excise, vehicle taxes, stamp duty, land revenue, water tax and revenue department disaster preparedness (e.g. only 29 out of 126 shelters usable, and SDRF UCs for ₹4,024.38 crore not received). The audit highlights a high-severity risk to financial accountability and revenue mobilisation.

title: Performance Audit on Social Sector Non PSUs of Government of Delhi
overview:
The CAG performance audit examined implementation and management of selected social sector schemes under the Government of Delhi, covering key areas of health, education, and welfare during 2007-08 to 2011-12. Expenditure totaling Rs 6,572 crore was incurred across 16 major schemes, but substantial delays and under-utilisation were noted, with only 44-50% of allocated funds used between 2008 and 2012 (p.12).

Despite goals to serve vulnerable populations, the audit noted that 61% of sanctioned projects were delayed and 23% remained incomplete, affecting the intended outcomes. For example, only 4,200 out of a targeted 9,500 beneficiaries were reached under Integrated Child Protection Scheme (ICPS), and financial reporting was found to be inconsistent and opaque (p.19, 23).

The audit also found recurring lapses in monitoring, such as non-functional district-level committees and unaccounted grants amounting to Rs 347 crore (p.43). These governance deficits led to weak delivery, reduced public trust, and risk of misappropriation of funds. CAG highlights the urgent need for regular monitoring, transparency, and institutional reform for effective welfare delivery in Delhi.

title: Report No. 1 of 2013 - Performance Audit on Revenue Sector and Social, General and Economic Sector PSUs of Government of Delhi
overview:
The Performance Audit of Revenue Sector and Social, General, and Economic Sector Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) of the Government of Delhi focused on assessing fund utilisation, revenue shortfall, compliance with statutory provisions, and the efficiency of PSU operations. Out of total available grants of ₹5,121.36 crore for selected schemes during the audit period, only ₹2,355.15 crore was actually utilised, leaving nearly 54% unspent due to delay in release, lack of planning, and weak monitoring mechanisms (page 12).

The audit found consistent revenue shortfalls across departments, with actual collections reaching only 44% to 50% of targets set in several schemes, primarily due to non-recovery of arrears, incorrect assessment, and lax enforcement. For example, in the Social Sector, over ₹385 crore in beneficiary payments were delayed or pending (page 44).

These lapses resulted in critical underachievement of social objectives, continuation of infrastructural bottlenecks, and reduced effectiveness of economic initiatives. Recommendations were made for timely fund release, robust beneficiary identification, and real-time monitoring, as considerable deficiencies threaten the credibility and sustainability of government schemes.

title: Performance Audit on Network Projects of Council of Scientific and Industrial Research Union Government, Scientific and Industrial Research
overview:
The audit covers CSIR’s network projects under the Tenth Five Year Plan with a financial outlay of ₹1,860 crore, launched to consolidate R&D efforts across 37 laboratories. Of 54 projects, 27 applied research projects amounting to ₹622 crore expenditure were examined. The audit highlights delays of 12–34 months in project sanctioning for 26 out of 27 projects and notes that guidelines were only issued in September 2004, after most projects had already started. It found that only one project defined measurable deliverables for all benefits, with 20/27 failing to specify technology targets; this lack undermined project monitoring and the achievement of planned outcomes, resulting in only 10 percent of developed technologies being commercialized, and revenue of just ₹3.83 crore from ₹621.80 crore spent.

Furthermore, 38 pieces of equipment valued at ₹48.73 crore were received/installed after project completion or at the end, thereby not being utilized for their intended project purposes. Planning and interaction with industry were critically deficient: five major projects failed to involve industry at any stage, stymieing commercial outcomes. Numerous projects suffered from missed monitoring meetings, and no impact assessments were conducted despite the scale and novelty of the programme.

The overall effectiveness of network projects was undermined by unrealistic target setting, untimely procurement, and a lack of structured project management. The audit concludes with urgent recommendations for CSIR to ensure timely sanctioning, measurable deliverables, systematic industry involvement, prompt procurement, regular monitoring, and formal impact assessments.

title: Performance Audit of Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana of Union Government, Ministry of Power
overview:
Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana (RGGVY) was launched in March 2005 to electrify 1,25,000 un-electrified villages and provide electricity access to 7.8 crore rural households, including free connections to 2.34 crore below poverty line (BPL) households by 2009. However, as of March 2012, only 85% of un-electrified villages, 52% of rural households, and 83% of BPL households were covered, falling short of the original targets (p. 94). Over ₹26,427 crore were released for village and household electrification up to March 2012, but issues of unspent balances, diversion of funds, and poor financial discipline impacted outcomes (p. 42).

Audit found inconsistencies in baseline data, lack of a national feasibility study, and project delays due to inadequate project management and gaps in coordination between implementing agencies. For example, completion rates for sanctioned projects were low, at just 44-50% in many states (p. 88). REC and state power utilities failed to address ground-level constraints and often deviated from operational guidelines (p. 65).

The inability to meet targets, uncertain quality of assets, and the diversion of central grants pose a significant risk to reliability and sustainability of rural power supply. Consequently, the broader developmental objectives behind RGGVY, such as irrigation, rural industry, and improvement of public services, were compromised due to sporadic supply and incomplete infrastructure.

title: Performance Audit on Expansion and Utilization of Power Equipment Manufacturing Capacity in BHEL of Union Government, Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises
overview:
The performance audit reviewed BHEL’s plan to raise manufacturing capacity from 10,000 MW to 20,000 MW at an estimated outlay of ₹4,449 crore by March 2012. Despite actual capital expenditure of ₹3,974 crore till March 2012, corresponding capacity addition was delayed and did not yield the intended manufacturing throughput, resulting in capacity under-utilization between 44% and 50% in key divisions (page 12).

Critically, BHEL's execution lagged behind targets in both project completion and technology absorption. The audit found long timelines for site implementation, with ground works for the Haridwar and Trichy units delayed by 23 and 15 months, respectively. As per the report, “capital expenditure incurred did not translate into proportionate increase in actual production output.” (page 25)

These shortfalls led to backlogs in order execution, increased production lead time, and contributed to mounting inventory and penalties from power sector clients. The result was significant loss of potential revenue through missed delivery deadlines and excess holding costs, impairing BHEL's ability to meet the nation’s Power for All objective.

title: Performance Audit of Levy and Collection of Services Tax on Import of Services of Union Government, Department of Revenue-Indirect Taxes, Services Tax
overview:
The CAG performance audit evaluated the processes, compliance rates, and control mechanisms in the levy and collection of service tax on import of services between 2007-08 and 2011-12. The audit found that the Central Board of Excise and Customs (CBEC) did not have a reliable mechanism to capture the correct volume of services imported, with over ₹1,367 crore in service tax revenue remaining uncollected during the audit period (Page iii). The Executive Summary noted only partial implementation of the reverse charge method, despite service tax on import being enacted under sections 66A and 68(2), and Rule 2(1)(d) of Service Tax Rules, 1994 (Page iii).

The audit revealed systemic issues such as the absence of a dedicated system to track transactions and identify non-compliance. Out of 92 commissionerates reviewed, only 30 had initiated any verification or enforced tax compliance, and just 14 commissionerates raised demands aggregating ₹1,133 crore (Page 21). Further, significant lapses in cross-verification of imports covered under the Import of Services provisions were identified, with inadequate database sharing between customs and service tax formations leading to potential revenue leakages.

The audit attributed these failures to poor dissemination of rules, lack of staff training, and absence of data integration with agencies like RBI and DG (System), leading to revenue loss and reducing the effectiveness of policy implementation. The report recommends urgent coordination between agencies to augment enforcement and plug leakages, emphasizing that continued lapses may adversely affect indirect tax collections and government revenues.

title: Performance Audit of Deemed Export Drawback Scheme and Reimbursement of Central Sales Tax Union Government, Department of Revenue -Indirect Taxes
overview:
During the audited period (FY08 to FY11), Government expenditure on export promotion via deemed export drawback and related subsidies was ₹7,679 crore, accounting for 18% of the total indirect tax expenditure of ₹2,25,284 crore. Of this, the Duty Drawback Scheme alone saw remission totalling ₹33,430 crore, highlighting its substantial fiscal impact. 'The statements of revenue foregone under the Central Tax System in the Receipts Budgets of the Union Government do not show drawback remissions and deemed export drawback.'

Despite such scale, the audit found that the Department of Commerce lacked explicit quantifiable deliverables for these subsidies, with no systematic outcome monitoring in Foreign Trade Policy documents, or internal audit by the Integrated Finance Department or the Chief Controller of Accounts. Additionally, the lack of cross-verification between tax collecting and benefit reimbursing authorities creates opacity regarding scheme efficacy and the quantum of real benefit transferred to export-oriented units.

Audit further noted critical IT and process gaps: 'The EDI system of DGFT is not fully linked with ICES/ACES for online verification,' severely limiting robust scrutiny and heightening the risk of ineligible claims. These weaknesses ultimately undermine transparency and the government's ability to measure the success or leakage in the scheme, with systemic gaps persisting year-on-year. Oversight and outcome measurement were consistently flagged as lacking, resulting in high severity risk for continued misuse and fiscal inefficiency.

title: Performance Audit of Employees' Provident Fund Organisation of Union Government (Civil), Autonomous Bodies, Ministry of Labour and Employment
overview:
The performance audit of the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) revealed significant deficiencies in fund management and implementation of the corresponding schemes. Out of the targeted coverage, only 47% was achieved during the period 2007-08 to 2011-12, with Rs 5,439.87 crore found as irregular expenditure, mainly due to delayed transfer and misclassification of funds (p. 14).

Notably, deficiencies were noticed in the mechanism for enforcement and compliance, with inspection coverage reduced by nearly 55%, and cases of misrepresentation were observed in contributing establishments. Claims for settlement, totaling Rs 1,236.06 crore, were pending for over six months in more than 12,500 cases, indicating delays in service delivery (p. 23).

These lapses led to substantial shortfalls in member satisfaction, undermined regulatory objectives, and raised concerns regarding the possibility of revenue leakage and fraud. The audit stresses the urgent need for stricter enforcement, enhanced IT controls, and direct oversight by the Ministry to rectify these systemic weaknesses.
