title: Performance Audit of Preservation and Conservation of Monuments and Antiquities of Union Government, Ministry of Culture
overview:
The performance audit scrutinized the Ministry of Culture and its key bodies, including ASI and major national museums, covering the years 2007-08 to 2011-12. The CAG physically inspected 1,655 monuments and reviewed records for 3,678 centrally protected monuments. It found serious inadequacies in identification, preservation, funding, and documentation. Notably, 92 centrally protected monuments were not traceable during inspection, much higher than numbers reported to Parliament.

The audit highlighted that the ASI did not maintain a reliable database of protected monuments, nor did it complete basic surveys or update lists regularly—impacting both transparency and effectiveness. Less than 1% of ASI’s expenditure was on exploration and excavation, despite this being a core mandate. Museums lacked systematic accession registers, and significant discrepancies existed between physical inventory and recorded antiquities, raising concerns of theft, loss, and authenticity. Further, there were cases of encroachment and unauthorized construction around World Heritage Sites.

Acute manpower shortages, poor governance, and ineffective responses to past recommendations were evident across organizations. In total, 131 antiquities were documented as stolen from monuments and 37 from site museums during the period, and efforts to retrieve them were deemed 'completely ineffective'. The audit concludes that without systemic reforms, India's tangible heritage remains at high risk of neglect and loss.

title: Performance Audit on Administration of Penalty and Prosecution of Union Government, Department of Revenue - Direct Taxes
overview:
The Performance Audit examines the administration and implementation of penalty and prosecution by the Department of Revenue – Direct Taxes for combating tax evasion. The Department levied penalties amounting to Rs 19,060 crore during 2007-08 to 2011-12, but only Rs 7,885 crore (41%) was actually collected, leaving Rs 11,175 crore unrealised. Discrepancies in imposition and follow-up of penalties, including significant delays and cancellations or waivers, were prevalent. For example, Rs 3,501 crore of penalties were cancelled and Rs 2,079 crore were waived in this period.

The audit also found that prosecution as a deterrent was weak: though 2,616 prosecution complaints were filed during 2006-07 to 2011-12, conviction rate remained below 6%. Delays in case initiation and ineffective monitoring caused pendency of 2,226 cases at courts, with many pending for over a decade. Internal controls for selection and tracking of cases were weak, resulting in varied practices across Commissionerates and field offices.

Consequences include a low deterrent effect against evasion, a large pool of unrecovered penalties, and dilution of prosecution's credibility as a tool for enforcing compliance, ultimately undermining voluntary compliance with direct tax law.

title: Performance Audit on Autonomous Bodies of Union Government, Civil
overview:
The Performance Audit covered 32 autonomous bodies under various Ministries and Departments of the Union Government for the period 2007-08 to 2011-12. The audit revealed major deficiencies in the utilisation of grants, with only 44-50% of allocated funds being effectively utilised across several years. For example, grants received by eight institutes of Ministry of Health and Family Welfare amounted to Rs 10,520 crore, but only 47% was utilised in 2011-12. Approximately Rs 5,400 crore remained unspent by the end of the audit period, indicating systemic inefficiencies (p. 12).

Significant lapses were observed in adherence to General Financial Rules, with several autonomous bodies having unspent balances for over five years. Many institutions had not established adequate internal audit mechanisms, and 19 bodies lacked regular Director Board meetings, impairing governance and accountability (p. 23). Delayed submission of Utilisation Certificates (UCs) persisted, with 63% of UCs pending as of March 2012, potentially impacting the release of future grants.

The consequences of these findings are severe: recurring under-utilisation of funds limits the achievement of objectives, delays vital projects, and may constitute violations of financial discipline. The lack of timely external and internal audit exposure increases risk of misuse and fraud. The audit recommends strict compliance monitoring and frameworks to ensure better fund management, and restoration of institutional accountability to the Government.

title: Performance Audit of Storage Management and Movement of Food Grains in Food Corporation of India, Union Government, Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution
overview:
The CAG performance audit examines FCI's storage and movement of food grains over a period of significant operational expansion between 2006-07 and 2011-12. Procurement for the Central Pool rose steeply—total stocks reached 823 lakh MTs in June 2012 compared to 410 lakh MTs in June 2007, nearly doubling FCI’s storage and movement obligations. The audit highlights that despite a sanctioned buffer norm of 317 lakh MTs as of July 2012, actual stocks exceeded operational requirements by 506 lakh MTs, causing acute pressure on storage infrastructure and increasing the risk of losses due to prolonged outdoor stacking.

Key findings reveal systemic gaps: 224 lakh MTs (27%) of food grains were stored in CAP (Cover and Plinth) facilities in June 2012 due to non-availability of covered storage—a practice discouraged due to higher risks of damage. Further, the audit observed continued high holdings of non-issuable stocks, which peaked at 32.39 lakh MTs (6.5% of total stocks) in June 2012 despite prior instructions to reduce such obsolete inventory.

The audit identifies recurring lapses including delayed evacuation, lack of scientific stock rotation, and significant operational inefficiencies. The financial consequences involved increased handling, transportation, and storage losses, with grain quantity and quality compromised in areas not meeting prescribed standards.

title: Performance Audit of Exemptions to Charitable Trusts and Institutions of Union Government, Direct Taxes
overview:
The performance audit examined the efficacy of income tax exemptions granted under sections 11, 12, and 80G to charitable trusts and institutions by the Union Government. Out of 21,850 trusts scrutinized, only 5,386 were audited, representing a mere 24.6% coverage. The audit highlighted Rs 1,123 crore in tax foregone during 2007-11 owing to exemptions, with notable shortfalls in due diligence and monitoring.

Major deficiencies included irregular grant of registration, inadequate vetting of activities, and lack of follow-up on cancellation of registrations. For instance, in several cases trusts claiming exemption were found engaged in non-charitable activities, with Rs 304.20 crore wrongly allowed as income exempt from tax (Page 31). Insufficient verification and inconsistencies in reporting led to repeated lapses across assessment years.

The consequences of these gaps resulted in substantial revenue loss, lack of accountability for fund utilisation, and potential misuse of exemptions. The audit emphasized the urgent need for robust oversight, standardized assessment practices, and timely action to mitigate misappropriation risks and protect revenue interests.

title: Performance Audit of Strengthening the Tax base through use of Information-Union Government, Department of Revenue - Direct Taxes
overview:
The performance audit reviewed the effectiveness of Government measures to widen and deepen the direct tax base through improved utilization of information available with the Income Tax Department (ITD). Audit reviewed 1,381 cases out of 2,85,547 high-value information records for FY 2008-09 and found that only 15.2 per cent were properly acted upon, pointing to insufficient use of third-party information (p. vii).

Key audit findings showed total unverified potential tax evasion of over Rs 1,016 crore, and an average delay of over 18 months in taking action on key information inputs (p. ix). Out of 25,618 non-PAN information cases, only 5.7 per cent were eventually matched, reflecting significant technical and procedural lapses. Serious cases of non-action included a single corporate taxpayer’s income of Rs 237 crore going unverified for three years.

Audit concluded that failure to systematize, prioritize and utilize available information resulted in a significant loss of potential tax revenue, underutilization of data analytics capabilities, and persistent manual bottlenecks despite an overall expenditure of Rs 243 crore on PAN and OLTAS systems during the audit period (p. 24).

title: Performance Audit of Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme of Union Government, Ministry of Rural Development
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS) revealed significant deficiencies in implementation between 2007 and 2012. The audit covered 3,848 gram panchayats across 28 states and 4 UTs. Funding was substantial, with total expenditure reported at ₹15,857 crore in 2007-08 rising to ₹38,035 crore in 2011-12. Despite this, there was a marked decline in average annual rural household employment from 54 days in 2009-10 to 43 days in 2011-12. Only 30% of planned works in the annual plans were completed during the audit period, and a considerable portion of central funds was underutilized, with Bihar, Maharashtra, and Uttar Pradesh (housing 46% of rural poor) utilizing only about 20% of central funds.

Institutional gaps were significant: annual plans were not prepared or completed in 31% of test-checked GPs, and five states did not formulate state rules as required by the Act, even seven years post-enactment. There were operational failures, including shortages of Gram Rozgar Sahayaks by up to 93% in some states and poor information and education activities critical for beneficiary awareness. Financial irregularities were prevalent, with ₹1,960.45 crore released in March 2011 against financial norms, excess releases totaling ₹2,374.86 crore to six states, and unaccounted expenditure or misappropriation in several instances.

Failure to follow key controls and prescribed processes led to substantial non-completion of works, wage non-payments of ₹36.97 crore, and extensive maintenance issues in program records. Monitoring from the Centre was found unsatisfactory, with the statutory Central Council failing its mandate. The consequences undermined livelihood security, affected asset creation, and raised serious risks regarding transparency and effective fund use.

title: Performance Audit of Planning and Management of Refits of Indian Naval Ships of Union Government, Defence Services Navy
overview: This performance audit covers the effectiveness, efficiency, and economy of the planning and management of refits for Indian Naval Ships from 2005-06 to 2009-10, with updates through 2012-13. The audit scrutinized 152 refits conducted at four Naval Dockyards/Ship Repair Yards, sampling 52 in detail, and highlighted substantial overshoots in both the planning and the actual execution time for these crucial maintenance operations. Specifically, delays led to an excess of 8,629 ship days lost for operational purposes, and 2,975 excess dry docking days costing Rs 167.49 crore were consumed. The report also identified recurring causes, such as spares shortages—only 24-69% of required spares were available in certain cases—and infrastructure bottlenecks. Inadequate adherence to Operational-cum-Refit Cycles (OCRC) contributed to major delays: 82% of refits did not commence as scheduled and 74% were completed late. Offloaded refits also suffered from non-transparent tendering and uneconomical repairs, causing extra expenditure of Rs 2.89 crore. The report concludes that shortcomings cited in CAG's 1999 audit continue despite assurances of corrective actions, leading to persistent adverse impacts on fleet combat readiness and asset availability.

title: Performance Audit of Disaster Preparedness in India of Union Government, Ministry of Home Affairs
overview:
This CAG performance audit reviewed disaster preparedness of India's Ministry of Home Affairs for the period 2007-08 to 2011-12, examining planning, institutional arrangements, funding, capacity, response, and specific hazards. The audit found that the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) had not completed major planned projects, with only one of several national initiatives fully implemented as of September 2012, despite lapses of up to five years (Paragraph 4.3, page vii). Several critical posts in NDMA remained vacant and consultants were used for day-to-day work instead of regular staff (Paragraph 4.6, page vii). This undermined coordination and capacity building for disaster response nationally.

There were major delays and mismanagement in State Disaster Response Funds (SDRF); States were irregular in sending utilisation details and failed to invest unspent balances as per guidelines, resulting in a potential loss of interest amounting to Rs 477.99 crore (Paragraph 5.1, page vi). In some States, significant amounts remained unspent due to procedural delays and lack of monitoring, with Rs 654.04 crore lying idle in Gujarat, Assam, and Goa (Paragraph 5.2, page vi). Major gaps existed in disaster planning: even after six years from enactment of Disaster Management Act, a comprehensive National Plan was not formulated (Paragraph 3.1.1, page vii).

Preparedness for major hazards—including floods, earthquakes, cyclones, and chemical disasters—was found lacking. Less than 10% of flood-prone areas covered by procurement of topographic information, only eight States prepared action plans for large dams, and key resilience projects for earthquakes and droughts were stuck in preparatory phases or shortfalls. The audit highlights systemic weaknesses, including lack of regular monitoring, unutilized resources, and failure to institutionalize key functions and guidelines for disaster mitigation.

title: Performance Audit on Ordnance Equipment Group of Factories of Union Government, Department of Defence
overview:
The performance audit of the Ordnance Equipment Group of Factories (OEFG), covering the years 2008-09 to 2011-12, uncovered systemic and persistent deficiencies in production planning, procurement, production execution, and quality control. The report found that factories faced significant mismatches between target fixation and real manufacturing capacity, leading to delays in supply to the Army, which received around 77% of these items. Procurement violations resulted in over-provisioning of stores worth Rs 165.54 crore and extra expenditure of Rs 12.31 crore due to improper tendering methods.

Production shortfalls were critical: in 116 out of 208 cases, shortfalls in issue and production to the Army ranged from 21% to 100%, with a cumulative value of Rs 1,147.13 crore during 2008-12. Issues also spilled over to subsequent years, affecting supplies worth Rs 493.08 crore, while only 2.62% of paramilitary needs were met. Factories also incurred overtime payments of Rs 48.68 crore despite underutilised man-hours, and suffered a net loss of Rs 226.09 crore over the audit period, adding pressure on the Consolidated Fund of India. Quality control remained a challenge, with high rejection rates and repeated failures reported at both factory and user ends.

Internal controls and top management monitoring were flagged as inadequate, with irregular accounting and persistent operational inefficiencies. The audit concludes that systemic weaknesses persisted despite earlier reviews and directives, emphasizing the need for structural improvements in planning, procurement, manpower utilisation, and quality management.

title: Performance Audit of Civil on Agricultural Debt Waiver and Debt Relief Scheme of Union Government, Ministry of Finance
overview:
The Agricultural Debt Waiver and Debt Relief Scheme (ADWDRS), announced in the Union Budget 2008-09, aimed to address the plight of indebted farmers. The initial allocation was Rs 60,000 crore, later revised to Rs 71,680 crore, covering nearly 3.69 crore accounts across Rural and Urban Co-operative Banks (RCBs/UCBs), Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs), and Regional Rural Banks (RRBs). According to the report, as of March 2012, total debt waiver and relief granted under the scheme amounted to Rs 52,516.86 crore covering 3.45 crore accounts.

The audit highlights significant lapses, including ineligible beneficiaries receiving benefits, discrepancies in records maintained by lending institutions, and instances of undue favour to certain categories of borrowers. Specifically, 'unscrupulous accounts' were detected and documentation was found lacking in numerous cases, raising concerns regarding the adequacy of internal controls and targeting of the intended beneficiaries. The audit also observes improper verification of claims, non-adherence to guidelines, and the risk of double/multiple financing in certain states.

Consequently, the scheme's effectiveness in achieving its core objectives was undermined, with a substantial quantum of eligible farmers not benefitting due to implementation lapses, while several ineligible accounts were granted waivers, highlighting the need for strengthened monitoring, audit, and transparency in future relief measures.

title: Report of 2012 - Performance Audit on District Boudh of Government of Odisha
overview:
The Performance Audit for District Boudh, Odisha, analyzed the adequacy and effectiveness of flagship socio-economic development programmes from 2007-12 across nine sectors including health, education, nutrition, drinking water, rural employment, housing, agriculture, roads, and electricity. Audit covered major offices, agencies, all three blocks, and a sample of 15 out of 63 Gram Panchayats. Boudh district, with a high poverty ratio (80% BPL households per 1997 survey) and literacy rates below State averages, received substantial programmatic funding: a total of ₹450.17 crore between 2007-12, but could utilize only 74% (₹333.89 crore), with significant misstatement due to advances and diversions.

Key headline findings include grave staff and infrastructure shortages in healthcare (24 centers short, 24 doctor and 61 paramedical vacancies), incomplete basic facilities in education (204 habitations without schools, 337 teachers short as per sanctioned strength, and 1,303 short as per RTE norms), high malnutrition rates (62% of children malnourished), and extensive fund mismanagement with fictitious utilization certificates totalling ₹34.85 crore. Numerous program committees failed to meet as required, with few or no meetings, or existed only on paper, undermining oversight and participatory planning at the local level.

Consequences included 61% of habitations remaining inaccessible by road, less than half of rural electrification targets met, 37 incomplete rural water supply schemes, and failure to provide basic nutrition/ICDS services in 221 villages. Routine monitoring lacked impact evaluation, and planning failed to involve Gram Panchayats or converge schemes. This led to unfruitful, misdirected, and often wasteful expenditure, undermining intended benefits to the rural poor. (Pages V-VIII, 1, 5, 14-17, 18-78)

title: Report of 2012 - Compliance and Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Odisha
overview:
The 2012 CAG Performance Audit evaluated key civil sector programmes, focusing on public funds, compliance, and major infrastructure developments. Five Minor Port projects (Astaranga, Chudamani, Dhamra, Gopalpur and Subarnarekha) were initiated via PPP between 1998-2012 with projected private investment of ₹12,594.02 crore. Concession agreements (CA) ranged from 30 to 34 years, but approvals of High Level Clearance Authority were not sought for projects exceeding ₹500 crore, failing mandatory policy checks. Exclusive selection by MoU instead of competitive bidding led to revenue shares below the legal reserve — Gopalpur's rate was 0–7.5%, causing ₹99.26 crore in lost revenue share.

Audit found critical lapses in institutional setup: Odisha Maritime Board (OMB) was never formed to monitor PPP port projects, contrary to Port Policy. Delayed environmental clearances and land acquisition, mostly due to developer actions, caused additional costs; e.g., Dhamra incurred extra ₹30.86 crore. Deficiencies included non-engagement of Independent Engineers, missing escrow accounts, and tariffs at Dhamra Port that were 153–799% higher than rates prescribed by the Tariff Authority for Major Ports (TAMP) and Paradip Port Trust.

The audit further revealed widespread avoidance of competitive price discovery in dal procurement for Supplementary Nutrition Programme (SNP) and MDM schemes. Ceiling prices were used as tender offer rates, resulting in losses of ₹43.61 crore at market prices, rising to ₹65.75 crore if average prices considered. Other compliance issues included 84% of Blood Banks operating without license, short supply and quality lapses in nutrition, and diversion of TPDS rice worth ₹2,655.61 crore. Oversight and monitoring by project and departmental units were routinely inadequate, enabling chronic underperformance and loss.

title: Report of 2012 - Performance Audit on Social, Economics, General Revenue and Economic Sectors of Government of Mizoram
overview:
This performance audit report covers the social, economic, general revenue, and public sector undertakings' activities of the Government of Mizoram for the financial year ending March 2012. The review highlights critical deficiencies in fund management, planning, and implementation across departments. For instance, a total budget allocation of ₹1363.20 crore in the Social Sector was matched by an actual expenditure of ₹1264.87 crore, reflecting underutilisation and inefficiencies in delivering services. Ad hoc planning and yearly resizing of plans were observed rather than a needs-based approach, leading to excess and avoidable expenditures, such as ₹28.52 crore parked under Civil Deposits to avoid fund lapse and extra expenditures of ₹1.39 crore due to delayed loan repayments, as well as irregular procurement of ₹0.71 crore requiring ex-post-facto approval.

Loan recovery was substantially deficient, with outstanding loan and interest of ₹3.65 crore against loanees, representing 83 per cent recovery shortfall. Moreover, the audit found the absence of technical inspection of completed works by the responsible engineers, raising concerns about quality assurance in public works. Examination of grants-in-aid found significant delays, up to 530 days, in release to implementing agencies, resulting in the inability to ensure timely execution of targeted programs. The report also assesses implementation of the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS), documenting chronic shortfalls in state matching share releases and delayed transfer to district authorities.

Throughout the audit period, notable service delivery metrics against targets were largely achieved in terms of civic amenities and housing loans, but systemic weaknesses in fund flow, monitoring, and procurement controls resulted in avoidable expenditure, poor loan recovery, and quality risks. The audit concludes that improvements in planning, fund release, monitoring, and procurement practices are essential to ensure effective service delivery and fiscal responsibility.

title: Report No. 5 of 2012 - Financial and Performance Audit on District Kinnaur of Government of Himachal Pradesh
overview:
This audit report examines the financial and performance aspects of selected schemes in District Kinnaur, including the Sarv Shiksha Abhiyan, Indira Awas Yojana, Mid-Day Meal Scheme, National Rural Health Mission, and several infrastructure projects. Total funds released to these schemes between 2006-07 and 2010-11 amounted to ₹99.23 crore, of which only ₹57.12 crore (57.6%) were utilised, leaving significant unspent balances. For example, under the Sarv Shiksha Abhiyan, out of ₹24.53 crore released, ₹11.18 crore remained unutilised by the end of March 2011.

The audit found headline lapses including improper fund management and delayed project execution. In the Indira Awas Yojana, only 920 out of 1,822 sanctioned houses were actually constructed within the review period, indicating a completion rate of just 50.5%. Delays in provision of materials, non-adherence to technical guidelines, and shortfall in staff deployment critically affected outcomes.

These lapses resulted in significant consequences for local beneficiaries. Non-utilisation of funds and incomplete infrastructure led to deprivation of intended services, with adverse effects noted in school attendance, delivery of health services, and rural asset creation. The audit stresses urgent need for strengthened management to prevent such recurring inefficiencies and ensure optimal public welfare.

title: Performance Audit on De-notification of land by Government and Allotment of sites by Bangalore Development Authority of Government of Karnataka
overview:
This report examines the denotification of land by the Government of Karnataka and the allotment of sites by the Bangalore Development Authority (BDA) between 2007 and 2012. Of the 34,527-17 acres acquired for 54 layouts, only 19,049-02 acres (44%) had been taken possession of by April 2012, leaving a significant shortfall due in part to delays and irregular denotifications. During the audit period, Government denotified 212-39 acres after possession had been taken, despite having no legal authority to do so, and withdrew acquisition for 1355-01 acres overall from January 1995 to March 2012. Multiple denotifications, totaling over 610-16½ acres during 2007-12, were executed without referral to the Denotification Committee, subverting established procedures and resulting in loss of public land and revenue.

The audit uncovered irregular denotification after sites were developed and in several cases where land had been allotted or sold, highlighting disregard for legal judgments and systemic weaknesses. Notably, betterment tax totalling Rs 51.30 crore and other revenue streams were compromised, while unauthorised exclusion of 91-35½ acres from compensation awards occurred. There was also evidence of significant irregularities in the allotment of 'G' category and alternative sites, resulting in at least Rs 36.83 crore in loss.

Systemic failures were observed in enforcing lease conditions for Civic Amenity (CA) sites, monitoring compensation payments, preventing encroachment, and maintaining asset inventories. As a result, BDA lost substantial land, revenue, and failed to deliver planned civic amenities, thereby undermining public objectives and exposing the Authority to recurring financial, administrative, and legal risks.

Para 1: The audit covered financial and operational performance of 21 public sector undertakings in Himachal Pradesh. As of March 2011, the investment by Government and others in these undertakings was ₹4,420.97 crore. Out of these, 16 companies and five statutory corporations were examined, reflecting a combined turnover of ₹1,044.97 crore in 2010-11. Notably, only seven PSUs generated profits during the period, amounting to ₹23.87 crore; the remaining entities reported aggregate losses.

Para 2: The headline finding of the audit is the consistently low fund utilization and recurring operational inefficiencies. "The average fund utilization for capital projects to actual allocation during 2006-11 remained below 50%" (page 12) due to delayed project implementation and inadequate capacity planning. Several PSUs, such as HPSIDC, failed to meet intended objectives resulting in incomplete projects, substantial idle funds, and non-recovery of advances.

The audit identified lapses in internal controls, long delays in finalization of accounts (up to 5 years), and risks of fund misappropriation.

title: Performance Audit on Revenue of Government of Karnataka
overview:
The performance audit of revenue receipts in Karnataka for the period 2006-07 to 2010-11 revealed substantial shortfalls in target collections, major delays in assessments, and significant lapses in enforcement. The report highlighted that revenue receipts for Commercial Taxes, State Excise, Stamps and Registration, and Other Taxes fell short of the budget estimates by Rs 3,622 crore in 2010-11 alone, representing an underachievement of 21% in crucial segments (p. 9).

A notable gap was identified in the recovery of arrears, where out of total arrears of Rs 6,144 crore as of March 2011, only Rs 1,028 crore was realised—a realization rate of just 16.7%. This underutilisation of available legal and enforcement provisions was repeatedly observed. The audit also detected instances of misclassification of receipts amounting to Rs 54.92 crore and improper grant of exemptions estimated at Rs 99.98 crore (p. 26), raising concerns of revenue leakage.

The consequences of these lapses included lower resource availability for state development projects, weakened fiscal health, and growing reliance on borrowings. The irregularities observed in registration fee collections, short levy of excise duties, and inadequate verification of inputs increased non-compliance risk and may encourage tax evasion, unless urgent systemic reforms are undertaken.

title: Report No. 3 of 2012 - Performance Audit on Revenue Sector of Government of Himachal Pradesh
overview:
The Performance Audit covering the period 2006-07 to 2010-11 assessed the efficiency and effectiveness of revenue collection in Himachal Pradesh. The audit examined major receipts under State Excise, Taxes on Vehicles, and Taxes and Duties on Electricity, highlighting substantial shortfalls and irregularities. Notably, between 2006-07 and 2010-11, State Excise receipts fell short by ₹43.59 crore, representing a 14.8% deviation from budget estimates (page 2).

The audit identified instances where the department failed to recover ₹22.87 crore due from defaulters and did not levy interest of ₹1.78 crore on delayed payments (page 18). There were also delays in finalising assessments, leading to revenue loss and weakening of internal controls. Furthermore, the audit observed lapses such as uncollected composition fees, improper grant of concessions, and diversion of funds totalling ₹11.24 crore (page 34).

These shortcomings hindered optimal revenue mobilisation, impacted financial planning, and risked further arrears. The lack of robust monitoring and control processes undermined the department’s credibility and jeopardised public finances in Himachal Pradesh.

title: Performance Audit on Social, General and Economic Sector (Non Public Sector Undertakings) of Government of Himachal Pradesh
overview:
The performance audit examined the implementation and outcomes of select schemes in the Social, General and Economic Sectors of Himachal Pradesh between 2006-07 and 2010-11. The report highlighted persistent underutilisation of allocated funds, with up to ₹129.62 crore remaining unspent in key schemes during 2010-11 alone.

One major area of underperformance was in the execution of rural connectivity and health sector schemes. For example, only 44 per cent of targeted habitations were actually covered under the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana up to March 2011 (page 12), leading to continued isolation of remote villages. In education and health, significant shortfalls in staff deployment and infrastructure were noted: only 61 per cent of sanctioned posts in rural health centres were filled as of March 2011 (page 40).

The audit found that delays in release of central and state shares to implementing agencies impaired project execution, and in several cases, ₹42 crore lapsed due to administrative delays (page 15). Consequences included incomplete works, denied benefits to target groups, and lower social and economic outcomes. The report stressed the need for improved planning, regular monitoring, and transparent, accountable fund management.

title: Performance Audit on Public Sector Undertakings of Kerala
overview:
This performance audit report covers the functioning of State Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) in Kerala, highlighting significant financial, operational, and governance issues across 116 PSUs (99 working, 17 non-working) as of 31 March 2012. The report notes that the total investment by the government in these PSUs was ₹9,097.98 crore, with the working PSUs registering a turnover of ₹16,171.31 crore, representing 4.95% of the State GDP. However, the cumulative losses of several major corporations have eroded the State’s capital investment, resulting in a present net worth of only (−)₹906.40 crore as per the latest finalized accounts, despite a capital and loan infusion of ₹5,880.68 crore by the Government.

The audit identified major gaps: only 44 out of 76 PSUs with finalized accounts posted profits (totaling ₹645.36 crore), while 29 incurred losses (₹477.88 crore), with particularly large annual losses at Kerala State Road Transport Corporation (₹376.89 crore) and Kerala State Cashew Development Corporation (₹68.50 crore). Quality of accounts was also flagged, with statutory auditors issuing only 16 unqualified certificates against 88 finalized accounts, and 106 instances of non-compliance with accounting standards in 42 accounts. Arrears in account finalization were significant, with 77 working PSUs collectively 207 accounts in arrear as of 30 September 2012.

Programme and project execution flaws were prevalent, especially within the Kerala State Electricity Board, where failure to prepare and act upon long-term plans, delays in project completion (leading to cost and time overruns), outdated grid management systems, and inadequate maintenance all contributed to service and financial inefficiencies. Avoidable expenditures and lapses in internal controls were observed, resulting in quantified losses or excess payments amounting to multiple crores. Many of the recommendations focus on planning, monitoring, internal controls, and financial management reforms.

title: Compliance and Performance Audit on General and Economic Sector of Government of Gujarat
overview:
This audit report highlights major deficiencies in fund utilization and programme implementation across key government sectors in Gujarat during 2010-12. For example, out of the ₹392.47 crore proposed for the coastal security scheme, only ₹58.43 crore was sanctioned and utilized, resulting in significant shortfalls in infrastructure, manpower, and surveillance capabilities. The report also found that vital health and social sector programmes, such as management of bio-medical waste and the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS), suffered from chronic under-coverage, non-availability of basic amenities, and non-functional infrastructure, leaving large populations without intended services.

Serious delays and deviations were noted in setting up coastal police stations and deploying patrol boats, with up to 91% shortfall in night sea patrolling and manpower shortages of up to 46 percent in crew members. In the health sector, only 19 out of 80 government healthcare establishments had proper authorizations for bio-medical waste management, resulting in unsafe disposal practices and environmental hazards (page 6).

Consequently, despite heavy investments and central funding, large-scale operational deficiencies persisted across departments. The absence of strategic planning, non-utilization of funds for core components, delays in execution, poor monitoring, and lack of trained personnel undermined key security, health, and social initiatives, directly compromising service outcomes and the safety of vulnerable populations.

title: Performance Audit on Revenue Receipts of Government of Gujarat
overview:
This performance audit presents a detailed analysis of revenue receipts of the Government of Gujarat for the year ended 31 March 2012, covering tax and non-tax revenues as well as central transfers. The report notes that the State Government raised Rs 49,528.81 crore in 2011-12, which constituted 79% of total revenue receipts, with the remainder from the Government of India. Tax revenue saw robust growth, particularly in Value Added Tax (VAT), which increased by 34.77% over the prior year to Rs 27,259.38 crore, making up 70.51% of total tax receipts.

Despite growth, serious gaps remain in audit compliance and revenue realization. Outstanding audit observations reached Rs 8,814.69 crore across 14,423 cases from 4,519 inspection reports at the end of June 2012. Recovery against accepted audit findings was low, with only Rs 43.39 crore recovered out of Rs 309.14 crore accepted by departments for the period 2006-07 to 2010-11. Additionally, clearance of past audit objections remains sluggish and departmental responses often lack timeliness and completeness.

The audit also highlighted significant financial irregularities including underassessment, short levy, and loss of revenue across VAT, land revenue, stamp duty, and mining receipts. In 2011-12, Rs 596.11 crore in 1,744 cases of underassessment or short levy were observed, but corrective recoveries during the year stood at only Rs 6.71 crore. Departments are advised to strengthen monitoring, enforce accountability, and expedite action on audit findings to safeguard public revenue.

title: Performance Audit on Revenue of Government of Assam
overview:
This report examines the performance of revenue administration in Assam for the year ended 31 March 2012, highlighting significant deficiencies in tax collection, audit response, and recovery mechanisms. The total receipts for 2011-12 were ₹27,455.39 crore, with only 38% raised by the state government; the remainder was from the Centre. Of particular concern was the failure by senior officials to promptly reply to audit queries, leading to 2,721 unresolved paragraphs involving ₹935.88 crore as of June 2012 (pg 4-5). Audit checks across 148 units found under-assessment and short levy in 498 cases, resulting in revenue loss of ₹1,864.50 crore (pg 11).

A performance audit of recovery offices in Sales Tax revealed poor arrear recovery rates of 1-2% from 2006-11, leaving ₹1,564.31 crore pending in 15,795 cases (pg viii, 15). Deficiencies included lack of property information, ineffective execution of coercive measures, and a century-old unrevised interest rate on arrears. The Motor Vehicles department was found to have failed to levy minimum fines totaling ₹518.73 crore due to widespread vehicle overloading (pg ix, 90).

Non-insertion of operational deduction norms in Petroleum and Natural Gas Rules cost the government ₹136.31 crore. Water Rate assessment was also lax, leading to non-realisation of ₹50.78 crore, while losses from water transit exceeded ₹325.64 crore (pg xi). Recovery in accepted audit cases remains very low—only 4.02% of the money value accepted by departments was actually realised. The report stresses urgent need for systematic follow-up, accountability, and mechanisms to expedite revenue recovery and audit settlement.

title: Performance Audit on Activities of Atomic Energy Regulatory Board Union Government, Atomic Energy
overview:
The report examined the functioning of the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) in India, focusing on regulatory oversight of nuclear and radiation facilities between 2005-06 and 2011-12. The audit revealed that AERB lacked statutory independence, operating as a subordinate office of the Central Government without legal powers for rule-making or enforcement. The maximum fine for violations was just ₹500, regardless of the severity, and AERB had no authority to determine penalties, underlining critical gaps in India's nuclear safety framework (p. v-viii).

A major concern was the weak consenting process for radiation facilities: about 91% of medical X-ray units (estimated over 56,000 nationwide) were not registered with AERB, leaving vast populations and workers outside regulatory oversight. The Supreme Court's 2001 directive to establish Directorates of Radiation Safety in all States was implemented in only 2 out of 35 jurisdictions by July 2012. Regulatory inspections for high-risk radiography and radiotherapy units had a shortfall of 85%, while diagnostic radiology inspections lagged by over 97% annually (p. vi-vii).

Radiation protection monitoring was left to plant operators, not the regulator, and AERB did not maintain a detailed inventory of sources or enforce strict disposal controls. Emergency preparedness and decommissioning lacked clear codes and mandates, with none of India’s nuclear power plants having a decommissioning plan after 13 years of AERB issuing the relevant safety manual. The Department of Atomic Energy acknowledged these concerns but offered no concrete timelines for remediation (p. ix-x, 73).

title: Performance Audit on Environment Management in Indian Railways Union Government, Railways
overview:
The Performance Audit found major deficiencies in the environment management practices of Indian Railways (IR). The audit period covered 2006-07 to 2010-11, examining air, water, and noise pollution, as well as resource conservation and waste management. The report highlights that IR, though one of the largest carriers in the world (handling 7,651 million passengers and 922 million metric tonnes of goods per annum), has not formulated comprehensive environmental guidelines to mitigate pollution from core activities including handling of coal, iron ore, cement, and petroleum (p. v-vi).

During audit checks, only 55% of surveyed sidings had obtained the statutory Consent for Operation from State Pollution Control Boards as required under the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981. Effluent Treatment Plants were installed in just one station per zone on average, with most major stations lacking any such equipment, resulting in unsafe effluent discharge into the environment (p. vii-ix). Further, of 212 stations checked, only 7 had implemented rainwater harvesting, evidencing poor compliance with basic water conservation directives. Animal mortality along tracks remained high, with 62 elephant deaths in the audit period due to train hits, notably in the Northeast Frontier and Southern Railways (p. viii).

Waste management was similarly weak—IR generates about 3,980 MT of human waste per day, most of which is discharged directly on tracks; and test checks in 54 stations found garbage was frequently burned or dumped, violating environment norms. Despite 20 years of experimentation, IR had not frozen a suitable 'green toilet' technology, resulting in premature renewal of 47 km of rail track and avoidable expenditure of ₹35.79 crores (p. vi).

title: Performance Audit on Rail Links to Kashmir in Indian Railways Union Government, Railways
overview:
The Udhampur-Srinagar-Baramulla Rail Link (USBRL) project, sanctioned in 1994-95 at an estimated Rs 1,500 crore, was designed to provide all-weather rail connectivity to the Kashmir valley. However, weak planning and the absence of proper geo-technical investigations led to massive delays and cost overruns. By 2012, the expected outlay for the project had soared to Rs 19,565 crore, with time overruns of up to 112 months on critical sections such as Udhampur-Katra. As of July 2012, only the Qazigund-Baramulla stretch was operational, leaving the main connectivity to Kashmir incomplete.

The primary causes of the delays were poor project planning, insufficient ground surveys, and the reliance on aerial mapping rather than thorough site investigations. This led to the abandonment of completed works, termination of multiple contracts, and arbitration liabilities estimated at Rs 1,514.40 crore. The detailed project report had excluded the cost of constructing 300 km of approach roads, resulting in underestimated financial needs and insufficient cost controls.

Despite being declared a project of national importance and funded through the Consolidated Fund of India, the USBRL saw progress on the critical Katra-Banihal section reach only 12-14% by July 2012, with numerous unresolved technical and financial issues. The oversight and lack of due diligence have ultimately resulted in further financial burden to taxpayers and continued delays in achieving the main goal of Kashmir rail connectivity.

title: Performance Audit of IT Applications in Income Tax Department
overview:
The Performance Audit of IT Applications in the Income Tax Department examined the planning, implementation, and effectiveness of five major IT projects — AST, OLTAS, CPC, AIR, and TMS — designed for expanding e-governance. Around ₹2,887 crore were approved for IT applications under the ITD’s 10-year plan, of which only ₹1,291 crore (44.7%) was actually spent between 2007-08 and 2010-11. The audit identified delays in completion of key modules and poor rollout coordination, with only 62% of new functionalities achieved against planned targets, impacting taxpayer services, scrutiny, and refund efficiency.

A critical finding was that the IT ecosystem could not ensure complete and reliable data, resulting in 12.5% erroneous records detected during cross-checks, affecting assessment and arrears tracking. Inconsistencies between the IT modules, lack of information flow between Central and field offices, and common issues such as non-standardized PAN databases were highlighted. The AIR system failed to generate annual lists for targeted scrutiny, weakening revenue augmentation and compliance measures, while the CPC module suffered from failure to automate refund bank upload processes for 18.3% cases.

Such gaps in IT deployment significantly reduced the effectiveness of direct tax administration, resulting in continued manual interventions and delayed refunds. The absence of robust data validation and quality assurance, incomplete integration, and insufficient monitoring mechanisms meant targets for taxpayer coverage, arrear realization, and audit trail generation were largely missed.

title: Performance Audit of Implementation of Public Private Partnership Indira Gandhi International Airport Delhi, Ministry of Civil Aviation
overview:
The Comptroller and Auditor General’s performance audit examined the implementation of the Public Private Partnership (PPP) model at Indira Gandhi International Airport (IGIA), Delhi, covering the period from 2006 to 2011. The report highlights that while the development notably improved airport services - with the new T3 terminal completed on schedule and the airport ranked second in the world for its category - numerous contractual and financial anomalies have resulted in significant undue benefit to the private concessionaire, Delhi International Airport Limited (DIAL). For example, land valued at approximately ₹24,000 crore was made available for commercial exploitation at a lease of only ₹100 per annum, while DIAL projected possible earnings up to ₹1,63,557 crore from this land over 58 years.

The audit revealed policy gaps and post-contractual concessions, such as allowing DIAL to levy a ₹3,415.35 crore Development Fee (DF) on passengers, which was neither in the bid documents nor OMDA. Furthermore, the concession period was extended to 60 years at DIAL's sole discretion—contravening Cabinet notes and sector comparators, where such periods are typically far shorter. The lease arrangements also involved highly concessional rates unmatched by government norms.

There were delays in mandatory capital projects and unauthorized diversions of security funds, with losses to the public exchequer and repeated deviations from agreed contractual norms, all of which reveal a pattern of decisions benefiting the private operator at the Government’s cost. The audit calls for significant improvements in contract management and safeguarding the Government’s interest in future PPPs.

title: Report No. 20 of 2012-13 – Performance Audit of Production and Sale of Iron Ore by NMDC Limited, Ministry of Steel
overview:
The performance audit of NMDC Limited, covering 2005-06 to 2011-12, highlights substantial production and revenue figures. NMDC achieved a production capacity of 32 million tonnes per annum by 2011-12, earning a profit before tax of ₹10,760 crore on an income of ₹13,278 crore during the year. Despite these achievements, the annual production targets were missed in four of seven years, except 2007-08, 2010-11, and 2011-12, largely due to evacuation constraints and delays in project implementation.

Capacity expansion projects, including Kumaraswamy and Deposit 11B, expected to add 14 MTPA, continued to face delays, leading to cost overruns from ₹592 crore to ₹1,506 crore. The delay primarily resulted from slow statutory clearances and inadequate project management, with Kumaraswamy project still in progress well beyond its planned completion (originally October 2009, now scheduled for January 2013). Evacuation facilities were also insufficient, with the Bailadila sector facing bottlenecks; options to enhance capacity, such as slurry pipeline and doubled rail lines, were not vigorously pursued, further restricting production.

The audit found deficiencies in governance and price fixation. Losses of ₹1,574.11 crore were incurred due to infirmities in price fixation from 2007-11. NMDC's domestic pricing mechanisms allowed customers undue benefits and exposed the company to avoidable losses, as domestic prices lagged behind export parity. The Board failed to proactively monitor progress or provide needed guidance until late, with only limited follow-up on critical issues such as project expansion and evacuation capacity. These shortcomings underline the need for strengthened project management and a transparent price fixation mechanism.

title: Performance Audit on Medical Establishments in Defence Services, Department of Defence
overview:
The Performance Audit reviewed the functioning of the Armed Forces Medical Services (AFMS) from 2006-07 to 2010-11, focusing on budget utilisation, manpower deployment, equipment, drug procurement, and the Ex-Servicemen Contributory Health Scheme (ECHS). The report found that allocations for local purchase of drugs increased significantly, by 135% from ₹157.73 crore to ₹371.34 crore, far outpacing the increase for central purchase (11%). This trend resulted in an increased share of local purchases (56% in 2010-11, up from 38% in 2006-07), raising concerns over cost and quality control (Page iv-v).

There was a documented overall shortage of 12% Medical Officers in hospitals, with critical shortfalls at field and zonal levels (up to 36% at Field Hospitals). Specialist cadre faced a 14% deficiency and high attrition, particularly in disciplines already understaffed, directly impacting patient care. Shortages also extended to nursing and paramedical staff in several major hospitals, where deficits ranged from 3% to 39% (Page v-vi).

Equipment and stores management remains a major challenge—by December 2010, at least 22,108 electro-medical equipment were deficient, and overstocking of drugs was rampant, with stocks of some medicines sufficient for 6-109 years. The report also flagged major non-compliance with the Bio-Medical Waste Rules (87% of Army and 61% of Air Force establishments lacked valid authorization as of March 2011), and severe infrastructure and manpower deficiencies in the ECHS, where only 15% of required polyclinics at non-military stations were appropriately established (Page viii-xi).

title: Performance Audit of Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission, Ministry of Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation
overview:
The Performance Audit of Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission (JNNURM) revealed substantial under-utilisation of funds, administrative delays, and incomplete projects. Out of Rs 37,243 crore committed by Government of India (GoI) under the Mission, only Rs 17,940 crore (48 per cent) were released and disbursed (Page 12). Of 1,536 projects sanctioned under JNNURM, only 353 had been completed by the end of audit period (Page 14), indicating severe delays in implementation and achievement of objectives.

Audit found that almost 40 per cent of projects suffered from major time overruns, with cost escalations amounting to Rs 2,386 crore, often due to lack of proper project planning and execution (Page 23). Further, the Mission failed to ensure sustainable urban development, as only 22 per cent of cities achieved the mandatory reforms stipulated under the programme (Page 36). This impacted the programme’s long-term effectiveness, resulting in continued deficiencies in urban infrastructure and basic service delivery.

The consequences of these lapses were manifold, including persistent issues of urban poverty, slum proliferation and inadequate access to sanitation and housing. The audit recommends strengthened project monitoring, prudent financial management and greater accountability on the part of state and city authorities.

title: Performance Audit of Operational Performance of Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Limited, Ministry of Commerce and Industry
overview:
This performance audit focused on the operational effectiveness of the Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Limited (ECGC) for the period April 2008 to March 2011, particularly reviewing underwriting practices, risk mitigation, and claim settlements.

Key findings reveal significant shortcomings: While ECGC generated a profit of ₹665.78 crore under Whole Turnover Packing Credit (WTPC) covers, it suffered a loss of ₹191.72 crore under Whole Turnover Post Shipment (WTPS) covers. Between 2008-09 and 2010-11, for 13 out of 29 banks, the Claims Premium Ratio under WTPS exceeded 200%, resulting in losses amounting to ₹309.27 crore. Audit also found that claims totaling ₹316.13 crore were paid despite banks submitting outdated or unsatisfactory buyer verification reports. Recoveries declined sharply from ₹151.29 crore in 2008-09 to ₹110.65 crore in 2010-11, and pending recoveries rose from ₹2,170 crore to ₹2,628 crore over the same period.

The system of appraising buyers and fixing overall limits was found flawed, with claims of ₹158.40 crore paid despite incomplete or poor information. Moreover, ECGC's reinsurance for medium and long-term exposures was insufficient—the company bore major losses including a single likely net claim of ₹1,047 crore related to Zoom Developers Limited. The overall recovery rate for short-term policies ranged from just 4.13% to 5.58% during this period. The findings indicate serious gaps in underwriting discipline, risk appraisal, claims management, and financial oversight, raising concerns about the company's financial sustainability.

title: Performance Audit on Hydrocarbon Exploration Efforts of Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas
overview:
The Performance Audit reviewed ONGC's hydrocarbon exploration efforts between 2007-08 and 2010-11, focusing on the effectiveness, planning, and execution relative to set targets and national goals. It was found that ONGC acquired 89 prospective blocks under the New Exploration Licensing Policy (NELP) but made only 11 discoveries in 8 blocks during the period, reflecting substantial underperformance.

In terms of physical progress, the company failed to complete its committed work in 25 blocks and drilled only 30 out of 90 committed wells within specified periods. Particularly concerning is that in 74% of highly prospective blocks acquired in NELP rounds I to V, work commitments were not met. Despite making 99 discoveries (in both NELP and Nomination blocks), only 80.93 MMToe of reserves were added, and just 73 out of 158 discoveries were monetized (with offshore fields underserving, as only 2 out of 56 offshore discoveries were monetized).

These failures have direct fiscal and productivity consequences for ONGC and the nation's hydrocarbon self-sufficiency. The company’s exploration cost indicators were concerning, with reserve accretion through exploratory, wildcat, and appraisal wells ranging only from 13% to 38% of MOU targets, and the cost per barrel of oil equivalent was understated by up to US$ 21.71. ONGC's headline Reserve Replacement Ratio (RRR) above 1 was achieved largely through reinterpretation and development drilling, not new discoveries, raising concerns over sustainability of reserves, missed targets, and financial inefficiency.

title: Performance Audit of Allocation of Coal Blocks and Augmentation of Coal Production, Ministry of Coal
overview:
The Performance Audit of Allocation of Coal Blocks highlights significant lapses by the Ministry of Coal in the evaluation and allocation of 194 coal blocks between 2004 and 2011. These allocations, with extractable reserves of approximately 44.80 billion tonnes, were distributed to government and private companies for captive mining but suffered from lack of transparency and standardised procedures. The Ministry failed to establish a fair, transparent, and objective system, resulting in alleged windfall gains of ₹1.86 lakh crore to private allottees, as computed based on average open market prices.

The report documents that out of 194 coal blocks allocated, only 28 commenced production by March 2011, indicating an implementation rate of just 14%. Consequently, targeted augmentation of domestic coal production was not achieved, leading to continued reliance on costly coal imports. Furthermore, the selection process for allocation did not include competitive bidding, and several blocks were awarded despite the absence of firm milestones or track records for the selected companies, further compounding delays in coal development and revenue loss.

These shortcomings have resulted in a significant loss of potential revenue to the government exchequer, long delays in coal production commencement, and missed opportunities for the power, steel, and cement sectors. The absence of a transparent screening mechanism also raised the risk of non-meritorious allocation, ultimately impacting public resources and critical sectoral growth.

title: Performance Audit of Ultra Mega Power Projects under Special Purpose Vehicles, Ministry of Power
overview:
The Performance Audit scrutinised the effectiveness and transparency in the award of Ultra Mega Power Projects (UMPPs) through Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs), covering four awarded projects: Sasan (Madhya Pradesh), Mundra (Gujarat), Krishnapatnam (Andhra Pradesh), and Tilaiya (Jharkhand). The audit found that contracts worth ₹1,67,784 crore (Mundra), ₹87,749 crore (Sasan), ₹1,71,169 crore (Krishnapatnam), and ₹1,29,862 crore (Tilaiya) were awarded based on tariffs ranging from ₹1.196 to ₹2.333 per unit. Several irregularities affected the transparency and competitiveness of the process.

The report highlighted that consultancy assignments were awarded to M/s Ernst & Young at higher prices even when M/s ICRA was technically qualified, violating General Financial Rules. The audit also found that bid documents were not vetted by the Department of Legal Affairs, and dilution of equity lock-in requirements, lower normative availability, and net worth requirements potentially increased operational and financial risks for UMPPs.

Major consequences included excess acquisition of land (1538 acres in Mundra and 1096 acres in Krishnapatnam), post-bid concessions regarding coal block allocation, and a financial benefit estimated at ₹29,033 crore (NPV ₹11,852 crore) to Reliance Power Limited (RPL) due to the diversion of surplus coal—actions that collectively vitiated the fairness and sanctity of the bidding process, raising serious concerns about future UMPP procurements.

title: Performance Audit of Integrated Child Development Services ICDS Scheme of Union Government, Ministry of Women and Child Development
overview:
The audit covering 22 States/UTs found significant deficiencies in the implementation of the ICDS Scheme with large-scale shortfall in the achievement of objectives, delivery of services, and utilisation of grant-in-aid. Out of the total allocation of Rs 35,221 crore during 2005-11, only Rs 16,330 crore was released and actual expenditure was far less, with utilisation ranging between 44 and 50 percent in many years placing the effectiveness of fund flow in question (p. xii).

There was a shortfall of 37 to 60 percent in the coverage of children under the Supplementary Nutrition Programme, and records showed inflated beneficiary numbers in several states. Direct observations found cases where nutrition was not provided regularly, and cross-checks revealed food quality defects, unsafe storage, and absence of mid-day meals on the audit day in 31 percent of visited anganwadi centres (AWCs).

Thirdly, monitoring was grossly inadequate with major gaps in reporting, supervision, and capacity building. Delays and lapses led to non-disbursement of take-home rations valued at Rs 211 crore. Persistent shortfalls in critical infrastructure, such as drinking water and toilets in more than 40 percent of AWCs, further undermined the scheme goals, severely impacting child health outcomes and nutritional status.

title: Union Government (Civil) Autonomous Bodies-Performance Audit
overview:
The Performance Audit, covering 188 Central Autonomous Bodies (CABs), highlighted significant mismanagement of grants, persistent accumulation of unspent funds, and chronic delays in the submission of accounts. During the audit period, the total grants released to these CABs amounted to Rs 11,404 crore; however, the cumulative unutilised balance at the end of March 2011 was Rs 4,139 crore, representing nearly 36% of funds disbursed.

Key findings disclosed that 62 CABs delayed the submission of accounts for periods ranging from one to 17 years, impeding timely parliamentary review and financial control. Furthermore, instances of diversion of government grants, irregular parking of funds in private banks, and non-adherence to prescribed financial norms were identified. For example, Rs 266.86 crore was irregularly parked in interest-bearing deposits, contrary to Rules.

These deficiencies have led to a substantial risk of misuse and lack of transparency in public fund management, adversely affecting the intended delivery of services and undermining financial accountability within autonomous bodies.

title: Performance Audit of Jalayagnam in Andhra Pradesh
overview: Andhra Pradesh launched the Jalayagnam programme in 2004 to bring 97.46 lakh acres under irrigation and stabilize 22.53 lakh acres, aiming to utilize 65.14 TMC of water for drinking purposes for 2.11 crore people and generate 2700 MW of power, with an estimated cost of ₹1.86 lakh crore covering 86 projects. Of the 74 irrigation projects sanctioned, 26 projects (representing 35% of projects and 85% of total capital outlay) worth ₹1.43 lakh crore were selected for audit scrutiny, but significant gaps were found in planning, water availability assessment, and project execution. There was evidence of premature commencement and lack of comprehensive feasibility studies; for example, major projects on river Krishna were undertaken without proper evaluation of flood water availability or Central Water Commission (CWC) clearance, risking large investments of ₹23,093 crore. As of 2004-05, only 125.65 lakh acres were irrigated out of a cultivable area of 362.90 lakh acres, and the State was utilizing just 70% (1933 TMC) of dependable river flows—underutilization especially acute for Godavari, where only 720 TMC out of 1480 TMC was tapped. These issues led to likely overlap and unsynchronized project activities, creating high risk of unachieved targets and inefficient public expenditure. The audit concludes execution was not sequenced, water availability was overstated, and large-scale projects were started without state and central clearances, posing significant financial and developmental consequences.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on National Rural Health Mission of Government of Uttar Pradesh
overview:
The National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) in Uttar Pradesh was launched to improve access, availability, and quality of rural health services. During the audit period, total fund utilisation fluctuated sharply, with only 44 to 50% of allotted funds being used between 2005 and 2011. As per the audit, the state received ₹5,772 crore under NRHM but only ₹2,865 crore was reported actually utilised (Page 12: "Against the available funds of ₹5772.31 crore, only ₹2865.67 crore was utilised.").

Critical human resource shortages were observed. For instance, vacant posts ranged between 48 and 65 percent for ANMs, doctors, and specialists; only 4606 staff nurses were working against 4948 sanctioned posts, despite a total requirement of 83,273 (Page 69: "The vacant posts ranged between 48 and 65 per cent as compared to those required to be at par with IPHS norms."). Further, targets for maternal health interventions like Janani Suraksha Yojana saw a persistent miss: only 38% of institutional deliveries achieved versus a 70% target in 2010-11—an overall 69% shortfall across years (Page 137: "Percentage shortfall in institutional deliveries in comparison to target of 70 per cent ... 38").

This audit highlights systemic weaknesses in planning, monitoring, and fund management. Shortfalls in staff deployment, underutilisation of funds, and gaps in critical health outcome targets point to high risk of continued poor maternal and child health outcomes. The consequences include sustained high maternal and infant mortality rates and delayed achievement of health access and quality benchmarks statewide.

title: Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Uttar Pradesh
overview:
The Performance Audit reviewed the implementation of Government civil works in Uttar Pradesh for the period 2005-10. Total budgetary allocation during the audit period was Rs 21,734 crore, of which Rs 10,895 crore (50 per cent) was actually utilised for completion of projects. The report recorded major delays in execution, with only 44 per cent of works completed within timelines, and highlighted the presence of unutilised funds across multiple departments.

Significant discrepancies arose due to lax monitoring of works, resulting in non-disbursement of Rs 3,687 crore earmarked for specific infrastructure initiatives. In 2,157 out of 4,955 projects reviewed, expenditure was incurred without proper technical sanction, resulting in incomplete or substandard works.

These lapses resulted in delayed benefits to intended communities, inflated project costs, and avoidable financial losses amounting to Rs 623 crore. The audit concluded that systemic weaknesses in fund flow, irregularities in procurement, and inadequate oversight were pervasive.

title: Performance Audit on Compliance with Environmental Laws in Lucknow, Government of Uttar Pradesh
overview:
This performance audit of compliance with environmental laws by the Lucknow Municipal Corporation (LMC) and other notified authorities in Lucknow identifies significant shortcomings in the implementation of key environmental regulations. The audit period was 2005–06 to 2009–10, focusing on municipal solid waste, water quality, air pollution, biomedical and hazardous waste management. Audit scrutiny revealed that during 2005–10, of the Rs 48.51 crore allotted for solid waste management, only Rs 22.41 crore (46%) was utilised, leaving Rs 26.10 crore unspent (p. 7).

The LMC failed to set up a proper landfill, composting unit, or a system for segregation and transportation of waste as mandated under the Municipal Solid Waste (Management & Handling) Rules, 2000. Less than 35% of the daily solid waste generated was being scientifically processed, and door-to-door garbage collection covered only select wards, as noted on p. 11. Monitoring of air and water quality remained sporadic due to equipment shortages and lack of trained manpower, resulting in failure to meet health and environmental benchmarks.

The lack of coordination between municipal agencies, state pollution control boards, and hospitals resulted in improper bio-medical and hazardous waste disposal. The audit saw repeated instances of contaminated surface and ground water and excessive air pollution levels in high-traffic zones. The consequences of these failings include continued risk to public health and violations of key statutory requirements. The audit recommends urgent systemic and administrative interventions to address these critical lapses.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Commercial of Government of West Bengal
overview:
This report examines the performance of State Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) in West Bengal for the year ended March 2011. As of 31 March 2011, there were 72 working PSUs with a turnover of Rs 23,319.08 crore, representing 5.07% of the State GDP. The total state investment in PSUs stood at Rs 39,535.42 crore, with power and finance sectors accounting for nearly 81% of it. However, 40 of 72 PSUs incurred total losses of Rs 812.38 crore during the year, outweighing profits of Rs 550.58 crore from only 30 PSUs; major losses were concentrated in transport and power entities.

Serious deficiencies were noted in financial management, operational efficiency, and quality of accounts. For example, only 31 of 72 PSUs finalized accounts up to 2010-11 by September 2011; the remainder had arrears of one to seven years, severely affecting transparency and the ability to track performance. Notably, energy losses in West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Limited amounted to 3,396 MUs valued at Rs 1,311.47 crore, exceeding regulatory norms, while delays and extra expenditure in rural electrification schemes cost Rs 102.08 crore and lost administrative charges of Rs 66.08 crore.

Overall, the audit finds "tremendous scope to improve the functioning and enhance profits" of the PSUs. Lapses in project planning, monitoring, revenue collection, and financial internal controls continue to result in significant avoidable losses, underutilization of public investment, and a lack of accountability in sectors critical to the state's economic development.

title: Report of 2011 - Compliance and Performance Audit on Civil of Government of West Bengal
overview:
The 2011 CAG report for West Bengal covers performance and compliance audits across major civil departments. In a district-centric audit of Dakshin Dinajpur, significant underspending and implementation deficiencies were identified across Health & Family Welfare, School Education, Development & Planning, Women & Child Development and Social Welfare, Panchayat & Rural Development, Public Health Engineering, Irrigation & Waterways, Power, and Urban Development departments. For example, utilisation of irrigation potential in government-operated Minor Irrigation schemes ranged only between 29% and 37% during 2006-10, primarily due to defunct schemes and insufficient maintenance, leading to poor returns on investment of public funds.

There were also instances where Rs 9.50 crore in water usage fees remained unrealized, and over 11,990 new schemes (command area 1.08 lakh hectares) were handed to unregistered committees with no effective maintenance or monitoring, risking further wastage of state resources. Persistent general irregularities were also found in cash management by drawing and disbursing officers, impacting programme delivery.

Consequences included long-term inefficiency in developmental work, substantial scope for misappropriation, and erosion of public trust. The report underscores that fund utilization in crucial sectors often hovered at 44-50%, leading to sizable gaps between targets and achievements—indicating a critical need for financial management reform and process redesign in major West Bengal civil programmes.

title: Performance Audit on Commercial of Government of Tamilnadu
overview:
This Performance Audit reviews the effectiveness of the commercial operations and development activities of various State Public Sector Undertakings, including the State Industries Promotion Corporation of Tamil Nadu Limited (SIPCOT) and Tamil Nadu Generation and Distribution Corporation Limited, for the period up to 2010-11. The audit found that SIPCOT did not have a long-term strategic or annual action plan for developing and operating Industrial Centres, resulting in only 0 to 36 percent sale of plots in five of the eight SEZs formed since 2006-07. Major financial inefficiencies were observed, such as a continuous decline in revenue from core industrial development activities (from 67% to 24%) and significant uncollected potential revenue: 2,124 acres of unutilised land with 195 entrepreneurs was not repossessed, leading to a revenue loss of ₹421.56 crore.

The audit also flagged a lack of robust systems for cost fixation of plots, failure to charge commercial rates to non-industrial allottees, and weak internal controls. Further, there was avoidable unproductive expenditure amounting to ₹7.89 crore and excessive incentives released due to inadequate verification of investment claims, totalling ₹297.75 crore in two notable cases. In the power sector, the gap between income and expenditure increased sharply, from ₹1,218.94 crore in 2006-07 to ₹12,950.56 crore in 2010-11, mainly from slow T&D loss reduction, under-billing, and unclaimed subsidies.

Consequences of these systemic issues included missed opportunities for industrial growth, ongoing financial losses, and heightened liabilities due to delayed land compensation. The report highlights that unless strategic planning, effective costing, and stronger monitoring are implemented, revenue losses will continue, undermining the commercial and developmental objectives of the state undertakings.

title: Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Tamilnadu
overview:
The Performance Audit Report No. 2 of 2011 covers several critical functions in the Civil Administration of Tamil Nadu, including the Co-operation, Food and Consumer Protection Department, Municipal Administration and Water Supply Department, and other selected entities. The report highlights total plan and non-plan expenditures, with the Grand Total increasing from ₹1,46,170 crore in 2008-09 to ₹1,95,890 crore in 2010-11 (Table 1, p.5).

Key findings included non-remittance of unspent funds by 22 District Collectors, excess allotment of rice in PDS, subsidy overpayments to co-operative societies, and delayed computerisation projects. The audit notes an excess payment of ₹0.99 crore in the Public Works Department, wasteful expenditure of ₹8.35 crore on Jatropha seedlings, and unfruitful outlay of ₹2.07 crore in Animal Husbandry, Dairy and Fisheries Department. Data validation gaps, incomplete systems, and underutilisation of expenditure targets across departments point to systemic inefficiencies and loss of intended public value (pp.31-41).

Additionally, infrastructure projects such as the Chennai seawater desalination plant show financial burden due to advance release of funds and lack of cost recovery measures. Lack of monitoring, incomplete record verification, and long-pending disposal of seized vehicles further contributed to irregularities. The overall severity is high, given substantial fund management lapses, inefficiencies, and target misses impacting service delivery.

title: Report No. 6 of 2011 - Performance Audit on Revenue Receipts of Government of Rajasthan
overview:
This Performance Audit examines the levy and collection of stamp duty and registration fees in Rajasthan for FY 2006-07 to 2010-11. During this period, stamp duty accounted for an average of 9.96% of Rajasthan's total tax revenue, growing from ₹1,293.68 crore in 2006-07 to ₹1,941.07 crore in 2010-11. Despite this, the audit found significant scope for increased collection, particularly on conveyance, developer agreements, mortgages, and transactions processed through public offices.

Audit scrutiny revealed irregularities totaling ₹9.04 crore, including undervaluation of properties, misclassification of instruments, and incorrect application of rates. Additionally, public offices failed to recover proper stamp duty and registration fees resulting in a further revenue loss of ₹20.74 crore. The report highlighted excess stock of stamps in treasuries, a backlog of adjudication cases, and systemic failures in enforcing rules and conducting effective internal audits.

The report concludes that weak internal controls, inadequate oversight of sub-registrar offices, and systemic misapplication of outdated notifications contributed to substantial revenue leakage. Recommendations focus on strengthening compliance, audit mechanisms, and clarifying legislative provisions to improve future collections and reduce arrears.

title: Report of 2011 - Compliance and Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Rajasthan
overview:
This performance audit report covers significant deficiencies and achievements in multiple civil departments of the Government of Rajasthan for the year ending 31 March 2011. Major areas examined include the National Horticulture Mission Programme, Drinking Water Supply Projects, Social Justice and Empowerment schemes, working of Rajasthan University of Health Sciences, and the utilisation of Twelfth Finance Commission Grants for maintenance of roads and bridges.

Audit observed substantial delays and cost overruns in water supply projects, with several schemes remaining incomplete well past rescheduled dates, resulting in denial of intended benefits to the population despite incurring heavy expenditure. The National Horticulture Mission was implemented in the absence of baseline surveys and perspective plans, leading to shortfall in both physical and financial targets for a variety of horticulture initiatives, hindering the holistic growth of the sector.

Critical issues reported included non-compliance with financial rules, irregular and avoidable expenditures amounting to over ₹20 crore, improper financial management with non-utilisation and blocking of funds, and widespread evidence of deficient monitoring and weak internal controls. Oversight failures led to irregular payments, unproductive expenditure, and lack of accountability as exemplified by funds remaining unutilised for social empowerment schemes and non-completion of capital works. These undermine financial discipline and efficient public service delivery.
