title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Tripura
overview:
The Performance Audit on Civil of the Government of Tripura assessed the effectiveness of fund allocation, project execution, and outcomes in key social and infrastructural schemes between 2005-06 to 2009-10. The report highlights substantial discrepancies in fund utilisation, with only ₹462.54 crore out of ₹1,016 crore released being spent, underscoring a critical gap of nearly 54.47% (Page 9). The audit also identifies major delays in implementation of public works, with 36% of projects sanctioned remaining incomplete at the time of review.

Further, it was observed that the monitoring and reporting mechanisms failed to ensure timely submission of Utilisation Certificates, resulting in a backlog of ₹108 crore for the period under review. Irregularities in procurement procedures, such as award of contracts without competitive bidding amounting to ₹22.65 crore (Page 16), raised concerns regarding transparency and accountability.

The consequences of these gaps include stagnation of intended developmental outcomes, continued deprivation of target beneficiaries, and the risk of financial misappropriation. The audit strongly recommends structural reforms in project planning, fund tracking, and procurement to enhance efficiency and coverage.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Pondicherry
overview:
This Performance Audit examines the processes and outcomes related to the acquisition and utilisation of land for public purposes by the Revenue and Disaster Management Department of the Union Territory of Puducherry. Covering transactions between 2006 and 2011, the audit found that out of ₹326.59 crore drawn for land acquisition, only ₹207.80 crore was disbursed, with a significant unspent balance of ₹118.79 crore kept in bank savings accounts, contrary to financial rules (page 14).

The audit highlighted a large backlog in utilisation, as 92% of the acquired land, including land acquired under emergency provisions, remained unutilised for periods between four and nine years (page 11). Notably, 336 hectares acquired at a cost of ₹73.39 crore for a Special Economic Zone were left unused for over four years, and ₹10.10 crore worth of land for Scheduled Caste housing went unallotted due to delays in beneficiary identification (page 11).

This led to blocked funds, administrative inefficiencies, and intends to signal risks of poor planning and policy execution. The audit also called attention to issues of non-maintenance of cash books and lack of effective monitoring, impairing accountability and transparency. Delayed or no action on previous recommendations remains a concern (page 9).

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Public Distribution System of Government of Nagaland
overview:
The Performance Audit on the Public Distribution System (PDS) in Nagaland for the period 2005-06 to 2009-10 revealed systemic deficiencies in allocation, distribution, and monitoring, resulting in significant shortfall and diversion of foodgrains. Against the allocation of 1,99,800 MT of rice, only 1,61,125 MT were distributed to beneficiaries, with the shortfall of 38,675 MT valued at Rs 68.26 crore not accounted for or explained (p. v, Executive Summary).

The audit found persistent lapses in transparent identification and issue of ration cards, with discrepancies between official figures and actual lists at FPS level, leading to denial of entitlements. Additionally, huge backlog in delivery was observed: "Test check disclosed that 23.08% of the population was not covered under PDS," with APL and BPL beneficiaries reporting irregular receipt (p. 17, Table 2.3 and narrative).

Leakages and misuse of funds further exacerbated food insecurity in the State. Audit noticed that financial irregularities of Rs 23.46 crore relating to freight, handling, and margins were not supported by documentary evidence. Consequences included reduced trust in government schemes and rising food insecurity among the targeted population (pp. vi-vii, Executive Summary).

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Agriculture Department of Government of Odisha
overview:
The audit reviewed the activities of the Agriculture Wing of the Government of Odisha from 2006-2011, covering an expenditure of ₹1974.49 crore (budget route) and ₹99.92 crore (off budget) on agriculture. It found strategic deficiencies: a long-term perspective plan was not prepared even three years after the State Agriculture Policy (SAP) of 2008, despite explicit instructions by state leadership. Annual plans were prepared at the Directorate without a bottom-up approach, failing to consult or integrate the district plans, and the State missed opportunities for synergy between centrally sponsored and state schemes, resulting in overlapping and duplication of efforts, notably ₹141.2 crore spent on the same machinery under different schemes.

Physical achievements lagged: Of the 30.36 lakh hectare irrigation potential, only 20.85 lakh hectares (69%) was actually under cultivation. The Seed Replacement Rate for paddy reached only 20.64% against a target of 25%, while non-paddy crops remained below 5%. Large scale vacancies of Village Agriculture Workers (44%) and Assistant Agriculture Officers (46%) hampered extension services when timely outreach was critical.

Budgetary focus did not align to critical needs: Marketing and crop insurance faced severe shortfalls in allocation (81% and 85% below plan projection respectively), while agricultural productivity for key crops such as rice, pulses, and oilseeds persistently trailed national averages. Systemic issues included inadequate monitoring, non-functioning soil labs, delay in infrastructure projects, and weak internal controls, raising concern on departmental capacity to meet its mandate.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Nagaland
overview:
The performance audit on the Civil Departments highlights persistent shortcomings in the implementation of development schemes by the Department of Under Developed Area (DUDA). Despite allocation of substantial funds by the Government of India, the Department reported an absorption capacity between 44-50% with Rs 344 crore out of Rs 776 crore released during 2006-11 actually utilised. This revealed large unspent balances impacting scheme rollout and service delivery.

The audit found irregularities in fund disbursement, with delays in Central fund release to State agencies and instances of payments without execution of works. Rs 3.73 crore was suspected to have been misappropriated in the Public Works Department (Roads and Bridges) South Division by recording inflated cash book entries against cheque disbursements. Additional fraudulent and improper withdrawals totalling Rs 18 crore by the Director General of Police (DGP), and about Rs 18 lakh in salary and arrear bills were also identified across three education department offices.

These findings reveal institutional weaknesses in financial control, monitoring, and evaluation across multiple civil departments, resulting in poor achievement of programme objectives, wastage of public funds, and lack of accountability for targets under critical development schemes. The summary recommends urgent reforms in planning, financial management, and project oversight to restore credibility and effectiveness in civil administration. (Ref: Executive Summary & Ch II, pp.8, 12, 23, 24)

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Revenue of Government of Odisha
overview:
This report covers major revenue receipts of the Government of Odisha for the year ended 31 March 2011, audited under Section 16 of the CAG Act. The audit examined receipts from VAT, CST, entry tax, motor vehicles tax, land revenue, stamp duty and registration fee, excise, forest, mining, and other departmental revenues. During 2010-11, the State's total revenue receipts were ₹33,276.15 crore, with 48% from State taxes and non-tax revenue (₹15,973.04 crore), and 52% from the Government of India (₹17,303.11 crore).

The report identifies 45 paragraphs and three performance audits relating to non/short levy or loss of revenue, totaling ₹1,032.61 crore. Outstanding audit observations amounted to ₹6,258.05 crore across 3,267 inspection reports. Test checking during 2010-11 and one case in 2011-12 revealed underassessment, short levy, and loss of revenue totaling ₹2,138.56 crore in 1,83,397 cases. Departments accepted deficiencies worth ₹1,635.29 crore in 33,615 cases and recovered ₹31 crore in 2,986 cases within the period.

The audit highlights serious issues in internal control, cross-verification of declaration forms, and computerisation in Motor Vehicles Department. It notes persistent non-compliance with audit observations, inadequacy in follow-up procedures, and delayed corrective actions, resulting in continued revenue loss and unrecovered demands.

title: Report of 2011 - Compliance and Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Odisha
overview:
This CAG report highlights extensive deficiencies in the acquisition and allotment of land, modernisation of police forces, implementation of JNNURM initiatives, and construction of roads and bridges in Odisha. During 2005-10, area under cultivation was reduced by 1.17 lakh hectares, with land diverted for non-agricultural use rising by 2.99 lakh hectares. The Revenue and Disaster Management Department provided 50,276.887 acres (including 33,355.127 acres of acquired private land) to 107 promoters or companies in 16 districts, often misusing emergency provisions and irregularly fixing market values, leading to `224.29 crore under-assessment of compensation in 35 land acquisition cases.

Performance audit of the Modernisation of Police Force scheme indicated that 55% of allocations were spent on buildings while only 11.5% went to operational components like communication and forensic science, crucial for combating rising left-wing extremism. Sophisticated weapons worth `14.80 crore remained unused, with shortages up to 61% in eight districts due to lack of trained personnel. Much infrastructure remained unutilised, and inflated utilization certificates of `90.06 crore were furnished to the GoI despite funds lying unused.

The JNNURM audit found poor spending efficiency, management deficiencies, unauthorised fund diversion, and delayed reforms. Only `613.78 crore (45%) out of `1,365.91 crore sanctioned project costs was utilised. Multiple departments failed to respond to audit queries, and outstanding audit paragraphs remain high. Overall, critical systems failures resulted in significant financial losses, poor governance, and service delivery setbacks. (Pages vii-xiii)

title: Report of 2011 - Financial and Performance Audit on Civil, Commercial and Revenue of Government of Mizoram
overview:
This Report covers 16 Audit Paragraphs, three Performance Reviews and one Chief Controlling Officer based Audit for the Government of Mizoram, examining financial and performance aspects in Civil, Commercial, and Revenue sectors. During 2010-11, the audit uncovered significant misappropriations, excess payments, doubtful expenditures, and ineffective program implementation. For example, failure by the Health & Family Welfare and School Education Departments in exercising routine checks resulted in an excess drawal of ₹9.91 lakh (pg viii).

Substantial irregular fund diversion was noted: funds totalling ₹14.95 crore (29% to 79% of available funds) meant for Out of School Children interventions were diverted to payment of honorarium to Education Volunteers between 2006-11. Poor planning and monitoring led to schools being overstaffed, with 2,883 excess teachers in primary and 4,625 in upper primary schools, and considerable funds parked in PW Deposits due to the department's incapacity to absorb released funds (pg vii-x).

Projects suffered from delays, quality issues and financial improprieties. Instances include unauthorised disbursement of ₹104.18 lakh to individuals not entitled, non-utilisation of cold storage facilities after ₹4.13 crore expenditure, and payment of huge compensation for land acquisition without proper award pronouncements. Additionally, operational efficiency issues in Public Health Engineering and Power Distribution resulted in excess losses of ₹13.80 crore and avoidable expenditure of ₹2.37 crore (pg vii-xiv).

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Revenue of Government of Meghalaya
overview:
The Performance Audit on Revenue of the Government of Meghalaya reviewed the assessment, collection, and remittance of major tax and non-tax revenues during 2005-2010. Total revenue receipts during the five-year period amounted to Rs 5,012.83 crore. However, audit scrutiny revealed persistent shortfall in collection targets across major revenue heads, with 54% of assessed dealers having no returns filed in two out of five years, resulting in a revenue leakage of Rs 112.65 crore (Page 2: Executive Summary).

The audit observed that in the mining sector, non/short-levy of royalty and cess on coal due to non-monitoring amounted to Rs 40.82 crore forgone. The Excise Department suffered from weak enforcement and incomplete reviews, leading to Rs 15.60 crore unrecovered from licensees. Registration of vehicles was marred by undervaluation, with at least 4,217 cases of under-assessment (Page 3: Executive Summary).

The consequence is serious revenue loss for the State, undermining its fiscal position and affecting public welfare delivery. The lack of effective monitoring in tax departments, together with manual systems and poor coordination among revenue departments, has enabled both willful evasion and administrative lapses on a significant scale.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on West Garo Hill District of Government of Meghalaya
overview:
This performance audit examined the functioning of major development programmes and the delivery of core services in West Garo Hills District, Meghalaya. The audit reviewed records pertaining to various flagship schemes including Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, National Rural Health Mission, and Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, across the audited years. The audit identified substantial under-utilisation of government funds, with utilisation ranging from only 44% to 50% for key development schemes during the period 2007-11 (p.12). For instance, out of total available funds of Rs 197.86 crore, only Rs 96.93 crore was utilised in the district for rural employment and health initiatives by the end of 2010-11.

Audit scrutiny revealed numerous deficiencies in service delivery, fund management, and project implementation, such as delayed release and diversion of funds, creation of unfruitful assets, and persistent vacancies in critical posts affecting health and education service delivery. The audit further revealed that the district failed to meet more than 30% of crucial targets across programmes, including rural infrastructure and maternal healthcare (p. 20-25). Instances of poor monitoring, irregularities in beneficiary selection, and the lack of concurrent social audits contributed to systemic weaknesses and outcome shortfalls.

The consequences of these deficiencies included compromised service delivery to intended beneficiaries, poor developmental outcomes in basic education, health, and rural employment, and significant risk of misappropriation due to weak internal controls. The audit concludes that urgent corrective measures are required to strengthen planning, execution, and monitoring to ensure optimal use of public funds and realization of intended impacts, particularly for vulnerable populations in West Garo Hills.

title: Report of 2011 - Financial and Performance Audit on Civil and Commercial of Government of Meghalaya
overview:
The Financial and Performance Audit of the Civil and Commercial departments of Meghalaya for the audit period revealed significant shortcomings in fund management and project execution. Of the Rs 920.17 crore available for utilisation by the various departments, only Rs 402.99 crore were actually utilised, resulting in underutilisation of allocated resources by over 56 percent. (Page 12)

Several departments, notably Public Works and Power, failed to achieve targeted outcomes, with delays and cost overruns observed in 23 out of 30 major projects audited. These lapses resulted in an estimated Rs 112.45 crore of excess expenditure and Rs 47.32 crore in unnecessary delays. The audit also detected inconsistencies in procurement and contract management leading to financial losses and suboptimal public service delivery. (Page 22)

The consequences of these management issues have led to incomplete infrastructure development, negative impact on the state’s economic growth, and aggravated public dissatisfaction. Persistent weaknesses in internal controls have increased the risk of fraud and misappropriation, raising concerns about accountability and governance in Meghalaya's civil and commercial sectors.

title: Report of 2011 – Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Maharashtra
overview:
This performance audit focused on critical housing, environmental, and infrastructure schemes in Maharashtra, with a particular focus on Slum Rehabilitation Schemes in Mumbai. As outlined, despite the establishment of the Slum Rehabilitation Authority (SRA) in 1995, only 1.27 lakh slum dwellings were rehabilitated against a target of 8.05 lakh over 15 years, reflecting a 16% achievement rate. Notably, only 9,547 beneficiaries had received photo identity cards as of September 2011.

The report also documented significant financial lapses, including short recovery of ₹133.54 crore in infrastructure charges and the non-recovery of ₹1,120 crore from Mumbai International Airport Limited (MIAL) for the construction of 28,000 tenements. Excess Transferable Development Rights (TDR) of ₹187.17 crore and excess land TDR worth ₹48.66 crore were further granted to developers in connection with the airport rehabilitation, indicating poor controls and irregular benefit to private parties.

Systemic weaknesses were also found in planning (no survey/data bank on slums; incomplete/invalid beneficiary lists), execution (projects awarded without tenders, major schemes stalled for years), and fund management (₹78.89 crore infrastructure charges lying idle with SRA). The report concludes that 15 years after scheme inception, the objectives remain largely unfulfilled, with significant risks to integrity, transparency, and value-for-money for the state.

title: Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Uttarakhand
overview:
The Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Uttarakhand reviewed multiple infrastructure projects and utilisation of allocated funds. A total of ₹342.50 crore was released, but only ₹186.74 crore (54.5%) was actually utilised during the audit period, leading to substantial unspent balances and augmentation failures (p.7).

The audit highlighted that out of 215 projects, only 112 were completed within the stipulated period, whereas 103 projects faced delays ranging from one to five years. The report also noted major deficiencies in project planning and execution, including lack of transparency in tender processes and inappropriate financial management, resulting in increased costs by 27% over the original estimates (p.18).

These shortcomings had negative consequences on developmental targets. The delays led to underachievement of household electrification, water supply connections, and educational infrastructure goals, disproportionately affecting rural populations and heightening funding wastage (p.23).

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Acquisition and allotment of land by Karnataka Industrial Area Development Board of Government of Karnataka
overview:
This performance audit scrutinised the acquisition and allotment of land by the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board (KIADB) during 2006-11, covering a period of rapid land acquisition and significant industrial activity. The Board acquired a total of 26,624 acres and 20 guntas of land for establishing industrial areas, disbursing ₹6,687.66 crore in compensation. However, the audit uncovered serious irregularities: regional imbalances persisted, with Northern Karnataka constituting just 9% of land acquired in these years, contrary to state policy aiming at equitable regional development. The audit highlighted that land acquisitions were often ad hoc and not preceded by feasibility studies, strategic planning, or proper consultation with local planning authorities, leading to both non-compliance with zoning laws and creation of industrial areas in restricted or special agricultural zones without sanctioned land use changes.

Further, compensation payments were marred by grave irregularities, including fraudulent disbursal: in one instance, compensation of ₹76.07 crore was paid for 235 acres in two survey numbers, despite prior notification from authorities that RTCs were manipulated and the matter was under investigation. There were cases where the Special Land Acquisition Officer disbursed compensation for land exceeding the area notified, resulting in an excess payment of ₹17.68 crore. Compensation of ₹14.40 crore was paid to nine persons with doubtful or no land title, and ₹26.70 crore was used to evict unauthorised occupants even after courts had nullified their claims.

The Board also exhibited a lack of transparency in allotment, violating its own regulations by allowing Zonal Development Officers to allot lands without proper oversight or policy for civic amenity site allocation. The audit concludes that the Board’s functioning did not effectively address regional imbalances or ensure accountable, lawful, and transparent land management processes.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Revenue of Government of Karnataka
overview:
This report, prepared under Article 151 (2) of the Constitution, contains 23 paragraphs including three Performance Audits, documenting non/short levy of tax, interest, and associated issues involving Rs 275.84 crore. The total revenue receipts of Karnataka for the fiscal year 2010-11 stood at Rs 58,206.23 crore, reflecting a substantial rise from Rs 49,155.70 crore in the previous year. The State raised 72% of this revenue (Rs 41,831.41 crore) through tax and non-tax sources, while the remaining 28% was sourced from Government of India as State's share and grants-in-aid.

Significant audit scrutiny conducted in 376 units uncovered 1,057 cases of under-assessments, non/short levy of taxes, and other irregularities aggregating Rs 905.66 crore. Notably, the Commercial Taxes Department alone had 2,462 cases of short or non-filing of declaration/statutory forms, leaving Rs 147.40 crore in assessed tax and interest unbooked as arrears. Additionally, the Departments accepted under-assessments worth Rs 122.62 crore in 259 cases, but recovered only Rs 18.89 crore in 550 cases as a direct result of audit findings.

Crucial areas identified for improvement include weak controls in cross-verification of inter-state transaction forms, performance deficiencies in excise and vehicle taxation, and persistently outstanding IRs totaling 7,610 audit observations with a notional value of Rs 2,205.10 crore. The audit underscores systemic risks of revenue leakage, inadequate tracking, and failure to act on audit recommendations, demanding urgent process reforms.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on District Mandi of Government of Himachal Pradesh
overview:
The performance audit of District Mandi in Himachal Pradesh covers the period 2006-07 to 2010-11 and examines execution across 19 departments. During the review, it was noted that out of the allocated funds totaling Rs 610.16 crore, only Rs 315.55 crore (51.7 per cent) were utilized, leaving a significant portion unspent (Page 5).

Major gaps were observed in planning and monitoring. As per the report, there was a shortfall of 27 per cent in achieving physical targets for rural infrastructure, with only 487 of the planned 670 works completed (Page 19). Further, delays of up to 24 months in project execution led to cost escalations of Rs 6.7 crore (Page 38).

The audit also found irregularities in procurement, including awarding contracts without proper tendering, resulting in avoidable expenditure of Rs 2.85 crore (Page 46). The consequences of these lapses have affected the delivery of essential services and deprived beneficiaries of intended outcomes as planned for the district, highlighting the urgent need for system improvements.

title: Report of 2011 - Compliance and Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Karnataka
overview: This report examines the compliance and performance management of civil departments in Karnataka during 2010-11, reviewing selected programmes and highlighting major deficiencies. Total Government expenditure for 2010-11 was ₹1,47,573 crore, marking an increase of 16.1% over the previous year, with capital outlay reaching ₹13,355 crore. Performance audits underline critical lapses in implementing the Comprehensive Computerisation Project of the Department of Food, Civil Supplies and Consumer Affairs, where, after an expenditure of ₹54.23 crore, project objectives were not met and the private partner left prematurely, leaving assets untransferred and database riddled with deficiencies. In Fire and Emergency Services, only 176 out of 201 required fire stations were functional by December 2011, with 43 housed in temporary buildings and severe shortages of vehicles and staff. Heritage conservation was hampered by lack of strategic coordination, inadequate resource allocation (40% of technical posts vacant), and poor identification and protection of monuments. Compliance audits revealed ₹27.45 crore of non-compliance cases, including failure to recover the net present value for forest land diversion and excess payments in public works. Persistent gaps in administrative oversight led to stalled projects and blocked assets, with ₹16.14 crore unutilised due to indecisiveness and lack of follow-up, affecting the intended outcomes for public benefit. Despite repeated audit findings, responsiveness of departments remained weak as 804 Inspection Reports with 3,508 paragraphs were still outstanding as of December 2011.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Sale of Sugar Mills of Uttar Pradesh State Corporation Ltd of Government of Uttar Pradesh
overview:
This performance audit reports major deficiencies in the disinvestment and sale process of 21 sugar mills belonging to the Uttar Pradesh State Sugar Corporation Limited (UPSSCL) and its subsidiary UPRCGVNL. The sale was executed between July 2010 and March 2011, covering 10 operating mills and 11 closed mills. Valuation discrepancies resulted in a combined shortfall of ₹1,179.84 crore, including unjustified reductions in land and plant valuation, and clubbing of assets.

The audit highlighted undervaluation of assets, such as land and plant machinery, with ₹243.48 crore reduced by reversing valuation weightages and ₹82.08 crore undervalued in machinery. Disclosure of expected price prior to bidding and change of bidding methodology mid-process adversely affected final bid prices. In 14 of 21 mills sold, bid prices were far below expected values.

Lack of competition in bidding was also observed, including concerted bidding, cartelization, and bidders related to each other. Stamp duty lapses caused revenue loss of ₹100.77 crore to the state exchequer. Severity is high given the extent of undervaluation, procedural lapses, and resulting financial loss to the public sector.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Revenue of Government of Himachal Pradesh
overview:
The Performance Audit of the revenue sector in Himachal Pradesh reviewed the efficiency, effectiveness, and accountability in assessment and collection of key state revenues, including State Excise, Value Added Tax (VAT), and Stamp Duty, among others. The audit covered departmental records for five years, highlighting significant under-assessments, short realisations, and cases of non/short levy of taxes and duties. For the audit period, total revenue receipts amounted to Rs 15,314.95 crore, but the CAG noted a persistent shortfall in collection and recovery processes, with Rs 391.91 crore remaining unrealised across assessed demands.

Notably, systemic weaknesses were found in both compliance and enforcement. Tax authorities failed to apply provisions consistently, resulting in 2,381 cases of under-assessment and a potential revenue loss of Rs 138.06 crore (p.13). Further, VAT administration suffered from inadequate monitoring and weak internal controls, leading to delayed scrutiny of dealer returns and non-detection of tax evasion in multiple instances. In addition, the audit pointed out the absence of a robust mechanism for periodic internal audit, which compromised revenue assurance.

Consequences of these weak controls and gaps in tax administration included impaired fiscal capacity, accumulation of arrears, and a decrease in the state's own tax effort ratio. The audit concludes that unless corrective action is taken to address compliance deficits, procedural lapses, and monitoring failures, collection efficiency will remain compromised, directly affecting the State's fiscal health and development priorities.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on State Excise Department of Government of Kerala
overview:
The performance audit of the State Excise Department of Kerala revealed significant issues in revenue collection and enforcement. For the audit period 2006-07 to 2009-10, the department failed to achieve the targeted revenue growth, with actual excise revenue collection being Rs 1,772.65 crore against the target of Rs 2,050 crore, representing a shortfall of 13.5 per cent. (Page 10)

Several cases of under-assessment, short collection, and irregularities in granting licenses were detected. Specifically, 69 cases of license renewals were found without proper verification, resulting in potential revenue loss of Rs 45 lakh. The audit also highlighted inefficiencies in monitoring, where inspection records were incomplete or not maintained, affecting effective follow-up on violations. (Page 23)

Consequences of these lapses included weakened enforcement, diminished deterrence for illegal liquor sales, and systemic vulnerability that may facilitate revenue leakage. The CAG emphasized the need for robust procedures, digital tracking of licenses, and proper maintenance of inspection registers to curb future irregularities. (Page 46)

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Himachal Pradesh
overview:
The Performance Audit of civil departments of the Government of Himachal Pradesh highlighted significant systemic deficiencies in planning, utilization of funds, and program implementation. Total expenditure of ₹4,329.21 crore was incurred during the audit period under various civil works, schemes, and programs; however, fund management was flagged as lacking efficiency as only 56% of allocated funds were actually utilized in key examined schemes (p. 4). Non-utilization led to large-scale parking of funds and delay in project completion.

The audit revealed shortfalls in achievement of physical targets, such as construction of health sub-centers, where only 171 out of 340 planned centers were completed (p. 23). Further, diversion of funds amounting to ₹32.76 crore was observed in certain projects, resulting in breach of financial propriety (p. 67). Execution of work without adequate survey and planning led to time overruns, with 37% of completed schemes suffering delays ranging from 6 months to 3 years (p. 59).

The consequences of these lapses included underutilization of assets, delays in service delivery, and denial of intended benefits to target beneficiaries. The audit recommended a systemic overhaul in planning, strict monitoring of implementation, and timely release of funds to mitigate such deficiencies in the future.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Revenue of Government of Jammu Kashmir
overview:
The Report presents a performance audit of revenue receipts for the Government of Jammu & Kashmir for the year ended 31 March 2011. Total receipts by the State grew to ₹22,233.65 crore, marking a 26% increase from the previous year. However, the State’s own revenue constituted only 21% of total receipts, with the remaining 79% comprising central funds, notably Grant-in-aid from Government of India (GOI) forming 65.62% of the total revenue, which raises concerns about dependency on external funds (Page v).

During audit, significant issues were uncovered including system and compliance deficiencies that led to non/short levy of tax, interest, and penalties, amounting to revenue implications totalling ₹39.90 crore. Inspection reports revealed 2053 outstanding audit paragraphs involving ₹1,726.88 crore, primarily due to lack of departmental response, indicating persistent failures by senior officials to enforce accountability (Page iii-v, 1.3.1).

Critical failures were noted in Commercial Taxes, Motor Vehicles, State Excise, and Stamp Duty departments. Performance Audits highlighted non-maintenance of databases, misuse of declaration forms causing revenue loss of ₹49.05 lakh, delays in system implementation, unreliable tax and vehicle records, and systemic shortcomings in assessment and levy procedures. Recovery in accepted cases remained minimal, with only ₹0.43 crore recovered out of ₹8.75 crore accepted by the departments, underscoring the lethargy in executing corrective measures (Pages v-vii, 6).

title: Report of 2011 - Financial and Performance Audit on District Baramulla of Government of Jammu Kashmir
overview:
This CAG report evaluates the financial and performance aspects of socio-economic development programs in District Baramulla, Jammu & Kashmir, for the period 2005-11. The audit covered all major sectoral offices, reviewing allocation and utilization of funds, infrastructure gaps, and program achievement. It highlights major deficiencies, including lack of perspective planning, poor fund management, incomplete infrastructure works, and inefficiencies in social service delivery.

Total expenditure on the social sector was Rs 243.44 crore and on the economic sector Rs 853 crore. The percentage utilization of funds ranged from 74% to 99% in key departments, but Rs 20.51 crore remained unspent under Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan as of 31 March 2011. Administrative expenditures in some sectors were as high as 92% of total spend, greatly reducing actual developmental impacts. Significant infrastructure gaps remain, with 974 school works incomplete and 516 schools operating from rented premises.

These lapses resulted in delayed program benefits, inflated unspent balances, and ineffective service provision. The audit stresses the urgent need for better planning, coordinated fund release, completing school infrastructure, and actionable targets for health and water supply services. Administrative inefficiencies and fund misallocation pose severe risks to development aims.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on District Jammu of Government of Jammu Kashmir
overview:
The Performance Audit of District Jammu revealed significant shortcomings in the implementation and monitoring of developmental schemes between 2007-08 and 2010-11. A total of Rs 119.24 crore was allocated to the district, but only Rs 53.71 crore (45.1%) was actually utilized, indicating major lapses in fund management (Page 3, Executive Summary). The audit found incomplete projects with 37 out of 95 works still pending beyond stipulated periods, leading to delayed benefits for intended communities (Page 17, Table 2.2). There were numerous instances of irregularities, including improper tendering and violation of norms in the PMGSY rural road scheme, resulting in cost overruns of Rs 5.22 crore (Page 22).

Poor record-keeping was observed, with discrepancies in beneficiary data for MGNREGA, where the reported number of job cards issued (23,781) did not match actual verified figures (Page 36). Audit also highlighted insufficient monitoring, evidenced by just 6% of planned inspections being conducted, raising concerns about oversight effectiveness (Page 39).

The consequences of these lapses included hindered access to welfare services, unproductive expenditure, and continued infrastructure gaps. The report underscores the need for stringent monitoring, timely completion of projects, and accurate reporting to ensure intended socio-economic outcomes are achieved for residents of Jammu district.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Civil and Commercial of Government of Jammu Kashmir
overview:
This report covers the performance audit of major civil and commercial departments for Jammu and Kashmir for the year ended 31 March 2011, highlighting both systemic and operational weaknesses. Across key sectors such as Education, Agriculture, Housing and Urban Development, and Power, there were substantial shortcomings in planning, timely fund utilisation, and outcome achievement. Audit observed poor utilisation of centrally sponsored programme funds, with huge unspent balances—between 32% and 72% of funds were released at the fag end of the financial years, severely hampering project completion and basic service delivery. In the Education sector, 65% of construction works initiated since 2002 were completed, but 485 were abandoned mid-way and 560 not started, resulting in widespread absence of basic amenities including toilets and drinking water. Similarly, Power sector reforms failed to achieve target reductions in T&D losses, which instead increased, compounding financial stress.

The Department of Housing and Urban Development's attempts at Dal Lake management were hampered by unscientific planning and under-utilisation of 32-60% of conservation funds. Poor monitoring, weak internal controls, and the absence of holistic planning led to idle investments—such as over ₹11 crore spent on non-functional sewage treatment plants, and further delays affecting rehabilitation and resettlement schemes. Furthermore, the State’s Public Sector Undertakings, with an aggregate investment of ₹5,225.63 crore, saw only 6 out of 21 working PSUs making profits, while 13 posted losses totalling nearly ₹154 crore for 2010-11. Key contributors to losses were the State Road Transport (₹52.52 crore loss) and Industries Limited (₹42.31 crore loss).

In summary, pervasive issues of poor fund management, ad-hoc project implementation, unauthorized diversions (e.g., ₹1.15 crore in one corporation), and mounting liabilities (unauthorised liability of ₹110.82 crore) undermined program outcomes and public accountability. The audit underscores urgent need for process reforms, better planning, and robust internal controls to avoid wasteful or unproductive public expenditure.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Revenue of Government of Gujarat
overview:
This Performance Audit report covers the revenue receipts of the Government of Gujarat for the year ended 31 March 2011, comprising sales tax/VAT, land revenue, taxes on vehicles, stamp duty and registration fees, and other tax and non-tax receipts. Total revenue receipts for 2010-11 amounted to ₹52,363.64 crore, with State-raised revenue accounting for 79% and central transfers and grants-in-aid contributing the remaining 21% (₹6,679.44 crore and ₹4,430.55 crore respectively).

Major revenue sources included Sales Tax/VAT (₹24,893.46 crore) and stamp duty & registration fees (₹3,666.24 crore). Non-tax revenue was dominated by receipts from non-ferrous mining and metallurgical industries (₹2,019.31 crore). Audit examination found significant lapses, including non/short levy of tax, penalty, and interest amounting to ₹462.98 crore across 50 paragraphs. Issues observed ranged from inadequate cross-verification of declaration forms, failure in internal controls, misapplication of tax rates, and irregular deductions.

The audit noted persistent weaknesses in Departmental accountability and follow-up. As of June 2011, 14,100 unresolved audit observations involving ₹8,718.32 crore remained pending, highlighting systemic inefficiencies in compliance and recovery. Government land allocation, vehicle taxation, stamp duty on large financial transactions, and entertainment tax exemptions were identified as critical areas of concern, resulting in significant lost revenues.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Commercial of Government of Gujarat
overview:
The Report of 2011 on the Performance Audit of Government Commercial Undertakings in Gujarat highlights serious governance, financial, and operational challenges within State Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs). As on 31 March 2011, working PSUs of Gujarat registered a turnover of ₹63,008.20 crore, which constituted 12.24% of the State's GDP, and employed 1.09 lakh people. Despite earning an aggregate profit of ₹2,662.94 crore, audit revealed ₹4,216.53 crore in controllable losses and ₹300.98 crore in infructuous investment due to deficient management practices (page vii/viii).

The audit found systematic issues in the power distribution segment, with aggregate technical and commercial (AT&C) losses significantly exceeding government norms. For example, DGVCL and PGVCL faced losses of ₹105.79 crore and ₹451.01 crore in excess of permitted norms, largely due to poor network maintenance and delay in implementing central schemes. Furthermore, ₹135.33 crore under RGGVY and over 75% of R-APDRP funds remained unutilised as of March 2011 (page viii). The audit also detected inefficient billing, collection, and financial management, with delays in revenue submissions, non-recovery of security deposits (total exceeding ₹520 crore), and unjustified premature loans causing direct losses.

Transaction Audit observations identified ₹17.66 crore lost due to non-compliance with procedures, ₹98.74 crore from failing to safeguard financial interests, and ₹14.60 crore from poor planning. Major cases included probable loss of ₹96.42 crore by Alcock Ashdown (Gujarat) Limited due to imprudent contract acceptance (page xii/xiii). The findings emphasize the need for urgent reforms, professionalism, and accountability to maximize public investments and minimize fiscal risks.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Gujarat

The Performance Audit reviewed the implementation and management of civil schemes and activities by the Government of Gujarat during the period 2007-08 to 2009-10. During this period, aggregate budget provision was ₹23,563.50 crore, but utilisation ranged between 44 to 50 percent, falling far short of both national norms and stated yearly targets (page 12, Executive Summary).

Major headline findings include persistent fund underutilisation, incomplete projects, delays in the release of funds, and weak internal controls. For instance, the audit revealed that up to ₹1,423 crore remained unspent at the end of 2009-10, and only limited physical progress was observed in core infrastructure areas, undermining the effectiveness of flagship programmes (page 18, Chapter I).

The consequences of these systemic weaknesses are severe: intended benefits of critical development schemes did not reach beneficiaries, large block appropriations were returned each year, and the risk of fund diversion or misapplication increased significantly. Accountability gaps, insufficient monitoring, and delayed administrative sanction further contributed to the lack of impact on the ground.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Revenue of Government of Haryana
overview:
The Performance Audit report for the year ended 31 March 2011 presents key findings on the Government of Haryana's revenue receipts. Total revenue receipts for 2010-11 stood at ₹25,563.68 crore, with ₹20,211.31 crore raised by the state—comprised of ₹16,790.37 crore tax revenue and ₹3,420.94 crore non-tax revenue. The increase of ₹4,571.02 crore (22%) over the prior year was attributed mainly to the state's own tax and non-tax revenue growth (Paragraph 1.1.1, page 2).

Test checks in the Sales Tax, VAT, State Excise, Motor Vehicles, and other departments revealed underassessments, non/short levies, and losses aggregating to ₹1,052.85 crore in 4,662 cases. Departments accepted audit findings for underassessments worth ₹222.79 crore across 2,176 cases, but recovered only ₹13.77 crore (Paragraph 1.5.1, page vii).

The audit found recurring issues such as a lack of internal audit, poor recovery rates on accepted cases (as low as 4-10%), and notable non-recoveries including exemption benefits and penalties from defaulting businesses. Absence of proper internal controls and data management contributed to repeated omissions, revenue leakages, non-realisation of taxes, and system lapses spanning multiple revenue streams.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Haryana
overview:
This report presents the findings from the performance audit of civil activities of the Government of Haryana for the year ending 31 March 2011, highlighting both significant successes and serious systemic failures. Audit covered 1,453 units and found widespread deficiencies, including non-utilization of large government grants, poor planning, and non-compliance with rules. For example, the Forest Department did not utilize Rs 109.18 crore received as compensatory afforestation and failed to prepare a long-term plan, directly contravening policy targets.

Kurukshetra University failed to prepare a balance sheet since inception and had unadjusted temporary advances of Rs 5.89 crore given to employees and an under-utilization of Rs 20 crore out of Rs 30 crore for student capacity enhancement. Key deficiencies across sectors included incomplete research projects, insufficient staff levels (26% shortage for general and 61% for self-financing courses), and delay in critical infrastructure projects.

Governance lapses resulted in unfruitful or idle expenditure of over Rs 515.91 crore in multiple cases, including public works and welfare schemes. Follow-up actions by administrative departments on CAG observations remained grossly inadequate, with 6,189 unresolved paragraphs worth Rs 278.91 crore and 354 Public Accounts Committee recommendations pending across decades.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit of Government of Goa
overview:
This Performance Audit for Goa highlights persistent lapses in forest protection, planning, and grant utilization. The Forest Department failed to achieve compensatory afforestation targets, with only 509.59 hectares (35%) completed out of the mandated 1,440.97 hectares for North Goa since 1983. Implementation of the Goa, Daman and Diu Preservation of Trees Act, 1984 was inadequate: just 9,000 trees replanted versus the required 203,000 for 59,000 trees permitted to be cut from 2005-11. A newly constructed shopping complex in Panaji costing ₹15.33 crore was encroached by vendors, causing a revenue loss of ₹98.97 lakh over seven years, while ₹2.80 crore of unspent grants-in-aid were not refunded by the Corporation of the City of Panaji.

Financial management showed regular savings, with a cumulative ₹4.08 crore (4%) underspent from 2006-11. Key schemes suffered from technical and administrative delays, with less than 54% achievement in nursery targets for rehabilitation schemes and 92% achievement in social forestry, according to departmental data. Fundamental structural issues pervade district planning, as the District Planning Committee (DPC) in North Goa met just twice in five years and failed to produce any development plans, leaving 386 Below Poverty Line families without housing under Indira Awas Yojana despite longstanding waitlists.

Repeated non-compliance with audit recommendations persists. As of June 2011, 369 Inspection Reports with 1,384 paragraphs remained unresolved. No administrative department furnished explanatory memoranda for 22 audit paragraphs as of September 2011. Audit highlights high severity due to missed critical afforestation and fund management targets, systemic regulatory failures, and persistent governance gaps.

title: Performance Audit on “Assessment, Levy and Collection of Major and Minor Mineral Receipts” of Government of Chhattisgarh
overview:
This Performance Audit examines the assessment, levy, and collection of major and minor mineral receipts by the Government of Chhattisgarh for the period 2006-07 to 2010-11. The mining sector contributed ₹2,470.44 crore in 2010-11, forming 64.41% of the non-tax revenue. However, the audit found widespread deficiencies including short realisation of royalty, misuse of transit passes, unauthorized excavation, and the absence of a mineral policy despite a model being circulated in 2009.

One of the most critical findings was that irregularities in management of leases, unauthorized excavation, and non/short assessment and realization of royalty aggregated to ₹294.54 crore. The Department's internal control was found weak: there was no separate Internal Audit Wing, inspections were insufficient, and government weighbridges were largely absent, heightening risk of revenue leakage. Additionally, a significant number of lease applications were pending, hampering mineral development and revenue realization.

Compliance mechanisms were lacking, as evidenced by receipt arrears of ₹1.80 crore, most of which pertained to pre-1996 leases to lessees no longer traceable. Further, environmental and infrastructure cesses due on both major and minor minerals were neither assessed nor realized, and a large number of stone crusher leases operated without environmental clearance, underlining the severe weaknesses in oversight, enforcement, and revenue protection.

title: Report of 2011 - Financial and Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Arunachal Pradesh
overview:
The audit highlights persistent deficiencies in public financial management in Arunachal Pradesh, covering civil departments for 2005-06 to 2009-10. The Government incurred an expenditure of ₹2,262.97 crore against the total grants received, with 44 per cent of the reviewed schemes showing underutilisation of funds. Delay in the release and utilisation of funds was observed, with Rs 576 crore lying unutilised at the close of the financial year 2008-09 (page 12).

A review of selected departments revealed shortfall in achievement of physical targets ranging from 35 to 68 per cent in core sectors like Health, Education, and Rural Development. Multiple instances of diversion, retention and misclassification of funds were noted, resulting in non-compliance with financial rules and General Financial Rules.

These deficiencies adversely affected delivery of public services and increased dependency on central grants. The risk of funds lying idle increased due to poor monitoring, weak internal controls, and delayed submission of utilisation certificates, raising serious concerns about transparency and accountability in state governance.

title: Performance Audit of XIXth Commonwealth Games
overview:
The performance audit of the XIX Commonwealth Games 2010 exposed critical governance and financial mismanagement. The total expenditure for the Games was estimated at ₹18,532 crore, a near 13-fold increase from the original bid estimate of ₹1,620 crore, due to frequent changes, delays, and lack of holistic planning. Delays in project initiation resulted in bunching of works, time and cost overruns, and avoidable extra expenditure.

Key findings include irregular contracting practices, arbitrary contract management, and serious lapses in the implementation of financial controls across multiple agencies. The Organising Committee's inability to finalise plans led to delay in finalising crucial arrangements, hurting revenue generation and overall efficiency. The audit also detected collusive behavior and cartelization in procurement, resulting in financial losses to public exchequer.

Consequently, the legacy of the Games was undermined by poor planning, cost escalations, irrecoverable liabilities, and numerous projects left incomplete or underutilized. The report stresses that "there were significant deficiencies in financial management and governance structure, resulting in enormous avoidable expenditure and loss to the government." [Executive Summary, p. 5-7]

title: Performance Audit of Fertilizer Subsidy in India of Union Government, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers
overview:
The Performance Audit of Fertilizer Subsidy in India highlighted substantial financial outlays between 2007-08 and 2009-10, with overall subsidy released amounting to Rs 1,13,813 crore. Specifically, the audit noticed the subsidy climbed sharply—from Rs 22,456 crore in 2003-04 to Rs 99,494 crore in 2008-09, demonstrating a 343% increase in just five years. This sharp rise placed significant budgetary pressure on the Government of India (GoI) and exposed the scheme to risks of inefficiency and leakage (p. xi).

The audit revealed systemic weaknesses in the control framework, including delayed recognition of imports, opaque procedures for production and dispatch certification, and insufficient controls on freight payments and input monitoring. For example, unvalidated or excess freight was reimbursed, and 49.3 lakh MT of indigenous urea unaccounted in the system during review, raising a high risk for diversion or misutilization (p. xv, xxiii). Additionally, the audit pointed out instances of overpayment, such as Rs 13,600 crore in excess freight due to the existing system (p. xxiv).

Consequences of these findings were seen in recurring mismatches between physical and financial performance, delayed subsidy releases, and potential loss of public funds. The report underlines a pressing need for independent verification mechanisms, improved data management, and restructuring of the subsidy administration to ensure the scheme reaches the intended beneficiaries without leakages or undue delays.

title: Performance Audit of Sale and Distribution of Imported Pulses in India of Union Government, Ministry of Commerce & Industry
overview:
This performance audit reviewed the implementation of two major schemes for the import and distribution of pulses in India from 2006-07 to 2010-11. The Government of India initiated large-scale imports through MMTC Ltd., PEC Ltd., STC, and NAFED, aiming to bridge a national supply-demand gap that reached between 10 and 50 lakh MT per year. The targeted import and sale volume was 53.10 lakh MT, but only 30.04 lakh MT was imported and 26.95 lakh MT sold, leading to significant shortfall and a cumulative loss of ₹ 1201.32 crore for the agencies involved (Pages v, 6.2, 6.8).

The audit found systematic failures: delays at ports incurred an additional ₹ 42.71 crore expenditure by March 2011, and the distribution strategy—lacking detailed Ministry guidelines—favoured large private traders due to high tender requirements, shutting out smaller entities. Specifically, 73% of a test-checked quantity was sold to just four large buyers (Page v, 6.5). The controversial decision to import large quantities of yellow peas caused losses of ₹ 897.37 crore, 75% of total scheme losses (Page v, 6.8.1).

Furthermore, the scheme intended for PDS reached only a fraction of its target. States often did not specify requirements, and a subsidy of only ₹ 10/kg allowed possible diversion to non-BPL and open markets. The overall result was that despite releasing subsidies of ₹ 781.10 crore, both price stabilization and increased availability objectives were not met (Page vii, Para 9).

title: Performance Audit of Water Pollution in India of Union Government, Ministry of Environment and Forest
overview:
This performance audit covers the period from 2006-07 to 2010-11 and examined the effectiveness of policies, programmes, and implementation mechanisms of the Ministry of Environment and Forest (MoEF) in tackling water pollution across India. Document review, physical sample testing, and analysis of records were conducted in 25 States, covering 140 river projects, 22 lakes, and 116 groundwater blocks. Key findings include failure to complete lake and river inventories and critical gaps in monitoring, leading to poor policy enforcement. For instance, only two of 22 NLCP lake conservation projects were completed, and 82% of National River Conservation Plan (NRCP) river projects were delayed, with 28 projects (worth ₹251.27 crore) not utilised.

Serious shortcomings were identified in risk assessment, planning, and enforcement—there was no basin-level approach, and the institutional setup was inadequate, resulting in weak controls and lack of measurable outcomes. Monitoring networks to track pollution were severely lacking, with insufficient stations and poor real-time data dissemination. Most water bodies continued to suffer from high organic pollution and the spread of waterborne diseases.

The financial situation was equally critical; available funds were inadequate to meet programme demands, major schemes were underfunded, and existing funds were inefficiently utilised. Despite efforts since 1985, pollution levels have not decreased in major rivers like Ganga, Yamuna, and Godavari, while most lakes remain under severe threat from eutrophication, posing ongoing risks to health, ecosystems, and livelihoods.

title: Performance Audit of Civil Aviation in India of Union Government, Ministry of Civil Aviation
overview:
This performance audit examines the civil aviation sector in India including Air India Limited (AIL), Indian Airlines Ltd (IAL), and the Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA). The review spans significant aircraft acquisitions, their merger into National Aviation Company of India Ltd (NACIL), and liberalised bilateral agreements from 2004-05 onwards. Audit revealed that AIL signed agreements on 30 December 2005 for 50 Boeing aircraft at an estimated cost of ₹33,197 crore, while IAL procured 43 Airbus aircraft at ₹8,399.60 crore. Notably, the aircraft purchase was funded mostly through debt, resulting in acute working capital issues: working capital loans rose 21 times between 2004-05 and 2009-10 reaching ₹18,524 crore, and interest burden increased 36 times to ₹2,434 crore. The merger lacked a validated financial case and was delayed, resulting in missed synergy opportunities and incomplete HR integration (98% staff below DGM not yet unified).

Major operational and financial parameters deteriorated: passenger/cargo revenues stagnated, available seat kilometre (ASKM), load factor (PLF), and route profitability dropped. By 2009-10, all international routes were loss-making, with India-USA routes alone contributing 41-90% of total operating losses. Government equity infusion was negligible—just ₹325 crore in 2005-06 and ₹800 crore in 2009-10—compared to huge borrowings. Liberalised bilateral agreements expanded rights for foreign carriers, notably Emirates, facilitating excessive '6th freedom traffic' and undermining Indian airlines. Performance Linked Incentive (PLI) payouts were not linked to operational achievements, and MoCA's oversight mechanisms failed, skewing MoU ratings and accountability.

The report recommends urgent measures including asset revaluation, HR harmonisation, restructuring PLI, freezing bilateral entitlements, infusion of government equity aligned with accountability, and enhanced operational controls. The situation is deemed critical: "The Airline has a debt liability of ₹38,423 Crore as on 31 March 2010", and piecemeal infusion will only delay collapse.

title: Report No. 17 of 2011-12 – Performance Audit of Autonomous Bodies of Union Government (Civil)
overview:
This performance audit presents a comprehensive review of five central autonomous bodies under various ministries between 2005-06 and 2009-10. Significant inefficiencies, unutilized funds, and failure to achieve objectives were found across critical schemes. For example, in the Marine Products Export Development Authority (MPEDA), against an allocation of ₹42.50 crore for sea freight assistance (2007-10), only ₹3 crore was released and ₹1.03 crore remained unutilized, indicating a major underutilization of resources and poor implementation.

Similar shortfalls were observed in Assam University and Jawaharlal Nehru University, where 17–39% and 11% of available postgraduate seats respectively remained vacant, and a high percentage of plan funds (up to 73% in Assam University) stayed unutilized. The National Institute for the Orthopaedically Handicapped suffered from severe faculty and infrastructure shortages, impacting its ability to achieve training and rehabilitation targets. At Delhi Development Authority, despite acquiring over 6,046 acres at a cost of ₹2,060 crore and expenditures of ₹2,612 crore, audit found recurring issues such as non-recovery of excess payments and delays hampering achievement of the Master Plan objectives.

The overall audit highlights systemic planning defects, inadequacies in scheme monitoring, scaling down of controls, non-achievement of scheme objectives, and absence of feedback and impact assessment mechanisms—pointing to a high risk of inefficiency and financial mismanagement.

title: Performance Audit of Hydrocarbon Production Sharing Contracts of Union Government, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas
overview:
The audit examined the oversight and performance of 10 Production Sharing Contracts (PSCs) covering key oil and gas blocks such as KG-DWN-98/3, RJ-ON-90/1, Panna Mukta, and Tapti. The total expenditure claimed in audited blocks exceeded Rs 76,000 crore, out of which Rs 45,000 crore was accounted for KG-DWN-98/3 alone. Notably, DGH failed to adequately verify cost recoveries and profit petroleum calculations, compromising government revenue.

On KG-DWN-98/3 (Krishna-Godavari basin), the audit found cost overruns reaching 2.04 times the initial estimates (Rs 45,200 crore versus Rs 22,254 crore), leading to significant loss of profit petroleum to the government estimated at Rs 6,016 crore. There were also major lapses in approval of contracts and technical evaluation, resulting in delays and inflated capital expenditure. For the RJ-ON-90/1 block, inflated cost recovery claims and incomplete relinquishment of areas caused the government to lose out on royalties and profit shares.

Key structural and compliance flaws include ineffective control by DGH, lack of transparency in contract administration, and frequent deviations from PSC provisions by operators. The consequences included loss of government revenues, reduction in profit petroleum share, and diminished public trust in petroleum sector governance. The audit recommended urgent corrective and preventive actions to restore integrity, financial discipline, and compliance in hydrocarbon PSC monitoring. title: Performance Audit of National Institutes of Technology of Union Government, Ministry of Human Resource Development
overview:
This performance audit covered the functioning of 19 National Institutes of Technology (NIsT) across India for 2005-06 to 2009-10, with a focus on admissions, academic quality, infrastructure, and fund management. The audit revealed that admissions in Civil, Electronics, Mechanical, Chemical, and IT Engineering streams remained much below intake capacities—1.38% to 42.31% of seats at the undergraduate (UG) level and 3.13% to 87% at the postgraduate (PG) level remained vacant in some years. New courses were often introduced without ascertained demand, leading to high vacancy rates of up to 83% in certain PG streams (Table-6/Table-7, p.12-13).

The audit further found that out of 88 UG and 191 PG courses offered, 45 UG and 137 PG courses lacked National Board of Accreditation recognition, undermining educational quality. On research output, only 27 out of 60 projects at NIT Calicut and Kurukshetra were completed by March 2010. Financial management showed inefficiency: although available funds were less than requested, the institutes still did not fully utilize grants, leaving an unspent balance of ₹293.69 crore at the reporting period end (Table-3, p.9).

Significant gaps were also found in infrastructure: 281.568 acres of land remained encroached, many NITs lacked adequate classrooms, lecture halls, computers, and hostel accommodations. Furthermore, statutory Council, BoG, and Finance Committee meetings frequently did not occur as required, resulting in unaddressed core issues and oversight lapses.

title: Performance Audit on Role of Tea Board in Tea Development in India
overview:
The performance audit of the Tea Board revealed severe lapses in both regulatory oversight and developmental support activities. The Board failed to discharge its basic regulatory duties, with more than 80% of small tea growers remaining outside the ambit of its registration. As of 2010, only 32,288 out of 157,504 small growers (roughly 20%) had been registered, and there was no data on applications received or permission status for the years under audit. The increasing share of commercially unproductive bushes—57% at the end of 2008—indicates an acute threat to productivity. Efforts to address this, including replantation or replacement, were grossly inadequate: clearing the backlog at the current pace would take an estimated 149 years.

Financial management remains weak, as cess revenue from 2005-06 onwards was not transferred to the Tea Fund, and revision of cess rates ranged widely from 3 to 14 years, indicating a lack of oversight or planning. The cost of production of Indian tea is the highest among major producers globally, with labour costs ranging from 32% to 50% in different regions. No meaningful initiatives for cost reduction or productivity improvement, such as worker training or incentivisation, were undertaken during the period.

Marketing and export promotion schemes lack benchmarks or accountability, with no means to correlate subsidies with export increases. Research activities funded by Tea Board showed no transferred deliverables or patents, with insufficient funds and poor monitoring of external projects. Overall, the Ministry accepted most recommendations, yet the auditors note that government action and funding need substantial revision for lasting, impactful reforms.

title: Performance Audit of Central Excise and Service Tax Union Government, Department of Indirect Taxes (Working of Commissionerates, Divisions and Ranges)
overview:
This performance audit evaluated the efficacy of the Central Excise and Service Tax administration in 46 commissionerates, 95 divisions, and 204 ranges for the fiscal period ending March 2011. It covered approximately three years of receipts, during which central excise collections totaled ₹3,35,215 crore and service tax receipts ₹1,70,663 crore. Key issues included non-adherence to prescribed procedures for broadening the service tax base, with 17 of 35 test-checked commissionerates failing to implement the DGST's action plan and more than 80% of unregistered service providers (1,622 out of 1,959) identified in prior years not verified by the department. Delays were widespread, with 25% of central excise and 19% of service tax registration certificates issued beyond the mandated seven days, in some cases by several months—a critical bottleneck for revenue administration.

The scrutiny revealed that out of 2817 central excise registration cases, 700 faced delays, and only limited scrutiny of central excise and service tax returns was occurring at range/division level. Internal audit processes were frequently compromised by staff shortages, improper risk-based selection, and lack of mandatory unit coverage. 10 commissionerates prioritized non-mandatory over mandatory audits, further reducing assurance on compliance and revenue protection. Weaknesses in the cancellation, conversion, and surrender of registrations put the system at risk of tax evasion and revenue loss.

The audit concludes that inadequate monitoring mechanisms, inconsistent practices, and lack of centralized record keeping undermined control over assessments, audit coverage, and identification of potential taxpayers. The CAG warns that without comprehensive and immediate reforms—including MIS integration, electronic information sources, and stronger guidelines—both revenue collection and taxpayer compliance will suffer, risking further loss to the exchequer.

title: Performance Audit on Security Management in Indian Railways Union Government, Railways
overview:
This audit examined the effectiveness of security management on Indian Railways for the period 2005-06 to 2009-10. The audit found that overall expenditure on security was only ₹6,698.61 crore over five years, including salary expenditure of ₹5,882 crore (89% of total expenditure), comprising just 2.55% of total IR expenditure in 2009-10. Funds utilization was inconsistent, with 1.3% to 12.53% of the allotted grants surrendered annually.

Despite the formulation of the Integrated Security System (ISS) in July 2008 to cover 137 stations by March 2010, implementation was absent in all zones up to March 2011. Boundary walls/fencing and adequate station lighting were excluded from ISS, and basic controls such as closure of unauthorized entry points were neglected: 30% of entry points at 74 checked stations were unguarded. Progress on elements like DFMDs, baggage scanners, and CCTV surveillance was slow and below international standards.

Serious concerns were raised about inadequate co-ordination between the Railway Protection Force (RPF), Government Railway Police (GRP), and State Police leading to large gaps in incident reporting and response. Across the zones, total crime rate more than doubled in five years, with passenger and goods areas most vulnerable. Escort security was provided to only 32% of daily train services, with no norms in place for selection or arming of escorts. Shortages in staff persisted: security force vacancy rates remained above 11% and, for GRP, increased from 6% to 16%. Indian Railways was found to have failed to collaborate effectively with State Governments for asset security planning.

title: Performance Audit of Export Promotion Capital Goods Scheme Union Government, Department of -Indirect Taxes
overview:
This performance audit evaluates the operation of the Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) Scheme, focusing on whether the DGFT and Customs implemented adequate controls in authorisation issuance, monitoring, and export obligation (EO) redemption. Between 2000 and 2008, 89,000 licences were issued, with the highest concentration (63%) in Mumbai, Delhi, Coimbatore, Chennai, and Bengaluru. The scheme led to a revenue forgo of ₹38,188 crore for the period 2005-06 to 2009-10.

The audit detected multiple weaknesses, including issuance of authorisations without complete documentation, lack of post-issue audits, and incorrect calculation of export obligations. A sample check revealed that out of 1,814 cases, 49 authorisations were issued without valid documents. Errors in EO fixation led to a shortfall of ₹3,060 crore due to miscalculations.

Crucially, no operational post-issue audit wings existed outside Mumbai, and ineligible applicants—including defaulters—received licences through improper use of refusal and abeyance orders. The total audit-identified revenue implication is ₹3,154.87 crore, highlighting substantial control and compliance gaps that pose high risk to government revenue.

title: Performance Audit of Service Tax on Banking and other Financial Services and Duty Drawback Scheme Union Government, Department of -Indirect Taxes
overview:
The Performance Audit of Service Tax on Banking and Other Financial Services, and Duty Drawback Scheme, revealed that during the period 2005-06 to 2009-10, there was a significant shortfall in revenue realization. The audit identified that out of the potential ₹15,000 crore service tax estimated for banking services, only ₹7,240 crore was realized, indicating a realization rate of just 48.3% (page 14).

Major issues highlighted include incorrect classification of taxable services and significant delays in verification of drawback claims. Notably, instances of irregular duty drawback claims totaling ₹215 crore led to an estimated revenue loss of ₹68.4 crore (page 25). These deficiencies pointed to systemic weaknesses and the lack of effective oversight within the Department of Indirect Taxes.

Consequences of these shortcomings included loss of revenue, persistently high pendency of audits, and ineffective deterrence against non-compliance. The report noted “substantial loss to the exchequer and erosion of deterrence due to gaps in monitoring and enforcement” (page 14).

title: Performance Audit of Recovery of Arrears of Tax Demand
overview:
This Performance Audit examined the recovery of arrears of tax demand by the Department of Revenue for the period 2005-06 to 2009-10, where outstanding arrears increased from ₹1,01,619 crore in March 2005 to ₹2,32,329 crore in March 2010. The assessment found that a major portion of these arrears, amounting to ₹1,52,481 crore (66 percent), was categorised as ‘difficult to recover’ due to reasons such as assesses not traceable, inadequate assets, or litigation pending.

A significant finding was the Department’s failure to effectively pursue collectible arrears—only ₹2,756 crore (1.2 percent of total arrears outstanding at the start of 2005-06) was realised over five years. The audit noted systemic weaknesses in monitoring cases, incomplete maintenance of registers, and delays in attaching assets for recovery. Additionally, it highlighted poor coordination between assessing officers and recovery officers, resulting in delayed or abandoned recovery actions.

The consequences of ineffective recovery include severe revenue loss and poor deterrence for tax defaulters. The lack of robust internal controls and absence of a centralised database impeded follow-up on high-value demands. Overall, failure to resolve arrear cases in a timely and consistent manner undermined public confidence in the tax administration system.

title: Performance Audit on Role and Functioning of Indian Coast Guard
overview: The audit reviewed the performance of the Indian Coast Guard (ICG) over the period 2004-05 to 2009-10, focusing on planning, organisational capability, infrastructure, acquisitions, and operational effectiveness. It found significant delays in approval and implementation of perspective plans and development plans, with the Xth Five Year Plan (2002-07) approved 33 months late, and the XIth Plan revised only after the 26/11 attacks. Despite allocations, only 50% of target acquisitions were achieved in the IXth Plan (1997-2002) and just 43% in the Xth Plan (2002-07), with not a single procurement fructifying within the Xth Plan period. Inadequate fund utilisation was evidenced by persistent savings in the capital head, with budgetary savings ranging from 15.48% to 65.28% over five years. As of December 2010, the Coast Guard operated at only 65% of its required force levels for ships/vessels and 48% for aviation assets. Infrastructure deficiencies persisted, with only 30 out of 42 stations activated and at least 16 stations lacking basic berthing and fueling facilities. Manpower shortages were critical, with deficits of 57% for officers and 43% for enrolled personnel against the envisaged levels. Additionally, repair and maintenance of ships suffered a shortfall of 62%, further impacting operational readiness. The audit concluded that ICG suffers from serious resource and planning constraints, affecting its ability to respond effectively to increasing maritime security challenges, especially highlighted in the aftermath of the 26/11 incident.

title: Performance Audit of Business of Civil Construction
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Business of Civil Construction under direct taxes examined compliance, assessment, and revenue collection across multiple states and zones. A detailed review covering 7,599 assessments found systemic omissions accumulating to a revenue loss of ₹1,246 crore. In 5,440 of these cases, deficiencies involved short levy of tax, incorrect allowance of expenditure, incorrect computation, and mistakes in the application of Section 194C.

A critical finding is that non-compliance in collection and remittance of Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) by contractees led to a revenue shortfall. For instance, TDS was not appropriately deducted or remitted in 12,500 cases, causing a potential loss of ₹684 crore (p. 7). Lapses in return scrutiny and underassessment were observed in over 32% of the sample.

These failures, if unaddressed, undermine the integrity of the tax system. The audit concluded that poor implementation both enabled significant revenue leakage and contributed to non-uniform tax burden distribution across the construction industry, with negative implications for government project funding and fiscal planning.

title: Performance Audit of Revival of Sick Central Public Sector Enterprises
overview:
This audit examines the Government of India’s performance in reviving sick Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) between 2002-03 and 2010-11, where accumulated losses among 67 CPSEs reached ₹82,477 crore against equity investment of ₹14,660 crore by 31 March 2011. Despite persistent efforts, only 251 out of 406 CPSEs earned net profit of ₹1,27,141 crore, while 127 registered combined losses of ₹23,264 crore, highlighting inefficiencies in revival mechanisms and fund utilization.

The audit reveals that the success rate of revival schemes for CPSEs was only 33.33%, significantly below the 66.85% rate for private companies, underscoring systemic weaknesses in public sector rehabilitation compared to private enterprises. The number of loss-making CPSEs fell insignificantly from 63 to 59 over five years, while aggregate annual losses increased from ₹6,845 crore in 2005-06 to ₹15,842 crore in 2009-10. Delays in insolvency processes and lack of a robust legislative framework exacerbated these challenges and led to substantial loss of national resources locked in proceedings.

Consequences of CPSE sickness included significant revenue loss to the government, underutilization of capital assets, mounting non-performing assets for banks, and adverse socio-economic impacts such as unemployment and public unrest. The inability to efficiently liquidate or revive sick units impacted the overall investment climate and led to increased public expenditure, undermining confidence in public sector management.
