title: Performance Audit of Coal India Limited Corporate Social Responsibility
overview:
Coal India Limited (CIL) and its subsidiaries allocated Rs 123.86 crore for Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) during the audit period, but only Rs 59.07 crore (47.72%) was actually utilised, resulting in a shortfall of Rs 64.79 crore. The shortfall is particularly notable given the requirement to allocate 5% of net profits for CSR activities and the consistently low utilisation rate reported across all subsidiaries. [pg 12]

The performance audit further revealed inadequate planning and unclear objectives for CSR, with many projects undertaken not directly linked to communities impacted by coal mining. The report highlighted that in some cases, projects were executed without proper needs assessment or involvement of local stakeholders. Additionally, there were delays in project completion, and monitoring mechanisms were found lacking or altogether absent, leading to incomplete outputs and questionable outcomes. [pg 23]

This underperformance led to serious consequences for affected local populations, notably in areas such as healthcare, education, and infrastructure. The audit identifies an urgent need for better planning, transparent fund utilisation, and enhanced reporting. The lack of synergy between subsidiaries and CIL headquarters further exacerbated inefficiencies and reduced the overall effectiveness of CSR initiatives. [pg 30]

title: Performance Audit of Management of Vessels (The Shipping Corporation of India Limited)
overview:
The Comptroller and Auditor General conducted a performance audit of vessel acquisition, management, and operations by The Shipping Corporation of India Limited (SCI) for the period April 2005 to March 2010. SCI’s fleet declined from 83 vessels in 2005-06 to 76 in 2009-10, with tonnage capacity remaining stagnant at around 50 lakh tonnes. Over these years, company profits plummeted from ₹1042 crore to ₹377 crore, and turnover remained nearly static. SCI aimed to acquire 39 vessels under the 10th Five Year Plan and 62 vessels in the 11th Five Year Plan, but achieved only 14 and 25 vessel acquisitions, respectively—a shortfall of 26 vessels even after accounting for orders placed in 2010-11. Delays of 14 to 34 months in government approvals escalated acquisition costs by an estimated ₹2100 crore and led to business loss opportunities.

The company faced significant issues in vessel operations: The liner segment shifted from a ₹100 crore profit in 2005-06 to losses of ₹225 crore in 2009-10, and overall idle days rose, producing standing charges and losses totalling ₹134 crore. The average age of SCI’s fleet was 15.63 years versus 11 years for private competitor Great Eastern Shipping Company, with 36 of 76 vessels nearing or surpassing their economic life, adversely impacting competitiveness. Government policy and oversight remained indecisive, with major concerns about tax burdens and slow policy responses, despite a 34% growth in India’s seaborne trade.

Ultimately, SCI failed to modernize its fleet and meet acquisition targets, lagging behind national trade growth. In maintenance, repair expenses ranged between 13-16% versus 9-10% for competitor Great Eastern, indicating inefficiency. Oversight mechanisms were weak, and poor documentation raised transparency concerns.

title: Performance Audit of Bharat Electronics Limited Procurement System
overview:
The Performance Audit of the procurement system at Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL), as conducted by the CAG, identified significant shortcomings in the planning, execution, and monitoring of procurement activities over the period 2006-07 to 2010-11. Of the ₹11,672 crore procured during the audit period, high-value items worth ₹7,420 crore (63.6%) were obtained through limited tenders instead of open competition, suggesting sub-optimal transparency and competitive rates, as detailed on page 12.

The audit found that BEL's procurement lead time exceeded the company’s norm in 34 per cent of cases, with delays ranging from three to 36 months, directly impacting project execution and deliveries to key defence customers. For instance, on page 23 it is noted that material procurement for Akash missile systems faced an average delay of 8 months per order. These inefficiencies resulted in liquidated damages amounting to ₹33.87 crore imposed by customers between 2006-07 and 2010-11, affecting profitability and customer satisfaction (page 29).

The audit also found that BEL often failed to update its Approved Vendors List (AVL) annually, with 43 per cent of items in sampled units procured from vendors not on the latest AVL, increasing risks of unreliable supplies. The systemic issues have led to recurring procurement shortfalls and increased strategic and financial risk for BEL’s defence business, as highlighted in Chapters II and IV.

title: Performance Audit of Capacity Expansion in Hydro Power Sector by CPSEs, Ministry of Power
overview:
The audit reviewed the performance of Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) under the Ministry of Power in the expansion of hydro power capacity during the 2007-12 plan period, focusing on NHPC Limited, SJVN Limited, THDC India Limited, and NEEPCO Limited. Originally, 11,813 MW of hydro power capacity addition was targeted for the XI Five Year Plan, but only 6,794 MW (57%) was actually planned for execution by these CPSEs, reflecting a substantial downward revision due to allocation to private developers, unresolved joint ventures, and project delays (p. 13).

Notably, actual capacity expected to be added in the XII Plan (2012-17) at the time of audit was only 3,774 MW (just 34% of the 11,129 MW planned), with several major projects slipping to subsequent plan periods, indicating persistent lags in preparedness and project execution (p. 14). Progress was also hindered by delayed clearances, environmental and forest permissions, as well as long durations for statutory approvals, with only two of 14 audited projects meeting prescribed pre-investment timelines (p. 15).

These delays have cascading effects on the overall capacity addition strategy of the Ministry of Power, raising significant risks to the reliability and expansion of hydroelectric generation, and highlighting inefficiencies in planning, approval, and execution mechanisms. The audit emphasizes the need for more robust coordination, long-term planning, and improved internal controls to avoid cost escalation and ensure timely project completion.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Revenue of Government of Andhra Pradesh
overview:
The Performance Audit on Revenue Receipts for the Government of Andhra Pradesh for the year ended 31 March 2011 highlights significant issues in tax administration and revenue realization. The report reveals that tax and non-tax revenue raised by the State during 2010-11 stood at ₹55,859.27 crore, representing 69% of the total receipts. However, ₹12,175.14 crore in outstanding audit observations across 32,322 paragraphs from previous Inspection Reports remain unsettled, indicating systemic gaps in compliance and follow-up (p. 7).

Major findings include large-scale evasion and fraud in VAT administration, especially relating to the use of fake 'F' and 'C' forms, leading to the non-levy and short levy of tax and penalties amounting to several crores (e.g., ₹73.07 crore via fake ‘F’ forms and ₹8.65 lakh via fake ‘C’ forms). Performance Audit reveals similar alarming gaps in the realization of land conversion fees, with ₹1,438.11 crore pending recovery due to lack of pursuance (p. xii).

Other notable gaps include non-renewal of vehicle fitness certificates resulting in loss of ₹59.56 crore in fees and penalties, and non-levy of electricity duty of ₹264.58 crore by the Chief Electrical Inspector. The compliance rate on audit findings and departmental notes is low, with cases pending explanation for up to 112 months (p. 10). This continued lack of enforcement and follow-up points to high risks to state revenue and fiscal discipline.

title: Report of 2011 - Performance Audit on Commercial of Government of Andhra Pradesh
overview:
The Performance Audit on Commercial activities of the Government of Andhra Pradesh comprehensively evaluates the functioning, efficiency, and financial implications of 72 State Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) for the period ending 2010-11. As on 31 March 2011, the State had 48 working and 24 non-working PSUs, collectively employing 2.64 lakh people and with a total investment of ₹50,165.06 crore, marking a 56.93% increase since 2005-06. The report highlights that despite a collective profit of ₹238.56 crore by working PSUs in 2010-11, they carried accumulated losses amounting to ₹2,711.66 crore, mainly due to mismanagement, inefficiency, and delayed execution of projects.

Serious deficiencies were noted in the financial management of critical sectors, with the Power sector accounting for 53.76% of total PSU investment by 2011. Issues such as underutilized funds—only 32.74% of RAPDRP funds used—and massive cost overruns, notably in mining operations and infrastructure development, were found. The quality of PSU accounts remains poor: out of 46 accounts finalized between October 2010 and September 2011, 28 received qualified certificates and 51 instances of non-compliance with accounting standards were observed.

Such systemic weaknesses led to significant losses. The report documents losses of ₹458.23 crore due to violations of rules and contract conditions, an additional ₹94.24 crore from poor financial safeguards, and ₹126.90 crore from particular real estate ventures. Moreover, audit identified urgent needs in internal controls, risk mitigation, and winding up of 24 non-functional PSUs as no public interest is served by their continued existence.

title: Report of 2011 - Compliance and Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Andhra Pradesh
overview:
This report comprises 13 chapters and covers both compliance and performance audits of civil departments in Andhra Pradesh, focusing on Central and State schemes, autonomous bodies, and departmental efficiency. For the audit year 2010-11, a total of 14,814 party-days were spent auditing 1,427 units across 23 key government departments, with the findings intended to inform corrective actions and improved governance.

Major lapses included unutilised funds, poor program implementation, non-compliance with statutory requirements, and instances of fraud and financial irregularity. Notably, there was a pending settlement of 29,689 audit paragraphs in 5,432 Inspection Reports as of June 30, 2011, indicating severe delays in response and systemic oversight issues. For example, the Deepam scheme resulted in an extra burden of ₹23.93 crore due to administrative failures, and only 53,457 of 75,474 sanctioned works under ACDP/CDP were completed, causing prolonged fund locks and denied benefits.

Critical operational gaps were also highlighted: several hospitals’ trauma care units remained non-functional, crucial equipment lay idle for years, and major development schemes such as the Integrated Handloom Development Scheme, Rajiv Udyogasri Society, and coastal security infrastructure remained mostly incomplete or operationally deficient, leading to significant wastage of public funds and denied service delivery.

title: Financial and Performance Audit on Local Self Government Institutions of Government of Kerala
overview:
During the period 2005-10, Local Self Government Institutions (LSGIs) in Kerala received ₹13,801.80 crore from the State Government, including ₹6,896.81 crore as development funds, ₹6,679.34 crore for maintenance, and ₹225.65 crore as General Purpose Grant. However, delays in release of development funds averaging 5 to 8 months led to poor planning and under-utilisation. Notably, only 44-50% of the annual plan outlays in Gram Panchayats were utilised in certain years, with even lower percentages in many Municipalities.

Audit found instances of misappropriation and other irregularities totaling over ₹3.04 crore, with 164 cases pending finalisation, out of which 62% were outstanding for more than three years. There were also significant deficiencies in accounting and reporting, as only 9% of LSGIs submitted accounts for audit within the due dates, leaving 91% either delayed or pending, thus impeding effective oversight and transparency.

The consequences of these issues were compounded by the lack of monitoring and absence of a comprehensive database on assets and liabilities. Delayed submission reduced the utility of audit findings, while ineffective internal controls and poor follow-up action on audit reports hindered remedial measures on financial lapses, leaving substantial risks in the LSGI financial system.

title: Report of 2010 - Performance Audit on Collection of Motor Vehicle Taxes, Fees and Fines of Government of West Bengal
overview:
The performance audit of Collection of Motor Vehicle Taxes, Fees and Fines by the Transport Department, Government of West Bengal for the period 2003-04 to 2007-08 revealed systemic deficiencies in tax assessment, collection, and monitoring mechanisms. Audit scrutiny found that the Department failed to realise revenue of ₹316.82 crore due to non-assessment and incomplete collection processes (Para 1.7.1, p.3). Further, test check in the offices indicated considerable delays and lack of compliance, especially in computation of arrears and enforcement of penalties for defaulting vehicle owners.

The Department did not maintain appropriate records or a robust database for tracking registered vehicles, which led to leakage of significant revenue. CAG found that, for example, there was an uncollected balance of ₹81.44 crore as arrears of taxes at the end of March 2008, showing persistent under-collection and hampered enforcement (Para 1.9, p.8). Moreover, the absence of reconciliation between Transport offices and Treasury resulted in mismatches amounting to ₹20.34 crore (Para 1.10.2, p.10).

As a result of these deficiencies, there was not just financial loss but erosion of public trust, as the resources meant to fund transport infrastructure and safety initiatives were instead left unrealised or unaccounted for. Unreconciled accounts and poor monitoring potentially incentivised non-compliance among transport operators, further weakening the system's integrity.

title: Report of 2010 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Uttar Pradesh
overview:
The Performance Audit on Civil for the Government of Uttar Pradesh revealed significant deficiencies in planning, fund utilisation, and implementation. For instance, out of the available outlay of ₹3134.07 crore during 2008-09, only ₹1574.84 crore was utilised (50%), reflecting low fund absorption capacity (p.12). Large sums remained unutilised due to delayed release and weak monitoring mechanisms, resulting in lapses of budgetary grants.

Physical achievements also lagged behind targets. For example, the target for construction of school buildings during 2007-09 was 1,800, but only 984 buildings were completed (p.54). In health infrastructure, only 44% of planned sub-centres were operationalised (p.67). This shortfall has adversely impacted access to basic services for vulnerable populations.

Further, audit scrutiny revealed procedural lapses, non-maintenance of essential records, and instances of diversion of funds or unauthorised expenditure. Such failures compromised the efficiency and effectiveness of state schemes, and pose significant risks to the intended social and economic outcomes for the people of Uttar Pradesh.

title: Report of 2010 - Performance Audit on Commercial of Government of West Bengal
overview:
The Performance Audit for the State Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) in West Bengal for 2009-10 reveals serious deficiencies in financial and operational management. As on 31 March 2010, the State had 72 working PSUs and 20 non-working PSUs, with an aggregate investment of ₹41,810.57 crore, up 22.76% from ₹34,057.55 crore in 2004-05. A total turnover of ₹21,674.57 crore equalled 5.90% of the state GDP. In 2009-10, only 32 PSUs made profits totaling ₹562.87 crore, while 36 incurred losses of ₹644.31 crore, and three reported no profit/no loss, highlighting an overall net loss for the sector.

Audit findings indicate both significant operational inefficiency and gaps in compliance. Only 31 PSUs out of 72 working units finalised their accounts, while 41 had arrears ranging from one to six years. The quality of accounts remains poor: out of 74 finalised accounts, 42 received qualified certificates and 23 had audit comments impacting profitability by ₹680.93 crore. Contract and project management failures led to time overruns (7–84 months) and cost overruns totaling ₹3,035.42 crore. Financial mismanagement increased borrowing by 408% (₹696.58 crore to ₹3,539.52 crore) with an interest burden of ₹588.01 crore.

Critical operational inefficiencies included short receipt of coal (19.54%–28.29%), excessive auxiliary and manpower costs, excess consumption of coal worth ₹1,384.47 crore, poor plant load factors below national averages (59.48–67.84% vs. 73.71–78.61%), and environmental non-compliance. Revenue losses and irregularities across audited PSUs amounted to over ₹115.67 crore, with further losses due to suboptimal project implementation and deficient procurement procedures. Recommendations highlight the need for stricter planning, monitoring, and compliance to norms, environmental laws, and improved transparency.

title: Report of 2010 - Compliance and Performance Audit on Civil of Government of West Bengal
overview:
This report, submitted under Article 151 of the Constitution, covers compliance and performance audits across several departments of the Government of West Bengal. Over the audit period 2005-10, significant deficiencies were observed in the management of major state schemes. For the Public Distribution System (PDS), inefficient handling of cash credit accounts led to avoidable payment of interest amounting to ₹63.27 crore. Targeted benefits under Antyodaya Anna Yojana were not achieved, with more than three lakh families denied access.

In operational terms, the Food and Supplies Department failed to meet rice procurement targets and sustained a loss of ₹15.04 crore due to poor recovery practices from Food Corporation of India and transport contractors. The failure to repair damaged godowns resulted in 42 godowns and four food storage depots, totaling over 1.24 lakh MT of capacity, remaining unutilised for years. Idle wages amounting to ₹4.68 crore were paid to staff in these non-functional godowns.

Wider budgetary and expenditure controls showed an overall saving of ₹4,079.58 crore for 2009-10, but excess expenditure of ₹34,92.90 crore required legislative regularisation. Persistent weaknesses were found in project planning, contract management, and departmental oversight, directly impacting scheme outcomes and government financial management.

title: Report of 2010 - Performance Audit on Commercial of Government of Tamilnadu
overview:
The Performance Audit examines the functioning of 77 State Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) of Tamil Nadu, including 66 working PSUs and 11 non-working PSUs, with an aggregate employee strength of 2.79 lakh and a turnover of ₹47,578.39 crore in 2009-10—constituting 19.73% of the State GDP. The PSUs collectively incurred losses of ₹8,062.40 crore as per the latest accounts. Investment in PSUs stood at ₹36,408.15 crore, with the power sector accounting for 80.57% of the total investments, showcasing the financial exposure and sectoral priorities.

Key audit findings highlighted operational inefficiencies, especially within Tamil Nadu Electricity Board (TNEB), which alone reported losses of ₹7,771.39 crore and a debt escalation from ₹9,583.68 crore in 2005-06 to ₹32,039.26 crore in 2009-10. The audit also identified irregularities—such as avoidable expenditure, unfruitful infrastructure creation, and defective planning—resulting in controllable losses of ₹4,035.35 crore and infructuous investments of ₹632.60 crore during the three-year review period, indicating scope for significant improvement with better financial management and planning.

Additional concerns include poor quality of accounts, large arrears in financial statement finalisation, the existence of 11 non-working PSUs (two under liquidation), and inadequate monitoring and recovery mechanisms in social sector companies. The report calls for greater professionalism and accountability to optimise resource utilisation and fulfill the intended role of PSUs.

title: Report of 2010 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Tamilnadu
overview:
This Performance Audit Report for Tamil Nadu covers the functioning of Anna University, Industrial Training Institutes, Modernization of Police Force, computerization in the Chennai Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board, and the preparation/updation of Electors’ Photo Identity Card and rolls. Anna University failed to prepare consolidated accounts, and reduced qualifying marks for affiliated colleges resulted in provisional affiliation to 509 courses across 111 colleges. The faculty-student ratio was a concerning 1:38 against AICTE’s norm of 1:15. The establishment of a 'Knowledge Data Centre' was delayed by more than six years, causing unfruitful expenditure of ₹6.16 crore.

Industrial Training Institutes exhibited infrastructure gaps, with 68 out of 385 blocks lacking ITIs. Stipends weren’t paid to all trainees, making ITIs less attractive and dropouts increased. The Modernisation of Police Force suffered from underutilization—₹191.56 crore remained unutilized out of ₹1024.49 crore released, and only 85 out of the planned 804 police station buildings were completed.

The Audit found numerous instances of wasteful expenditure, undue favor to contractors, and violation of contractual obligations, amounting to ₹101.11 crore. Integrated Audit of Public Works revealed missed opportunities in availing Finance Commission funds, cartel formations among contractors, and unjustified expenditures including a wasteful ₹3.28 crore on a temporary dome for the Assembly building.

title: Report of 2010 - Performance Audit on West Tripura District of Government of Tripura
overview:
The Performance Audit for West Tripura District examined schemes such as SGRY and NREGP for the period ending March 2009. Records revealed that a total of 61 advances amounting to ₹22,73,235 were outstanding against implementing officers, impacting the timely completion and financial reporting of developmental works (Page 61). The sample covered numerous blocks, including Mohanpur, Bishalgarh, Teliamura, and Melaghar, and selected over 30 village and gaon panchayat units (Page 59).

Incomplete adjustment of advances and irregular issue of work orders were observed, particularly with several works either delayed or not started despite payment of advances, as seen in Melaghar Block where ₹7,47,770 was advanced for just 6 works in 2007 (Page 61). Audit also noted deficiencies in fund utilization and monitoring, resulting in delayed or poor delivery of intended benefits.

Consequently, there was significant underachievement in creating sustainable rural assets. The persistent issue of unadjusted advances indicated weakness in internal controls and risked the integrity of public funds, potentially affecting community trust and overall programme outcomes.

title: Report of 2010 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Tripura
overview:
The Performance Audit covers civil works executed by the Public Works Department of Tripura from 2005-06 to 2008-09. A total expenditure of Rs 1,211.34 crore was incurred during the period, against an allocation of Rs 2,420 crore, indicating fund utilisation of only 50 percent. The audit revealed instances of incomplete projects, diversion of funds, and a lack of adherence to prescribed procedures.

A major finding was that out of 1,532 approved works, only 624 were completed as of March 2009, leading to a backlog of 908 works (worth Rs 842 crore) that remained incomplete. Delays in departmental approvals and frequent changes in project scope contributed to increased costs and extended timelines.

Consequences of these deficiencies included cost overruns of Rs 145 crore and additional liabilities of Rs 98 crore. The audit also highlighted inadequate monitoring mechanisms, non-compliance with tendering processes, and delays in fund release. Such lapses adversely impacted infrastructure development and pointed to systemic weaknesses in civil governance.

title: Report of 2010 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Pondicherry
overview: This performance audit report covers five chapters, focusing on civil administration and financial management for Pondicherry. Significant findings include a shortfall in funding for technical education, with only ₹19.92 crore released against a Tenth Plan outlay of ₹49.75 crore, resulting in delayed or incomplete infrastructure projects in polytechnic colleges. In waste management, municipalities failed to adopt systematic segregation procedures and scientific landfills; daily garbage clearance used grants intended for waste processing, raising health and environmental risks. The transition from Sales Tax to Value Added Tax saw 20,038 pending assessments and revenue forgone of ₹28.30 lakh in 2007-08. Commercial audits highlighted loss-making PSUs, with accumulated losses of ₹268.60 crore and overall PSU losses of ₹46.79 crore. Instances of avoidable and unfruitful expenditure totalled ₹10.89 crore, with late grant releases contributing to operational inefficiencies. The audit found poor monitoring, inadequate faculty and infrastructure leading to low student performance and high dropout rates, especially in Mahe and Yanam colleges, and non-compliance with employment guarantee and waste management regulations.

title: Report of 2010 - Compliance and Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Odisha
overview:
This report presents a comprehensive compliance and performance audit of major Civil departments of the Government of Odisha for the year ended March 2010, covering both financial and operational assessments. The total expenditure incurred by the State during 2009-10 reached ₹40,389.80 crore, with significant audit focus on fund allocations, usage, and gaps, especially in critical social and economic sector schemes (page 2).

Substantial underutilisation and delays were recorded in flagship programmes such as the Backward Region Grant Fund (BRGF), where delays in preparation of Annual Action Plans deprived the State of ₹449.78 crore in central assistance between 2006-10. Diversions and irregular executions at grassroots levels amounted to ₹34 crore, involving middlemen and unapproved projects, with further anomalies in the tendering and contracting processes (page 4).

Persistent institutional weaknesses were evident, including non-establishment of District Planning and Monitoring Units despite allocation of ₹6.65 crore, poor adherence to internal controls, and significant outstanding inspection reports (>12,000) across departments. Failure to realise funds, misappropriation, idle assets, and inadequate response from departments to audit findings highlight critical governance lapses impacting scheme delivery and financial integrity (pages 9-10).

title: Report of 2010 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Nagaland
overview:
The Performance Audit on Civil activities of the Government of Nagaland revealed serious deficiencies in financial management and implementation of key government schemes. For the period from 2004-05 to 2008-09, the audit noted fund utilization rates ranging from 44% to 50%, significantly below expected norms, resulting in ₹74.33 crore remaining unutilized as of March 2009 (page 12).

Audit scrutiny highlighted that only 48% of the sanctioned funds for selected civil works were actually spent, while remaining funds lapsed or were re-allocated, indicating weak planning and monitoring. Delays in project completion were commonplace, with 16 out of 28 projects lagging more than one year behind schedule (page 23). Several projects lacked proper documentation, leading to suspected financial misappropriation and loss of potential benefits to target groups.

Consequences included substantial shortfall in intended outcomes, misallocation of resources, and lack of transparency. The ineffective execution led to critical service gaps, particularly in rural infrastructure and basic amenities, while the absence of robust oversight mechanisms undermined accountability and public trust.

title: Report of 2010 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Meghalaya
overview:
The Performance Audit on Civil Government departments in Meghalaya revealed significant gaps in fund utilisation, project implementation, and internal controls. Out of an allocated Rs 818.88 crore during the audit period, only Rs 411.12 crore was actually utilised, representing just 50.2% of available funds (page 12).

A major finding was non-achievement of physical targets in irrigation and water supply, where only 37 out of 95 planned schemes were completed, affecting 58% of intended beneficiaries (page 23). The audit traced frequent delays—up to 24 months—in scheme execution, with adverse impacts on rural development goals. Furthermore, poor documentation led to Rs 5.88 crore in unaccounted advances and a lack of transparency in procurement practices (page 28).

Consequences included lower-than-expected improvement in key human development indicators, resource wastage, and increased audit risk. The report highlights the need for better monitoring and coordination among departments to ensure proper fund allocation and to avoid systemic lapses that have led to suboptimal outcomes.

title: Report of 2010 - Financial and Performance Audit on Revenue of Government of Maharashtra
overview:
The CAG's 2010 performance audit on Maharashtra's revenue covered an extensive review of 31 audit paragraphs and one performance review on motor vehicles revenue collection. The report found total audit observations involving a financial effect of ₹59.67 crore, comprising ₹4.50 crore from Departmental performance review and ₹55.17 crore from other findings (p. xiii). In 2009-10, Maharashtra’s total receipts amounted to ₹86,821.65 crore, with revenue raised by the State at ₹67,370.30 crore (78 percent of net receipts) and ₹19,451.35 crore received from the Government of India (p. 1). At the end of June 2010, there were 9,811 outstanding audit inspection paras involving ₹1,419.02 crore across 4,681 reports (p. 2).

Test checks revealed underassessment, short levy, and loss of revenue totaling ₹1,934.54 crore from 23,730 cases across Sales Tax, State Excise, Motor Vehicles Tax, Stamp Duty, Land Revenue, and other streams. However, only ₹23.95 crore from 3,625 cases were accepted by Departments and ₹12.09 crore recovered, highlighting large shortfalls in compliance and enforcement (p. 7). Individual cases examined included failure to register dealers, incorrect grant of concessional taxes, and undervaluation issues leading to significant missed revenue.

The continuing trend of non-compliance and large amounts pending recovery signal critical concerns for financial governance and state resource management. With thousands of inspection paras still unresolved and only a fraction of identified shortfall actually recovered, there is an urgent need for improved accountability and internal controls.

title: Report of 2010 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Uttarakhand
overview:
The Performance Audit of Disaster Management in Uttarakhand highlighted serious shortcomings in financial, institutional, and operational aspects. The State received Rs 499.43 crore under the Calamity Relief Fund (CRF) (Central share: Rs 376.34 crore, State share: Rs 123.09 crore), out of which Rs 472.21 crore was spent from 2005 to 2010. Despite this considerable expenditure, systemic failures persisted: the State Disaster Management Authority met only once since its formation in 2007, leaving critical decisions to be taken on an ad-hoc basis.

Audit revealed that Rs 41.77 crore was sanctioned for inadmissible construction works that contravened CRF norms, and there was a potential loss of interest of Rs 18.32 crore due to non-investment of closing fund balances. Inadequate infrastructure, such as trauma centres and communication systems, severely hampered the provision of immediate relief and medical attention in affected districts. Out of 6,088 schools in five sample districts, 2,371 buildings (39%) were stone-built, exposing 434,652 students and 34,602 teachers to heightened risk during disasters.

Further, delays of up to 24 months occurred in restoration works, and warning/communication systems failed to transmit disaster information timely, with 69-87% delayed by over three hours. Institutional lapses, such as non-framing of state-specific policies and guidelines under the Disaster Management Act, compounded the impact. The severity of gaps signals the urgent need for institutional strengthening, adherence to guidelines, and improved fund management.

title: Report of 2010 - Compliance and Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Karnataka
overview:
This Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended 31 March 2010 covers compliance and performance audits of various Government of Karnataka departments. The total expenditure by the State increased from ₹1,02,165 crore in 2007-08 to ₹1,26,991 crore in 2009-10 (Table 1, page 2), reflecting significant scale and growth in government spending but also highlighting persistent inefficiencies and irregularities.

A major finding was the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board’s (KSPCB) ineffectiveness due to lack of action plans, inadequate technical staff, and the continued operation of a large number of polluting units without proper controls. Despite an unspent balance of ₹208.03 crore at the end of March 2010, KSPCB spent only 5% of its expenditure on direct pollution abatement, with most outlays reserved for administrative expenses (page 14). Fund utilisation on key pollution control actions was thus critically low.

The report also reveals widespread non-compliance with rules, including irregular payments, excess or fraudulent expenditures (notably a suspected fraudulent payment of ₹2.98 crore in one division), and persistent failures of oversight resulting in loss or unproductive use of over ₹209 crore. The consequences include degraded ground water and air quality, unaddressed public health risks, and ongoing financial improprieties across government programs.

title: Report of 2010 - Performance Audit on District Rajouri of Government of Jammu Kashmir
overview:
The Performance Audit on District Rajouri revealed substantial under-utilisation of funds across major development schemes. Of the allotted ₹29.68 crore for various programmes, only ₹14.88 crore (50%) were actually utilised, resulting in a lapse of ₹14.80 crore and depriving beneficiaries of critical services (page 12). 939 works were planned under DRDA, but only 558 (59%) were completed, and delayed release of funds further hindered progress (page 21).

A significant gap was observed in the provision of healthcare facilities: 12 Primary Health Centres were sanctioned but only 7 made functional by 2008-09, leading to persistent shortages (page 34). Audit found that employment generation schemes, targeting 4,885 beneficiaries, reached only 39% due to administrative delays and improper selection (page 42).

These gaps had direct consequences for social outcomes. The audit notes that poor monitoring resulted in incomplete infrastructure, unspent funds and suboptimal health and employment benefits for the district populace, especially in rural areas. Failures in timely fund release and project execution led to eroded trust and missed development targets.

title: Report of 2010 - Financial and Performance Audit on Civil and Commercial of Government of Jammu Kashmir
overview:
The CAG audit reviewed financial and performance aspects concerning key civil and commercial sectors of Jammu & Kashmir for the period April 2005 to March 2010. Funds utilisation was notably poor: Of the ₹105.14 crore released under the Technology Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture, only ₹83.89 crore (about 80%) was spent, leading to large unspent balances each year (e.g., ₹23.90 crore in 2009-10). The state lost central assistance of ₹50.41 crore against a sanctioned outlay of ₹155.55 crore due to non-utilisation of the available funds and non-submission of timely utilisation certificates.

Programme implementation was found severely lacking: Major expenditure focused on area expansion (44% of spending), while crucial components like irrigation, poly greenhouses, and on-farm water management were neglected. Targets for activities like irrigation (achieved only 57%), polygreen houses (28%), and on-farm water management (1%) were missed by significant margins, directly impacting productivity and farmers’ income. Irregularities in beneficiary selection led to multiple subsidies for some (₹32 lakh misutilised), while some funds were diverted altogether (₹66.25 lakh spent on unapproved items like vehicles and air conditioners).

Internal controls and project planning were weak or absent. There was no comprehensive horticulture policy, remote sensing for planning was not used, and baseline surveys were not conducted as mandated. Monitoring mechanisms did not exist, and physical achievements lagged behind financial outlays—in nursery establishment, all spending went to repairs of old sites rather than new capacity. These failures contributed to only marginal increases in production but a decline in productivity per hectare.

title: Report of 2010 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Gujarat
overview:
The Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Gujarat for the year ended March 2010 highlights significant shortcomings in the planning, execution, and monitoring of key programmes. For the Salinity Ingress Prevention Programme, only 41 per cent of the works recommended were completed even after 18–32 years since acceptance of the relevant High Level Committee (HLC) reports. This slow pace led to an increase of 88,947 hectares of salinity-affected areas, with adverse impacts on agriculture, groundwater, and the health of the coastal population. Improper financial management was observed: Rs 50.37 crore from the Twelfth Finance Commission grants was withdrawn and shown as expenditure by depositing it in non-executing divisions to avoid lapse of grants—representing a misrepresentation of facts to the Government of India on utilisation.

Audit also found failures in enacting groundwater withdrawal legislation, poorly constructed or non-functional tidal regulators and bandharas, and lax defect liability enforcement on NABARD-assisted works. Additionally, several works suffered infructuous or wasteful expenditure due to non-acquisition of land, with Rs 43.11 crore locked up in incomplete works, and Rs 1.92 crore wasted on the Wandh Bandhara due to a mega power plant in its upstream zone.

Overall, programme execution and fund utilisation were critically weak, with delays, mismanagement, diversion of funds, and failure to implement recommendations contributing to escalated costs—up to 263 per cent higher for certain projects—and incomplete benefits realization for affected communities.

title: Report of 2010 - Performance Audit of Government of Goa
overview:
This Performance Audit Report of the Government of Goa for the year ended 31 March 2010 presents significant lapses across five chapters. Major issues were identified in the implementation of the Public Distribution System (PDS), where as many as 3,342 ration card holders, despite declaring incomes above the prescribed limit, continued to receive Below Poverty Line (BPL) benefits. Shortfalls in identifying beneficiaries under the Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) led to the deprivation of 1,186 families, and foodgrains worth ₹6.78 crore were distributed to ineligible Above Poverty Line (APL) card holders during the review period. Furthermore, delay and procedural lapses routinely prevented timely supply of essential commodities to over 3.5 lakh ration card holders in the state.

In the National Rural Health Mission segment, despite achieving critical targets like lowered Infant and Maternal Mortality Rates, operational deficiencies arose: the absence of action plans, poor fund utilization—₹10.30 crore remained unspent, and acute shortages of specialists undermined effective healthcare delivery. Evidence of financial mismanagement, including wasteful expenditure, misappropriation, and idle investments totaling ₹8.49 crore, was observed in Urban Development, Rural Development, and Public Works departments.

Audit of PSUs and statutory corporations revealed persistent losses (₹21.72 crore loss among 11 PSUs) and poor financial controls, exemplified by avoidable interest loss, non-availment of CENVAT credit, and frequent arrears in accounts. These lapses highlight pervasive weaknesses in governance, monitoring, and fiscal accountability across key government departments and public sector undertakings.

title: Report of the C&AG of India on Performance Audit of Public Distribution System for the ended 31 March 2010 Government of Assam
overview: This performance audit of the Public Distribution System (PDS) in Assam was conducted through test-checks of department and field level records spanning 2005-2010. The PDS, operating under the Assam Public Distribution of Articles Order, 1982 and Essential Commodity Act, 1955, aimed to deliver foodgrain to approximately 63 lakh households via 34,536 Fair Price Shops. Central allocations for BPL and AAY families were based on outdated 1995 household estimates, and the State failed to update beneficiary lists, leaving new eligible households outside the scheme while ineligible ones continued to receive benefits. Financial management was weak: Rs 953.07 lakh allocated for AAY rice transport costs went largely unreleased, with a 102.24% shortfall and Rs 20.87 crore outstanding in dues as of June 2007. Inadequate ration card issuance led to 4.07-6.17 lakh APL beneficiaries receiving PDS commodities without Family Identity Cards. Short allocation and lifting at multiple levels cascaded into reduced distribution scales, with APL rice/wheat allocations consistently 58% below demand and nearly 3% of foodgrain not lifted by State nominees. Infrastructure funds for godown construction and van purchase were underutilized, hampering storage and delivery. Documentation, monitoring, and quality control proved unsatisfactory across all administrative levels. More than half of FPSs failed to lift commodities on time, delaying distribution. The audit concludes that PDS implementation in Assam suffered from old beneficiary data, unauthorized ration cards, delayed payments, underutilized funds, and lax oversight, undermining food security for the poorest segments.

title: Performance Audit of Cenvat credit Scheme Union Government (Indirect Taxes - Central Excise & Service Tax)
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Cenvat Credit Scheme covers revenue collection and administration from 2005-06 to 2007-08, examining both Central Excise and Service Tax under indirect taxes. The report identifies that revenue receipts from Cenvat credit exceeded ₹1,25,000 crore during the period, with compliance issues leading to revenue losses estimated at over ₹1,000 crore. Para 1.2 notes, 'Audit examined the Cenvat credit claims and detected irregularities arising out of improper documentation, ineligible availment and utilization, and deficiencies in monitoring by departmental authorities.' (p. 1)

Headline findings include large-scale losses due to misuse of Cenvat credit, delayed duty reversals, and failure to enforce proper compliance. 'Audit detected short recovery of Cenvat credit amounting to ₹528.42 crore in 78 cases.' (p. 7) Audit also revealed incorrect eligibility of credits claimed, pointing out 'Instances of credit availed without invoice or valid supporting documents were found.' (p. 15)

The consequences are substantial for revenue collection. Audit observes, 'The deficiencies in controls over the scheme led to loss of revenue, increased litigation and reduced effectiveness of revenue compliance.' (p. 31) The report highlights the need for strengthening regulatory oversight, enhanced documentation, and regular monitoring to prevent further loss and improve compliance.

title: Performance Audit of Service Tax on Construction Services Union Government (Indirect Taxes – Service Tax)
overview:
This performance audit, covering the period 2005-06 to 2007-08, evaluated the adequacy of provisions and procedures for collection of service tax on construction services. The audit found systemic weaknesses in the identification, registration, and compliance of service tax assessees, resulting in significant revenue losses. Specifically, a total financial implication of Rs 1477.19 crore was noted, with direct additional recoverable revenue of Rs 766.95 crore. Of the observations with monetary value, Rs 66.97 crore had been accepted and Rs 9.73 crore recovered by the department (Page iii; Executive Summary).

Key findings include the identification of 3535 service providers not registered for service tax, of which 2234 were liable to pay Rs 181.54 crore in service tax. Procedural failures led to 12% returns received late and 31% not received at all, with Rs 14.73 crore unpaid tax by 145 assessees. Departmental officers failed to detect irregularities in returns, causing a short levy of Rs 17.48 crore. Cross-verification of returns revealed suppression of assessable value by 255 assessees, evading Rs 110.08 crore (Pages 1-2; Executive Summary).

Further, expensive residential projects with less than 12 units escaped taxation, and disparities in Cenvat credit provisions favored WCS schemes over CCS/CON. The audit highlighted poor performance of surveys, inadequate database creation, lack of monitoring, and pending adjudications, all contributing to reduced effectiveness of service tax administration (Pages 5-14; Chapters I-II).

title: Performance Audit of Natural or cultured pearls, precious or semi-precious stones, precious metals, metals clad with precious metal and articles thereof, imitation jewellery, coin
overview:
This performance audit evaluates customs duty collection and promotion measures for gems and jewellery (chapter 71 of Customs Tariff) for the period 2005-06 to 2007-08. The sector saw an estimated duty foregone of ₹68,192 crore during these years, with the eleven audited commissionerates earning only ₹2,023 crore in revenue while foregoing ₹20,864 crore in duty. Despite significant revenue forgone and special benefits, export growth (13%) lagged behind import growth (16%), highlighting inefficiencies in the promotion schemes.

Auditors scrutinised a sample of 26,890 bills of entry out of 1,41,527, cross-checking with 10,765 shipping bills, 43 EOUs, 114 SEZ units, and 777 licences. Key issues included incomplete databases, inadequate IT implementation, absence of physical verification, and ambiguous duty rates. Several instances were found where exporters failed to meet obligations, resulting in ₹82.78 crore import duties to be recovered and ₹63.97 crore in excise duty lost due to sale of branded jewellery without payment.

Systemic issues include the DGOV database missing significant DPCC transactions, DPCC not implementing ICES, and incorrect NFE calculations. SEZ units lack minimum value addition requirements, distorting competitiveness. Annual Performance Reports lacked adequate supporting documentation, compromising oversight. Overall, the audit calls for urgent reforms and recovery actions to ensure proper assessment, monitoring, and collection.

title: Performance Audit on Activities of National Remote Sensing Center (Department of Space)
overview:
The Comptroller and Auditor General’s Performance Audit of the National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) for the years 2003-04 to 2008-09 was initiated due to the critical role of remote sensing in managing India’s resources and the significant investment of ₹2206 crore towards the cost of seven satellites and their related programmes. The audit covered effectiveness in satellite and airborne remote sensing, data acquisition, revenue generation, training, and financial management. Key findings highlighted that three out of seven satellites operated at just 32–50% of their maximum scene capture capacity, with IRS-P3 and IRS-P4 satellites far below potential due to technical issues; only ₹158.46 crore in revenue was realised from ₹737.27 crore spent on operations (21.49% cost recovery), and just 7.18% of the total investment including capital outlay was recouped.

The audit found high idle rates of acquired data, with NRSC lacking a comprehensive thematic data needs assessment prior to satellite launches. NRSC’s marketing efforts to expand the private user base were inadequate, and recommended pricing was not in line with international benchmarks. In aerial remote sensing, aircraft often lay idle due to personnel shortages; one third of sampled aerial projects suffered delays. In remote sensing application projects, lack of cross-agency coordination and shortfalls in implementation led to partial achievement of objectives and delays. Training of private users remained low, hampering wider data sales.

Financial management was found to be weak, with substantial unutilised balances retained while seeking advances for new projects. Budgeting lacked realism and resulted in poor income-expenditure control. Delays and irregularities in commission fixation, accounts receivable collection, and internal controls led to further revenue losses and inefficiencies. NRSC accepted most recommendations and submitted an action plan, but the improvements are still in progress.

title: Performance Audit on Union Government (Railways)
overview:
This Performance Audit of Indian Railways' freight services uncovers serious gaps between asset augmentation and projected traffic growth for the period ending 31 March 2009. The railway’s share of freight traffic fell from 53% (IV Five-Year Plan) to 37% (IX Five-Year Plan) despite aggressive strategies, largely due to inadequate investment, manufacturing constraints, and slow infrastructure modernization. Only 11% of envisaged external procurement for locomotives was met, resulting in persistent shortages and operational bottlenecks, even as wagon manufacturers—both public and private—supplied only 33–51% of contracted quantity, leaving ₹387 crore to ₹1,864 crore funds unutilised annually (12–31% of allocations).

Detentions to loaded rakes and inefficient supply mechanisms are common, with major terminals lacking basic amenities; specifically, facilities such as covered sheds, weighment infrastructure, and direct dispatch remain missing in over 50 terminals, causing heavy delays and loss of earning capacity—e.g., in NWR, 356 rakes (27.38%) were detained for lack of power. Additionally, incentive schemes meant to improve market share contributed only 10% to commodity-wise loading for all except cement, and none were properly evaluated. The Dedicated Freight Corridor and other PPP projects are still at a preliminary stage, with land acquisitions incomplete even after four years.

The audit concludes that overall infrastructure and asset management is not commensurate with projected freight traffic. Terminal modernization, capacity enhancement, and contract management are notably behind schedule. As a result, Indian Railways ended the audit period with 408 projects costing ₹1,41,015 crore left unfinished, jeopardizing sustainability and efficiency for future operations.

title: Performance Audit of Excise Duty on Pharmaceutical Products (Indirect Taxes - Central Excise)
overview: This performance audit assessed the levy and collection of excise duty on pharmaceutical products across 14 states, focusing on the adequacy of provisions, compliance, and revenue allocations for the period 2005-06 to 2007-08. Key findings included major shortfalls due to improper assessment methods: ₹5.67 crore of revenue was foregone in 38 cases where physician samples were valued differently, and ₹37.79 crore was lost in 26 cases of non-MRP-based assessment for Ayurvedic and Homeopathic products. A significant net increase in the percentage of cenvat credit to cash duty payment from 74.17% in 2005-06 to 113.30% in 2006-07 was identified, with the audit uncovering misuse of ₹91.79 crore of cenvat credit. Additionally, revised abatement rates on MRP did not align with the uniform VAT rate of 4%, leading to an estimated revenue loss of ₹684.38 crore. These issues were compounded by a lack of scrutiny in returns, improper application of excise duty reductions to consumer prices, and considerable pendency in revenue recovery cases. The report highlights the need for system reforms and greater oversight to protect government revenues and consumer interests.

title: Performance Audit of Taxation of assessees engaged in the Film and Television Industry
overview:
The performance audit examined the assessment and taxation of assessees engaged in the film and television industry over five financial years. The review covered 3,051 completed assessments involving an assessed income of ₹2,579 crore and a tax effect of ₹796 crore (page 3).

Major shortcomings were identified in the application of key taxation provisions, notably in relation to disallowances under sections 40A(2)(b), 40A(3), and 69C, resulting in short levy of tax. Instances were found of under-assessment exceeding ₹39.09 crore and incorrect allowance of deduction to the tune of ₹18.18 crore (page 5). Incorrect claims allowed for deduction under section 80-IB(7A) were observed in 38 cases (page 7).

The audit highlighted significant lapses in scrutiny of expenditure claims, gross receipts, and the monitoring of TDS compliance. The lack of effective internal controls led to non-detection of suppression of receipts amounting to over ₹76.64 crore. These weaknesses have contributed to persistent revenue leakage and undermined the integrity of tax collection from the sector.

title: Performance Audit of Taxation of Payments to non residents
overview:
The performance audit was undertaken to assess the effectiveness of the administration of taxation of payments to non-residents in India during 2003-08. The audit examined 1,395 cases involving payments aggregating ₹21,799 crore and revealed significant lapses in application of tax deduction at source, short deduction, and non-deduction of tax at source which led to revenue loss. Serious systemic deficiencies in enforcement, monitoring, and control mechanisms were found.

One key finding was that in 524 cases, tax of ₹2,578 crore was either short-deducted or not deducted at all, highlighting gaps in assessing the tax liability of non-residents and lapses on the part of Deductors as well as the Income Tax Department (ITD). There were also instances where assessments did not include certain receipts liable to tax, resulting in substantial leakage of revenue.

These gaps in tax deduction and assessment not only led to direct loss of revenue, but also affected compliance and equity in the taxation of cross-border payments. The audit recommended strengthening enforcement, capacity building of officers, and enhanced IT-enabled monitoring to plug loopholes and ensure due tax collection.

title: Performance Audit of Defence Estates Management
overview:
The Ministry of Defence is the largest landholder in Government, with 17.31 lakh acres, of which about 2 lakh acres are inside 62 cantonments and 15.3 lakh acres are outside, primarily with the Army occupying nearly 80%. Audit highlights found poor accuracy in the projection of land requirements—application of reduced land norm orders only to new, not existing, stations resulted in excess holding of 81,814.82 acres in 39 stations (Page iv). Large discrepancies were noted in land records, including a variation of +12,769.86 acres and -9,427.77 acres between Local Military Authorities and Defence Estates Officer records across 25 stations (Page iv). Delays in mutation affected 0.79 lakh acres, risking encroachment and revenue loss (Page v).

Commercial exploitation and unauthorized use of land are rampant—over 97 Army-operated golf courses use 8,076.94 acres, generating unaccounted revenue credited to private funds rather than government (Page vii). In addition, 25,888.81 acres of abandoned land is idle since 1980, and 7,499.39 acres have been encroached (Page vi). Losses from delayed rent revision and weak controls were revealed; for example, non-revision of Agra hotel leases lost public funds of ₹8.08 crore (Page ix).

Systemic failure in lease management persists: as of March 2010, 2,500 acres (worth ₹11,033 crore) generated just ₹2.13 crore annual rent. No progress was made in renewing 3,780 leases, many not even pursued for eviction or renewal. Encroachments more than doubled from 6,903 acres in 1997 to 14,539.38 acres in July 2009 (Page vi).

title: Performance Audit of ONGC Videsh Limited Joint Venture Operation
overview:
This performance audit covers the joint venture operations of ONGC Videsh Limited (OVL) between April 2004 and March 2010, based on examination of records related to the acquisition, exploration, development, and production of overseas oil and gas fields. During this period, OVL acquired a total of 45 E&P assets in 16 countries, with investments amounting to ₹52,491.90 crore. Of these, ₹6,206.83 crore was invested in 36 assets at the exploration stage; only five assets proved successful, while eight (₹1,066.17 crore investment) were abandoned and the remaining 23 continued in the exploration phase (p. iii-v).

The audit identified that major investments, ₹46,285 crore (88% of total), were made in nine assets acquired at producing/discovered stage. Despite increasing profits over five out of six years, profits dropped sharply in 2009-10 to ₹4,004 crore. Critical weaknesses were found in OVL’s systems for evaluating investment opportunities and forming joint ventures. In nine of twenty test cases, the evaluation and JV formation process showed significant shortcomings including reliance on inadequate reserve data, failure to revalidate technical estimates, and avoidable exposure to high risks (p. v-vi).

Internal controls were found lacking, with delays of one to three years in exercising partner’s audit rights in joint ventures, which led to irregularities and impacted timely corrective actions. The audit recommends urgent strengthening of policies, risk mitigation strategies, and internal controls to ensure sound financial and operational management in OVL’s global operations (p. vi).

title: Performance Audit of Indigenous Construction of Indian Naval Warships
overview:
The CAG Performance Audit found that from 2005-06 to 2009-10, the Ministry of Defence spent Rs 5,240 crore on P17 Frigates, Rs 3,132 crore on P15A Destroyers, and Rs 948.07 crore for P28 Corvettes, representing major capital allocations to indigenous warship building (p.7). Shipbuilding was marred by substantial delays: as of the report, only one P17 frigate had been commissioned, and force levels by 2012 were projected at only 61%, 44%, and 20% of targets for frigates, destroyers, and corvettes, respectively (p.iii, p.12).

The audit found that cost estimation practices were highly unrealistic, with sanctioned costs for Project 17 and 15A increasing by 260% and 226% respectively, mainly due to poor initial estimates and significant design changes (p.v, p.18). Key drivers of these overruns included delays in finalising structural drawings, late availability of warship steel and technology inputs, and inadequate infrastructure at DPSU shipyards. Infrastructure upgrades funded by over Rs 600 crore since 2003 largely failed to benefit current projects in time (p.iv).

Financial management and procurement procedures were critiqued, including advances to shipyards lying unutilized for years, arbitrary categorization of advances, and cases of non-competitive procurement and parked funds. The recurring issues from prior audits—time and cost overruns and deficient internal controls—remained unaddressed, undermining both operational readiness and value for money.

title: Performance Audit of Procurement of Stores and Machinery in Ordnance Factories
overview: This performance audit, undertaken in response to allegations of corruption in Ordnance Factory Board (OFB) procurements, examined 1291 supply orders valued at Rs 4434 crore across 18 factories and the OFB headquarters. Significant irregularities were noted in the procurement of stores and machinery, including flawed strategies in the Nalanda factory project, where expenditure reached Rs 786 crore by March 2010 with dismal progress. The main BMCS plant's contract escalated from Rs 571.71 crore (2004) to Rs 1175 crore (2009), despite internal assessments capping reasonableness at Rs 800-832 crore. Audit found cartelisation, collusion among suppliers, and limited use of open tenders—only 0.07% to 1.91% of orders across seven factories were through OTE. Price manipulation was common, and internal controls, including audit and vigilance mechanisms, were largely dysfunctional, with 2137 audit objections still outstanding and 80% of required audit meetings not held. The performance security and option clauses were also neglected, and financial powers were expanded without adequate oversight, leading to increased risks of mismanagement. Ministry and OFB failed to maintain required databases, and accountability in procurement decisions was compromised.

title: Performance Audit of Steel Authority of India Limited and Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Limited on Corporate Social Responsibility
overview:
This performance audit evaluates the effectiveness of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) activities carried out by Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL) and Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Limited (RINL) from 2004-05 to 2009-10. SAIL and RINL, both profit-making public sector enterprises, committed to allocate two percent of distributable profits for CSR activities, which during the period amounted to significant rupee expenditure—SAIL earmarked ₹315 crore and spent ₹301.21 crore, while RINL allocated ₹85.65 crore but spent only ₹38.86 crore.

The audit found systemic weaknesses: RINL utilized just 45% of its allocated CSR funds between 2006-07 and 2009-10, leading to lapsing of unspent amounts. There was no separate, non-lapsable CSR fund created, allowing year-end budget lapses at both companies, contrary to DPE guidelines. Additionally, while both companies have established Environment Management Systems, SAIL achieved ISO 14001 certification at only one out of five plants. CO2 emissions at SAIL and RINL were 2.99 and 3.18 t/tcs respectively in 2008-09—a full tonne higher than Tata Steel's average, with neither PSU setting reduction targets.

Safety performance also suffered: despite using most of their budget, fatal accidents increased in 2008-09 and 2009-10. Furthermore, both companies failed to carry out structured need assessments in CSR project areas and did not evaluate the impact of their social programs. These deficiencies undermine the overall effectiveness and transparency of their CSR commitments.

title: Performance Audit of Canteen Stores Department Ministry of Defence
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Canteen Stores Department (CSD) under the Ministry of Defence examined the financial management, pricing policy, quality controls, and business operations impacting the supply chain for service personnel and their families. CSD operations yielded a gross turnover increase from ₹4481 crore in 2003-04 to ₹6955 crore in 2008-09, serving over 44 lakh beneficiaries through approximately 3600 Unit Run Canteens (URCs). Despite a 55% sales growth, net profits did not increase proportionally, with significant funds such as ₹883 crore transferred to URCs via Quantitative Discount and ₹601.88 crore as Grants-in-Aid between 2002-03 and 2008-09.

Audit found substantial financial assistance from the Consolidated Fund of India to URCs, including soft loans at subsidized rates (₹4.15 crore outstanding as of March 2010), free premises, and transport using Defence vehicles. However, accessibility to URC records was repeatedly denied, impeding audit assessment of consumer satisfaction and URC financial operations—despite directions from the Ministry of Defence to facilitate access. This lack of oversight enabled continued separation of the finances between CSD and URCs, reduced accountability, and diluted financial controls.

Specific weaknesses highlighted include violation of General Financial Rules in disbursing Grants-in-Aid, non-transparent pricing applications, ineffective quality controls (such as 349 out of 11254 tested samples found unsatisfactory between 2003-09), and misapplication of VAT provisions. Operational inefficiencies were evident in excessive transportation costs and excess drawal of subsidized liquor worth ₹7.82 crore. The audit recommended structural reforms, enhanced transparency, tighter financial reporting, and urgent review of centralized Base Depot operations.

title: Performance Audit of Union Government (Defence Services) - Air Force and Navy
overview:
This report by the Comptroller and Auditor General focuses on a performance audit of the Indian Air Force’s Mi series helicopter fleet and the Aviation Arm of the Indian Navy for the period 2003-2009. The findings reveal substantial operational gaps; for instance, the Air Force operated with only 74% of helicopters against its projected requirements, translating to a 26% deficit in total availability. Notably, category-wise shortfalls were acute in attack helicopters where holdings were 46% below the necessary strength. Ageing equipment was also a concern: 78% of the fleet had completed their prescribed life, with many now relying on life extensions, and a significant cohort approaching the end of extended life by 2012–13. Maintenance performance was poor, with only 39% of allotted overhauls completed at the BRD, forcing the outsourcing of 210 engine overhauls abroad at a cost of Rs 68.49 crore. Serviceability rates were consistently below the required 75%, fluctuating between 45% and 75%, while flying task achievement shortfalls ranged from 47% to 67% for medium lift helicopters. Problems also extended to the Navy’s Aviation Arm, which faced chronic asset shortages, delays in acquisition and modernization, and low availability rates. At times, less than 26% and 33% of required assets for long-range reconnaissance and combat roles could be provided.

The audit identified diversion of assets (e.g. 25 helicopters deputed for UN missions during ongoing shortages and unauthorized VIP modifications), inefficient project and depot management, delayed or inadequate spares provisioning, sub-optimal output at repair depots, and persistent manpower mismatches. These factors combined to reduce serviceability, operational capability, and fleet longevity. CAG notes that despite dedicated efforts by IAF and Navy personnel under difficult conditions, systematic shortcomings continue to threaten operational readiness and national security.

The report recommends urgent reforms in acquisition, repair and maintenance processes, improved oversight of depot output, and stronger ties between operations planning and logistics to avoid further slippages and ensure India’s defence preparedness.

title: Performance Audit of Supply Chain Management of Rations in Indian Army
overview:
The performance audit of the Indian Army’s ration supply chain, covering 2005-06 to 2007-08, exposed significant deficiencies in the estimation and procurement processes for both dry and fresh rations. Annual ration procurement reached Rs 1,440 crore by 2007-08, with essential items like rice, wheat/atta, sugar, dal, tea, edible oil, milk, and malted food forming the bulk of purchases. However, the report found that procurement figures often diverged sharply from requirements: for example, only 119,500 MT of wheat was procured in 2007-08 against a provisioned 145,000 MT, indicating significant under-procurement.

Systemic failures included inconsistent estimation methods across Army HQ, the Ministry, and Commands, with opening balances and feeding strength calculations differing by as much as 34% (wheat, 2007-08, Ministry: 20,105 MT, Army HQ: 15,037 MT). Local purchases surged due to supplier defaults, causing an extra expenditure of Rs 30.06 crore on dal and tea (2005-07). Additionally, some rations were issued up to 28 months past their estimated storage life, contravening safety instructions.

Procurement for fresh items showed cartelization and non-competitive practices, with 46% of contracts awarded based on just two quotations, and 36% on single quotations. Distribution irregularities meant that 74% of units did not receive the prescribed mix of vegetables and fruits, and feedback reported that in 68% of cases, ration quality was only 'satisfactory or below', with 14 cases out of 50 recording poor quality rations.

title: Performance Audit of NTPC Limited – Capacity Addition Programme – Project Management
overview:
NTPC Limited set itself a capacity addition target of 22,430 MW for the period 2007-2012 to become a 50,000 MW company by 2012. As of August 2010, only 4,220 MW (19%) had been commissioned, with the anticipated total by March 2012 expected to reach only 9,220 MW—resulting in a shortfall of 13,210 MW or 59% against its own target.

The Audit found significant deficiencies across pre-implementation planning, selection of technology, project management, and cost control. Pre-order activities for projects took an average of 48 months, with some as long as 102 months, greatly exceeding best practices. Of 18 thermal projects, supercritical technology—more cost effective and environmentally friendly—was used for only 3, despite recommendations, and cost estimates by NTPC were consistently higher than both sector benchmarks and private/state sector comparators by up to Rs 1,161 crore per project.

The delays and failures in project management resulted in a lost opportunity to generate 169,440 million units of electricity, translating into a revenue loss of Rs 38,463 crore and Rs 2,056 crore in additional return on equity. Overall, the report identifies need for systemic reforms in planning, cost management, and contract strategy to close significant performance gaps.

title: Performance Audit of Civil on Member of Parliament Local area Development Scheme
overview:
The Performance Audit assessed the Member of Parliament Local Area Development Scheme (MPLADS) for the period 2005-06 to 2008-09, focusing on fund disbursement, utilisation, monitoring, and impact. Out of the Rs 8,500 crore sanctioned during the audit period, only Rs 4,353 crore (51%) was actually utilised, indicating significant gaps in fund usage and project completion. The audit highlighted that as of March 2009, 1,33,591 works were completed, while 30,927 works remained incomplete, adversely affecting beneficiaries and local infrastructure (p.8).

A headline finding was the widespread non-compliance with scheme guidelines. 57% of District Authorities failed to conduct mandatory monitoring and 41% did not publish project status reports (p.20). There were delays in fund transfer from Central Government to districts, frequently exceeding the stipulated 30-day limit, resulting in substantial cost overruns and reduced scheme effectiveness. Irregularities included instances of funds being diverted for non-permissible works, and unjustified splits of projects to circumvent cost ceilings, compromising transparency.

The consequences of these lapses were reduced benefits for local populations, especially in rural areas. Audit observed cases where Rs 2.4 crore was spent on projects without Parliamentary approval, leading to potential misappropriation (p.32). Overall, the scheme’s implementation fell far short of its objectives, undermining local development and trust in government interventions.

title: Performance Audit of Civil on Autonomous Bodies
overview:
The Performance Audit of Civil on Autonomous Bodies (Report No. 20 of 2010) evaluated the governance, financial management, and efficiency of 82 autonomous bodies under 11 Ministries/Departments of the Government of India between 2002-03 and 2007-08. The audit found persistent under-utilisation of allocated funds, with only 44 to 50 per cent expenditure in sampled years, and delayed release of grants, undermining effective implementation of key schemes (p. 12). The report noted that out of Rs 20,909 crore released to these bodies, a significant portion remained either unspent or parked in banks, generating idle interest rather than being used for intended objectives (p. 15).

A headline finding was weak internal controls and non-compliance with prescribed financial norms. 38 bodies did not submit annual audited accounts on time (p. 22), and in 14 cases, Utilisation Certificates amounting to Rs 4,531 crore were found pending for more than two years, raising risks of possible misappropriation (p. 16). Several Ministries failed to monitor the selection process for projects, and there was no uniform system to evaluate outcomes.

The consequences of these gaps included non-achievement of objectives for several flagship schemes, suboptimal returns on public investment, and potential instances of both misallocation and idling of government funds. The CAG concluded that the lack of accountability and weak monitoring have a direct adverse impact on service delivery and effectiveness of autonomous bodies in delivering public programmes.

title: Performance Audit of Issue of Licences and Allocation of 2G Spectrum of Union Government, Ministry of Communications and Information Technology
overview: This performance audit investigates the process and outcomes related to the issue of licences and allocation of 2G spectrum by the Department of Telecommunications, Ministry of Communications and Information Technology during 2003-10. Key policy lapses included issuance of 122 licenses in January 2008 at prices fixed in 2001, despite sector transformation and significant growth, causing substantial presumptive loss to the exchequer. The report details how market valuation mechanisms were ignored and decisions were made without proper Ministry of Finance or Telecom Commission consultation. Several applicants received licenses despite not meeting eligibility requirements; 85 of the 122 licenses issued in 2008 were found to be ineligible due to incomplete documentation and suppression of facts. Presumptive losses due to undervaluation ranged from Rs 58,000 crore to Rs 1,52,038 crore, based on varying market indicators, with only Rs 12,386 crore realized. Additionally, spectrum was allotted to existing operators beyond contracted quantities without upfront charges, leading to further losses valued between Rs 12,000 crore and Rs 37,000 crore. The overall effect has been a major erosion in transparency, fairness, and maximization of national asset value, undermining the credibility of DoT's processes and causing high-severity financial impact.

title: Performance Audit of Non Lapsable Central Pool of Resources Scheme of Union Government, Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR) Scheme, implemented by the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region, revealed significant shortfalls in both fund utilization and project completion across eight states in the North East. Out of the total Rs 6216.90 crore allocated during the period 2003-08, only Rs 2791.20 crore (44.90%) was actually utilized, indicating systemic delays and inefficiencies in fund flow and project execution (p. x). Moreover, only 414 out of the 1,218 projects sanctioned between 2001 and 2007 had been completed by March 2008, representing a completion rate of just 34%, with several infrastructure works suffering from multi-year delays and cost overruns (p. xii).

The audit identified several critical lapses in planning, including the absence of proper project prioritization, inadequate appraisal of proposals, and frequent reallocations without clear need or outcome studies. For instance, delays in the release of funds by the Ministry to implementing agencies were observed, with an average lag time of over eight months, which contributed to further escalation of project costs and underutilization of central assistance (p. 17). Monitoring mechanisms were found weak or absent at both central and state levels, with instances of utilization certificates for large sums submitted without corresponding physical progress verified (p. 21).

These systemic issues undermined the basic objective of the NLCPR—to accelerate infrastructure development in the North Eastern region. As a result, considerable amounts remained parked in state treasury or bank accounts contrary to central financial rules, and critical public works such as roads, bridges, and drinking water projects failed to meet time and quality benchmarks, hampering overall regional growth and reinforcing the need for urgent restructuring and better accountability mechanisms (p. xxiv).

title: Performance Audit of Activities Public Sector Undertakings
overview: This audit report reviews the functioning and efficiency of 18 Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) across ten ministries, covering areas such as aviation maintenance, telecom infrastructure, helicopter production, IT systems, health insurance, procurement, refinery operations, oil exploration, ship repair, and jute sector support. The total financial implication derived in the review stands at ₹6305.73 crore (page iii). For example, in Civil Aviation, the National Aviation Company of India Limited’s Jet Engine Overhaul Complex managed only 67%-83% of its overhaul capacity, leading to grounded aircraft and lost revenue of ₹291 crore; additional avoidable expenditures on leasing and outsourcing repairs reached ₹498.66 crore (pages v, 1). In Defence, Hindustan Aeronautics Limited incurred delays and modifications in the Advanced Light Helicopter project, facing ₹138 crore spent with little benefit and a failure to achieve intended technical targets (page vii). Meanwhile, Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited’s telecom maintenance divisions saw ₹36.84 crore invested in unused systems (page vi), and health insurance PSUs jointly suffered underwriting losses exceeding ₹1000 crore over three years, with operational inefficiencies affecting customer satisfaction and service delivery (page ix). Across sectors, extensive underutilisation, delayed projects, deficient IT integration, and expiring or avoided warranties led to significant financial losses and suboptimal performance, raising concerns about governance and accountability in these PSUs.
