title: Performance Audit of Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme AIBP of Union Government, Ministry of Water Resources
overview:
The Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme (AIBP) was launched by the Ministry of Water Resources to expedite completion of ongoing irrigation projects. Between 1996-97 and 2008-09, Rs 36,341 crore was released for 266 major/medium projects and 10,132 surface water minor irrigation schemes, as well as for Command Area Development and Water Management (CAD&WM) projects. Despite these allocations, the audit found that fund utilisation ranged from only 44 to 50 percent, and physical achievements were significantly below targets, with only 8.85 lakh hectares of new irrigation potential actually created out of the targeted 28.42 lakh hectares by March 2009.

The audit identified delays in granting central assistance, inadequate project monitoring, and lack of clear guidelines for project selection and approval. Numerous projects suffered from time overruns (averaging more than five years), and frequent revisions in cost estimates were observed, with cost escalations up to 223 percent in some cases. These weaknesses contributed to incomplete works, delayed benefits to intended populations, and inefficient use of public funds.

The consequences of these lapses included continued water scarcity in critical regions, financial burden on states, and increasing gap between irrigation potential created and actually utilized, undermining the stated objectives of the AIBP and overall agricultural productivity.

title: Performance Audit of National Library, Union Government, Ministry of Culture
overview:
The performance audit of the National Library highlighted serious lapses in financial and administrative management. Out of the total plan allocation of Rs 34.31 crore during 2004-09, only Rs 16.76 crore (49%) was utilized for the intended purposes, reflecting significant underutilisation of allocated funds and depriving the library of crucial infrastructure and service upgradation (p. x, Executive Summary). Non-utilisation of allocated plan funds resulted in stalling of critical modernization, acquisition, and conservation works for several years.

Key audit findings included lack of transparency in procurement, with only 48% of the books and periodicals acquired through the prescribed selection procedure. Drastic delays in the computerisation project led to only partial completion of digitisation targets, with less than 30% of rare books digitised against the set goal (p. 27, Chapter II). Additionally, Rs 2.15 crore was blocked in idle equipment, and Rs 89 lakh worth of procurement was questioned due to irregular procedures (p. 34, Chapter III).

The overall deficiencies have adversely impacted the Library’s ability to provide modern services, meet users’ expectations, and preserve invaluable heritage collections. The lack of skilled manpower, improper planning and procedural violations resulted in inefficient delivery and risked the preservation and accessibility of the national archival resource.

title: Report of 2010 - Performance Audit on Revenue Receipt of Government of Andhra Pradesh
overview:
The performance audit of the revenue receipts of Government of Andhra Pradesh identified significant shortfalls in the realisation and collection of taxes, fees and dues. The audit covered the period from 2004-05 to 2008-09 and examined records relating to major revenue departments such as Commercial Taxes, Stamps and Registration, State Excise, Land Revenue and Transport, revealing a cumulative shortfall of ₹2,354 crore in revenue collection against budget estimates.

The audit found that the Department of Commercial Taxes alone reported revenue losses of ₹1,011 crore due to non-detection of suppression of turnover, incorrect application of rates and irregular grant of concessions. There was delay in issuance of demand notices and weak monitoring which contributed to accumulation of arrears amounting to ₹2,227 crore as of March 2009. Further, the audit observed instances of misclassification of receipts, under-assessment, and lack of coordination among departments.

The consequences of these deficiencies included erosion of the State’s resource base, inadequate funds for planned development works, and loss of public trust in tax administration. The audit recommends immediate corrective measures to plug systemic gaps, ensure effective monitoring, and enhance transparency in revenue administration.

title: Report of 2010 - Performance Audit on Revenue of Government of Andhra Pradesh
overview:
The report covers revenue receipts of the Government of Andhra Pradesh for the year ended 31 March 2010, highlighting results from the audit of sales tax/VAT, state excise, taxes on motor vehicles, stamp duty and registration fees, land revenue, entertainment and betting tax, as well as other tax and non-tax receipts. The audit identified a financial impact of Rs 1,168.41 crore across 46 paragraphs and a performance review on ‘Interest Receipts on loans’ worth Rs 976.82 crore. Notable findings include short levy, non/short realisation, and misapplication of rates in several tax categories, such as Rs 23.38 crore unrecovered from industrial units availing sales tax incentives and Rs 306.06 crore unrecovered interest due to weak internal controls.

The overall revenue receipts for 2009-10 were Rs 64,678.35 crore, with 66% raised by the State and 34% received from the Central Government. The audit discovered serious gaps in departmental accountability, overdue Inspection Reports totaling Rs 11,916.66 crore from 28,990 outstanding audit observations, and major delays in departmental responses. Audit committees met infrequently, with only seven meetings settling 727 paragraphs out of thousands pending.

Consequences include significant unrealised revenue and persistent weaknesses in accountability mechanisms, undermining the State’s financial position and effectiveness of revenue collection departments. The government is urged to strengthen audit response systems, internal controls over loans and receipts, and enforce timely recovery processes.

title: Report of 2010 - Performance Audit on Commercial of Government of Andhra Pradesh
overview:
This Performance Audit reviews the functioning of Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) in Andhra Pradesh for 2009-10. As of March 2010, the State had 44 working PSUs and 24 non-working PSUs, employing 2.61 lakh people. These working units reported a turnover of ₹52,822.45 crore—equivalent to 12.84% of the State GDP. Despite the large scale, PSUs collectively posted an aggregate loss of ₹15.50 crore for the year and carried accumulated losses of ₹3,103.07 crore. Major profit contributors included Andhra Pradesh Power Generation Corporation Ltd. (₹288.66 crore), The Singareni Collieries Company Ltd. (₹268.01 crore), and Transmission Corporation of Andhra Pradesh Ltd. (₹70.19 crore). Conversely, Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation and State Housing Corporation suffered heavy losses totalling ₹514.55 crore and ₹341.13 crore, respectively.

Audit highlights inefficiency and mismanagement as root causes for recurring losses, with ₹5,087.82 crore in cumulative losses over three years identified as controllable through better management. PSUs across the state are noted as needing professionalism and accountability to ensure financial self-reliance and to curtail deficits. The power sector dominated investments—accounting for 52.81% of total PSU investment, which rose 45.37% in five years to reach ₹44,894.92 crore by March 2010, with government contributions of ₹8,639 crore in this audit period.

Serious weaknesses were observed in quality of accounts: 32 out of 47 finalized accounts received qualified certificates and there were 41 instances of non-compliance with Accounting Standards. Audit arrears remained high, with 25 working PSUs delayed by 64 accounts, and 24 non-working PSUs cited as providing no public value and recommended for rapid winding up.

title: Performance Audit of Income Tax Refunds
overview:
This performance audit focused on income tax refunds processed between 2005-06 and 2008-09, aiming to assess the timeliness, accuracy, and internal controls in the functioning of the Income Tax Department regarding refunds. The audit found procedural irregularities in refunds aggregating ₹5,803.5 crore, with the tax effect of erroneous refunds amounting to ₹135.8 crore (p. v). While the quantum of refunds increased by 30% over the period, the incidence of refunds (as a percentage of gross tax collections) declined, reflecting an apparent improvement in the tax assessment process. However, despite automation, the pendency rate of refund claims worsened, with a 37% pendency and a backlog exceeding six months by 2008-09 (p. 7).

Significant issues included persistent delays, particularly affecting small taxpayers and senior citizens, and continuing trends of excess advance tax payments by corporates and PSUs—public sector undertakings accounted for 92% of ₹436 crore in excess advance tax payments found in 21 corporates across 6 states (p. 6). Internal controls in both manual and automated systems were inadequate, with substantial amounts lying in suspense accounts due to invalid PANs and unsatisfactory manual reconciliation (p. 10). Interest outflows on delayed refunds increased at a pace higher than the refunds themselves, compounding the monetary impact on public finances.

The Ministry acknowledged audit findings, agreeing that internal control lapses and gaps in IT systems were significant impediments. Audit recommendations emphasized urgent improvement in automation, strengthened monitoring, accountability for errors, and prioritization for vulnerable taxpayer groups. The CAG stressed that correcting these systemic gaps is essential to bolster taxpayer confidence and fiscal transparency.

title: Report No. 15 of 2009 - Performance Audit Natural or cultured pearls,precious stones,precious metal,coins Union Government, Department of Indirect Taxes-Customs
overview:
This performance audit examines the levy and collection of customs duty on 'natural or cultured pearls, precious or semi-precious stones, precious metals, metals clad with precious metal and articles thereof, imitation jewellery, coin (chapter 71 of Customs Tariff Heading)' for the period 2005-06 to 2007-08. The report highlights that the estimated duty foregone by the Government during this period was ₹68,192 crore. In the eleven audited commissionerates, revenue earned amounted to ₹2,023 crore, whereas the duty foregone totaled ₹20,864 crore, reflecting significant gaps in revenue collection compared to benefits given.

Despite numerous exemptions and growth in imports (16%), export growth lagged behind at only 13% from 2005-06 to 2007-08. Systemic and procedural issues were uncovered, such as incomplete data collection, gaps in IT system implementation (notably at the DPCC in Mumbai, which handles the bulk of the trade), and lack of physical examination of SEZ exports. Cases were found where importers/exporters failed to meet obligations after availing duty exemptions, leading to recoverable import duties of ₹82.78 crore.

The audit identifies ambiguity in customs notifications (e.g., for gold coins), loopholes in NFE calculations, and disparities between EOU and SEZ requirements—resulting in a lack of a level playing field. The consequences include risks of undervaluation, possible duty evasion, and weak regulatory oversight, undermining government objectives for boosting exports while safeguarding revenue.

title: Performance Audit of The Appeal Process-Union Government-Direct Taxes
overview:
This performance audit evaluated the appeals process under Direct Taxes for the years 2006-09, highlighting critical deficiencies that directly impact government revenue and taxpayer experience. As of the review period, Rs 2.2 lakh crore—amounting to 87% of the revenue deficit for 2008-09—was locked up in appeals pending across various appellate levels. The audit found that 48% of tax demands raised remained uncollected, with disputes accounting for 45% of these uncollected amounts; 22% of all assessment demands were disputed, pointing to systemic dissatisfaction within the taxpayer base and especially among small taxpayers, who constituted 66% of total appeals (with demands below Rs 1 lakh) but were least equipped to handle the cost and duration of litigation (page v).

Over the audit period, the number of appeals preferred annually averaged 1.4 lakh, of which 74% originated at the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) [CIT(A)]—the base of the appellate pyramid. Despite a reduction in new appeals, the inventory of pending cases with CIT(A) increased by 46% between 2006 and 2009, as disposal rates lagged at just one-third of the Central Action Plan’s target. Each CIT(A) bench averaged 637 pending appeals, translating to a 2.4-year clearance cycle at current disposal rates (page 7).

The audit also exposed weak internal monitoring, with only 49% of required records produced nationwide (as low as 5% in Delhi), and wide inconsistencies in departmental data systems. Poor implementation of appellate orders resulted in ₹1,456 crore in mistakes across 385 cases, with 97% of errors leading to under-assessment of tax, thus benefiting taxpayers and casting doubts on the process’s integrity (page vi). Major system and legislative lacunae, discretionary decisions by AOs, and weak internal controls were found to underpin these outcomes.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Performance Audit on Compensatory Afforestation in Himachal Pradesh (English)
overview:
The Performance Audit reviewed Compensatory Afforestation (CA) in Himachal Pradesh over April 2006 to March 2021, with special scrutiny of CA implementation efficacy and financial management. Records at the offices of the Principal Chief Conservator of Forests, State CAMPA Authority, APCCFs, and nine sampled divisions were examined. Notably, there was a 20% shortfall in utilisation of funds approved by the National Authority, totaling ₹169.73 crore between 2016-17 and 2021-22. Despite formation of a State Fund, user agencies deposited money into the National Authority account from February 2019 to March 2022, violating Compensatory Afforestation Fund Rules, 2018.

Further, out of 1,018 forest clearance proposal cases, 766 remained pending, with 17% stuck within the State Forest Department and the remainder awaiting user agency action. Delays in processing approvals at various levels reached up to 93%. There were considerable lapses in the execution of CA, as only 4,284 ha were afforested against a stipulated 5,213 ha in sampled divisions, with delays leading to cost escalations and environmental loss. Encroachments and plantation of CA outside designated open degraded forests were also prominent issues.

Overall, the audit reveals lack of coordination, deficient monitoring, inaccurate and delayed reporting, and financial rule violations, all resulting in non-compliance with statutory objectives. The consequences include creation of additional liabilities over ₹8.72 crore due to delay, significant cost and time overruns, unauthorized expenses, potential misappropriations, and unfulfilled ecological obligations. Serious gaps in catchment area treatment plan monitoring and geospatial mismatches further highlight risks to the integrity of forest wealth and associated funds.

title: The Performance Audit on “Waste Management in Urban Local Bodies”
overview:
Municipal Solid Waste Management in urban areas is increasingly challenging due to rapid urbanisation, with ULBs (Urban Local Bodies) lacking systematic planning and consistent infrastructure creation. During the audit period, none of the test-checked ULBs had prepared a comprehensive MSWM plan or a Contingency plan, leading to fragmented waste management and environmental health hazards. DPRs (Detailed Project Reports) were not prepared according to guidelines, with baseline waste analysis often ineffective or outdated, and duplication seen across DP₹

Though funds were available and DPRs approved, infrastructure projects failed to materialise within prescribed timelines. In two ULBs, even the identification/procurement of sites for projects was pending. Bioremediation or capping of legacy dump sites occurred in only one out of five ULBs audited, leading to significant accumulation of old waste and environmental concerns. On an average, 5–8% of waste generated was not collected statewide, and 8–16% remained uncollected in sample ULBs (see Table 3.1, p. 37). Only 3.13% of collected waste was segregated, with ragpickers generally not integrated into the process. Most vehicles for waste transport (64%) were not covered, and workers often lacked uniforms or personal protective equipment. Transfer stations were typically sited near homes, highways, canals, or open grounds, and only two sanitary landfill sites exist, resulting in open dumping across most areas (13 dumpsites, 3,63,019 tons of waste).

Financial management was inconsistent, with substantial idle funds and serious underutilisation of grants. The audit found that SWM projects often failed to meet deadlines, and expenditures did not match available funds. The lack of proper segregation and scientific disposal increases public health risks, visible through widespread improper dumping, burning of waste, and contamination of agricultural lands. Overall, the audit period reflected systemic mismanagement and insufficient compliance with the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, leading to a heightened risk profile for both environment and urban populations. [Executive Summary, p. vii-xiii](https://cag.gov.in/uploads/download_audit_report/2024/2.-Report-No.-3-of-2024_WM-ULBs_Marathi-&-English-067e4e5899fb3d5.89416086.pdf)

title: Performance Audit on “Functioning of Delhi Transport Corporation”
overview:
Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC) operated a fleet of 3,762 buses in 36 depots as of 31 March 2022, carrying an average of 15.62 lakh passengers daily. The audit period revealed persistent financial distress, with accumulated losses increasing from ₹ 25,299.87 crore in 2015-16 to ₹ 60,741.03 crore in 2021-22. Operating revenue declined due to non-revision of fares and shrinking commuter base, exacerbated by rising operating and manpower expenditures not proportional to revenue.

A significant finding is the lack of a Business Plan or Perspective Plan for the Corporation, leading to directionless efforts and degraded operational efficiency. DTC continued to suffer from heavy interest payments on GNCTD loans, comprising 72.90% of total expenditure for 2021-22, with only ₹ 122.43 crore as real operating loss after excluding unpaid interest, which itself was booked on accrual basis and never paid since 2011-12. Despite receiving ₹ 13,381 crore in revenue grants from GNCTD over the period, the gap between operating revenue and expenditure remained at ₹ 817.78 crore, resulting in increased dependency on government support.

Operational inefficiencies were highlighted by the failure to benchmark against other State Transport Undertakings (STUs), absence of studies on profitability/sustainability, and delays in procurement and project implementation. Route rationalisation was inadequate, with DTC operating on only 468 out of 814 routes as of 31 March 2022. The overall financial and operational sustainability of DTC is at risk without strategic planning and strong control mechanisms.

title: Performance audit of Public Health Infrastructure and Management of health Services in Rajasthan
overview:
The Performance Audit covers the period from 2016-22, assessing Rajasthan's public health infrastructure and management. The report finds consistent underfunding, with total health expenditure comprising only 6.95% of total State expenditure in 2021-22, and health spending as a percentage of GSDP ranging from just 1.08% in 2016-17 to 1.36% in 2021-22, falling well short of the National Health Policy’s target of 2.5% of GDP by 2025. (Table 1.1, page 5)

There are major gaps in human resources; only 15,121 doctors are available against a sanctioned strength of 22,018 (31.32% shortfall), with persistent vacancies at all levels and district-wise shortages documented in Appendix 2.1 (page 117). Shortfalls extend to nurses and paramedics, compromising service delivery.

Infrastructure remains inadequate across several areas: 12 out of 34 district hospitals lack radiology, 18 lack dietary services, and ambulance services are absent in 7 DHs (Executive Summary, page vii). Equipment and drugs are frequently unavailable or distributed below demand; delays in procurement and testing lead to critical service disruptions. Capital expenditure constitutes only 6.67% of total healthcare spending, limiting upgrades and expansion. Though out-of-pocket expenditure as a proportion of total health spending declined in 2016-20, it was still alarmingly high at 47.40% in 2019-20, indicating low financial protection for households (Executive Summary, page viii).

title: Performance Audit on Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services
overview:
The report examines the adequacy of public health infrastructure, fund allocation, and management of health services in Himachal Pradesh from 2016-17 to 2021-22, with updates for human resources up to March 2023. It highlights that the State spent only 6.35% of its total expenditure and 1.70% of GSDP on health services during 2021-22, which is below the 8% and 2.5% targets set under National Health Policy 2017. Significant shortages exist in health sector human resources, with overall vacancies at 41.87% across all categories. For example, specialist shortages in Medical College hospitals ranged from 15% to 49% and exceeded 33% in several District Hospitals (DHs).

Infrastructure gaps were evident, with the actual increase in beds during 2016-22 at 20.60%, despite a sanctioned increase of 45.02%. Double and triple occupancy of beds was commonly observed, and 113 works valuing ₹60.49 crore were not initiated due to delays. Stock-outs and expired drugs plagued primary and secondary institutions—19 to 32 essential drugs were unavailable for up to 1,422 days and 341.59 lakh quantities expired from 2017 to 2021 according to DVDMS records. Out of 2,136 notified Health Wellness Centres, only 1,468 were operational as of March 2023.

Regulatory weaknesses were noted: all private clinical establishments operated on provisional registration only. Major deficiencies were also found in drug testing and sample analysis. The audit reveals that shortcomings in management, resource allocation, and regulatory enforcement have led to compromised healthcare quality and availability across Himachal Pradesh.

title: Performance Audit on Functioning of Bengaluru Metropolitan Transport Corporation
overview:
The CAG performance audit of Bengaluru Metropolitan Transport Corporation (BMTC) covers financial and operational functioning from 2017-18 to 2021-22. During this period, BMTC’s fleet strength was 6,799 buses (as of March 2022) and operated 5,547 schedules, but suffered significant declines in passenger base and operational revenue even before the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. Average daily ridership dropped from 44.37 lakh in 2017-18 to 33.10 lakh in 2019-20, and further to about 14.38 lakh during the pandemic years (2020-22), a reduction of 61.63 percent.

Operational losses increased year-on-year. Operating ratios rose from 133.59 percent in 2017-18 to 222.62 percent in 2021-22, with ticket revenue accounting for 63 percent of BMTC’s total income and personnel and fuel costs forming 87 percent of all operational expenditure. Due to a lack of fare revision since 2014-15, BMTC lost an estimated ₹649.74 crore in possible additional revenue, and had to rely heavily on financial assistance from Government of Karnataka, which provided ₹1,980.60 crore during pandemic years but still fell short of covering annual operational losses.

Audit found operational inefficiencies including use of overaged buses, unscientific schedule planning, excessive dead kilometres, delays in repairs and maintenance, and underutilization of land assets. BMTC’s inability to recover operational expenses threatens long-term sustainability, leading to critical recommendations for improved financial support, more scientific scheduling, and maximization of non-operational revenue.

title: Performance Audit on Preservation and Conservation of State Protected Historical Monuments and Antiquities in Karnataka
overview:
Karnataka houses 1,453 notified protected monuments as of March 2022, with 844 under state protection and the remainder managed by the Archaeological Survey of India. During 2017-18 to 2021-22, ₹123.65 crore was spent by the Department of Archaeology, Museums and Heritage, out of a budgeted allocation of ₹146.81 crore; ₹37.22 crore (30%) was administrative expenditure, while only ₹1.68 crore was generated as revenue from various fees. Conservation and maintenance activities accounted for just 54% of expenditure, and only ₹39 lakh was allocated specifically for monument maintenance over five years.

The Audit observed absence of any long-term or annual conservation planning, leading to ad hoc allocation and execution of works. Moreover, the Directory of protected monuments was found to be inaccurate, with physical verification revealing several listed sites missing and inadequate records of non-notified monuments. Public amenities and protective measures such as signage boards, fencing, and CCTV installation were lacking at many significant sites, with joint inspections uncovering unauthorized constructions and encroachments adjacent to state-protected monuments.

The department operated without scientific criteria for budget proposals or assessments of technical manpower required for its mandate. This resulted in neglect of essential maintenance activities, and administrative overheads consumed a disproportionate share of financial resources, undermining the primary objectives of preservation and conservation. The Government of Karnataka accepted all audit recommendations, initiating corrective action as noted in August 2023.

title: Performance Audit on Role of Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation (MIDC) in Industrial Development of Maharashtra
overview: The Performance Audit covers the role of MIDC in Maharashtra's industrial development covering 2014-2021. MIDC was in possession of 79,317 hectares across 289 industrial areas as of March 2021. The report finds major shortcomings in corporate governance, planning, land acquisition, pricing, allotment, and revenue recovery. During the period, 7 out of 15 Board seats were vacant, and direct allotments to ineligible parties led to loss of transparency and financial detriment. Key issues include lack of systematic planning—MIDC had no perspective or annual plans despite SIP targets. There were no databases to track whether land allottees met investment or employment goals, and unutilized land was not reclaimed as required. Arbitrary relaxations to land price or charges in favor of private parties reduced MIDC revenue. Instances of cancelled tenders and re-tendering increased costs. MIDC failed to recover GST on non-exempted receipts, and did not revise water/service charges in time, leading to short recoveries. The absence of an effective monitoring system allowed encroachments and unauthorized sublettings to persist. Overall, lapses have caused financial loss to the public exchequer and undermined Maharashtra's industrial growth objectives.

title: Performance Audit of Protection, Conservation and Management of Wildlife Sanctuaries in Gujarat
overview:
The audit covered the functioning of 23 wildlife sanctuaries across Gujarat. Out of ₹312.37 crore sanctioned between 2018-19 and 2022-23, only ₹138.90 crore was actually utilised, equating to a fund utilisation rate of 44%. The report notes shortages in staffing with only 59% of required forest guards posted, contributing to insufficient patrols and exacerbating poaching and habitat degradation risks. The audit found that out of 2,215 sanctioned anti-poaching camps, merely 1,276 were operational, and only 31% of GPS tracking devices were functioning, hampering monitoring effectiveness.

A major finding was the absence of updated Management Plans in 18 out of 23 sanctuaries, which directly impacted habitat restoration and species conservation outcomes. Irregularities in eco-development committee functioning were noted; only 30% of targeted local communities were reached for sustainable livelihood interventions and awareness programs. Shortfalls in fire protection measures resulted in avoidable losses—with three sanctuaries reporting over 700 hectares of burnt area in 2021-22 alone.

The consequences include persistent threats to flagship species such as Asiatic lions, wild ass, and significant migratory birds, along with fragmentation and degradation of critical habitats. These gaps have led to declining wildlife populations, increased human-wildlife conflict, and limited progress towards biodiversity targets set under national policies. The audit concludes that the Department needs urgent action to address fund utilisation, capacity building, and planning gaps to safeguard Gujarat's natural assets.

title: Performance Audit of Conservation and Management of Coastal Ecosystems
overview:
The audit reviewed the conservation and management of coastal ecosystems in Gujarat for the period 2015-16 to 2019-20, focusing on institutional mechanisms, regulatory compliance, and implementation of major projects. Gujarat, with 1,600 km coastline across 16 districts, spent ₹410.91 crore on the Integrated Coastal Zone Management Project (ICZMP), of which 77% was funded by World Bank, 13% by Government of India, and 10% by the State. The report highlighted delays in reconstitution of the Gujarat Coastal Zone Management Authority (GCZMA), shortage of dedicated staff, and lack of transparency and monitoring. Notably, delays of up to 175 days in GCZMA reconstitution led to periods with no project clearances issued (Table 2.1, page 13).

Out of 32 reported violations in Coastal Regulation Zones (CRZ), 14 remained unresolved and GCZMA failed to frame any Standard Operating Procedure for complaint disposal. Major issues included large-scale destruction of mangroves with shortfall of 1,968.80 hectare against reported plantation, irregularities in project vetting, non-compliance in post-clearance monitoring, and improper use of high-cost equipment—impairing effectiveness (Executive Summary, pages v-viii).

The consequences included absence of robust mechanisms to identify illegal constructions, continued discharge of untreated wastewater in CRZ areas due to shortage of treatment capacity, and underperformance on SDG-14 indicators. The report concludes that ineffective institutional mechanisms led to significant regulatory lapses, with high deficiencies in conservation outcomes and project implementation.

title: Performance Audit on Planning and Contract Management of Road Works in Public Works Department
overview:
The Performance Audit of Planning and Contract Management of Road Works in the Public Works Department (PWD), Karnataka, for the years 2016-21, reviewed capital expenditure of ₹17,046.97 crore on State Highways and Major District Roads. The report highlights that the Department did not achieve the Karnataka Road Sector Policy, 2009 goal of developing a Core Road Network with minimum two-lane width. Only 26% of SHs met the two-lane standard, and 79% of MDRs were single lane as of March 2021. Estimates sanctioned for road works contained serious deficiencies including inaccurate traffic census, improper soil testing, and unreliable measurements, leading to avoidable excess expenditure and losses amounting to ₹38.63 crore in test-checked works (page 16).

Contracts worth ₹2,738.86 crore (75% of sampled works) were awarded when only one or two bids were received, with no retendering undertaken, depriving the State an opportunity for competitive rates (page vii). Another headline finding was ₹1,480.37 crore released in 333 cases for establishing field labs where contractors failed to comply, and quality control test reports were not submitted (page vii).

Other issues included non-conduct of Road Safety Audits before sanction, non-recovery of royalty, and lack of systematic annual and five-year planning. The absence of up-to-date road data in key systems like KRAMS and RIS hampered planning, monitoring, and transparency. The report recommends comprehensive road data management, strict compliance to technical standards, disciplinary action for irregular tender acceptance, and mandates for online measurement reporting.

title: CAG Report on Performance Audit on Karnataka Rural Infrastructure Development Limited, Government of Karnataka
overview:
This performance audit reviewed Karnataka Rural Infrastructure Development Limited (KRIDL) for the period 2016-17 to 2020-21 and found systemic lapses in project implementation, financial management, and regulatory compliance. Despite receiving total funds ranging from ₹2,604 crore to ₹4,610 crore annually from 2016-17 to 2020-21, KRIDL utilised only 13.97% to 38.79% on works per year, resulting in significant underutilisation.

The report highlights that KRIDL completed only 24,014 out of 84,574 works during the five-year period (28%), and as of 2020-21, ₹17,320.30 crore remained unutilised. Key causes included delays in commencement of works, absence of procurement planning, subletting of works without tendering, and misuse/mismanagement of advances and suspense accounts. Audit revealed ₹389.90 crore in unsettled mobilisation advances, ₹303.76 crore where no work codes were allotted, and ₹238.89 crore of interest on scheme funds not credited to government accounts.

Entrustment violations included splitting of large works to bypass tender norms, award and execution of ineligible works, and payments made without sufficient monitoring or quality control. The report calls attention to deficient accounting practices, lack of real-time project monitoring, and outdated standing orders, all cumulatively resulting in poor transparency, accountability, and financial discipline.

title: CAG Report on Performance Audit of Functioning of Kalyan Karnataka Region Development Board , Government of Karnataka
overview:
The performance audit of the Kalyana Karnataka Region Development Board (KKRDB), which covers the period 2016-17 to 2020-21, was conducted to evaluate the Board’s effectiveness in addressing persistent regional developmental imbalances. The audit reveals that over the five-year period, the Board spent only 74% of the released fund amount, with actual physical progress on approved projects reaching just 70%. In terms of fund allocation and planning, the Board did not appropriately ascertain sector-wise development backlogs and failed to collect or use relevant socio-economic data for targeted interventions, directly hampering measurable progress in key areas like per capita income, health, nutrition, and education.

The audit further highlights a lack of strategic planning, as no long-term plans were implemented to redress deep-seated regional disparities. Annual action plans were often delayed and lacked quantifiable targets or defined timelines. Financial management was found to be weak, particularly around the Board’s inability to prepare annual budget estimates, track fund utilization and advances, or ensure timely completion and quality control of works. Crucial Board functions—inclusive of policy recommendation, backlog determination, and institutional development—remained largely unaddressed, partly due to multi-year gaps where no nominated Board was in place to provide oversight.

The consequences of these governance and operational failures are evident: the socio-economic status of Kalyana Karnataka’s districts remains below state averages, especially by indices such as the Human Development Index, NITI Aayog Aspirational District indicators, and Multidimensional Poverty Index, with 21 of the 38 most-backward taluks in Karnataka still located in this region. The lack of robust monitoring, quality assurance mechanisms, and social audit frameworks persists, impeding impactful delivery and public accountability on Board-led projects.

title: Performance Audit of Outcomes in Higher Education in Andhra Pradesh, Government of Andhra Pradesh.
overview:
The Performance Audit covered higher education outcomes in Andhra Pradesh from 2014-15 to 2018-19, focusing on student employability, progression to higher studies, quality of teaching, and adequacy of governance. During this period, the State's expenditure on higher education as a percentage of GSDP decreased sharply from 0.47% in 2014-15 to 0.25% in 2018-19, failing to meet policy targets of 1.5% by 2022 and 2.5% by 2029. Out of 10 state universities, 3 major universities and their 9 constituent colleges, along with 26 out of 607 affiliated colleges, were analyzed.

Key shortcomings identified include that less than half (46%) of test-checked affiliated colleges had placement/career counseling facilities, and only 27% maintained student progression data. Pass percentages in undergraduate courses showed a worrying decline in Andhra University (23.49% in BA and 23.54% in BSc for 2018-19) and Adikavi Nannayya University (19.27% in BA and 21.77% in BCom in 2018-19), far below desirable levels and down from previous years. Furthermore, only 7% of affiliated colleges were NAAC-accredited as of 2018-19, a critical gap against the state’s target of 100%.

Infrastructure was found severely lacking: most colleges missed minimum requirements for buildings, laboratories, libraries, and facilities for differently abled students. There was also a significant shortage of permanent teachers, with only 6 out of 281 teachers in 19 private colleges holding a Ph.D. Programmes for professional faculty development were grossly inadequate. The data management for tracking student outcomes and institutional adherence to statutory guidelines remained weak across the evaluated institutions.

title: Report of 2009 - Financial and Performance Audit of Local Self Government Institutions of Government of Kerala
overview:
The 2009 report on the Financial and Performance Audit of Local Self Government Institutions (LSGIs) in Kerala presents a detailed account of the decentralisation process, flow of funds, and accountability mechanisms for the years leading up to 2010. The resource base of LSGIs included own revenues, central grants, and State devolutions under various heads. Total receipts of LSGIs doubled from Rs 2,763.03 crore in 2005-06 to Rs 5,263.47 crore in 2009-10, reflecting a 114% increase in five years. Notably, State grants constituted 70% of total receipts, while Central grants and own funds comprised 13% and 16%, respectively.

The audit identified significant issues in fund utilisation, internal controls, and the execution of legislatively devolved responsibilities. Despite the transfer of 26 functions to PRIs and 17 to ULBs, certain mandated subjects like minor forest produce and distribution of electricity were not devolved. Numerous lapses were noticed in scheme implementation, beneficiary selection, and financial record-keeping. Specific cases included deficits in physical and financial executions, and frequent shortfalls in the internal audit and inspection mechanisms at the LSGI level.

Consequences included delayed or incomplete project implementation across sectors, poor asset maintenance, and non-utilisation of significant portions of available funds. The audit recommends strengthening internal control systems, completing the devolution of all mandated functions, and enforcing stricter performance and financial reporting protocols to ensure effective governance and transparency in LSGIs.

title: Report of 2008 - Financial and Performance Audit of Local Self Government Institutions of Government of Kerala
overview: This audit covers the structure, finances, and performance audit of Local Self Government Institutions (LSGIs) in Kerala. In 2008-09, the actual utilisation by LSGIs against the `1848.22 crore available for development expenditure was only `1476.66 crore, resulting in underutilisation of funds and a lapse of `60.21 crore. Financial achievement for key schemes, including SJSRY, IDSMT/UIDSSMT, and JNNURM, remained below 50% during 2005-06 to 2008-09, indicating critical deficiencies in both fund absorption and project implementation. The audit also found significant arrears in the submission and audit of annual accounts, with only 66% of required accounts received in 2008-09 and 32% pending audit as of July 2009. Supplementary audits revealed widespread lapses in record maintenance and budget preparation, non-adherence to prescribed accounting standards, and lack of IT audit practices or training. Major inefficiencies were detected in flagship schemes such as Indira Awaas Yojana and water supply programs, where misutilisation and retention of funds, false reporting, and unspent balances led to denial of benefits for intended recipients and unproductive investments. The audit concludes that persistent underperformance and institutional weaknesses have resulted in recurring loss of revenue, denied benefits, and blocked funds throughout the period reviewed.

title: Report of 2007 - Financial and Performance Audit of Local Self Government Institutions of Government of Kerala
overview: The audit report covers the structure and finances of Local Self Government Institutions (LSGIs) in Kerala, with a special focus on fund utilisation, irregularities, and compliance. As of 31 March 2008, there were 1223 LSGIs with accounts arrears dating back up to 12 years. Against a budget provision of ₹452.74 crore under State and Centrally Sponsored Schemes (Category 'B'), only ₹154.22 crore (34.06%) was actually utilised, leading to lapse of ₹298.52 crore under Plan and ₹42.46 crore under Non-plan heads. Similarly, only 71% of maintenance grants were used during 2004-08; 8 LSGIs irregularly utilised ₹2.72 crore for maintenance of assets not owned by them, and there was diversion of ₹8.24 crore between asset categories in test-checked units. The delay in submitting accounts persisted, with 1724 accounts pending and 4532 audit reports in arrears. In the distribution of electricity and water, Thrissur Municipal Corporation incurred avoidable interest of ₹2.58 crore, failed to realise ₹11.64 crore in electricity charges, and lost ₹78.24 lakh in meter rentals, amongst other lapses. Multiple cases of failed projects, excess payments, and unauthorized fund transfers were also flagged, indicating systemic weaknesses. These lapses have resulted in significant shortfalls, fund lapses, and missed opportunities for effective decentralization and delivery of public services.

title: Report of 2006 - Financial and Performance Audit of Local Self Government Institutions of Government of Kerala
overview:
This audit report presents comprehensive findings on the financial management and performance of Kerala's Local Self Government Institutions (LSGIs) from 1996-97 to 2006-07. A critical issue was arrears in accounts submission: as of December 2007, 3633 annual accounts from 1996-97 to 2006-07 were in arrears, comprising 38.24% of accounts receivable for the year (p.4). These delays led to lapses in financial oversight and failure to detect misappropriation and fraud. In 79 LSGIs checked, cash books were not properly closed in 41, leaving cash balances unverifiable and undermining internal controls (p.5).

Fund utilisation remained below target and centrally sponsored schemes saw low implementation. Though ₹260.80 crore was available for seven schemes, only ₹70.63 crore (27.08%) was utilised (p.ix-x). Category 'A' funds (plan funds) also had unspent balances—out of ₹1400.36 crore transfer credited in 2006-07, ₹178.99 crore remained unutilised, with only ₹1221.37 crore actually spent (p.8).

Audit revealed major gaps in regulatory compliance: no officer was authorised to collect DP, Municipality, or Corporation accounts (p.2); budget and accounting rules remained unframed despite repeated recommendations. The lack of timely accounts and audit reports, poor record keeping, unaddressed irregularities, and widespread internal control failures have undermined LSGI accountability, resulting in unfruitful expenditures, diversion of funds, and loss to public finances.

title: Report of 2005 - Financial and Performance Audit of Local Self Government Institutions of Government of Kerala
overview:
This audit report presents a comprehensive performance review of the finances and governance of Local Self Government Institutions (LSGIs) in Kerala for the period 2002-03 to 2005-06. The audit identified significant lapses in consolidation and submission of annual accounts—17.42% of PRIs submitted 2004-05 accounts by September 2006 and only 6.09% for 2005-06, indicating systemic weaknesses. Of the ₹5357.16 crore state plan outlay for 2005-06, actual disbursements were ₹4017.49 crore, with just ₹1008.15 crore (25.09%) actually transferred to LSGIs. Utilisation of central scheme funds was equally poor: of ₹217.43 crore available across 17 schemes in 2005-06, only ₹107.65 crore (49.51%) was expended.

Asset management practices were found lacking—six asset projects were abandoned and 45 incomplete, wasting ₹6.51 crore, while maintenance grants of ₹21.07 crore remained unutilised in 2004-05 and 2005-06. There were further large gaps in release of General Purpose Grants (shortfall: ₹154.43 crore, 25.88%) and Maintenance Grants (₹456.82 crore, 48.71% shortfall), limiting LSGIs’ ability to meet obligatory expenses and asset upkeep. Notably, 73% to 82% of LSGIs failed to submit their accounts within a year of close, raising risks of misappropriation.

Transaction audit detected misappropriation of ₹15.49 lakh in Thiruvananthapuram Municipal Corporation and uncovered persistent internal control failures. The report concludes that delays, incomplete releases, poor planning, and unattended assets caused substantial financial leakage and inefficiency, undermining decentralisation and local development objectives.

title: Report of 2004 - Financial and Performance Audit of Local Self Government Institutions of Government of Kerala
overview:
This performance audit highlights substantial deficiencies in the finances and functioning of Local Self Government Institutions (LSGIs) in Kerala. Out of 10,931 accounts of LSGIs receivable during the period 1996-2005, 4,256 accounts (39%) were in arrears as of November 2005, indicating a persistently weak financial reporting mechanism and failure in timely submission and audit of accounts. Though ₹51.73 crore was reportedly spent on asset creation by LSGIs in 2004-05, details of assets created could not be verified due to incomplete recipient-wise records, further undermining transparency and accountability.

Despite decentralisation, only 29% of the annual plan outlay for 2004-05 (₹1,092.74 crore out of ₹3,755.25 crore) was devolved to LSGIs, illustrating the gap between policy intent and actual fund flows. Technical Guidance and Supervision audits revealed non-maintenance/improper maintenance of accounts, lapses in safeguarding assets, and widespread non-compliance with statutory requirements. Additionally, the report documents instances of fund misappropriation, inflated provision of own funds, and major shortfalls in project execution, especially in key sectors such as water management, women development, and welfare schemes for Scheduled Castes.

The consequences include continuing arrears, substantial misappropriation (e.g., ₹12.89 lakh embezzled in Adoor Municipality), unfruitful expenditures (e.g., ₹30.58 lakh on electric crematorium in Kollam), and projects stalled or not achieving intended objectives. The lack of clarity in the regulatory framework, weak asset management, and failure to integrate centrally sponsored schemes further compounded the issues, leading to serious risks to local governance and accountability.

title: Report of 2009 - Performance Audit on State Excise Department of Government of Uttar Pradesh
overview:
This report on the performance audit of the State Excise Department of Uttar Pradesh evaluates records audited from October 2008 to December 2009, covering the period 2004-05 to 2008-09. Test checks revealed irregularities including low recovery of alcohol from molasses, non-lifting of the minimum guaranteed quota (MGQ) of country liquor, non-realisation of licence fees, and non-levy of interest, resulting in a total revenue impact of ₹1,344.56 crore. A significant finding was the absence of a mechanism to monitor actual sales by retailers, leading to a loss of licence fee amounting to ₹2.07 crore. Excise duty losses due to unverified MF 4 passes from sugar factories were calculated at ₹58.09 crore, and incorrect accounting for molasses further resulted in a short accountal affecting ₹21.40 crore.

The audit also identified that distilleries had not achieved mandatory minimum production standards, causing additional excise revenue losses of ₹133.30 crore, with non-imposition of prescribed fines for alcohol over-production compounding the issue by ₹788.78 crore. Other irregularities, such as the unauthorised storage of spirits, faulty security deposits, and weak internal audit practices, were noted.

The cumulative effect of operational lapses, system deficiencies, and weak financial controls has resulted in significant arrears and low recovery rates of previously identified dues. As of March 2009, revenue arrears totaled ₹56.73 crore, the majority of which was pending recovery for over five years. Internal control weaknesses, such as unfilled posts and poor internal audit execution, further hinder departmental effectiveness.

title: Report of 2009 - Performance Audit on Commercial of Government of West Bengal
overview:
The CAG performance audit examined the functioning and financial management of Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) in West Bengal as of 2008-09, covering 72 working PSUs and 23 non-working PSUs, with a combined turnover of ₹17,304 crore, constituting 5.59% of the state's GDP. Total state investment in PSUs reached ₹40,970.41 crore, showing a 30.26% increase since 2003-04, with power and finance sectors alone accounting for 81% of this sum.

Significant operational deficiencies included persistent delays: only 29 of 72 working PSUs finalized accounts for 2008-09 on time, while 43 had arrears of 1-5 years. Out of 70 PSU accounts finalized in the audit year, 37 received qualified auditor certificates, and audit comments affected reported profits by ₹263.20 crore. Notable losses stemmed from management failures—for example, the Calcutta Tramways Company posted a ₹195.25 crore loss, while slippages and revenue shortfalls in West Bengal Housing Infrastructure Development Corporation led to a ₹371.75 crore loss.

The audit also highlighted frequent non-compliance with procedures (₹574.09 crore), defective planning (₹100.51 crore), and serious arrears in audit report discussions. Recommendations include improved pricing policy, stronger internal controls, and rapid winding up of dormant PSUs to prevent continued financial drain.

title: Glossary of Report of 2009 - Compliance and Performance Audit on Civil of Government of West Bengal
overview:
This CAG audit report evaluates the performance of the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) and other civil functions in West Bengal, focusing on the audit period from 2006-07 to 2008-09. The report highlights serious issues in fund utilisation, implementation, and monitoring of critical schemes. For NRHM, only 37% to 64% of available funds were utilised annually between 2005-09, leaving Rs 424.66 crore parked and unutilised as of March 2009. Across five test-checked districts, 34% of untied funds at health centres remained unutilised, indicating inefficiency in financial management.

Compliance audits show cases of avoidable expenditure and losses. For example, failure to install individual electric meters at government quarters led to Rs 4.52 crore wasted, and diversion or non-utilisation of scheme funds resulted in blocked investments and interest losses. The report further documents the lack of baseline surveys, Perspective Plans, and delayed Project Implementation Plans, undermining the mission's ability to meet targets for accessible rural healthcare. Audit observations extend to the State Urban Development Agency (SUDA) and Housing Department, revealing inefficient fund management, shortfall in scheme achievement, and administrative lapses.

Consequences include overall savings of Rs 2875.96 crore across government accounts, significant delays needing legislative regularisation for excess spend (Rs 28200.65 crore pending regularisation), and persistent failure to submit Action Taken Notes across 45 departments. The report concludes that major system-level weaknesses, poor oversight, and non-compliance have impaired effective scheme delivery, exposing gaps in governance and financial management.

title: Report of 2009 - Performance Audit on Commercial of Government of Tamilnadu
overview:
The performance audit of Tamil Nadu State PSUs for 2004-09 identified significant operational and financial challenges. By 31 March 2009, there were 75 PSUs—64 working and 11 non-working—with an aggregate investment of ₹28,549.79 crore. The Power Sector alone accounted for 78.60% of total investments. However, PSUs recorded accumulated losses of ₹13,207.60 crore, highlighting persistent financial stress. The total turnover reached ₹42,535.07 crore, equal to 18.62% of the State's GDP, employing 2.75 lakh people (page ix). Despite their importance, 20 PSUs were in arrears of 31 accounts, with substantial accumulated losses in entities like TNEB (₹3,512.08 crore) and State Transport Corporations.

Audit noted inadequacies in operational efficiency and internal controls. For instance, State Transport Undertakings accumulated an overall loss of ₹3,884.99 crore as of 31 March 2009. Excess manpower and suboptimal bus productivity led to idle wage and extra fuel costs exceeding ₹542.38 crore and ₹33.76 crore, respectively. Several PSUs faced large storage losses, unnecessary expenditures on private hulling agents, and inefficient use of godown space, adversely burdening the State exchequer (page xii-xiv).

The audit revealed substantial room for improvement in financial management and recommended reforms in MIS, realignment of fare policy, tapping non-conventional revenues, minimisation of avoidable costs, and creation of an independent regulator. The persistent lapses indicate that required fiscal discipline, efficiency, and accountability were not being achieved, impacting both public service delivery and State finances.

title: Report of 2009 - Performance Audit on Commercial of Government of Rajasthan
overview:
This report details the results of audit of Government Companies and Statutory Corporations in Rajasthan, covering 29 working PSUs (26 companies, 3 statutory corporations) and 4 non-working PSUs as on 31 March 2009. The working PSUs registered a turnover of ₹17,510.67 crore for 2008-09, equal to 9.12% of State GDP, highlighting their significant role in the Rajasthan economy. Investment in PSUs reached ₹28,485.12 crore, a 102.35% increase since 2003-04. Out of this, the power sector accounted for over 93%.

Performance audit revealed major deficiencies: Only 13 PSUs earned profits totaling ₹348.40 crore, 3 incurred losses of ₹34.41 crore, while 5 power sector PSUs showed 'No Profit No Loss' using revenue gap recoverable from the government, which was not as per accepted GAAP. Heavy losses were noted in Rajasthan State Road Transport Corporation (₹23.57 crore), with overall state PSU losses of ₹1005.55 crore deemed potentially avoidable with better management.

Other critical issues include substantial arrears in accounts, quality problems in financial statements (21 of 22 accounts received qualified certificates), and transaction audit observations indicating losses exceeding ₹650 crore across six cases due to non-compliance with rules, and persistent gaps in billing and monitoring systems in power and transport corporations. Recommendations span professionalisation, tighter controls, better monitoring of losses, and tapping non-conventional revenue sources.

title: Report of 2009 - Performance Audit on West Tripura District of Government of Tripura
overview:
The performance audit of West Tripura district for 2004-09 examined the planning, implementation, and impact of socio-economic developmental programmes covering sectors such as education, health, urban development, employment generation, road connectivity, and general services. The report highlighted that the absence of a consolidated Perspective Plan or Annual Plan led to disjointed sectoral planning; no shelf of projects was maintained, and the District Planning Committee (DPC) failed to convene a single meeting post-constitution in September 2008 (p. v). The report found that targeted outcomes were not met in critical areas: for instance, the goal to bring all children aged 6-14 into school by 2003 was not reached even by 2009, with basic school infrastructure shortfalls persisting.

Financial management in the district was highly fragmented; neither the district administration nor any agency held consolidated records of funds received or expended, and accounting was often on the basis of releases rather than actual usage, resulting in a distorted picture of development outcomes (p. vi). Mismanagement also extended to employment schemes — under NREGA, guaranteed 100 days of wage employment for card holders during 2007-09 fell short by 36.71 to 78.40 days. Only 38% of PMGSY road works taken up since 2004-05 were completed, and just 32% of habitations were provided new connectivity, far below the minimum targets (p. viii).

This lack of effective planning, inadequate monitoring, and perfunctory supervision led to incomplete projects, underutilisation of funds, and significant delays in realising scheme benefits for local citizens. The decentralisation intended under constitutional reforms was not fully actualised, and accountability mechanisms, such as dedicated grievance redressal and monitoring committees, were largely absent. The audit concludes with a call for robust, community-driven planning and transparent fund management to bridge critical development gaps in the district.

title: Report of 2009 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Tripura
overview:
This CAG Performance Audit Report covers six performance reviews and multiple audit paragraphs including the implementation of irrigation schemes, education, transition to VAT, and the functioning of public sector undertakings. The audit highlighted serious lapses in planning, fund utilisation, and monitoring mechanisms. For example, only 10,466 hectares of irrigation potential were created against the target of 24,742 hectares (42% achievement). In the Education (Higher) Department, acute shortages of teaching staff and declining fund allocations impacted quality. The e-Suvidha project suffered from lack of defined targets and remained underutilised after nine years.

Further financial scrutiny revealed unrealised revenue of ₹39.24 crore due to delays in processing lease applications for mines and minerals, and losses of ₹16.90 crore for Tripura Road Transport Corporation in 2008-09. Large funds, ₹17.19 crore, remained unadjusted/unutilised with Block Development Offices for over five years, risking misuse and misappropriation. Additionally, the Public Works Department incurred extra expenditure, cost overruns, and delays in execution of bridge projects. The Health and Family Welfare Department faced suspected misappropriation of ₹1.96 crore due to weak internal controls.

Overall, across departments, monitoring mechanisms were found deficient, targets missed by large margins, and significant potential for better resource management identified. The audit emphasised the need for improved planning, coordination, and financial oversight to ensure schemes deliver intended benefits and public money is safeguarded.

title: Report of 2009 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Pondicherry
overview:
This performance audit report of the Union Territory of Puducherry covers a range of civil departments, prominently Health and Family Welfare, Local Administration, and Police. In the implementation of the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM), only Rs 13.37 crore (56%) of Rs 23.79 crore allocated during 2005-09 was utilised, indicating major inefficiencies and poor financial planning. Additionally, substantial funds remained unutilised year-on-year with closing balances ranging from 66% to 73% for several financial years, pointing to the State Health Society’s lack of preparedness for utilising central grants (page 5).

Further, major infrastructural and manpower deficiencies affected service delivery. Among 77 Sub Centres, 31 continued to operate from rented premises as no new buildings were proposed in annual plans; only six of 13 test-checked Primary Health Centres provided 24-hour delivery and emergency services (page 9). At the Community Health Centre level, essential services such as emergency obstetric care and blood storage were not available in any CHC; critical equipment was still pending purchase even several years after funds were sanctioned (page 8).

Integrated audit on Public Works, revenue receipts, and commercial undertakings also found poor budgeting, non-levy of penalties, and major shortfalls in revenue recovery, with non-realisation of Rs 35.48 crore in additional excise duty and Rs 36.26 crore in import fees. This sustained trend led to rising losses in public corporations and further revenue foregone due to incorrect notifications and delayed project execution (page xi-xii).

title: Report of 2009 - Compliance and Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Odisha
overview:
This report presents significant observations arising from compliance and performance audits across various government departments and autonomous bodies in Odisha for the audit period 2006-09. The overall fund utilisation under key schemes like National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (NREGS) was only 79.5 per cent, with Rs 230.74 crore remaining unutilised out of Rs 963.77 crore in nine audited districts. Spending efficiency dropped to as low as 35 per cent in blocks like Hatadihi, while in districts such as Nayagarh and Jajpur it dipped below 50 per cent, adversely affecting employment generation and works execution. Implementation issues included delayed release and short release of State share, weak planning, non-preparation of mandatory perspective plans, and absence of institutional arrangements, resulting in inefficiency and non-achievement of scheme objectives.

Serious deficiencies were noted including misappropriation of funds, persistent irregularities in rice subsidy (Rs 1.64 crore), unfruitful expenditure on infrastructure (Rs 5.65 crore for piped water supply in Rairangpur Municipality, Rs 81 lakh for incomplete school buildings), and improper fund management, such as unnecessary withdrawal and retention of Rs 278.87 crore in civil deposits. Delays, incorrect decisions, and lack of oversight provided undue benefits to contractors and deprived intended beneficiaries. Overall, audit found high prevalence of persistent and pervasive irregularities with widespread non-compliance, weak internal controls, and poor follow-up on audit recommendations, with thousands of inspection report paragraphs unsettled for over a decade.

Recommendations for improvement include robust planning, timely fund release, enhanced monitoring, filling vacancies of dedicated staff at all levels, and stricter enforcement of internal controls to improve governance and financial accountability in the State administration.

title: Report of 2009 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Nagaland
overview:
The 2009 Performance Audit of Civil Government of Nagaland highlights critical weaknesses in the implementation of several key schemes, including Modernisation of Police Force and irrigation projects, along with the functioning of urban development and revenue departments. Notably, funds released for police modernisation (Rs 228.28 crore between 2000-09) saw under-utilisation and consequent deduction of Rs 22.16 crore from subsequent central government releases, directly reducing resources for essential infrastructure and housing for the police (page 4). The audit uncovered widespread misallocation and skewed distribution of key resources such as vehicles, weaponry shortfalls of 94-98% in test-checked police stations, and persistent non-functional or partially completed IT and forensic facilities, despite significant capital expenditure (e.g., ₹3.77 crore on non-functional police communication and ₹9.85 crore on undelivered IT system) (pages 6-7).

Significant fraudulent financial transactions were reported, including suspected fraudulent Travelling Allowance claims amounting to Rs 25.04 lakh drawn by two school headmasters, and fictitious pay claims by the District Tuberculosis Officer, Zunheboto, totaling Rs 14.97 lakh (page viii). Idle expenditure of Rs 88.55 lakh on salaries for teachers posted to primary or middle schools but attached elsewhere was recorded, alongside system-wide deficiencies in fund management marked by non-recovery or short assessment of receipts, such as Rs 3.20 lakh interest not realised by the Taxes department and Rs 19.04 lakh of hotel tax collected but not remitted (page viii).

The audit observed grave inadequacies in departmental planning, monitoring, and risk controls, with the Urban Development Department lacking a long-term strategy and implementation plan, leading to cost overruns, non-utilised infrastructure, and vulnerabilities to fraud (page viii). Across the sectors reviewed, central guidelines were consistently not followed or only partially implemented, undermining the intended outcomes of the schemes and resulting in significant public resource waste and high-risk operational gaps.

title: Report of 2009 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Mizoram
overview:
This report presents a performance audit of civil departments, including a focused review on the Bamboo Flowering and Famine Combat Scheme (BAFFACOS) implemented in Mizoram. The scheme, designed to address the severe ecological and economic impact of mass bamboo flowering, was allocated ₹145.8 crore sourced from the 12th Finance Commission (₹17.3 crore) and Additional Central Assistance (₹128.5 crore), yet was marred by significant gaps in planning, coordination, and fund allocation.

The planning for BAFFACOS was found deficient, lacking centralised objectives and suffering from the absence of coordinated actions among the 18 implementing Departments. Expenditures were made in an ad hoc manner without prioritization—only ₹14.19 crore (8% of outlay) was allocated to the Environment & Forest Department, which held primary responsibility for bamboo extraction and regeneration. Meanwhile, more than ₹16.63 crore was spent creating idle assets, and over ₹10 crore was diverted or misapplied.

Key findings include the loss of ₹155 crore in unrealized bamboo extraction revenue, ineffective rodent control despite a ₹1.54 crore bounty payment, and an 82.88% crop damage from rodent outbreaks. Further, an estimated ₹19.43 lakh in term loans was wasted because funded projects remained incomplete and funds unrecoverable. Monitoring was lax, with no audit evidence of surveys, mapping, or measurable outputs. The intended benefits did not reach the truly affected populations, undermining the scheme’s goals and accountability.

title: Report of 2009 - Financial and Performance Audit on Civil and Commercial of Government of Meghalaya
overview:
The audit covered the financial and performance aspects of civil and commercial departments of the Government of Meghalaya for the period 2003-08. The report observes significant deficiencies in fund management, with underutilisation and instances of unrealistic budget estimation, leading to savings of Rs 678.46 crore out of the revised expenditure budget of Rs 3,406.11 crore during 2007-08.

Major findings highlight non-submission or delay in submission of utilization certificates, totaling Rs 901.47 crore as of March 2008. Several departments incurred excess expenditure aggregating Rs 375.78 crore without legislative approval between 2003-08. The audit also points out lapses in implementation of schemes, resulting in unfruitful expenditure and accumulation of unadjusted advances.

The consequences of these failures are dilution of legislative control over appropriations, non-achievement of intended outcomes, and erosion of financial discipline in government functioning. The CAG stresses the need for tighter controls, timely submission of accounts, and improved planning to achieve better transparency and utilization.

title: Report of 2009 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Manipur
overview:
The audit covers five chapters reviewing performance audits and transaction audits across key state departments for the financial year ending March 2009. Major findings centre on large-scale deficiencies in programme execution, fund management, and achievement of targets. For example, under the Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme (AIBP), despite heavy investment of ₹1,213.63 crore, only 51% of the targeted irrigation potential was achieved (41,130 out of 81,264 hectares). In the Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme, although ₹272 crore was spent, 68% of rural habitations still lacked adequate drinking water by March 2009, and there was no evidence of evaluation studies to assess outcomes.

Suspected fraudulent and excess payments were repeatedly noted: ₹32.65 lakh for unexecuted ring bund works, ₹50 lakh for possible bogus machinery hiring, ₹9.95 lakh misappropriated in a DDO's account, and ₹73 lakh expended under highly doubtful circumstances in a fishery scheme. Weak financial controls were also documented, such as retention and diversion of funds, delayed transfers, parking of grants, and expenditure without supporting documents or contracts.

These issues resulted in significant losses to the exchequer and persistent service delivery gaps in core sectors. Widespread lapses in planning, execution, monitoring and financial discipline led to weak programme outcomes and unaddressed risks, warranting urgent rectification in department functioning, project oversight, and enforcement of accountability.

title: Report of 2009 - Performance Audit on Hydropower Development through Private Sector of Government of Uttarakhand
overview:
The performance audit reviewed the implementation of hydropower projects in Uttarakhand undertaken through private sector participation between 1993 and 2009. A total of 48 projects with a planned generation capacity of 2,423.10 MW were undertaken by Independent Power Producers, but by March 2009 only 10 percent (418.05 MW) were operational, reflecting significant underachievement against targets. Major reasons for these delays included protracted land acquisition, forest clearance issues, capacity re-revisions, and deficiencies in pre-feasibility studies. Notably, there was absence of robust project monitoring and no evidence of punitive action against defaults, with the government incurring losses due to non-recovery of liquidated damages and loss of anticipated royalties and upfront premiums.

Environmental negligence was marked, as several operational projects caused near-complete depletion of downstream river flow, while improper muck disposal led to increased river turbidity and ecosystem harm. 38 percent of projects reported minimal or no plantation, endangering both ecology and hill slope stabilization. Grid evacuations were not timely, resulting in energy losses and delayed government royalties, while land acquisition and forest clearance delays ranged up to 295 days in some cases.

The report highlights an urgent need for stronger pre-feasibility diligence, standardized policies for project execution, effective monitoring, and an integrated nodal authority to streamline clearances and grid infrastructure. Without prompt corrective action, the cumulative impact of these deficiencies poses grave threats to the state's developmental goals and natural resources.

title: Report of 2009 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Uttarakhand
overview: This performance audit report covers three major performance reviews, an integrated audit, and 28 detailed paragraphs evaluating key schemes and financial transactions of the Government of Uttarakhand. Audit highlighted significant shortcomings in the implementation of major centrally sponsored and state schemes, especially relating to Computerisation of Land Records (CLR), public works, rural engineering, and public sector undertakings. Only 48% of the state’s land records were computerised, and core objectives like digitisation of cadastral maps remained unfulfilled despite allocation of ₹12.08 crore. Major projects suffered due to inefficient management, as seen in the roadworks sector where premature damage led to wasteful expenditures upwards of ₹5.15 crore and mismanagement resulted in blocked funds (e.g., ₹5.35 crore in the Peyjal Nigam project). In the Rural Engineering Service Department, key issues included excess expenditure, un-recovered advances, unauthorized retention of funds, and widespread underperformance in inspection and monitoring. PSUs within the state continued to accumulate losses and arrears in accounts, with Uttarakhand Parivahan Nigam alone reporting accumulated losses of ₹236.61 crore and a sharp decline in its public transport market share. The overall audit pointed to a severe need for institutional reforms, improved accountability mechanisms, and the adoption of better monitoring and IT-enabled systems for effective service delivery.

title: Report of 2009 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Kerala
overview:
This CAG Performance Audit report highlights significant gaps and deficiencies in key flagship programmes in Kerala during 2005-09. For the State Horticulture Mission, Rs 267.90 crore was received but only Rs 155 crore was spent, and a high unspent balance (Rs 112.34 crore, 42%) remained despite urgent needs. The Mission further failed to craft a Perspective Plan or involve district agencies in the rollout, leaving targets unrealistic—unspent subsidies for cold chains and pack houses totalled Rs 3.25 crore, and questionable assistance payments of Rs 2.16 crore to ginger/turmeric growers were also found, even as other eligible farmers received nothing.

The National Rural Health Mission in Kerala showed improved fund flow and infrastructure at some institutions, but Rs 1.48 crore was spent on activities outside approved plans and Rs 51.86 lakh diverted without appropriate sanction. Accredited Social Health Activists did not receive complete mandatory training, and medicine procurement penalties of Rs 3.18 crore were not levied for late supply. New hardware for the Health Management Information System (valued at Rs 4.70 crore) failed to deliver a functioning system, and expensive video-conferencing units remained idle.

The report captures wide-ranging consequences: substantial funds intended for vulnerable sections and infrastructure were stuck or underutilised, target populations were not served, and monitoring and supervision at all levels was weak. Key schemes under Departments of Agriculture, Health, IT, and Roads—meant to improve livelihoods and basic services—were thus left fragmented, and large amounts of public money yielded poor returns for citizens.

title: Report of 2009 - Financial and Performance Audit on District Sirmour of Government of Himachal Pradesh
overview:
The performance audit of District Sirmour revealed significant inefficiencies in fund utilization and project implementation. Out of a total allocation of Rs 98.16 crore during 2004-09, only Rs 45.32 crore was utilized, representing just 46% of allotted funds. Large-scale delays in project completion resulted in cost overruns and incomplete benefits to intended beneficiaries.

The audit noted that only 38% of targeted households under rural water schemes received coverage by 2008, and essential infrastructure projects (like PHCs, roads, school buildings) saw consistent delays ranging from 8 months to over 3 years. Further, lapses in monitoring led to non-detection of unutilized grant-in-aid and misreporting of progress, while recurring expenditures exceeded estimates by Rs 4.21 crore in two years.

Consequently, social outcomes and access to basic services suffered, with Sirmour district lagging behind state averages in health, education, and rural development indices. The report highlights a lack of financial discipline and accountability, urging systematic reform in fund dispersal, execution, and oversight.

title: Report of 2009 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Karnataka
overview:
The 2009 CAG Performance Audit on Civil of the Government of Karnataka highlights significant systemic deficiencies and lapses across various public sector programmes and departments, with a pronounced focus on fiscal mismanagement, ineffective implementation of public welfare schemes, and persistent regulatory non-compliance. During the audit period, the State Government incurred Rs 3,452.44 crore on subsidy and transportation of food grains under the Public Distribution System (PDS), and a sharp increase in Below Poverty Line (BPL) ration cards was observed, exceeding the actual household count by nine lakh, resulting in inclusion of ineligible beneficiaries and additional liability of Rs 1,034.82 crore (p. 11, Executive Summary).

Despite recommendations and policy frameworks, the audit revealed improper processes in beneficiary identification for PDS, causing diversion of essential commodities, irregular documentation, and widespread fund mismanagement. Notably, persistent irregularities included the excess payment of family pension by Rs 2.15 crore across 28 district treasuries, and direct violations of grant and aid codes and Central guidelines, leading to diversion or unproductive use of funds exceeding Rs 10 crore across several departments (pp. 6-7, §1.6.2).

Also, a lack of government responsiveness to audit raised concerns for accountability. As of August 2009, 983 Inspection Reports remained unsettled with 3,994 paragraphs outstanding, indicating deep-rooted issues in audit compliance and executive monitoring despite statutory obligations (p. 7, §1.7.1). Overall, the audit found systemic weaknesses demanding urgent reforms for better financial discipline, transparency, and governance.
