title: Report of 2009 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Himachal Pradesh
overview:
This performance audit reviewed 32 paragraphs, three performance reviews, and one integrated audit of key civil departments in Himachal Pradesh for FY 2005-09. Major findings include chronic fund underutilisation, gaps in infrastructure, and instances of unfruitful or infructuous expenditure.

For the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM), only 25–39% of budgeted funds were utilised (Rs 80.53 crore spent out of Rs 119.85 crore released); between 61% and 75% of available funds each year remained idle. District-level fund utilisation was as low as 6–41%. Significant audit findings include non-preparation of household surveys (critical for bottom-up planning), lack of Perspective/Annual Action Plans, and failure to appoint required medical or paramedical staff—all resulting in deprived rural populations and poor service delivery.

The absence of adequate planning and community participation led to routine blockages in implementation. Even with a surplus of health centres above population-based norms, basic facilities and staff were inadequate: 44 para-medical posts for 117 centres remained vacant, only 1 out of 24 PHCs audited had both Medical Officer posts filled, and 139 PHCs functioned without any staff nurse. Overall, the report highlights major deficiencies in fiscal management, capacity building, and failure to deliver intended social benefits.

title: Report of 2009 - Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Gujarat
overview:
This performance audit covers key government schemes and institutional performance in Gujarat across the Home, Social Justice, Health, and Forest sectors. The Modernisation of Police Forces Scheme, with an annual plan size of ₹100 crore, suffered from under-utilization of funds (5%-68%), routine delays in annual plan submissions by up to 128 days, and the misallocation of vehicles and grant diversions. Despite substantial central assistance, the department replaced condemned vehicles, contrary to scheme norms, and faced critical shortages: 24% less manpower, 20-78% shortage in modern weapons, and persistent ammunition shortfalls. For the Juvenile Justice Act, Child Welfare Committees were not constituted in two districts, and 963 children remained untraced after transfer, revealing alarming system gaps.

NRHM implementation lagged; no facility surveys were conducted at any Sub Centre till March 2009, ₹103.77 crore remained unutilized by 31 March 2009, and key grants were not released at CHCs and PHCs. The report noted continued procurement from blacklisted suppliers, insufficient infrastructure in test-checked facilities, and persistent staff shortages (12-100%) in the health sector.

The Forest Department had a 28% shortfall in plantation targets, with a net loss of 99 sqkm forest cover and 2965 km tree coverage outside forest (2003-2005). Monitoring and internal controls were weak or absent across departments, resulting in cost overruns, delays, and savings not reported to the Centre. The report underscores structural, financial, and administrative lapses producing missed targets, non-functional systems (e.g., POLNET), and poor scheme delivery, with unfruitful and wasteful expenditures aggregating over ₹49 crore.

reportNo: Report of 2009 - Performance Audit on Commercial of Government of Andhra Pradesh
title: Report of 2009 - Performance Audit on Commercial of Government of Andhra Pradesh
overview:
This CAG Performance Audit analysed the financial and operational results of 66 Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) in Andhra Pradesh as of 31 March 2009. The working State PSUs registered a turnover of Rs 44,180 crore for 2008-09, amounting to 14.13% of the State GDP, demonstrating their significant role in the economy. Aggregate profit for the year was Rs 701.56 crore, while accumulated losses stood at Rs 2,351.72 crore; a review of three years’ reports showed that Rs 1,238.09 crore in losses were controllable through better management.

As on 31 March 2009, the State’s investment in PSUs (capital and long-term loans) was Rs 40,469.51 crore—an increase of 31.22% from Rs 30,841.99 crore in 2003-04, with the power sector accounting for 49% of the total and government contributions reaching Rs 12,466.34 crore in 2008-09. 26 PSUs earned profits totalling Rs 1,015.71 crore, but 8 PSUs incurred losses of Rs 314.15 crore, highlighting continued issues of professionalism and accountability.

Quality and timeliness of PSU accounts remain problematic: out of 46 accounts finalised during October 2008 to September 2009, 33 received qualified certificates, and 26 working PSUs had 70 arrear accounts pending. Transaction audits identified losses of Rs 36.95 crore caused by rule violations, poor planning, inadequate monitoring, and transparency failures, underscoring the need for sharper controls, winding up of non-working PSUs, and improvements in governance and financial management.

title: Compliance Audit Report of Government of West Bengal for the year ended on 31 March 2024.
overview:
The 2026 CAG Compliance Audit for West Bengal highlighted significant deficiencies in the infrastructure and functioning of the Animal Resources Development Department. For example, expenditure in Animal Resources Development increased from ₹855.09 crore in 2021-22 to ₹1,164.50 crore in 2023-24 (19.02% of total departmental spend), but this did not translate to provision of key policy documents or maintenance strategies for critical infrastructure such as veterinary hospitals and laboratories. The audit found 46% of surgical equipment in randomly checked Block Animal Health Centres (BAHCs) was non-functional (p. ix), and critical facilities like radiographic digital systems and anaesthesia machines for large animals were missing or inoperable for extended periods.

Shortfalls were acute in the supply of medicines—the majority of facilities did not receive sufficient drugs to meet minimum treatment requirements, contributing to gaps in effective care provision and delayed treatment during outbreaks (p. vii). Staff shortages were profound: 62.74% of sanctioned posts in Animal Resources & Animal Health were vacant as of August 2024. Only 176 of the state's 2,054 Animal Development Assistance Centres (ADACs) were operational due to lack of sanctioned staff, leaving 91% of centres effectively defunct (p. ix).

The consequences included assets falling into disuse, such as the ₹50.27 lakh Jalpaiguri feed-testing laboratory built in 2019, which was never commissioned for lack of manpower (p. vii). Other observed issues were improper bio-waste disposal, lack of disaster SOPs, and chronic failures in capacity utilization at meat processing plants and feed factories, with no active remedial analysis by management, ultimately resulting in wasted investment, suboptimal animal health services, and failure to meet rural livelihood objectives.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Compliance Audit for the year ended 31 March 2024 (Report No. 3 of 2026)
overview:
The Compliance Audit for the year ended 31 March 2024 covers instances of lapses and deficiencies in various Government Departments and Autonomous Bodies in Maharashtra. The audit found persistent delays in utilisation and transfer of funds to implementing agencies. During the period audited, fund utilisation ratios in key schemes were found to be as low as 44% in critical sectors, with Rs 352 crore from centrally sponsored schemes remaining unutilised as of 31 March 2024 (page ix).

Headline findings include non-adherence to scheme guidelines, cost overruns, unnecessary delays, and significant failures in fund management. Audit highlights instances of wrongful extension of benefits to developers amounting to Rs 18.56 crore, non-levy of penalty on contractors resulting in a revenue loss of Rs 7.2 crore, and diversion of scheme funds in violation of allocation norms (page x-xi).

The consequences are significant: critical public services and infrastructure projects stagnated, leading to direct impact on targeted beneficiaries. In the case of tribal girls' hostels, incomplete works led to non-creation of intended capacity, affecting over 17,000 students. Delays and irregularities in relief payments under disaster management schemes resulted in genuine claimants waiting over a year in some districts. The audit concludes that timely compliance with financial controls and reporting mechanisms needs urgent strengthening to address these systemic issues. [Executive Summary, pages ix-xii]

title: Performance and Compliance Audit Report of the Government of West Bengal for the year ended March 2023
overview:
This Performance and Compliance Audit examined the Swasthya Sathi Scheme and infrastructural accessibility in educational institutions in West Bengal. An amount of ₹6,882.06 crore was expended under Swasthya Sathi during 2018-23, benefitting more than 2.25 crore families. However, the audit noted persistent gaps in eligibility protocols and financial oversight, raising serious questions about the integrity of beneficiary databases and payment mechanisms (p.1-2). The report highlighted that as of March 2023, the number of enrolled families exceeded ration cardholder families by nearly ten percent, introducing the risk of ineligible claimants. No annual action plans or comprehensive guidelines existed for the core programme until July 2024, undermining outcome-based monitoring and fund utilisation (p.4). Additionally, empanelled government super speciality hospitals did not achieve Grade-A status, which led to lower treatment packages and loss of revenue, while private hospital billing irregularities saw nearly two-thirds of test-checked cases approved for higher packages without proper justification (p.7).

The report’s compliance audit across educational institutions found incomplete implementation of prescribed accessibility norms for children with special needs. Nearly 58% of audited schools lacked basic infrastructure, such as accessible toilets and ramps, while none had prepared school-level accessibility action plans (p.25). These deficiencies risk ongoing exclusion and non-compliance with the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act. As a result, the report recommends robust beneficiary management, action plan formulation, and regular audits to safeguard both financial and social objectives.

The extent of irregularities, exceeding 30% in several categories (such as schools without essential infrastructure and private hospitals breaching payment rules), and the existence of systemic financial control failures, lead to assessment of the situation as high severity and in need of urgent corrective action.

title: Report No. 06 of 2025-Compliance Audit Report of Government of West Bengal for the year ended 31 March 2023.
overview:
This Compliance Audit Report by the CAG covers material audit findings from 24 West Bengal government departments for the year ended 31 March 2023, focusing on e-procurement (Finance Dept., PWD, PHED) and tourism infrastructure. The report highlighted that, as of 31 March 2023, out of 52 major state departments, 18 PSUs, and 68 autonomous bodies remained unregistered on the mandatory e-Procurement portal, posing significant transparency and accountability risks. Critical modules such as tender evaluation and contract award in e-procurement were not implemented, resulting in manual and offline practices for award processes. For instance, out of 90,928 tenders floated by PWD and PHED between 2018-19 and 2022-23, 4,012 tenders failed to impose minimum submission timelines, and in 7,137 cases, automated value calculation discrepancies were detected.

In the Tourism Department, from 2017-2023, 471 projects were sanctioned worth ₹976.4 crore for infrastructure and asset upgrades, but only 330 (70%) have been completed as of 31 March 2023—significant delays are ascribed to land issues and planning weaknesses. For certain flagship schemes such as Swadesh Darshan, project utility remained low due to non-transfer, poor maintenance, and CRZ violations, incurring avoidable expenditures (e.g. ₹1.84 crore worth of assets left unused or demolished). On the financial front, various departments failed to recover or safeguarded revenue—e.g. a ₹15.02 crore loss in royalty from lease holders due to delayed rate notification and ₹6.36 crore lost by not commencing toll collection on a completed bridge.

The report underscores systemic risks: lack of strategic planning, insufficient IT controls, misapplication of government instructions, and weak contract enforcement. Recommendation stress robust system controls, proper departmental coordination, and policy enforcement to ensure targeted development outcomes and safeguard state finances.

title: Compliance Audit Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the period ended March 2023 Government of Himachal Pradesh Report No. 4 of 2025 (Hindi)
overview:
This CAG compliance audit report details institutional gaps, regulatory failures, and financial irregularities in Himachal Pradesh between 2018 and 2023. University faculty vacancies ranged from 27-37%, resulting in heavier workloads and reduced student guidance. Over ₹11.19 crore worth of Enterprise Resource Planning System modules stayed non-functional through December 2023 due to lack of use or adaptation, with maintenance issues preventing effective academic administration (see page vi).

Mining sector revenue regulation proved weak: ₹1,236.66 crore mining sector contribution to state revenues in five years (2018-2023), yet royalty collection was short by ₹1.81 crore across 27 mining leases, with widespread unsupervised activity. District Mineral Foundation Trusts received ₹239.21 crore but only 19.66% was released for projects (page x), and none operated a mandated website or published annual budgets. Audit found 40,000+ instances of illegal mining, and monitoring frameworks (eg. GPS-based vehicle tracking) were not implemented (page ix).

Irrigation projects suffered delays: Of 163 examined schemes, only 72 were completed, 31 with delays up to 45 months, and 18 with cost overruns totaling ₹8.83 crore. Technical surveys often lacked essential hydrological, geological data, causing failures and waste. Disaster Response Fund utilization averaged only 69-92%, and ₹61.07 crore was withheld by the Government of India due to persistent misutilization, while training targets for emergency volunteers missed by over 50% (page xv).

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended 31 March 2024 Union Government (Commercial) No. 39 of 2025 (Compliance Audit Observations)
overview:
This Compliance Audit examines the financial activities and adherence to regulations by twelve Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) under seven Ministries/Departments for the year ended 31 March 2024. The audit revealed avoidable and infructuous expenditures totaling ₹14,777.92 crore, primarily due to non-compliance with rules, defective planning, and poor monitoring. Specific cases include Central Coalfields Limited’s (CCL) violation of Forest regulations, resulting in an additional ₹21.22 crore penalty, and Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited’s (BPCL) aborted Polyol project, incurring a loss of ₹300.15 crore.

Other major findings highlight cost overruns and operational inefficiencies, such as NTPL's cost overrun of ₹2,383.94 crore due to delays and lack of project planning, and NHAI’s substantial undue burden on road users through excess toll collection. Industry and infrastructure clusters also reflected significant gaps, including non-recovery of advances that led to a loss of ₹6.58 crore at Instrumentation Limited.

In total, the report underscores systemic shortcomings in project management, procurement, and regulatory compliance, recommending procedural reforms and stricter monitoring to avoid repeat lapses and improve CPSE performance.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended March 2024 Union Government Report No. 36 of 2025 (Compliance Audit – Civil & Commercial)
overview:
This CAG compliance audit examined the conservation and preservation of monuments and antiquities by the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) in Uttar Pradesh, covering five circles—Agra, Jhansi, Lucknow, Meerut, and Sarnath—across 741 Centrally Protected Monuments (CPMs). The gross expenditure for Civil Ministries and five Constitutional bodies was ₹16,26,975.07 crore in 2023-24, with ASI circles spending only 0.41-0.76% of their budgets on excavation and exploration, despite PAC's assurance to increase this to 5%.

Audit revealed critical lapses: 86% of notifications lacked legal boundary details, and only 6.4% of CPMs had proper ownership documentation. ASI operated 456 CPMs (94%) without legal title. Encroachment was reported at 96 monuments, and 31 CPMs remain untraceable as per ASI records. Antiquities were stored in deteriorating conditions with only 20% digitised. Staff shortages were acute: 57% in technical cadre, 41% in Monument Attendants, and up to 96% in security. Additionally, 81% of Adarsh monuments lacked cafeterias, 90% lacked professional guides, and 86% lacked Wi-Fi connectivity.

The consequences were ongoing vulnerability to misuse, boundary erosion, and litigation risks for monuments. Despite field actions such as constructing grills and gates at 195 sites, lack of revision to notifications left these protective measures legally unrecognized. The report calls for urgent reforms in notification, documentation, staffing, and encroachment removal to halt the deterioration of national heritage.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended March 2024 Union Government Report No. 37 of 2025 Union Territories without Legislatures (Compliance Audit - Civil)
overview:
The CAG report highlights critical compliance and financial management issues across five Union Territories without Legislatures—Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Ladakh, and Lakshadweep. Collectively, these UTs reported a gross expenditure of ₹21,028.78 crore for 2023–24. Audit found that major infrastructure projects at ANIIMS in Andaman & Nicobar Islands suffered severe delays, with only 8 of 29 sanctioned works completed as of October 2024, due to lack of a comprehensive funding plan and poor project oversight. The resulting backlog meant crucial facilities like the Science Block and residential quarters remained incomplete after 7+ years, pushing unit costs up more than 58% and burdening the exchequer with extra HRA payments and project escalation costs.

In the revenue sector, the audit revealed significant legacy arrears in VAT in Chandigarh, with systemic lapses such as non-revalidated bank guarantees and weak enforcement mechanisms. Audit scrutiny in Dadra and Nagar Haveli/Daman and Diu exposed avoidable expenditures and regulatory non-compliance in critical departments. Across UTs, the audit pointed out non-release and inefficient utilization of central grants, evident in the 4% overall underutilization and ₹1,298.25 crore surplus capital funds (22.8%).

Systemic delays, shortfalls in asset creation, and non-adherence to financial rules compromised service delivery and represent a high risk to fiscal discipline, with over ₹69 lakh in excess pay and ₹95.24 lakh avoidable penalties directly cited for urgent recovery. These failures undermine the objectives of national healthcare and welfare schemes in the UTs and necessitate immediate corrective action.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the period ended March 2022 (Compliance Audit - Civil and Commercial)
overview:
This audit report highlights substantial deficiencies in the implementation of the Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT) in Telangana. Notably, there was a lack of coordination among the State Mission Directorate, Engineer-in-Chief (Public Health & Municipal Engineering), and Urban Local Bodies, with the mandated Tripartite MoU never executed. For example, assets worth crores created under the Mission were pending takeover in both Karimnagar and Ramagundam as of 2022, reflecting accountability failures (Page 23).

Audit revealed that planning for the Mission was inadequate, with assessments of service gaps lacking scientific rigor and sanctioned works often unsupported by authenticated estimates. In the test checked cities, there was significant underachievement in providing House Service Connections (HSCs). Service Level Benchmarks (SLBs) for water supply and sewerage were not met—the executed connections were not fully handed over, and many remained nonfunctional, directly affecting intended beneficiaries (Page 27).

A critical financial finding was the use of Mission funds for inadmissible items, such as price adjustments and road restoration, in violation of both Mission Guidelines and state orders, resulting in excess payments running into crores. Further, the payment sanctioning process failed to detect overpayments due to incorrect calculations for POL, DI pipes, and DI fittings. Overall, the audit concludes that monitoring and implementation weaknesses resulted in critical gaps in financial management, project delivery, and service improvement, potentially causing leakages and a waste of public funds totaling over ₹55 crore (Page 7).

title: Compliance Audit Report-Civil for the period ended March 2023 (Report No. 5 of 2025)
overview:
The Compliance Audit Report-Civil for the period ended March 2023 (Report No. 5 of 2025) by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India presents critical findings on Central Government ministries and departments. Total irregular expenditure of ₹4,753.21 crore was detected across 35 cases, with major observations on misutilisation and diversion of scheme funds, excess procurements, understatement of liabilities, and unfruitful investments in public projects. The audit also found several instances of non-compliance in procurement, contract execution, and recurring delays in submission of utilisation certificates and completion of infrastructure initiatives.

A recurring issue is that more than 47% of allocated funds during the audit period remained unutilised or were diverted, pointing to systemic shortcomings in planning and implementation. Many departments failed to maintain asset registers, leading to thousands of assets unaccounted for as per physical verification. The audit also reported on lapses in adherence to General Financial Rules and failure to recover outstanding advances, with implications for accountability and transparency. Cases involving unproductive expenditure due to abandoned or incomplete works ran into hundreds of crores.

The report underscores that such persistent lapses in compliance, weak internal controls, and delays have a cascading effect on public service delivery targets. They resulted in loss to exchequer, delayed or denied benefits to intended beneficiaries, and increased litigation risks against the government. The CAG recommends system reforms, regular monitoring, and strict enforcement of financial discipline for all Central Government ministries and implementing agencies.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme, Government of Maharashtra (Report No. 7 of 2025)
overview:
The audit covers Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme implementation in Maharashtra from 2019-20 to 2023-24, examining financial management, planning, execution, and monitoring across six selected districts. Of the Rs 13,957.47 crore available for the Scheme, Rs 13,518 crore was utilised, representing 96.8% fund usage. Despite high expenditure, only 52.81% of the 25.72 lakh approved works were completed, with Rs 6,725.65 crore spent on finished projects and Rs 5,361.02 crore on incomplete works. As of March 2025, over 7.10 lakh works had not commenced, while 2.48 lakh projects remained pending for over three years.

Employment generation under MGNREGS fell significantly short of targets. Although registered households increased by 46%, only 19% demanded work, of which just 8.7% (1.71 lakh of 19.65 lakh average per year) completed 100 days. Delays in wage payments persisted, with Rs 35.32 crore for unskilled labour outstanding as of October 2024. The audit also notes Rs 5.88 crore in rejected compensation claims, despite no provision in the Act for denial.

Further deficiencies include gaps in record-keeping (52% received job cards late and 44 of 48 panchayats issued duplicate cards); staffing shortfalls (Gram Rozgar Sahayaks missing in 2,258 of 28,279 gram panchayats); and monitoring lapses—65% of verified works lacked display boards and 30% of works had not been geo-tagged. Social Audit Unit flagged 1,084 cases of misappropriation, with Rs 11.22 crore to be recovered; action remained pending in 314 cases involving Rs 4.44 crore. These cumulative weaknesses undermine Scheme effectiveness and transparency, with persistent delays, incomplete asset creation, and accountability concerns impacting rural livelihoods.

title: Compliance Audit Report (Civil) of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the period ended March 2024 (Report No. 7 of 2025)
overview:
This report examines the implementation of the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) in Punjab and reviews compliance audits across several departments for the period ending March 2024. The audit reveals significant weaknesses in planning and fund utilisation: while the total budget outlay was ₹2,96,345 crore, actual application of resources reached ₹3,00,517 crore during 2023-24, with revenue expenditure increasing by 54.77% from ₹75,860 crore in 2019-20 to ₹1,17,407 crore in 2023-24. Fund under-utilisation hampered Central Share releases, largely due to unverified baseline data and inaccurate Annual Action Plans.

Audit found an alarming backlog of 17,245 Inspection Reports containing 67,816 outstanding observations with a money value of ₹73,534.62 crore, 12,608 of these over five years old. In the JJM, 11.27 lakh households with their own drinking water source were wrongly reported as 'covered', inflating results without actual service delivery. There is a critical under-provision of infrastructure: only 7 out of 153 required Block Laboratories exist (95% shortfall). Water quality monitoring is compromised: in some districts, up to 97% of positive samples were not escalated for advanced testing.

Over-extraction of groundwater remains unchecked in 78% of districts, contrary to JJM’s vision, with minimal adoption of sustainable practices or technology integration. Poor committee functioning, delayed SOPs, and severe shortfall in emergency response vehicle deployment (86% below requirement) further impede effective service delivery. Recommendations urge immediate attention to planning, accountability, laboratory capacity, and real-time water quality tracking to ensure clean and safe water for all.

title: Compliance Audit Report (Civil) of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the period ended March 2024 (Report No. 7 of 2025)
overview:
As against the total budget outlay of ₹ 2,96,345 crore, the application of resources was ₹ 3,00,517 crore during 2023-24, with expenditure increasing by 29.51% from ₹ 94,471 crore in 2019-20 to ₹ 1,22,346 crore in 2023-24. Revenue expenditure rose by 54.77%, comprising 80-96% of total expenditure for the period, whereas capital expenditure remained low, except in 2019-20 due to UDAY loan conversion.

The audit highlighted severe lapses in implementation of the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) in Punjab, including inaccurate annual action plans and failure to re-verify baseline data, resulting in underutilisation of funds and inflated reporting of Functional Household Tap Connection (FHTC) coverage. Over 11.27 lakh households were wrongly reported as covered, although they had not received piped water supply; critical planning steps like Village Action Plans and a State Action Plan were omitted, leading to unrealistic proposals and objectives.

Water quality monitoring was found wanting, with a 95% shortage of block-level laboratories (only 7 for 153 blocks), and poor sample follow-up. Arsenic, nitrate, iron, fluoride, and uranium contamination remained high in several districts. Audit noted delays in water quality results (45.57% samples delayed over 31 days) and a lack of real-time monitoring, affecting supply safety and timely response. The government's lack of timely action not only hampers service delivery but increases the risk of continued exposure to unsafe water and hampers long-term rural water sustainability.

title: Composite Audit Report (Civil) of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the period ended March 2023
overview:
This Composite Audit Report presents significant findings of performance and compliance audits for Punjab covering two major performance audits—in Information Systems Audit of e-Procurement and Quality of School Education—and sector-specific compliance audits including Jails Department and Punjab Labour Welfare Board. The total financial implications from compliance audit observations were ₹209.47 crore, with individual cases of avoidable expenditure, unrecovered water cess, and delayed payments leading to interest and penalties.

Fund utilisation and expenditure trends highlight notable growth: Punjab’s total expenditure increased by 53.72% from ₹79,177 crore in 2018-19 to ₹1,21,710 crore in 2022-23. Revenue expenditure grew by 50.74%, while capital expenditure surged 176.41% between these years, indicating higher resource commitment but ongoing issues in spending efficiency. Departmental response to audit observations has been slow, with 17,844 inspection reports containing 64,482 observations (₹79,727.63 crore money value) pending as of June 2023, and more than five years of unresolved audit queries.

Performance audits indicate persistent system design deficiencies, unaddressed recommendations from previous CAG reports, and inadequate training or controls in critical systems like GePNIC. Education audits revealed a decline in higher secondary retention rates from 106% to 66% (2018-19 to 2022-23), substantial shortages in SCERT and DIET staff (up to 88%), and adverse pupil-teacher ratios—30% of primary schools in Punjab affected in 2022-23. Compliance audits expose critical gaps in jail amenities and welfare administration, from overcrowding and health infrastructure deficits to delayed benefit processing and missing accountability mechanisms.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Functioning of Regional Transport Offices (Report No. 8 of 2025)
overview:
This statewide compliance audit examined the functioning of Regional Transport Offices (RTOs) in Uttarakhand's Transport Department between 2019-20 and 2023-24. The audit found significant gaps in regulation, revenue, and enforcement: For instance, 67,603 vehicles—including ambulances and school buses—were found without valid fitness certificates as on 31 March 2024, and 43,821 non-transport vehicles were overdue for registration renewal. Additionally, over ₹361.86 crore in vehicle tax arrears accumulated during the period, with more than ₹176.81 crore pending beyond five years.

Revenue collection targets were not met except for 2022–23. Only ₹10 crore of the ₹209.20 crore green cess collected was actually utilised for eligible projects, and only 39% of required road accident relief funds were transferred (₹30.02 crore of ₹76.38 crore). The audit revealed weak controls over driver licensing, as 144 individuals received more than one driving license, and process deficiencies such as granting hill endorsements without required tests and irregular inspections of driving schools.

Findings highlight systemic data and IT weaknesses, including 1,110 vehicles registered in more than one RTO, 15 cases of vehicle registration predating purchase date, and poor integration between enforcement IT systems and the Vahan database. These failings led to reduced compliance, service delivery gaps, and lost government revenue, demanding urgent reforms for transparency and accountability.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the period ended March 2022 (Report No. 3 of 2025)
overview:
The CAG audit covers the compliance performance and financial transactions of 60 Departments and 32 Public Sector Undertakings of Uttarakhand, accounting for over 48,000 auditable units. For the year under review, audit scrutiny was performed on 503 units across 39 departments, examining major schemes like PMKVY 2.0, PRASHAD, Swadesh Darshan, GST operations, disaster recovery, and public sector enterprise management.

The total financial impact of audit findings is noted as ₹3,101.07 crore. Serious lapses included unfruitful or wasteful expenditure—such as ₹2.98 crore on abandoned works in Transport, ₹10.79 crore on a failed communication media project, and ₹3.94 crore wasted on Five Heritage Circuit assets due to site misselection. Further, procedural weaknesses led to failure in recovering ₹252.26 crore in mining penalties and systemic loopholes enabled GST non-compliance and fraudulent placement claims under PMKVY.

Audit traced repeated recurring weaknesses: prolonged unsolved contractor disputes after 69 months, non-adjustment of ₹1.61 crore with failed TPs in skill development, and severe delays in tendering, award, and infrastructure use—many components and assets remained unutilised or even locked after years. Recoveries effected at audit’s instance were just ₹0.02 crore out of ₹275.57 crore accepted, showing limited corrective action in practice. The report underscores that ineffective departmental oversight, lack of due diligence, and unaddressed recommendations from previous audits continue to place a significant financial and governance burden on the State exchequer.

title: Combined Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the period ended March 2023
overview:
Part I of the Combined CAG Report No.6 of 2025 covers compliance and revenue audit observations for the Government of Kerala for the period ending March 2023. Total revenue receipts for 2022-23 amounted to ₹1,32,724.66 crore, out of which the State’s own revenue was ₹87,086.12 crore (66%). However, revenue arrears across principal heads accumulated to a critical ₹28,398.10 crore—over 21% of annual receipts—indicating persistent collection challenges. At the end of June 2023, 14,953 audit observations spanning 2,524 Inspection Reports and involving a money value of ₹5,062.52 crore remained unsettled, reflecting slow rectification and weak response from departments (p.9).

The audit found systemic lapses in tax administration for GST, excise, vehicles, and stamp duties. Notably, deficiencies in GST monitoring led to losses amounting to ₹1,671.25 crore, with slow scrutiny and non-issuance of notices exacerbating revenue leakage. Specific instances—including non-renewal of fitness certificates for transport vehicles (₹8.82 crore loss), non-collection of service charges (₹4.24 crore), and non-levy of green tax—were found to undermine statutory revenue streams.

Part II highlighted short/non-transfer of ₹279.3 crore to the Road Safety Fund, pervasive lapses in forest plantation management, and significant audit follow-up backlog. The magnitude of outstanding inspection reports and unresolved audit paragraphs signals ongoing weaknesses in financial discipline, internal controls, and accountability mechanisms.

title: Report No. 10 of 2025, Government of Madhya Pradesh-Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the period ended March 2023
overview:
The audit report highlights critical deficiencies in the human resource management of school education in Madhya Pradesh for the years 2018-19 to 2022-23. A key finding is the inability of the Government of Madhya Pradesh to maintain the mandated Pupil-Teacher Ratio (PTR), with ratios reaching 37:1 in Middle, 40:1 in Secondary, and 54:1 in Higher Secondary schools, against norms of 35:1, 30:1, and 30:1 respectively. Teacher shortages were most acute in Higher Secondary (45% shortfall) and Secondary schools (40%), while even Primary schools experienced a 10% shortage despite being better staffed overall.

Deployment of teachers is inefficient, with rural schools experiencing greater staffing deficits, undermining equitable educational access. Training programs also suffered, both due to substantial shortfalls in trainer posts—between 57.45% (Lecturer) and 80.85% (Assistant Professor) at District Institutes of Education and Training—and due to financial mismanagement. Notably, ₹35.71 crore, constituting 21.64% of ₹165.09 crore allotted under Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan for capacity-building, lapsed during 2018-23.

Further issues include delayed transfer of employee pension contributions, with a shortfall of ₹303.11 crore to ₹555.86 crore annually not deposited on time into NSDL accounts, poor functioning of HRMIS modules, and inadequate school monitoring resulting in thousands of grievances pending and incomplete inspection routines. Transfers and postings were found to be non-transparent and in violation of government orders, compromising staff rationalization and quality outcomes.

title: Government of Madhya Pradesh-Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Management of Town and Country Planning
overview:
This compliance audit reviewed the functioning of the Directorate of Town and Country Planning (T&CP) and five key Municipal Corporations of Madhya Pradesh, focusing on the management of urban and regional development for the period 2018-2023. The audit revealed that the Directorate failed to prepare Regional Plans for seven out of eight statutory regions, and no new Development Plan for Bhopal has been approved since 2005, despite a population increase of 77% in the municipal area and a 175% rise in unauthorised colonies since 2000, resulting in outdated, ineffective planning tools.

The report highlighted irregularities including non-collection of data from stakeholder departments, reservation of land without railway requirements, repeated delays in approval of the Bhopal Development Plan, and several violations in land use and building permits such as unauthorized constructions, non-maintenance of required open spaces, and diversion of land in violation of legal provisions. Municipal Corporations failed to monitor developments, allowing irregular building permissions without completing required internal development or preparing zoning plans. Over 33,000 building permissions were issued between 2018 and 2021 without ensuring occupancy certificates, increasing risks of safety, regulatory violations, and loss of municipal revenue.

Internal controls were found severely lacking, with up to 96% shortfall in required planning and supervision committee meetings, no mechanism to trace unauthorized development, and significant shortage of skilled manpower. The audit concludes that the Department of Town and Country Planning was largely non-functional, resulting in unregulated growth, significant public risk, and loss of revenue.

Implement a GIS-based and IT-enabled monitoring system for real-time tracking of permissions, developments, and compliance.
Regularly inspect authorised and unauthorised constructions and act promptly against non-compliance.

title: Report No. 9 of 2025 of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the period ended March 2023, Government of Madhya Pradesh
overview:
This report of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) for Madhya Pradesh covers significant findings from compliance audits of multiple state departments including General Administration, Higher Education, Revenue, and Backward Classes & Minorities Welfare for the period 2020-23. Of notable concern, 14,102 Inspection Reports containing 57,600 audit paragraphs remained unsettled as of March 2024—of these, 21.55% had not received any departmental reply, highlighting considerable delays and systemic inaction with financial implications exceeding ₹124,000 crore in audited expenditure between 2020 and 2023.

Fund management and recruitment processes were notably deficient. For instance, the Public Service Commission failed to timely verify and process 101 departmental vacancies, with delays ranging from 31–68 months in some cases. Examination and selection timelines were routinely missed, with 22 of 44 exams unheld as scheduled and significant appointment delays adversely affecting both candidates and state capacities. Further, compliance issues included unreconciled advances totalling over ₹30 crore at Barkatullah University left outstanding for up to two decades, and persistent failures in furnishing UCs led to a reduction in sanctioned grants (₹5.68 crore received out of ₹14.21 crore sanctioned by UGC).

The ramifications include compromised governance, loss of revenue, and breach of statutory and regulatory frameworks. Substantial lapses in land diversion compliance, non-recovery of affiliation fees, and deficient financial controls contribute to a climate of inefficiency and unaccountability, risking loss to the public exchequer, delayed access to public services, and potential fraud.

title: Government of Goa - Report No. 4 of Year 2025- Compliance Audit Report of C&AG for the period ending March 2023
overview:
This Compliance Audit Report assesses critical government operations in Goa, including Social, General and Economic Sectors, the Revenue Sector, and Public Sector Undertakings, for the period ending March 2023. Total government expenditure rose sharply by 31.66% between 2020-21 (`14,842.08 crore) and 2022-23 (`19,541.24 crore), while revenue expenditure alone rose by 23.09% to reach `14,884.48 crore in 2022-23. Revenue expenditure's share of total outlay decreased from 80% in 2021-22 to 76% in 2022-23, driven by increased capital spending.

Key findings include systemic shortcomings in Solid Waste Management (SWM) in Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), with only 78% of waste treated on average across 14 ULBs, leaving substantial quantities dumped untreated. Test-checked municipal councils often lacked council-approved SWM plans, under-collected user charges, and had inadequate treatment facilities – for example, Margao MC ran a 5 TPD facility for 35 TPD waste. Audit also exposed deficiencies in GST oversight, excise collections, improper award of contracts, and poor loan recovery and reporting practices in government-owned NBFCs.

Consequences of these lapses encompass mounting arrears, uncollected revenue, creation of new waste dumpsites, ineligible waivers to defaulters, and substantial unaddressed risks to public health and state finances. The audit underscores the urgent need for robust planning, improved oversight, strengthened financial controls, and accountability across government operations.

title: Audit Report for the period ended March 2024
overview:
The Performance Audit of the University of Calicut highlighted major administrative, academic, and financial shortcomings amounting to ₹1394.64 crore across several departments. The University’s strategic plan lacked Syndicate approval and did not define timelines or milestones for its seven strategic priority areas. Key mechanisms such as the College Development Council (CDC) were improperly constituted, lacking State Government and Principal representation. Syllabi of 24 out of 45 programme categories were not revised as per UGC norms, undermining academic quality.

Critical lapses in financial management resulted in delays of four to five months in annual account preparation and seven to eight months in submission to Kerala State Audit Department, with audit delays ranging from 10 to 19 months. Failure to establish a self-sustaining pension fund for 47 years, and advances drawn totalling ₹6.79 crore remained unsettled from 1975-76 to 2023-24. Non-compliance with UGC norms affected Ph.D. admissions and research outcomes; 41 out of 145 researchers did not submit theses despite substantial funding. The University’s ranking in the NIRF consistently declined, dropping to 89th position in 2024 and distance education for 32,651 students lacked UGC recognition.

Infrastructural deficiencies persisted, with classrooms and accessibility features inadequate and 74 out of 169 buildings constructed without Kerala Panchayat Building Rules approval, classifying them as unauthorized. Additionally, incorrect deduction by Water Resources Department resulted in undue benefit of ₹53.78 lakh to contractors. Multiple cases of misappropriation, wasteful expenditure, and loss of government assistance/revenue were identified, underscoring the need for improved oversight and strict adherence to statutory guidelines.

title: Performance Audit of Jal Jeevan Mission
overview:
The Performance Audit of the Jal Jeevan Mission in Kerala, covering 2019-24, found significant gaps in planning, implementation, and community participation. Despite an administrative sanction to provide Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTCs) to 54.45 lakh rural households at a total cost of ₹44,714.79 crore, only 52.46% coverage was achieved by March 2024—falling far short of the targeted 100%. Of the total 5,318 works planned, only 51% were completed, and 17% had not even commenced, impacted largely by critical administrative hurdles such as road cutting permissions, for which over half of the 7,458 applications were still pending. Financial management issues included a pending contractor bill backlog of ₹3,578.47 crore and ₹3,625.72 crore worth of work packages remaining unawarded due to poor fund mobilization and lack of contractor interest.

Community involvement, a core tenet of the Mission, remained superficial, with Village Water and Sanitation Committees (VWSCs) constituted in only four of 21 test-checked Grama Panchayats, and community contributions totaling merely ₹131.40 lakh. The absence of baseline surveys led to large numbers of disconnections—2,13,991 (52.92%) of 4,04,404 FHTCs—occurring within just one month of provision, exposing a lack of need-based planning. Essential schemes for vulnerable SC/ST groups and water-quality affected areas were not prioritized, and comprehensive policies for operation and maintenance had not been framed.

Water quality was not systematically monitored, and third-party oversight was weak. The State had not formulated source sustainability or greywater management plans, which, along with delays in release of matching State shares, convergence failures, and inadequate institutional mechanisms, led to overall underperformance and sustainability risks.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the period ended March 2023 on Development of Multi-Functional Complexes and Commercial sites by Rail Land Development Authority- Report No.26 of 2025 Government (Compliance Audit-Railways)
overview:
This audit examined the development of Multi-Functional Complexes (MFCs) and commercial sites by the Rail Land Development Authority (RLDA) during 2018-19 to 2022-23. The RLDA earned ₹2,138.06 crore during the audit period, with a substantial shortfall of ₹1,661.52 crore (43.73%) against the revised earnings target of ₹3,799.58 crore, indicating significant underachievement in financial performance. Further, out of 188 proposals received for 657.10 hectares of land, only 59 proposals (203.83 hectares) were entrusted to RLDA, and just 35 sites were awarded to developers, with none of the commercial sites developed as of March 2023.

Physical progress also lagged: of the 53 MFC sites awarded to developers, only 14 had been completed by March 2023. Audit found systemic flaws, including non-preparation of five-year plans for the period 2022-27, slow project pipeline clearance, recurring delays, and persistent land-related issues such as encroachment and unclear land title. Further, RLDA failed to transfer ₹233.44 crore in earnings to Ministry of Railways (MoR) and retained ₹3.92 crore in excess margin money.

These shortcomings have hampered RLDA’s core mandate of generating non-fare revenue from railway land. The lack of clear timelines, inconsistent valuation methodologies, ineffective oversight of consultants, and persistent administrative lapses threaten public asset monetization and jeopardize long-term railway infrastructure funding.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the period ended March 2023 on Levy and recovery of charges on Private Sidings in Indian Railways and Working of Signalling Systems in South Western Railway, Report No. 24 of 2025- Government (Railways) (Compliance Audit)
overview:
The CAG audit uncovered critical inefficiencies in the Indian Railways’ management of charges on private sidings and the maintenance of signalling systems. As of March 2023, outstanding charges totalling ₹4,087.33 crore (including ₹1,461.47 crore in interest) remain unrecovered from 269 private siding owners. Land License Fee (LLF) alone accounted for ₹2,016.20 crore, primarily from Central Railway, constituting 95% of LLF outstanding balances. The period saw delays in billing up to 1,825 days, attributable to poor coordination and the absence of IT systems to monitor levies and recoveries. Charging errors and lack of maintenance of basic records like siding registers impeded accountability and collection.

In the South Western Railway, substantial incidents of signal failures (an average of 2,961 per year) were noted, despite full completion of scheduled maintenance. Repeated irregularities in inspection and maintenance practices were highlighted, signaling weak internal controls and monitoring, with some critical safety upgrades and asset replacements still pending. There is no comprehensive upgradation plan for signalling infrastructure, and IT solutions such as Signal Maintenance Management Systems and Computerised Train Signal Registers remain unimplemented as of March 2023.

The audit concludes that systemic failures in enforcing contract stipulations, poor record keeping, and administrative lapses have led to mounting arrears, operational risks, and adverse impacts on the reliability and safety of Indian Railways’ network.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended March 2023 Government Scientific and Environmental Ministries/Departments Report No. 29 of 2025 (Compliance Audit)
overview:
This Compliance Audit report covers seven Scientific and Environmental Ministries/Departments for the year ended March 2023, focusing on transactions, financial management, project efficiency, and regulatory compliance. The total expenditure for these Ministries during 2022-23 was ₹72,725.54 crore, an increase of ₹3,876.93 crore (5.63 per cent) compared to the previous year. Despite this, overall fund savings amounted to ₹8,917.85 crore (10.92 per cent of budget allotment), with the Ministry of Earth Sciences accounting for the highest unspent proportion (40.33 per cent).

Critical audit findings include sustained manpower shortages in the National Biopharma Mission (Para 2.1), unproductive expenditure of ₹0.78 crore for idle prototypes (Para 3.2), and avoidable penalties and non-realisation of charges amounting to ₹8.86 crore in the Ministry of Earth Sciences (Paras 4.1–4.3). The Zoological Survey of India failed to develop a Survey Manual seven years after assurance, and 77% of specimens from the last five years remained unidentified (Para 5.1). Infrastructure gaps, slow digitisation, and inadequate capacity building were pervasive, impacting scientific outcomes and biodiversity conservation.

There are widespread deficiencies in procurement, contract and project management, delays in monitoring and evaluation, and irregular grant payments, with ₹5.46 crore released without milestones. Outstanding Utilisation Certificates for grants totaling ₹16,905.17 crore (41,526 due) signify systemic issues in grant management and accountability. The report recommends intensifying project monitoring, implementing structured feedback mechanisms, and improving compliance and governance frameworks across departments.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Customs for the period ended March 2023 Government Department of Revenue (Indirect Taxes-Customs) Report No. 21 of 2025 (Compliance Audit- Civil)
overview:
The report presents the results of the compliance audit of the Department of Revenue – Customs and the Director General of Foreign Trade for the year ended March 2023. During FY 23, Customs receipts realised were ₹2,13,372 crore, marking a 6.83% year-on-year increase and an overall 81% growth over the last five years. Exports through 417 Customs ports amounted to ₹36.22 lakh crore, while imports through 432 ports reached ₹57.50 lakh crore. A total of 203 inspection reports, covering 1,894 observations amounting to a revenue implication of ₹1,779 crore, were issued to various Commissionerates and Regional Licensing Authorities. However, arrears in Customs revenue pending recovery as of March 2023 increased to ₹55,853 crore—up 7.86% compared to March 2022—with more than ₹3,526 crore unresolved for over five years.

The Subject Specific Compliance Audit on the Merchandise Exports from India Scheme (MEIS) and Service Exports from India Scheme (SEIS) uncovered persistent systemic issues, including manual intervention delays in 39-44% of sampled cases and continued issuance of scrips to ineligible entities, leading to incorrect incentive outflows totalling ₹724.96 crore. The Department’s automation and internal control recommendations from earlier audit reports remained unimplemented as both schemes were being phased out, yet significant irregularities continued during wind-down.

Overall, the report highlights non-compliance, under-assessment, and slow recovery mechanisms within the Customs administration. Despite partial rectifications with recoveries of ₹14 crore in 39 cases, the continued accumulation of arrears, inefficiencies in scheme administration, and irregularities in the application of Customs law indicate high compliance risk and the ongoing need for systemic reforms.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the period ended March 2023, Government, Department of Revenue (Indirect Taxes, Goods and Services Tax), Report No. 25 of 2025 (Compliance Audit)
overview:
This compliance audit covers oversight of GST payments and return filing by the Department of Revenue (CBIC) for the period 2018-19 to 2022-23. The audit revealed significant deficiencies in monitoring mechanisms, with the Indirect taxes collections increasing by ₹93,612 crore (7.22%) during FY23 over FY22; however, Central Excise collections fell by 18% (₹71,808 crore) in the same period. There was a decline in Indirect Taxes to GDP ratio from 5.47% in FY22 to 5.15% in FY23 mainly due to that drop, despite CGST revenues rising 22% in FY23 (₹1,51,796 crore).

The compliance verification mechanism for Composition Levy Scheme (CLS) taxpayers was found inadequate, specifically regarding Rule 5 requirements, signage, and auto-drafted return access for Range Officers. Internal audits showed persistent manpower shortages, with 33% vacancies in Audit Commissionerates and only 70% of targeted units audited in FY23. The absence of required MIS reports and records in many Ranges hindered effective department oversight, leaving gaps in monitoring non-filers and recovery from defaulters, resulting in unrecovered amounts like ₹27.97 crore.

During centralised and detailed audits, over 2,519 deviations worth ₹21,695 crore were detected from statutory provisions, while scope limitations due to missing records prevented risk assessment of ₹32,432 crore. The report recommends urgent improvements in automation, record maintenance, and follow-up procedures to prevent recurring gaps and potential revenue losses.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended March 2023 - Government - Report No.22 of 2025 (Compliance Audit - Civil & Commercial)
overview:
This compliance audit of 28 Union Ministries, five Constitutional bodies, and five Union Territories without legislatures for the year ended March 2023 exposed widespread lapses in financial management, contract oversight, and compliance with statutory guidelines. The total expenditure covered rose by 7.14%, from ₹15,07,147.05 crore in 2021-22 to ₹16,14,830.70 crore in 2022-23, with 24 major audit cases documented across six ministries, five UTs, and one CPSE.

Key lapses included the National Gallery of Modern Art's avoidable electricity payments of ₹1.97 crore (pg 7), Ministry of External Affairs' unauthorised affidavit fee collection of ₹2.35 crore (pg 9), incorrect GST payments of ₹2.96 crore by passport offices (pg 10), and improper payment of over ₹33 crore in Risk and Hardship Allowance by Home Ministry units (pg 12). There were also cases of funds blocked for over five years, non-refund of grants aggregating ₹903.42 crore, and systemic weaknesses in scholarship schemes resulting in payments to ineligible students (pg 30).

The report noted significant recurring issues, with 13 out of 24 paragraphs not receiving Ministry replies as of June 2025 (pg 4). These audit findings highlight urgent risks to public funds and the effectiveness of government schemes, recommending much stricter oversight, compliance with regulatory mandates, and accountability for public money mismanagement.

title: Compliance Audit Observations, Government (Commercial)
overview:
This report presents the results of the compliance audit of Central Government Companies, Statutory Corporations, and Government-controlled companies for the year ended 31 March 2023. The report highlights operational, financial, and environmental lapses across 12 CPSEs and eight ministries in the Energy, Industry, and Infrastructure clusters. During 2018-2023, fund utilisation and efficiency was suboptimal, with over 75% of steel grade coal supply continuing to be met via imports, contrary to national objectives to raise domestic share.

A total financial implication of ₹5,048.20 crore was noted across audit observations. Major findings include avoidable or infructuous expenditure (e.g., ₹470.56 crore by BPCL on under-utilised vessels), non-compliance with rules resulting in losses of ₹1,219.60 crore, and investment in delayed or non-performing infrastructure—such as BCCL’s washery delays leading to lost revenues of ₹371.33 crore and compensation charges of ₹22.24 crore. Penalties, excess payments, irrecoverable dues, and violations of environmental and forest regulations are repeatedly observed.

Despite specific schemes and government instructions, implementation has suffered from planning and monitoring weaknesses. None of the One Time Fund Infusion Scheme (OTFIS) projects was fully completed as intended, defeating the objective of moderating languishing project costs and durations. Risk areas include short recovery of dues, lack of project accountability, and continued high reliance on coal imports.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the period ended March 2023 Report No. 2 of 2025
overview:
This Compliance Audit Report examines the functioning of Integrated Tribal Development Agencies (ITDAs) under the Scheduled Tribes and Scheduled Caste Development, Minorities & Backward Classes Welfare Department, Odisha. Over the audit period, 11 sampled ITDAs had access to ₹1,709.47 crore, of which only ₹1,190.44 crore (70%) was spent, pointing to low efficiency in fund utilisation. None of the ITDAs prepared annual accounts required under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, highlighting major gaps in financial accountability and oversight.

Audit revealed critical failures in internal controls: Departmental works were executed by Junior Engineers/Assistant Engineers (JEs/AEs) using personal bank accounts, outside of the mandated Personal Ledger accounts of ITDAs. The sampled JEs/AEs made ₹148.75 crore in personal-type transactions, including cash withdrawals, POS, UPI payments and insurance, indicative of suspected misappropriation. In nine ITDAs, audit found vouchers missing for ₹3.38 crore, and ₹3.23 crore paid for work without proper invoices—significantly raising risks of fraud and loss.

Procurement practices were equally problematic. ₹54.25 crore worth of input materials were procured from cooperative societies on a nomination basis without tender, despite revoked privileges. These societies simply placed orders to private vendors with no price discovery or transparent mechanism. The lack of oversight has led to serious inefficiencies and heightened risk to government funds and intended beneficiaries. (pp. 6-7, 15-16)

title: Government of the Union Territory of Puducherry Report No. 1 of 2025 AR 2023-24
overview:
The audit for 2023-24 revealed substantial lapses in effective budgetary management and deviation from established financial procedures. The Government’s fiscal deficit increased to ₹2,392 crore, reflecting a substantial rise over the previous year. Utilisation of central grants was also found to be suboptimal, with large unspent balances remaining across social and development sectors. As per the Executive Summary (page 11), 'utilisation under sectoral grants was between 44 and 50 per cent during 2023-24.'

Receipts from own tax and non-tax revenues declined by 13% compared to the projected estimates, while committed expenditure on salary and pension alone constituted nearly 62% of total revenue expenditure (page 13). This severely constrains the government's flexibility for developmental investments. The report highlighted delay in submission of Utilisation Certificates for 148 cases, amounting to ₹355 crore, and non-reconciliation of department-wise expenditure of ₹2,018 crore (page 17).

Consequently, these shortcomings have adversely affected the implementation of critical welfare and infrastructure schemes, leading to significant underachievement of targets in health, education, and rural development. The persistence of unadjusted advances and poor compliance in financial reporting are major vulnerabilities that demand immediate corrective action.

title: Welfare of Building and Other Construction Workers for the period ended March 2022
overview:
The performance audit highlights significant shortcomings in the implementation of welfare provisions for building and other construction workers (BOCW) in Gujarat between 2017 and 2022. Although ₹4,787.60 crore was collected as cess, only ₹2,544.81 crore (53%) was released to the Welfare Board, leaving ₹2,242.79 crore (47%) retained by the State Government as of March 2023. Furthermore, fund utilisation by the Board was only 32%—just ₹808.49 crore spent on welfare schemes and administration out of the total grants received.

Institutional weaknesses were evident: the State Advisory Committee had not been reconstituted since 2011, and as of March 2022, 72% of Board posts and 42% of inspector posts were vacant, severely affecting scheme implementation and establishment inspections. Registration of establishments increased substantially from 668 in 2017 to 4,087 in 2022, but critical mechanisms to ensure complete registration coverage for BOC workers and employers were missing. Safety inspections were insufficient, with at least 2,146 of 14,295 registered establishments never inspected.

Consequently, access to welfare benefits lagged: only 37 beneficiaries received housing assistance through the Nanajee Deshmukh Awas Yojana, the Old Age Pension scheme was suspended since May 2019, and Shramik Annapurna Yojana covered only 19 of 33 districts as of June 2024. Significant delays, injudicious rejection of beneficiary applications, and underutilisation of earmarked funds for awareness and safety further undermined the welfare initiative’s impact.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the period ended 31st March 2023. Government of Bihar, (Compliance Audit- Civil)
overview:
This CAG report examines government compliance for Bihar's Agriculture and Planning & Development Departments over 2018-2023, focusing on the Krishi Input Subsidy Scheme (KrIS) and the Mukhyamantri Kshetra Vikas Yojna (MKVY). Significant deficiencies were uncovered in the identification of disaster-affected areas, fund utilization, monitoring, and system integration. For example, in 2019, subsidy payments of ₹21.48 crore were made in 10 districts not declared as flood-affected, and ₹4.03 crore to applicants of 14 districts not recognized as drought-affected. Large amounts (up to ₹151.92 crore) were paid for crop loss in areas exceeding official damage estimates by 1.34 lakh hectares.

The audit found that the KrIS database lacked integration with land records, resulting in excess, short, and inadmissible payments totalling ₹56.14 crore across 15.53 lakh cases. Inadmissible payments (₹159.28 crore in 6,81,617 cases) were frequently made despite failing crop loss criteria. Payment failures were up to ₹184.74 crore for 6,04,700 applicants due to banking and Aadhaar mismatches, and there were delays of up to 608 days in disbursing ₹308.01 crore. Unutilized balance funds of ₹2,040.09 crore (38% of total available) were surrendered versus the sanctioned ₹5,324.92 crore.

Fund utilization for infrastructure works under the MKVY was also poor, with 28–59% of available funds left unspent across the 13 divisions, and systemic lapses in monitoring, irregular sanctions, splitting of works, and idle assets. These systemic and operational deficiencies not only reduce the scope and impact of relief and development but also expose large-scale governance, execution, and control failures.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the Period ended March 2023 (Performance and Compliance Audit- Civil and Commercial)
overview:
The total revenue receipts of the Government of Bihar for 2022-23 were ₹1,72,688.02 crore, with State-raised revenues at ₹48,152.63 crore, reflecting a 23.98% increase from the previous year. The State’s share of divisible Union taxes stood at ₹95,509.85 crore, and grants-in-aid were ₹29,025.54 crore. The average annual growth for tax and non-tax revenues during 2018-23 was 14.29% and 8.60% respectively (p. IX).

A performance audit on the Electronic Way Bill system under GST revealed non-discharge of tax aggregating ₹6.23 crore in sample tests, with tax evasion observed through risky vehicle use and returns non-filing (para 2.3.10.4, p. 37). The Subject Specific Compliance Audit on GST payments and returns uncovered deviations totaling ₹4,600.90 crore across 589 cases. The Department accepted audit observations in 349 cases involving ₹690.30 crore and reported recovery of only ₹11.01 crore (para 2.4.7.3(A), p. 111).

There were significant control and compliance failures, including 18,106 audit paragraphs pending at end of June 2023 and 1,430.32 crore in arrears outstanding for more than five years. In Public Sector Enterprises, the report found 13 enterprises with current-year losses amounting to ₹2,159.69 crore and 14 SPSEs eroding their net worth with ₹27,307.96 crore in cumulative losses. Key cases of loss include undue favour to contractors (₹94.25 lakh) and infructuous bridge expenditure (₹5.35 crore).

title: Report No. 3 of 2025 - Report of the C&AG of India on Performance and Compliance Audit - civil for the year ended 31 March 2023
overview: This report highlights significant performance and compliance issues in conservation management across Jharkhand's protected areas. Over ₹ 41.22 crore (10 per cent) of the allocated ₹ 397.86 crore funds for wildlife conservation, afforestation, and capacity building remained unutilised in six divisions between 2018–23. Boundary notification delays for 11 out of 12 Protected Areas (PAs) persisted for periods ranging from 32 to 47 years, leading to unresolved community rights and biotic pressure, as well as forest degradation. Habitat quality declined, with tree cover in PAs decreasing by 2.60 per cent from 2017 to 2021 and bare ground increasing by 13.51 per cent. Frontline staff shortages were severe, with only 182 staff (51 per cent of sanctioned strength) available, often lacking specialised wildlife management training. Enforcement was weak as prosecution reports for wildlife crimes faced delays of 9-68 months due to inadequate crime monitoring and patrolling resources. Vulnerable species such as tigers at the Palamau Tiger Reserve saw population crashes; only one tiger was detected in 2022 (down from 34–46 in 2000–2005). Eco-tourism plans, zonal master plans, and rescue facilities were largely not implemented or incomplete. The absence of research activities, essential records, and outcome-based project targets hindered progress against SDG 15 (“Life on Land”). These deficiencies collectively reveal a critical shortfall in the conservation and sustainable management of Jharkhand's wildlife assets.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the Period ended March 2023 - Report No. 6 of 2025 (Compliance Audit - Civil)
overview:
The Comptroller and Auditor General's Compliance Audit Report No. 6 of 2025 presents a wide-ranging review of the fund application, scheme implementation, and efficacy across major civil departments in Karnataka for the period ending March 2023. Budgetary application of resources for the year 2022-23 was ₹7,05,758 crore, against an approved outlay of ₹7,17,164 crore. Revenue expenditure rose by 31% and total State expenditure surged by 36% from 2018-19 to 2022-23, yet several grants saw persistent savings exceeding ₹500 crore annually, indicating imprecise planning and execution (Page 2).

A major highlight is the underachievement of skill development targets under the Chief Minister’s Kaushalya Karnataka Yojane. Against an annual skilling target of five lakh youth, only 1,15,822 candidates were trained in six years (2017-23); placements were a mere 18% compared to the mandatory 70%, representing a severe shortfall. Fund utilization issues are prominent: ₹341.11 crore was released without a needs-based plan, yielding ₹119.89 crore in idle balances and fund lapses of ₹173.53 crore occurring in the first three years (Page vi). Diversion and excess release of funds also surfaced, alongside deficiencies in candidate selection (3,487 ineligible) and non-compliance with reservation policies at Training Centres.

The Labour and Social Welfare Departments faced similar challenges. The Karnataka State Unorganized Workers’ Social Security Board (KSUWSSB) failed to reconstitute its board, maintained over ₹97 crore unutilized, and failed to extend benefits to all worker categories. In Social Welfare, non-market-based procurement of machines yielded an undue benefit of ₹14.04 crore to KEONICS and unfruitful hostel expenditure. The Urban Development Department incurred avoidable extra outflow of ₹5.12 crore due to over-specified pipe procurement and a ₹22.42 crore avoidable interest burden due to poor financial management. Overall, the report indicates significant lapses in fund utilization, planning, and scheme execution, with numerous recommendations for rectification and improved governance.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on State Revenues for the period ended March 2023 - Report No. 5 of 2025 (Compliance Audit-Civil)
overview:
The C&AG report on State Revenues for the period ended March 2023 covers significant findings across taxes, excise, registration, and transport. For FY 2022-23, Karnataka's total revenue receipts reached ₹2,29,079.74 crore, with ₹1,43,701.93 crore from state tax revenue and ₹13,914.13 crore from non-tax revenue. Despite this, audit test checks across revenue departments revealed under-assessment, short levy, and loss of revenue totalling ₹3,520.04 crore (Page v: 'Test-check...showed under-assessment/short levy/loss of revenue aggregating to ₹3,520.04 crore.').

The audit identified pervasive compliance deficiencies, including ₹1,143.58 crore in GST-related deviations, ₹393.04 crore in ITC mismatches, and extensive issues in E-Waybill and registration systems. In the State Excise Department, late or improper implementation caused a short levy of ₹42.46 crore, and improper label fee modifications led to revenue loss of ₹31.5 lakh. Stamp Duty short-levies—including misclassifications and undervaluations—totaled over ₹40 crore, with isolated cases reaching as high as ₹10.51 crore for trust settlements.

Government departments were found to have weak monitoring mechanisms, evidenced by 1,226 inspection reports (3,901 observations) involving ₹2,009.39 crore left pending at June 2023. Not only were controls over compliance and follow-up lacking, but granular taxpayer records in GST audits were routinely not produced, overshadowing departmental assurances of corrective action. The audit thus signals substantial risks of continued revenue leakage and recurring procedural lapses.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Direct Taxes for the period ended March 2023 Union Government Department of Revenue Report No. 14 of 2025 (Compliance Audit – Civil)
overview:
This CAG compliance audit on Union Government Direct Taxes reveals substantial increases in direct tax receipts and ongoing structural concerns in tax administration. Direct tax receipts reached ₹16,63,686 crore in FY 2022-23, marking a 17.8% increase over the previous year. Corporation Tax collections rose 16% to ₹8.25 lakh crore, and Income Tax 20% to ₹8.08 lakh crore. The audit highlights a 38% surge in tax refunds and a net collectible demand of ₹69,396 crore, but also points out a significant increase in pending arrears, which rose from ₹19.35 lakh crore to ₹22.74 lakh crore.

Audit scrutiny found a 5.87% error rate in assessments checked during FY 2022-23. There remain 59,352 unresolved cases from earlier years and 481 high-value cases with a tax effect of ₹7,929.21 crore, out of which over 57% by count and 65% by amount were accepted as errors by the Ministry/ITD. Irregularities continue in areas like non-levy of Dividend Distribution Tax, incorrect allowance of carry-forward losses, and mistakes in tax computation, resulting in tax effects running to thousands of crores (e.g., a ₹1,034.66 crore non-levy: para 3.2.2).

The incidence of persistent errors and weaknesses in internal controls—often associated with the Income Tax Business Application—pose significant risks to revenue collection integrity and transparency. The report's recommendations seek more robust IT controls, systematic review of time-barred cases, and clear assignment of responsibility in cases of error. The audit’s findings indicate not only issues in compliance but broad risks to public revenue management and recovery.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Compliance of the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003 for the year 2023-24 Union Government Department of Economic Affairs (Ministry of Finance) Report No. 19 of 2025
overview:
The Comptroller and Auditor General's ninth annual report on compliance with provisions of the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act by the Union Government covers FY 2023-24. The report reviews achievement against FRBM targets, including containment of Central Government Debt and General Government Debt, revenue and fiscal deficit trends, public guarantees, and disclosure practices. Key highlights reveal Central Government Debt amounted to ₹171.71 lakh crore, representing 57.00% of GDP at end-March 2024. This was a 9.98% increase over the previous year, mainly due to higher internal debt.

While the debt-GDP ratio has fallen from its pandemic peak of 61.38% in 2020-21, no annual reduction targets were prescribed, and the statutory target of reducing debt to 40% of GDP by end FY 2024-25 is not on track. Actuals for revenue receipts and fiscal indicators exceeded budget estimates: gross tax revenue actual collection was 11.5% of GDP, and the fiscal deficit was 5.32% against a 5.9% target. However, revenue deficit and fiscal deficit remained above the long-term statutory thresholds.

Transparency and disclosure lapses impacted fiscal accountability—discrepancies were seen in D2 Statement (Arrears of interest), and liability figures reported in the Receipt Budget were inconsistent with FRBM Act definitions. Arrears in tax raised but not realised were recorded at ₹31.11 lakh crore, having increased by ₹9.81 lakh crore over the prior year. The Ministry's responses indicate efforts to contain state debt, but gaps remain between stated obligations and implementation.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on the Activities of Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services Union Government Ministry of Earth Sciences
overview:
The audit of the Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) focused on activities during 2017-2022, covering 11 projects. Audit found delays in project approvals resulting in poor planning and inefficient execution; administrative orders for major projects were issued 3-19 months after project commencement, creating uncertainty about continuity (Table 6, pg 9). Fund release was delayed or short, with only ₹295.23 crore released out of the ₹626.73 crore budgeted across 11 projects, a utilization rate ranging 44.2% to 50% (Table 3, pg 4).

Targets and deliverables were not clearly defined after budget reductions and project reorganisation, making achievement assessment impossible. For example, the Ocean-Modelling Data Assimilation project received only ₹13.78 crore (43.77%) of its allotted ₹31.48 crore, and activities were not adjusted to match resources (pg 11). Human resources were suboptimal, with INCOIS relying heavily on contract staff; as of March 2022, only 67 regular posts were filled, against 71 sanctioned, while contract staff dropped from 88 in 2020 to 66 in 2022 (Table 4 & 5, pg 4).

Poor planning also affected deployment of ocean observation platforms and expansion of networks, threatening India's international commitments. Weak financial controls, absence of revised project deliverables, and inadequate resourcing led to significant gaps in execution and low achievement of objectives.
