title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Accounts of the Union Government for the year 2022-23 Union Government Ministry of Finance
overview:
FY 2022-23 was marked by notable fiscal consolidation, with India’s nominal GDP growing by 14.21% and real GDP by 6.99%. Tax receipts increased by 16.28%, driven primarily by direct taxes, which constituted 53.50% of Gross Tax Receipts (GTR). Total revenue receipts reached ₹27,13,267 crore, while total expenditure was ₹45,50,514 crore – a 7.36% increase over the previous year. Repayment of debt was the largest outflow from the Consolidated Fund, accounting for 61.27% of the total outgo (₹71,99,701 crore).

Despite improvements, major financial reporting issues persist. Transfers to four reserve funds were grossly delayed or nearly absent: only ₹344 crore was transferred out of ₹2,41,220 crore of receipts (FY 2018-19 to FY 2022-23). Several dormant reserve funds with ₹6,065 crore remain un-repurposed. Misclassification of expenditure led to a ₹49,948 crore overstatement of capital expenditure; over 50% of receipts (₹4,136 crore) and expenditure (₹5,572 crore) were booked under omnibus Minor Head 800, undermining transparency. Additionally, ₹74,241 crore in loans and advances are in arrears for principal and interest as of year end.

Several suspense and remittance account imbalances persist, impacting the accuracy of accounts: netting balances understated Suspense Account (Civil) by 61.99% and PSB Suspense by 74.72%, and ₹4,597.11 crore in cash balances remain unreconciled with RBI. Overspending was noted in the 'Repayment of Debt (Capital Charged)' head by ₹53,871.01 crore; excesses and persistent savings across numerous grants and appropriations indicate weaknesses in financial forecasting and budget execution.

Improve budget estimation accuracy to prevent persistent large savings in grants.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Accounts of the Union Government for the year 2023-24 Union Government Ministry of Finance Report No. 16 of 2025 (Financial Audit)
overview:
The CAG reported that in FY 2023-24, the Union Government saw robust financial growth with nominal GDP increasing by 12.02%, reaching ₹3,01,22,956 crore, while real GDP grew by 9.19%. Revenue receipts grew by 13.82% over the previous year, with tax revenue up 10.93% and non-tax revenue surging 23.81% largely due to a 71% increase in dividends and profits. Despite increased government spending from ₹39,07,647 crore in FY 2020-21 to ₹48,52,572 crore in FY 2023-24, the spending as a percentage of GDP fell from 19.68% to 16.11%.

Significant issues arose in financial reporting quality: incorrect discharge accounting understated internal debt by ₹372.64 crore; ₹15,103 crore was pending for disbursement to State/UT compensatory afforestation funds; netting practices understated balances pending clearance by over 68% in Suspense Account (Civil) and 54.89% in Reserve Bank Suspense Central Accounts Office. Dormant reserve funds with ₹834.37 crore and short transfers of ₹3,69,307 crore to designated reserve funds highlight lapses in fiscal discipline.

Budgetary management showed savings of ₹17,81,873.44 crore under 102 Grants/Appropriations, excess expenditure in some capital transfers, and persistent delays in the submission of Utilisation Certificates—₹72,764.09 crore outstanding as on 31 March 2024. Over-utilisation and injudicious re-appropriations were also noted, compromising budget transparency and compliance. These findings point to significant weaknesses in fund deployment, fiscal reporting, and required corrective action to improve accuracy and transparency.

title: Union Government Economic and Service Ministries (Compliance Audit - Civil)
auditPeriod: 2021-22 (with references to actions up to July 2024)
overview:
This CAG compliance audit covers Economic and Service Ministries of the Union Government for the year ending March 2022 and highlights persistent gaps and irregularities in multiple schemes and bodies. Across 16 audit paragraphs in 10 ministries, the audit uncovered losses, excess payments, and procedural lapses exceeding ₹88 crore, along with major cases of underutilised infrastructure and unfruitful expenditure. For instance, direct losses included ₹11.77 crore in lost interest due to improper parking of government funds (“Coal Controller’s Organisation”), ₹10.79 crore and ₹1.88 crore in irregular medical allowance payments by MSME and Chemicals & Petrochemicals bodies, and ₹32.46 lakh and ₹2.41 crore in inadmissible bonuses by academic institutes.

Systemically, only 0.68% of the ₹5,714.51 crore Investor Education and Protection Fund was refunded since inception, with over 98% of transferred shares still lying unrestituted as of March 2023. Infrastructure projects suffered severe delays: the IIFT's Maidangarhi campus faced a 7-year delay resulting in an unproductive ₹5.32 crore spent in ground rent, while FDDI Ankleshwar’s campus costing ₹101.48 crore is severely underutilised (11% seat fill) with only 94 out of 825 seats filled over seven academic years. Additionally, the Ministry of Tourism failed to realise the intended objectives of multiple institute-creation projects despite disbursing crores.

These failures were compounded by non-compliance with Central Pay Commission and Ministry of Finance norms for allowances, ad-hoc incentives, and post creations, as well as inadequate mechanisms for refund processing, monitoring, and performance assessments. Despite repeated audit observations, ministries have not acted swiftly enough to recover excess reimbursements or enforce financial discipline, causing continued leakage and under-achievement of scheme objectives.

title: Union Government, (Railways) Railways Finances
overview:
Indian Railways reported total expenditure of ₹4,41,642.66 crore in 2022-23, an increase of 11.34% over the previous year, with capital expenditure rising by 7.21% and revenue expenditure by 15.15%. Gross traffic receipts rose by 25.51% to ₹2,39,982.56 crore, mainly due to a 61.72% jump in passenger earnings, 15% in freight, and 40.06% in sundry earnings. However, passenger operations still incurred a loss of ₹5,257.07 crore, which had to be cross-subsidised by freight profits. MoR generated a net surplus of ₹2,517.38 crore in 2022-23, reversing a deficit from the previous year. Yet, the Operating Ratio remained high at 98.10%.

Despite supplementary budget allocations, MoR incurred ₹13,615.30 crore more than sanctioned under revenue grant, and unsanctioned expenditure of ₹6,483.71 crore involving 1,932 cases was recorded. There were repeated misclassifications between revenue and capital grants, and delays or inaccuracies in the handling of accounting heads—including ₹68.30 crore in income tax deductions wrongly booked and significant backlog in renewals worth ₹31,852.60 crore.

Public sector rail enterprises’ net profit grew to ₹12,056.61 crore, but only 11 out of 33 profit-making enterprises declared the required dividend. Budgetary and accounting controls at zonal levels were weak, with issues such as excess budget releases to frozen or completed projects, delayed productivity tests, misclassification of deposits, and outstanding stock sheets rising by 13%. Workshop accounting also revealed substantial inaccuracies, inflating debits and understating costs by hundreds of crores.

title: Report No. 1 of 2025 of Government of Goa
overview:
The audit report for Goa details significant lapses in compliance, planning, and execution across Social, General, Economic, Revenue, and Public Sector domains. Total expenditure of the State increased by 24.87%, from ₹14,321.25 crore in 2019-20 to ₹17,882.94 crore in 2021-22, with revenue expenditure rising by 22.41% from ₹11,622.66 crore to ₹14,226.88 crore. The shift in expenditure saw revenue share decrease from 81% to 80%, while capital expenditure rose from 19% to 20%.

Major audit findings include misappropriation of ₹15.86 lakh in the Public Works Division VI, Margao, and poor fund utilization in the National Social Assistance Programme, resulting in loss of central assistance. Deficiencies in project planning and execution were evident, such as the unfruitful procurement and relocation of sound and light show equipment worth ₹3.94 crore, and ineffective operation and maintenance of tourist infrastructure built under the Swadesh Darshan Scheme.

The Revenue Sector audit uncovered systemic issues, including irregular allowances of input tax credit, short-levy of VAT (₹56.50 lakh), luxury tax and excise duty, and loss of revenue due to departmental oversight. Urban Development faults resulted in losses exceeding ₹45 lakh from non-renewal of advertising agreements and ₹86.81 lakh from unauthorized road repairs. Persistent lack of responsiveness from departments to audit recommendations, with 743 Inspection Reports and 3,212 paragraphs pending compliance, indicates widespread issues in accountability and follow-up.

title: Report No. 2 of year 2025 Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended 31 March 2022 (Compliance Audit- Civil)
overview:
This Compliance Audit report for Madhya Pradesh reviews the financial and regulatory oversight across five key departments: Commercial Tax, Mineral Resources, MSME, Forest, and Public Works. The audit period covers transactions for the year 2021-22, with select findings from prior years and significant emerging issues post-2021-22.

Major issues include delayed departmental responses, critical lapses in GST oversight (only 69.92% of non-filers received notices), loss of revenue in Excise Duty (₹9.58 crore unrecovered), non-recovery from excess mineral extraction (₹630.06 crore lost), and irregularities in subsidy payments to MSMEs and capital projects. The Forest Department saw delayed working plan preparations, resulting in delayed revenue realisation worth ₹15.77 crore, and widespread encroachment on forest land caused considerable losses.

Public Works exhibited overpayments and excess expenditure totalling ₹30.66 crore, unsurrendered savings of ₹13.66 crore, and short levy of supervision charges with deficits up to ₹20.10 crore. Monitoring and reconciliation failures across departments continue to threaten transparency and efficient delivery, as evidenced by 6,705 outstanding IRs and 38,010 unresolved paragraphs pending compliance as of 31 March 2022.

title: Report no. 3 of 2025, of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Compliance of the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003 for the year 2022-23
overview:
The CAG's eighth annual compliance audit of the FRBM Act reviewed the Central Government's adherence to fiscal targets set by the FRBM Act, 2003, as amended in 2018. The audit period covered FY 2018-19 to FY 2022-23, examining achievement against debt reduction and deficit criteria. During FY 2022-23, Central Government debt represented 57.93% of GDP, having declined from a pandemic peak of 61.38% in FY 2020-21 but still exceeding the pre-pandemic level and the statutory target of 40% by FY 2024-25. Total debt increased by ₹17.48 lakh crore (12.61%) over the previous year, with internal debt rising ₹16.12 lakh crore, external debt by ₹0.90 lakh crore, and public account liability by ₹0.13 lakh crore (page 5).

Significant discrepancies were observed between debt disclosures in Union Budget documents and FRBM Act definitions, including a ₹3.89 lakh crore gap in FY 2022-23 between computed Central Government debt and figures presented in Budget 2024-25. Extra Budgetary Resources (EBR) disclosure across years saw reconciliation issues, with unreconciled variations of ₹1,418.70 crore in Statement 27 of Expenditure Profiles and discrepancies regarding NSSF loans outstanding, which were not acknowledged in parliamentary documents (page 9). In addition, transparency concerns were noted in tax raised but not realized (₹21.30 lakh crore, up ₹5.47 lakh crore over previous year, page v), and incomplete fiscal projections, with government omitting three-year rolling targets in medium-term fiscal policy statements post-pandemic (page 13).

Although the Central Government's additional guarantees fell well within statutory limits (₹0.61 lakh crore or 0.23% of GDP), high debt-to-GDP ratios and increased allocation of revenue receipts to interest payments (35.35% in FY 2022-23) signal elevated fiscal stress. Debt sustainability analysis found the stabilization indicator positive for 2022-23, indicating gradual improvement in fiscal resilience but substantial gaps remain to meet the FRBM targets by 2024-25.

title: Report No. 2 of 2025- Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Compliance Audit for the year ended 31 March 2022, Government of Maharashtra
overview:
The Compliance Audit Report for the year ended 31 March 2022 covers the audit of Government Departments, Autonomous Bodies and Public Sector Undertakings of Maharashtra, with findings based on test audits conducted in 2021-22. The report highlights cases where financial rules, regulations, and prescribed procedures were not complied with, resulting in losses to the exchequer or non-achievement of intended outcomes. Audit scrutiny revealed irregularities in contract management, financial sanctioning, and execution of works in multiple departments, resulting in avoidable expenditures and liabilities for the state government.

Significant lapses included diversion and misutilisation of funds, irregular payments, non-adherence to tendering processes, and deficiencies in monitoring. For example, in certain departments improperly awarded contracts and deficient supervision led to excess payments of over ₹18.72 crore and avoidable liability exposure of more than ₹10 crore. Audit also detected non-recovery of dues, including non-levy of penalties and interest, leading to further financial loss to the state.

Wide-ranging recommendations have been issued to address these gaps and to improve internal controls. Unaddressed, such deficiencies impair public service delivery and erode public trust. Failure to institute robust compliance frameworks exposes the government to financial risk and recurring losses, which was evident from repeated observations made in earlier years. Follow-up on compliance to past recommendations also remained inadequate, highlighting the need for better accountability mechanisms. title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the period ended March 2023, Report No. 5 of 2025- Union Government (Railways) (Compliance Audit)
overview:
The audit report reviews compliance issues across the Ministry of Railways, covering significant financial lapses and operational inefficiencies for the period ending March 2023. The Report comprises 25 audit paragraphs with money value implications totaling ₹543.17 crore. Notable lapses include non-realisation of shunting charges worth ₹50.77 crore in East Central Railway, loss of ₹17.47 crore due to continuing poorly-patronised trains in South Western Railway, and repeated failures to upgrade critical infrastructure and notify routes for higher axle-loads, causing revenue loss exceeding ₹6 crore in Western Railway alone (p.v-vii).

Widespread systemic gaps were seen in resource recovery including ₹148.61 crore in short land license fee from government-aided schools, ₹55.51 crore of non-recovered District Mineral Foundation contributions across nine zonal railways, and loss of ₹11.02 crore due to ineligible freight concessions. Failings in contract management also resulted in avoidable liabilities—for example, a delayed renewal of VHF licenses led to ₹23.16 crore in late fees in South Central Railway (p.viii-x).

The report highlights both the failure to adhere to existing codal and Ministry instructions and the lack of internal controls for preventing recurring fiscal errors. It recommends fixing responsibility on relevant officials, a systemic review of all zones for similar lapses, and strengthening the Railways’ policies to ensure such losses do not recur. The cumulative impact indicates significant governance and oversight shortcomings, underscoring a need for urgent reform and accountability across the Indian Railways administration (p.v-xv).

title: Compliance Audit Report for the year ended March 2022, (Report No. 1 of the year 2025), Government of Maharashtra
overview:
The Compliance Audit Report for Maharashtra (Report No. 1 of 2025) provides a detailed review of Government departments and agencies for the year ending March 2022. The audit covers lapses from the Excise, Stamp Duty and Registration, Goods and Services Tax, and Public Works departments.

Serious lapses in the Excise Department led to substantial revenue shortfalls. The State lost Rs 20.15 crore due to incorrect assessment of licence renewal fees, and Rs 70.22 crore in interest. Undervaluation of production cost in Canteen Stores Department products resulted in a further Rs 38.34 crore loss in excise duty. Errors in imported liquor calculations led to Rs 14.37 crore loss between 2017-22. Departmental exemptions and delays in analysis cost Rs 73.18 crore in tax recovery. Short/non-levy of privilege fees for change in ownership and partnership led to Rs 26.93 crore deficit, while failure to apply supervision fee revisions lost Rs 1.20 crore. Operational inefficiencies across Stamp Duty resulted in property undervaluation and wrong zone classification, causing additional losses to state revenue.

Overall, the audit found revenue miscalculations, exemptions without government approval, undervaluation practices, and delays causing total losses over Rs 170 crore. The systemic gaps in internal control, oversight, and record maintenance contributed to missed collection targets and undermined financial integrity. There are critical recommendations for rectifying assessment and procedural flaws, improving real-time oversight, and updating rules to prevent recurring losses.

title: Report No. 4 of 2025 – Report on Performance and Compliance Audit (Civil & Commercial) for the period ended 31 March 2022, Government of Chhattisgarh
overview:
This audit report covers significant findings from the implementation of major government schemes in Chhattisgarh, including the Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT), NABARD-assisted irrigation projects, agricultural schemes, skill development, and management of degraded forests. The performance audit observed systemic deficiencies in planning and execution: Out of 114 AMRUT works, 19 works costing ₹1,712.07 crore remained incomplete until March 2023, and 20 works faced delays of 3 to 33 months. Incomplete works resulted in the target of providing potable water in 8 of 9 cities remaining unachieved; particularly, the pipeline at Rajnandgaon costing ₹62.53 crore was unused due to lack of civil work commencement, and Bilaspur laid a pipeline of ₹84.87 crore with canal linking unfinished (p.xi-xii).

In the NABARD RIDF irrigation projects, only 15 of 60 projects sanctioned between 2019-22 were completed; 45 remained incomplete, leading to a shortfall in irrigation potential creation—17,715 ha (48%) missed against a designed 36,776 ha. Wasteful expenditure included ₹28.02 crore for a river diversion scheme in Surajpur and ₹2.06 crore for the Kalmahar project where canals were not constructed (p.xiii-xiv). For skill development, only 65% of the target was achieved between 2014–23, with certificates not recognized for government jobs and 31% candidates not allocated training, while ₹1,358.53 lakh allocated funds were unutilized due to administrative lapses and pandemic interruptions (p.xv-xvi).

Serious lapses like premature release of performance security, wasteful expenditure on incomplete infrastructure, substandard compliance in GST oversight (203 out of 532 cases, ₹245.91 crore), and only partial achievement of service benchmarks highlight a high severity across sectors. The cumulative effect is a loss of efficiency, fund wastage, and delayed benefit delivery for citizens, warranting urgent systemic corrections.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Working of Mancheswar Carriage Repair Workshop in East Coast Railway and Construction of 5th and 6th line between Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT)-Kurla Station
overview:
This compliance audit examines the operational efficiency of the Mancheswar Carriage Repair Workshop (CRW/MCS) under East Coast Railway and the construction progress of the 5th and 6th rail lines between Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT) and Kurla Station. Between 2016-17 and 2022-23, CRW/MCS consistently underachieved, overhauling between 86 and 113 coaches per month—substantially below its enhanced capacity of 150 per month. Despite a sanctioned augmentation expenditure of ₹181.78 crore from 2018-19 to 2022-23, this failed to yield improved outturn, and workshop budgeting was found excessive and not linked to unit costs or actual POH projections (p. iv). Projections of coaches due for Periodical Overhaul (POH) were routinely overstated by 20–38% across three years, then revised downward mid-cycle due to factors such as changes in POH periodicity and errors in coach-holding data, leading to unreliable planning and reporting (p. 6–7). Significant delays were found: 52% of coaches exceeded stipulated POH cycle time, with 191 instances of idle periods from 10 to 171 days, resulting in an estimated loss of earning capacity of ₹7.69 crore (p. 14).

In the CSMT-Kurla expansion, audit observed persistent delays: as of January 2024, only 26% of the sanctioned work was completed despite 56.22% of funds (₹500.93 crore out of ₹890.89 crore) already spent. Land acquisition and PAP rehabilitation were major contributors to the slippage, compounded by lack of coordination among agencies and contract awards without assured access to sites or finalized designs, postponing completion from the original March 2021 deadline to a further extension beyond March 2024 (p. v).

The audit concludes there was poor project planning, weak internal controls, and ineffective monitoring in both projects. Incorrect coach inventory data, failure to follow codal provisions, and non-realistic targets affected utilization and service delivery, while critical recommendations target capacity planning, quality monitoring, and inventory system transparency.

title: Report No. 5 of the year 2025 - Compliance Audit Report for the year ended 31 March 2023
overview:
The CAG Compliance Audit Report for the year ended March 2023 identifies substantial lapses and irregularities in the implementation of key government schemes in Kerala, particularly the Integrated Child Protection Scheme (ICPS) and other child protection schemes. The audit revealed that ₹22.94 crore was involved in cases of non-adherence to codal provisions, unfruitful expenditure, and idle investment. For example, unspent Central funds each year ranged from ₹216.95 lakh to ₹783.85 lakh, leading to inefficient use and even revalidation of funds without effective results. The audit also noted significant delays in the renewal of registration for 165 Child Care Institutions (CCIs), with renewal processes delayed at the District Child Protection Unit (DCPU) level and subsequent cascading inspection delays.

Other major findings included the continued absence of State-specific rules for Child Protection implementation, with Kerala relying solely on central model rules almost a decade after the relevant legislation. The Child Protection Management Information System (CPMIS), despite a payment of ₹2.67 lakh, remained non-functional as of March 2024, undermining monitoring efforts. Moreover, essential welfare services were not delivered: regular inspections of CCIs were nearly non-existent, and only two out of fourteen Specialised Adoption Agencies were equipped with cradle points to receive abandoned children. Children with special needs were found housed in facilities failing to meet mandated standards, and processes (such as social investigation reports and post-adoption follow-ups) regularly faced delays of several months.

The audit’s consequences are serious; government assets intended for vulnerable populations are left idle, financial assistance is disbursed to ineligible recipients (including ₹20.78 lakh paid to 56 SC and six ST children already receiving aid), and cases of direct misappropriation (such as ₹1.28 lakh at the Coconut Nursery, Valiyathura) signal weak internal controls and systemic deficiencies. These shortcomings leave children exposed to greater risk and erode public trust in government systems.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Working of Mancheswar Carriage Repair Workshop in East Coast Railway and Construction of 5th and 6th line between Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT)-Kurla Station
overview:
This CAG Compliance Audit examined the efficiency and effectiveness of the Mancheswar Carriage Repair Workshop in East Coast Railway (ECoR) and the construction of the 5th and 6th lines between Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT) and Kurla Station, covering financial years 2020-21 to 2022-23. The workshop’s periodical overhaul (POH) outturn ranged between 86 and 113 coaches per month, falling short of its augmented capacity of 150 coaches, resulting in actual output being 20% to 38% below projected figures despite further investments of ₹181.78 crore. Only 47.9% of coaches met the prescribed POH cycle time, with 52.1% experiencing delays, some exceeding three years, leading to an earning capacity loss of ₹7.69 crore due to idle coaches (page 14).

The audit found chronic issues in capacity and resource planning. Projections sent to the Railway Board for coaches due for POH were systematically overstated, and incorrect coach holding data contributed to unrealistic planning and repeated downward revisions. Four high-value machines valued at ₹4.15 crore remained idle for years, and persistent shortfalls in stores procurement were noted, with repeated user complaints about shortages. The Workshop Information System (WISE) was found unreliable, with multiple data mismatches between manual and digital records.

In the CSMT-Kurla 5th/6th line project, only 26% of physical work was completed despite 56.22% of funds (₹500.93 crore of ₹890.89 crore) being spent as of January 2024, and land acquisition and stakeholder coordination failures further delayed the project. The report expresses concern that completion deadlines will again be missed due to these systemic issues.

title: Performance and Compliance Audit Report No. 5 of 2025
overview:
The audit evaluated performance and compliance of key Uttar Pradesh departments, notably the State Agricultural Produce Market Board and Market Committees, over 2017-18 to 2021-22. The Board reported total receipts of ₹7,654.78 crore during this period, with the Board itself incurring ₹4,173.17 crore in expenditure and Market Committees ₹3,124.19 crore. The funds available for centrally sponsored schemes (e-NAM and RKVY) saw low utilisation rates, with only 49.14% and 9.62% respectively being spent from 2017-18 to 2021-22, indicating critical underperformance.

Audit identified outstanding premium of ₹81.96 crore on shop allotments, unrecovered rent and user charges totaling ₹13.11 crore, and advance payments lingering for over five years (₹5.61 crore yet to be adjusted by six DDC offices). Major infrastructure built under the Board, such as principal market yards and Agricultural Marketing Hubs, remained idle: in 12% of Market Committees principal yards were not constructed, and 29% of AMHs built during 2011-12 to 2014-15 were non-operational as of January 2024. Minimal activity on the e-NAM platform left intended outcomes unachieved.

The report concludes that significant lapses in governance, weak fund utilisation, and lack of operationalisation of market initiatives have severely undermined efficiency. Recommendations emphasize need for nomination of stakeholders to committees, systemic reforms in fund management, bottom-up infrastructure development, and prioritisation of unutilised assets. The severity of audit findings is high due to substantial target shortfalls and large misapplied/idle funds.

title: Welfare of Building and Other Construction Workers
overview:
The audit examined the Welfare of Building and Other Construction Workers in Uttar Pradesh for the period 2017-22, focusing on implementation of the Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996 and associated rules. As of March 2022, the Uttar Pradesh Board had registered 1.44 crore workers and executed 25 distinct schemes. However, systemic deficiencies led to significant underutilization of the collected welfare cess, administrative lapses, and dilution of benefits.

Fund utilization was notably poor with large sums remaining unspent and delays in distribution to intended beneficiaries. For instance, active beneficiary counts remained low despite a surge in registrations from 2020-22, and eligible workers often did not receive timely assistance. Collection, assessment, and transfer processes for the mandated construction cess were inefficient and inconsistent: assessments ranged from zero to only 24% of targeted establishments in sample districts.

Audit also found widespread non-compliance with statutory mandates regarding registration of establishments, identification of eligible workers, and enforcement of health and safety norms. The Board failed to conduct required social audits, did not prepare annual reports and accounts since inception until 2021, and multiple mandatory Board functions were omitted from state rules. These recurring lapses in governance and administration led to ineffective delivery of intended welfare outcomes, as detailed throughout all chapters of the report.

title: Audit Report No.1 of 2025: Solid Waste Management in Urban Areas
overview: This performance audit examined Solid Waste Management (SWM) in urban areas across Uttar Pradesh for the period 2016-17 to 2021-22, covering regulatory compliance, financial management, planning, segregation, processing, disposal, and special waste streams. The audit found critical underutilisation of allocated funds: during 2016-22, only zero to 63% of available SWM funds, zero to 20% of Capacity Building/Administrative & Office Expenses (CB & AOE), and three to 62% of IEC&PA component funds reached ULBs, causing substantial unutilised balances at the State Mission Director SBM (Urban) level. There was persistent delay in fund release, ranging from 55 to 236 days for SWM and 11 to 1,098 days for CB & AOE (2017-21). Only 27% ULBs framed SWM bye-laws by 2022, most lacking uniformity and failing to address key issues of the SWM Rules, 2016. In terms of coverage, 93% of test-checked ULBs had no SWM plan, and 89% lacked weighbridges; only 67% tippers had partitions, indicating continued mixing of segregated-waste. Waste processed ranged from 26-71% of collected at State-level and 0-63% in sampled ULBs, well below national and regulatory targets. Land allocation for SWM facilities was deficient, and only 72 of 651 ULBs assessed legacy waste, revealing 84,57,782 MT dumped. Gaps resulted in ineffective segregation, incomplete processing plants and delays, poor monitoring, shortfall in plastic and C&D waste infrastructure, and systemic issues in managing bio-medical waste (with 17-43% operators unauthorised). Overall, ineffective fund flow, poor planning, inadequate infrastructure and deficiencies in stakeholder engagement combined to impede service quality and regulatory compliance, leading to environmental and operational risks and missed national benchmarks.

title: Report No 1 of 2025 - Compliance Audit (Civil) Report for the year ended March 2023 - Tamil
overview:
The Compliance Audit (Civil) Report No 1 of 2025 for Tamil Nadu highlights major irregularities and deficiencies in the enforcement of schemes and fund management across Health, Social Welfare, Finance, and Higher Education departments. The audit reviews periods from 2019-20 to 2022-23 and includes specific audits such as on the Integrated Child Development Services and Food Safety regulations. Notably, the fund utilisation across several schemes ranged only between 44% and 50%, leading to unspent balances of up to ₹124 crore in selected departments (p.12).

Among headline findings are excess payments on electricity bills, delays in renewal and regulation enforcement, and inadequate use or idling of approved assets. For example, there was a delay of over 2 years in construction of sports infrastructure (p.61), leading to cost increase and suboptimal asset usage. The Health & Family Welfare department saw non-installation of Telecobalt machines in tertiary hospitals, causing additional financial liabilities of ₹34.7 crore (p.73). States failed to initiate timely adjudication for food safety violations, resulting in delayed penalty collections (p.95).

Consequences include systemic financial inefficiencies, service delivery gaps, and risks of fraud and misuse. Substantial amounts blocked in idle investments or underutilised assets were not recovered, while failure to comply with statutory timelines has increased exposure to regulatory action and potential loss to the exchequer. The report highlights the need for tighter fund oversight and improved project execution to safeguard public resources and ensure intended benefits.

title: Report No 1 of 2025 - Compliance Audit (Civil) Report for the year ended March 2023
overview:
The Compliance Audit Report No. 1 of 2025 for the Central Government covers the financial and performance audit of Ministries including Electronics and IT, Communications, Finance, and Statistics for the year ended March 2023. The audit highlights significant lapses in fund utilization, monitoring and project delivery, including delays and under-achievement of scheme objectives. Key schemes examined include the National Knowledge Network (NKN) and Modified Special Incentives Package Scheme (M-SIPS). For example, the NKN project was delayed by more than two years resulting in cost overruns of ₹138.62 crore, while around 47% of the allocated funds for key digital infrastructure remained unutilized between 2018-23 (p. 12).

Irregularities cited include non-recovery of GST by the Department of Posts, non-deduction of TDS by Kerala Postal Circle, under-billing and wasteful expenditure by BSNL, and loss due to non-availing of GST input tax credit. Ministry responses indicated inadequate efforts to address sustaining gaps, especially in contract management and financial controls. Recovery at the instance of audit was reported at ₹26.38 crore but with persistent issues noted in monitoring compliance and quality of accounts of PSUs and autonomous bodies (p. 13).

These lapses have resulted in considerable loss of government revenue, delayed service delivery, and compromised transparency. The consequences include blocked funds, inefficient project management, and undue favour to contractors, critically undermining public trust and fiscal discipline. The audit recommends strict enforcement of control mechanisms and timely corrective actions for all ministries involved.

title: Report No. 01 of 2024-Performance and Compliance Audit Report of Government of West Bengal for the year ended 31 March 2022.
overview:
The Performance and Compliance Audit Report for West Bengal presents a detailed review of the Swasthya Sathi Scheme between 2018-19 and 2022-23, covering Rs 6,882.06 crore in expenditure. The audit found that the number of families registered under the scheme (2.43 crore as of March 2023) was around 10% higher than the 2.21 crore families with ration cards, indicating considerable risk that ineligible beneficiaries were availing scheme benefits. Notably, the State Nodal Agency had neither prepared comprehensive guidelines nor annual action plans as of July 2024, affecting operational effectiveness and monitoring.

A test check of 50 private hospitals revealed 31 were assigned higher grades than justified, resulting in excess payments of Rs 14.48 crore, with actual payments made at inflated rates rather than those warranted by the hospital’s real infrastructure and services. The audit also observed that only 2,605 hospitals had been empanelled against a target of 3,038, reducing patient access to covered facilities and decreasing scheme reach.

Procedural gaps included the non-completion of Aadhaar-linkage for beneficiaries, hampering verification and increasing the risk of duplicate or bogus enrolments. Furthermore, Rs 47 crore of extra expenditure went on hurried or improper smart card generation and enrolment. The combination of poor guidelines, infrastructure shortfalls and verification lapses resulted in substantive financial irregularities and undermined the scheme’s intended purpose of inclusive, targeted health coverage.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Welfare of Building and Other Construction Workers for the year ended March 2022
overview:
The audit revealed significant governance and financial lapses in the administration of welfare for building and other construction workers. Of the ₹164.25 crore collected by Urban Local Bodies and one Urban Development Authority, only ₹59.86 crore (36%) was remitted to the Board; ₹104.39 crore (64%) remained untransferred as of the audit, directly contradicting statutory requirements. Annual accounts have not been prepared by the Board since 2018-19, undermining fiscal transparency and legislative oversight. Out of 1,38,908 welfare claims filed, 45,047 claims remained pending and 10,125 were rejected, but applicants generally received no notification of rejection, severely impacting benefit delivery.

The Board failed to constitute itself with the minimum required members after 2018, functioning with only three out of the mandated eight members, and conducted just 8 board meetings out of 20 required, impeding strategic direction and oversight. Suspect double registration of beneficiaries and benefits paid to unregistered workers were identified; for example, ₹18.95 lakh disbursed to 27 unregistered beneficiaries (2018-22). Significant fund diversion occurred: ₹32.43 crore spent on non-permissible advertising, ₹40.07 crore diverted to a state social security scheme with only partial reimbursement, and ₹1004.82 crore advanced for COVID relief but with just ₹258.04 crore disbursed to BOC workers.

There was also a severe shortfall in regulatory action: only 432 of 14,530 (3%) establishments due for inspection were checked, and the mandatory State Advisory Committee was not constituted for nine years after state formation. Government schemes approved but unimplemented, delays in claim processing, and gaps in grievance redressal all contributed to significant under-delivery of benefits, exclusion of beneficiaries, and high financial risk.

title: Implementation of National Social Assistance Programme through Direct Benefit Transfer Scheme (Report No. 03 of 2024)
overview:
This report assesses the effectiveness of implementing the National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) through the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) Scheme in Gujarat from 2017-18 to 2020-21. During this period, the State Government serviced an average of 9.96 lakh beneficiaries and incurred an expenditure of ₹2,398.80 crore on all four NSAP components. However, audit findings highlight systemic shortcomings such as absence of a centralised eligible beneficiary database, with implementation operating on a demand-driven basis, potentially excluding many deserving citizens.

Significant delays in pension disbursement were noted—3,820 beneficiaries experienced one to 38 month delays, leading to a cumulative shortfall of ₹1.81 crore. Additionally, lapses in follow-up for failed DBT transactions resulted in stoppage of pensions worth ₹1.57 crore for nearly 5,000 people, while errors in migration between scheme components caused losses up to ₹25.04 lakh for 380 beneficiaries.

The State also failed to contribute matching NFBS grants, depriving 27,801 families of ₹55.60 crore. Further, 774 eligible widows missed out on ₹1.55 crore under NFBS due to lack of proactive outreach, and continued payments were made to 1,072 ineligible beneficiaries, wasting ₹32.60 lakh. Widespread issues with social audit implementation, IT systems, and convergence with related schemes exacerbate the risk of exclusion, double payments, and fund leakages, with overall control and oversight rated as inadequate, jeopardising the intended social impact of NSAP.

title: Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Service (Report No. 05 of 2024)
overview:
This report assesses the performance of Gujarat’s public health infrastructure between 2016-17 and 2021-22, focusing on fund utilisation, staffing, and service delivery. Out of a cumulative allotment of ₹9,538.42 crore as per State’s Programme Implementation Plan, ₹7,717.50 crore (81 per cent) was provided by the Government of India and Government of Gujarat during 2016-22. However, only ₹4,792.18 crore (56 per cent) was expended by the Project Implementation Unit on infrastructure, while Gujarat Medical Services Corporation Limited spent ₹4,111.16 crore (78 per cent) of the available funds on procurement of drugs and equipment (p. xi).

Despite recruitment of 9,983 healthcare personnel, there was a shortage of doctors (23%), nurses (6%), and paramedics (23%) in public health institutions as of March 2022. Vacancy rates for specialist doctors were 28% in Medical College Hospitals, 36% in District Hospitals, and 51% in Sub-District Hospitals. Uneven geographic distribution of staff persisted, with shortages exceeding 25% for doctors in 22 districts and paramedics in 19 districts (p. ix).

The audit revealed critical gaps in availability of OPD, IPD, emergency, and auxiliary services across tested facilities. Only 10 of 19 District Hospitals offered all essential OPD services, and emergency services were partially available in 13 of 19. Infrastructure construction was notably slow: out of 5,332 approved works, only 24% were completed, and 70% were dropped or not started (p. xi-xii). Persistent deficiencies were found in drug procurement, quality control, and regulatory mechanisms, affecting service accessibility and health outcomes.

title: Implementation of Integrated Child Development Services Scheme (Report No. 06 of 2024)
overview:
The audit examines the implementation of the ICDS Scheme in Gujarat between 2015-23, focusing on delivery coverage, infrastructure, and financial management. The Scheme, implemented via 53,029 Anganwadi Centres, targeted a population of 5.53 crore, with an average enrolment of 40.34 lakh children against the 77.77 lakh census figure, indicating substantial coverage gaps.

Financially, funds totalling ₹18,649.19 crore were allocated, but only ₹14,986.14 crore was utilised. Significant unspent grants were observed: ₹242.39 crore remained unspent in seven of eight audit districts and 12 of 22 blocks, while inaccurate utilisation certificates to GoI masked ₹69.73 crore parked as spent. Infrastructure gaps included 3,381 AWCs operating out of temporary structures and 8,452 in dilapidated buildings; only 27% of sanctioned ramps for disabled access were constructed.

Key service delivery issues included 86% SNP coverage, shortfall in immunisation (94%), ECCE service gaps (pre-school education not provided to 18.79% children), and increasing antenatal/postnatal service shortfalls. Persistent manpower shortages were detected: 56.70% of CDPOs and 14.35% of Lady Supervisor positions vacant, directly undermining Scheme effectiveness.

title: Report No. 11 of 2024 of Government of Madhya Pradesh on Welfare of Building and Other Construction Workers for the year ended 31 March 2022
overview:
The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) conducted a performance audit of implementation of welfare measures for building and other construction workers in Madhya Pradesh. As of March 2022, there were 13.33 lakh registered construction workers in the state, and benefits worth ₹1,568.71 crore were disbursed to 11.81 lakh beneficiaries between 2017-18 and 2021-22.

The audit found multiple long-standing systemic deficiencies: key rules under the BOCW Act and constitution of the Welfare Board were delayed by 6 years, field offices were not established in any district for almost two decades, and no mechanism existed to identify or register all eligible establishments or beneficiaries. The audit also highlighted significant disparities between state rules and central legislation, notably lack of penalty provisions for safety lapses, and non-compliance in cases of accidental worker deaths.

Fund utilization was critically low, ranging between 13% and 37% during the audit period, with between ₹1,839 crore and ₹2,453.70 crore remaining idle in FDRs and bank accounts. The Board also diverted ₹416.33 crore towards unrelated state schemes in violation of the BOCW Act and Supreme Court directives. Suspected fraudulent payments totaling ₹2.07 crore, delays in sanctioning benefits, and failure to obtain utilization certificates for major fund transfers were also reported. These lapses deprived workers of entitled benefits and compromised safety oversight.

title: Report No. 10 of 2024 of Government of Madhya Pradesh for the year ended 31 March 2022
overview:
This report presents the significant findings from the compliance audit of the Revenue and Labour Departments of the Government of Madhya Pradesh for the period ending March 2022. The primary objective was to assess the effectiveness, regularity, and propriety of financial assistance schemes, especially those targeting victims of natural calamities and social welfare interventions.

A headline issue in the audit was the detection of serious cases of fraudulent disbursement. Notably, ₹23.81 crore was fraudulently siphoned by crediting relief funds for natural calamities into the accounts of unauthorized persons, including officials and their relatives across 13 districts. Weaknesses in the global budgeting system and Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS) enabled employees to manipulate records and bypass eligibility checks, resulting in the creation of fake beneficiary lists and forged sanction orders.

The report further finds large-scale operational lapses, such as payment of ₹164.31 crore to cooperative societies in Khandwa in violation of direct benefit transfer mandates and delays of up to 29 months in distribution of ₹563.72 crore meant for drought and pest relief. Overall, systemic deficiencies in scheme design, monitoring, and IT controls have led to financial losses, delays in relief, and widespread risk of fraud, ultimately undermining both the intended impact of welfare schemes and the credibility of public expenditure management.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended 31 March 2022 - Government of Rajasthan (Compliance Audit-Civil & Commercial) (Report No. 5 of the year 2024)
overview:
The CAG Compliance Audit for Rajasthan inspected enforcement of safety, health, and welfare provisions under the Factories Act, 1948. The Department was responsible for oversight of 7.06 lakh factory workers as of 31 March 2022, with a 38% increase in workers from 2017-18 to 2021-22 [page 9]. There was a critical shortfall in inspections, as only 68% of scheduled audits were conducted, leaving an overall shortfall of 32% as per the Central Inspection System [page viii]. Joint audit inspections of 60 factories revealed widespread non-compliance, including lack of fencing on machines, absence of protective equipment, expired fire extinguishers, and missing accident registers [page vii]. No prosecution cases were filed against violators.

Financial impact totaled ₹8.74 crore in losses and unrecovered taxes across departments, including ₹1.42 crore in short-realised lump-sum tax on motor vehicles, ₹6.49 crore in unpaid Motor Vehicle Tax, and ₹83 lakh unrecovered from illegal mineral excavation [page viii]. Audit committees failed to convene the minimum four meetings per department, with 22,961 audit paragraphs unresolved across 5,243 outstanding Inspection Reports for ₹68,387.60 crore [page 3].

The Factories and Boilers Inspection Department did not have an effective mechanism to monitor compliance or enforce corrective action. Crisis management groups failed to meet as scheduled, and factory owners did not submit required annual returns or maintain accident registers. Only partial recovery was achieved: as of June 2024, departments had accepted observations for ₹7.91 crore but recovered only ₹2.31 crore [page 7]. Total recoveries at the instance of audit reached ₹57.56 crore for the year, including prior years and ongoing inspections.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Compliance Audit Report II for the year ended March 2022 (Government of Haryana Report No. 3 of 2024)
overview:
This CAG Compliance Audit Report for Haryana examines state revenue receipts, GST administration, stamp duty, excise, and financial systems for the year ended March 2022. The total revenue receipts during 2021-22 were ₹78,091.69 crore, showing an increase of ₹10,530.68 crore (15.59%) over the previous year. Of this, tax and non-tax revenue accounted for 77.82%, while receipts from the Government of India contributed 22.18% (Page 1).

Audit scrutiny of 104 units covering Sales Tax/VAT, State Excise, and Stamp Duty revealed under-assessment, short levy, and revenue loss of ₹1,103.94 crore across 2,552 cases. Departments accepted deficiencies amounting to ₹643.07 crore and recovered only ₹3.52 crore during 2021-22 (Page vii). Major GST-related compliance failures resulted in inconsistencies and deficiencies totaling ₹678.22 crore, with issues like ITC mismatches, turnover discrepancies, and improper return verification (Page viii).

Significant lapses included short recovery of excise penalties (₹7.46 crore), irregular exemption of stamp duty (₹3.11 crore), and large arrears in revenue, notably ₹35,639.25 crore with ₹6,378.97 crore outstanding for over five years (Page 6). The Integrated Financial Management System audit found weak controls, invalid PANs, and double withdrawals, underscoring systemic risk and the need for improved financial governance.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Compliance Audit Report -II for the year ended March 2022 (Report No. 3 of 2024)
overview:
This report presents a detailed compliance audit of Haryana’s major revenue earning departments for the year ending March 2022. The State's total revenue receipts reached ₹78,091.69 crore in 2021-22, marking a 15.59% increase from the previous year. Of these receipts, 77.82% was raised from tax and non-tax sources within the state, highlighting significant dependence on internal resources, while the remainder came from the Government of India as the State’s share of Union taxes (₹9,722.16 crore) and grants-in-aid (₹7,598.24 crore). Audit of 104 units revealed instances of under-assessment, short levy, and loss of revenue aggregating to ₹1,103.94 crore in 2,552 cases, with only ₹3.52 crore actually recovered during the year.

Key audit issues were identified across tax administration (₹4.99 crore under-assessment due to misclassification), input tax credit errors (₹10.91 lakh excess benefit allowed), and evasion due to stock mismatches (₹73.11 lakh). The audit also revealed a significant compliance gap in GST oversight, with deficiencies totaling ₹678.22 crore identified due to lack of verification mechanisms for GST payments and returns.

In other sectors, the State Excise department had not initiated appropriate steps for recovery, leading to a shortfall of ₹7.46 crore, while several irregularities were found in stamp duty and registration fee cases, resulting in revenue losses exceeding ₹20 crore. The IT audit of the Integrated Financial Management System (IFMS) exposed system control weaknesses, double withdrawals, and inadequate audit trails. The recurring theme of weak enforcement and process gaps has led to a high severity rating, with a total compliance deficiency of ₹724.46 crore impacting state finances.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Welfare of Building and other Construction Workers
overview: The performance audit evaluates the effectiveness of welfare schemes for Building and Other Construction Workers in Jharkhand, covering the period from FY 2017-18 to FY 2021-22. The audit found that the Board had not utilised more than half of its allocated funds for welfare schemes, with actual expenditure remaining at 50 percent of allocations. Cess collection and transfer were inefficient, leading to a shortfall of ₹504.67 crore not transferred to the Board as of March 2022. Registered workers increased from 5.96 lakh in March 2017 to 12.57 lakh in March 2022, but the estimate was 16.99 lakh in June 2013, indicating poor registration coverage. Many welfare schemes such as loans for house construction and group insurance premiums had not been implemented even after over a decade. Out of 1,869 construction works in sampled districts, none were registered with the Board, and identity cards were not issued as per requirements. Delays in reconstitution and meetings of the State Advisory Committee further hampered oversight. Major consequences include delayed scheme benefits, unspent welfare funds, missed pension coverage, and large gaps in regulatory enforcement and scheme delivery.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India - Union Territory Finances for the year 2022 - 23 - Govt UT of Puducherry Report No. 4 of 2024(UT Finances Audit Report)
overview:
The audit report critically examines the financial management of the Government of Puducherry during the period 2019-20 to 2022-23, revealing persistent lapses in fund utilisation and compliance with statutory and procedural requirements. Total receipts for 2022-23 amounted to ₹8,912.09 crore, but significant gaps were noted in disbursement and allocation of grants-in-aid, with utilisation rates consistently below the national average.

Auditors identified major deficiencies in the Reliance on Central grants, which constituted 56.4% of total revenue receipts in 2022-23, indicating excessive dependency and vulnerability to reductions in central transfers. The report highlights a mismatch between budget estimates and actual expenditure, notably in capital outlay, which was only ₹336.99 crore against a budgeted ₹621.13 crore—a shortfall of 45.7%.

Consequences of these deficiencies include delayed implementation of infrastructure projects, reduced efficiency in social sector spending, and heightened fiscal stress. The audit stresses that "non-utilisation of funds led to accumulation of liabilities and compromised service delivery" (page 13). Urgent corrective actions are recommended to strengthen budgetary controls, streamline fund release, and enhance transparency.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India - Compliance Audit Report for the year ended March 2022 - Government of the Union Territory of Puducherry Report No. 2 of 2024
overview:
The Compliance Audit Report for the year ended March 2022 examines fund utilisation, contract management, and scheme implementation across multiple departments of the Government of the Union Territory of Puducherry. The audit reviewed ₹2,520 crore of expenditure, highlighting significant lapses in financial controls and non-compliance with regulations. Only 47% to 50% of allocated funds were utilised on key social and infrastructure projects, leaving ₹1,110 crore unspent. Para 1.3 notes: 'Out of the total grants available, only 47 per cent were actually utilised, indicating underutilisation and delays in key works.'

The audit identified irregularities in tender processes and project execution, including 16 cases of improper award of work, delayed execution, and non-compliance resulting in avoidable extra expenditure of ₹74 crore. In Chapter II §2.2, the report states: 'Multiple works were delayed beyond stipulated timelines, causing additional expenditure.' In addition, the absence of internal audit in several departments led to undetected deviations and persistent issues.

The consequences include delayed benefits to beneficiaries, risk of misappropriation, and lost opportunities for economic development. As highlighted: 'Due to non-utilisation and procedural lapses, several communities did not receive timely interventions,' undermining the objectives of welfare schemes and infrastructure development.

title: Compliance Audit on (Public Sector Undertakings) for the year ended 31 March 2022
overview:
This CAG compliance audit report examines four Madhya Pradesh PSUs for the financial year ended March 2022, focusing on road construction, loan management, power generation, and power transmission. For the Madhya Pradesh Road Development Corporation Limited, serious lapses were identified in the inclusion of ineligible State Highways under ADB V projects, violating selection criteria and resulting in an irregular expenditure of ₹652.21 crore. Audit also found unwarranted dowel bar works leading to an extra burden of ₹13.35 crore, and omission of mandatory fly ash usage inflating project cost by ₹18.06 crore.

Additionally, failure to impose delay penalties contributed to an unrecovered amount of ₹30.11 crore, while inflated measurements and improper consultancy extensions led to further excess payments of ₹10.20 crore and ₹39.68 crore respectively. Across PSUs, non-compliance in loan disbursement, poor NPA management, and suboptimal plant performance led to substantial losses and excess costs, with audit observations totaling ₹1,876.32 crore. The lack of timely responses and delayed remedial actions pose risks of financial irregularities and inefficiency in governance.

Overall, the report calls attention to institutional weaknesses, recommending strict adherence to funding criteria, improved penalty recoveries, and enhanced oversight mechanisms to prevent recurring lapses and ensure greater transparency. The severity remains high due to major target misses and fund misappropriation in these PSUs.

title: Report of 2010 – Compliance and Performance Audit on Civil of Government of Maharashtra
overview:
The 2010 CAG Audit Report on Civil Departments of the Government of Maharashtra highlights significant deficiencies in fund utilisation, persistent lapses in planning and monitoring, and numerous compliance shortfalls. During the audited period of 2005-06 to 2009-10, notable amounts such as Rs 18,326 crore remained unutilised, representing up to 41% of plan funds released in several key departments (p. viii).

Audit scrutiny disclosed that schemes faced chronic delays, such as only 59% physical targets being achieved for vital rural infrastructure projects, with Rs 123 crore surrendered due to incomplete works (p. 6). Weak internal controls led to irregular sanctioning of projects and advances, with instances of Rs 78 crore being diverted to unrelated purposes (p. 12). The report also documents 2,421 cases where financial rules were violated, raising serious concerns about transparency and accountability (p. 38).

These failures resulted in tangible negative impact: non-completion of projects meant denial of intended benefits to citizens, significant cost overruns, and accumulation of unspent balances. The report concludes that unless systemic reforms are instituted, such inefficiencies and violations will persist, impairing public service delivery and financial discipline.

title: The Performance Audit on “Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services in Maharashtra”
overview:
As the second most populous and third largest state by area, Maharashtra faces critical challenges in ensuring adequate public health infrastructure. The report notes substantial shortages in medical manpower and facilities. For instance, there was a 27% shortfall in doctors, 35% in nurses, and 31% in paramedical staff across key cadres, with even starker gaps in rural and specialist domains. Specifically, only 1,906 Primary Health Centres and 10,740 Sub-Centres serviced a population of over 120 million, well below national norms (Table 1.2, p.5).

Capital expenditure remained low, with only ₹602 crore spent on capital health works in 2016-17, rising to ₹1,612 crore by 2021-22. Despite increasing outlays, Maharashtra’s health expenditure was just 0.49% to 0.66% of Gross State Domestic Product, compared with a normative benchmark of 8% under the National Health Policy (Table 1.1, p.4; Executive Summary, p.xiv). The audit found that up to 70% of sanctioned facility construction and 90% of expansion works were incomplete as of September 2022 (Executive Summary, p.xiv).

The consequences include severe overloading of existing public health facilities—some serving 2 to 3 times their design population—leading to overcrowding, reduced quality, staff burnout, and long wait times. Essential services such as specialist care, diagnostic and radiology facilities, and basic infrastructure such as kitchens and fire safety measures were found lacking in many facilities. Moreover, of the medicines demanded by health facilities, only about 71% were supplied on time, with ₹2,052 crore unutilized with Haffkine Bio-Pharmaceutical Corporation (Executive Summary, p.xv). Overall, weak planning, underfunding, and poor execution threaten the state’s ability to deliver effective health care.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the period ended March 2022, Government of Uttar Pradesh, Report No. 6 of 2024 (Compliance Audit-Civil & Commercial)
overview:
This report presents compliance audit findings for 16 departments, 53 Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs), and 19 other entities in Uttar Pradesh. PSUs under review recorded annual turnover of ₹76,189 crore, contributing 4.09% to the state's GSDP for 2021-22. Government investment in these 37 PSUs stood at ₹2,80,732.97 crore, with 58.51% as equity and 41.49% as long-term loans. Losses were significant: 21 PSUs posted a combined loss of ₹15,856.93 crore, while only 16 earned a profit of ₹378.18 crore, highlighting deep fiscal stress among state enterprises (major loss-makers included Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited at ₹8,305.27 crore).

The CAG flagged large arrears in submission of PSU accounts: of 72 functional PSUs, only 11 submitted their accounts for 2021-22, while arrears totaled 308 accounts among active PSUs, with ₹8,610.52 crore in state support provided during periods of non-compliance. Asset erosion has resulted in 10 PSUs posting negative net worth of (-) ₹62,779.27 crore, despite a cumulative equity input of ₹1,37,041.97 crore.

Audit traced procedural lapses, such as delays in land handovers (up to 38 months), late applications for regulatory NOCs, non-deduction of statutory dues (losses of ₹2.01 crore), short recovery of liquidated damages (₹63.39 crore forgone), and regulatory violations leading to ₹144.75 crore in lost revenue. The total quantified financial impact of findings in this report is ₹322.97 crore. These stress the urgent need for system-wide improvements in compliance, monitoring, and strategic intervention.

title: Report No.6 of 2024, Report on Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services for the year ended 31 March 2022
overview:
This audit examines the state of public health infrastructure and management of health services in Madhya Pradesh for the period 2017-18 to 2021-22. The Public Health and Family Welfare Department did not deploy human resources as per Indian Public Health Standard (IPHS) norms, resulting in a critical shortage of 22,845 healthcare workers, and over 11,500 staffing gaps in 1,775 institutions. Facilities at all levels, particularly Primary Health Centres (PHCs), Community Health Centres (CHCs), and District Hospitals (DHs), suffered major shortfalls in manpower and essential drugs—a key reason for suboptimal service delivery, especially during emergencies and maternal care.

On the infrastructure front, only about 52% of target PHCs and 68% of targeted Sub Health Centres (SHCs) have been established, with a shortage of 1,147 PHCs and 4,904 SHCs. District Hospitals also face bed shortages, with 5,345 beds missing from 33 out of 51 DHs. Crucial life support equipment and drugs faced regular shortfalls and procurement delays, affecting core services. Of the allotted budget of ₹52,068.83 crore, only ₹45,326.05 crore was spent (87%)—leaving ₹6,742.78 crore unutilized and sectoral expenditure stuck at just 0.94–1.05% of GSDP against an NHP target of 2.5%. Unspent balances in the National Health Mission reached up to 42% in some years.

These persistent issues in human resources, drugs availability, budget utilization, and regulatory mechanisms have led to serious consequences, including high maternal mortality rates (173 vs. India’s 97) and failure to achieve SDG health indicators. Trauma care centers and several regulatory gaps, such as expired licenses and unlicensed machinery, further compound risks to public health.

title: Compliance Audit Report on Examination of assessments of companies dealing in the business of ‘Distilleries and Breweries’ by the Income Tax Department of Union Government, Department of Revenue - Direct Taxes
overview:
The audit, covering the assessments of eleven companies in the distilleries and breweries sector across Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Delhi, reviewed income tax returns processed between AY 2009-10 and AY 2018-19. The CAG found significant tax shortfalls due to under-reporting of sales, with the cumulative tax impact estimated at ₹12,781.22 crore. In one case, a distillery in Uttar Pradesh was found to have under-reported sales by ₹1,378 crore, resulting in a tax loss of ₹448 crore (excluding interest). "While the distillery had reported sales in its profit and loss account at ₹4,036 crore, whereas information made available by UP excise dept revealed that sale reported by assessee was ₹5,414 crore" (p. 28).

The audit revealed that three companies did not get their accounts audited under section 44AB of the Income Tax Act, 1961, nor did they offer income from business under the 'Profits and gains from business or profession' head. Audit also noted that the information available within the Income Tax Department was not effectively utilised by assessment units, resulting in missed tax recoveries and lack of reconciliation with assessees. "Assessing Officers did not exercise power to call for the information, as envisaged in section 133(6) of the Income Tax Act" (p. 33).

These lapses led to the possibility of sale proceeds not being accounted for tax due to opaque agreements and systemic vulnerabilities. Errors in quantitative reconciliation, mistakes in assessments, and over-allowance of rebates and discounts further compounded revenue losses, raising significant concerns about the effectiveness of departmental checks and audit controls in the sector.

title: Compliance Audit Report (Commercial) for the year ended 31 March 2022 - Union Government
overview:
This CAG Compliance Audit Report (Commercial) details 30 audit paragraphs covering 16 CPSEs under eight ministries, grouped in Energy, Industry, and Infrastructure clusters. Total financial implication across findings is ₹3,437.30 crore, with cases spanning non-compliance, defective planning, poor monitoring and failure to safeguard financial interests. In the Energy Cluster, Central Coalfields Limited (CCL) violated environmental regulations, exceeding production limits and operating without valid Environmental Clearance, resulting in avoidable expenditure of ₹12.32 crore and two years of production disruption (p.1). Eastern Coalfields Limited failed to recover coal shortage dues, causing a loss of ₹17.39 crore (p.5). Industry Cluster highlights include India Infrastructure Finance Company Ltd’s non-adherence to Credit Policy, leading to a net loss of ₹393.37 crore (p.33), while National Highways Authority of India (Infrastructure Cluster) blocked ₹533.96 crore in land compensation funds for over six years due to delays (p.75).

Audit found ₹484.01 crore lost in six paras from non-compliance with contract terms, ₹435.09 crore from failure to safeguard financial interest, and ₹1,894.96 crore due to defective planning. Delayed actions and inadequate monitoring led to ₹623.24 crore of missed targets, including avoidable payments, unrecovered tolls, and unaddressed defects.

Report highlights recoveries at the instance of audit totaling ₹3,435.12 crore over ten years, corrections by CPSEs, and recommends robust controls, stricter policy adherence, and accountability for lapses to prevent recurrence. The severity of issues—marked by critical fund misutilisation, contract violations, and systemic gaps—demands high-level intervention from ministries and CPSE management.

title: Government of Karnataka Report No. 7 of 2024 (Compliance Audit - Civil)
overview:
This CAG Compliance Audit on Karnataka’s civil departments for the period ending March 2022 surfaces systemic and persistent issues in grant management, programme implementation, and revenue recovery. Notably, out of a total budget outlay of ₹6,96,660 crore in 2021-22, actual application of resources stood at ₹6,45,281 crore. Revenue expenditure alone, at ₹2,02,718 crore, comprised 79% of total expenditure that year, with a 42% increase over five years. Persistent underutilisation of budgetary grants is demonstrated by 10 out of 29 grants showing savings of more than ₹10 crore (5%+ of total grants) for five consecutive years (e.g., Agriculture and Horticulture, Health and Family Welfare).

The audit highlights delayed completion or non-utilisation of key infrastructure (like buildings and internet infrastructure), failure to recover statutory dues, and lapses in contract, tender, and maintenance processes across departments—including Water Resources, Higher Education, Revenue, Social Welfare, and Minority Welfare. For example, non-recovery of operation and maintenance (O&M) costs in the water sector and undue payments to contractors led to government losses and project underperformance.

A large backlog of audit observations remains outstanding, with 7,680 Inspection Reports (41,193 paras) pending response as of March 2022. Accountability is further constrained by significant delays in submission of action-taken notes and finalisation of accounts by autonomous bodies, increasing risks of financial irregularity and undermining transparency.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India Compliance Audit (Local Government) for the year ended March 2022 (Tamil) - Report No. 01 of 2024
overview:
This report evaluates the compliance and financial management of Local Governments (PRIs and ULBs) in Tamil Nadu for the period 2019-20 to 2022-23, highlighting major shortcomings in audit responses, fund utilisation, and project execution. During 2019-20, 74,722 audit IR paragraphs raised against Village Panchayats remained largely unaddressed, with only 43,664 (58%) acted upon, and among 863 Block Panchayats, less than 52% were addressed (p.6). In Urban Local Bodies, of 47,000 total IRs, 28,488 (61%) remained pending in Municipal Corporations, with analogous gaps in Municipalities and Town Panchayats (p.7).

Significant lapses were observed in asset and fund management: Out of substantial capital expenditures such as ₹6.33 crore spent on ULB slaughterhouse and market infrastructure, facilities were not put to use, resulting in idle assets and potential revenue losses (p.109). Rural infrastructure also suffered—delays and defective execution in Multi-Community Compost yards (MCC), with incomplete works and non-functional assets recorded in multiple districts well beyond the scheduled implementation date (p.68). Instances of avoidable/unauthorised expenditure ranged from ₹1.05 crore due to deficient site selection (p.114), to over ₹69 lakh on unused equipment (p.96).

Persistent failure to respond to audit findings compromises transparency and accountability, with outstanding audit issues hampering effective governance. The audit recommends urgent remedial measures to avoid wastage, improve compliance rates, and set up robust monitoring mechanisms. The severity of observed lapses is indicated as high due to systemic underutilisation, recurring financial mismanagement, and unresolved audit queries.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India Compliance Audit (Local Government) for the year ended March 2022 - Report No. 01 of 2024
overview:
This report presents comprehensive compliance and subject-specific audits of Panchayat Raj Institutions (PRIs) and Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) in Tamil Nadu for the financial year ending March 2022. Audit coverage included the functioning, accountability, and financial reporting of local government bodies, with a focus on major schemes such as the Chief Minister’s Solar Powered Green House Scheme and Pooled Assigned Revenue.

Key findings include ineffective impact of flagship schemes—such as the Green House program, which failed to provide accessible housing for the rural poor due to non-revision of unit costs and delays in supply chains. Delays and lapses in financial planning led to significant underutilisation and idle investment, such as ₹1.51 crore spent on a rural bus stand that has been unused for over six years. There were also cases of excess and avoidable expenditure totaling several crores, with ₹2.25 crore excess payment for earth works and ₹1.54 crore for over-priced chlorination units among the most prominent cases.

The audit further revealed high pendency of audit paragraphs (over 74,000 in Block Panchayats alone) as well as many unresolved CAG and PAC recommendations. ULBs were found to have created ₹6.33 crore in community assets that remain unused, and there have been notable revenue losses, such as the non-collection of ₹7.04 crore in profession tax. These findings highlight major systemic issues in transparency, monitoring, and internal control across local government entities, with serious implications for public spending and service delivery.

title: Public Health Infrastructure and Management of Health Services in Uttar Pradesh
overview:
The State Government of Uttar Pradesh incurred ₹1,11,929 crore on healthcare from 2016-17 to 2021-22, but only 82% of revenue budget and 60% of capital budget were utilised out of a provisioned ₹1,43,610 crore. Despite an annual compound growth rate of 9.65% in healthcare expenditure, public health spending remained between 1.10% and 1.30% of the GSDP—well below the National Health Policy 2017 target of 2.5% by 2025. For SDG 3 programs, of ₹18,253 crore provisioned during 2017-21, only ₹9,651 crore (53%) was actually spent. Substantial gaps exist in both infrastructure and staffing: rural CHCs, PHCs, and SCs were all short by 44-51% relative to state norms, and 38% of doctor positions and 46% of nurse positions remain vacant.

Tertiary hospitals increased from 17 to 33, but completion of new health facility construction lagged up to 1,789 days, with quality issues flagged in 53% of sampled facilities. Serious bottlenecks were reported in drug supply (41-68% non-availability in sampled GMCs, 2018-21) and idle equipment was found due to HR shortages.

As a consequence, patient loads at District Hospitals far exceed national norms (average 587/day per registration counter), and institutional capacity to absorb funds and deliver quality care remains insufficient. Program implementation (Janani Suraksha Yojana, urban mapping, NQAP, etc.) is not meeting targets, with the state lagging behind national averages in almost all maternal and child health indicators as of 2021.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India Compliance Audit for the year ended March 2022 (Government of Odisha, Report No. 3 of the year 2024)
overview:
This Compliance Audit Report covers Government of Odisha departments for the year ended March 2022 and highlights significant lapses in financial management, process adherence, and scheme implementation across several sectors. Notably, the audit found sub-optimal fund utilisation of major rural infrastructure schemes, with the Mukhya Mantri Sadak Yojana achieving only 83% of its targeted spending over five years (₹1,573.03 crore utilised vs ₹1,888.74 crore budgeted), and only 1,238 out of 3,295 identified rural habitations receiving road connectivity as of 2021-22. The report also reveals weaknesses in internal controls over scholarships for ST/SC students, including the disbursement of ₹97.32 lakh on fabricated caste certificates and ₹40.51 lakh on fabricated income certificates, in Khurda district alone.

Major compliance failures were detected in land acquisition and compensation, where excess payment of ₹76.51 crore was made due to incorrect valuation, and ₹4.82 crore of private lands were acquired without compensation in Bhadrak. Multiple instances of wasteful expenditure were noted, such as ₹17.58 crore incurred on inactive Land Acquisition Offices and ₹11.03 crore paid via questionable procurement practices, with works split to avoid tendering. Revenue loss to the State was linked to the injudicious rejection of highest bids in quarry leases and concessional land allotments, totalling several crores.

The audit notes a chronic lack of departmental response: as of June 2022, 43,430 audit paragraphs in 11,535 Inspection Reports remained unsettled, including 1,014 serious irregularity cases totalling ₹2,305.29 crore. The findings underscore the need for strengthened internal controls, improved transparency, recovery actions, and greater accountability to safeguard public funds.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Compliance Audit of Public Sector Undertakings for the year ended March 2022
overview:
This compliance audit report evaluates the financial and operational performance of 82 Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) in Odisha, including 64 Government Companies, 15 Government Controlled Other Companies, and 3 Statutory Corporations, for the period ending March 2022. The audit covers aspects such as government investment, returns, compliance, and deficiencies in management, highlighting cases of fund misutilisation and avoidable losses.

The PSUs registered a turnover of ₹38,504.42 crore in 2021-22, accounting for 6.03% of Odisha’s GSDP. Out of 32 SPSEs reviewed, the State government investment totalled ₹25,204.22 crore, with profit earning companies reporting ₹3,289.86 crore and loss making entities racking up ₹2,423.12 crore. Notably, 11 companies reported accumulated losses of ₹8,980.85 crore, eroding net worth and jeopardising viability.

Detailed compliance audits exposed significant financial lapses: GRIDCO lost ₹1,065.55 crore owing to delayed surrender of high-cost NTPC power, while a ₹3,257.40 crore loss ensued from non-optimal procurement strategies. Many smart city initiatives failed to utilise more than 36% of approved project funds due to poor planning, and several PSUs incurred substantial regulatory penalties, indicating widespread management shortcomings and urgency for reforms.
