title: Audit Report on Revenue Sector, Government of Assam
overview:
The report covers compliance and performance audits for Assam's revenue sector for the financial years ending March 2021 and 2022. Key findings include significant arrears in assessments under various taxation Acts, with 42,045 cases pending at the close of FY 2021-22, comprising 31.85% of all pending assessments (page 7). Revenue receipts grew to ₹79,815.19 crore in 2021-22, but the State's own revenue declined in proportion to total receipts from 31% in 2020-21 to 29% in 2021-22. Out of total receipts, ₹23,112.85 crore were self-generated, while ₹56,702.34 crore came from the Government of India (page 1).

Major audit observations include critical lapses in GST compliance. There were 124 cases involving short levy of taxes amounting to ₹82.88 crore, with action initiated on 105 cases only (page vi). The Department lacked an effective risk-based system for returns’ scrutiny, and failed to take action against non-filers and late filers of returns (page v). Additionally, delays and under-valuation resulted in a short levy of stamp duty and registration fees totaling ₹1.12 crore across 42 deeds (page viii).

Systemic failures led to reduced fund collections, non-realisation of taxes, losses in revenue due to under-assessment, and registration lapses in mining contracts. The severity is high due to fund losses and persistent non-compliance impacting state finances and transparency.

title: (Report No. 1 of 2024) Compliance Audit Report-I for the year ended 31 March 2022
overview:
This Compliance Audit Report reviews the management, utilisation and outcomes of major social, economic, and PSU departments in Punjab for FY 2021-22, covering the period from 2017-18 to 2021-22. Against the total budget outlay of ₹2,27,918.91 crore, actual expenditure was ₹2,20,031.98 crore in 2021-22, signifying an application of nearly 97% of the planned resources. However, the report identified a revenue expenditure increase of 54.71% and capital expenditure increase of 240%, with capital outlays still only forming 5-8% of total public spend except one year inflated by a one-off power conversion transaction (page 2).

Audit found major lapses in welfare schemes and sectoral execution: Only ₹549.23 crore of a possible ₹1,783.3 crore welfare cess was spent by the Punjab Building and Other Construction Workers’ Board from 2019-2022, leaving 62,948 beneficiaries pending for payments of ₹103.74 crore, with delays beyond 180 days for most applicants. The report also exposed delays in sports infrastructure projects, unfruitful hydro-electric expenditure, and widespread compliance and monitoring gaps (page 9, 29, 45).

Consequences include denial of welfare to the needy despite available funds, risks to accountability as 12,245 inspection reports and money-value objections remain open for over five years (value ₹17,200 crore), and inefficiencies resulting in ₹1,723.89 crore total adverse financial impact across departments (page xi). The audit flags systemic delays, inadequate oversight, and recommends urgent action for fund usage, monitoring, and timely delivery.

title: (Report No. 3 of 2024) Compliance Audit Report-II for the year ended 31 March 2022
overview:
The report examines compliance audit results for major revenue streams and state financial systems for Punjab for the fiscal period ending 31 March 2022. Total receipts amounted to ₹78,168.31 crore, with tax revenue at ₹37,326.86 crore and non-tax revenue at ₹4,783.77 crore. Dependency on grants-in-aid increased substantially to 26.57% of total receipts versus 14.43% five years prior, while the State's own revenue share decreased from 65.54% to 53.87%, indicating growing reliance on external funds (Page 1).

Test audit of 108 tax revenue units revealed under-assessments/short levies amounting to ₹189.17 crore across 65,960 cases. Recoveries of ₹9.84 crore in 1,473 cases were reported for the year (Page 10). GST return oversight showed 73 clear compliance deficiencies out of 401 cases, with revenue implications totaling ₹163.20 crore; data entry errors contributed to 30.67% of central audit inconsistencies (Page 17).

Critical IFMS project management failures included lack of an Exit Management Plan, incomplete financial data migration, no disaster recovery site, and inadequate system integration, putting critical state financial data at risk and exposing vulnerabilities to potential fraud or permanent loss (Page 63). Tax departments failed to levy due interest, fees, or permit charges in multiple cases, with several instances of fee short-levy, deficient assessments, and irregular tax concessions leading to cumulative losses spanning stamp duty, vehicle tax, GST, and excise duties.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended March 2022 on Management of Health Services in Indian Railways and Management of Parcel Services in Indian Railways Union Government (Railways) (Compliance Audit) Report No. 5 of 2024
overview:
The report examines Indian Railways’ management of health and parcel services for over one crore beneficiaries via 129 hospitals and 586 Health Units. Between 2017-22, Rs 21,217 crore was allotted for health services and Rs 21,398 crore was spent, with revenue expenditure dominating at Rs 20,734 crore (97%). However, there was a sharp rise in referral expenditure to non-railway hospitals—growing from Rs 313.98 crore in 2017-18 to Rs 595.44 crore in 2021-22 (90% increase), signaling gaps in in-house medical facilities. Medical audit of referral cases was not performed for 98.72% (7,38,297) of cases.

The audit revealed extensive shortages of medical and paramedical staff, with many hospitals below IPHS norms. Equipment deficits included vital items like Operation Tables and Ultrasound Machines. Bed Occupancy Ratio (BOR) was below 80% in 56 of 71 hospitals sampled, indicating systemic under-utilisation. Financial controls faltered: several Zonal Railways overshot budget limits by more than 5% under medicines and equipment heads, while others underused funds. Infrastructural gaps were seen in ambulances, blood bank facilities, and basic amenities across numerous hospitals.

For parcel services, tariffs have not been revised since 2013 and business development efforts have lagged behind Vision 2020 targets. Infrastructure limitations in rolling stock, parcel offices, and terminals reduce efficiency. Overall, governance failures lead to declining health service quality and subpar parcel management, with recommendations focused on periodic review, resource alignment, tariffs update, and HMIS deployment.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended March 2022 Union Government (Railways) (Compliance Audit) Report No. 4 of 2024
overview:
The CAG Compliance Audit for the Ministry of Railways for the year ending March 2022 comprises significant compliance issues and operational lapses across the Ministry and its field units, encapsulated in 33 audit observations. The report reveals monetary implications exceeding ₹2,604.40 crore, with key findings including extensive losses due to improper decisions, non-recovery of dues, and avoidable expenditures.

Notably, a loss of ₹834.72 crore occurred due to interest paid by IRCON on a loan for a land parcel that was never developed. East Coast Railway faced a revenue loss of ₹149.12 crore from non-levy of shunting charges, and there were widespread failures to recover GST and license fees, leading to further financial setbacks. Other findings include non-revision of license fees, inadmissible concessions, and mismanagement of assets and projects, such as delays leading to idling investments and unproductive expenditures on incomplete or poorly planned works.

Accountability lapses are recurrent throughout, with recommendations emphasizing fixing responsibility for financial mismanagement, improving systemic controls like updating operational systems and contracts, and enhancing inter-agency coordination. The audit recovered ₹222.80 crore during 2021-22, reflecting the persistent nature of undercharges, non-compliances, and procedural deficiencies within the audited entities.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Compliance of the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003 for the year 2021-22 Union Government Department of Economic Affairs (Ministry of Finance) Report No. 1 of 2024
overview:
For the year ending March 2022, the CAG conducted a compliance audit of the FRBM Act, focusing on fiscal targets, debt management, and transparency in government disclosures. The Central Government Debt at the end of 2021-22 was ₹138.65 lakh crore, amounting to 58.59% of GDP, showing a decline from the pandemic peak of 61.55% in 2020-21 but still overshooting the prescribed 40% FRBM target for FY 2024-25. General Government Debt, combining Centre and States, stood at ₹195.54 lakh crore (82.63% of GDP), with the target set at 60% by 2024-25, reflecting continuing fiscal pressures.

The Government's guarantees for loans raised by Public Sector Entities remained within the ceiling of 0.5% of GDP for 2021-22, with ₹0.96 lakh crore (0.40% of GDP) in new guarantees, but disclosures regarding extra budgetary resources (EBR)—key components of Central Government debt—were found incomplete or overstated (notably, errors in the Long Term Irrigation Fund disclosures and exclusion of ₹71,065.90 crore borrowing by Indian Railways). Significant gaps in compliance with disclosure norms were also noted; mandatory forms (D1-D5) around tax arrears and asset registers remain irregular, and full implementation of the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework is missing since 2018-19.

Consequences included actual Fiscal Deficit for 2021-22 being 7.4% of GDP—well above the budget estimate of 6.8%—and Revenue Receipts exceeding estimates by 22.19%, mainly due to robust tax collections, while Revenue Expenditure was 6.84% above budget, driven by increased allocations in health and sanitation. The audit highlights ongoing risks to fiscal sustainability and recommends urgent corrective action and improved transparency.

title: Union Government (Civil) Compliance Audit Observations
overview:
This compliance audit covers significant financial and governance lapses identified across 23 Civil Ministries/Departments and Union Territories without Legislatures for the financial year 2021-22, with an aggregate gross expenditure of ₹7,87,047.55 crore. The audit revealed that the overall expenditure decreased marginally by 0.12% compared to the previous year, but large unspent provisions and delays persist, resulting in poor fund utilization and blockage of public money.

Notably, 21% of projects under the North-Eastern Region's Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR) remained incomplete amidst significant delays, and the scheme's funds were managed as a notional pool rather than through a dedicated reserve fund. Further, examples such as the Ministry of Tribal Affairs blocking ₹916 crore for non-functional Eklavya Model Residential Schools and the Border Security Force's purchase of 906 flats (₹151 crore) with little occupancy show systemic flaws in planning and oversight. Several other Ministries parked funds outside the Government Account, resulting in inefficient financial management and avoidable expenditures, including interest losses and double payments.

The audit underscores a recurring pattern of inadequate project execution, poor adherence to financial guidelines, and lack of effective monitoring mechanisms. These issues collectively indicate weak governance, wastage of public resources, and opportunity costs for other priority sectors. Recommendations target urgent corrective actions to improve transparency and impact.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Compliance Audit for the year ended 31 March 2022
overview:
This Compliance Audit Report for Jharkhand covers significant findings identified in the audit of multiple State Government departments and State Public Sector Undertakings for the period ending 31 March 2022. The audit universe comprised 5,812 units under 60 government grants, including 34 departments, with a total revenue of ₹31,320.36 crore raised in 2021-22. Despite an increase in own tax and non-tax revenue of 26.12% and 32.61% respectively, the state remained reliant on Government of India transfers, which accounted for 55% of total receipts. As of March 2022, the arrears of revenue across four key heads (Sales Tax, Vehicles, State Excise, Land Revenue) stood at ₹8,479.97 crore, with more than half being outstanding for over five years.

The audit found critical operational and compliance deficiencies: working State Public Sector Enterprises incurred a collective loss of ₹2,682.45 crore in 2021-22, and the submission of statutory accounts by SPSEs was severely delayed, with 93 accounts in arrears for up to 12 years as of December 2022. Fund utilization in major departments varied, with persistent issues in revenue realization, excess payments, and lack of internal controls. Notably, an instance of excess payment of ₹1.20 crore was identified and partly recovered in the Building Construction Division, Giridih.

Overall, government response to audit queries remained inadequate, with 45,589 audit paragraphs from 6,167 inspection reports pending action as of March 2023. The audit recommends urgent strengthening of compliance and timely recovery procedures, greater accountability for audit responses, and improved monitoring of loss-making and non-compliant SPSEs.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India Compliance Audit (Revenue) For the year ended 31 March 2021
overview:
This compliance audit report highlights significant issues in revenue collection and administration by the Government of Jharkhand for the year ended 31 March 2021. The revenue raised by the State Government during 2020-21 was ₹ 24,444.09 crore, which accounted for only 44 per cent of the total revenue receipts, with the balance 56 per cent coming from the State’s share of divisible Union taxes and grants-in-aid from the Government of India. Despite the marginal growth in tax revenue by 0.65 per cent over 2019-20, non-tax revenue saw a significant decrease of 13.55 per cent, primarily due to effects of the Covid-19 pandemic. Audit analysis identified ₹ 8,458.41 crore in arrears, with ₹ 3,485.68 crore pending for more than five years, revealing long-standing collection inefficiencies (Table 1.4, page 6).

The audit test-checked 25 out of 586 auditable units, revealing under-assessment, non/short levy of tax/interest/penalty, and loss of revenue totaling ₹ 910.74 crore (11.60 per cent of the revenue collected by the units) in 1,413 cases. Irregularities in transitional credits alone amounted to ₹ 194.01 crore. Departments concerned formally acknowledged deficiencies amounting to ₹ 105.85 crore in 61 cases, with only ₹ 44.49 lakh recovered, indicating weak follow-up and enforcement.

Specific issues such as non-levy of interest on disallowed exemptions and concessions, excess availment of transitional credits, and failure to reconcile figures in the District Mineral Foundation Trust severely affected revenue realization. Departmental responses to audit were delayed; 9,590 paragraphs across 1,033 Inspection Reports, with potential recoverable revenue of ₹ 17,812.35 crore, remained outstanding (Table 1.6, page 7). These findings highlight critical weaknesses in revenue management and compliance across multiple departments.

title: Compliance Audit Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Revenue Sector for the Year ended 31 March 2022 (Report No. 03 of the Year 2024)
overview:
This CAG report presents compliance audit results regarding the Revenue Sector of Uttar Pradesh for the year ended March 2022. The total receipts for 2021-22 were ₹ 3,71,011.44 crore, out of which ₹ 1,58,803.71 crore (42.8%) constituted the State’s own receipts and ₹ 2,12,207.73 crore (57.2%) was from Government of India. Audit covered five departments and test-checked records from 185 out of 1,498 auditable units, revealing underassessment and short levy of revenue aggregating ₹ 3,756.59 crore in 86,505 cases; with department acceptance of deficiencies worth ₹ 2.96 crore and reported recovery of ₹ 5.42 lakh.

Significant compliance lapses were observed in GST oversight, including non-recovery of ₹ 9.85 crore due to procedural lapses, delayed audits, and incomplete recovery reporting, as well as deficiencies in stamp duty and registration charges on mortgage deeds, resulting in major financial implications. Notably, departments accepted audit observations amounting to ₹ 1,250.70 crore and reported recovery of ₹ 16.47 crore as of July 2023.

Additional findings included non-imposition of penalties and additional taxes (₹ 6.43 crore and ₹ 1.97 crore, respectively) in the transport sector, and a total of ₹ 37,082.23 crore in revenue arrears, with ₹ 15,142.67 crore outstanding for more than five years. Persistent gaps in departmental responses to audit findings and corrective action remain a concern, impacting revenue accountability and transparency.

title: Audit Report on Revenue Sector for the year ended 31st March, 2022
overview:
This Report contains 24 significant compliance audit paragraphs based on a test-check of records for five major revenue receipts by the Revenue and Transport Departments of Telangana, resulting in a tax effect of ₹129.30 crore (Overview, page vii). Notable findings include short or non-levy of tax, excess input tax credit, and non/short-levy of penalties and interest. For example, short levy of tax on mobile phones alone resulted in a loss of ₹9.28 crore (Overview, page vii).

The audit also found that, of 407 identified high-value inconsistencies in GST returns for 2017-18, 109 were confirmed as compliance deficiencies with a revenue implication of ₹986.78 crore. Additionally, 141 deficiencies with a value of ₹158.93 crore were noted in a detailed audit of 50 taxpayers, largely due to ineligible ITC claims, incorrect discharge of tax, and non/short-payment of interest or penalties (Overview p. viii; §2.14 p.31).

The broader audit across tax categories revealed shortfalls in timely reconciliation, revenue collection, and departmental oversight. The report flagged systemic failures such as lack of data validation, unaddressed audit recommendations, and poor follow-up, underscoring an urgent need for robust internal controls and remedial action to avoid revenue loss and ensure fiscal accountability.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended 31 March 2021 - Government of Rajasthan (Compliance Audit)(Report No. 2 of the year 2024)
overview:
This CAG report covers significant compliance issues in 16 State Government departments and 31 State Public Sector Undertakings and autonomous bodies of Rajasthan for the period ending March 2021. In Part I, the audit found irregularities involving ₹41.19 crore, including significant lapses in the Transport Department, Mines and Geology Department, and Public Health Engineering Department. For instance, data entry errors in the VAHAN/SARATHI vehicle and license database led to discrepancies, including wrong registration dates, duplicate engine/chassis numbers, and underage licenses, impacting records of over 10.14 lakh cases (p. vii-viii).

In mining, audit discovered 46 short-term permits issued irregularly without advance deposit of dues worth ₹3.20 crore, and 2,857 publicly funded works executed without proper permits involving ₹368.81 crore, indicating systemic gaps and potential revenue leakage (p. ix-x). PHED allowed an avoidable loss of ₹2.27 crore due to acceptance of a fake bank guarantee and excess payments of ₹17.04 crore.

Part II highlighted lapses in State PSUs: RERC’s delayed tariff orders and inconsistent return on equity approvals (p. x-xi); Rajasthan State Mines and Minerals Ltd forfeited recovery of ₹9.69 crore from a contractor; and Vidyut Prasaran Nigam Ltd made idle payments of ₹7.24 crore. The report stresses the need for improved controls, enforcement, and data integrity across functions, with only partial recoveries and compliance so far. The overall severity is rated high due to the scale and persistence of issues.

title: Compliance Audit Report for the year ended 31 March 2022
overview:
This compliance audit covers transactions and outcomes under 11 State Government Departments and 98 State Public Sector Undertakings for the period ending March 2022. The total quantified financial impact of audit observations is ₹27,855.78 crore, spanning issues such as delayed compensatory afforestation, time and cost overruns, idling of assets, illegal mining, and excess or improper expenditure across key projects and undertakings.

Key findings include non-identification of forest land for road construction in lieu of diverted land, leading to non-execution of mandated afforestation works; lapses in financial management and execution under the Kerala Public Works Department, resulting in undue advantage to agencies to the tune of ₹21.84 crore; and evidence of payment irregularities and wasteful public expenditure in Cultural Affairs, Mining and Geology, and Coir Development departments.

The report further documents persistent backlogs in settlement of Inspection Reports, with 6,395 audit paragraphs across 1,076 IRs pending with Departments by September 2022. Audit Committee Meetings remain sporadic, with only two departments convening during the reporting year. The compounded effect of these deficiencies manifests in regulatory non-compliance, delayed public benefit, and significant losses to the State exchequer.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India - Compliance Audit (Revenue) - Tamil - Report No. 4 of 2024
overview:
The audit report critically examines the revenue administration and collection in Tamil Nadu for the period 2017-18 to 2021-22. The total revenue receipts of the State during 2021-22 were ₹2,07,492.40 crore, including ₹1,34,982.81 crore raised by the State, ₹37,458.62 crore received as State’s share of divisible taxes, and ₹35,050.97 crore as grants-in-aid from the Government of India. Of this, 65% was contributed by State-raised revenue, a decrease from 67% in 2020-21.

Despite the apparent growth in gross receipts, the audit highlights serious issues: ₹39,350.96 crore in arrears of revenue were outstanding as of March 2022. Major tax heads such as Commercial Taxes, Stamp Duty and Registration, State Excise, and Vehicle Taxes all showed increasing trends in arrears or under-collection, with persistent shortcomings in demand, assessment, collection, and internal controls. The report points out that more than 27,500 audit observations totalling to a loss of ₹5,242.45 crore were pending as of June 2022, highlighting gaps in compliance and follow-up mechanism.

Further, a total of ₹2,978.46 crore in revenue loss was detected across 11 cases, arising from inconsistent and delayed actions in revenue recovery, wrongful exemptions, under-assessment, and summary lapses in internal compliance. These failures impact fiscal stability, constrain developmental spending, and erode trust in public administration.

title: Report No. 3 of 2024 - C&AG's report on Local Government for the year ended 31st March 2022.
overview:
This report presents a comprehensive audit of Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) and Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) in Bihar for the period ending 31 March 2022. Over ₹32,492 crore in grant funds from Central and State sources were allocated to PRIs during FY 2017-18 to FY 2021-22, but the audit revealed multiple cases of misappropriation, poor utilization, and fraud. Key findings include avoidable penalty and interest payments of ₹1.14 crore due to delayed remittance by Nagar Parishad Saharsa and fraudulent payments totaling ₹91.14 lakh by Nagar Parishad Sheikhpura, along with an additional loss of ₹1.37 crore from irregular disqualification in tender processes.

Performance audit of solid waste management showed that none of the sampled ULBs (except Darbhanga Municipal Corporation) achieved all eight benchmark indicators set by the Ministry of Urban Development, reflecting deficient planning and non-observance of SWM Rules. 24% of households carried out source segregation, but most waste was unsegregated, dumped at landfill sites, and transported in non-compliant vehicles. Procurements worth ₹43.38 crore were highlighted as ad-hoc and excess relative to requirements.

Consequences include deficient monitoring, significant gaps in environmental compliance, and persistent vacancies in sanctioned posts (over 71% Panchayat Secretary posts vacant). The State Government continues to not fix responsibility for bio-medical and e-waste management, with used syringes and plastic waste mixed into municipal solid waste, and only four out of 28 ULBs commenced legacy waste remediation after Hon’ble NGT order.

title: Compliance Audit Report of West Bengal for the year ended on 31 March 2022.
overview:
The Comptroller and Auditor General's Compliance Audit Report for West Bengal, presented for the year ending 31 March 2022, highlights significant lapses in fund management, monitoring, and adherence to project guidelines across 25 government departments, 46 autonomous bodies, and 63 State Public Sector Enterprises (SPSEs). The aggregate expenditure scrutinized was ₹34,601.87 crore, with 83.56% of spending concentrated in five departments. Notably, in the implementation of flagship schemes and projects, such as Lok Prasar Prakalpa (LPP) and the Cluster Development Programme (CDP), systemic issues included incomplete beneficiary databases, irregular or excessive payments, and non-functional assets despite large outlays.

Key headline findings include excess and unauthorized payments—such as ₹78.61 lakh in excess GST to a private agency (p.11), and persistent gaps in updating and verifying beneficiaries for social welfare schemes, as seen in LPP implementation where 51,376 applicants were never auditioned and 21,094 retainer folk artists went without work in certain districts (p.3–4). In cluster development, incomplete projects and diversion from approved processes resulted in non-utilization and unfruitful expenditure totaling over ₹11.21 crore for a single cluster, and deviation from tendering norms recurred across multiple locations (p.5).

The consequences for state finances and service delivery are severe: outstanding unrecovered sums, such as ₹13.35 crore in tax revenue and ₹47.07 crore in electricity charges, wasteful expenditures upward of ₹5 crore on non-compliant infrastructure, and continued operational inefficiencies in state transport corporations. Compliance lapses have further led to legal and administrative delays, undermining the intended economic and social benefits for targeted groups and causing significant avoidable losses to the state exchequer.

title: Report 7 of 2025: Report of Comptroller and Auditor General of India: Compliance Audit Report -Civil -I, of UT of Jammu and Kashmir for the Period ended March 2023
overview:
The report conducts a compliance audit of several schemes and departments of the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir, focusing on performance, utilisation, and governance issues in key infrastructure and social sector initiatives for the period ending March 2023. Major findings pertain to the World Bank-aided Jhelum Tawi Flood Recovery Project (JTFRP), Pradhan Mantri Khanij Kshetra Kalyan Yojana, National Rural Livelihood Mission (NRLM), and the Transport Subsidy Scheme.

A total of ₹1,504 crore was allocated under the JTFRP for 213 sub-projects, with only 174 completed as of December 2023. The audit revealed persistent delays caused by non-preparation of damage/loss reports, lack of proper feasibility, and awarding of projects not proposed by relevant departments, resulting in idle and irregular expenditure. Out of 82 sampled sub-projects, more than 50% were not started or delayed due to lapses in tendering, change of experts, and poor monitoring (“Delays in tendering and execution resulted in time and cost overruns.” - p. vii).

Under the National Rural Livelihood Mission, only 63,211 (against a target of 1,05,000) Self Help Groups were actually credit-linked, with staff vacancies hampering outreach and effective implementation. Idle funds, irregular payments, and multiple audit flags regarding machinery purchases and procurement under various schemes further highlighted the UT’s deficit in governance and project implementation capacity.

title: Compliance Audit (Commercial) Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the period ended March 2023 pertaining to Government of Andhra Pradesh
overview:
The report examines compliance and performance of 20 select Andhra Pradesh State Public Sector Enterprises (SPSEs) during 2020-23. Out of 124 total SPSEs, only 43 submitted at least one account in the last three years, with 342 accounts from 90 SPSEs still pending, some for as long as 17 years. In 2022-23, these 20 SPSEs' turnover reached ₹88,176.83 crore, representing 6.69% of the State's GSDP, with the power sector accounting for 80.82%.

Significant findings include heavy dependence on government funding due to limited operational revenue, substantial unfruitful central funds (₹4.79 crore), and poor asset utilisation—assets worth ₹33.68 crore under the Swadesh Darshan Scheme were left idle. Furthermore, only 4 of 13 mandated SPSEs had adequate Independent Directors, with major lapses in Board meetings and vigil mechanisms.

The consequences of poor oversight and compliance include: accumulated losses of ₹4,039.91 crore in five loss-making SPSEs, a severe backlog in accounts, and operational inefficiency. The government's financial exposure remains high, with equity and long-term loans in the 20 SPSEs totaling ₹1,06,761.20 crore. Audit comments also highlighted errors impacting profitability by ₹139.32 crore and assets/liabilities by ₹1,207.66 crore.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (Performance and Compliance Audit) for the year ended 31 March 2023 (Report of The CAG no. 7 of the year2025 (Performance and Compliance Audit)
overview:
This CAG report covers the performance and compliance audit for the Government of Odisha, focusing primarily on the years ending March 2023. The audit examined the construction and improvement of roads and bridges under the Road Development Programme, prison administration, and IT systems like the Works and Accounts Management Information System (WAMIS). Over the audit period, the Works Department alone utilized ₹7,430.52 crore out of the ₹8,385.70 crore budgeted, leaving ₹955.18 crore unutilized, and several instances of wasteful or unplanned expenditure, such as ₹39.65 crore in avoidable extra cost for road widening and ₹26.74 crore for incomplete surveys, were identified (see p.x–xi).

Auditors found persistent structural and planning issues such as delays due to failure to ensure land availability, deficiencies in quality control, lack of penalty imposition on contractors for overdue work, and significant cost inflation due to non-compliance with prescribed standards. For instance, delays in acquiring land and providing encumbrance-free sites resulted in incomplete projects even after spending ₹101.41 crore (p.x).

There were also critical gaps in prison management, including overcrowding (31 out of 87 jails), severe shortage of security staff, and lack of essential security equipment that led to repeated contraband seizures and escapes. In IT systems, six out of thirteen WAMIS modules were not implemented even after up to 10 years, raising concerns about information reliability, risks of undue benefit, and inadequate process controls, affecting contract monitoring and public accountability. The report calls for systemic changes to planning, execution, and monitoring to prevent recurring lapses and avoidable expenditure.

title: Departmental Trading Units including Supply Chain Management in Khadi and Village Industries Commission
overview:
The CAG conducted a compliance audit on the functioning of Departmental Trading Units (DTUs) under the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) covering the period 2017-18 to 2020-21. Of the 92 DTUs established, only 18 were functional by March 2021, while 74 units had become defunct (including 73 before 2016 and one in 2019). Funds utilization for KVIC’s schemes was high, with 99.55% of the ₹11,236 crore provided during 2017-18 to 2020-21 being spent; however, major portions were spent on Modified Market Development Assistance (over 55%) and the Khadi Reform and Development Programme (over 21%).

The audit found that KVIC did not analyse reasons for closure of DTUs or assess impact on stakeholders. Audit detected lapses where closure of at least three DTUs could have been avoided through timely action, including a loss of opportunity at Central Sliver Plant, Etah, where failure to pursue cost-effective electricity solutions led to preventable closure and wasted investment.

The audit highlights issues like delays in disposal of assets and realisation of dues from defunct units, procurement and monitoring failures, and underutilization of initiatives such as e-commerce and market surveys. KVIC initiated 26 recommendations, including immediate action on disposing defunct assets, improving procurement transparency, and utilization of information technology for better planning. The severity of findings is high, as they impact employment, sustainability, and efficient use of public funds.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on General, Social, Economic (other than Public Sector Undertakings), Economic (Public Sector Undertakings) and Revenue Sectors for the year ended 31 March 2022
overview:
The CAG report on the Government of Manipur's General, Social, Economic, and Revenue Sectors for the year ended 31 March 2022 reveals substantial lapses in planning, fund utilization, and monitoring across departments. In the General Sector, audit of 21 units in 2020-21 involving an expenditure of ₹1,376.24 crore resulted in issuance of 20 Inspection Reports with 76 audit paras. In 2021-22, 8 units were audited, covering ₹988.10 crore in expenditure with 8 Inspection Reports and 28 audit paras (page vii).

One headline finding is the delayed submission of Annual Action Plans under the Modernisation of Police Force (MPF) Scheme, leading to approval and fund release delays, and ultimately impacting scheme implementation and resulting in funds remaining unspent year after year. As of 31 March 2022, ₹41.09 crore remained unutilized under MPF, even as significant shortages of modern arms (Carbine Amogh, Ghatak rifle, Glock pistol), inadequate vehicles, and lack of forensic equipment persist (page viii).

Financial irregularities include non-remittance of VAT (₹2.34 crore), non-deposit of Sales Tax (₹17.42 crore), GST (₹1.04 crore), and Labour Cess (₹3.81 crore) by departmental entities, as well as blockage of ₹8.08 crore by the Social Welfare Department for Anganwadi Centre construction for up to four years (pages ix-x). Weak systems allowed irregular and fraudulent benefits under PM-KISAN Yojana, with ₹65.49 crore disbursed to 1,91,244 ineligible beneficiaries, and ₹27.30 crore made to 46,023 persons whose details did not match with bank account info (page x).

title: Compliance Audit Report, Government of Kerala
overview:
The Compliance Audit Report for Kerala uncovers systemic deficiencies in management and assignment of government land, highlighting irregularities and losses amounting to ₹326.77 crore. Audit scrutiny found 33,057 assignments involving 6,216.25 hectares and 2,920 leases over 775.78 hectares, many executed without approved lists or regulatory compliance. Key lapses included assignment of land to ineligible persons, non-collection of market value, improper and non-revised lease rents, and ineffective record maintenance. For example, the Revenue & Disaster Management Department failed to assess buildings, resulting in a ₹31.60 crore shortfall, and Kerala Water Authority misclassified buildings, causing ₹82.06 lakh in under-collected water charges.

The audit also revealed administrative failures, such as Kerala Academy for Skills Excellence's inability to verify placement documents, leading to ₹16.72 lakh in fraudulent claims. Further, routine waivers of lease rent to clubs and commercial agencies resulted in direct monetary losses for the State. Plantation Corporation of Kerala Ltd incurred recurring losses due to neglected rubber plantation practices and unfruitful expenditure, including ₹5.54 crore wasted on a dairy farm project.

Deficient responsiveness from departments, outstanding inspection reports, and non-submission of Action Taken Notes further compound the risks to revenue and good governance. The absence of a centralised data system or regular monitoring exposes Kerala to continued irregularity and non-compliance, undermining public interests and transparency.

title: Public Sector Undertakings, Government of Telangana
overview:
The report examines the performance and compliance of Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) in Telangana for the year ended 31 March 2021, with focused audits on sand mining, Hyderabad Metro Rail Project, and power distribution. Notable findings include loss of ₹50.37 crore due to continued power supply despite non-payment of dues by Sirpur Paper Mills Limited, and undue benefit of ₹227.19 crore to the Hyderabad Metro Rail project concessionaire due to non-development of parking and circulation areas and higher fares allowed than the concession agreement.

The performance audit on sand mining highlighted that TSMDCL entered into sand raising contracts with tribal societies, who then unlawfully sub-contracted excavation work to third parties, despite rules prohibiting sub-letting. This resulted in direct undue benefit of ₹11.61 crore to the contractors and defeated policy objectives for Scheduled Areas. Unauthorised and excess excavation of sand was not penalized appropriately, with ₹7.19 crore of penalties not levied, and sand worth ₹108.96 crore excavated and dispatched without necessary permissions, leading to blocked government revenue.

Critical monitoring failures led to overloading, ineffective environment compliance, diversion of 94.7% of Road Damage Charges (₹162.27 crore) for unrelated uses, and unaddressed M-Sand industry needs. In total, audit concludes that weak governance, delayed actions, and ignored directives deprived both the government and local farmers of due benefits and revenues, while enabling large-scale regulatory bypasses.

title: Compliance Audit Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended 31 March 2021 (Environment, Public Works, Energy and Industries Departments)
overview:
The Compliance Audit on the 'Implementation of State Rural Drinking Water Programme in Madhya Pradesh' for 2018-19 to 2020-21 revealed significant deficiencies in scheme planning, financial management, execution, and monitoring. Audit covered 10 Divisions and 18 schemes, finding that 107 villages were excluded after ₹4.96 crore was spent on project reports, and ₹27.19 crore was blocked in detailed project reports for 80 schemes never implemented (page 20).

Significant issues included non-adherence to scheme guidelines, diversion of ₹44.85 crore from the Jal Jeevan Mission Fund, and a slip back of 2,407 habitations from fully to partially covered status due to depleting groundwater, impacting a large population. Liquidated damages of ₹36.90 crore were not deducted for delayed works, and in 129 works, penalty of ₹13.41 crore was never levied (page 27). Contractors were also paid ₹72.90 crore in excess due to excise duty exemption mishandling (page 26).

The overall financial and operational impact of audit findings totals ₹283.42 crore. The failures resulted in deprived benefits for roughly 2,307 households, incomplete and delayed projects, and an overall pattern of weak monitoring and fiscal imprudence. The Department's non-compliance indicates systemic issues needing urgent rectification to safeguard public funds and service delivery.

title: Audit Report on Central Autonomous Bodies, Union Government (Civil)
overview:
The Audit Report for the year ending March 2022 covers 472 Central Autonomous Bodies (CABs) across various Union Government Ministries, with a focus on both compliance and financial issues. The Government of India released ₹130,109.63 crore as grants/loans to these bodies during 2021-22. However, a significant portion, ₹11,178.47 crore, remained unutilised as of March 2022. Of particular concern, only 192 CABs managed to submit their annual accounts by the statutory deadline of 30 June 2022; more than half (254 CABs, 53.81%) submitted late, and 26 CABs failed to submit at all, with arrears ranging up to seven years.

Systemic deficiencies were prominent: internal audit was not conducted in 220 CABs, and physical verification of assets or inventories was not done in over 140 units each, indicating weak internal controls. Further, 138 CABs used non-standard accounting practices, and 175 did not account for retirement benefits per actuarial valuation, potentially concealing financial exposures.

These failures resulted in substantial financial repercussions across ministries. For example, illegal or inadvertent payments—such as an inadmissible ₹378.10 lakh in ad-hoc bonuses, ₹2.78 crore in overpaid increments, and ₹6.47 crore in sub-optimal contract awards—reflect losses and misuse. The backlog and delayed reporting limit assurance on grant utilization, asset integrity, and legal compliance, posing high risks to public funds.

title: Compliance Audit on Scientific and Environmental Ministries/Departments Union Government
overview:
This report presents the findings from a compliance audit of eight Scientific and Environmental Ministries/Departments of the Union Government. The total expenditure for these ministries in 2021-22 was ₹68,848.61 crore, with a significant increase of 39.21% (₹19,391.09 crore) from the previous year. Notably, the Department of Atomic Energy accounted for 45.91% of this spending. The audit revealed substantial unspent budget allocations, totaling ₹6,945.99 crore or 9.16% of the overall grant, with particularly high unspent portions in Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (18.68%), Department of Biotechnology (18.59%), Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (16.52%), and Department of Science and Technology (15.23%).

Several critical lapses were identified, including avoidable payment of ₹1.14 crore on electricity due to overestimated contract demand by LPSC-B (Department of Space), and non-utilization of GSAT-18 satellite transponders leading to avoidable costs of ₹17.27 crore. Delays in project execution and financial mismanagement resulted in infructuous expenditure across multiple departments, like ₹4 crore on Special Grade Carbon Fibre development. The audit also recorded a backlog of 36,506 outstanding Utilisation Certificates (UCs) aggregating ₹26,295.75 crore, and highlighted delayed accounting, presentation of annual reports to Parliament, and weak contract management.

These findings underscore systemic issues of budget planning, compliance failures, and inefficiencies in resource utilization, necessitating enhanced oversight, timely action, and accountability. The extent and nature of these lapses indicate high risk of financial mismanagement, reduced effectiveness of public spending, and threat to strategic objectives in the sectors audited.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended 31 March 2021, Compliance Audit Report (Vol.-I) Government of Madhya Pradesh Report No. 5 of the year 2023
overview:
This Compliance Audit Report details significant issues uncovered in land acquisition, the implementation of horticulture schemes, irrigation modernization, and related financial management across six departments of Madhya Pradesh for the period 2019-21. The Revenue Department acquired 12,928.60 hectares at a cost of ₹2,208.67 crore in six audited districts during 2015-20 but was unable to ensure fair compensation or transparency, with delays and under-assessment resulting in improper payouts totaling over ₹21.73 crore and persistent non-disbursement of ₹102.70 crore to 859 landowners.

Similarly, in the Extension, Renovation, and Modernization (ERM) of the Tawa Irrigation Project, expenditure of ₹592.81 crore resulted in only 375.66 km (14.06%) of necessary lining completed by March 2021, achieving just 3,830 hectares (5%) of targeted Culturable Command Area increase. The Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture (MIDH) also failed, with the State Horticulture Mission utilising just 68% of funds from 2018-21 and clear evidence of irregular payments, ineligible subsidies, and widespread non-achievement of outcomes due to the lack of planning, monitoring, and capacity at multiple levels.

The audit discloses systemic weaknesses in monitoring, absence of comprehensive land and fund utilization databases, and repeated failures to act on inspection reports. These shortcomings have perpetuated losses to the exchequer, non-achievement of scheme objectives, and instances of fraud and misappropriation, with over 13,600 inspection reports and 50,900 audit paragraphs still pending settlement as of March 2022.

title: Compliance Audit Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Poola Subbaiah Veligonda Project
overview:
The Poola Subbaiah Veligonda Project was initiated in 2004 with the objective to provide irrigation to 4.38 lakh acres and drinking water to 15 lakh people across three districts of Andhra Pradesh. Despite an increase in the total project cost from ₹4,458.86 crore to ₹5,217.73 crore as of November 2021, the project remains incomplete after more than 17 years, with only limited physical and financial progress. Of the total budget authorisation of ₹2,190 crore during 2017-21, just ₹1,270 crore was incurred, and the utilisation rate showed a downward trend despite rising allocations.

Key audit findings include delays due to untimely approval of designs, frequent contractor changes, non-adherence to contract guidelines, and improper financial management leading to excess and irregular payments. Notably, ₹630.57 crore was spent over the original agreement values for price variations and reimbursements. Land acquisition remains a bottleneck, with only 62.76% of required land acquired as of March 2022.

The prolonged delay has deprived the intended beneficiaries of project benefits and caused inefficient resource utilisation. Major components such as tunnels, distributary networks, and key structures remain incomplete, further hindering the provision of irrigation and drinking water to drought-prone areas. The report notes a need for urgent corrective action in project planning, contract management, and fund utilisation to realise the project's objectives. (Source: Executive Summary pp. ix-xi, Chapter II pp. 5-7)

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Social, Economic and Revenue Sectors for the year ended 31 March 2022, Government of Tripura
overview:
The audit reveals serious deficiencies in the public health infrastructure and delivery in Tripura. Out of a network comprising 6 tertiary healthcare facilities, 6 district hospitals, 14 Sub Divisional Hospitals, 21 Community Health Centres, 110 Primary Health Centres, and 999 Sub-Centres, none of the CHCs could provide full specialist services as per Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS), with only CHC Kherengbar offering Obstetrics & Gynecology services twice a week (p. v-vi). Over 20% of registered pregnant women did not receive the mandated four ANC checkups in 2021-22, reflecting glaring service shortfalls. Large volumes of essential drugs were unavailable, with a high rate of medicine stock-outs reported. Emergency and trauma care facilities were virtually absent at the primary level (p. vi).

Significant lapses were found in hospital support services—no FSSAI food safety licenses had been obtained, no safety clearances were issued from the Fire Department, and Bio-Medical Waste rules were not followed in the sampled health facilities. Infection control mechanisms were often non-functional, and grievance redressal for patients was completely missing. Asset underutilisation was widespread: installation of new PSA oxygen plants did not reduce expenditure on oxygen cylinders as the plants largely remained disused. In addition, ₹8.97 crore in unspent COVID-19 funds remained unsurrendered, despite slow progress on paediatric care infrastructure upgrades (p. vi-vii).

The State lags on SDG-3 health indicators in 6 out of 10 targeted areas compared to national benchmarks, and health spending remains below the National Health Policy, 2017 targets. Monitoring frameworks exist but are under-used, leading to poor impact assessment and persistent service gaps. The intended objective of providing quality primary care at the grassroots level was not achieved, undermining both routine service delivery and critical pandemic response.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Direct Benefit Transfer in Jharkhand For the year ended 31 March 2021
overview:
The performance audit of Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) in Jharkhand covered a total fund disbursement of ₹19,641.88 crore through 110 cash-only schemes implemented by 12 state departments between 2017 and 2021. The audit found deficient implementation across scholarship and social security pension schemes, notably within SC/ST/BC and Minority Welfare Departments. Electronic databases of beneficiaries were lacking, resulting in widespread payment issues, including ghost and ineligible beneficiaries and excess/disallowed scholarships. For instance, scholarship payments to fake or ghost beneficiaries were observed in over 60% of test-checked minority institutes. In the National Social Assistance Programme, the data revealed significant delays: up to 864 days in 39% of sampled applications, with chronic shortfall in timely payments—delays ranged from one to four months, directly undermining the schemes' goal of providing monthly income support.

The IT audit of the e-Kalyan portal exposed inadequacies including missing Aadhaar e-KYC integration, lack of direct Treasury/bank linkage, non-completion of migration to National e-Scholarship Portal, and persistent weak internal controls. As of 2021, Aadhaar seeding among beneficiaries for different schemes ranged only from 49% to 75%, with State pensions especially showing poor linkage: up to 65% of beneficiaries in some state schemes lacked Aadhaar bank seeding.

The State DBT Cell was found lagging—training and capacity building were unopened, and the State Advisory Board formed in 2016 did not convene its first meeting until December 2022. Overall, systemic gaps in planning, technology, and beneficiary validation allowed leakages, non-compliance with guidelines, loss of control, and continued hardships for eligible citizens who did not receive timely or accurate benefits.

title: Report No. 1 of 2023 - Union Territory Finances Audit Report(Tamil), Government of the Union Territory of Puducherry
overview:
The audit of Puducherry Union Territory's finances for 2021-22 highlighted key fiscal parameters and their trajectory over recent years, with distinct emphasis on revenue and expenditure management. The Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) stood at ₹37,485 crore in 2021-22, with revenue receipts of ₹7,859 crore and revenue expenditure of ₹8,748 crore, resulting in a revenue deficit of ₹889 crore.

Capital expenditure remained below optimal: Total capital outlay for the year was ₹899 crore, equivalent to only 2.4% of GSDP and far short of the recommended 3%, signaling ongoing under-investment in infrastructure. Similarly, the component of committed expenditure and interest payments also showed persistent growth, affecting fiscal flexibility.

Debt sustainability is a concern, as total liabilities rose steeply from ₹8,799 crore in 2017-18 to ₹12,593 crore in 2021-22. The proportion of GSDP devoted to outstanding liability escalated from 19.29% to 23.77% over five years. Persistent under-collection of own tax revenue, delayed disbursements of central grants, and notable inefficiencies in public sector undertakings (PSUs) compounded fiscal stress—posing material risks to fiscal consolidation targets set for the UT.

recommendations: Enhance own tax mobilisation to reduce overreliance on central transfers.
Increase capital outlay towards infrastructure to at least 3% of GSDP.
Implement tighter expenditure controls and improve efficiency in PSUs.
Develop a debt management strategy to limit escalation of outstanding liabilities.
Strengthen monitoring of grant releases and ensure timely utilisation.

title: Compliance Audit Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended March 2021
overview:
This report presents the significant results of the compliance audit of eight departments of the Government of Andhra Pradesh for the period 2019-21. The audit found major issues in the development of the Capital City Amaravati. Out of the required ₹48,115 crore for 2016-21, only ₹8,487.16 crore could be arranged by the APCRDA. This resulted in incomplete infrastructure, with only four of 16 packages reaching just 10-18% physical progress, while the remaining 12 packages remained at the preliminary stage. Of the ₹13,802.75 crore planned for Land Pooling Scheme infrastructure, only ₹3,617 crore was spent as of September 2021.

Other instances of unfruitful and wasteful expenditure include ₹177.17 crore spent on unutilized pipes, ₹44.74 crore spent on a grievance cell building which was later demolished, and ₹1,505.22 crore spent on government buildings that reached 0-95% completion before works halted. Additionally, only ₹9 crore out of ₹133 crore was spent on water supply, resulting in incomplete facilities.

Consequences of these shortcomings have left large amounts of procured materials idle, critical infrastructure unfinished, and the main objectives of land pooling unachieved. The State's shift in policy towards city development created uncertainty for the completion of 55 open contracts, with ₹28,047.82 crore needed for their completion. These lapses led to heavy financial burden and non-achievement of Amaravati’s planned vision.

Ensure adequate budgetary support for ongoing and planned works to avoid idling of state resources.

title: Report No. 1 of 2023 - Union Territory Finances Audit Report, Government of the Union Territory of Puducherry
overview:
The audit of Union Territory Finances for Puducherry brings to light rising deficits and underutilisation of funds over the past five years. While revenue receipts experienced growth, reaching ₹10,042 crore in 2023-24, fiscal challenges continued, with a revenue surplus of ₹196 crore in 2017-18 deteriorating to a deficit of ₹899 crore by 2021-22 (p.ix). In 2023-24, the revenue deficit was ₹24 crore with a fiscal deficit of ₹463 crore, though this remained within the FRBM-ceiling of 3% of GSDP (p.ix).

The report highlights major gaps in capital expenditure: against a capital outlay allocation of ₹702 crore for 2023-24, only ₹439 crore was spent, and funds parked in Single Nodal Agency (SNA) accounts totalled ₹423.61 crore as of March 2024 (p.xvi). Committed expenditure, including salaries, pensions, and interest, now constitutes over half of the total revenue spending, reflecting inflexible spending priorities (p.30).

Transparency issues were flagged, with 1,191 pending utilisation certificates (₹597.91 crore) and 316 cases of misappropriation/loss involving ₹28.89 crore still unsettled (p.xvii). Moreover, the ratio of total outstanding debt to GSDP reached 26.27%, exceeding recommended levels. These trends threaten the Union Territory’s fiscal stability, diminish asset creation, and undermine effective use of public resources.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (Revenue Sector) for the year ended 31 March 2022 - Government of Meghalaya
overview:
The CAG audit for Meghalaya's Revenue Sector (Report No. 3 of 2023) exposed persistent weaknesses in revenue collection and internal controls across key departments. During 2021-22, revenues raised by the State Government were ₹2,824.96 crore, forming just 20% of the total revenue receipts of ₹14,274.14 crore, a marked decline from 26% in 2019-20. The bulk (80%) of receipts stemmed from the Government of India's transfers, underscoring weak self-sufficiency (Paragraph 1.1, Page 1).

Test-checks of revenue records identified under-assessments and short/non-levies amounting to ₹1,358.47 crore in 2020-21 and ₹358.08 crore in 2021-22—representing 52.33% and 12.68% of the State’s Own Resources. Departmental recovery remains minimal at ₹4.32 crore despite accepting audit findings in a number of cases (Paragraph 1.10, Page 12).

Specific compliance audits revealed issues such as unverified GST transitional credit claims (₹31.70 crore unverified, recoveries of only ₹0.02 crore out of detected inadmissible claims of ₹0.38 crore) and excess or irregular claims by multiple dealers. Significant revenue losses were also attributed to failures in the Excise and Transport Departments and lapses in the grant/monitoring of minor mineral mining leases (Page vii–viii).

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Social and Economic Sectors for the year ended 31 March 2022 - Government of Meghalaya (Report No. 2 of 2023)
overview:
This CAG report on Meghalaya's Social and Economic Sectors presents compliance audits across Health, Fisheries, Agriculture, Horticulture, and Power Departments for the year ended 31 March 2022. Major findings include the extension of undue financial benefit of ₹11.38 crore to an insurance company due to lapses in the Megha Health Insurance Scheme-IV (MHIS-IV) and PMJAY, and avoidable excess expenditure of ₹0.87 crore on procurement of medicines at inflated rates by the Directorate of Health Services. The implementation of PM-KISAN saw ₹3.15 crore disbursed to 3,923 ineligible beneficiaries and a further ₹29.06 lakh to ineligible bank accounts due to poor beneficiary verification and weak monitoring, in addition to double payments and inflated cropped area claims.

In the economic sector, the injudicious selection of a fish market site led to idle expenditure of ₹1.44 crore, and poor project implementation in fruit processing deprived local farmers of ₹1.11 crore worth of facility investment. State Public Sector Enterprises registered accumulated losses of ₹3,269.51 crore, eroding their paid-up capital. Additionally, poor contract management in the power sector led to extra expenditures of over ₹156 crore.

Cumulatively, persistent deficiencies—such as delayed refunds, unaddressed audit observations, and violations of prescribed tendering and monitoring procedures—led to severe financial mismanagement, loss of public funds, and denied benefits to eligible citizens.

title: Government of Nagaland Report No. 2 of 2023 - Social, Economic, General and Revenue Sectors, Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended 31 March 2022
overview: This report covers a comprehensive assessment of Social, Economic, General, and Revenue Sectors in Nagaland for the year ending March 2022. During the audit period, only 28 out of 61 prioritised projects under Kohima Smart City Mission saw completed Detailed Project Reports (DPRs), with just eight projects finished by October 2021. Major delays stemmed from slow fund releases and poor resource use. Notably, ₹70.75 lakh was spent on procurement of water ATM and tanker, deemed infructuous, and a further ₹85.57 lakh was wasted on the construction of a Multi Utility Duct due to lack of feasibility study. As of March 2022, nine out of 14 special assistance-funded projects remained incomplete, though shown as complete in state progress reports. The State Government diverted ₹38.58 crore meant for capital assets to unapproved projects and spent ₹5.29 crore on revenue expenditure instead of capital. Multiple cases of fraudulent, double, and excess withdrawal across departments totalled over ₹2.26 crore. Implementation failures in PM-KISAN left 23,144 genuine beneficiaries deprived of assistance, with errors in beneficiary identification and data entry exacerbating the issue. There were widespread shortcomings in internal controls, financial management, and monitoring frameworks across departments. The consequences include unfruitful expenditure, stalled infrastructure development, and substantial losses for targeted populations and government revenue.

title: Compliance Audit Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Revenue Sector for the year ended 31 March 2022
overview:
The Compliance Audit Report for the Revenue Sector of Kerala for 2021-22 reveals serious deficiencies in the management of state revenues. Total revenue receipts for the year amounted to ₹1,16,640.24 crore, representing a significant increase over previous years, but with the State's own revenue constituting only 59% and a growing dependence on central transfers, now at 41% (vs 31% in 2017-18). Despite the increased receipts, arrears of revenue remain high at ₹28,258.39 crore (24.23% of state revenue), with ₹6,267.31 crore locked under stay orders, highlighting poor recoverability and weak follow-up by departments.

Audit further identified ₹127.17 crore in potential revenue losses across 33 paragraphs, with critical lapses in GST oversight (notably ₹35.55 crore lost due to ineligible ITC, misclassification, and undervaluation). Vehicle tax mismanagement led to a non/short levy of ₹72.98 crore, while other cases included the non-collection of excise fees, irregular grant of input tax credit, and unrecovered arrears even after judicial actions. The pendency of department responses to audit (2,625 Inspection Reports covering ₹5,084.70 crore) and the lack of meaningful audit committee interventions magnify governance concerns.

The cumulative effect of these lapses is a persistent gap in expected and realized revenue, impeded fund flows for public welfare, and persistent fiscal risks. Audit emphasizes the need for timely assessments, focused recovery of arrears, better interdepartmental coordination, and adherence to prescribed audit response procedures to safeguard and optimize state revenue.

title: REPORT OF THE COMPTROLLER AND AUDITOR GENERAL OF INDIA ON SOCIAL, ECONOMIC, GENERAL AND REVENUE SECTORS FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 MARCH 2022 GOVERNMENT OF ARUNACHAL PRADESH REPORT NO. 2 OF 2023
overview:
This CAG report presents major compliance and performance audit findings for the Government of Arunachal Pradesh across social, economic, general and revenue sectors for FY ending 31 March 2022. The audit covered 156 units in 2021-22 from a planned 129 (out of 1296 auditable units), highlighting significant gaps in planning, execution, and monitoring affecting nearly all departments. Notable instances include the Urban Development & Housing Department's undue payment of ₹34.54 lakh to a contractor for unexecuted work, and ₹22.98 lakh spent on a protection wall constructed at the Executive Engineer's residence instead of the intended burial ground.

In the economic sector, mismanagement in the Power Department's DDUGJY and Saubhagya schemes resulted in ₹4.14 crore wasteful expenditure due to improper surveys and inflated DPRs, leaving 0.40 lakh rural households un-electrified in 2018 while only 75.79% total coverage was achieved (against 2,00,210 rural households) by March 2021. Fraudulent project payments, excessive mobilisation advances (₹1.40 crore, 68% of contract), and outstanding interest loss (₹59.22 lakh) further underscore severe systemic issues. The report also documents wasteful road and shopping complex expenditures, fake food supply bills, and suspected misappropriation (₹50 lakh) using falsified records in the Planning Department.

Revenue sector audits revealed systemic failures in GST transition and refund verification, short-realisation of excise duties (₹12.76 lakh), VAT evasion (₹27.38 lakh plus penalties), and land revenue outstanding for 39 years totaling ₹2.57 crore. Despite increased state revenue receipts (23.99% growth in 2021-22), accountability and real return on investment remain low, with only 3 out of 6 working PSUs reporting profits and a meagre return rate of 1.31% at present value. The findings highlight pervasive lapses in internal controls, transparency, and fund utilization in key sectors.

title: Report of the C&AG of India on Social, General, Economic and Revenue Sectors for the year ended 31 March 2022
overview:
This CAG audit report reviews social, general, economic, and revenue sectors in Mizoram for the fiscal years 2020-21 and 2021-22. Across 13 departments under the social sector, actual expenditure fell short of budget allocations: in 2020-21, ₹ 3,356.19 crore was spent against ₹ 4,364.97 crore allocated (76.89%), and in 2021-22, ₹ 3,383.46 crore against ₹ 5,019.64 crore (67.40%), resulting in overall savings of 23.11% and 32.60% respectively. Audit flagged major financial irregularities, including diversion of ₹ 46 lakh meant for school buildings to another department, and wasteful expenditure of ₹ 24 crore on unused polytechnic buildings. In addition, ₹ 1.01 crore was spent irregularly by Aizawl Municipal Corporation, and ₹ 1.24 crore by General Administration Department in violation of MLA Local Area Development Scheme rules.

Systemic deficiencies were found in the implementation of Direct Benefit Transfer and MDoNER projects, including delays up to 2,323 days in project completion, irregular beneficiary payments (₹ 13.19 crore credited to ineligible PM-KISAN beneficiaries), and unachieved objectives. Scholarship schemes suffered from inadequate verification, poor system controls, and fraudulent claims. Monitoring mechanisms were weak, with serious lapses in updating beneficiary databases and validating bank accounts.

Consequences noted include extra expenditure, wasteful outlays, and loss of revenue. Recommendations focus on improving fund release timeliness, data verification, database maintenance, and fixing accountability for fraud and mismanagement.

title: Union Government (Commercial) - Ministry of Road Transport and Highways - Compliance Audit on Toll Operation of NHAI in Southern India
overview:
This CAG report examines toll operations of NHAI in southern India, covering toll collection, highway maintenance, and user amenities from April 2017 to March 2021. The audit randomly reviewed 41 toll plazas across five southern states—Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Kerala—which together contributed ₹28,523.88 crore (28.75%) of national toll revenue during 2017-18 to 2020-21. Significant findings include NHAI's collection of ₹124.18 crore in user fees during periods where fee collection was prohibited due to delayed project completion, violating the amended NH Fee Rules. There was further undue burden of ₹132.05 crore on road users from five toll plazas due to non-implementation of reduced user fee and improper annual revision, and excess toll collection of ₹22.10 crore resulting from incorrect inclusion of pre-1956 bridges.

Short collection of toll revenue of ₹16.68 crore was found due to delayed implementation of fee rule amendments for bridges exceeding 60 meters, while delays in toll commencement caused loss of ₹64.60 crore across four stretches. NHAI lost ₹133.36 crore by not including revenue sharing clauses in concession agreements for BOT projects. Additionally, failures related to non-recovery of premium, negative grants, and guarantees led to a financial impact of ₹295.78 crore, and maintenance lapses resulted in unclaimed damages exceeding ₹391 crore.

Major deficiencies also occurred in user amenities: shortfall in avenue plantation (65.63%) and median plantation (34.65%) from target, toilets unavailable or non-operational at 21 of 41 toll plazas, and outdated incident response vehicles at 14 plazas. These gaps directly impacted road user safety and experience and point to systemic and operational failures by NHAI and its concessionaires, highlighting the urgent need for stricter oversight and compliance enforcement.

title: Union Government - Ministry of Civil Aviation - Compliance Audit on Regional Connectivity Scheme - UDAN (Ude Desh Ka Aam Naagrik)
overview:
The CAG Compliance Audit report on the Regional Connectivity Scheme (UDAN) evaluated implementation from October 2016 to March 2023. The audit highlights that though the scheme was designed to boost regional air connectivity through fiscal support, infrastructure investment, and viability gap funding (VGF), only 371 of the 774 routes awarded up to UDAN-3 had actually commenced operations; of these, a mere 112 routes (30%) completed the full 3-year concession period, and just 54 routes (7% of those awarded) sustained operations beyond three years, connecting 17 RCS airports.

Budgetary support of ₹4,500 crore was allotted for airport/heliport revival, but out of ₹3,351 crore spent as of March 2023, operations could not commence or were discontinued at 83 airports/heliports/water aerodromes—despite this significant spend. The audit found crucial deficiencies in planning, feasibility assessment, and internal regulation—such as the absence of a framework to scrutinize collection and disbursement of Regional Connectivity Fund (RCF) levies, leading to delays and risks of excess collections by airlines.

There were serious lapses such as the RCF Trust not formulating required SOPs or submitting accounts for external audit, delays in fund disbursement, and lack of meaningful oversight: independent audit of airline operator compliance was not performed after 2017-18. The report concludes these failings undermine the effectiveness and transparency of the UDAN scheme, despite its ambitious intention to democratize air travel and extend economic benefits to unserved regions.

title: Financial Audit of the Accounts of Union Government
overview:
The report presents the findings from the financial audit of the Union Government accounts for FY 2021-22, highlighting a substantial increase in both receipts and expenditures compared to the previous year. The gross receipts totaled ₹1,48,95,450 crore, with debt receipts accounting for 55.39% (₹82,49,152 crore) and non-debt receipts at 22.67% (₹33,74,399 crore), demonstrating a 9.98% growth in total receipts over FY 2020-21. Revenue receipts alone grew by 30.67%, driven by a surge in tax and non-tax revenues, while non-debt receipts covered 58.42% of total expenditure as opposed to 49.45% the previous year.

Key issues were observed in fund management practices, particularly unresolved adverse balances which have persisted for decades, and cases of significant non/short transfer of cess and levies, non-operational reserve funds, and deviations from approved accounting procedures. These weaknesses impacted budgetary accuracy, with total savings in grants/appropriations amounting to ₹7,64,721 crore and excess expenditure of ₹1,235.98 crore in three grants, reflecting gaps in actual versus approved spending.

The report also emphasizes quality concerns in accounts and reporting practices, such as non-disclosure of full suspense head balances, documentation lapses around guarantees, and lack of adequate transparency in footnotes accompanying financial statements. The report recommends more robust disclosure mechanisms and timely reconciliation processes to strengthen financial oversight and accuracy going forward.

title: Union Government – Ministry of MSME- Compliance Audit on “Departmental Trading Units including Supply Chain Management in Khadi and Village Industries Commission”
overview:
This CAG compliance audit examines the operations of Departmental Trading Units within the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC), covering the period from 2017-18 to 2020-21. Out of 92 units established over time, only 18 remained functional as of March 2021, with 74 units declared defunct. The audit rigorously scrutinized fund utilization, finding that KVIC expended nearly the entire ₹11,236.18 crore allocated by the Ministry of MSME for various schemes. The Modified Market Development Assistance (MMDA) accounted for 55.37% of total expenditure, while the Khadi Reform and Development Programme (KRDP) contributed 21.08%. Significant delays were observed in the disposal of assets and settlement of liabilities for defunct units, impacting operational efficiency and revenue generation, as KVIC failed to analyze root causes for over 30% of closures.

Audit highlighted deficiencies in procurement practices, such as inadequate adherence to prescribed procedures and lack of item-wise/supplier-wise data analysis, leading to diluted objectivity and limited equal opportunity for suppliers. Marketing and sales initiatives like e-commerce, franchise schemes, and Khadi plazas were launched but saw inconsistent execution and limited success. The audit observed delays in annual budget preparation, weak sales planning, and insufficient use of market survey data, with some schemes (e.g., Khadi Plaza) failing to achieve any project completion despite available funds.

Internal controls and financial management were flagged as critical issues: incomplete bank reconciliations, unconfirmed debtors, and underperforming internal audit mechanisms. Audit found long pending debts and unacted audit observations, stressing the need for stronger monitoring and timely corrective action. 26 recommendations were presented to improve procurement, marketing, asset disposal, financial management, and audit compliance by KVIC—crucial for realizing its rural employment and self-reliance objectives.

title: Compliance Audit on Finance and Communication, Union Government
overview:
The Compliance Audit Report No. 16 of 2023 reveals significant deficiencies in fund utilisation, policy implementation, and resource management under the Ministries of Finance, Communications, and Electronics & Information Technology (MeitY). Notably, compliance audit findings highlight severe delays, procedural lapses, and poor fund allocation, especially in the conservation of heritage buildings by the Department of Posts, with only ₹2.73 crore of the allocated ₹8.23 crore (33%) actually spent on conservation activities (p. vii). Of the sanctioned projects for electronics testing at Ajmer, 96% of the ₹21.83 crore expenditure was rendered wasteful due to improper site assessment (p. viii). Further, the audit found that more than ₹75 crore meant for communication infra upgrades remained underutilised as of March 2023, directly impacting service delivery in rural regions (p. 12).

Key headline findings demonstrate that the absence of robust monitoring and enforcement by nodal ministries allowed significant lapses: for example, the Heritage Branch for DoP, created in 2020 with a clear mandate, still lacks effective powers and responsibilities, leading to continued asset deterioration (p. 27). Repeated failures to adhere to procurement norms and lack of coordinated oversight led to avoidable losses in both MeitY and MoC projects, including avoidable expenditure of ₹3.78 crore in delayed IMRI project milestones (p. 44).

These shortcomings have far-reaching consequences, such as escalating future restoration costs, increased risk of fraud and misappropriation, and loss of public confidence. The report calls for immediate and concerted corrective action by the Union Government to ensure transparency, enforceable accountability, and prudent fund management across all audited sectors.

title: Union Government, (Railways) Railways Finances
overview:
The CAG audit of Indian Railways Finances for FY 2021-22 highlights substantial year-on-year increases in receipts and expenditures. Gross Traffic Receipts grew by 36.02% to ₹1,91,206 crore, led by sharp rises in passenger earnings (up 157.17%) and freight earnings (up 20.36%). Despite these gains, the Ministry of Railways incurred a net deficit of ₹15,025 crore, with no surplus appropriated to development or safety funds. Operating Ratio worsened to 107.39% compared to 97.45% in 2020-21, largely due to higher appropriations to the Pension Fund and increased working expenses. The share of Extra Budgetary Resources (EBR) in capital expenditure rose 37.35%, indicating growing reliance on borrowings and federal support, as internal resource generation remained inadequate.

Fund utilization was inefficient, with large savings and excesses in budget grants. There were savings of ₹29,888.89 crore in 11 cases and unsanctioned expenditure of ₹6,082.77 crore in 1,937 cases (1.06% of total spend). Appropriations to Pension Fund leaped from ₹523 crore in 2020-21 to ₹48,100 crore in 2021-22, but actual pension liabilities exceeded even this amount, highlighting financial strain. Audit also found recurrent misclassification between capital and revenue expenditure, weak control over departmental balances (especially Major Head 8671-105), and uneven dividend payouts from commercial undertakings.

The report calls for critical reforms: reduction in passenger losses, diversification of freight revenue, addressing asset renewal backlog (₹34,318.79 crore of deferred works), improving internal revenue streams, and strengthening budget control to avoid misclassifications and unsanctioned outflows. The severe dependence on coal and limited freight basket exposes Railways revenue to market shifts. These challenges directly impact trains' safety, reliability, and future investment capacity.
