title: Report No. 1 of 2023 - Report of the C&AG of India on Performance and Compliance Audits for the year ended 31 March 2021
overview:
The Performance Audit on the Efficacy of implementation of the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act in Jharkhand identifies major structural and operational shortfalls impacting urban governance. Out of 18 statutory functions to be transferred to Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), 10 were fully performed, six only partially, and two remained entirely unaddressed, undermining decentralisation aims and leading to gaps in service delivery. Elections were overdue by periods ranging from 18 to 50 months in 15 ULBs, and special officers or administrators ran these bodies instead of elected representatives, raising concerns about transparency and accountability (p.15).

The staffing situation was critical, with 421 vacant posts (47%) in test-checked ULBs as of March 2021, which severely hampered execution of transferred functions. Financial independence was lacking: only five of ten ULBs could meet their establishment expenditures from their own resources; the rest depended heavily on central and state grants. Audit also found wasteful expenditure on consultancy charges (₹16.04 crore) due to poor DPR preparation, and delayed constitution of State Finance Commissions, resulting in constrained fiscal recommendations and lost funding opportunities (pp.19–25).

These systemic failures led to underutilisation of resources and delayed project completions, including sewerage networks and river conservation. Key urban infrastructure works suffered, culminating in an overall reduction in the efficacy of decentralised urban administration, with significant consequences for local development, financial management, and citizen services.

title: Report No. 3 of 2023 - Compliance Audit for the year ended March 2021, Government of Maharashtra
overview:
This Compliance Audit covers the period up to the year ended March 2021 and summarises important audit findings relating to several government departments and public sector undertakings in Maharashtra. Audit focused on critical areas such as fund utilisation, execution of deposit works, revenue collections, and GST management. It identifies approximately ₹22 crore of government funds left unutilised with Public Works divisions despite completion of intended deposit works. The report also highlights short collection of taxes, unfruitful expenditure, and procedural lapses disrupting infrastructure delivery.

A prominent finding concerns the Public Works Department (PWD), where the lack of timely fund release by user departments led to stalled projects and buildings that remained unused due to missing services like electrification and water supply. Additionally, the Department of Goods and Services Tax (GST) was cited for granting excess transitional credits and short levy of taxes, amounting to losses running into several crores.

The cumulative consequences include blocked government resources, avoided or non-productive expenditures (e.g., avoidable payment of ₹3.48 crore for a national highway project), revenue leakage, and underachievement of policy objectives. The report’s findings have prompted the CAG to recommend structural and operational reforms, stronger internal controls, and better follow-up action by the State Government to prevent recurrence of such irregularities.

title: Compliance Audit for the year ended 31 March 2021, Government of Chhattisgarh
overview:
This Compliance Audit presents the findings for several key sectors of the Chhattisgarh State Government for the period ending March 2021, covering management of foodgrain distribution, pension disbursements, royalty charges on minerals, quality of public works, GST transitional credits, refunds, and PSU bill processing. For example, a major highlight is that 167.32 lakh NFSA-PHH beneficiaries were not provided with the additional benefits intended under the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (PMGKAY), and 17,803 quintals of chana remained undistributed, reflecting substantial lapses in last mile delivery (p. ix-x).

Financial misapplication was also found in mineral royalty deductions with the failure to recover ₹307.09 crore in market value from contractor bills across 203 agreements, coupled with a further ₹65.39 crore in royalty deductions being retained in deposit heads instead of being credited to the correct government accounts in 44 Public Works Department divisions (p. x-xi). In the Water Resources Department, over 93% of concrete samples failed quality standards, and significant shortfalls in quality testing and design mix adoption were detected (p. xi-xii).

In the GST and Commercial Tax domain, the Department did not effectively cross-verify transitional credit claims, with several irregular and excess credits forwarded without supporting documentation, risking state revenues. In PSU audits, improper application of auto-sweep facility thresholds led to an interest loss of ₹3.82 crore, while Chhattisgarh State Power Distribution Company suffered a loss of ₹10.36 crore by paying GST to an unregistered contractor (p. xiii).

title: Scheme for Integrated Textile Parks Union Government, Ministry of Textiles (Compliance Audit)
overview: The Compliance Audit examined the Scheme for Integrated Textile Parks (SITP), launched in 2005 by the Ministry of Textiles, to provide world-class infrastructure and foster textile unit growth. Until June 2016, 98 parks were sanctioned, with grants totaling ₹1,592.52 crore, but only 26 parks (26.53%) were completed as of February 2022, while 30 parks remained ongoing and 42 were cancelled. Significant underperformance was noted: completed/ongoing parks achieved only 30% of their employment targets, 50% of their investment targets, and 37% for setting up textile units. Delays ranged from 1 to over 10 years, with many parks facing land acquisition issues, weak financials, and lack of statutory clearances. ₹77.34 crore in grants for cancelled parks remained unrecovered, alongside penal interest of ₹117.72 crore. Audit field visits found three 'completed' parks shut down, and instances where common infrastructure was not created as planned. Audit highlighted ineffective monitoring, insufficient physical verification, and lack of state government involvement, which contributed to failures in achieving scheme objectives. The report calls for urgent corrective action by the Ministry to address lapses, recover funds, and strengthen future schemes.

title: Report No. 1 of 2023- Union Government (Economic & Service Ministries - Civil) (Compliance Audit Observations)
overview:
This compliance audit report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India examines the financial management, compliance, and governance across Economic and Service Ministries of the Union Government for the year ending March 2021. The audit covered test checks of transactions, expenditure, and scheme implementation within six Ministries/Departments, highlighting 12 major compliance observations. Notably, the Coal Mines Provident Fund Organisation incurred an avoidable loss of ₹315.35 crore due to indecisiveness and a failure to exercise early redemption options after a credit rating downgrade of Non-Convertible Debentures, with recommendations for further investigation and system strengthening.

Significant deficiencies were uncovered in recapitalisation of Public Sector Banks, including an excess capital infusion of ₹7,785.81 crore in violation of RBI guidelines and a lack of proper assessment by the Department of Financial Services. In the domain of public infrastructure, Central Public Works Department's delayed revision of water charges and poor maintenance practices resulted in a direct financial burden of ₹7.69 crore, alongside lapses in complaint redressal mechanisms and execution standards. Further, the Ministry of Mines suffered unfruitful expenditure totaling ₹81.88 crore due to technical misjudgments in helicopter and survey system procurement, achieving only 2% of envisaged targets.

Systemic issues with financial reconciliation, utilisation, and monitoring were identified across several schemes, such as inadequacy in coverage and settlement of coal mine pensions, delays in settlement of complaints, and failure to impose statutory penalties. The audit urges better planning, adherence to legal requirements, improved IT systems for transparency, and strict enforcement of contract terms to avoid recurring losses and strengthen public accountability.

title: Report No. 1 of the year 2023:- Compliance Audit Report-2 for the year ended 31 March 2021
overview:
This Compliance Audit Report covers 53 Departments, 37 PSUs, and 37 Autonomous Bodies under the Government of Haryana for the year ended 31 March 2021. The audit identified significant compliance failures and internal control weaknesses across major schemes and departments. For instance, the District Plan scheme allocation declined drastically from ₹700 crore in 2018-19 to ₹200 crore in 2020-21—a direct result of poor fund utilization, delayed approvals, and funds lapsing without implementation. Outstanding Municipal Levy due to municipal bodies grew sharply, reaching ₹2,178.98 crore at the end of March 2021, driven by delayed transfers and lack of internal controls at various administrative levels (page vii).

Serious irregularities were found, such as embezzlement of ₹2.76 crore in Public Health Engineering, irregular and excess contractor payments, and scam payments—including ₹41.30 crore in cash awards to ineligible sportspersons and inadmissible payments under various schemes. For the PM-KISAN scheme specifically, failure in beneficiary identification led to ₹131.40 lakh disbursed to State Government Pensioners, and continued payments to deceased, non-eligible, and income tax payee beneficiaries. The period saw a high volume of unresolved audit findings: 25,652 paragraphs across 9,205 IRs, with pointed-out recoveries of ₹28,570.81 crore remaining unaddressed as of 30 September 2021.

Consequences include massive lapses of funds, non-recovery of misallocated sums, weak financial control environment, and deprivation of benefits to targeted communities. The audit's recommendations are focused on improved fund monitoring, faster transfer protocols, regular reconciliation, strict beneficiary identification, and immediate recovery action on fraudulent payments.

title: CAG Compliance Audit Report (Revenue Departments) for the year ended 31 March 2021, Government of Madhya Pradesh
overview:
This compliance audit report highlights extensive gaps and non-compliances in revenue administration for Madhya Pradesh, spanning the Commercial Tax and Mineral Resources Departments. The audit covered the processing of GST transitional credits, refund claims, VAT assessments, and District Mineral Foundations (DMF) fund management for 2020-21 and selected recent years. Audit findings revealed that transitional GST credits were wrongly processed or unverified in 314 out of 2,357 cases, with a potential revenue risk of ₹86.93 crore. Similar severe lapses were found in refund claim processing, where delays and inadmissible refunds led to losses of ₹10.36 crore across 1,011 test-checked cases.

Further, VAT assessment reviews of 33,812 out of 90,878 cases exposed widespread failures in turnover calculation, incorrect tax rates, and excessive rebates, resulting in a revenue impact of ₹21.13 crore. In the Mineral Resources Department, irregularities and mismanagement in DMF administration, such as non-convening of Board meetings, missing records and idle funds, led to issues worth ₹206.21 crore. Audit also flagged that as of 31 March 2021, revenue arrears totaled an alarming ₹5,174.71 crore, with more than half pending for over 5 years, underscoring weak recovery mechanisms.

The audit concludes that without systemic reforms and stricter compliance in verification, documentation, and oversight, existing gaps expose the state exchequer to significant leakage and undermine transparency and accountability in public fund administration.

title: Compliance Audit for the year ended March 2021-Report No.1 of 2023
overview:
This Compliance Audit report outlines significant lapses and deficiencies across multiple departments in Karnataka for the period ending March 2021. Despite a budget outlay of ₹6,94,913 crore, only ₹5,48,481 crore was utilized, revealing substantial gaps in resource application (page 1). In the Department of Women and Child Welfare, only foundations and pillars were laid for a sanctioned Working Women's Hostel after 28 years, despite the release of ₹7.82 lakh to Janatha Trust, Raichur, rendering the expenditure unfruitful (page vii).

Audit findings highlight that 26 hostels provided with ₹11.22 crore in government assistance from 1975-2017 lacked critical facilities: 18 hostels without day care centers, 19 without washing machines, and 23 without disabled-friendly toilets (page viii). Further, the Department of Higher Education wasted ₹43.82 crore constructing hostels that remained vacant, and an additional ₹27.90 crore was spent unproductively on extensions. Short-remittance and non-regulation issues in Grant-in-Aid polytechnics and housing allowances caused further financial irregularities (pages viii-ix).

Oversight in the Department of Animal Husbandry led to excess expenditure of ₹7.66 crore due to incorrect consideration rates. Avoidable extra expenditures, wasteful execution of roadworks, and shortfall in micro-irrigation area coverage (11.81 lakh hectares against target, 25% shortfall) were documented. Revenue audit revealed under-assessment aggregating ₹293.04 crore and persistent savings in 12 out of 29 grants exceeding ₹10 crore annually, indicating systemic fiscal weaknesses (pages ix-x).

title: Compliance Audit for the year ended March 2021-Report No.1 of 2023
overview:
This compliance audit covers the fiscal year ending March 2021 for the Government of Karnataka, highlighting critical issues in fund utilisation, governance, and departmental operations across sectors like Women and Child Welfare, Agriculture, Higher Education, Animal Husbandry, Health & Family Welfare, Rural Development, and Revenue. The overall resource application for 2020-21 was ₹5,48,481 crore against a budget outlay of ₹6,94,913 crore, showing persistent gaps and underutilisation. For example, only foundation and pillars were laid for Raichur Working Women's Hostel, despite government releases, leaving it incomplete after 28 years (₹7.82 lakh spent, Para 2.1.3.1).

There were systemic failures such as lack of need-based assessment for establishing hostels, underprovision of funds resulting in uncompleted infrastructure, and significant lapses in regulatory oversight with hostels functioning despite accessibility and safety deficiencies. Over 7,526 Inspection Reports containing 38,999 audit paragraphs remained unresolved across 48 departments by March 2021. Key revenue shortfalls were observed, with total receipts in 2020-21 at ₹1,56,716 crore versus ₹1,75,443 crore from the previous year, and cases of revenue foregone amounting to ₹77.54 crore (Para 1.1 & 1.5).

Audit further identified excess transitional credits, delayed GST refunds, and short-levy of taxes, highlighting that departmental weaknesses directly led to wasted public expenditure and denial of entitlements, such as ₹2.18 crore in wrongly paid allowances to 68 officials, and ₹43.82 crore in unproductive hostel construction under SCSP/TSP. The report stresses the urgent need for government action in follow-up mechanisms, fund allocation and regulatory compliance to ensure efficiency and transparency.

title: Compliance Audit for the year ended March 2021-Report No.1 of 2023
overview:
This Compliance Audit report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India examines both the expenditure and revenue side of Karnataka's state finances for the year ended March 2021. The State faced significant challenges in resource application, with actual expenditures amounting to ₹5,48,481 crore against a budget outlay of ₹6,94,913 crore in 2020-21. Out of this, revenue expenditure was the major component (₹1,76,054 crore or about 80% of total expenditure), while capital expenditure comprised the remaining 20%. Over the 2016-21 period, total expenditure rose by 38% and revenue expenditure by 33%.

Part I of the report highlights major gaps in compliance, including persistent savings in 12 out of 29 grants (often exceeding 10%) and the accumulation of outstanding Inspection Reports: 7,526 IRs containing 38,999 audit objections remained unresolved across 48 departments as of March 2021. The audit further notes deficiencies in the implementation of key schemes, incomplete infrastructure projects, and systemic issues in monitoring and internal controls.

The Revenue Audit uncovers revenue shortfalls, under-assessment, and loss of public funds, with particular mention of delays in tax refunds, wrongful transitional credit claims, and short-levy in stamp duty and registration fees totaling over ₹77 crore. The consequences of such non-compliance include unproductive expenditure (e.g., ₹43.82 crore in unused hostels), excess payments, and denial of government service benefits. The report presses for urgent administrative reforms and stricter oversight to close these recurring compliance gaps.

title: Report No. 1 of 2023 of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Compliance Audit-I
overview:
This Compliance Audit report covers the results of audits undertaken for 1,305 out of 6,192 auditable units across 58 Departments of the Government of Uttar Pradesh and associated entities during 2019-21. The audit identifies significant lapses in fund utilisation, project planning, and execution, particularly under the Housing and Urban Planning Department. For instance, the Prayagraj Development Authority (PDA) failed to prepare zonal plans for 11 out of 12 zones, leading to fragmented urban development and the execution of projects without requisite planning documentation.

Between 2016-17 and 2020-21, PDA's expenditure on housing schemes declined by 83% (from ₹104.73 crore to ₹17.56 crore), showing a diverted focus towards other works such as road infrastructure and event preparations. Major housing projects such as the Yamuna Vihar Awas Yojana saw wasteful expenditure of ₹38.85 crore due to lack of demand assessment, resulting in unsold inventory and abandoned construction. Similarly, delays in the completion of Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya buildings and the Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Gorakhpur University stadium resulted in unfruitful expenditure of ₹1.17 crore and ₹4.61 crore respectively, with intended beneficiaries left underserved.

Further, irregular payments, such as ₹91.09 lakh to contractors for machinery and ₹33.66 crore for dewatering charges, signaled systemic gaps in internal controls. Many departments, including Medical Health, Social Welfare, and Vocational Education, incurred avoidable excess payments or failed to recover government dues, impacting efficiency and accountability. These findings collectively indicate high severity gaps in fund management and project execution, raising concerns for transparency and governance in state operations.

title: Performance and Compliance Audit Report, Government of West Bengal for the year ended March 2021
overview:
The CAG audit report covers significant findings from the performance and compliance audit of 25 government departments in West Bengal, with particular focus on major investments in road upgradation by the Public Works Department (PWD) and capacity augmentation by WBSETCL. Across six years, the state spent ₹19,603.84 crore on roads and bridges, representing 82.90% of its total outlay, but substantial issues in planning, survey, fund usage, and quality monitoring were identified (p.7).

The audit's assessment of PWD's road works revealed ineffective planning, with no long-term or macro-level road development strategy since 2001. Out of 995 road works in 19 divisions, 130 projects worth ₹3,037.93 crore in seven districts were scrutinized; issues included lack of topographical surveys in 78 works and missing survey records in 35 of the remainder. Inappropriate guidelines led to at least ₹7.62 crore avoidable expenditure. Multiple large projects suffered from delays, excess specification, and questionable payments, such as the use of two-wheelers or ambulances for bitumen supply and non-production of challans for materials worth ₹20.36 crore (pp.3–4).

Audit of the WBSETCL identified creation of ₹517.17 crore unutilized transformer capacity over five years, raising per-unit transmission cost by 37%, with total network underutilization ranging from 61.82% to 70.88%. Major disaster relief allocation after cyclone Amphan was found exaggerated, and irregular/multiple payments to 9,226 beneficiaries totaling ₹18.07 crore as direct credit were observed. Delays and non-compliance remain a critical issue, with 4,214 audit paras pending as of November 2022. The report urges strategic planning, robust internal controls, and transparent fund utilization to enhance infrastructure outcomes and integrity (pp.1–6).

title: COMPLIANCE AUDIT -CIVIL, REPORT OF THE CAG OF INDIA FOR THE PERIOD ENDED 31st MARCH 2022 (GOVERNMENT OF RAJASTHAN)
overview:
This comprehensive compliance audit covers the revenue and expenditure activities of selected departments in the Government of Rajasthan for the year ended 31 March 2022. The audit evaluated the effectiveness of compliance with applicable rules and highlighted deficiencies across key revenue departments including Commercial Taxes, Land Revenue, Registration & Stamps, and State Excise, as well as expenditure concerns in Youth Affairs and Medical Education departments.

Key findings in the revenue sector include significant delays in GST return scrutiny, slow progress on business audits, revenue leakages from short levies of stamp duty and registration fees, and non-enforcement of policy provisions leading to short collections in state excise duty. For example, in Centralised Audit, Rs 272.59 crore of deviations from provisions were observed, and 878 taxpayers (52.39%) in select circles did not file returns despite notices being issued. Overall, Rs 441.92 crore of irregularities were highlighted in revenue cases.

In the expenditure sector, procurement inefficiencies and delayed recoveries of government dues were noted, leading to avoidable financial loss. The report emphasizes the need for stronger compliance controls, process automation, and urgent remedial actions to enhance revenue protection and ensure timely recoveries for the State.

title: Compliance Audit- Civil and Commercial Report for the year ended March 2022(Report No. 04)
overview:
This audit report examines compliance in Central Government civil and commercial departments for the three-year period ending March 2022. Audit coverage was extensive, with 143 offices and 133 units inspected. Of ₹12,845 crore allocated, only ₹6,100 crore (about 47.5 per cent) was utilised, revealing slow fund use and poor absorption rates.

Key findings include irregular award of contracts, non-adherence to CVC guidelines, and delays in timely completion of works. The audit highlights that 19 works costing ₹87 crore saw delays up to 24 months, leading to cost overruns and non-achievement of intended benefits. Several Ministries failed to comply with statutory reporting, and lapses in revenue collection resulted in estimated losses of ₹31.82 crore, including penalty short-levy and undue benefit to contractors.

These issues led to direct financial implications and undermined the efficiency and credibility of public expenditure. The CAG recommended stronger monitoring, regular reviews, and timely action on audit objections to address recurring weaknesses and safeguard public funds going forward.

title: Report No. 3 of 2022 - Revenue Sector, Government of Telangana
overview:
This Compliance Audit Report for the year ended March 2021 highlights significant issues in the revenue administration of Telangana across four major receipts—Commercial Taxes, Stamp Duty & Registration Fee, Motor Vehicle Taxes, and Land Revenue. The audit covers a test-check of records in the Revenue and Transport departments with a total tax effect of ₹221.74 crore, revealing 29 significant compliance audit paragraphs.

Key findings include excess or incorrect allowance of Input Tax Credit (ITC) worth ₹3.88 crore, short levy of tax on various goods and dealers totaling ₹26.91 crore, and non-realisation or short levy of revenue in areas such as refunds under GST, transitional credits, registration fee miscalculations, and motor vehicle taxes. For example, in GST refunds, 149 excess/incorrect claims worth ₹31.06 crore were allowed, and a lack of robust mechanisms in checking transitional credits led to excess/incorrect credits of ₹55.8 crore.

The report stresses consequences such as weak internal controls, repeated underassessment, and delayed recoveries—of the ₹51.88 crore of audit observations accepted by departments, only ₹5.02 crore (10%) had been recovered as of April 2022. These findings require immediate policy attention to prevent revenue leakage and ensure stronger financial management and compliance.

The report covers compliance audits for nine departments, including Housing, Minorities Welfare, Animal Husbandry, Dairy Development, Fisheries, Agriculture, Municipal Administration, Planning, School Education and Youth Advancement, Tourism & Culture. Observations include deficiencies in fund utilisation, suspected frauds, and wasteful and avoidable expenditures. Notably, the Sheep Rearing Development Scheme (SRDS) under Animal Husbandry saw fraudulent withdrawals amounting to ₹1.57 crore by manipulating beneficiary data, while the Planning Department processed fraudulent bills of ₹89.58 lakh.

Implementation gaps in the Two Bedroom Housing Scheme in Greater Hyderabad led to only 44 per cent of the sanctioned units being completed as of March 2021, despite ₹3,315 crore being released, reflecting serious shortfalls in target achievement. Additionally, wasteful expenditure totaling ₹3.46 crore was incurred on biometric attendance devices by the School Education Department, as devices were procured but remained idle due to lack of compliance with procedural requirements.

Systemic inefficiencies were also seen in delayed remittances of EPF in Panchayat Raj and Rural Development Department, leading to an avoidable interest liability of ₹1.52 crore. The cumulative audit highlights inadequate oversight, lack of robust internal controls, and delays in follow-up action by departments, posing a high risk to public funds and service delivery. title: Composite Compliance Audit Report for the period 2019-21
overview:
This Report presents the significant results of compliance audits carried out for the period 2019-21 across State Government Departments and State Public Sector Undertakings in Kerala. A total of 11 paragraphs pertaining to departments with a combined financial impact of ₹145.69 crore were discussed. Audit observations were accepted by the government on ₹44.12 crore, reflecting both revenue loss and procedural lapses (page vii).

Key issues included a non-achievement of intended benefits from ₹1.02 crore investment in IT projects by the Directorate of Museums and Zoos, an avoidable loss of ₹76.07 lakh in input tax credit by the Forests and Wildlife department, and excess payment of ₹11.86 crore in employer’s EPF contributions, all resulting from procedural failures and non-compliance with statutory requirements (pages vii-viii).

The audit also found that as of September 2021, 6,177 paragraphs across 1,041 Inspection Reports remained outstanding, indicating systemic issues in resolution and accountability. Projects for rejuvenation and revival of PSUs, with an investment of ₹200.17 crore, failed to achieve their intended benefits due to deficient project evaluation and fund diversion (page ix). Overall, weaknesses in financial management and persistent follow-up gaps revealed high severity and call for prompt corrective action.

title: Report No 7 of 2022- Compliance Audit- Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended 2021 (Tamil)
overview:
The report covers compliance and audit observations for the period 2019-20 to 2021-22 across Central and State government departments in Tamil Nadu. Out of the total Rs 3,421.53 crore allocated, only Rs 1,584.29 crore (46%) was utilised, leaving a significant shortfall in expenditure and implementation effectiveness, especially across sectors like rural development, health, and education (Page 12).

A headline finding was fund misutilisation and delayed implementation, such as Rs 118 crore earmarked for infrastructure improvements remaining unutilised at year end (Page 23). Moreover, priority schemes saw lapses: e.g. the Midday Meal Scheme reported discrepancies in beneficiary data, with a shortfall of nearly 10% compared to official targets (Page 33).

Consequences of these gaps include delays in scheme benefits, loss of intended impact, and continued socio-economic deprivation among target groups. Audit also noted lack of compliance with statutory norms, resulting in critical revenue loss and procedural lapses that need immediate rectification (Page 44).

title: Compliance Audit Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Revenue Sector for the Year ended 31 March 2021 (Report No. 4 of the Year 2022)
overview:
This Compliance Audit covers the significant results of audit for the revenue sector in Uttar Pradesh, highlighting findings from the financial year ending 31 March 2021. The report details a total financial implication of ₹1,551.08 crore across audit paragraphs, including compliance audits on transitional credits, GST refund processing, stamp and additional stamp duties, mining receipts, vehicle taxes, and state excise. Of these, audit observations amounting to ₹80.87 crore were accepted by the Commercial Tax and Stamps & Registration Departments; other departments did not submit replies through June 2022.

During 2020-21, total government receipts were ₹2,96,176.33 crore, but the state's own receipts declined sharply by ₹72,787.46 crore to ₹1,31,743.45 crore, negatively impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic. The audit identifies wide variation between budget estimates and actuals—44.48% of total receipts were the state’s own while 55.52% originated from the Government of India—showing continued unreliability in the budgeting process. Systemic deficiencies in the management of transitional GST credits (excess/irregular availment, non-verification, and recovery failures) and persistent issues in Stamps, Mining, Excise, and Transport highlight major areas of non-compliance and revenue loss.

Notably, ₹1,683.30 crore of underassessment/short levy/loss of revenue was identified from 18,351 cases (out of 22,497 test-checked) in only 115 units audited. The audit pointed out lack of timely departmental action: as of March 2022, 48,800 audit paragraphs in 13,190 inspection reports remained unresolved, and replies to new audit findings are often absent, which severely affects accountability, revenue recovery, and overall fiscal health.

title: Report No.8 of 2022- Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India Compliance Audit (Revenue) for the year ended 31 March 2021 (Tamil)
overview:
The CAG report details the compliance audit of revenue for the financial year ending 31 March 2021, covering a period from 2016-17 to 2020-21. In 2020-21, total revenue realised was ₹1,06,152.96 crore against a target of ₹1,16,574.81 crore, reflecting a shortfall of ₹10,421.85 crore or 9% below the target. Over five years, the revenue realisation remained below target with a range of miss from 1.13% to 21.67% across various streams, particularly showing a 19.62% decrease in certain segments (p.2).

The report highlights critical compliance issues, including irregularities in refund payments, short realisation of revenue due to improper tax collection, and gaps in assessment procedures. For example, tax collection from 31 March 2021 was ₹38,124.75 lakh while actual recovery was only ₹19,273.15 lakh, indicating a difference of ₹18,851.6 lakh or nearly 49% of anticipated collections (p.5). The audit also flagged delays in registration, suboptimal processing of tax cases, and mismatches in declared versus collected revenue.

Consequences of these gaps include reduced state financial capacity, potential encouragement of tax evasion, and administrative inefficiency. The report notes ongoing COVID-19 impact affecting revenue flows, a total of 1,079 cases pending amounting to ₹675.87 crore, and systemic challenges in timely recovery and compliance enforcement. Recommendations stress urgent procedural reforms, stricter monitoring, and prompt disposal of pending cases to align revenue collection with targets (pp.12, 16).

title: Government of Tamil Nadu Report No. 4 of 2022- IT Audit of STAR 2.0 Application in the Registration Department, Tamil Nadu
overview:
The STAR 2.0 Application was implemented in the Registration Department of Tamil Nadu to streamline property registration and delivery of services. It was intended to cover 575 Sub-Registrar Offices (SROs) across the State, involving a total IT investment of ₹58.23 crore.

CAG found severe delays in implementation. Only 360 SROs (62.6%) were fully migrated to STAR 2.0 by October 2021, despite a deadline to migrate all offices by June 2019. The audit observed incomplete digitization of legacy records, resulting in inconsistent availability of digital services. On audit scrutiny, only ₹27.54 crore (47.3%) of the allotted funds were productively utilized, mainly for hardware and software acquisition, while significant portions remained unutilized or were used for non-core activities.

Consequences included poor integration between legacy and new modules, duplication of processes, and sub-optimal user experience. The lack of robust security for sensitive public records was highlighted as a risk. These lapses led to delayed registration timelines and reduced transparency in service delivery, directly impacting citizens in Tamil Nadu.

title: Report No.8 of 2022- Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India Compliance Audit (Revenue) for the year ended 31 March 2021
overview:
The Compliance Audit (Revenue) for the year ended 31 March 2021, Government of Tamil Nadu, reveals significant issues in revenue collection and administration across Commercial Taxes, Registration, and Transport Departments. The state's total revenue receipts in 2020-21 were ₹1,74,076.30 crore, with tax revenue at ₹1,06,152.96 crore and non-tax revenue at ₹10,421.85 crore. Sales tax and GST contributed ₹81,431.41 crore, representing 77% of tax revenue, while interest receipts and other sources formed 75% of non-tax revenue (Page vii).

Test checks uncovered under-assessments, short levy, and loss of revenue totaling ₹675.87 crore in 1,079 cases (Page 11). Arrears of revenue as of 31 March 2021 reached ₹38,124.75 crore, with ₹19,273.15 crore outstanding for over five years (Page 4). GST refunds processing exhibited excess payments (₹366.88 crore) due to incorrect ITC determinations, delays in refund issuance, and procedural inconsistencies. Stamp Duty and Registration audits highlighted undervaluation and short fees collection, with delays in property deed disposals and inconsistencies in land valuation, affecting ₹3.53 crore in stamp duty fees (Page 44).

Transport audits revealed non-levy of Green Tax for vehicles, resulting in revenue loss of ₹4 crore (Page 52). The audit observed systemic weaknesses in addressing audit queries, with over 31,000 unreconciled audit observations pending, indicative of persistent governance and compliance gaps.

title: Report No. 9 of 2022- Compliance Audit for the year ended March 2021, Government of Tamil Nadu
overview:
The Compliance Audit Report No. 9 of 2022 covers the audit findings relating to the Government of Tamil Nadu for the year ending March 2021. The report highlights significant lapses in resource allocation, utilization, contract management, and compliance with statutory guidelines across various departments. Audit scrutiny uncovered instances of unutilized funds amounting to ₹163.16 crore, delays in project implementation, and irregular sanctioning of funds, resulting in avoidable expenditures and foregone benefits to intended beneficiaries (p. vii, Executive Summary).

Specifically, in the Health and Family Welfare Department, the audit found that ₹43.73 crore remained undisbursed, affecting the upgrading of health infrastructure and delivery of health services. Further, discrepancies were noted in the execution of infrastructure projects, where delays led to cost overruns, up to 22%, and incomplete works. The Education sector audit revealed that only 44% of sanctioned hostels under the Post-Matric Scholarship Scheme were operationalized, directly impacting 1,752 students (p. xi, Executive Summary).

The consequences of these lapses included delayed benefits to vulnerable sections, accumulation of idle funds, non-adherence to financial propriety, and sub-optimal use of government resources. The audit recommended systemic improvements to enhance internal controls, ensure timely completion of projects, and strengthen accountability mechanisms to avert such deficiencies in future.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Social, Economic and Revenue Sectors for the year ended 31 March 2020
overview: This report presents significant audit observations from the performance and compliance audits of the Government of Tripura's Social, Economic, and Revenue sectors, covering an expenditure of ₹15,052.70 crore against a budget provision of ₹19,925.00 crore in FY 2019-20. Out of 1,680 auditee units, 186 were planned and 63 were actually audited, involving expenditure of ₹10,443.73 crore. The Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) were found to lack autonomy, as the State Government retained powers pertaining to assessment, revision, and procedure of property tax, affecting their ability to generate revenue. Functioning of Ward Committees and District Planning Committees remained deficient, impacting implementation of devolved functions. Vacancies ranged from 14% to 57% among various categories, compromising ULB service delivery. The State Property Tax Board was constituted but remained non-functional, leaving ULBs without technical guidance. Lack of a second State Finance Commission and non-submission/acceptance of subsequent SFC reports weakened the institutional framework. Across Economic and Revenue Sectors, significant shortfalls were found in creation of water harvesting structures, integrated pest/nutrient management, post-harvest infrastructure, and processing industries, with a marginal increase in horticultural production despite declining cultivated area. In Power sector, key rural electrification schemes saw reduced scope and shortfalls from 2% to 83% on planned outputs, leaving 13.4% rural households un-electrified. Monitoring mechanisms were weak, fund misutilisation was noted, and recovery rates of audit observations remained critically low at just 3.56%.

title: Report No.35 of 2022 Vol II - Compliance Audit on Union Government (Railways) for the year ended March 2021
overview:
This CAG compliance audit focused on the Ministry of Railways, examining operational efficiency, policy implementation, and fund management across numerous areas, including sundry revenues, major projects, and procurement. Despite the introduction of the Nav Arjan drive (2016-17), sundry earnings as a percentage of receipts fell from 4.85% in 2017-18 to 4.22% in 2020-21, and Non-Fare Revenue (NFR) dropped sharply as a share of both sundry earnings and total receipts. Actual sundry earnings consistently missed budget estimates—falling short by up to 66% and repeatedly failing to meet both original and revised targets. The audit uncovered significant lapses and avoidable expenditures including ₹141.70 crore on mismanaged land acquisition for the Dimapur-Kohima Project and cases such as avoidable contractual liability of ₹7.09 crore in East Coast Railway.

The audit revealed severe operational and financial inefficiencies: targets were set without Zonal input; even revised, lowered targets frequently went unmet; and most initiatives to enhance non-core revenue produced much less than projected. Large segments of allocated funds were used improperly or without tangible results—₹12.13 crore of Institutional Finance for NFR was spent on ineligible purposes, and major projects such as the Dimapur-Kohima rail line suffered cost overruns, delays, and repeated surveys resulting in huge waste.

Consequently, Indian Railways remains far from global benchmarks, with sundry and non-fare revenue comprising less than 5% of receipts compared to international railways generating 10%–20% or more. The report calls for urgent reform in policy setting, project execution, monitoring, and accountability to prevent further inefficiency and resource wastage.

Fix realistic, evidence-based revenue targets and actively monitor their achievement at the Zonal level.

Strictly follow MoR directives on leasing charges and fund earmarking, with responsibility fixed for lapses.

title: Government of Nagaland Report No. 2 of 2022 - Social, Economic, General and Revenue Sectors, Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended 31 March 2020
overview:
The performance audit of Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) within Nagaland covering April 2017 to March 2020 revealed significant systemic and operational deficiencies. Out of 65 centrally sponsored schemes operational across 15 departments, just two high-expenditure schemes from the Municipal Affairs and Rural Development Departments were intensively reviewed. Despite budget outlays, timely and full implementation of DBT protocols lagged: for example, only 11.60% of Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS) payments were direct, while 88.40% routed through intermediary Village Development Boards—primarily due to lack of banking access.

The State DBT Advisory Board, set up in July 2017, failed to conduct mandatory quarterly meetings, and the State DBT Cell neglected to upload complete scheme data to central and ministry portals. Delays in fund release and improper beneficiary targeting were noted; in PMAY-Urban, ineligible beneficiaries received payments, highlighting control failures. These inefficiencies led to poor achievement of DBT goals, undermining government efforts to ensure direct and transparent benefits to the people.

Consequences include significant delays in benefits to legitimate recipients, fund leakages, and weak accountability. There is also an elevated risk of fraud and loss of public trust, necessitating urgent reform in DBT processes to ensure compliance, transparency, and timely delivery of entitlements. title: Report No. 3 of the year 2022 - Compliance Audit for the year ended 31 March 2021, Government of Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir.
overview:
This Compliance Audit report highlights significant deficiencies in financial management and governance across various departments and PSUs in the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir. During 2020-21, UT government’s own revenue was only ₹12,953.37 crore—just 24.68% of total receipts, with the remaining 75.32% received as Grants-in-aid from the Government of India. Capital expenditure stood at 16.67% of total expenditure, with the majority (83.29%) being revenue expenditure; over ₹21,964.27 crore and ₹14,842.46 crore were spent on Social and Economic Services respectively, making up 58.27% of total spending for the year.

Audits found systemic delays and irregularities: for example, refund acknowledgements under GST were delayed up to 477 days in multiple cases, with average delays of 52 days (page 11-12). Refund sanctions were also delayed, with interest not being paid to claimants as required. Several crores were lost or doubtful for recovery due to mismanagement in PSU operations, excessive advances, and non-recovery of taxes and penalties—for instance, the J&K Bank had ₹140.22 crore in unutilised land and questionable recoveries totaling over ₹100 crore.

Major governance lapses were identified, such as irregular appointments and promotions in agricultural universities, wasteful expenditure on social welfare infrastructure, and non-compliance with audit recommendations—12,414 outstanding inspection reports with 56,053 unresolved audit paragraphs noted at year-end. The audit highlights the urgent need for improved controls, corrective procedure implementation, and stricter compliance monitoring across government entities.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Social, Economic and Revenue Sectors for the year ended 31 March 2020
overview:
This CAG report covers key compliance and performance audits across Mizoram’s Social, Economic and Revenue sectors for FY 2019-20. The total budget allocation across 13 social sector departments was ₹4,006.26 crore, while actual expenditure reached ₹3,564.61 crore, resulting in overall savings of 11.02%. Notably, certain departments, such as Medical and Public Health Services and Social Welfare, underutilised funds with an expenditure of only 78% of allocation, against the benchmark of over 80% utilised by most departments.

Critical findings include avoidable and irregular expenditures, with ₹5.30 crore spent avoidably by the Directorate of Hospital and Medical Education resulting in a further committed liability of ₹4.20 crore. Additionally, ₹82.62 lakh was expended on training 1,021 ineligible persons, and significant revenue losses and execution irregularities were also noted.

Consequences of these lapses include violations of CVC guidelines, risks of recurring liabilities, and systemic failures in scheme implementation and oversight. Recommendations target stricter adherence to procedures, better fund management, stronger monitoring, penal action against culprits, and improved transparency to avoid such losses in the future.

title: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on General, Economic (other than Public Sector Undertakings), Economic (Public Sector Undertakings), Revenue and Social Sectors for the year ended 31 March 2020 (2019-20) Government of Manipur
overview:
This report covers audit findings as of 31 March 2020 for the State of Manipur, encompassing ₹ 3,740.78 crore total expenditure under the General Sector (against a budget of ₹ 4,940.09 crore for 17 departments) and ₹ 2,033.12 crore in the Economic Sector across 18 departments. Audit scrutiny revealed delays, idle investment, and process bottlenecks across Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) schemes, PSUs, and social and economic sector spending. The State DBT Cell was found under-resourced, limiting its ability to coordinate or monitor 78 beneficiary schemes, while delays and fund flow inconsistencies affected timely pension and subsidy transfers. In the Fisheries Department, ₹ 16.73 lakh was suspected misappropriated, and Commerce & Industries had ₹ 3.26 crore worth of equipment lying idle.

PSUs in Manipur also showed severe weaknesses: as of March 2020, 54 out of 103 overdue PSU accounts were concentrated in two agencies, and five out of 10 working PSUs reported accumulated losses totalling ₹ 159.26 crore, eroding their paid-up equity. The audit noted an increase in idle, incomplete investments across the Food Industries Corporation and social sector infrastructure. Monitoring of schemes was found inadequate, and fund flow from the Centre was delayed, resulting in late beneficiary payments — in some cases up to 44 months for pensions or over 800 days for maternity benefits in PMMVY.

Revenue sector observations included significant delays (41 to 354 days) in processing GST refunds, non-compliance with State Finance Commission recommendations, and continued State Government control undermining municipal autonomy. The cumulative effect is a high risk of misappropriation, missed service delivery targets, and erosion of public trust in State financial management.

title: Compliance Audit Report (Commercial) for the year ended 31 March 2021 - Union Government
overview:
This Compliance Audit Report includes 26 individual observations relating to 23 CPSEs under seven Ministries/Departments, with a total financial implication of ₹4,068.64 crore identified. Notable findings include NLC India Limited's Board approval of non-monetary perquisites of Concessional Electricity resulting in irregular payment of ₹17.22 crore to its executives and subsidiaries, in contravention of the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) guidelines. Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited incurred avoidable expenditures of ₹16.93 crore due to delays in lease renewal, while Indian Oil Corporation Limited, ONGC, GAIL, and ONGC Videsh Limited extended undue benefit of ₹2,609.47 crore to executives by paying vehicle expenses over the prescribed limit. Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited's decision to create additional propylene handling facilities led to infructuous expenditure of ₹11.50 crore, despite the customer lifting product directly from Visakh Refinery.

Damodar Valley Corporation was unable to recover damages amounting to ₹693.24 crore from the concessionaire due to failure to enforce contract terms. National Highways Authority of India failed to recover toll revenue and enforce contractual provisions, leading to doubtful recovery of ₹21.35 crore. These cases demonstrate widespread issues of non-compliance with rules, defective planning, inadequate monitoring, and loss of financial interest. Of the 26 paragraphs, 12 remained without response from the respective Ministries/Departments, highlighting gaps in accountability and risk management.

The report emphasizes the recurring nature of irregular payments and the erosion of capital due to poor adherence to guidelines and defective project management. Significant amounts remain unrecovered or written off across multiple CPSEs, impacting public sector revenues and overall financial integrity.
